14421-wilson-s-tales-of-the-borders-and-:
This twenty-fourth volume of Wilson's Tales of the Borders and of Scotland, revised by Alexander Leighton and published in 1884, gathers short historical and legendary tales from the Anglo-Scottish border country. A glossary helps with Scots words.

The minstrel's tales include romances of knights and ladies, legends of haunted halls, and ballads such as the tale of Ailie Faa, told in verse and prose. Love, revenge, and supernatural dread recur across the stories. The collection preserves border storytelling for Victorian readers, mixing antiquarian care with popular romance. Leighton's revision kept Wilson's tales in print for new readers.
15471-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's children's weekly reaches April 22, 1897 in this number, still five cents, still from West 18th Street in New York. An advertisement for The Sportsman's Magazine, an eighty-page monthly by sportsmen for sportsmen, fills an early page, offering guns, rods, and bicycles as premiums for new subscriptions.

The news itself opens with Cuba: reports confirm the capture of General Ruis Rivera, as Spanish forces press the island's rebels. That lead shows the paper's method, taking a hard foreign story and telling it plainly for school readers. The number captures a moment when American children followed the Cuban war in their own weekly paper, weeks before their country joined the fight.
18746-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
The Great Round World, a weekly newspaper for boys and girls, issued this number, volume two, number twenty-four, on June 16, 1898, at five cents a copy. Its masthead gives the New York publisher's address and terms of a dollar and a half a year, with bound volumes sold at stores from Philadelphia to San Francisco.

Advertisements fill the front pages, offering a three-dollar-and-fifty-cent talking machine, premiums for a two-cent stamp, and notices for bicycles and bound volumes. The issue belongs to a paper that mixed news of the world with matter for young readers, week by week through the year. Its news pages lie beyond the excerpt, but the masthead and advertisements alone sketch a lively children's weekly of 1898.
28555-the-virginia-company-of-london-160:
The Virginia Company of London, 1606 to 1624, is Jamestown 350th Anniversary Historical Booklet number 5, copyrighted in 1957. Its subject is the company, not the colony: the adventurers in England whose hopes shaped Jamestown and carried it through early disappointment. The story runs only eighteen years, from the first charter to dissolution.

Two companies began the venture, one at London and one at Plymouth, under a charter stretching from Cape Fear to mid-Maine. Plymouth's Sagadahoc colony, planted in August 1607, failed by spring 1608, while London persisted. Readers learn how London backing, more than luck, separated Jamestown's fate from Roanoke's.
29574-seven-minor-epics-of-the-english-r:
Paul W. Miller edited this 1967 volume of seven minor epics of the English Renaissance, printed in Gainesville, Florida, by Scholars' Facsimiles and Reprints. Its texts span 1596 to 1624: The Love of Dom Diego and Ginevra by Richard Lynche, Mirrha and Hiren by William Barksted, and Amos and Laura by Samuel Page. Pyramus and Thisbe by Dunstan Gale and The Scourge of Venus by H.A. stand beside them, with Philos and Licia by an anonymous hand.

Each poem appears in facsimile, with Miller's introduction to guide the reader. The set shows Renaissance poets working the erotic epic in short, vivid form. Students of early modern verse will find a rare, useful gathering of poems seldom read outside libraries.
30780-the-first-seventeen-years-virginia:
Charles E. Hatch Jr. wrote this short history of early Virginia, published by the University Press of Virginia at Charlottesville, with a 1957 copyright held by the Virginia 350th Anniversary Celebration Corporation of Williamsburg. The copy held here is a tenth printing from 1991. Its span, as the title says, is the first seventeen years, from 1607 to 1624.

Contents move from the establishment of Jamestown through the summer and fall of 1607, the three supplies of 1608 to 1610, and a critical hour for the colony. Later sections treat order and more stable ways, tobacco, Yeardley and Argall, Yeardley and Wyatt, Virginia and the dissolution, and the spread of settlement. It is a compact, clear guide to Virginia's hard founding years.
31809-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Volume twenty-four of the Swanston Edition of the Works of Robert Louis Stevenson, published in London in 1912 by Chatto and Windus with Cassell, Heinemann, and Longmans, is a volume of letters. The edition as a whole ran to twenty-five volumes. Two thousand and sixty copies were printed, and two thousand offered for sale.

Its frontispiece shows Tembinoka, Apemama's king, with the heir-apparent, and its letters include a writer remembering a friendship that began with mirth years ago and ended with sorrow. Readers get Stevenson in his own voice, writing to friends about his life, his work, and the people he loved, in a handsome collected edition.
5298-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
Jean de La Fontaine's Tales and Novels continue in this twenty-fourth volume, in English verse translation. Its contents are The Indiscreet Confession, The Contract, and The Quid Pro Quo, or The Mistakes. The first opens in Paris with Aminta, famed for youth, beauty, temper, and fortune, kept beneath her mother's wing.

Damon, struck by love's dart, offers Aminta his heart, and the tales that follow turn on confessions, contracts, and comic mistakes. Readers get three tales of Parisian gallantry, in which lovers bargain, blunder, and confess, all in La Fontaine's polished, ironic verse.
5927-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Camacho's wedding continues in chapter twenty-one alone, the whole of this Don Quixote installment. While Quixote and Sancho pursue the discussion of the last chapter, loud shouts and great noise rise from men on mares galloping to receive bride and bridegroom. The couple approaches with musical instruments, pageantry, priest, relatives, and the most distinguished people of surrounding villages.

Sancho, seeing the bride, exclaims that she looks not like a country girl but like a fine court lady, in rich coral and green Cuenca stuff. Readers get a festive interlude of love, wealth, and peasant pageantry, before Quixote's ideals meet the wedding's real choices. The single chapter suits readers following volume two, since Camacho's feast tests romance against marriage, money, and merit.
70741-a-decade-of-negro-extension-work-1:
A Decade of Negro Extension Work, 1914 to 1924, is a report of the United States Department of Agriculture, issued at Washington in October 1926 as Miscellaneous Circular number 72. It was written by Martin, the officer in charge of cooperative extension work in the southern states. A picture message at the front says land ownership and home improvement are vital in developing Black farm life in the South.

The report tells how Black extension agents were organized, how their numbers and funds grew, and what they achieved. Club work for boys and girls, the movable school, farm and home demonstration results, and stories of achievement fill the pages. It closes with statistics and an outlook. The circular is a plain official record of a real service.
abrege-de-la-doctrine-de-paracelse-et-de:
Abregé de la Doctrine de Paracelse, printed in 1724, is Francesco Maria Pompeo Colonna's French summary of the doctrine of Paracelsus and his Archidoxes. It adds an explanation of the nature of the principles of chemistry, meant to clarify the treatises of Paracelsus and of the other philosophers. The preface is signed with an anagram of the author's name, Sum incola francus.

After the summary comes a practical treatise on different manners of operating, by the dry way and by the wet way, the two great routes of the laboratory. The book thus joins theory to bench work for French readers of Paracelsian chymistry. At over four hundred pages in small format, it is a full handbook, not a pamphlet.
adler-practice-theory-radin-1924:
Alfred Adler published The Practice and Theory of Individual Psychology in German in the 1920s. The English text here is P. Radin's translation of 1924. The book gathers Adler's mature system in papers on therapy, childhood, and social life. Birth order, social interest, and style of life are its key ideas.

Adler argues that each child builds a unique style of striving for significance. Health lies in social interest: caring for others as equals. Case studies show his method of early recollections and dream reading. The book shaped counseling, education, and parenting advice. Adler's influence runs wide though his name is less known than Freud's.
al-baladhuri-origins-islamic-state-murgo:
Francis Clark Murgotten finished the English Futuh al-Buldan of al-Baladhuri in 1924, taking up the work Philip Hitti had begun. This second part completes the ninth-century Arabic account of the conquests that built the caliphate. Al-Baladhuri wrote at the Abbasid court from records, reports, and named chains of witnesses.

The later campaigns run east and west: the frontiers of Persia, the marches of Armenia, Sicily, and the far Maghreb. Murgotten adds the taxes, garrisons, and land terms that made conquest into a state. Together the two parts give the fullest early picture of how the Islamic empire was won and run. Hitti's project stands whole in this volume.
apocryphal-new-testament-james-1924:
M. R. James gathered the standard English collection of apocryphal New Testament writings in 1924. James, better known for his ghost stories, was also a leading manuscript scholar. His volume translates non-canonical gospels, acts, letters, and apocalypses.

Readers meet the child Jesus working miracles in the Infancy Gospel. Paul battles sorcerers, and apostles tour heaven and hell in vivid detail. These texts show how wide and varied early Christian storytelling became. Some were treasured by churches for centuries before exclusion. James's introductions explain each work's age, sources, and survival. Anyone studying early Christianity beyond the canon starts with this collection.
arabische-alchemisten-ii-gafar-alsadiq-1:
Arabische Alchemisten II, published in 1924 by the orientalist Julius Ruska, studies the alchemical writings ascribed to Ja'far al-Sadiq. It is the second volume of Ruska's series on Arabic alchemists. Ruska built the book in three parts, and its structure is itself a small edition of the source.

The first third gives introduction and commentary in German. The middle third translates the medieval Arabic text into modern German, and the last third prints the medieval Arabic itself, the sixth imam's attributed sayings on the art. Scholars can thus move from Ruska's guidance to the source in one volume. The book remains a tool for the study of early Arabic alchemy.
arnim-svf-vol4-1924:
A set of fragments gathered from hundreds of old books is only as good as its index. Maximilian Adler built the index volume for Hans von Arnim's Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, and it appeared in 1924 as the fourth volume of the set. It keys the Greek and Latin material of the first three volumes.

Adler listed names, subjects, and Greek terms so a reader can track one idea, such as fate or impulse, through every passage that names it. With these lists the huge collection becomes a tool a scholar can search by hand. The volume closes von Arnim's project, the standard source book for the early Stoa.
arxiv-2412-00124:
MinKyu Lee and co-authors sharpen AI photo enlargement in a 2024 paper. Super-resolution rebuilds a large, detailed image from a small one, and generative methods make results look real. But the loss that enforces closeness to the original photo also blurs, a known tug of war between fidelity and looks.

The team dissect that loss and isolate exactly which part causes the blur. An auto-encoder, trained with the same loss, separates the blurring part from the harmless part, so their new loss guides training only by the safe part. The result aims at enlargements that stay both faithful and crisp, without the usual workarounds that never fixed the root cause.
arxiv-2412-00224:
Saurabh Mishra and four co-authors presented an AI-driven data mesh platform in twenty twenty-four for infrastructure construction and public procurement. The sector — an industry of industries tied to government spending — loses enormous value to fragmented information. Their ecosystem standardizes and ingests diverse sources into structured knowledge, organized by data mesh and service mesh principles.

The platform rests on a training corpus the team calls the largest for this domain, exceeding one hundred billion tokens spanning publications, activities, and risk data. A knowledge graph feeds domain-specific multi-agent question answering, supporting early planning, research, market analysis, and qualitative assessment. The web-scalable design lets AI agents reason under uncertainty. The authors frame it as a template for dragging traditional industries into digital workflows.
arxiv-2412-00324:
Daomin Ji and co-authors tackle table integration in data lakes as three linked tasks, published in 2024. Merging tables into one comprehensive table requires judging whether two rows can join, finding all joinable groups, and settling conflicts among rows. Each step carries its own traps, from typos to meaning differences.

For the first task they train a classifier, and, since labeled data is scarce, a self-supervised method that creates its own training examples, including adversarial ones. Joinable groups then look like dense communities in a graph whose edges are the pairwise judgments, so community detection methods are compared for the second task. The third task resolves conflicts when many rows merge. The authors present the pipeline as an end-to-end treatment of a common data engineering problem.
arxiv-2412-00624:
Yogesh Kulkarni and Pooyan Fazli teach video language models to improve themselves without human labels or paid model judges. Standard tuning needs ranked pairs of answers, which are costly to collect for video. Their pipeline, VideoSAVi, has the model critique its own first answers, spot reasoning errors, and write better versions. Those before-and-after pairs then train the model through preference optimization, round after round.

The self-trained model gained 4.2 points on MVBench, 3.9 on PerceptionTest, and 6.8 on the hard EgoSchema benchmark over its starting point. It needs only thirty-two video frames per question, keeping compute modest. The method works with different base models, since nothing in the loop depends on one architecture. The authors present self-critique as a cheap route to sharper video reasoning where labeled data is scarce.
arxiv-2412-00824:
Ishwar Kant and five co-authors work backward from scattering data to the forces behind it in a 2024 paper. When a helium nucleus scatters off a hydrogen or helium-3 nucleus, the pattern of phase shifts encodes the interaction potential. The team wanted that potential for two specific resonant states.

They built a candidate force from three smooth curve segments, covering short-range nuclear pull, mid-range behavior, and the long-range electric barrier. A standard numerical method then computed the phase shifts the candidate predicts. A genetic algorithm tuned the candidate's knobs until predicted and expected shifts matched closely. The recovered resonance energies and widths for the hydrogen system came out in line with known values. Inverse problems like this let physicists describe reactions that resist direct measurement, and the fitted potentials feed later calculations of nuclear structure.
arxiv-2412-00924:
Tomer Ravid presents a 2024 review arguing that a popular theory tool for strange metals is being used outside its valid range. Patch bosonization rewrites the physics of a Fermi surface, the boundary of filled electron states, in terms of wave-like variables. Physicists hoped it could describe a two-dimensional metal at a quantum critical point, where standard theory fails. Ravid contends the formalism fundamentally cannot handle that problem.

It survives, he argues, only in contrived limits, such as when the number of fermion flavors is very small or very large. Around those limits, step-by-step expansions can at least be written down. Once the flavor count nears the realistic value of one, effects beyond expansion take over. The review is a caution about mistaking a tidy formalism for a solved problem.
arxiv-2412-01024:
Sherry Qiu, Holly Rushmeier, and Kim Blenman studied how guided data displays affect the experts who use them, in this 2024 arXiv paper. Guided systems steer users toward key trends in large, tangled datasets. Less is known about how that steering shapes the way experts read charts and later share what they found.

The authors ran two user studies with domain experts. Experts did better with a guided structure that moves from the broad picture down to fine detail. That coarse-to-fine path matched the way experts already tell others about their findings. The work suggests that guidance helps most when it follows the shape of expert communication, not just the shape of the data.
arxiv-2412-01124:
Qingtian Zhu, Yinqiang Zheng and their co-authors present SUICA, a tool for spatial transcriptomics data, in 2024. Such data link gene activity to spots in tissue, but the spots are sparse and each one holds a huge list of gene values.

SUICA models the data as a smooth, compact map using implicit neural representations. A graph-based step first gives each spot context from its neighbors. The team also treats skewed values by sorting them into classes for training. In tests across common platforms, SUICA beat prior methods on accuracy and on keeping true biological signals. Its output also boosted gene signatures for later study.
arxiv-2412-01324:
Pfeiffer and colleagues present in twenty twenty-four a solver that fuses robot motion planning with the discrete choices planning usually handles apart. A robot arm may need to pick which handhold or target to use while shaping its whole-body motion, and mixing both in one nonlinear problem is heavy. Older routes split the choice from the motion maths or used blunt approximations.

Their sparse hierarchical solver exploits the problem's layered structure and a strict count of active joints, a tool rarely used in robotics. It handles cases like planning a reach while picking the best end point from many candidates, or choosing two-handed grasps on a turned box, in one pass. The authors claim speed, range, and accuracy gains over mixed-integer and split approaches.
arxiv-2412-01524:
Yuhan Suo and co-authors design cost-aware online learning for agent networks under attack. Connected device networks learn together, but hostile agents can poison the process. Blocking bad neighbors helps, yet it can desync honest agents nearby.

Their framework rejects suspect neighbor data with strict rules. It also counts the cost of repeated corrective adaptation. A two-time-scale regulator then steadies long-term learning rates. The outer layer adjusts pace so honest agents stay in step. The design targets persistent attacks during early learning stages. It keeps convergence while cutting wasted effort across the network. The work suits sensor and device fleets that must learn in hostile settings.
arxiv-2412-01724:
Kaya Unalmis and four co-authors build a fast, highly accurate algorithm for averaging particle motion in fusion devices, designed so its derivatives come free, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Bounce-averaging simplifies the kinetic models used to design stellarators, machines that hold plasma in twisted magnetic fields. Optimization over many design knobs needs gradients that older tools supplied slowly or not at all.

Built into the DESC design suite, the algorithm reaches exponential accuracy and supports reverse-mode automatic differentiation. That makes gradient cost independent of how many knobs are tuned. The team used it to directly shrink a ripple transport measure in a working-pressure stellarator, a first. They also point to gains for particle confinement and turbulence studies.
arxiv-2412-01824:
Zeyi Sun and co-authors give a vision-language model the power to make images from examples, not just captions. Their twenty twenty-four paper, X-Prompt, brings in-context learning to image generation. Show the model a few pairs, and it should grasp a new style or task without retraining.

The design squeezes the useful traits out of example images into a compact form the generator can use. One unified model then handles seen and unseen generation jobs. Prompt craft shifts from words alone to curated examples, the way people teach by showing. Flexible image tools that learn a house style from three samples would serve designers far better than fixed filters.
arxiv-2412-01924:
Kattel, Zhakenov, and Andrei model a magnetic impurity where superconductivity fights the Kondo effect in twenty twenty-four. The Kondo effect clouds an impurity spin with a screen of electrons. Here the wire's own pairing, which drives superconductivity, tugs the other way. Their model sets the impurity at the wire's edge with strong bulk pull.

At strong Kondo coupling, a many particle screen holds and a Kondo scale emerges. At matched strengths, a mid gap state screens the spin in the spectrum, yet the ground state leaves it bare. Where pairing wins, no screening survives. A novel phase with a near zero energy edge mode sits between regimes.
arxiv-2412-02024:
David Kaplan and Srimoyee Sen argue that a five dimensional setup for chiral gauge theory can ease two long puzzles at once. They place the four dimensional theory on the edge of a five dimensional space, a form that can live on a finite grid. Odd traits appear that a flat four dimensional view misses.

When the strong force theory sits inside the standard model this way, both a known axial puzzle and the strong CP puzzle can fade. Light modes far off in the fifth depth play the key role. The result breaks the usual claim that all grids agree.
arxiv-2412-02124:
Long Wang presents a 2024 paper on simulating triple star systems with high accuracy. Such systems drive events from blue stragglers to gravitational wave sources. A leading integrator handles single orbits very well by transforming time. Wang shows it is far less accurate for ranked triples, where a close pair is orbited by a third body. It can even drive false long-term change in the inner orbit.

Hybrid methods work better: one rule for the inner pair, another for the outer bodies. Wang adds a new hybrid that needs no time sync and is time-symmetric. It is built into a few-body code. Rules for switching between methods in general triples are explored. The aim is faster, truer runs for ranked systems.
arxiv-2412-02524:
Juhee Lee and co-authors build a general theory in 2024 for a process where a whole group restarts, not just one member. In the classic setup, a lone particle wanders and is now and then sent back to a start point. Here, the restart is driven by the group as a whole, for instance by its most extreme member.

Settings like this show up in bacteria facing antibiotics and in robot swarms that search an area. The team treats the group's center as a single stand in particle and writes an equation for how it spreads. From that they get exact formulas for where the center settles and how widely it spreads. They also study a case where the group must steer clear of a bad region. The theory gives a shared base for group restart problems that were solved one at a time before.
arxiv-2412-02624:
Paolo Baglioni and Francesco Di Renzo investigate, in a 2024 paper, noise troubles in a computational method for a classic field theory. The theory, a nonlinear sigma model, lives on a curved target space and shows asymptotic freedom. High-order calculations for it rely on a stochastic perturbation method.

That method's random fluctuations grow with each order, above all in low dimensions. In some models the noise can drown the signal entirely. The authors show the trouble depends strongly on the model's size parameter. Larger values make higher orders feasible again. Their simulations map where the method can be trusted. Taming such noise decides which theories can be computed perturbatively at all.
arxiv-2412-02824:
Gilderlan Tavares de Araújo and André de Almeida tackle channel estimation for a new kind of smart radio surface, in a 2024 paper. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces help wireless signals reach their targets. A newer design, called beyond diagonal, links its elements in richer ways, and standard estimation methods do not fit it well.

Most existing methods lean on pilot signals sent in advance. The authors instead build a semi-blind receiver that learns the channels and the data symbols together, with no pilot stage first. Their method rests on a tensor model of the received signal and alternates between estimates in three directions. Early numerical tests show the approach works for chosen setups. Its error rates are compared against a receiver that magically knows the combined channel perfectly.
arxiv-2412-02924:
Indu Kant Deo and Rajeev Jaiman present a way to improve long-range wave forecasts from deep neural networks. Their paper came out in 2024. Networks can predict waves quickly, but small errors in timing and height build up as the forecast runs longer.

Their method splits the training loss, the score the network tries to lower, into two separate parts. One part grades the phase, which is where each wave crest sits in time. The other part grades the amplitude, which is how tall the waves are. Grading the two parts apart steadies training and slows the build-up of error. Long forecasts of wave motion stay much closer to the truth.
arxiv-2412-03224:
Brain-computer interfaces read brain waves to steer devices, but each new user supplies only a small calibration set. That scarcity starves decoding models. Ziwei Wang and co-authors propose a simple fix called channel reflection. The method augments training data by flipping electrode channels in ways that respect how brain signals are laid out for each task type.

The trick adds no parameters and needs no tuning. Across eight public datasets and four kinds of tasks, from imagined movement to seizure detection, it reliably raised classification accuracy. It beat existing augmentation methods and stacked well with them, adding further gains. The authors argue such augmentation should be a standard step in brain-wave decoding.
arxiv-2412-03424:
Daniel Armstrong and co-authors speed up computer planning of chemical synthesis, in a 2024 paper. Planners work backward from a target molecule to starting stuff, but users often must start from a set stock, such as waste or plant-based feed. A two-way search method exists for that case, yet it is complex.

Their method, Tango*, guides a standard one-way search with a value score rich in chemical sense. Tuning a single knob let it beat prior methods on both speed and solve rate. Routes it found were as short as rivals', a common mark of route quality. The score also sped up the two-way methods when added there.
arxiv-2412-04024:
Pierre Tapie and co-authors mimic a fingertip with a bubble of gas in soft rubber. Touch sensors in skin turn pressure into signals that let us judge texture. Their stand in is a gas cavity buried in a half round of elastic. As the pad presses or slides on rough model surfaces, cameras watch the cavity bend and wobble.

A math model forecasts the bend under load and shows the skin stress runs stronger one way than the other. In sliding tests, the cavity's shape jitter was rich enough to tell textures apart. The authors muse on what the stress pattern might mean for real touch cells.
arxiv-2412-04224:
Mazzolari and co-authors check whether black hole systems found by the James Webb Space Telescope shine in radio waves. The team used deep radio data at five frequencies for one northern sky field. None of the thirty-seven broad-line systems was seen at any frequency, and stacking all of them still gave no signal.

The silence is odd. For most single sources, the limits still fit what quiet systems should emit, but the stacked limit and the total blank make chance a poor excuse. The authors weigh causes such as a dense veil soaking up the waves, or a missing magnetic field or corona, perhaps from feeding too fast. Far deeper radio data are needed, they say.
arxiv-2412-04424:
Jiuhai Chen and co-authors present a 2024 paper on a vision-language model family called Florence-VL. Most such models see images through encoders trained by matching pictures to captions. Florence-2, the vision base used here, is instead a generative model that can describe images at many levels of detail.

The authors fuse features taken from several depths of the vision model and under several prompts, a scheme they call depth-breadth fusion. Training first ran end to end on a broad mix of image and instruction data, then tuned the connector and the language model. Visual checks showed tighter alignment between image features and words than rival encoders give. Benchmark scores rose across many multimodal and vision-focused tests.
arxiv-2412-04524:
Davood Momeni and Ratbay Myrzakulov develop, in a 2024 paper, a modified theory of gravity in a geometric language built for torsion. General relativity describes gravity through curvature alone, but the theory they study, named for Myrzakulov, lets spacetime also twist, and blends both effects into the equations. They rewrite it using vielbeins, a set of local frames at each point, which suits a kind of spacetime where the twist does the work curvature usually does.

With the theory in this form, the authors explore what the twist changes for black holes, gravitational waves, and neutron stars. The modifications could shift how black holes store heat-like quantities, how waves travel, and how dense matter holds up. They offer the work as groundwork for tests that might one day separate their theory from Einstein's, and as a fresh angle on how spacetime is built.
arxiv-2412-04624:
De la Reza, writing in 2024, tackles a long puzzle in star studies: why about one percent of giant stars hold far more lithium than the rest. The work merges two large catalogues, one with more than ten thousand lithium-rich giants and one that detects infrared sources. It looks for signs that these stars are losing mass.

The merged data show hundreds of clump giants and first-ascent giants with extra infrared light, a sign of mass loss. The author proposes that all low-mass giants gain lithium in a brief phase tied to shell ejections, driven by fast movement of matter inside the star. Helium flashes in clump stars may add still more lithium, which could explain why those stars are the richest of all.
arxiv-2412-04724:
Jixun Yao and his six co-authors, publishing in 2024, build a voice converter that can borrow one person's tone and another's style independently. Voice conversion usually copies a voice's sound onto new words. Mixing timbre from one unseen speaker with speaking style from another, without training examples of either, is harder. Their system, StableVC, first splits speech into content, timbre, and style.

A flow-matching module then rebuilds the sound from those parts. A dual attention mechanism with an adaptive gate picks out timbre and style features cleanly. Because the design avoids step-by-step generation, it runs far faster than real time, about twenty-five times quicker than word-by-word rivals. Tests show it beat leading systems on quality and similarity while keeping the flexible control. The authors target dubbing, assistants, and accessibility tools.
arxiv-2412-04824:
Anar Dosi studies joint spectra for representations of the quantum plane in a 2024 paper. The quantum plane is a noncommutative version of flat space, where the order of multiplication matters. Modules over it that live in Banach spaces carry several operators at once, and their shared spectrum needs a careful definition.

Dosi builds that spectrum from a homology based comparison with simple modules, yielding a well defined Taylor spectrum. A projection property is proved in a noncommutative form that stands in for the classic commutative result. Key examples show the new modules lack the forward and backward projection traits of the older theory.
arxiv-2412-04924:
Enrico Maria Fenoaltea and co-authors grade AI reach into jobs by trail of startup cash in a 2024 paper. Old grades score which jobs AI could do in theory. They say less on which jobs AI firms chase in fact. The team built an index from job task lists and the goods of startups in a famed fund program. That lens shows what the market builds, not just what labs can build.

High-skill jobs face wide swings in the new grade. Routine desk tasks, such as data work and office care, score high. High-stakes roles such as judges and surgeons score low, held back more by social bars than by tech bars. The authors say AI spread will be slow and shaped by want as much as by skill. The index gives policy teams a live gauge of that spread.
arxiv-2412-05024:
Thomas Sievers and Nele Russwinkel test how a social robot's dialect affects people who talk with it in 2024. The robot is a humanoid used in public service settings. Smooth talk and user trust matter for its success. The team compares the robot speaking standard German with it speaking Low German, a regional form from the north.

The words' content stays the same in both forms. Only the variety of speech changes. Seventeen adults took part, with a wide age range. A standard scale scored warmth, skill, and discomfort. The Low German form scored far higher on warmth. The authors link the gain to cultural identity and familiarity. The work hints that local speech can aid robot acceptance.
arxiv-2412-05224:
Andrii Liashyk, Stanislav Pakuliak, and Eric Ragoucy derive new recurrence rules in a 2024 math paper on quantum integrable models. Bethe vectors are the key states in these models, and building them step by step is a core task. The models here carry one of two symmetry types, both classic in the field.

Their method adds one fresh parameter to set parts of a Bethe state at a time. The new state comes out as a mix of matrix entries acting on states free of that parameter. Those entries sit in the upper right block of the matrix, hence the rectangular name. The build runs inside the zero mode method, a known frame. The rules should ease work on spectra of such models.
arxiv-2412-05324:
Mario Amrein wrote a math note on steering nonlinear maps in two thousand twenty-four. Many tasks need the output error of a map driven toward zero. Examples include finding roots and cutting costs in optimization. Amrein asks for a path from a start point to a target value. Along that path, the error must stay under control. The bound should rest only on the starting error.

The note extends an earlier result by another mathematician. It assumes the map's slope can be written via a helper operator. That operator acts on the starting error to guide the path. A simple choice of operator recovers known continuation results. The proof yields a rough inverse function statement as well. Such tools underpin solvers used across science and engineering.
arxiv-2412-05524:
Zhi-Qiang You and co-authors reconstruct the birth mass distribution of neutron stars from ninety measured masses. Their 2024 paper corrects each star's present mass for material it may have gained from a companion, since many weighed neutron stars are recycled pulsars in binaries. Birth masses encode how supernovae work and how matter behaves at extreme density.

One smooth distribution fits best: masses switch on near a lower edge, peak at a modest value, then fall steeply. That shape beats the popular two-bump model at strong significance. The steep fall implies that single stars above a certain starting mass rarely leave neutron stars behind. The pattern may descend from the birth distribution of massive stars themselves, filtered by which explosions succeed.
arxiv-2412-05724:
Neha, Deepshikha Bhati, Deepak Kumar Shukla, and Md Amiruzzaman generate Monet-style paintings with a tiered GAN that refines its output in stages. Their paper from twenty twenty-four walks random noise through successive tiers toward detailed artistic images. Each stage enhances quality progressively, a design aimed at classic GAN ailments: unstable training, mode collapse, and weak fidelity. Downsampling and convolutional blocks keep the compute bill in check.

Experiments show the architecture producing foundational artistic structures in Monet's manner. The authors are candid that realism and true fidelity to Monet need further work. Training methods and model complexity are the named frontiers. The tiered idea itself is the contribution: many small improvements stacked, rather than one monolithic generator.
arxiv-2412-06024:
Asaad Daher and co-authors (2024) extend the equations describing hot, dense matter flowing like a fluid. Such matter appears in heavy-ion collisions, where a baryon current and a nonzero chemical potential matter. Earlier second-order theories often skipped those features or used a toy equation of state. Starting from quantum theory, the authors use a quasiparticle picture of the medium. They connect it to the Wigner formalism and expand the kinetic equations to second order.

The result is a closed set of equations for the stress-energy tensor and the baryon current. All transport coefficients follow from one recipe respecting thermodynamics. They depend on the chosen equation of state, so realistic matter models can plug in. The authors present it as a firmer base for simulating collision fireballs. It should serve studies of dense matter in neutron star mergers, where chemical potential cannot be ignored.
arxiv-2412-06124:
Nicholas Pritchard and co-authors use brain-like spiking networks to detect radio interference in astronomy data, in a paper from 2024. Interference from human technology pollutes the faint signals radio telescopes collect. Automated detection must run in real time with little power.

The task was reshaped as labeling a time series segment by segment, a form that suits spiking networks. Several ways of encoding spectrograms into spikes were tried, with two kinds of spiking neuron models. A normalization step inspired by vision science improved results across encodings. On synthetic data the method rivaled standard tools. First tests on real data from a European low-frequency array were promising. The authors position spiking networks as a path to live, low-power detection.
arxiv-2412-06224:
Jiazhao Zhang and co-authors build one model in 2024 that can handle many kinds of robot navigation at once. A useful home robot must follow spoken directions, hunt for objects, answer questions, and track people, often in one long task.

Earlier models were tied to one task setup or to maps with fixed waypoints. Their model, named Uni-NaVid, learns from video and language and outputs actions directly, with one shared format for every task. Training used 3.6 million samples drawn from four navigation sub tasks, so the tasks could teach each other. The model led on standard benchmarks and also worked in real world rooms it had never seen.
arxiv-2412-06724:
Cleaning a messy spreadsheet by hand is slow and slip-prone, even in good tools. Lan Li, Liri Fang, Bertram Ludäscher, and Vetle Torvik built a system in 2024 that hands the job to a language model. Given a raw table and the purpose the clean table must serve, it writes a sequence of cleaning steps in a popular tool's language. The steps cover six common flaws, from bad formats to duplicates.

To judge it they built a benchmark of 142 purposes over ninety-six tables, scoring the final answer, the table itself, and how human-like the steps are. Three open models all lifted data quality over the baseline; the largest wrote the best tables, its smaller sibling the most human-like workflows.
arxiv-2412-06824:
Clifton Cunningham and colleagues settled a normalization question for p-adic groups in a 2024 representation theory paper. Groups over p-adic numbers, a number system based on divisibility by a prime, have their representations sorted into packets. One construction of packets, the ABV construction, seemed to depend on an auxiliary choice called a Whittaker datum, which would be an unwanted freedom.

The team proves the packets themselves do not depend on that choice, while the labeling map from packet to a fundamental group does, and they pin down the change exactly. For classical groups they prove a genericity conjecture, and for open parameters the packets match the Langlands picture. A conjecture of Vogan on Arthur packets for tempered representations follows.
arxiv-2412-07024:
Gonzalez-Gutierrez, Casana, and Santos find compact self-dual solitons in a gauged baby Skyrme model under an outside magnetic field. Their paper from twenty twenty-four uses the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield frame, which sets an energy floor and equations that meet it. The catch is size: the method works only when the soliton and the field's zone are matched in a set way. Two setups are treated.

In one, the field sits inside the compacton like an impurity. In the other, the field rings it in full. Both let the team fix the self-dual potential and the BPS equations. Radial solutions are then computed with step and Gaussian field shapes. Profiles show how the field shifts the compacton's size, flux, and fields. The work widens the soliton census for this model family.
arxiv-2412-07124: Wenxuan Chen and Linjie Zhao study the random fluctuations of particles that hop along a line and now and then leap far, in a 2024 paper. Their model is a weakly asymmetric exclusion process with endless reservoirs at the two ends. They prove that the stationary swings follow a generalized Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process or the stochastic Burgers equation. Which one holds, with fixed boundary conditions in both cases, turns on how strong the asymmetry is.
arxiv-2412-07724:
Inkit Padhi and co-authors introduce a 2024 family of guard models that screen what goes into and out of large language models. Safety filters often miss newer risks, such as jailbreak attempts and the grounding failures that plague retrieval-based systems. The guard models were built to cover those gaps.

They check prompts and replies across many risk types: bias, profanity, violence, sexual content, unethical acts, and jailbreaks. For retrieval systems, they also judge whether a reply stays grounded in its sources and answers the question. Training mixed human labels from varied sources with synthetic examples. Reported scores show strong detection on harmful content and on retrieval-specific tests. The guards can pair with any base model.
arxiv-2412-07924:
Emily Robitschek and nine co-authors present a 2024 paper using language models to measure how social factors sway liver transplant decisions. A patient's housing, support, and work life shape both health and access to care, and transplant committees weigh those factors case by case. The influence is real but hard to quantify from prose notes.

The team had language models extract 23 social and psychosocial factors from transplant evaluation notes. These snapshots of a patient's circumstances were then tested against the care path that followed. The framework turns unstructured judgments into data that can be audited for disparity. The paper reports how strongly the factors tracked with eligibility outcomes.
arxiv-2412-08124:
Xi Wang, Xiaoyi Wang, and Victor Solo develop, in a 2024 paper, a method for steering rotating bodies under randomness, with a global best strategy. Attitude control keeps spacecraft and robots pointed where they should. Noise makes the steering problem far harder than the deterministic version.

The authors first write a stochastic version of the classic optimality equation on the rotation group. They then build a numerical solver that expands the solution in special rotation functions. Policy iteration wraps the solver into an efficient scheme. Simulations of attitude stabilization show the method works. A global strategy matters because local fixes can strand a tumbling craft in a bad orientation.
arxiv-2412-08724:
Julien Pinske and co-authors write a new kind of master equation that watches entanglement being born inside noisy quantum systems, moment by moment. Open systems leak and decohere, so judging when their states are truly entangled — not just classically correlated — is notoriously slippery. Most tests compare inputs to outputs after the fact. Their 2024 equation instead bans entanglement at every instant.

The separability Lindblad equation forces trajectories to stay within classically correlated states. Any real process that departs from its predictions must be manufacturing entanglement en route. The authors solve it for key examples, pricing the dynamical contribution exactly. Dissipation, usually the enemy, becomes a benchmarked engineering tool. Quantum engineers get a stopwatch and a purity gauge for entanglement built in messy conditions.
arxiv-2412-09024:
Robert Rugg, Shambel Sahlu, and Amare Abebe let dark matter and dark energy trade energy in two simple models, then ask the data which version it prefers, in this 2024 paper. The universe's late acceleration is usually blamed on a constant dark energy. Interacting models, where the two dark components exchange energy linearly, might ease puzzles like why their densities are comparable today.

Fitting both models with Markov chain Monte Carlo against two datasets produced a split verdict. Expansion-history data favored strong interaction, leaving matter at forty-four to fifty-six percent of the universe with a low Hubble constant near sixty-six. Supernova data reversed the interaction's sign, giving eighteen to twenty percent matter and a Hubble constant near seventy-two. The authors revisit the coincidence problem in light of the disagreement, and flag the tension between datasets as the story.
arxiv-2412-09324:
Yunchen Yuan, Junyuan Xiao, and Xinjie Li ask a pointed question in their 2024 paper: are a popular class of image models really well suited to fixing damaged photos? The models they test build images step by step from learned patterns.

The authors compare those models with older, more direct repair tools across many tests. The newer models do well at grasping the broad sense of a scene. Yet they often add drift and error, and older tools beat them when damage is light. Tests of design choices show where the loss comes from. Readers get a clear case for rethinking how these models are used for repair work.
arxiv-2412-09624:
Taiming Lu and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on GenEx, a system that generates explorable 3D worlds from a single image. Understanding and moving through the physical world is a core challenge for artificial intelligence. GenEx grows one photo into a full, consistent environment that an agent can wander, shown as panoramic video.

The model learned from scalable 3D world data built in a game engine. It can capture a continuous 360-degree scene with little effort. Tests show high-quality generation and strong loop consistency over long paths. Agents guided by a large language model use the imagined world to plan. They form expectations about unseen areas, then refine their beliefs as they explore. The work links world generation to goal-driven navigation in one system.
arxiv-2412-09724:
Yankı Lekili and Jenia Tevelev compute algebra families tied to surface singularities in a 2024 paper. Smoothing a certain kind of singularity is known to produce a one-parameter family of algebras. Those families were found by abstract geometry, which makes them hard to compute explicitly. Mirror symmetry offers a concrete route in.

Using mirror symmetry for genus-one fibrations, they spot a notable immersed curve with extra data in a punctured torus. The algebra built from that curve inside a category of surfaces matches the family in question. That match lets them compute the algebra family explicitly for the classic case, turning an abstract existence result into formulas specialists can use.
arxiv-2412-09924:
Han-Gyeol Yun and co-authors stir a young planet-forming disk with vertical shear. Their 2024 paper deals with the vertical shear instability, spun up by rotation speed that shifts with height in the disk. Heat layers, or thermal stratification, bend the instability's shape. A semi-global linear study sorts the modes that grow.

Two mode kinds appear: surface modes hug strong shear zones, while body modes span the disk. In layered disks the surface kind splits in two, and the mid-height branch grows fastest. Heat layers boost both kinds and push energy into radial motion. Simulations should meet surface modes first, then body modes, the team says.
arxiv-2412-10424:
Grading a language model with fixed test questions can miss how it behaves in real conversation. Kim and co-authors propose the interview instead: a second model questions the candidate over several turns, gives feedback, and follows up on weak spots. The interviewer also rewrites the starting questions on the fly, which guards against memorized answers from leaked test sets.

They interview six models on math and depth-question tasks and find the method exposes how well each model starts, adapts, and handles clarification. It also dodges two known flaws of the judge style, runaway praise for long answers and inconsistent scores. An interview report sums up each model's strengths and gaps.
arxiv-2412-10524:
Minhyeok Lee proves that a recommender system with no ideology at all will still split its users into camps, in a 2024 paper. Platforms feed people content similar to what they already like, and echo chambers are usually blamed on bias in users or algorithms. Lee strips the system to a minimal model: users and items are points in a space, and each user drifts toward the median of the items recommended by nearest-neighbour similarity.

Under that rule alone, the mathematics guarantees users coalesce into distinct, stable clusters. Simulations confirmed the clustering and measured how population size, adaptation speed, fresh content, and noise change its pace and strength. The uncomfortable moral: fragmentation is the default physics of similarity-based recommendation, not a pathology needing villains. Designing against it means engineering against the drift itself.
arxiv-2412-11024:
Zeeshan Patel, James DeLoye, and Lance Mathias compare two leading ways to train image-generating models, diffusion and flow matching, inside one shared framework. The two methods look different: one learns to remove noise step by step, the other learns a flow that carries noise into data. A recent framework, called Generator Matching, claims both are cases of one scheme.

Recasting both methods in that single frame, the authors derive why flow matching often proves more robust in practice. They also show how mixing steady and random parts creates new model types that sit between the two. The comparison gives builders a clearer map of the design space for generative models.
arxiv-2412-11624:
Irek Mukhamedshin and co-authors probe in 2024 the local magnetic order in a kagome metal that hosts Weyl physics. Such a magnetic material could allow control of its topological traits through its magnetism. Yet it was unclear whether a second, non aligned magnetic phase or a glassy state coexists with the main ferromagnetic state below its transition point.

Using nuclear magnetic resonance, the team reads the local field at cobalt sites. All sites look the same at low heat levels, and the field follows the bulk magnetization while tilting a few degrees. Above a point, a new shoulder in the signal suggests tilted in plane moments grow. The authors rule out a coexisting in plane antiferromagnetic phase.
arxiv-2412-11724:
Researchers propose a diode-like device built from a single magnetic swirl moving in a thin strip. The swirl, called a skyrmion, is a tiny knot of magnetism that can carry data. A diode lets flow pass one way but not the other. Their 2024 simulations shape the strip, made of an antiferromagnet, with slanted zones of stronger magnetic grip.

The swirl crosses those zones going forward but is blocked coming back, just like current in a diode. The slant angle of the zones steers how well the trick works. A sweet spot of current strength and grip lets the swirl pass cleanly without bouncing back or winking out. The authors say the design could serve future spin-based electronics.
arxiv-2412-12124:
Yves Gabellini, Thierry Grandou, and Ralf Hofmann calculate a key quantity in Yang-Mills theory in a 2024 paper. Yang-Mills theory describes the strong force in a simplified form without quarks. When the coupling is strong, standard step-by-step math fails, and the gluon propagator, which tracks how gluon effects spread, is hard to obtain.

The authors build on a property called effective locality, first found in the fuller theory of the strong force. In Yang-Mills theory this property takes a simpler shape, which they recall from a recent letter. They then use it to compute the propagator in the strong regime. The paper is theoretical and offers a path around a long-standing block in non-perturbative work.
arxiv-2412-12524:
Shuta Funakoshi, Tatsuo Kobayashi, and Hajime Otsuka present a 2024 study of flavor rules in D-brane models of particle physics. Such models place matter on crossed or magnetized branes in a curled space, and the matter types carry labels from an orbifold group. Those labels yield fusion rules that are richer than plain group rules.

At the base level the matter fits a D4 flavor pattern when flux counts are even. Loop effects leave that pattern intact, a surprise the team proves. Effects past perturbation reach, tied to brane flashes, are studied as well.
arxiv-2412-12624:
Haoran Sun and Michael Galperin wrote this 2024 physics paper on steering a qubit that sits in a warm environment. Fast, faithful control of qubits underpins quantum technology, and optimal control theory designs the driving pulses. Real devices leak energy to their surroundings, so the control problem is an open-system one.

Standard practice simulates that leakage with a memory-free master equation. The authors instead use the nonequilibrium Green's function method, which keeps the memory of the bath. Even where the simple equation should apply, the two descriptions give sharply different optimal pulses for mixed states. The fuller description reaches the target state much faster. The reason, they argue, is that driving itself reshapes dissipation, an effect the memory-free picture misses.
arxiv-2412-12824:
Yi-Fang Ren, Janarbek Yuanbek, and Yusuf Turek present a 2024 physics paper on improving the quantum character of pair coherent states, a two-mode form of light. A measurement trick that keeps only selected outcomes can sharpen such states. The authors test whether that trick boosts the states' most useful quantum traits.

They computed squeezing, photon count patterns, and the entanglement between the two modes, before and after the trick. Both the non-Gaussian character and the broader nonclassical behaviour grew stronger. A scaled Wigner function picture, a standard map of quantum states, confirmed the gains across settings. The scheme offers a practical route to better light sources for quantum technology.
arxiv-2412-12924:
Eduardo Flandez and Victor Munoz wrote a 2024 space physics paper forecasting the Sun's twenty fifth activity cycle with network methods. Sunspot counts rise and fall in roughly eleven year cycles, and predicting the next peak matters for satellites and power grids. Their approach turns solar time series into complex networks.

Visibility graph methods map each data point to a node, linked when the points can see each other on the plotted curve. Network measures then trace patterns across cycles. During solar minimum, the decay exponents of several solar indices lined up with the next cycle's peak sunspot count, making them candidate precursors. Applying the method to current data predicts a peak of 179 sunspots. A classic curve fit then dates that maximum.
arxiv-2412-13024:
Daniel Patnaude and co-authors present a 2024 arXiv paper on the fading glow of supernova 1996cr, an oxygen-rich explosion still interacting with its surroundings decades on. Fresh optical spectra from 2017 and 2021 look nothing like 2006. Broad twin-peaked lines of oxygen, argon, and sulfur race out at thousands of kilometers per second. Their red sides are dimmed by dust inside the debris.

X-ray brightness from Chandra slips slowly downward, a sign the shock has burst through the dense shell around the star into thinner space. Re-reading the evidence, the authors argue the parent star was heavily stripped before exploding.
arxiv-2412-13224:
Hongpeng Cao and co-authors train safer control policies in a 2024 paper by hunting for worst cases. Learning systems often fail at rare corner cases, yet training usually starts from one fixed state or random easy ones. Their method uses a physics model to sample the dangerous states that matter most.

The sampler plugs into a physics-regulated learning framework, making training both safer and more data-efficient. Tests span a simulated pole-balancing rig, a two-dimensional drone, and a four-legged robot in simulation and in reality. Policies trained this way handled safety-critical cases far better than those from standard setups, the authors report.
arxiv-2412-13724:
Muhammad Sohail Ibrahim, Muhammad Usman and Jeong-A Lee wrote a 2024 paper on running neural networks on small edge devices. Such networks are key in many tools, but small devices have tight memory and power. Their design, called USEFUSE, joins several network layers into one step. That cuts trips to off-chip memory.

The design uses fast bit-by-bit math units for the core work. It can also spot and skip steps that add little after a key stage. Two builds serve two needs: one favors speed for urgent jobs, the other saves resources. Tests showed fewer wasted steps and better use of each pass over the data.
arxiv-2412-13924:
Ibrahim Merad and co-authors build a translator for a language almost no software supports, in a 2024 paper. Monégasque, spoken in Monaco, lacks the large text collections that modern translation needs. Their system, LYRA, fine-tunes an open large language model, adds retrieval of similar examples, and transfers knowledge from a related high-resource language, French.

Everything was trained on a single graphics card to keep the recipe adoptable. The team translated both ways between French and Monégasque. LYRA frequently beat and consistently matched strong encoder-decoder translation models on this rare pair. The study is a template for other small languages. Combine a fine-tuned open model with retrieval and a helpful big sibling language, rather than waiting for a giant corpus.
arxiv-2412-14224:
Gunindra Krishna Mahanta and co-authors hunt the radio counterpart of a mystery cosmic accelerator in a 2024 paper. A Chinese observatory had caught photons up to PeV energies from twelve sources, proof that something nearby accelerates particles to extreme energies. One source matched nothing at any other wavelength.

The team scanned the spot with a large radio telescope array in India at six hundred fifty megahertz. Inside the source's blur circle they found spread out radio emission shaped like a disk with a jet. Given the position and size match, they argue this radio source plausibly does the PeV acceleration. The find gives follow up studies a concrete target at last.
arxiv-2412-14324:
Asapanna and co-authors report a 2024 optics test of edge states in a lattice driven in steps. The setup uses light pulses in a double fibre ring, which act like steps on a two-way grid. In still lattices, the count of edge states follows bulk traits of the grid. Step-driven walks may break that rule.

The team found that the count also turns on a trait tied to the step operators at the edge itself. That extra trait lets users change the edge count without closing the energy gap, a step older routes needed. The result stretches the usual link between bulk and edge in physics. It also opens new ways to shape guided light modes in walk-based devices.
arxiv-2412-14424:
Five authors present FedPIA, a method for fine tuning large vision-language models across sites, in this 2024 paper. Hospitals and clinics hold valuable data they cannot share, so models must learn on local devices with small data and weak computers.

Standard federated learning trains small adapter parts locally and merges them on a server, but adapters trained on unlike data and tasks merge poorly. FedPIA permutes and integrates the adapters on the server using Wasserstein barycenters, a way to average shapes fairly. The aim is to draw more value from diverse local adapters while keeping data private and compute light. The method targets real multi-modal health settings.
arxiv-2412-14724:
Vummintala, Das, and Gujar address in twenty twenty-four how to make a trained scoring model fair to two protected groups at every cut-off point. Users pick a cut-off to trade off false alarms against missed cases. A model can look fair at one cut-off yet treat one group worse at another, which is a real risk in lending, hiring, and health tools.

They define fairness across the whole trade-off curve, not just at one point. They then give a fast method that adjusts a model's scores, with some randomness, to meet that standard. They prove the method loses as little accuracy as theory allows, under stated conditions. Tests on real datasets with many trained models support the claims.
arxiv-2412-14924:
Gopal Datt and Ramanpreet Kaur open a new line of study on how repeated use of harmonic mappings behaves, in a 2024 note. Harmonic mappings are built from two smooth parts and arise in complex analysis. For classic smooth functions, repeated use splits the plane into calm and wild zones, named for Fatou and Julia. No such study existed for the harmonic case.

The note sets up those two zones for harmonic mappings and proves basic traits of each. Some traits match the classic case, while others stand in sharp contrast. The authors also build a harmonic mapping with a wandering domain, a zone that never returns to itself. That case marks a clear split from some classic behavior.
arxiv-2412-15024:
Alison Warman and four colleagues design a spin chain that can host every phase allowed by a new kind of symmetry, in a 2024 paper. They also sketch how to build it with atoms. Categorical symmetries, including non-invertible ones, generalize the old Landau picture of phases of matter. Testing their predictions needs a model that is rich yet buildable.

Their chain realizes all gapped phases and second-order transitions governed by the symmetry of the dihedral group's representation category. The model stays simple enough for the lab. The proposal uses neutral atoms in optical tweezers, two species working together, with Rydberg blockade interactions driving a digital simulation of the dynamics. Several nontrivial phases become reachable in the plan. The authors offer the design as a bridge between abstract symmetry theory and tabletop experiment.
arxiv-2412-15224:
Ruimin Peng and co-authors classify seizure subtypes from brain wave recordings in a 2024 paper. Naming the exact subtype matters for precise diagnosis of epilepsy, but deep learning tools usually need far more labeled data than clinics have.

Their transformer has several branches that teach each other. One branch reads the raw brain signal, while others read its wavelet views at different frequency bands. Knowledge passes between the branches so a small labeled set goes further. Every second encoder block is replaced by one of these multi branch blocks. On two public data sets, the model beat both classic machine learning and recent deep learning tools.
arxiv-2412-15324:
David Robinson and co-authors test in 2024 if a smart learn stand in for gas heat and cool rates shifts a fake twin of a near galaxy. True rates cost too much to run raw in such sims. Two stand ins face off: a curve fit to a chart of exact runs, and a learn form with sharp marks.

One fake galaxy runs on each. The learn run's thin gas sits hot ter in a set span. A cross curve marks where both runs hold the same gas share. Glow rates for one lit gas split a shade tween runs. Beam true checks are owed next.
arxiv-2412-15524:
Xinxi Lyu and co-authors build a benchmark for how well language models follow instructions, in a 2024 paper. Most tests use a strong model as judge, which can bias scores away from human judgement. The team rechecks many design choices for automatic evaluation across a wide range of tasks.

Methods that use human written responses raised agreement with human judges by up to a few percent. Human responses also gave a view that model responses lack, so they help as extra context in comparisons. Their benchmark holds more than four thousand samples across eleven task types and is kept free of contamination. A live leaderboard tracks models on a private test set.
arxiv-2412-15624:
Rudrajit Choudhuri and co-authors reported in two thousand twenty-four on how software students use generative AI tools. Tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot are now common in class and in coding work. The team held long reflective talks with sixteen students about their real use of these tools.

Students said the tools help in some tasks, such as learning new ideas and speeding up routine code. They also cause trouble in other spots, where answers can mislead or block real learning. Teachers checked the findings as well. The paper gives clear advice on where these tools should and should not be used in teaching.
arxiv-2412-16124:
Shujie Gu and co-authors present the first statistical study of harmonic EMIC waves in near-Earth space in a 2024 paper. These waves are electromagnetic emissions tied to ion gyration, and some carry strong extra tones at multiples of the base note. Data came from the Van Allen Probes satellites.

The team sorted waves into three kinds: plain, with electric harmonics, or with magnetic harmonics. Both harmonic kinds favored the dayside, beyond the plasmasphere's edge. They appeared where plasma density was low relative to the magnetic field, protons ran hot, and the base wave was strong. Knowing where these waves thrive helps explain how they scatter radiation belt particles, a factor in satellite safety.
arxiv-2412-16224:
Khan Reaz and Gerhard Wunder put a voucher protocol to a formal proof in a 2024 paper. The protocol guards who may enter shared systems, with signed vouchers as the keys. In high-stakes fields, such guards must be proven sound, not just tested by trial.

Their check runs on a top symbolic prover under a strong foe model, where the foe reads and bends all traffic. Traits checked span who is who, secrecy, whole data, and blocks on replayed notes. The prover bore out the protocol's strength against tamper, fake IDs, and replays. Weak spots tied to trust links are also named.
arxiv-2412-16324:
Paul Masanja and co-authors computed the structure and electronic traits of lithium peroxide from first principles in a 2024 paper. Lithium-air batteries promise very high energy storage, and lithium peroxide is the key discharge product inside them. Knowing its bulk properties precisely guides cathode design.

The simulations use numerical atomic orbitals, a basis well suited to large systems. The team reports lattice structure and electronic behavior for the solid. Such data feed models of how the peroxide forms, conducts, and breaks down during charging. Slow charging and early death plague lithium-air cells, and both trace back to this material. The paper adds reference-grade numbers for battery modelers.
arxiv-2412-16724:
Six authors present in 2024 a neural network that uses physics rules to track the charge level of lithium-ion batteries. Charge tracking guides power control and helps extend battery life. Pure physics twins and pure data models each have weak spots, so the team merges the two paths.

One branch reads sensors to give the charge now, and a second branch forecasts charge later from the load ahead. Battery equations guide training so the model holds up across forecast spans. On two public data sets the merged model beat pure data models and topped prior work with a smaller build.
arxiv-2412-17024:
Yaoting Gui and co-authors wrap a model universe in an orderly family of surfaces, then weigh its center of mass two ways to prove they agree. In asymptotically Schwarzschild spaces, the geometry of distant cousin of a black hole spacetime, surfaces of constant harmonic mean curvature are the natural rulers. The authors run a volume-preserving flow from a large coordinate sphere.

The flow exists for all time and converges exponentially to such a surface. Those limit surfaces foliate the space outside a large ball, leaf by leaf. Using the foliation to define the center of mass, they show it matches the classic ADM definition, a consistency check general relativity quietly depends on.
arxiv-2412-18324:
Chunhua Zeng and co-authors did a global study of spin effects in particles in two thousand twenty-four. The work fits three sets of functions that describe how quarks carry spin inside nucleons and how they break into new particles. It uses a framework that tracks sideways motion as well as forward motion.

The fit adds the newest data from deep inelastic scattering, Drell-Yan events, and W and Z boson production, from the COMPASS and STAR teams. With the new data, the fits for down quarks and their antiquarks became much sharper. So did the tensor charge, a key number that sums part of the quark spin effect.
arxiv-2412-18524:
Mohammed Hamdan, Abderrahmane Rahiche, and Mohamed Cheriet present HTR-JAND, a lean reader of handwriting in two thousand twenty-four. Historical pages mix many hands, faded ink, and worn paper, and readers must stay fast across tongues and eras. Their design attacks all three strains at once.

A gated image network with squeeze-and-excitation blocks pulls features with care. A joint attention block blends two attention styles for sequence sense. Knowledge distillation then squeezes the big model into a small one, trained by a staged curriculum with synthetic pages. A context-aware language model polishes the output. Error rates near one percent on test sets set new marks, the authors report, while the distilled size suits wide use.
arxiv-2412-18724:
Andrei Grekov and Nikita Nekrasov extend a classic limit shape problem into richer settings in a 2024 math paper. The Vershik-Kerov problem asks what large random partitions look like at scale, and its answers link to string theory and gauge theory counting. The authors focus on circular and linear quiver theories, a family of gauge setups arranged in chains or rings.

They also touch on a double elliptic version tied to six dimensional gauge theory on a torus. In that setting they prove the limit shape is ruled by a genus two algebraic curve. The result hints at surprise dualities between counting data and symmetry data.
arxiv-2412-18924: Jacob Bradd, Nigel Higson, and Robert Yuncken prove an equivalence between two deep results in a 2024 mathematics paper. The first is David Vogan's theorem on representations of real reductive groups. It says each representation of a maximal compact subgroup appears exactly once, as the minimal type, inside a tempered representation of the whole group. The second is the Connes-Kasparov isomorphism in operator K-theory. The authors show the isomorphism is equivalent to a K-theoretic form of Vogan's result.
arxiv-2412-19024:
Hayato Kanayama and Suguru Otani gauge how well a spot gig platform matches workers to jobs in a 2024 paper. Timee, a private Japanese app, fills short flexible shifts. Public Hello Work posts give the old style match point.

Data span 2019 to 2023 on users, posts, and hires. A form free method reads match efficiency and response pulls. The private app matched far better, most of all after 2022. Response pulls for users and posts differed by platform type. Three prefectures moved alike early, split, then partly rejoined. Digital matching reshapes how spot work finds its people.
arxiv-2412-19124:
Valay Bundele and co-authors benchmark self-supervised learning for medical imaging in this 2024 paper. Such methods train models on unlabeled scans, a draw in health care where labeled data are scarce. Past tests tended to cover one data set or one trait, leaving open how sturdy the models are across settings.

Using a standard collection of medical data sets, the team tested eight leading methods across eleven data sets. They checked accuracy inside each field and skill at spotting odd samples that do not belong. They also varied the starting point, the model shape, and the share of labels, down to one percent. Cross-data-set tests measured how well learning carries over. The authors hope the shared benchmark helps others pick methods with clearer eyes.
arxiv-2412-19424:
Alberto Maté and Mariella Dimiccoli teach video models to keep their action forecasts in order, in this 2024 paper. Long-term anticipation means naming the actions still to come in a video, and for how long, after watching only the start. Their encoder-decoder builds on parallel decoding with two additions.

A regularizer checks neighboring forecast segments for a coherent story, running both ways along the timeline. A learned transition table then polishes the whole sequence at once, favoring plausible action orders. On four kitchen and activity benchmarks, the method matched or beat leading systems, including language-model rivals.
arxiv-2412-19624:
The Belle II Collaboration measures a rare B meson decay in a 2024 paper. The decay sends a neutral B meson into two charged rho mesons, and its rates carry clues to a core angle of the quark mixing scheme. Sorting such decays at a collider takes huge data sets and fine timing.

The team reports the branching share of the decay, how its spin states split, and how its rate shifts with time in a CP linked way. Those values then hem in the CKM angle phi2, a key test of the standard model of particles. Tight bounds help check whether new physics hides in B decays.
arxiv-2412-19824:
Haoyi Zhang and co-authors build AnalogXpert, a language-model agent that designs analog circuit layouts, in a 2024 paper. Analog design resists automation, and choosing the topology, which parts to use and how to wire them, is its hardest step. Earlier model-based attempts took vague wishes as input and returned idealized sketches far from factory practice.

AnalogXpert instead writes topologies as SPICE code and draws on a library of ready subcircuits, the way veteran designers reuse trusted blocks. The job splits into picking blocks and connecting them, guided by chain-of-thought prompting and in-context examples. The design brings detailed structural demands and real device models into the loop, aiming at practical synthesis rather than toy demos.
arxiv-2412-19924:
Tobias Strauch designs a way to test computer chips while they work, without interrupting them. Chips in cars, spacecraft, and military systems must be checked in the field for radiation hits and aging faults, because failures there can be life threatening. Pausing a running system to test it is itself risky, and checkpoint-based recovery can lose vital data when a strike corrupts memory.

His solution repurposes a performance technique called System Hyper Pipelining, which blends fast context switching with a retiming method, so test operations ride along invisibly. The chip gains an upset-detection circuit with ultra-fast recovery, plus a test-generation framework that writes software self-tests covering all testable stuck-at faults. Reported results on performance per area and test cycles per net look promising. Strauch argues the architecture also fits production testing and other uses.
arxiv-2501-00024:
Mohamed Osman and Tamer Nadeem present LoRaFlow, a method that rebuilds weak radio signals sent with LoRa. LoRa links serve low-power networks over long ranges, but heavy noise can wreck them. Most past fixes aim to sort signals by type. Their method instead restores the signal itself, using a rectified flow model. The cleaned signal still feeds standard decoding steps.

The design pairs a hybrid neural network with fake training data and tough noise drills. It slips into current LoRa setups with little change. The authors argue it can stretch range and trust in harsh sites. They also note the core trick could aid other radio systems. The paper offers a fresh path for hardy Internet of Things links.
arxiv-2501-01424:
Gaurav Parmar and co-authors let users compose images from object pictures, not just words, in a 2025 paper. A cook could drop in photos of a specific chair and lamp and ask for a room built around them. Keeping each object recognizable while varying the scene is the hard part.

Their method splits the guiding signals inside the image model. Layout keys come from a tight encoder, while look details come from a roomier one, and mixing the two keeps identity with freedom of arrangement. Extra guidance at run time sharpens layout and faithfulness. Results show varied scenes that preserve each prompt object's character across styles, widening the creative range of text-to-image tools.
arxiv-2501-01624:
Andrea Erdas computes a quantum vacuum effect for fermions in a theory that bends relativity, in a 2025 paper. The Casimir effect is a force between close plates caused by empty space's own energy. Erdas studies it for a massless fermion field under Horava-Lifshitz rules, which treat space and time unevenly at tiny scales.

The fermion is boxed between two plates under bag-style boundary rules, in contact with a heat bath. A zeta-function method yields clean formulas for the free energy and the pressure between plates. Both low- and high-heat limits are worked out, for even and odd values of the relativity-breaking parameter. Exact results like these give benchmarks for testing exotic gravity ideas in tabletop settings.
arxiv-2501-01724:
Ravshan Ashurov and Ilyoskhuja Sulaymonov prove a clean fact about the Mittag-Leffler function, a special function that shows up whenever diffusion runs slower than usual. They show that as the parameter of the function grows, its values move in one steady direction, with no reversals.

That steady behavior then solves a practical puzzle. In a subdiffusion equation, the order of the fractional derivative is often unknown. Earlier work had gaps in showing it could be pinned down from a single measurement at one point in space and time. Ashurov and Sulaymonov fill in the missing conditions and cover a wider class of equations than before. They also give an example where the unknown order is the only possible one.
arxiv-2501-02124:
B Laikhtman, G Belenky, and S Suchalkin propose a new way to tune a semiconductor laser in this 2025 study. Their design gives the laser a third contact, placed inside the layered stack.
