One pair of contacts powers the light gain as usual. A voltage across another pair drives a special current through the lower layer, piling up charge there.

That stored charge changes how the layer bends light, and so shifts the laser's color. Because the link between voltage and color comes out straight, sweeps of color are naturally even, with no extra correction gear. The authors work through an example laser that emits far-infrared light. Their numbers show shifts in the gigahertz range, with speed set by outside electronics, not the device.
arxiv-2501-02224:
Kingman Cheung and co-authors gauge in 2025 if a future muon collider could find a heavy dark twin of the Z boson. The dark twin would mix with plain light in a faint way. In muon hits it can be born next to a photon, which gives a clean trace.

The photon's bounce mass lets the dark mass be read with care. Cut picks tuned by mass lift the hunt odds at three scope strengths. Jet and electron end forms both get a pass in the plan. For heavy dark forms the bounce cuts bite most, while light forms gain from pair mass cuts.
arxiv-2501-02324:
Hua-Chao Liu and Rong-Xin Miao study traversable wormholes in a curved space setting in a 2025 physics paper. A wormhole that a traveler could pass through usually needs exotic matter, which breaks a standard energy rule. Recent work found such wormholes with normal matter in flat space, using a theory that mixes gravity, electrons, and electric fields.

The authors extend that work to anti-de Sitter space, a space with constant negative curvature. They find wormholes with both ball-shaped and flat-shaped openings. Using a known link between gravity and field theory, they compute how entanglement grows for strips and disks on the two edges of the wormhole. As the region grows, the entanglement shows a sudden shift in behavior.
arxiv-2501-02424:
Jack Logan and four co-authors ask what makes folded proteins take the shapes they do, in a 2025 paper. Proteins are chains that fold into compact three-dimensional forms. Certain measures, such as size and core packing, follow clear patterns across proteins. The inner scaling of size along the chain breaks the simple pattern, though.

The team built simple computer models of chains, adding detail step by step. Spheres stand in for chain units and side parts, with set bend angles. The fullest model matched the key measures for thousands of known protein structures. It captured both core traits and the odd inner scaling. The work shows that chain bend limits alone explain much of protein shape. Simpler models missed some of those traits.
arxiv-2501-03124:
Mingyang Song and four co-authors build an examination for the graders that grade reasoning, in this 2025 paper. Process reward models score each step of a language model's chain of thought, catching errors before they compound. The graders themselves need grading, and existing benchmarks mostly check whether they spot wrong steps, which is too crude for the subtler failures of real reasoning.

Their benchmark, PRMBench, holds 6,216 problems and 83,456 step-level labels, designed to probe distinct abilities: noticing redundancy, honoring soundness, and staying sensitive to small planted errors. Fifteen models sat the exam, from dedicated reward models to big chatbots asked to play critic. All showed real weaknesses somewhere. The authors publish the weak spots as a research agenda: until the graders can pass a fine-grained test, trusting them to supervise machine reasoning is premature.
arxiv-2501-03324:
Sabine Wehnert, Muhammet Ertaş, and Ernesto William De Luca study bias in Swiss court data in two thousand twenty-five. The dataset predicts Swiss Federal Supreme Court judgments. Biased training facts could skew such legal predictions badly. Fair, neutral case facts are the base the models need.

The team scans the set with Holistic Bias descriptors. Attention views show how dispreferred terms steer model outputs. Bias shows up in the data and moves predictions in tests. Dataset imbalance and token limits also drag performance down. The findings warn legal model builders to audit their sources.
arxiv-2501-03424: Ethan Eugene Wynner, writing alone, offers a condensed tour of Soergel bimodules and what they bought for Kazhdan-Lusztig theory, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The bimodules give a concrete, categorical home for Hecke algebras. Wynner follows the path laid out in a well-known textbook treatment and explains Soergel's headline results, including his fresh proofs of the Kazhdan-Lusztig conjectures. The paper is openly a survey, pitched at readers who want the shape of a vast subject without years of detour.
arxiv-2501-03624:
Gaoussou Youssouf Kebe and co-authors benchmark language models on real psychiatric interviews, in a paper published in 2025. Their test set, LlaMADRS, comes from a corpus of clinical interviews scored by experts. It holds over five thousand annotations across 541 sessions, and the task is to rate depression symptoms from dialogue the way a clinician would.

They ran twenty-five open models, from small to very large, making over four hundred thousand predictions. Strong models reached item scores close enough to expert ratings for clinical use. Asking the model to score each symptom in its own call, then sum, beat asking for a total at once. Gains credited to reasoning models mostly came from prompt design, the authors found, since plain models with structured prompts matched them. Longer reasoning traces did help within reasoning models.
arxiv-2501-03724:
Fermion fields linked to discrete series representations are studied by Vasileios Letsios, Ben Pethybridge, and Alan Rios Fukelman in a 2025 paper. The representations belong to the group SL(2,R) and have half-integer scaling dimension. At the classical level, the authors show that these representations live in the mode solutions of spinor fields with imaginary mass on a fixed two-dimensional de Sitter background.

With the mass tuned in this way, the field gains a fermionic shift symmetry, which the authors characterize. In the Euclidean section, zero modes appear and block a standard two-point function. The team proposes a way to handle those modes and define a function with the right singular form. They close by proposing two interacting theories that hold these fermions in their spectrum.
arxiv-2501-03924:
Guillaume Delord works on Schur's orthogonality relations for the free group, in a mathematics paper from 2025. The paper deals with the quasi-regular representation of a finitely generated free group. Such relations state how matrix coefficients of a representation pair up when averaged over the group.

Delord shows that integrals of these products over larger and larger balls in the group settle to an explicit limit once they are scaled in the right way. The result gives a precise large-scale picture of the coefficients. Readers in group theory and representation theory get a clean convergence statement for a group where many sums fail to behave so well.
arxiv-2501-04124:
Marie-Therese Huebsch, Fabien Tran, and Martijn Marsman fix a gap in a widely used way of computing material properties, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Standard approximations for electron interactions miss a twisting effect that acts on electron spin. That effect matters for magnetic materials and spin-based devices.

Their fix builds the effect into a broader theory that tracks spin currents as well as charge. They coded the new method into a major simulation package. Tests on a small chromium molecule and a bulk oxide matched the strength of costlier methods. Surprisingly, the effect also shifted energy in simple aligned magnets. Cost per step stayed like that of similar methods, with fewer steps needed overall.
arxiv-2501-04524:
Dani de Boe, Fabiano Santos, and Jackson Levi Said test the stability of a modified gravity theory in this 2025 paper. The theory adds scalar fields to gravity and serves as a dark energy candidate. It grows from Horndeski gravity as used in string theory, with two dilaton fields.

The team studies the scalar sector's wobbles around allowed background states. They set those results beside the tensor sector's, studied before. Entropy from particle creation and from the apparent horizon gives bounds to compare as well. A single-field background gets the closest look. The paper checks whether the theory's cosmos can hold together without runaway modes.
arxiv-2501-04724:
Joe Omatoi, Abdul M. Mohammed, and Dennis Trujillo use causal inference, rather than correlation, to ask what actually changes how long breast cancer stays away after treatment. Randomized trials pin down causes but only in narrow groups. The authors instead apply a causal discovery method called LiNGAM to records from a Duke breast cancer imaging dataset with more than forty recorded features per patient.

Two effects stood out. Adjuvant anti-HER2 therapy added about 169 days of local recurrence-free survival, underlining its value for HER2-positive patients. Tumor involvement of the skin or nipple cut that survival by about 351 days, marking a high-risk group that may need targeted intervention. The authors argue that causal models over broad observational data can guide personalized treatment strategy where trials cannot reach.
arxiv-2501-04824:
Auvity and co-authors present a 2025 lab study of how waves snap thin floating sheets, a stand in for sea ice. Sheets of a brittle stuff ride on water and take wave driven bends. The team asked where the break starts and what sets the load at which it gives.

Breaks came at the spot of peak bend, and the snap point swung with wave traits. A fixed stress cap could not explain the data. An energy rule fit far better: a crack runs when the freed elastic energy beats the cost of new surface. That cost depends on the wave shape, which ties the break rule to the forcing. The authors urge ice modelers to retest stress based rules in sea ice sims.
arxiv-2501-05124:
Michael Ridley and co-authors study how noise can boost, rather than blur, a weak signal in a tiny circuit. Their 2025 paper works with a junction made of two quantum dots, a speck-scale link for current. They use an exact math frame for current under a bias that shifts in time. First they weigh heat against a steady drive with random swings, then they add a smooth wave drive on top.

At some drive settings, the swings lift the net current instead of washing it out. That lift is the resonance effect in the title. Tint in the noise, set by how long its swings last, also shifts the effect. Light-aided flow, they show, can be tuned by the noise around it.
arxiv-2501-05224:
Tomas Goldsack, Carolina Scarton, and Chenghua Lin test language models as plain-language summarizers in a 2025 paper. Research papers in biomedicine are hard for non-experts to read. A lay summary restates the work in everyday words, and models could draft them without task-specific training.

Their two-stage method mirrors how humans write such summaries, and human judges preferred its output more as models grew larger. They also tested models as judges of summaries and found their choices matched human panels well. Early trials on computing papers show the skill transfers to a new field. The work sets out early best practice for zero-shot lay summary.
arxiv-2501-05424:
Christophe Morisset and co-authors model the glow of gas in star-forming galaxies in this 2025 paper. Galaxies shine through thousands of glowing gas clouds around young stars. Adding up those clouds' light by hand is slow, and each cloud differs.

Their approach trains a neural network on runs of a physics code that simulates one cloud. The network then predicts each cloud's emission lines fast. They build 250,000 fake galaxies from up to 3,000 clouds each, with dust and a diffuse gas share mixed in. Varying the inputs shows how the total glow shifts. The method makes galaxy spectra easier to read.
arxiv-2501-05624:
Fei Li, Arul Rhik Mazumder, and Max Zhao tackle shipment rerouting, a logistics problem that bundles many hard sequencing and packing problems into one. Goods must move by truck between hubs from sources to destinations, and the solver must choose trucks and routes that minimize total cost. The problem is NP-hard, and only classical approximate methods existed for its variants with limited truck capacity.

The authors design both classical methods and quantum annealing algorithms for the task. Their edge comes from new mathematical programming formulations that exploit the network's structure, the shipments, and truck capacities together, handling sequencing and packing at once rather than separately. In extensive experiments across scenarios, the quantum annealing solver reached optimal or near-optimal solutions much faster than the standard solver. The team presents the work as evidence that quantum annealers can compete on real logistics optimization.
arxiv-2501-05724:
Companies guard their code fiercely, yet they still need it translated when languages shift. Jahnavi Kumar and co-authors study a workaround in this 2025 paper: a shared translation model trained without anyone handing over their code. Each client trains locally and only model updates travel, the federated learning pattern.

The joint model translated between C# and Java far better than models each client trained alone, lifting one quality score for a known code model by over 40 percent. Pooling knowledge helped every participant while code stayed home. The authors call it one of the first tests of federated language models for this task. They see the pattern spreading to other guarded software jobs.
arxiv-2501-05924:
R Nagy and co-authors compare how stars drift across a galactic disk under two rival laws of gravity. In the dark matter view, unseen mass shapes the pull; in MOND, the law itself changes at weak pull. Spiral arms and bars push stars inward or outward through resonances, a process called churning.

The team ran a two-dimensional simulation of a Milky Way-like galaxy with two million stars over six billion years. They tracked each star's guiding radius and its motion phases. Migration ran far stronger in the MOND runs. Up to five times as many stars shifted their guiding radius by a large margin there than in the dark matter runs. The contrast gives observers a fresh way to test which gravity law better matches real galaxy data.
arxiv-2501-06424:
Matheus de Morais Leça and Ronnie de Souza Santos sort out three kinds of software testing that often blur together. Their 2025 paper deals with fairness testing, which checks whether a system treats people even-handedly. Fairness matters most in data-driven systems, yet in practice its borders with usability testing and accessibility testing are muddy, which makes it hard to build into daily development work.

Theirs is a study of studies: they draw on twelve systematic reviews published over the past decade. From those reviews they map how the three testing kinds overlap and where each one stands on its own. The aim is a clearer, user-focused picture of cross-domain testing, so teams can plan fairness checks without confusing them with the other two. The paper speaks to researchers and practitioners who build and test modern software systems.
arxiv-2501-06724:
Takamasa Terada and Masahiro Toyoura denoise ECG signals with wavelets in two thousand twenty five. Wearable heart monitors use dry electrodes for convenience. Those sensors suffer heavy noise distortion in daily use. ECG and noise bands overlap, so plain filters fail.

Their network adds a wavelet transform layer to a CNN. The layer pulls clean ECG frequency features to the fore. Noise traits shift with intensity and type in the design. Tests span signal to noise ratios from minus ten to ten. Gains grow largest where the noise is worst.
arxiv-2501-07224:
A robot's touch can be scripted by a chat model, Qiaoqiao Ren and Tony Belpaeme show in a 2025 study. Touch carries feeling in human contact, yet most robots can only open and close a hand. Their test rig is a sleeve with a five-by-five grid of buzzers worn on the arm.

Prompt chains coaxed the model into ten-second buzz patterns for ten emotions and six gestures, from pats to rubs. Thirty-two volunteers rated each pattern for pleasantness and intensity. Sparse buzz patterns can carry social touch signals, earlier work hinted. A language model as choreographer could give care robots a richer, safer touch vocabulary.
arxiv-2501-07324:
Buse Sibel Korkmaz and co-authors present AutoRefine, a method that fine-tunes foundation models with reinforcement learning driven by measurable task gains, in a 2025 paper. Fine-tuning normally needs human feedback, which is costly to gather. Their method instead takes its feedback from direct measures of downstream performance.

They show it on hiring platforms, where biased wording in job posts skews which candidates a matching engine returns. A generative model rewrites job specs, and the system steers it toward posts that draw more diverse candidate matches. Tests on a public hiring data set and a real platform show how large language models can spot and soften bias in practice.
arxiv-2501-07624:
Isaac Wang, Xun-Jie Xu, and Bei Zhou probed a new range of neutrino self interaction with space neutrinos. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, starts from a fresh case. One neutrino type may weigh less than the heat of the cosmic neutrino sea. Then part of that sea moves at near light speed. That spread smears the dip such neutrinos carve into space neutrino spectra.

Past work, with a cold sea, foresaw a sharp dip. The team solved the flow math for both loss and regrowth of neutrinos. The broad dip opens reach to far lighter go between particles than the old range. Future reads of supernova neutrinos round the sky could test it.
arxiv-2501-08224:
Turner and co-authors report 26 new galactic radio transients in a 2025 paper. A live search pipe on the MeerKAT scope catches lone pulses as they land. Most new finds are rotating radio transients, stars that flash at odd gaps. Three finds match stars known from next surveys. Two sources' spread marks strain the galaxy's own share, a hint they sit far.

Fine pulse fits and snap shots give sky posts to arcsecond truth. Five sources earn full time marks, with ages of millions of years and weak fields. One source turns each 17.5 seconds, a slow spin. Most flashed once and hid on past returns.
arxiv-2501-08624:
Oliver Li wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on weighted blowups in algebraic geometry. A blowup replaces a chosen center inside a geometric space with a richer structure that records incoming directions, resolving singularities. Weighted blowups allow the directions to carry different weights, which suits more delicate singularities.

Li proves a semi-orthogonal decomposition theorem for the weighted blowup of an algebraic stack along a Koszul-regular weighted center. Such a decomposition breaks the derived category of the blowup into ordered, simpler pieces. The result generalizes a classic theorem of Orlov for ordinary blowups. His approach builds on work by Bergh and Schnürer. Decompositions like this are a basic tool for comparing the geometry of related spaces.
arxiv-2501-08724:
Sergiu Arapan and co-authors show how to carry fine atomic-level magnetism into the coarser simulations engineers actually run, in a 2025 paper. Their test case is a three-layer stack of cobalt, ruthenium, and cobalt, a sandwich used in magnetic devices. The layers talk to each other through the middle one, and the strength of that talk is set at the buried interfaces. Atom-scale calculations can find the strength but cannot model a whole device.

The authors compute the interface coupling and other material values from first-principles and spin simulations at several temperatures. Those values then feed a continuum model of the magnetisation, called micromagnetics. The work demonstrates the hand-off on the cobalt sandwich. Such bridges matter because real magnetic memory and sensors are designed at the device scale, while their key behaviours are born at the atomic one.
arxiv-2501-08924:
Benoit Brummer and Christophe De Vleeschouwer release a dataset of raw camera images and methods that clean, reconstruct, and compress them in one go, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Camera pipelines usually polish finished pictures, discarding raw sensor data early. Raw files keep more information but need special handling.

The dataset pairs raw shots designed to help denoisers work across sensors, shooting styles, and development paths. One method cleans the raw mosaic directly for speed. Another works on linear color data for wider sensor reach. Both beat approaches that start from finished images. Merging denoising with compression at the raw stage also improved the size-versus-quality trade and cut computing cost. The authors argue for raw-first workflows.
arxiv-2501-09024:
Amirreza Payandeh and colleagues taught a robot to read social situations in words in 2025. A robot moving through a crowd must act in ways people find acceptable, but hand-written rules and demonstrations alone leave a gap between seeing a scene and choosing a socially sound action. The team used language as the bridge, in the style of human reasoning.

They built a dataset of forty thousand human-annotated question-and-answer pairs drawn from two thousand recorded interactions in busy public spaces, covering perception, prediction, step-by-step reasoning, action, and explanation. Fine-tuning a vision-language model on it produced Social-LLaVA, which outscored leading commercial models on average across a battery of human-judged questions. The model was then deployed on a real mobile robot, showing the approach works outside the lab.
arxiv-2501-09224:
Kaiyan Li and co-authors set a ceiling on how well fast MRI methods can ever perform on a given task. Their 2025 paper uses an ideal observer, a math judge that makes the best possible call from raw scan data. No rebuild method can beat that judge, so its score bounds every method. The worry is real. Learning-based rebuilders can yield clean images that hide lost detail when scans skip too much data.

A neural stand-in for the ideal judge does the scoring from raw data. Past work built such judges for X-ray scans. Here the team extends the idea to multi-coil MRI, the standard form for modern scanners. Tests on a styled case show how the bound can expose scan plans that doom a task. Designers can use the check before trusting sharp-looking rebuilt images.
arxiv-2501-09424:
Julian Göttsch and eight co-authors set out a new way to gain test data on light states that, in a strict sense, never were there. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Small cat-like states of light can be made by a chance signal that a photon was cut from a linked field. Full tests then give the state's shape, but with few photons. A second path picks out events with an exact photon count. The new path starts from a batch of such heralded states, splits them at a beam splitter, and reads two field traits at once at the two ends. It yields data for states with far more linked photons on the mean.
arxiv-2501-09524: Jaak Peetre's 1981 technical report from Lund, reissued here in 2025 with Per Nilsson as typist, treats H-infinity spaces and complex interpolation, two tools of advanced analysis. The note is an exact copy of the original report, with some newer general references added, a few references updated, and misprints corrected. It preserves a compact piece of interpolation theory in its original form for current readers.
arxiv-2501-10224:
Erol Gelenbe and Mohammed Nasereddin design a defense that keeps vehicle-network gateways working during packet flood attacks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Gateways for the Internet of Vehicles must spot attacks while holding delays and losses low, yet floods can bury the very detector meant to catch them. The authors first measure how floods degrade a gateway in practice.

Their answer pairs a smart forwarder at the gate with an adaptive mitigation system that wakes once an attack is flagged. The system samples the incoming stream to check whether the flood persists, and drops batches of packets to drain the backlog. A cost balance weighs sampling effort against good packets lost. Tests and theory both show the tuned version blunts attacks well.
arxiv-2501-10324:
Andrea Avogaro and four co-authors survey research from 2025 on forecasting how new fashion items will sell. Fast fashion makes huge runs of new styles, which wastes cloth and harms the environment. Better forecasts could cut overproduction, but taste shifts fast and old trends return in new forms, so the task is hard.

Their survey sorts past work into the first full taxonomy of learning-based methods for this task. It reviews ways to join image, text, and sales data, and lists the data sets teams can use. The authors close with open problems and paths for greener, sharper forecasting tools.  The survey follows a standard, open method for sorting and screening the past studies it covers.
arxiv-2501-10824:
Zsolt Pocze wrote a theoretical paper in 2025 on how much information a finite pattern contains. Standard information theory grew up around Shannon's ideas, which fit signals from well-behaved random processes such as ergodic Markov chains. Many real patterns do not come from such processes, so Pocze seeks definitions of information content and entropy that apply more broadly while agreeing with the traditional ones where those work.

Working from a combinatorial viewpoint, he compares the information content of different finite patterns and derives general properties any such quantity should have. From those properties he builds normalized estimation methods based on compression algorithms and Kolmogorov complexity. He then redefines entropy in the same spirit, in a way that matches traditional entropy in the large limit.
arxiv-2501-11324:
Ben Snow and co-authors simulate the churning boundary where a cool solar prominence meets the million-degree corona, and find the mixing cools more than it heats. Their 2025 paper models the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability along a prominence thread. Observers see brightened emission at intermediate temperatures in such layers and usually blame turbulent heating.

The simulations say otherwise: radiation at those temperatures is so efficient that the layer loses energy overall, even while glowing brighter in warm lines. The authors synthesize what telescopes would see in several spectral lines. One magnesium line probes the mixing layer itself, while hydrogen and calcium lines trace the thread and its edge. The proposed signature of mixing is cooler lines dimming as hotter lines brighten, a pattern heating cannot mimic.
arxiv-2501-12124:
Simon Blackburn, Yeow Meng Chee, Tuvi Etzion, and Huimin Lao extend a classic randomness construction to two dimensions in a 2025 paper. A well known sequence type, prized for its balance, has a grid analogue where every small pattern appears exactly once as a window.

Some polynomials yield whole sets of sequences that share the good properties even when the usual recipe fails. The paper builds the grid version of those sets. The arrays also obey a shift and add rule: adding two arrays, or shifted copies, lands on another array of the set. Two proof methods are given. One folds sequences into arrays. The other generalizes an older argument and reaches parameter choices never built before.
arxiv-2501-12424:
Wang, Liu, and Liu present a collaborative learning framework for multimodal sentiment analysis in twenty twenty-five. The task reads sentiment from video by combining face, voice, and text. The three modes differ a lot in nature, which limits feature capture. Their framework aims to learn shared and specific features together.

A parameter free module splits each mode into common and specific parts. Policy models, guided by a joint reward, mine extra features from the specific parts. Attention within each mode highlights key components of the common parts. Experiments on four databases check overall gains and each module's role. The framework beat prior methods by a clear margin in their tests. Code is shared by the authors for reuse.
arxiv-2501-12724:
Shubham Purwar and co-authors investigate a metal to insulator switch in an iron selenium compound in a 2025 paper. They prepared samples with several selenium contents and tracked structure, electrical behavior, and magnetism across temperatures. As selenium content rose, the lattice constants and cell volume grew. Around each sample's switching temperature, the lattice changed in an unusual way.

The team argue that this anomalous lattice effect is what triggers the switch. Computer calculations of the electron states backed the claim: the low temperature structure looked metallic, while the high temperature structure opened a gap at the Fermi level, as an insulator should. The paper ties a structural quirk directly to an electronic phase change.
arxiv-2501-12824:
Alessio Quercia and co-authors present a 2025 paper on judging depth from a single photo. Depth maps guide robots and cars, but labeled depth data are costly and scarce. The team borrows data from sister tasks, such as labeling image regions. A shared decoder on a pre-trained vision model trains in turns on depth and helper tasks, with depth weighted most.

Across wide tests, helper data lifted depth quality by about 11 percent on average. Not all helper tasks helped alike, so choice matters more than volume. Region labeling data, recast as a dense multi-label task, often added extra gains. The method also kept quality while cutting depth data needs by at least 80 percent. Code is public, the team notes.
arxiv-2501-12924:
Bran Knowles and co-authors ask how the field of human-computer interaction talks about age and ageing. Rather than treat age as a simple number, they argue that work with older adults needs a fuller view of what age means in daily life.

The team looks at ten years of papers from a major conference and builds a typology with many parts. The typology shows which traits of older adults designers tend to stress. The authors then urge a more careful and social view of age, and use it to think again about the gap in digital access faced by older people.
arxiv-2501-13024:
Fabrizio Canfora and co-authors show in 2025 that a certain gravity theory can host wormholes and other exotic ground states that a plainer theory cannot. Their setting pairs Einstein gravity with a Skyrme matter field that carries a baryonic charge. The wormholes are of Euclidean type in a space with a negative cosmological constant, a setup used to study dual quantum theories.

A known block stops such wormholes in a simpler theory when their edges curve the wrong way, but the Skyrme field lifts it. The wormhole free energy does not depend on the free constants, like a topological soliton, and its linked stress measure vanishes. Other states act as distinct vacua and switch phases above a set heat level, much like heat driven transitions known in gravity theory.
arxiv-2501-13224: Daniel Acosta Soba, Alessandro Columbu, and Giuseppe Viglialoro wrote a math paper from 2025 on cells that chase a chemical they also eat. In such a model, a cell crowd can pile up without bound, which breaks the math. Their model adds damping terms tied to how steep the crowd and signal are. They find starting conditions that keep every solution bounded for all time, marking where the damping can hold the pile-up in check.
arxiv-2501-13324:
Neal Ma and co-authors study how battery owners bid in California power markets in a 2025 paper. Using market data from July 2023 to October 2024, they ask whether storage firms hold back supply to lift prices. The concern grows as more batteries join the grid and can shape prices.

Bids tracked market prices closely and rose sharply during price spikes. Tests showed a strong link between spikes and held-back capacity, which suggests firms can foresee surges. A daily pattern also stood out when bids were compared with the best bids made with hindsight. Readers get clear evidence of profit-driven holding back, plus a case for tighter market rules as storage grows.
arxiv-2501-13824:
Yuan and co-authors asked in 2025 whether hallucinations from language models can help drug discovery, under a head title that poses that question directly. Hallucinations are plausible but wrong text, usually seen as a fault. The team tested them as input for predicting molecule properties, an early step in drug work.

Models wrote natural language descriptions from molecule codes, and those often wrong descriptions fed sorting tasks. For some of seven tested models, accuracy rose clearly when the text was included. One model beat all baselines, and text from the strongest model gave the largest gains across models. Structural misdescriptions helped most, the authors found.
arxiv-2501-13924:
Hao Dong, Eleni Chatzi, and Olga Fink adapt models at test time for mixed data in this 2025 paper. Models often meet data unlike their training set, with classes never seen before. Test-time adaptation tunes the model on the fly, without labels.

Their setting joins several data types at once, like image and sound, which older methods barely touch. Their framework leans on entropy, the model's uncertainty score. Known and unknown samples differ in that score, and the method uses the gap to guide updates. It filters and weighs samples with care. The aim is robust adaptation that does not collapse when strangers appear.
arxiv-2501-14124:
Rostamijavanani, Li, and Yang find bent modes of sway sets from response data. Core modes let one read, sum, and mark how a set acts. Straight mode swaps fail for bent sets, which lack one fix form. Bent modes, called NNMs, stretch the straight frame to such sets. Past roads need the full sums or tight test rigs to find them. Both are oft out of reach in field use of gear.

Their road folds law caps in a flow net trained on data. Flow nets hold split hid spaces that ease mode splits. Their turns can flip back, which aids the mode map build. Hid spaces map one-to-one to modes in the trained net. Swap rules for the modes come out of the same net. Response reads alone feed the whole build.
arxiv-2501-14224:
Jiaxin Bai and a big team charted ten challenges in twenty twenty-five on the road to agentic neural graph databases. Graph databases store linked data well. They cannot infer, though. Neural graph databases add learned prediction over noisy graphs with gaps. Yet they still wait for queries set in advance. The next step the team backs adds autonomy. A system would build its own queries. It would run them neurally and keep on learning.

The authors name the blocks in the road. They hold how to represent semantic units and how to do abductive reasoning. They hold scalable execution and links to foundation models. Their piece is an agenda for the field. It says these ten challenges will decide if self-improving data systems can be built. If built, agentic graph databases would serve uses that need flexible, autonomous care of linked data.
arxiv-2501-14324:
Sofia Forsblom and four co-authors report X-ray polarization measurements of the pulsar Vela X-1 in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Polarized X-rays reveal the geometry of the gas falling onto a neutron star. The space telescope IXPE has unlocked this view for several pulsars. Vela X-1 stood out for a sharp twist: its polarization angle swings by ninety degrees between low and high energies. That twist had blocked any firm reading of its geometry.

The team split the analysis by energy and by pulse phase. The split reveals two spectral parts with crossed polarization. With the parts separated, the pulsar's geometry comes into reach. The result sharpens how we picture accretion near a neutron star's magnetic poles.
arxiv-2501-14524:
Image generators based on Stable Diffusion can restyle a picture, but keeping the content while changing the style is a balancing act. Ludovica Schaerf and co-authors locate where that balance lives inside the network in a 2025 paper. They dissect the skip connections, the side channels that carry detail across the U-shaped architecture.

One channel does most of the work: the link from the third encoder block carries the image's spatial content. Style rides in the opposing stream at the decoding side. Injecting that block's representation into a generation lets users edit by text, make precise changes, and transfer style, all without any retraining. Benchmarked against leading editors, their SkipInject method scored the best trade-off between honoring the prompt and preserving the original structure.
arxiv-2501-15124:
Licheng Zhang and co-authors bounded crowding in claw-free drawings in two thousand twenty-five. Some graphs draw on the plane with one crossing per edge. A claw is one hub joined to three leaves. Forbidding claws as subgraphs tames the structure. The team asked how dense such graphs can get. Degree and connectivity limits were the targets.

No vertex can exceed degree ten, and that is tight. Special families push the cap down to eight. Connectivity cannot reach seven without forcing a claw. So claw-free versions stay at six or below. The paper also sharpens some older planar results. Graph theorists gain exact extremal numbers. Such bounds guide network design constraints.
arxiv-2501-15224:
Xiao-Tong Li, Guang-Yu Wang, and Qi-An Zhang study a particle that may be made almost wholly of glue-like force carriers, in a paper from 2025. The particle, called X(2370), was probed in decays of another particle by a large experiment in China. Its mass and spin traits match what theory expects of the lightest glueball of its kind. Glueballs are rare states where the strong force binds to itself.

The team propose a new test ground: decays of heavy B mesons. Treating the particle as a glueball, they compute the rates for several such decays. Some rates land high enough for a running facility, Belle II, to detect. A sighting pattern there would support or shake the glueball claim. The paper maps a fresh route into a long open question of strong-force physics.
arxiv-2501-15424:
Li and co-authors report a 2025 physics study of a magnet made from iron and germanium, with a layered kagome pattern. They measured a very large anomalous Hall effect, a sideways voltage that appears in some magnetic materials. The effect is tied to curves in the energy states of the material, which grow strong near flat bands of states.

The team found a Hall response far larger than in other kagome materials of this kind. They link the size of the effect to a sheet of touching states in the material. The result points to a new place to search for large Hall materials for spin based devices and future quantum tools.
arxiv-2501-15524:
Bijo Anand and co-authors pin down a domination number in graph products in 2025. A dominating set touches every vertex outside it, and here the leftover vertices must also form a weakly convex set. The smallest size of such a set is the number under study.

Earlier work on this number left gaps for combined graphs. The paper settles the value for two graphs joined by three product rules: the Cartesian, strong, and lexicographic products. Along the way, the authors note further counting results of interest. The work sits in pure graph theory, where such numbers guide network design intuition.
arxiv-2501-15624:
Eduard Barbu and co-authors report a language technology study, published in 2025, on making Estonian text easier to read. Estonian has few resources for this task, so the team first built a new dataset. They combined texts simplified by hand with versions made by a large language model, giving both systems the same material to learn from.

Two approaches were compared: a translation style neural system and a fine-tuned large language model called LLaMA. Judges rated the language model higher on grammar, ease of reading, and keeping the original meaning. The team also released its dataset, training scripts, and tests, so others can adapt the method to other low resource languages.
arxiv-2501-16024:
Richard Beanland and Robin Sjokvist extend their diffraction rules for tilted perovskites in this 2025 paper. Perovskites with tilted oxygen octahedra show extra faint spots, called superstructure reflexions. A first paper derived simple yes-no rules for those spots.

That work assumed tilts were vanishingly small and kept only the first term of an expansion. Real crystals tilt enough that the second term matters. It creates a fresh set of spots with a half-even-even-odd index pattern. The authors derive yes-no rules for when those second-order spots appear. The rules help readers decode real diffraction patterns from tilted perovskite materials without heavy computation.
arxiv-2501-16124:
Xiao-Yu Qi, Qi Wu, Xing-Dao Guo, and Dian-Yong Chen estimated rare decays in two thousand twenty-five of a family of charm particles called D-wave charmonia. Two members of this family were spotted in recent experiments, which filled out the group. The team studied how these particles decay into lighter charm particles while hiding their charm inside.

They use a meson loop model, with its key setting fixed from a known decay rate. Estimates cover several decay paths for three family members. One path is predicted at about ten percent of a known gamma-ray path. Future runs at BESIII, Belle II, and LHCb can test these numbers directly.
arxiv-2501-16224:
Abdoulatif Cisse and co-authors present in 2025 BORA, a helper that pairs a chance based search method with a large language model for lab work. Many lab tasks pair many knobs with slow, dear tests. Plain search can trap in poor zones of a bent field.

The model feeds field sense into the search to point it at rich zones. It also talks the user through each step in live notes, with its grounds laid out. Fake tests with up to fifteen knobs and four real lab tasks back the blend. Bias risk in human hints is one spur for the tool.
arxiv-2501-16424:
Amornrat Aungwerojwit and co-authors report new observations of three little-studied ultracompact binary stars in a 2025 paper. AM CVn stars pair a white dwarf with a helium-rich companion in orbits under about an hour. They are rare, and some members have barely been watched since discovery.

Blending ground-based telescopes with the TESS space telescope, the team gathered light curves for three such systems and pinned down their orbital behavior, including outbursts called superoutbursts. These binaries are future sources for space gravitational wave detectors, so every measured period sharpens forecasts. Small, patient follow-up papers like this one build the census on which that new astronomy will stand.
arxiv-2501-16624:
Ali Safarpoor Dehkordi and Ahad Zehmakan study fake accounts in social networks, in a paper published in 2025. Fake, or sybil, accounts befriend real users to spread spam and scams. Graph methods spot fakes from connection patterns, but the team add a new signal: how strongly a real user resists friend requests from fakes.

They built a generator that makes test networks under varied attack plans, using that resistance signal. Then they tackle a budget problem: reveal the resistance of a chosen few users so as to clear as many real users, and expose as many attack links, as possible. Their algorithms carry proven guarantees. In large experiments, using the method as a first step notably improved several existing detectors. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2501-16724:
Seven researchers, led by Yoojin Jang and Junsu Kim, built a new test set in twenty twenty-five for a vision task. The task asks a program to spot how a person and an object act on each other in an image. The old main test set, HICO-DET, has flaws that can warp scores.

Their new set, called B-RIGHT, fixes two flaws. Some classes had far more test images than others, and class counts were uneven. B-RIGHT gives each class the same count, using a balance method plus made-and-checked images. It also adds a fair test for unseen cases. When old models were retested, score gaps shrank and ranks changed, which shows that balance matters.
arxiv-2501-16924:
David Marín and Jordi Villadelprat study closed paths in flat systems of change in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their focus is a path type called a hemicycle, which runs off to the edge of the plane. Seen on a disc, it joins a straight line with half of the rim. It holds two saddle points far out at the rim.

The authors prove four main results about how many closed loops can grow from such a path when the system is nudged. The first result keeps the saddle links in place. The rest treat square-degree systems with two hemicycles, each around a center point. They count loops that grow from one path, from both at once, and in three set cases. The work aids the study of how loops are born in smooth systems.
arxiv-2501-17024:
Alessandro Midolo and Massimiliano Di Penta test whether a large language model can clean up Python code in the idiomatic style of the language. Python favors certain expressive constructs, and tools based on static code analysis already exist to rewrite clumsy code into those forms. The authors reran a published study design with GPT-4 in the tool's place, asking it to spot and suggest such rewrites.

The model not only found the idiomatic chances well, it often beat the benchmark tool, proposing fixes where the older method had failed. A hand check of a random sample confirmed the suggestions were correct. The authors say the result shows language models can handle a task that used to need complex hand-built code analyzers. They frame the study as a differentiated replication: same questions as the original work, new engine under the hood, and a careful audit of what changed.
arxiv-2501-17224:
Macon Magno and a large team of co-authors present a radio atlas of active galaxies in a 2025 paper. Active galactic nuclei are bright galaxy cores fed by black holes. This survey imaged 231 nearby examples chosen by hard X-ray emission, using a radio array at high frequency and sharp resolution. It is the third phase of the largest such survey to date.

Nearly every target, about 98 percent, was detected in radio. Shapes fell into three families: compact sources, extended sources tied to star formation or one-sided jets, and two-sided jet systems. Radio power spanned over a million-fold range. The ratio of radio to X-ray output matched that of active stars, a curious parallel. Extended glow in quiet objects often traced star birth rather than jets.
arxiv-2501-17324:
Lee Carlin and Yuval Benjamini published a research paper in 2025 on a generative model for tables whose category columns explode with distinct values, like product codes or place names. Standard encodings for such high-cardinality features either balloon or blur them, and mixed-type tables add imbalance on top. Their variational autoencoder swaps one-hot encoding for learned embedding layers on both sides.

The embeddings are trained jointly and can depend on the row's other values, giving a compact shared language for categories. The model needs far fewer trainable parameters than rivals, so it scales. On real and simulated data it produced synthetic tables that preserved rare and imbalanced categories better than competing generators.
arxiv-2501-17524:
Jiaping Lu and Martyn Quick counted generators for iterated wreath products in 2025. Start with a chain of groups, each an alternating, symmetric, or cyclic group. Fold them one into the next by wreath products, letting each new group act on the last by permutations.

The question is the smallest number of generators each product in the chain needs. The pair determine that number for every step. Wreath products pile up fast in size, so a tight generator count is a real structural fact, not a formality. Their answer covers all mixes of the three group families in the chain. The work sits in pure group theory, where such counts drive later classification results.
arxiv-2501-17624:
Alan Koch and Paul Truman build new algebraic objects from old ones in this 2025 math paper. Skew braces, built from abelian maps, are known structures in abstract algebra. Skew bracoids, a looser cousin defined by Martin-Lyons and Truman, were less explored.

Koch and Truman show the braces spawn whole families of bracoids. Under the right conditions, those bracoids yield solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation. That equation began in physics and now anchors a branch of algebra. New solution families are prized test material. The paper is brief and construction-focused, giving algebraists fresh examples to study.
arxiv-2501-17824:
Christian Skalka and Joseph Near present a type theory that checks the safety of secure multi-party computation programs, in a 2025 paper. Such programs let several parties compute on pooled data without exposing anyone's private inputs.

Their framework covers a language pair built for this kind of low-level work. Types in the system promise three things at once: the protocol runs correctly, secrets stay secret, and data stays untampered. Each promise rests on automated checks by a solver working over finite fields. The method composes across program parts and scales to large key and data sizes. It also works for any prime field, the authors note.
arxiv-2501-18024:
Robert Dicks and Hui Xue work in number theory, on where the zeros of certain polynomials fall. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The polynomials come from modular forms, and their values encode key numbers of an attached L-function.

For the classic case, all zeros lie on one neat circle, a pattern much like the famous Riemann hypothesis. The authors build a matching polynomial for the symmetric powers of the L-function, when the level is squarefree. Their version keeps the same symmetry between two linked points. They then prove the circle result holds when the weight is large enough. For very large weights, they also show the result holds once the level grows large.
arxiv-2501-18124:
Liangjing Shao, Benshuang Chen, Shuting Zhao, and Xinrong Chen present REMOTE, a system that tracks an endoscope's motion in real time by learning from several visual cues at once. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Knowing where the scope tip is helps doctors navigate and robots assist. The view inside the body is slippery, dark, and deformable.

Their network reads motion flow, scene features, and a joint feature from two neighboring views. An attention-based extractor fuses the stacked frames along their channels. A new decoder then turns the fused map into the pose change between frames. Chaining those changes yields the scope's full path. On three data sets of varied scope scenes, REMOTE beat the best rivals. It runs faster than video rate, meeting the real-time bar.
arxiv-2501-18324:
Wiradee Imrattanatrai and co-authors release VDAct, a dataset of dialogues grounded in videos of everyday activities, plus a metric to score answers, in a 2025 paper. Unlike earlier sets, its videos run longer and show layered events that demand real context tracking. The set holds 3,000 dialogues and over 30,000 question-answer pairs drawn from 1,000 videos.

State-of-the-art vision models stumbled on several question types, the team found. Their scoring metric, VDEval, judges a reply using the whole session history plus knowledge-graph summaries of the video. It matched human judgments far better than metrics that look at one turn alone.
arxiv-2501-18924:
Ying Wen, Ziyu Wan, and Shao Zhang urge language games as a road to machine minds past human reach, in a 2025 paper. Smart tools grow by making, sifting, and relearning their own text. Trapped in fixed human text, that loop just stirs old facts and stalls.

Games break the loop with three tricks the team names in plain terms. Roles shift, prizes vary, and rules morph as play goes on. Spread to world scale webs of folks and tools, games could pour fresh data in a stream with no end. Growth then stays open, not locked in a ring.
arxiv-2501-19024:
Vuksanović tours stacked nets as brain build tools in this twenty twenty-five piece. Brain reads span scales and modes that one flat net can not hold at once. A stacked net holds each mode as its own coat with links tween coats.

Inside, the tour starts with flat net roots, then builds the stacked frame step by step. Stacked builds can split form from act in brain scans with new fine grain. Ill reads gain too, as coats track how a fault spreads cross modes. Scale blends, from cell to whole brain, fit the same stacked frame. She shows how the frame bares traits flat nets hid in the past.
arxiv-2501-19124:
Monojit Chatterjee, Viktor Holubec, and Rahul Marathe write a 2025 physics paper on tiny heat engines. Engines made of one jiggling particle can turn heat into work in cycles. Past tuning methods fixed settings at set points, which made the best cycles hard to run in a real lab.

The team adapts control theory into an algorithm that tunes the whole cycle at once, within real bounds on stiffness and heat. It also sets cycle length itself rather than taking it as given. On a trapped particle test case, the method held up in the thick-fluid regime and stretched to all damping levels. Thin damping killed peak power, while tuning the heat path lifted efficiency in the middle range.
arxiv-2501-19224:
BaoLinh Tran and Van Vu speed up the exact recovery of a noisy matrix from a few of its entries, judging error by the worst entry instead of the average. Their 2025 paper works on matrix completion, a core task in data science. Classic methods recover a clean low-rank matrix exactly, but with noise they return only a near miss in average error.

Turning that near miss into an exact hit is the hard part. Recent work showed the worst-entry, or infinity-norm, view can do it when the true matrix has bounded precision. The present paper builds on those results toward a fast method, keeping the standard assumptions: low rank, spread-out singular vectors, and enough sampled entries. The goal is exactness with noise, at practical speed.
arxiv-2502-00024:
Ke Yuan, Yaoxin Liu, Shriyesh Chandra, and Rishav Roy present a retail market analysis project in a 2025 paper. The project studies market trends using three data sources: historical sales records, search trends, and customer reviews. Combining them gives a fuller view than any one source alone.

By spotting patterns and trending products, the analysis aims to guide inventory choices and marketing strategy. Better stocking decisions cut waste and missed sales, while sharper marketing raises customer satisfaction. The authors frame the work as actionable insight for retailers who want data, not guesswork, behind everyday decisions.
arxiv-2502-00124:
Shuang Liang, James Nakamura, Geoffrey Gardner, and Michael Manfra settle a puzzle about electron interference, in a 2025 physics paper. In a quantum Hall device shaped like a ring, the outermost channel of electrons interferes with itself, and its pattern repeated at half the expected magnetic period. Some had read that halving as a sign of exotic electron pairing.

Their device was built to feel both bulk-to-edge and edge-to-edge coupling at once. At two integer filling levels the half period appeared, yet the interfering charge measured exactly one electron, which rules out pairing. The authors show the halving comes instead from capacitive coupling between the isolated neighboring channels and the interfering one. The result gives experimenters a cleaner way to read charge in such devices while they run.
arxiv-2502-00824:
Zohre Mashayekh Bakhsh, Yasaman Omid, Gaojie Chen, Farbod Kayhan, Yi Ma, and Rahim Tafazolli study direct phone-to-satellite links, in a 2025 paper. Future networks aim to let an ordinary phone reach satellites overhead when towers are out of range. A cluster of satellites can listen together and combine the faint signal, if they can share what they hear.

The team weigh two ways for satellites to swap signals: terahertz radio and free-space laser links. Both are imperfect, and each has its own capacity limits, which the authors compute. They also propose how to pick one satellite as the hub that does the combining, based on both the phone link and the shared links. Standards-based settings keep the work close to real deployments.
arxiv-2502-01024:
Nianyi Chen and a team of co-authors use a large universe simulation to predict a hum of gravitational waves in a 2025 paper. Timing of pulsars has recently revealed very low frequency waves, likely from pairs of massive black holes. The signal is stronger than light based estimates suggested, so better models are needed.

The simulation tracks black hole motion as it happens, rather than adding it later, which curbs excess growth by mergers. Its predicted background reaches under half the observed level at low frequencies. Much of the signal comes from the heaviest pairs at modest distances, with a fair share from uneven mergers.
arxiv-2502-01424:
Bénédicte Haas and Vincent Viau study a frozen variant of a classic random network in a 2025 paper. In the classic model, links form at random until one giant web spans the graph. Here a rule freezes any cluster the moment it gains a single loop, which blocks the giant web from forming. A dial slows the growth of looped clusters by a set amount. The process stops once every cluster carries its one loop.

The pair ask what the network looks like when the graph grows huge. They show that the main counts settle onto smooth curves given by a set of rate laws. Their proofs adapt a standard method for such limits. As a payoff, they pin down how the final freeze time behaves for large graphs. The work sorts a model built to study how gels set in soft matter.
arxiv-2502-01924:
Javier Borquez and three co-authors present a control method from 2025 that keeps robots both safe and fast. Sampling-based predictive control plans well in complex settings but can stray into unsafe states. Their method, DualGuard MPPI, mixes that planner with reachability analysis, a formal tool that maps which states a system can safely reach or avoid.

Safety checks are built into the sampling step, so every trial plan the controller weighs is provably safe. With unsafe samples filtered out, the same number of samples explores good options better, cutting noise in the search. Simulations and hardware tests beat standard methods on performance with no loss of safety.
arxiv-2502-02024:
Weiren Zhao and co-authors let a segmentation model decide the order in which it reads an image, starting where it is least sure. Their 2025 paper adapts the Mamba architecture, a state-space sequence model prized for long-range reasoning at linear cost, to medical image segmentation. Standard scanning reads pixels in fixed raster order, wasting effort on easy background and starving the ambiguous boundaries that decide diagnoses.

Their uncertainty-driven design scans rows and columns in orders set by a pixel-level uncertainty map, clustering hard regions together and alternating between certain and uncertain ground. Learnable weights balance the scan strategies, and a consistency loss smooths the transitions. Across pathology, skin lesion, and cardiac datasets the method proved robust. Medical images are mostly obvious and partly treacherous; an architecture that spends its attention budget on the treacherous part mirrors how radiologists actually read.
arxiv-2502-02124:
Nicolas Kaufmann, Octavio Guilera, Yann Alibert, and Irina San Sebastián model the first growth of planets in rings in a 2025 paper. Small bodies can form in clumps where pebbles pile up in a young disk, often in local rings. The team ask whether bodies in those rings can grow fast enough to start sweeping up pebbles with ease.

Their semi analytic model tests rings at varied distances from stars of varied mass. Inner rings made embryo sized bodies quickly, while outer rings showed little growth. Growth also slowed around lighter stars. The authors conclude that making pebble ready seeds far out in a disk is hard within the disk's lifetime.
arxiv-2502-02424:
Reemt Hinrichs and Jörn Ostermann shrink the neural nets that squeeze sound for cochlear implants, without losing speech clarity. Their 2025 paper deals with implants that stream audio wirelessly to a processor worn on the head. A deep autoencoder can cut the bit rate at no delay, which saves power, but past work ignored the size of the model itself.

Size matters in hearing gear, where compute is scarce. The team adds a loss term that feels the effect of pruning, the cutting of weak links, while the net still trains. Against the standard cut-by-size route, their way kept speech scores far higher at steep cut rates. After fine-tuning, scores held near flat up to cuts of about half the model.
arxiv-2502-03024:
Masato Tsuboi, Takahiro Tsutsumi, Ryosuke Miyawaki, and Makoto Miyoshi track the motions of maser stars near our galaxy's central black hole to ask which structure they belong to. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The stars shine in a silicon oxide line picked up by the ALMA array. Two observing rounds, years apart, let the team measure drift across the sky.

Thirty-seven maser stars were found, and most yielded full three-dimensional motions. Their drifts were not random: they tended to run along the galactic plane. Many speeds also ran too high for bound orbits in the central star cluster. Those traits point instead to the nuclear stellar disk, a flatter, wider structure. The result reshapes the census of the galaxy's crowded heart. It shows masers can sort membership where starlight blurs together.
arxiv-2502-03324:
Some shapes in symplectic geometry can be bent but not broken, and Joe Brendel and Joontae Kim classify a family of them by an unlikely route: billiards. Their 2025 paper concerns Lagrangian tori in the product of two spheres. These doughnut surfaces split as a product of two circles.

With a non-monotone symplectic form on the space, classifying such tori up to Hamiltonian motion turns out to be exactly a billiard problem in rectangles. A bouncing ball's path encodes the torus. The dictionary pays off three ways. It answers a question on Lagrangian packing numbers. It describes the shape of the space of all such tori. And it tells which split tori arise from ball embeddings of known examples. The authors let a game of rebounds do the heavy classification work.
arxiv-2502-03824:
Search engines need training data that says which passages answer which questions, and human labeling is slow. Minsang Kim and Seungjun Baek build that data synthetically with a large language model. They use only its text replies rather than its internal scores, which the newest models do not expose. In the first stage, the model writes relevant passages, near-miss passages, and extra questions, then checks its own output for invented facts.

A retriever is trained on that data with a loss that pulls good passages together. In a second stage, the retriever is aligned to the language model's own ranking tastes. The alignment uses a partial ranking method, with a guard that keeps it from straying too far from the first stage. Across benchmarks from several domains, the approach the authors call Syntriever reached the best reported scores, showing synthetic data can carry a retriever far.
arxiv-2502-04024:
Charging electric vehicles both cheaply and fast is modeled by Tran and co-authors in a 2025 paper. The catalog record lists three authors, while the head byline lists more, so the work is a wider team effort. Charging stations must balance user cost against rapid power delivery, and prices can swing in ways that a fixed plan cannot handle.

The team proposes a robust optimization model that joins a cost goal with a fast charging goal. Uncertainty in charging cost is built in through an L2-norm set, so the plan stays resilient when costs fluctuate. Tests under real-world scenarios are reported. The authors argue the model offers efficient and flexible charging. Station operators get a tool that protects users from price swings.
arxiv-2502-04124:
Débora Senise and Pavel Shumyatsky wrote a 2025 paper in finite group theory. A conjugacy class groups elements that mirror each other inside the group. In 1954, Neumann showed that if all such classes stay small, the derived group is finite with bounded size.

Later work by Dierings and Shumyatsky cut the condition down to commutators alone. This paper cuts it further, to commutators whose order is a prime power. The main result says the second derived group still has size bounded by the class limit. Each cut sharpens a classic line of results. Such bounds tell algebraists how much control a weak size condition can exert.
arxiv-2502-04224:
Jiate Li and co-authors build the first explanation system for graph neural networks with a proof of robustness. Their 2025 paper concerns tools that explain why a graph model reached its answer, which builds trust in high-stakes uses. The authors noticed a weak point: a tiny tweak to the graph's structure can swing the explanation wildly, even when the answer barely moves.

Their system, XGNNCert, guarantees that under the worst allowed tweak, the explanation stays close to the untampered one. The guarantee is mathematical, not sampled, which sets it apart from earlier defenses. The work opens a line on certifying not just what graph models say, but why they say it.
arxiv-2502-04524:
Donato Francesco Falcone and co-authors present a chip that both trains and runs AI in a 2025 paper. Most past analog chips did one task or the other, not both on one base. Their device uses memory cells that switch resistance, built into the chip's back layers.

The cells switch at low voltage and hold over thirty stable levels with low noise. That calm makes weight transfer near ideal, far better than rival memory types. Tests on a grid array show error far lower than rivals, even years after setting. A single base that trains and then keeps running could cut the energy cost of AI.
arxiv-2502-04824:
Joshua Blake and co-authors (2025) estimate how long a COVID-19 infection stays detectable by PCR testing. Knowing that duration lets health agencies turn survey positives into counts of new infections. The data came from the United Kingdom's long-running Coronavirus Infection Survey. Its records are awkward: test dates bracket the true start and end, some infections slip between visits, and tests can miss. The team built a Bayesian method that handles all three problems at once.

Their model estimates the whole distribution of detectable days rather than one average. It borrows prior information from a companion study. Simulations showed the method recovers the truth and tolerates wrong assumptions fairly well. Applied to the survey, it gave the first full duration distribution for a general population. The authors offer the approach for future outbreaks of other infections, where the same censoring problems will appear in prevalence surveys.
arxiv-2502-04924:
Banks, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, sets out a fluid-based view of gravity, where each patch of space holds a small quantum system. The work grows from results of the past century's last decade.

In this view, a classic path of Einstein's rules sets the state of each patch, tied to a diamond of cause and effect. Each patch's parts form a finite algebra, like a thin field theory on the patch's edge. The edge's grain is set by a link between its area and a charge count, which makes the edge fuzzy. The full quantum play is set in a bundle over the paths of fall. Patches nest along a path, with maps that embed each in the next.
arxiv-2502-05324:
Edyta Bogucka, Sanja Šćepanović, and Daniele Quercia build a storytelling atlas that explains artificial intelligence risks to non-experts, in a 2025 paper. Existing risk displays dwell on technical faults like biased data and target technical audiences. Job loss, surveillance, and other social harms get less room, and lay readers get little help.

Two crowdsourcing studies shaped and tested the Atlas. Forty participants first defined what lay decision-makers need from a risk display. Then 140 participants, matched to the United States population, tried the tool on facial recognition. The Atlas proved friendlier than a baseline display, with a more classic, expressive feel. It also presented risks and benefits of the technology in better balance. The authors argue the design travels: an incident database behind it covers many technologies, so the same narrative frame can map risks far beyond the test case.
arxiv-2502-05524:
Francesco Mele, Giovanni Barbarino, Vittorio Giovannetti, and Marco Fanizza compute how fast quantum messages can be sent when only a finite number of tries is allowed. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Most past theory assumed endless channel uses and vanishing error. Real devices get neither, so practical rates need a sharper treatment.

They give easy-to-compute lower bounds for three tasks: sending quantum bits, creating shared entangled pairs, and making secret keys. Two new tools support the result. One bounds the chance that a light-based state holds more photons than a set cap, and shows it falls off fast. The other is the first algorithm that measures the distance between two such states to a set precision. Both tools have uses beyond this paper.
arxiv-2502-05824:
Geng Sun and co-authors sent a swarm of drones in 2025 to act as one floating antenna, beaming stronger signals to moving phone users on the ground. A single drone's range is capped by its small battery and antenna, but a coordinated swarm can focus energy like a much larger dish.

The catch is a tug of war: fly and beam harder for speed, or save energy and last longer. The team modeled user movement as a memory bearing random walk, then taught a learning algorithm to hunt the best trade offs rather than one perfect answer. The learner uses a memory network to read movement patterns. Simulations showed a rich spread of trade off plans beating older schemes.
arxiv-2502-06124:
Pawel Renc and co-authors present a computing paper from 2025 on risk scores in hospitals. Hospitals struggle to foresee bad turns in patients. Older warning scores use fixed facts and fixed cut-offs, so they adapt poorly to each patient.

The team built a system on a model that reads a patient's health timeline as tokens. It predicts how the timeline will unfold and turns that into personal risk scores. It also names the facts that drive each score, so doctors can see the reasons. They tested it on a large public hospital data set with over 285 thousand timelines. The system beat older scores and other smart models at foreseeing admissions and long stays. Scores held up across patient groups. Real clinic value still needs proof in live wards.
arxiv-2502-06824:
Simbarashe Aldrin Ngorima, Albert Helberg, and Marelie H Davel study noise in training data for vehicle channel estimation in a 2025 paper, using the byline given in the text. Cars move fast and their radio channels shift quickly, so receivers must estimate the channel on the fly. Neural methods are often trained only on clean, high-quality signals, on the hope that they will generalize.

The team tested five estimator designs trained either on clean data alone or on a mix of clean and noisy data. Mixed training often won, above all in noisy conditions where clean-trained models fell behind. The authors say the noise range of the training set should be treated as a tunable choice, not a fixed rule, when building such estimators.
arxiv-2502-06924:
Arghadip Das and co-authors bring state space models to the small neural chips built into AI laptops. These models rival transformers on long texts but sip far less compute. The catch is that each new network breed tends to demand its own fresh chip.

Their XAMBA frame instead tunes the models for chips already on sale. First it gets the models running, then it speeds them up, then it trades a little accuracy for more speed. Two tricks swap step-by-step sums for matrix math, which the chips love. A third trick swaps costly curve functions for straight-line chunks, cutting wait with little loss.
arxiv-2502-07024:
Vedran Brdar and three co-authors study collider prospects for a neutrino magnetic moment portal in this 2025 physics paper. The portal is a transition magnetic moment that lets an active neutrino flip into a sterile one. The idea is well motivated beyond the Standard Model. The authors focus on the lab side, at proposed lepton colliders. They revisit the older LEP machine and add four future designs, among them FCC-ee, CLIC, and a muon collider.

Working in an effective field theory frame, they map the parameter regions each machine could reach. Reach depends on which lepton flavor couples to the sterile neutrino. New production processes with large rates at high energy sharpen the outlook. The expected sensitivity lands near ten to the minus seven per giga electron volt for the moment.
arxiv-2502-07224:
Baopi Liu, Lu Chen, and Wenjun Xu study how tail shape affects swimming in tiny swimmers in this 2025 paper. Such swimmers push themselves by spinning whip-like tails. Tail shape shapes their speed, energy use, and control of direction. The team first simulated full three-dimensional swimming paths. They read the motion traits of swimmers from those runs. Flow fields around a swimmer were then visualized in detail.

The runs showed swimmers can steer by changing the angle of their tails. The interplay between body and tail flows explained much of that control. Speed and stability shifted with the form of the tail in clear ways. The authors treat tail design as a key lever for micro-scale robots. Their findings may guide devices meant to swim in blood or other fluids. The study is based on simulation rather than live microbes.
arxiv-2502-07424:
Alan Saji and co-authors peek inside multilingual language models and catch them thinking in Roman letters, in a 2025 paper. Models trained mostly on English still handle languages in other scripts suspiciously well. Probing token by token, the team find middle layers often sketch a target word in Romanized form before rendering it in the native script, a habit they name latent Romanization.

Patching experiments show the model holds the same concept whether the script is native or Romanized, one shared representation beneath both. For translation into non-Roman targets, Romanized forms also surface earlier in the layers. Romanization, quietly, is the bridge the model walks across languages.
arxiv-2502-07524:
Emmanuel Deruty, a solo author, studies how a classic drum machine shapes the keys of hip-hop songs, in a 2025 music paper. The Roland TR-808 bass drum has a prized deep sound, but its usable pitch range is narrow. Producer Scott Storch flips the usual workflow: he keeps the drum as is and shifts every other track to fit it. Deruty asks what that choice costs and what it buys.

He reviews drum tuning habits, tests samples of the drum sound, and weighs how speakers and ears handle deep bass. The drum's tone seems to rest more on its sound color and register than on exact pitch. Shifting the song protects that color and boosts bass punch. The paper frames a studio habit as a window on how modern pop values sound texture.
arxiv-2502-07724:
Alex Wilkinson, Radi Radev, and Saúl Alonso-Monsalve test in 2025 whether a learning trick from image work can make neutrino models more robust. Neutrino studies lean on huge simulated data sets, since real detector events are rare and hard to label. A model trained on simulations must still work on real data, whose spread differs.

The trick, called contrastive learning, trains a model on altered copies of each data item. The model learns traits that survive the alterations, which tend to be the true traits of the event. The team applies the method to neutrino data and weighs the gains in tests and in theory. Models that carry over from simulation to the real detector save years of tuning. The paper maps where the trick helps in this field.
arxiv-2502-07924:
Matthew Stephenson and co-authors study a classic bind in deals over new ideas, in a paper from 2025. An inventor must reveal an idea to get paid or funded. Yet once revealed, the idea can be taken without pay, so inventors hold back and deals fail.

The team models talks between a seller and a buyer under that threat. They show that secure computing hardware, paired with AI agents, can act like an ironclad non-disclosure agreement. The seller can hand choices about revealing and payment to tamper-proof programs. That allows full sharing and a fair transfer at the end. Even when the idea is worth more than the hardware can fully secure, partial sharing still beats silence. Caps and checks keep most of the gains even when agents err.
arxiv-2502-08424:
Chee, Etzion, Ta, and Vu build sequences that cover every pattern to a set tolerance. A covering sequence is a cyclic string whose runs of consecutive symbols form a code: every possible block of length n sits within a distance R of some run. Shorter sequences make better tests and storage schemes, so the authors improve the known upper bounds on their length for small block lengths and radii.

They then stretch the idea two ways: to a set of sequences whose blocks jointly cover, and to two-dimensional arrays whose sub-rectangles do the same. Their constructions cover these cases too. Finally, they prove that, asymptotically, covering sequences can reach the sphere-covering bound within a constant factor, closing most of the gap between theory and practice.
arxiv-2502-08624:
Benjamin Bedert settles a long-standing problem in additive combinatorics in this 2025 paper. A set is called sum-free when no two of its members add to a third member of the same set. Erdős asked how large a sum-free subset every set of integers must contain. The plain bound gives a third of the set, and beating it by a growing margin resisted proof for decades.

Bedert shows a constant exists so that any set of n integers holds a sum-free subset of size at least n/3 plus a term that grows like the double logarithm of n. The proof runs through sharp estimates for trigonometric series in the first-power norm. The result closes the Erdős problem in the form posed, the paper reports.
arxiv-2502-09024:
Sangjoon Park, Cook Hyun Kim, and B. Kahng ask where to add spare inertia in a power grid so it steadies the system without triggering worse failures. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Renewable sources spin less than the turbines they replace, so modern grids carry less inertia. Adding fast frequency response helps, but careless placement can spark avalanche blackouts, a Braess-style paradox.

The team tests placements on a standard coupled-oscillator model of the grid. They score each spot by weighing failure relief against the harm done. Across sizes of reinforcement, the network's periphery came out as the effective zone. Edge stations give support without disturbing the core's balance. The strategy offers planners a rule of thumb for the renewable era. It also warns that more inertia is not always better.
arxiv-2502-09224:
Marković and Denecker propose an extension of order-sorted logic in a 2025 paper. Subtyping lets programs built for a general type work safely with subtypes. The authors ask how knowledge representation can use the same idea.
