They note two limits in order-sorted logic. It cannot speak about a concept itself rather than its values, and it lacks tools to constrain the type of a term. Their answer is guarded order-sorted intensional logic. Guards carry typing notes on terms, while the intensional part allows quantification over concepts. The paper sets out the new logic and its aims. It bridges programming language ideas and formal knowledge systems.
arxiv-2502-09524:
Terrance Savitsky and three co-authors tackle a practical problem in survey statistics in this 2025 paper. Analysts often merge a proper random survey with a convenience sample, whose members volunteer rather than being drawn at random. Estimating each convenience member's chance of taking part lets the two sources be combined into one weighted estimate for a subgroup.

The catch is that convenience members who look nothing like the survey members can add bias or noise instead of sharpening the estimate. The authors develop a rule that drops convenience members whose chance of appearing in both samples is low, choosing the cut to minimize the variance of the combined estimate. In simulations with two kinds of overlap between the samples, their rule beat other cut rules. The result is a cleaner way to borrow strength from convenience data without letting its odd corners hurt.
arxiv-2502-09824:
Bagoren, Micatka, Skinner, and Marburg tackled robot grasping underwater in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Underwater sensors return patchy, noisy views of objects. A gripper that trusts every reading equally will grab at the wrong spots. Their method, PUGS, measures how unsure the 3D reconstruction is at each point.

Uncertainty from many camera views is carried through the rebuilding process. Grasp choices then favor spots the robot can actually see well. Tests ran on both simulated scenes and real underwater data. Accounting for doubt made grasp picks hold up against noise and missing views. The authors plan to release the code for other teams.
arxiv-2502-10124:
Zhipeng Li and co-authors model when VR users notice avatar redirection in a 2025 paper. Virtual worlds can subtly shift an avatar motion to enable new interactions. Shift too far and the user feels the mismatch. Past work blamed avatar traits; this team studies the scene around the user, tracked through eye gaze.

Two user studies linked gaze patterns to how noticeable shifts felt. A regression model fed with gaze features predicted noticeability with tiny error on fresh scenes. An adaptive version that eased off when gaze warned of detection left users less strained and more embodied. Readers get a gaze-driven dial for believable VR.
arxiv-2502-10224:
Waldemar Bauer and Jerzy Baranowski compare two kinds of neural networks for spotting motor faults from sound, in a paper from 2025. Faults in electric motors can halt work in homes and plants, and sound offers a cheap way to listen for harm. The team recast sound in terms of its tones and fed the result to each network.

Both networks were built and tested on real sound clips from home devices, taped with phones. The network that tracks its own doubt gave the best scores, above all when fault clips were rare next to healthy clips. The authors say doubt aware nets suit plant checks well, since they flag when a call is unsure. More tests of cost and speed are still needed.
arxiv-2502-10324:
Lee and co-authors analyze in 2025 wireless coverage and channel rank for drone networks in rural areas with dense foliage. Drones are set to serve next generation vehicle links that need high rates and low delay. Trees block and scatter signals, above all at low flight heights.

Ray tracing simulations over a university field lab used modeled trees from map and 3D tools. Results show tree blockage cuts coverage and channel rank at lower altitudes. A 3D interpolation scheme based on Kriging fills channel rank across space, using its observed spatial pattern. Error scores beat baseline interpolation methods in their tests.
arxiv-2502-10424:
Rishabh Tiwari and co-authors present a faster way to run large language models on edge devices in a 2025 paper. Long texts fill a memory store that must be loaded at each step, slowing replies and eating memory. Guessing ahead methods can speed things, but poor memory handling keeps gains low. Their system, QuantSpec, lets a draft model share the main model's shape while using compressed memory and weights.

The draft guesses are accepted more than ninety percent of the time, the authors report. End to end speed rose up to about two and a half times, beating rival guessing methods. Memory use fell as well compared with those rivals. Readers learn how shrinking the memory store, not just the model, unlocks speed for long texts.
arxiv-2502-11224:
Patrick Popescu-Pampu and Dmitry Stepanov introduce local tropicalization, a local cousin of a known geometry tool. Their 2025 paper explains the idea from four viewpoints. Global tropicalization turns shapes inside torus spaces into spiky combinatorial shadows; the local version does the same near a point.

The tour starts with plane curve singularities, where the ideas can be drawn and grasped fast. It then lifts the same viewpoints to any dimension. Formal germ pieces inside toric germs supply the objects under study. The paper closes with variants and extensions of the local notion. As an introduction, it aims to give newcomers several doors into the same room, each door stressing a different facet of the tool.
arxiv-2502-11324:
Cullen Anderson and Jeff Phillips present a 2025 empirical study of robust mean estimation when data are scarce. Robust statistics aims to summarize data even when some of it is corrupted arbitrarily. The mean is the basic target, and recent theory has produced near-optimal algorithms for high-dimensional corrupted data. Every one of them, though, assumes sample sizes that grow large with dimension.

In practice, high-dimensional data often come in small batches that break those assumptions. The authors run extensive experiments across mean estimation techniques in exactly that low-data regime. The study maps which methods hold up and which fall apart when theory's data requirements are not met. The authors frame the work as a reality check for a fast-moving theory area.
arxiv-2502-11624:
Dmitry Miserev, Joel Hutchinson, Herbert Schoeller, Jelena Klinovaja, and Daniel Loss argue that the range of the attraction between electrons changes the rules of superconductivity, in a 2025 paper. Classic BCS theory says any attraction, however weak, opens a gap and makes a metal superconduct. That prediction assumed the attraction acts at a point. The authors study attractions spread over a finite range, much wider than the electron wavelength.

With only the spread-out attraction, they show no gap opens at all. Instead, the tendency to pair up grows as a power law toward a critical state with no true long-range order. Adding the short-range attraction that real materials always have restores superconductivity. In a layered material where sound-like vibrations supply the pull, their model yields the dome-shaped curve of critical temperature against doping seen in high-temperature superconductors, with a muted isotope effect.
arxiv-2502-12324:
Airey and co-authors run the first large color survey of the belt of satellites that hover over the equator, using a scope that takes four colors of light at once. The color of the light a satellite reflects can hint at its build, which helps sort and describe the many objects in that belt.

Over two months in 2023 they took full night color curves for 112 live satellites. Maps of those curves let them compare satellite families. Two bus kinds could be told apart by color maps, though mean color alone was a weak guide. One bus kind showed a hint that color shifts with years in orbit.
arxiv-2502-12724:
Zhuoqun Chen, Xiu Yuan, Tongzhou Mu, and Hao Su wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It speeds up diffusion policies, a way to teach robots by copying shown moves, which can be slow to react since they act on stale plans.

Their method keeps a buffer of actions at rising noise levels and cleans them one step at a time, in sequence. The head of the line is always a fresh, clean action based on the newest view, while new noisy actions join the tail. This keeps motion smooth yet quick to respond. Tests on fast-response tasks show a clear gain in success rate over the standard policy. On plain tasks it also beats the best known speedup trick.
arxiv-2502-13124:
Weizhe Yuan and co-authors released in 2025 a vast set of hard reasoning questions drawn from real life. Training models to reason beyond math and code is held back by a lack of varied, high-quality questions. Their set holds 2.8 million questions across science, economics, social science, and more, each with a reference answer.

Tests show the set can pass reasoning skill from a strong teacher model to a smaller one. It also helps models train themselves, judged by outside reward models or by self-scoring. The authors offer the set as shared raw material for the whole field.
arxiv-2502-13424:
Pawel Garncarek, Dariusz Kowalski, Shay Kutten, and Miguel Mosteiro speed up deterministic algorithms for beeping networks. In this model each node can send at most one bit per round, a setup drawn from biological processes. Fast randomized algorithms exist for many problems, but every known deterministic method costs at least polynomial time in the maximum node degree. The team treats network communication as distributed coding to beat interference.

Their simulator replays one round of any CONGEST algorithm in far fewer beeping rounds than past methods needed. Any efficient CONGEST algorithm can thus run on a beeping network with that overhead. The gain improves the best known deterministic beeping algorithm for maximal independent set by a polynomial factor.
arxiv-2502-13824:
Gaetano Agazzotti and co-authors test a market model that mixes shifting volatility with sudden double-sided jumps, in a research paper from 2025. Option prices depend on how well a model fits market quotes, above all for short-dated deals. The model had been proposed before but never fully vetted.

The team calibrates it against rivals with similar features and prices many option types with fast Fourier methods. It fits the short-term price smile better than challengers. Its uneven jump sizes capture richer market moves, and each setting carries a clear meaning for risk managers. All code is public, inviting others to adopt and extend the work.
arxiv-2502-13924:
Reading the Sun's magnetic field from its light is an inverse problem: from polarized spectra, infer the field that made them. Robert Jarolim and co-authors bring physics-informed neural networks to that task in this 2025 paper, under a standard simplifying model of the solar atmosphere. Their network maps time and place coordinates to the field parameters that best reproduce what telescopes see.

The network builds the instrument's blur into the fit, and its built-in coupling across space and time damps noise. Tests on synthetic spectra from a realistic simulation, and on real observations, show clean, coherent maps that resolve fine features in both strong and weak field areas. The method also stays light on memory for wide fields of view.
arxiv-2502-14024:
Yifan Zhou and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a young planet that is still gathering material. The PDS 70 system hosts two directly imaged protoplanets, a rare live view of planet birth. A glowing hydrogen line, H-alpha, traces gas falling onto each planet. The team watched that glow change over time.

Hubble telescope images from 2020 and 2024 caught both planets with high clarity. For the outer planet, PDS 70 c, the glow more than doubled between the two epochs. Ground-based data confirm the brightening trend through 2023 and 2024. Such swings point to unsteady feeding, shaped by the disc around the planet or by bursts of inflow. The findings warn that single snapshots can mislead when judging how fast young planets grow.
arxiv-2502-14124:
Cristina Andrade and co-authors study how the Vera Rubin Observatory's scan rhythm affects its chances of catching kilonovae, the fast fading glows from merging neutron stars. Only one such joint catch, in 2017, has been confirmed with gravity wave and gamma ray partners. Rubin's wide survey could find many more, with or without those triggers.

Their 2025 work adapts a fast transient metric proven on an earlier sky survey. They vary filter picks, revisit gaps for the same sky patch, and whole rhythm families. Baseline rhythms paired with triplet visit families, called presto gap, gave the best odds of a catch. The paper weighs cadence as a design lever for rare events.
arxiv-2502-14624:
Daniel Halpern, Alexandros Psomas, Paritosh Verma, and Daniel Xie settle open questions linking fair division over time with a balancing problem in vector geometry, in a 2025 paper. In the fair division problem, goods arrive one by one and must be handed out at once, keeping envy between agents low. In the geometry twin, vectors arrive and must be colored so the color groups stay close in size.

Any bound for the geometry problem gives the same bound for envy. Against a foe who adapts, both share one best possible answer. What was open is whether this holds against a foe who commits in advance. The authors prove the two problems are fully equivalent in that setting. They give matching upper and lower bounds for the many-color case, closing the gap left by earlier work.
arxiv-2502-14724:
Natalia Koliou and George Vouros rank team strategies in games by their long-run staying power in this 2025 paper. Classic game theory seeks Nash equilibria, yet real play often never settles there. The authors instead recast a dynamic game in empirical form, treating whole strategies as the units of play. An evolutionary method then scores each joint strategy by how well it persists over time.

The ranking also weighs payoffs, and the method explains why top strategies rank high. In tests, learning agents played varied styles on a random graph-coloring task. Simulations built the payoff table, and the evolutionary ranking picked out the joint styles that held up best across long interactions.
arxiv-2502-14924:
Ibrahim Alabdulmohsin and Andreas Steiner asked whether large language models copy the fractal shape of human language in a 2025 paper. Natural language shows self-similar complexity across scales, with links that stretch far across a text. The team measured such patterns in model output under varied heat settings and prompts.

Human text kept its fractal measures in a narrow band, while model text swung widely. That gap suggests fractal measures could flag a fair share of machine-written text. The findings held across three model families of different sizes. The authors also released a data set of over 240,000 model-written articles beside human matches. They frame fractals as a new lens for judging and detecting synthetic text.
arxiv-2502-15024:
Finding hidden communities in a network has a famous cliff edge: above the Kesten-Stigum threshold, fast algorithms recover the groups; below it, recovery is thought impossible in reasonable time. Jingqiu Ding, Yiding Hua, Lucas Slot, and David Steurer prove that cliff in 2025, assuming a leading conjecture about low-degree tests.

For the symmetric stochastic block model, they show no polynomial-time method can beat random guessing below the threshold, even slightly, with steady probability. Known algorithms succeed above it, so the transition is sharp. A stronger form of the conjecture extends the wall to models with many blocks. The result also exposes a gap between what statistics allows and what computation can reach.
arxiv-2502-15124:
Joyce Chew, Willem Diepeveen, and Deanna Needell adapt a basic data tool to data that live on curved surfaces. The catalog creator field glues the authors' email addresses to their names, so the clean head byline governs here. Their tool is a cousin of nonnegative matrix factorization, which splits data into simple parts that add up. Curved data, such as brain scan tensors, do not follow flat rules.

Their method, called CC-NMDF, adds a correction for the surface's curvature so the parts stay faithful to the geometry. They give a step-by-step algorithm that computes the split efficiently. Tests use real diffusion tensor MRI data, which records how water moves in tissue. The work, published in 2025, adds a building block for analysis of data that live on manifolds rather than flat grids.
arxiv-2502-15224:
Tingting Chen and co-authors build a testbed that isolates one skill AI agents need before they can do science: keeping track of what they have learned. Their 2025 paper introduces Auto-Discovery-Bench, where an agent recovers a hidden structure through repeated rounds of guessing, intervening, and receiving exact feedback from an oracle.

Three puzzles stand in for discovery itself: finding a directed graph, an undirected relation web, and a symbolic equation. Performance falls as variables, round counts, and distractors grow. A stripped-down tracking test then removes choosing and guessing entirely, leaving only memory of the feedback stream. Many models still fail there. The authors read this as a bottleneck diagnosis: agents stumble less at cleverness than at holding structured state over long interactions. The bench is deliberately artificial, a microscope for one capability rather than a mock laboratory.
arxiv-2502-15324:
A learning equation from behavioral science describes how an animal's response builds with experience, mixing the unknown function's values at blended time points, which makes it nonlocal with shrinking delays. Four authors generalize that equation and ask the basic questions first: does a solution exist, and is it the only one, within the space of Hölder continuous functions?

They prove the answer is yes on both counts, in the function space they argue is the natural home for the problem. Then they build a collocation scheme that pins the solution at chosen points and fills the gaps by interpolation. They prove the scheme converges at a rate tied to the solution's smoothness. Computer runs confirm the predicted rate. Side results about how interpolation behaves in these spaces round out the work, which serves modelers of learning in animal behavior.
arxiv-2502-15724:
Halil Ibrahim Ergul, Selim Balcisoy, and Burcin Bozkaya test whether a fine-tuned language model can guess what a bank customer will buy next. Banks hold long records of past payments, and the next merchant type, such as groceries or fuel, is a useful signal. Their 2025 study turns each customer's history into plain text and fine-tunes an open model on it. Training data came from one bank and test data from another, a harder and more honest check.

The tuned model beat classic sequence models and simple baselines on the three main merchant types. Scores were higher where it counts for banks: spotting spending shifts early. The authors credit the model's vast prior reading, reshaped by light tuning. They share the method as a template for other prediction tasks on text-shaped data.
arxiv-2502-15924:
Raj and co-authors tackle a trust problem for large language models: the same question, reworded, can draw different answers, in this 2025 paper. People will only rely on these systems if equal meanings get equal treatment. No built-in dial for consistency existed at inference time.

Their method, Chain of Guidance, prompts the model through steps that steer it toward stable outputs. Fine-tuning on synthetic pairs of matched inputs and outputs strengthened the habit. The tuned models were more than twice as consistent as the base versions. The skill also carried to datasets never used in training. The authors compare their route with template answers and majority voting.
arxiv-2502-16024:
Dilong Zhou and co-authors sharpen a multiscale method for flow through stubbornly uneven rock. Simulating reservoirs means solving pressure and flux on fine detail too costly to grid whole. Their base method, a Robin-coupled scheme with oversampling and smoothing, already cut flux errors to about one part in ten thousand on the SPE10 benchmark field, a standard trial by fire.

Two new iterative variants build informed correction spaces online, refreshing them with each round's own boundary values. The payoff is steep: errors fall by roughly six more orders of magnitude within a few steps. Parallel structure keeps the cost in check. Head-to-head tests against each other and a published iterative rival show both variants converging fast and holding their accuracy.
arxiv-2502-16124:
Aditi De proposed a theory framework in 2025 for AI that acts without being asked. Zero-Input AI predicts user intent from gaze, brain and heart signals, and context such as time, place, and past use. The aim is help that arrives before a command, within a tenth of a second.

The design joins these streams with cross-modal attention, estimates its own uncertainty in a Bayesian way, and adapts through reinforcement learning. Shrinking tricks such as quantisation and pruning fit it to edge chips, and a linear attention variant cuts computing growth. Theory bounds the prediction error and shows fusion beating single signals. Expected accuracy reaches eighty-five to ninety percent with brain signals, for uses in access, health, and consumer tech.
arxiv-2502-16324:
Alireza Nourbakhsh and Hoda Mohammadzade present a deep learning method for aligning many time series at once in a 2025 paper. Signals in the real world often arrive shifted or stretched in time, which throws off classification done on the raw data. Older tools mostly align sequences of letters, like proteins, or handle just two signals at a time.

Their method warps all signals together. It bends time through piecewise linear pieces whose complexity can vary, while obeying the classic rules of warping: fixed ends, steady forward motion, and no breaks. A convolutional network drives the process with a new loss that sidesteps flaws of the standard warping score. On a large public archive of more than a hundred data sets, alignment with their method raised classification accuracy on most sets and ran faster.
arxiv-2502-16824:
Many science problems ask for the best input to a costly black-box system, from drug doses to robot settings. Taeyoung Yun and co-authors present DiBO in a 2025 paper, a method built for such searches in high dimensions. Classic Bayesian optimization is sample-thrifty but wilts as dimensions and trials grow.

DiBO alternates two stages. First, a diffusion model learns the shape of good inputs while helper networks predict values with honest uncertainty. Second, picking the next trial is cast as a posterior inference problem, which the diffusion model is tuned to solve directly. That balance of exploring and exploiting held up across synthetic and real tasks, beating strong rival methods.
arxiv-2502-17524:
Tasfiq Alam and co-authors present a 2025 method to detect bearing faults in rotating machines under changing conditions. Bearings reduce friction and carry heavy loads, and their failure accounts for a large share of machine faults. Reliable early detection keeps equipment running and avoids costly breakdowns.

Their approach feeds two signals, vibration and motor current, into a one-dimensional neural network. Combining the signals gives the network more to work with than either one alone. Transfer learning helps the model adapt when working conditions change. The method is aimed at factories that need fault checks they can trust across varied machines.
arxiv-2502-17624:
Christopher Zerafa, Pauline Galea, and Cristiana Sebu present a 2025 paper on seismic imaging rebuilt as a neural network task. Full waveform inversion maps the deep earth from wave echoes, but its solvers strain in hard ground and full angle data are rare. The team ports the pseudo-spectral form of the method, a past leap in the classic field, into deep learning for the first time.

A loop-shaped network runs the theory-led steps, so physics rules the fit rather than raw data alone. Tests run on made-up data and on a standard two-part model, set against both classic and time-domain learned rivals.
arxiv-2502-17724:
Your friends have more friends than you do, on average: that statistical quirk is the friendship paradox, and Rajat Subhra Hazra and co-authors take it several steps out. In sparse random graphs, they measure the bias not just between a vertex and its direct neighbors. They extend it to vertices reached by a walk of length k, following paths that may or may not retrace their steps. For backtracking and non-backtracking explorations they pin down the limiting distribution of these multi-level biases as the graph grows, and as the walk lengthens.

For non-backtracking walks the two limits commute across a wide class of graphs, so the order of taking them does not matter. Where they fail to commute, the walk's mixing time explains why. The results extend the team's earlier single-level analysis.
arxiv-2502-18024:
Hanbo Sun and co-authors show how to switch a flat magnetic material into a new magnetic state, in a 2025 paper. The new state, altermagnetism, splits electron spins by energy while keeping no net pull, unlike both plain magnets and antiferromagnets. Their test sheet is a single layer of a compound called VPSe3.

Three levers do the work: an electric field, a one-sided Janus build, and a ferroelectric base. Together they unbalance the selenium atoms on the two faces, breaking a symmetry and waking the spin split. The sheet also splits its valleys by a small energy gap. Each lever can tune or flip that valley split, a step toward valley-based devices.
arxiv-2502-18124:
Gopal Hazra reviews how planets lose their atmospheres to space, in this 2025 paper. Escape sculpts which worlds keep air and water. Light-based spectra of passing planets now catch the outflow directly, and it proves common.

Young planets under fierce starlight shed gas fastest. Hazra walks through each escape mechanism and the models behind them. Star flares, winds, eruptions, and magnetic fields all push or shield, while the planet's gravity, heat, and own field push back. The balance decides long-term air evolution. The survey links single escape events to the patterns seen across the exoplanet census.
arxiv-2502-18324:
Jemma Bennett and colleagues tested a pairing of two quantum methods in 2025. One method, a parity embedding, rewrites hard problems with long-range links so they fit real quantum hardware. The other, a continuous-time quantum walk, searches for good answers and can dodge a slowdown that hurts rival methods.

The team simulated walks on small spin-glass problems with four, five, and six logical qubits placed on the parity layout. The walks kept working well, and rules for picking the best hopping rate held up. Some ways of cleaning up the readout after the walk clearly raised the chance of success. The findings guide future tests on real machines.
arxiv-2502-18724:
Etim and Szefer show how plain black and white stickers can fool road sign readers in this twenty twenty-five paper. Most past attacks needed a fresh trick mark for each image, which is slow and hard to use. A shared mark that works on many signs at once would pose a much larger risk.

Inside, the authors build one set of sticker marks that can be placed the same way on many types of signs. They test the marks on street view photos rather than on real signs on real roads. The marks fool common sign-reading models at a high rate on United States sign data. The work flags a cheap and real risk for self-driving cars.
arxiv-2502-18924:
Ziyue Jiang and co-authors present a speech synthesis system that clones voices from brief samples in a 2025 paper. Aligning text with sound is the hard part of zero shot speech tools. Forced alignment can sound stiff, while no alignment can sound sloppy. Their system feeds sparse alignment hints to a diffusion transformer.

Hints bound the search without fencing it in, which keeps speech natural. A guidance trick tunes accent strength on demand. A fast flow method cuts sampling steps sharply. One minute of high grade speech takes just eight steps. Tests place the system at the front of zero shot speech quality rankings.
arxiv-2502-19124:
Changhong Li wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It ties the energy scale of a big bounce cosmos to the hum of gravitational waves it would leave, and bounds that scale with real detector reach.

Big bounce models swap the big bang's singular start for a contraction that rebounds. A sea of gravitational waves could test the idea. The author derives a clean link between the bounce scale and the wave spectrum's shape. Data from space, pulsar, and ground detectors then fence the scale in. A wide band of contraction styles is ruled out. One slim window, near a matter-led squeeze, could still sing loud enough to hear.
arxiv-2502-19524:
Six authors led by Letizia Ferbel study what happens when platinum slips under a graphene sheet in a 2025 paper. Graphene is a one-atom-thick carbon sheet, here grown on silicon carbide. A buried metal layer under it can tune the sheet for spin tools, catalysts, and more. Past work showed platinum can slip in at the seam, but the shape of the buried layer and the path it takes were unclear.

The team laid platinum on the surface and heated it in cycles, then tracked shape, chemistry, and electron traits. Under the bare buffer layer, one flat platinum layer formed and smoothed its ridges. Under full graphene, two layers formed, with a wide repeat pattern on top. The buried atoms bonded with silicon from below, forming silicide-like links. The sheet charge stayed near neutral after the change.
arxiv-2502-19824:
Vidhi Lalchand and Anna-Christina Eilers build a shared model for the light spectra of quasars and their known traits. Quasars are very bright galaxies with huge black holes at their cores. Their 2025 paper joins two kinds of data for each object in one model.

The model hides each quasar in a shared low-size space, then rebuilds both its spectrum and its labels from that space. Labels include black hole mass, feeding rate, and brightness. The method can train even when many values for an object are missing. Tests rebuild test spectra and labels with high fidelity. The authors also note what the hidden space may mean for quasar science.
arxiv-2502-20124:
Yujie Li and co-authors explore open-world continual learning, where a model must keep learning new classes while flagging ones it has never seen, in a 2025 paper. Real deployments face incomplete training data and unknown samples at test time. Earlier methods split detection and learning into separate chores, and they ignored what unknown samples might teach.

The authors define four distinct scenarios and run wide experiments on them. Their tests show detection of unknowns and sorting of knowns shape each other, defying a common assumption that the two are independent. Building on this, they propose HoliTrans, which joins a nonlinear projection for cleaner feature space with distribution-aware prototypes. The framework treats knowns and unknowns as one shared source of knowledge.
arxiv-2502-20424:
When two neutron stars merge, the debris glows as a kilonova, and its spectrum carries fingerprints of the heavy elements forged in the blast. Kitovienė and co-authors compute the atomic data needed to read one such fingerprint: doubly ionized thorium.

Using relativistic atomic structure methods, they calculated energy levels and electric dipole transitions for seven electron configurations of Th III. Their levels match measured values with a root-mean-square deviation of 436 wavenumbers, a good score for so heavy an atom. Plugged into radiative transfer simulations, the data show that a thorium mass fraction of only a few hundred-thousandths would stamp absorption features near 18,000 angstroms on a kilonova spectrum. The tables give observers a concrete target to hunt in future merger light.
arxiv-2502-20524:
Mirko Mizzoni, Pieter van Goor, and Antonio Franchi join two drive modes in one law for bent path craft in a 2025 note. Rich-input craft oft hold cheap inputs for the main task and dear ones for a spare task. A wheel craft with all-side wheels is their case in point for the frame.

One mode tracks the main task on cheap inputs while dear ones rest at zero. One mode wakes the dear inputs to track the spare task as well. The law pledges firm main-task tracks in both modes.
arxiv-2502-20624:
Genta Furuya and Kazumasa Hattori use Monte Carlo simulation to show that fluctuations can quietly strangle a current-driven magnetic response. Their 2025 paper studies a metal hosting chiral quadrupole order on a distorted kagome lattice. The ordered orbital moments break mirror symmetry and couple to conduction electrons, so an electric current induces magnetization.

Mean-field thinking would tie that response to the order parameter's own curve. The simulations disagree: fluctuations in the order parameter suppress the induced magnetization strongly across a broad range below the transition. The team also trace how Fermi surface shape and matrix elements tune the effect. Their warning is general: near ordered phases, fluctuation effects can rewrite the temperature story of a response. Experiments reading such signals must budget for them.
arxiv-2502-20724:
Arup Sarker and a large team glue data work, deep learning, and job flow into one pipeline for big science rigs. Fields like genetics, climate work, and astronomy drown in preparation work before a model can train. Their 2025 pipeline, Deep RC, runs the full chain, preparation, training, and later work, across cloud and top-tier sites as one run. A task pilot steers the steps on mixed rigs with accelerator chips.

Link libraries let nodes talk at scale in three dialects. One end-to-end run drove 11 storm forecasting models in one frame and water models in the next, on the same system. End-to-end time fell sharply in both runs. The team pitches open, flexible pipelines over locked shops.
arxiv-2502-21024:
Questions about the past need documents from the right time, not just the right topic. Abdallah and co-authors present TempRetriever, a search engine that embeds the query's date and each document's timestamp into its dense retrieval process. Passages must match both the meaning and the moment the question asks about.

On two large archive test sets, the method beat standard dense retrieval by about seven to ten points on top-hit accuracy, with gains in ranking quality as well. A training trick that picks negatives from the wrong time sharpened the model further. The authors set a new benchmark for time-aware passage search in question answering.
arxiv-2502-21224:
Sidney Wong and co-authors test if social posts can chart how tongues shift in a place. In New Zealand, census counts are the lone stock source on tongue use, and they age fast. Their 2025 chapter sets census truth next to a vast post trove tagged by place. Tongue tags for each post are checked by two tongue-spot models.

Diversity is then read at land, shire, and town scale in both sources. Posts prove keen to crowd and rule shifts at fine scales, the team finds. Such feeds could fill the gaps between census rounds. The case warns too: post crowds skew young and loud, so counts need care. Still, the match at small scales marks a fresh well for tongue maps.
arxiv-2503-00024:
Yanran Chen and Steffen Eger present a 2025 paper asking whether emotion really makes arguments more convincing. Psychology says feelings sway judgment, but language technology research has barely tested the claim, and earlier work used static setups. The pair borrow the manipulation check from social science, using language models to dial an argument's emotional charge up or down.

Human judges rated arguments across languages, topics, and text types under different emotional tones. In over half the cases, stronger emotion changed nothing about how convincing an argument felt. When it did matter, emotion helped more often than it hurt. Eleven language models mostly mirrored the human pattern but missed subtle shifts in individual judgments.
arxiv-2503-00124:
Nikita Soni and co-authors asked in 2025 how best to turn a writer's text into numbers that capture the writer's state of mind. Language models store inner states as they read, and those states can serve as a portrait of the author. Yet teams differ on which part of the model to draw from.

The team tested many ways to build portraits of single texts and of whole users, across tasks such as mood, empathy, and distress. Averaging the inner states of all words in a text worked best in most cases. A stored portrait of the user rarely won on its own, but adding it made other portraits stronger. The results guide teams building tools that read people, not just text.
arxiv-2503-00224:
K O T Erziev wrote a 2025 paper reporting a strange skill in large language models: they can read meaning into symbol strings that look like nonsense to people. One string of Byzantine music symbols, for instance, was read by a leading model as a magic word phrase. Some models can even talk to each other in such strings, the paper reports.

Erziev tested a wide range of current models for the trait and traces part of it to the way models chop text into tokens, which breeds false links. The paper warns that hidden channels like this could matter for the safety and security of systems built on these models.
arxiv-2503-00324:
Sk Tanzir Mehedi and co-authors build DySec in this 2025 paper, a behavior watcher that catches malicious Python packages as they install. Attackers hide bad code in the open PyPI store through tricks like look-alike names and delayed payloads. Static scans and metadata checks miss such moves. DySec instead traces live behavior with kernel and user probes during installation.

It records thirty-six signals, from system calls to network traffic and folder access. The team built a set of over fourteen thousand packages, half of them malicious traces, run in isolation. DySec scored about ninety-six percent accuracy with sub-second delay, cutting missed attacks sharply versus static methods. It even flagged eleven packages PyPI had passed; hand checks confirmed six, and four were removed after the team's report.
arxiv-2503-00424:
Zeyi Niu, writing alone in 2025, forecasts typhoons with a hybrid that weds a machine learning model to a physics-based one. The system couples the FuXi learning model, strong on large-scale patterns, with the Shanghai Typhoon Model, strong on storm-scale detail, through spectral nudging. The dual design aims at track, intensity, and rainfall accuracy together.

On super typhoons Yagi and Krathon, both from 2024, the hybrid improved all three forecast targets over its parents. A perturbation method then mapped the regions where the hybrid is most sensitive, showing where dense satellite data buys the most extra skill despite the learning model's grip on the large scale. Niu frames the work as a signpost: operational forecasting is shifting toward fused systems, and the fusion itself is becoming the research object.
arxiv-2503-00524:
Denis Blessing and co-authors let a sampler learn a better starting point for drawing from tricky distributions, in a 2025 paper. Diffusion samplers generate samples by running a noisy process from a simple prior shape. When that starting shape poorly matches the target, sampling wanders and errors pile up. Learning the prior naively invites collapse onto a few modes.

Their answer is a learnable mixture of Gaussians, trained end to end with the sampler itself. The mixture can stretch to cover the target's support and keeps exploration broad. Training adds mixture components step by step where they help most. Across synthetic and real benchmarks, sampling improved markedly with no extra target evaluations. Better priors make diffusion sampling practical for harder problems.
arxiv-2503-00724:
Tianyi Huang and co-authors compare ways to use large language models as lie detectors for online falsehoods in a 2025 paper. False claims spread fast on social media and do real harm. Language models read and reason well, so many teams have tried them as fact checkers.

The review sorts methods into three kinds: text-only, mixed media, and agent teams that check step by step. It weighs tuned models, no-example use, and strict checking routines across health, politics, and finance topics. Each style has weak spots, from made-up facts to attack tricks and high compute cost. The authors back hybrid designs that pair firm check steps with models that keep learning. Future work may track falsehoods live.
arxiv-2503-00824:
Sarthak Satapathy, Sumit, and Salman Ahamad Khan compute the behavior of ultra-dense quark matter threaded by a strong magnetic field. Such matter may sit in the cores of neutron stars and magnetars, where pressure, heat, and magnetism decide the star's fate. The team uses a loop-based perturbation method built for dense matter. They calculate the free energy of quarks and gluons, then derive pressure along and across the field, magnetization, a count of how quark numbers respond, and the speed of sound.

The numbers show pressure along the field rising with both density and field strength, while the sideways pressure falls. At the highest densities the sound speed along the field climbs toward the speed of light, as theory expects at the limit. The authors offer the results as input for models of magnetized star interiors.
arxiv-2503-00924:
Xinyu Zhang and co-authors make preference-based optimization fast enough to chat with. Their 2025 paper works on preferential Bayesian optimization, which learns what a user likes by asking them to compare pairs of designs. The classic version refits a heavy statistical model after every answer, far too slow for interactive use with a person waiting.

Their method, PABBO, amortizes the whole loop: a transformer neural process is meta-trained to act as both the surrogate model and the chooser of the next pair. Reinforcement learning plus tailored extra losses shape that training. On synthetic and real-world benchmarks the system ran orders of magnitude faster than the Gaussian process standard. It also often won on accuracy, not just speed. The authors aim the work at design tools where taste, not a formula, is the objective.
arxiv-2503-01124:
Vision transformers read images through attention, but their inner feed-forward blocks use plain multilayer perceptrons. Shreyas S and Akshath M swap those blocks in 2025 for Kolmogorov-Arnold networks. Such networks build complex functions from sums of simple one-variable curves. The team tests five flavors, from vanilla to sine- and Fourier-based versions, plus a fast attention variant.

On the MNIST digit benchmark, the sine, fast, and well-tuned vanilla versions all passed ninety-seven percent accuracy, though training cost more than the standard block. A plain perceptron and a small convolutional net serve as baselines. The authors publish code-level detail so others can weigh the accuracy-for-compute trade themselves.
arxiv-2503-01424:
Zekun Zhou and a large team of co-authors survey systems that use AI to support research from first idea to published paper. Research drives human progress but eats time and effort. The survey sorts the field into three stages: forming hypotheses, validating them, and publishing manuscripts.

Forming covers knowledge synthesis and idea generation. Validating covers claim checking, theorem proving, and experiment testing. Publishing covers writing help and peer review support. For each stage the authors map tools, benchmarks, and open challenges. They also point to future directions. The paper serves as an entry guide for newcomers and a reference for active builders, with resources posted online.
arxiv-2503-01524:
Kiyoon Eum wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on point processes on curved spaces from complex geometry. A determinantal point process scatters points with a built-in repulsion, governed by a kernel. Eum studies the total weight, the partition function, of such processes on polarized Kähler manifolds.

The paper gives the full asymptotic expansion of that weight as the process scales up. Each coefficient turns out to be a geometric functional of the Kähler metric, tied to the Bergman kernel's own expansion. These functionals generalize two famous ones, the Mabuchi functional and the Liouville functional. Eum also shows that holomorphic invariants can block the functionals from having critical points. The last section connects the formulas to the quantum Hall effect in physics.
arxiv-2503-01824:
David Klindt and four co-authors argue that the tangled internal code of neural networks can be untangled into features people can name, in this 2025 paper. Networks seem to store concepts in superposition, many features sharing the same neurons, overlaid like transparencies. That overlap makes their reasoning hard to inspect, a problem for both artificial intelligence and neuroscience.

The perspective rests on three steps. First, theory shows that networks trained to classify recover the true hidden features of their data, up to a simple linear remixing. Second, sparse coding techniques, borrowed from signal compression, can undo that remix and pull the features apart. Third, the authors propose quantitative scores for how interpretable the recovered features really are, checked against human judgment. The result is the outline of a science of reading networks: measure first, name second, trust last.
arxiv-2503-02024:
B. Kapanadze, A. Gurchumelia, and M. Aller mine fifteen years of gamma ray observations of a nearby blazar in a 2025 astronomy study. The space telescope Fermi watched the galaxy Markarian 421, whose jet points nearly at Earth, from the late two thousands into the early twenty twenties. Six stretches of stronger activity stand out against the rest of the record.

Across those stretches the baseline brightness drifted over months to years, with shorter flares of varied shapes on top. The authors read that layering as evidence for several distinct unsteady processes at work in the jet. Long, even coverage is what lets such slow patterns emerge.
arxiv-2503-02524:
Jotin Gogoi and Mrinal Kumar Das test patterns of enforced zeros in the neutrino mass matrix inside a model that also hosts dark matter. Neutrinos are far lighter than other particles, and seesaw models explain that lightness with heavy partners. The team works in a minimal inverse seesaw setup shaped by a discrete symmetry, with an added triplet of scalar fields whose neutral members could serve as dark matter. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they ask which zero patterns in one of the input matrices survive contact with measured neutrino mixing and with the observed amount of dark matter.

Of fifteen candidate patterns with two zeros, only two reproduced all measured mixing angles within allowed ranges. For those favored cases the team computed the expected dark matter abundance. The paper narrows a large model space to a small testable corner.
arxiv-2503-03124:
Ping He and Bo-Qiang Ma set limits on possible violations of Lorentz invariance for protons, using the highest-energy cosmic rays. Lorentz invariance is a core rule of modern physics, but some theories allow small breaks in it. Such breaks could let protons decay in new ways or change how they make pions when they strike light.

Observations of very fast protons already rule out strong effects in the faster-than-light direction. The confirmed cutoff in cosmic ray energy, linked to pion production, bounds effects in the slower direction as well. Together the two sides give tight, two-way limits. The work shows how cosmic rays serve as a sharp test of basic physics.
arxiv-2503-03224:
Johann Rafelski and Cheng Tao Yang explored the Higgs particle in the early universe in two thousand twenty-five. After the electroweak phase transition, the cosmos held a hot quark-gluon plasma. Most particles in it stayed in full thermal balance as the universe expanded.

The authors show the Higgs was an exception at certain stages. Its decays into heavy gauge bosons kept it out of chemical balance. At lower temperatures, fast formation and decay reactions also shaped its momentum spread in a non-balanced way. As heavy particles vanished, the Higgs coupled too weakly to light particles for collisions to restore balance. The paper is a theoretical account of that special case.
arxiv-2503-03824:
Siddhartha Gurung-Lopez and co-authors separated this 2025 tangle of light: what a galaxy's own gas does to its brightest emission line versus what the gas between galaxies does. Lyman-alpha light from young galaxies gets scattered and partly eaten at every stage of its journey. The team fit 313 observed line shapes, from nearby to when the universe was young, with a neural tool trained on simulated spectra.

Nearby galaxies showed almost no intergalactic dimming. Beyond redshift three, the space between galaxies swallowed much of the line's blue side. Once that fog was removed, the galaxies' own line shapes barely changed across cosmic time. The measured escape share fell from near total nearby to about fifty-five percent at the far end, matching other probes of the cosmic fog.
arxiv-2503-03924:
Prakash Shukla and co-authors warn that design help from smart tools can dull the very skills it aids, in a study from 2025. Such tools now draft screens and text at a tap. Gains in speed are real, but old lore on auto aids lists ironies: skills fade, thought is offloaded, blame lands wrong.

The team read more than 120 posts and chats from design forums. Hands-on designers told of both hope and dread: joy at less grind and more spark, fear of lean on the tool, thin thought, and lost craft. The team ties those tales to the old irony lore and to the split of work between human and tool. Their charge: judge the tool by craft years from now, not by this week's speed.
arxiv-2503-04024:
Philip Charles and co-authors build a neural operator framework based on an optimal formulation for solving partial differential equations, in work from 2025. Such equations govern heat, flow, and many other processes. The optimal method gives the best answer within a chosen function space, but it needs weighting functions that are hard to build for complex problems.

Their network is shaped to mimic the optimal weak form of the equation, so it learns the weighting functions on its own during training. Training uses labelled pairs of equation data and solutions. The team proves error bounds that separate the sources of error, including the learned weights. Tests on a standard equation mixing drift and spread show the method works well and generalises beyond its training data.
arxiv-2503-04124:
Shinya Fujita and Boram Park set tight limits on a graph measure in a 2025 math study. A hop dominating set is a set of points such that every point outside it sits exactly two steps from a point inside. The hop domination number is the size of the smallest such set. The team studies connected graphs with no triangles and at least fifteen points, where each point has at least two neighbors.

For such graphs they prove the number is at most two fifths of the point count, and the bound cannot be improved. They also give tight bounds for graphs that hold a path or a cycle through all points. The results pin down how sparse a two-step watch set can be.
arxiv-2503-04924:
Jonathan Auerbach and co-authors fix a bias in field timing data in a 2025 paper. Volunteers who watch plants report bloom or leaf states on visit days, but the true event may fall between visits or be misread. Plain methods then place the event date off target, which warps studies of plant timing and climate.

Their Bayesian model uses smooth rising curves to infer the true event time and correct both error types. Tests on fake data show the fix works. Applied to lilac blooms watched in the northeast United States, it moved peak bloom far later than plain methods said. Some sites also stood out as truly late once the bias was stripped away.
arxiv-2503-05224:
Baris Yilmaz, Erdem Akagündüz, and Salih Tileylioglu predict a key ground property from earthquake recordings in a paper from 2025. The property, average shear wave speed in the top thirty meters of soil, guides seismic hazard work but is rarely measured directly at recording stations in Türkiye. Rule-of-thumb estimates miss local variation, so the team turned to deep learning.

Their hybrid model joins convolutional and memory networks to read both the shape and the time course of strong motion records. Better picking of the first wave arrival raised accuracy. The study shows the model learning tangled, site-specific patterns that simple formulas miss.
arxiv-2503-05324:
Ofir Cohen, Jose Yallouz, Michael Schapira, Shahar Belkar, and Tal Mizrahi wrote a 2025 networking paper on routing data inside data centers that train large machine learning models. Training moves huge volumes of data in repeated rounds. Those flows are unusually regular and persistent, since the same training steps cycle again and again.

That regularity is an opening for smarter routing. The authors present an algorithmic framework that first quantifies how efficient the whole network is under a given routing. It then periodically re-optimizes routes against that global metric, rather than tuning one link at a time. The work targets the communication bottleneck that grows as models scale. Better routing squeezes more training out of the same hardware.
arxiv-2503-05424:
Niklas Penzel and Joachim Denzler present a 2025 arXiv paper on explaining single predictions by gently changing the input. Most explanation tools report associations, not causes. Their framework uses modern image editing models to slide one trait at a time, blush on a cheek, say, or age in a face, and measures how the prediction glides in response. A new score captures the strength of that response.

Tests first proved the method finds planted biases in a synthetic setup. Real studies followed: skin lesion classifiers, the inside story of network training, and a large vision-language model probed with real edits. The authors argue property-level interventions reveal behavior that heat maps miss.
arxiv-2503-05924:
Tanmay Tirpankar, Arnab Das, and Ganesh Gopalakrishnan present Satire in two thousand twenty-five. Satire bounds floating point rounding error in mixed precision programs. Numerical code needs such hard bounds to be trusted. Few tools handle branches and mixed precision in one pass.

Abstraction lets users trade bound tightness for analysis speed. That trade helps while they search design options in a routine. New gauges track instability jumps at conditional branches. Mixed precision runs show how error shifts with the precision mix. A conjugate gradient case shows step and direction effects. The tool is free for evaluation.
arxiv-2503-06024:
Ying Zhang seeks pattern rules in quark mass matrices in a 2025 paper. Why quarks come in three families with steeply rising masses is one of particle physics' open flavor puzzles. Zhang shows that a quark mass matrix can be split, in a model-independent way, into a phase part that varies by family and a real symmetric part set by only two parameters.

That split yields general rules any such matrix must obey. In the limit where the first two families count as equal in mass, a large CP violation phase, a measure of matter-antimatter asymmetry, appears naturally. Zhang then tests a flat pattern, where the symmetric part's entries sit close to one, against measured quark masses and mixing values. The fit describes flavor structure well with few inputs.
arxiv-2503-06224:
Edgar Assing and Radu Toma bring a physics-born method to number theory in a 2025 paper. The orbit method, in a sharp form by Nelson and Venkatesh, has powered recent wins on L-functions. The target here is the sup-norm problem: how large a wave form can grow.

The pair prove a new joint bound for fresh forms of large prime-power level and large eigenvalue. The bound matches a classic spectral result and beats the local record in the depth side for the first time in this open setting. The note also teaches the fine-scale tools used, through the classic case. It serves both as proof and as a guide.
arxiv-2503-06424:
An AI tutor can sound wise while the student learns little, since it was trained to sound like a teacher, not to cause learning. Alexander Scarlatos and four co-authors retrain the tutor on outcomes in 2025. For each turn, the system drafts several replies and grades them two ways.

One grade comes from a student model that forecasts the chance of a right answer next. The other is a teaching rubric scored by a large model. Wins and losses among the drafts then teach an open model by direct preference tuning. The result speaks to lift the odds of a right reply while keeping sound teaching form. Trials in live chats test the claim.
arxiv-2503-06924:
Michael McGuire, writing alone, graded five leading speech recognition systems on how well they transcribe non-native English, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such systems power language learning and testing tools, so their accuracy on accented speech matters. McGuire used a standard speech collection with speakers from six first-language backgrounds.

The test covered read sentences from twenty-four speakers and story recordings from twenty-two. For read speech, two systems, Whisper and AssemblyAI, came close to human accuracy. For free speech, RevAI led the pack. Systems differed a lot in how they handled filler words, repeats, and self-corrections. Speed also varied widely, and slower did not mean more accurate. The results help teachers and researchers pick a system for each job.
arxiv-2503-07324:
Zhiyu He, Saverio Bolognani, Florian Dorfler, and Michael Muehlebach study optimization problems where the decision itself changes the data that future decisions rely on. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, gives this feedback a dynamic form: the population or environment shifts over time in response to choices, following rules that can be nonlinear. Earlier work often treated the shift as a fixed map tied to each single decision. The authors instead follow how the whole distribution moves and settles.

They design an online method that both adapts to the moving distribution and steers it toward better outcomes. The analysis covers when their method finds the best decision and how well it generalizes. Two examples ground the theory: shaping opinions in a divided population, and tuning a recommender system where user tastes shift in response.
arxiv-2503-07824:
Alessio Russo, Yichen Song, and Aldo Pacchiano wrote a 2025 paper on learning the best option when each try reveals only part of the picture. In their setup, a learner picks an action and sees feedback on related actions too. A graph spells out those links, covering cases from full feedback down to almost none. The goal is not to earn the most during learning, but to name the best action with confidence using few tries.

The authors derive a floor on how many samples any method needs for a given problem. The floor holds even when the graph itself is random and unknown. They show cases where the best action cannot be pinned down at all. Their results spell out how the needed samples grow with features of the graph. Last, they give a method that meets the floor in the long run, and test it across graph shapes.
arxiv-2503-07924:
Three researchers route wireless network traffic with a quantum-inspired machine in a paper from 2025. Multi-hop wireless networks must balance several goals at once, such as speed and energy. The team recasts routing as a binary optimization problem and maps it onto an Ising model. A coherent Ising machine, which uses light to settle into low-energy states, then searches for good routes.

The machine handled varied network shapes without custom adjustments. It found feasible, near-optimal routes in networks with hundreds of nodes and thousands of links. Classic quantum algorithms need more tuning per shape, the authors note. Efficiency improved as networks grew. The work tests quantum-inspired hardware on a practical telecom problem.
arxiv-2503-08124:
Five authors present a 2025 paper on how research on statistical methods itself should be classed and reported. Studies of real-world topics are often split into two modes: open-ended work that builds ideas, and strict work that tests set claims. That split is well known in fields such as medicine, but method research in statistics has rarely used it.

The authors first view method studies through that split. Then they survey 115 papers from biostatistics to see how current practice handles the line between the modes. They close with advice on design, reading, and reporting. Both modes matter for progress, they argue, but they should not be blurred.
arxiv-2503-08624:
Klusek-Gawenda, Gonçalves, and Szczurek estimate inelastic contributions to light-by-light scattering in heavy ion collisions, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Theory currently underpredicts the scattering rates measured by ATLAS and CMS. Missing channels where nuclei break up may explain the gap. Photons coupling to single nucleons are added to whole-nucleus coupling.

Both ground-state and excited nucleon couplings enter the calculation. Inelastic fluxes use modern photon-in-nucleon distribution functions. Corrections reach twenty to forty percent of standard predictions in ATLAS regions. They grow with photon pair mass and rapidity gap. Factorization scale uncertainty is quantified alongside the estimates.
arxiv-2503-08924:
Gonzalez-Vega and co-authors build tools to study the curve where a torus meets a quadric surface. The torus is taken as centered at the origin, with its axis along the z direction. That setup loses no generality for the analysis.

Most attention goes to the curve's shadow on the z equals zero plane, called the cutcurve. Getting that projection right is key for lifting back to the true 3D curve. The authors characterize singular points on both curves in detail. They also settle when double tangents exist. Resultant and subresultant polynomials supply the core machinery behind the tools.
arxiv-2503-09524: Bin Shen and six co-authors squeeze a kagome-lattice magnet under pressures up to fifty gigapascals and watch a strange metal phase appear, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Strange metals, whose resistance grows in a straight line with temperature, often precede superconductivity and remain poorly understood. The material, CrNiAs, starts as a ferromagnet. Under pressure its ordering temperature falls in a straight line toward a quantum critical point, and the strange phase opens around it.
arxiv-2503-09624:
Marius F R Juston, Alex Gisi, William R Norris, Dustin Nottage, and Ahmet Soylemezoglu present a control design that adapts to the person working with the machine, in a 2025 paper. Human-in-the-loop systems, from assistive devices to shared driving, must respect limits while fitting each operator's style.

Their design sets clear bounds on the controller's behavior so key control properties hold by construction. They study worst-case training losses and how to weight them for effective learning. In simulations, the adaptive controller beat the human operator's results by about four and a half percent. It beat a plain neural network controller, trained the same way, by about nine percent. The authors offer the design as a safer path to personal machine help.
arxiv-2503-09724:
Shubhayan Sarkar and co-authors show that real and complex quantum theory can differ without bound in this 2025 paper. Standard quantum theory uses complex numbers to describe quantum systems. A rival version built only on real numbers was already known to fail some network tests.

The team study a star network with many parties sharing quantum systems. They build a multipartite Bell test suited to that setup. The gap between the two theories grows in a straight line as parties are added. That growth means the difference is not a small edge case. Experiments can use the test to show why complex numbers are needed.
arxiv-2503-09924:
François Golse and Jakob Möller test a smoothing tool on a quantum kinetic equation in a 2025 paper. The Wigner equation tracks a quantum version of a particle distribution as it evolves. Velocity averaging theorems say that mixing over velocities smooths the density, but whether they hold for Wigner functions was open.

For mixed states with a stated size condition, the authors prove the density gains fractional smoothness in one dimension. Pure states behave worse: they give settings where averaging fails outright for rank-one states under the standard quantum evolution. A side result re-derives the Madelung fluid equations quickly, explaining the key assumption behind the failure.
arxiv-2503-10124:
Taekyun Kim and Dae San Kim present a study from twenty twenty-five on a family of polynomials tied to counting split sets. The Lah-Bell polynomials grow out of counts of ways to split a set into ordered blocks. A known type of recurrence, named for Spivey, steps such counts from one size to the next. The pair seek that recurrence for these polynomials.

They use two operators: one that multiplies by the variable, and one that takes its slope. The two swap with a fixed gap, which drives the proof. They get the recurrence for both the plain and the weighted forms. A third form, with a new dial, is handled by a unlike route with no operators.
arxiv-2503-10224:
Pierre Bikorimana and Stephane Tchuiaga proved a geometry result in this 2025 paper. Their setting is cosymplectic manifolds, spaces that mix traits of two classic kinds of geometry. On such a space sits a group of maps that act like Hamilton's flow in mechanics. The pair ask whether that group is simple, meaning it has no smaller group nested inside in a tidy way.

Their answer is yes, echoing a famed theorem of Banyaga for the symplectic case. A key step shows the space's Reeb flow always runs in a cycle. That cycle forces a linked flux group to sit in discrete steps, which feeds the proof. The paper also rebuilds known facts about these spaces as layered maps, proves a full set of conserved paths for steady systems, and pins down the commutator part of the larger group.
arxiv-2503-10424:
Norbert A'Campo and Pablo Portilla Cuadrado survey, in a 2025 paper, how a drawing-like device called a divide illuminates the topology of plane curve singularities. Divides are wavy curves drawn in a disk under set rules. From them, one can build knotted loops whose twisting pattern is written out directly.

Singular points of plane curves carry a classical fibered link of their own, the Milnor fibration. The survey gathers decades of work connecting divides to that structure, its twisting map, and its vanishing cycles. Putting the pieces in one place shows how a simple drawing encodes deep knot theory. Students of singularity theory gain a map of a rich meeting ground between pictures and proofs.
arxiv-2503-10824:
Simulating flowing fluids in full detail is slow, so engineers learn compact models from data, but those models can break the physics, leaking energy that should stay fixed. Leonidas Gkimisis, Igor Pontes Duff, Pawan Goyal, and Peter Benner work on quadratic models, whose curved terms model many flows. A twisted matrix layout, called skew-symmetric, guarantees the energy stays put.

They prove every energy-keeping quadratic term can be rewritten in that layout. They also give a method to convert any such term into the layout. Folded into a data-driven modeling tool, the layout is enforced through a chain of simple fitting steps. On a standard fluid test, the learned model stayed accurate and true to the physics, unlike the classic version.
arxiv-2503-10924:
Moslem Uddin, Huadong Mo, and Daoyi Dong survey how to keep cyber-physical systems trustworthy in a 2025 review. These systems weld computers to machines: power grids, factory floors, smart vehicles. When the weld cracks, the physical world pays.

The review sorts reliability work into three crafts. Modeling comes as equations, as simulation, or as a blend. Evaluation runs from fault trees to Markov chains to uptime measures. Improvement leans on fault tolerance, live reconfiguration, and smart resource allocation. The authors map each craft's tools, then flag the open challenges and coming trends, writing a field guide for engineers and policymakers alike.
arxiv-2503-11024: Imane Jarni, Ayoub Laayoun, and Badr Missaoui prove that a stable outcome exists for a class of mean field games with bounced-back dynamics. Mean field games model many small players who react to the crowd average. Here each player's motion follows a reflected stochastic equation, which keeps it inside a set region. The proof uses relaxed controls and a martingale problem frame, as stated in the short abstract.
arxiv-2503-11624:
Adrià Labay-Mora and co-authors design a quantum code that traps its own errors, in this 2025 paper. Their chiral cat qubit stores information in a single light or microwave oscillator, extending the known Kerr cat design with stronger nonlinear effects. The system's phase space holds four long-lived states: two carry the data, and two form an error space.

Thanks to a twist in that layout, bit-flip errors fall into the error space without touching the stored data, where they can be spotted and fixed. The trick shines under heavy dephasing, the authors show, and gates stay fast.
arxiv-2503-11824:
Tuomas Jalonen, Mohammad Al-Sa'd, Serkan Kiranyaz, and Moncef Gabbouj proposed a semi-supervised learning method in twenty twenty-five for time-series data with few labels. Labeled signals are costly to get, yet tasks like bearing fault diagnosis need them. Their method, Dual-Domain Fusion, trains on both a signal's raw time form and its time-frequency picture at once.

Three model parts handle the time view, the frequency view, and their fusion, teaching each other through co-training. At test time the extra parts are dropped, so running cost matches a plain time model. On two public fault data sets it beat five known semi-supervised methods, with accuracy gains from eight to forty-six percent. The framework is model-agnostic, built to wrap around existing time-series classifiers.
arxiv-2503-11924:
Kun Su and a team of co-authors release a data set for conversational recommendation, in two thousand twenty-five. Recommenders that chat with users need data on how people steer a search in words. Older data sets track only the sequence of items picked, which misses that steering.

Their set extends a large product review collection with two added text types. Critiques capture the user's steering words before each pick. Narratives give rich text for each suggested item, including praise, reasons to buy, and a summary of tastes. Their benchmark model generates picks and narratives together from user history. Adding critiques improved recommendation quality in their tests.
arxiv-2503-12024:
Byeongjun Park and co-authors present SteerX in a 2025 paper on making 3D and moving scenes with sound geometry. Past methods fix alignment at each stage apart, so small errors from one stage slip past the next. SteerX folds scene rebuilding into the making step itself, with no new training.

Two score rules grade how well a scene's shape holds up, based on pose-free rebuilding models. Those scores tilt the making process toward scenes whose parts line up in space. Broad tests show the steering lifts the grade of both still and moving made scenes.
arxiv-2503-12124:
Yingying Deng, Xiangyu He, Fan Tang, and Weiming Dong introduce Z-Magic in this 2025 paper. Their tool makes images with more than one chosen trait at once, such as style, color, or content. Past tools could add traits, but the traits did not always fit well with each other in the final image. The work also tackles the case where no training examples cover the trait mix.

The authors frame the task with chance and condition rules. Each new trait should follow from the traits set before it. That view keeps the traits in step and links the task to multi-task learning, which cuts the computing cost. In tests, Z-Magic beat prior models at this zero-shot task.
arxiv-2503-12424:
Zeng, Chen, and Deng put forth a math frame in twenty twenty-five for clean single-bit gates in quantum chip rows. Bits that are linked at all times help pair gates but spoil single gates with cross-talk. Past fixes work when links are weak next to the drive.

Their frame draws the gate path as a closed loop on a ball whose curve is set by the tune gap. A zero-net-area rule for the loop kills cross-talk, and pulse shape maps to loop curve. In two- and three-bit chains their pulses held up to shifts in link and tone. They beat a past pulse by more than ten-fold when links were strong.
arxiv-2503-12624:
Zubankov and a large team of co-authors test a prototype granular neutron detector inside the BM@N experiment at the NICA complex. Their paper from twenty twenty-five describes a time-of-flight design: absorber and scintillator plates interleaved, fine transverse cells, timing near a hundred fifty picoseconds. The full detector will tag neutrons from nucleus collisions and weigh their energies. The compact prototype first had to prove the concept on beam.

Xenon projectiles struck a cesium iodide target in the trial runs. Simulations with two event models supplied acceptance and efficiency estimates. Measured energy spectra of forward spectator and dissociation neutrons matched the simulated shapes. The calibration methods proven here now carry over to the full-scale detector's commissioning.
arxiv-2503-12724:
Xing Huang and co-authors map the magnetism of a cobalt compound with a honeycomb skeleton, in a 2025 paper. The material grows as chains of cobalt-oxygen octahedra arranged in honeycomb pattern layers. Cooling it reveals two magnetic transitions close together, around fourteen and sixteen kelvin. Neutron scattering let the team read the spin arrangements behind each transition.

The ground state proved to be a tilted zigzag pattern, with nearby cobalt ions carrying unequal moments. Raising a field along the easy direction triggered a chain of spin flips. Those flips melted the ordered states and left behind extra disorder. Such field-tunable frustration makes the compound a prized test case for odd magnetism. The full synthesis and structure work is reported alongside.
arxiv-2503-12824:
Paul Djangang, Summer Han, and Nilotpal Sanyal compare methods, in a 2025 preprint, for survival analysis when several endings compete. A patient, for instance, may die of the disease, die of other causes, or live. Standard survival tools blur those endings together. Competing risk methods keep them apart. With gene-scale data, the count of possible predictors dwarfs the count of patients. No one had compared the methods head to head in that regime. The authors run simulations to fill the gap.

They test penalized regression, boosting, random forests, and a deep learning method. Each is scored on picking variables, accuracy, and calibration. One boosting method gave the steadiest results with strong control of false finds. Certain penalized methods calibrated best when patients outnumbered predictors. Forests and deep learning caught curved effects but calibrated weakly. A melanoma gene dataset shows the methods at work. The paper ends with picking guidelines.
arxiv-2503-12924:
Artur Solomonik and Hendrik Heuer map how people move between social platforms in a 2025 paper. Platforms rise and fall, but the act of leaving one for another has drawn little study. The team asked 32 guests at a science festival to draw journey maps of the platforms they had used and why they moved.

The maps were read with content checks and redrawn as graphs of moves. Peer driven fame, the timing of new feature uptake, and felt causes like safety shaped most moves. The work aims to guide future platforms toward richer and more humane online lives, rather than churn driven by hype alone.
arxiv-2503-13024:
Trueman, Pignatari, Cseh, and a team of co-authors use the chemical history of the Milky Way to interrogate how white dwarf stars explode. These blasts, called Type Ia supernovae, forge much of the galaxy's iron family of elements, yet which star systems trigger them is still unsettled.

The team ran more than a thousand simulations of the disk's chemical growth, each pairing a candidate explosion mechanism with a choice of yields from massive star deaths. Comparing the fossil record in real stars, they found most element ratios could not separate the mechanisms. One ratio, nickel to iron, favored explosions of lower-mass white dwarfs under one yield choice. The authors warn that the answer leans heavily on uncertain inputs, and urge caution in drawing firm conclusions.
arxiv-2503-13124:
Mayengbam Kishan Singh and Nimai Singh build a model of neutrino mixing with one sterile partner, in their 2025 arXiv paper. The scheme adds a triplet of right-handed neutrinos under a flavor symmetry, plus a single light sterile neutrino, all governed by a combined discrete symmetry group. Four scalar fields set the mixing pattern.

The model reproduces the measured oscillation parameters within their experimental ranges. It also predicts the effective mass that neutrinoless double beta decay experiments should see. A built-in antisymmetric interaction breaks the symmetry between muon and tau flavors. The total active neutrino mass stays under the cosmological bound for both mass orderings.
arxiv-2503-13324:
Karlheinz Gröchenig and Irina Shafkulovska extend uncertainty principles to a wider family of signal views, in work from 2025. An uncertainty principle limits how sharply a signal can be pinned in both time and frequency at once. New signal views need their own versions of that limit.

The authors give a transfer method that carries a known principle to the wider views. Starting points include principles for the short-time Fourier view and for Fourier pairs. Two classic forms, tied to Beurling and to Hardy, are carried over in full. The work is pure theory aimed at harmonic analysis specialists. It widens the toolbox for modern time-frequency methods.
arxiv-2503-13424:
Xinyu Lian and ten co-authors present Infinite Mobility, a method that creates detailed articulated objects, objects with moving joints, by procedural generation. Their paper came out in 2025. Robots that learn in simulation need many such objects, but existing sets are limited by hand labeling or costly simulation work.

Procedural generation builds each object from rules and parameters, so scale is not limited by manual effort. In user studies and measured tests, their objects matched or beat current state-of-the-art sets. Quality was comparable to human-annotated datasets, on both physical properties and mesh detail. The team also shows the synthetic objects work as training data for generative models. That opens a path to still larger datasets for embodied artificial intelligence.
arxiv-2503-13524:
Joseph Loffredo and Suyeol Yun show how AI agents can aid the study of political institutions, in this 2025 paper. The catalog title carries stray footnote text, but the head gives the clean title.
