Large language models are spreading through political science, yet plain chat use wastes much of their power for research chores.

The authors equip a model with set functions and tools, so it can fetch data, clean it, summarize documents, code transcripts, classify variables, and run statistical models. This style, called agentic retrieval-augmented generation, lets the model act on outside knowledge bases, not just chat. Their example agent, CongressRA, serves scholars of the United States Congress. They argue such agents cut the cost of repeating, testing, and extending studies built on the field's data.
arxiv-2503-13824:
Pulsar beam shapes for stars with interpulses are mapped by the authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Pulsars are dense stars that sweep radio beams as they spin. Some show a second pulse half a turn from the main one. A big China dish caught polarization profiles for twenty-three such stars. A vector model then gave beam tilt and pass angles for sixteen.

For five stars, both pulses seem to come from the same pole. For eleven, they come from facing poles. Beam fill ran from low to near full, and pulse heights above the star split by tens to thousands of kilometres. Some beams run very wide.
arxiv-2503-13924:
Hyuntai Kim and Seong-Yong Cho analyze interference and cavity resonance in top emission quantum dot displays in a 2025 paper. Such displays are studied for augmented and virtual reality use. A Fabry-Perot resonance effect in them is well explored, and multi beam interference in the emission layers has been treated in theory, but often with simplified simulations that drift from experiment.

A full investigation of multi beam interference was still lacking. The authors give a theoretical analysis backed by numerical simulation, examining the cavity resonance and comparing it with interference between upward and downward emission parts. Findings aim to guide design of more efficient display architectures.
arxiv-2503-14124:
Ragheed Alhyder, Mikhail Lemeshko, and Alberto Cappellaro study electron flow past twisted molecules in a 2025 paper. Chiral molecules lack mirror symmetry, and their twist can sort electron spin. The team models a flat electron system over a magnetized surface with such molecules. Dipole tilt angle turns out to steer the whole effect.

Tilted mirror forms give uneven sideways conductance, a clear chiral mark. That mark persists even without spin orbit coupling, which points to plain scattering as its source. With coupling active, twist enables spin flips in the flow. Charge and spin signals thus report molecular handedness. The model offers a lean frame for lab tests of chiral electronics.
arxiv-2503-14424:
Superconducting qubits vary from chip to chip, and the cause may sit in the materials, not the design. Akshay Murthy and a large team of co-authors ran a blind study across three labs. Qubit chips with known lifetimes were examined with many material probes, gentle and invasive. Three features stood out together: the depth of the etched trench in the base, the thickness of the surface oxide, and the sidewall shape. Combined, they tracked with how long each qubit held its state.

The study crossed different metals and base materials, so the pattern is not one recipe's quirk. Makers gain concrete knobs to turn for steadier qubits. The work comes from a national quantum research center's coordinated program.
arxiv-2503-14624:
Tristan and co-authors report radio views of flares on a nearby young red dwarf star, watched for seven days across the spectrum. Red dwarfs are the most common stars near the Sun and many flare violently. Their 2025 paper focuses on high-frequency radio light curves from two telescope arrays, which trace fast electrons spiraling in flare loops.

Nineteen flares appear in the radio data, from a thirty-second spike to a five-hour fade. Spectra rose and fell in ways that show both thick and thin emitting gas. Thick cases point to loop-top magnetic fields near a thousand gauss and steady electron counts. Energy in the electrons of thin cases can cover the light seen at all wavelengths. The values match modern flare simulations better than older estimates.
arxiv-2503-14724:
Sebastian Zhao and co-authors introduce a proactive coding assistant in a 2025 paper. Most AI coding tools wait for the user to ask. Their tool, CodingGenie, sits inside the code editor and offers help on its own, based on the code on screen.

Suggestions range from bug fixes to test writing. Users can steer the tool with a task note and pick which kinds of tips appear. The authors show several use cases and measure the cost of running the tool without being asked. The code is open for others to build on. Readers get an early look at editors that speak up at the right moment.
arxiv-2503-15124:
Korbinian Kuhn, Verena Kersken, and Gottfried Zimmermann test whether speech software can flag its own errors in a 2025 paper. Speech-to-text tools give each word a confidence score for how sure the tool is. In theory, low scores could point users to likely errors. The team checked that idea with model tests and a user study.

They tested end-to-end speech models and ran a study with 36 users. Scores did track accuracy to a degree, but error spotting was weak. Tools built on scores missed many errors or flagged many right words. Users did not fix text faster with the flags and did not find them helpful. The authors say better methods are needed to guide users.
arxiv-2503-15424:
Alain Govaert and co-authors study growth with scale-free saturations in a 2025 paper on how real growth processes level off. Growth regimes split into types driven by steady positive feedback, and a sublinear type driven by efficiency where growth slows as resources run short.

The team proposes a simple network growth process that mimics the sublinear regime. They characterize how its scale-free saturation zones shape the diversity and fairness of network structure. Scaling laws seen across complex systems emerge from the model. The work links resource limits to fairer, more varied network shapes. Systems scientists get a clean model of growth that stops itself.
arxiv-2503-15624:
Hot, dense plasmas can build their own magnetic fields, and those fields then change how heat flows through the plasma. The authors simulate a laser-driven plasma as it ablates, expands, and magnetizes, using a particle-in-cell code with a laser ray-tracing module. Their flat geometry suppresses one known field source, the Biermann effect, so they can isolate fields driven by uneven particle motion. Laser strength varies across the range used in high-energy-density and fusion experiments, where collisions matter.

Above a threshold strength, the plasma magnetizes itself within a few hundred picoseconds through an expansion-driven Weibel process. The resulting fields are strong enough to bend electron paths and alter heat transport. When the team reruns the simulation with the fields artificially switched off, the temperature profile changes clearly. The work offers an explanation for the megagauss filaments seen in several experiments.
arxiv-2503-15724:
Linji Wang and three co-authors present a 2025 method that tunes helper rewards for robot learning on the fly. The catalog author field garbles the names with stray marks, so the byline follows the head of the text. Robot training leans on hand-built bonus rewards, which take effort, bake in bias, and cannot shift as the robot improves.

Their teacher-student setup watches the student's growth and reweights each bonus to serve the main goal best. On tight-space navigation and rough-ground driving in simulation, it beat expert-built rewards and trained faster. On real robots it won all five trials against two for the expert set, and cut tilt angles nearly in half. The authors frame the method as training wheels that adjust themselves.
arxiv-2503-16024:
Ruihan Yang and seven co-authors present Critique-Guided Improvement, a two-model setup where one language model acts and another coaches it with written feedback. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Scores and verifiers can rank an agent's moves, but they say little about how to do better. Words, by contrast, carry rich, usable advice.

The critic is trained to give fine-grained judgments and concrete revisions. The actor is trained to actually use that coaching. Together they explore more widely and dodge local ruts. Across three interactive worlds, the pair beat rival methods by a wide margin. Even a small critic outcoached a far larger famous model. The resulting actor set new best marks. The work argues that explicit, repeated guidance is a strong engine for agent skill.
arxiv-2503-16124:
Xin Yue Yu and co-authors examine in 2025 what detecting tau neutrinos at the DUNE experiment adds to searches for non-standard neutrino interactions. Such interactions would alter how neutrinos change flavor while traveling. Tau neutrino appearance channels turn out to carry the strongest observable effect for one key interaction parameter in their analysis of the far detector.

They study how these channels affect mass ordering, charge-parity violation, and octant questions. They also project limits on interaction strengths and phases. Finally, they test how tau detection constrains whether the neutrino mixing matrix is truly unitary. The work argues tau channels deserve full weight.
arxiv-2503-16224:
Wei Wei and co-authors present a review, published in 2025, on the magnetic field strength that destroys superconductivity in high temperature superconductors. That upper critical field reveals how Cooper pairs break apart, how large they are, and how they bind, all central to the unsolved pairing puzzle in these materials. The review gathers studies across the three great families of the field.

Cuprates, iron based materials, and the newer nickelates are compared side by side. The field's behavior is traced against temperature, chemical doping, and direction, since these crystals conduct differently along different axes. By lining the families up, the authors hope shared patterns will point toward the common mechanism behind high temperature superconductivity.
arxiv-2503-16324: Bostan and three co-authors test natural inflation inside a modified gravity family, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They work in the Palatini formulation, with a gravity function that also takes the inflaton's kinetic term as an input. Such models flatten the inflation hill on their own, without forcing odd kinetic terms later. Feeding in a natural inflation potential and computing the microwave background signal, they find the model stays compatible with observation across a wide class of these gravity functions, including the quadratic case.
arxiv-2503-16524:
Patrick Callaghan, Reid Simmons, and Henny Admoni study how a robot learner can ease the load on its human teacher, in this 2025 paper. When a robot's feedback confuses the teacher, both sides build wrong beliefs about each other. The teacher may misjudge what the robot knows, and the robot may misread how the teacher sees it. Those crossed beliefs raise the effort teaching takes.

The team gives the learner a second-order theory of mind: a model of how the teacher views the learner and its goal. Perceived rationality serves as the source of the mistaken beliefs in their model. The learner then picks feedback that accounts for those beliefs. The goal is feedback that draws out efficient teaching and cuts the teacher's burden.
arxiv-2503-17224:
Giacomo Savazzi and co-authors test, in 2025, whether structured scene descriptions can improve made-up training images for visual models. Training data is costly and scarce in special fields, and synthetic data still lags real data as tasks grow harder. Scene graphs record objects and their relations in a formal way.

The team used those graphs to guide image generation for a model that itself predicts scene graphs. Adding the synthetic data raised standard recall scores by up to a few points. The gain suggests the graphs add structural information that real data alone did not supply in the same form. The approach offers a route around data scarcity.
arxiv-2503-17324:
Courtney Watson and co-authors check a far-off galaxy cluster candidate with the Hubble Space Telescope. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses a grism, a tool that spreads galaxy light into spectra. The candidate came from a survey of clusters marked by bent radio jets.

Seven galaxies sat in a tight range of redshifts near the same value, within a small radius. That match marks the group as a real cluster at great distance. Its spread of speeds gave a rough total mass. The find is strong above the background field of galaxies. Readers see how one sharp follow-up can confirm a cluster seen when the universe was young.
arxiv-2503-17624:
MohammadAmin Zaheri, Michalis Famelis, and Eugene Syriani study in 2025 how people bend software forms that refuse to accept the data they need to enter. Workarounds get the job done, but they flag design flaws, slow people down, and can quietly corrupt the data a system holds.

Through a descriptive user study, the authors watched where workarounds come from when real information clashes with rigid form fields. They trace how those tricks affect both system design and data quality. Designers who understand workaround habits can spot unmet needs early and build forms that fit real work instead of fighting it.
arxiv-2503-17724:
Four researchers in China present a stealthier attack on image making models in a 2025 paper. Such models build pictures from text prompts, and a hidden trigger can force a set output. Past attack samples left traces: their pictures stayed alike when prompts changed, and their inner focus maps looked too steady.

Their method, Trigger without Trace, uses sentence structure as the trigger to break the first trace. A math rule then aligns the focus maps of attack samples with clean ones. Tests show a high attack success rate, and most samples slipped past three top detectors. The authors frame the work as a warning about weak spots in current defenses.
arxiv-2503-17824:
Danisbel Herrera and co-authors map where faint early galaxies cluster to learn what kind of dark matter halos host them, in work from 2025. The ODIN survey photographed about 14,000 Lyman-alpha emitting galaxies in three slices of cosmic time.

After correcting for distortions and contamination, the team measured how strongly the galaxies bunch together at each epoch. Later samples cluster less, yet their inferred halo masses run slightly higher, around a hundred billion solar masses. Only about 3 to 7 percent of matching halos actually hold such a galaxy. The pattern traces how the link between young galaxies and their halos evolved as the universe aged.
arxiv-2503-18124:
Igor Ovchinnikov argues that the butterfly effect, the seed of chaos, is topological at heart. The paper from twenty twenty-five works inside the supersymmetric theory of stochastic dynamics. That frame rewrites general stochastic equations as a cohomological field theory. Chaos then reads as the spontaneous breaking of a topological supersymmetry. Ghost fields in the frame keep track of the long dynamical memory that defines the effect.

Ovchinnikov builds the effective theory of that breaking by a background field method. A supergauge field couples to the theory's currents and symmetries. The Goldstone theorem forces the result to be a conformal field theory. Its operator products explain the one-over-f noise seen as chaos's fingerprint. A holographic dual picture is also drawn. The claim reframes chaos as a symmetry story, not a mere sensitivity tale.
arxiv-2503-18324:
Basim Azam and Naveed Akhtar present a computing paper from 2025 on image generators that take text prompts. Such models can make unfair or unsafe images, so guardrails are a must. Past guardrails handle one concern at a time and hide how they work. Many also require changes to the model itself, which can hurt quality.

Their method adds a plug-in unit that learns a control space for many concerns at once. The space is built to stay readable, so users can see what each control does. It can plug in at two points: where text is encoded, or inside the image-building core. Tests showed strong control of fairness and safety themes without retraining the base model. The authors say the design scales to fresh concerns as they arise.
arxiv-2503-18424:
Zekiye and co-authors (2025) propose ED-DAO, a decentralized organization for donating energy to people who cannot get it when they need it. The system is designed to be fully transparent and community-driven. The team first sorts donation approaches by where the energy and the money come from, then builds a hybrid algorithm that draws on all of them.

The hybrid takes energy in a set order: first surplus energy from peers, then grid energy paid for by outside donors such as charities, then direct peer-to-peer donations. In experiments on their dataset, the hybrid delivered at least 0.43 percent more donated energy, some 64 megawatts, than any single-route algorithm. The authors present the design as a more effective way to fight energy poverty by pooling every source at once.
arxiv-2503-18824:
Radek Zavorka and co-authors carried out long radio measurements in 2025 to support communication for autonomous ground vehicles. Such vehicles need reliable links close to the ground, where signals behave differently than at head height. The team recorded indoor channels over long runs at two high frequency bands.

Each recording ran twenty minutes and captured the full impulse response of the channel. They tracked how key traits, such as the spread of signal delays and a factor describing the strength of the direct path, changed over time and between bands. The data set aims to ground realistic channel models for near-ground vehicle links.
arxiv-2503-19024:
Kohki Uno and co-authors report, in a 2025 astronomy paper, polarized light measurements of a nearby stellar disruption event, AT2023clx. A star wandered too close to a black hole in the galaxy NGC3799 and was torn apart, and the glow from the wreckage carries clues about its shape.

Three rounds of measurements found two signals mixed together. One steady part came from the lopsided outflow of the event itself. The other, bluer part came from light bouncing off dust near the galaxy's core. Between rounds, the signal's angle flipped by ninety degrees, showing the outflow ran across the dust plane rather than along it. The dust also seems made of fairly large grains.
arxiv-2503-19124:
Ibrahim Yildirim and Tho Le-Ngoc fight beam drift in terahertz wireless in a 2025 paper. Future systems will use huge antenna arrays at very high frequencies. Wide channels then suffer beam split: each sub-band's beam points a bit off target.

Their fix uses rough angle knowledge rather than exact models. Beams per sub-band are steered with the user's angular spread in mind. Spreading the beam on purpose covers the split, so no costly delay hardware is needed. Simulations showed clear gains in data rate and beam accuracy. Compute and hardware stayed light. The method suits next-generation links where arrays are large and beams are needle thin.
arxiv-2503-19224:
Barata, Salgado, and Silva gave a talk in twenty twenty-five on how early crash matter in atom smashes may twist the spray of parts in jets. Right after a heavy crash, the hot matter can pull more in one cross way than the other. That pull should show in the spread of parts in each jet.

They study a quark pair born from a gluon as it moves through such lopsided matter. The final spread of parts shows a wave-like swing with angle that tracks the lopsided pull. That swing also ties to the spin of the end parts. Spin reads could thus probe the matter in a new way.
arxiv-2503-19424:
Ruonan Cao and Nianyu Yi build a steadier solver for liquid crystal flow in a 2025 paper. The Ericksen-Leslie model describes how rod-like molecules align and move, as in display screens. Solvers must respect the physics' energy decay or they blow up. Their scheme reaches second-order accuracy while staying linear and fully split into easy steps, with no stability limit on step size.

A pressure correction handles the flow part, and a scalar helper variable keeps the energy bookkeeping honest. The authors prove the energy stability outright, not just for small steps. Numerical tests confirm the accuracy order, the stability, and the speed. Such schemes let engineers simulate texture changes in liquid crystal devices over long times without babysitting the math.
arxiv-2503-19524:
Subhashree Patra and Subarna Bhattacharjee show in 2025 how a special math function helps simulate certain probability distributions. Some distributions in the Weibull family lack quantile formulas that the standard inversion method can solve. Without such formulas, generating random samples is hard to do exactly.

By adding the Lambert W function, a transcendental tool, they solve those quantile equations in closed form. The same inversion approach then works where only approximations were known before. Their work extends exact simulation to non-Weibull cases as well. The Lambert function has a record of unlocking closed forms in many fields, they note.
arxiv-2503-19624:
Bart van Lith, writing alone, offers a 2025 math paper on a playful family of functions tied to a square circle. These squigonometric functions mimic sine and cosine for a square-shaped geometry. Their derivatives turn out to be polynomials in two basic members of the family, a tidy pattern worth pinning down.

Van Lith gives a framework that finds those polynomials step by step, plus a direct formula for every coefficient. The same work yields the power series coefficients for all functions in the family. Methods to compute the functions to any desired accuracy, across the whole real line, are also discussed. The paper rounds out the calculus of this curious family.
arxiv-2503-19824:
Jiazhi Guan and co-authors generate whole-body human videos from a single photo plus a voice track. Earlier tools moved mostly the face, leaving head and body stiff and out of step. Their framework, AudCast, aims for true lip-sync and natural talking gestures across the full figure, built from cascaded diffusion transformers.

A first stage, a holistic human model fed by the audio, drives the whole body's motion with lively gesture. Hands and faces, the hardest parts to render, then pass to a regional refinement stage. That stage borrows signals from three-dimensional fitting to rebuild fine detail. Tests show high-fidelity clips with steady timing and sharp hands and faces. The team posts its resources online for others to build on.
arxiv-2503-19924:
Athokpam Langlen Chanu and co-authors classify brain states, in a 2025 paper, by measuring how disordered brain-wave patterns become. They focus on the main flow of phase signals running front to back in the scalp recordings. A measure called permutation entropy scores that disorder.

Two datasets test the idea. One follows people through general anesthesia, where awareness fades and returns. The other compares resting recordings from healthy adults and people with inattentive-type attention disorder, eyes open and closed. Disorder patterns shifted clearly with brain state in their analysis. A cheap, math-only marker of awareness level could aid both anesthesia monitoring and attention research.
arxiv-2503-20024: Oleksandr Manzyuk wrote a 2025 paper showing that four standard monad transformers of functional programming are instances of one categorical construction. The state, reader, writer, and error transformers, usually each built by its own recipe, all arise from translating a monad along an adjunction. The paper's title states the method plainly: these programming tools can be calculated with category theory rather than invented case by case.
arxiv-2503-20124:
Zergham Ahmed and co-authors present a learning agent that builds its own world models in this 2025 paper. Game-playing systems can master complex games, but they need huge amounts of practice and adapt poorly to new games. A theory-based approach instead gives the agent a causal model of the world, like a small theory, to plan with.

Their system, called TheoryCoder, writes that low-level model as a computer program, made from what the agent observes with help from a large language model. Broad moves, such as going to a target, sit above that model. A two-level planner uses both layers to solve large grid-world games. Tests show this beats methods that write a direct policy.
arxiv-2503-20224:
Zhenhua Yuan, Junhao Peng, and Long Gao study how well merged networks move things from place to place, in a 2025 paper. Their networks form when several graphs are joined through a single shared node. Transport matters in many real systems, from data to travel. The authors ask how the joined shape affects search and spread.

They study random walks on the joined networks. Three measures track how long a walk takes to first reach a target. The authors derive exact formulas for all three. Each measure turns out to depend on the same traits of the parts that were joined. They also give a method to pick the joining node and tune links for faster transport.
arxiv-2503-20924:
Quentin Blomet, a solo author, asks a logic question in a 2025 paper about how two formulas can share a middle step. The classic result behind the work is Craig's theorem on interpolation. Blomet studies a split form of that result, where the middle formula must link to one side in one logic and to the other side in a second logic.

Both logics use three truth values and the same basic rules for joining statements. The paper finds which choices of truth tables and proof rules make the split property hold. Each case where it holds sharpens the classic theorem for these weaker logics.
arxiv-2503-21224:
Matthieu Meunier, Christoph Reisinger, and Yufei Zhang speed up learning in decision problems with a Monte Carlo ladder in a 2025 paper. Entropy-regularized Markov decision processes soften the hunt for the best policy by rewarding randomness, which suits exploration. Learning them in huge or continuous state spaces is costly. The team's algorithms climb a multilevel scheme: cheap coarse simulations are corrected by rarer fine ones, wrapped around fixed-point iteration on the value function.

They measure exactly how the choice of approximate Bellman update bends the error. A biased plain estimate yields quasi-polynomial sample needs, while an unbiased randomized multilevel version reaches polynomial needs, in expectation. Strikingly, neither bound grows with the size of the state or action spaces. Numerical tests back the theory.
arxiv-2503-21324:
Ivan Korneev and Vladimir Semenov study how noise shapes sync in excitable systems in 2025. They work with FitzHugh-Nagumo units, a classic model of nerve-like spikes. In the coherence resonance regime, noise alone can make the spikes fire in a near-regular rhythm.

Using computer simulation, the pair test three setups under Levy noise. First comes a single unit driven by a steady external rhythm. Next come two coupled units, then large groups with local or global links. Levy noise can create or destroy forced sync at a fixed drive strength. In some ranges a stronger drive even pushes the unit out of sync, a surprise result. For groups, noise shifts the coupling strength where sync begins. For just two units, its effect stays small.
arxiv-2503-21424:
Suyang Zhong and Manuel Rigger present a way to test many database systems with one tool in a 2025 paper. Automated testers have found hundreds of logic bugs in mature databases, but each tester needs generators tuned to that system's dialect of SQL. Building them takes weeks, so most database teams never adopt the approach.

Their platform, SQLancer++, pairs existing test oracles with a self-teaching statement generator. The generator tries SQL features freely, then learns from the database's replies which ones it accepts, so over time most of its statements are valid. Across eighteen database systems the tool found 196 distinct bugs that nobody had reported before. Nearly all were fixed after disclosure. The authors call it a first step toward testing that scales, with open problems left for follow-up work.
arxiv-2503-21724:
Ke Xu and co-authors report a 2025 astronomy finding: gas being torn from galaxies in a young cluster at redshift 2.51. Local clusters are full of old, quiet galaxies, and astronomers still debate whether they shut down star birth on their own or had it forced on them.

Data from the ALMA telescope show long gas tails stretching past the starlight in five galaxies, caught by the JWST view. The tails point one way, and the galaxies show no signs of mergers or close passes. That pattern fits ram-pressure stripping, where hot cluster gas sweeps a galaxy's own gas away. The find proves this outside force was already at work early in cosmic time.
arxiv-2503-22224:
Huixiang Zhen, Xiaotong Li, Wenyin Gong, and Xiangyun Hu wrote a 2025 paper on a frugal way to solve design problems with more than one objective. In such problems, each true evaluation of a design is expensive. A surrogate model, a guess model, stands in for the true evaluation. The difficulty is choosing which few designs deserve the true evaluations.

The plan of the team first breeds a crop of candidates with a known algorithm, scored by the surrogate models. A new combined score then ranks the crop on three marks at once: how close to optimal, how diverse, and how evenly distributed the set is. The top ranks win the true evaluations. Part-by-part tests showed that each element of the score earns its place. On three known benchmark sets and on real-world problems, the plan beat five leading plans of its kind.
arxiv-2503-22824:
Pranav Kumar, Fritz Körmann, Blazej Grabowski, and Yuji Ikeda compute how a titanium-chromium alloy soaks up hydrogen, in a 2025 paper. The alloy forms Laves phases, tidy crystal patterns that can store hydrogen in their gaps, a trait of interest for storage tanks. Two crystal forms, cubic and hexagonal, were studied across the full range of hydrogen loading. Exact quantum calculations are slow, so the team trained machine learning potentials on them and let the fast models search.

The searches found the lowest-energy hydrogen arrangements and the order the atoms settle into. Phase changes at zero temperature matched low-temperature experiments. Along the way, the team predicted two crystal symmetries for loaded phases that no one had reported, plus limits on how much hydrogen the dilute phases can hold. Hydrogen atoms shun each other's shared gaps, which steers the ordering.
arxiv-2503-22924:
Youjin Sung and Yang Liu derive standard errors for reliability coefficients under item response theory, in a 2025 paper. Reliability tells how much trust to place in a test score. Recent reviews split reliability measures into two families. Both families need honest measures of their own sampling error. Existing formulas cover only part of that error.

Test scores wobble from two sources at once. Item parameters are estimated with error, and population moments get replaced by sample ones. The authors give a general strategy that counts both sources together. Worked cases show how to apply the formulas. Test developers can then report reliability with proper uncertainty. That matters for high-stakes exams and clinical scales alike.
arxiv-2503-23224:
Yiqian Wu and seven co-authors present SmartFL, a tool that hunts for faults in software. Their 2025 paper works on test-based fault localization: given passing and failing runs, find the faulty lines. Full meaning analysis is precise but slow; simple spectrum methods are fast but crude. SmartFL aims for the middle.

The tool models only whether program values are right, not their full meaning, using probability. On a real-world bug set, its top guess hit the faulty line in fourteen percent of cases. That rate more than doubled the best older methods. Its average run time was about half that of spectrum methods. Mixed with other tools, it lifted their scores further.
arxiv-2503-23424:
As AI systems grow stronger, judging their danger takes tests, and judging the tests takes care. Gil Gekker, Meirav Segal, Dan Lahav, and Omer Nevo write from practice about what makes a safety evaluation worth trusting. They start with threat modeling: naming what harm you fear, then shaping the test to match that fear, drawing examples from cybersecurity.

They list the traits and settings that make a test useful, such as clear targets and honest difficulty. Then they turn to the wider problem of building a full suite of tests that covers a system rather than a single skill. The piece is a field guide for teams who must decide, from test results, whether a model is safe to release.
arxiv-2503-23524:
Economists who estimate demand build structural models that predict what would happen in markets that never existed, such as after a merger or a new tax. Jiafeng Chen asks what quietly licenses those predictions. He rewrites the models' assumptions as statements about the joint spread of potential outcomes. He finds a strong one hiding inside: the link between outcomes under different conditions is taken to be the same in every market.

That sameness cannot be weakened without losing the market-level predictions the models are built for. Without it, Chen shows, the predictions can still be read as careful extrapolations from average effects that causal methods do identify. The paper builds a conceptual bridge between structural modeling and causal inference.
arxiv-2503-23724:
A team including Sajid Husain and Maya Ramesh shows greatly boosted spin transmission through an all-antiferromagnetic stack, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Magnons, the quanta of spin waves, are studied for spintronic logic and memory devices. Controlling magnons in standard antiferromagnets has stayed hard. Their layered system can be controlled by electric means instead.

The stack places bismuth ferrite between lanthanum ferrite layers, all antiferromagnetic. Using spin-orbit-driven spin-charge transduction, the team traps magnons in the very thin layers. This trapping raises the output voltage from magnon transport by several orders of size. The device is also non-volatile, which enables ultralow-power logic-in-memory work. Magnonic devices could be reset through spin currents under electric control. The authors present this as a pathway to magnetoelectric memory and logic.
arxiv-2503-23824:
Search engines that learn sparse word weights struggle with long documents, and add-ons claim to fix that. Emmanouil Lionis and Jia-Huei Ju re-ran those claims in this 2025 study. The base method scores documents by learned term weights. Long texts are chopped into segments, and add-ons merge segment scores with tricks like nearby-word matching.

Their reruns confirmed that one factor dominates: the first segment. Early text carries most of the retrieval signal. Two recent merging methods were retested on documents from two segments to many. New comparison methods of the authors' own design joined the field. Reproducibility checks like this keep search research honest about what actually helps.
arxiv-2504-00024:
Changshuai Wei, Ming Li, Yalu Wen, Chengyin Ye, and Qing Lu built a new chart in 2025 for gene-based risk forecasts. As gene reads grow cheap, models can weigh huge sets of variants at once to call who faces a disease. A known chart shows how well one mark sorts risk across a crowd. Most diseases rest on many marks, though, so a one-mark chart falls short.

Their curve takes in many marks at once and can be drawn for case-control data with no strict shape assumed. Two scores sum it up: one for the whole crowd and one for the slice doctors care most about. Tests showed the main score beat three rival scores on bias and steadiness. On rare-variant disease models, the slice score did best. A nicotine study shows the tool at work.
arxiv-2504-00124: Gustavo Arciniega and co-authors present a modified theory of gravity they call Geometric Cosmology. The change begins with redefining the coupling constant that multiplies the curvature term in Einstein's action, together with adding a family of generalized quasi-topological gravity terms. Their 2025 paper sets out the framework and offers four example models whose key functions converge exponentially, spread across three different gravities inside the new class.
arxiv-2504-00324:
Man Ho Chan wrote a 2025 physics paper arguing that Earth's atmosphere can absorb a form of dark matter in a resonant way. Dark matter is usually assumed to touch ordinary matter only faintly. Chan focuses on dark photon dark matter, a candidate that mixes slightly with normal light, and shows the air itself could soak it up at set energies.

That soaking would deposit a little extra heat in the upper stratosphere, which Chan links to reported temperature oddities there. The link pins down a narrow mass range and mixing strength for the particle for the first time. The paper also draws out wider effects, from heating planets to giant dark stars.
arxiv-2504-00424:
Long chains of thought help chat models solve hard problems, but most of the words in those chains are filler that costs time and money. Jianshu She and co-authors build a team approach in a 2025 paper: a large model writes a short, dense plan, and a small model expands it into the full reply. The plan keeps the steps that matter and drops the rest.

Training teaches the large model to squeeze its reasoning by scoring how much each part earns its place. With plans at about a third of the full length, reply quality held level while clarity rose. On hard math the team ran several times faster end to end and cut costs by more than half. The split plays to each model's strength: judgment up front, fluency after.
arxiv-2504-00824:
Yubo Wang and co-authors build a tool to help write research papers with sound sources in 2025. Good papers need clear text and exact links to past work. Many writing tools add sources at the end, which can lead to wrong or weak links. Their tool, called ScholarCopilot, decides while it writes when it needs a source.

At that point the tool searches a store of past papers and feeds the best matches back in. It was trained on a large set of papers from an open archive. Tests show it finds the right source far more often than older search tools. Human judges also rated its drafts and its source choices above a well known chat tool.
arxiv-2504-01224:
Alexsandre Ferreira, Nelson Pinto-Neto, and Vanessa Xavier study in 2025 whether eternal inflation can be completed by a bounce. A known theorem says a spacetime with average positive expansion cannot extend forever into the past. Past eternal inflation would thus seem to need a singular start.

Using frames of non-comoving observers in flat de Sitter space, the authors test all options the theorem allows. Either a curvature singularity must occur, or the past must approach a de Sitter state. In the second case, an extension exists that respects energy rules. That extension, they show, must contain a bounce.
arxiv-2504-01524:
Mark Knudsen and four co-authors warn, in a 2025 paper, about a quiet flaw in a popular survival model. Cox models that track only a patient's current treatment are often read as if they showed what would happen under a set treatment plan. That reading needs a Markov property: the risk ahead must not depend on treatment history once the current level is known.

The team show, in continuous time, exactly when that property can hold for both the group a doctor sees and the true group, hidden frailty included. It demands no interplay between treatment and frailty on one scale, an assumption that can never be checked, since frailty is unmeasured by definition. They build a case where the model fits perfectly yet the plan reading still fails.
arxiv-2504-01824:
Yuchen Meng and co-authors find a pairing pattern in the Fisher zeros of topological materials. Fisher zeros are points, in an extension of temperature or time, where a system's partition function vanishes; their pattern reveals phase behavior. The team studied two topological models and a magnet model that maps onto one of them. They show that boundary zero modes, the protected states at the edge, correspond to pairs of these zeros in real time.

The pairing survived when the models were made non-Hermitian, a form of controlled imperfection, and produced braiding pictures and crystal-like patterns in imaginary time. Interactions, by contrast, dissolved the topology in a fractal pattern of zeros. The authors present zero-pairing as a statistical-mechanics lens on topology, a field read through other tools. It connects edge physics to the partition function's structure, a new diagnostic for model builders.
arxiv-2504-01924:
Andreas Panayiotou, Panayiotis Charalambous, and Ioannis Karamouzas present Gen-C, a system that fills virtual worlds with crowds that act out rich plans, in a research paper from 2025. Older crowd simulators handle low-level tasks well, like avoiding bumps and following paths. They struggle with the higher-level behavior that grows from long contact among people and places.

Gen-C stands for Generative Crowds and builds crowd scenes as time-expanded graphs of actions, contacts, and places. To train it, the team used large language models to draft synthetic crowd data, avoiding costly video labeling. Two linked learning parts then learn the graph links and the node traits from text and structure. Tests on a campus and a train station gave mixed crowds with coherent, context-fitting plans.
arxiv-2504-02024:
Pedro Bittar, Subhojit Roy, and Carlos Wagner compare ways to compute heat effects in a model with two Higgs fields. Good heat sums matter for claims about sharp phase shifts in the early universe. Poor sums can give the wrong story.

They test a careful self matched method against two older ones on the same model. The choice of method changed whether the shift looked sharp and whether heat kept the old symmetry at high heat. It also changed the hum of waves such a shift would leave. Future space probes and colliders may test the favored zone.
arxiv-2504-02524:
Yunhao Lv and four co-authors pretrain a model to outline organs in CT scans in a 2025 paper. Masked image modeling teaches networks by hiding patches and forcing rebuilds. Prior attempts masked patches at random, which wastes effort on easy regions.

Their framework first predicts which patches will be hardest to rebuild. Those hard patches become the next masks, so training focuses where the model struggles. A helper loss predictor guides the choice inside the self-training loop. Tests cover belly scans and whole-body scans from public sets. The method beat rival approaches on both multi-organ tasks. Smart masking may help medical models learn more from unlabeled scans, where expert outlines are scarce.
arxiv-2504-02824:
Zhong, Roy, and Jing wrote in twenty twenty-five about observing defect-bound states in a non-Hermitian acoustic lattice. Non-Hermitian systems gain or lose energy, unlike closed textbook systems. Crystal defects like dislocations can trap special states in such lattices. The team built a two-dimensional acoustic lattice with active elements. Those elements set hopping and gain or loss with fine control. They inserted a matched pair of edge dislocations into the lattice.

Robust states appeared pinned at the dislocation cores. Spectral tests confirmed bulk exceptional points where states merge. The defect states survived moderate disturbance but spread out under stronger changes. Under some conditions the core also showed weak skin effects, where states pile toward an edge. The work opens acoustic routes to study defect-based topology.
arxiv-2504-02924:
Medina and a large team of colleagues share a first-year list of pulsing stars from a big sky survey in this twenty twenty-five paper. These stars swell and shrink in a set beat and serve as mile posts for mapping our galaxy. The list holds more than six thousand of them, some far from the galaxy core.

Inside, the team models how each star's light traits swing with its beat from a single snap. That lets them infer true speeds and mean heat for each star with no repeat visits. Far stars sort into two broad kin groups with unlike metal shares and unlike paths. One group fits a past merger that helped shape the galaxy halo.
arxiv-2504-03024:
Jannis Blueml and co-authors tackle a weakness of game playing agents in a 2025 paper. Agents trained on raw screen pixels often latch onto background clutter and fail when the scene shifts even a bit.

Their agent masks the screen so only task linked objects stay in view, guided by a bias toward simple accounts of the scene. On classic arcade tests, the masked agent shrugs off fresh twists far better than pixel agents. It also learns from fewer tries while matching or beating their scores. The team offer the result as proof that built in structure, not word like symbols, can carry broad skill.
arxiv-2504-03424:
Adam Moss presents an agentic AI system that runs cosmology data analysis on its own, in a 2025 paper. The system covers the full research loop. Specialized agents plan, write code, run experiments, analyze results, and draft reports. Unlike standard auto-tuning tools, it invents varied strategies rather than searching a fixed menu. It also repairs its own execution errors.

Tests spanned several machine learning tasks in the field. The system explored solution spaces and iterated on outcomes. Winning elements from different attempts were combined into new approaches. Example papers produced by the system appear in the appendix. Code and experiment data are public. Moss argues such agents can automate parts of research. That could speed discovery, though human judgment still frames the questions. The work is a first installment in a planned series.
arxiv-2504-03724:
Zhiqiang Wang and six co-authors teach in 2025 a vision-language model to count crowds more honestly, by rewarding almost-right answers. Counting people in dense photos is a classic hard vision task, and the reinforcement method they borrow usually pays only for exactly right counts, a reward too sparse to learn from.

Their fuzzy reward gives partial credit that fades smoothly with the size of the error, guiding the model like a patient teacher. Plain group-relative training with all-or-nothing rewards actually did worse than ordinary fine-tuning. With fuzzy rewards, their models beat every baseline they tested, at two sizes.
arxiv-2504-03824:
Anacleto, Silva and Casarini build thin-shell gravastar models inside a BTZ spacetime that carries a minimum length. A gravastar is a black hole stand-in: a dark-energy core, a thin shell of matter, and an outside that looks like a black hole. Here both core and outside use anti-de Sitter forms shaped by the smallest allowed length, entered two ways, through a hydrogen-like probability spread and through a Lorentzian spread.

The team checks the shell's energy, pressure and entropy, and finds stable setups in both models. Stability survives even when the cosmological constant is set to zero. They also work out the heat behaviour of the matching black hole and test its stability.
arxiv-2504-04024:
Yifan Li and co-authors slim down the image data fed into vision-language models, so the models run faster. Such models turn pictures into long strings of tokens, and the length slows every answer. Their method, WiCo, glues neighboring image tokens inside a small sliding window into single tokens.

Plain gluing can blur fine detail, so the team fine-tunes the last layers of the image reader to make tokens within a window more alike before merging. A plus version later splits tokens back apart inside the language model for detail-hungry tasks. Tests on two well-known model families beat rival token-cutting methods on both coarse and fine tasks. The code is public, and the approach keeps a wide field of view at low cost.
arxiv-2504-04224:
Factory software built from snap-together parts must still run safe when the parts come from many hands. Gustavo Quiros and five co-authors set out in 2025 what two joint projects with a big plant tech firm learned. Their test bed was the firm's open edge platform, where app blocks from many makers meet. A coordination language from their lab supplied the rules that keep blocks in step.

Four tasks frame the report: build plants that are modular and safe by design, not by patch. An event-driven standard orders how the blocks fire. Big plants spread across many sites must stay in sync, with timing tuned to the best plan. The report gathers the concepts and know-how the team built across four years of joint work.
arxiv-2504-04324:
Some machines are flat: from a few chosen outputs, every part of their motion can be planned and steered, which makes control design far easier. Fengjun Yang, Jake Welde, and Nikolai Matni ask what happens when engineers bolt a learned correction onto such a machine's model. A careless correction can quietly destroy the flatness that made control easy.

They show that corrections with a staircase structure, each layer depending only on earlier ones, keep flatness intact for the pure-feedback machines they study. They also give a recipe to rebuild the key change of variables for the corrected model from the original one. On a simulated quadrotor with unmodeled air effects, the learned flat model tracked paths five times better than the nominal one.
arxiv-2504-04524:
Xuerui Su and co-authors propose a reinforcement learning method to improve reasoning in large language models. Their 2025 paper compares two training styles. Reward-based methods score well on reasoning but can be gamed by a model that hacks the reward. Preference-based methods avoid that trap, yet they have lagged on hard reasoning tasks.

Their algorithm, called TRPA, joins rule-based checks with preference learning inside a trust region, which keeps updates stable. Since it learns from preferences rather than raw rewards, the hacking problem fades by design. The authors present the method as simple and stable. They aim to close the reasoning gap between the two training styles without giving up alignment gains.
arxiv-2504-04624:
Miles Blencowe, Michael Casey, and Kimberly Tan report on turning quantum physics data into sound and music in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Sonification lets the ear catch signals that visual plots can hide.

One strand converts measurements from mesoscopic mechanical oscillators cooled near their quantum ground states into soundscapes. The other generates music with a programmed quantum computer that rotates a single qubit in patterns designed to test macroscopic realism. Listeners trained beforehand can hear when the qubit data violates the Leggett-Garg inequality, the statistical test involved. The authors frame the work as an open window into the quantum realm for non-experts.
arxiv-2504-04824:
Some diffusion problems degenerate at a boundary, meaning the spreading slows to a crawl exactly where the domain ends. Hyungsung Yun studies a model equation of this kind on a flat boundary. Equations like it arise when analyzing the porous medium equation, which governs flow through sponges, soil, and gas in rock. He asks how smooth solutions can be right up to that edge when nothing is allowed to cross it.

Yun proves the best possible smoothness in each direction and shows it cannot be improved. For the clean case with no source term, solutions gain one more degree of smoothness across space, and a rescaled version of the solution varies smoothly along the boundary and in time. The result sets the benchmark for this class of equations.
arxiv-2504-05024:
Antonia Holzapfel and co-authors present in 2025 ECLAD-ts, a method that explains how neural networks sort time series by pulling out concepts. Such networks now sort series for quality checks and medical tasks. Their inner steps stay hidden, and they can learn shortcuts that break trust.

Concept methods name groups of inputs the model treats alike at each layer. The new method clusters step-wise maps of network activity and scores each concept by its effect on the output. Tests on fake and real data show the concepts track what the model truly uses. Limits of the approach are also weighed in the results.
arxiv-2504-05124:
Silvano Pitassi wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on computing the loops that generate a cohomology group of a triangulated surface. Cohomology is a tool of algebraic topology that counts holes and handles in a shape. For a surface with boundary, the relative version tracks loops relative to a chosen part of that boundary.

Pitassi proposes a graph-based algorithm that constructs representative loops for a basis of the group. Unlike the earlier construction of Hiptmair and Ostrowski, it also works for non-orientable surfaces such as a Möbius-type geometry. Its worst-case running time is linear in the number of mesh edges, so it scales to large meshes. Such generators are critical building blocks in computational electromagnetics and other simulation software that solves equations on surfaces.
arxiv-2504-05824:
The authors present a neural system that links each pronoun and name in a chat to the folk it points to. Such links are a first need for machines that read talk. At big scale, the work must be both fast and right. Their system reads a chat end to end in one pass, with watch tools that weigh the full text at each call.

Speed tricks trim the cost of each read with no loss the team could find. On set test chats, the system beat past ways on grade while keeping its runs quick. Hard tests back its use in live, large gear. The work sets a mark for the next builds in this line, they say. The catalog name field runs the team's names into one string; the head byline, used here, lists them apart.
arxiv-2504-06024:
Cheraghi and Davoodi Yeganeh introduce AriaQuanta, an open-source program for quantum computing. Their 2025 paper aims to make circuit design and simulation open to users at all skill levels. The first version ships with a compiler that can build a range of quantum circuits and algorithms.

The program also supports circuits with adjustable values, which suit variational methods used on near-term hardware. Noise models let users test how errors would affect a run before real hardware is used. The authors ran many simulations, covering both plain algorithms and noisy circuits. They report that the results compare well with widely used rival tools in speed and quality.
arxiv-2504-06124:
Benjamin Christie and Dylan Losey plan robot behavior that stays safe however unpredictable the human partner acts in a 2025 paper. Rather than forecast people, they frame the encounter as a zero-sum game where the human plays against the robot. The equilibrium of that game is a policy robust to the worst plausible moves.

Exact game solvers are too heavy, and linear shortcuts too crude. Their method starts from the linear game, then refines with Monte Carlo search toward the true equilibrium. A dial tunes how paranoid the robot should be. Simulations and a user study back the approach for real-time use.
arxiv-2504-06224:
Alex Kehagias and Antonio Riotto derive the fading tail of waves from a ringing black hole in this 2025 paper. A disturbed black hole settles by shedding gravitational waves. At any fixed place, that signal fades as a power of time.

The classic Price law covers the first-order fading of each wave pattern. This work pushes the calculation to second order, where waves feed on themselves. The new tail fades more slowly than the linear one for each pattern. Its form is fixed by how the second-order source falls off with distance. Longer-lived tails could show up in precise waveform models. Detector teams use those models to read real merger signals.
arxiv-2504-06324:
Monika Jotautaitė, Mary Phuong, Chatrik Singh Mangat, and Maria Angelica Martinez probe the moral leanings of large language models with a fresh dilemma set, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The set rests on moral foundations theory, which sorts human morals into six core bases. Models answered a range of real-world style dilemmas to reveal their leanings.

Top models leaned in much the same way as each other. Yet their answers lacked steadiness across like cases. Shared lean plus shaky hold is the core worry the authors raise. As such models enter daily tools, that mix shapes user trust. Readers get a new gauge for machine morals and a warning about its wobble.
arxiv-2504-06424:
Bryna Kra and three co-authors prove a new theorem in this 2025 arXiv paper at the meeting point of number theory and dynamics. Hindman's classic result says that any large set of whole numbers, split any way, contains a rich pattern of sums. This paper asks for a density version: take any set that fills a positive share of the numbers in a strong sense.

Inside a shifted copy of that set, they find all sums of up to any fixed count of distinct elements drawn from one infinite pool. In other words, finite sum patterns of every bounded size hide inside dense sets, once a single shift is allowed. The proof weaves together sumset theory, the dynamics behind arithmetic progressions, and the geometry of nilpotent Lie groups. The result strengthens a central theme of Ramsey-style mathematics: density alone forces deep structure.
arxiv-2504-06524:
Satoshi Ikegaya, Shingo Kobayashi, and Yasuhiro Asano study an odd topological phase in a thin superconducting film, in a 2025 paper. The film sits on a high-temperature cuprate superconductor whose pairing has a cross-shaped pattern. Flat bands of trapped states form at the edges of such a material.

As the film narrows, those edge states mix across the film and open an energy gap, helped by spin texture in the film. The gapped state carries a winding number — a topological count — that grows with film width, reaching unusually large values. Crowds of zero-energy states appear, and they carry charge perfectly through dirty junctions in the team's tests. Wide-tunable topology could serve future quantum devices.
arxiv-2504-06624:
Janne Nurminen and Suman Kumar Sahoo solve a recovery problem in pure mathematics in a 2025 paper. The problem runs backward: from measurements at the edge of a region, can one work out an unknown rule acting inside it? Their rule sits inside a nonlinear fourth-order operator, a class tied to bending and vibration models.

Building on earlier work in this line, they prove the unknown term can indeed be recovered from local edge data. The proof first simplifies the problem to a linear one, then leans on an approximation trick and on known uniqueness results for the simpler case. Inverse problems like this matter wherever inner properties must be inferred from surface data alone.
arxiv-2504-06724:
Stockmans and co-authors describe a design toolbox for tiny Earth-watching instruments, in a 2025 paper. New detector chips carry color and polarization filters on each pixel, shrinking a satellite spectrometer to camera size. Flying fewer filter passes saves time but leaves holes in the data cube.

Software must fill those holes, and the filter layout decides how well it can. The toolbox trains a neural filler and the filter values together, so layout and reconstruction improve as a pair. Training used airborne measurements over Earth from a sister instrument. The paper reports an optimized layout from that training. End-to-end design, where optics and algorithms are tuned jointly, is the authors' broader pitch for cheap space instruments.
arxiv-2504-07224:
Samarth Chawla, Kwinten Fransen, and Cynthia Keeler extend the double copy idea into coordinates built around light rays, in a paper from 2025. The double copy links gravity solutions to simpler gauge theory ones. Working near a light path gives a local view that suits curved spacetime.

Expanding around a null geodesic, the leading term recovers a known limit-based copy. For spacetimes with an exact copy, the structure extends to all orders. For generic spacetimes, obstructions appear at second subleading order, so a local copy holds at least to first subleading order near any light ray. A gauge mismatch blocks one further extension, they note.
arxiv-2504-07324:
Godrick Oketch, Rachel Fewster, and Jesse Goodman study the cost of an approximation in statistics in two thousand twenty-five. The saddlepoint approximation can stand in for a likelihood when the true one is too hard to compute. But the estimate from the approximation will differ somewhat from the true maximum likelihood estimate.

Past work sized that gap by simulation, or by tackling the hard likelihood anyway. The authors instead give an explicit formula that can be computed directly. Readers can use it to judge whether the saddlepoint estimate is close enough. They test the formula in cases where the true likelihood is known. They also give asymptotic results that show how the gap behaves in a suitable limit.
arxiv-2504-07624:
Joel Barmettler, Abraham Bernstein, and Luca Rossetto present ConceptFormer in two thousand twenty-five. Language models need world knowledge from knowledge graphs. Textifying graphs wastes tokens and strains context windows. Editing model internals is the other costly route.

ConceptFormer works in the model's own embedding space instead. Knowledge graph nodes become concept vectors injected at input. A lookup table maps each node to its vector. The language model itself stays frozen during training. Factual recall on GPT-2 jumped sharply in their tests. One vector alone beat graph text retrieval at a fraction of tokens.
arxiv-2504-07724:
Penglei Sun, Yixiang Chen, Xiang Li, and Xiaowen Chu present a diagnostic framework in two thousand twenty-five for medical language models. Retrieval-augmented systems deploy fast and protect privacy, but patients describe symptoms in everyday words while knowledge bases use formal terms. That gap hurts diagnosis.

They built a knowledge graph, DiagnosGraph, covering eight hundred seventy-six common diseases in modern and traditional Chinese medicine. It also recasts real case complaints into formal records to bridge the wording gap. Their framework then refines diagnoses over several dialogue rounds, mimicking a doctor's reasoning. Tests on four benchmarks, judged also by human physicians, showed better diagnostic performance. The authors aim for automated diagnosis that is both accurate and human-aligned.
arxiv-2504-08024:
Fabian Retkowski and co-authors survey the field of speech summarization. Their 2025 survey notes that spoken and video content keeps piling up, and summaries are the practical way through it. Yet the task itself stays loosely defined, sprawled across speech recognition, text summarization, and uses like meeting notes.

The survey maps data sets and scoring habits, which decide how progress gets judged. It then traces the field's shift from stitched pipelines toward tuned end-to-end systems that hear and summarize in one pass. Open problems close the account: fair test sets that reflect real recordings, more languages, and summaries of very long material. The authors aim to give newcomers and veterans one shared map of a scattered field.
arxiv-2504-08124:
Nikita Sharma and co-authors published this study in 2025. It examines two high entropy alloys that superconduct. Each mixes five metals in equal shares, built on tantalum, niobium, vanadium, and titanium. The fifth metal is zirconium in one alloy and hafnium in the other. Both form the same cubic crystal structure. Tests of magnetism, resistance, and heat capacity show true bulk superconductivity.

The zirconium alloy starts superconducting near 6.2 kelvin, the hafnium one near 5 kelvin. Computer modeling backs the picture of a moderate, even pairing state. It also confirms the alloys are stable and metallic. One striking result: the hafnium alloy's upper critical field passes the usual Pauli limit. The team ties that to stronger spin-orbit coupling. Hardness and field strength make both alloys candidates for future devices.
arxiv-2504-08224:
Ishwar S. Kaushik, Peter J. Ehlers, and Daniel Soh designed a computer made of light in 2025, built on a scheme called an echo state network. Reservoir computers like these let a fixed, tangled system do the hard processing while only a simple output layer is trained. Software versions are capable but spend energy on arithmetic that optics might do almost for free.

Their design performs the needed matrix multiplication with optical components and gets its nonlinear response from stimulated Brillouin scattering, a light-sound interaction in optical media. Because the nonlinearity happens inside the physics, no measurement step interrupts the computation. Simulations checked the system's memory capacity, its nonlinear processing strength, and its ability at polynomial algebra. Performance matched software echo state networks on the benchmark tasks, suggesting a feasible, scalable route to optical machine intelligence hardware.
arxiv-2504-08324:
Achim Ahrens and five co-authors offer a plain introduction to double, or debiased, machine learning, in this 2025 paper. The method tackles a common research problem: estimating the effect you care about while nuisance parts of the model, needed for identification but not of interest, are estimated by flexible machine learning. Two kinds of bias creep in when those nuisance estimates are plugged in naively.

Double machine learning removes those biases by design, through a scoring trick and by splitting the data so predictions and evaluation never share the same rows. That frees researchers to use powerful learners, even on text or images, without the usual penalty in accuracy of the final estimate. The introduction works through simulations and real examples, and closes with practical advice. A companion website gathers code and further material, making the paper a doorway into a widely used causal toolkit.
arxiv-2504-08424:
Iuliia Grotova and fifteen co-authors catalog the stars torn apart by black holes in X-ray surveys, in this 2025 paper. When a star wanders too close, its shredding flares bright. The team mined the first two sky sweeps of a German-Russian X-ray telescope for flashing sources that were not known active galaxies, then tied each to an optical host.

Thirty-one candidates passed the tests for clean, single-flare events with soft spectra, nearly all true tidal disruptions and one set off-center. Their brightnesses span a wide range, and the count by brightness breaks at the natural cap for orderly feeding. The implied rate is about one event per hundred thousand galaxies per year. Host galaxies lean green and quiet, the team notes.
arxiv-2504-08624:
Matteo Spanio and Antonio Roda present TorchFX, a software library for audio work, in a twenty twenty-five paper. Audio signal processing today faces heavy real-time demands, and classic libraries do not use graphics chips well. They also blend poorly with AI models.

TorchFX is built on PyTorch, so it runs on GPUs and sits well beside AI code. It offers filters of both main kinds, FIR and IIR, with a focus on multi-channel audio. A pipe operator lets users chain filters in a clean way. Benchmarks show clear speed gains over SciPy, above all with many channels. The library is free on GitHub for others to use and extend.
arxiv-2504-09024:
William Schupbach and Kannan Premnath build a simulation method for substances that ride on the boundary between two fluids in a 2025 paper. A key case is soap-like surfactant, which gathers on drop surfaces and changes how drops deform and break. Modeling that transport is hard because the substance lives only on a moving, thin interface.

Their method uses a lattice Boltzmann scheme, a grid-based flow solver, built on a transformed equation that avoids singular terms. A companion scheme tracks the interface itself. Benchmark tests checked the solver, and the full system was then applied to surfactant-covered drops in shear flow. The simulations captured drop stretching and breakup at several settings. The tool should help study sprays, coatings, and other multi-fluid processes.
arxiv-2504-09124:
Fabrice Baudoin, Nizar Demni, Teije Kuijper, and Jing Wang study random motion on a curved space of flags, in a math paper from 2025. A flag here is a nested set of planes, and random motion on it is hard to track in a direct way. The team seeks exact laws for areas swept out along the way.

They show the motion can be built from a simpler random walk on matrices. That link yields a clear formula for the joint law of the swept areas. In the long run, those areas follow a known heavy-tailed law with separate parts. The work also gives new results on winding around spheres.
arxiv-2504-09224:
Tatarinova and co-authors lower the power needed to start a special light oscillation in a tiny ring, in a 2025 paper. In a microring fed by two pump colors, a degenerate parametric process can lock into one of two phases, a bit made of light, and shed nonclassical light as well. The team modeled the full mode family to find the cheapest start.

Careful choice of settings cut the threshold power, and reshaping the ring's dispersion, as in coupled rings or patterned crystals, can cut it further by nudging chosen modes. Lower thresholds bring photonic computing bits and quantum light sources closer to practical chips.
arxiv-2504-09324:
Lukin and co-authors build in 2025 a light matter system where disorder itself creates new behavior. Inside a polished silicon carbide ring, light circles for long stretches and meets an ensemble of atomic defects. The defects vary in tone and place, a mess that here becomes a feature.

That disorder breeds a handedness in how light and atoms interact. The host crystal's own nonlinearity then links four photons at once, leaving readable traces in atom photon correlations. The setup shows solid state defects can host Hamiltonians once confined to cleaner platforms. It opens a bench for few body quantum optics.
arxiv-2504-09724:
Gaurav Shinde and five co-authors survey methods to make vision language models cheaper to run, in a 2025 paper. These models join image and text input for tasks such as caption writing and visual question answering. Their high computing cost blocks real time use on phones and other small devices.

The survey reviews tricks to trim model size and speed up inference on limited hardware. It also covers compact model designs and software frameworks, and weighs the trade off between performance and memory use. The authors maintain a public list of the surveyed papers and plan to keep it updated. Their aim is to spur more work on models that run well outside large data centers.
arxiv-2504-10124:
Biswajit Das, Sreekanth Manikandan, and Ayan Banerjee traced how information moves inside a driven microscopic system in 2025. Their laboratory model is minimal: two colloidal particles in water, coupled through the fluid itself, with a fluctuating drive, an exponentially correlated noise, applied to only one particle. The question is whether data alone can reveal which particle is driven and how influence flows between them, a generic problem for interacting systems far from equilibrium.

Applying mutual information and its directional relatives, the authors dissect the flow systematically. The measures identify the driving node and rebuild the directional dependency structure between the particles. They also explain a puzzling earlier observation, that making the coupling stronger can appear to reduce irreversibility once the description is coarse-grained. The work offers a template for exposing hidden structure in other nonequilibrium systems from measurements alone.
arxiv-2504-10324:
When a layer of two fluids is heated from below, surface tension and buoyancy can team up to set it swirling. Anubhav Dubey and co-authors study that instability in a fluid pair whose willingness to mix changes with temperature. They built a phase-field model that tracks the mixing boundary and lets surface tension follow the local degree of mixing.

A spectral method then solved the linearized equations to find when flow starts and whether it begins as steady rolls or oscillations. The window for oscillatory onset widened or narrowed with miscibility. Stresses at the mixing boundary, they find, set how much heating the layer needs before convection begins.
arxiv-2504-10424:
Scholarly journals that charge neither authors nor readers can run on a tiny budget, Joppe Bos and Kevin McCurley argue in a 2025 paper. The catalog record lists no creator, while the head names both authors. Many societies struggle to adapt to this diamond open access model, and cost is often cited as a main barrier to making the switch.

The authors built a publishing workflow that minimizes human labor, plus software to run it, and launched a journal on that system. Their estimated cost is about seven hundred dollars per year, plus about a dollar per article and a few minutes of volunteer labor per article. Two factors helped: authors in their field use LaTeX, and volunteers built and run the system. The software is open source.
arxiv-2504-10924:
Yue Tan and co-authors probe a rare four quark state in a quark model in a 2025 paper. New lab finds of odd particles have stirred the hunt for four quark states. One state, seen in recent tests, may be a loose pair of mesons or a tight four quark knot.

The team model two such pairs with a chiral quark model and a sharp few body method. One pair stays unbound, a mere pass through state. The other pair binds, thanks to a strong two quark core and light meson swaps. Size reads show the bound form is a compact knot, not a loose pair.
arxiv-2504-11024:
Andrea Simonelli, Norman Müller, and Peter Kontschieder simplify the job of picking objects out of 3D scenes with clicks, in work from 2025. Interactive 3D segmentation serves editing, robotics, and reconstruction, but tools must stay fast and work in unfamiliar settings.

Easy3D pairs a sparse voxel encoder with a small transformer decoder that folds user clicks into its features implicitly. The plain design beat earlier state-of-the-art systems on four standard benchmarks, indoors and on street scenes. It also held up on geometry from Gaussian Splatting, a distribution it was not trained on. The authors stress that simplicity, handled well, can outperform heavier machinery in both accuracy and efficiency.
arxiv-2504-11324:
Larizgoitia and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a prototype gas detector for ghost particles called neutrinos. The planned GanESS experiment will watch neutrinos bump whole nuclei at a European neutron source. Its chamber holds noble gas under high pressure and boosts faint charge signals with a light flash step. The prototype, GaP, tests the craft at low energies before the full build.

Jobs for the prototype include gauging how much signal each gas keeps and where the detection floor sits. First runs used argon gas at moderate pressure with an iron source for calibration. A floor below 2.9 kilo-electronvolts was seen. Low floors matter, since the neutrino bumps of interest are tiny. The prototype steers the full detector's design.
arxiv-2504-11924:
Francesco Zola, Jon Ander Medina, Andrea Venturi, and Raul Orduna study how coin mixers operate inside the Bitcoin network. Their paper came out in 2025. Mixers shuffle coins between addresses to hide who owns what, and criminals also use them to launder money.

The team mapped addresses and transfers as a network and looked for dense clusters with shared shapes. They also added data on known exchanges to see what role exchanges play. Applied to one large mixer, the method found the same structural patterns again and again. Exchanges turned out to play a key and regular role, which raises questions about their checks against money laundering.
arxiv-2504-12124:
Camilo Riano-Rios, George Nehma, and Madhur Tiwari design a spacecraft controller that also watches for faults in this 2025 paper. Keeping a craft pointed right is key to mission success. Its reaction wheels can wear down, and such failures often end missions early.

Their controller adapts as it flies, judging wheel wear and making up for it at the same time. A learning term gathers flight data to pin down unknown values on the fly. The design promises steady pointing even as wheels degrade. Computer simulations test how well the scheme performs. The work joins control and health checks in one unit.
arxiv-2504-12224:
Achille Fiore, Ludovica Crosato Menegazzi, and Giulia Stratta published this review in 2025. Some gamma-ray bursts, the brightest explosions known, coincide with powerful supernovae called hypernovae. One burst lasted seven hours, far beyond normal, and its partner supernova was classed superluminous, outshining galaxies. The authors ask whether such pairings reveal a distinct population: superluminous hypernovae driven by ultra-long bursts.

They survey the events, the stars that might produce them, and the galaxies hosting them. A leading explanation invokes a magnetar, a newborn neutron star with a monstrous magnetic field, spinning down and pumping energy into the burst and the explosion. That engine fits luminous, long-lasting cases well. The authors stress that rival explanations remain alive. Neither the progenitor path nor the explosion mechanism is settled. More observations and sharper theory are needed before the classical burst-supernova link can be extended to these giants.
arxiv-2504-12324:
Mengying Yuan and co-authors define a harder version of a classic language task and build the first dataset for it, in a 2025 paper. Natural language inference asks whether one statement follows from another. Their version spreads the evidence across several documents written in different languages, the reality of cross-border news, law, and research. The dataset holds over twenty-five thousand examples in twenty-six languages.

Their method reads each document's rhetorical structure, how its parts argue, explain, or concede, and fuses those structures in a graph network. Lexical chains align meanings across languages. The system also explains itself by pointing to the exact discourse units behind each verdict. Early results show the structure-aware approach beating flat baselines. The work opens a benchmark for machines that must reason across documents and tongues at once.
arxiv-2504-12724:
Some integrals with knobs on them obey tidy equations in the knobs, and finding those equations is a craft of its own. Hadrien Brochet, Frédéric Chyzak, and Pierre Lairez speed that craft in 2025, in the tongue of D-modules. Their method stretches a classic cut-down trick from lone integrals to whole systems.

The build runs in the Julia language. On the field's home ground it does not yet beat the reigning method, the authors grant. But it opens systems the old craft could not touch. As a proof, they pull out an equation for the count series of a strict graph family, one past reach before. Wider reach, not raw speed, is the claim.
arxiv-2504-12924:
Anthony Bloch and Tudor Ratiu connect an optimal transport problem to geometry and matrix theory in a 2025 mathematics paper. The Monge Kantorovich problem asks for the cheapest way to move mass between distributions.
