In its discrete form, the authors link it to minimizing linear functions over the orbit of a matrix under conjugation, the territory of the Schur Horn theorem.

They then generalize to smooth area preserving rearrangements of an annulus, the diffeomorphism setting of the title. In both settings the problem ties back to permutohedra, the shapes whose corners are permutations, and to majorization, the partial order comparing how spread out vectors are. Gradient flows under a chosen metric complete the picture.
arxiv-2504-13024:
Daniel Gonzalez-Alvarado and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on labeling data that sits on a graph. Each node starts with rough local labels, and the goal is a labeling that agrees across the whole graph. Their approach works with a dictionary of labeled patches that compete to cover the data.

Label assignments and labels then move together under a flow on a curved geometric space. The flow follows a Riemannian ascent toward the most consistent assignment, guided by an action principle. Careful numerical steps keep the motion stable. Experiments show how the method behaves, including a way to state how unsure each label assignment is. The work serves labeling tasks where local guesses need global agreement.
arxiv-2504-13324:
Rui Huang, Jackson Fogelquist, and Xinfan Lin present a sturdier way to gauge battery health in a paper from 2025. Knowing a battery's state of health matters for cars and grid storage. Model-based methods often need slow, gentle test cycles that real use rarely allows.

Errors in the model can also throw off the health estimate. The new method stores the voltage curve of a fresh battery under a set test pulse. Years later, the same pulse is run and the new curve is compared with the stored one. The gap between curves corrects for model error. That gives a health reading that holds up better in real use.
arxiv-2504-13724:
Michael Ramsey-Musolf and Jiang Zhu build a first-principles framework for a problem from the early universe, in a 2025 physics paper. In a first-order phase transition, bubbles of a new phase grow through the hot plasma of the young cosmos. How fast their walls move decides many later effects, and two kinds of friction set that speed: bulk fluid forces and direct hits from particles.

Past work usually treated one source or the other. The authors start from a quantum framework that tracks particles out of balance, and they show the usual flow equations and both friction forces fall out of it under the right approximations. Applying the framework where particles fly freely between hits, they compute a new friction from particle-particle scattering. That force grows in step with the wall's speed factor, which rules out runaway walls in this setting.
arxiv-2504-14224:
Yongguang Li and six co-authors proposed VLM-OpenXpert in twenty twenty-five, a training-free way for vision-language models to reject images from classes they never learned. Such models assume every test image fits a known label, yet new classes appear constantly, and only unlabeled data may be at hand. Retraining to repel unknowns can warp the model's native structure.

The authors name the core snag Semantic Affinity Anchoring: some unknowns sit stably near known classes because they truly resemble them. Their two plug-in modules avoid retraining entirely. One extracts an 'unknown subspace' from confident unknowns and softly removes it from each feature. The other fixes skewed scores and fits a two-humped model to choose a threshold on the fly. Tests span nine benchmarks and three model backbones.
arxiv-2504-14324:
Acacia Chong and co-authors built in 2025 a virtual reality escape room that teaches sustainable food habits. Climate lessons often fail to connect daily choices with distant harm. Their game, Meltdown, drops players into a grocery trip and a food waste challenge, with story feedback on each choice.

Thirty-six university students in Singapore played through it in a user study. Afterward, their factual knowledge of sustainable consumption rose firmly, and so did their confidence and their stated intent to act. The authors argue that hands-on virtual worlds can make abstract climate ideas feel immediate and personal.
arxiv-2504-14424:
Lott, Magyar, Petridis, and Pintz proved in twenty twenty-five that dense sets of prime grids hold all curve-shaped step patterns of a set form. Past work had shown such patterns in plain dense prime sets. Their set is a multi-dim grid built from primes in each axis.

Any dense share of that grid holds the full pattern set, they show. The steps follow fixed curve rules from a shared start and pace. A side rule keeps the patterns from going flat or trivial. They also bound how soon the first such pattern must show up.
arxiv-2504-14524:
Preetam Kumar Ojha presents a method for spotting bad data in large pipelines where totals are built up level by level. The 2025 paper notes that fixed check rules often fail to scale across users, sessions, accounts, and regions. His approach applies a robust form of principal component analysis at each level of the stack.

At each level, the method splits the data into a clean low-rank part and a sparse part that holds the odd values. Those odd values flag errors, outliers, and totals that do not line up. Tests on made-up data sets with planted faults show the method beats rule-based checks at finding corruption. The design is modular, so it can grow with the pipeline.
arxiv-2504-14624:
Polina Gordienko, Christoph Jansen, Thomas Augustin, and Martin Rechenauer study group belief updates in a 2025 paper. Groups must merge member probabilities into one view, and that view should update cleanly when new facts arrive. Static rules miss that dynamic need. Their frame rests on propositional probability logic and a shared common ground.

Any rule that respects consensus and independence on a non-nested agenda must be linear, they show. If members start by agreeing on a common ground and new facts stay inside it, updating before or after merging gives the same result. A health and immigration policy case runs through the paper as an example.
arxiv-2504-15224:
Rafael Holanda, Victor H Jorge-Pérez, and Victor D Mendoza-Rubio study extension modules of finite homological dimension. They ask what that finiteness buys. Their 2025 algebra paper works with Ext modules, which measure how far one module is from splitting cleanly off another. The dimensions in play are the projective and injective ones, plus their Gorenstein counterparts, each gauging how complicated a module's resolutions must be.

The team establishes several criteria under which these dimensions stay finite. Under such conditions they prove their main result. It is a new duality for certain Ext modules tensored with canonical modules. Canonical modules act as a balancing weight in duality theory. The paper is a compact contribution to commutative algebra, sharpening when the Ext machinery behaves tame enough to dualize.
arxiv-2504-15524:
Qiyao Wang and co-authors benchmark language models on intellectual property in 2025. Patent and trademark work blends deep legal and technical knowledge. Past test sets covered patents alone or only slices of the field. Their IPBench is billed as the first broad taxonomy of such tasks.

The bilingual set spans eight property mechanisms and twenty distinct tasks. Tasks mirror real work, from drafting to analysis of filings. Leading models were scored to expose gaps in this specialist domain. A shared yardstick should help law and tech teams judge which models can aid real property work safely.
arxiv-2504-15924:
Alycia Carey and Xintao Wu bring theories of justice into the math of federated learning. In federated learning, many clients train one model together, and fairness can mean equal results, or results matched to contribution. Practitioners pick a notion with little guidance, the authors note.

Their framework, UDJ-FL, weights clients by the noise inherent in their data and borrows rules from fair resource division. One set of dials then reaches four justice standards: strict equality, greatest total good, priority to the worst-off, and reward for desert. Tests show the framework matching or beating specialist fair methods at their own games. The paper also proves error bounds and explains why the uncertainty weighting is load-bearing.
arxiv-2504-17124:
Ming Du and four co-authors show an artificial intelligence workflow that speeds up a key X-ray technique for probing materials. Their demonstration appeared in twenty twenty-five. The technique reads a material's chemical state from how it absorbs X-rays, but it needs readings at many energy points.

Their sampler knows what these spectra look like, including sharp edges and small pre-edge peaks. Guided by that knowledge, it picks the most telling points next. It rebuilds the full curve from only fifteen to twenty percent of the usual readings. Key energy values land within tiny error bounds. Tests on battery materials and catalysts, still and changing, show the method tracks chemistry in motion with far less beam time.
arxiv-2504-17224:
Zhifeng Wang, Qixuan Zhang, and Peter Zhang lead a team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five, whose text adds Niu, Zhang, Sankaranarayana, Caldwell, and Gedeon. It boosts how vision language models read feelings in video, by feeding them richer prompts.

Past methods zoom on the face alone and miss body language, scene, and the feelings of others in the shot. The frame, SoVTP, packs spatial marks such as boxes and face points, face muscle signals, and scene cues into one prompt plan. The whole scene stays in view while fine face moves can still be read. Broad tests show large gains over past visual prompting tricks, with no training on the target task.
arxiv-2504-17724:
Nicolas Heintz and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on an algorithm that can tell from brain waves whether a person is truly listening to a sound. It needs no training labels at all. Knowing when attention is on or off helps hearing tech adapt. Supervised decoders need long, tedious calibration sessions for each user.

Their method pairs a correlation-based feature step with a lightly informed classifier, both unsupervised. On test data it beat a leading supervised model by a clear margin. The win comes from adapting cheaply to each person's drifting signals at test time. The door opens to attention tracking that sets itself up.
arxiv-2504-18024:
Yiwei Zha introduces SMARTFinRAG in a 2025 paper on evaluating retrieval augmented generation for finance. Such systems fetch documents before a language model answers. Banks are adopting them fast, yet testing specialized systems in finance remains hard, and research code often differs from deployed tools.

The platform has three features. Its parts can be swapped live, thanks to a modular design. It builds domain questions from newly added financial documents, centering tests on documents. Its interface is meant to be easy for both researchers and practitioners. Tests show wide performance gaps across configurations, which the open source system makes visible.
arxiv-2504-18224:
Peter Danchev and Zahiri define new families of rings that satisfy the McCoy condition. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A ring meets that condition when zero-product patterns behave tamely. The authors call an element weakly reversible when some power of it is reversible. A ring of such elements is weakly reversible. The class turns out to be broad and well behaved.

Every weakly reversible ring is an abelian McCoy ring. Such rings are also 2-primal in the abelian sense. The authors build one that is not reversible, marking the class as strictly wider. Polynomial rings over these rings inherit strong properties. Zip behavior transfers between a ring and its polynomial ring. Ring theory gains new, workable classes.
arxiv-2504-18624:
Ali SaraerToosi and Avery Broderick tune lean black-hole flow mocks so the great scope's shots of our core hole can be read with true doubt bars. Full flow mocks cost too much to run per fit. A learn tool, trained on a shelf of such shots, spins fresh flow shots fast for set dials. Their 2025 study runs that tool to price the doubt from two un-mocked plays: star haze bend and the hole's own flicker.

Priced doubt then pads the fit bars. Mock scope sets, built from the heavy mock shelf, test the bars. Lean mocks can thus serve real fits with doubt that owns its gaps. True bars keep scope reads from bold claims.
arxiv-2504-18724:
Entanglement in light beams is famous, but entanglement inside solid magnetic materials is far less mapped. Marcin Wieśniak, Ankit Kumar, and Idriss Hank Nkouatchoua Ngueya explore that terrain in a 2025 paper. They study a chain that alternates small and larger spins, a pattern called ferrimagnetic.

Exact computer methods found that simple two-part entanglement stays between nearest neighbors only. Yet a richer kind, genuine multipartite entanglement, reached across distant spin pairs. A shortcut picture based on tiny magnetic ripples, called micromagnons, approximated the ground state quickly. The results show that long-range quantum links can hide in materials where simple measures see none.
arxiv-2504-18824:
Ju Gao and Fang Shen rethink the electron spin qubit by treating the electron as a physical wave, not a point particle. In their picture, a qubit is a pattern of current density whose direction is set by relative phase, rather than a particle holding up and down states at once with set odds. Their 2025 paper works through the magnetic moment that follows from this current in a cavity.

The wave view yields a richer spread and topology of moment density than the standard fixed dipole picture. Both views give the same total moment, one Bohr magneton, and match in uniform fields. They part ways for structured fields and spin to spin coupling. The authors point to Aharonov-Bohm like effects as tests that could separate the two pictures.
arxiv-2504-18924:
Qing-Ping Ding and co-authors study, in 2025, how a kagome metal acts as a magnet. A kagome metal is a crystal whose atoms sit in a woven lattice. The team used nuclear magnetic resonance on aluminum nuclei in the metal. With this tool, they tracked the pull that the nuclei feel inside the metal as the temperature changed. Most readings matched the bulk readings, but one rise at low heat did not. That rise came from outside the metal, not from the metal itself.

More readings showed the stuff is a metal at the small scale too. Set side by side, the relaxation data and the shift data point one way. Ferromagnetic fluctuations rule how the metal acts. In this state, spins side by side lean the same way for a time. These shifts are slow. They move at kilohertz rates, or at rates below that.
arxiv-2504-19224:
Tensors from machine learning need a home in knowledge graphs, and Piotr Marciniak, Piotr Sowiński, and Maria Ganzha propose one in a 2025 paper. Embeddings produced by learning methods, including language models, come as tensors. Hybrid uses that join learning with knowledge graphs need a robust, efficient way to store and query those tensors inside a graph database.

The authors introduce a scheme for representing tensors as literals in RDF. They also extend SPARQL with specialized functions for such literals, adding dozens of functions and several aggregates. A tested, open-source implementation based on Apache Jena supports the scheme. An exemplary knowledge graph and query set are provided. Readers get a working bridge between tensor data and semantic queries.
arxiv-2504-19624:
Yizhe Zhang and co-authors present a system that builds live 3D maps of underground spaces in this 2025 paper. Lava tubes, mines, and tunnels are hard to survey, yet robots and safety teams need accurate models of them. Neural surface methods can mesh such scenes as they are scanned, but fixed settings make them brittle in wild, uneven places.

Their framework, ARMOR, adapts the meshing as it goes, guided by reinforcement learning that tunes the reconstruction to the scene. The team tested it over more than three thousand meters of tunnels, caves, and lava tubes. Shape error fell by about four percent against the best rival methods, while the system kept up in real time. The authors say the adaptive step is what lets one system handle both neat engineered tunnels and rough natural caves. They aim it at inspection, structural checks, and safety monitoring underground.
arxiv-2504-20024:
Wufei Ma and six co-authors present a vision-language model built for reasoning about three-dimensional space, in a 2025 paper. Top models still struggle with such reasoning, even on questions humans find easy. Past fixes trained models on spatial question data, but the reasoning stayed hidden inside. Errors were hard to trace that way.

Their model, SpatialReasoner, uses clear 3D descriptions shared across its stages. Seeing, computing, and reasoning all work on the same descriptions. That shared form helps the model handle new question types. The team also read its step-by-step traces to find where models go wrong. Tests beat a leading rival by a wide margin on one benchmark. Gains held on novel spatial questions as well. The study links older 3D parsing tools with modern language reasoning.
arxiv-2504-20124:
Abul Ehtesham and co-authors listen for childhood asthma in two-second clips of breathing, in a 2025 paper. Early asthma hides behind ordinary coughs, and late care breeds emergencies. Their pipeline borrows Google's HeAR model, a foundation system trained on hundreds of millions of health sounds, to turn each clip from a children's sound library into a rich numeric fingerprint.

Simple classifiers trained on those fingerprints sorted asthma-like sounds from normal ones with over ninety-one percent accuracy. Error hunts, waveform replays, and score charts checked where the system trips. The recordings are short and cheap to gather. The team pitch the tool for screening in clinics light on specialists, even far from big hospitals.
arxiv-2504-20624:
Social chatbots wait for users to start, which cuts chats short, and Zihan Niu and co-authors give them a way to open and steer topics, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their frame first folds the user profile and chat past into a model that sharpens the user's aim. Fresh topics then grow from that aim.

Those topics guide a live fetch from a social app, and the fetched text grounds the bot's next lines. The frame ran in a live product for more than a month. Mean chat length rose by more than a fifth. The team frames the gain as proof that bots which plan topics can hold people longer than bots which just reply.
arxiv-2504-20724:
Hossein Allahverdizadeh and Karim Achouri write the math for how a patterned surface scatters light from any angle, on any backing. Metasurface modeling breaks down when neighbor coupling, multipole effects, or a substrate enter, and older tools assumed head-on light in a uniform medium. Their formalism lifts all three limits at once. An exact spherical multipole expansion, carried to octupole order, handles toroidal effects for free.

Unequal media above and below the sheet are built into the scattering bookkeeping. Test surfaces, dielectric and plasmonic, matched full-wave simulations closely, including sharp bound states in the continuum. Designers gain a fast, trustworthy predictor.
arxiv-2504-20824:
Melzer and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about simulating an interacting particle model on a trapped-ion quantum computer. The Schwinger model is a toy version of quantum chromodynamics in one dimension. With several particle flavors and nonzero density, classical methods hit the sign problem. That barrier makes even small systems intractable classically. Their variational simulation ran on a shuttling-based ion processor. A parameterized circuit searched for ground states across parameter regimes.

The runs mapped out a quantum phase transition central to the model. State tomography revealed how correlations change across that transition. From the data they determined the model's phase boundaries. The work shows quantum hardware tackling a genuine high-energy physics problem. Noise-era processors can already address sign-problem cases, they argue. Larger simulations could follow as hardware improves.
arxiv-2504-21124:
Marco Abate and Ian Short present a 2025 math paper on iterated function systems of holomorphic maps. Such a system applies a set of maps over and over to points on a curved surface. The authors unite and extend many past works on these systems for maps of hyperbolic Riemann surfaces.

Their main result widens a little-known theorem of Heins on iteration in the unit disc to left systems. Uses reach work on transcendental dynamics, hyperbolic steps, and left semiconjugacy in the disc. They also extend work on compact left systems and prove a distance inequality that widens a known theorem. An open question from past work is answered, the need for Bloch domains is removed, and a right-system form of the theorem is added.
arxiv-2504-21224:
Yiling Yun, Stephanie Stacy, and Tao Gao test how people choose signals when cooperating in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Humans manage rich communication with sparse, ambiguous signals. Two theories explain the skill: reasoning about what a partner will infer, and weighing the pair's joint payoff. The authors ran a cooperative grid-world task where players picked ambiguous signals. Behavior was recorded and compared across theories.

The results favored the joint payoff account. A standard pragmatics model, Rational Speech Acts, was also fit to the choices for contrast. Knowing which mechanism rules helps design agents that talk well with people. The study serves cognitive scientists of language and cooperation. It links lab behavior to formal models of meaning.
arxiv-2504-21424:
Shaykin works out how shaped light packs and lone waves run in a twin fiber whose two strands bend light with unlike signs. In such a pair, the plain wave band holds a gap. His 2025 study shows the gap shuts when the waves wear a shaped wrap. Lone waves are then sought as skins of fast-shaped packs, through the packs' own spread law.

Splits of that law give waves from unlike band parts. Count runs match the hand calls well. Twin fibers with split signs could thus host lone waves where plain bands bar them. The craft is a sums-first path to fiber wave design.
arxiv-2504-21524:
Wei Ji, Changhao Xu, Guofeng Qu, and Dmitry Budker build a levitated magnetometer in two thousand twenty-five. Floating particle systems sense with low loss, since no touch means less noise. Most room heat float tools sense motion, not magnetism. Magnetic tricks in use fail in normal air and field.

Their device floats a magnet by diamagnetic force and reads its motion with light. Strong spin lattice links curb spin noise in the magnet. Low loss from floating helps as well. Sensitivity reached a level on par with top cryogenic and atomic tools. It works at room heat and in Earth's own field.
arxiv-2504-21724:
Wei Guo and co-authors computed this 2025 set of corrections to the thermodynamics of spinning black holes. The setting is a Kerr black hole in anti-de Sitter space, a curved backdrop common in theory work. Extra terms in the gravity action, up to the cube of the curvature tensor, tweak the hole's heat behavior. The authors find the first-order tweaks with a simpler method than the standard heavy machinery.

They subtract a background instead of building counterterms, and split the action to ease the math. A check with the well-known Gauss-Bonnet term confirmed the answers. Comparing with two other formula families let them read off facts about the corrected hole itself. The work sharpens theory tools for quantum gravity studies.
arxiv-2504-21824:
Agrawal and co-authors characterize the range of the spherical mean transform in a 2025 mathematics paper. The transform averages a function over spheres, a step used in imaging and inverse problems. Knowing exactly which outputs can occur is key to rebuilding the input.

Earlier work by the same team settled the odd-dimension case for functions in the unit ball. The new result covers even dimensions with symmetry relations alone. Those relations use elliptic integrals of the spherical harmonic coefficients of the function. The paper also proves two fresh identities for normalized Bessel functions. A cross-product integral identity for integer order rounds out the pair of tools.
arxiv-2505-00124:
Michele Tammaro and Jure Zupan give an introduction to hunting axions at particle colliders. Their 2025 notes cover axions and axion-like particles, light hypothetical particles tied to dark sector physics. The text is written as a teaching guide rather than a single experiment report.

The notes start with the basics of collider physics, with stress on how new particles are made and caught. They then survey searches for dark sectors, contrasting light candidates with heavy dark matter hunts. The final part works through a full example: a search for a light-loving axion-like particle in electron-positron collisions. The example mirrors a real early analysis at the Belle-II experiment, step by step.
arxiv-2505-00324:
Yuri Shtanov and Yurii Sheiko revisit how scalaron dark matter interacts with normal matter. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in f(R) gravity, a modified gravity theory. The scalaron is an extra scalar degree of freedom in that theory. It could form all dark matter if its mass sits in a certain range. Its coupling to Standard Model particles is set to the minimum.

The team recalculated the scalaron decay rate into two photons. Past results on that loop process disagreed with each other. Direct loop evaluation with proper regularization removed the ambiguity. They then estimated background radiation from decays across cosmic history. Primordial scalarons added a negligible share of today's dark matter. Results support the original picture of a coherently oscillating field.
arxiv-2505-00524:
Mikhail Rybakov proves undecidability results for fragments of classical and non-classical first-order logic, in a 2025 paper. Rather than attacking each logic head-on, he routes the proofs through recursive inseparability, a property of two problem sets that no algorithm can pull apart. A new domino problem serves as the tool for catching that property.

With it, he shows that classical logic with a single binary predicate and three variables is inseparable from the theory of its finite symmetric models. The same fate meets monadic fragments of many modal and intuitionistic predicate logics, even with one unary predicate and two variables. The paper closes by answering related decidability questions for special fragments.
arxiv-2505-00624:
Chaitali Bhattacharyya and co-authors shrink big language models for special fields in a 2025 paper. Training a domain model from scratch is costly, and plain pruning of a large model dulls its skill. Their framework, FineScope, uses sparse autoencoders to read which features a domain needs. Structured pruning then cuts the model under domain constraints, keeping what the field requires.

Lost skill is restored by fine-tuning on data the autoencoder itself curates from the domain. The pruned models rival far larger systems on specialty tasks, they report. The curated data even sharpens unpruned models. The route promises cheaper, sharper tools for narrow jobs.
arxiv-2505-00724:
Lucas Bordeu and Javier Castro compute best play and best betting in blackjack with formal math, in a 2025 paper. They model the game as a Markov decision process, where each state calls for a choice. Expected utility theory then scores choices by the player's taste for risk, from steady to bold.

Dynamic programming yields the top policy for both card play and stake sizing. Simulations show the best play policy only edges out the classic basic strategy, which speaks well of that folk system. Betting by exact deck makeup slightly beat the Hi-Lo counting scheme. The authors supply both brain-friendly versions and full computer versions. Rule changes and more players remain open ground.
arxiv-2505-01324:
Yukai Yang asked in 2025 whether one randomised trial can reveal the true average effect of a treatment. That average is taken over hidden random settings, yet one trial shows only one draw of those settings. A sound design alone does not promise the truth can be recovered.

Yang shows that when units depend only weakly on near neighbours, a helpful averaging property appears. Averaging across many units then recovers the average over hidden settings. The usual trial estimates stay accurate, their spread can be pinned down from the single trial, and the estimates settle toward a bell shape. That spread result breaks with classic practice, where only cautious upper bounds were possible.
arxiv-2505-01524:
Zexi Yao, Natasa Krco, Georgi Ganev, and Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye show that a shortcut for judging the privacy of synthetic data does not work. Synthetic data sets are shared as safe stand-ins for sensitive records, and the gold-standard check is an attack that guesses whether a record was in the training set. Practitioners instead use distance-to-closest-record scores, which pass a data set when its rows are no closer to the training data than real rows are. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team tests that shortcut across data sets and generator types, from classic models to diffusion models.

Data sets that passed the distance test fell to membership attacks, again and again. Both the pass-fail version and the continuous score failed to track risk under settings. The authors give a leaking example the metric misses and call the approach flawed by design.
arxiv-2505-01924:
Yudin and co-authors build a model in 2025 for a resonance effect used in atomic clocks and sensors. The effect, called coherent population trapping, appears when atoms are lit by a laser whose strength is modulated in time.

In such light, only two frequency parts sit close to the atomic transitions, while many others sit far off. Their model treats the two close parts exactly and the rest with a second order approximation. The off resonant parts fold into two new operators, one for shifts and one for relaxation. Tests on a three level system matched exact calculations closely. The model also shows that a common view of the resonance shift is, in general, wrong.
arxiv-2505-02024:
Minjie Shen and co-authors survey Manus AI, a general-purpose agent launched in early twenty twenty five that aims to close the gap between thinking and doing. Large language models plan well but usually stop at text. Manus, from a Chinese startup, is built to execute whole tasks end to end and hand back finished outcomes.

Their 2025 overview walks the system's architecture and tests its reach across healthcare, finance, manufacturing, robotics, and gaming. Strengths in autonomous multi-step work sit beside current limits in reliability and scope. The authors frame the agent as a preview of a coming shift: software that takes intentions, not instructions, and returns work rather than words.
arxiv-2505-02124:
Comparing two networks, whether road maps or molecular webs, often comes down to graph edit distance: the cheapest set of changes turning one graph into the other. Finding that optimum is notoriously hard, and learned predictors need costly ground truth and act as black boxes. Verma, Goyal, Mathur, Anand, and Ranu flip the approach with GRAIL. Instead of predicting the distance, a large language model writes a program that computes it.

Automated prompt tuning improves the generated code over time, with no ground-truth answers needed for supervision. The resulting program can be read and audited, unlike a neural predictor. On seven datasets, GRAIL beat the best existing approximation methods in quality. It also carried across graph types without retraining. The authors pitch program generation as a more open, portable path for hard combinatorial measures like this one.
arxiv-2505-02424:
Jinxian Guo and co-authors report progress toward a near-perfect quantum memory in a 2025 paper. Such a memory stores light-based quantum states and returns them on demand. Good devices should keep over ninety percent of the signal, yet noise has held real devices back.

The team maps how light converts into a spin wave inside warm rubidium vapor. They then squeeze that spin wave with a light-guided method that adapts as it works. The squeeze raises conversion strength while holding noise down. Lab tests of the Raman memory show the approach beating the old trade-off. The result points toward more useful quantum networks.
arxiv-2505-02524:
Hannah Middleton and co-authors find free sensitivity for a gravitational wave hunt by shuffling a telescope schedule. Their 2025 paper concerns the MeerKAT pulsar timing array, which watches a set of pulsars for the slow ripple of waves from giant black hole pairs.

Evidence for that ripple has just emerged from several arrays. Holding total observing time fixed, the team uses a greedy algorithm to shift minutes between pulsars, giving more time where it buys the most signal. Under stated assumptions about the signal and pulsar noise, the reshuffle lifts the signal-to-noise ratio by about twenty percent over a ten-year array life. The change is small enough to leave the current program nearly untouched.
arxiv-2505-02624:
Louis Bastogne and Philippe Ghosez present an interatomic potential for lead titanate in two thousand twenty-five. Lead titanate is a benchmark ferroelectric with strong polarization. It shifts phase at high heat in ways labs prize. Density functional theory models it well but costs too much for big runs.

Their second principles potential is open source and fully atomistic. It matches the costly theory on key traits of the material. Domain wall motion and polar textures come out right in its runs. The model stays predictive across a wide span of settings. Big, accurate studies of memory grade uses are the target.
arxiv-2505-02724:
Hisato Matsukawa builds a spectrum that reads geometry back out of abstract categories with actions. His 2025 paper defines the relative Matsui spectrum for a stable infinity category carrying an action. The construction merges Balmer tensor spectra and Matsui triangular spectra into one frame for sorting thick submodules.

Core traits include universality, comparison with older spectra, and descent. A natural map links the new spectrum to the Balmer spectrum of the base. In test settings, the spectrum recovers the classic geometric space hidden in the category data. Those settings span perfect complexes on schemes, twisted derived categories, singularity categories, and matrix factorization categories. Matsukawa argues the tool extends tensor triangular geometry past purely tensor settings.
arxiv-2505-03824:
Jiarui Chen presents a 2025 paper on personalizing recommendations from large language models with a memory store. Language models can grasp user taste, but stuffing a whole history into each prompt is costly and slow to update. Chen proposes MAP, a memory-assisted system. It first builds a profile of each user's past ratings and choices. At request time it pulls only the memories most similar to the current need.

A new test task varies memory size in two settings: same-domain and cross-domain, such as movie memories guiding book picks. MAP beat recommenders that paste history straight into prompts. Its edge grew as histories lengthened, in both settings. The author presents the design as suited to ongoing personal service, where user histories keep growing. The work points toward cheaper, fresher personalization for language-model products.
arxiv-2505-04124:
Nozomi Nakatsuyama and Masatomo Takahashi define, in a 2025 geometry paper, a new class of surfaces in plain three-dimensional space. A framed surface is a smooth sheet that carries a moving frame, a set of axes that ride on it. The pair builds a Bertrand form of such sheets, in the same spirit as Bertrand curves, a classic pair form where two curves share their main axes. For this class they find two linked sheets: the caustic, where light rays from the sheet pile up, and the involute, an unwind form.

Each of those can be set straight from the sheet, with no extra frame work. The pair gives terms for when the two acts undo each other, as with Legendre curves. A sheet is in the class just when a second caustic of its involute exists, under set terms. A fresh act, the tangential form, closes the work.
arxiv-2505-04224:
Kittikun Surawuttinack, Suppanat Supanyo, and Sikarin Yoo-Kong argue, in a 2025 paper, that Einstein's relativistic formulas can grow out of a tweaked classical framework. The multiplicative Lagrangian adds a spare parameter to the usual action, yet yields the same equations of motion. For a free particle the freedom is especially stark.

By varying that parameter and averaging over it, the authors find the statistical mean of the framework takes a new shape. Out of that average, the relativistic Lagrangian and Hamiltonian appear on their own. On the action level, Einstein's spacetime seems to emerge from a statistical reading of the classical setup. The authors present the framework as a bridge between classical and relativistic physics, richer than either view alone.
arxiv-2505-04324:
Mirgita Frasheri, Prasad Talasila, and Vanessa Scherma extend a digital twin platform toward federation in two thousand twenty-five. Digital twins mirror real systems to tune work and run cyber physical gear. Twins hold models and data that others could reuse. Reuse cuts cost and sparks joint work across teams.

Their platform, DT as a Service, now links many copies of itself. Users on distinct copies can find and share twin assets. They can also reshape and alter assets made by peers. The paper is a demo of that linked mode. It shows the blocks that make twin growth and care easier across sites.
arxiv-2505-04424:
Jing Hu and six co-authors teach a small agent to restyle pictures in a 2025 paper. Style transfer paints a photo with the look of an artwork. Heavy models do it well but cost much compute, and each fresh look can take a fresh run.

An agent trained by trial and reward steers the paint step by step instead. One shared policy handles any style thrown at it, and the results flow as a smooth series of frames. A side trick shifts the loss weights on its own as training moves, balancing content and style. Tests at many sizes show crisp, varied art at low cost.
arxiv-2505-04724:
Alana Cavalcante and Fernando Lourenço study when the bundles tied to a holomorphic distribution split into simple parts, in a paper from 2025. The spaces at hand are Grassmann manifolds, which collect all flat subspaces of a fixed size, and smooth quadric surfaces in space. A distribution is a field of tangent planes across such a space. Its singular set marks where the field breaks down.

The pair prove split results for the tangent and conormal sheaves of these fields. Their work extends past results on simpler spaces like projective space. They also tie the geometry of the singular set to traits of the sheaves. Such links let geometers read a field's flaws from its algebra. The paper adds to the toolkit for complex geometry in higher dimensions.
arxiv-2505-04824:
Masahito Mochizuki reviews theory on steering magnetism with light in a 2025 article. Shining light on a magnet is an appealing way to flip or tune it for future devices. The catch is that light's magnetic field couples to magnetization only feebly, far too weakly to cause dramatic change.

The way around, Mochizuki explains, is light's electric field, which acts on electron charges a hundred to a thousand times more strongly. In materials where spin and charge are tightly linked, such as multiferroics, pulling the charges drags the spins along. The review walks through three recent lines of theory showing how light can switch magnetization in these coupled systems, and weighs what they promise for devices.
arxiv-2505-05024:
Ziyu Fang, Xiangru Li, and Haining Li publish a catalog in 2025 of rare carbon-rich, metal-poor stars. Such stars are fossils of the early universe, born from gas seeded by the first stars, and their carbon excess records ancient element making. Finding them in huge survey archives is a needle-in-haystack task.

Using low-resolution spectra from a Chinese survey telescope's eighth data release, the team trains a deep learning scheme to flag candidates. The search yields 12,766 candidate stars. For each, the catalog gives estimated temperature, surface gravity, iron content, and carbon content. The authors offer the list as a reference for studies of galaxy history and the origin of elements.
arxiv-2505-05224:
Charbel Bou Chaaya and Mehdi Bennis work on a hard split: how to share radio resources in next-generation wireless nets that must serve calls, sensing, and computing at once. Choices are many, discrete, and high in number, so hand rules scale poorly. Their 2025 work builds a learning loop that tries patterns, scores them, and learns from the scores.

A flow network that favors high-reward patterns draws each new set of choices. Those draws are tested, and the results update a stand-in model of the net. The loop then finds good splits in fewer rounds. Tests showed gains of about twenty percent over rival methods. The loop also needed less than half the test rounds of those rivals.
arxiv-2505-05524:
Lorenzo Damenti reports the status of a detector upgrade for the CMS experiment, in this 2025 paper. The Large Hadron Collider will soon run in a high-luminosity mode, smashing particles together far more often. To cope, the CMS team is replacing its entire silicon tracking system, with the inner tracker at the heart of the rebuild.

The report walks through the main design and technology choices for the new inner tracker. It also covers how prototypes are being checked and how the team is preparing for large-scale production. The upgraded detector must survive harsh radiation while still tracking particles with precision.
arxiv-2505-05824:
Jhuma Sannigrahi and nine co-authors probe an odd magnet in this 2025 study. Most ferrimagnets owe their pull to unlike ions or unlike sites. In their compound, identical nickel ions in like settings grow unequal moments purely from their surroundings. Neutron beams and first-principles math were combined to find out why.

Two nickel sublattices share the same charge but differ in shape of life. One forms near one-dimensional chains, bonds more strongly to oxygen, and carries a shrunken moment. The other stays near two-dimensional with a full moment. The authors credit spin shape and local warps for the split, widening the known routes to ferrimagnetism.
arxiv-2505-06124:
Cruz Velasco and Javier García de Abajo propose a new quantum sensing method using free electrons in a 2025 paper. Quantum sensors beat classic ones by using odd quantum states of light. But making and reading states with many photons is hard.

Their design pairs photons with electrons that skim past a light guide. Each electron can trade many photons with the guide, thanks to strong coupling. Splitting the electron beam and letting it interact twice could sharpen phase sensing tenfold with current tools. Picking out certain electrons after the interaction could also build large entangled light states at fast rates. The work opens a fresh path for quantum measurement.
arxiv-2505-06224:
Plachouras and co-authors argue for a broader way to judge what AI models learn, in this 2025 paper. The usual test checks whether a model's inner codes hold facts needed for a task. That misses traits like stability under change, which matter when models meet the real world.

The team propose a shared protocol that scores four traits: how much useful information codes carry, and how they handle shifts, swaps, and tangled factors. They run it on image and speech models of many designs. Models with equal task scores behaved very differently on the new traits. The framework aims to make such comparisons standard and clear.
arxiv-2505-06324:
Vipula Rawte and three co-authors study how language models cite documents in this 2025 paper. Models increasingly answer from supplied documents, and their citations must actually support the text. The team proposes two checks. The first treats attribution as a plain entailment question and asks a model whether the cited passage implies the claim. On a standard benchmark, that zero shot method edged past the best baselines on both in domain and out of domain sets.

The second check reads the model's own attention. Using a small model, attention based scores beat the baseline at nearly every layer. Two layers ranges lagged, a detail the authors report openly. The work matters because fluent answers with fake support are worse than no citation at all. Cheap entailment checks could run as a live filter on model output.
arxiv-2505-06424:
Adam Snyder and Anthony Tyson sim how bright satellite streaks look in sky survey cameras as orbit height changes, in a paper from 2025. Streak glare can spoil star photos, and its strength rests on range, satellite size, lens width, and streak speed.

For a large lens focused at far distance, a low satellite blurs out of focus, which spreads its light. In the Rubin Observatory camera case, the effects near cancel out. A big satellite moved from a mid orbit down to a low orbit ends up about as bright in streak form.
arxiv-2505-06624:
Sorting documents into classes often starts with only a handful of labeled examples and a mountain of unlabeled ones. Arezoo Hatefi and co-authors extend a teacher-student method for that bind in this 2025 paper. In the base method, a teacher model labels the unlabeled texts, a student learns from them, and the teacher improves by watching the student's score on the gold examples.

Their addition is an unsupervised pretraining phase built on masking tied to the task's objective, run before the labeling loop begins. They compare the original model, the extended one, and several baselines in depth. Tests span three datasets in two languages, English and Swedish, to check that the gains are not tied to one tongue or topic.
arxiv-2505-07124:
Many learning tasks show only samples of a crowd, never the hidden cost that shaped it. Francisco Andrade, Gabriel Peyré, and Clarice Poon build a way to learn that cost back, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their trick turns the forward problem's own shortfall into a loss with clean shape. A sharpened form adds a data term that keeps scores honest.

The error splits neatly into three parts: measure noise, forward wobble, and fit bend. Two crowd-flow cases get recovery bounds with high odds. In the flow case, the sharpened loss collapses to a known transport form, which ties old and new tools together. Tests show the sharpening at work.
arxiv-2505-07224:
Tim Zolkin and co-authors show how near-conserved quantities in symplectic maps can be recovered from discrete symmetry, in a 2025 paper. Noether's theorem links smooth symmetries to exact conservation laws. Reversible symplectic maps hold a discrete symmetry instead, and it can seed approximate invariants. Building functions that respect the symmetry order by order uncovers those hidden quantities. This second part of the work applies the method to wide-ranging motion.

Once averaged, the approximate invariants trace resonances and the edges of stable regions with care. In fully integrable cases, the method recovers the exact invariants. One unified function yields phase portraits, rotation numbers, and tune maps that match direct tracking across wide settings. Against a rival matrix method, the new technique proved more accurate in resonant, strongly nonlinear regimes. Uses in beam physics are highlighted.
arxiv-2505-07624:
Alexandre Moreira, Patricia Silva, Miguel Heleno, and Andre Marcato ask where long-duration energy storage pays off in the United States, in a 2025 paper. Such storage can firm up wind and solar power for days. The technology is young, and future costs are unsure. The team worked state by state.

For each of the 48 mainland states, they found the top cost at which storage stays worthwhile. Under a federal cost target, only four states could drop firm fossil plants without raising total costs. States with high storage value tended to have little thermal power and lots of wind. The map helps planners see where long storage helps first and where costs must fall further.
arxiv-2505-07824:
Kritika Babbar and Amit Maji classify a family of analytic functions in a 2025 operator theory paper. A classic model theory pairs such functions one to one with a class of contractions, up to a change of basis.

The authors pin down exactly which of those functions give a contraction that is a power partial isometry of the special kind. As a use of the result, they name a class of contractive polynomials whose linked operator splits into a clean block form. Two blocks are shifts, in opposite senses, and one is nilpotent. They also characterize the symbols for which a Toeplitz operator on a vector valued Hardy space is a partial isometry.
arxiv-2505-07924:
Dylan Folsom and co-authors argue that dark matter speed near Earth is better pinned down than feared in a 2025 paper. Underground detectors listen for dark matter particles striking atoms, and their reach depends on how fast those particles move locally. Modeling that speed takes simulated galaxies, but collecting enough look-alikes was long out of reach.

Nearly one hundred Milky Way twins from the TNG50 simulation now form the largest sample at this sharpness. A new scaling step sets each galaxy's rest frame to match our own local standard. The pooled speed curves hug the standard halo model well, though single galaxies stray at the high-speed tail. Detection limits drawn from the spread vary by about sixty percent. That spread, the authors say, now sits at or below the detectors' own systematic error.
arxiv-2505-08024: Nate Harman writes an informal, mostly expository note in 2025 on the shape of q-binomial coefficients. These coefficients extend the familiar binomial coefficients with a parameter q. The note describes their long run behavior and qualitative traits in a friendly question and answer style. Most results are not new, Harman states, but the overall story is not well known. All diagrams in the note are new, he adds, giving readers a fresh visual route into a classic topic.
arxiv-2505-08124:
Laszlo Szilagyi, Francis Engelmann, and Jeannette Bohg speed up language-tagged 3D scene building for robots. Scenes stored as clouds of Gaussian blobs can carry word tags from vision-language models. Such tags aid search and rescue, city scans, and mining, but tagging big scenes is slow. Their framework, SLAG, spreads the work across many graphics cards at once.

Tags are drawn from two known vision models and fused into the 3D scene. No loss-based fitting is needed, since tags come from a weighted mean of scene values. A vector data base stores tags for fast lookup later. On sixteen cards, tagging ran eighteen times faster than a prior system. Tag quality held on two standard scene sets.
arxiv-2505-08324:
Elena Morotti, writing solo, presents a 2025 algorithm for sharpening medical images. Many imaging tasks are framed as inverse problems: recover a clean image from blurred or partial data. Adding a penalty term that favors sharp edges gives good results, but the math becomes non convex, with many false valleys that trap solvers. Morotti's framework pairs a neural network with a classic solver to dodge those traps.

The network makes a strong first guess at the image. The solver then refines it step by step under the penalty rule, in an incremental way. Tests covered image deblurring and tomographic reconstruction, on synthetic pictures, brain scans, and chest and belly scans. The hybrid beat both plain solvers and pure learning methods on accuracy and stability. Training without true reference images cost little, which the author calls a practical plus.
arxiv-2505-08524:
Pratibha Kumari and co-authors present a computing paper from 2025 on tissue slide reading. Software can sort whole slide images of tissue, but it falters when the source changes. A new organ, disease, or hospital can shift the data and break the model. Retraining from scratch wastes past learning.

Their method lets the model learn new domains in steps without storing old slides. It makes fake versions of past slide summaries from a mixture model. A filter based on attention keeps only the most telling patches. That keeps the fake samples sharp and protects patient privacy. Tests on public sets for disease markers showed the method kept old skill while learning new domains. It matched methods that do store old data.
arxiv-2505-08824:
Varun Sahni wrote a 2025 memoir of the cosmologist Alexei Starobinsky, his former doctoral advisor. The two worked together for nearly forty-five years, starting in Moscow. Sahni recalls thesis days and the birth of inflation theory in that period. Starobinsky early work reshaped how the young universe is pictured.

He also visited India often and worked closely with its scientists and students. Topics ranged over inflation, cosmic structure, and dark energy. The joint work yielded over a dozen papers and several doctorates. Two diagnostic tools, Statefinder and Om, grew from that teamwork. The essay is both tribute and history of a fertile partnership.
arxiv-2505-09224:
Leineweber and co-authors map the ethical debate around social robots in elderly care, from the viewpoint of those who must decide on their use. Robots are proposed as one answer to scarce care resources, with real benefits and real risks. Their 2025 review screens over fifteen hundred publications and keeps 248, sorting findings into hazards, opportunities, and open questions.

At least sixty broad ethical aspects emerged, touching three groups of stakeholders. Some issues, like deception and privacy, are widely discussed, while many others surface only at the margins. The authors argue that sound decisions need case by case review of each setting, not blanket rules. They also suggest decision makers must grasp how this debate is structured before they can weigh it well.
arxiv-2505-09824:
Jason Yang develops, in a 2025 preprint, exact algorithms for splitting tensors into simple pieces over finite fields. The decomposition, called canonical polyadic decomposition, sits under fast matrix multiplication. Random search has found many record decompositions lately. But when search fails, it cannot prove nothing better exists. Famous gaps, like the true rank of three-by-three matrix multiplication, stay open for that reason. Yang's algorithms keep exactness: they can certify that a tensor has a given rank or not. They run in polynomial time and save a large factor over brute force.

A companion algorithm hunts border decompositions, a relaxed variant used in the same field. The paper also gives new upper and lower bounds on the maximum rank for families of tensor shapes. With extra pruning, the exact search can still attack the three-by-three problem. It does not crack it, but it sharpens the tools that might.
arxiv-2505-10124:
Ziad Kheil and co-authors reconstruct breathing motion for tumor radiotherapy in a 2025 paper. Treating chest and belly tumors needs images at breath phases never actually scanned. Standard interpolation stitches slices into volumes, but irregular breathing and lag between the breath signal and organ motion leave artifacts.

Their framework registers known images with their conditions to estimate the missing phase image directly. A conditional U-Net takes the condition in fully, with no fixed reference frame required. On clinical four dimensional scans, the method produced artifact free volumes at real time speed. The authors release the code openly. The goal is cleaner targeting of moving tumors during treatment planning.
arxiv-2505-10324:
A large team of co-authors reports an astronomy paper in two thousand twenty-five on a planet drifting into a forbidden zone. Space missions have found thousands of planets a bit smaller than Neptune. Almost none sit very close to their stars, a gap called the evaporation desert, where starlight should strip their air away.

The team confirms a planet, TOI-5800 b, on an eccentric, stretched orbit that carries it toward that zone. A few hot Neptunes do survive inside the desert. Such planets let astronomers watch migration and air loss in action. The paper presents the data that confirm the planet and pin down its orbit.
arxiv-2505-10624:
Yunwen Ji, Mark van der Laan, and Alan Hubbard sharpen the error bars on causal estimates, targeting the variance itself with their targeted learning machinery. Standard practice reads variance off the estimated influence function, but that read runs optimistic in small samples or when treatment is rare, inflating false positives. Their fix treats variance as its own estimand.

In their 2025 paper, a one-step targeted maximum likelihood estimator aims at the variance of the log causal risk ratio. The construction first derives the efficient influence function for that variance, then builds the substitution estimator along a least favorable path. The method extends to other causal parameters. Better variance, they argue, is better inference: honest intervals that cover at the promised rate.
arxiv-2505-11224:
Eva-Maria Ahrer and co-authors read in 2025 the air of a hot Jupiter whose orbit runs backward around its star. Such planets should not form where they sit, so their chemistry is a fossil of where they began. The team used the Webb telescope to capture a transmission spectrum as the planet crossed its star.

The air looked fairly clear, with water and carbon dioxide firmly detected, plus hints of carbon monoxide and a sulfur gas. The carbon-to-oxygen ratio came out below the star's, and the metal content near the star's own. Those numbers sketch a birthplace and migration path the authors compare with formation models.
arxiv-2505-11524:
Midhun Augustine gives an overview of data-driven model predictive control in this 2025 paper, with code level detail in MATLAB. Model predictive control steers a system by planning its next moves over a short horizon, again and again. The classic form needs a written model of the system. The data-driven form learns the needed behavior straight from past data instead.

The review first covers the classic linear and nonlinear forms. It then turns to data-driven linear control, with subspace methods and prediction error methods. Next come neural network based forms for the nonlinear case. Each approach is shown with its numerical steps, so readers can build it themselves. The paper closes with recent advances and open paths for future work in the field.
arxiv-2505-11724:
Kai Zhu and four co-authors present a 2025 model for judging the visual quality of video game images without a reference picture. Games suffer their own defects: aliasing, texture blur, and detail-level switches, unlike the compression flaws photo metrics know. The model pairs a distilled feature extractor, trained to spot game-specific distortions, with semantic gating that weighs features by scene content, using a vision-language model's embeddings.

Trained on gameplay recorded across quality presets, its scores align with human perception. The extractor generalized to distortion levels it never saw in training, and semantic gating steadied the predictions. The model beat out-of-domain baselines and tracked quality monotonically on unseen games of the same genre. The authors offer it as a base for automated graphics quality checks.
arxiv-2505-11824:
Minsu Kim and seven co-authors give reasoning chains a lie detector in 2025. Step-by-step reasoning helps language models, but a single false step can poison the answer while sounding smooth. Their idea attaches a hidden correctness tag to every step and infers the tags from the model's own likelihoods.

A search algorithm explores tag assignments efficiently, scoring them by how well they explain the final answer. Those inferred tags then train a fast predictor that flags errors in new problems without search. On logic, math, and commonsense benchmarks the method caught errors reliably, and the flags fed self-correction loops that improved answers.
arxiv-2505-11924:
Yu-Ting Lee and co-authors explain how language models correct their own moral judgments in a 2025 paper. When prompted, models often refine ethical answers on their own, a trait called intrinsic moral self correction. It works across many tasks, but the inner mechanism was unclear, so the team turned to mechanistic interpretability tools that read hidden model states.

Their hypothesis is that correction prompts steer hidden representations along readable latent directions. Across six models and four morality tasks, prompt induced shifts aligned with contrast steering vectors, even when those vectors came from a separate corpus. Adding those shifts directly changed behavior even more strongly than the prompts themselves.
arxiv-2505-12424:
Lior Broide and co-authors mix large language models with evolutionary search to write stronger unit tests for software. Their 2025 paper tackles a known flaw of search-based test writing: it stalls early and its test suites lack variety. Language models write tests in a fresh style, but they do not optimize a suite as a whole.

Their system, EvoGPT, seeds the search with suites drafted by a model. It forces variety by varying the model's heat and prompts, and it repairs each test in a loop while adding checks aimed at code coverage. When the search stalls, fresh model tests target the branches still missed. On a standard Java bug benchmark, the blend lifted both coverage and fault-finding scores by about ten percent.
arxiv-2505-12724:
Hyunseong Kim and co-authors review progress in Josephson junctions, the core parts of superconducting quantum computers, in this 2025 paper. A Josephson junction lets paired electrons tunnel through a thin barrier, giving the nonlinear response qubits need. Scaling to useful machines demands junctions that are uniform, low-loss, tunable, and compact. This survey covers how materials and fabrication advances chase those goals.

The authors trace fabrication from classic multi-angle evaporation toward foundry-ready processes. New junction materials and better testing methods get full treatment. They also rethink which figures of merit matter for the next generation. The review frames progress in junctions as the pace setter for industrial-scale quantum processors, linking lab craft to factory practice.
arxiv-2505-12824:
Renato Leme, Carlos Olarte, Elaine Pimentel and Marcelo Coniglio revisit the modal cube with a semantics that uses no possible worlds. The modal cube gathers the standard modal logics built from common axioms. Their framework gives each logic a modular, uniform set of multi-valued non-deterministic matrices, where the necessity rule is captured by level valuations.

The semantics rests on an eight-valued system and yields a sound and complete decision method for each logic in the cube. Earlier semantics appear as special cases of this one. A new model view links the matrices back to relational, Kripke-style semantics, and speaks to old conjectures on how modal axioms match semantic conditions in non-deterministic settings.
arxiv-2505-13024: Allem and co-authors show in 2025 that a threshold graph needs at most four distinct eigenvalues in its best matrix. For any such graph and any nonzero target value, they build the matrix by hand. Its spectrum sits inside a four-value set built from that target. The construction works for any threshold graph the reader picks first.
arxiv-2505-13124:
Francesco Innocenti, El Mehdi Achour, and Christopher Buckley scale a brain-like learning rule to very deep networks in a paper from 2025. Predictive coding learns from local signals only, unlike backpropagation. Such networks have long failed beyond modest depth. The authors analyze why standard versions destabilize as layers pile up. Their fix adapts a depth-aware parameterization from mainstream deep learning.

The resulting method trains residual networks beyond one hundred layers reliably. Performance on simple classification tasks rivals current benchmarks with little tuning. Learning rates transfer across widths and depths without re-searching. Code ships in an open library. The authors call it a first step toward complex architectures for local learning rules.
arxiv-2505-13324:
Galit Shmueli, David Martens, Jaewon Yoo, and Travis Greene compare one idea, the counterfactual, across two fields that use it very differently, in this 2025 paper. Both causal inference and explainable AI ask what would have happened otherwise. Yet their answers serve different masters: one estimates effects in the world, the other explains a model's behavior.

The authors give a formal definition broad enough to hold both uses. They then walk through how each field frames, generates, evaluates, and deploys counterfactuals. Causal versions answer to data and identification assumptions. Machine learning versions answer to plausibility and closeness to the case at hand. By setting the two side by side, the paper hunts for cross fertilization: methods each field can borrow from the other without confusing their goals.
arxiv-2505-13424:
Moussa takes stock of the middle path in atomistic simulation. Semiempirical quantum mechanics simplifies the full equations with fitted parameters, a practice as old as quantum theory itself. Such methods once dominated the software market, but over three decades the field has polarized toward costly first-principles methods at one end and fast, narrow force fields at the other.

Looking from the middle ground, the author reviews why the older methods succeeded and where they might grow again. Active work marries them to machine learning, and he sees untapped room in joining them more tightly with first-principles theory, using flexible frameworks and modular software. The essay argues the middle path is far from exhausted.
arxiv-2505-13824:
David Lin, Daniel Hall, Giannis Fikioris, Siddhartha Banerjee, and Éva Tardos improve robust guarantees for online resource sharing in two thousand twenty-five. Agents share a resource in rounds with no money changing hands. Past work showed each agent can lock in half their ideal gain. That bound held no matter how rivals act, but gains past it looked hard.

A simple randomized bid in a first price auction lifts the floor. Agents bid at random when their value sits in a top slice. The new floor sits close to a known hardness cap. Static bid rules cannot pass a set bar, so the trick is near tight.
arxiv-2505-14024:
Di Wu, Qian Li, Heng Yang, and Yong Han built a shield for federated learning. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with training shared models across spread out clients. Each client keeps its data local and sends only model updates. That setup is open to broad attacks that aim to drag the shared model down, not to flip one class. Past shields lose force when client data differ a lot.

The team chose to spot and cut attacks, not just blunt them. They found that spread between class embeddings marks how well a client truly learns, better than raw scores with thin data. A Gram matrix on embeddings turns that spread into a test. Readers who run shared training get a shield built for messy real data.
arxiv-2505-14124:
Big teacher networks can train small ones, but teachers are costly to build and store. Hongjun Choi and co-authors drop the teacher entirely in a 2025 paper, using a patch-swapping trick to let one network teach itself.

The trick swaps patches between two images of the same class, making paired versions of differing confidence. The network then learns by aligning its own predictions across those pairs, a stand-in for a teacher's guidance. Nothing is added to the model: no extra parts, no new parameters, just one augmentation step. Across image classification, segmentation, and detection tests, the method beat other teacher-free approaches and even many teacher-based ones. Simplicity, the authors argue, is the point.
arxiv-2505-14224:
Atanu Manna and Bhakti Bhusan Manna prove a sign-flip path exists for a bent spread equation in a 2025 paper. The equation pairs a spread term with a pull that fades by a set power of range. Signs in the path flip by zone, and its shape holds two round symmetries.

The team lifts the task to a curved ball frame, where it takes a cleaner form. A kept-still sub-room of paths with the right symmetry hosts the hunt. Pack maths then yields the flip path in that room, they show.
arxiv-2505-14324:
Saulo Diles, Miguel Angel Martin Contreras, and Alfredo Vega use holography based models of the strong force to study heavy mesons, particles made of a heavy quark and its anti-partner. Such models give the masses of these particles and how fast they shed light, through sums done in a higher dim space.

The authors turn those results around to pull out new facts. From a known rule of non-relativistic theory they get the mass of the heavy quark itself, plus widths for decays into three photons, or into light and glue carriers. They extend the work to excited states and compare the numbers with real data where it exists.
arxiv-2505-14424:
Levin Hornischer and Hannes Leitgeb explain neural networks by the reasons their neurons carry in a 2025 paper. Interpretability tools usually say which inputs mattered, not what a neuron stands for. Their method assigns each neuron a reasons vector, built from a mathematical philosophy of evidence. Reading that vector against a claim, like this image shows a two, tells how strongly the neuron speaks for or against it.

The scheme handles polysemantic neurons, single units serving several concepts, which break simpler labels. It runs on forward passes alone, so it scales, and nudging a neuron along its reasons vector changes outputs as predicted, a faithfulness check. The authors also show networks can be trained to sharpen their reason structure, with gains in robustness and fairness among the payoffs.
arxiv-2505-14524:
Sending each user question to the right language model is a sorting chore with a safety twist: stray, foreign, or unsafe queries must be caught, not misrouted. Richard Šléher and co-authors release in 2025 a benchmark for guarded query routing across law, finance, and healthcare, with seven extra datasets of out-of-domain traps. They race model-based routers, guardrail systems, and plain classifiers.

A simple wide network with out-of-domain detection won the balance: eighty-eight percent accuracy in under four milliseconds. A classic embedding method was fastest, under a millisecond, at eighty percent. Big models scored highest, ninety-one percent, but answered hundreds of times slower.
arxiv-2505-14724:
Michał Jabłonowski settles an open problem about moves on surface links and adds new tools for them. His 2025 paper deals with surfaces knotted in four-dimensional space, drawn as flat diagrams. A known list of ten moves is meant to turn any diagram of a surface into any other of the same surface.

He proves the fifth move on the list can never be faked by the other nine plus plain shifts. The proof uses a marker that only the fifth move can change. He then builds a counting tool from an algebra called a biquandle. With it he shows endless pairs of ribbon knots that share a group but differ in a finer trait.
arxiv-2505-14924:
Shashwat Khandelwal and a co-author present SecCAN, a 2025 design that builds attack detection into a car network controller itself. Cars talk over a bus protocol called CAN, which attackers can spoof. Existing detectors sit on separate chips or computers, so each message must travel to the detector, adding delay and software load. SecCAN taps messages inside the controller as they arrive, so detection overlaps with reception.

A small built-in machine learning engine does the checking. Built on a programmable chip, the design hid detection fully inside the reception window for every message size. It caught multiple attack types at top accuracy with no software overhead for the car's computer. The extra hardware stayed modest, under 30 percent more lookup tables than a standard controller.
arxiv-2505-15024:
Furong Jia, David Sontag, and Monica Agrawal audit where medical chat models get their knowledge in a 2025 paper. Models never trained on hospital records still answer clinical questions well. Their smarts came from giant scraped text piles, and nobody had checked how the piles' makeup shapes the answers.

The team tested models on clinical jargon and on shaky medical claims, then counted matching material in the training piles. Jargon skill tracked how often terms appeared in the piles, yet terms thick in real hospital notes are often rare there. Worse, a real slice of the piles backs disputed claims that models then repeat. The audit argues for deliberate menu planning in training data.
arxiv-2505-15224: Jianing Li studies towers of number fields where the arithmetic eventually stops changing. In Iwasawa theory, Fukuda showed that class groups along a cyclic p-tower stabilize. Li widens the stage to what he calls potential cyclic p-towers, where the Galois group mixes a p-part with an arbitrary second group, as in radical towers built by stacking p-th roots. He extends Fukuda's stabilization result to this broader family of towers. The paper also carries Iwasawa's class number formula over from the classic setting to potential Zp-extensions.
arxiv-2505-15424:
Yan-Shuo Liang, Jia-Rui Chen, and Wu-Jun Li help large language models learn new tasks in sequence without erasing old ones, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Their method builds on LoRA, a popular trick that fine-tunes a model by adding small low-rank patches instead of retraining the whole network.

The usual recipe adds a fresh patch for each new task, but then old and new patches sway old tasks equally, which invites forgetting. The team's method, GainLoRA, also adds a patch per task, yet it routes them through small gating modules. The gates blend the patches while damping the new patch's effect on old tasks. That restraint protects what the model already knows. The authors report better overall performance across a run of tasks. The work targets assistants that must keep absorbing new skills over their working life.
arxiv-2505-15524:
Lang Gao and co-authors find a way in a 2025 paper to grade bias in language models with no hand-made test sets. Past grades build labeled cases group by group, a slow craft that catches few kinds of bias. Their lens looks inside the model own map of ideas instead.

Bias shows when two pole ideas, such as good and bad mood, lean in a lopsided way toward a third idea, such as a food kind. A fair model should hold the third idea even. The team reads those leans straight from the idea map. Model teams gain a cheap, wide bias check that needs no fresh case craft.
arxiv-2505-15624:
The authors of this study dig into grokking, the odd delay where a network first memorizes its training data perfectly and only much later learns the general rule. Working with modular arithmetic tasks, they show the embedding layer is the engine of the delay. Adding embeddings to a simple multilayer network creates grokking where none occurred, while removing them lets the network generalize at once.

Two mechanisms explain it. Rare tokens get few updates, so their embeddings stall under weight decay. And the coupling between embeddings and later weights is bilinear, which plants saddle points and makes training sensitive to the starting point. Balancing how often tokens are sampled, and giving embeddings their own learning rate set by a derived ratio, eased both problems. The authors argue the lessons reach beyond this puzzle, since the same coupling sits inside every transformer.
arxiv-2505-16224:
Chuan-Ren Chen, Cheng-Wei Chiang, and Leon de la Vega study a dark matter model with a dark force carrier in a 2025 paper. Their dark Z boson mixes with the known Z boson of the Standard Model. That mix lets dark matter talk to normal matter. The setup grows from an extra dark Higgs pair and a lone scalar.

Those roots give new exotic scalars that can end dark matter clashes. The team checks the model against Higgs data and dark matter bounds. Each check rules out a distinct part of the space. Future hunts for odd Higgs decays at the upgraded LHC will probe more. Heavy scalar searches will test the same ground. The model stays testable with near-term data.
arxiv-2505-16424:
Anton Kluge and Andrea Stocco rerun famed web test tools that re-find page parts after a site change. Web tests break when a button or box moves or is renamed in a fresh build. Such tools score part traits to re-match the lost part on the new page. The pair reran the two lead tools, Similo and its heir, and probed soft spots in the first tests.

The heir bred more false matches than its sire in their fair rerun. Fixes to scores and match rules then lifted the sire tool by over five points on its home test set. A test ground twenty-three times the first size was built for the field. A blend tool that weds both lines found 98.8 percent of lost parts there.
arxiv-2505-16724:
The authors present an upgraded foundation model for brainwave recordings, built around a learned codebook of signal patterns. Their 2025 model answers a weakness of earlier large brainwave models: many fail to capture the rich rhythm content of neural oscillations. That gap caps their skill across brain-computer interface tasks.

The new design, LaBraM++, rests on firmer signal-processing choices than its parent model. It posts large gains across a spread of tasks. Results beat the original design throughout and rival other open brainwave models. Training runs faster as well. The authors offer the model as a strong base for future interface and health tools that read brain signals.
arxiv-2505-16824:
Yongick Cho and William Jacobs show that the skin between phases rules how fuel driven fluids separate, in a 2025 paper. When chemistry feeds a separating mixture, the result can settle into steady patterns no equilibrium rule predicts. Models often assume small scales sit near equilibrium, but burning happens at both molecule and droplet scales.

Microscopic simulations showed flows near phase boundaries shaped by out of equilibrium wobble at the interface itself. A first principles theory then predicted coexistence curves, where flows gather, and how droplet size scales, all matching the simulations. Interface behavior, the authors conclude, is the missing lever.
arxiv-2505-16924:
Pembe Ipek Al, Zameddin Ismailov, Fuad Kittaneh, and Satyajit Sahoo wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on ways to measure operators. Operators are rules that transform spaces of functions or signals, and analysts use special numbers to gauge their size and reach. Two such numbers are at the center here: a numerical radius and a Crawford number, each in a version tuned by a fixed operator and a parameter.

The authors give estimates for both numbers in terms of simpler versions of the same measures. The setting is broad: any complex space with a weakened inner product.
