They then study what happens when two operators are combined into a larger one by a tensor product. They also examine how the numbers behave when a sequence of operators settles toward a limit. Worked examples show the estimates in action. A final section applies the results to classes of operator-valued functions.
arxiv-2505-17524:
Reading a protein's sequence straight from a mass spectrometer is detective work with missing clues. The instrument smashes peptides into fragments, but some fragments never appear. Ye Du and co-authors tackle the gaps before guessing the sequence. Their method, LIPNovo, first repairs the model's internal picture of the spectrum.

Instead of inventing raw data, the method imagines the missing peaks in latent space, guided by what the true peptide's peak pattern should look like. A set of learnable queries reasons about which peaks are absent and fills their representations in. On three benchmark datasets the repaired-then-read approach beat the best existing sequencers by wide margins. The code is public.
arxiv-2505-18424:
Tianyi Ren and co-authors describe how careful image preparation, more than a fancy model, won a major stroke imaging contest, in a 2025 paper. In the ISLES 2024 challenge, teams received hospital-arrival CT scans. They had to outline stroke damage as it would appear on MRI days later. That is a hard forecast, since early CT often hides the lesion. Annotations came from the follow-up scans.

Their winning pipeline first strips the skull away with a deep learning tool, then applies custom brightness windowing tuned for stroke tissue. A standard large segmentation network did the rest. The system reached a mean overlap score of 28.5 on the test set, with wide variation across cases. The authors present the result as a lesson for medical imaging: thoughtful preprocessing can matter as much as architecture, especially when the signal is faint.
arxiv-2505-18624:
Arslan Sikandar and Jamil Aslam compute rare decays in which a B meson sheds a photon and a tensor meson. The decays cover the K2*(1430), f2(1270), and a2(1230) mesons. Their tool is soft-collinear effective theory, applied at next-to-leading order, which sorts the calculable parts of the process from the stubborn ones and tames large logarithms.

A two-step matching yields the soft-overlap function that the rates depend on. For the K2* channel, the predicted branching ratio lands close to measured values. The other two decays, suppressed by the weak mixing of quarks, come out far rarer. They are still within reach of running and future B physics experiments, the authors note.
arxiv-2505-18724:
Shrinking a large language model to a few bits per weight lets it run on small devices, but teaching it afterward is awkward. The teaching weights live at full precision, clash with the shrunk ones, and lose accuracy when merged back. Junyu Chen and six co-authors propose a way around all three problems in this 2025 paper.

Their method, LoTA-QAF, teaches with ternary weights, just three values, snapped to the same grid the shrunken model already uses. Because the two grids align, the teaching weights merge into the model with no loss, and every shrunken weight can still be adjusted. The paper pairs the three-valued teaching weights with a merging scheme built for the same end. The aim is fine-tuning that keeps both the small footprint and the accuracy.
arxiv-2505-18824:
Zhang and co-authors present FlatAttention, a way to run the attention step of transformer models faster on tile-based accelerator chips, in this 2025 paper. Attention is the workhorse kernel of modern AI models. On chips built from many small processing tiles, how data flows decides how much of the hardware actually works.

Their design cuts trips to main memory by using messaging built into the chip's network fabric. It reached high hardware utilization and ran several times faster than a leading baseline layout, while moving far less data. The team also searched for the best chip shape to pair with the method. Their favored design rivals a flagship GPU while needing less memory bandwidth.
arxiv-2505-18924:
Chenxi Li and co-authors use chat models to build label trees that guide which points of a 3D scan to hand tag, in a paper from 2025. Hand tags for 3D scenes cost dear, so teams tag a few points and let a model learn the rest. Past picks treat tags as flat, which wastes the rank that links broad kinds to fine ones.

The chat model drafts a rank tree of labels on its own. A spread rule then pours doubt scores down and up that tree, so picks stay spread in space and rich in kind. On two room scan sets the method lifts scores by up to four points at tag shares as low as a few in ten thousand. The authors cast rank doubt as a strong new frame.
arxiv-2505-19324:
Luca Sandrock and Thomas Schick compute a motion-planning measure in 2025 for a broad class of spaces. Topological complexity counts how hard it is to plan continuous motion in a space. The spaces here carry a special cohomology class that vanishes on every torus map yet has a nonzero power, a property called atoroidally symplectic in the paper.

The pair prove every such complex of dimension two n has topological complexity exactly four n. Their result extends an earlier theorem for smooth manifolds to general complexes. New values follow for many products of three-dimensional manifolds and for group presentation complexes. The paper ties an algebraic shadow of symplectic geometry to a concrete robotics-flavored invariant.
arxiv-2505-19924:
Takaaki Nomura, Yusuke Shimizu, and Towa Takahashi revisit a 2025 flavor model of particle physics, one built on a set of symmetry rules for leptons. Their version adds new fields so the model can match the measured mixing angle that the first version missed. The team then asks whether the same model can also explain how the universe ended up with more matter than antimatter.

At the lowest order, the model gives no matter excess at all, because its neutrino mass pattern is too simple. The authors therefore add the next order of terms and scan the settings by computer. They find ranges that fit both the measured neutrino data and the seen matter excess. In one case, the lightest neutrino must weigh at least a small lower bound that differs between the two mass orderings.
arxiv-2505-20124:
Fanheng Kong and colleagues build a benchmark that grades video models on time itself: how actions, scenes, cameras, and objects change together. Existing video tests isolate one aspect or skim surfaces. Their suite uses dense, dynamic clips and poses two tasks, captioning and question answering. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team designed interpretable, robust scoring criteria and varied the scenarios widely. Several leading models were then graded dimension by dimension, giving a fine-grained report card rather than a single number.

The weaknesses are specific. Models describe actions thinly. They lose track when several subjects act at once. They barely notice camera motion. Each failure mode points at a concrete fix for the next model generation. Data and code are public, so the benchmark can be rerun as models improve.
arxiv-2505-20224:
Shripad Garge and Deep Makadiya settled in 2025 an open case in the theory of Chevalley groups, a family of groups built from Lie theory. Splitting such a group into triangular and unitriangular parts is a basic structural fact. For one twisted family, the result was known only over special fields, not over general rings.

They introduce two new classes of rings with helpful properties and give examples of each. Their main result proves the factorizations for the remaining family over a wide class of rings, covering all fields and local rings with mild conditions. The paper closes a gap that had resisted the methods used for other cases.
arxiv-2505-20324:
Md Arman Islam and co-authors measured in 2025 how much energy the code from twenty large language models burns compared with careful human code. They ran the models on 878 coding problems of mixed difficulty from a popular practice site. Correctness was only half the question; the electricity bill was the other half.

Most models produced working code, yet their solutions often ran far heavier than the human reference versions. Two models, DeepSeek-v3 and GPT-4o, came closest to human efficiency. Two others burned more than twice the human energy on average. In hard corners such as dynamic programming, machine code could use up to 450 times the energy of the human version. The authors say efficiency belongs in how these models are judged.
arxiv-2505-20524:
Alejandro Hernández-Cano, Dhia Garbaya, Imanol Schlag, and Martin Jaggi present a 2025 paper on training large language models entirely in low-precision FP8 arithmetic. FP8 promises big speed gains, but training in it usually wobbles at scale, so engineers keep sensitive parts in higher precision and lose the benefit. The team designs model architectures where every matrix multiplication inside the transformer blocks runs in FP8, in both the forward and backward passes.

Their design tames the large outlier activations that usually destabilize low-precision training. The result trains stably over long runs while matching the downstream quality of standard sixteen-bit training. They also name the metrics worth watching to foresee divergence before it strikes. The authors present the work as the first full-FP8 recipe that holds at scale, unlocking the format's throughput for real pretraining.
arxiv-2505-20624:
Usman Naseem and a large international team release POLAR, a dataset for studying online polarization across languages and cultures. Most past work is monolingual, culture-bound, or tied to a single event. POLAR holds over 110,000 instances in 22 languages from varied platforms and real events. Each item is labeled for detection, type, and manifestation of polarization, with annotation adapted to local context.

The team fine-tuned six small pretrained language models and tested large models in zero-shot and few-shot modes. Results show how unevenly current tools read polarization across languages. The benchmark aims to widen computational social science past its English core.
arxiv-2505-20724:
Il Gyeong Choi and Dong-han Yeom probe a cosmic censorship puzzle in a 2025 paper. The weak cosmic censorship idea holds that singularities stay hidden inside black holes, never naked to outside view. A classic gravity collapse model, named for Oppenheimer and Snyder, offers a test bed.

Metric models with a naked singularity do allow such a collapse while respecting an energy condition. But those metrics are not true solutions of Einstein's equations, so the setup stays a toy. Adding a thin shell makes the model a real solution, yet the shell must break the energy condition near the singularity. The authors find no fully physical counterexample. They note modified gravity might yet supply one, which keeps the question productively open.
arxiv-2505-20824:
Kai Chen and co-authors stress-test teams of medical AI agents for safety. Hospitals are beginning to let several language-model agents consult together, but a single bad actor might poison the group's advice. Their benchmark, MedSentry, throws five thousand adversarial medical prompts at four common team layouts, spanning twenty-five threat categories.

Layouts differed sharply in resilience. The open shared-pool design, where every agent reads everything, fell easiest to contamination. Spread-out designs with redundant, semi-isolated agents held up best. The team then built a guard that profiles agents' personalities, spots the malicious ones, and corrects them, restoring safety close to baseline. The authors offer the bench and the guard as design guidance for safer medical AI teams, where a poisoned consensus could harm real patients.
arxiv-2505-21024:
Charles London and Varun Kanade prove that pause tokens strictly increase the expressivity of constant depth transformers. Pause tokens are simple filler symbols that reliably improve transformer performance on language and math tasks, with no theory to explain why. A formal separation result settles what the tokens actually add.

With bounded precision activations, transformers without pause tokens compute only a strict subset of a basic circuit class. Adding polynomially many pause tokens lets them express the whole class. With logarithmic precision, pause tokens reach a stronger class that matches known upper bounds. Empirically, two layer masked transformers learn parity with pause tokens but appear unable to learn it without them.
arxiv-2505-21124:
Rohit Kanchi and co-authors release UniFoil in this 2025 paper, a vast public data set of airfoil flows for machine learning. Airfoils are wing cross-sections, and predicting air flow over them drives aircraft and turbine design. Most existing sets cover only smooth, fully rough-turbulent flows at low speed. Real design also needs the tricky shift zone where smooth flow turns turbulent, plus shock waves at high speed.

UniFoil holds over half a million simulated cases across wide speed and size ranges. It spans more than 4,800 laminar-flow airfoils and 30,000 turbulent ones. Flow physics come from standard engineering solvers with a transition model for the shift zone. The set is free under an open license, aimed at data-driven aerodynamics research.
arxiv-2505-21224:
Abderrahmane Issam and co-authors look inside translation models to see how they survive grammatical errors in the input, in a 2025 paper. Neural machine translation often copes with typos and broken grammar, but earlier work mostly catalogued failures or patched them. The inner mechanism of the coping was unknown.

The team probed internal representations layer by layer with error detection tests and similarity analysis. The encoder appears to flag the error first, then shift the faulty word's representation toward its correct form. Attention analysis found specific heads, dubbed Robustness Heads, that track meaningful language units when errors appear. Fine-tuning for robustness made models lean harder on exactly those heads. The findings suggest error handling is a localized, learnable circuit rather than a diffuse property. That localization, the authors note, could guide cheaper robustness fixes.
arxiv-2505-21524:
Amitai Yacobi and three co-authors showed that shared representations across kinds of data can be learned from unpaired samples, in a paper published in 2025. Shared representations let a text search fetch a photo, and more. Standard methods lean on matched pairs, which are hard to obtain. Their path builds a drift map for each kind of data alone, then reads the deep shape of each map.

The two shapes turn out to hold the same cross-kind links. Tests in vision and language work support the claim. The representations did well at retrieval tasks, made cross-kind generations, and sorted new kinds with no fresh training. To their knowledge, no earlier work has shown this from bare samples alone. The authors present the representation as nearly universal, free of the kinds it was built from.
arxiv-2505-21624:
Elena Rasia and co-authors model the gas content of galaxy clusters in a 2025 paper. Galaxy clusters are the largest bound systems in the cosmos. The share of normal matter in a cluster can help pin down cosmic values, while the hot gas share shows how cluster plasma and galaxy growth affect each other.

The team used computer runs of about 300 massive clusters from a joint project. They modeled how each share changes with cluster mass and with time, back to when the cosmos was younger. Simple power laws fit poorly, missing the flattening at high mass and the drop at low mass. Curved forms in log space fit far better. Shares measured in smaller inner zones changed more over time than those in larger zones.
arxiv-2505-21924:
Kamyar Rashidi and Matthew Sfeir present a 2025 method for reading material traits from terahertz light tests. Such tests probe low-tone light traits, but the key constants hide inside the signal and need math to extract. Past fixes lean on narrow guesses that fail off their home turf.

Their take pairs a wave transfer matrix with a breeding-style search that tunes the fit. The pair pulls the bend index of a sample straight from the test trace. Across wide index, shape, and tone spans it matched or beat top methods in the checks shown.
arxiv-2505-22024:
Long-Khanh Pham and co-authors build RESOUND, a system that reconstructs speech from silent video of a talking face. Lip reading is hard because the same mouth shapes serve many sounds, and tone, accent, and rhythm leave few visual traces. Their design splits the job along a theory of voice production. One path predicts the sound's prosody, its melody and timing, while a second path extracts the words' content.

Splitting the task lets each half learn on its own terms. The system feeds in speech units, learned without labels, beside the usual sound pictures when it builds the waveform. That mix helps the output keep the speaker's identity while sounding natural and clear. On two standard test sets, RESOUND beat rival methods on every scoring measure. The authors present the split design as the reason for the gain.
arxiv-2505-22124:
Si Zhang and co-authors tackle nurse staffing under shifting demand in a 2025 paper. Rosters must meet patient needs, nurse wishes, and strict regularity rules. A large Singapore hospital time policy anchors the study. Bounded flexibility is their middle path between rigid and loose schedules.

They model the problem as a multi-stage stochastic program. A two-stage rewrite with block structure cuts the computing cost. A generative AI-guided algorithm then solves real cases. Hospital data showed real savings and happier flexibility. Regularity of shifts barely suffered in the trade, a key win for staff morale.
arxiv-2505-22224:
Senne Berden and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on training prediction models for planning tasks without calling a solver at every step. In many jobs, a model first guesses the numbers a plan needs, then a solver picks the best plan. Training the guesser to serve the plan, not just to be accurate, works better but costs huge computing time.

Their trick uses the shape of straight-line plans: a plan is best only if it beats its nearest neighbor plans. They precompute those neighbors and grade guesses against them, skipping the solver. Tests show training runs far faster with little loss in plan quality. The method targets the linear plans used across much of logistics.
arxiv-2505-22624:
Ryan French and co-authors take the first spectra in two decades of dark rain above solar flare loops in this 2025 paper. These features, called supra-arcade downflows, appear as dark tendrils sinking through bright flare fans. Their origin is unknown, partly for lack of spectral data since 2003. A 2022 mid-sized flare gave the team its chance with two space instruments.

Iron lines revealed faster downward speeds and broader motion inside the dark features than around them. Their temperatures matched the fan's. Combining two viewing angles gave full 3D speeds for four features, which spread apart above the loops. The team also found stealth versions visible only in spectra.
arxiv-2505-22724:
Ralph Pudritz and co-authors wrote this 2025 review on how planets get their makeup. Surveys have now measured thousands of planets around other stars, including rough readings of their air and cores. The review asks how those traits trace back to the discs of gas and dust where planets form.

The authors gather fresh views of young discs from the ALMA array and the Webb space telescope, plus the latest theory and simulations. They argue that winds driven by magnetic fields, not swirling turbulence, steer how discs evolve. Those winds shape rings, gaps, chemistry, and how planets drift. The same processes stamp the sizes, orbits, and air of the planets that result.
arxiv-2505-22824:
Classical mechanics often assumes we can see the full state of a system, but real machines give us only partial views. Dongzhe Zheng, writing alone in a 2025 paper, builds a geometric theory for such half-seen systems. The key idea is a fiber bundle induced by observation, which layers possible full states over each partial reading.

Within that frame, Zheng extends Dirac's theory of constrained motion to cover both state and observation constraints at once. Results sort out when such bundles exist and describe their Poisson structures and symmetry reductions. The paper also gives exact conditions for when a system stays integrable, with a method to build its conserved pairs. The classic link between symmetry and conservation is extended as well, with uses from mechanics to safety-critical control.
arxiv-2505-23224:
Zhitao He and co-authors present a 2025 paper on teaching image-language models to know the edge of their own knowledge. These models reason in steps, but if confidence is judged only on the final answer, early errors snowball into invented facts. Each step needs its own confidence check.

Their framework scores confidence step by step, using two reward signals: one from the text itself and one that crosses between image and text. Training starts with guided fine-tuning on those signals, then a reward-based stage aligns the model's sense of its limits. The goal is answers that pause or hedge where the model is unsure, rather than bluffing.
arxiv-2505-23524:
Rui Xia and four co-authors present a 2025 computer vision paper on finding when actions happen in videos, with no labels at all. Temporal action localization normally needs hand-marked boundaries, which are expensive. Unsupervised methods struggle because pretrained features fixate on the most distinctive frames and video alone gives weak boundary cues. Their method brings in two helpers: a vision-language model and the audio track.

Language-guided and classification features are enhanced together so attention spreads beyond the flashiest moments. Sound supplies context that sharpens where actions start and stop. A self-supervised scheme then aligns the multiple views without any annotation. On two public benchmarks the system beat several state-of-the-art rivals. The authors target video retrieval and analysis pipelines drowning in unlabeled footage.
arxiv-2505-24124:
Jiuyu Sun, Yongping Du, and Erjun Kan proposed a way to spot a new class of magnets in a 2025 paper. These materials, called altermagnets, split electron spin by direction while showing no net magnetism. That trait makes them hard to tell apart from a more common class of magnets.

The team shows that stretching such a material in one direction breaks its symmetry in a useful way. Light can then pick up signals that the common class does not give. Tests by computer on two sample materials, one thin layer and one bulk solid, gave signals strong enough for normal lab tools. The authors offer this as a fast, gentle screen for new candidates.
arxiv-2505-24424:
Amit Peleg, Naman Deep Singh, and Matthias Hein worked on teaching CLIP to grasp how concepts relate in two thousand twenty-five. CLIP links images and text and does well at sorting and search. Yet it often misses composition, which words go with which objects or actions in a scene.

Their fine-tuning method, CLIC, trains on groups of images with their captions at once. It improved both word-level sensitivity and deeper meaning on a hard test, across several CLIP versions. Search results also got better, not worse, which past attempts often caused. After short training, their model was the best compositional CLIP on that test, and the code and models are public.
arxiv-2505-24524:
Callum Berry adds in 2025 a new member to the known set of lone symplectic singular points in geometry. The new case sits in a chart of a partial smoothing of a four-dimensional quotient space. It stands alone and its local shape has no loops, like its known peers.

Berry shows the new case differs from all known ones by one trait. The cone that touches it at its point fails a basic reduced test that the others pass. All twelve best partial smoothings of the new case are found. In the same work, twice that count is found for the parent quotient case, which widens the full map of this corner of geometry.
arxiv-2505-24624:
Georgios Amanatidis and co-authors open the study of buying mechanisms that learn from a prediction, in a 2025 paper. In a budget-feasible mechanism, a buyer with a hard budget limit purchases services from self-interested sellers and wants the most value for the money. A modern twist gives the algorithm a prediction, possibly wrong, of the best achievable value, and asks it to do well when the guess is right without collapsing when it is wrong.

The authors work in the online version, where sellers arrive in random order. They design mechanisms that stay truthful and inside budget while beating the best known guarantees without predictions, for both monotone and non-monotone value functions of the submodular kind. Their gains lean on the predicted optimum. A matching negative result shows that in the offline version, predictions barely help approximation at all. The contrast marks where prediction power actually lives.
arxiv-2505-24724:
Ethereum payments can secretly carry chat, and Xihan Xiong and five colleagues read millions of them to see what people say. Every Ethereum transaction has an input field meant for talking to smart contracts. Users also tuck plain-language notes into it, and the team sifted the chain's whole history through February 2024.

They found 867,140 messages worth reading. English notes often warned about scams and sounded gloomy. Chinese notes leaned warm and social, with small symbolic payments attached. Senders formed small, loose clusters. The team also shows how attackers abuse the channel during on-chain scams.
arxiv-2505-24824:
Old maps record how land was used centuries before satellites existed, but reading them by machine is hard. Marta López-Rauhut, Hongyu Zhou, Mathieu Aubry, and Loic Landrieu release a dataset in 2025 that covers all of metropolitan France. It holds map collections from the eighteenth, nineteenth, and twentieth centuries. Modern land labels come free, and the team hand-labeled nearly 23,000 square kilometers of the older maps. Styles shift between eras, and the land itself changed, as marshes gave way to forest.

They test three segmentation approaches: one trained on the hand labels, and two that lean only on modern labels, one translating old maps into modern style first. The authors discuss how such tools can track landscape change over centuries.
arxiv-2506-00024:
Ying-Ying Jin and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on gyrogroups, a twist on groups where the join rule need not commute. Their case adds a topology, so shape and algebra meet. They ask when such a gyrogroup can sit in a product of many small, well behaved ones. The product view is a standard test of how tame the space is.

They give full terms for when the fit works, for two grades of separation. The terms mix a separation trait, a balance trait, and a count trait for how tight the space is near its identity. Proofs run both ways, from the traits to the fit and back. The work pins down the shape of these odd algebraic spaces.
arxiv-2506-00224:
Bernardo Subercaseaux and co-authors present a computer method for symmetric point sets in geometry, in a 2025 paper. Some classic puzzles ask for point sets that meet strict rules and are as large or small as a set type allows. Past computer searches used logic solvers but did not build in rotational symmetry.

Their method codes symmetry straight into the search, which cuts the variables to solve. A second local search tool then turns the abstract design into real points. The pair found new best sets for two known puzzles, one with twenty one points where twenty three was the prior best. Symmetry also makes the sets easier for people to read.
arxiv-2506-00324:
Cameras and AI systems judge depth and motion by matching pixels between two views, but some spots are far harder to match than others. Jisoo Jeong and co-authors improve that training in a 2025 paper from Qualcomm AI Research. Standard training treats every pixel the same, which wastes effort on easy spots and starves the hard ones.

The team maps how unsure the model is at each pixel and uses that map in two new training losses. One loss pushes the model to spend more effort on hard pixels. The other steers it away from spots hidden in one view, where no true match exists. Tests on both motion and depth tasks showed clear gains from the paired losses.
arxiv-2506-00424:
Chamika Sudusinghe and co-authors present COGNATE, a tool to speed sparse tensor programs on new hardware, in a research paper from 2025. Such programs sit at the core of deep learning and graph work. New chips for them are costly to test, since early tests rely on slow simulators, and cost models need much data.

COGNATE trains its cost model on cheap data from standard chips first. It then fine-tunes the model with a small set of samples from the new chip. The tool needs only a small share of the usual data for like accuracy. Tests show clear speed gains on two core sparse tasks.
arxiv-2506-00524:
Hui Li and co-authors demonstrated generalised quantum fluctuation theorems in a 2025 experiment. Such theorems extend the second law of thermodynamics into a statistical form, linking forward and reverse process probabilities. Their quantum version, with coherence and varied quantum noise, had stayed open.

Using a photonic system, the team validated a theorem that applies to general quantum processes with nonclassical traits. The ratio between quasi-probabilities of the forward process and any of several time-reversed ones obeyed the predicted rule. Coherence created imaginary parts of entropy production, which govern a phase factor in the theorem. The work gives a basic toolkit for noisy quantum information work.
arxiv-2506-00724:
Siddharth Prabhu, Srinivas Rangarajan, and Mayuresh Kothare bring a multiple shooting method to neural ordinary differential equations. Their 2025 paper works on models that learn the rules of a changing system from data. In multiple shooting, a trajectory is cut into short pieces that can be solved in parallel, then stitched by equality constraints.

That stitching is the hard part for neural models, which is why the method saw little use there. The authors use a condensing trick to fold the stitch rules into the training problem. First-order optimizers such as Adam can then train the model directly. The payoff is stability: multiple shooting handles wiggly and long trajectories far better than a single long integration.
arxiv-2506-00924:
Three authors led by Parsa Hassani build a two-lens gauge for how good a video stream feels to its viewers. Network teams know line marks such as loss and lag, yet those only hint at felt quality. User comments on live streams hold the felt side, but they pour in as raw text at huge scale. Their frame reads both sides and rolls them up per operator for fair checks.

One lens trains a model on lab mean scores to call felt quality from line marks alone. The next lens sifts live comments with a language model and scores the apt ones on the same scale. A set of near 48,000 comments, with fake operator tags and time stamps, backs the build. A gap score then sets felt and line reads side by side.
arxiv-2506-01024:
Xiaochen Hong and a team of co-authors use ultrasound to probe how a magnetic field bends sound waves in a honeycomb magnet. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies a cobalt compound with a flat, near-two-dimensional lattice. Sound speed and damping are tracked across temperature and field. Both shift in ways that expose strong spin-lattice coupling.

Below its Néel point, the material takes an out-of-plane ferrimagnetic order. Careful study of the full data set backs a triple-Q ground state for the compound. The team also sets their sound data beside published heat-flow results. That match teases out how much of the flow is carried by phonons, the sound quanta themselves. The work promotes ultrasound as a sharp probe of magnetic traits. Frustrated honeycomb magnets are a live test bed for exotic order.
arxiv-2506-01124:
Bankim Chandra Das and co-authors show strong interplay between single light particles sent toward each other, in a 2025 physics paper. Making photons interact is a key step toward computers that run on light. The clash range is usually tiny, which forces a trade-off between strength and pulse length. The team sent photons through matter made of excited atoms, moving in opposite directions.

The setup stretched the interplay range to a record length, over a millionth of a second. Whole light pulses could then block each other fully, with timing that tunes the effect. With three photons, the interplay grew stronger still when one met a pair. Theory and simulations match the lab results. The work points to firm, on-demand control of light with light.
arxiv-2506-01324:
Junghyun Lee and co-authors study how to group movement paths by which hidden chain made them in a 2025 paper. Each path comes from one of several unknown Markov chains, which step between states by fixed chances. The task is to sort long sets of such paths into the right groups, without knowing the chains in advance.

The authors first set a floor on the error rate that depends on how far apart the chains are. They then give a two stage method, a spectral grouping with a new embedding for chains, followed by one likelihood based reassign step. Math proof shows near best error under fair conditions, and early tests support the approach.
arxiv-2506-01424:
Yujun Shi and Xiaoting Feng ask whether magnetic flux concentrators still work when they are cut from solid blocks into discrete pieces. Concentrators gather and focus magnetic fields for sensors and instruments, but solid designs waste material and weight. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the pair ran finite element simulations comparing chopped-up structures against solid counterparts at guiding and concentrating flux. Even an unoptimized design cut along one dimension performed comparably to the solid version while using about a tenth of the material.

Extending the chopping to two dimensions in three-dimensional devices promises savings of about a hundredfold in material, by their simulations. Nothing in the design was tuned, so better layouts should do more. The authors pitch the approach for applications where weight and cost dominate, such as portable instruments and large sensor arrays.
arxiv-2506-01724:
Tong Wang, Jiaqi Wang, and Shu Kong wrote a 2025 computer science paper on teaching vision-language models with less hand-labeled data. Such models learn from huge web data first, then need labeled examples for each new task. Labeling costs money and often takes expert skill.

Active learning cuts that cost by picking only the most useful examples to label. The team's twist is to also pull in free open data that matches the task. They call the method Active Learning with Open Resources. Adding these found examples raised scores by a lot in their tests. They also compare ways to tune the model once the data is picked.
arxiv-2506-01824:
Pedro Zuidberg Dos Martires (2025) studies probabilistic circuits through the lens of quantum information theory. Circuits of this kind build probability models by nesting sums and products, and they are prized because questions like the total probability of partial evidence can be answered quickly and exactly. The paper asks what happens when the numbers flowing through such a circuit are replaced by matrices of the kind used to describe quantum states.

The result is a new model class, positive unital circuits, in which evaluations run over positive semi-definite matrices rather than plain positive numbers. The author shows this class strictly contains ordinary probabilistic circuits and also contains a recently proposed circuit family built on the same matrix idea. The quantum viewpoint thus unifies and extends several tractable model families, and may point to new algorithms for reasoning under uncertainty.
arxiv-2506-01924:
Tim Linke, Dane Sterbentz, and three colleagues couple two simulation methods that see matter at very different scales, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Molecular dynamics tracks individual atoms, while direct simulation Monte Carlo follows representative particles in a gas flow. Many problems, like hypersonic flight, need both views at once.

Earlier couplings decided cell by cell in a limited way. The new framework generalizes that decision and adds operators that translate between the two descriptions, lifting detail up and restricting it down across length and time scales. The authors verify the coupling against basic conservation laws. They then demonstrate it on a hypersonic flow case and weigh its accuracy gain over plain Monte Carlo simulation. Strengths, limits, and further uses are discussed. The goal is one seamless simulation where atoms matter locally but the flow is vast.
arxiv-2506-02024:
Serving large language models means handling sudden surges in demand without missing response-time goals. One fix is to run a precise FP16 model normally and switch to a faster FP8 model during surges, but keeping two full copies of the model wastes memory. Haeun Lee and co-authors present NestedFP, a method that stores the FP8 weights inside the FP16 weights so both share one memory footprint.

The overlay uses a compact data format, and a specialised matrix kernel reads it with little loss of speed. Quality and speed stay close to the separate models in both modes. The result is a flexible platform that can shift precision up or down as load changes, helping services meet their response goals without buying extra memory. The code is public, so other serving teams can test the method on their own models and traffic patterns.
arxiv-2506-02224:
Darc and co-authors report a long optical follow-up of a gravitational wave event in work from 2025. Most such events come from merging black hole pairs, and none has a confirmed light counterpart yet.

Mergers inside the disk of an active galaxy might flare in visible light. The team searched with a southern telescope, focusing on known active galaxies in the event zone. No candidate passed as a real counterpart. Using their timing and depth, they constrained three flare models and mapped where detectable flares are most likely. The framework can guide future joint searches.
arxiv-2506-02324:
Blockchains promise systems that run without trusted middlemen, yet no one knew whether crypto networks were actually becoming more or less spread out over time. Harang Ju, Ehsan Valavi, Madhav Kumar, and Sinan Aral build a framework for measuring how control is shared in crypto systems and compare the measures in common use.

They apply the framework to seven large crypto ecosystems, across five parts of each system, over more than 15 years. The broad trend is toward wider sharing of control. Recent years, though, show movement the other way in three areas: the consensus layer that validates transactions, markets for non-fungible tokens, and the developer community. The authors offer the framework as a shared, repeatable base for researchers, regulators, and builders who track how these systems evolve.
arxiv-2506-02624:
Bruno Felipe Costa and Taufik Abrao design a combined communication and sensing system for satellites in low Earth orbit in a 2025 study. The framework pairs a modulation built for fast motion with a sharing scheme that splits signals among users. Satellite links suffer imperfect channel knowledge and leftover interference after cancellation, which the authors build into their measures.

They derive sharper signal quality formulas and fundamental sensing limits through an estimation bound that includes echo gain. Resource allocation is then posed as a fairness problem, maximizing the worst user's share under those limits. The results guide waveform and power choices for orbit networks.
arxiv-2506-03024:
Madhusudan Srinivasan and Jubril Abdel present a fairness testing tool in a 2025 paper. Language models can carry biases from their training data, and unfair outputs are hard to catch. Bias that hits people at the overlap of traits, such as age plus gender, is missed most often by older test methods.

Their tool, GenFair, builds test cases in a systematic way, splitting inputs into groups, mutating them, and probing edge values. Changed versions of each case are then compared by tone to expose unfair shifts in the replies. On two leading models, GenFair found far more fairness faults than template or grammar-based rivals. Its cases were also more varied and more coherent. The authors offer it as a scalable way to audit models before release.
arxiv-2506-03224:
Jinwei Zeng and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on forecasting carbon emissions block by block in a city from open data. Fine maps of emissions guide plans to cut them. Hand counts are slow and costly to build. Once trained, an open data model can map new areas from data on hand.

Their model, OpenCarbon, joins two open sources. Satellite shots give the broad, still view of a place. Point of interest data adds fine facts on what each site does. A cross type module blends the two and weighs how site uses mix. A neighbor module catches how emissions clump in space. Tests show a clear gain over rivals in fit.
arxiv-2506-03424:
Nicole Schneider and three co-authors give language models a way to reason about distance in a 2025 paper. Models are weak at judging how far apart places are, which hurts tasks like trip planning and local search tips. Their method, DistRAG, stores real distances between towns in a graph.

When a question arrives, the system pulls the part of the graph that matters and hands it to the model as context. The model then answers with true distance facts instead of guessing from text patterns alone. The authors call this a flexible first step toward a basic world model for models. It can cover any set of places the graph holds. Tests show the model answering distance questions it could not handle before.
arxiv-2506-03524:
The ByteDance Seed team lets a code model curate its own training data in a 2025 paper. Code data lifts not just coding skill but general smarts. Human filtering rules are costly and hard to scale. Their pipeline uses models to score and filter code instead.

The result is Seed-Coder, a family of open 8B models. Base, instruct, and reasoning versions share the data recipe. Fine-tuning and preference tuning polish the instruct model. Long chain-of-thought training powers the reasoning version. Scores top open models of similar size across code tasks. Some much larger models are beaten as well. Editing, completion, and reasoning tasks all shine.
arxiv-2506-03924:
Particles that jostle in a line cannot pass each other, and rare swings in their flow obey set laws. Xiaofeng Xue and Linjie Zhao prove such laws for a weakly lopsided version of that system in a 2025 paper. Two quantities are tracked: the total current across a point and the path of one tagged particle. The system starts from one of its steady states.

The laws they prove sit between everyday wobble and the rarest swings, a range called moderate deviations. Proofs cover whole paths, not just end values. The argument leans on, and shortens, their own earlier proofs for the symmetric case. The work is pure probability theory aimed at specialists in particle systems.
arxiv-2506-04324:
Jonathan Kroth and Srimoyee Sen present a theory paper from 2025 on placing a lone Weyl fermion on a lattice. Physicists use grid models to study such particles, but getting a single unpaired one on a finite grid is tricky. Past work used a wall defect; the new work uses a string defect instead.

The string is the grid form of a known continuum object tied to axion physics. The authors work in a time-based setup and show the lone particle emerges for the basic case. They note the step to curved settings and higher cases is direct. Readers get a fresh route that may aid work on exotic gauge theories and the early universe.
arxiv-2506-04624:
Takashi Wada and colleagues published a computer science paper in 2025 on representing sentence meaning cheaply. Their method uses fixed word vectors instead of large neural encoders. A sentence is represented by simply averaging its word vectors. That costs almost nothing to compute at run time.

The team started from vectors inside a trained sentence model. They refined those vectors with sentence-level statistical analysis. Two further training methods sharpened them still more. The analysis strips out parts that matter little for sentence meaning. It also rescales words by their real influence on meaning. Tests in one language and across languages beat older static models. The method even topped a basic transformer model on one benchmark.
arxiv-2506-04924:
Han Wang and many colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on a computer model that flags intensive care patients at high risk of death. Early warning helps staff aim scarce time and beds at those who need them most. Past tools often used simple chart data and plain sorting methods.

Their model, called ALFIA, builds on a BERT language model tuned for the task. It blends features from many layers of the network, weighting each layer as it learns. The team trained it on a strict 24-hour data window they built for fair tests. ALFIA beat top chart-based tools on a key score for rare-event tasks. The design is modular, so parts can be swapped or updated.
arxiv-2506-05024:
Bogna Kubik and co-authors present a low-noise method to estimate light flux for the Euclid space mission, in work from 2025. Euclid maps the dark universe, and exact brightness measures drive its science. Its infrared detectors record counts that follow Poisson statistics with linked noise.

The proposed fit has a closed-form answer, so it runs fast and stays unbiased. It also yields a sound quality score for each measure, which flags suspect data. The team compares the method with rival estimators on flight-like detectors. Anomaly hunting on those detectors is shown as well. The approach should suit any mission using like infrared sensors.
arxiv-2506-05424:
Guo-Hua Liang and three co-authors track a spinning particle on curved paths in a 2025 physics paper. A spin one half particle is confined to a curve drawn on a curved surface. The geometry of both path and surface bends its motion. Curvature terms act like gauge and scalar potentials in its Hamiltonian.

Path curvature, normal curvature, and torsion shape the gauge part. Surface curvature shapes the scalar part. The resulting spin precession is worked out with and without a slow change approximation. Under that approximation, surface topology fixes the spin's rotation along a boundary. Helix paths show how geodesic and non geodesic routes differ. A classic closed curve, Viviani's, shows pure surface dependence. The theory points to spin control through shaped nanochannels.
arxiv-2506-05524:
Zoe Godard, Derek Moulton, and Sarah Waters model a soft porous material squeezed and released in cycles. Poroelastic response depends on boundary conditions, pore structure, and stiffness in tangled ways, and real materials add uneven properties on top. Their one-dimensional nonlinear model pairs Darcy flow through the pores with a neo-Hookean solid skeleton. A Gaussian bump imposes smooth variation in stiffness or permeability.

The system faces cyclic stress or cyclic displacement at one end, across a range of frequencies and bump positions. Stress-driven and displacement-driven runs answer in qualitatively different ways. Diseased tendon behavior inspired the work, though the framework is general.
arxiv-2506-05624: Siddharth Mulherkar builds weights that meet sharp Mizohata-Takeuchi type estimates, in a mathematics paper from twenty twenty-five. Such estimates are weighted Fourier restriction estimates. Using tools from high-dimensional probability, he builds a large class of weights meeting the sharp bound. Read as a statement about chance, a generic weight meets the sharp inequality with high probability, up to a small epsilon loss. The abstract is brief, stating the construction and how to read it, without further detail.
arxiv-2506-05724:
Joshua Holroyd studies how solutions of a discrete Painlevé equation behave far out in a 2025 math paper. The Painlevé family of equations sits at a crossroads of physics and pure math, with solutions that resist plain formulas. The q-version replaces smooth change with jumps scaled by a factor q. Holroyd looks at the second equation of the family when q lies very close to one.

In that regime, the leading behavior of most solutions is written in elliptic functions, the classic doubly repeating functions. The slow drift of that behavior is captured by complete elliptic integrals. Classical Painlevé theory has a matching story, and this paper builds the discrete twin. Such limiting maps help compute and classify solutions that cannot be written directly.
arxiv-2506-06124:
Lukas Gehring and Florian Tschorsch design a data trustee that learns as little as possible. Trustees sit between data owners and data users, passing answers across while keeping the raw records private. Most designs still let the trustee see more than it needs. Their system, PrivTru, flips the flow: before asking sources for anything, it computes the smallest amount of information that could answer the user's query.

The authors prove this amount is optimal in a strong sense. No matter what the trustee already believes, PrivTru leaks no more than that minimum to it, while the answer's usefulness stays intact. Privacy here is a property of the design, not of promises or policy. The paper offers the construction as a technical template for the data trustee roles now being written into data-sharing law.
arxiv-2506-06224:
Cesare Vianello, Matteo Ferraretto, and Luca Salasnich study a tiny system of atoms split between two wells. Their 2025 paper works at temperatures above zero, not just in the coldest state. The two wells are not equal, and that lack of balance is a key part of the study. The authors use a two-site model for the atoms.

They compute a range of measures by computer, from heat-related entropy to shared quantum links and visible coherence. They track how these shift with heat and with the gap between the wells. For strong tunneling, they build a phase model that lets some averages be worked out by hand. That shortcut uses a modified heat weight with an effective temperature.
arxiv-2506-06424:
Michael Jones and co-authors (2025) introduce Pavo, a galaxy whose gas refuses to sit still. Pavo is newly found and extremely low in mass. Radio observations with the MeerKAT telescope found neutral hydrogen that older single-dish data had missed. Its gas mass, about ten to the power 5.79 in solar units, is the smallest yet measured in an isolated galaxy with a firm distance. Pavo has no neighbor within seven hundred kiloparsecs.

Despite that isolation, the gas is highly disturbed. It shows no rotation, its center of mass sits 320 parsecs from the starlight's center, and its peak is offset by 82 parsecs. Something stirred it. With no neighbors to blame, the likely culprit is the galaxy's own star formation blowing gas around: stellar feedback in action. The galaxy still fits the usual link between gas size and mass, which helps the authors judge how violent the stirring has been.
arxiv-2506-06524:
Sam Earle, Ahmed Khalifa, and colleagues present a system that designs small puzzle games on its own in a 2025 study. Automatic game design has leaned on large pre-trained models under constant human watch. Letting a system generate, test, and revise games over longer stretches, linked directly to a game engine, remains an open goal.

Their system, ScriptDoctor, uses a language model plus tree search to write games in PuzzleScript, a tight language for tile-based puzzles. Generated games are played and tested inside the engine without a person in the loop. The work shows a fuller pipeline for machine game creation.
arxiv-2506-06624:
Mojtaba Mollahossein and three co-authors build a featherweight neural network that reads leg movements from muscle signals, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The model takes surface electromyography from several channels and sorts walking, standing knee bends, and sitting knee extensions. An attention block helps it weigh the channels that matter.

With only about sixty-three thousand parameters and no heavy preprocessing, the network is built for real-time use on small hardware. Leaving one subject out at a time during training kept it honest about new wearers. It scored about eighty-seven percent on validation and eighty-five percent on held-out tests. The authors aim it at controllers for assistive robots and rehab devices.
arxiv-2506-06824:
Chi Liu and five co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on planning energy use in green buildings in real time. Such buildings make their own power and store it in fixed batteries. Parked electric cars can store power too, but car batteries wear out in ways that differ from fixed ones.

The authors use a learning method that improves by trial and error, with no fixed model of the building. They join the fixed store and the car fleet into one shared system. The method weighs battery wear, cost, and the travel needs of car users. A forecast step helps plan how the shared store trades power with the building.
arxiv-2506-06924:
Andrew Elvey Price and co-authors count discrete surfaces as both their size and their genus grow large. Their objects are unicellular maps, drawings on surfaces with a single face, whose counts obey a tidy recurrence. Finding how such counts behave when two measures swell at once is the core problem.

The team attacks the recurrence by way of random walks, a detour that turns counting into tracking steps. The route pays off beyond maps: the paper proves a general theorem that hands back growth formulas for whole families of similar recurrences once a few conditions hold. Results of this kind feed the study of random surfaces and two-dimensional geometry at large scales.
arxiv-2506-07124:
Daniel Alcantara and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on smart surfaces that can steer wireless signals, and on how to estimate the channels they create. Such surfaces can boost modern wireless systems, but their gain depends on setting each element's phase well, which in turn needs accurate channel estimates. Past work used ideal models or fixed tables of phase values. None had studied how the circuit traits of the surface shape channel estimation.

The authors model each surface element as a small resonant circuit with resistance, capacitance, and inductance. Resistance and capacitance can be set on their own and changed as needed, which leads to a full impedance picture of the surface. From that, they build a phase matrix that reflects how the circuit actually responds. The aim is phase control that stays honest to the hardware, not just to an ideal sketch.
arxiv-2506-07324:
Weather forecasts made by neural networks give one answer, but forecasters also need a spread of likely outcomes. David Millard and co-authors present a method that adds that spread with a diffusion model. The model creates varied starting conditions for the forecast. It can run again and again, and a guidance term sets how strong the variation is. Any single-answer neural forecaster can gain a range of outcomes this way.

Tests used a global weather dataset at coarse grid size, built from records since the nineteen sixties. The spread-out system built up less error over long forecasts. Its range of outcomes also stayed reasonable. The approach frees ensemble design from methods built only for physics-based solvers.
arxiv-2506-07424:
Kyeonghyun Kim and co-authors present in 2025 a way to lend a small language model some of a big model's skill. Big models know more and generalize better, but they cost too much for tight settings. Small models are cheap yet narrower. Their frame, PiFi, plugs one frozen layer from a big model into a small one.

Only the combined model is then fine-tuned for the task at hand. Scores rose across a range of language tasks, both understanding and generation, with little added cost. The borrowed layer also helped the small model handle topics it had never seen, which shows that big-model knowledge can transfer through a single layer.
arxiv-2506-07624:
Ali Hariri and a team of co-authors revisit ChebNet, one of the first graph neural networks, in a paper from 2025. Most graph models pass notes between near nodes, which works well for local shape but poorly for links across a whole graph. ChebNet, built on a spectral method, had been largely set aside for years.

The team found that plain ChebNet already beats many newer models on long-range tasks, while staying fast. Yet its math can turn unstable in training. Their fix, Stable-ChebNet, treats the model as a steady system that spreads facts in a calm, controlled way. It needs no graph rewiring or added position codes, and it scored near the top on several test sets.
arxiv-2506-07824:
Yao Yan wrote this 2025 paper peering inside a language model as it adds numbers, layer by layer. Multi-digit addition is a clean probe of real computation, and Yan dissected the forward pass of LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct with linear probes and a logit lens. Four stages surfaced, like movements in a piece of music.

First, the shape of the formula becomes readable in the activations while the answer still ranks low. Core computational features then flare up. Deeper in, the numeric value of the result sharpens until each digit can be decoded almost perfectly. Near the output the model tidies up and the correct token takes the top rank. The arc favors genuine internal computation over memorized answers. Code and data were released for others to replay.
arxiv-2506-07924:
Zhizun Xu, Baozhu Jia, and Weichao Shi describe YellowCube, an underwater robot built from swap-ready parts, in a 2025 paper. Robots of this kind serve offshore work and ocean study. Most older designs make it hard to add or upgrade a sensor. YellowCube splits the craft into sections that can be changed to suit each mission, so one body can carry many tool sets.

Unlike rival modular craft, YellowCube has no single central brain for its software. Its parts talk to each other as peers, each sharing data with the rest. The team ran tests in the lab to check the design. They then took the craft to sea for trials. Both rounds supported the design, and the paper lays out how the peer links and part swaps work in practice.
arxiv-2506-08024:
Laksh Patel and Neel Shanbhag design an optimization method for supply chains whose partners cannot stay in sync. Their 2025 paper tackles flow allocation across a directed network of suppliers, distributors, and retailers. Real networks suffer late messages, packet loss, and agents spread across the globe, so methods that demand lockstep updates fail.

Their scheme lets each edge agent update its flow and each retailer update its prices from possibly stale information, with no global clock. They prove the process still settles at a saddle point, with a duality gap that shrinks at the best known rate. Tests on three-tier networks beat synchronous and rival asynchronous methods on speed and message cost. The method also held up under heavy staleness and drifting costs.
arxiv-2506-08124: Amartya Goswami, Elena Caviglia, and Luca Mesiti extend a classic algebra idea in a 2025 arXiv paper. They carry Jacobson's notion of a primitive ring over to quantales, a related structure used in logic and algebra. They show that every primitive ring gives rise to a primitive quantale of ideals. They then prove a density theorem for strongly primitive quantales. Two further results round out the paper: primitive quantales are prime, and commutative strongly primitive quantales turn out to be field quantales.
arxiv-2506-08224:
Osman Ridwan and co-authors present an AI tool that grows crystal structures toward a chosen local setting, in a 2025 paper. Classic crystal prediction samples many shapes, then refines each with costly energy methods. New AI generators are faster but often ignore crystal symmetry and periodic order. They also handle only small unit cells.

Their tool, LEGO-xtal, builds symmetry into the generation step. It starts from AI models trained on a small, expanded data set. Machine learning descriptors, not energy checks, then refine each structure. As a test, the team grew a set of known carbon forms into a far larger set of low-energy candidates. The approach suits materials built from modular blocks.
arxiv-2506-08524:
Weiguo Wang and co-authors teach in 2025 language models to hear the physical world. Text-trained models know nothing of effects like the pitch shift of a passing siren. Their framework, ACORN, uses sound as the teaching channel, since sound carries rich physical clues.

A physics-based simulator mixes real sound sources with modeled channels to make varied training data without endless recording. On it they built an audio question set and an encoder that reads both the loudness and phase of sound. Linked to leading language models, the system handled tasks like judging whether a path is blocked, estimating speed from pitch shift, and locating a sound's direction, in both simulated and real settings.
arxiv-2506-08824:
Yulia Mukhina and Gleb Pogudin bound, in a 2025 mathematics paper, the size of the simplest equation hidden inside a dynamical system. Given equations for how variables change and a chosen observable built from them, elimination asks for the smallest differential equation the observable alone obeys.

Their earlier work handled the case where the observable is a single variable and no unknown parameters appear. The new bound allows any polynomial observable and symbolic parameters throughout. Computer experiments test how tight the bound is. The support bound turns elimination into a concrete algorithm, solving cases beyond the reach of current software.
arxiv-2506-09024:
Felix Wagner, Pramit Saha, Harry Anthony, Alison Noble, and Konstantinos Kamnitsas present DIsoN, in a 2025 preprint, a privacy-safe way to flag odd medical images. A deployed model must warn when an input looks nothing like its training data. Comparing against that data would help, but hospitals cannot ship patient scans with the model. The authors' base method asks how hard a new image is to separate from the training set. Their decentralized version swaps only model parameters between the training site and the clinic. No images move.

A class-aware variant compares the image only with training cases of its predicted type. Tests covered skin, chest, breast, and tissue images across twelve tasks. DIsoN matched or beat existing methods while keeping data private. The authors imagine vendors selling a remote oddity-check service alongside their models. The training data would help from afar without ever leaving home.
arxiv-2506-09624:
Zehavi, Obolski, Chowers, and Nevo set out a way in twenty twenty-five to weigh how germ drugs affect later drug-proof infections. Some patients may live under one drug but not the other, which clouds a fair match. They frame the task as two risks that race each other in time.

They name a group of patients who would live or catch the infection under both drugs. That group is wider than past groups used for such tasks. For that group they give a clean effect to aim at, with bounds and two model routes to find it. They show the way on real hospital data.
arxiv-2506-09824:
Johan Erbani and four co-authors guard shared learning, where many holders train one model with no data shared, against bad actors who send poisoned updates. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The shared plan looks safe for privacy, but a rogue holder can warp the shared model. Past guards drop odd updates, on the guess that rogue ones stray most. When holders' data differ a lot, though, honest updates stray too, and such guards can fail. The team weights each holder's loss in a new way, to keep the shared model sound when data are mixed. The aim is shared learning that stays true in the wild.
arxiv-2506-10024:
Elena Sofia Ruzzetti, Giancarlo A Xompero, Davide Venditti, and Fabio Massimo Zanzotto turn a known AI weakness into a shield for privacy. Large language models memorize chunks of their training data, including private details about real people. Attackers can sometimes pull those details back out.

Their method, Private Memorization Editing, first finds memorized private data inside a model. It then edits the model's knowledge to blunt that memory. The edited model keeps its normal language skill, they report. At the same time, extraction attacks recover far less private data, in some setups none at all. The work suggests that knowing what a model memorized can help protect the people in its data.
arxiv-2506-10224:
Alejandro Diaz and three co-authors develop a clearer way to build small stand-in models of complex systems, in a 2025 methods paper. Engineers often shrink a big simulation into a reduced model that runs fast. Label-free methods learn the small model's rules from data alone, but the learned rules can be hard to read. The new method uses kernel interpolation, a smooth fit method tied to a chosen function space.

Careful choice of features inside the kernel lets the small model keep the shape of the big one. Added general terms can close gaps the features miss. The team also derives a bound on the total error that users can compute after the fit. Tests on several problems, with two ways of shrinking the state, show the method at work. The authors stress both clarity and flexibility.
arxiv-2506-10424:
Kaiyuan Zhang and ten co-authors defend fine-tuned language models against detectives who can tell whether a given text was in the training set. Their 2025 paper first measures the danger. Membership inference attacks exploit the loss drop that fine-tuning stamps on its own data. That makes them highly effective at exposing membership, a real privacy leak for sensitive corpora.

Their defense, SOFT, obfuscates selectively: influential training points are chosen and masked with an adjustable dial trading privacy against usefulness. Experiments across six domains and several model sizes showed privacy risk falling while performance stayed competitive. The authors bill it as practical and scalable, built for the common case where fine-tuning data cannot be public. The study is billed as the first full audit of this attack surface.
arxiv-2506-10724:
Haiyan Wang and co-authors offer a way to spot the shift from calm to chaos in population models in this 2025 paper. They study two classic growth equations with randomness added, described by a gamma distribution. When the spread is small, the random versions hug their deterministic twins.

The analysis finds two branches of growth rate, giving alternative stable states with higher and lower growth. The logistic model never tips from a steady state into chaos. The Ricker model does, when the distribution's shape parameter is small. The authors say the approach sharpens understanding of how populations behave under noise. They also pitch it as a general detector for chaos in complex systems.
arxiv-2506-10824:
Sebastián Rojas-Innocenti and co-authors present a planning method for factories that use huge amounts of power, in a 2025 study set in a cement plant. Prices, solar output, and demand all shift without warning, so a fixed schedule can fail or cost too much. Their framework plans for many possible futures at once, not just one forecast.

The model weighs average cost against worst-case cost, so planners can dial risk up or down. It coordinates batteries and shiftable production steps. Tested on day-ahead price swings, the schedules held up better, with steadier costs and operations. The authors offer the method as a risk-aware tool for industry.
arxiv-2506-10924:
Quang Huy Nguyen and three co-authors develop a space time interface fitted method for moving subdomain control problems with energy regularization. The moving interface optimal control problem is reformulated through its optimality conditions into a variational problem in state and adjoint together. That problem is shown equivalent to the original control problem.

Fully unstructured space time interface fitted meshes support a Petrov-Galerkin approximation. An optimal error estimate in a discrete norm is proven under a stated regularity assumption on state and adjoint. Numerical results back the theory. The fitted mesh tracks the moving subdomain exactly, which avoids the smearing that fixed grids suffer at interfaces. The work serves control problems in fluids and materials with moving internal boundaries.
arxiv-2506-11724:
Dimitrios Konstantinides, Jiajun Liu, and Charalampos Passalidis bound ruin chances in a multi line risk model, in work from 2025. Lines share one renewal claim clock and face steady interest on held funds. Claim sizes form random vectors with linked heavy tailed parts across business lines.

Estimates track the chance that discounted total claims enter rare high sets. Local uniform bounds hold near fixed times, then extend across all time spans. Heavy tail classes used here go beyond plain regular variation cases alone. Worked distribution examples show which claim laws fit the wide tail frame. Results serve actuaries who price linked lines with fat loss tails.
arxiv-2506-12124:
Yu-Ching Chen and co-authors use in 2025 the Webb space telescope to reveal the home galaxies of very red, dust-hidden quasars. A quasar's glare normally drowns out its host, above all for these red ones at cosmic noon, when galaxies grew fast. The team observed six such quasars plus two dust-hidden ones at nearer distances.

By splitting the light across the full spectrum, they parted quasar glow from starlight and mapped each host. The hosts proved compact, with masses in a range that fits what theory expects for quasar hosts of that era. Most quasars sat off-centre in their hosts, a hint of past mergers or patchy dust. The black holes looked heavy for their hosts.
arxiv-2506-13024:
Andrew Cullen and co-authors argue, in a 2025 position paper, that a certified shield against trick inputs does not yet make an AI model secure. Certified robustness promises proof that small input tweaks cannot flip a model's answer. Such proof is often sold as a fix for adversarial attacks. The authors say real deployment still faces deep gaps between the promise and the practice.

They name three trouble spots. A system may spot an attack without telling friend from foe. Practitioners lack clear rules for judging rival certification schemes. Worst, users may over-trust a guarantee and drop their guard. The paper calls on the research community to close these gaps with concrete steps, so that certified models can earn a real place in secure systems.
arxiv-2506-13124:
Jong-Ho Shinn, Rory Smith, and Kyuseok Oh stress-test an astronomy analysis tool in this two thousand twenty-five paper. IZI is a Bayesian program that reads emission lines from ionized gas regions and star-forming galaxies and estimates metallicity, ionization parameter, and dust reddening. The authors created mock datasets with IZI itself, in idealized and realistic variants, then ran the estimation back on the mocks to see whether the true parameters were recovered.

Recovery was biased: estimates missed the truth by about one standard deviation or more once model error was included, even using every available emission line. The cause is substantial model error inside the likelihood that varies with the parameters. The authors strongly recommend users run their own recovery tests before trusting IZI output, and they share a script for doing so. The warning extends to similar tools such as NebulaBayes.
arxiv-2506-13624:
Luyao Zhang, Chenghuai Lin, and Sergio Grammatico build a graphics chip solver for branch model predictive control, used to plan robot paths, in a paper from 2025. The branch form weighs many future splits at once, which makes the math heavy for plain chips.

Their solver grows from a repeat linear quadratic method, states the motion in split steps, and folds in path limits with a penalty method that allows warm starts. Two inner solvers tap the tree shape of the problem at split levels of parallel work. On large tasks the chip solver beat a top plain chip solver.
arxiv-2506-14324:
Saveliy Skresanov, a solo author, works on a math question about Rota-Baxter operators on compact simple Lie groups and their algebras. Such an operator is a smooth map on a group that meets a fixed rule linking the images of two group members.

Skresanov shows that on these groups the only such maps are two simple ones: the trivial map and the inverse map. He gives a like result for the same kind of operator, of weight one, on the algebras that go with the groups. The proof closes off the search for more complex cases in this setting.
arxiv-2506-14424:
R. Schussnig and colleagues compare computer methods for simulating fluids whose thickness varies from place to place, such as blood or industrial liquids. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses a high-order grid method that needs no stored matrices, which saves memory on large problems. They test two broad strategies. One solves for speed and pressure together in a single coupled system. The other splits the work into a sequence of simpler steps, such as flow, diffusion, and a pressure equation.

Splitting methods are cheaper per step but face stricter limits on step size. Fully coupled methods cost more yet stay stable with larger steps, sometimes needing costly nonlinear solves. The authors map out when each approach wins on speed and reliability, using several test flows. Their accelerated solvers and multigrid techniques aim to make high-order simulation practical for real engineering problems.
arxiv-2506-14524:
Nadezhda Alsahanova and co-authors improve the outlining of multiple sclerosis lesions in brain scans by adding texture features to deep learning. Their 2025 paper starts from a diagnostic need: exact lesion maps guide care, but current networks falter on varied scans. The team fuse hand-crafted image statistics with the raw scans.

They devise two new features that capture how lesion types differ in concentration and disorder. The fused input feeds two network designs across scans from dozens of patients and over a thousand slices. One design gained clear accuracy, precision, and sensitivity over the scan-only baseline. The other grew more stable, with smoother training curves and less variable scores. Richer inputs, not just bigger networks, drove the gains.
arxiv-2506-15024:
Frank Verheest and Willy Hereman study lone waves in a dusty plasma in a 2025 paper. The waves ride on sound-like pushes in a gas of charged grains, dust, and free charge, and they can hold their shape over long runs.

Two tools go to work on the same model. One treats the full push and pull but needs a machine to draw each wave. The next trims the model step by step and lands on a named rule that blends two wave rules, one square and one cube in shape. That rule gives the wave's shape in a clean closed form. With a picked set of mix values, the two waves match well. The authors weigh where the trimmed form can stand in for the full one.
arxiv-2506-15524:
Vasluianu leads a very large team reporting the NTIRE 2025 Image Shadow Removal Challenge, in a 2025 paper. Shadow removal is a step in cleaning up photos and computer vision inputs. The challenge drew hundreds of registered participants.

Seventeen teams submitted full solutions for final scoring. The contest had two tracks, one judging how faithful the rebuilt image is, the other judging visual quality through a user study. Test images came from the WSRD+ data set. They show self shadows and cast shadows across many objects, textures, and materials. The report sums up the methods and results. It gives a benchmark for future shadow removal work.
arxiv-2506-15724:
Kunxi Li and co-authors trim the memory cache of multimodal language models so long conversations fit on real hardware. Their 2025 paper targets the key-value cache, which grows with every token and every image an AI processes. Standard trimming rules were built for text only and miss a key fact: different attention heads care about different modalities.

Their method, MadaKV, senses each head's taste for image versus text and keeps the tokens that matter for that head. A layered compensation step softens the loss from dropping the rest. Across long-context multimodal tests, memory fell sharply and decoding sped up by roughly a third to a half. Accuracy held against rival trimming methods. The authors present cache design as a modality problem, not just a size problem.
arxiv-2506-16024:
Zhihan Guo and co-authors teach models to write long texts with targeted rewards in a 2025 paper. Research on long context mostly tests reading, not writing at length. Training long-form generation lacks gold references, and past rewards graded output only in general terms, blunt feedback for a demanding task.

Their ProxyReward framework builds training data by simple prompting and scores each answer for completeness and accuracy against its specific question. The tuned model surpassed GPT-4 on their open-ended long-context tests. Reports, briefings, and long answers are where language models are headed; this work sharpens the feedback that gets them there.
arxiv-2506-16124:
Mathieu Gonod and co-authors test a hair-thin detector that tracks a radioactive source during radiation therapy. In high-dose-rate brachytherapy, a source dwells at spots inside the body, and a positioning slip can overdose healthy tissue. The detector packs seven tiny scintillator cells onto optical fibers in a bundle under half a millimeter wide. Each cell flashes as the source passes, and a camera reads the pattern of flashes.

The team ran the device against a standard treatment machine over 4,040 dwell positions. Gaps ran from ten to thirty-six millimeters, and dwell times from a tenth of a second to nearly twenty. It found 99.5 percent of the positions, with average placement errors near two tenths of a millimeter. Nearly all readings fell within the one-millimeter safety line. The few failures clustered at the first dwell of each run, traced to the machine itself.
arxiv-2506-16324:
Borrowed memory that must be handed back intact sounds like a trick, yet it can boost what a computer can do. Harry Buhrman and co-authors define that trick for quantum machines in a 2025 paper. Qubits are scarce and costly, so using space well matters a great deal. Past quantum work on borrowed bits either needed special states or wrecked the borrowed memory.

The team sets out a clean model of quantum catalytic space, where borrowed space is restored after use. They show this kind of log-sized space can always be run in polynomial time on a quantum machine. The matching classical question is still open, which makes the quantum result stand out. They also show the model can mimic a class of shallow circuits. The work opens a new branch of space study.
arxiv-2506-16424:
Sankalp Kumar, Sumiran Pujari, and Jonathan D'Emidio study a spin chain that looks critical but is not quite.
