Their paper from twenty twenty-five treats an SU(N) version of the Heisenberg antiferromagnet. Such chains can show pseudocriticality: near scale-free conduct with slow drift. A recent view ties this to a true critical point with complex values nearby.

Working in one space dimension plus time, the team tunes the closeness to that complex point through N. Quantum Monte Carlo runs track the central charge in fine detail. A new loop estimator, built on a work-based trick, gauges entanglement entropy. The counts match field theory forecasts with high care. Past N of two, the real part of the complex charge is still read off well. The spin-1 chain's dimer phase gains a fresh reading.
arxiv-2506-16524:
Piotr Dulian, Stanislaw Kurdzialek, and Rafal Demkowicz-Dobrzanski wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five presenting a Python package for quantum metrology. Quantum metrology uses quantum effects to measure quantities with extreme precision. Finding the best measurement strategy for a given setup is a hard optimization problem.

Their package, QMetro++, searches for protocols that maximize a key quantity called quantum Fisher information. It accepts custom setups: input states, encoding channels, noise, controls, and measurements can all be specified. Tensor networks and an iterative algorithm keep large cases, around a hundred channel uses, tractable. Built-in bounds let users judge how close their result sits to optimal.
arxiv-2506-16724:
Measuring what a model does not know is hard when a question has many valid answers. The authors study how prompt bias distorts uncertainty estimates in vision-language models, and how a model's own confidence changes that distortion. Experiments use visual question answering with two large models.

Removing prompt-introduced bias improved uncertainty measurement in one model. Across both, every bias studied hit harder when the model's bias-free confidence was low. Low confidence also made models underestimate their knowledge uncertainty, which yields overconfident answers, while effects on the other uncertainty type had no steady direction. The authors say the pattern deepens understanding of bias in uncertainty work. The text head gives the fuller title, which names vision-language models.
arxiv-2506-16824:
Thomas Marwitz and twelve co-authors use large language models to forecast fresh research directions in materials science. Their 2025 paper starts from a flood problem: papers now appear faster than any scientist can read, even inside one field. Hidden links between ideas may sit unread in the pile.

The models pull the main concepts from paper abstracts and weave them into a concept graph. A learning model trained on past data then predicts which concept pairings are about to emerge as new topics. Adding the meaning of concepts, not just keywords, sharpened the forecasts. Experts interviewed with tailored suggestions said the ideas sparked their thinking. The authors frame the tool as a creativity aid for working scientists.
arxiv-2506-17124:
Josiah Hanna and Nicholas Corrado ask when plain trial-and-error learning, with no world model, can produce behavior that looks like thinking. Their paper appeared in 2025. Language models trained this way have begun to reason aloud, which is odd: thought steps earn no reward and change nothing outside. The team builds a minimal theory by adding a thought state and thought actions to the classic decision model.

They prove the starting policy decides whether thinking emerges at all, and that a thought step equals one round of self-improvement of the policy. Open language models meet the conditions their theory requires. They then propose what might let thinking arise beyond language, with a toy test case.
arxiv-2506-17424:
Nikolaus Salvatore and Qiong Zhang show that sequence-to-sequence translation models with attention mirror the shape of a leading model of human memory search. Human search is guided by context, and context-based models explain many memory facts, yet why such a design arises was unclear. Translation models, shaped purely by task performance, land on like mechanisms.

The attention steps of the translation model map onto the context upkeep and retrieval steps of the CMR memory model. Built as a memory model, the translation system matched human behaviour, both average and optimal patterns, as well as the classic models do. Splitting the model apart also showed how search skill grows from its parts working together.
arxiv-2506-17524:
Many models in science are written as differential equations, and splitting a hard equation into simple parts is a classic way to solve it on a computer. Arun Banjara and co-authors build a framework in this 2025 paper that freezes all but one variable at a time, turning each step into an easy one-variable problem.

They combine old product formulas with these frozen sub-steps to form update schemes of several orders, and they count the cost of each scheme. Tests on three famous systems, from predator-prey to the Lorenz model, compare accuracy and effort against a standard solver. The results map out the trade-offs a user faces when picking a scheme.
arxiv-2506-17624:
Nakagawa, Ohmura, and Kuniyoshi teach a robot to move its neck while it handles objects in this twenty twenty-five paper. Most past work used fixed cameras, so the robot could only act inside one set view. A moving neck lets the robot look past that view and take on more tasks.

Inside, the team built a teaching setup that records neck moves while a person guides the robot from a distance. They also built a new network that learns hand tasks and neck moves at the same time. In tests the robot reached a win rate near ninety percent. It did best when objects sat at the edge of, or just past, the plain view.
arxiv-2506-17824:
Cultice and co-authors test quantum-tied sort tools for flaw hunts in plant nets. Plant nets feed data that guards key works like power and water. Flaw hunts flag bad or rogue data in those feeds fast. Learn tools do much of that hunt work in live nets. Quantum core tools show skill at hard flaw shapes in past work. Their wide state space gives that skill its base strength.

Three known sets from plant-type nets test the mixed tools. The mixed tools beat stock core tools by 13.3 percent on F1. Noise runs on real IBMQ gear cap the flaw at 0.98 percent. That flaw trims sort scores by 1.57 percent on mean. Aim fit for the cores jumps 91 percent past stock tools. The team reads that jump as a hint of quantum edge.
arxiv-2506-18024:
Thien Tran and colleagues split computing across cloud, fog, and shipboard layers for robot boats in 2025. Unmanned surface vehicles must spot and classify collision risks in real time, but onboard processors are weak and links to shore are slow, so heavy analysis cannot live in one place. Their design follows a cloud-fog automation pattern with three tiers.

Sensors at the waterline gather data with low delay, nearby edge nodes run the fast AI decisions, and the cloud aggregates data and refines models for later use. Experiments showed gains in efficiency, responsiveness, and scale over conventional setups, with classification accuracy in the mid-eighties and better latency. Layered computing suits maritime autonomy where seconds matter.
arxiv-2506-18124:
Shaoxiu Wei, Mingchao Liang, and Florian Meyer blend neural networks into Bayesian multi-object tracking. Their paper from twenty twenty-five weighs two camps. Model-based trackers work anywhere but lean on plain motion and sensor models. Data-driven trackers shine where labeled data abound but travel poorly. Their hybrid keeps the Bayesian frame and upgrades its weak parts with learned nets.

Belief propagation keeps the math tractable in high dimensions. Sequential Monte Carlo steps handle the low-dimensional parts with care. The nets enrich the motion and measurement models where hand forms fall short. Tests on the nuScenes driving set reach top-tier scores. The authors claim the mix keeps model-based range while gaining data-driven sharpness. Uses span driving, ocean study, and air surveillance.
arxiv-2506-18624:
Zejian Li, Anna Delmonte, and Rosario Fazio study entanglement in watched quantum systems in a 2025 paper. When a quantum system is continuously monitored, its behavior can switch phases, and entanglement between parts can change abruptly. Earlier work saw those switches numerically in small systems. Here the setting is bosons with infinite range interactions, examined in the limit of huge particle numbers.

Under gentle assumptions, the quantum fluctuations along a single monitored run settle into a deterministic pattern that can be solved exactly, for both jumpy and smooth monitoring styles. A layered structure in the equations explains why entanglement transitions and dissipation transitions coincide. Examples on a two site boson model and a collective spin system illustrate the theory.
arxiv-2506-18824:
Islem Bouzenia and Michael Pradel studied how coding agents think in two thousand twenty-five. AI agents now fix bugs and resolve issues on their own. They loop through thoughts, tool calls, and results. Little was known about patterns inside those loops. Failure modes were likewise poorly understood. The pair gathered logs from three leading agents.

The agents were RepairAgent, AutoCodeRover, and OpenHands. Logs were merged into one common format for study. The set held over a hundred full repair trajectories. Thousands of model interactions were included. The team measured action patterns and token use. They also read trajectories closely for quality signals. Recurring loops and dead ends came to light. The findings can guide safer, cheaper agent design.
arxiv-2506-18924:
Al Mhdawi and co-authors link traffic vision to carbon counting in a 2025 paper on road design. Their system extends the YOLOv8 detector to find, segment, and track vehicles in live traffic video. Counting traffic well is a first step toward honest street-level emission estimates.

Once a vehicle is boxed, a separate module reads its license plate and refines its type. A deep optical character reader handles the plate text, since the base detector cannot do such fine work. Behavior and vehicle mix then feed the emission estimate. City teams could judge road designs by the carbon they truly produce, not by rough traffic guesses alone.
arxiv-2506-19024:
Alessio D'Errico and co-authors run quantum walks on looped lattices with light in a 2025 paper. Quantum walks spread a particle over a lattice in steps set by a unitary rule. Few platforms can be reprogrammed, scaled, and given wrap-around edges at once. Their platform works in reciprocal space, where sampling the rule enforces the looped shape.

They program walks on one-dimensional rings and on two-dimensional cylinders and tori. Lattice size is tuned by sampling density. Localized states refocus and breathe in ways that reflect the topology, they show. A two-dimensional walk on a cylinder can also be recast as a one-dimensional walk with a rich coin.
arxiv-2506-19824:
Jacob Pierce and co-authors propose a discrete flying focus to drive laser wakefield acceleration, in a 2025 paper. The method may enable future colliders at very high energies, but reaching them likely needs many stages. Staging brings alignment and matching problems and lowers the average gradient.

Their scheme uses a sequence of laser pulses with staggered focal points and delays. The pulses drive a plasma wave in which an electron beam feels a near-constant push over long distances. Simulations show a single short stage could transfer large energy per electron to a beam. Fewer stages would simplify future accelerators.
arxiv-2506-19924:
Yoav Zigdon derives a new charge rule in a known matrix model of quantum gravity in a 2025 paper. The model is a gauged quantum system with a top share of saved symmetry. Past work showed its count of states grows fast with size from the ground state that keeps the full gauge group.

Zigdon shows that the truth of the linked heat-like count forces one charge part to vanish. That holds for any saved sector that keeps the full gauge group in place. The rule may help judge if a dual black hole with a wave-like far zone can exist.
arxiv-2506-20024:
Salva Rühling Cachay and co-authors build a rolling diffusion forecaster for weather and fluid flow. Their 2025 paper starts from a weakness of diffusion forecasts: they predict each future step alone and lose the thread of growing doubt. Rolling schemes add more noise to farther steps, which matches how uncertainty grows.

The team merges that rolling frame with a leading diffusion design. A new loss weighting aims capacity at mid-range times, where order gives way to chance. A pretrained model seeds the first window, and a hybrid network reads space and time together. On fluid tests and global weather data it beat close rivals.
arxiv-2506-20124:
Blend models, which cast data as a mix of hidden groups, force a basic choice: how many groups to use. Hien Nguyen and TrungTin Nguyen tweak a classic score for that choice in 2025. The score was long known to pick the right count, but only under stiff demands on the data, such as smooth shapes and rich spread.

Their two new scores weigh the classic penalty by a tiny log factor that barely moves it in practice. That small shift buys the same right-pick promise under far weaker demands. When the true model lies outside the set on offer, the scores still settle on the best near pick. The pair also show two hard limits: no smallest penalty works for all, and right picks can clash with other goals.
arxiv-2506-20324:
Torben Berndt and co-authors work on graphs that change over time, such as networks where both the links and the node traits keep shifting. A recent tool adapted a type of neural model to follow such paths on graphs. The new work adds one firm rule: swapping the labels of nodes should not change the result.

Adding that rule cuts the number of settings the model must learn, while keeping its power to fit the data. Training then runs more lean, and the model tends to work better on new cases. The team tested the idea on made-up systems that change over time and on real tasks, in both gap-filling and forecast settings.
arxiv-2506-20824:
Toshiya Namikawa, Kai Murai, and Fumihiro Naokawa set limits on axion like particles from space data in a 2025 paper. Such particles could twist the light of the early universe as it travels, an effect called cosmic birefringence. Fresh measures hint the twist is real, but its source is not yet known.

They built a joint test from the Planck satellite's high band channels that lets the twist leave its own shape on the data. The test also folds in a tool aim error and dust from our own galaxy. If the particles cause the twist, whole bands of their mass are ruled out at strong confidence. The paper shows how the shape of the signal, not just its size, ties down the model.
arxiv-2506-21024:
Mallory Flynn, Paul Gustafson, and Michael Irvine tackle a hidden count problem in a 2025 preprint. They want to know how many opioid overdoses took place in British Columbia in a set period. Many cases are hard to count, yet the total guides health funds and policy choices.

Care data in the province form a tree, with each path showing steps a person took after an overdose. The authors compare two ways to work back from those paths to the full total. One blends path based estimates with weights, while the other builds a full model that states doubt at each level.
arxiv-2506-21124:
Finding the lowest point of a many-input function is a core task in physics, logistics, and machine learning. Intoccia and co-authors present a hybrid method, Quantum Adaptive Search, in a 2025 paper. A quantum state holds a map of how good each region looks, coded in its wave heights.

The map guides a steady narrowing of the search bounds toward the best region. A classic solver then polishes the final answer inside that tight space. The authors prove the bounds shrink toward the true best point with bounded cost. On test functions, the method beat classic rivals on accuracy. It also used less time and space, they report.
arxiv-2506-21224:
John Debes and a large team used the Webb telescope to image four dead stars that show traces of rocky debris, in a 2025 paper. Such stars, white dwarfs, are polluted by the remains of small bodies torn apart nearby. The bodies were likely nudged by planets that survived the star's death.

Deep images in mid-infrared light were sharp enough to catch cold giant planets. Two candidate companions turned up. Two stars also glowed more than expected at one wavelength, a first at that band. The team weighs dust against planets as the cause and leans toward giant planets on close orbits. If the candidates hold, such dead stars often keep at least one giant planet.
arxiv-2506-21624:
Blaž Škrlj and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a recommender model that serves over half a billion predictions per second. Systems like this rank ads and content for huge platforms. The base design, Deep and Cross, is a sturdy production standard, but it loses some information inside its cross layers.

Their upgraded design, DCN squared, adds three fixes. Learnable weights at the lookup level manage collisions between features more openly. A custom layer models pairwise feature likeness in the style of factorization machines. The authors detail how each change behaves at scale. In live A/B tests the new model beat the old one online as well as offline. Four public benchmarks backed the same result.
arxiv-2506-21824:
Shine swirling light on a sample and the scattered colors can betray its hidden symmetries. Hikaru Watanabe and co-authors analyze Raman optical activity with circular light. Two setups matter: crossed and parallel circular polarizations between incoming and scattered beams. Working through the magnetic point groups, they map which symmetries allow each signal. The response can diagnose traits like chirality and axiality in a sample.

Stokes and anti-Stokes scattering turn out to be linked by time-reversal symmetry, combined with mirror reflection. The authors present the analysis as a systematic guide. Lab teams can use it to read a sample's symmetry class from its optical answer.
arxiv-2506-21924:
Zhao Jin and co-authors build an agent that finds objects in 3D rooms from spoken descriptions, without ever training on labeled 3D data. Grounding language in a point cloud normally demands pricey annotation. SPAZER instead reasons in stages, mixing a rendered 3D view with ordinary camera photos, and leaning on the knowledge inside large vision-language models.

It first turns the scene to its best angle, then screens candidates with anchors for a rough fix. Finally it cross-checks the shortlist against real 2D images before naming the one object that fits. On the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks, the staged approach beat earlier zero-shot systems by roughly nine to eleven points of accuracy. The authors argue that progressive, two-stream reasoning beats either stream alone.
arxiv-2506-22224:
Emma Fraxanet and co-authors present a 2025 data set from an Austrian news site. The data cover ten years of reader activity, from 2013 to 2022. They hold tens of millions of comments and hundreds of millions of votes. Article facts and topic tags from editors are also included. The source is DerStandard, a major paper in Austria.

Comments keep their thread shape, so readers can trace who replied to whom. Votes are signed as up or down, which shows praise and pushback plainly. Names are hidden with salted codes, and raw comment text is not shared. In its place the team shares number forms made by a strong text model. Researchers can study debate flow, network shape, and word meaning in German. The set fills a gap for mid-size languages, which often lack large open data.
arxiv-2506-22724:
Niyati Bafna and co-authors argue that language models often fail in other languages at a hidden translation step, in a 2025 paper. Output quality drops for mid- and low-resource languages. The causes are poorly understood. The team shows models seem to work in two stages. First they solve the task in a mostly language-neutral way. Then they translate the answer ideas into the target language.

The authors name failure at that second stage the translation barrier. They measured each stage's share of errors on a word translation task. The test spanned one hundred eight language pairs. The barrier explained most errors for a majority of pairs. It hit low-resource languages hardest. The finding points builders at a clear bottleneck. Fixing the inner translation step could lift multilingual quality broadly. It also suggests testing the stages apart, not just final answers.
arxiv-2506-22924:
Pratyush Mishra and Tolulope Oke build a two way map on a resolution for a family of algebras in a 2025 paper. One member of the family is a cluster tilted algebra of type D4, a class drawn from a four point diagram. Such maps matter because they shape the ring that tracks an algebra's self extensions, a core tool in the field.

They lay the map out with the idempotents tied to the quiver's points. A chain homotopy then spells out how the ring multiplies for the first family member. A star product they define gives the cup product for every member of the family. The work links one concrete case to a whole family in a single frame.
arxiv-2506-23024:
Jerry Liu and co-authors add a polynomial layer to physics-informed neural networks and expose a trade-off between precision and conditioning. Their 2025 study asks why such networks stall far above machine precision. The fault may lie in the equations or in the standard network shape itself.

The new layer models solutions by barycentric interpolation and can sit atop a network or replace it. On a plain interpolation task, big standard networks stall eight orders above machine precision. Adding the layer lifts that cap and cuts errors by large factors on five test equations. A full swap reaches near machine precision on three of them. Error math for linear cases guides training choices.
arxiv-2506-23424:
Forecast tools trained once can drift as the world shifts, and a live fix at test time can cost a lot of memory. Heitor Medeiros and co-authors offer a lean fix in a 2025 study, named PETSA. Their method tunes only small plug in blocks at the mouth and tail of the tool, not the whole bulk.

Small rank blocks and a smart gate shift the tool's marks as fresh data stream in. A three part loss keeps the fix true: one part fights wild points, one keeps the beat of the series, and one keeps the shape of each patch. On set tests, the lean fix matched or beat full retrain tools across all spans. The code is free for others to use.
arxiv-2506-23724:
Chang'an Yi and co-authors let small models guide large ones at test time in a 2025 paper. Test-time tuning bends a trained model to new data on the fly, with no labels to lean on. Past work tuned one model alone, and the team asked what peer models could add to the mix.

Even a small model, they found, can steer a far larger one with fair, sure facts the big one lacks. Size gaps did not block the help. Their frame, called COCA, has models teach each other as tests roll in. Joint tuning beat lone tuning across shifts.
arxiv-2506-24024:
Nicolas Heintz, Tom Francart, and Alexander Bertrand add a smoothing step to tools that read listening focus from brain waves, in a 2025 paper. Their setting is a room with several speakers, where a device must guess which voice a listener follows. Current tools judge short slices of signal, and their guesses jump around too much for real use.

The fix is a hidden Markov model, a method that weighs what came just before. Since people rarely switch focus from one moment to the next, the model steadies the guesses. Tests showed gains in accuracy and speed of response, in both live and offline modes, beating older smoothing steps.
arxiv-2506-24124:
Sixun Dong and co-authors teach time series models to use pictures and text in this 2025 paper. Forecasting from raw numbers alone can miss high-level patterns. People, by contrast, read charts by eye and grasp shapes at a glance.

Their method turns each numeric series into both a visual view and a text view. Contrastive learning then aligns the two views in a shared space. A selection module picks the most useful variables for multi-series forecasts. Tests on fifteen short-term and six long-term benchmarks beat strong single-mode rivals. The gains suggest aligned views give a richer signal than numbers alone.
arxiv-2507-00124:
Sebastian Harris wrote this solo 2025 arXiv paper in theoretical physics, on a method called the conformal bootstrap. The method pins down what kinds of quantum field theories can exist by demanding that their math stays consistent. Most work uses links between four points, but recent work pushed to six points, which can give new and strict bounds.

The six-point version needs huge matrices, and that size has held the method back. Harris shows the matrices have a sparse, banded shape that can be split into small pieces. With that trick, a one-dimensional six-point problem turns into a standard four-point one that existing tools can solve. He then derives new bounds and matches the edge cases to known free-particle theories. The paper makes a promising method far more practical to run.
arxiv-2507-00224:
Changsoo Jung and three co-authors study how computers can track hand-held objects while students work in groups, in a 2025 paper. Hands-on group tasks help schoolchildren learn, and smart classroom tools need to follow what students do with real objects. That calls for estimating each object's full position and tilt in 3D from video, a task called 6D pose estimation.

The team built a video data set, FiboSB, of trios solving a task with small cubes and a balance scale. Filming whole groups from afar makes the cubes tiny in frame, which strains current methods. The team tested four leading pose estimators on the set and mapped where they fail. The paper frames the data set as both a benchmark and a call to build trackers that can keep up with busy, real classrooms.
arxiv-2507-00324:
Speech synthesis tools can now imitate a person's voice well enough to fool many listeners, and public figures are frequent targets of such impersonation. Malik and co-authors describe how they built a dataset of real and fake speech for ten public figures, including political leaders, and they document the problems they met along the way. Their pipeline gathers high-quality real speech samples on its own and uses transcription-based segmentation to cut the audio into clean pieces, which raised the quality of the fake clips.

The team tried several synthesis routes, from single-speaker training to zero-shot methods, and records how its approach changed over time. The resulting dataset pairs real and synthetic samples and reached a naturalness score of 3.69 on a standard quality scale. In listening tests, people misclassified the fake speech 61.9 percent of the time, which shows how hard such fakes are to spot.
arxiv-2507-00424:
Marcos Vasconcelos and Behrouz Touri study how a group of agents can act as one when each sees just a noisy stream of counts. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, uses a class of games with partial facts.

The agents must pick acts that pay off best when they line up, yet none sees the true state of the world. The team takes the counts to follow a known chance law, with a prior on the state. They prove a stable point exists among plans that switch acts at a set mark, for pay that grows in a straight line with acts. To find the mark, they study a form with an endless count of agents. The work fits germ groups that sense their own density.
arxiv-2507-00824:
Matthieu Pigaglio and eight co-authors present PANDAS for data availability sampling in Ethereum in two thousand twenty-five. Layer two data must spread and be sampled within four seconds. That bound comes from the consensus slot clock of the chain. No past system met it at planetary scale in their account.

PANDAS uses light, direct peer exchanges to spread and sample data. It needs no change to consensus or discovery protocols. Loss, node failure, and silent peers are all handled in design. A thousand node prototype and larger simulations test the build. Sampling met the deadline under global latency in those runs.
arxiv-2507-00924:
Chase Cooper and co-authors chart how Saturn's moon Titan brightens and dims across its phases. Cassini watched the hazy moon for thirteen years. The team built a pipeline to merge thousands of whole disk infrared snapshots into smooth phase curves. At crescent phases, Titan flares far more than optical data suggested.

Thin air windows let light stream forward through the haze, boosting the crescent glow. Spectra near full phase double as a measure of the moon's reflectivity. The results give modelers a test case for hazy worlds around other stars. They also warn that strong forward scattering can skew readings of distant planets.
arxiv-2507-01524:
Johannes Lengler and Tom Offermann introduce a way to use crossover in evolution without draining variety, in a 2025 paper. Crossover mixes two parent solutions to make new ones. It works best when the pool is varied. Yet using it tends to shrink that variety. This self defeating loop limits many genetic methods. Their paradigm keeps variety high. It still exploits the gains of mixing.

The resulting method was proven to solve a standard benchmark, LeadingOnes, in notably fewer scoring runs than classic genetic methods need. Only artificial, hand tailored methods had broken that barrier before. Simulations confirmed the theory. Tests on other benchmarks showed the method stays competitive beyond its home example. The authors argue the paradigm deserves systematic study.
arxiv-2507-01924:
Samirah Bakker, Yao Ma, and Seyed Ziabari hunt odd bills in mental health care with hybrid deep learning, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Billing tangles hide fraud, but labels are scarce and classes skewed. Fake labels from two scout methods feed the learners.

A memory net scout combo caught about ninety-six percent of odd declaration-level bills. On finer operation-level data, the hybrid scout model led recall at about seventy-four percent, with weaker precision. No prior work had tried this mix on health billing. The authors frame fake labels as the bridge over label scarcity. Readers get a fraud net tuned for messy real books.
arxiv-2507-02324:
Jintae Kim, Yizhi You, and Jung Hoon Han extend noninvertible symmetry ideas to one-dimensional phases guarded by patterned charges, in this 2025 paper. Such modulated phases protect order through symmetries that vary along the chain. Their hidden dualities were only partly charted.

Starting from a cluster model, the team builds the two classic duality transforms for charge, dipole, and exponential symmetries. Each lands on a symmetry-broken twin, and the twins interlink. New phases emerge that the standard domain-wall picture misses. A holography map then ties each chain phase to a two-dimensional bulk theory built from toric codes.
arxiv-2507-02524:
Diab Abueidda, Mbebo Nonna, Panos Pantidis, and Mostafa Mobasher wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It learns solution operators for time-based partial differential equations from sparse, uneven data, free of any fixed time grid.

Their network, NCDE-DeepONet, puts a neural controlled differential equation in the branch net. The load history is coded as the path of that equation, driven by a smooth curve through the samples, so any sampling rate gives the same code. The trunk net takes raw space and time points, so answers can be asked on new meshes and steps with no retraining. Tests on heat, elastic, and coupled heat-elastic tasks show fast, sound forecasts.
arxiv-2507-02624:
Six authors, Antoine Honoré, Borja Rodríguez Gálvez, Yoomi Park, Yitian Zhou, Volker Lauschke, and Ming Xiao, wrote this 2025 paper on predicting how gene variants change drug response. Tools that judge variant effects often rely on alignments of like proteins across species. That route assumes natural variants are fit, which can fail for drug genes under weak evolutionary pressure.

Lab data from deep mutational scanning offer a second route, since they score many variants directly. The team built a transformer-based model, called matVAE, that learns from such data with a structured prior. They tested it on 33 scanning data sets covering 26 drug target and drug-processing proteins from the ProteinGym benchmark. Trained on alignments, their model beat the top rival, DeepSequence, at zero-shot prediction. It did so with far fewer parameters and less compute.
arxiv-2507-02924:
David Li tests whether street view images can model urban food insecurity, in work from 2025. Food insecurity harms health in many city areas worldwide, yet surveys that track it are hard to scale. Street level images may offer a cheaper signal tied to place.

The project predicts food insecurity at census tract level from street images. A two step method first extracts image features, then joins them with gated attention across views. The team compares model designs, reads learned weights, and runs a case study for checks. Scores fell slightly short of rival designs on raw prediction power. Li still argues the approach can support survey methods and help planners target aid.
arxiv-2507-03024:
The largest in-vivo toxic gene database has gaps, and filling them by shape may beat filling them flat. Tan Nguyen and Guojing Cong test that idea in a 2025 paper on the DrugMatrix database. The data form a three-way block: tissue, treatment, and gene response. Older methods flatten that block into a table, which can lose the block's structure.

Their tensor method keeps all three axes and learns the missing entries in place. It matched the true data spread better and caught organ-specific patterns more faithfully. Error scores beat both a classic tensor method and flat table methods. The approach also revealed links among tissues. The authors say it may help study drugs that cross from rats to humans.
arxiv-2507-03524:
Janmejoy Sarkar and co-authors describe a heat filter for a solar telescope in this 2025 paper. The telescope sits on an Indian satellite built to study the Sun, and it images the Sun in near-ultraviolet light across eleven bands. Sunlight in that range is strong and varies a lot by band, so heat is a major problem.

The filter sits at the telescope's front opening, facing the Sun directly. It lets through only a tiny share of the incoming light, which controls heat and keeps the camera sensor in its sound working range. Choosing the base and coating was hard, due to risks of dirt, rust, and wear. The paper covers the design, making, and testing of the part.
arxiv-2507-03724:
Zhiyu Li and a very large team propose giving language models an operating-system-style memory, in a 2025 paper. Today's models remember only what fits in their weights and the current prompt, so they forget user preferences, lose track of long projects, and cannot update knowledge cleanly. Retrieval add-ons fetch text but manage nothing: no lifecycle, no consistency checks, no structured store.

Their design, MemOS, treats memory as a managed resource with layers, echoing how a computer's memory hierarchy cuts cost by keeping hot data close. The paper argues that an explicit memory layer between model weights and external retrieval can serve long-context reasoning and steady personalization. The proposal is architectural: a shared way to store, update, and retire what an AI system knows.
arxiv-2507-04224:
Haining Wang and co-authors test whether AI chatbots treat library users fairly when they differ in sex, race, or campus role, in a 2025 paper. Libraries are eyeing large language models for online reference desks, where equal service is a core promise. A biased bot could quietly break that promise.

The team posed reference questions to six leading models, varying the stated identity of the asker. Answers showed no split by race or ethnicity, and only a slight stereotyped tilt against women in one model. Models did adjust tone for campus roles, shifting formality, politeness, and jargon in ways that mirror professional norms rather than bias. The authors judge current models fairly ready for reference work, with watchfulness still advised.
arxiv-2507-04624:
Claudianor Alves, Zhentao He, and Chao Ji study normalized solutions of a nonlinear Schrödinger equation on bounded domains. 'Normalized' means the solution's total mass is fixed in advance, and the frequency term in the equation appears as an unknown to be solved for rather than a given value. The equation allows very general boundary rules, covering several standard edge cases in one setup. The authors adapt a perturbation method to prove that such solutions exist and that several distinct ones can be found.

Their results go further than the first equation. The same approach covers equations with critical growth in two dimensions, equations with magnetic fields, higher-order biharmonic equations, and Choquard equations, which involve interaction terms that reach across space. The paper thus gives one method that handles a wide family of mass-constrained problems.
arxiv-2507-04924:
Rakesh Arora and Sergey Shmarev studied a hard growth equation with two unlike powers. Their paper, from twenty twenty twenty-five, deals with a double phase evolution problem in a bounded zone. The spread weights are rough: not smooth, with change rates held in an L class. The powers shift from point to point. Data and start state come with set bounds. The team proves that solutions exist for the same value edge problem.

Global regular order of the solutions is proved with it. The weight pair is kept from both dying at once by a floor sum rule. Readers in partial equations get an existence and polish result for a class where rough weights break stock proofs.
arxiv-2507-05024:
Kai Yang and Daniel Schwalbe-Koda teach a generative AI to design glasses and other disordered materials atom by atom, in a 2025 paper. Diffusion models have changed the design of molecules and crystals, but amorphous materials, with no repeating pattern, resisted them. The team's model generates amorphous structures up to a thousand times faster than standard practice, across compositions and processing conditions.

For silica glass, the generated structures matched real ones in short- and medium-range order, variety, and bulk properties, checked by simulation and by an information-based test. Guiding the model let it build large samples cooled very slowly. It showed a switch from ductile to brittle and porous silica forms. The method also worked for metallic glasses, reproducing structures from both computed and lab data. The authors present it as a roadmap for making disordered materials that computers could not reach before.
arxiv-2507-05224:
Athanasakis-Kaklamanakis and co-authors report the first study of a radioactive actinium molecule in a 2025 paper. Heavy molecules can probe whether the strong force of nature breaks a deep symmetry. This question is tied to why matter dominates the universe. Such forms were put forth as keen probes for this test, but most lay beyond technical reach.

The team made the gas-phase molecule actinium monofluoride. They saw its predicted strongest light transition, the line needed for future readout. Calculations on its electronic and nuclear structure then gauged how well it can sense several symmetry-breaking effects. A realistic near-term experiment, they estimate, would tighten current limits on those effects. The paper is a large collaboration's step toward a new class of precision tests.
arxiv-2507-05424:
Yufei Tao, Adam Hiatt, Rahul Seetharaman, and Ameeta Agrawal measure how language models weigh a provided passage against what they already know, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Their framework, CoPE, scores contextual knowledge and built-in parametric knowledge separately across models and languages.

They built a dataset from Wikipedia facts in English, Spanish, and Danish, then watched how models answer open questions. A clear pattern emerged, which they name lost-in-the-later: models tend to overlook information placed late in a passage. That positional bias weakens how well answers are grounded in the given text. Reasoning models leaned on context even less. So did ordinary models told to think step by step. The findings warn that longer context windows do not guarantee that late facts get used. Anyone building retrieval systems should test where in the passage the answer sits.
arxiv-2507-05624:
A research team presents ADMC in a 2025 paper, a model that fills in missing parts of multimodal data. The catalog and text author lists differ, so the work is best credited to the team as a whole. Multimodal systems that read emotion and intent study speech, text, and pictures to call a user's state, for machines that deal with people on their own.

Parts go missing when sensors fail or data comes in short. Older rebuild methods often bind the parts too tightly and make sloppy stand-ins. ADMC trains a feature-picking network for each part on its own, which keeps what makes each part distinct. A diffusion network with attention then builds the missing features so they sit close to real multimodal spreads. Readers get a design that keeps the parts distinct while it fills the gaps.
arxiv-2507-06124: Manuel Mancini and co-authors build two new notions of action inside a class of algebraic categories, in work from 2025. The categories are called ideally exact, and the notions extend how rings and algebras act on other objects. One notion is named coherent action, and the other is named ideal action. The authors prove that every ideal action is also coherent. They also show the reverse holds in some key ideally exact settings. A link to a known notion of semidirect product in such categories is drawn out as well.
arxiv-2507-06324:
Arash Azizi builds a general method for dual forms on spheres in a 2025 paper. In higher dimensional theories, extra dimensions are often curled into a sphere. Fields living on that sphere need their mirror forms computed with care. Sloppy handling can break the lower dimensional theory built on top.

Azizi derives a closed formula for the dual of a form of any degree under the sphere constraint. Test cases in three dimensions check the formula in flat and slanted settings. The result gives builders of gravity and string models a steady tool. Steady use matters most where models are trimmed to fewer fields.
arxiv-2507-06424:
Yairon Cid-Ruiz wrote this 2025 algebraic geometry paper introducing the mixed Segre zeta function, a power series that packages the Segre classes of a whole sequence of ideals at once. By extending the ideals into projective spaces of growing dimension, the series records intersection-theoretic data that classically came one ideal at a time, unifying work of Kleiman, Thorup, and Aluffi.

Three theorems anchor the paper. The series is always a rational function, and its poles sit exactly at the degrees of the generators of the ideals. It depends only on the integral closures of the ideals, so cosmetic changes wash out. And after a small modification, its numerator, homogenized, is a denormalized Lorentzian polynomial in the sense of Brändén and Huh, importing their log-concavity machinery into Segre theory. The results hand geometers a compact invariant with unexpectedly rigid behavior.
arxiv-2507-06724: Jan Moser, a solo author, works on deep links between famous math results in a 2025 paper. He connects the Riemann zeta function with the Fermat-Wiles theorem. That theorem settled a claim about whole-number equations that stood open for centuries. Using a tool he calls Jacob's ladders, he builds new endless families of statements. He also uses a classic set of orthogonal functions. Each new statement is shown to be equivalent to the famous theorem.
arxiv-2507-07024:
Weijia Shi and co-authors build language models whose data can be switched in and out in a 2025 paper. Owners of private data often cannot share it for joint training, yet everyone wants the gains of pooling. FlexOlmo trains separate expert modules, each on its own closed data set. It then joins them in a mixture-of-experts model. A router, taught which expert fits which domain, needs no joint training on the raw data.

At use time, any expert, and with it its data, can be included or dropped with no retraining, honoring licenses and permissions. Tested at up to thirty-seven billion parameters across thirty-one tasks, adding closed-data experts lifted scores by about forty-one percent on average over the public-data expert alone. The method also beat model merging and matched unrestricted training.
arxiv-2507-07124:
Leonardo Dos Santos and co-authors present a science case in two thousand twenty-five for watching exoplanet atmospheres escape with a future space observatory. The Habitable Worlds Observatory is planned to hunt and characterize Earth-like planets. Air leaking to space shapes how small planets evolve and whether they can stay habitable.

Using ultraviolet transit spectroscopy, the observatory can catch escaping gas as a planet crosses its star. The team argues for a UV spectrograph with moderate-to-high resolution, coverage of key lines from one hundred to three hundred nanometers, and detectors that handle high count rates. Such an instrument would test how well small planets hold their air and search for signs of Earth-like atmospheres. The article adapts a working-group document for the mission.
arxiv-2507-07324:
Kirill Tuchin wrote a 2025 theoretical physics paper on chiral Cherenkov radiation when the chiral chemical potential changes over time. Cherenkov radiation is the glow a fast particle emits in a medium. In a chiral medium, theory predicts a resonance in photon emission for one polarization, tied to a magnetic conductivity driven by the chiral imbalance.

Tuchin studies particle decay into a photon when that imbalance varies with time. He shows the adiabatic approximation holds for ultra relativistic particles. For two model time profiles, he derives the photon spectrum in closed form. The first model can show up to two resonances, depending on the signs of the imbalance early and late. The second shows none. Numbers use quark gluon plasma settings.
arxiv-2507-07424:
Jingjing Jiang and co-authors present Corvid, a multimodal language model built for step-by-step reasoning. Their 2025 paper notes that open multimodal models perceive well but lag on complex, structured problems. Such tasks need a chain of thought that joins image and text evidence.

Corvid pairs a hybrid vision encoder with a connector designed to align image and language features. The team built a large instruction data set of multimodal reasoning examples, cleaned from public sources. Training ran in two stages with reasoning-formatted data to grow the skill gradually. At inference, a self-check strategy guards against both over-thinking and under-thinking a problem. Tests show Corvid beating like-sized multimodal models, with notable strength on hard reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2507-07624:
Qu, Wang, Lin, and Li study a layered cluster Mott material under pressure in a 2025 paper. The compound is built from niobium trimers in a chloride lattice. Pressure shrinks its charge gap in experiments, and the reason was unclear.

Combining two theory methods, the team compare normal and high-pressure forms. Pressure breaks the local symmetry of each trimer, widens the bands, and lifts band degeneracy. Even so, the cluster Mott state survives the distortion. The smaller gap comes from both wider bands and weaker Coulomb effects under pressure. The authors call this the first full account of how pressure-driven symmetry change acts on such a state.
arxiv-2507-07824:
Gianluca Vico and Jindrich Libovicky introduce a way to build tokenizers, the tools that chop text into pieces for language models, using parallel texts in two languages. Their paper came out in 2025. Standard tokenizers are trained on one language at a time, so the pieces rarely line up across languages.

Their method conditions the target language's piece choices on the source language's pieces, aiming for pieces that carry matching meaning. They tested four language pairs from different families and resource levels. The new tokenizer kept the same basic statistics as the standard one. It did not improve machine translation, but it consistently lowered perplexity, a measure of model surprise, in language modeling. The authors suspect a data-efficiency bottleneck and suggest other designs for cross-language tokenization.
arxiv-2507-07924:
Jack McKechnie, Graham McDonald, and Craig Macdonald argue that search evaluations miss half their error story. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Retrieval systems are ranked using human relevance judgments. Those judgments are costly, so cheaper sets are proposed. A cheaper set must still tell systems apart correctly. Past work counted how often sets flag real differences. It also quantified false positives, the Type I errors.

The authors insist Type II errors matter just as much. Those are real differences the test set misses. Missing them yields false comfort about a weak benchmark. The paper measures both error kinds together. Evaluation practice gains a fuller account of statistical risk. Benchmark builders can no longer cherry-pick one error type.
arxiv-2507-08324:
Mengjiao Rao and co-authors settled a question in 2025 about when a large network must contain a blown up copy of a tree. The blow up takes a graph and pads each link with new points, making a uniform hypergraph, and the question is how connected each point must be to force such a copy.

The authors find near best degree thresholds for all such blown up trees with bounded branching. Their answer refutes a published guess that a lower threshold would do. The surprise is a parity snag: trees whose points all have odd degree need higher thresholds. If a tree has even one even degree point, the needed threshold drops a lot, a split the paper also proves.
arxiv-2507-08824:
Raymond Pierrehumbert, Helene Brogniez, and Remy Roca explain why Earth's air is mostly far from saturated with water vapor, in a book chapter held in the catalog. Dry air aloft matters: it shapes how strongly water vapor amplifies warming and whether a planet can tip into a runaway greenhouse. The chapter asks what keeps the air subsaturated despite oceans below.

Drawing on observations, full climate models, and small idealized models, the authors trace the processes that dry the air. Sinking air, mixing, and the way clouds form and rain out all play parts. Though Earth is the focus, the same physics governs any condensible vapor on other planets. The chapter gives climate students a compact tour of a core topic.
arxiv-2507-08924:
Tests for chatbots often stop at school topics, yet jobs demand licensed expert knowledge too. Seokhee Hong and co-authors built two Korean test sets for that deeper level in this 2025 paper. One set rebuilds an older Korean test from national technical qualification exams, with serious errors cut out. The other is new and draws on national professional licensure exams in Korea.

Together the sets cover both study-based and work-based knowledge in Korean. The authors ran current large language models on the sets to check how well they capture expert skill. Their trials showed the tests do reflect industrial knowledge in Korea. Both sets are released in public for other teams to use. Harder, job-true tests can push models toward real workplace use.
arxiv-2507-09424:
Jiao leads a team introducing DATE-LM, a benchmark for judging data attribution methods in language models, in a 2025 paper. Attribution methods score how much each training example shaped a model's output. Uses include dataset curation, interpretability, and data valuation.

The benchmark grades attribution through three tasks: selecting training data, filtering toxic or biased data, and factual attribution. The tools let researchers run large evaluations across tasks and model designs. In a large-scale test, no single method won across all tasks. Simpler baselines sometimes traded blows with fancy methods, and scores shifted with task design. A public leaderboard supports comparison. The authors offer the benchmark as a base for future attribution work.
arxiv-2507-09524:
Yunwei Lan and co-authors present a method for clearing haze from real-world photos, in this 2025 paper. Many tools learn from paired hazy and clear shots of the same scene, which are hard to gather outdoors. Tools trained without pairs often rely on contest-style setups with weak image transport. That weakness caps the quality they can reach on real haze.

Their method, DehazeSB, rests on a math frame called the Schrödinger Bridge, drawn from optimal transport theory. It links the spread of hazy images to the spread of clear ones directly. That link lets the tool move an image from haze to clear in fewer steps. The design also guards the scene's structure, so edges and layout stay true while the haze lifts.
arxiv-2507-09824:
Mingya Huang and Soham Ghosh wrote a 2025 paper on a flaw in test scoring models. Such models assume each test item stands alone, but in some tests the items link up in real ways. In nature surveys, people who know one species in a place often know its neighbors too. In author tests, knowing one science fiction writer predicts knowing others.

Older models handled these links only for yes-or-no answers and with rigid rules about which items count as near each other. Huang and Ghosh propose a model that uses smooth spatial curves instead, so the link can bend in more complex ways. Their method widens the kinds of tests that can be scored fairly when items cluster by place or topic.
arxiv-2507-09924:
Tuan-Luc Huynh and co-authors propose a 2025 method for keeping generative search up to date as new documents arrive. In generative retrieval, a model itself acts as the index, so adding documents can demand costly retraining. Their system mixes several small adapter experts that can be added over time. New experts are brought in only when the system spots enough documents that fall outside what it knows.

This growth plan keeps the added size well below one expert per new batch of documents. Tests use two large question and passage collections. The authors report that their method beat full model update baselines. It did so with little added size and much lower training cost. The design is meant for collections that change often, where retraining the whole model each time is not practical.
arxiv-2507-10124:
Thomas Hills, writing solo, tests a one-line prompt as a cure for bias in language models and people. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Models store facts about bias and counterarguments from their vast training. Those facts surface only when the model is pushed. Human decision research faced the same problem earlier. Its fix was metacognitive prompts that make latent knowledge active.

The prompt studied here is simply: could you be wrong? After a first answer, it leads models to add reasons and caveats. They explain why they answered as they did. They also raise points that cut against the first answer. Hills argues such general prompts will outlast any single model version. The approach borrows tools from psychology rather than new training. It may help human choices made with model advice.
arxiv-2507-10324:
Amit Chopra, Samuel Christie, and Munindar Singh present a software suite for building multiagent systems around communication protocols, in a research paper from 2025. In their approach, designers first model how the roles in a system should talk. Agents are then built to play those roles and follow the exchange rules.

The suite includes tools that check protocols for safety and liveness traits quickly. Middleware in the suite eases the work of coding agents that obey the protocols. The paper walks through parts of the suite built over recent years. It aims to make protocol-first design practical for working system builders.
arxiv-2507-10424: Omer Sella and Thomas Heinis wrote this short computing paper in 2025 on decoding LDPC codes, the error-correcting codes used in modern links. The Min-Sum decoder that reads them is usually built for one fixed parity matrix. The pair instead treat the matrix as an input. They map the decoder's work onto reduction steps, a shape that graphics chips handle well, and build it as CUDA kernels. Their version runs on any parity matrix of the right size, with no rebuild for each new code.
arxiv-2507-10524:
Sangmin Bae and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on making large language models cheaper to run. Big models cost a lot to train and serve. Two known savings are sharing the same layers more than once and letting easy words take fewer steps than hard ones. Their method, called Mixture-of-Recursions, joins both savings in one design.

A small router decides, for each word, how many passes through the shared layers it needs. Words that finish early stop taking part, which saves memory and time. The team also offers a variant that reuses saved attention data from the first pass. The result is a model that spends effort where the text is hard and skims where it is easy, without growing in size.
arxiv-2507-10624:
Zheng Zhang argues that language models grasp principles they cannot reliably apply, in work from 2025. The models speak fluently yet fail at symbol tasks, arithmetic, and strict logic. Zhang calls the split a computational split-brain syndrome.

Controlled tests and architecture review support the diagnosis. Models often state a rule correctly, then break it in execution. The fault lies in how the systems compute, not in missing knowledge. The same gap recurs across math and relation tasks, even with ideal prompts. Models act as strong pattern completers without scaffolding for stepwise reasoning. Zhang urges designs with self-checking control built in. The paper maps where today's models truly end.
arxiv-2507-11124:
Maxime Faymonville and Carsten Jentsch studied in 2025 a resampling method for time series of counts, such as daily numbers of events. Models for such data use a thinning step that carries past counts forward and add fresh random counts at each step. A flexible method can estimate both parts without fixing their shapes in advance.

Their bootstrap version mimics that flexible estimate and is shown to be jointly sound for both parts. Uses covered include fit checks, forecasts, and a joint study of spread. Computer tests with several fresh-count shapes showed how the method behaves in small samples. Real data cases close the work and show the method in use.
arxiv-2507-11924:
Hyeongmin Choe and SooJean Han study sensor networks that track a moving target, and ask what is gained when the central unit sends information back to the sensors, in a 2025 paper. Sending less data saves power, but the data that arrive must stay accurate. Their feedback method lets each sensor drop repeats.

The authors compare feedback and non-feedback setups in a strict way, tracking error and power cost per sensor. They map when feedback is workable and when it wins, under varied delay, power cost, wait time, sampling rate, and noise. Readers get clear conditions for choosing an architecture, rather than a blanket claim. The work speaks to designers of low-power tracking networks.
arxiv-2507-12124:
Artur Riazanov and co-authors prove a hard limit on teamwork in a 2025 paper. Two parties hold pieces of a puzzle: a random logical formula, built from short clauses over many variables, that no assignment can satisfy, plus an assignment to test. Their shared job is to find one clause the assignment breaks. Randomized chatter is allowed, and the formula's shape follows the classic random pattern at logarithmic clause width.

The result is a wall: any randomized two-party protocol needs communication growing linearly with the number of variables. In plain terms, no clever shortcut of hints and summaries can shrink the search; the parties must effectively pool a constant share of everything they hold. The bound hardens a known frontier in proof complexity and communication, where random formulas at this width resist every distributed shortcut.
arxiv-2507-12224:
The optimizer that trains a neural network is usually judged by how fast it learns, and Razvan Pascanu and co-authors say that misses half the story. Because network loss surfaces are nonlinear, different optimizers land on genuinely different solutions, not just the same answer at different speeds. The choice quietly encodes inductive biases and can change what a model class is able to express.

The authors argue the field should map the biases of existing optimizers on purpose. Better still, new optimizers could be designed to push solutions toward wanted properties directly. They frame optimizer design as a lever beside architecture and data in shaping what models become.
arxiv-2507-12524:
Micha Berkooz, Trivko Kukolj, and Josef Seitz reinterpret a set of quantum field theory quantities through a simpler chaotic model. The quantities are Schur half-indices, counting tools for certain supersymmetric gauge theories, here for a basic SU(2) theory with extra matter and line defects inserted.

The authors show these half-indices can be read as transition amplitudes inside a model known as DSSYK, a toy system of randomly interacting fermions much studied for its links to quantum gravity. In the chord diagram language of that model, the gauge theory objects come from summing diagrams with special segments. Those segments act as coherent states of a deformed oscillator algebra. One case yields an especially clean match: the half-index equals the partition function of a particle living on a quantum disk. The authors offer these matches as a dictionary between gauge theory and the chaotic model.
arxiv-2507-12624:
Wang and co-authors introduce a new score for judging computer-made tissue stains, in this 2025 paper. Virtual staining turns one microscope image into the look of a chemically stained one, saving time and reagents. Older scores, built for photos, often miss the cell details that pathologists care about.

Their score, called PaPIS, learns features from cell shape data and splits images in a way inspired by light correction. In tests it matched expert judgment better than rival scores and caught fine cell structures others missed. Used as a training guide, it also made staining models produce more faithful images. The work pushes virtual staining toward clinic-ready quality.
arxiv-2507-12724:
Richard Sproat, Tianyu Zhao, and Llion Jones build a translation judge that reasons before it scores. Their twenty twenty-five system, TransEvalnia, prompts a large language model to grade translations on fine quality dimensions drawn from the MQM framework. It names a winner and gives numbers per dimension and overall.

Tests cover English-Japanese and several shared-task language pairs. The system matched or beat the leading ranker, MT-Ranker. Human raters found its judgments highly acceptable, and its scores tracked human scores well. Machine translation improves fastest when grading is trustworthy; a judge that shows its reasoning can be audited, not just believed.
arxiv-2507-12824:
Tattwamasi Amrutam, Artem Dudko, Yongle Jiang, and Adam Skalski studied a rigidity property of operator algebras built from certain groups, in a 2025 paper. The property asks whether every invariant subalgebra of a group's algebra must come from a normal subgroup. Groups with the property are rare, and friendly groups with it were not known.

The groups in play arise as semidirect products from algebraic actions on groups built from two-torsion parts. The team presents the first example of an amenable group with the rigidity property that still has a non-trivial abelian normal subgroup. Another example has exactly one invariant subalgebra that no normal subgroup explains. They also work out the invariant subalgebras of the standard lamplighter group. The results widen the known map of this rigidity notion.
arxiv-2507-13124:
Jafar Olimov, Yi-Chan Tsai, and Hao-Yu Yang model how uneven bribery can, at times, raise output. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, studies firms choosing between capital-heavy and labor-heavy technology. Data from one hundred forty-eight countries show bribery hits the two types differently. A general equilibrium model builds that unevenness in.

When bribes burden weak labor-heavy firms more, resources shift to stronger capital-heavy rivals. Capital stock and total output can rise as a result. Removing bribes only for capital-heavy firms beats removing them everywhere, in their model. The effect is larger in rich countries than poor ones. The findings complicate the view that graft always harms growth.
arxiv-2507-13224:
Keerthi Veeramachaneni, Praveen Tirupattur, Amrit Singh Bedi, and Mubarak Shah detect AI-made videos with pre-trained vision models, in a paper from 2025. Video generators now make clips far beyond face swaps, and detectors built for deepfakes miss general content. A fresh approach that needs little new training would help fight false media.

Features from models trained on vast real footage carry subtle signs that split real from made clips. With no extra training, those features already detect well. Adding a simple linear layer on top lifts accuracy further. On a new set of about ten thousand made videos and four thousand real ones, accuracy topped ninety percent on average.
arxiv-2507-13424:
Sarang Shah studies the moduli space of a singular monopole in this 2025 mathematics paper. The object at the center is an SU(2) monopole with a Dirac singularity, built in earlier work by Durcan and by Cherkis and Durcan. The moduli space collects all such monopoles, and Shah asks what shape that space has.

Shah builds the tangent directions to the space from the monopole's phase and translational zero modes, using the Nahm transform to construct them. From those modes he computes parts of the metric on the space and finds that the space is the Taub-NUT space. He then computes the moduli space of the matching Nahm data in a second way, through a quotient construction. The two spaces turn out to be isometric, and an inner product formula gives a direct link between them.
arxiv-2507-13624:
Daniel Commey, Kamel Abbad, Garth Crosby, and Lyes Khoukhi propose FedSkipTwin, a way to cut communication in federated learning by letting unhelpful clients sit out rounds, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Bandwidth is the main bottleneck for learning on phones and sensors.

Each client gets a lightweight digital twin on the server, a small LSTM that studies its history of gradient norms. The twin forecasts the size and uncertainty of the client's next update. The server requests updates only when a forecast clears a threshold. On UCI-HAR and MNIST benchmarks, total communication fell by twelve to fifteen percent while final accuracy slightly improved over standard federated averaging.
arxiv-2507-14224:
Benoît Brebion and seven co-authors build a diffusion method to translate between newborn EEG and fetal MEG signals, in work from 2025. Brain study in premature babies rests on EEG, but development starts before birth, where only fetal magnetoencephalography can record activity. That data are scarce and noisy, so a bridge between the two signal types has clear value.

Dual diffusion bridges carry the unpaired translation, with numerical steps tuned for quality at lower cost. Training used bursts from 30 newborn EEG records and 44 fetal records. The method beat GAN results on time-domain error and removed mode collapse in frequency. The authors claim a new best for this translation task.
arxiv-2507-14324:
Yao Ma and co-authors advance a 2025 method for proving identity without revealing secrets. Checking who someone is underpins banking, health care, and online services. Passwords and PINs can be stolen by fake login pages. A recent line of work uses zero knowledge proofs based on graph coloring. The proofs are sped by the limits of relativity. Two provers who cannot signal each other in time can be forced to answer honestly.

The team eased the distance demand of the setup from sixty meters to thirty. They also made the demonstration steadier and easier to scale. For long term safety against provers who share quantum entanglement, they propose a modified protocol at similar cost and bound its cheating risk. They further extend the design from two provers to three, with security shown for that case as well.
arxiv-2507-14424:
Modules over a ring can be swapped for simpler stand-ins that keep the key traits of the first. Richard Bartels, writing alone in 2025, studies such stand-ins for a class of rings named for Cohen and Macaulay. He links two kinds of stand-ins, called MCM approximations and FID hulls, when the ring has a special dual module and a mild extra trait.

He then broadens a known result of Kato about rings that meet a depth rule named the SC condition. For higher levels of that rule, he gives a test that reads the trait off a module's first derived partner. The test works when that partner meets the rule one step down. The result helps algebraists sort rings and modules by depth.
arxiv-2507-14824:
Kunyu Yu and co-authors benchmark large pre-trained models on public health records, in work from 2025. Such models can take in mixed record types, from notes to codes and measures. The team tests how well they predict, how fair they are, and how clearly they can be read.

Records came from a well-known public intensive care data set. A shared cleaning pipeline put the mixed records into one ready form. Eight models were compared, some single-type and some mixed, some medical and some general. Mixed-type models predicted better across tasks, with no added bias found. The authors share their code and aim to guide builders of clinical tools that doctors can trust.
arxiv-2507-15324:
H. M. Heidema, H. J. van Waarde, and B. Besselink work out the control theory of neural networks built from memristors, circuit parts whose resistance remembers past current. Crossbar arrays of memristors can run a neural network directly in hardware, saving the energy that digital chips spend shuttling data. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors describe one such circuit design and settle three practical questions. How to compute what the circuit outputs for a given input, how to read the hidden resistance values from measurements at the terminals. How to steer those resistances to desired values with applied voltages.

They demonstrate the answers on a small teaching example and on a network trained to read handwritten digits. The results supply the missing operating manual for learning in hardware networks, a step toward low-power analog computing.
arxiv-2507-15724:
A team of researchers compares ways to control where generated images place things in a paper from 2025. The catalog creator field includes an email address, and the head byline lists five authors against four in the catalog, so team framing is used here. Users guide generation with edge maps or poses, but papers differ too much for fair comparison. The team ran controlled tests on a standard data set across diffusion, flow, and autoregressive transformers.

A simple trick, prefilling control tokens, proved a strong general baseline. Extending guidance to the control signal and truncating the softmax both sharpened obedience. Adapters prevented forgetting on small data but lagged full training on consistency. The paper aims to give builders clear takeaways.
arxiv-2507-15924:
Mary Rawcliffe, Nathan Griffiths-Janvier, and Richard Parker argue in two thousand twenty-five that hidden biases may distort what we know about double stars in birth clouds. Most stars form in pairs or multiples. In the general field, pair separations follow a smooth log-normal curve across a huge range, but young star-forming regions show a confusing mix, with an apparent excess at middle separations.

The authors show the field's smooth curve can be rebuilt from several sub-populations whose own starting distributions look nothing like it. They also note that one famous cluster's excess need not clash with the field, since the field sums over many regions. Simulation limits near one astronomical unit add fog. They urge more spectroscopy of close pairs in young regions to complete the picture.
arxiv-2507-16024:
Rafikul Alam, Volker Mehrmann, and Ninoslav Truhar show how to peel dangerous vibrations out of damped spring-mass models before computing the rest, in this 2025 paper. Such systems yield quadratic eigenvalue problems whose borderline values, at zero, infinity, and on the imaginary axis, sit exactly where stability is lost. Solvers handle them badly if left in place.

The authors give structure-preserving deflation steps that remove those values through a trimmed linearization, keeping the model's physics intact. They treat fully hyperbolic problems in detail and analyze how a damping tweak moves the purely imaginary values.
arxiv-2507-16424:
Hui Xiang and co-authors present a method that picks the best samples to label when labels are scarce, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Active learning saves labeling cost by asking for the most useful cases first. With very few labels, the learned border between classes can drift far from the true one.

Their method uses unlabeled samples to build prompts that shift with each sample. Those prompts pull the model's border closer to the target layout. Picks then blend doubt with variety, both local and global. Tests on nine data sets beat nine rival methods. The code is shared in public.
arxiv-2507-16524:
The authors build a vision-language model with a sharper sense of 3D space. Most such models squeeze a whole scene into one summary or chop it into objects, losing layout. Their system grows its view step by step, widening the perception field while stamping location data into the scene features.

Two new tasks test the skill: measuring distances between objects and editing a room's layout. A fresh instruction dataset supports the tests. The model tops prior systems across many 3D tasks, and the gains trace to the step-wise spatial scheme. Code is public.
arxiv-2507-16624:
Meng Lou, Yunxiang Fu, and Yizhou Yu present A2Mamba, a hybrid network for recognizing images, in a 2025 paper. The design weds two lineages: transformer networks, which weigh which image parts matter, and state space models from the Mamba family, which scan efficiently. Earlier hybrids merely stacked the two kinds of layers in turn, with no real conversation between them.

Their new mixing block feeds attention maps at several scales into the state space scan, letting the scan gather its hidden states by place. That deepens the model's grip on two-dimensional layout while keeping its speed. On the standard ImageNet test the largest version reached about eighty-six percent top-one accuracy. The hybrid also beat strong rivals at outlining objects and scenes, in one case with forty percent fewer parameters.
arxiv-2507-16724:
Hu, Cao, Wu, Luo, and Yang present SALM, a spatial audio language model with structured embeddings, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Understanding where sounds come from is vital for perceiving acoustic scenes. Prior audio-language models handle spatial audio poorly. SALM bridges spatial audio and language through multimodal contrastive learning.

A dual-branch encoder splits sound into semantic and spatial components. Structured embeddings keep those components separable yet jointly usable. The model aligns spatial audio with natural language descriptions. Zero-shot direction classification works without task-specific training. Text-based editing can modify directional audio flexibly. Experiments show well-structured embeddings and strong cross-modal alignment.
arxiv-2507-16924:
Yueyao Xu and Yize Chen read a grid's true wire map from a few meter draws by a subset-sum trick in tiers. Grid maps are oft lost or part-told, yet load watch and break hunts need them true. Their 2025 way casts the map hunt as sums that must match meter facts. Tier craft splits the big hunt into small sums that chain to the whole.

Fewer draws then pin the map than past ways ask. Swift calls suit live yards where wires swap oft. Noise in the draws bends the call by no real span in their tests. True maps from scant draws can cut the cost of grid sense at scale.
arxiv-2507-17024:
Chase Stokes, Kylie Lin, and Cindy Xiong Bearfield compare ways to ask readers what a chart says in a 2025 paper. Chart design steers takeaways, but mapping that link needs crowds of readers writing free responses, which are slow to analyze. The team tested four elicitation methods on line charts, dot plots, and heat maps: free writing, two ranking styles, and salience rating.

No shortcut fully matched the free-response picture. Rankings plus ratings together formed a decent proxy at scale. Rankings bent toward favorite chart types and toward the offered conclusions. Ratings missed the fine differences between chart types. A side study used GPT-4o as a stand-in reader; it proxied ratings best and stumbled elsewhere. The authors warn that method choice shapes findings. Pick deliberately, combine methods, and mind the trade-offs.
arxiv-2507-17524:
Jiahao Tang and a large team of co-authors built a net that reads feelings from brain waves across new heads. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with EEG emotion reads for brain computer links. Each new user shifts the wave marks, and tagged data for them is scarce. Their net, SDC-Net, adapts with no tags on the new side at all. A mix trick blends trials of one user to grow the train set with no tag fog.

A live align step keeps sense and shift in step as domains move. Readers in feeling tech get a tag free path to emotion reads that hold from one skull to the next.
arxiv-2507-17724:
Joseph McDonald studies implication algebras and their links to quantum logic in a math note from 2025. The algebras, introduced by Hardegree, capture a weak form of logical implication. Orthogonality relations, which say when two elements clash, can be built from them in several ways.

McDonald adapts classic constructions from ortholattices to this setting. He then adds an operator to the algebras, creating monadic versions. Quantum monadic algebras pair a lattice with a closure operator that acts like a quantifier. Each such algebra converts into a monadic implication algebra through Sasaki implication. The note ties abstract implication to the logic of quantum systems. Converse results complete the bridge between the two frameworks.
arxiv-2507-17924:
Cities need forecasts of how people flow between every pair of places, at a grain fine enough to act on. Hongrong Yang and Markus Schläpfer present UrbanPulse, a deep learning system that treats each point of interest as its own node rather than clustering places together. A graph encoder reads the city's rhythm over time, and a transformer decoder predicts the flows.

Transfer comes in three stages: pretraining on large urban graphs, cold-start adaptation to a new city, then reinforcement fine-tuning.
