Jichen Feng, Ethan Abraham, Joseph E. Subotnik, and Abraham Nitzan show in 2025 that chiral molecules can rectify vibrational energy transfer under controlled driving. Chirality means a molecule's mirror form differs from itself, like left and right hands. Rectification means energy flows more easily one way than the other, like a one-way valve.

Classical models cover a single helical chain and a more realistic double helix of polyethylene. Drive frequency, polarization, and temperature all shape the effect. The favored direction and its size hinge on drive frequency and phase. The effect persists at room temperature, which raises hopes for molecule-scale energy control.
arxiv-2509-00524:
Gavin Wong joins four co-authors, Ping Shu Ho, Ivan Au Yeung, Ka Chun Cheung, and Simon See, in using known biology to guide machine learning. Biological pathways map how genes interact, yet many models treat genes as loose tokens and throw that structure away.

Wong and his co-authors build a graph attention network, a model that weighs links between genes, so each pathway is modeled at gene level rather than as a bag of genes. Their model cuts prediction error sharply on unseen treatments compared with simpler networks. Tests that encode drug action as edge changes boost robustness, and the model rediscovers all five known links in a key feedback loop from raw gene data.
arxiv-2509-01124:
Social media data form huge graphs, with users and posts as nodes and links between them. Wei Jiang, with five co-authors, builds a general learning framework for tasks such as spotting rumors, finding bots, and modeling influence. Many past models were built for one task and broke down on noisy social data.

Their design uses two encoders, one for graph structure and one for context, plus a module guided by kinetic ideas, meaning rules for how things spread. That module tracks how information moves through the graph over time. By learning from spread itself, the model aims to work across tasks and data sets without fresh design each time, and to resist the noise common on social platforms.
arxiv-2509-01224:
Quantum computers need special resource states, called magic states, to do tasks beyond a simpler class of circuits. Kwok Ho Wan and Zhenghao Zhong apply a cutting technique that splits hard quantum states into sums of easier Clifford pieces, using a diagram language called ZX-calculus. They target states made by magic state cultivation, a recent error-correction scheme.

For the two circuit sizes studied, the resulting states became sums of just four and eight Clifford diagrams, after fixing measurement outcomes for simplicity. Such small sums make simulation of the circuits far cheaper. Wan and Zhong suggest that tweaks to these decomposition methods could improve simulation of circuits with a moderate number of T gates, a key cost driver in quantum error correction work.
arxiv-2509-01324:
Legal questions often need several linked steps of reasoning across many provisions, and standard tests rarely check that skill in open-ended form. Jihyung Lee, with four co-authors, introduces KoBLEX, a Korean benchmark for explainable legal question answering grounded in real provisions. It holds two hundred twenty-six scenario-based questions with their supporting provisions, built by a pipeline mixing language models and human legal experts.

The team also proposes ParSeR, a method that drafts parametric provisions from a model's own knowledge to guide retrieval in three stages. That structure supports multi-hop reasoning over complex questions. A new scoring method, LF-Eval, judges how faithful answers stay to the law. Lee and the co-authors aim for legal systems whose answers can be traced to the provisions they rest on.
arxiv-2509-01424:
Maximum entropy is a classic rule for choosing the least biased probability distribution that fits known averages, and it yields the Gibbs-Boltzmann form. Amir R. Asadi extends that rule to hierarchical systems, models with many levels, common in physics and machine learning. The new framework is called hierarchical maximum entropy.

Asadi shows that distributions which are Pareto optimal, best across all levels at once, arise from renormalization group procedures borrowed from theoretical physics. Multilevel versions of two variational principles support the construction. Special settings with hierarchical invariances make the computation much simpler, including quadratic, logarithmic, and nearest-neighbor losses. A notion of parameter flows carries out the simplification. The work links a core idea of statistical inference with tools built for scale in physics.
arxiv-2509-01924:
Sakshi Arya and Wentao Lin design adaptive fertilizer guidance that balances crop yield against environmental harm. Nitrogen boosts growth but drives emissions, runoff, and rising costs when overused. Their tools must stay principled, affordable, and clear enough for farm practitioners to trust. The approach uses bandit algorithms, which learn by trying options and favoring winners, grounded in classic crop response models.

Mechanistic terms like peak yield and nutrient efficiency keep each recommendation readable in biological terms. Theory gives regret and sample cost results for the well matched case, plus checks under mismatch. Simulations scored by profit and a replay of Midwest corn trials test the methods. Biologically grounded versions learn faster and earn more as data grow.
arxiv-2509-02024:
Nikos Giakoumoglou, Andreas Floros, Kleanthis Marios Papadopoulos, and Tania Stathaki add fake hard test pairs to the training of image models that learn on their own. Such models learn from raw photos with no labels by matching pairs of views. Hard pairs look close but do not match, and they force the model to learn sharp traits. Past work made such pairs by code but not for this kind of image model.

The team folds fake hard pairs into the training of two model types in the study. That one small change makes the learned traits much more sharp and clear. Both a small model and a windowed model gain from the change. The paper frames itself as a study of a missed trick, not a new method. It makes the case to look at hard pairs once more.
arxiv-2509-02324:
Changshi Zhou and nine co-authors wrote a 2025 robotics paper on teaching a robot arm to fold cloth step by step from spoken-style instructions. Cloth bends in many ways, so long folding plans need both careful planning and sharp vision.

Their system joins three parts. A large language model breaks a broad command into small action steps. A vision-language module then locates the right cloth features for each step, tuned with a low-rank method that changes few weights. A final module carries out the moves. Tests in simulation beat prior methods on seen and unseen tasks. A real robot also folded varied cloth pieces, showing the plan transfers beyond the lab setup.
arxiv-2509-02524:
Zhipeng Liu, Chen Ma, and Tejaswi Tripathi wrote a 2025 probability paper on the directed landscape, a universal random geometry behind many growth models. They study its geodesic, the optimal path between two points, when the path length is forced to be huge.

Earlier work showed the geodesic stays inside a thin strip and wiggles like a Brownian bridge when rescaled. This paper zooms further into the endpoints under that conditioning. A critical scaling window emerges, with different powers of the length governing time, position, and length fluctuations. Inside the window, position and length share a nontrivial joint limit law. As time grows, that law splits into two independent Gaussian parts, matching earlier results, and it links to tail behaviour of the KPZ fixed point.
arxiv-2509-02624:
Minja Axelsson and three co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on wellbeing robots. These are machines meant to coach healthier habits. Real-world use raises ethical and social questions. Lab studies often skip those questions.

The team ran workshops with three groups. Such groups are usually left out of robot design. They were science festival visitors, women computer scientists, and humanities researchers. A co-design canvas structured the ethical debate. Thematic analysis then grouped the results. Four questions emerged. Is the robot safe, and how could anyone tell? Who is it built for, and with whom? Who owns the robot and its data? And why a robot at all? The authors offer those questions as a working framework.
arxiv-2509-02924:
Nefeli Manoudaki and 3 co-authors described a 2025 media installation called Simulacra Naturae. The artwork turns recorded activity from brain organoids into a living, changing environment. Organoids are small lab-grown clusters of nerve cells. Here their signals help shape sound, images, plants, and clay objects in one shared space.

Rather than treating the signals as simple switches, the system lets neural rhythms steer software agents modeled on termites and slime molds. Clay pieces fitted with small vibrating devices add physical sound, while live tropical plants fill the room. Visitors step into a scene guided partly by nonhuman activity. The piece frames data display as an act of care that shares authorship beyond people.
arxiv-2509-03324:
Yixiong Jing and 5 co-authors presented InfraDiffusion in 2025, a training-free method for restoring depth maps of masonry infrastructure. Inspectors use point clouds, three-dimensional point sets from scanners, to monitor bridges and tunnels. Brick-level damage like spalling and mortar loss is usually graded from photos, yet tunnels are too dark for good images.

Point clouds work in the dark but arrive sparse and noisy. The method projects them into depth images from virtual cameras, then restores those images with an adapted diffusion model, a generative technique that rebuilds detail step by step. No task-specific training is needed. On bridge and tunnel datasets the restored maps sharply improved brick-level outlining by a general segmentation model. The authors release their code and data.
arxiv-2509-03424:
Ó. Jiménez-Arranz, S. Lilleengen, and M. S. Petersen showed in 2025 that the S3 stellar stream likely belongs to the Milky Way, not the Large Magellanic Cloud. Stellar streams are ribbons of stars torn from clusters or dwarf galaxies. S3 is long, narrow, and far away, nearly aligned with the Cloud, which had suggested an origin there.

Using Gaia data, a neural network classifier picked out over fifteen hundred high-confidence new member candidates, widening the stream's apparent width several-fold. A list of red clump candidates offers targets for follow-up spectroscopy and precise distances. The authors evolved stream models inside time-dependent, deforming halos of both galaxies, accounting for their interaction. Closest approach speeds exceed the Cloud's escape velocity, so an LMC origin looks unlikely. S3 becomes the most distant extended Milky Way stream known.
arxiv-2509-03624:
In a 2025 research paper, N. Godoy and nine co-authors refine the mass, age, and physical properties of kappa Andromedae b, a companion object orbiting a bright star. The companion sits near the boundary between giant planets and brown dwarfs, the heavier objects that never quite became stars. Age and mass estimates had swung widely for a decade.

New mid-infrared images from the James Webb Space Telescope's MIRI instrument capture much of the object's emitted heat. Combined with recalibrated near-infrared measurements, they pin down temperature, surface gravity, and radius more tightly. Cloudy atmosphere models fit best, matching its spectral type and its place among similar field objects. A combined model average gives an age near 47 million years and a mass near seventeen Jupiter masses. That mass sits just past the limit where deuterium burning begins, and the age agrees with the Columba stellar association.
arxiv-2509-04524:
Anh Tuan Nguyen and one co-author, Viet Anh Nguyen, prove learning guarantees for shrinking quadratic optimization problems with data in a 2025 research paper. Projection methods compress a problem's dimension so solvers scale better. A recent data-driven idea learns the compression matrix from past problem instances drawn from the same application. For linear programs that learning is understood, but convex quadratic programs are harder, since their optima can sit inside faces rather than at corners.

Using Carathéodory's theorem, the authors localize solutions inside a region tied to a special active set. An unrolled active set method then models value computation as a bounded-complexity algorithm, yielding generalization guarantees. Extensions cover matching the optimal solution itself and instance-aware mappings.
arxiv-2509-04824:
Light field images record both position and angle of light, and raising their resolution requires using links across both. Haosong Liu, lead author with five co-authors, propose a hybrid Mamba-Transformer framework for light field super-resolution in a 2025 paper. Existing Mamba scanning strategies extract features inefficiently from such complex data.

Their design adds a subspace scanning strategy and blocks that model spatial-angular features in two stages. A parallel branch then refines epipolar features, the geometry linking views, using both Mamba and transformer parts. The framework aims for fuller use of non-local correlations at lower computational cost.
arxiv-2509-05024:
Cops hunting an invisible robber on a graph need a strategy that does not waste time or memory. Igor Potapov, lead author with two co-authors, study that zero-visibility game in a 2025 paper. Unlike the classic game, the robber's location stays hidden until capture.

An earlier solution used pathwidth decomposition. Their alternative rests on a separation hierarchy. It improves capture time and space use without raising the cop number in most cases. They also improve bounds on the approximate zero-visibility cop number for several graph classes, where strategies must be computable in polynomial time.
arxiv-2509-05224:
Curvature bounds for spaces shaped by relativity get a new discrete test in a 2025 paper by Tobias Beran and Felix Rott. They work with Lorentzian length spaces, which model space-time distance where time-like paths have length instead of ordinary shortest paths.

The authors prove a version of Reshetnyak's majorisation theorem for two future-directed time-like curves with the same endpoints. A flat model region and a distance-shrinking map link the model curves to the real ones while keeping their lengths. One special case describes an upper curvature bound through four-point configurations. That form suits discrete settings, where space-time is built from finitely many points.
arxiv-2509-05324:
Augmented reality headsets used in tactical settings can be attacked through the user's own perception. Rongqian Chen with five co-authors propose a way to reason about that risk in a 2025 paper. Cognitive attacks quietly distort what a user sees, which can steer decisions in dangerous ways.

Their Perception Graph model first mimics how a person picks out key information from a mixed reality scene. It then records the outcome in a structure with clear semantic labels. From that graph the model computes a score for how distorted perception has become. A measurable score gives defenders a way to detect attacks and study their effects, rather than relying on user reports.
arxiv-2509-05424:
A ring made of iron and dysprosium atoms may let scientists directly prepare and read a swirling magnetic state, Alessandro Soncini and ten co-authors report in a 2025 chemistry and physics paper. Such rings host closed vortex patterns carrying a toroidal moment, attractive for electric control of spins.

Opposite swirl directions look identical in ordinary fields, so direct detection has stayed out of reach. The authors model the ring's huge low-energy state space with a transfer-matrix method informed by first-principles work. The model matches measured heat and field data and finds a strongly toroidal ground state that survives at real temperatures. A proposed light-based prep and readout plan falls within sensor reach.
arxiv-2509-05624:
What an agent wants is far easier to read from its behaviour than what it believes, Jason Starace and Terence Soule report in a 2025 paper on behavioural inference. Inferring hidden values from action sequences matters for evaluating artificial agents, yet how much can be recovered at scale was untested.

Language model agents with assigned profiles, mixing nine belief systems with four motivations, generated over a million action sequences in grid worlds. Classifiers recovered motivations at near-perfect accuracy and most of their information. Belief systems plateaued far lower, even for transformer models, giving a sixfold gap in extraction efficiency. Confusion centred on a neutral zone where behaviour carries little signal. Signal boosts barely helped the weaker models.
arxiv-2509-05724:
Learning from simulators breaks when the simulator is wrong, and Matthew O'Callaghan, Kaisey S. Mandel, and Gerry Gilmore build a repair in a 2025 methods paper. Neural methods estimate posteriors for models too tangled for direct maths, but real simulators always bend the true process a little.

Their method, robust variational neural posterior estimation, bridges the gap to reality with variational methods and plain error modelling. It recovers robust posteriors from the data itself, without extra tuning knobs or priors on the mismatch. Benchmark tasks and real astronomy data test the method. Sound results under imperfect simulators matter wherever costly models stand in for reality.
arxiv-2509-05924:
Learning a detector for quantum entanglement straight from data is the goal of a 2025 paper by Mohammad Rezaei Shokou and Hossein Davoodi Yeganeh. Entanglement witnesses are measurements whose values certify that a state is entangled, but hand-designing them is hard. Their hybrid system pairs a continuous-variable quantum neural network with a small classical network that outputs one witness score.

The quantum side combines interferometers, squeezers, and Kerr gates, which supply the needed nonlinearity. Simulations on two- and three-mode families, Gaussian and non-Gaussian, pure and mixed, reach classification accuracy above ninety-nine percent and pull ahead of strong classical baselines as modes grow. The authors also quantify survival under photon loss and prove the model can approximate any continuous witness-like rule when measurements are complete.
arxiv-2509-06024:
Rewarding a language model only for the final answer can leave its reasoning sloppy, and Haoyang He and seven co-authors add a reward for reasoning quality in a 2025 paper. Rule-based rewards on math and code tasks check format and correctness, but never whether the chain of thought actually helped. Their framework, Dynamic Reasoning Efficiency Reward, plugs into reinforcement learning to fix both gaps.

One part scores reasoning chains that demonstrably raise the chance of the right answer, crediting helpful steps. Another decays the advantage of answers whose length strays from a validation-derived target, stabilizing training. The team also releases Logictree, a generated deductive reasoning benchmark. Their seven-billion-parameter model reaches a leading system's level on it within a few hundred training steps, with broader gains on logic and math tests.
arxiv-2509-06124:
Computing all trade-off-optimal solutions, the Pareto set, for problems with several goals is the subject of a 2025 paper by Joshua Könen and two co-authors. Their tool is dynamic programming over tree decompositions, a standard parameterized technique whose power for multiobjective problems was unclear. The team first settles the multicriteria s-t cut problem.

The same machinery then handles a polygon aggregation problem from cartography, the multiobjective minimum spanning tree, and the traveling salesman problem. Running times depend on treewidth and the largest intermediate Pareto set. An implementation with a purpose-built data structure and heuristics solves real polygon instances of treewidth up to twenty-two, and a preprocessing study compares decomposition choices. The work shows tree-based dynamic programming can carry multiobjective optimization further than expected.
arxiv-2509-06224:
Three standard models for how ice reflects sunlight are graded against real Antarctic snow and glacier ice in a 2025 paper by Aditya R. Khuller and Al Emran. Predicting albedo, and inferring grain size from it, matters for the climate of ice-covered worlds. The test set is well-measured firn and bubbly glacier ice from East Antarctica.

The delta-Eddington model strays least from measured albedo, then Shkuratov, then Hapke. For inferring grain radius the order flips, with Shkuratov closest on average. The authors trace the errors to missing physics: absorption inside dense ice, specular surface reflection, and nonspherical bubbles, all worse for coarse grains. Their recommendation is delta-Eddington for solar-system ices, as the least wrong with realistic parameters.
arxiv-2509-06324:
Checking a running Python program against formal rules gets a general platform in PyMOP, a 2025 system led by Zhuohang Shen with six co-authors. Runtime verification has found hundreds of bugs in Java projects, but Python tools were domain-bound or slow. PyMOP supports five specification logics, five monitoring algorithms, and dozens of ready specifications for popular libraries, with three instrumentation strategies.

The evaluation is large: hundreds of thousands of unit tests across nearly fifteen hundred GitHub projects. The fastest Java-default algorithm is often not fastest for Python, PyMOP outruns two recent dynamic analysis systems by orders of magnitude, and dozens of the bugs it helped find are already fixed. The authors position it as infrastructure for Python verification research.
arxiv-2509-06424:
Plethysm coefficients, among the most mysterious numbers in representation theory, settle into a simple pattern as one parameter grows, proves Tim Kuppel in a 2025 paper. These coefficients count how representations decompose when one representation is substituted inside another, symmetric power inside symmetric power. For large d they are given by quasi-polynomials, computable in one special case by Pieri's rule.

Kuppel shows that for all but an explicit finite list of cases, the leading term is constant, and the coefficient approaches a clean ratio involving the dimension of a smaller representation. In particular, a conjecture of Kahle and Michałek, going back to Howe, is answered. The result tames the asymptotics of a notoriously wild family.
arxiv-2509-06524:
Choosing which data should fine-tune a language model for one special field is the bottleneck addressed by Jian Wu and six co-authors in a 2025 machine learning paper. Raw data is plentiful, but training on all of it adds noise and can hurt results. Existing selection methods struggle to be both accurate and cheap.

Their method, LAMDAS, treats selection as asking whether a candidate belongs to the target domain, using the pretrained model itself as the judge. A small reference set defines the domain, and no separate feature engineering or heavy optimization is needed. Across many tests, models trained on the selected fraction beat models trained on everything, and the method outperformed nine leading rivals. The authors stress its balance: strong gains at modest computing cost, which suits teams with limited budgets.
arxiv-2509-06724:
Safety monitors that juggle sensor streams arriving at different speeds are protected by a new type system from Florian Kohn and three co-authors in a 2025 formal methods paper. Monitors watch drones and other cyber-physical systems in real time. The specification language RTLola lets designers state synchronization policies precisely, but subtle runtime errors can still slip in.

Pacing types, as the system is called, check that a monitor specification will behave well at runtime despite asynchronous inputs. The authors formalize the core of the idea for a fragment of RTLola and prove soundness using a new logical relation, a proof technique linking types to behavior. The system is implemented inside RTLola itself. For safety-critical monitoring, catching synchronization mistakes at design time is far cheaper than meeting them in flight.
arxiv-2509-06824:
Light patterns that grow inside a laser cavity because of filtering are studied by Minji Shi and four co-authors in a 2025 optics paper. The resonators mix quadratic and cubic nonlinearity, two ways light acts on a material. Modulation instability, where a smooth beam breaks into sidebands, is the effect under study.

Losses that treat frequencies unevenly, relative to the steady beam's frequency, can trigger sideband growth even in the normal dispersion regime, where it would not normally occur. The authors work out the parametric gain and show the pattern growth that follows. The same process can be used to make optical frequency combs, sets of evenly spaced frequencies useful as precise rulers for light, with a tunable spacing between teeth. Theory and computer work together support the picture, pointing to filtered hybrid resonators as comb sources.
arxiv-2509-06924:
Working out what a layered sample looks like from neutron reflections, quickly and with honest uncertainty, is the advance from Max D. Champneys and six co-authors in a 2025 instrumentation paper. Neutron reflectometry probes surfaces and interfaces, but reading a sample's structure from its reflection pattern is an inverse problem. Standard sampling methods are slow, and machine learning surrogates discard the physical model.

Their Bayesian inversion keeps the true reflectivity model and computes exact gradients through it for the first time in this field. Gradient-based sampling then explores far more efficiently than Markov chain Monte Carlo, and variational inference gives approximate uncertainties in seconds rather than hours. Tests on a thick oxide film and on multilayer organic LED devices showed strong performance, including fitting several datasets together. An open-source Python library of reflectometry kernels accompanies the work.
arxiv-2509-07024:
Yadi Cao and 9 co-authors present a lean stand-in for a costly fusion model in a 2025 paper. The source model, TGLF, forecasts how turbulence moves heat and particles in a tokamak, a ring-shaped fusion device. A full device run needs that forecast thousands of times, which is far too slow, so a neural net stand-in is trained to give fast, smooth answers in its place.

Their net, TGLF-WINN, is built to learn from few cases. First, smart feature choices shrink the range the net must learn. Next, rules drawn from wave physics keep its answers sane when data are thin. Last, a Bayesian step picks the most telling new cases to train on, based on where the net is most unsure. The goal is a stand-in that stays true even when each training case is costly to make.
arxiv-2509-07324:
Transformer models sometimes focus their attention on too few words, missing links across a long text. Nakyung Lee and 6 co-authors propose a fix called SAOBP in a 2025 research paper. Their method runs one step of belief propagation, a technique that passes messages between connected items, through the attention graph. The goal is to spread multi-hop relationships into each attention decision.

The team also defines Global Token Dependency, a measure of how much multi-hop links contribute inside attention. Experiments show the method prevents entropy collapse, where attention becomes too narrow in deep layers. It keeps the dependency measure near task-appropriate levels. Gains were clearest in small models. That makes the approach promising for capable language models that must run on limited hardware.
arxiv-2509-07424:
Hyunseung Lim and 4 co-authors present Feed-O-Meter in 2025, a practice tool that lets design students rehearse giving feedback to AI mentees. Studio design courses depend on critique, but students often hold back from fear of judgment and low confidence, which stunts a core skill. AI role-play could offer low-stakes practice, yet language models often fail to act like real people when given a persona.

Feed-O-Meter uses carefully designed language model agents as mentees, and the student plays the mentor, critiquing the agent's design work over several turns. The design goes beyond pasting a personality onto the model, addressing how the agent reasons and reacts so practice feels genuine. The goal is a safe rehearsal space where feedback skills can grow without time pressure. Such tools could help design schools scale critique practice beyond the studio.
arxiv-2509-07524: Leena Mondal and 2 co-authors prove the Nagell-Lutz theorem for imaginary quadratic fields of class number one in a 2025 number theory paper. The Nagell-Lutz theorem is a classic result in the arithmetic of elliptic curves. Class number one fields are number fields whose ideals factor in an especially clean way.
arxiv-2509-07724:
Lujia Wang, writing alone in 2025, extends a conjecture of Erdős and Gallai to signed graphs. A signed graph assigns a plus or minus sign to each edge of a network. The negative girth tracks the shortest cycle whose overall sign is negative. The balanced chromatic number is a coloring measure adapted to the signed setting.

Wang proves a two-sided bound. For every natural number p, consider signed graphs on n vertices with balanced chromatic number at least p. Among them, the maximum negative girth lies between two explicit bounds. Both bounds grow like a small power of n, with the same power. So the growth rate is pinned down up to constant factors. Results of this shape link coloring strength to short negative cycles. They force such cycles to appear once coloring demands grow.
arxiv-2509-07924:
Quantum machine learning is often pitched for security tasks, but squeezing real data into few qubits can strangle it. Huu Phu Le and 3 co-authors test hybrid quantum classifiers on unseen ransomware in a 2025 research paper. Their system pairs a variational quantum classifier with principal component analysis, which compresses the data first. Ransomware the system never trained on is the target.

Even the best twelve-qubit version recalled less malware than classical baselines. Performance also moved oddly with size: it worsened from four to eight qubits, then improved at twelve. The authors read that pattern as a serious training problem, not just data loss. They conclude that progress needs better compression methods and sturdier quantum optimization together. The study is a useful reality check on near-term quantum security claims.
arxiv-2509-08024:
Social media posts mix words with images, so judging a post's stance on climate change needs both. Lata Pangtey and 3 co-authors present a two-stage multimodal framework in a 2025 research paper. First, a large language model pulls stance-relevant summaries from the source text. In parallel, a domain-aware caption generator describes the image in topic context.

A specialized transformer then models the source text, the image reading, and the reply text together. The team evaluates on the MultiClimate benchmark, which pairs video frames with transcripts. Their method beat existing state-of-the-art approaches on accuracy and related scores. The design shows how hierarchical fusion, combining each mode at the right level, steadies stance detection. Such tools help researchers track public opinion on contested issues at scale.
arxiv-2509-08824:
Large language models speak English best because their training data is mostly English, leaving other languages to improvise. Thales Sales Almeida, Rodrigo Nogueira, and Helio Pedrini tackle that gap for Portuguese in a 2025 research paper. They build a huge new Portuguese corpus from Common Crawl web snapshots. Then they test how data choices affect a model shifted from English to Portuguese.

Their pipeline filters for educational and technical content and removes toxic material. The resulting corpus rivals an industrial-grade dataset in downstream performance. Language-specific filtering, they show, is not decoration: it drives the gains. Adapting a model to its target language measurably improves it. Although Portuguese is the case study, the authors offer the recipe to builders of models for the many languages the web underserves.
arxiv-2509-09224:
Yuan-Pei Yang argues long period radio transients arise in magnetic white dwarf pairs in a 2025 paper. These sources pulse on scales from minutes to hours. Two of them are confirmed to sit in white dwarf and M dwarf binaries with two to three hour periods.

The pairs are in a pre-cataclysmic phase with a very low inflow rate, so their magnetospheres stay clean. A gap between white dwarf spin and orbit lets an inductor type process or magnetosphere clash speed up particles. A maser process then makes the pulses, beamed by the pair's magnetic shape. Laws for period and brightness spreads are predicted for future samples to test.
arxiv-2509-09324:
Shoppers can imagine a dress but cannot describe its fine details in words a generator understands. Hui Li and 4 co-authors propose a workflow to close that gap in a 2025 research paper. Their framework uses a large multimodal model to turn images into rich prompts automatically. Users chat with the system and refine designs at a fine-grained level, without professional fashion knowledge.

The workflow aims to free creative potential that text alone bottles up. It also lowers the barrier to clothing design and editing, with no further human expert in the loop. To test it, the team built the FashionEdit dataset, which simulates a real design workflow. Evaluation covered generation similarity, user satisfaction, and quality. Code and dataset are public. The study shows generative AI moving from novelty images toward tools a garment business could actually run.
arxiv-2509-09524:
Daniil Ignatev and 4 co-authors report the DeMeVa team's entry to the LeWiDi-2025 shared task in a 2025 system paper. The task, now in its third edition, concerns learning from disagreements, where annotators may honestly label the same item differently. Rather than forcing one gold answer, the team models separate perspectives directly.

Two directions are compared. In-context learning with large language models is tested under different ways of choosing examples, and it predicts individual annotators' labels well. Grouping those predictions into soft labels stays competitive. Label distribution learning with a RoBERTa model is also tried under several fine-tuning schemes. The authors argue that route deserves more attention from the perspectivist community.
arxiv-2509-09624:
Dark energy might not ignore dark matter; the two dark sectors could trade energy as the universe expands. Atul Ashutosh Samanta, Abhijith Ajith, and Sukanta Panda constrain that coupling in a 2025 research paper. Their model is quintessence, a dynamic dark energy field, interacting with dark matter with a time-dependent strength. A warm dark matter component is also considered.

The team fits the model to the cosmic microwave background, baryon acoustic oscillations, and supernova data, including the newest survey releases. One statistical criterion strongly prefers the coupled model with warm dark matter. The Bayesian evidence, a stricter referee, favors the standard cosmological constant model instead. The split verdict is itself informative. It shows how model comparison in cosmology can hinge on the statistic chosen. It also keeps the coupled-quintessence idea alive, but unproven, pending sharper data.
arxiv-2509-09924:
Weisheng Wu's 2025 paper builds equilibrium states for a geodesic flow in curved geometry. The states are built from measures placed on the boundary at infinity. The stage is a closed rank one space. Its curvature never goes positive. An earlier result gives one such state for smooth potentials. Wu's aim is to build that state in the open. He uses the Patterson-Sullivan style.

New notions sort the boundary points by how they behave. One is a core limit set. One is a regular radial limit set. The measures are built in two settings. The state is then put together from them, step by step. That path yields the Bernoulli property, a strong form of chance. The same tools then count weighted loops in the curved world.
arxiv-2509-10124:
Marie Dorchain and 2 co-authors prove that Turing's pattern-forming idea survives on networks whose links keep adapting in a 2025 applied mathematics paper. Spots and stripes across nature are often explained by two reacting substances spreading at different rates, a story told on plain domains and on fixed networks alike. Real links, from synapses to social ties, rewire and reweight themselves in answer to the states they connect, and that feedback was missing from the theory.

For adaptive networks with symmetric, positive weights, the authors give general conditions for the instability that seeds patterns, resting on the spectrum of the network Laplacian together with the reaction parameters. Two classic model systems then grow a rich zoo of motifs: the Brusselator reaction scheme and the FitzHugh-Nagumo equations. The result ties pattern birth firmly to evolving topology.
arxiv-2509-10824:
Aghiles Kebaili and five co-authors forecast the growth of gliomas, aggressive brain tumors, in this 2025 medical AI paper. Clinical MRI follow-up is sparse and irregular, so predicting how a tumor will evolve at an arbitrary future date, with honest uncertainty, is genuinely hard. Their multi-task diffusion framework predicts pixel by pixel rather than by a single date-stamped image.

One task generates the future FLAIR scan at any chosen time; another produces a probability map of tumor evolution built from signed distance fields. A pretrained deformation module carries motion between scans, and a targeted augmentation pipeline fabricates complete follow-up sequences and fills missing scan types to fight data scarcity. A radiotherapy-weighted loss makes the model care most about regions the radiation plan cares about. Clinicians can then query progression risk at any future milestone.
arxiv-2509-11024:
Lingwen Li bounds graph pebbling numbers with an optimization trick in this solo-authored 2025 paper. Pebbling a graph is a game. Tokens move along edges, and two tokens are spent for one step. The pebbling number is the smallest stockpile with a guarantee. From any arrangement, a token can reach any target vertex. Exact values are scarce, so good bounds matter.

Li applies Hurlbert's linear optimization technique. Cleverly chosen weight functions on the graph certify upper bounds. A weight function lemma does the computational heavy lifting. Case studies include the Petersen graph, a famous ten-vertex network. The Bruhat graph and several families of trees appear, too. The paper offers concrete numbers for those families. It also offers a worked demonstration of a general method. Other researchers can aim that method at their own graphs.
arxiv-2509-11724:
Wa-Kin Lei, Jun-Cheng Chen, and Shang-Tse Chen show a privacy leak in split AI models. This 2025 machine learning security paper treats split inference. An edge device runs the first layers of a model. It ships the middle results to the cloud. The raw input is meant to stay private.

Their attack is DRAG. It rebuilds the input from those middle results. A latent diffusion model guides the rebuilding. The guide brings rich image knowledge from its own training. Past attacks were tested on small image classifiers. This one targets deep layers of a vision foundation model. It beats the state of the art in scores and in looks. Split deployments of large models need stronger protection.
arxiv-2509-11924:
Judging whether a carotid artery plaque is likely to rupture, straight from a 3D MRI scan, challenges radiologists and standard vision networks alike. Bo Cao and seven co-authors tackle that diagnostic problem in 2025 with a learning method that borrows how clinicians actually work.

In practice, specialists combine several imaging views with written reports and accumulated expertise, so the proposed network does the same. Its design pairs variational inference with knowledge distillation across modalities, letting cross-modality prior knowledge from a small set of labeled scans and reports guide predictions on unlabeled ones. Experiments on the group's own collected dataset, the authors report, confirm that the strategy lifts diagnostic performance for this difficult screening task.
arxiv-2509-12124:
Neutral atom arrays need loading, cooling, and photographing, sometimes inside a magnetic field that ordinary imaging dislikes. Emily H. Qiu and eleven co-authors show in 2025 how electromagnetically induced transparency solves that for rubidium-87 arrays.

Their method blends EIT cooling with fluorescence imaging, so the same light that calms the atoms also reveals them. Readout fidelity averaged about 99.7 percent while nearly all atoms survived. Single atoms loaded stochastically with success up to about two thirds of attempts. All of this ran in a field of a few gauss and was checked up to ten. Cooling works along both axial and radial directions. A survival model matches several other groups' experiments, and the technique points toward atom processors that run continuously.
arxiv-2509-12224:
Parsa Vatani and 3 co-authors present TripOptimizer in a 2025 paper on faster car aerodynamics design. Standard fluid dynamics model runs are costly, which limits how many shapes engineers can explore. TripOptimizer is a fully differentiable deep learning system that works directly from vehicle point cloud data, a set of points outlining a shape.

Its variational autoencoder uses a triplane-based representation to reconstruct three-dimensional geometry accurately and to predict the drag coefficient, a measure of air resistance. Training used DrivAerNet++, with eight thousand vehicle geometries and drag values from detailed model runs. An optimization method steers a starting shape toward a target drag value. In case studies, optimized designs cut drag by up to about a tenth, with results later checked by further model run.
arxiv-2509-12324:
Sayed Shafaat Mahmud and 3 co-authors present VADER in a 2025 paper for reading planet and disk properties from telescope images. The images come from ALMA observations of protoplanetary disks, the gas and dust around young stars where planets form. Rings in those disks can hint at unseen planets.

VADER is a variational autoencoder, a probabilistic deep learning model that reports uncertainty along with its estimates. It was trained on over one hundred thousand synthetic images built from simulations and post-processing. From a dust image alone, it infers planet mass plus disk traits such as viscosity, dust-to-gas ratio, and number of planets. Applied to twenty-three real disks, its mass estimates matched literature values and revealed correlations that reflect known disk physics.
arxiv-2509-12924:
Shipeng Liu, Ziliang Xiong and two co-authors present MATTER in 2025, a method to grade how well two point clouds line up. Good grades matter for mapping and tracking, but past methods sorted grades into a few coarse classes.

MATTER instead predicts the error as a smooth score, which gives finer detail. It pulls traits at many scales and joins them with a focus step. Tests on varied sets are strong, most of all where point density shifts across a scene. Used to guide mapping, it raised map quality for the same repair budget versus the best class-based rival.
arxiv-2509-13024:
Haohan Min and 4 co-authors propose DVDP, an end-to-end policy for visual docking of mobile robots, in a 2025 paper. Automatic docking is a longstanding challenge in mobile robotics. Visual methods offer higher precision and lower deployment cost, but they impose strict requirements on the robot's initial position at the start of docking.

DVDP uses only a binocular RGB-D camera, which captures color and depth, installed on the robot to directly output the docking path. That design achieves end-to-end automatic docking without the usual positioning constraints. The team also collected a large-scale visual docking dataset combining virtual and real environments, built with a three-dimensional platform and actual robot setups. They developed a series of evaluation metrics to quantify performance of end-to-end visual docking methods.
arxiv-2509-13124:
Ryo Sato and Shintarou Yanagida compute Zhu algebras in 2025 for superconformal vertex algebras via Huang's broad definition. Huang's form needs no Hamiltonian or Virasoro piece. That breadth suits super cases where such pieces vary or are absent.

Two goals anchor the note. First, Zhu algebras for N equals one through four and big N equals four are fixed. Second, Zhu algebras for supersymmetric families are introduced. The note shows the payoff of the broad definition in concrete cases. Readers gain a ready table for later representation work and a base for module counts.
arxiv-2509-13224:
Quoc Thai Tran, Duc Truong and two co-authors solve large 3D Poisson tasks on complex shapes in 2025 with tensor trains. Shape-aware solvers keep true geometry but cost much memory. Low-rank trains can compress both shape maps and operators.

Their TT-IGA frame builds all parts in train form. Geometry and discrete operators both stay low rank. Tests on the Poisson equation cut memory and time by large shares. Accuracy holds against full builds. Past low-rank work needed structured domains; this frame takes general shapes. Device-scale uses gain a lean path.
arxiv-2509-13624:
Shambhavi Krishna and five co-authors study transfer learning for large language models in a 2025 paper. Fine-tuning a model on one dataset often changes its skill on other tasks, for better or worse, and practitioners cannot collect perfect training data for every possible request. The team asks what actually drives these cross-task effects.

They trained and analyzed ten models, built a transfer matrix between tasks, and used dimension reduction to uncover latent abilities such as reasoning, sentiment classification, and arithmetic. Gains often defied surface similarity between datasets or source data quality. Instead, hidden traits like class balance, typical answer length, and specific language features mattered more, a finding that points toward more predictable model adaptation.
arxiv-2509-13724:
Jan Janak and 6 co-authors describe methods for mission-critical voice tests in a 2025 paper. Mission-critical voice communications have been a critical tool for the public safety community for over eight decades. Users expect these systems to operate reliably and consistently, notably in challenging settings such as fires and emergencies.

A national standards institute's public safety research division has sought to correlate impairments in such systems with user quality of experience. Earlier research studied voice quality and intelligibility in controlled settings, but emulating real-world settings is inherently difficult, and the best metric for quality of experience remains an open question. The paper describes method and tools for human-subject tests using automated speech recognition and crowdsourcing, illustrated in emulated real-world settings.
arxiv-2509-13824:
Jiazhuang Si and six co-authors explain a magnetic puzzle in a 2025 materials paper. Two layered chromium trihalides look alike, yet chromium chloride prefers its magnetization lying in the plane while chromium bromide prefers it pointing out of the plane. Which energy wins that contest decides the easy magnetization axis.

Density-functional calculations separate two contributions: a spin-orbit-driven crystalline anisotropy and a shape anisotropy from dipole interactions. The chromium orbitals behave similarly in both compounds, so the difference comes from the halogens. In the chloride, competing spin-flip channels nearly cancel, leaving shape effects in charge and an in-plane axis. In the bromide, stronger spin-orbit coupling and hybridization make the crystalline term dominate, standing the axis upright.
arxiv-2509-14224:
Louis-Philippe Coulombe and twenty-seven co-authors report observations of TOI-270 b in 2025, a warm rocky planet larger than Earth. Rocky planets with low density for their size may hold large amounts of light materials, called volatiles, that could help them keep an atmosphere.

Using the James Webb Space Telescope, the team measured the planet as it crossed its star and updated its density, which no longer fits a pure Earth like mix of rock. The data instead point to a small share of water by mass, held on the surface or inside. The spectrum also shows possible signs of a steam rich atmosphere, though the strength of that sign depends on how the data are handled. Checks using a larger planet crossing at nearly the same time helped rule out a trick of the starlight itself.
arxiv-2509-14624:
Linxi Xie and four co-authors propose Reveal-and-Release in 2025, a way to make language models forget data without ever holding the forget set. Unlearning usually assumes full access to what must be removed. Such data are often private, rare or legally controlled, so access is impractical.

Their method prompts the model with optimised instructions to reveal what it knows about the target. Self generated examples then stand in for the missing forget set during unlearning. The stand ins can match how the model itself stores the information, not just how a data set lists it. Iterative rounds reveal and release further traces. Privacy law compliance could get easier if a model own disclosures suffice to erase them.
arxiv-2509-14824:
Sander de Jong, Rune Møberg Jacobsen, and Niels van Berkel argue that confirmation bias can help group decisions when large language models are involved, in a 2025 paper. Language models are joining group decision-making, but they can push people toward conformity and lower everyone's guard. Confirmation bias, usually treated as a flaw, is reconsidered here as a resource.

Drawing on the Argumentative Theory of Reasoning, the authors propose a three-step process. People first form ideas on their own, away from the group. They then use a language model to sharpen and state those ideas clearly. Finally, the model plays critic, raising the objections the group is likely to make. Framed this way, the model prepares individuals for sharper, more productive discussion instead of flattening disagreement.
arxiv-2509-15024:
Xuanting Xie and five co-authors bring Transformer attention back to the task of grouping graph nodes, in a 2025 paper. Graph neural networks group nodes well but lean too hard on near neighbors, which washes node traits into sameness. Transformers swing too far the other way and stress far nodes at the cost of local pattern. The team asks if attention is of any use at all for this task.

A broad test study shows the two flaws side by side. Their model, the Attentive Graph Clustering Network, treats the graph itself as a form of attention. By tying attention to the graph's links, it keeps both reach and local detail. The aim is node traits that stay sharp and groupable where both parent designs fail.
arxiv-2509-15524:
Marcello Lanfranchi, writing alone, builds a formal frame for a geometry like branch of category theory. Tangent categories copy the tools of calculus into abstract settings: tangent bundles, fields, and links between spaces. In the past decade the field sprouted new flavors, from tangent monads to reverse forms. How those flavors mesh with the classic constructions was unclear.

Lanfranchi uses tangentads, objects from his past work that capture all flavors at once. He pins down the right universal property for vector fields in that wide setting. The frame also lifts known bridges, such as the Grothendieck construction, into the tangent world. The paper is formal and aimed at category theorists.
arxiv-2509-15724:
Davide Ettori leads a team that shrinks large neural models for use on small devices. Models like BERT and ResNet score high but cost much to run at the edge. Their method, RMT-KD, uses random matrix theory to judge which inner directions carry real information. Only those directions are kept when a big model teaches a smaller one.

The cutting runs layer by layer, with the model teaching itself to stay stable. On a language test suite and an image set, the method cuts up to four fifths of the parts. Accuracy drops by only about two points. Inference runs well over twice as fast, and power use nearly halves. The math gives the cutting a firm base.
arxiv-2509-16024:
Two special values describe much about a network: one tracks its overall growth, the other how well it holds together. Silvia Noschese and Lothar Reichel study how both values, and their partner vectors, shift when the weight of a single link in the network changes. Their math points to the links whose change would move the values most.

That guide helps find the links that matter most for keeping a network strong. Past work covered shifts in the values alone; this study adds the shift in the vectors themselves. The results aid anyone who must judge which links to guard or reinforce first.
arxiv-2509-16124:
Precise tests of the strong force need exact math for how heavy quarks shape deep scattering data. J. Ablinger and six co-authors compute these heavy-flavor effects to three-loop order for two key structure functions, one plain and one spin-based. The work covers the range of large energy transfer, where such terms matter most for world data sets.

The new terms will sharpen measures of the strong coupling and of parton maps inside the proton. They should also cut the error on the charm quark mass drawn from scattering data. A fast public code shares the results for use at future colliders.
arxiv-2509-16324:
Online ad systems bid on their own, but the true worth of each ad view is never known for sure. Jiale Han and six co-authors add honest doubt bounds to this auto-bidding task. Their method wraps past bid data in a prediction tool that gives intervals for each view's value, with no need to assume the data are independent draws.

From those intervals they build an adjusted value estimate with proven performance promises. Plugged into standard bidding methods, it keeps return-on-spend breaches low while lifting reward. Tests on simulated and real industry data back the claims, at modest compute cost.
arxiv-2509-16424:
Linear codes protect data with built-in redundancy, and new ways to measure them can expose traits that old measures miss. Eduardo Camps-Moreno, Elisa Gorla, and Hiram H. López introduce code distances, a fresh family of such measures. They prove basic traits and bounds, and show the new measures are not fixed by the code's matroid or its rank-metric cousin.

Examples show the measures split apart codes that look identical under classic parameters. No mirror rule links a code's measures to its dual's. Greedy and long-run versions are also defined and tied to known measures like covering radius.
arxiv-2509-16524:
Ellis R. Owen, Leonard E. C. Romano, and Kentaro Nagamine study gas flowing out of busy galaxies in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Such outflows carry energy and matter from a galaxy into its halo. The team asks what role a halo full of cosmic rays plays in launching and shaping those flows.

Their results show that a cosmic ray halo can hold back large winds. Instead, the rays push feedback into smaller local recycling flows. Young galaxies with weak halos may drive slow outflows more easily. In fierce starbursts, momentum takes over and halo rays matter far less. The findings help explain why outflow speeds differ.
arxiv-2509-17324:
Chi Zhang, Mengxin Zheng, Qian Lou, and Fan Chen tackle a training snag for quantum algorithms in a 2025 arXiv paper. Variational quantum algorithms run on today's noisy quantum hardware, and where their parameters start decides how well training goes. Past learning-based starters work in one task area only and train on just a few hundred samples.

The team reframes the choice of starting values as a generation problem. Their initializer, DiffQ, is built on a denoising diffusion model that learns to produce good starting points. To train it, they built a data set of more than fifteen thousand cases across three domains and five tasks. In tests, DiffQ cut the starting loss by a wide margin next to baselines. It also trimmed the steps needed to converge, which matters when quantum hardware time is scarce and costly.
arxiv-2509-17424:
Antoine Alaguero and seven co-authors probe the dust ring around the young triple star V892 Tau. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that many young stars sit in multiple systems, so planet birth there shapes the wider exoplanet census. The team set out to pin down the dust in this system's circumbinary ring, the reservoir from which planets could form.

They joined archival ALMA and VLA data across wavelengths from just under a millimeter to about a centimeter. Maps of the spectral index hint at non-dust emission near the central pair and dust that likely stays optically thick out to longer wavelengths. Full three-dimensional radiative transfer models then constrained the ring's shape and how grain traits change with radius. The best model matches the observed brightness at every wavelength. Dust density and temperature both fall with distance, a profile that planet formation models can now use.
arxiv-2509-17624:
Asem Abdelraouf, writing alone, counts points on a family of algebraic varieties over finite fields. His 2025 arXiv paper studies hypersurfaces built from a small set of monomials inside algebraic tori, in two compactified forms. Such point counts are basic data in arithmetic geometry, and closed formulas for them are prized.

Under stated general conditions, Abdelraouf proves the count equals a finite hypergeometric sum. To get there he defines a gamma triple, which extends finite hypergeometric sums to prime powers tied to the field where the monodromy representation lives. The Dwork family falls out as a special case, with its own point-count formula. The results generalize work by Beukers, Cohen, and Mellit, who treated sums over the rationals. The paper links the geometry of toric hypersurfaces to a classical special-function calculus.
arxiv-2509-17724:
Tillmann Buttersack leads a team of fourteen co-authors on a 2025 arXiv paper that films a fast reaction where two waters meet. Heavy water and normal water exchange protons and deuterons at blinding speed, even across long distances. The team measured the birth of HDO, the mixed molecule, inside the first hundred microseconds at the liquids' interface.

A fast-flowing flat jet lays the two waters side by side, and infrared imaging reads the chemistry as it runs. Early on, the reaction is limited by the scarcity of the ions that mediate the exchange. As ion counts rise, the rate nears the diffusion limit, and the extracted rate constant matches the picosecond scale of the single exchange step. A surprise emerges: the waters mix fully by diffusion while HDO still lags far below equilibrium, a true non-equilibrium state. The imaging method opens fast interface kinetics to direct study.
arxiv-2509-17924:
Xiuqi Ge, Zhibo Yao, and Yaosong Du blend two simple medical models to spot fetal gene faults. Their 2025 paper deals with non-invasive prenatal tests, where a miss can have grave results. Clear rules help doctors trust a tool, but clear tools can miss hard cases, while strong tools can be opaque.

Their blend, called Medical Priority Fusion, mixes a chance-based model with a rule-tree model under set medical limits. On more than a thousand real test samples, most of them normal, the blend caught most fault cases. It also kept a high score for how clear its logic stays.
arxiv-2509-18024:
Dunyao Xue and 3 co-authors speed up a classic method for filling in missing values in a big table. Their 2025 paper deals with alternating least squares, used in recommender systems to guess what a user may like. The method fits a low-rank form to user-item data, but cost grows with scale.

Their plan picks a core set of entries, not whole rows, and works with sparse maths on that set. Proofs back how close and how steady the shortcut stays. Sims and real data tests show like scores in far less time. The gain matters most for large shops and media sets.
arxiv-2509-18124:
Edmund Agyemang and 5 co-authors guess coffee scores from review text and numbers. Their 2025 study asks which traits in a review drive a coffee's rating. Clean text, word-weight scores, and a top-trait pick step prepare the data for the models.

Six model types were trained and tuned, from a plain tree to boosted forests. Group methods and a multi-layer net beat the plain tree and nearest-neighbour picks. Score checks used a blend of fair class and curve measures. The team says firm trait picks and tuning are the key to a sound guesser for taste goods.
arxiv-2509-18324:
Quantum error correction protects fragile quantum states by spreading them across many parts. Dongjin Lee and Beni Yoshida present a new family of codes called chiral color codes in this 2025 paper. The codes live in three dimensions and are built from simple stabilizer rules. They realize exotic states of matter known as topological orders, including fermionic ones.

For qubits, the code gives a single copy of the fermionic toric code phase. For larger units called qudits, a tuning knob called the chiral parameter shapes the particle types that appear. On closed spaces the code has one ground state once stray particles are removed. The authors prove the bulk state can be prepared by a local process in many cases. The codes also inherit single-shot error correction from the color code family. That makes them a handy platform for handling fermions and chiral particles.
arxiv-2509-18724:
Zero-sum problems ask how long a sequence over a group can run before a part of it must sum to zero. Guoqing Wang extends a key invariant of that theory in this 2025 paper. The invariant, defined through a group algebra, bounds the length of sequences that avoid a certain algebraic zero-sum. Wang carries it from groups to commutative semigroups, a looser structure.

He sets the invariant for semigroup algebras and proves the best possible lower and upper bounds in general. For finite semigroups over a field, sharper results follow. Equality holds for several named classes, including Clifford and Archimedean semigroups. Those classes cover all the building blocks in the standard decompositions of such semigroups. He also applies the invariant to other zero-sum questions. A conjecture for algebraically closed fields of zero characteristic is stated and partly proved.
arxiv-2509-18924:
Kartik Teotia and five co-authors present a way to build a moving, talking head avatar from sound alone. Past methods mostly turned speech into changes in head shape, and they missed how speech also changes how the face looks. Their system needs no prior model of the specific person. It pairs a general speech model with a learned prior for head avatars, trained on videos of many people seen from many angles.

The speech model turns raw audio straight into codes for facial expression. Those codes carry both shape and look, including eyebrow moves, gaze shifts, and the inside of the mouth. A light encoder then adapts the system to a new person from a single camera view. Tests show sharper lip sync and more lifelike images than shape-only methods.
arxiv-2509-19224:
Tariq Abdul-Quddoos and two co-authors compare six large pre-trained language models on a clinical task: pulling medication events and their context out of hospital notes. The data come from a 2022 national clinical language challenge, built on annotated electronic health records. The models range from general BERT to versions trained on biomedical and clinical text, plus a long-document model. Each was fine-tuned for three jobs: spotting medications, detecting events, and classifying the context around them.

Models pre-trained on clinical data proved better at detecting medications and events. General-domain BERT Base, though, was the most effective at classifying event context, a split result that resists a simple more-domain-training story. The authors also detail how the long records were broken into pieces each model could accept. Scores use precision, recall, and F1, giving a practical guide for clinical text mining.
arxiv-2509-19824:
Model predictive control plans ahead under uncertainty by keeping the true state inside a safety tube. Sabin Diaconescu and three co-authors slim down how that tube is described. Their tubes are zonotopes, symmetric shapes that scale elastically along the plan. New inclusion conditions remove constraints that older designs had to fix in advance.

A full complexity analysis compares their zonotope tubes with polyhedral ones. The trade is explicit: a wider region of safe operation costs more computing. Numerical tests back the design across many runs. Tube control serves constrained systems from robots to power converters. Cheaper tube math widens the class of hardware that can run it in real time.
arxiv-2509-20124:
Junjie Yao and Zhi-Qin John Xu wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on how language models organize meaning. Inside these models, each token is a point in an embedding space. Points for digits, for example, line up in their natural order. Why such structure forms has stayed unclear.

The authors propose probability signatures, summaries of how tokens appear together in data. These signatures, they argue, mirror the semantic links between tokens. In small models trained on a composite addition task, the signatures shaped the embedding layout strongly. Theory on gradient flow backed up the experiments. The team then trained a Qwen model on parts of the Pile corpus. There too, signatures aligned closely with the learned embedding structure, above all for strong pairwise links.
arxiv-2509-20424:
Radio waves bent by plasma clouds can magnify or dim distant bursts. Yu-Bin Wang, Xia Zhou, and Abdusattar Kurban rework that lensing theory in a 2025 arXiv paper on fast radio bursts. The classical model treats image position as independent of frequency. Their analysis shows that assumption fails inside structured plasma: position and dispersion both shift with frequency.

The fix builds frequency-dependent dispersion into the framework through a power-law relation. Magnification then falls steadily as frequency drops. That trend matches the frequency-dependent peak brightness seen in several fast radio bursts, notably a known repeating source. The authors suggest such bursts may originate in the magnetized surroundings of compact stars. Accounting for lensing across sub-pulses should sharpen estimates of what the bursts are intrinsically like.
arxiv-2509-20624:
Diffusion language models write in parallel but usually need hundreds of refining passes. Amin Karimi Monsefi and five co-authors cut that to a handful of steps in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their model, FS-DFM, treats the step budget as an explicit dial. Training makes the model consistent across budgets, so one large move lands where many small ones would.

A careful update rule shifts probability in the right direction without overshooting. Teacher guidance, distilled from long sampling runs, steadies the few-step behavior. With eight sampling steps, the model matched the perplexity of a baseline using over a thousand steps on long generations. Sampling ran up to one hundred twenty-eight times faster as a result. Code and pretrained checkpoints accompany the release. The work narrows the speed gap between diffusion and autoregressive text generation.
arxiv-2509-21424:
Drug design often optimizes binding to one target while ignoring wider effects on cells. Transcriptional profiles show how a compound shifts gene activity across the system. Ran Song and Hui Liu use those profiles to guide molecular design in a 2025 paper. Their framework pairs a chemistry large language model with expression data. The aim is phenotype aware generation.

PhenoMoler conditions generation on drug induced differential expression signatures. That links chemical structure to transcriptional response directly. It masks and rebuilds set substructures, such as scaffolds, side chains, or linkers. Fine grained control over edits follows from that design. Experiments show the system generates chemicals with desired phenotypic effects, going beyond target binding alone. The work treats the whole cell response as a design goal, not just one binding score.
arxiv-2509-22324:
Andrea Montessori, Marco Lauricella, Aritra Mukherjee, and Luca Brandt simulate turbulence filled with bubbles, a flow met in industry, weather, and oceans. Classic turbulence theory, due to Kolmogorov, describes how energy cascades from large swirls to small ones. Their 2025 paper asks whether that picture survives when a dispersed gas phase is mixed in. Using high-resolution simulations based on the lattice Boltzmann method, they examine the forced, uniform turbulence both as a whole and phase by phase.

For the mixture as a whole, the classical cascade largely held. Separated by phase, the story split. The liquid kept a structure close to classical expectations, even at high gas shares. The gas phase departed strongly from Kolmogorov's predictions: its energy spectrum ran nearly flat at large scales. It then followed a steeper law at intermediate scales, a signature of localized bursts spread between two wavelengths.
arxiv-2509-22624:
Ziyu Liu and 7 co-authors let a model grade its own answers while it learns to answer better. Reinforcement learning from human feedback is costly and can mismatch the policy. Learning from verifiable rewards avoids that, but throws away rollouts and correctness signals after each update. Their framework, SPARK, recycles those rollouts to train the model as its own reward judge.

Mixed objectives teach scoring, pairwise choice, and reflection-based review. Better judging gives better policy updates, which yield better rollouts to learn from. The loop removes the need for a separate reward model or human preference data. SPARK gained on reasoning, reward, and general benchmarks across language and vision-language models.
arxiv-2509-22924:
Erin Ellefsen, Rana Parshad, and Vaibhava Srivastava study two rival species in a stream with a steady drift. Classic theory says the faster spreader always drives out the slower one. Their twist is a much faster spreader, modeled with a p-Laplacian term. They ask whether extreme speed can backfire.

The three prove that valid solutions exist for any starting state in their range. Then they show the much faster species can in fact lose for some starting states. Computer runs back up the proof. The result matters for refuge design and pest control. Habitat breaks and climate shifts make such speed gaps more common.
arxiv-2509-23024:
Loss curves say little about how a model's inner geometry grows during training. Melody Zixuan Li and 6 co-authors track that geometry from pretraining to post-training. They use spectral tools, effective rank and spectrum decay, on OLMo and Pythia models. Three phases appear in a steady order. First comes rapid representational collapse.

Next, an entropy-seeking phase expands the code space as n-gram memorization peaks. Then a compression phase keeps variance on top directions and shrinks the rest, as task scores jump. Fine-tuning styles push the geometry in opposed ways. Reward-based tuning compresses, while instruction tuning expands at some cost to robustness.
arxiv-2509-23324:
Small phone models are weak, big ones are hungry, and the phone's neural chip sits partly idle during inference. Zixu Hao and 7 co-authors put that idle compute to work with parallel test-time scaling. Extra samples at test time can lift a small model's quality. Mobile neural units, though, handle fine quantization poorly and grind on general math. Two techniques answer those limits.

A tile quantization scheme aligns groups with the chip's memory access pattern. Lookup tables replace costly operations like softmax and dequantization. On Snapdragon platforms, kernel speeds rose sharply. Small models with scaling matched or beat larger models on accuracy.
arxiv-2509-23524:
Judging whether a completely locked-in patient is aware calls for tests that need no movement at all. Nicoli Leal and 3 co-authors design an EEG-based check of reflex and perception levels for such patients. Their concern is that weak executive function, memory, and alertness may block brain-computer interface use even when awareness remains. The test battery reads brain responses tied to sensing and perception.

The tasks draw on mismatch negativity plus steady-state responses to sound and sight. Five healthy volunteers piloted the battery. The runs show that a report on cognitive state at both levels can be produced, a step toward matching patients with the right communication tools.
arxiv-2509-23824:
Smart contracts move real money, so code generators must be judged on whole contracts, not toy functions. Zhifan Ye and 5 co-authors built SolContractEval, a contract-level benchmark for Solidity generation. It holds one hundred twenty-four tasks drawn from real on-chain contracts across nine domains. Each task gives full context dependencies, a structured contract frame, and a short prompt, all annotated and cross-checked by experienced developers.

A dynamic evaluation framework replays historical transactions to score functional correctness. Six mainstream models were tested; Claude-3.7-Sonnet led overall. Models handled standard patterns well but stumbled on complex logic, cross-contract dependencies, and Solidity-specific features.
arxiv-2509-23924:
Masked diffusion language models generate in parallel, but training tricks borrowed from left-to-right models fit them badly. Jingyi Yang and 3 co-authors ask whether that naive transfer is ever optimal, and propose fixes on both decoding and learning. Their EOS Early Rejection and Ascending Step-Size scheduler let full diffusion-style decoding compete with block-wise schemes in fewer steps. A new reinforcement learning method keeps rollout and optimization trajectories consistent.

Tests on math and planning benchmarks use the LLaDA-8B-Instruct model. The combined recipe tames the models effectively, the authors report. They argue masked diffusion needs its own training discipline rather than borrowed habits.
arxiv-2509-24024:
Transformers power large language models, yet what they can and cannot do stays unclear. Anthony W Lin and Pablo Barcelo survey fast gains in this area in an invited piece. Their guide leans on logic and automata, with help from the study of circuit cost.

Logic gives a clear way to state what a model can compute. Automata, the simple machines of computer science, give a second lens on the same limits. The pair also point to open problems where logic, automata, and program checks meet transformer research. Those open ends show how much basic theory still has to explain.
arxiv-2509-24324:
A partition splits a whole number into a sum of parts, and coloring the parts creates richer counting rules. M P Thejitha and S N Fathima study a counting function where even parts come in one color only, while odd parts may use any of several colors. Hirschhorn and Sellers defined this function in recent work.

The pair prove several new infinite families of congruences for the counts, modulo three and modulo five. Their proofs rest on a result of Newman and on the theory of modular forms. Infinite families matter here because they settle the counts for whole arithmetic patterns at once, not just single cases.
arxiv-2509-24824:
Electrons leaving a quantum dot do not fly straight when the material twists their spin, show Szafran and Wójcik in a 2025 arXiv simulation study. In a waveguide made of indium antimonide, the spin orbit force bends the path, and spin precession turns the bend into a snake like wiggle.

The wiggle's shape depends on the electron's starting state, which means the path itself can report the state stored in the dot when read at a T junction. The pattern survives a small magnetic field and imperfect spin preparation. Hand calculations with a classical model matched the full quantum simulations well.
arxiv-2509-24924:
Jaekwon Im and Juhan Nam present an audio upgrade model that restores high notes missing from low-rate recordings. Speech, music, and sound effects all lose sparkle when stored at low sample rates. Past diffusion methods often drifted from the true meaning of a sound or rebuilt high parts unevenly. Their 2025 model, SAGA-SR, takes two kinds of guidance.

Text labels guide what the sound should be, while a spectral roll-off cue guides its brightness shape. The model lifts any input rate in a wide range up to full studio rate. In both measured and listening tests, it beat current rivals across cases. The authors share sound samples and code online for others to check.
arxiv-2509-25124:
David Smith Sundarsingh and co-authors present a 2025 robot planner that stays safe in unknown places despite fuzzy perception. A robot must reach target spots while keeping set distances from labeled objects. Sensor readings are unsure, so maps built on the fly carry error. Older planners either ignore that error or demand a known sensor model.

Their planner measures map uncertainty with conformal methods. It then plans paths that meet a user-set chance of success. No knowledge of sensor noise is needed. Semantic maps grow as the robot senses its surroundings. The method is the first of its kind for such reach-avoid tasks. It suits robots in homes, hospitals, and disaster zones.
arxiv-2509-25324:
Scott Hagen and seven co-authors mined a three-year, near-daily watch of the active galaxy Fairall 9 in 2025, tracking light from optical to X-ray bands. Midway, the ultraviolet glow rose over about fifty days in step with the X-rays, reshaping the galaxy's spectrum. Outside that episode, the team used frequency-resolved timing to test how fluctuations travel through the accretion flow. Standard models expect ultraviolet changes to drive later X-ray ones.

The data disagreed. Hard X-rays barely tracked the ultraviolet and even seemed to lead it slightly. The pattern fits two mostly separate flicker sources, one slow in the disc and one fast near the center, loosely linked by light travel time. The authors say this reshapes how accretion flows are pictured. It also sets design rules for the next long monitoring campaigns.
arxiv-2509-26224:
Six authors led by Alessandro De Bellis tackle link prediction in knowledge graphs, where new items appear all the time. A knowledge graph stores facts as links between things, and the task is to guess links that are not yet shown. Type labels for items could help, but they are often missing, coarse, or wrong. The team asks whether large language models can supply the missing type hints.

Their method, called TyleR, adds type hints drawn from language models to the features of each item. It stays type-less in its inputs yet type-aware in how it reads each item. Tests on standard data sets show it beats prior best methods when type labels are scarce and graphs are sparse. The team shares its code for others to check.
arxiv-2509-26624:
Tiangang Cui, Josef Dick, and Friedrich Pillichshammer sharpen the math for averaging functions over endless space, in a 2025 paper.
