They include realistic nonlinear and random dynamics. The authors ran five optimization methods on the benchmark. Three were leading Bayesian optimization algorithms. Two were simpler baselines. The tool serves algorithm developers and city model builders alike.
arxiv-2510-19124:
Thomas Blommel and three co-authors build a many-body perturbation theory for open quantum systems that are driven and losing energy at the same time. Real materials under light or current flow are never closed systems, yet theory often treats dissipation, correlations, and driving with separate tools that do not fit together cleanly.

Their Keldysh-Lindblad approach adds diagram rules for dissipative lines that carry quasiparticle flows and fluctuations, while keeping the structure of standard equations intact. Existing solvers can then be reused directly. The authors derive dissipative versions of two common approximations and identify what their self-energy terms mean physically.
arxiv-2510-19224:
Benjamin Horowitz, Carolina Cuesta-Lazaro, and Omar Yehia present BaryonBridge, a model that quickly turns cheap dark matter simulations into realistic maps of ordinary matter. Linking dark matter runs to costly hydrodynamical outputs is a long-standing bottleneck, since full physics simulations are far too slow to run for every question astronomers ask.

A stochastic interpolant learns the mapping in three dimensions, conditioned on cosmology and astrophysics settings, at a cost of only minutes of graphics time per volume. Trained on a multifield dataset, it reproduces hydrogen absorption statistics accurately down to small scales. Fast baryon maps widen the range of surveys theorists can confront with models.
arxiv-2510-19324:
Loay Abdelrazek, Leyli Karaçay, and Marin Orlic address how to authorize software agents inside intent-based network management systems planned for future networks. Such systems translate high-level goals into low-level settings automatically, and their agents monitor the network, gather data, and enforce actions, so their permissions must be secure and finely graded.

Classic access models based on roles, attributes, or relations often lack the flexibility for shifting, multi-tenant settings. The authors examine authorization for knowledge-base agents in that context, aiming for control that adapts as context changes. Getting this right is a precondition for trusting automated network management.
arxiv-2510-19724:
Claudio Campagnari and twenty-eight co-authors present a way to predict afterpulses in the light sensor of the SUBMET experiment, which hunts for proposed millicharged particles. Afterpulses are delayed extra pulses that trail a strong signal in the sensor. They can fake or mask real events. SUBMET pairs a plastic scintillator with a Hamamatsu photomultiplier tube, and the extra pulses show up most after large primary pulses.

The team's method rests only on quantities that can be measured. It reproduces the seen afterpulse rate to within about twenty percent. Knowing this background in advance makes the experiment's background estimates more trustworthy. That matters because SUBMET probes an unexplored range of millicharged particle masses and charges, where every background must be pinned down.
arxiv-2510-19824:
Luke Staszewski and three co-authors bring a Krylov space viewpoint to periodically driven quantum systems, asking how fast they settle into their long-time behavior. Driven many-body systems either thermalize or freeze dynamically, and computing infinite-time averages is notoriously hard. Their perspective yields both insight into convergence rates and a practical algorithm for those averages within the diagonal ensemble.

The method is demonstrated on the driven mixed-field Ising model at sizes up to thirty spins. It cleanly resolves the boundary between the ergodic and dynamically frozen phases and reveals the structure of the Floquet eigenstates across the phase diagram. The long-time behavior, they show, is encoded in how the algorithm's Ritz vectors localize under the driving.
arxiv-2510-19924:
Skylar Grayson and four co-authors introduce RAFIKI, a suite of galaxy simulations designed to pull apart how black hole feedback works. Cosmological simulations need active galactic nucleus feedback to stop massive galaxies forming too many stars, but the details are poorly pinned down. RAFIKI builds on the SIMBA-C simulation and varies the mass loading of black-hole-driven winds.

Unlike the base simulation, RAFIKI separates the efficiencies of the two kinetic feedback modes, so their effects on galaxies, black holes, and surrounding gas can be studied independently. Even with stronger loading, the slower quasar-type mode cannot quench massive galaxies, though it regulates black hole growth and star formation in mid-sized ones. The runs also expose parameter degeneracies that future observations could break.
arxiv-2510-20124:
Lifang Feng, Bin Pei, and Yong Xu study a shaking system with one mode of motion, driven by noise with long memory. The noise is called fractional Gaussian noise. Its long links in time make the response non-Markovian. The classic Fokker-Planck tool can not be used in its plain form here.

The team builds a new form of that tool with memory built in. It has mixed terms and rates that shift with time and state. A local mean step helps gauge those rates in a stable way. A grid scheme then solves the tool. Tests on linear and non-linear cases match known results and Monte Carlo runs well, for both joint and edge spread curves.
arxiv-2510-20424:
Patrick O'Toole, Christian Rohrbeck, and Jordan Richards group tail links of multi-part random sets by a new score. A known frame, conditional extremes, tells how tails act as a pair. But its marks are hard to read or match across many sites or traits. Their score is a closed-form gap gauge for tails, built from a skew-geometric Jensen-Shannon split.

The score works in any size of set. Stock group steps on the pair gap grid give clean groups with like tail links. In sim tests, the way beats past ways for two-part tails and also works for more parts. On Irish rain and wind data, groups form clear zones on the map with like joint peaks.
arxiv-2510-21224:
The Belle II Collaboration, listed with 402 named members alongside the collaboration itself, measures a tiny matter-antimatter imbalance in charm meson decays. The team uses electron and positron collisions recorded from 2019 to 2022. The decay under study turns a neutral charm meson into two charged pions and one neutral pion.

A linked charged pion reveals the meson's flavor at birth. That lets the team compare decay rates for the matter and antimatter versions. A second, well-understood decay serves as a control sample. It cancels effects created by the detector itself. The result is a small positive value near three tenths of one percent. The errors are of similar size. The value matches no imbalance, and it stands as the most precise measurement of its kind so far.
arxiv-2510-21524:
Ilija Lichkovski and three co-authors build a test for whether AI agents break European Union law while carrying out innocent-looking requests. Agents given tools can drift into unlawful actions, from mishandling personal data to biased decisions, so the team measures that tendency directly rather than guessing at it.

Their benchmark, EU-Agent-Bench, is human-curated and checkable: each scenario admits both a lawful and an unlawful way to comply. A rubric anchored in citations to the actual legislation scores the agent's tool calls against the law. Categories span data protection, discrimination, and scientific integrity. Frontier models are compared with and without the relevant legal excerpts placed in their instructions. A public preview set is released while a private set is held back to keep future scores honest.
arxiv-2510-21624:
F. Herzog and four co-authors look back on one of the heaviest calculations in particle physics: the five-loop beta function, which tracks how the strong force's grip changes with energy. Completed at the end of 2016, the result feeds nearly every precision prediction made with quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons.

The review recalls the tools built for the job and the analytic and numerical answers obtained, covering quantum electrodynamics and general non-Abelian gauge theories alongside the strong force itself. The machinery later powered even harder five-loop work, including Higgs boson decay into hadrons and the splitting functions that evolve quark distributions inside protons. Those in turn gave the first realistic estimate of a key quantity, the quark cusp anomalous dimension, at the same order.
arxiv-2510-22024:
Evangelos Bitsikas, Jason Veara, and Aanjhan Ranganathan probe the cellular security of connected cars through a black-box study of Tesla's Model 3 and Cybertruck. Cars now lean on always-on LTE links for remote diagnostics, over-the-air updates. Safety-related services, yet phone-network flaws have rarely been tested in a setting where a failure rides at highway speed.

The team found the telematics stack open to IMSI catching and rogue base station hijacking, with insecure fallback paths that can quietly degrade service. Older control-plane settings also allowed silent text message injection and spoofed broadcast messages the driver would never see. Although the tests targeted Tesla, the authors argue the lessons reach the whole industry, especially since safety regulations already assume telematics that are secure and traceable.
arxiv-2510-22124:
Shiji Zhou leads a seven-author team on machine unlearning, the task of making a trained model forget sensitive or harmful material without retraining it from scratch. The difficulty is the tug of war: erase the target thoroughly, but leave the model's ordinary usefulness untouched. Earlier multi-objective methods could land anywhere on that trade-off curve with no fine control.

The team reframes the problem as constrained optimization: maximize forgetting while capping how much utility may slip. Solving that problem turns out to equal a one-sided surgery on the forgetting gradient, adjusting it only where it would wound utility. A cheaper implicit version of the surgery follows, avoiding the heavy computation the direct form demands. The framing gives practitioners a dial with a promised bound rather than a hopeful compromise.
arxiv-2510-22424:
Mouyang Cheng and five co-authors combine reinforcement learning with physics simulation to raise the critical current of high temperature superconductors. That current limit depends on defects inside the material, and the best mix of defect type, density, and spacing is hard to guess. Their workflow lets a learning agent propose defect layouts and scores each one by simulation.

The simulations produce current voltage curves that serve as the reward guiding the agent. In flat thin film shapes, the agent found layouts that pin vortices better and lift the current well above random starts. The approach offers a scalable route to defect design for fusion magnets and accelerators.
arxiv-2510-22524:
Army ants build living walls that keep foraging trails from tangling with each other. Shenbagaraj Kannapiran, with four co-authors, borrows that trick in 2025 for robot swarms that must stay separated while doing different tasks at the same time.

One controller uses a finite state machine, a simple rule set that switches states after encounters, to form rigid stable walls. A second controller adds a Deep Q-Network, a learning method, creating flexible buffer zones instead. In simulation both reduce mixing between subgroups. The learning version adapts better, cuts mixing by roughly forty to fifty percent, and settles faster.
arxiv-2510-22824:
Generative adversarial networks pit a maker against a checker. Mirco A Mannucci, writing alone in 2025, gives that checker a logic budget. The system is called LOGAN, for Logical GANs. Its checker can only probe to a fixed logical depth. It hunts small, legible faults in samples.

The maker must match a target theory for k rounds. Games of this type come from Ehrenfeucht Fraisse logic. Tools include a probe simulator and graph checkers. A logical loss mixes game resilience with cheap certificates. Simulation tests show high property satisfaction. Real neural training improved hard properties. Failures stay interpretable under this design.
arxiv-2510-23024:
Chuan Yan and six co-authors measure privacy practices across virtual reality app stores. VR apps can collect body data, behavior, and scans of the room around a user. Rules for handling that data are still thin, so practices vary widely between stores run by firms like Meta, Pico, and Microsoft.

The team carried out a multi-store measurement of the VR app ecosystem to compare what apps gather and disclose. Their findings map where protections lag for sensitive VR data. The study gives regulators and store owners a concrete base for tighter, VR-specific privacy rules.
arxiv-2510-23324:
Sebastian Maier, Manuel Schneider, and Stefan Feuerriegel run a randomized experiment on how people co-create with generative AI under different interaction modes. Language models can support creative work, but interface design may decide who leads. They compare two reflective, human-led modes, where the model prompts elaboration with suggestions or questions, against a proactive model-led mode that rewrites ideas on its own.

With four hundred eighty six participants, they assess idea quality and diversity across modes. The results show how much initiative to give the model. Designers of creative tools can use the evidence to balance human control against AI drive.
arxiv-2510-23624:
Tiago Mendonça dos Santos, Rafael Izbicki, and Luís Gustavo Esteves make random forests faster by keeping them shallow. A standard forest grows hundreds of deep trees, which predict well on tabular data but answer slowly and eat memory. That cost blocks uses where replies must be instant or hardware is small.

Their two methods, DiNo and RanBu, squeeze a few depth-limited trees into distance-weighted predictors after training ends. DiNo measures how far apart two cases sit by their most recent common ancestor in a tree, while RanBu smooths over a classic proximity measure with a kernel. Tuning the width parameter needs only light matrix work. Across three synthetic benchmarks and twenty-five datasets, RanBu matched or beat full forests, especially with noisy data, while cutting time by up to ninety-five percent. Both methods extend to quantile regression, and the code is open source.
arxiv-2510-24124:
Yotam Sherf and three co-authors build a global system to measure chlorophyll a in inland waters from the Sentinel-2 satellite. Chlorophyll a signals algae and water health, but telling water from clouds, glint, snow, ice, plants, and land in satellite images is hard. Their classifier learns from nearly one hundred water bodies spread around the world.

On top of that classifier, they train a model on more than thirteen thousand matched points with United States Geological Survey field data. Scenes the classifier marked as true water gave more accurate chlorophyll estimates than those it rejected. The two step system aims for stable performance across regions and water types.
arxiv-2510-24224:
Yichen Gao and two co-authors develop theory for the climate of hycean planets, hypothetical worlds with water oceans under hydrogen rich air. These planets are top targets in the search for signs of life, since they pair liquid water with air that is easy to observe. Their oddest trait is convective inhibition, which can reshape the temperature profile.

Most earlier studies used one dimensional models that ignored this effect. The authors build pen and paper theory for moist convective inhibition and check it against a one dimensional radiative convective model. They show the climate can settle into multiple stable states and can oscillate, findings that affect how hycean planets should be modeled and observed.
arxiv-2510-24324:
Ivan Tolkachev and four co-authors ran computer trials of damage cascades in iron made of many tiny crystals. Such fine grained iron is a candidate for fusion reactor walls. Its many grain borders may soak up the defects that radiation makes. The team built samples in two ways and hit them with cascades of fast atoms. They also ran the same tests on plain single crystals with no defects at the start.

The trials show a healing effect from the radiation itself. After about two hits per atom on average, all samples turn into a single crystal state. The defects strain the grid, so the team tracked stored energy as a gauge of harm. The results test whether the fine grained edge holds up under heavy exposure.
arxiv-2510-24424:
Louis-Pierre Arguin and Jad Hamdan study the Fourier coefficients of critical Gaussian multiplicative chaos, a random measure used to model rough, multifractal fields. They continue work recently begun by Garban and Vargas on how these coefficients decay. The setting is critical chaos on the unit interval, the borderline case where the measure is most delicate.

The authors show that the coefficients, scaled by any power of the logarithm of the index below one quarter, converge to zero in probability as the index grows. This quantifies the smoothness of critical chaos in frequency terms and adds to the mathematical theory of random measures arising from log correlated fields.
arxiv-2510-24724:
Nazmun Nahar, Ritesh Harshad Ruparel, Shariar Kabir, Sumaiya Tasnia Khan, Shyamasree Saha, and Mamunur Rashid made AmarDoctor, a health app for Bengali speakers. Big health apps tend to serve users in rich lands and main tongues, while Bengali speakers face gaps in care and in tech ease. Their app speaks and listens, and serves both sick users and care staff.

For users, a step wise ask flow weighs signs of ill health and points to the right kind of doctor. Voice help guides users who find screens hard to use. For staff, the app adds AI tips for care calls. It works in three main Bengali speech forms.
arxiv-2510-25024:
Ian McConachie leads a team with twenty seven co-authors who ask where huge, dead galaxies sat in the young cosmos. Now, such dead giants most oft sit in rich clusters. At high past times, when the cosmos was young, the trend is less clear.

With Webb scope light reads, they picked out a set of dead galaxies from two sky fields at a far past span. A map tool built from both shot and light based ranges found a set of dense peaks and large young clusters in those fields. The dead giants sat most oft in those peaks and in those large groups. That hints place drove their fast birth and death, even then.
arxiv-2510-25224:
Ziyi Liu, Bahar Sarrafzadeh, Pei Zhou, Longqi Yang, Jieyu Zhao, and Ashish Sharma built ProMediate, a test frame for AI agents that step in to help group talks reach a deal. Such help agents must juggle clashing wants across folks and topics, and build pact step by step. Past test ways for this kind of pro help were scarce.

Their frame pairs a fake talk test bed, built on real deal cases with three set hard tiers, with a plug in help agent. The agent is grounded in known help theory from social and thought work, and can pick when and how to step in. Scores weigh how the agent aids pact, not just talk.
arxiv-2510-25624:
Nils B de Vries, Adrian J Barker, and Rainer Hollerbach study tidal dissipation. Rotating giant planets and stars are the setting. Tidal dissipation occurs through various mechanisms in systems. It destabilizes laminar flows forced by axial precession.

A rotating, oblate, spin-orbit misaligned body forces those flows. Inertial waves get excited in convective regions. They constrain its contribution to tidal dissipation. Cartesian hydrodynamical runs model a small planet patch. Effect with turbulent convection is also studied. Without convection, flow is laminar at low rates. Convection shifts turbulent thresholds to lower rates. Hot Jupiter interior models test the scaling laws. Precessional instability drives spin-orbit matching within a gigayear.
arxiv-2510-26224:
Naufa Nazar, Mashhoor A. Al-Wardat, Ahmad Abushattal, and Hassan B. Haboubi determine the physical parameters of the subgiant binary star system HIP 72217. A subgiant is a star that has exhausted core hydrogen and begun to expand. They apply Al-Wardat method, a technique that fits the combined light of both stars to model atmospheres to extract each component properties.

Nazar and the team find the two stars are near twins, with masses of about one point one four and one point one two times the Sun mass. Their surface temperatures are about six thousand one hundred twenty five and five thousand nine hundred fifty kelvin. The system age is estimated at about three point five billion years, consistent with a subgiant evolutionary stage.
arxiv-2510-26324:
Zhiyang Xun, Shivam Gupta, and Eric Price ask a sharp question about working backward from noisy data. A sensor gives a blurred, noisy view of some hidden signal, and a good model of the signal exists. When can a computer draw fair samples of what the signal might have been, given that view? Such sampling helps with tasks like filling in missing parts of a photo or cleaning up scans.

Xun and his two co-authors focus on a class of smooth, bowl-shaped distributions where older methods can work but break easily when scores are slightly off. They prove that mixing diffusion models, which learn to undo noise step by step, with a heated form of Langevin dynamics works in fast time. Their method also needs only a weaker bound on score error.
arxiv-2510-26824:
Magdalena Lederbauer, Siddharth Betala, and twenty-three co-authors built a toolbox for materials data in 2025. Synthesis means the steps used to make a material in a lab. Those steps sit scattered in papers, in text and figures, hard to search.

Their parser uses large language models and vision models to pull steps and scores out. It built a set with fifty-eight thousand procedures from eighty-one thousand open papers. The set spans thirty-five methods and sixteen material classes. Experts and a model judge checked how well the pulls matched the source. One test links maker steps for catalysts to their heat-driven work. A second test checks the shift point where materials turn superconducting. Both the parser and the data set are shared in public.
arxiv-2510-27024:
Maria Kazachenko, Yuhong Fan, and Andrey Afanasyev offer a new lens on solar flares, the sudden blasts from the Sun that can disturb satellites and power grids. The three-dimensional change of coronal magnetic fields during a flare is hard to track because the corona cannot be measured directly. The team pairs data-driven simulations of a known active region with observations of flare ribbons and dimmings.

Their tool, L-maps, records the logarithm of magnetic field-line lengths across the region. Shortening lines mark ribbons, while lengthening lines mark dimmings, and both match telescope observations closely. Grouping the time patterns reveals three stages, from slow rise to reconnection and expansion. The maps give researchers an intuitive bridge between simulations and sky data.
arxiv-2510-27224:
Mahmoud El Hussieni, Bahadir Gunturk, Hasan Ates, and Oguz Hanoglu evaluate YOLOv11 for finding buildings and estimating their heights from satellite images. Accurate building outlines and heights support urban planning, three-dimensional city models, and infrastructure monitoring. The study gives a detailed analysis of the newest YOLO model applied jointly to instance segmentation and discrete height classification.

On a dataset with over a hundred thousand annotated buildings across twelve cities, the model posts strong segmentation scores and robust accuracy across five height tiers. It handles occlusions, complex shapes, and class imbalance well, including rare high-rise cases. Comparisons show it beats earlier multitask frameworks on both accuracy and inference speed, suiting large-scale, real-time urban mapping and geospatial intelligence.
arxiv-2510-27424:
Qianhang Ding, Minxi He, and Hui-Yu Zhu show how gravitational waves can reveal dark dense environments around black holes. Dark matter can condense into superradiant clouds or ultracompact mini-halos around black holes, and a companion object plowing through feels dynamical friction that alters its orbit and the emitted waves. The team defines a novel quantity capturing those effects through wave amplitude, frequency, and their time derivatives.

Density profile information can be extracted from that quantity, characterizing the condensate type and hence the underlying dark matter property. Multi-wavelength observation with ground-based and future space-based detectors could probe these environments, potentially illuminating the dark sector and the primordial origin of stellar-mass black holes. A null detection would still place strong constraints on relevant dark matter parameters.
arxiv-2510-27624:
Todd Elder, Matt Landremann, Christoper B. Smiet, and Robert Davies design a divertor for stellarators in 2025 by shaping coils around a surface with sharp corners. A stellarator confines hot gas with twisted magnetic fields. A divertor guides waste heat to set spots. The twisted fields can tangle escape paths into chaos, which spreads heat in unwanted ways.

By cutting the stray field that crosses the sharp target surface, the team aims for a clean split line akin to a large prior device. Their coils are modular, not helical, a first for this divertor type. Escape lines show far less chaos than in that prior device. Extra steps also make the coils more fit to build.
arxiv-2511-00324:
Isaac Meza extends a causal inference method to a harder setting. Approximate residual balancing estimates average treatment effects by weighting cases so treated and control groups compare fairly. The original framework handled linear outcome models, leaving open the problem posed by Athey and co-authors in 2018. What happens when outcomes follow a nonlinear model, as in generalized linear models for counts or binary results?

Meza derives a new bias breakdown for the nonlinear case and shows a second-order correction is needed, to account for the curve of the link function. New balancing weights control both first- and second-order bias sources. He proves the estimator stays consistent at the standard root-n rate and settles into a normal distribution, under standard high-dimensional assumptions.
arxiv-2511-00524:
Jihao Gu, Kun Li, He Wang, and Kaan Akşit build a system that does more than flag odd moments in video: it explains them. Subtle anomalies show as weak cues in space and time that conventional detectors miss, and their usual output is a bare yes-or-no with no evidence. Large vision-language models can talk about a scene but cannot point precisely at faint signals.

Their framework, T-VAU, joins the two strengths. A heatmap decoder aligns visual and textual features to extract pixel-level anomaly heatmaps. A region-aware encoder then turns those heatmaps into structured prompts, so the language model can detect, localize, and explain in one reasoning pass. A new fine-grained dataset, built from two standard benchmarks with detailed object and motion labels, supports the training, and results improve across the board.
arxiv-2511-00724:
Shuxiang Zhou, Kevin Vallejo, and Krzysztof Gofryk hunt for new materials in an old structural family. Antiperovskite nitrides are compounds with a flipped perovskite layout and a record spanning superconductivity, magnetism, and topological behavior. They seed the family with lanthanides, whose f-electrons bring strong correlations, local magnetic moments, and spin-orbit coupling, all rich and all hard to compute well.

A double-screening framework handles the ambiguity by treating f-electrons as fully itinerant in one pass and fully localized in another. High-throughput density functional calculations then sift candidates by heat and motion stability. Thirty-seven stable lanthanide antiperovskite nitrides survive. Several show nontrivial topology, with Dirac and semi-Dirac cones near the Fermi level in one erbium compound. The family opens a fresh playground where antiperovskite structure meets f-electron physics.
arxiv-2511-01024:
Masanori Nakazato offers a new geometry built on a simple new definition: an angle is the difference of the slopes of two lines. From that starting point, plus a set of axioms for angles, he argues an angle can be treated as a basic geometric notion, with no need for circles or rotations underneath it.

Inside the system he defines triangles, norms, bisectors, perpendiculars, and inner products. Strange traits appear: the triangle inequality always holds with equality, and the interior angles of any triangle sum to zero. Classical Euclidean figures, including Brocard type ones, reappear in new dress. The main theorem gives the first explicit, rigorous proof of a suggested concurrency in the parabolic Miquel configuration. The author presents the system as a candidate fourth geometry, after the Euclidean, hyperbolic, and elliptic ones.
arxiv-2511-01524:
Yan Yu and four colleagues prepare image-cleaning tools for the China Space Station Survey Telescope, whose survey images will be peppered by cosmic ray hits. The telescope revisits each patch of sky only rarely. So the usual trick of stacking several frames to spot the damage will not work. Each image must be cleaned on its own.

The team retrained the DeepCR detection model on simulated telescope images, reaching recall near 97.9 percent and precision near 98.7 percent on cosmic ray detection. A second, morphology-aware step repairs the damage: a UNet++ network restores scientifically valuable regions such as stars and galaxies, while adaptive median filtering handles plain background. Corrected targets end up with measurement errors close to clean ones, and detection rates rise about 13.6 percent over simple masking.
arxiv-2511-01724:
Yi Zhang and seven colleagues launch PRBench. It is the first shared test set for probabilistic robustness in image classifiers. Adversarial robustness asks if any tiny change can fool a model. Probabilistic robustness asks a softer, statistical question: how likely is a random change to fool it? Training methods for the second kind exist. But they were scored under mismatched rules, and rarely against strong adversarial training.

PRBench scores the common methods side by side. It checks clean accuracy, both kinds of robustness, training speed, and generalization error. A theory section covers the last. One headline result: adversarial training lifts probabilistic robustness more than expected. The set gives a scattered subfield one yardstick at last.
arxiv-2511-02024:
Rachel Lee and seven colleagues ask whether a proposed far-infrared space observatory could settle how stars gain their mass. Protostars may grow steadily or in violent accretion outbursts; if outbursts dominate, they reshape planet formation too. The PRIMA concept observatory's guest observer program is the test bed.

The team built ensembles of synthetic protostars from Herschel 70-micron flux data. They evolved them with a Monte Carlo toy simulation. The runs cover steady growth, and large accretion bursts too. Synthetic observations at several epochs measured how many large outbursts the proposed program could actually recover and recognize. The verdict is clear. Observing an ensemble of at least 2,000 protostars, with PRIMA's proposed program, would suffice. It would determine whether bursts contribute at least half of a star's final mass. That settles the assembly question, within the toy model's premises.
arxiv-2511-02224:
Yan Li, a researcher in decision theory, shows that a popular way of making sequential decisions robust is computationally hard at its core. Distributionally robust Markov decision processes choose a policy that performs well even when the true transition probabilities are only known to lie in an ambiguity set. Li studies the static formulation and constructs explicit problem instances that expose the difficulty.

When policies must be Markovian and non-randomized, finding the optimal policy for these instances is NP-hard. Allowing randomized Markovian policies does not rescue the problem: the robust value function develops strict local minimizers that are not global optima, and finding the optimal policy remains NP-hard. Strikingly, the hard instances need an ambiguity set containing only two possible transition kernels.
arxiv-2511-02424:
Jae-Woo Choi and six co-authors give language-model agents a way to plan long jobs without drowning in their own history. Most planners keep one continuous trajectory in which every past decision and observation is tangled together, and performance collapses on long-horizon tasks. Their method, ReAcTree, breaks a complex goal into subgoals arranged in a tree that grows dynamically as work proceeds.

Each subgoal is handled by its own agent node, which can reason, act, and expand the tree further, while control-flow nodes coordinate how the agents execute. Two memory systems support the tree: episodic memory supplies goal-specific examples to each node, and a shared working memory passes environmental observations around. On two embodied benchmarks the method consistently beat strong baselines, nearly doubling one baseline's goal success rate, reaching sixty-one percent against thirty-one.
arxiv-2511-02524:
Michiel Snoeken and six co-authors compute what a magnetic field lying in the plane does to the light absorbed by a thin semiconductor. The materials are transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers, and the absorbers are excitons, bound pairs of an electron and a hole. Some excitons are bright, coupling directly to light, and some are dark, invisible; the field's orientation relative to the layer is the experimental knob the authors turn.

An in-plane field mixes the bright and dark transitions, so the dark excitons light up in the absorption spectrum. The authors work out analytically how resonance energies shift, how lines broaden, and how the brightness ratio between the two species behaves. For a molybdenum diselenide monolayer with a radiatively limited linewidth, they find an intricate interplay between the dark-bright energy splitting and the difference in linewidths. It gives experimentalists a map of what to look for.
arxiv-2511-02624:
Liang Kong, Yilong Wang, and Hao Zheng introduce finer ways to say that two quantum phases of matter are the same. Fusion categories organise the anyons of two-dimensional topological phases, and Morita equivalence is the standard sameness relation among them. Witt equivalence plays the matching role for nondegenerate braided fusion categories, which describe the phases themselves. Both relations are coarse, lumping structures that differ internally.

The authors define a family of new equivalence relations among fusion categories that are less refined than Morita equivalence, and quotienting by them produces new abelian groups. Upgraded to the braided setting, the relations become more refined than Witt equivalence, yielding new groups that sit strictly inside the usual Witt group picture. Those groups expose structure hidden within each Witt class. The authors expect them to serve the classification programme for fusion categories and the study of gapless edges of topological orders.
arxiv-2511-02924:
Haranath Rakshit, Rajkumar Bhandari, and Subhasis Banerjee present a light way to refresh encryption keys for small Internet of Things devices. Static shared keys are cheap but risky: they get reused, allow replay attacks, and never expire. Their 2025 protocol, DSEKP, derives a fresh AES-GCM key for each session using a standard key derivation function, with a one-step handshake to prove both sides agree.

They ran it on an ESP32 sensor node talking to a Raspberry Pi 5 edge server through an MQTT broker, over more than 6,500 packets per setup. Speed and reliability nearly matched the static baseline. Session setup cost about 27 percent extra once, and packets grew by about 10 percent, in return for per-session isolation and replay protection.
arxiv-2511-03024:
Fabian Levican-Santibanez and Pedro Montero classify a family of algebraic varieties that admit a large additive symmetry. A variety is additive if the additive group of the same dimension acts on it with an open orbit, and uniquely additive when that action is the only one of its kind. Their 2025 paper covers smooth Fano toric varieties, a class built from fans of cones, in dimensions up to six.

The classification was done by computer, with fine detail given through dimension four. It extends an earlier list of threefolds by Huang and Montero. The engine is a new Macaulay2 package, AdditiveToricVarieties, for working with such group actions. The math rests on Demazure roots of the fan, which control when actions exist. They also prove every Picard rank two case is additive.
arxiv-2511-03324:
Tom R Hepworth, Simon L Cornish, and Philip D Gregory chart routes through the crowded state space of ultracold molecules. Each spin state of such a molecule splits into many fine levels, leaving hundreds of possible jumps between two spin states. Picking the best path through that maze is slow work for experimenters today.

A simple heuristic joined with graph theory finds near-best state sets and paths quickly. The method balances speed of preparation against how true the final state stays. The team also studies small networks where several couplings act at once and some states stay isolated. Cleaner state control supports quantum chemistry, simulation, and computing with molecules. The graph view turns a bewildering level jungle into a map that can be searched.
arxiv-2511-03924:
Ekin Ugurel, Cynthia Chen, Brian H Y Lee, and Filipe Rodrigues ask whether personal traits can be shown from mobility signals to help transport planners use passively gathered travel data. Links between movement patterns and traits such as age, income, or household structure are weak, inconsistent, and often fail to transfer across settings.

Higher-order measures from directed mobility graphs capture trip sequences, travel modes, and social co-travel, and they beat baseline features. New metrics and visual tools compare how sure a model is with how right it is, supporting honest uncertainty. A shared framework that predicts several traits together beat single-task models, most with limited data or shifted test periods.
arxiv-2511-04124:
Giorgio Morales and John W Sheppard present decomposable neural symbolic regression, a method that explains a trained opaque regression model by turning it into readable math expressions. Plain symbolic regression often chases prediction error and returns bloated or wrong formulas.

A multi-set transformer drafts one-variable skeletons showing how each variable moves the opaque model's response. Genetic search selects strong skeletons, genetic programming merges them while keeping structure, and coefficients are tuned last. Tests under set, varying noise check whether the recovered formulas track the true links rather than merely fitting points.
arxiv-2511-04224:
Yurij V Kalyuzhnyi, writing alone, offers a simpler scheme for computing traits of associative fluids whose particles are strongly anisotropic in shape, a long-standing challenge for Wertheim's multi-density perturbation theory. The method joins thermal perturbation theory with the interaction site model for molecular fluids due to Chandler and Andersen.

A primitive model of Laponite suspension, a clay system proposed recently, serves as the demonstration case. Phase behaviour and percolation traits are worked out with the new scheme. Fast computation for highly anisotropic bonded particles matters well beyond one suspension, since such models appear across soft matter where shape and bonding act strongly.
arxiv-2511-04324:
Eugenia Pyurbeeva and Ronnie Kosloff write an engineering guide to quantum dot thermal machines. These devices exchange particles continuously between hot and cold reservoirs, with a quantum dot as a narrow energy filter. Theory shows Carnot efficiency can be approached when passive heat flow is suppressed, and experiments have already reached a large share of that limit.

Practice, the authors stress, rewards maximum power, efficiency at maximum power, and low output noise over peak efficiency alone. Internal dot dynamics shape all three through few parameters: overall conductance and three asymmetries of the dynamics. Those parameters tell engineers which quantum states to build, improving performance beyond the simplest spin-degenerate transmission level.
arxiv-2511-04524:
Seungjoo Baek and his co-author propose bulk theories for two-dimensional minimal models. One family is supersymmetric, the other is built on W_N algebras. Both extend earlier work by Gang, Kang, and Kim from 2024.

Each model is matched to a Seifert fibered space over a sphere with three special fibers. The 3D-3D correspondence then realizes the bulk theory from that geometry. For unitary cases, the bulk flows to a gapped phase holding the chiral model at its edge. Non-unitary cases flow to a twisted topological theory, tying geometry to abstract algebra.
arxiv-2511-04724:
Thomas Chillery leads fifteen authors testing a prototype neutron detector for deep-underground studies. The target science is the s-process, a slow neutron capture chain that builds heavy elements. The array pairs an EJ-309 liquid scintillator with six helium-3 counters around it.

Tests ran at the FRANZ facility in Frankfurt using a lithium proton reaction. Neutrons spanned fifty to seven hundred twenty kiloelectronvolts in energy. The team's lowest detectable neutron energy came out at one hundred sixty-three kiloelectronvolts. Coincidence counts match simulations, supporting a larger array now under construction for a key magnesium-forming reaction.
arxiv-2511-04824:
Kosei Horikawa leads six authors studying how AI coding agents refactor real software. Tools like Codex, Claude Code, and Cursor now act as autonomous teammates on development tasks. Refactoring, improving code structure without changing behavior, is a core maintenance job.

How agents refactor in practice, and how they compare with humans, was largely unknown. The team mines agent-made refactorings across real open-source Java projects at scale. Their study weighs usage patterns and code quality effects together. The findings give engineering teams early evidence on where agent refactoring helps and where oversight stays essential.
arxiv-2511-04924:
Ziyang Yuan leads nineteen authors introducing Nuclear Ptychoscopy for phase-sensitive nuclear spectroscopy. Knowing a nuclear response needs both its amplitude and its phase. Phase retrieval was shown possible in time-and-energy spectra.

Ptychography, borrowed from coherent imaging, exploits redundancy across overlapping measurements. Their framework adapts those algorithms to rebuild the full complex response function. Three rebuild schemes fit three test situations. One uses a known analyzer response, one works blind, and one folds in extra constraints. Richer response data would sharpen how X-ray light probes nuclear transitions. The schemes are presented as complementary tools rather than rivals.
arxiv-2511-05124:
Felix Divo and co-authors present QuAnTS, a data set for answering questions about time series, a field that has drawn far less work than image or text questions. Text can open dense numeric records to users and aid choices.

QuAnTS asks many kinds of questions about human motion, given as tracked skeleton paths over time. Models track the moving joints and reply in words. The set is built to be hard, so scores show real skill at linking numbers to language. It gives builders a shared test for time-aware question systems.
arxiv-2511-05224:
G. Lombardi and co-authors test how squeezing a crystal along one axis changes the anomalous Hall effect in Mn3Ge, a frustrated antiferromagnet with a hexagonal form. Tunable traits in such materials could serve in new spin-based devices.

X-ray tests show the crystal's axis ratio shifts in a straight line with strain along one axis, and the crystal is much stiffer along the other. That straight-line shift mirrors what pressure from all sides does. The Hall response under one-axis strain gives a clean knob for probing how lattice change steers electron flow in this magnet.
arxiv-2511-05524:
Ruiying Chen describes EviBound, a guard system for AI research agents that claim work is done when it is not. Such agents may mark a task complete even when files are missing, numbers clash, or code failed to run. EviBound blocks a claim unless machine-checked proof backs it up.

Two gates do the checking. One gate reviews the plan and its success rules before code runs. The other checks the outputs after the run, using stored run records and required files. On eight test tasks, a prompt-only setup let every false claim through. EviBound let none through, with only a small rise in run time.
arxiv-2511-05724:
Mariane Souza-Gomes and co-authors simulate inertial waves inside the Sun and other stars. Such waves were recently detected in the Sun through helioseismology, but what excites them and what they do to solar plasma and magnetism is poorly understood. The team uses global computer simulations to watch them start and evolve.

First they check their setup on a rigidly rotating sphere, where an imposed wobble excites neighboring wave modes as theory expects. Then, with realistic differential rotation switched on, they find the waves grow mainly through baroclinic instability. High-latitude vortices spin backward near the poles, while weaker Rossby waves appear at the equator. Stronger shear lets the polar modes stir stresses that can move angular momentum.
arxiv-2511-06224:
Anmar Kareem and Alexander Aue test whether classic time series tools can forecast Bitcoin prices. They compare four models: ARIMA and SARIMA for price trends, plus GARCH and EGARCH for volatility, the size of price swings. Daily Bitcoin data from 2010 to 2020 supplied the test bed, with the last tenth held back for scoring.

Models were judged by error measures and information criteria that reward accuracy and simplicity. ARIMA gave the strongest short-run forecasts of log prices. EGARCH fit volatility best because it captures lopsided responses to shocks. Even with Bitcoin's extreme swings, the authors find classical models still useful for short-run forecasting.
arxiv-2511-06324:
Lukas Flajsman and colleagues grew thin films of erbium-substituted yttrium iron garnet and measured their magnetic and structural behavior. The material pairs the low magnetic loss of yttrium iron garnet with erbium's light emission in the telecom band. That mix suits hybrid devices linking microwaves to light, including quantum signal conversion.

Films with a range of erbium levels were grown by pulsed laser deposition on garnet substrates. Careful measurements confirmed clean single-phase growth with sharp interfaces throughout. More erbium lowered the saturation magnetization and widened the resonance line through added damping. Lightly substituted films stayed close to pure material behavior, keeping the low-loss traits that optomagnonic uses need.
arxiv-2511-06424:
Amit Vaisman and co-authors speed up image compression that uses diffusion models without any training on the target image. Zero-shot diffusion compressors have improved lately but remain notoriously slow. Their starting point, DDCM, compresses by picking noise vectors step by step from reproducible codebooks so the denoiser rebuilds the target picture.

Turbo-DDCM blends many noise vectors at each denoising step, cutting the number of steps sharply, and pairs that change with a better encoding protocol. Two flexible variants follow: one favors regions a user marks as important, and one targets a chosen quality level instead of a file size. Experiments place the method among the practical leaders.
arxiv-2511-06524:
Haihui Gao and colleagues stabilize an unknown linear system using only recorded inputs and outputs. The plant is a continuous-time system with several inputs and outputs, and no model equations are available. Recent output-feedback methods lean on special realizations but demand a uniform observability index, a strong assumption many systems fail.

Their key move reinterprets Kreisselmeier's adaptive filter as an observer for a stabilizable non-minimal realization of the plant. Filtering the collected experiment data through it produces a linear matrix inequality whose solution is the feedback gain of a dynamic stabilizer. The result covers a broad class of multi-input, multi-output systems without the observability restriction.
arxiv-2511-06624:
Soumyadip Patra and colleagues show that every Bell inequality hides a standard version untouched by a standard data cleanup. Bell tests probe whether nature admits local realistic descriptions, and raw data often carries faint signalling that analysts project away onto the no-signalling set before judging results. Whether that projection distorts the verdict matters for device-independent uses.

For any setup with several parties choosing among binary-outcome measurements, a canonical form of the inequality exists whose violation the projection leaves unchanged. The team derives a general closed formula for the projection, far cheaper to evaluate than older procedures. Non-standard versions of interest for particular uses fit the same generalization.
arxiv-2511-06924:
Simone D'Onofrio, Sergei Odintsov, and Tiziano Schiavone test an exponential version of f(R) gravity, a modification of general relativity, as a system for dynamical dark energy. The model behaves like the standard cosmological model at early times and departs smoothly later. The authors fit it jointly with the total mass of neutrinos, a quantity cosmology can constrain.

A Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis combines cosmic chronometers, the DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation data, the cosmic microwave background acoustic scale, and the Pantheon+ supernova compilation. The exponential model stays consistent with all observations while slightly easing the Hubble tension and the neutrino mass problem compared with the standard model. Its neutrino mass limits are tighter than those of a common phenomenological alternative.
arxiv-2511-07124:
Zhikang Chen and five co-authors stabilize the hidden reasoning of large language models. Chain-of-thought prompting reasons in visible tokens, which propagates errors and constrains expression, so recent work lets models reason in continuous latent space before answering. Those latent trajectories, however, can diverge and contradict themselves, because nothing enforces consistency between steps. The proposed EBM-CoT system calibrates latent thoughts with an energy-based model.

The energy model scores latent thought states, and calibration nudges trajectories toward low-energy regions where steps agree with each other. The base language model itself is left unmodified. Across mathematical, commonsense, and symbolic benchmarks, the system greatly improved both the consistency and the efficiency of multi-step work, suggesting latent reasoning benefits from an explicit consistency check before decoding.
arxiv-2511-07224:
Gabe Hoshino and six co-authors ask whether the Large Hadron Collider can hunt axions through their supersymmetric partners. In the supersymmetric DFSZ axion model, the axino couples at tree level to the Higgs sector. If R-parity is conserved, heavier neutralinos should decay into lighter, mostly axino states with displaced vertices, a distinctive signature. The team simulates a scenario where mostly higgsino states decay to a mostly axino lightest particle.

Using MadGraph event creation and MadAnalysis5 detector simulation with kinematic cuts, they map the experiment's reach. For higgsino masses below one teraelectronvolt, the collider with 140 inverse femtobarns of data can probe axion decay constants below a hundred billion gigaelectronvolts. The reach complements direct detection and astrophysical searches, opening supersymmetric axion models to current collider data.
arxiv-2511-07324:
Andrea Autieri and four co-authors refine predictions for Z boson production at hadron colliders like the LHC. The transverse momentum distribution of the Z is a precision yardstick, but computing it requires adding up large logarithmic effects from radiation emitted before the collision. This work performs that summing with quantum chromodynamics and quantum electrodynamics radiation treated together, a mixed calculation, at next-to-next-to-leading logarithmic order.

Adding the mixed corrections on top of the pure QCD result, the authors find percent-level effects on that spread. Percent-level shifts matter here because Z production is a standard candle for collider physics, used to benchmark detectors and to pull out basic parameters. The paper measures exactly how much the combined strong and electromagnetic radiation changes the expected spectrum.
arxiv-2511-07524:
Bruno Bucciotti, Felipe Figueroa, and Guilherme Pimentel map the heavy states of the open bosonic string. String theory predicts towers of massive particles organized in Regge trajectories, where spin grows with mass. Writing each state explicitly has long been laborious.

Using light-cone quantization, the authors give oscillator recipes for single states and whole trajectories. Transverse oscillators combine into clean rotation representations, and a climbing method adds oscillators step by step from seed states. Composition coefficients follow simple level patterns, yielding closed forms for infinitely many states. The catalog helps theorists test duality and scattering ideas against exact spectra.
arxiv-2511-07624:
Hristo Dimitrov, Viktorija Pavalkyte, and Giulia Dominijanni package motion tracking for non-specialists. Tracking without markers now serves behavior, clinic, and biomechanics studies, yet current toolkits demand heavy skill or fit only narrow tasks. TrackStudio merges proven open-source parts into one guided pipeline.

A simple screen covers recording and syncing, plus automatic pose tracking in two and three dimensions out of the box. Modular design lets users swap parts as needs grow. Labs without programmers can still capture animal or human movement well. Open tracking widens who can run movement studies, from small clinics to field researchers.
arxiv-2511-07824:
Zhiyao Zhang, Zhuqing Liu, and Xin Zhang formalize learning problems with two layers of conflicting goals. Modern systems stack decisions: an upper level chooses preferences or designs, a lower level optimizes within them, and several objectives pull against each other at once. Multi-objective bilevel learning names that structure, but its theory is young.

The study builds theoretical and algorithmic foundations, clarifying when such problems are tractable and how preference guidance at the upper level shapes lower solutions. Many applications, from hyperparameter tuning to policy design, hide this shape. Naming and analyzing it gives practitioners algorithms instead of improvisation when layered goals collide.
arxiv-2511-08124:
Alin Morariu, Jess Bridgen, and Chris Jewell present gemlib, a Python library for building and calibrating stochastic epidemic models. Deterministic outbreak models are simpler, but random state transition models capture chance events that matter in real epidemics. Their cost has kept them out of fast pandemic response work, despite their clearer interpretation.

Gemlib splits a model into three ingredients that fully define it and drive the computation. Simulation uses Gillespie and tau leaping methods, while Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers connect directly for calibration. Built on JAX and TensorFlow Probability, the library uses modern hardware so modelers can focus on structure and assumptions during an outbreak.
arxiv-2511-08324:
Pier Luigi Silvestrelli and co-authors use density theory to compare sliding in bilayers of transition metal dichalcogenides, layered materials valued as solid lubricants. Easy shearing between layers makes these compounds slick, and van der Waals forces dominate the grip between layers. Fourteen bilayers are studied, from molybdenum and tungsten compounds to vanadium, tantalum, titanium, hafnium, and zirconium variants, plus two mixed pairs.

Van der Waals corrected calculations confirm those forces supply most of the interlayer binding, though functional choice shifts exact numbers. Most bilayers bind more strongly and show greater surface corrugation than the molybdenum disulfide reference. A few, including titanium and zirconium sulfides, slide more easily, and links to electronic traits are explored.
arxiv-2511-08624:
Andrés Ledesma and Karo Michaelian ask around which kinds of stars carbon-based life is most likely to start. Their lens is non-equilibrium thermodynamics: life begins, on this view, when ultraviolet light drives molecules into ordered structures that dissipate energy.

For Earth-like planets around star types from hot O stars to cool M dwarfs, they compute surface photon fluxes in helpful and destructive ultraviolet bands. They then track how fast basic molecules build up under different decay rates. Sun-like G stars and their F and K neighbors give the highest molecule levels within weeks to months. Quiet M dwarfs fare far worse, and flaring ones damage the surface. The authors conclude life most plausibly starts around F, G, and heavy K stars.
arxiv-2511-08824:
Yi Yang and twenty co-authors caught a supernova in the act of breaking out of its star, and measured the shape of that breakout with light polarization. The nearby type II supernova 2024ggi was observed by spectropolarimetry starting only about one point two days after explosion, earlier than such measurements usually begin.

The polarization reveals a well-defined symmetry axis for the shock breakout itself. The same axis persists in the hydrogen-rich envelope that appeared once the ejecta swallowed the surrounding circumstellar material. A single stable axis running through the whole event favors explosion mechanisms that act coherently on large scales, whether neutrino reheating or jet power drives them. How massive stars launch their death shock has puzzled astronomers for decades, and this geometry is a fresh constraint.
arxiv-2511-09124:
Ryan Babbush and eight colleagues from the Google Quantum AI team lay out what it will actually take to make quantum computers useful. Their perspective separates promising paths from hard hurdles. They organize the road into five stages, from early theoretical studies of quantum advantage through compilation and resource costing for real machines.

Two middle stages get flagged as both essential and under-resourced: naming concrete problem instances where quantum advantage should appear, and tying those problems to genuine real-world uses. The essay also weighs criteria for a compelling advantage demo, the help AI itself might give this research, and how code translation changes as early fault-tolerant machines arrive. Each stage mixes scientific goals with social roadblocks, and the authors are frank about both.
arxiv-2511-09424:
Henrique de Oliveira and Jeffrey Mensch characterize when an inattentive decision-maker's information costs take a clean closed form. The agent has rationally inattentive preferences over menus of acts, meaning information is valuable but costly to process. The question is which extra assumptions force the cost into that form, depending only on beliefs before and after learning.

Two axioms, Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives and Ignorance Equivalence, turn out to be necessary and sufficient. The cost must also meet a mild smoothness requirement the authors define. Reading the problem as Bayesian persuasion, the same axioms characterize solvability by a unique hyperplane. When costs stay fixed across priors, the axioms yield costs of that same form everywhere.
arxiv-2511-09724:
Yunqian Cheng and two co-authors upgrade a floor-plan-based indoor localization system. It works where GPS cannot, using only a phone camera and a map. The earlier PALMS system needed a stationary scan and was limited by smartphone LiDAR's short range and by ambiguous indoor layouts. Emergency response and assistive navigation motivate something better.

PALMS+ reconstructs scale-aligned three-dimensional point clouds from posed photographs. A monocular depth foundation model supplies the depths, and convolution matches layouts against the floor plan. It outputs a probability distribution over position and orientation. On benchmark and campus datasets it beat PALMS and F3Loc at stationary localization with no training. A particle-filter version tracked real trajectories more accurately too.
arxiv-2511-09924:
Hu Zhang, Zhien Dai, Zhaohui Tang, and Yongfang Xie propose MDMLP-EIA, a forecasting model for time series built from multilayer perceptrons rather than attention. Perceptron models are lean and robust, but they can lose weak seasonal signals, run short of capacity when channels multiply, and fuse channels poorly. The design answers each weakness with a named mechanism.

An adaptive dual-domain seasonal module separates strong and weak seasonal parts and fuses channels with little noise. An energy invariant attention focuses on different feature channels while keeping total signal energy constant, which fits the decompose, predict, and rebuild pipeline. A dynamic rule scales neuron counts with channel count. Across nine benchmark datasets, the model reached state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency.
arxiv-2511-10024:
Ayush Sahu, Richa Arya, Sergio E. Jorás, and Karim H. Seleim study warm inflation, a version of cosmic inflation where the inflaton stays coupled to a radiation bath. Their model uses a quartic potential and a dissipation coefficient built from two terms that dominate at different scales. The early term governs the large scales seen in the cosmic microwave background, while the second term grows key at small scales.

Inflation then runs in two stages: a strongly dissipative first phase producing a red-tilted spectrum matching microwave background observations. Then a second phase, with a blue tilt, amplifies small-scale power enough to form primordial black holes. The authors vary phase durations and dissipation strength to map the spectrum, and check the model against swampland and trans-Planckian conjectures from quantum gravity.
arxiv-2511-10224:
Udvas Das, Binayak Dutta, Satyabrata Jana, Debabrata Pal, and Sasanka Roy study witness sets in polygons, a visibility concept from computational geometry. Two points in a polygon see each other when the segment between them stays inside. A witness set is a set of points such that every point of the polygon is visible from at most one of them. Finding the largest witness set is the problem, in continuous and discrete variants.

The authors give a polynomial-time method for the discrete variant in general polygons. For monotone polygons they discretize the continuous problem, generating a candidate point set that must contain a large witness set if one exists. That yields an exact method and also an approximation scheme with strong guarantees for the monotone case, building on earlier work on monotone mountains.
arxiv-2511-10324:
Matteo Taffetani and Matteo Pezzulla build a theory for thin elastic shells that change shape under non-mechanical stimuli, such as growing tissue or swelling matter. Large deformations, rotations, and incompatible internal strains are the norm in such systems; the eversion of the Volvox embryo is their motivating example. Starting from a fully nonlinear 3D model, they derive a reduced 2D morphoelastic energy for naturally curved shells.

Earlier morphoelastic theories covered flat plates; this one handles curvature and stimuli acting through the thickness. Two matter laws, incompressible Neo-Hookean and compressible Ciarlet-Geymonat, show how compressibility and curvature steer snap-through and global shape change. Applications include everting spherical shells and vesiculation in living systems.
arxiv-2511-10824:
Inga Girshfeld and Xiaohui Chen build a regression method for data whose inputs and outputs are whole probability distributions. Standard approaches lean on a single global transport map or on linearizing around a tangent space. Those choices can restrict what the model can express and warp the geometry, especially in several dimensions.

Their Neural Local Wasserstein Regression works locally, in analogy with kernel regression. Kernel weights built from the Wasserstein distance focus each estimate near a reference distribution, while neural networks parameterize the transport maps so they can adapt to complicated geometries. Training uses DeepSets-style architectures with Sinkhorn-approximated losses and a greedy scheme for choosing reference points. On synthetic and image-based tasks, the method captured nonlinear distributional relationships that existing methods missed.
arxiv-2511-10924:
Lise Waldek, Brian Ballsun-Stanton, and their colleagues ask when scholars may use hacked data with a clear conscience. Their case is research on far-right violent extremism online, where leaked files can show groups that hide from open study. Rules made for older kinds of research give little firm guidance here.

Through the case, the authors show the doubts that such work raises for safety, consent, and harm. They argue that ethical use is possible in some settings, but only if scholars keep weighing those doubts at each step. The study offers a careful path for others who face the same hard choice with leaked data.
arxiv-2511-11124:
Tuochao Chen, Bandhav Veluri, and their colleagues present AV-Dialog, a spoken dialogue system that listens and watches at the same time. Voice-only systems falter in noisy rooms with many speakers, giving off-topic replies and awkward turn-taking. Seeing the speaker's face gives cues that sound alone cannot supply in such settings.

AV-Dialog uses sound and vision together to track the target speaker, judge when a turn ends, and form apt replies. Training mixes solo, synthetic, and real dialogue data in stages. Tests show fewer transcription errors, better turn-taking, and higher human ratings than sound-only models, which points to richer agents for real noisy rooms.
arxiv-2511-11424:
Simon Badger, Matteo Becchetti, and their colleagues compute one hard part of a precision prediction. The process is top-quark pair production with an extra jet at a hadron collider. The order is next-to-next-to-leading in quantum chromodynamics. The part computed here is the double virtual part. It comes from two-loop amplitudes, with infinite terms subtracted off.

The finite rest is extracted in exact form. The extraction uses evaluations over finite fields. A basis of special functions carries the result. The team then builds the summed interference with the tree-level amplitudes. They release a C++ library ready for use in physics studies. New techniques evaluate the special functions by direct numeric integration. They perform well across the full phase space.
arxiv-2511-11524:
S. K. Steensen and thirteen co-authors tackle a practical headache in materials computing: density functional theory codes each speak their own input and output language, so results are hard to compare or reuse. Workflow tools such as AiiDA, PerQueue, Pipeline Pilot, and SimStack all face the same translation problem.

A common input and output standard lets those tools convert jobs into one unified schema that runs across codes including CASTEP, GPAW, Quantum ESPRESSO, and VASP. As a test, the team computes open-circuit voltages for several battery cathode materials and documents where energies from different engines disagree. The standard is a step toward results that others can check and build on.
arxiv-2511-11824:
Zhongping Dong and four co-authors present SOTFormer, a deliberately minimal transformer that tracks a single object and predicts its short-term path in one unified model. Occlusion, scale change, and drift over time break the temporal coherence real-time perception depends on.

Constant memory is the design constraint: a ground-truth-primed memory and a burn-in anchor loss stabilize identity from the start, and one lightweight temporal attention layer refines features across frames. Detection, tracking, and trajectory forecasting share the same end-to-end framework with fixed graphics memory. Results on a Mini-LaSOT benchmark subset test whether minimal machinery can hold identity as reliably as heavier stacked encoders.
arxiv-2511-11924:
Yongkang Huo, Fulvio Forni, and Rodolphe Sepulchre present a neuromorphic control design built from one motif. The motif is the rebound winner-take-all circuit. It is scaled from cells to whole systems. Brains mix discrete choices with smooth tuning with ease. Built controllers usually force a pick between the two styles.

Winner-take-all state machines supply the discrete side. Excitable biophysical circuits supply the smooth tuning side. Both are described in one physical modeling language. Rhythm generation and decision making share one event-based frame. A snake robot's nervous system shows the design in action. It shows versatility, robustness, and modularity in one build.
arxiv-2511-12324:
Naomi Fokkens and Fei Xue show a new route to flipping a perpendicular magnet reliably without an external magnetic field, a key step for spintronic memory. Standard schemes need explicit symmetry breaking to make the switch deterministic. Their idea uses higher harmonics of spin-orbit torque, the twist exerted on magnetization by a current.

Expanding the torque in vector spherical harmonics reveals extra fixed points away from the equator, and those points allow clean reversal when the higher harmonics are strong enough. First-principles work on the Weyl ferromagnet PrAlGe supports the picture: its band structure and strong spin-orbit coupling make the higher terms sizable, while the usual terms stay weak.
arxiv-2511-12424: Montserrat Vite proves a result about extremal divisors on the Hilbert scheme of points in the plane. That scheme is a space that describes finite sets of points. She takes point counts of two specific triangular forms. For those counts, being extremal is preserved under residuality. That operation passes between a divisor and its residual pair on the scheme.
arxiv-2511-12724:
Nazmiye Alemdar, Hürmet Fulya Akız, and Halim Ayaz develop connectedness ideas inside soft topology, a framework where sets come with a parameter attached. They define a soft version of the usual topology on the real line and use its interval to define a soft path. With paths in place, they define soft connectedness and soft path connectedness, study how the two notions relate, and show both survive under soft continuous mappings between spaces.

The paper then follows these properties into soft topological groups, where the group operations and the topology must fit together. It closes by building the category of such groups, naming its morphisms, and proving the category is symmetric monoidal, a structure that supports well-behaved combinations of objects. The contribution is foundational: it extends familiar topology language into the soft setting and gives later work a checked set of definitions and preservation results.
arxiv-2511-13024:
Aneesh Sivasankaran and eight co-authors simulate what black hole winds do when galaxies collide. Using the SMUGGLE model plus refinement that follows black hole feedback down to tens of parsecs, they compare merging and isolated galaxies, with and without the winds. The comparison spans three galaxy types: Milky Way analogues, gas-rich Sbc galaxies, and Small Magellanic Cloud analogues.

Feedback and merging amplify each other most in the Milky Way-like systems, where winds grow stronger as the merger thickens the disks. In the vigorously star-forming Sbc mergers, the winds matter mainly after star formation fades. The sharpest surprise concerns small galaxies: their clumpy medium knocks low-mass black holes off center, wandering kiloparsecs away, starving them of fuel and feedback.
arxiv-2511-13124:
Changxi Chi and six co-authors predict how a single cell's gene expression will shift under a drug or genetic perturbation, without ever seeing the same cell twice. Sequencing destroys the cell, so data are inherently unpaired: control cells and perturbed cells are different cells. The authors model the trip from one population to the other with a Schrödinger bridge. The entropy-regularized optimal transport process that finds the most plausible stochastic path between two distributions, conditioned on each perturbation.

Earlier bridge approximations inferred the coupling between source and target by modeling both directions, which is ill-posed. This work pairs cells with minibatch optimal transport instead, directly guiding bridge learning, and trains two bridges jointly, one for discrete gene activation states and one for continuous expression levels. The pairing makes the approximation scalable and more precise.
arxiv-2511-13224:
Devina Mohan and Anna M. M. Scaife test whether natural gradient descent improves Bayesian neural networks that classify radio galaxies. Such networks are most often trained with simple first-order methods. The authors argue that second-order detail can give a more direct path through the space of distributions and faster learning.

They use the iVON algorithm and compare it with a recent benchmark that includes strong methods such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Networks trained with iVON matched the best methods on accuracy and gave the best sense of their own uncertainty. They also flagged very different optical galaxy images, though not images from a new telescope.
arxiv-2511-13624:
Rajesh Karmakar, Ruth Heller, and Saharon Rosset design multiple testing procedures that keep strong control of the family-wise error rate while gaining power. Testing many hypotheses at once risks false claims, so error control is mandatory, but crude control wastes real discoveries. They first characterize the optimal procedures for several power goals under reasonable assumptions.

Those optima are rarely computable, so they propose a bottom-up recipe that builds consonant closed testing procedures level by level with the power goal in view. The resulting methods stay practical to run and design. Simulations and a real data study showed substantially improved power over existing procedures, without loosening the error guarantee.
arxiv-2511-13724:
Omkar Desai and 4 co-authors present Seneca, a data loading system that removes preprocessing bottlenecks when many multimedia training jobs run at once. Starved accelerators often wait on decoding and augmentation rather than on model math. Seneca treats the storage and ingestion pipeline as a resource to be shared with intent.

A performance model splits cache space among encoded, decoded, and augmented data forms for the best total throughput. During random batch sampling, Seneca favors cached items so concurrent jobs quietly help each other fill the cache. Built into PyTorch, it cut total job time by roughly forty-five percent against stock loading and multiplied processing throughput against the next best loader.
arxiv-2511-14024:
Jaskirat Singh and Rohan Chandra propose FACA, a collision avoidance method for robot teams in tight, urgent spaces. Robots delivering medicine or aiding rescues must move fast through small gaps while other robots, each with its own priority, crowd the same passages. Priorities can also change mid-mission without warning. Safety alone is not enough; the team must stay agile.

In FACA the robots coordinate by talking in natural language, much as people do. A modified potential field method creates an automatic roundabout pattern whenever paths conflict, keeping motion fair and fluid. Experiments show missions finished more than three and a half times faster than baseline methods, with time cut by over seventy percent and safety maintained.
arxiv-2511-14124:
Sabiha Afroz, Redwan Ibne Seraj Khan, Hadeel Albahar, and two co-authors present 10Cache, a memory manager for training large language models in the cloud. GPU memory is scarce and pricey, so training spills tensors to CPU memory and fast storage, but slow transfers and wasted space inflate both time and cost. 10Cache coordinates all three tiers with knowledge of how training actually uses tensors.

The system profiles tensor execution order to prefetch ahead, sizes pinned memory buffers from the tensor size distribution, and reuses buffers to cut allocation overhead. Across varied training workloads it doubled training speed at best, raised GPU cache hit rates sharply, and lifted memory use on both CPU and GPU over prior offloading methods.
arxiv-2511-14524:
Venkat Chandar, Aslan Tchamkerten, and Shashank Vatedka prove a compression result with a strong privacy demand. A binary source must be stored in compressed form above its entropy rate. At the same time, decoding any single symbol must reveal nothing about all the others. That joint demand creates a delicate consistency problem for code distributions.

The authors solve it with a geometric view of how codeword probabilities are arranged. Their method shows lossless recovery is still possible under the privacy rule. The geometric technique may help in other coding problems as well. The result separates the cost of privacy from the cost of compression in this basic source setting.
arxiv-2511-14624:
Giulia Janzen and five co-authors argue that active matter physics can guide the design of living like robots. Robophysics studies physical rules for robots in complex real settings. Single robots still move inefficiently, and swarms struggle with shared purpose, coordination, and cost. Biology and active matter offer principles that engineering alone has missed.

As a perspective, the article surveys key challenges for bio inspired robot collectives. It highlights recent work that imports active matter ideas into swarm modeling and design. Collective motion, self organization, and energy use are central themes. The authors aim to connect physicists and roboticists. Their roadmap targets swarms that coordinate robustly without central control.
arxiv-2511-14724:
Vitaliano S. Amaral, Marcio Antônio de A. Bortoloti, and two co-authors design optimization methods for curved spaces where the objective is rough and bent in hard ways. The problems live on Hadamard manifolds, complete spaces of nonpositive curvature. The objective mixes smooth, convex, and merely well-behaved parts, which covers a wide family of hard tasks.

Two variants of an adaptive proximal point method are offered. One uses a known smoothness constant for the gradient, while the other needs no such knowledge and so applies more broadly. The authors prove convergence, bound the cost, and test both versions on numerical examples. The work widens the reach of reliable manifold optimization.
arxiv-2511-15824:
Lewis Burke, Mark Greenaway, and Joseph Betouras study how high order Van Hove singularities reshape exciton and trion energy dispersions in two dimensional semiconductors. Van Hove singularities are points where electronic density of states spikes. High order versions arise from Mexican hat or monkey saddle band shapes.
