The results feed into Olson's spectral order, a way of comparing positive matrices, and into comparisons between the symmetric modulus and its quadratic variant. One consequence completes a line of work begun by Ando: the sum of two positive matrices sub-majorizes their Kato supremum. The paper closes with open questions about the smallest number of orthogonal conjugates needed for exact orbit averages. Such norm comparisons are quiet workhorses, underpinning estimates throughout matrix analysis and quantum information.
arxiv-2606-16024:
Avraham and colleagues construct an O(4)-breaking bubble solution for false vacuum decay in 2026, the first explicit example of its kind. Coleman's theorem makes the dominant saddle, the bounce, O(4)-symmetric, but fixes only the minimum-action one. Mathematics had non-constructive existence proofs of less symmetric solutions, their physics unknown. For a simple sextic potential, the authors build one outright.

The solution is nonradial: two bubble-tubes of opposite sign wrap orthogonal rings, kept invariant by two rotations and a parity exchanging the rings. It admits valid initial data for real-time evolution and supports an odd number of unstable modes. That odd count gives the saddle an imaginary Gaussian factor and a nonzero weight in the decay rate, set by its action excess over the bounce. The associated Stokes ambiguity is left unresolved. An existence proof becomes a physical object whose decay role can now be studied.
arxiv-2606-16324:
Didier and co-authors demonstrate in 2026 a chip-scale source of mid-infrared frequency combs whose color can be tuned electronically. Mid-infrared combs, evenly spaced laser lines, enable sensitive molecular spectroscopy because molecules absorb strongly in that band. Compact tunable sources are needed for compact sensing platforms. The device is built in thin-film lithium niobate, a photonic material that mixes light frequencies efficiently.

A telecom-band electro-optic comb, made by double-pass phase modulation, feeds a patterned poled waveguide. There, difference frequency generation converts it into the mid-infrared. A near-infrared pump is amplitude-modulated through an integrated Mach-Zehnder modulator to allow lock-in detection. Tuning the seed laser and the chip temperature shifts the mid-infrared comb's center wavelength by over 200 nm, with a bandwidth near 6 nanometers. The comb's line spacing is set directly by the applied radio-frequency drive.
arxiv-2606-16824:
Tiwari and colleagues study how to serve coding agents efficiently in a 2026 systems paper. Coding agents run long sessions where model generations alternate with tool calls, unlike short chat exchanges. Their behavior under real workloads had not been measured, so serving systems were tuned for the wrong shape of traffic.

The team collected real coding assistant traces and found sessions repeatedly reuse large, growing prompt prefixes. That reuse strains the key-value cache, the stored attention state that lets a model avoid recomputing context. Their system, CacheWise, adds a management layer inside the vLLM serving stack. Prefix-aware scheduling favors requests that can reuse resident cache, and reuse-aware eviction keeps prefixes that tool-call metadata predicts will be needed soon. On the collected traces, cache evictions fall by more than half and total session completion time improves several-fold at best.
arxiv-2606-17024:
Xiang and colleagues prime language models for hard reasoning in a 2026 paper on reinforcement learning. Sparse-reward training only pays off when the base model already samples diverse plausible attempts. On hard problems it usually cannot, so rewards stay at zero and nothing is learned.

Their method, ExpRL, performs reinforcement learning during mid-training, using large collections of human-written questions and answers. The reference solutions are never shown to the model to copy. Instead, each reference is turned into a grading rubric, and a judge model scores the model's own attempts for partial progress, both on outcomes and on process. Training on those dense rewards builds the strategy coverage hard problems demand. Afterwards, the model reaches non-trivial correctness under the sparse outcome reward alone. ExpRL thus serves as a well-primed starting point for later sparse-reward training, automating a priming stage that usually needs hand-designed traces.
arxiv-2606-17424:
Kumaranathunga, De Livera, and Prendergast present a 2026 arXiv paper warning meta-analysts about a quiet statistical trap: estimating missing standard deviations from three-number summaries. Many studies report only a median with quartiles or a range, and popular conversion formulas promise means and spreads from those scraps. The authors show the three-number case simply does not carry enough information about the data's shape. The converted spread can then be badly wrong, quietly poisoning any combined inference built on it.

A sensitivity analysis is offered so researchers can see how fragile their conclusions are to the unknown shape. The paper also tests whether naming extra shape information can rescue the estimate, introducing an estimator built on a scaled Beta distribution. Simulations and a real data example weigh the gains and limits of that fix. A web application helps researchers run the sensitivity checks themselves.
arxiv-2606-17724:
Ablikim and hundreds of collaborators in the BESIII experiment report a 2026 particle physics measurement on how a charged D meson decays. Their study uses electron and positron collision data gathered with the BESIII detector in China. The focus is the decay of a D+ meson into a pion and two eta mesons, and the shape of the a0(980) resonance inside it.

Carrying out the first amplitude analysis of this decay, the team finds a prominent chain where the D+ first makes an a0(980)+ plus an eta, and that resonance then decays onward. No extra conventional resonance was needed to explain the signal. They also measure the overall branching fraction for the decay, giving hadron physicists a sharper test of how this unusual resonance is structured.
arxiv-2606-17824:
Kühn and colleagues describe a 2026 workflow that splits 3D models into meaningful parts with a person guiding the process. Splitting assets this way is hard because what counts as a part depends on the intended use, so full automation often misses the point. Their pipeline serves media, game, and extended reality production, and it was built at Fraunhofer IGD in Germany.

The method first picks a small set of rendered views that together cover the whole surface. A user then marks regions in those views, with help from the SAM 2 segmentation model. Those masks are projected back onto the model to form one segmented atlas, ready for tasks like assigning materials per part or style transfer. Tests on eight cultural heritage objects worked well, though fine structures and cavities still needed hand fixes.
arxiv-2606-17924:
Yang and Shan tackle a speed versus thoughtfulness trade-off in robot control models, in a 2026 paper. Vision-language-action models that decode actions directly are fast but shallow, while models that reason in words or pictures plan better yet run slowly. Their system, PearlVLA, moves the deliberation into the model's latent space, where no text needs to be generated.

A plan branch refines a rough semantic draft round by round. Each round asks a small frozen world model to imagine the future the current plan implies. A refinement network then folds that preview back in as scheduled updates. The edits move from coarse fixes to fine ones. The finished plan is decoded in parallel into an action chunk, keeping execution quick. A reinforcement method with process rewards from imagined futures further trains the refinement path itself.
arxiv-2606-18024:
Hidekel and Raviv argue that when a model learns a new task and forgets an old one, the damage lives in surprisingly few directions, in a 2026 theory paper. Catastrophic forgetting is usually tracked through drifting parameters or fought with replay, views that never say which outputs are at risk. Working in the neural tangent kernel regime, the authors look at forgetting in function space instead.

New-task training pushes old-task predictions through the cross-task kernel, and that link yields a closed-form prediction of the forgetting vector before a single new gradient step is taken. In frozen-backbone, linear-head adaptation the predictor is exact. The same formula shows forgetting concentrates in a handful of old-task kernel modes, with a scaling rule for the vulnerable rank. The lesson is aimed at practice: regularizers guarding parameter space can miss the real, low-rank interference.
arxiv-2606-18224:
Maslova and colleagues compare how an excited quasiparticle spreads in quantum models against classical wandering models, in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. Several of their quantum systems are exactly solvable. That lets them compute the full time-dependent probability spread with no approximation. The surprise is how familiar the quantum spreading looks: its shape echoes classical continuous-time random walks, including Lévy walks and diffusing diffusivity models.

When quasiparticles share a flat phonon reservoir, the exact distribution turns U-shaped. That shape signals a strong ballistic component. That component survives because quasiparticle speed has a hard ceiling, letting coherence effects from the shared reservoir matter. The authors benchmark the phonon-assisted hopping model against three rivals. These are a plain tight-binding chain, a disordered ensemble of chains, and a chain with randomly fluctuating hopping. The comparison maps where quantum and classical transport part ways.
arxiv-2606-18324:
Ganesaraja and colleagues publish a candid post-mortem of their language model, in a 2026 retrospective. SWave is a complex-valued recurrent model of about one hundred seventy million parameters. It rests on three bets: that waves encode language more richly than real numbers. A unitary transition stops the state from decaying or exploding, and a rotating hidden state preserves signals over very long contexts. It trained on FineWeb-Edu across two H100 accelerators.

Across three development phases, one founding component failed structurally. The Resonance Head, which tied output embeddings by phase matching, provably admits collapse of the imaginary channel as a global loss minimum, a failure the authors name cos-domination collapse. Replacing it with untied real and imaginary embedding tables fixed training, and the final model reached a perplexity of 15.6 in its last configuration. The actionable lesson targets anyone building complex-valued models: check the head first.
arxiv-2606-19124:
Onglao and colleagues assess in 2026 whether the proposed CHRONOS detector can observe gravity-gradient noise and prompt gravity signals from earthquakes. Ground detectors at sub-hertz frequencies are limited by Newtonian noise, gravity shifts from nearby moving mass. That same band offers a rare window on seismic and atmospheric gravity effects. CHRONOS is a cryogenic torsion-bar detector with a quantum non-demolition speed meter, designed for that low band.

The team models gravity-gradient inputs from Rayleigh-wave seismic fields, atmospheric infrasound, and mass shifts during quakes, then projects them onto the detector response. Rayleigh-wave noise dominates below about half a hertz, while air-driven noise stays far smaller across the band. They also gauge how close and how large a quake must be for its prompt gravity signal to stand out. The study maps where CHRONOS can double as an earth-science sensor.
arxiv-2606-19224:
Lee and colleagues present a conjugate gradient form of the ensemble Kalman filter in 2026 for data assimilation. Ensemble Kalman methods blend numerical forecasts with incoming data over time, accounting for model error and noisy measurements. Their cost can be high for large dynamical systems, and many variants trade accuracy for speed. The new algorithm reformulates a matrix inverse step with a classical conjugate gradient method, keeping cost comparable to efficient variants.

The authors derive an upper error bound under the gradient method and show error convergence to the classical filter result. They also analyze computational complexity in detail. A reduced variant is even cheaper for high-dimensional systems with small ensembles. Numerical examples compare the new filters against benchmark ensemble methods. In select cases the gradient form achieves better state estimation at like cost. Parallel structure is preserved, which matters for operational forecasting centers.
arxiv-2606-19324:
Dantam and colleagues settle the strategy complexity of optimal play in two-player stochastic games in 2026, focusing on lifting strategies from simpler models. Earlier work showed optimal memoryless strategies for a broad class of objectives can be lifted from Markov decision processes to two-player games, at exponential memory cost.

The authors prove the matching lower bound. The extra exponential memory is required in general, even for randomized strategies. For mean-payoff-parity the picture is kinder. In decision processes, the maximizer has optimal memoryless random strategies, while deterministic ones need far more memory. In stochastic games, optimal random strategies need exactly linear memory, equal to the number of even colors. A further result blocks a tempting shortcut. A known construction for lifting deterministic strategies cannot be extended to randomized ones, shown by a crafted objective where both players have memoryless random optima in decision processes but not in games.
arxiv-2606-19424:
Meyer and colleagues characterize a symmetric-facet dual-ruled grating for spatial heterodyne spectroscopy in 2026. Dual-bandpass spectrometers measure two widely separated passbands at high resolution at once. They need one beam to span two adjacent gratings with distinct ruling densities and blaze angles. The gap between ruled sections cuts throughput. Dual-ruled gratings solve this by integrating multiple ruled panels onto a single substrate.

The team validates a first-generation grating made by Bach Research. It was mechanically ruled at two densities. Using a stabilized deuterium source and a reference monochromator, they measured diffraction efficiency into several orders across a wide wavelength range. Comparison with rigorous coupled-wave theory infers a small facet asymmetry and a duty cycle near seventy percent, signs of minor manufacturing defects. The work demonstrates that mechanically ruled dual-ruled gratings are viable. It gives makers feedback to tighten the next generation.
arxiv-2606-19624:
Hongxuan Liu leads a large team auditing a molecule discovery benchmark in 2026. MassSpecGym tests machine learning models that identify molecules from tandem mass spectrometry data. Faulty benchmarks can crown weak models and mislead a whole field.

The audit reviews papers that reported MassSpecGym results in the benchmark's first year. At least 17 of 26 papers carry evaluation issues, the team find. Three failure classes emerge: data leakage, shortcut learning, and code bugs with metric drift. Replication runs and fresh experiments measure how badly each issue distorts scores. Distilled recommendations generalise to other spectrometry challenges and custom setups. A repaired release, MassSpecGym version 1.5, puts those fixes into the suite itself. Careful evaluation hygiene, the authors argue, is part of the science, not clerical detail.
arxiv-2606-20024:
Dongmei Wei, Junxiang Wang, Hanxiu Xu, Cancan Chen, and Jiaying Wu simulate memory-laden quantum dynamics with a fractional Schrödinger equation in 2026. Non-Markovian systems remember their past, which changes how fast they can evolve; the quantum speed limit time sets the minimum evolution time. Wei's time-fractional equation is applied to a resonant dissipative Jaynes-Cummings model, a qubit coupled to light in a lossy cavity.

Solving the speed limit shows how environmental memory speeds evolution up. Tuning the fractional order, coupling strength, and photon number together optimizes the acceleration. Across the full fractional range the fractional model tracks the true dynamics, where Naber's variant works only in a narrow band, and trajectory calculations run faster as well. Fractional calculus earns a concrete role in open-system simulation.
arxiv-2606-20224:
Luis Thomas and a large international team confirm two eccentric warm Jupiters first spotted by the TESS space telescope. Their 2026 paper characterizes TOI-2147 b and TOI-6019 b, planets with periods between ten and two hundred days. Warm Jupiters show a wide spread of eccentricities and layouts, hinting at varied formation and migration histories. TOI-2147 b has a radius near ten and a half Earth radii and a mass of about 116 Earth masses, orbiting a slightly metal-poor star.

Ground-based follow-up did the confirming: multiband photometry from LCOGT and MuSCAT2, speckle imaging to rule out contaminating stars, and precise radial velocities from the MaHPS spectrograph. Both candidates proved to be genuine planets on eccentric orbits. Such planets are informative, because gentle disk migration should leave circular orbits, while violent scattering can pump eccentricity up.
arxiv-2606-20424:
Shikuan Shi, Chunran Zheng, Jiaming Xu, Tianyong Ye, Tao Yu, and Yukang Cui make 3D Gaussian splatting maps survive bad lighting by adding a thermal camera. Their 2026 paper presents LIT-GS, a LiDAR-inertial-thermal splatting framework. Existing pipelines that fuse LiDAR, inertial, and visual data lean on RGB cues and falter when light changes or scenes lack texture. Thermal images see heat rather than light, but low contrast makes them hard to align alone.

LIT-GS uses LiDAR-derived plane geometry to constrain pose refinement and Gaussian optimization. Visual map points serve as anchors linking thermal and LiDAR data, and point-to-plane residuals enter bundle adjustment to refine poses under weak thermal supervision. A plane-regularized splatting objective keeps rendered points on observed planes, fighting surface thickening and drift. On public and private sequences, LIT-GS beat baselines on accuracy and rendering quality, especially in challenging light.
arxiv-2606-20524:
Diogo Gorgulho, Jacob Litterer, and João Rosa show that the string axiverse boosts dark matter production around light primordial black holes. Their 2026 paper studies both evaporation and superradiance, the process where a spinning black hole amplifies bosonic fields into a cloud.

Realistic string constructions predict between a hundred and a hundred thousand light axion species, and their Hawking emission raises black hole spin, which significantly enhances superradiance efficiency. The axiverse thus expands the parameter regions where a sizeable fraction of dark matter could sit in micro-boson stars, the self-gravitating remnants of superradiant clouds. Conversely, the same effect constrains where such black holes can hide. String theory's particle zoo turns into a lever on dark matter production.
arxiv-2606-20624:
Kejiang Qian and Fengxiang He argue in 2026 that language models can be irrational even after their values are aligned. Alignment trains a model toward a target value function, a scoring rule for good answers, but the model may still fail to pick answers that maximize that score during reasoning. They formalize the gap as rational value risk, the utility lost between the deployed reasoning strategy and the best possible response.

Qian and He split estimation error for that risk into three parts: limited candidates, limited prompts, and imperfect verifiers. Tests cover Llama, Qwen, and Tulu families, plus GPT and DeepSeek systems. Rational value risk appears widely. Alignment reduces but does not remove it. Longer reasoning helps, with shrinking gains.
arxiv-2606-20724:
Aagam Sogani and five colleagues study web agents that finish tasks yet still fail in 2026, using a new benchmark called Parallel WebBench. Long web tasks hide failures behind final-answer scores. An agent may visit useful pages and answer confidently. It can still miss fields, add unsupported items, or use stale evidence. Their benchmark holds 1,679 verified records, with curated tasks and reconstructed trajectories.

Agents are trained with reinforcement learning under three data mixes. The best model raises completion from 50.7 to 96.0 percent. Element-wise scores also improve. Yet binary accuracy stays far below completion. Trace analysis finds three stubborn failure modes. Agents loop in search, stop early on partial answers, or collapse during synthesis after finding evidence. The gap between finishing and being right argues for trace diagnostics in evaluation, so builders can see where a run went wrong instead of only scoring its final text.
arxiv-2606-20824:
Yan Fyodorov and Bertrand Lacroix-A-Chez-Toine study how spectra move together in 2026 in non-Hermitian quantum chaos, using random matrix theory. Interest has grown in such matrices as a model for quantum systems that lose energy to their surroundings. Their question is how spectral densities change together when a parameter varies. The setting is a family of complex Ginibre matrices.

They derive an explicit closed-form result for the covariance in that setting. It applies to eigenvalues in a round region with a finite average count. The behavior is expected to be universal, meaning shared across many systems. Tests on other matrix families support that hope. They also discuss a link to how far eigenvectors depart from orthogonal form. Shared spectral patterns help physicists tell when complex behavior reflects deep structure rather than details of one model.
arxiv-2606-20924:
Qingtao Pan and four colleagues propose ELDiff in 2026, an evidential learning method for text-to-image diffusion with multiple objects. Generated images must match the prompt in meaning. That consistency is often underweighted during denoising. Token-supervised models learn object consistency from segmentation maps. But maps can be biased, and object meanings can overlap and conflict, especially with many objects.

ELDiff uses uncertainty metrics and conflict detection to tolerate unreliable maps. A pixel evidence loss restrains overconfidence in shaky labels through evidential regularization. A token conflict loss weakens contradictions between object meanings. Object-wise consistency learning is thereby strengthened. Better handling of flawed supervision matters for busy scenes, where a model must place several named objects correctly and a biased map could otherwise teach systematic mistakes.
arxiv-2606-21024:
Hanchun Wang proposes negative knowledge as shared memory in a solo 2026 paper for AI-assisted research systems. Such systems generate many failed attempts. Failures rarely become a durable, shared asset. A curator agent converts each failed attempt into a bounded, typed record in a shared bank. A downstream research agent then explicitly adopts or rejects those records before proposing its next experiment.

Two settings are evaluated: retrying the same task on a science benchmark, and cross-task research on nonlinear math-physics problems. The memory layer beats standard baselines while using fewer tokens. Agents with the bank solve new tasks that all baselines fail. A bank from earlier work can also transfer to different problems. Treating failure as maintained knowledge, alongside positive findings, could stop research agents from repeating dead ends that human teams would pass on as hard-won lore.
arxiv-2606-21124:
Rajat Agarwal, Suvidha Tripathi, and Shubham Sharma introduce PulseCX in 2026, a framework that frees customer experience chatbots from a closed-world limit. Service agents usually ignore fast external shifts such as viral trends or outages. Ad hoc web search can bridge that gap, but adds latency and can poison context. PulseCX separates knowledge acquisition from knowledge use.

An asynchronous agent linearizes signals into a temporal knowledge graph. Reinforcement and decay dynamics manage the life cycle of each fact, so stale items fade. Hierarchical intent gating couples that memory to conversations. Synchronous search bottlenecks disappear, with overhead kept very low. Reported gains cover intent resolution and customer satisfaction in dynamic settings. Currency matters in support: an agent that does not know about a live outage will confidently misdiagnose hundreds of customers reporting the same fault.
arxiv-2606-21524:
Achraf Azize, Mathieu Molina, Hugo Richard, and Vianney Perchet open a new problem in 2026. It is the classic prophet inequality and optimal stopping, but with every arriving value hidden behind local differential privacy. Platforms from hiring to auctions want good pick-one decisions without learning sensitive personal values, and local privacy means each value is scrambled on the spot, with no trusted curator. The decision maker designs the scrambling and must stop irrevocably based on noisy reports alone.

The authors characterize the optimal stopping rule and show simple binary mechanisms suffice: a randomized-response report plus a dynamic-programming threshold rule. Against the best non-private online policy, the tight competitive ratio moves smoothly from one over n at full privacy to one at no privacy. Intriguingly, stronger privacy erodes the all-seeing prophet's edge faster than it hurts the online rule.
arxiv-2606-21824:
Renzo and colleagues publish, in 2026, a grid of stellar models for the fast-spinning massive stars thought to end as stripped supernovae or long gamma-ray bursts. How a massive star's core looks at collapse strongly shapes the explosion, yet few progenitor grids include rapid rotation and magnetic effects. Their grid fills that gap with models that mix their interiors as they spin.

Using the open MESA code, the team computed 113 single-star models with starting masses from thirty to ninety times the Sun's mass. Each star began rotating at half to nearly the critical break-up rate, at low metal content, and followed a 128-isotope reaction network through silicon burning. By construction the stars evolve chemically homogeneously, staying well mixed, and reach collapse carrying large, structured amounts of angular momentum. The grid gives explosion simulations a uniform starting point.
arxiv-2606-22024:
Kawauchi's 2026 paper works in knot theory. It introduces a quantity called non-trivialization probability for arc systems in three-dimensional space. An arc system is a set of disjoint polygonal arcs, like several bent wires that never touch. Earlier work defined a knotting probability for arc diagrams using chord diagrams of ribbon surface-links in four-dimensional space.

Kawauchi modifies that notion into the non-trivialization probability. He generalizes it from single arcs to whole arc systems. The definition extends an earlier method that turns a polygonal arc in space into a unique arc diagram, up to isomorphism. With the definition in place, he proves several properties of the new probability. The work quantifies how likely a configuration is to be genuinely knotted rather than trivial, now for interacting families of arcs instead of single strands.
arxiv-2606-22124:
De Jong and colleagues present, in 2026, a dataset and a model for recognizing anatomy in surgery video. Safe guidance during operations depends on this kind of perception. Annotated surgical data is scarce, and most methods were designed for natural scenes. Their ATLAS-120k dataset holds over 120,000 annotated frames from one hundred videos. The videos span fourteen procedures and both laparoscopic and robot-assisted surgery.

The labels were built with a scalable pipeline. It mixes expert manual labelling, automated propagation, refinement, and surgeon verification. Alongside the dataset, the ATLAS model labels anatomy across video frames. It uses foundation-model embeddings plus lightweight temporal reasoning. Context cues such as procedure type and phase keep its predictions consistent over time. The model also stays fast enough for real-time use. Both are released publicly.
arxiv-2606-22224:
Ji and Su reanalyze, in 2026, lattice QCD data for the proton's isovector parton distribution function, the gap between its up-quark and down-quark distributions. Several lattice groups have computed this quantity through large momentum expansion. Lattice artifacts and less advanced analysis, however, kept the results from strict comparison with measured data.

Using state-of-the-art tools, Ji and Su correct the artifacts empirically and reanalyze the published datasets. Excited states, unphysical pion masses, discretization effects, and large logs all receive updated treatment. The new distribution, taken to the physical limits, agrees with global fits within about one sigma. The authors read this as compelling evidence that large momentum expansion can predict the distribution's shape once ideal lattice data become available.
arxiv-2606-22424:
Yufei Zhang and Changhao Chen tackle robot navigation under poor visual conditions in this 2026 paper. Their setting is vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments, where an agent follows instructions through unseen spaces. Large models have improved such navigation, but real-world visual corruptions, such as blur or noise, degrade their performance badly.

The pair introduce FlowDec, an image restoration framework built for this task. It uses a hybrid temporal conditioning strategy, which aligns image cleaning with earlier frames. An action-centroid guided filter then judges and integrates each restored image. In their experiments, FlowDec beat the best existing cleaning methods on both navigation accuracy and generation latency, meaning it cleaned images better and faster. The authors present it as a practical route to robot navigation that stays reliable when conditions turn rough.
arxiv-2606-22524:
Hamidou Tembine rebuilds information theory around risk in this 2026 paper. Shannon's classical theory measures information with expectations, plain averages that treat all outcomes neutrally. Tembine replaces the expectation with expectiles, a risk-sensitive generalization that weighs outcomes by how much an agent fears or seeks extremes.

From that swap come expectile versions of entropy, divergence, and mutual information, the three core quantities of the field. These quantities behave in ways Shannon's framework forbids. Divergence, a measure of how far apart two distributions sit, can turn negative under risk-seeking regimes. The new mutual information also separates fundamentally from the classical one, rather than reducing to it. In multiuser systems, the framework induces a mean-field-type game of information exchange, where achievable rate regions depend on each user's risk-sensitivity index. Tembine argues Shannon information alone cannot quantify the extreme risks that drive advanced machine intelligence.
arxiv-2606-22624:
E. Yu. Shchetinin, A. A. Shevchuk, and S. I. Salpagarov analyse transport through membranes in this 2026 mathematics paper. Their system follows Maxwell-Stefan diffusion, where species move together and hinder each other, plus reactions. A finite occupancy constraint caps how much material each site can hold, leaving vacancies as the free volume.

That cap induces a Boltzmann-Fermi entropy and entropy variables. The mobility splits into a composition channel, redistribution at fixed filling, and a mass channel, change in the filling fraction. The mass channel can lose coercivity, the grip solutions need. A single rank-one augmentation restores it while leaving the composition block untouched. On that basis the authors prove four results. They show a coercivity estimate, global existence of entropy weak solutions, and a weak-strong stability estimate with uniqueness. They also prove convergence of an implicit finite-volume scheme that preserves the occupancy structure.
arxiv-2606-22724:
Neranjan Senarath, Rohit Muralitharan, and Sadia Asif study a geometry problem in federated fine-tuning in this 2026 paper. Federated LoRA lets many clients adapt a shared model privately, each training a low-rank update. With heterogeneous client data, those local updates can point into misaligned subspaces, so averaging them destroys progress.

Their method, Subspace-Reg, adds a regularizer that keeps each client's update close to a shared global subspace. They evaluated it on RoBERTa-large and SmolLM-360M over HellaSwag, with ten clients on non-identical data and twenty-four runs. On RoBERTa-large it achieved the strongest accuracy, about forty-five percent at best, and the lowest loss, beating three baselines widely. On the smaller model plain FedAvg led instead, so gains are model-dependent. Basis overlap between local and global subspaces stayed near one under their method, against 0.96 to 0.99 for baselines, supporting the alignment hypothesis.
arxiv-2606-22824:
Nikhil Navas, Sergio Chevtchenko, Talisson Damiao, and Saeed Afshar present a compact speech recognizer in this 2026 paper. Their target is phonetic transcription in the International Phonetic Alphabet, which records pronunciation rather than spelling. Large multilingual systems do this well but are big, and scores are sensitive to how outputs are normalized before comparison.

Their model, BranchShine, pairs a light convolutional front end with a nineteen-block encoder using rotary position embeddings. It has about thirty-three million parameters and reads raw audio directly. On a multilingual test set of 16,660 utterances covering 41 language labels, it scored a 9.19 percent character error rate. That beat a rival model with 575 million parameters, which scored 9.78 percent under the same scoring rules. A side test on children reading aloud showed a different profile: BranchShine was more cautious about wrong readings, while Whisper-Medium accepted correct readings more exactly.
arxiv-2606-23124:
Jiaqiang Wu, Zhouan Zhu, and Shangfei Wang shrink empathetic chatbots through distillation in a 2026 paper. Large language models reply to emotional conversation with diverse, context-aware warmth. Their size blocks deployment on modest hardware. Distillation compresses them into smaller students, but plain distillation misses the subtle cues that guide human connection. Their method, PRIDE, gives the student privileged information during training only. Expert psychology notes and summaries of future events teach empathy at training time, then disappear at run time.

Wu and colleagues add three components. A reasoning prompt makes the teacher spell out feeling understanding and situation analysis step by step. A multi-source attention mechanism helps the student blend the privileged material in. A dual-alignment loss matches teacher and student at both the output and feature levels. Experiments on multimodal and text-only datasets show the approach transfers empathetic skill to small models.
arxiv-2606-23324:
François Impens and David Guéry-Odelin speed up quantum-state transfer in interacting topological chains in a 2026 physics paper. The Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain is a standard model with protected edge states. Shortcuts to adiabaticity already move a single particle's edge state quickly without errors. Interactions spoil that trick through nonlinear phase buildup. The authors remove the obstruction by making the phase of a next-nearest-neighbor shortcut hopping adjustable. In the mean-field regime, one part of that hopping keeps the state on its ideal path. The other part cancels the interaction-induced phase twist exactly.

Impens and Guéry-Odelin then test the shortcut against full many-body Bose-Hubbard dynamics. The mean-field version still helps but saturates below perfect fidelity, exposing genuine many-body corrections. Optimizing the transfer directly in the many-body space, with complex phase-tunable hoppings, recovers near-perfect fidelity.
arxiv-2606-23424:
P. S. Houdayer and M. Rieutord build a mean-field theory of stellar convection from phase space in a 2026 paper. Convection inside stars remains an uncertain link. It sits between fluid simulations and the one-dimensional models used to evolve stars. Mixing-length recipes prescribe the mixing instead of deriving it. The authors take another route. They describe the flow as a swarm of mesoscopic fluid particles, each tracked in position and velocity. A conservation law for that swarm defines the average. It also yields the standard mean-field equations as moments over velocity.

Houdayer and Rieutord identify the phase-space divergence as a local measure of how nearby paths contract or expand. Near the adiabatic limit, its sign falls back to the classical Schwarzschild stability test. Away from that limit, the tool stays velocity-resolved. It can tell apart distinct parts of the convective population within one layer.
arxiv-2606-23524:
Agbeti-Messan and colleagues examine how a Mamba-based optical character recognition system scales from single lines to full paragraphs, in a 2026 document analysis paper. Optical character recognition, or OCR, turns images of text into machine-readable words. Mamba is a state-space model, a sequence model that processes text in linear time rather than with the costly attention step used by Transformers, which slows sharply on long inputs.

Tuning four main settings on synthetic paragraphs up to one thousand characters, the team finds the recurrent state size and expansion factor matter most for long text. On clean synthetic paragraphs, each model keeps its character error under one percent, and Mamba finishes up to four and a half times faster. On real handwriting Mamba trails clearly, and controlled tests show much of that gap comes from too little training data rather than the design itself.
arxiv-2606-23624:
Gomberoff, Henríquez-Baez, and Vera study how an expanding universe like ours could decay by spawning black holes with patterned horizons, in a 2026 paper on theoretical cosmology. De Sitter space describes a universe whose expansion accelerates under steady vacuum energy. It is unstable: black holes can nucleate within it, though very rarely. The matter clothing those black holes can carry vortices, swirling defects whose winding is counted by a whole number called a topological charge.

The authors build the instanton, the Euclidean solution that governs such a decay, by generalizing the classic Nariai case to vortex dressed horizons. Its geometry joins a two sphere with a surface shaped by the vortex arrangement. Decay rates are organized by the discrete topological charge itself. Matter vortices therefore open a new family of decay channels, each labeled by a whole number.
arxiv-2606-23724:
Gu and colleagues build a visual tool for auditing the answers that language models give about financial reports, in a 2026 paper on visual analytics. Analysts now ask models questions over annual reports, earnings decks, and notes. A fluent answer can quietly mix well grounded statements, weak synthesis, and outright unsupported claims drawn from text, tables, and charts. Ordinary chat interfaces hide those differences behind coarse citation links or none at all.

EvidenceLens breaks each answer into atomic claims and lays them against their evidence in a matrix. Rows meet source passages, table cells, and chart regions, making coverage, contradiction, and missing support visible at a glance. Summary views show support composition and gaps, while a ranking steers reviewers to claims most needing inspection. A JSON artifact schema keeps the audit reproducible. Scenarios show analysts separating grounded claims from overconfident synthesis.
arxiv-2606-23824:
Hao, Yang, and Yu narrow the gap toward a conjectured bound on a demanding kind of graph coloring, in a 2026 paper on graph theory. A strong edge coloring paints a graph's edges so that same colored edges form an induced matching: no two may touch, or even be joined by another edge. The fewest colors needed is the strong chromatic index. For bipartite graphs, Brualdi and Quinn Massey conjectured the index never exceeds the product of the two sides' maximum degrees.

The authors prove the index is at most about 1.676 times that product, whenever the product is sufficiently large. The conjecture itself stays open, but this is a concrete step toward it. Strong colorings model interference free channel assignments, where nearby links must all differ.
arxiv-2606-23924:
Atzori, Cacciari, Marzani, and Soyez give the first full theoretical treatment of a new way to measure how evenly a particle collision sprays its energy. Their 2026 paper treats collider physics. Event isotropy scores how closely a collision's energy pattern resembles a uniform spread. It builds on the Energy Mover's Distance, a metric treating events as piles of energy to be rearranged into one another. Until now the observable lacked precision predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics.

The authors compute the distribution for electron positron collisions at leading and next to leading order. They then resum soft and collinear emissions to all orders at next to leading logarithmic accuracy. Matching the pieces yields combined NLL plus NLO predictions, turning a geometric idea into a precision observable for experiments.
arxiv-2606-24024:
McCaw and colleagues tackle a common problem in medical follow-up studies: patients can suffer the same event again and again, such as repeat hospital visits. Their 2026 statistics paper builds a regression method around the mean cumulative function, a curve that tracks how events pile up over time for each person. The work also covers the area under that curve, which gives one summary number for total event burden before a chosen cutoff time.

Rather than invent new estimation machinery, McCaw's team converts each patient's curve into pseudo-values, which are leave-one-out style scores that can then be fed into standard regression tools. Simulations check accuracy, interval coverage, false-positive control, and power across several repeated-event settings. An application to the ORATORIO trial tests the approach on ocrelizumab, a drug for primary progressive multiple sclerosis, a disease where the nervous system slowly worsens.
arxiv-2606-24424:
Xiao and colleagues survey how to open the black box of neural networks inside next generation wireless systems. Future networks are expected to be AI native. Neural networks sit throughout the physical layer, the radio-facing part of the stack, improving spectral efficiency, latency, and autonomy. The obstacle is opacity. Deep models make decisions engineers cannot inspect.

Their 2026 survey organises explainable AI for the wireless physical layer, from basics through the state of the art to open challenges. Explanation methods are mapped onto physical layer tasks. Practitioners can see which interpretability tools fit which signal processing problems, and where the mismatches lie. The authors frame explainability not as an optional garnish, but as a deployment requirement for AI native networks. They catalogue the research problems, from trustworthy explanations to real time constraints, that must be solved before operators will trust neural receivers at scale.
arxiv-2606-24824:
Peiyan Hu and eight colleagues attack inverse problems for chaotic systems: infer the starting state from the final one. Chaos makes this hard, since small errors explode exponentially and many starts can end alike. Their method, Bidirectional Conditional Flow Matching, learns maps between the distributions of initial and final states, both ways. Working with distributions captures the randomness of chaotic evolution and limits error blow up. A variant adds conservation law constraints for systems that conserve quantities.

Tests cover the classic Lorenz system, a circuit system, and the high dimensional Lorenz 96 model. The method improves five distribution level metrics over baselines. It also runs more than a hundred times faster. On the three body planet scattering problem, the constrained variant respects conservation laws about as well as ground truth. Real globular cluster observations provide the final test. The authors present the results as a scalable route to chaotic inverse problems.
arxiv-2606-25124:
Self testing certifies a quantum object from measurement statistics alone, with no assumptions about how the devices work inside. Victor Barizien and four colleagues extend the method from states, measurements, and channels to quantum supermaps. These are operations that act on channels themselves, and can combine them in a fixed or even an indefinite causal order.

Two levels of certification emerge, set by the experiment's network structure. When each slot of the supermap takes a single uncharacterised black box, the supermap is identified up to local embedding combs. When several boxes sit inside each slot, identification sharpens to local extracting and injecting maps. Four worked examples include the identity comb, an error correcting comb, and the comb behind Grover's algorithm. The quantum switch example gives the first self test of a causally indefinite process, a new device independent way to certify causal indefiniteness.
arxiv-2606-25524:
Two attempts at the same maths problem by one model can split early: one token lands badly and the whole trace derails. Jaeyong Ko, Pilsung Kang, and Yukyung Lee hunt for that exact token in 2026, calling it a cliff token. Their detector watches a per token success potential and flags sharp drops using a statistical test with a threshold that adapts to the local level. Seven models and three benchmarks, from grade school word problems to olympiad questions, supply the traces.

Deleting the first cliff token and resampling restored perfect success rates in their tests, while keeping it capped recovery well below that. Cliff tokens sort into three kinds by how the token was chosen and how uncertain the model was, and the kinds behave differently. Training preferences only at cliff positions improved accuracy across benchmarks, with two of the three kinds carrying the benefit.
arxiv-2606-25924:
Hao Chen and Scott Howard work on sharpening fluorescence microscopy images, pictures of glowing tagged molecules inside cells. The standard Richardson-Lucy method undoes some blur from diffraction, but the task is fundamentally ill-posed: many sharp images could produce the same noisy measurement. At low photon counts the method amplifies noise, while common smoothing fixes erase fine detail.

Guidance comes instead from a learned diffusion prior, a generative model that knows what plausible cell structures look like. Chen and Howard insert that prior into the Richardson-Lucy iterations while keeping the method's Poisson data consistency intact. Across varied biological samples, noise amplification drops and weak thread-like and dot-like structures survive better under dim imaging. The gains hold for structures that smoothing regularizers such as total variation tend to wash away.
arxiv-2606-26324:
Efthymios Costa flags outliers in datasets that mix continuous and ranked variables. Real tables often pair measurements with ordered categories, like star ratings or severity grades. Outlier hunters built for pure numbers stumble there. His method takes a multivariate Gaussian as the reference for normal points. Ordinal variables are treated as shadows of hidden Gaussian ones, seen only through their category cut-offs.

Robust fitting drives the algorithm. A minimum covariance determinant estimator, extended to handle the half-seen ordinal data, fits the clean majority without bending toward the outliers. A breakdown theorem promises extreme outliers stay detectable no matter what gets replaced. Simulations under varied contamination hit high detection with few false alarms. An Airbnb listings application shows the method earning its keep on real mixed data. Robust statistics gains a tool shaped like the data analysts actually hold.
arxiv-2606-26424:
Qiyuan Wu and four colleagues dig into a mismatch inside trajectory forecasting. That task predicts where nearby cars, cyclists, and pedestrians will go next. Forecasters are usually built as mixture models. Such models spread probability across several possible futures. But training uses a winner-take-all rule. It credits only the single closest guess. Wu traces several practical headaches back to that mismatch.

Winner-take-all training slices the space of futures too finely, the authors argue. It ignores how nearby guesses relate to each other. It also flips its choices under tiny changes. Their fixes need no retraining. One merges nearby candidate paths at test time, using the model's own probabilities. The other softens hard training labels through one expectation-maximization step. That algorithm alternates between assigning and updating probabilities. Across several forecasting systems, both steps gave better ranked and stronger final predictions.
arxiv-2606-26824:
Adhiraj Banerjee and Vipul Arora present wav2tok 2.0, a scalable way to turn speech into discrete tokens for audio search. Query-by-example search finds spoken terms from a spoken sample. Tokens must keep similar sounds similar, even across utterances of different length. The earlier wav2tok tied its clustering and alignment training tightly together, limiting scale.

The new version trains in stages. It first learns speaker-invariant sound features by contrastive learning and quantisation. Alignment training then enforces pairwise token consistency between related utterances. Two objectives, a connectionist temporal classification loss and a time-warped frame prediction loss with adaptive weighting, do that job. Experiments show steady gains over the previous backbone and over general-purpose tokenizers. Efficiency and scalability are retained.
arxiv-2606-27024:
Pandey, Ansari, and Singh introduce a new family of rings in commutative algebra, the study of number-like systems with addition and multiplication. Their family, called Nil-S-Noetherian rings, widens two older families at once. One older idea weakens the classic Noetherian rule, which demands that chains of ideals cannot grow forever. The other focuses on ideals tied to nilpotent elements, which become zero when raised to some power. The new family blends both weakenings through a chosen multiplicative set S.

For this wider family, the authors prove fresh versions of four classic results. These include theorems named for Cohen, Levitzki, Hilbert, and Lasker and Noether. Hilbert's basis result concerns when adding variables keeps the chain rule intact. The Lasker-Noether part shows ideals can still be split into primary pieces, which are simpler building blocks.
arxiv-2606-27124:
Ohto and colleagues check whether a popular quantum bug collection still reproduces its bugs years later. Bugs4Q gathers real defects from quantum programs, letting researchers test debugging and repair tools fairly. Earlier work on classical collections showed bugs often stop reproducing as software environments drift. The team ran tens of thousands of executions across many versions of the Qiskit core library. Thirty-seven artefacts were exercised to see which reported bugs still trigger in 2026 conditions.

Reproducibility fell steeply as the library moved from an old release toward the newest one checked. Manual root-cause inspection blamed dependency drift for the overwhelming share of failures. Unlike classical cases, most failures here need source edits, not just version pinning. Import paths and renamed calls must be migrated by hand. The team therefore releases Bugs4Q-Robust, a patched edition restoring most lost reproducibility.
arxiv-2606-27224:
Crosta, Saubanere, and Huber improve guaranteed approximations for Quantum Max Cut using real atomic hardware. That problem seeks the ground energy of an anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg system, a benchmark so hard it resists even quantum computers in general. Their hybrid algorithm pairs Rydberg atom dynamics with semidefinite programming and randomised rounding. The resulting guarantee beats the best purely classical semidefinite ratio known before in this quantum algorithms paper from 2026, reaching above sixty-five hundredths of optimal in the stated conditional result.

Robustness matters as much as the headline ratio. The advantage survives even when the atom annealer reaches only eighty-nine percent of its true ground energy in the runs considered. Imperfect hardware therefore does not erase the gain. Combining natural quantum evolution with classical rounding opens a fresh design route. Hybrid schemes gain a provable edge, not just heuristic promise.
arxiv-2606-27824:
Peptides promise drugs that combine small-molecule tunability with protein-like specificity. Designing ones that bind a chosen antigen without toxicity is the hard part. Takashi Fujiwara and four colleagues present Pepti-drift in 2026. The framework generates candidates through an antigen-conditioned drift step in embedding space. Generated peptides are pulled toward known binders. They are pushed away from harm-linked regions.

Binding-friendly features often overlap toxicity-linked ones, so the two forces compete. A warm-up strategy stabilises training. Binding attraction is learned first, and harm repulsion rises afterward. Speed is a headline result. Generation runs about sixteen times faster than PepMLM and over a thousand times faster than PepTune. The peptides show validity and ninety-eight percent uniqueness. Diversity is the highest among compared methods, with near-zero reuse across antigens. Toxicity and hemolysis risk fall across most length ranges, while target binding signal is retained.
arxiv-2606-27924:
China's electric-vehicle sales share rose from about one percent in 2015 to roughly forty-five percent in 2024. Yu Hao and Jinge Li evaluate that transition in 2026 with an equilibrium model of the Chinese auto market. The model covers differentiated products. Attribution, welfare, and reallocation effects are quantified. Subsidy effects receive special attention.

Every yuan of 2024 subsidy delivered about three point four yuan of private surplus. The surplus was unevenly shared, though. Removing subsidies would hit big-city consumers about five times harder per person than others. About half the welfare loss from removal runs through learning effects, not the cash itself. A Shapley decomposition credits product quality gains most, at about forty-five percent. Wider choice and cheaper batteries follow. The subsidy block is negative because subsidies were phased down over the period. Removing the 2024 subsidy entirely would cut the EV share by twenty-three to thirty-three percent.
arxiv-2606-28124:
Sparse learning problems carry size limits that make them NP-hard. Morteza Kimiaei, Shima Shabani, and Michael Breuß introduce an algorithm in 2026 for minimising over sparse symmetric sets. Their method blends several moves. Coordinate search and symmetry-aware swap updates keep points feasible. Random subspace search escapes poor supports. A reservoir of past feasible points injects fresh directions.

Sparse projection is built into its setup, keeping geometric diversity. Convergence guarantees accompany the method. Under stated assumptions, every full-support accumulation point is zero-coordinatewise stationary, almost surely. A safeguard can extend that to all limit points. After the support stabilises, a local linear rate holds. Experiments on synthetic sparse learning problems follow. The method improves robustness and solution quality over three named competitors. It stays computationally competitive with them.
arxiv-2606-28224:
M. Horoi tackles a computation at the heart of double-beta decay, a rare nuclear process where a nucleus changes by two steps at once. Interpreting experiments requires nuclear matrix elements, numbers that encode how likely each step is, and the two-neutrino version of the decay is both allowed by standard physics and already observed.

Horoi presents a faster strength-function method built on Lanczos iterations, a way to extract the needed sums without fully diagonalizing the nuclear Hamiltonian. The method avoids the slow, costly summation over countless intermediate states while matching explicit calculations where those are feasible. He tests it on several experimentally important emitters and different effective Hamiltonians, and extends it to higher-order matrix elements used in related decay treatments.
arxiv-2606-28524:
Pamela D. Rivière, Cameron Jones, and Sean Trott watch language models grow up. Models can pass false belief tasks, the classic test of understanding that someone can believe something untrue, but doubters question whether the success means real mentalizing. The team traces reasoning across training stages in two open model families, much as developmental psychologists track children.

Above-chance false belief performance needed both size and enough training, arrived late in pretraining, and improved most from post-training in the most diagnostic implicit condition. Yet the skill stayed fragile: verbs like thinks inflated false belief attributions even when beliefs were true. A plainer ability, situation modeling, reporting the facts of a scene, emerged earlier and stronger, but models still confused one character's knowledge with another's. Capability arrives in a sensible order, with coherence lagging behind.
arxiv-2606-29024:
Singh adapts a strong open translation system, IndicTrans2, so it can handle casual conversation in its 21 Indic languages. The system was trained on general text and sounds stiff on chat and subtitles. Using only public data, Singh fine-tunes it for conversational register. Then he fights the side effect: plain fine-tuning improves casual scores but makes the model forget the general domain.

Mixing general data back into training, called experience replay, and then averaging the tuned weights with the base model, called a model soup, removes the trade-off. The adapted model beat the original on conversational scores in all 21 languages, while matching it on FLORES. Tests confirm the casual gains are real and general scores are not significantly worse. Singh is candid about scope: human and model judges did not confirm a quality gain, so it may be register matching, not better translation.
arxiv-2606-29124:
Singha and colleagues present CornerCase, a tool that hunts bugs at the edges of network protocol specifications. Many critical bugs live near boundaries: inputs just inside or outside allowed ranges, or messages valid alone but invalid in a given state. Famous exploits from Heartbleed to TCP Christmas Tree packets came from such corners, yet fuzzing and model-based testing under-test them.

CornerCase works in two stages. First, large language models extract explicit validity constraints from protocol documents section by section, in structured form. Then the tool generates extremal test cases at or near each constraint's boundary. Tests run across multiple implementations, and differential testing flags inconsistencies between them. The team applied it to widely used HTTP, DNS, BGP, SMTP and QUIC implementations, finding many previously unknown bugs, including a redirect loop in the h2o server. They filed 42 anomalies; 26 were acknowledged as bugs, with 18 fixed.
arxiv-2606-29524:
Punzo and four co-authors model circular data, measurements such as wind directions that wrap around a full circle. Ordinary methods stumble when some readings look odd. They split mild anomalies, points that merely spread wider than usual, from gross anomalies, points scattered anywhere.

Starting from a symmetric reference model, they build mixtures. Adding a uniform part captures the gross ones. Mixing in a wider copy of the model captures the mild ones. A double-contaminated model combines both. Model-based posterior odds classify each reading, with no hand-set thresholds. Tests plus three real datasets, covering animal movement and wind directions, show that modelling both types jointly improves fit and reveals latent structure that simpler methods miss.
arxiv-2606-29624:
Laha and van Loock study how to transfer quantum states between two bosonic oscillators through a single two-level ancilla, a helper system with restricted access. The puzzle is identifying which collective mode the ancilla actually controls when the two oscillators couple to it with opposite signs.

In the normal-mode basis, the symmetric mode stays dark, meaning the ancilla cannot touch it. Transfer between the physical modes becomes equivalent to synthesizing parity, a symmetry property, on the antisymmetric bright mode. That reduction yields exact transfer formulas, finite sums, for Fock states and their superpositions. It also explains why resonant transfer hits a recurrence limit beyond the single-photon sector. Detuned Jaynes-Cummings evolution then offers a native route with two parameters to high-fidelity parity synthesis at finite cutoff. The authors quantify residual excitation, calibration sensitivity, and noise separately.
arxiv-2606-29724:
Kruse and four colleagues simplify normalizing flows, generative models that learn an invertible map between complex data and a simple latent distribution, usually a standard normal. That usual choice can mismatch the data's topology, forcing the learned transformation to work harder. Training slows and generation quality suffers as a result.

They propose MPPCA, mixtures of probabilistic principal component analyzers, as the latent density instead. Starting closer to the data distribution, in the sense of KL divergence, simplifies the flow transformation the model must learn. MPPCA models fit quickly and cheaply with the expectation-maximization algorithm, making them practical even for high-dimensional tasks. Validation covers tabular and image datasets. The method gives steady gains in training efficiency and generation quality over baselines. The broader lesson is that latent choice is a design lever: a better-shaped starting distribution can matter as much as a more powerful flow architecture.
arxiv-2606-29824:
Zhao and five colleagues address a gap in AI agents built on large language models: the agents lack lasting procedural memory, the know-how of how tasks are done. The usual fix is to paste written instructions into the prompt, but words alone often fail to switch on the right internal behaviour.

Their framework, Neural Procedural Memory, needs no training. It distils skills from past good and bad attempts into steering vectors, small pushes applied inside the model's activation space, the internal numbers that carry its processing. Across four agent benchmarks the method matches instruction-based baselines, and combining the steering with written workflows works better than either alone. Analysis shows the vectors organise into consistent task patterns.
arxiv-2606-30324:
Marius Smytzek and Andreas Zeller test whether richer execution data helps developers find bugs faster. Statistical fault localization ranks suspicious lines from pass and fail patterns. Lines alone cannot explain why a failure happens. Data flow, values, and branch conditions carry that missing information. The 2026 study asks whether such execution features measurably improve localization.

Features are extracted with the EFDD tool across Tests4Py projects. Per-subject random forests score feature importance for each program. Importances are mapped back onto source lines for ranking. The weights combine with established statistical localization formulas. Accuracy is measured against the reference patches that fixed the bugs. Line-level and function-level inspection effort are also tracked. A confounder-adjusted mixed-effects model handles the statistical analysis. Paired tests and outcome-neutral quality checks corroborate the conclusions.
arxiv-2606-30524:
Abu Saleh and five colleagues test whether splitting a documentation task among many AI agents beats using just one. README files introduce GitHub projects to newcomers. Language models now draft them automatically with retrieval support. Multi-agent systems promise gains from dividing the work. The team compares a single agent, a specialized multi-agent setup, and a developer-guided planning variant. A heuristic baseline and human originals anchor the comparison.

The single agent matches the multi-agent system on word quality. It uses eighty-six percent fewer tokens doing so. It also runs twice as fast. The multi-agent system wins on structure instead. Its formatting consistency reaches ninety-eight percent in manual analysis. Single-agent outputs show more formatting problems by contrast. Autonomous planning emerges as the main bottleneck throughout. Adding lightweight human plans yields the best documentation quality. Complexity, the title concludes, is largely an illusion here.
arxiv-2606-30624:
E. Kyritsis, A. Zezas and K. Kovlakas, in a 2026 analysis, quantify a sampling nuisance in galaxy astronomy. The X-ray glow of a star-forming galaxy comes mainly from high-mass X-ray binaries, where a compact object feeds on a massive star. Galaxies hold few of these bright sources, so random sampling makes total luminosity jump around.

Using Monte Carlo simulations, repeated random draws on a computer, the trio mapped luminosity distributions over wide grids of star-formation rate and metallicity. They fitted surfaces to the upper and lower bounds, turning the scatter into ready-made prescriptions. Users can now estimate expected luminosity, with randomness included, without rerunning costly sampling. Applied to galaxy samples, the prescriptions show randomness can lift luminosity well above the mean at low redshift, even into the range of weak active nuclei.
arxiv-2606-31124:
Jana, Mukherjee, and Rajesh estimate a subtle spin effect for the future Electron-Ion Collider. The Sivers asymmetry describes how unpolarized gluons inside a transversely polarized proton prefer one side over the other. The gluon Sivers function is still poorly known. The team studies two reactions where an electron and proton collide and produce a J/psi meson back-to-back with either a photon or a jet.

The calculation uses transverse momentum dependent factorization. It also folds in TMD evolution, which describes how these distributions change with energy scale, through the Collins-Soper-Sterman approach. The production itself is modeled with non-relativistic QCD. The gluon channel dominates both reactions. The key result is durability: the asymmetry stays sizable even after evolution is applied. For the photon channel it barely depends on uncertain model inputs at all, which makes both reactions robust probes.
arxiv-2606-31324:
Hashim and three colleagues test whether exponential infrared f(T) gravity can explain late cosmic acceleration. This teleparallel theory bends gravity through torsion rather than curvature and adds no new free parameters beyond the standard six. It admits two branches: a phantom-like one and one where the effective dark energy density flips sign.

Both branches are fitted to cosmic microwave background data from Planck, ACT, and SPT, plus DESI distance measures and Pantheon+ supernovae. The main branch eases the Hubble tension but is still disfavoured overall. The second branch is ruled out decisively: once distances fix the expansion history, its other parameters are forced into shifts that wreck the microwave fit. Perturbation data, not expansion alone, deliver the killing blow.
arxiv-2606-31424:
Anempodistov and two colleagues study what happens to Lin-Lunin-Maldacena geometries when their droplet develops a cusp. These geometries are supergravity duals of huge half-BPS operators in a supersymmetric gauge theory. The cusp mirrors a generic feature of eigenvalue densities in the dual complex matrix model, tied to two-dimensional quantum gravity.

Near the cusp tip the metric takes a universal symmetric form, with a naked singularity running along a half-infinite line. Almost every particle trajectory, light or massive, gets trapped by that line. Generic paths reach it in finite affine time, even as the observer's clock time diverges. Exact solutions for many light paths, and no sign of stochastic behaviour nearby, hint that the cusp problem may be integrable after all.
arxiv-2606-31524:
Wu and three colleagues prove convergence for a regularized version of the SAIL algorithm for online language model alignment. SAIL tackles distribution shift by collapsing a bilevel alignment problem into an efficient single-level method, and it works well in practice. Its objective, though, is not guaranteed to be strongly concave, which blocked any formal guarantee.

Their SAIL-RevKL adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler penalty, a divergence term that reshapes the optimization landscape. The regularized objective satisfies the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition on a bounded parameter space, which yields global convergence with near-linear sample complexity. Experiments on MuJoCo control tasks and on language model alignment back the theory: the regularized version beats plain SAIL and stays stable, giving self-improving alignment a firmer footing.
arxiv-2608-00024:
Zhang and co-authors seek more diversity from text diffusion models. Diffusion models give high quality and strong guidance in image work. Text is discrete and sequential, so control there stays hard. Current sampling tweaks token odds with no view of semantic shape. The fidelity-diversity balance suffers as a result.

Their SAKE guidance needs no training. It computes Rényi entropy over a kernel Gram matrix. That matrix captures cross-token semantic links and token positions. A linearized form yields a usable guidance signal in embedding space. Sampling flattens to explore when output turns redundant. It sharpens for fidelity when output is diverse. Tests show a better Pareto frontier than temperature scaling, they report. Multi-sample gains showed on code and math tasks.
arxiv-2608-00324:
Steiger and the BICEP/Keck Collaboration report bandpass filters for the BICEP Array. The array measures polarization of the cosmic microwave background from the South Pole. It uses small-aperture polarimeters in the long BICEP/Keck line. Each detector couples serially to a bandpass filter to fix its frequency response. The filters serve the 220 and 270 GHz bands.

Their circuits use series and shunt capacitors plus series inductors. Leaving out shunt inductors simplifies fabrication. Designs were simulated in Sonnet and tuned for noise from atmosphere and CMB loading. Several 220 GHz modules have been measured at the South Pole. The 270 GHz modules are now in lab testing. Receiver measurements for those follow this winter.
aurobindo-isha-upanishad-1924:
Sri Aurobindo translated the Isha Upanishad and wrapped it in close analysis, in the edition printed at Calcutta in 1924. The Isha is among the shortest and deepest of the Upanishads, opening with the claim that all this is clothed in the Lord. Aurobindo reads it line by line, word by word.

The work first appeared in 1921 and grew from his Arya years, when he was forging his philosophy in print. Seeds of Integral Yoga lie in these pages, in his way of joining world and spirit. Readers meet both a classic text and a modern master's mind at work.
black-bartlemy-s-treasure-pg2424:
Jeffery Farnol opened Black Bartlemy's Treasure in a galley, where his narrator rows chained beside a dead Frenchman and cannot die himself. Martin Conisby, escaped and vengeful, reaches England, falls in with the one-eyed sailor Adam Penfeather, and hears tell of the pirate Black Bartlemy's buried hoard. A voyage on the Faithful Friend, dogged by a nameless black ship, carries them toward Bartlemy's island.

Farnol fills the contents with fights in the dark, a bloody hand mark, fire at sea, and a secret cave. The Lady Joan Brandon supplies the love interest, and Penfeather's narrative the pirate lore. It is full-blooded treasure romance in the Stevenson line, told in hearty, old-fashioned prose that never hurries past a marvel.
brazilian-constitution-1824:
Brazil received its first constitution in 1824, granted by Emperor Pedro the First two years after independence from Portugal. An elected assembly had drafted a charter the emperor disliked, so he dissolved it and issued his own through a council of state. The result made Brazil a constitutional monarchy, the New World's great exception.

The text divides power among legislature, executive, and courts, then adds a fourth, the moderating power, held by the emperor above the rest. Catholicism is the state religion, with other faiths tolerated in private. Property and civil rights receive formal guards. The charter governed Brazil for sixty-five years, longer than any later Brazilian constitution. It was the empire's founding law, order and hierarchy under the Braganza crown, and it steadied a vast new nation through a difficult century.
byron-don-juan-1824:
Lord Byron began Don Juan in 1818 and kept adding cantos until his death in 1824. He wrote it in ottava rima, an eight-line stanza that suits jokes as well as high drama. Sixteen cantos were published in his lifetime, and the poem was never finished.

Young Juan is sent abroad after a scandal and stumbles through shipwreck, slavery, love affairs, and war. Unlike the cold seducer of older tales, Byron's Juan is mostly the one being seduced. The narrator keeps interrupting with witty attacks on poets, politicians, and British manners. Many readers call it Byron's masterpiece and the greatest comic poem in English.
carnot-reflexions-puissance-motrice-1824:
Sadi Carnot asks how much work heat can do in his Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire, in French from 1824. A young engineer studies the steam engine's limits with a philosopher's depth. His cycle of expansion and compression sets the most that any heat engine could ever yield in theory.

From that simple model grew the second law of thermodynamics in time. Carnot died young, and his book was nearly lost before men of science grasped it. Few works of physics match its reach from so slim a start. Written at twenty-eight, it stands as the founding text of a whole science of heat and energy.
cia-0000012324:
Senior officers talked shop in January 1962, and a discussion record preserves it: the Soviet division's chief of operations, his deputies, and one name blacked out. Their subject was the chief's European trip, the travel that case management at that level required. Europe was where the Penkovsky operation's meetings, couriers, and allied partners all lived.

Only initials and office codes name the men in the room. Behind closed doors they weighed the next moves of a case nearing its crisis. For readers, the record is the conference room's echo: deliberation by officers whose names stay hidden.
cia-0000013224:
A printed questionnaire used on American prisoners survives in a CIA file from August 1969. The form belonged to the Military Proselyting Section of Front 7, the enemy unit charged with turning captives. Its questions are set out in cold order: unit, mission, family, beliefs. The printed form reveals the interrogators' minds better than any memoir, because it shows what they wanted before a word was spoken.

The file preserves the inquisition's paperwork intact. Questions printed in advance mean answers planned for in advance. For readers, the form is a chilling artifact: captivity reduced to blanks waiting to be filled.
cia-0000013924: An American pilot was captured in Son La Province, in a CIA note dated January 1, 1968. Son La lies in the hills of northwest North Vietnam. Pilots downed in that rough country were hard to reach and harder to rescue. The note adds a New Year capture to the rolls of men held in the north.
cia-0000015424: Thomas B. Scott Jr. wrote to the CIA, and on March 1, 1962, his letter was sent onward to Air Force headquarters. The packet went to Major Carl R. Hart and held Scott's letters plus a reply dated April 20, 1962. A young observer's report thus got a formal answer from the service in charge. The routing slip alone shows how citizen mail moved through two agencies.
cia-0000020424: Letelier del Solar, Orlando, is the full name filed on a CIA record dated in 1975. The entry is little more than a name in the catalog, with no event attached. Yet the name belonged to Chile's former envoy, then living in exile in America. A bare name file shows how a watched man's paper trail could begin with almost nothing.
cia-0000036824:
A CIA record dated January 6, 1970 links Havana with General Creighton Abrams, the American commander in Vietnam. The subject line points to an interview connected with Abrams and his command. Havana watched the war closely, and Cuban interest in its leaders was itself news.

The record preserves that pairing as the agency filed it, an interview item from wartime monitoring. Files like this came from tracking foreign broadcasts and press day after day. They show how much of the intelligence record is built from open sources, carefully clipped and kept. The pairing of Havana and a Saigon commander is odd, yet that oddness is part of the file's interest.
cia-0000044424:
A Jesuit linked the priests' deaths to the Romero killing, in a CIA record dated October 5, 1989 in the catalog. Archbishop Oscar Romero had been murdered in 1980 while saying Mass. His death opened the war's long season of violence against the church.

Inside, the comparison between the two crimes is drawn by a fellow Jesuit. Nine years apart, the killings seemed to him one story. Both struck men of the church who had spoken for the poor. The file preserves that act of linking, which shaped how many Salvadorans read the new murders from the day they were first reported.
cia-0000044524:
Prospects for Eastern Europe are weighed in a CIA record dated May 5, 1977. Eastern Europe then lay inside the Soviet bloc, state by state. Analysts in 1977 looked for cracks in that settled and guarded order.

Inside, the region's outlook is judged country by country in brief. Such forecasts tried to spot change before it reached the streets. Few readers in 1977 foresaw how fully the bloc would fall, or how soon its fall would come once it began in earnest. The file is worth reading against that ending, since it shows careful experts measuring a system that had only twelve years left to stand.
cia-0000045224:
The government expected new contact with the kidnappers, in a CIA record dated September 4, 1985. Contact was the crisis's lifeline and its scarcest resource. Days without word from the captors were the hardest to bear.

Inside, the expected approach from the kidnappers is noted. Governments in such cases live by the telephone and the messenger. A promised contact raised hopes that days of silence had beaten down. Hope, in that crisis, was always one phone call away from rising or falling again. The file preserves that state of waiting, which filled more of the kidnapping's long course than any dramatic event, for the family and for the country alike.
cia-0000049324: Declassified CIA document 0000049324, dated March 5, 1991, is titled El Salvador: Examining Foreign Relations and carries a Truth Commission note. The paper takes up El Salvador's foreign relations as its subject.
