The loss usually comes from reversible controls, chemical marks and regulators such as NFkB, IRFs, and NLRC5, rather than from broken genes. Reversible means restorable. The review catalogues the mechanisms and then the strategies to switch display back on and reawaken adaptive immunity. Readers get a hopeful angle on a major escape route: the tumor's invisibility cloak is held by clips, not welded shut.
europmc-pmc7462924:
Chadt and Al-Hasani review glucose transporters in fat tissue, liver, and skeletal muscle. A family of carriers, the GLUTs, moves glucose into tissues. Their work keeps blood sugar steady across the body.

GLUT2 is the main controller of sugar flow in the liver. GLUT4 does the heavy lifting for insulin-driven uptake in muscle. When transport activity falls, fuel use goes wrong. That failure links with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. How insulin commands transport across cell membranes is still not fully clear. Blood-borne signals and extra transporters fine-tune flow between organs as energy needs shift. The review gathers what is known and marks the open gaps in the mechanism.
europmc-pmc7490424:
Zhao and co-authors review chitinase-3 like-protein-1, a protein known as CHI3L1, and its roles in disease. It binds chitin, heparin, and hyaluronic acid but has no enzyme action. Many cell types make and release it, from macrophages to tumor cells.

CHI3L1 helps steer tissue injury, inflammation, repair, and remodeling. It links with asthma, arthritis, sepsis, diabetes, liver fibrosis, and heart artery disease. In cancer it is overproduced in many human tumors and animal models. Its signals drive tumor growth, spread, vessel growth, and immune skewing. Several receptors for it are now known. Targeted treatments based on CHI3L1 are in study for glioma, colon cancer, and rheumatoid arthritis. The review maps paths and treatment ideas.
europmc-pmc7502724:
Ganguli and co-authors build a rapid, portable test system for SARS-CoV-2 that skips the central lab. Standard RT-PCR is the gold standard but needs lab steps to free and clean viral RNA. Those steps cost time and hands.

Their system uses isothermal RT-LAMP, which copies RNA at one steady heat. A printed cartridge holds the sample work. A smartphone-based reader reports the result at the point of collection. The design cuts the labor and gear of lab testing. It aims for speed, accuracy, and ease in one package. Such tools could widen testing in clinics, airports, and field sites. The authors frame it as a proof of a new testing class for outbreaks.
europmc-pmc7511224:
Ramaswamy and co-authors compare patient satisfaction with video visits and in-person visits during COVID-19. New York City was the pandemic's early epicenter. Clinics shifted fast from office visits to video calls.

The team analyzed 38,609 Press Ganey survey outcomes at one large urban medical center. Video visits numbered 620 against 37,989 in-person visits in the data set. Video visits scored higher on satisfaction than office visits did. Both video format and the pandemic period linked with higher scores after adjustment. Younger age, female gender, and new visit type linked with lower scores. The authors say satisfaction is no barrier to wider telemedicine use. More quality measures should guide the shift, they add.
europmc-pmc7518324:
Zhang, Parmigiani, and Johnson present ComBat-seq, a batch fix for RNA-seq count data. Joining data batches boosts power, but batch effects add unwanted variation. Technical gaps between batches drive the problem.

Many fix methods assume smooth, bell-shaped data curves. RNA-seq counts are skewed and over-dispersed, so that assumption fails. ComBat-seq uses a negative binomial model instead. It keeps the integer nature of the counts intact. That makes fixed data fit standard differential expression tools. In realistic simulations, it gave better power and false positive control than rival methods. On real data, it removed batch effects and recovered the true signal. The authors offer it for large merged genomic studies.
europmc-pmc7610724:
Munafò and co-authors set out a manifesto for reproducible science. Unreliable research wastes effort and slows discovery. Their paper argues for changes across the research process.

Measures target methods, reporting and dissemination first. Reproducibility, evaluation and incentives are also covered. Threats include low power and publication bias. Data dredging and poor sharing add to the problem. One estimate says 85% of biomedical effort is wasted. A survey found 90% saw a reproducibility crisis. The authors review proof for each proposed fix. Wide adoption needs funders, journals and institutions to act. Stepwise testing of the measures is urged. The goal is more credible published science.
europmc-pmc7645624:
Chen and co-authors build a deep learning model to detect COVID-19 pneumonia on chest CT scans. CT is a favored imaging route for this pneumonia. Fast and accurate reading can aid busy clinicians.

Training used 46,096 images from 106 admitted patients. Cases included 51 confirmed COVID-19 pneumonia patients. Controls numbered 55 patients with other diseases. Per-patient accuracy reached 95.24% in the test set. Per-image accuracy reached 98.85% in that set. A prospective test covered 27 consecutive patients. There the model matched an expert radiologist in performance. An outside hospital test gave 96% accuracy overall. With model help, radiologist reading time fell by 65%. The system may speed clinical work in pneumonia care.
europmc-pmc7688124:
Alsoufi and co-authors survey medical students in Libya on online learning during COVID-19. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE. Students came from more than 13 medical schools across the country. The survey asked about knowledge, attitudes, and daily use of electronic learning. It also covered devices, study status during the shutdown, and mental health.

In all, 3,348 valid replies came back from the students. Most doubted that e-learning could be rolled out with ease in Libya. Few had joined an online medical program during the pandemic months. Most also doubted that online tools could teach hands-on clinical skills. Yet 65% used the internet to join study groups and talks with peers. The authors see a lasting disruption that schools must plan for.
europmc-pmc7731724:
Landrigan and co-authors examine how ocean pollution harms human health. Pollution overall causes an estimated nine million early deaths each year. Ocean pollution is a large but poorly tracked part of that toll. It mixes toxic metals, plastics, chemicals, oil, and sewage.

More than 80% of it comes from land, by rivers, runoff, and direct discharge. An estimated 10 million metric tons of plastic enter the seas each year. Mercury from coal burning and small-scale gold mining is the metal of chief concern. The authors urge leaders to act and set clear priorities for control and prevention.
europmc-pmc7745124:
South and co-authors engineer tobacco plants to waste less energy in the field. Their study tested synthetic paths for handling glycolate, a toxic byproduct of photosynthesis. In C3 crops such as soybean and wheat, this cleanup, called photorespiration, can cut yields by 20 to 50%. The team placed new paths inside the leaf's chloroplasts.

They also blocked export of glycolate into the old path, to force flow through the new ones. The best designs raised photosynthetic efficiency by 20%. In repeated field trials, many plant lines grew 19 to 37% more biomass. The authors say such redesign could lift yields of major C3 crops under real farm conditions.
europmc-pmc7816624:
Bayati and co-authors show that SARS-CoV-2 enters cells through clathrin-mediated endocytosis. The virus first grips the cell surface with its spike protein. What happens next was unsettled. Many coronaviruses get pulled inside the cell. Whether SARS-CoV-2 needs that step was unknown.

The team used pure spike protein and harmless test viruses wearing spike. After surface contact, uptake was rapid. It ran through the clathrin pathway, a standard cell entry route. Viral RNA likely passes to the cell interior from inside those compartments. Blocking clathrin heavy chain cut infection sharply. The authors name this entry step a key part of infectivity. It is also a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc7895824:
Ochocka and co-authors report a single-cell study of immune cells in brain tumours called gliomas. Microglia are the brain's own immune cells. Other immune cells enter from the blood. Both kinds gather in gliomas and can help the tumour grow. Their full variety has been unclear.

The team used single-cell RNA sequencing on immune cells from healthy and glioma-bearing mouse brains. They found distinct groups: microglia, invading monocytes and macrophages, and border-associated macrophages. Each group had its own gene profile and place in the tumour. Male microglia switched on more immune-display genes than female ones. The same pattern showed in human glioma data. The authors suggest sex-linked immune differences may help explain why gliomas are more common in men. The work maps targets for future treatment research.
europmc-pmc7898624:
Tilg and co-authors present a review that revisits a leading theory of fatty liver disease after ten years. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease affects about one quarter of the world's population. It ranges from simple fat build-up to inflamed, scarred liver and cancer. The multiple parallel hits idea tried to explain that wide range.

The idea holds that many insults strike the liver at once, rather than one cause acting alone. Diet, gut signals, fat tissue, and genes can all hit in parallel. The authors review how the idea has held up over a decade of new data. They weigh fresh evidence on inflammation, fibrosis, and metabolic links. The review also notes that noninvasive scans have cut the need for liver biopsy. Readers get an updated frame for a very common disease.
europmc-pmc7933824:
Litchfield and co-authors report a meta-analysis of what makes tumours respond to checkpoint inhibitors. These drugs free the immune system to attack cancer. Some patients gain lasting benefit, while others gain none. The team pooled genetic and clinical data to weigh the rival explanations for that split, inside both the tumour and its T cells.

The data covered more than 1,000 treated patients across seven tumour types. Clonal mutation burden was the strongest predictor of response. Total mutation burden and one immune signal, CXCL9, followed. Several favoured markers failed to hold up across cancers. Two gene changes also stood out: one loss tied to response, one gain tied to resistance. Single-cell work named two further T-cell markers of sensitivity. The study gives trial designers a ranked list of what to measure.
europmc-pmc7945924:
Burget presents a biographical study of Stephen Hales, who lived from 1677 to 1761. The paper was read before a medical history club in Portland in November 1924. Hales was born at Bekesbourne in Kent on September 7, 1677. He was the sixth son of Thomas and Mary Hales. Little is known of his early years, Burget admits.

In 1696, at nineteen, he entered Bennet College, Cambridge. He took his first degree and won a fellowship around 1702. A friendship with William Stukeley shaped his student days. The two roamed the countryside with a plant catalogue in hand. Fossils, butterflies, and dissections of frogs and dogs all drew them. Chemistry lectures by Vigani added a further pull. Burget traces how a country parson became a founder of experimental physiology.
europmc-pmc8005924:
Page and co-authors present the PRISMA 2020 statement, an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. It replaces the PRISMA statement from 2009. Systematic reviews answer questions that single studies cannot settle. But their value depends on clear, complete reporting of why the review was done, what the authors did, and what they found.

The statement gives a 27-item checklist for review reports. An expanded checklist spells out the guidance for each item. The authors also supply an abstract checklist. Revised flow diagrams cover both new and updated reviews. The new guidance reflects advances in how studies are found, chosen, appraised, and combined.
europmc-pmc8027624:
Wauters and co-authors profile single immune cells from lung washes to separate mild from critical COVID-19. How innate and adaptive immunity miscommunicate in severe disease stayed murky. The team sampled bronchoalveolar lavage from 5 patients with mild and 26 with critical illness. Samples from non-COVID pneumonia and healthy lungs served as comparisons. Pseudotime methods traced how T cells and monocytes matured.

In mild disease, resident-memory CD8 and helper-17 CD4 T cells expanded late and worked well. In critical disease, those cells stayed naïve-like. Helper-1 and exhausted-like cells showed stress signs in critical cases. Harmful hyperinflammatory monocytes built up, while protective alveolar macrophages thinned out. Monocytes also left a signaling footprint tied to lung fibrosis. Viral RNA turned up in epithelial cells, neutrophils, and macrophages.
europmc-pmc8041624:
Nayfach and co-authors assemble a genomic catalog of Earth's microbiomes. Most microbes have never been grown in a lab. Genome-resolved metagenomics rebuilds their genomes from environmental DNA instead. The team applied it to more than 10,000 metagenomes. Samples spanned every continent and ocean, plus human and animal hosts. Soils, farms, and engineered systems joined the haul.

The catalog holds 52,515 metagenome-assembled genomes. They represent 12,556 novel candidate species-level groups across 135 phyla. Known diversity of bacteria and archaea grows by 44%. The resource supports comparative analysis, metabolic modeling, and bulk download. The authors show its value in two test cases. They mine secondary-metabolite potential across the genomes. They also resolve thousands of new links between viruses and their hosts.
europmc-pmc8062524:
Huang and co-authors review the extracellular matrix and its promise as a cancer treatment target. The matrix gives tumors their physical frame and much of their signaling. Its amount and cross-linking set how stiff a tissue feels. Tumors often stiffen their matrix, and cells read that stiffness as a growth cue. Faulty force sensing then feeds further malignant change.

The review starts with the main matrix parts and their jobs in health and cancer. It then traces the two-way talk between cancer cells and matrix. Key force-sensing receptors and their shifts during cancer come next. The closing section surveys drugs aimed at the abnormal matrix. Some attack its building blocks, others its stiffness signals. The authors frame the matrix as part of the disease itself. Treating the tumor's scaffold may slow the cells it holds.
europmc-pmc8080624:
Baik reviews how stress bends the brain's dopamine reward system toward depression. Dopamine runs reward behavior through the mesolimbic pathway. Stress shifts dopamine levels and the firing of its neurons. Such tuning helps an animal pick the right response to threat. Both reward and harsh events can excite the system, which complicates the picture.

Acute stress sharpens reward sensitivity and aids coping. Chronic stress does the opposite, dulling the sense of reward. That blunting shows up as anhedonia, a core mark of depression. The review weighs animal and human evidence line by line. It asks which circuits flip the system from coping to collapse. Receptor-level changes in the reward path get close attention. The author frames the reward system as a stress sensor. Protecting its tuning may guard against stress-born depression.
europmc-pmc8128724:
van Leeuwen and co-authors catalogue 100 commercial AI products for radiology and audit their evidence. All carried the CE mark for clinical use in Europe. They came from 54 different vendors in the team's census. Tasks spanned image types, body regions, and reading jobs. Deployment and pricing models varied just as widely. The science behind the sales pitches varied most of all.

For 64 of the 100 products, no peer-reviewed efficacy evidence existed at all. The other 36 products shared 237 papers between them. Most of those papers, 65%, stopped at diagnostic accuracy. Only 18 products showed evidence of real clinical impact or beyond. Half the evidence was independent of the vendors involved. The sector, the authors conclude, is still in its infancy. Hospitals are buying promises faster than proof. Buyers should demand outcome data, not accuracy alone. Regulators may need to raise the evidence bar.
europmc-pmc8131624:
Zhang and co-authors build a light-activated nanoparticle that both kills tumors and degrades a shield protein. The particle, SPNpro, pairs a semiconducting polymer with a PROTAC unit. Under near-infrared light it makes singlet oxygen on command. That burn kills tumor cells in an immunogenic way. Dying cells then advertise themselves to the immune system. A second weapon wakes only inside cancer tissue.

A tumor marker, cathepsin B, switches the PROTAC part on. The switched-on unit targets IDO, an enzyme tumors use for cover. IDO normally drains tryptophan to paralyze effector T cells. Destroying it reopens the metabolic road for attack. In living mice the double action shrank tumors and curbed spread. Always-on degraders risk damage at healthy sites. Gating the degrader by tumor signals fixes that flaw. The platform points toward smarter protein-degrading drugs.
europmc-pmc8139424:
Zhang and co-authors solve the structural puzzle of the D614G spike change that swept the world early in the pandemic. One letter of the spike protein flipped at position 614. The G form outran the D form on every continent. Oddly, it binds the human ACE2 receptor less tightly. The team built the full-length G614 spike trimer. Cryo-EM tests compared it with the old form.

New contacts inside the G614 spike hold its S1 subunit in place. S1 carries the receptor-binding machinery of the virus. In the D form, S1 sheds too early and is lost. Stabilized spikes therefore stay armed far longer on the surface. More working spikes per virus means easier infection overall. The variant won by durability, not by grip strength. That lesson guides how later variants get judged. Small structural mercies can move a pandemic.
europmc-pmc8249424:
Luu and co-authors show that microbial short-chain fatty acids boost cancer-killing T cells. Gut microbes make these fatty acids during digestion. The team tested pentanoate and butyrate on cytotoxic and CAR T cells.

Both compounds reprogrammed the cells through metabolic and epigenetic routes. They raised mTOR activity and blocked class I histone deacetylases. Treated cells made more CD25, IFN-γ, and TNF-α. Their tumour attack grew markedly stronger in tests. The effect held for antigen-specific cells and engineered CAR cells. Feeding T cells these molecules may sharpen adoptive therapy. The strategy needs no genetic change to the cells themselves.
europmc-pmc8356424:
Wu and co-authors survey data mining in clinical big data, its databases, steps, and models. Public sets such as SEER, NHANES, TCGA, and MIMIC feed many studies. Their data are rich but messy, sparse, and uneven in time.

Mining methods help turn that mass into patient risk scores. They also aid diagnosis and treatment choices. The paper lists the databases most often used. It then lays out the mining workflow stage by stage. Model families are compared for clinical tasks. The authors stress how much value sits unused in these sets. Better mining could free it.
europmc-pmc8480024:
Hu and co-authors review ways to target mutant p53 in cancer therapy. The TP53 gene is a key tumor suppressor, mutated in over half of human cancers. Mutations do not just switch off its guard role. The faulty protein gains new cancer-driving powers of its own.

Direct drugs try to restore normal p53 action or wipe out the mutant form. Their success turns heavily on tumor shape and drug type. Indirect paths attack the backup systems mutant cells lean on. Synthetic lethality is one such idea, where paired gene losses kill the cell. Noncoding RNAs add fresh angles. The review sorts these direct and indirect strategies.
europmc-pmc8557524:
Jiang and co-authors sum up work on CD47 as a target for cancer immunotherapy. Blocking this protein helps immune cells attack tumors. Much progress has come in solid tumors and blood cancers alike. The review analyzes the trial landscape in the United States and China.

As of August 28, 2021, a registry held 23 related agents in 46 clinical trials. Most trials sat in early phases. Designs split between single-target and dual-target agents. Tumor types ranged from stomach cancer to leukemias and lymphomas. New-generation CD47 antibodies have shown promising results. The authors expect some agents to reach clinic use and meet urgent patient needs.
europmc-pmc8604724:
Feng and co-authors search for immune markers that predict protection from SARS-CoV-2 infection. Data came from a United Kingdom trial of the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine. If a marker level can stand in for protection, new vaccines can be judged faster. The team measured binding and neutralizing antibodies 28 days after the second dose.

Higher levels of all markers linked to lower risk of illness with symptoms. A set level of binding antibodies matched 80 percent vaccine efficacy. The markers did not predict infection without symptoms at the set test level. Most cases in the trial were the alpha variant. The authors say these levels can help extend results to new vaccines and groups.
europmc-pmc8612924:
Karvelis and co-authors show that a transposon protein called TnpB can cut DNA under RNA guidance. Transposons are DNA pieces that move within genomes. Their TnpB gene was not needed for movement, and its job was unknown. Clues hinted it might be an early form of CRISPR enzymes.

Tests used TnpB from the bacterium Deinococcus radiodurans. An RNA from the transposon end guided the protein to a DNA site. It cut next to a short motif with the letters TTGAT. The team then reprogrammed TnpB to cut chosen sites in human cells. The work supports TnpB as a forerunner of CRISPR cutting tools.
europmc-pmc8660024:
Markello and co-authors introduce abagen, a software toolbox that standardizes work with brain gene expression data. Gene activity shapes the structure and function of the human brain. Open atlases let teams study this link in living people. Yet each group processed the data its own way, so results varied.

The team tested 750,000 distinct processing pipelines on one atlas. Pipeline choice had a large effect on findings. Some choices swung result correlations by a full point or more. Steps that set gene normalization mattered most. The toolbox gives the field one shared, open route. The authors argue this base will make imaging transcriptomics more sound.
europmc-pmc8664924:
Kozlowski, Crook, and Ku review ways to grow organoids without Matrigel, the gel most labs now use. Organoids are small cell clusters that copy organ function. They serve as stand-ins for organs such as liver, gut, and brain. Matrigel comes from mouse tumor cells and is poorly defined.

That vague mix hides which factors guide organoid growth. The review covers defined options to replace it. Teams can use processed tissue matrix from real organs. Synthetic gels offer a second path with known content. Gels made from engineered proteins form a third. The authors weigh each path for growth and care of organoids.
europmc-pmc8718224:
Wolchok and co-authors report 6.5-year outcomes from a trial of immune drugs in advanced melanoma. Patients with untreated, inoperable disease were split into three groups. One got nivolumab plus ipilimumab, one got nivolumab alone, and one got ipilimumab alone. Group sizes were near equal, at just over 300 each.

Median survival was 72.1 months in the combo group. It was 36.9 months with nivolumab and 19.9 months with ipilimumab. Survival rates at 6.5 years also favored the combo. Gains held in tumors with and without the BRAF mutation. The authors frame the combo as a durable gain for this cancer.
europmc-pmc8728224:
Varadi and co-authors introduce the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, a free store of predicted protein shapes. The system uses DeepMind's AlphaFold v2.0 to predict structure from sequence. This has vastly widened the share of known proteins with a structure model. Each entry gives atomic positions plus confidence scores for the model.

The first release holds over 360,000 predicted structures. They span 21 model organism proteomes. Plans call for growth to most of the 100 million-plus reference sequences in UniRef90. Users can view models in an interactive display. Programmatic access is also offered for large-scale work.
europmc-pmc8866424:
Wei and co-authors review smart biomaterials that respond to signals while healing bone. Bone defects often come with tumors, infection, or other disease. Standard grafts can bring complications of their own. Worse, the diseased surroundings can sabotage regrowth. A material that treats disease and rebuilds bone at once is the goal. Stimuli-responsive designs promise exactly that.

Some materials answer outside triggers. Light, electric and magnetic fields, ultrasound, and force all serve. Others answer the defect site itself. Tumor acidity, bacterial enzymes, and excess reactive oxygen species can flip the switch. Multi-responsive designs combine both logics. The authors explain how each design is built. They clarify the mechanisms and clinical uses so far. They also state the limits plainly. The review serves bone engineers and clinicians alike.
europmc-pmc8935224:
Wang and co-authors test forsythoside A, a plant compound, against Alzheimer's-like disease in mice and cells. The compound comes from Forsythia suspensa. It is known for calming inflammation and oxidation. Alzheimer's involves both ferroptosis and neuroinflammation. The team used APP/PS1 transgenic mice as the disease model. Three cell systems probed separate mechanisms. Memory tests tracked the animals' cognition. Brain tissue was read for amyloid and tau.

Treatment eased memory and thinking deficits in the mice. Amyloid deposits and phosphorylated tau fell. Iron buildup and fat oxidation in brain dropped. Inflammatory factors fell while calming factors rose. In cells, the compound blocked ferroptosis and inflammation. A pathway through Nrf2 and GPX4 proved key. Dopamine signaling also strengthened. The authors propose the compound as a drug lead. Human proof, they note, is still to come.
europmc-pmc9039924:
Masyita and co-authors review terpenes and terpenoids, the main active compounds in essential oils. These plant oils show antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer effects in studies. The review covers green methods for extracting and purifying the compounds. It also explains how the body absorbs them and how well they reach target tissues. Compounds named include linalool, limonene, and eugenol.

The authors then weigh essential oils as natural food preservatives, a use backed by their microbe-fighting action. Limits remain, including dose control and stability in food. The review maps where these natural compounds could realistically replace synthetic preservatives.
europmc-pmc9134924:
Zhang and co-authors demonstrate that neutrophil extracellular traps drive a form of cell death in sepsis-linked lung injury. Traps are DNA webs that neutrophils cast out to fight microbes. The team found more traps in patients and mice with sepsis-linked acute lung injury. A death process called ferroptosis rose alongside them.

Experiments in cells and in a mouse sepsis model pinned down the chain. The traps raised an enzyme-driven mark on RNA, called m6A, through the protein METTL3. That mark lowered GPX4, a guard against ferroptosis, in lung lining cells. Mice lacking METTL3 fared differently, confirming its key role. The findings name a new target chain for a lung injury with few good treatments.
europmc-pmc9287124:
Banta and co-authors explain why blocking both TIGIT and PD-1 works better than either alone against tumors. Both are brake receptors on T cells, and dual blockade shows early promise in patients. The team studied how each brake controls the gas-pedal receptors CD28 and CD226. Tests ran in mouse tumors and in lung cancer patient samples.

PD-1 was found to damp both CD226 and CD28 signals directly. TIGIT instead blocks CD226 by stealing its shared binding partner. Either drug lost effect when CD226 was absent. CD226 levels also tracked with patient benefit from anti-PD-L1 therapy. Full revival of CD226 signaling needs both brakes off. That gives a clear reason for combined treatment in the clinic.
europmc-pmc9442924:
Hambleton and co-authors give a rapid review of the psychiatric and medical conditions that occur with eating disorders. Eating disorders are severe and can be life threatening. Death rates run high, driven by medical complications and suicide. The review aimed to sum up the evidence and find gaps.

The team searched three databases for studies from 2009 to 2021. A total of 202 studies entered the review. Of these, 58% dealt with psychiatric conditions and 42% with medical ones. Anxiety reached up to 62% and mood disorders up to 54% among patients. Substance use and post-traumatic stress each reached up to 27%. Medical problems spanned hormone, bone, gut, dental, and reproductive systems. Early spotting of these added conditions may improve care, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc9499024:
Brown and co-authors build mobileOG-db, a curated database of proteins from bacterial mobile genetic elements. These elements carry core and accessory gene modules. Accessory genes often look like ordinary immobile genes. That likeness floods older databases with false positives.

The team analyzed 10,776,849 protein sequences from eight source databases. From them they built 6,140 manually curated protein families. Each family ties to a step in an element's life cycle. Steps span entry, copying, transfer, and defense roles. Entries carry tiered notes and an element class label. The finished database holds over 700,000 deduplicated sequences. They sort into five major and more than 50 minor categories. Users can pull custom subsets from the web portal. The tool aims to make element annotation simple and sound.
europmc-pmc9640124:
Bass sets out the sources of hookworm infection and how infection takes place, in a paper read in May 1910. Knowing the worm's life facts is the base for tracing each case. Two species infect man, he notes. One is the Old World kind and one the New World kind.

The New World species was first found in material from Porto Rico. It proved to be spread wide across the Southern United States. Adult worms live only in the human gut, where they lay eggs. The eggs leave the body in feces and cannot hatch inside the gut. Hatching takes twenty-four to thirty-six hours in the open. Young worms then need at least four or five days to reach the stage that can infect. Every case thus traces back to the waste of an infected person. One heavy case was estimated to pass over 4,000,000 eggs in a stool.
europmc-pmc9646524:
Bera and co-authors show that thicker extracellular fluid makes cells move faster and helps cancer spread. Cells answer physical cues such as stiffness and fluid shear. Viscosity shifts in health and in cancer states. How cells sense those shifts was unknown until now.

Higher viscosity raised cell motion on flat surfaces and in tight spaces. It also pushed more cells out of tumor spheroids. Thick fluid loads the cell surface with more force. That load builds a dense actin web through the ARP2/3 complex. The web lines up the exchanger NHE1, which swells the cell. Swelling raises membrane tension and opens the TRPV4 channel. Calcium flows in and RHOA driven grip power climbs. Breast cancer cells kept a memory of thick fluid exposure. That memory raised their spread in fish, chick, and mouse tests.
europmc-pmc9991924:
van Lengerich and co-authors describe a TREM2-activating antibody built to cross the blood-brain barrier. Loss-of-function TREM2 variants raise Alzheimer's disease risk. That fact suggests that switching TREM2 on could help patients. A normal antibody reaches the brain poorly, so delivery needed work.

The team fused a high-affinity TREM2 antibody to a transferrin receptor binding site. This transport vehicle carries it across the barrier in mice. Brain exposure and signaling beat a standard anti-TREM2 antibody. In human stem-cell-derived microglia, the antibody switched on cell programs. It enhanced microglial metabolism in disease models. The design shows how brain delivery can unlock immune targets. It offers a template for other barrier-blocked antibodies.
europmc-pmc9995824:
Hu and co-authors review the JAK/STAT pathway, a central route for signals from outside the cell. The pathway carries cytokine and growth signals to the cell nucleus. It shapes immunity, blood formation, and tissue growth. Faults in its parts link to cancer, immune disease, and inflammation.

The hosted text for this record is dominated by the article's reference list. That list spans trials of JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib and fedratinib. It also spans work on STAT signaling in tumors and immune cells. From the title and record, the review covers extracellular signals, disease links, and immunity. Treatment regimens built on pathway blockers form its practical side. Readers should note the text here gives the bibliography more fully than the body.
flamel-hieroglyphicall-figures-1624:
Nicholas Flamel was a Paris bookseller of the fourteenth century whom legend turned into the immortal alchemist. His Exposition of the Hieroglyphicall Figures, in this 1624 English translation, explains the alchemical paintings he set on an archway of the Holy Innocents' churchyard in Paris. The book founded his deathless fame.

Flamel reads dragons, serpents, and a field of corpses as a coded recipe for the philosophers' stone. Later seekers hunted Paris for the archway and for the treasure the figures were said to hide. The legend of Flamel, the poor scribe made rich and undying, still draws readers to his exposition.
fludd-utriusque-cosmi-vol-2-naturae-simi:
Fludd's second tract, De Naturae Simia, appeared in 1624 as part of his history of both worlds. Its Latin title calls man the ape of nature. Fludd argues that human arts copy nature's own work.

He surveys crafts, sciences, and skills that imitate natural powers. Mirrors, music, and machines all find ranked places. The scheme folds human making into his cosmic order. Readers meet a mind that saw no wall between art and nature. The tract is a curious, learned tour of Renaissance craft through one believer's eyes. The conceit is strange, the learning behind it real.
ford-conrad-remembrance-1924:
Ford Madox Ford and Joseph Conrad worked together for a decade, co-writing novels and shaping each other's style. Ford's 1924 remembrance, published soon after Conrad's death, is the inside account of that odd, fruitful partnership.

Ford recalls their Kentish years: the talk, the methods, the doctrine of the impression that governed their fiction. He writes with grief, pride, and some score-settling, and scholars check his memory carefully. No other source shows the workshop of early modernism this closely. The book is both a memorial and a claim: that the modern English novel was built by two men in conversation.
ford-some-do-not-1924:
Some Do Not..., published in 1924, opens Ford's Parade's End sequence, the great tetralogy of Christopher Tietjens. Tietjens is a brilliant, principled civil servant, often called the last Tory, trapped in a marriage to the faithless, glittering Sylvia.

On a golfing weekend he meets Valentine Wannop, a young suffragette, and a bond forms that honor forbids him to use. Around them, England drifts toward a war that will break their world. Ford renders thought itself, in looping time and shifting impressions. The volume sets up one of the century's major works of fiction, often ranked with the best war literature.
forster-passage-to-india-1924:
E. M. Forster traveled in India before and after the First World War, and those trips shaped A Passage to India, published in 1924. Forster had already written four novels set in England and Italy. This one tests British rule in India directly.

An English visitor, Adela Quested, accuses an Indian doctor, Aziz, of attacking her in the Marabar Caves. Nobody, perhaps not even Adela, knows what really happened in the dark cave. The trial splits the town along racial lines and exposes the cruelty of empire. The novel asks whether friendship can survive across the gulf that colonial power digs between people.
frost-challenge-of-the-klan-1924:
Stanley Frost, a journalist, published The Challenge of the Klan in 1924, when the second Ku Klux Klan was near its peak. The new Klan had grown fast in the early 1920s, claiming millions of members and real political power. Frost set out to report how it worked and why it spread.

Frost traced the Klan's leaders, money, recruiting, and use of fear, and he reported on violence linked to its robes and secrecy. He treated the Klan not as a passing scare but as a test for American law and public life. His account remains a close, early look at the movement from outside its ranks.
frus-1861-d124:
William Dayton wrote from Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 27 May 1861. The dispatch is document 124 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two Dayton reports in one week show a post finding its rhythm. The French stance on the war was being set in those very weeks. His letters gave Seward the feel of Paris talk, which no formal note could fully carry. French talk ran through salons and banks as much as through the foreign office. Salon and bank talk reached Dayton's ears long before it reached print.
frus-1861-d224:
Seward's incoming mail for 3 June 1861 held a dispatch from Mr. Fay. The printed record keeps it as Document 224 in the President's message volume for 1861. The letter comes from the opening months of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d24:
Henry Sanford wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 July 1861. The dispatch is document 24 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The first July of the war found every Union envoy pressing the same plea: treat the South as rebels, not as a nation. Sanford carried that plea in Belgium and beyond. His letter shows the plea being made in one small court among many. King Leopold's court prized trade, so the blockade's bite on commerce filled much talk there. Commerce, more than pride, set the tone of Belgian talk in that year.
frus-1862-d124:
On 8 August 1862, the State Department wrote to all its officers posted in foreign lands. The printed record keeps it as Document 124 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text speaks to the whole foreign service at once, not to one man in one capital. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d224:
On 23 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart in a letter printed as Document 224 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart handled British business in Washington while Lord Lyons was away from his post.

Late July was a low point for Union hopes, with the army regrouping after the failed Richmond campaign. In London and Paris, ministers weighed whether to propose a pause in the fighting. Seward's frequent notes to Stuart formed one side of the talks that would decide the question, and they show a secretary refusing to look beaten. Each note was numbered and docketed by clerks, which is why the file reads so evenly.
frus-1862-d24:
21 February 1862 is the date on a dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 24 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the winter of the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d324:
A Dayton report dated 10 September 1862 stands as Document 324 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, wrote it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Mid-September reports from Paris reached Washington in October, landing amid the emancipation debate's foreign echo. What Dayton sent was still valuable: his account of French intentions guided Seward's talks with the French minister at home. This letter is one of the file's many proofs that old news, well judged, could still steer policy. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d424:
On 1 August 1862 Horace J. Perry wrote from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 424 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record of the year's foreign dealings.

August 1862 was a month of strain, with a second call for troops at home and intervention talk rising in London and Paris. From Madrid, Perry could report whether Spain would follow a Franco-British lead or hold its own course. His letters also guarded practical points: Confederate access to Spanish ports and the safety of Union commerce near Cuba. The report is one strand of the watch Washington kept on every court that summer.
frus-1862-d524:
James Shepherd Pike reported from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 October 1862. The dispatch is Document 524 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

By mid-October the news of Antietam and emancipation had reached the Netherlands, and Pike could report the Dutch response to both. Antislavery Holland received the emancipation order warmly, which strengthened the Union's moral position there. His report also kept up the file's practical side, the port and trade questions that never paused. Seward's map of Europe brightened that autumn, and letters like this one, from a friendly and observant post, were among the reasons.
frus-1862-d624:
The Turkish file opens on 31 March 1862 with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Edward Joy Morris, the American minister at Constantinople. It is Document 624 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Morris, a Pennsylvania scholar who had served in the Ottoman capital before, represented the United States at the court of the sultan. American interests there were commercial and protective: trade, missionaries, and travelers under the capitulations. Seward's opening order set the year's line for the most distant of his European posts, where the war was a rumor from another world. The letter begins a file colored by that distance and by Morris's long local knowledge.
frus-1863p1-d124:
On 19 March 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 124 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Paired letters let Adams give each head of news its own room. One might hold a talk; the next, the press or the yards where Southern ships rose. This letter is the second of the day's pair. Read with its mate, it shows the London post at its spring pace, feeding Washington the facts it needed to hold Britain at arm's length.
frus-1863p1-d224: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 29 June 1863. It is document 224 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d24:
William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 5 January 1863, and a second letter to him bears the same date. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 24 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward's first London letters of 1863 came just after the freedom edict took force. The act made the war a fight over slavery in plain terms, and envoys abroad had to speak to that change. This letter is one of the pair that opened the year. It shows the secretary resetting his London brief for a war whose meaning had grown.
frus-1863p1-d324:
The British minister in Washington, Lord Lyons, took up his pen on 24 November 1862 to write Secretary of State William H. Seward. His note is document 324 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Cases in these notes can look small, one ship or one arrested man, yet each tested the rules of neutrality. Both governments treated the precedents as serious business. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d424:
On 25 March 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 424 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The channel between Lyons and Seward was the main safety valve of Anglo-American relations in the war. Papers like this one are the valve at work. It dates from the spring when British debate over aiding the South was still live, and every note counted. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d524:
Writing on 21 May 1863, Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons addressed Secretary William H. Seward in an official letter. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d624:
A letter of 26 September 1863, from William H. Seward to William Stuart, stands as document 624 in the printed record. Stuart was Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863. Stuart was holding the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was away on leave, so the channel ran through him that season.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Alone it is one note among hundreds.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d124: Ambassador Harriman wrote to Harry Hopkins on November 12, 1943, choosing the President's special assistant as his channel that day. The letter is Document 124 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Writing to Hopkins was often quicker than writing to the president, and nearly as sure of being read. The record gives the date and the two men and no topic. The letter rests in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d224:
Charles Bohlen, first secretary at the American embassy in Moscow, wrote a memorandum on 16 November 1943 recording a conversation between Ambassador Harriman and Soviet foreign minister Molotov. The two men first marked ten years of diplomatic relations between the United States and the Soviet Union.

Harriman says he will leave on 19 November to meet Roosevelt, who reaches Cairo on 22 November. Since the President is at sea under radio silence, he cannot say how large the American military staff will be. He lists likely topics: the second front that spring, Turkey in the war, forces freed once the line north of Rome settles, the Dodecanese, and the Dardanelles. Molotov counters with news that thirteen German divisions had shifted from the west to press the Soviet front at Fastov.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d24: Writing for the third day in a row, Churchill sent Roosevelt another message on August 12, 1943, now Document 24 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Quebec Conference was about to open, and the two governments were lining up their positions. The record supplies the date and the names and leaves the topic to the text. In the published volume it helps show the tempo of allied business that summer.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d324:
General Dwight Eisenhower, commander in chief at Allied Force Headquarters in Algiers, sent the Combined Chiefs of Staff an extract from a letter by General Giraud on 26 November 1943. Circulated as paper C.C.S. 413, it asks that the French high command be heard at the Cairo Conference.

Giraud argues from France's place in the coming operations in western Europe. His knowledge of the country, and the weight of the underground and resistance groups there, entitle him to help study them. He holds himself ready to come in person to Roosevelt and Churchill. Failing that, he asks that one officer of his staff present his views to the chiefs. Failing even that, he relies on Eisenhower to defend the interests of France and the French army.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d424:
The Military Agreement of the Tehran Conference, headed Military Conclusions, was initialed on the evening of 1 December 1943 by Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill. An editorial headnote notes that the text stayed secret for years and was released to the press on 24 March 1947.

Its five points fix the war plan. The Partisans in Yugoslavia will be supported with supplies, equipment, and commando operations to the greatest extent. Turkey should come into the war before the end of the year, and if Bulgaria then attacks her, the Soviet Union will at once be at war with Bulgaria. Overlord will be launched during May 1944 with a companion operation against southern France. It will go in at whatever strength landing craft permit. Soviet forces will attack at about the same time, to stop German troops moving west. The three staffs will keep in close touch, and concert a cover plan to mislead the enemy.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d524:
President Roosevelt replied to Ambassador Averell Harriman in Moscow on December 21, 1943, the day after Harriman's report reached him. The exchange, cable out and answer back within a day, shows the President's direct line to his Soviet embassy at full stretch. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Roosevelt guided the Soviet relationship personally, and Harriman was his chosen instrument in Moscow. A presidential answer at this speed signals business the President considered his own. For readers, the pair of messages, this one and Harriman's of December 20, show how the most delicate channel in American diplomacy actually worked in practice.
frus-1944-quebec-d124:
Under the heading "The Polish Problem," State Department planners gave Roosevelt a blunt reading of Stalin's aims in September 1944. The paper argues the Soviet leader had decided the London Polish government's forces in Poland must be destroyed. Only then could his sponsored Lublin Committee gain the upper hand in the country.

The authors call Stalin's refusal to help Warsaw a political decision, not a military one. They rate Premier Mikołajczyk's chances of forming a coalition government as very small. For American policy they urge continued pressure for a compromise, steady support for Mikołajczyk, and great slowness in recognizing any Soviet-installed group. World opinion, they warn, will judge the outcome.
frus-1944-quebec-d224:
Cherwell wrote to Morgenthau from Quebec on September 16, 1944. His purpose was to pin down four disputed words: "or sold for profit." He set out his recollection of their meaning in the September 14 conversation. Britain, he understood, should not sell lend-lease goods for more than their book price plus a reasonable allowance for transport and similar charges.

Cherwell asked Morgenthau to confirm the reading. He added that Britain habitually kept well within such a limit, thanks to America's generous desire to keep the dollar sign out of lend-lease. Morgenthau's reply, given in the editors' note, declined a precise restatement: the principles that had governed sales would be retained unless changed circumstances made reconsideration desirable.
frus-1944-quebec-d24:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to Harry Hopkins on August 10, 1944, using the channel to the President's closest aide. Churchill valued Hopkins as a friend and as the fastest route into Roosevelt's mind. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

A month before the Quebec Conference, the Churchill-Hopkins channel carried both business and the warmth that oiled the alliance. Hopkins could soften a disagreement or speed a decision as no formal note could. For readers, the message shows summit preparation running through personal trust, in a correspondence that mixed statecraft with genuine affection between the two men.
frus-1945-50-intel-d124:
Hoover wrote to Attorney General Clark again on 12 August 1946. Four days after the authority's letter, the FBI director was still putting his case to his chief. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Persistence was Hoover's method: a lost round was followed by a fresh statement of the bureau's rights, building a file no later decision could ignore. His August letters to Clark form the bureau's brief in the Latin American case. Readers can judge the result in the volume's later papers, where the hemisphere's work was divided in fact. Win or lose on the day, Hoover's paper made the bureau's claim permanent, and permanence in files is its own kind of victory.
frus-1945-50-intel-d224:
On 23 September 1947, Acting Secretary of State Lovett sent a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 224, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. That season, the talk in Washington was of one big law to join up defense, foreign policy, and intelligence.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d24:
Tamm wrote to Hoover again on 4 October 1945, keeping up the near-weekly rhythm of inside FBI papers in this part of the volume. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

By October, the first shock of the OSS order had passed, and the fight settled into positioning for whatever central system the president might build. Tamm's memoranda kept Hoover current on that slow game. Readers should notice the bureau's patience: Hoover rarely rushed, preferring to let rivals spend themselves while his own claims stayed fresh. This paper is one more entry in the bureau's careful log of a contest it expected to last for years.
frus-1945-50-intel-d324:
Formal minutes cover the 16th Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board, held on 11 September 1947. It survives in print as document 324 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act was moving through Congress that year, and it would soon replace the wartime setup with the CIA.

The text is the meeting as the secretaries kept it, topic by topic, with the results marked as they were reached. For a reader now, the draw is the nearness: this is the meeting as its own staff chose to keep it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d424:
Dated 12 December 1947, National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 6 is document 424 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A numbered directive bound every agency that did intelligence work, not just the CIA. The set issued that December formed the first rule book for the postwar system. This one helps readers see how much of the Cold War state rested on short, formal orders few outsiders ever saw. The rules in this set governed how secret reports were shared, graded, and kept across the government. Each fresh order also told the older services that the new system was here to stay.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d124:
How the Treasury plan for Germany reached the cabinet table is traced in this 28 September 1944 paper. James Riddleberger, chief of the Division of Central European Affairs, wrote it for Under Secretary Stettinius. It is titled “Developments in the Formulation of American Policy for the Post-War Treatment of Germany.”

On 1 September, Harry Hopkins passed on the President's wish for a Cabinet Committee on Germany. At a meeting the next day, Dr. Harry White produced the Treasury plan. As White explained it, the Rhineland and a strip north to the Kiel Canal would be placed under world control. Poland would take East Prussia and Upper Silesia, France the Saar and lands along the Rhine and Moselle. The rest of the Reich would be split into two separate states.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d224:
Two draft replies to Harriman's credit cables are the subject of this excerpt from Grew's report of 27 January 1945. Sent to the traveling Secretary of State, it is the first message of the series since Stettinius left Washington. The excerpt is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The papers on postwar credits and 3-C terms, Grew reports, were given to Alger Hiss for the conference files. One draft has since changed course. The Treasury has withdrawn its suggestion that fresh 3-C terms, with no interest, be offered to Moscow. So the instruction sent to Kennan on the 3-C matter tells him to take no action until further word comes. The other reply, carrying the facts on postwar credits, went out with only small changes of wording.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d24: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on 23 November 1944, which was Thanksgiving Day in the United States. His message stands as document 24 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta, issued by the Department of State. Late November brought the summit planning to a sharper point, and a letter from the Soviet leader in that week carried more than routine courtesy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d324: One short question carries the weight of a February 3, 1945 note from the Joint Chiefs of Staff. It was addressed at Yalta to General Antonov of the Soviet General Staff. The American staff wished to discuss details of Soviet entry into the war against Japan. They asked whether Antonov could obtain approval for talks. Few messages in the volume open a larger bargain. Soviet entry against Japan was a prize Washington had sought for years. Asking leave to raise it, through staff channels, was the careful first step.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d424:
Molotov broke in early in Matthews's minutes of the February 9, 1945 plenary. Stettinius had begun reading the foreign ministers' report. At the end of the Poland section, Molotov asked to speak at once. The meeting agreed to hear him before the rest of the report.

We accept the American proposal as a basis, Molotov said. He wanted agreement, with only some amendments. The first sentence should say the provisional government would be reorganized on a wider democratic basis. Democratic statesmen in Poland and Poles abroad would be included. A second amendment touched the holding of elections. Matthews catches the ice beginning to crack on Poland.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d124:
Secretary Byrnes formally invited Ambassador Harriman to the Berlin meeting in a telegram dated July 5, 1945. The message, only a few lines long, is document 124 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Part of the telegram is not printed in the volume.

Byrnes writes that he would like Harriman present at the coming meeting of the three heads of government, and that Edward Page should accompany him. He adds that the State Department party expects to arrive in Berlin on July 13. The invitation put into official form what Bohlen had told Harriman the day before. Harriman, the American ambassador who knew Stalin's circle best, would serve at Potsdam as both adviser and interpreter of Soviet moves.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d224:
A briefing book paper laid out Britain's plan for a Western European bloc, written for Truman before the conference. The paper is document 224 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It describes the scheme, urged by General Smuts, as a hedge against the failure of Big Three cooperation after the war.

The idea was to draw France, Belgium, Holland, Norway, and Denmark into something like dominion status in the Commonwealth. It would mean a common foreign policy, joint military planning, combined boards for finance and supplies, a customs union, and shared stands on aviation and colonies. The Russians oppose the plan, the paper says, seeing a British sphere of influence; London claims it is aimed at Germany. The Joint Chiefs warned that building rival blocs was the likeliest road to a British-Russian conflict.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d24:
Hopkins met Stalin at the Kremlin at 8 p.m. on May 26, 1945, and Bohlen's memorandum records the first conversation. Stalin expressed great pleasure at seeing Hopkins again. Talk turned briefly to Hopkins's flight in over Germany. Hopkins asked Molotov if he had recovered from the battle of San Francisco; Molotov replied he recalled no battle, merely arguments.

The listed subjects map the crisis: Roosevelt's death, Soviet-American relations, a meeting of heads of state, Germany, the Far East, the Poles, and Hitler. Before giving Truman's reasons for the mission, Hopkins set out his own ground. The memorandum opens the fullest surviving record of the spring's most important negotiation.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d324:
Instruction No. 698, sent to Ambassador Harriman on July 6, 1945, transmits a State Department policy paper on American property used for reparations. The enclosed paper, dated June 22, is titled on the use of American property by satellite countries for reparation. Harriman's mission was to be guided by it in all such matters.

The paper starts from the armistices signed by Finland, Rumania, Hungary, and Bulgaria. Those deals obliged each state to pay for war damage, much of it to the Soviet Union. The question was what happened when the goods or plants handed over belonged to American owners, a problem that ran through the whole reparations fight.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d424:
Coal famine drives a Washington cable to Pauley in Moscow dated July 3, 1945, signed by Secretary Byrnes. The Potter-Hyndley mission's report on northwest Europe, it says, concludes that without immediate and drastic steps, next winter will bring a coal famine there and in the Mediterranean area. Its severity would destroy all semblance of law and order.

The American government, the cable states, concurs in the report's major findings. It backs instant action on two points: reach maximum coal production in Germany early, and export to northwest Europe and the Mediterranean all coal above German needs. The President, it adds, proposes a directive to the American commander to that effect.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d524:
Soviet cooperation in Europe's recovery is sought in a briefing book paper on solving immediate European economic problems. Its recommendation: the Soviet Union should be urged and encouraged to participate actively with the United States, the United Kingdom, and other countries in combined endeavors on relief and reconstruction. The steps it calls particularly important begin with organizations.

The paper seeks Soviet agreement to participate fully in four bodies: the Emergency Economic Committee for Europe, the European Coal Organization, the European Central Inland Transport Organization, and the United Maritime Authority. Soviet representatives would cooperate in their day-to-day work. A second section turns to UNRRA, and the terms on which Soviet agreement should be sought there.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d624:
Secretary of State Byrnes wrote to Harold Ickes, the wartime petroleum chief, on July 6, 1945. The top secret letter is document 624 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It brings Ickes up to date on the oil situation in Eastern Europe.

Byrnes says reports of Ickes's interest in eastern oil for Western Europe have reached him. He encloses three papers for Ickes's use. One is the Department's airgram to Moscow of June 29. The others cover the use of U.S. property by satellite states for reparations, and a goods deal between Rumania and the Soviet Union. The airgram, he notes, shows Ambassador Harriman fully briefed on the oil picture. It also stresses the link between reviving that industry and the world output needed for war and civil needs alike.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1024:
Philip Mosely sent this secret memorandum to Assistant Secretaries James Dunn and William Clayton on July 17, 1945. It sums up the plan to create a Rhineland-Ruhr state, then tests the case for and against. Most plans would make the area a lasting separate unit, run by France, Belgium, and the Netherlands under the Security Council.

Supporters claim separation would keep Germany's basic resources out of German hands forever. A weaker Germany would also tempt no outside power as an ally. Mosely answers that maps cannot erase a people's numbers, skills, and drive. Germans, he argues, would never sincerely accept partition. Holding it would demand permanent unity among the four great powers, which partition itself would strain.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1124:
A second message from the Acting Secretary of State went to Assistant Secretary Clayton on 20 July 1945. It followed the first by two days. Clayton led the State Department's work on trade, loans, and the money terms of the peace.

Money questions sat near the top of the Potsdam agenda. What Germany would pay, how trade would restart, and who would fund relief all ran through Clayton's office. Repeat contact of this kind shows how central that track was to the summit. The message is one more link between the talks in Germany and the staff who ran the home office.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1224:
Togo cabled Sato again on 17 July 1945, a second message the same day. Tokyo's foreign minister was pressing his Moscow envoy hard at the very start of the Potsdam talks. Japan's leaders knew the summit would speak to their fate.

The traffic between Tokyo and its Moscow embassy ran through American hands in secret. Codebreakers broke Japan's codes, and the Potsdam team read the pleas as they flew. That hidden fact gives these plain cables their drama. This second note of the day shows Tokyo's urgency. Japan sought Soviet help to end the war on terms softer than surrender, and every day counted.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1324:
The United States team tabled this proposal on 25 July 1945. It came the day before the Allied terms to Japan went out and the British government changed hands. The summit's drafting machine ran at full speed that week.

A proposal at this stage aimed at closing text: words the other teams could sign. The paper is one of the American moves in the drive toward the final protocol. Kept in the official record, it lets readers follow the drafting fight clause by clause. Its fate, kept or cut, can be traced in the approved texts printed near it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1424:
A text submitted to the heads of government themselves forms document 1424, dated 24 July 1945. Papers addressed to the leaders, rather than to the conference staff, were meant for the highest eyes at Potsdam. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Most summit paper moves among officials; a text laid before Truman, Churchill, and Stalin directly marks a question the staffs could not settle. Readers should note the channel as much as the words: escalation to the top was the summit's way of breaking deadlocks. This paper belongs to the crowded middle of the talks, when the leaders' days filled with points their aides had failed to close below.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-124:
A rapporteur reported on July 27, 1945, summing up a working group's progress for the Potsdam Conference's senior levels. The report dates from the final week, when subcommittees raced to close their files. It was printed among the conference papers in the second Potsdam volume. Rapporteur reports were the hinges between detailed work and top-level choice.

Inside, the group's gains and gaps stand side by side. Leaders could see at a glance what a final push might settle. The form teaches readers how the conference processed hard problems in layers. Few documents show the method as clearly as these short, factual reports.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-24:
Robert Murphy, political adviser in Germany, memoranda'd an experts' session on German economics dated July 19, 1945. The memo is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The subcommittee of experts agreed to work informally and to report back only its disagreements.

Soviet delegate Maisky led off by asking what decentralization meant. Will Clayton tied it to breaking up trusts, cartels, and monopolies. Another U.S. man tied it to ending tight central control of industry and commerce. A joint definition was agreed on the spot. The German economy would be decentralized to end the excessive concentration of economic power. Maisky had no quarrel with a relief principle that followed. He did ask what relief of liberated areas meant, and he made no comment when asked if Germany meant her 1937 frontiers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d724:
Document 724 is Byrnes's reply to his acting deputy, sent July 16, 1945 as he settled at Potsdam. The Secretary of State answered Joseph Grew, who held the Department in Washington. Their exchange frames the volume's Washington channel. This letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Replies from the field show what the traveling team needed most. A secretary at a summit depends on home for facts, drafts, and calm judgment. Readers see that dependence in writing. The document pairs with Grew's letter of the same day. Together they show the two ends of one working line.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d824:
Cannon wrote from Lisbon to Assistant Secretary Dunn on July 28, 1945, in document 824. The first secretary at the Lisbon embassy now reported to a higher desk. His letter dates from the conference's final days. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

A report routed to an assistant secretary gains speed. Dunn could carry a point straight to the Secretary's circle. Readers see Cannon's Lisbon view climbing the ladder at a key moment. The document shows the Department's wiring at work: a quiet post, a senior reader, and a summit drawing to its close in the same week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d924: Emile Despres, adviser on German economic affairs, wrote to William Clayton on July 24, 1945, about safeguards in a possible reparations deal. If the Russians gain a free hand in their zone plus set removals from the Ruhr, he says America should insist on two protections. Looted property that can be identified must be returned, and Allied teams must be free to locate it. Allied-owned property in Germany must not be removed without the owners' government's consent, and fair payment must be arranged.
frus-1955-57v24:
The Soviet Union and the Eastern Mediterranean share Volume XXIV of the 1955–1957 set. Policy toward Moscow leads, in a short block. East-West exchanges of persons and information follow, also brief.

Cyprus takes a long run, as Washington worked to settle the island's fight between Greece and Turkey. Greece and Turkey close the volume in their own country blocks. Argued in the files, the island's fate pitted two allies against each other. Each offer of terms was weighed for what it would cost the alliance as a whole. Island talks ran through London, Athens, and Ankara files.
frus-1961-63v24:
The Laos crisis fills Volume XXIV of the 1961–1963 set on its own. The handover from Eisenhower to Kennedy leads. War or talks is weighed through the spring of 1961 in these files.

Geneva's conference on Laos opens in May, beside the Vienna summit. Harriman's mission and the drive for a coalition follow. Sanctions on Phoumi and the Nam Tha crisis fill 1962. Marines deploy at the crisis's height. The record shows a small kingdom used as the Cold War's test case, its neutrality built by threat, aid cuts, and talk. The coalition's signing closes the volume's main arc in Geneva.
frus-1964-68v23-d24: A Central Intelligence Agency telegram dated September 19, 1960, went from headquarters to the station in the Congo. It is document 24 in Volume XXIII of the 1964-1968 Foreign Relations series. The cable sets out secret meeting plans for a man who would arrive from Paris and name himself as Joe. Editorial notes tie the cable to a plot against Congo leader Patrice Lumumba. The notes cite later Senate inquiry testimony on toxic materials prepared for that plot.
frus-1964-68v24:
Africa fills Volume XXIV of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964-1968. Opening chapters cover North Africa, with sections on Algeria, Libya, Morocco, and Tunisia. Later chapters treat Ghana, the Horn of Africa, and Nigeria. Long closing chapters cover Rhodesia and South Africa. Sections on Portuguese Africa and the southern region round out the volume.

The documents are cables and memos on coups, wars, and race. Nigeria's slide toward civil war runs through its chapter. Rhodesia's white regime and its break with Britain fill many pages. Across the volume, U.S. officials weigh Cold War aims against support for majority rule.
frus-1969-76v24:
The Middle East region and the Arabian Peninsula fill Volume XXIV of the 1969-1976 series, for 1969-1972. Sections cover the region as a whole, the Indian Ocean, and the Persian Gulf states. Saudi Arabia and the two Yemens get sections of their own. A long final part covers Jordan in September 1970. It runs to more than 130 documents on the civil war there.

The Gulf chapters follow British withdrawal and the rise of local states. Oil and bases run through the Saudi chapters. The Jordan chapters show Washington backing King Hussein against the fedayeen and Syria. The volume pairs quiet regional work with one sharp crisis.
frus-1977-80v24:
Volume XXIV of the 1977-1980 series covers South America and the Latin America region. A regional section opens the volume. Country sections follow for Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela. Argentina takes the largest share. Its papers deal with the junta, human rights, and the grain trade. The Chile section covers ties under Pinochet and the Letelier case's long shadow.

Human rights reports run through the volume, country by country. The Brazil section is short, dealing with nuclear and trade friction. Oddly, a stray talk record on Sadat and Begin sits deep in the files. The volume maps a continent under military rule.
frus-1981-88v24:
North Africa fills Volume XXIV of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1981-1988. A regional section opens the volume. Sections then cover Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, and the Western Sahara. Morocco takes a long share. Its papers deal with base access and arms. One memo urges talks without delay on access to Sidi Slimane and Mohammed V air bases. It offers to make up part of a Moroccan military building program there.

The Western Sahara section follows the war between Morocco and the Polisario Front. Algeria's covers gas, trade, and its role backing Polisario. The volume shows the Maghreb as a quiet but armed contest.
galsworthy-white-monkey-1924:
John Galsworthy opened his second Forsyte trilogy, A Modern Comedy, with The White Monkey, published in 1924. The Forsytes return, but the center shifts to the younger generation. Soames's daughter Fleur is now married and restless in postwar London.

Fleur and her husband Michael Mont drift through parties, publishing work, and marital strain. A Chinese statue of a white monkey, holding a squeezed fruit, becomes the symbol of their grasping age. Meanwhile Soames, older and less sure, watches his daughter repeat family patterns. Galsworthy mixes satire of the 1920s smart set with real sympathy for people trapped by wealth.
gao-gaoreports-b-297524:
NVT Technologies protested an Air Force award for lab support work in GAO decision B-297524, dated February 2, 2006. The winner was SelectTech Services. The site was Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio. The work was lab runs and gear upkeep. The firm hit its past work marks. It also said the winner took bars to key call terms.

GAO denied the protests. Past work marks and the pick fit the call terms. They also fit the buy rules. The firm had shown less close fit to this work than it claimed. That gap backed the lower mark. No bar by the winner to key terms was shown that would void its bid.
gao-gaoreports-b-299424:
Global Solutions Network protested a Treasury call to cancel a solicitation. The Bureau of the Public Debt ran the buy. The work covered administrative and clerical support services. GAO decided B-299424 on April 20, 2007.

The firm said the cancel call lacked a sound base. The agency judged that its terms might no longer fit its needs. Needs had shifted since the terms were drawn.
