GAO found that judgment fair on the record. An agency may scrap terms that drift from true needs. It need not push ahead with a stale buy. The firm's claim gave no ground to block the move. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299624:
Tennier Industries protested terms in an Army solicitation for fire resistant clothing. The gear sets span shirts, base layers, jackets, and cold weather wear. The firm claimed the terms were vague or flawed in many spots. GAO decided B-299624 on July 12, 2007.

GAO read the terms as a whole, not line by line. Read that way, the terms made sense. They gave firms a sound base to draft their bids. A term need not spell out each small point. It must let a firm grasp the need with fair clarity. These terms met that bar. Broad claims of flaws did not hold up. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-306424:
Sound gear for a rented hall is the subject of this GAO decision, B-306424, dated March 24, 2006. The Presidio Trust runs the Presidio site in San Francisco. The Trust rents space for public and private events. A board meeting of the National Academy of Public Administration used the site in 2005. The event needed rented sound gear and help.

The cost at issue came to $2,685.00. GAO held that Trust funds could pay it. Congress gave the Trust power to lease and run the site. Event service is a normal part of that work. Sound gear and help are a needed part of such service. The ruling shows how a small cost can fit an agency's funds when it serves the mission.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-224:
HUD Rental Assistance, GAO-05-224 of February 18, 2005, is the full report form of work summed in a later Senate statement. In fiscal year 2003, the Department of Housing and Urban Development paid about $28 billion to help some 5 million low-income tenants. Three plans carry the aid: vouchers, public housing, and project-based Section 8.

Some rent sums come out too high or too low each year. HUD set up a project to size the errors and find their roots. GAO, at the ask of Congress, checks the size and sources found. It checks the fix steps HUD has in train, and bids to make rent math simpler.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-324:
Aviation Security, GAO-05-324 of February 23, 2005, sets the tests for a plan to screen flyers with trade data. The Transportation Security Administration builds a new screen, called Secure Flight. It would take from the airlines the task of match of flyer names to terror watch lists. Trade data on each flyer could sharpen the match. Law bars a test of that data till fair tests exist.

Congress told the agency to write those tests first. It told GAO to grade them. GAO did, and briefed staff on January 11, 2005. The report puts that grade on record: how to weigh gains in safety next to harm to rights and speed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-424:
Paperwork Reduction Act, GAO-05-424 of May 20, 2005, asks if a law meant to curb federal forms has lost its bite. Folks spend billions of hours a year on federal forms, polls, and asks. The act aims to weigh that load next to the gain of each ask. Each agency's tech chief must bless each new ask first. The bless vows the ask meets 10 set tests in the act.

GAO read a land-wide sample of asks. It read the path at four arms that hold much of the load. It dug deep on 12 asks let through. A new path may be owed, the title holds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-724:
Air traffic costs at the Federal Aviation Administration are the focus of GAO-05-724, dated June 23, 2005. Air traffic work cost about $6.5 billion a year. That was over 80 percent of the agency's running costs. A new Air Traffic Organization took over in February 2004 and made cost control a top goal. GAO checked its outlook, its cost steps, and other options.

GAO found a grim outlook. Costs rose $1.8 billion in real terms from fiscal years 1996 to 2004. A gap of nearly $4 billion was projected through fiscal year 2010. Current savings steps covered only about 12 percent of that gap. GAO urged the group to weigh bigger moves, such as merging sites, and to finish its delayed business plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-24:
Down payment help on government-backed home loans is questioned in GAO-06-24, a report dated November 9, 2005. The Federal Housing Administration lets buyers take down payment aid from third parties. Studies have linked such aid to weaker loan performance. GAO tracked how fast the use of aid grew on insured loans. It asked how aid shapes sale prices and the deal itself.

Some aid flows through groups that recycle seller money, which can inflate prices. Loans with aid have shown higher claim rates. In a September 2005 report GAO urged the agency to test aid as a factor in its loan models. In October 2005 the agency added it to its yearly review for the first time. Thin data on aid sources may still hide the full effect. The report presses for tighter grip on a risky corner of home lending.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-324:
Cash offers to shrink and reshape agency staffs are surveyed in GAO-06-324, published March 31, 2006. A 2002 law lets agencies seek permission to offer buyouts and early retirement. The personnel office grants that authority case by case. GAO counted how many agencies won it and how often they used it. It asked how agencies view the personnel office's help. It checked whether agencies follow the habits tied to good use of the tools. It also gathered the hurdles agencies see ahead.

Use is climbing fast, GAO found. The count of agencies using the tools rose from 28 to 51 across fiscal 2003 to 2005. GAO urged the personnel office to spread word of what works. Buyouts can cut skills an agency still needs if aimed poorly. Aimed well, they let a workforce change shape without layoffs. The report weighs the tool's spread against that risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-624:
Federal support for new uses of wood is surveyed in GAO report GAO-06-624, released on June 15, 2006. More wood is used each year in the United States than all metals, plastics, and masonry cement combined. Forest product firms rely on research to find better ways to use wood. At least 12 federal agencies backed wood research and product work, led by the Forest Service.

GAO grouped the federal work into five types, from basic research to product testing. Agencies made at least $54 million a year available in fiscal years 2004 and 2005. GAO also reviewed how scientists share results with firms through field visits, training, and publications. The report maps a little-known research network that supports rural jobs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-724:
Breast cancer screening capacity is measured in GAO report GAO-06-724, issued on July 25, 2006. Mammography uses X-rays to spot small breast tumors early, when treatment works best. In 2002, GAO found that screening capacity was generally adequate across the nation. This update tracked certified facilities over a recent three-year span. GAO also asked why facilities were closing.

GAO found that closures outpaced openings during the period. Certified facilities fell from 9,306 on October 1, 2001, to 8,768 on October 1, 2004. Some 1,290 facilities closed while 752 opened. Financial strain was the reason cited most often for closures. GAO concluded that nationwide capacity stayed adequate. But access problems may exist in certain locations where closures hit hardest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-824:
Awards meant to spur lending in poor areas are weighed in GAO-06-824, which GAO issued on July 31, 2006. The Treasury Department's Bank Enterprise Award program began in 1994. It pays cash awards to banks that raise their investment in community development lenders and in distressed areas. Those lenders serve places and people that banks often pass over. GAO asked whether the awards change bank behavior in a measurable way.

GAO found that the program reportedly produces benefits for communities. But the available evidence suggests its impact has likely not been significant. The program's own performance measures likely overstate its effect. GAO also found weaknesses in Treasury controls meant to ensure proper award payments. The report questions whether small awards can move large bank portfolios.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-224:
Wartime deployments are straining the Army's supply of young officers. GAO examined the problem in GAO-07-224, a report dated January 19, 2007. Officers enter through academies, campus ROTC programs, or candidate schools. GAO compared accessions for fiscal years 2001, 2003, and 2005 with service needs. It also reviewed retention and foreign language skills. The Army drew the closest look.

The Army missed its officer needs in fiscal years 2001 and 2003, GAO found. It met them in fiscal year 2005. Its ROTC pool held 25,100 cadets in fiscal year 2006. The Army said it needed at least 31,000 to hit its goal. West Point's class of 2006 commissioned 846 graduates, short of a 900 goal. Candidate school output was near its ceiling. The services also struggled to recruit doctors, nurses, and minority officers. GAO urged a strategic plan for the Army. The department partly agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-24:
Estimates of the dead in Darfur range widely, and policy turns on which figures are sound. GAO put six estimates to expert review in GAO-07-24, a report dated November 9, 2006. Fighting in Darfur, Sudan, began in 2003 between rebels and government-backed militias. Published tolls ran up to about 400,000 deaths. GAO and the National Academy of Sciences convened the experts. They judged each study's methods and accuracy.

No estimate earned high marks across the board, GAO found. Experts trusted most an estimate built on about 30 mortality surveys. That work came from a Belgian disaster research center. The State Department's estimate ranked next. Experts said its write-up lacked detail needed to check it. The three highest tolls drew the least trust. They spanned 253,573 to 396,563 deaths. Experts faulted fixed death rates applied to all places and times. They urged fuller public methods.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-424:
Computer spending at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is the topic of GAO-07-424, a GAO report from April 27, 2007. For fiscal year 2008, DHS sought about $4 billion for information technology. That was the third largest such request among federal departments. GAO judged the department against its own investment management frame.

DHS had built the basic structure to steer its tech funds. But many rules were still vague or missing. Project-level checks were weak, and portfolio-wide review barely existed. After almost 4 years in operation, the department still lacked a mature way to pick and watch its projects. GAO warned that poor control raises the odds of blown costs and missed goals. The report urged DHS to finish and use its full set of rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-424:
Emergency response plans for underground coal mines are the focus of GAO report GAO-08-424, issued April 8, 2008. After the mine disasters of 2006, Congress passed the Mine Improvement and New Emergency Response Act of 2006. The act requires mine operators to plan for trapped miners, including backup air and wireless communications. The Mine Safety and Health Administration approves the plans.

The agency's shifting, vague guidance slowed approvals; guidance on refuges of air came 6 months after the first plans were due. Some plans never said what protection miners in certain areas would get. By January 2008, most plan parts were in place, but air systems awaited gear that does not yet exist, and wireless systems awaited a ruling on what technology counts. The agency agreed with GAO's call for clearer guidance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-624:
Pension checks for millions of private workers rest on one small federal body, the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation. It runs with about 800 federal staff plus some 1,500 hired workers. GAO-08-624, dated June 12, 2008, studies how well the body hires and keeps the skilled staff it needs.

From fiscal years 2000 to 2007, hiring and retention matched the rest of the government for most key jobs. Gaps showed in top posts and senior finance jobs. Nearly one-quarter of key staff could retire within 4 years, and pay lags some rival agencies. GAO urged better workforce planning, better data, and full use of pay options.
ghazali-mishkat-anwar-gairdner-1924:
Al-Ghazali, the great Muslim theologian of the eleventh century, wrote Mishkat al-Anwar, The Niche for Lights, as a commentary on the Quranic Light Verse. Gairdner's 1924 translation for the Royal Asiatic Society is the classic English rendering. The short work is among the most prized in Sufi thought.

Ghazali unfolds the verse's image of God as the Light of the heavens and the earth through layers of symbol. Niche, lamp, glass, and oil become stages by which the soul rises toward true sight. Readers meet here a mind that joined strict theology to deep mystical longing.
gide-strait-is-the-gate-bussy-1924:
Strait Is the Gate, published by André Gide in French in 1909, was the first of his books Englished by Dorothy Bussy, in 1924. Jerome loves his cousin Alissa, a devout girl who believes earthly love bars the road to heaven. The title quotes the hard, narrow gate of the Gospels.

Alissa renounces Jerome again and again, urging him toward a purer life without her. He waits, writes, and hopes across many years of separation. Her diary, read after her death, reveals the cost of her choice. Gide tells the story quietly, letting faith and desire wound each other. Many readers judge it his most perfectly made short novel.
goldman-further-disillusionment-russia-1:
Emma Goldman returned from Soviet Russia with her hopes broken, and My Further Disillusionment in Russia tells why. The 1924 book follows her first account of the Russian Revolution's betrayal. Goldman had gone to Russia as a supporter of the revolution. She left as a critic of the Bolshevik state.

She describes the crushing of the soviets and the Kronstadt rising of 1921. Free speech, unions, and rival socialists all faced prison or worse. Her case is the anarchist case against Bolshevism, from a witness. The book angered many on the left who still defended Moscow. It stands as a primary record of dissent.
guillaume-traditions-islam-1924:
Alfred Guillaume, an English scholar of Islam, wrote this first English guide to the hadith books in 1924. Hadith are the tales of the words and deeds of the Prophet Muhammad, passed down by a chain of names. They form the Sunna, the model life that stands by the Quran in the faith.

Guillaume tells how the tales were gleaned, sifted, and set in the great books of the Sunna. He gives samples in English so the reader can see their form and range at first hand. The book is the first door in English to a vast field of Islamic lore.
haldane-daedalus-1924:
John Burdon Sanderson Haldane was a young British biologist when he gave the lecture printed in 1924 as Daedalus. He used the Greek maker Daedalus as a sign of science pushing past old limits. The talk looks a century ahead at what biology might do.

Haldane foresaw babies grown outside the body, new foods, and vast changes in energy and daily life. Some of his guesses missed, but the method of bold, reasoned forecast struck home. The book is often named as a founding text of speculation about remaking human life. He meant the lecture to stir debate, and it did so at once.
henrietta-s-wish-or-domineering-pg5124:
Charlotte M. Yonge opens Henrietta's Wish; Or, Domineering at Teignmouth railway station on a warm July afternoon. Henrietta, sixteen, waits in the carriage with her book, checking the clock every few minutes. The train brings her twin brother Frederick home. The two faces, exactly alike, press together for one public moment.

Their mother lies unwell at home, teased by business letters she should not write. Henrietta rules the household with loving energy, and therein lies the fault of the title. Yonge studies a girl whose wish to manage everyone must be schooled into gentleness. Frederick's steadier temper and the family's invalid mother frame the lesson. The novel is domestic moral fiction of Yonge's characteristic kind, where a besetting sin, not a villain, supplies the conflict.
history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-babylonia:
Gaston Maspero devoted this fourth volume of his ancient history to a turning age. Its theme is the first Chaldean empire and the Hyksos in Egypt. Sayce edited and McClure translated the English text. Syria's hard fate, trapped between great powers, opens the account.

Maspero maps Lebanon, the Orontes valley, and the coast in detail. Babylon rises, the Hyksos rule Egypt, and Ahmose drives them out. Later pages weigh old masonry at Jerusalem and Beersheba. The dating of such remains is handled with care. Readers follow the chessboard of the ancient east as empires trade blows across Syria.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol4-1924:
William Holdsworth's History of English Law reached its fourth volume in the 1923 third edition. Holdsworth, an Oxford professor, spent his life on this vast history, which grew to many volumes. The work traces English law from its medieval roots toward modern times, court by court and doctrine by doctrine.

Volume 4 covers the later medieval law: the growth of the central courts, the rise of the legal profession, and the law books of the period. Holdsworth writes with steady command of the records, showing how procedure and pleading shaped the substance of the law. His history became the standard account of how English law grew, and lawyers still cite it as an authority. The volume shows the medieval common law in its mature, working form.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol5-1924:
The fifth volume of Holdsworth's History of English Law, in its 1923 edition, takes the story into the sixteenth century. Holdsworth's multi-volume history was already the standard account of English law's growth. Each volume follows the courts, the profession, and the books of the law through one stretch of time.

Volume 5 covers the Tudor revolution in law. The Reformation changed the courts and the church's place in the legal order, while the common lawyers rose to new power and wealth. Holdsworth unfolds the transformation with vast learning and calm judgment. He shows how old forms bent without breaking under religious and political upheaval. For the legal history of the Tudor age, this volume remains a first port of call.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol6-1924:
Holdsworth published the sixth volume of his History of English Law in 1924. The Oxford historian was building, volume by volume, the fullest account of English law ever written by one man. By this point the history had reached the century of civil war and revolution.

Volume 6 takes up the 1600s: Coke on the bench, the king's prerogative courts, and the struggle between crown and Parliament fought through law. Holdsworth tells the legal side of England's revolution with a master's authority, showing how courtroom battles over jurisdiction became battles over the constitution itself. The courts appear as a true battleground of English liberty. Students of the period still start with Holdsworth, whose learning has never been matched in a single-author history.
houdini-magician-among-spirits-1924:
Harry Houdini, the most famous magician of his age, spent his last years hunting fake spirit mediums. His A Magician Among the Spirits, published in 1924, reports that hunt in detail. Houdini had hoped the dead might speak, and his failure to find honest proof made him fierce.

He describes seances he attended in disguise, slate tricks, spirit photos, and messages faked by hidden hands. As a stage magician he could copy every effect the mediums claimed came from ghosts. The book stands as the landmark skeptical investigation of Spiritualism by an insider of the craft of illusion.
huizinga-waning-middle-ages-hopman-1924:
Johan Huizinga's The Waning of the Middle Ages appears in F. Hopman's translation of 1924. Huizinga, a Dutch historian, portrays France and Burgundy in the 1300s and 1400s. Chivalry, court love, tournaments, and vivid religious life fill his pages. Yet beneath the color he finds weariness and a sense of ending.

He calls the age an autumn: ripe, ornate, and overripe. Forms of ritual and symbol govern thought so fully that fresh life stirs elsewhere. The book created a model for cultural history of an age's mood. Its prose, even in translation, is rich and melancholy. It remains a beloved classic on the medieval mind's last flowering.
jeffers-tamar-1924:
Robinson Jeffers published Tamar and Other Poems in 1924, the book that made his name. Jeffers wrote long narrative poems set on the wild coast near Carmel, California. The title poem, Tamar, is a tragedy of passion and doom in a farming family. Its story involves forbidden love, ghosts, and fire.

Other poems in the book also deal with violence, desire, and fate. Jeffers used loose, rolling lines and stark images of hawks, rocks, and sea. He saw human pride as small against the vast natural world. The book shocked readers and won strong praise. It marks the start of his major career.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-24:
Jogues goes back to the Mohawk in Volume 24, from 1898. Thwaites covers Quebec and the Hurons across 1643 and 1644 in this book. The priest returns in peace to the very men who tortured him.

He carries the cross this time, not a sword, by choice. Old wounds mark his hands as he greets his former captors. The act strikes many readers as the most Christlike in the set. Priests at Quebec weigh the risk and bless his hard road. Readers know how his story ends, and they read on in awe. His courage shames and lifts them at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-bar-abba-1: Abba bar Abba was a Babylonian amora of the second and third centuries, noted for piety, kindness, and learning. He is known chiefly through his son, Mar Samuel, head of the Academy of Nehardea. For that reason he is almost always called simply Samuel's father. Abba traveled to Palestine and dealt with Judah I, the patriarch. He was a close friend of Judah's pupil Levi bar Sisi. When Levi died, Abba gave the funeral speech in his honor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abel-solomon-be:
Solomon ben Kalman Halevi Abel was a Russian teacher and moral writer, born on March 11, 1857, in the Kovno government. He died at Telsh on October 12, 1886. His work as a teacher at the Yeshibah of Telsh raised that school to the top rank in Lithuania. His fame rests on a book printed after his death.

That book, "Bet Shelomoh," came out at Wilna in 1893. It sums up rabbinical law on business and inheritance, with rules on the Sabbatical and Jubilee years and on almsgiving besides. It was meant for plain use, in a clean new Hebrew style. Abel stresses the moral side most. Interest taken from non-Jews, though not banned, he treats as a thing that can still stir moral disgust, and so fail a higher test.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abiob-aaron-pro: Aaron Abiob wrote "Shemen ha-Mor," the Oil of Myrrh, a commentary on the Book of Esther. He flourished in Salonica about the year 1540. His work was first printed in that same city, in 1601. That book, that city, and those two dates are the whole of this very brief entry. It gives no teacher, family, post, or other work of his, and it cites a note by Steinschneider in the Jewish Quarterly Review for the name as it is given here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-eli: Abraham ben Eliezer was a commentator, probably a peer of Elijah Mizrahi. He lived in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, probably at Constantinople. He wrote a supercommentary on Rashi's Bible commentary. Only a small piece of it survives in print, covering the weekly portion Mas'ey. It appeared in Jacob Canizal's rare collection of Rashi supercommentaries. Abraham died in 1525, at a very old age, the entry states.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-mes: Abraham ben Meshullam of Modena was a Hebrew scholar. He worked as one of the correctors of the first edition of the Zohar. That edition came out at Mantua in 1558-60. Verses he wrote in praise of the book were printed in its preface. The entry warns that he is often mixed up with Abraham Abigdor ben Meshullam. That other man wrote several philosophical treatises, which are not this scholar's work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abramovich-mikh: Mikhail Solomonovich Abramovich was a Russian poet born at Berditchev in 1859. He was the son of Solomon Abramovich and studied at the Gymnasium of Jitomir. Tied to a revolt, he was banished to Archangel, Samara, and Kazan. He finished his studies in 1887 and worked as a lawyer by 1901. His first poems ran in journals such as "Voskhod." A book of them came out in 1889. The entry says his poems on Judaism and Bible themes stand apart from his less fresh work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-accommodation-o:
Accommodation of the law means easing a law's strict edge to fit new facts of life. The Bible shows the pattern early. Men made unclean by a corpse could not keep Passover on its set day. A second Passover was set for them a month later. King Hezekiah used that same late date when the Temple was not yet made holy in time.

Hillel the Elder made the Prosbul for debts. The Sabbatical year wiped debts clean, so men stopped lending to the poor. His court note kept a debt alive past that year. A second case concerns wives with missing husbands. One witness could prove a death, so the wife could wed again. Rules that need two witnesses were eased for her sake. The close weighs how far this soft path can serve reform in Jewish life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-lazarus-l:
Lazarus Levi Adler was a German rabbi of a time of change. He was born at Unsleben, Bavaria, on November 10, 1810. He died at Wiesbaden on January 5, 1886. His father taught him Bible and Talmud as a boy. He spent five years at a rabbinic school in Gelnhausen. He then heard Talmud talks at Würzburg and read for a degree. He took that degree at Erlangen in the winter of 1833.

In 1840 he was chosen district rabbi of Kissingen. His charge held twenty-four towns. He wrote memos and open letters on the civil place of the Jews in Bavaria. In 1852 he took the chief rabbi post of Hesse, at Cassel. He led the rabbi meet at Cassel and spoke at synods in Leipsic and Augsburg. His last book, of 1878, pleads for wise reform with peace. Its title sets Hillel and Shammai side by side.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agricultural-co:
Agricultural colonies in the Argentine Republic were set up by the Jewish Colonization Association of Paris. Baron and Baroness de Hirsch founded that body and held near all its stock. In August, 1891, the baron bought land for the work. Some 3,000 square leagues cost $1,300,000. In all, more than 17,000,000 acres were got. Settlers from Russia came to farm them.

Two tracts were marked out first. Mauricio lay in Buenos Ayres province. Moïseville lay in Santa Fé. By the end of 1891 the settlers numbered 2,850. Locusts ate the crops, and water ran short. Quarrels with far-off managers shook the whole plan. Some 800 men were sent off to the United States in two years. By October, 1893, just 2,683 souls were left. Since then the counts have grown at a slow, steady pace. A table at the end lists the colonies and their folk, 4,885 in all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aguilar-jacob-d: Jacob de Aguilar was a pupil of Abraham de Fonseca. Fonseca taught at Hamburg. Aguilar served as hakam in Brazil. His post was in one of the Brazilian communities. The date was about 1640. The entry gives no more than these facts. No writings or later life are recorded there. That is the whole of his brief entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-ii-po:
Alexander II. was pope from 1061 to 1073. His family name was Anselmo Baggio, and he was born at Milan. He died on April 20, 1073. Hildebrand proposed his election, and Hildebrand's spirit guided his whole reign. An anti-pope, Honorius II., was set against him, but a council at Mantua deposed the rival.

In spite of his many duties, Alexander gave real thought to the Jews. In all emergencies he stood ready to protect them. In 1063 he praised the Viscount Berengar of Narbonne for stopping an outbreak against them. He also told the bishop of Narbonne to guard them in future. Two years later he rebuked Prince Landulph of Benevento for forcing Jews into baptism. He cited the rule against forced conversion laid down by Gregory the Great.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-algum-or-almug-: Algum, also called Almug, names a tree that no one can now pin down. Some writers take it for coral-wood. Others say brazil-wood or red sandal-wood. The Bible says the wood came from Ophir. One passage instead brings algum trees from Lebanon. The entry weighs both claims with care. Solomon used the wood for stairs and rails. He also used it for harps and other music tools. The entry ends by pointing readers to the main notes on each verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-altaras-david-b: David ben Solomon Altaras was an Italian rabbi and editor. He worked at Venice from 1675 to 1714. He wrote the short Hebrew grammar in a Venice Bible. That Bible came out in 1675-78. He edited a daily prayer-book in 1696. He also made a pointed Mishnah with short notes. That set came out in 1756-60. His will was printed at Venice in 1714.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amos-book-of-14:
Book of Amos is one of the twelve Minor Prophets. It opens with a threat of doom for wrongdoers. Land after land is called to account in turn. Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, and Edom head the list. Ammon, Moab, and Judah come next. At last the charge lands on Israel itself.

God had freed Israel from Egypt, Amos recalls. He had cleared the Amorites from their path. Israel still shut its ears to his prophets. Rich men crush the poor while wives urge them on. Rites and gifts will not save such a land. Visions of locusts, fire, and a plumb line close the book. Words of hope end its last page.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anglo-israelism:
Anglo-Israelism is the theory that the Anglo-Saxon race descends from the Lost Ten Tribes. Its followers hold that the promises made to Israel will be kept for England and America. The entry puts their numbers at 2,000,000 across England and the United States.

Most believers stayed inside the Church of England, holding the theory as an extra pious opinion, not a sect. The entry traces the movement to Richard Brothers, who in 1794 claimed descent from David and a coming reveal as prince of the Hebrews. His 1822 book tied the Saxon invasion to the lost tribes. J. Wilson's work of 1845 then set the theory on its lasting basis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antonio-de-vero: Antonio de Verona, also called Maria Antonio, was an Italian Jew who lived in England from 1623 to 1625. He seems to have taught, most likely Hebrew, at King's College, Cambridge. The college books record a grant of two pounds to him in 1623-24. Queen Henrietta Maria gave him a letter of recommendation to Oxford University on January 19, 1625. He is likely the same Jew who held a pension of forty pounds at Cambridge, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arta-or-larta-1:
Arta, chief city of the Greek district of Arthamania, stands on the river Arta about 7 miles from its mouth. It is the ancient Ambracia. In 1890 it held 4,328 people, of whom about 200 were Jews. Little is known of the community's early days. An old synagogue called of the Corfiotes hints that Jews from Corfu settled there after Roger I of Sicily seized that island.

Benjamin of Tudela, about 1170, counted 100 Jews at Arta under leaders named Solomon and Heracles. After the expulsion from Spain, Jews from Calabria, Apulia, and Sicily formed congregations and set up a college. Its early heads included Rabbi Caleb and Benjamin ben Mattathias, who died before 1539 and wrote Binyan Zeeb. He traded as well as studied, and argued law with rabbis in Venice, Constantinople, Salonica, and Corfu.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-ben-david:
Asher ben David, a son of Abraham ben David of Posquieres, flourished about the middle of the thirteenth century. He studied under his uncle, Isaac the Blind. The entry counts him among the earliest writers of the Cabala. Two works of his are named, one explaining the thirteen attributes of God in Exodus chapter 34, the other explaining the four-letter name of God and the Sefirot.

Only small parts of these works were ever printed, so their exact relation stays unclear. He seems to have tried to square the ten Sefirot with the thirteen attributes named in the Talmud. The ten Sefirot he matched to the ten spheres of the philosophers. The thirteen attributes he derived from the three middle Sefirot, which he called fundamental principles: love, justice, and mercy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asphar-2024: Asphar was a pool in the wilderness of Tekoah. Jonathan and Simon Maccabeus pitched their tents there when they fled before the army of Bacchides, as First Maccabees chapter 9 tells. Josephus tells the same flight. Where the pool stood is not certain. The evidence, the entry judges, points toward matching it with the modern Bir-Selhut, though Buhl's geography of ancient Palestine is noted against the match.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auerbach-menahe:
Menahem Mendel Auerbach was an Austrian rabbi, banker, and commentator. He was born in Vienna at the start of the seventeenth century. He died at Krotoschin, Posen, on July 8, 1689. Both his father and his mother's father belonged to the Vienna ghetto families. He studied under Joel Särkes and other noted teachers.

Auerbach served for years as a judge of the Cracow community, while running a banking business with his brother. He later returned to Vienna. The expulsion of the Jews from Vienna in 1670 drove him out. He became rabbi at Rausnitz in Moravia, then in 1673 at Krotoschin. There he served sixteen years as rabbi and district head, and he built a school that drew students from across Poland. His commentary on part of the Shulḥan 'Aruk, "'Aṭeret Zekenim," was printed at Dyhernfurth in 1720.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azriel-ezra-ben:
Azriel, also called Ezra, was a founder of the speculative Cabala. He was born at Gerona in 1160 and died in 1238. Men called him the Saint. Drawn to the mystic studies spreading in Spain, he went young to southern France. There he studied under Isaac the Blind, the famed cabalist of Posquières.

Azriel then traveled across Spain preaching the Cabala. He tried to win the philosophers over and failed, as he admits in his own preface. Thinkers, he says, believe only what logic can prove. He came home to Gerona and founded a school. Naḥmanides learned the Cabala there from him. His works include a commentary on the Ten Sefirot, written as questions and answers. Two other commentaries of his long went under Naḥmanides' name. His system rests on God as En Sof, the Endless One, from whom all things flow.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baena-juan-alfo:
Juan Alfonso de Baena was a Spanish troubadour of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, born at Baena in Cordova. He worked as a notarial secretary at the court of John II. His fame rests on a song-book he gathered, the "Cancionero del Judino Juan Alfonso de Baena." It holds poems from the courts of John I, Henry III, and John II of Castile.

The entry calls that book the oldest Castilian court song-book and the only one of its kind. It holds work by fifty-five authors of the Sevillan school, friars, knights, masters of theology, and others. Their verses picture court life and were meant to amuse the king. The book was first printed at Madrid in 1851.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bamberg-samuel-:
Samuel of Bamberg was a halakist and liturgist who lived about 1220. Born in Metz, he was taught by his father, Baruch ben Samuel, and by Eliezer b. Samuel of Metz. He became one of the best known German Talmudic scholars of his day. Meïr of Rothenburg was his pupil and, it seems, his kin. Of his private life nothing is known, beyond two daughters, Yiska and Gentil.

As a legal scholar Samuel leaned toward a liberal reading of the Law where no direct Bible command stood in the way. His famous pupil sometimes called him to account for it, yet praised him in verse. No book of his own on Halakah survives. His rulings live in the works of others. The entry clears him of two false credits, then quotes his saying that a gift for teaching the young outranks a gift for keeping up the synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barges-jean-jos:
Jean Joseph Leandre Bargès, honorary canon of Notre Dame of Paris, was an abbé and Orientalist born in 1810 at Auriol and died in 1896 near Marseilles. From 1835 he belonged to the Asiatic Society of Paris. He lectured on Arabic at Marseilles, then traveled widely in Algeria. In 1842 he became professor of Hebrew in the faculty of theology at the Sorbonne. He held the chair until the faculty was abolished in 1885.

Bargès put his Arabic at the service of Hebrew literature. With Beer Goldberg he published Judah b. Koreish's letter to the Jews of Fez in 1857. His other works include the Book of Ruth with two French translations (1854), "Les Samaritains de Naplouse" (1855), and Japheth b. Heli's Psalms in 1861. He also wrote on Hebron and Abraham's tomb, on a Hebrew-Samaritan Pentateuch fragment, and on six Phenician inscriptions. A study of Marseilles' Arabic inscriptions came in 1889.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bashyazi-moses-:
Moses ben Elijah Bashyazi was a Karaite scholar born at Constantinople in 1537. He was a great-grandson of Elijah Bashyazi. At sixteen he already showed deep learning and skill in foreign tongues, and he traveled in Palestine and Syria to gather old manuscripts.

Moses died in 1555, yet he left many works. Four survive in manuscript. They deal with barred marriages, the Passover rite, the history of the Karaite split, and points of belief. The entry names the cities where copies are kept. His travels were made, the entry says, for the love of knowledge alone, not for office or gain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beddington-maur:
Maurice Beddington was an English communal worker born in 1821, who died at Carshalton on Sept. 9, 1898. All his life he stayed tied to London's Jewish institutions. He helped found the Board of Guardians and chaired its inquiry board.

Beddington also helped found the Central Synagogue and sat on the United Synagogue council for life. He gave freely to the Jews' Hospital and Orphan Asylum as its vice-president. Beyond Jewish work, he sat as a justice of the peace for Surrey and for London. He also served the Anglo-Jewish Association and societies for the blind and for the spread of religious knowledge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belle-assez-or-:
Belle-Assez, also called Rachel, was a daughter of Rashi, the famed commentator who lived from 1040 to 1105. She married a rabbi named Eliezer. Like her sisters, she was well versed in Hebrew and in rabbinic books, the entry reports.

An old claim held that she or a sister wrote down Rashi's legal answers. Zunz showed that claim rests on a misreading and points to a grandson instead. A ruling by her nephew Jacob Tam shows her marriage was unhappy. She gained a divorce from her husband. That claim about the daughters was held for a time by the historian Graetz, the entry reports.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benedict-xiii-p:
Pedro de Luna, called Benedict XIII, was an antipope born in Aragon about 1334. Elected on Sept. 28, 1394, he was deposed by the Council of Constance in 1415 and died at Peñiscola in 1424. The entry stresses his drive to convert the Jews and the suffering it caused.

He summoned Jewish leaders to a forced debate at Tortosa, which ran from Feb. 6, 1413, to Nov. 12, 1414. His bull of 1414 then banned Talmud study, seized copies, and barred Jews from offices and crafts. It also forced badge wearing and attendance at Christian sermons three times a year. Two converts had urged him on. One was the former rabbi Pablo de Santa Maria. The other was the physician Geronimo de Santa Fé. Both claimed they could prove his case from the Bible and the Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berachah-blessi: Berachah is a name that the entry treats in two separate senses. First, it was a Benjamite who came to David and joined his forces at Ziklag, as First Chronicles records. Second, it was a valley where Jehoshaphat and his men gathered after despoiling the Ammonites and Moabites. That valley is identified with the modern Berekut, west of Tekoa. The entry is a short double identification, one person and one place, each with its biblical citation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernhardt-marti: Martin Bernhardt, a German nerve doctor and medical author, was born at Potsdam on April 10, 1844. He studied at Berlin under Virchow and Traube and took his degree in 1867. Posts at Königsberg and at the Charité in Berlin followed. War service with the Landwehr in the Franco-German war won him a medal for bravery under fire. From 1872 he taught medicine at Berlin as a specialist in nerve disease. He also edited a central medical journal from 1885 and wrote on skin feeling and brain tumors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bethesda-3224: Bethesda was a pool in Jerusalem. John is the only source that mentions it. He places it by the sheep market. That puts it north of the Temple-hill. Its exact spot cannot be fixed firmly. Early writers describe a double pond. Its water was reddish in color. Five colonnades surrounded it. That matches two ponds near the Sisters of Zion. In the Middle Ages another pond was favored. It lay by the French church of St. Anne.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-births-3324:
Births compares birth-rates among Jews and Christians. Its tables cover many lands and decades. At first sight Jews show fewer births per thousand. Algeria and Hungary are exceptions in the table. The entry calls the result surprising. Jewish population still grows faster almost everywhere. Fewer deaths under age five explain much of it.

That survival swells the share of children. Rates reckoned on all people thus dip. Later tables treat the sex ratio at birth. Boys predominate among Jews more strongly. Russia shows 129 boys to 105 girls. St. Petersburg shows an even wider gap. Scholars' proposed causes remain unproved.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blumenfeld-aron: Aron Wolff Blumenfeld was a German composer. He was born at Kurnik, Posen, on February 29, 1828. In 1846 he went to Berlin. Rungenhagen taught him composition there. He settled as teacher and composer. His opera "Künstlerleben" is his largest work. A cantata was first performed in 1851. His piano pieces are mostly salon morceaux. Titles include "La Fée Dansante" and "L'Espérance." His "Blumenlese" is a curious compilation. It arranges concert music for six to twenty instruments. Ninety-six separate books hold its contents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brainin-simon-3:
Simon Brainin was a Russian physician born at Riga, Livonia, on July 15, 1854. He studied medicine at Dorpat and Berlin. He served as physician to the Jewish community of Riga and as a director of it.

Brainin sat on a government committee on Jewish rights in Riga in 1885. In 1892 he went as a delegate to a rabbinical conference at St. Petersburg. In 1895 he emigrated to New York and practiced medicine there. His books include a Hebrew work on popular medicine, printed at Wilna in 1883. A guide for physicians and a study of kefyr followed in the next three years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-briviesca-not-b: Briviesca, the ancient Virovesca, is a city in Old Castile, not far from Burgos. A Jewish community dwelt there and was taxed 11,700 maravedis in 1290. Ferdinand III. gave the taxes of several named Jews there to a Burgos convent for ever. In the civil war that followed, Jews defended the city walls bravely. Attack from the rear killed or captured them all, one account says. Of two hundred heads of families, none stayed alive in that telling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-california-3924:
California, a Pacific coast state, has no firm record of Jewish life before 1849. In that gold year large numbers of Jews rushed to the new fields. They came from the eastern and southern states and from as far as Australia. First services met on Kippur Day 1849 in a San Francisco tent, with about ten people present.

Mining camps across Placer, Amador, and Yuba counties formed congregations and aid societies. When many camps failed, their Jews moved into San Francisco, whose community dated from 1850. The long entry then follows cities, synagogues, and charities across the state. Its tail notes Jewish officers in the Spanish American War era and in the state militia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carcassonne-ado: Adolphe Joseph Carcassonne was a French poet born at Marseilles in 1826. He died on Sept. 22, 1891. The entry is almost all a list of his works in print order. Poems came first, in a first volume of 1852 and a later one of 1869. Stage works fill most of the list: an opera, dramas in verse, and a siege play on Marseilles. Much of his later output was theater for the young, with short comedies and pieces for girls and teens. One verse piece marks the loss of Alsace in 1871.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castelli-david-:
David Castelli, an Italian scholar, was born at Leghorn, in Tuscany, on Dec. 30, 1836, and died in 1901. He trained at the rabbinical college of Leghorn. From 1857 to 1863 he taught Hebrew and Italian in the Jewish schools there. He then served as secretary of the Jewish congregation in Pisa.

From January 1876 until his death, Castelli held the chair of Hebrew at an institute of higher studies in Florence. His many books, all in Italian, treat Ecclesiastes, Talmudic legends, the Messiah in Jewish thought, and biblical poetry. He wrote a history of the Israelites in two volumes, issued at Milan in 1887-88. Later works cover the Song of Songs, the Book of Job, and a short political and literary history of the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chamberlain-hou: Houston Stewart Chamberlain, an Anglo-German musical critic and antisemitic writer, was born on September 9, 1855, at Portsmouth, England. Schooled in France and in science at Geneva, he settled in Austria and taught philosophy at Vienna. His chief work, issued at Munich in 1899, reads all history as a clash between Aryans and Semites. It casts the Jew as a type of the Semite and fears Jewish world rule. It even denies the Jewish origin of Jesus, whose character he admired.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cloud-4424:
Cloud gets a word study first. Hebrew holds five terms for it, from the everyday anan to the heavy dark arafel. The entry gives chapter and verse for each and notes which books favor which word. Poetic books lean on ab and shahak, the last often standing in for the heavens themselves.

Palestine's climate made clouds matter. Rain fell from October to May, then skies stayed clear for months. A rain cloud rose slowly from the sea in the west before the downpour. Later sections gather cloud images in speech and lore: clouds over Sarah's tent, a cloud that carried Moses upward, and rabbinic wordplay tying each Hebrew term to a trait. Glory clouds at death close the survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohn-leopold-45:
Leopold Cohn, a German author and philologist, was born on Jan. 14, 1856, at Zempelburg in West Prussia. He took his philosophy doctorate at Breslau in 1878. He became a privat-docent there in 1884, a librarian in 1889, and gained the professor title in 1897.

Greek literature fills his first book list, on Aristophanes of Byzantium, the Plato scholia, and the proverb collectors. His Jewish work centers on Philo of Alexandria. He edited Philo's work on the making of the world in 1889. With Paul Wendland he then issued Philo's surviving works in four volumes from 1896 to 1902. Essays on the latest Philo research and on Greek word study close the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cozbi-deceiving: Cozbi, whose name is glossed as deceiving, was a Midianitish woman. The entry gives only a few facts about her. She was a daughter of Zur, the leader of a tribe. She was put to death along with the Israelite Zimri. Phinehas carried out the killing. The entry cites Numbers, chapter twenty-five, verses 14 to 18, for the account. No family story, speech, or further act of hers is recorded here. Readers get her parentage, her partner in the story, and her death, and nothing more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cypros-4824: Cypros was a woman of a noble Arabian family. About 75 B.C. she married Antipater, the Jewish governor. She bore him five children: Phasaelus, Herod, Josephus, Pheroras, and Salome. When Herod had to go to Augustus, he placed his mother and sister in his brother's care at Masada. His wife Mariamne went elsewhere, since she looked down on them. Herod built a fortified retreat near Jericho and named it Cypros for his mother. That stronghold was destroyed at the start of the Jewish war under Nero.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-4924: David was an Oriental rabbi who lived at Mosul toward the end of the twelfth century. He was a nephew of the exilarch Daniel ben Solomon, who died in 1175 leaving no male offspring. David claimed the office of exilarch against his cousin Samuel, but Samuel ben Ali ha-Levi stepped in ahead of both and obtained the post. Some writers identify this David with David ben Hodaya, exilarch of Mosul. The traveler Pethahiah reported finding the nasi David at Mosul in 1176.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-disna-5224: Disna was a town in the government of Wilna, Russia. The census of 1897 counted 6,739 people there, about 5,600 of them Jews. The entry says most of those Jews worked as traders, while about 265 were day-laborers. A few families farmed rented land, and Jews owned some 437 deciatines nearby. The town had the usual charities and a Jewish public school for boys and girls, with 170 pupils on its register.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-edel-judah-low-:
Judah Löw ben Moses ha-Levi Edel was a Russian preacher born at Zamoscz, in the Lublin government. He studied under Elijah of Wilna, the famed Gaon. He showed great gift as a preacher. He was also a Hebraist and a sound Talmudic scholar. He died at Slonim in 1827.

Edel's first book was a short Hebrew grammar for beginners, printed at Lemberg in 1793. His Afike Yehudah gathered his sermons, though only one volume came out, in 1802. It held twenty-four sermons. Two commentaries of his treat the laws of purity in Maimonides and the Mishnah. His son Solomon later edited his essays on the Haggadah at Ostrog in 1835.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-b-abina: Eleazar ben Abina was a Palestinian haggadist of the fourth century C.E. He belonged to the fourth amoraic generation. He was a younger peer of Aha the Third, whose sayings he repeats. A later teacher, Yudan, in turn reports sayings in his name. The entry gives one of his homilies in full. In it he argues that keeping the Sabbath equals all other commandments joined. He builds the proof from all three parts of the Bible. He cites Exodus, Ezekiel, and Nehemiah in turn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-ben-sam: Eliezer ben Samson was a rabbi and prayer poet of Cologne. He lived in the twelfth century. He was kin to the tosafist Eliezer ben Nathan. He studied at Speyer and at Mayence. He sat among the leaders of a great synod of rabbis. That synod drew 150 rabbis under Jacob Tam and Rashbam. Two of his prayer poems are still in hand. One is for the Feast of Tabernacles and runs to seven stanzas. The other, in Aramaic, runs to thirty-two verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-embezzlement-57:
Embezzlement is the false use of goods held in trust. A man turns to his own ends what was left in his care. It differs from theft in one key way, the entry says. In theft the holding itself breaks the law from the start. The Law of Moses treats the crime in a narrow case. A man denies goods left with him and swears to the lie. He must pay back the whole sum if found out. He must add one-fifth of its value on top. He must also bring a ram as a guilt gift.

The Mishnah takes the topic up in one of its tractates. It sets rules for keepers who swear false oaths on a loss. If he swears to a loss that would clear him, he is caught. The entry works through those cases in set order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-evora-5924:
Evora was a Portuguese city and seat of the rabbi of the Alemtejo province. In 1490 its Jews met a royal bride-elect in solemn march and gave her cows, sheep, and hens. Seven years later King Manuel decreed there that all Jewish children under fourteen be seized on Easter Sunday. They were to be scattered and raised as Christians.

In April 1506 the crowd tore down Evora's synagogue. Many rich Marranos lived there when the Inquisition was proclaimed on October 22, 1536. Its work began in the city in 1542. Among the first brought to the stake was David Reubeni. The entry rests on Kayserling's history of the Jews in Portugal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-farissol-judah-: Judah Farissol was an Italian mathematician and astronomer who worked at Mantua at the end of the fifteenth century. In 1499 he wrote Iggeret Sefirah, a description of the astronomical sphere with diagrams. That book and its date are the whole factual core of the entry. No birth or death dates, teachers, or other works are named. The entry rests on two sources: Steinschneider on Jewish literature and Neubauer's catalogue of Hebrew manuscripts in the Bodleian Library. A reader learns his field, his city, his century, and his one book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-finzi-6124:
Finzi is an old Italian family whose name likely comes from Pinehas, through the Latin Finea. The earliest known bearers helped set up the first Jewish money-lending office in Padua in 1369. Sons of that line bought land in 1380. One of them may be the Isaac Finzi who spoke for his congregation at Bologna in 1416. A family Bible held the line's genealogy.

Branches spread to many Italian towns over the centuries. Members served as rabbis, bankers, printers, and poets. One Mantua physician of the fifteenth century also won note as a mathematician and astronomer. His tables of the length of days were printed at Mantua. Later Finzis taught noted pupils and wrote responsa, sermons, and legal works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-franklin-jacob-:
Jacob Abraham Franklin was an English journalist and philanthropist born at Portsmouth in 1809. He died on August 3, 1877. On retiring from business he moved to London and took an active part in its Jewish affairs. He set up a weekly paper, the first organ of the Anglo-Jewish community. In it he stated his views against the Reform movement of 1842. He spoke for the Manchester community at the Board of Deputies. He helped found the Anglo-Jewish Association.

Franklin cared deeply for Jewish schooling. He worked to set up a Jewish board school in London. He also won a share of state grants for the Jewish schools. He read papers on decimal coinage and on education. At his death he left most of his property for school projects. Works on natural religion and Jewish history came out under his fund.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fundam-isaac-64: Isaac Fundam, a Spanish author and publisher living in Amsterdam about 1723, issued a volume of plays and pleasant pieces there that year. He also wrote a treatise on the world from its start up to Moses the prophet. That work survives only in manuscript. With Aaron Hezekiah Querido he edited a communal order book. In 1724 he printed a catalogue of Spanish and Portuguese books and manuscripts at Amsterdam.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gambling-10124:
Gambling means playing games, above all games of chance, for money. Ancient Israel names no such games and made no rule against them. Dice play came in with foreign ways late in the Second Temple age. Rabbis hated the new habit. The Mishnah barred a gambler from giving witness in court. They classed gambling as a form of robbery, though losses could not be sued for in court.

Dice, lotteries, bets, and cards spread among Jews in medieval Europe. Towns passed many bans against them. Even scholars fell to the habit. Venice rabbis in 1628 banned card play for six years under pain of the ban. Play for pastime, though, was allowed, even on the Sabbath for women and children.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gaster-moses-65:
Moses Gaster, haham of the Spanish and Portuguese congregation in London, was born in Bucharest on September 16, 1856. He took a degree at home in 1874, then studied at Breslau. There he won a doctorate in 1878 and rabbinic leave to teach in 1881. His great work is a Rumanian reader and word book that spans the tongue from its dawn to 1830.

Rumania drove him out in 1885, and he settled in England. In 1887 he became haham in London. He led the two hundredth year feast of Bevis Marks Synagogue. His books treat Jewish folk lore, an old magic text, and chronicles. He also stood high in the Zionist cause and sat as vice president at the first Basel Congress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gershon-ben-sol: Gershon ben Solomon ben Asher, a French Talmudist who flourished at Beziers in the twelfth century, wrote a case-law work called Sefer ha-Shalmon. His son Samuel finished that book after him. Isaac ben Sheshet quotes it in his Responsa. A second title, Sefer ha-Shulhan, may name the same work. Gershon also left a set of legal replies, cited by Abudarham. The entry records no birth or death dates for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gottheil-gustav:
Gustav Gottheil was an American rabbi. He was born at Pinne in Prussian Posen on May 28, 1827. He died in New York city on April 15, 1903. He studied under Plessner, Holdheim, Zunz, and Steinschneider. In 1860 he left Berlin to serve progressive Judaism in new fields. Manchester's Reform congregation took him as rabbi for thirteen years.

In 1873 New York's Temple Emanu-El chose him as assistant. He soon became its senior rabbi. He rebuilt its religious school and helped found a theological training school. His 1886 hymn-book was the first Jewish one printed in America. It fed the later Union Hymnal. In 1889 he started the first Sisterhood of Personal Service. He also helped found the Jewish Publication Society and the Federation of American Zionists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hagege-abraham-: Abraham Hagege was chief rabbi at Tunis, where he died in 1880. His entry is short and rests on his one book. After his death, Israel Zeitoun of Tunis and Aaron ben Simon of Jerusalem brought out his notes on most of the treatises of the Babylonian Talmud. The work came out at Jerusalem in 1884 under the title "Zar'o shel Abraham." Nothing of his early life, training, or other writing is given here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haman-the-agagi:
Haman the Agagite, son of Hammedatha, was chief minister of King Ahasuerus. His name marks him as a descendant of Agag, king of the Amalekites. Stung because Mordecai would not bow to him, he resolved to wipe out the Jews of the whole kingdom. Lots set the day: the 13th of Adar. He offered the king ten thousand talents of silver for the right, and letters went out to every province.

Esther undid him. At her banquet Haman, sure of favor, built a gallows for Mordecai. That night the king's mood turned, and Haman had to lead Mordecai through Shushan in royal dress, crying his honor. At the second banquet Esther exposed the plot, and Haman was hanged on his own gallows. His house went to Esther, and his ten sons were executed. The entry adds the Talmud's legends: Haman as astrologer, as barber, and as Mordecai's onetime slave.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hannathon-7224: Hannathon was a city of Zebulun. Its one verse, Joshua xix, 14, puts it on the tribe's northern boundary. It lay about midway between the Sea of Galilee and the valley of Jiphthah-el. That is the entire entry. It offers no history. It offers no later mention. It offers no modern site. The name survives in this single boundary notice. The entry's work is only to fix the town's rough position from the one verse that names it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hast-marcus-732:
Marcus Hast, born at Warsaw in 1840, was a London cantor and composer. He went to Germany in 1864 to study music. At Breslau he became cantor of the chief Orthodox synagogue. There he taught many pupils who later won fame as cantors. In 1871 he moved to London as chief cantor of the Great Synagogue.

Hast printed many settings of Hebrew melodies and much music of his own. His works include a sacred cantata, an oratorio, and a piece on the death of Moses sung at Queen's Hall in 1897. Another work marked the fall of Jerusalem in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hazor-7424:
Hazor was a fortified city on high ground above Lake Merom, between Ramah and Kadesh. Its king Jabin led a league of kings against Israel. Joshua beat the allied force and burned the city to the ground. The entry calls Hazor the head of all those kingdoms.

The city rose again. A second Jabin ruled there in the days of Deborah and Barak, and Israel fell under his power for a time. Hazor later went to the tribe of Naphtali. In the end, Tiglath-pileser carried its people off to Assyria. Four lesser places of the same name are also listed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heldai-7524: Heldai is the name of two men in the Bible. The first was a captain in the Temple service for the twelfth month in David's time. He came from Netophah and traced his line to Othniel. A parallel list calls him Heled instead. The second Heldai returned from exile with Zerubbabel. With others he gave Zechariah gold and silver for making crowns as memorials. In one verse his name shifts to Helem. Other old versions give still other forms of it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herz-henri-7624:
Henri Herz, born at Vienna on Jan. 6, 1806, was an Austrian pianist trained first by his father and Hünten at Coblenz. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1816 and won its first piano prize. Concerts by Moscheles in 1820 shaped his brilliant style.

Herz toured widely in Europe and, from 1845 to 1851, through the Americas. In Mexico he wrote a hymn that became its national anthem, the entry says. Back in Paris he taught at the Conservatoire and built pianos that won first prize in 1855. About 200 pieces by him were once popular but were seldom played later. He died at Paris on Jan. 5, 1888.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-alphonse: Alphonse Hirsch, born in Paris in 1843, was a French painter and pupil of Meissonier and Bonnat. He began with sketching and etching, leaving many fine etchings. His chief merit, the entry says, was as a colorist. He showed work at the annual salons. Seven of his best paintings are listed by French title. His portraits include a chief rabbi of France, dated 1877, and writers dated 1878 to 1884. He died in Paris on July 15, 1884.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-holofernes-holo:
Holofernes was a general of Nebuchadnezzar in the apocryphal Book of Judith. He was killed at Bethulia, as Judith tells it. His name seems Persian in origin, the entry notes. Scholars have tried to link him to several Cappadocian figures of the same name. No single link is settled here.

As Judith tells it, Holofernes led 120,000 foot and 12,000 horse to punish the earth. He seized Bethulia's wells to force surrender. Judith visited his camp, feasted with him, and cut off his head once he was drunk. His army then fled in disorder before a Jewish attack. A shorter Hebrew version swaps in Seleucus, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hospitality-692:
Hospitality in Jewish law and life is the theme of this long article. Bible law guards the sojourner from oppression and deceit and commands love for him. He shares in festivals and tithes, and one law covers native and stranger alike. God himself is said to love the stranger.

Stories show the virtue in practice. Abraham feeds three strangers, Lot risks all for guests, and the Shunammite woman keeps a furnished room for Elisha. Hosts washed guests' feet, fed their animals, and guarded their safety. Rab Huna opened his door at meals and called in the hungry. Later ages built lodging houses for poor travelers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hull-7924:
Hull is a seaport in Yorkshire, England. In 1901 it held over 241,753 people, about 2,500 of them Jews. The first trace of Jews there comes late in the eighteenth century. They took over a Catholic chapel wrecked in the Gordon riots of 1780 for a synagogue.

Splits and reunions shaped the community. One congregation built a synagogue in Robinson row in 1826 and moved to Osborne street in 1903. Russian immigration brought a second synagogue in 1886 and a Western Synagogue in 1903. Charities included a ladies' benevolent society from 1861 and a girls' school from 1863. Many migrants passed through Hull on the road to Liverpool.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-shu-aib-joe: Joel ibn Shu'aib was a rabbi, preacher, and commentator of the fifteenth century, born in Aragon and later living at Tudela. His sermon book, arranged by the weekly Sabbath readings, was written in 1469 and printed at Venice in 1577. He wrote on Lamentations at Tudela in 1480. That note appeared in print with Galante's work on the same book. He also commented on Job, on Canticles, and on the Psalms. His son Samuel prefaced the Psalms volume, printed at Salonica in 1568 or 1569.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-tyrnau-82:
Isaac Tyrnau was a Hungarian rabbi and ritualist of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. He studied under Abraham Klausner of Vienna and R. Shalom of Neustadt. A schoolfellow of his was Jacob Mölin, the MaHaRiL. Grätz concluded that he died before 1427. David Gans, however, cites him as still living in 1460, and the entry leaves the two reports side by side.

Like his teachers, Isaac recorded the customs of communities that used the Ashkenazic rite. His book, the "Minhagim le-Kol ha-Shanah," was printed at Venice in 1616 and also appeared in German. Attached to it is his own treatise on morals, the "Orhot Hayyim," in 132 sections. Mordecai Jaffa quoted him at the end of the "Lebush" on Orah Hayyim. An 1857 story even made Isaac and his daughter its heroes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ishmael-b-elish:
Ishmael b. Elisha was a tanna of the first and second centuries, from a wealthy priestly family of Upper Galilee. As a youth the Romans carried him off. Joshua b. Hananiah bought his freedom and brought him home, and a close friendship grew between them; Joshua called him brother. The entry dwells on his gentle temper. He clothed poor maidens well and dowered them so they could marry.

Ishmael sat in the Sanhedrin at Jabneh and followed it to Usha, though he lived at Kefar Aziz. He built a system of halakic reasoning that ran beside Akiba's and was judged the more logical. He held that the Torah speaks in the language of man, so a spare word alone cannot ground a big ruling. He also taught early marriage even under Roman rule, asking how a man could teach his sons' sons if he waited.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israelitische-w: The Israelitische Wochenschrift was a weekly journal published at Breslau and later at Magdeburg. Its first number appeared on Jan. 5, 1870, and its last toward the close of 1894. A. Treuenfels edited it first, and M. Rahmer after him. Three supplements came with it: a family paper, a literary paper, and a homiletic supplement. Its theological position was conservative, the entry notes. The journal's full title promised coverage of religious and social interests.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-judah:
Jacob ben Judah, called Hazzan of London, was an English codifier of the thirteenth century. In 1287 he wrote the "Ez Hayyim," a ritual code in two parts of sixty and forty-six sections, covering the whole field of Halakah. He follows Maimonides' Mishneh Torah most of the way. He also used the "Halakot Gedolot," Amram's Siddur, Moses of Coucy, Alfasi, and the tosafists.

The entry calls the "Ez Hayyim" the chief literary work of an English Jew before the Expulsion. It preserves the rite the Jews of England actually used in his day. The manuscript, once Wagenseil's, now sits in the town library at Leipsic. Only one section has been printed, in an edition by H. Adler. A few verses of Jacob's own also survive, the entry notes in passing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-of-chart: Joseph of Chartres, also called Joseph b. Asher, was a French poet of laments born in the second half of the twelfth century. He was a pupil of R. Tam and of Rashbam. A great-nephew's book tells of his sharp answer to a monk who asked why God showed Himself in a bush and not a tree. Joseph replied that no crucifix can be made from a bush. He wrote an elegy on the killing of the Jews of York in 1191.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ben-simeo: Judah ben Simeon ben Pazzi, also called Judah b. Pazzi, was a Palestinian amora and haggadist of the start of the fourth century. He often passes on sayings in the names of his father, Joshua b. Levi, Johanan, and Simeon b. Lakish. In his own tales he liked parables. One tells of a wolf that seized a kid and a strange dog that fought it off. The wolf asks why the dog barks, since nothing of its own was taken. So, Judah said, was Balak toward Israel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kiera-esther-43:
Esther Kiera was a Jewish favorite of the sultana Baffa. Baffa was the wife of Murad III and the mother of Mohammed III. Kiera, the widow of Elias Chandali, died in 1600. Under Baffa's shield she gained great weight at court. A firman of 1618 still confirmed her grants to her grandchildren.

Through Kiera, many posts and deals were arranged. Envoys of the European powers sought her help for favors. She also aided Jews hit by riot and fire. She paid for the printing of Hebrew books. Her dealings, though, bred hate, and some rested on bribes. In 1600 mutinous soldiers seized her and her sons at the palace. They killed them and nailed her severed limbs to the doors of men she had advanced.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-krochmal-nachma:
Nachman Kohen Krochmal, an Austrian philosopher and historian born at Brody on Feb. 17, 1785, died at Tarnopol on July 31, 1840. Married at barely fourteen, he lived with his wife's family at Zolkiev and studied on his own. He read Maimonides, then German philosophy, Latin, French, Arabic, and Syriac. Overwork broke his health in 1808.

One Hebrew book carries Krochmal's fame. Moreh Nebuke ha-Zeman, printed at Lemberg in 1851 after his death, runs to seventeen chapters. It divides Jewish history into three epochs tied to seeking God. Later chapters treat Bible books, tradition, and the growth of Halakah and Haggadah. The entry calls the book a true guide for students of Jewish science in the nineteenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-landsberger-hug: Hugo Landsberger, a German novelist who wrote as Hans Land, was born at Berlin on Aug. 25, 1861. His first novel appeared at Dresden in 1891. A joint play followed in 1893, and that year his novel Die Richterin made his first success, reaching a sixth edition the next year. More novels treat mother right, modern love, and mine life. In 1898 he founded a weekly journal whose first number came out that October. Two later novels are dated 1899 and 1900. The entry lists no family or death facts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-leone-9824: Leone Levi, an Italian author and journalist, was born at Nizza-Monferrato in 1823. He died at Turin on Nov. 8, 1876. He was schooled at the Collegio Foà at Vercelli. He was a man of affairs and a lawyer by trade. Still, he found time for letters. His chief work was "Lampi della Società Contemporanea," a faithful picture of modern life. His "Massime a Casaccio" and his last work, "Il Tempio di Torino," both ran in the "Corriere Israelitico" of Triest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lewinstein-jose: Joseph Lewinstein, a Russian rabbi and author, was born at Lublin in 1840. He came from a family of rabbis and Talmudists. At twenty he became rabbi of Karol. In 1868 he moved to Zaklikov, and since 1875 he has served at Serotzk. His books include commentaries on Talmud tracts and on Genesis, and a note on the Passover Haggadah. His "Dor Dor we-Dorshaw" gathers 6,600 names of Israel's great ones, with the dates of their deaths. His family-tree articles are prized as a source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lissa-called-fo:
Lissa, once called Polnisch Lissa, was a town in Prussia that became a town in 1534. Jews settled there soon after with leave from Count Andreas Lescynski. A first privilege is dated March 10, 1626, and a synagogue and cemetery already stood there.

Jews at Lissa traded and worked in many crafts, from tailoring and gold work to dyeing and tanning. They suffered in Poland's wars and in Cossack attacks. In its best days the town held between 4,000 and 5,000 Jews and a famed school that drew students from far away. By 1904 about 1,200 Jews remained.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ma-arabi-nahum-:
Nahum Ma'arabi, a Moroccan Hebrew poet and translator, is the subject of a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His surname means the western one, or the Moroccan. He worked in the thirteenth century. His poems survive only in Moroccan collections, and two liturgical pieces were printed by L. Dukes.

The article values him most as a translator from Arabic into Hebrew. He rendered Maimonides' Letter to Yemen under the title Petah Tikwah, adding a preface in verse. He also translated a commentary on the Sefer Yezirah and Joseph ibn Zaddik's Microcosmos. A fourth translation covered Saadia's notes on the thirteen rules of Rabbi Ishmael. Some of these works are anonymous, and the entry weighs the evidence for his hand in them. It preserves the name of a poet who carried Arabic Jewish thought into Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malaga-10324:
Malaga, a Spanish seaport on the Mediterranean, is given a Jewish history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Said to be founded by the Phoenicians, it was a trading town under Rome with Jews from a very early date. Under Moorish rule its Jews enjoyed full equality. In Samuel ibn Nagdelah's time they were held in high esteem.

The article admits its sources are scanty, then tells a grim end. When Spanish forces took the city in August 1487, converted Jews who had fled there were tortured and killed. The town's own Jews, some 450 souls, were enslaved with the rest of the population. Young Solomon ibn Verga raised 20,000 gold doubloons across Spain for their ransom. They were redeemed and shipped to Africa. After 1492 no Jews could live in Malaga at all. The entry also claims the city as the birthplace of Solomon ibn Gabirol.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marks-david-woo:
David Woolf Marks, called the father of Anglo-Jewish Reform, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in London on November 22, 1811, he studied at the Jews' Free School. He taught at a Hammersmith boarding school, then served synagogues at St. Alban's and Liverpool. At Liverpool he refused to read the Law on second festival days.

The article follows that stand into a movement. About 1840 London's founders of a Reform synagogue noticed his sympathy. At twenty-nine he became minister of the West London Synagogue of British Jews. His ministry there ran for sixty years. He furthered education, regular preaching, and decorum in public worship. From 1848 to 1898 he held the Hebrew chair at University College, London. He published three volumes of sermons and compiled the Reform order of service. The entry honors the man who gave British Reform its pulpit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mazzah-plural-m:
Mazzah, the unleavened bread of Passover, is explained in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein. It is dough kneaded with water alone, without yeast, and baked in haste so it cannot ferment into hamez. The article calls it the primitive form of bread: leavening made loaves tastier, but mazzah stayed the poor man's bread, since the poor could not wait a day for dough to rise.

Scripture gives it two great roles. It is the bread of sudden hospitality, served to Abraham's angel guests and baked by the witch of Endor for Saul. And it is the bread of the Exodus, eaten with the Passover lamb and through the festival's seven days to recall the flight from Egypt. The article adds its symbolism: purity in the sacrifices, where leaven figures the evil impulse, and, in the Zohar's phrase, a sign of freedom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-eli:
Menahem ben Elijah was a Turkish liturgical poet of the fifteenth century. He came from Kastoria. Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn catalogue him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His surviving hymns are feats of construction. Two of them spell out in acrostic his own name, his father's, and his town's. One runs twelve strophes. Each strophe begins and ends with the same letter.

The marvel is his prayer "Shirat ha-Yad ha-Hazakah." It is also called "Malkiel." The prayer has 140 lines of five words apiece. The first ten lines all begin with one letter, the next ten with the next, and so through his name fifty times over. The entry also weighs another claim. Some would identify him with a Menahem ben Elijah of Crusade times. That man's letter, full of Salonica, survives among the Egyptian fragments. Neubauer published those fragments. Zunz rejects the identification.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mi-kamokah-who-:
Mi-Kamokah, Hebrew for Who is like unto Thee, names the verse from Exodus chapter fifteen sung as a response in Jewish daily services. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on its music in 1906. The verse, with the chapter's closing line, sits between the Shema and the Shemoneh Esreh prayers.

Most days the verse takes the melody pattern of the service around it, the article explains. But for the penitential evening service between New Year and the Day of Atonement, its own later, major-key setting sets the tone for everything else. The entry prints that melody and traces how such tunes became signature themes reused across the northern liturgy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morrison-lewis-:
Lewis Morrison was an American stage actor born in Jamaica, West Indies, in 1845. His Jewish Encyclopedia entry, written by Cyrus Adler and Edgar Mels, follows a career that began in uniform. When the Civil War broke out he joined the Federal Army and served four years as an officer.

Morrison went on the stage in 1865, appearing with Lawrence Barrett in New Orleans. He played Iago opposite Salvini's Othello and supported stars such as Edwin Forrest, Edwin Booth, and Charlotte Cushman. Later he toured with his own company in Faust, and his Mephistopheles became his best known role. The sketch also notes his wife, the actress Florence Roberts, and his daughter Rosabel, also an actress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munsterburg-hug:
Hugo Münsterburg was an American psychologist born at Danzig on June 1, 1863. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Jacobs wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He took a philosophy doctorate at Leipsic in 1885 and a medical degree at Heidelberg in 1887. In 1892 Harvard made him its professor of psychology.

Münsterburg wrote many papers for the specialist journals and a shelf of books for wider readers. They include Psychology and Life, the Grundzüge der Psychologie, and American Traits. Die Amerikaner, his two volumes on the Americans, appeared in 1904 in German and English. In 1898 he was president of the Psychological Association of America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nard-11324:
Nard is an eastern Asian plant whose root gave the ancient world its prized spikenard perfume. Joseph Jacobs and Immanuel Löw wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it. In the Bible the word occurs only in the Song of Songs. The plant never grew in Palestine; it belongs to the poet's imaginary garden there.
