Field tests on a real tracked vehicle followed. Speed and trajectory tracking both confirmed the design works outdoors, not only in simulation. Cheaper computation means smaller onboard computers can steer heavy machines precisely.
plos-pone-0346924:
Welelaw Necho Mulatu and a large team interviewed twenty-three supply chain workers and experts across Ethiopia about why contraceptives, maternal, newborn, and child health goods run out at small clinics. National reforms improved the upper levels of the system, but the last mile, health centres and tiny health posts, still fails patients. Interviews were coded into themes by setting, farming regions and pastoral regions alike.

Six bottlenecks recurred: erratic deliveries, poor data that nobody uses, sloppy stock keeping, weak forecasting of need, too few staff, and broken infrastructure. Pastoral areas added bad roads and thin cold storage, while health posts often fetched goods themselves. Extra hand-offs through district offices added delay everywhere. The authors map these frictions so reform money can be aimed at the exact points where supplies stall.
plos-pone-0347324:
R. Srivats and his team fused four known image nets to find landslides in shots from space and drones. One net can miss a faint slide or blur its edge. Bad maps can slow aid when hills fall. The fused net adds a fifth part, a rival pair that sharpens the edge of each slide it finds.

On three test sets, the scores ran from near ninety-four to near ninety-seven per cent. The sets span fine drone shots, mid space shots, and quake slides. The fused net beat each lone net by a clear gap. It also draws map-ready charts fast, fit for use right after a slide.
plos-pone-0348124:
Nigar Sultanova, Rasim Bayramov, and Narmin Maharammova measured face soft tissue thickness on three hundred CT scans of adults in Azerbaijan. Thickness at twenty landmarks, midline and paired, was split by three age bands, sex, and body weight class. Such tables guide face reconstruction from skulls in forensics and surgery.

Averages, spreads, and ranges were tabled for every landmark, with differences by age, sex, and weight reported. The set forms the first such database for Transcaucasia populations. Using tables from distant populations can distort a reconstructed face; local data give investigators and surgeons a truer starting point for Azerbaijani adults.
plos-pone-0348624:
Felipe do Carmo Jorge, Gabriel Politzer Couto, and Berndt J van Rensburg spent nights listening to an Australian open forest. Or rather, they let recorders listen. Then they asked whether simple sound measures can stand in for biodiversity after dark. Night ecology is understudied because sampling in the dark is hard. The team compared several acoustic indices, numbers that summarise a recording, against hand-counted insect sound types.

No single index did the job, but a blend of four, covering activity, evenness, and how full the soundscape is, tracked the richness of insect sounds well. Index patterns also matched how sites differed from each other. The authors caution that the recipe will not transfer unchanged to other habitats, yet they offer their procedure as a cheap way to watch nighttime ecosystems over long stretches.
plos-pone-0348724:
EDITORIAL NOTE: This notice updates an earlier Expression of Concern about a published study of virus communities found in fluid around the heart of patients with unexplained heart inflammation. The PLOS One Editors explain that the journal investigated whether the original study, which used samples from patients including minors, had proper ethics approval.

A university ethics representative in Marseille reported that an internal investigation found the study met ethical standards, since it only reanalysed samples taken during routine care. The journal, however, found that one of the study's authors sat on the very ethics board that approved the work. Because of that conflict, the editors say they cannot confirm the study received independent ethics review.
plos-pone-0349024:
Wenyan Xiao, Lin Zhang, and Yangshuyi Xu built a network that reads feelings from video by letting the words lead. Judging emotion from face, voice, and speech together trips many systems, because the channels disagree in quality and timing. Their design uses the transcript as an anchor: a gated attention step aligns sound and image against the text while damping noise. A second gating stage balances each channel's contribution before merging.

A contrastive learning scheme, also anchored on text similarity, keeps the merged representation honest to both shared and unique signals. On the two standard benchmark collections for this task, the system set new best scores for accuracy and robustness. The authors argue that giving text the anchor role, rather than treating all channels as equals, is the design lesson.
plos-pone-0349124:
Matthew M Harper and Nickolas A Boehme tested whether repeated short spells of low oxygen could shield mouse eye nerve cells from blast injury. Blast waves can harm the retina cells that carry vision signals to the brain, leading to slow nerve loss. Mice received six low oxygen sessions over two weeks, then a blast or sham blast, with eye function, structure, and cell counts checked a month later.

Blast mice lost signal strength and nerve layer thickness versus sham mice. Mice pretreated with low oxygen spells looked like sham mice on both measures, and surviving cell counts held up. Training the body with mild oxygen stress beforehand, the authors conclude, can at least partly protect vision nerves from blast harm.
plos-pone-0349224:
Tao Luo, Qingpeng Huang, and Jingyan Mai studied young people who have newly taken up farming in Guangdong Province, China, asking how their job skills are developing. Drawing on interviews and questionnaires across twenty-one cities, they traced three stages of a farming career: entering the field, putting down roots, and growing a business. Skill needs differ at each stage.

Young farmers' abilities fell into three layers: hands-on professional skills, general abilities useful anywhere, and core qualities such as judgment and commitment. Each layer grows best with its own kind of training. As more young people enter farming, matching training to career stage could help them stay and help villages renew their workforce.
plos-pone-0349624:
Ryo Murata and Kenji Tanaka propose a way to fill the gaps in pedestrian flow data by blending real measurements with simulation. Cities track crowds to plan streets and marketing, but sensors miss people, while simulations are complete yet ignore real human quirks. Their method borrows data assimilation, the fusion trick used in weather forecasting, and applies a particle filter to an agent-based crowd model.

Virtual pedestrians are continually nudged toward whatever the real sensors did capture, so the finished picture is both complete and realistic. The team tested the approach against three kinds of missing data. Better crowd pictures matter for evacuation planning and station design, where decisions are only as good as the flow data beneath them.
plos-pone-0350024:
Wenxin Jiang and Peng Liu compared two chemotherapy regimens for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, a fast-growing blood cancer, in patients whose tumors showed a high growth marker. One regimen adjusts doses upward over cycles, and the other is the long-standing standard. Earlier records from three hundred seventy-six patients set the marker level that counts as high.

Twenty-nine patients received the dose-adjusted regimen in a forward-looking study, matched against similar patients who got the standard one. Survival without the disease returning, and overall survival, did not differ meaningfully between the groups. Enrollment stopped early because benefit looked unlikely and recruitment was slow. For doctors, the result argues against choosing the harsher regimen on growth marker alone.
plos-pone-0350124:
Qiuyu Li led a study of two skills in Chinese undergraduates. One skill is computational thinking: breaking hard tasks into clear steps. The other is AI literacy: grasping what AI can and cannot do. Past work linked the two at one point in time. This team tracked two hundred sixteen students over time. They asked if the first skill builds the second.

Both skills grew across the study span. The modeling showed a clear push from the first skill to the second. The link held steady as both rose. The team says courses that teach step-wise problem solving lay real ground for AI smarts. They offer the design as a guide for course planners.
plos-pone-0350224:
Mohammad Abdul Karim Khan and four colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on blood flow and aneurysms. It is a computational investigation of nanoparticle effects on hemodynamics, the forces of moving blood, inside patient-specific aortic aneurysms, ballooned sections of the body's main artery shaped from individual patients' scans.

Alongside simulation, the authors use machine learning to predict those effects more quickly. Nanoparticles are studied as possible drug carriers, so knowing how they alter flow inside a weakened aorta matters for safety. Biomedical engineers and vascular specialists share the audience for a model built on real patient anatomy.
plos-pone-0350624:
José Alejandro Valdevila Figueira and co-authors tested what Ecuadorian health students know about Alzheimer's disease in 2026. With populations ageing, tomorrow's doctors, nurses, and psychologists will all meet dementia, and training gaps are easiest to fix early.

More than a thousand students, mostly nursing, took a standard knowledge scale. Average correct answers sat near fifty-five percent, a limited level. Medical students scored highest, with nursing and psychology behind. The authors call the gap urgent and propose stronger dementia teaching across all three programs. Knowing the baseline by discipline lets universities aim the remedy where it is weakest.
plos-pone-0350824:
Brown and colleagues compared gut microbes of Eastern indigo snakes, wild and captive, in a 2026 study. The snake is a threatened species native to the American Southeast. Samples from the rear opening stood in for gut samples across three groups: captive snakes with a gut parasite, captive snakes without it, and wild snakes.

Gene sequencing measured microbe variety and mix in each group. Captivity and infection each can reshape a reptile's gut community, and separating their effects matters for breeding programs. Knowing the normal microbe profile helps keepers spot illness early and may guide release choices for captive-bred snakes.
plos-pone-0350924:
Hai Huang and co-authors built a way to score how much cultural value a heritage building holds, working in Longxing Ancient Town in Chongqing, China. Conservation teams often argue about value without a shared yardstick. The team reviewed two decades of writing on cultural value, then interviewed shop owners and visitors in the town and convened heritage experts to shape the criteria.

The finished scale sorts value into five kinds: local, historic, sustainable, scientific, and aesthetic, with twenty-four finer measures beneath them, weighted by a structured ranking method. Because owners, visitors, and experts all fed into it, the scale reflects how a town actually experiences its old buildings, not only how specialists do. Other historic towns could adapt the same scaffold when deciding which buildings to protect first and why.
plos-pone-0351124:
Rudy Brogi and colleagues asked whether the ways scientists catch wild chamois quietly filter which animals get studied. If bold animals walk into nets more easily, behavior research built on caught animals would lean bold. The team compared two methods, drug darts and drop nets, in an Alpine herd, then watched twenty-five tagged adults alongside untagged herd mates.

Key behaviors like eating, standing, and resting proved consistent within each animal, so they could fairly test for bias. Neither capture method ended up over-sampling the risk-takers: shy and bold chamois alike turned up in the caught group. That all-clear matters because personality studies across wildlife rest on the assumption that traps do not pick personalities. At least for this large herbivore and these two methods, the assumption held.
plos-pone-0351224:
Cecilia Camacho-Hubner and seven colleagues survey doctors across Latin America about a stealthy heart disease. Their 2026 study concerns transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, where misfolded protein stiffens the heart. The disease is progressive, fatal, and badly under-recognised. Four hundred seventy physicians in eight countries answered questionnaires during 2023. They described their knowledge, attitudes, and the barriers they hit in diagnosis and treatment.

Knowledge was thin. Only about half the doctors understood the disease's basic mechanism. Patients reportedly consulted four or five physicians before anyone confirmed the diagnosis. Cardiologists carried most day-to-day management. Genetic testing for the transthyretin gene was available to barely a quarter of respondents. The key drug's cost and access blocked treatment often. Most local practice simply borrowed international guidelines. The authors map a fixable problem: train front-line doctors to suspect the disease sooner, and widen access to testing and therapy.
plos-pone-0351324:
Linking power grids flexibly lets regions share electricity and cuts waste, but planners must first forecast demand well. Xiaoyan Zhao and colleagues paired a hybrid forecasting network with a chaos-driven search method to design such links, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

The forecaster reads past load at several time scales, mixing pattern-spotting and memory layers. A new measure scores how well regions' demands complement each other hour by hour. The search algorithm then tunes the system's layout against balance, reliability, cost, and that complementarity score. Tests showed very small forecast errors, and the authors claim the combined approach designs cheaper, steadier interconnections.
plos-pone-0351424:
James Dickson Fiagborlo, Mexoese Nyatuame, and Stella Ahone Ntoko surveyed just over one thousand farm households across five areas of Ghanas Volta Region. Land wear harms soil and deepens rural poverty, yet uptake of better land care stays uneven. The survey asked how training and farm size shape what farmers would pay for such care, split by gender.

Training raised willingness to pay, and the effect ran stronger for men. Larger farms also paid more, since owners had more means to invest. Women started lower but gained fast when land access and training improved. Gaps thus look driven more by blocked access than by lack of interest. Fair training and land rights, the authors argue, are central to wider uptake.
plos-pone-0351624:
Justin Ofosu-Dankwa, Cristina Sisu, and Rhona Anderson examine the genomes of British nuclear test veterans in this 2026 study. These men served at Cold War nuclear test sites decades ago. Many worry the radiation left marks on their DNA. The team compared thirty veterans with thirty age-matched control veterans. Whole-genome data were processed with standard best-practice pipelines.

Somatic mutations, the small DNA changes gathered over a lifetime, were counted and classified. No variant type appeared more often in the test veterans. Tight mutation clusters, a suspected radiation fingerprint, were also no commoner. The dominant mutation signatures in both groups were the usual ones left by ageing itself. The null result cannot rule out every possible harm. Still, it offers these veterans evidence that their genomes carry no obvious excess burden.
plos-pone-0351724:
Rules against sexual harassment are clear on paper at a large Swedish university, yet Jack Palmieri, Frida Pilgaard, and Anette Agardh found daily norms tell another story. Their 2026 PLOS One study ran ten staff discussion groups, split by whether members managed others.

One theme covered everything: harassment is viewed through silence, power, and shifting boundaries. Staff described limits being negotiated on the spot, with women often checking with peers while men called the same behavior harmless. Prestigious senior researchers were seen as untouchable, and managers felt unsure how to act. Silence, many said, protected careers more than honesty would.
plos-pone-0351924:
Wonil Chung and Keonwoo Koo studied how GPT language models handle focus, the spotlight inside a sentence. Focus tells a listener which piece of news is at issue. The team used cut-off sentences with two possible completions. A question before the sentence set one spotlight. The small word only set another, placed before different items. Word-by-word surprise scores showed which ending each model expected.

The question's spotlight ruled in the first tests. It beat even a competing only. When only stood before the second object, the word-level spotlight grew stronger. It began to bend the expected endings its way. The models weigh the two cues in a graded tug-of-war, not by fixed rules. That matters wherever emphasis changes meaning in a text.
plos-pone-0352024:
Magreth Theophil, Ally Lyimo, and Joel Ambikile surveyed four hundred twenty-six adults on HIV treatment in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, asking whether their kidneys were being screened as guidelines advise. HIV and its medicines both strain kidneys, and catching damage early changes care. Records and questionnaires fed a search for what separates the screened from the missed.

Screening uptake was surprisingly high, about ninety-four percent. Patients with stronger immune counts were more likely screened, while those attending clinic only every six months were far less likely, an obvious contact effect. Oddly, patients who recalled a provider recommending screening had lower odds, a puzzle the authors flag rather than explain. In a system straining to follow its own guidelines, attendance rhythm, not distance or wealth, marked who slipped through.
plos-pone-0352124:
Zelan Wu and seven colleagues hunt for gene patterns linking inflammation, platelets, and heart failure. Their 2026 study merges bulk and single-cell gene data from human heart tissue. A protein pair called NEK7 and the NLRP3 inflammasome sits at the centre of their suspicion. Platelets, famous for clotting, also stoke inflammation. The team used network analysis and machine learning to find genes moving with both processes. A diagnostic scoring chart was drafted from the results.

Four genes formed the signature. All were turned up in failing human hearts. A mouse model of heart failure, driven by a hormone infusion, echoed the pattern for most of them. The signature also tracked with scarring genes, fitting the fibrosis story. The authors are explicit that this generates hypotheses, not proof. Still, a blood-or-tissue signature tying platelet activity to heart failure could eventually guide both diagnosis and anti-inflammatory treatment choices.
plos-pone-0352324:
Hong Nguyen-Thi and four colleagues tackle secure, energy-saving wireless design in a 2026 engineering study. Their setting is a future 6G network. Smart reflecting surfaces bounce signals to where they are needed. Several users share the same channel under a scheme called NOMA. A friendly jammer interferes with a hidden eavesdropper.

The goal is twofold: keep messages secret while wasting little energy, and treat the worst-off user fairly. The team trained a Double Deep Q-Network, a reinforcement learning method, to set power levels and surface angles. Its performance was compared with a standard learning method and with random settings. Simulations covered both shared-channel and separate-channel designs. The results highlight the shared design's edge in balancing secrecy against energy use.
plos-pone-0352424:
Shahab MohammadEbrahimi and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One spatial analysis of heart and circulation hospital admissions in Mashhad, Iran's second-largest city. More than fifty thousand admissions from 2016 to 2020 were mapped and tracked over time to find when and where the burden concentrates.

Admissions followed a repeating yearly rhythm and rose steadily until late 2019, when they dropped sharply. Men accounted for slightly more than half of cases, and the typical patient was in the mid-sixties. Mapping showed clear clustering: the city center formed a high-risk zone where admission risk ran many times higher than elsewhere. The authors say prevention and hospital resources should target that core, and offer the analysis as a template for other cities.
plos-pone-0353524:
Oronel and colleagues, in a 2026 animal study, trace how blocking a hormone system in newborn rats disturbs the growing kidney. Some adult diseases, including high blood pressure and kidney trouble, are now thought to start with early-life stress on development. The hormone endothelin helps kidneys form, and the team blocked its receptors during the first days of life.

Treated male pups showed more oxidative damage in the kidney and a worse balance between a protective gas, nitric oxide, and harmful oxygen radicals. Activity tied to nitric oxide fell in the very structures that become the kidney's filters. Female pups were partly protected, with differences in several protective enzymes and hormone signals. Cell growth and cell death also fell out of balance. The authors argue these early chemical shifts may be the first steps toward the adult kidney problems seen in earlier work.
plos-pone-0354124:
Dongmiao Zhang and colleagues present a protocol, published in 2026, for mapping which surface types of a dangerous newborn bacterium dominate around the world. The bacterium is a strain of E. coli that escapes the gut. It is a severe threat to newborns. Its O antigen, a variable coat component, is the leading candidate target for a protective vaccine. Yet nobody has charted its global variety in this age group.

The planned study will fuse two evidence streams. One is published serotype reports from four databases. The other is serotypes predicted from genome sequences in three public archives. Each strain's disease, site, year, and origin will be extracted. The verdict it seeks is strategic: one multivalent vaccine for the world, or regional recipes.
plos-pone-0354524:
Liu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, examine natural killer cells inside triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive form that lacks the usual drug targets. These immune killer cells should attack tumors, but in this cancer they often arrive immature and weak. Using public single-cell data, the team sorted the killer cells found in tumor tissue into three subtypes.

One subtype, the strongest killer, was scarcer and weaker in triple-negative tumors than in other breast cancers. Its cells carried more of a brake receptor that switches them off. Signals from neighboring immune cells appeared to set that brake. A second subtype, marked by an alarm gene, was more active in these tumors, and high levels of that gene tracked with worse patient outcomes. The strong subtype's signature, by contrast, tracked with better outcomes. The authors say releasing the brake on killer cells is a concrete target for new treatments.
plos-pone-0354724:
Kelsey Thompson led a team of six authors on this 2026 focus group study of clinicians who treat children with pediatric feeding disorder. In this condition, eating breaks down for medical, nutritional, skill, or emotional reasons. Twenty-five providers in seven groups described their training and daily work across all four areas of the condition.

Training varied wildly between professions, clinics lacked easy access to specialist backup, and everyone wanted fuller yet workable care that honors family views. Thompson calls for earlier teaching, mentorship, and ready evidence-based resources to lift patient care.
plos-pone-0354824:
Gökşen Polat and four colleagues published this 2026 interview study in Türkiye of people whose chronic diseases leave them disabled. Twelve adults holding official disability reports described their daily limits and what they expect from disability services. Recruitment ran through clinics and personal referrals during 2024.

Disability spilled into social, cultural, school, and work life. Although services are a legal entitlement, many participants barely knew what existed or could not reach it. Polat argues the gap is informational and structural, and that fixing awareness and access matters as much as passing laws.
plos-pone-0354924:
Kaiyue Du and colleagues built lifestyle-based risk models for keratoconus, a disease that thins and bulges the cornea. They used records from 711 patients at a Chinese eye center, 275 of them with the disease. Their 2026 study combined standard regression with seven machine learning models. The models were fed demographic and habit data. The team then asked the models to explain which factors mattered most.

Seven risk factors stood out. They included male sex, higher body mass, and less schooling. A more distant childhood home and allergic conjunctivitis counted too. Above all stood rubbing the eyes, harder and more often. The best model sorted patients with fair accuracy. Because eye rubbing is changeable, the authors see a practical opening. Flag high-risk patients early, and coach the habit away before corneas deform.
plos-pone-0355124:
Rogers Kamulegeya and seven colleagues systematically review artificial intelligence models that predict whether tuberculosis treatment will fail, in this 2026 meta-analysis. Failure fuels transmission and drug resistance, so early warning matters. Searching two major databases for a quarter-century of work, they gathered thirty-four studies, most published since 2019, and pooled the accuracy of nineteen of them covering over one hundred thousand patients.

The pooled discrimination looked promising, but the ground beneath it was shaky. Results varied enormously between studies, models performed notably worse in groups including people with HIV, and only a quarter of studies had validated their model on outside data. Just one study earned a low overall risk-of-bias rating, and the analysis detected signs of publication bias. The authors conclude these tools are not ready for routine care and prioritize rigorous external validation in high-burden settings.
plos-pone-0355224:
Rafael Borges and three colleagues examine whether who you have worked alongside predicts reaching ministerial office in Portugal, in this 2026 network study. They scraped the membership of Portuguese governments and parliament over a decade, plus officials' interest registers, and built a network linking people who shared institutional venues. Then they asked whether network position, computed before the fact, screened out future ministers better than chance or a simple career-ladder rule.

It did. Their centrality-based screen caught over half of the in-network ministerial appointments, far above the baselines. Ministers also showed systematically higher institutional reach than colleagues who never made cabinet, with the sharpest gap inside party structures, where ministers scored about double on one key centrality measure. The authors are careful to call the work exploratory, but it suggests appointments flow through relational position, not just résumés.
plos-pone-0355724:
Mirjana Grdinić-Rakonjac and Vladimir Pajković survey more than thirteen hundred licensed drivers in a developing country, in this 2026 case study. They asked about four risky behaviors: speeding, drunk driving, seatbelt use, and phone use. Because crash deaths fall hardest on poorer countries, and because habits differ by road type, they compared men and women separately on high-speed, regional, and urban roads, adjusting for age and experience.

Men were generally more prone to speeding and drinking and driving. Yet women reported significantly more extreme speeding, far over the limit, on high-speed roads, a reversal of the usual pattern, while also buckling up more reliably on regional and urban roads. Both sexes texted and used social media behind the wheel at similar rates, and overall risk awareness was higher than the authors expected. They recommend campaigns aimed at men in cities and at speed among women on fast roads.
plos-pone-0356524:
Pooja Panth and three colleagues studied cancer patients at Bhaktapur Cancer Hospital in Nepal, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. How patients view their illness shapes how they cope, seek care, and keep going through treatment. Panth's cross-sectional study linked those views to resilience, the capacity to bounce back under strain.

The team surveyed patients and compared illness views with measures of resilience. Some beliefs track with stronger coping, while others track with despair. Knowing which views help lets counselors support the beliefs that sustain patients, and gently challenge those that drag them down. In a setting with few support services, that guidance helps staff focus scarce time where it lifts patients most.
plos-pone-0356624:
Alexandra N Sheldon and colleagues reviewed 173 infected artificial joints treated at one center over nearly a decade. All were treated with a joint-saving operation. Surgeons cleaned the implant and kept it rather than replacing it. The team asked which germs doom that approach. Their 2026 retrospective study graded success as lasting eradication without further surgery. It tested fungal, resistant, mixed, and culture-negative infections against the odds.

Two thirds of cases were cured. Fungal infections almost always failed, carrying heavier illness burdens besides. Infections where no germ could be grown were nearly four times likelier to clear. That is a hopeful sign for a frustrating category. Resistant and common skin bacteria also dragged success down. The authors suggest microbe identity should steer the choice between saving and replacing a joint.
plos-pone-0357124:
John Adeleke used Nigeria's 2024 national health survey to ask whether household wealth protects children equally against two kinds of undernutrition. One is stunting, the slow height loss of chronic deprivation. The other is wasting, the rapid weight loss of acute shortage. His 2026 analysis covered more than nine thousand children. It adjusted step by step for other social and geographic factors.

Wealth showed a clear graded link with stunting. Each step up the wealth ladder came with less of it. For wasting, wealth showed no link at all. Adeleke reads the split through one idea. Money buys protection against slow, cumulative harms more readily than against sudden illness or food shocks. Programs fighting wasting, he argues, need tools beyond poverty relief.
plos-pone-0357824: Agrawal and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on sleep apnea using electronic health records. Obstructive sleep apnea makes breathing stop and start during sleep, and it is tied to stroke risk. The team measured how common it is, split by age and sex, along with related conditions. The data set was large and cross-sectional. Clear rates help clinics plan screening for a disorder often missed.
plos-pone-0358224:
Quan Pham Hong leads a team of five designing a neural network that listens for damage in structures, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Bridges and towers betray cracks through subtle changes in how they shake. The warning signs are brief blips in narrow frequency bands. Models that read only the time signal miss the frequency story; models that transform the whole signal lose track of when each frequency occurred. Their network, SpectralTCN, is built to keep both.

Inside each layer of a temporal convolutional network sits a wavelet gating module. It splits the signal into sub bands that correspond to vibration modes. The network then decides how much of each band to keep. Then it rebuilds the signal before moving on. Because wavelets preserve timing and frequency together, a short damage signature keeps its moment and its pitch. The design targets inspection of structures that cannot afford missed hints.
plos-pone-0358424:
Mohamad Kazem Dehghani, Reza Ghasemi-Fasaei, Sajjad Abbasi, and Amin Mojiri wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on plants and pollution. Working with spinach grown in water rather than soil, they study nanoplastics sprayed on leaves. The question is how these tiny plastic particles change the plant's handling of cadmium, a toxic metal.

The responses depend on both time and concentration, so the authors track uptake and the metal's movement from root to shoot under different doses. Cadmium in leafy vegetables is a food safety concern, and plastic particles are now common on farms. Plant scientists and food regulators share an interest in how these two pollutants interact.
plos-pone-0359224:
Sivarama Prasad Tera and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents an explainable AI framework for detecting cancer from skin lesion images. Explainable means the system shows its reasoning, not just a verdict, which doctors rightly demand before trusting software with diagnosis.

Skin cancer caught early is usually curable, so faster and more reliable screening saves lives. An imaging framework that explains itself can also teach, showing trainees which features drove a decision. Dermatologists and medical imaging researchers are the readers weighing whether this framework is ready to support real clinics.
plos-pone-0359424:
Darío López-Delgado and eight colleagues published this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a review that will gather studies systematically and pool them in a meta-analysis, on infections passed through sex, among women who are pregnant and who are migrants or refugees. Pregnancy plus displacement is a double vulnerability, and infections in pregnancy endanger both mother and child.

The review will gather prevalence figures, how common these infections are in this group, from studies worldwide. Migrant and refugee women often fall outside routine screening systems, so pooled prevalence can expose a hidden burden. Maternal health services designing outreach for displaced women are the audience waiting for this synthesis.
plos-pone-0359524: The PLOS One Staff published a 2026 correction notice in PLOS ONE. It amends an earlier scoping review about coach learning in youth participation sport. A correction keeps the public record straight when a detail in a published paper was wrong. Readers who cited the review can now check what changed. Notices like this are a small but real part of how science fixes its own record.
plos-pone-0359624:
Naim Gheymoumi and four colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies experimental allergic rhinitis, the laboratory version of hay fever's nasal inflammation. The treatment candidate is kynurenic acid, a natural compound made from the amino acid tryptophan, tested for whether it attenuates, or eases, the allergic response.

The authors tie the effect to the AhR receptor, a pathway that keeps immune activity in the nose in balance. A natural compound that calms nasal allergy through this pathway interests drug developers seeking gentler options than steroids. Allergy researchers are the core readers.
pmc-10652624:
Dongli Li and co-authors test in 2023 leg buzz cues from a worn gear to ease walk freezes in Parkinson's ill. Such cues can free a stuck gait, yet plain forms add load or fail in the wild. A loop form that fires just at a freeze could give the right nudge with no hand work.

Seventeen folk with daily freezes walk four hard paths with four cue plans: loop fire, crew fire, gear with no fire, and no gear. Loop fire cut path time the most in the read. On board chips log each freeze and step marks. Gear tweaks roll in block by block.
pmc-10655324:
Rana Ibrahim and co-authors mine a traditional Ayurvedic root for drug leads in 2023. Akarkara root has long been used as a remedy. The team pulled it apart step by step, testing each fraction for antioxidant power and for blocking enzymes tied to inflammation and Alzheimer's disease.

The most active fraction yielded 41 compounds, and four main ones were isolated in pure form. Each showed strong antioxidant action and slowed the target enzymes in lab tests. They also calmed inflammatory signals in immune cells. Computer studies suggested the compounds fit the enzyme pockets well and could reach the brain. The authors present them as promising starting points for new drugs.
pmc-10656524:
Shujuan Zhao and a large team of co-authors published a study in 2023 hunting the genetic roots of the vein of Galen malformation, the most severe congenital tangle of brain blood vessels. The team sequenced the protein-coding genes of 310 affected families and mined over three hundred thousand single-cell profiles of developing human brain vessels.

One gene towered over the results: a brake on the Ras growth pathway carried new, damaging variants at over two thousand times the expected rate. Variants passed down through families clustered in a partner receptor gene, and a handful of other vascular pathway genes appeared as well. Developing vessel-lining cells emerged as the likely scene of the defect, and mouse experiments supported the story. Prevention and early detection now have concrete molecular addresses.
pmc-10657124:
Hilary Short and co-authors test a quality of life form in rehab services in Canada in 2023. The EQ-5D-5L form is a short standard way to rate health related quality of life. Alberta community rehab programs collect it at intake and at discharge. The team used that routine data to profile who uses the services.

They tracked how scores changed across care and classed each change by a standard scheme. Gains were judged against the smallest change patients would feel. Traits tied to benefit were also explored. Routine outcome data like this can show funders what community rehab truly delivers.
pmc-10657424:
Niloofar Najafi and co-authors present a 2023 journal article that compares antibody responses to three COVID-19 vaccines used in Iran. A Tehran university cohort of 462 adults received Oxford-AstraZeneca, COVIran Barekat, or Sinopharm shots. The team measured virus-targeting IgG levels after each dose.

AstraZeneca drew the strongest response at both steps, with median levels and the share of people testing positive clearly ahead. Sinopharm trailed the other two vaccines. A past infection lifted levels further in every group. The authors rank AstraZeneca the superior candidate among the three for this population, while noting all three raised responses sharply after the second dose.
pmc-10659724:
Yao Wang and co-authors report two cases where back teeth were saved by taking them out and putting teeth back. Their 2023 case reports cover lower jaw molars with serious lesions at the root tip. Both methods, deliberate replanting of the same tooth and transplanting a tooth into a new spot, are last resorts when standard root work fails.

In the first case, a cracked molar held a broken instrument deep in one canal. The tooth was gently lifted out, the fragment removed, the root tip sealed, and the tooth replanted. The second case used a transplanted tooth for a similar lesion. Follow-up checks track how each repair settled.
pmc-10670224:
Anna Florowska and co-authors compare ways to set inulin hydrogels for food use, by heat and by newer cold methods. Inulin gels add texture and fiber to food products. How a gel is induced changes its feel and stability.

All methods tested produced gels in the study. Cold methods formed gel structure faster than heating. Ultrasound and pressure routes both counted as cold methods. Gels from cold routes were more stable overall. Their flow traits shifted toward a firmer, more solid balance. Elasticity and thickness indexes improved in most cold cases. Their structure was also finer and more delicate. The findings help food makers pick induction routes.
pmc-10675324:
Algal blooms in a Florida lagoon carry toxins whose fingerprints in human cells vary by place and season, in a 2023 assessment by Esther A. Guzmán and co-authors. The Indian River Lagoon, a 156-mile estuary, blooms as heat and human pressures build.

Water from twenty sites was gathered in wet and dry seasons across three years. A panel of human cell lines measured killing power, joined by tests for blood cell clumping, red cell bursting, and blocking of a key enzyme. Blooms in the south and north traced to different algae, each leaving a steady cell-killing pattern. Away from blooms, the patterns looked mixed or matched no known toxin. The survey maps where bloom toxins threaten people most.
pmc-10687424:
A dog's two jaw halves meet at a joint that can wobble, and a 2023 study by Sergio Minei and co-authors measures how much wobble is normal. Knowing the healthy range helps vets judge injury and disease at the mandibular symphysis, the chin joint.

The team reviewed records for 567 dogs of ninety-five breeds seen for mouth and dental work under anesthesia between 2015 and 2021. Each joint was scored for sideways and up-down movement on a zero-to-three scale, and X-rays showed whether the joint was fused or open. Sideways movement was absent in about seventy-one percent of first checks, and up-down movement in about ninety-seven percent. The study also weighed links with breed, weight, age, sex, and skull shape.
pmc-10689324:
Doctors in Vietnam charted the wider health load and drug use of people with psoriasis in two hospitals. This skin disease is driven by the immune system and often travels with other long-term illness. Local real-world data were scarce, so care plans leaned on foreign studies. The team read the charts of 661 adults first seen between early 2020 and late 2021, and logged their other diseases, drugs, and costs.

Near half of patients had poor fat levels in blood, and near a fourth had high blood pressure. One in ten had joint disease tied to the skin disease. About 44 percent took modern biologic drugs, which stayed in use far longer than older drugs. Patients on biologics also bore more added illness, yet few stopped the drug. Costs and stay times are laid out for planners.
pmc-10690824:
Husain Shakil and co-authors review central cord syndrome and degenerative cervical myelopathy, and go against a long-held idea on how the cord is laid out. Their 2023 review deals with spinal cord injury that is not full. Its mark is weakness of the upper limbs out of scale with the rest.

New proof hints that the syndrome is most like a diffuse injury, not a focal lesion. That puts right the old somatotopic model of cord layout. The marks used to spot it still lack a shared view, and how it is set out shapes which patients are picked out and what care they get. Proof in favour of early surgery has grown, but when to act still splits from doctor to doctor. As groups age, the zone where this syndrome and degenerative myelopathy meet grows. The team sets out tools to gauge the state and work still needed.
pmc-10692024:
Zikang Xu and nine co-authors report a new battery material made from manganese dioxide, in a 2023 paper. The base material can store ions with more than one charge, such as magnesium and aluminum. Its frame tends to break down as those ions move in and out. That leads to fast loss of charge over a few cycles.

The team placed potassium ions into the material before use, along with some water. The new form held a high charge in tests with a magnesium salt bath. It also kept working at fast rates and over more cycles than the base form. Aluminum ions could enter the same material as well. The result offers a simple fix for manganese-based materials in water-based batteries.
pmc-10692124:
Paige Helmer and Richard B. Vallee report a brain study, published in 2023, on how new nerve cells are made before birth. Cells called radial glial progenitors can divide in two ways. One way makes more stem cells, and the other makes neurons. Keeping the right balance builds a working cortex while saving enough stem cells.

The pair found that two related motor proteins pull this balance in opposite ways. One protein, Kif1A, favors making neurons. The other, Kif13B, favors divisions that copy the stem cell instead. Both act on the spindle, the frame that splits a cell in two, and both belong to the same protein family. Their opposed roles offer a new way to explain how the young brain controls its own growth.
pmc-10692324:
Marzia Di Donato and co-authors study why muscle weakens with age and how male hormones may help. Their 2023 paper looks at a hormone sensor in muscle, called the androgen receptor, and a partner protein named filamin A. Muscle samples came from 20 men, young and old.

Young muscle held more of the sensor, and the sensor paired with its partner far more in young samples. In lab muscle cells, hormone treatment built the pair fast and blocked cell aging from stress. A peptide that broke the pair brought the aging signs back. Blocking the sensor also shut off key growth signals in the cells.
pmc-10693124:
Arcobacter bacteria ride along in farm animals and can sicken people who eat contaminated food, yet data from African farms are thin. The authors sample poultry and livestock on commercial and smallholder farms in one Ghanaian municipality and one Tanzanian town council. Over 2,600 samples go through enrichment culture and mass spectrometry checks, and confirmed isolates face antibiotic susceptibility testing. Ghana shows the higher burden: 7.0 percent of samples carry the bacteria, against 2.0 percent in Tanzania.

Commercial farms carry more than smallholdings in both countries, and in Ghana pigs, ducks, and quails lead the list. One species, Arcobacter butzleri, makes up over nine in ten isolates. Nearly all Ghanaian finds come from the rainy season. Resistance to three common antibiotics is widespread, and multidrug resistance appears in about half the isolates from each country. The authors call for urgent, joined-up action against resistance in these farm settings.
pmc-10693224:
Yasser Alrefaie, Ali Alraddadi, Yazeed Alhathal, and Hanaa Bamefleh report an uncommon skin case in this 2023 paper. Lichen planus is a long-lasting inflammatory disorder of skin and moist inner surfaces. Its inverse form appears in skin folds rather than on open surfaces, which makes it easier to miss.

Their patient was a healthy fifty-year-old man who came to a dermatology clinic with violet to dark patches in both armpits and the groin. The patches had been present for three months. A skin biopsy confirmed inverse lichen planus. Later, his fingernails became damaged in a pattern that matched nail lichen planus. The authors stress that nail disease of this kind needs early spotting and treatment, because delay can leave permanent scarring that cannot be undone.
pmc-10693624:
Ziqing Zhang and five co-authors film single chemiluminescent reactions as they happen in solution, in a two thousand twenty-three chemistry paper. Light-emitting reactions were earlier readable only as bulk readings, hiding molecule-level conduct.

Single-molecule imaging under catalytic settings showed double-substrate Michaelis-Menten kinetics governing the flashes. Different catalyst particles, and even varied sites on one particle, behaved in varied ways. The imaging also yielded the catalytic system's activation energy resolved at the single-particle level. The authors offer the method as a direct window on reaction dynamics and a useful tool for checking catalysts one particle at a time.
pmc-10694924:
Arne Diehl and six co-authors tested how the rules for picking patients change results in ECPR, a last-resort heart restart method, in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. ECPR uses a machine to take over heart and lung work during cardiac arrest. The team reviewed one hundred ninety-nine cases from three Australian centers over eight years, then applied five common rule sets, from strict to loose.

About one in five out-of-hospital patients and two in five in-hospital patients lived to leave hospital. Strict rules gave the best survival rates but covered few patients, so fewer lives were saved in total. Loose rules saved more people at a lower rate. For in-hospital arrests, most survivors would have failed the strict rules. The authors warn that rule sets built for one group may fit the other poorly.
pmc-10695924:
Laura Battistel, Andrea Vilardi, Massimiliano Zampini, and Riccardo Parin test how finely people can feel air temperature, in a 2023 study. Most past work probed single spots on the skin. This team instead moved volunteers between four climate rooms whose air drifted up and down by about one degree, and asked after each move whether the new room felt warmer or colder.

Twenty-six people gave more than three thousand judgments. They proved strikingly sharp: on average they could spot a gap of well under half a degree, and nearly everyone performed alike. The point where warmer and colder answers balanced sat close to zero. The authors say such fine sense data could help design smart heating and cooling systems that keep people comfortable with less wasted energy.
pmc-10696024:
Nine authors build a 2023 gene score from T cell markers to forecast outlook and drug response in stomach cancer. T cells shape the tumor setting, but their exact role in this cancer was unclear. From single-cell data the team found 322 marker genes tied to T cells.

A five-gene score split patients into high-risk and low-risk groups with good accuracy at one, three, and five years. Checks in other patient groups and data sets held up. A chart that adds the score gave like values, and the marker genes may serve as drug targets in care.
pmc-10696824:
Kathryn Jordan and co-authors published a study in 2023 on what young people think about exercise and dirty air. Staying active is a core part of asthma care, yet exercise in polluted air means breathing more of it in. Children may be more at risk from such exposure than adults.

The team interviewed twenty-five youths aged seven to seventeen, some with asthma and some without. Most named traffic and factories as top sources of outdoor pollution. All viewed pollution in a negative light, and half tied it to harm to the lungs. Only about half knew that indoor air can be polluted too. Views split on exercise in dirty air: many called it more harmful than helpful, while a quarter said the gains of exercise win. The authors call for teaching that helps youth weigh both sides.
pmc-10697424:
Tianheng Wang and co-authors retest the claim that warm climates shape languages toward more sonorous sounds, in a 2023 study. Sonority is how open and ringing a speech sound is, and earlier work hinted that heat favors it.

The team scored basic word lists from over five thousand languages on a shared sonority scale. Across world regions and language families, warmer places did show higher sonority. Inside single families the pattern vanished, suggesting change is slow and small temperature gaps do little. Digging deeper, the authors argue cold does the damage: low temperatures seem to weaken sonority over long spans.
pmc-10697624:
A baseball swing wrecks a young player's shoulder in a new pattern, Jacob Cohen and co-authors report in a 2023 case study. An eighteen-year-old college player hurt his lead shoulder mid-swing, dislocating it backward. The tear of the shoulder's rim cartilage ran a full circle, the widest class.

Earlier reports of batter's shoulder covered narrower harm, so this case stretches the known picture. Scope surgery repaired the rim, and the player returned fully to sport. Trainers and team doctors gain a warning: the swing's twist can tear the whole rim, and imaging should check the full circle when a batter's shoulder fails.
pmc-10698924:
Naomi Tschirhart and seven co-authors asked undocumented migrant women about reaching maternal care along the Thailand-Myanmar border in a 2023 study. Many women worldwide give birth without a trained attendant, and legal status can shut migrants out of normal services. Groups were held with sixty-four pregnant women at three migrant clinics.

Women learned of care through community networks and trusted providers. For many, choice was narrow: no antenatal care near home, little knowledge of other services, and fees they could not pay. Travel ran up to four hours by foot, bike, tractor, motorbike, or car, and border closures at night plus heavy rain made trips harder. A clinic insurance plan could open referral to state hospitals. Access, the authors show, shifts with time, weather, and transport.
pmc-10700224:
Maria van Noordwijk and colleagues trace reproductive success of male Bornean orangutans, finding fatherhood scattered in time but clustered in space. Their 2023 genetic study reports twenty-one assigned paternities at an Indonesian research site.

Orangutan mating systems remain poorly understood: females keep overlapping home ranges while males roam widely and mature in two forms. All infants with identified fathers since mid-twenty oh three were sired by fully developed cheek-padded males. Yet fathers were not consistently dominant, and several sired multiple infants over roughly a decade. Sires spent most time within the home ranges of the females whose infants they fathered, linking success to location rather than lasting dominance.
pmc-10700324:
Doaa Mousa, Nourhan Zayed, and Inas Yassine track brain network change in Alzheimer's disease in this 2023 study. The disease unfolds in stages, from mild lapses to full dementia. How brain regions rewire their links across those stages is still unclear. The team applied a new link measure to resting scans gathered over three visits.

Groups covered healthy elders and three disease stages, with about two dozen people each. Healthy brains showed no standout links across visits. Early stages showed many strong links flowing from the cerebellum. Links from the memory hub grew in the late mild stage, then vanished in full disease. The measure may flag stage shifts earlier than standard tools.
pmc-10701924:
Surgeons in Taiwan reviewed a hand-grip method used while fixing the thumb base joint with a plate. The joint wears out in arthritis, and joining its bones is one known fix, though past work found high rates of failed joins. How the hand is held during surgery can shift the result. The team tested their grip method with a T-hook plate on patients with stage III disease, the class named in the study.

The review checked pain scores, hand use scores, wrist scores, and how far the thumb could touch the small finger. Scores were read before and after surgery for each patient. The aim was to judge both the plate and the grip method by these gains. Young surgeons face many grip choices, so a tested method with clear steps has clear worth for training and care.
pmc-10702124:
Yuanzhi Chen and six co-authors published a cancer cell study in twenty twenty-three on the transcription factor RUNX1 in high-grade serous ovarian cancer. The disease causes most ovarian cancer deaths, and RUNX1 is overproduced in its cells. What the factor actually does there was poorly understood.

Whole-transcriptome analysis and cell experiments showed RUNX1 keeps the cancer cells alive and mobile. Knocking it down triggered cell death through a FOXO1 and Bcl2 pathway. It also blocked the shape-shifting process cells use to spread, through an EGFR, AKT, and STAT3 pathway. Silenced cells became more sensitive to standard drugs. The authors propose RUNX1 as a diagnostic marker and drug target.
pmc-10703024:
Harun Bingol and three colleagues published a 2023 study on teaching computers to read kidney CT scans. Kidney disease can grow quietly, since early stages often cause no clear signs. Specialists use CT images to spot stones, tumors, and cysts, but reading many scans takes time.

The team built a hybrid deep learning model for sorting these scans by disease type. A feature-picking step, based on the Relief method, trims the input first. They also ran known pre-trained models on the same images for contrast. The aim is faster, earlier flags for kidney problems. Good machine sorting could help doctors catch disease while treatment works best.
pmc-10703124:
Anne Warren Peled, Rie von Eyben, and Ziv M Peled report that feeling can survive breast reconstruction. Their 2023 study follows forty-seven women, seventy-nine breasts, treated with nipple-sparing mastectomy and immediate implant reconstruction combined with nerve repair.

Surgeons preserved the chest wall nerves where safe, or bridged them to the nipple area with grafts when they could not. Pressure tests tracked sensation before surgery and at set points after. By six months, over eighty percent of patients scored good to excellent on both moving and static touch, averaged across test areas. No one developed lasting painful sensitivity or a nerve tumor. The authors call it the largest series yet for this combined approach, with most patients keeping a high degree of breast sensation.
pmc-10703224:
Shibu Vijayan and co-authors share lessons from an AI screening program in a 2023 implementation paper on tuberculosis in India. Software that reads chest X-rays for TB signs promises faster case finding, but real clinics bring installation snags, workflow friction, weak networks, and too few staff to act on results.

A program in Nagpur paired the qXR software with eight private X-ray laboratories. Informal providers referred more than ten thousand people with suspected TB for imaging. Radiologist or AI readings flagged about two thousand three hundred as presumptive cases. The authors estimate the AI lifted overall TB yield notably, and they detail the workarounds.
pmc-10704624:
Jingjing Ding and co-authors adapted a stress scale for nursing students in China in this 2023 study. Interns face stress in clinic training, but few scales capture the full range of those pressures. The team revised a 14-item scale with expert input for local use.

They surveyed 414 undergraduate nursing interns in three cities. The revised scale kept all 14 items and split into two factors, though the split differed from the source scale. Fit tests were good, and scores were steady across split halves and over time. The authors say the scale is sound for local interns. Its scores could guide training plans and support steps by nursing managers.
pmc-10704724:
Kang Yao and co-authors trace how breast cancer spreads to bone, with focus on support cells in the tumour, in work from twenty twenty-three. Breast cancer often spreads far, and bone is a favoured site. The team mines several public cohorts to find molecules tied to bone spread. Lab tests then check how those molecules act in cancer cells. Movement, growth, and invasion assays cover the main checks.

Six molecules track with patient outlook and sit mostly in support cells called CAFs. Those support cells switch on many cancer growth paths at once. They also trade signals with cancer, vessel, and immune cells nearby. In that way they reshape the tumour setting and boost bad cell behaviour. One molecule, MMP13, is picked for deeper study. Raising it makes cancer cells act more aggressively in the lab. Immune entry patterns around it are also mapped.
pmc-10705024:
Nasreen Jessani and co-authors share stories of joining research with policy work on chronic diseases in Africa, in this 2023 viewpoint. The method pairs researchers with users of research from the start, so findings fit local needs. Partners in five countries in sub-Saharan Africa applied it to curb long-term diseases.

Their stories stress four habits. Teams built skills on purpose and over time. They formed honest, strong ties with partners. They shaped outreach with users and stayed flexible as needs changed. They drew in many sectors at once. Some of these moves grew stronger during the COVID-19 years. The authors offer the cases as a guide for like work elsewhere.
pmc-10705324:
Doğan Narinç and Ali Aygun test whether sound played to chick embryos changes hatching and growth in a 2023 study. They exposed broiler embryos to recordings of sounds that embryos and a mother hen make around hatching. The sound pattern ran in cycles of five minutes of sound and five minutes of silence, played through late incubation.

A total of 750 eggs were split into three groups in separate incubators. One group heard sound from an earlier hour, one from a later hour, and one heard none. Early sound shortened the hatching window to twenty-eight hours, against forty hours in the silent group. Chicks from the early sound group also scored higher on a standard quality score. The study weighs sound as a tool in hatchery practice.
pmc-10706424:
Elizabeth Edwards and four co-authors studied how anxiety, worry, and depression jointly shape attention in melanoma survivors, in this 2023 study. The sample held 187 survivors, mostly women, averaging about thirty-seven years old. Each completed measures of trait anxiety, cancer-related worry, depression, and attentional control, the skill of shutting out distractions and shifting focus.

An odd pattern emerged. Survivors with high anxiety and worry reported sharper attention when depression was low, yet worse attention when depression was high. In other words, depression flipped the sign of the anxiety effect. The authors say the twist gives clinicians a marker: treating depression may matter most where anxiety runs high. They also flag lessons for primary care follow-up.
pmc-10708324:
Yi Chen and eleven co-authors tracked in 2023 how a pest-killing protein from engineered corn moves through farm food webs. The corn makes a bacterial protein that kills target pests, cutting spray use, but safety rules require knowing where the protein ends up. Field plots in northeast China grew the engineered corn beside a near-identical plain line.

Protein levels were measured in leaves, pollen, and roots across the season, and in the insects and spiders collected from the plots. The trail shows which non-target creatures actually ingest the protein, guiding which species future risk tests should watch.
pmc-10708624:
Malik Summair Asghar, Saad Arslan, and HyungWon Kim present a circuit design for the math at the heart of neural network chips, published in twenty twenty-three. The multiply-and-add units that do this math eat up most of the chip area and power, so the team built them in analog form to save both.

Their design pairs small current-steering circuits that turn digital values into currents with tiny storage cells that add the results up. A symmetric layout gives better accuracy in less space and with less power than the usual design. The unit takes nine-bit input data and filter weights, works out the filter result, and adds it to past results. The work points toward neural network chips that run on far less power.
pmc-10709324:
Fateme Fooladi Talari and co-authors measured this 2023 rate of a DNA-repair glitch in Iranian stomach cancers. Some tumors carry microsatellite instability, a marker that predicts a better outlook and different treatment response. World rates vary, and Middle East data were missing. The team collected 53 tumor samples from a Tehran hospital, gathered between 2015 and 2020, and tested tumor against normal tissue.

Only about 7.5 percent of samples showed the high-instability pattern, four patients in all. That small group differed significantly from the rest on some clinical traits. The authors compared age, sex, tumor type, stage, and spread against the marker's status. Their low rate suggests this favorable subgroup is uncommon in Iranian patients, which matters for planning immunotherapy trials there.
pmc-10709624:
Fazal Abbas and a large team test grafted cucumber plants under salty water in this 2023 study from Pakistan. Much of the ground water pumped for crops there is brackish, and salt builds up in the soil. Cucumber is a key crop, yet it handles salt poorly.

The team grafted cucumber onto hardy local types of related plants. They then tracked growth, body traits, and salt ion levels in the plants. Grafting gave the plants more salt tolerance and raised fruit yield. The method uses local plant stock and no chemicals. It offers growers a low-cost way to keep crops going on salty land.
pmc-10709924:
Pieternella Pieterse and Federico Saracini present a scoping review, published in 2023, on unpaid health workers in Sierra Leone. About half of the country's health workforce works without a salary, after hospitals take on medical and nursing graduates with a promise of paid posts later. The practice sits inside a world facing a deep shortage of health workers.

The review gathered thirty-six texts, from journal papers to ministry documents, that held data on these workers. Findings sorted into themes covering what the workers do, how patients fare, and how the workers themselves cope. Readers learn how much unpaid labor props up care delivery, and what that means for fairness to both patients and staff.
pmc-10710124:
Chen and six co-authors link knee force grades to jump height in top boxers in this twenty twenty-three study. Leg drive feeds punch force, and knee strength keeps a boxer's stance firm. Weak straight-leg force can bend form and raise joint harm risk in bouts.

Inside, a small squad of top male boxers took knee tests at three crank speeds. Straight-leg force grades fell as crank speed rose in the tests. Bend-to-straight force shares rose with speed in the same runs. Jump height tied most hard to straight-leg force at the top crank speed. The team backs blast-force drills at that top speed for boxers.
pmc-10710624:
Naosuke Nonoguchi and fourteen co-authors present a 2023 conference abstract on two young brain tumor patients who developed a hormone complication while freezing their eggs. Women with malignant gliomas may store eggs before chemotherapy. Fertility drugs can then overdrive the ovaries, which swell and leak fluid into the belly and chest, a syndrome graded mild to severe.

The abstract explains the chain: excess hormone lifts a growth factor that opens vessel walls, shifting fluid out of the blood. Severe cases can drop blood pressure, stall the kidneys, and seed clots. Early spotting and graded care are the defense. The two cases ground the warning in this rare pairing of tumor care and fertility care.
pmc-10712124:
Elham Mansouri and five co-authors review how nanoparticle coatings change radiosensitization in cancer therapy in this 2023 paper. Metal particles placed in a tumor boost the local dose from radiation. Coatings are added to cut toxicity, stop clumping, and guide particles to tumor cells. Yet the coat itself alters the physics and chemistry of the boost. Under low energy photons, a coat can absorb the low energy electrons that drive local dose gains, shielding the particle.

The coat seems to act more on the chemical stage, where reactive oxygen species form, than on the first physical stage. Irradiated coated particles lowered cancer cell survival more than normal cell survival in the studies reviewed. The authors frame coat design as a trade: delivery gains against dose losses. Coat choice must fit the radiation energy in use.
pmc-10712324:
Elanda Fikri writes a letter weighing a Yemen survey on public knowledge of mpox. The 2023 letter praises the study as the first of its kind in Yemen. Its call for targeted education campaigns and its policy value earn credit.

Four limits draw fire. Social media sampling skews toward internet users and the young in the capital, so the sample may not mirror Yemen. Answers may bend toward what respondents think others expect. The survey also never links knowledge to actual preventive behavior. Fikri urges field surveys that reach offline and varied groups, plus deeper study of how knowledge shapes action. The letter aims to sharpen the next round of mpox research in Yemen.
pmc-10714024:
Nine authors report a program that turns emergency department waiting time into social help in this 2023 study. People arriving at the emergency department often carry unmet social needs, from food to housing, that quietly drive their health.

Undergraduate volunteers screened waiting room patients with a questionnaire and referred those in need to community resources through a statewide database. Over one year the program reached 3,297 patients; 398 agreed to screening, and ninety-three percent of them had at least one unmet need. Nearly all wanted help, and sixty percent of positive screens were enrolled in the database. The study shows waiting time can be working time for social care.
pmc-10714124:
Minobu Ito, Atsuko Nishigaki, and Masami Hasegawa test how first carrion beetles shift scent goods from dead beasts, and how those shifts shape the bugs that come in late. Their 2023 lab and field tests link two views of the line of kinds on dead flesh.

A carrion beetle from Japan was the early kind on dead rats. Gas checks set plain dead beasts next to hurt ones, to ones fed on by beetles, and to beetles on their own. In the wake of half a day and more, dead beasts fed on by beetles sent out more high grades of two key sulphur goods that draw bugs in. Field traps with those goods as bait drew in more kinds and more bugs that eat flesh. The finds hint that early kinds steer the line by a shift of the scent cloud of the dead beast.
pmc-10714224:
Julia Stowe, Heather Whitaker, Nick Andrews, and Elizabeth Miller measure the risk of heart rhythm problems and cardiac arrest after COVID-19 vaccination in England. Their study came out in 2023. It covers forty million vaccinated adults and well over a hundred million doses.

Using a method that compares each person's risk just after vaccination with their own later risk, they found one clear signal. Admissions for rhythm problems, mostly palpitations without heart inflammation, rose briefly after second and booster messenger-RNA doses in younger adults. No rise appeared for cardiac arrest or any other rhythm outcome, for any vaccine, dose, or age group. In contrast, catching the virus itself raised the risk of all rhythm problems consistently. The authors call the findings reassuring on vaccine safety.
pmc-10714324:
Junichi Saito and co-authors test a therapy app for psychogenic erectile dysfunction in a 2023 feasibility study. The condition mixes body and mind, yet care often ignores the mental side. A phone app based on acceptance and commitment therapy could reach men who avoid clinics.

Eight men with situational symptoms used the app, called Dr App, through eight weekly modules. Six finished and completed the outcome surveys. Erectile function scores improved significantly, and satisfaction measures trended up, with a third to two-thirds of men crossing the line for meaningful change. Desire and orgasm scores did not move. The authors judge the app feasible and acceptable, and use the results to size a larger randomized trial.
pmc-10714624:
Sarah Abu Fadaleh and co-authors lay out the protocol for a trial of a newborn care kit in Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan, a remote mountain region with high newborn death rates. Pakistan has among the highest rates in the world. Bundling proven care steps into one kit, delivered by community health workers, could save lives at low cost.

In the planned trial, health workers give pregnant women a kit with a clean birth set, antiseptic gel, and skin oil. It also holds a temperature sticker, a blanket, a reusable warmer, and medicine tablets, plus picture guides. Villages are randomized to kit or standard care. The main outcome is death in the first month of life.
pmc-10715824:
Ihor Kuzin and twelve co-authors report from the field on the wartime spread of drug proof germs in Ukraine in twenty twenty-two, in a notes report. Drug proof bacteria kill more people worldwide than HIV or malaria, the authors note. The report came out in twenty twenty-three.

Ukraine entered the war with high proof rates, then saw more trauma wounds and strained hospitals. Proof germs were found more often and spread into Europe. A joint effort was set up mid year between the CDC, Ukraine's public health center, local teams, and world partners. Its aim was to boost lab strength and curb spread even as war went on.
pmc-10716124:
Boram Cha and co-authors look for what raises the risk of gallstones in patients fed through a tube placed into the stomach. Such feeding, called percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy, is common for bedridden patients who cannot eat. The team reviewed records from one Korean center for patients treated from 1996 to 2021 whose scans could confirm gallstones.

Of 576 patients, 161, or 28 percent, had gallstones. Being bedridden and having high levels of a blood marker of inflammation at the time of the tube placement both raised the risk on their own. Among bedridden patients, the share with stones rose to nearly 31 percent. Yet few of those with stones, only 5.6 percent, went on to inflamed gallbladders. Larger body size and higher cholesterol tracked with larger stones, and the authors advise scans for high-risk patients.
pmc-10717324:
Joan Fitzgerald and co-authors ask a practical question about cell therapy: does the liquid used to grow mesenchymal stromal cells change what the cells become? The team grew human bone marrow cells in five widely used culture media and compared colony formation, growth speed, and the ability to turn into other cell types. They also measured how well the cells calmed immune responses, and screened the cell surface with a panel of 243 markers.

The medium mattered a great deal. Cells grown in different media differed in cloning ability, growth, differentiation, and immune effects, and about a third of the surface markers changed with the medium. Yet every preparation still showed the standard markers CD73, CD90, and CD105. The findings help explain why results vary so much between laboratories.
pmc-10717624:
Chao Xu and co-authors adapt a pain questionnaire for Chinese patients in this 2023 study. The form asks about signs that the nervous system has become over-sensitive to pain. Their version was made for patients with knee arthritis who were set for a knee replacement at a large center in Xi'an.

The form was translated, translated back, and reviewed by experts to check its fit. In all, 325 patients filled it in, and 100 did so again a week later. The final form holds 25 items in five groups, covering mood, head and jaw signs, body signs, bladder signs, and tiredness and sleep. Scores were steady over time and lined up with pain and life quality scores.
pmc-10719324:
Heba Youssef, Salah Kamel, and Mohamed Hassan wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-three about managing energy in smart homes. Homes use a large share of electricity, and demand response lets households shift use to help the grid. The goal is to cut bills, flatten peaks, and import less power, while selling surplus from home solar and wind units.

The authors improve a nature-inspired search method modeled on how manta rays forage, adding a long-term memory step. They first test it on standard benchmark problems against rival methods. They then apply it to a smart home with a wind turbine, solar panels, and storage. Case studies show the plan lowers cost and peak load while using local renewable power well.
pmc-10720024:
Burning coal and oil shale leaves huge piles of ash, and the ash itself is a waste problem on top of the smoke. The four authors ask whether heat treatment can upgrade oil shale bottom ash so it can stand in for cement in concrete. Treating the ash changes its traits, which could make oil shale burning pay better while easing the waste burden.

The paper frames the work as a step toward greener building and greener energy use. If ash can replace part of the cement, builders would need less fresh cement and power plants would send less waste to dumps. The authors present the findings as useful for both the economics of oil shale burning and for waste handling in the energy and building trades.
pmc-10725924:
Negar Moradian, Mansoo Ko, Christopher Hurt, and David Brown study how walkers adjust their push-off force when a treadmill pulls backward against them. Their 2023 study uses a split-belt treadmill, where each foot rides its own belt. Keeping position on the belts while resistance grows demands a clear motor control strategy from each leg.

Eighteen healthy young adults walked against five levels of backward pull, from none to twenty percent of body weight. The team measured propulsive forces from each limb as resistance rose. Their aim was to reveal how the split of push between legs changes. Such findings inform gait rehabilitation methods that use resistance training.
pmc-10726724:
Reinhard Friedrich and co-authors measure jaw symmetry in patients with a nerve tumor syndrome in a 2023 study. Neurofibromatosis type 1 breeds tumors along nerves, and the plexiform kind can warp the growing face and count as precancerous. The team asked whether the jaw's shape betrays where such a tumor sits.

Rear-view head X-rays from one hundred sixty-eight patients were measured at three jaw landmarks. Patients with facial tumors were compared with patients whose tumors were scattered skin lumps, and with people free of the syndrome. Facial tumor patients showed clear, patterned departures from the midline planes. The departures shifted with which branches of the trigeminal nerve the tumor had colonized. The authors argue the jaw reads like a map of the tumor's local pressure on growing bone.
pmc-10727624:
Gao Chen and five co-authors describe the first eighteen patients treated for the new coronavirus pneumonia in Deyang, China, in a study published in 2023 covering the outbreak's first weeks. Half the patients had arrived from elsewhere, and half caught the virus from close family contact.

Most cases were of the normal type. Fever and cough were the common symptoms, and blood tests showed low white cell counts. Chest scans found hazy ground-glass patches in two thirds of the patients. All eighteen got antiviral and symptom-directed care. Their tests turned negative within 9 to 23 days, and all were cured and discharged by March 5, 2020. The authors offer the series as an early reference for diagnosis and control.
pmc-10728724:
Ning Zhang and eleven co-authors search the genome of Escherichia coli for the genes that decide whether it survives being hunted. Its predator, Myxococcus xanthus, is a bacterium that swarms and devours other microbes, and the pair is a lab classic. What the prey does to defend itself was the open side of the story. The team screened a library of Escherichia coli mutants, each missing a chunk of chromosome, for ones the predator could not eat as easily.

One mutant stood out. Its deleted stretch held seven genes, and two mattered: fis and dusB. Losing fis cut the prey's production of flagella, the whipping tails it swims with, and bought resistance. Losing dusB made the prey worse at provoking the predator to produce its antibiotic, myxovirescin A, and slightly harder for that antibiotic to kill. The authors read both genes as levers in a complex chemical arms race.
pmc-10729224:
Brian Schmidt and co-authors track limb loss after bone infection in a 2023 study. Bone infection can lead to amputation, but long term rates were not well known. The team followed more than one thousand hospital patients with the infection over two years and sorted them by infection site.

People with diabetes faced far higher odds of leg amputation, return to hospital, and longer stays, and a higher risk of death.
