Male sex, Black race, past smoking, heart disease, poor blood flow, and kidney disease each raised amputation risk on their own. Leg risk and arm risk did not share all the same drivers. Clinics can use the list to watch high risk patients closely.
pmc-10734024:
Min Zhuang and co-authors date the last gasps of a giant ancient lava province in northwest China in a 2023 study. The Tarim flood basalts erupted in the Permian, and the Puchang granites, tied to a vanadium-titanium magnetite deposit, record its late stage. The team analyzed two granite types' chemistry, zircon ages, and hafnium isotopes.

The porphyritic granite crystallized about two hundred seventy-six million years ago from enriched mantle material; the biotite monzogranite followed about seven million years later from mantle melts with crust stirred in. Both are silica- and potassium-rich with distinctive rare-earth patterns. Their setting was a post-collision stretch as the mantle rose beneath Tarim. The results pin down how a large igneous province winds down into granite-making.
pmc-10734224:
Francesco Galassi and five co-authors write a letter asking whether a tale in Boccaccio's Decameron holds an early account of indigestion. The piece was published in twenty twenty-three, blending medical history with a classic of Italian literature.

Dyspepsia, the modern term for a cluster of upper belly pain and discomfort, affects a large share of people and costs health systems dearly. A third of patients test positive for a stomach germ now known to drive many cases. Yet the history of the ailment is patchy: Greek doctors mentioned it, but its true cause stayed hidden for centuries. The authors turn to the fourteenth-century Decameron for a possible medieval witness. Their letter invites readers to weigh literature as a source for disease history.
pmc-10734624:
Teens and young adults with cancer often carry heavy worries alone, and meeting peers is hard when patients are few and spread out. A Danish team built a phone app with patients, holding facts, a symptom tracker, and a peer community. Their 2023 study gave the app to young patients for six weeks and measured quality of life before and after.

Eighty-one people joined across Denmark; most finished the study period. Among those in active treatment, role functioning improved clearly over the six weeks. Pain scores moved in a better direction as well. The study tests whether a shared digital space can support young patients through a lonely stretch of care.
pmc-10735424:
Eva-Maria Trinkaus analyzes how a German television series portrays home care work squeezed by the clock, in a humanities paper from twenty twenty-three. The series follows an in-home caregiver through ten-minute episodes. Its very title blends the words for carer and legionnaire, framing daily care as front-line combat.

Trinkaus focuses on the relationship between caregiver and patient, and what interaction can survive inside a tightly rationed visit. By shadowing the nurse through ordinary tasks, the show makes both her pressure and the patients' needs visible. Rather than quick glimpses, the short episodes open real insight into the job's duties through personal, fictional stories. The analysis sits where media studies meet care research.
pmc-10735824:
Darlingtina Esiaka and Elizabeth Luth test pathways from neighborhood disorder to cognition in older adults in a 2023 study. Messy surroundings, from graffiti to public drinking, link to worse cognition and dementia risk. Sleep quality and social cohesion might carry that effect. A national aging survey from 2021 supplied the sample.

Over twenty-five hundred adults aged seventy and up were studied. Staff rated physical disorder on a short scale. Those taking part rated trust where they live and their recent sleep. Thinking was tested across memory, orientation, and executive tasks. Greater disorder tied clearly to worse scores on those tasks. Social cohesion carried much of that link in the models. Sleep quality did not carry the link, though better sleep still tracked better thinking. The authors highlight local bonds as a protective channel. Spending on the area may defend thinking in part through such bonds.
pmc-10736024:
Jennifer Kaufman, Yiyi Wu, Jasmine Manalel, and four colleagues report interview research with adults living with HIV, published in two thousand twenty-three. Some newer antiretroviral regimens are associated with weight gain in groups already at risk for obesity. The team interviewed sixty-one people in a Medicaid managed care plan, aged twenty-three to sixty-five, about half of them fifty or older. The sample was majority non-Hispanic Black and about a third Hispanic, and included cisgender men, cisgender women, and transgender or nonbinary participants.

Many participants linked weight gain to their HIV medications, but attitudes split by age. Younger people, including transgender participants, often welcomed gain as a sign of better health and focused on appearance. Older participants more often framed gain as natural aging and acceptance, while worrying about mobility and other health conditions. The authors advise providers to tailor weight counseling to these differing perspectives.
pmc-10736124:
Nirmala Lekhak and co-authors ask whether meditation eases anxiety and low mood in older adults, in a 2023 study set during the COVID-19 pandemic. Their survey drew 1,861 older adults from across the nation. The team frames the work with a theory that good feelings widen a person's outlook and build lasting inner resources.

Adults who meditated felt more loved than those who did not. That feeling of compassionate love, in turn, linked to fewer signs of depression and anxiety on standard scales. The path from practice to calm ran through love, the models show. For care programs, the study points to meditation as a low-cost support that works partly by strengthening felt bonds with others.
pmc-10736224:
Jennifer Bugos reports a 2023 study on whether short music training can sharpen mental control in older adults. Earlier work linked music training to better inhibition, the skill of holding back a wrong response, but little was known about which kind of training helps or how much is needed. Bugos compared a piano course with a music listening course in adults new to music.

Eighteen older adults were split at random between the two courses and tested over twelve weeks. The piano group made fewer errors and answered faster on control tasks than the listening group. The gap grew clear after eight weeks of training. Bugos suggests that playing with both hands places a heavier load on the mind than listening alone, and that this load may drive the gain.
pmc-10736324:
Dillon and five co-authors shared methods in this paper from twenty twenty-three for research with people near death. Such patients are often left out of health studies for practical, ethical, and cultural reasons. The authors draw on studies with home hospice patients and people with advanced cancer. They review what blocks inclusion and what helps.

Illness swings cause cancellations and dropout, and home visits eat time and budget. Worries about vulnerability and taboos around naming death add friction. Partnerships with community groups and care teams opened doors in their projects. Flexible designs, careful wording, and staff support also helped. Using family interviews and existing data widened the reach further.
pmc-10736424:
Richard Allsopp and co-authors test whether a longevity gene variant blunts high blood pressure's harm to the brain, in a 2023 study. Brain autopsies from 809 men of Japanese ancestry in a Honolulu cohort were checked for tiny strokes called microinfarcts, and the results were set against genes and risk factors.

Overall, body mass was the clearest predictor of microinfarcts, with hypertension borderline. Splitting by the FOXO3 variant changed the story: without the longevity-linked G allele, hypertension more than doubled the odds of microinfarcts, while carriers showed no added risk at all. The authors read the gene as a shield and call for checks in other populations.
pmc-10736624:
Samaneh Farsijani and six co-authors studied meal timing and muscle health in older adults in a 2023 paper. When people eat, not just what they eat, can set the body's daily clock, yet its link to muscle has been little studied. The team used data from 828 adults averaging 76 years old in the SOMMA study.

Eating windows ran about eleven hours a day, from roughly 8 in the morning to 7 in the evening. Longer windows and later last meals went with greater muscle mass. A longer window also went with stronger leg power. The finding runs against fasting claims drawn mostly from animal work. The authors call for more study of meal timing in aging and care settings.
pmc-10736724:
Allison Marziliano and co-authors describe building a web platform to ease loneliness in dementia caregivers in a 2023 paper. Caregivers of people with Alzheimer's disease often feel isolated, and proven help is scarce. The team adapted ideas from meaning centered therapy, which raises a sense of purpose and has helped cancer patients and caregivers.

Development ran in three stages: rewriting scripts from six therapy videos, gathering feedback from 15 caregivers in interviews, and building the site with web specialists. The platform, RELOAD-C, joins six short videos, seven virtual peer meetings, and written material. Caregivers shaped wording choices and asked to drop hard talk prompts with the care recipient.
pmc-10736824:
Taylor Bucy, Tetyana Shippee, and Nidhi Kohli published this 2023 study on measuring quality of life in assisted living homes. Minnesota funded a public report card for such homes, built with a state university, and rolled out a resident survey statewide in 2021-22. This study checks whether the survey truly measures what it claims.

The survey covers seven areas of daily life: food, staffing, setting, engagement, choice, culture, and safety. Using pilot answers from 1,392 residents, the team tested how consistently the questions of each area hang together. Four areas, food, staff, safety, and engagement, scored acceptably. Three areas wobbled, and their scores overlapped heavily with each other. The results tell the state which parts of its report card are solid and which need rework.
pmc-10736924:
Christine Fruhauf and six co-authors hear from grandmothers raising grandchildren through the COVID-19 years. Care loads that were already heavy grew under lockdown rules. Their 2023 talk shares group chats with fourteen such grandmothers, drawn from a wider survey of custodial grandparents.

Many said the virus was hard, yet not harder than the daily work of raising the kids. School fights over online class, custody cases, and home visits all ran through the fear of catching the virus. Parenting style stayed the same, they said, but inner resolve grew. Time shut in also brought new shared fun and closer bonds. Gains sat beside losses, the team notes, and grit ran through both.
pmc-10737024:
Snehal Kulkarni wrote a study from 2023 on hand grip strength in older adults in India. Grip strength is a quick sign of muscle health and of how well a person may cope with daily life as they age. Kulkarni used a large national survey of ageing in India from 2017 and 2018. The study covered more than twenty-seven thousand people aged sixty and over.

On average, men gripped much harder than women. Grip was weaker in people who lived in rural areas, had trouble with daily tasks, or moved slowly. It was also weaker in those with poor balance, a past fall, or bone and joint disease. Kulkarni argues that a grip test should be a routine part of health checks for older adults at high risk.
pmc-10737224:
Janie Taylor and Renee Zucchero compare hospice nurses with nurses elsewhere on wellbeing and work life, in a 2023 paper. Nursing strains people: populations age, chronic illness grows, and the pandemic stretched staff thin. Whether end-of-life specialists fare better or worse than colleagues was unknown.

Seventy-two nurses, thirty-one in hospice and forty-one elsewhere, completed an online survey gathered by snowball sampling. Hospice nurses reported healthier work settings, stronger self-awareness, more trust in their palliative skills, and more compassion satisfaction, with less burnout. Two measures did not differ: flexibility and secondary stress. The portrait complicates the assumption that death work is simply the hardest nursing.
pmc-10737324:
Hyeyoung Park and co-authors study the sleep of people who care for dying loved ones at home. Their 2023 mixed-methods work follows five caregiving cases, for advanced and chronic illness, mixing surveys, a month of personal sleep monitoring, two weeks of sleep journals, and interviews.

On standard scales the caregivers scored 6.1 for sleep quality, a poor range, while devices recorded about 7.4 hours of sleep a night. They woke roughly twenty times across the month, and average fatigue sat high. Device readings looked alike across caregivers, yet self-ratings spread from fairly bad to very good. Interviews surfaced themes of vigilance, self-reliance, emotional labor, and being the linchpin, all under one heading: not having control. A patient's day, good or bad, set the caregiver's night, which the authors say makes support hard to standardize.
pmc-10737424:
Ashleigh Holmes, Weijun Wang, and Yu-Ping Chang compare the inner lives of older adults grouped by how pain limits them. Pain in later life ties to disability, low mood, shrinking social worlds, and higher care costs, but pain varies so much that group patterns stay hidden. Using a national survey of 3,381 older Americans from 2021, the team split people into three groups: no recent pain, pain without limits, and pain that limits activity. Ten regression models then weighed mood, sleep, and outlook measures.

The limited group stood apart. Against the pain-free group, they showed clearly higher depression, anxiety, and fear of falling. They also struggled more to start and keep sleep and used more sleep medicine. Their positive feelings and sense of self-realization ran lower. The authors argue support should target the limited group first.
pmc-10737524:
Huai Cheng, a solo author, reports a 2023 study with fourth-year medical students. The students were asked, but not required, to finish six online tasks before class. Cheng checked whether doing the tasks was linked to two kinds of learning. One kind was skill shown with a practice patient who had fallen. The other kind was real behavior in clinic, seen in chart notes.

The study used simple links between task scores and the two outcomes. It asks a plain question for teachers: does homework before class show up later as better skill and better care? The work fits the flipped class model, where facts are learned at home and class time is used for practice. Teachers can use the findings to judge whether pre-class work is worth keeping and how to track it fairly.
pmc-10737624:
Kuan-Ching Wu and co-authors listen to older adults describe how they adapt to urinary problems in daily life. Their 2023 study draws on interviews with twenty-nine people averaging seventy-seven years old. The team coded the conversations against a framework about engaging with aging, letting new themes surface as they went.

Six themes emerged, covering the experience of urinary concerns, emotional responses, and the tactics people build. Participants reshaped routines, timed medications and drinks, scouted restroom locations, and set reminders or used aids. The pandemic added a sharp edge when public restrooms closed and outings shrank. Knowledge gaps and personal resources rounded out the picture. The authors say these homemade strategies deserve respect in person-centered care, since patients often solve problems long before clinics hear about them.
pmc-10737724:
Makenna Green, Jamie Mayer, and Laura White review what speech-language experts and their students think about caring for people with dementia. Their review is from two thousand twenty-three. These experts help patients with speech, language, and swallowing, all of which dementia can harm. Their training needs in this area were not well mapped.

The team searched ten databases and kept twenty-nine sources. Most were journal papers, and most used one-time surveys. Students at several degree levels took part alongside working clinicians. Five themes dominated: experience, attitudes, roles, knowledge, and confidence. Education and training came up most often as both a barrier and a help. The review names gaps in core skills and in how confidence is measured.
pmc-10737824:
Beatrice Crettenand Pecorini and Emmanuel Duplaa describe, in a 2023 study, a project where older adults and young people build digital life stories together. Ageism, judging people by age, remains widespread, and shared projects are one way to soften stereotypes on both sides.

Each elder-youth pair met to turn the elder's spoken life story into a digital narrative, with the younger partner supplying media skills from a training workshop. Interviews, journals, and the finished stories were studied for effects. Early results matched the team's 2019 findings: better well-being, weaker generational stereotypes, and less loneliness among participants. The method treats storytelling as a bridge, not a lesson.
pmc-10737924:
Elizabeth Gallagher and co-authors studied older adult children who care for very old parents with dementia, in a 2023 paper. These caregivers are often past sixty five and may juggle their own health needs, grandchildren, or retirement. A parent with dementia can show hard behavior and mood symptoms, and the study asks what caregivers do day to day in response.

The team held deep interviews with one hundred caregivers whose parents were ninety or older. They found seven main strategies, from setting the record straight to going along with the parent. Other strategies were distracting, ignoring, telling small lies, giving medicine, and changing the home setting. Telling small lies and distracting often went together in the same families.
pmc-10738124:
Francesca Marino and co-authors report a 2023 study on heart rhythm spread and daily activity, tracked at home, and their links to thinking skill. Low spread in heart rhythm and low activity link to poor thinking in clinic tests. Whether those links hold in free daily life for older adults had not been checked.

The study drew 1,590 adults aged 72 to 94 from a long heart study, who wore a chest patch for 14 days. The patch read heart signals and motion at once. Neither heart rhythm measure linked to test scores or to mild loss and dementia. More daily motion did link to higher scores and to far lower odds of mild loss and dementia. The team calls for more work on which heart measures count.
pmc-10738424:
Barrón and co-authors mine nurses' free-text notes for early signs of dementia in home health patients. Formal diagnoses often come late. Nurses, though, see patients at home and write down what they observe. The team applied language-processing tools to about 1.8 million notes. The notes covered more than fifty-six thousand patients of a large home care agency.

Among patients who started care without a dementia diagnosis, twenty-three percent received one within four years. The more symptoms such as confusion or memory loss appeared in the notes, the higher the later diagnosis rate. Patients with both signs were diagnosed at about five times the rate of those with none. Note mining could trigger earlier referrals.
pmc-10738524:
Babatope Ogunjesa and co-authors study older adults' pandemic lives in a 2023 paper. Lockdowns and distancing shielded older people from the virus but cut the family and friend contact that well being rests on. Whether the harm fell evenly across racial groups was an open question.

Survey data on 1,051 adults aged fifty and up, gathered by a national research center, were reanalyzed. Quality of life reports were modeled against contact with family and friends, with race in view. Logistic modeling and margin estimates did the weighing. The results show both the protection that contact gave and the uneven ground groups started from, a guide for fairer crisis support.
pmc-10738824:
Yitao Xi reports the prevalence and correlates of depression among older drivers in the LongROAD study, publishing in twenty twenty-three. Depression is well studied in younger people, but data on rates for older adults are scant. LongROAD tracked nearly three thousand drivers aged sixty-five to seventy-nine across five American sites. They were tested with a standard patient-reported outcomes tool.

About six percent had depression at enrollment, while life-long prevalence reached about twenty percent. Only about a fifth of those with depression were taking antidepressants. Rates ran higher among women, the unmarried, and those with low home income. Diabetes and anxiety disorder also tracked with depression. City and rural dwellers were much the same. Xi ends by saying that screening and treatment programs are needed, since most depressed older adults go untreated.
pmc-10738924:
Linda Sawyer and six co-authors ask whether rural older veterans liked getting full geriatric checkups by video in a 2023 study. Comprehensive assessments are hard to reach in rural areas, so the veterans health system piloted them over its video platform. The team phoned veterans who had completed a video assessment and ran a ten item satisfaction questionnaire.

Sixty three veterans answered, mostly white men around seventy six years old. Nearly all said communication was easy, information was clear, and privacy felt adequate. Three quarters felt comfortable with the technology. Many said they would still prefer in person visits, yet about seventy one percent would do video again. The authors conclude rural veterans were satisfied overall with the virtual process.
pmc-10739024:
Melissa O'Connor, Margaret Brace, and Kathryn Bowles present a 2023 paper on a decision support project for home health care discharge calls. Nurses and doctors must judge when an older patient can safely leave home health services. No national, proof based tool exists to guide those frequent calls.

Expert teams, each with two nurses and one doctor, reviewed 500 case studies on a secure website. For each case, they chose discharge or more care. The case mix matched the national home health population by sex, race, and main diagnosis. The experts voted to renew care in over 44 percent of cases. Their judgments form the seed data for the support tool.
pmc-10739524:
Giacomo Maria Cioffi and three co-authors watch cardiologists' eyes to learn whether AI guidance helps them read artery scans faster, in this 2023 study. Optical coherence tomography gives exquisite pictures inside coronary arteries during stenting, but reading them live takes expertise many operators lack. The AI-assisted Ultreon 2.0 software promises to close that gap.

Eighteen interventional cardiologists and fellows at McMaster reviewed scans on the AI platform and on its predecessor while eye trackers recorded every glance. With AI help, eyes landed on the region of interest in zero point nine seconds, against one point six. Total reading time fell from twelve point six to ten point two seconds. The share of attention inside the target zone rose from 41 to 58 percent. Gains were the same for veterans and novices. Accuracy, crucially, did not slip: the software sped the search without dulling the judgment at its end.
pmc-10740024:
Wen-ting Yin and co-authors compare two ways to roast sesame seeds in a 2023 food study. Sesame oil's flavor comes from roasting, usually with hot air. Microwave roasting is a greener option, but its effects on aroma, nutrition, and harmful compounds were unclear. The team roasted seeds both ways and compared the oils in detail.

Microwaves opened more pores in the seeds and freed more of a protective compound, gamma-tocopherol. The oil carried more aroma compounds and, at six minutes, tasted more strongly roasted with less bitterness than hot-air oil. Harmful heat products, including two bitter alkaloids and a known carcinogen, came out lower under microwaves. The study makes microwave roasting look like a cleaner route to better oil.
pmc-10740424:
Muhammad Wasim Iqbal and co-authors report a 2023 study of how grazing and cud-chewing time links to milk output in pasture dairy cows. Automated collars tracked 162 spring-calving cows, across three breeds, through whole lactation seasons over three years. The cows grazed ryegrass and clover pasture with some extra feed in summer and autumn, under once-a-day milking.

More grazing time came with more milk, fat, and solids, though with lower live weight. Rumination time linked even more strongly to milk yield and its parts. Collar data of this kind, the authors argue, can flag cows that convert pasture well and guide breeding and feeding calls on pasture farms.
pmc-10740924:
Per Peetz Nielsen and Ewa Wredle test whether shade helps dairy cows in Swedish summers in a paper from 2023. Heat stress raises body temperature, cuts feed intake, and lowers milk yield. Twenty high-yielding cows on pasture were split into two groups. One group could use shade, and the other could not. Milk output was recorded daily, and pasture weather was logged every ten minutes.

Cows in early lactation without shade suffered most when hot days preceded measurement. Heat two days earlier and heat on the day itself both cut their yield. Shaded early-lactation cows were also affected, but less strongly. The authors conclude shade benefits cows in early lactation during Swedish summers. The work guides pasture planning in cool climates.
pmc-10741424:
Natacha Malu Miranda da Costa and nine co-authors test a bone scaffold dressed with an anti-fibronectin aptamer, in work from 2023. Aptamers are short binding molecules that can pull chosen proteins onto a material surface. Scaffolds with and without the aptamer were set into rat skull defects to form a blood clot, then seeded with bone-forming cells.

The aptamer group grew a denser fibrin network and drew in more stem cells and white blood cells. Bone markers such as alkaline phosphatase and bone sialoprotein lit up more strongly, and a key growth factor gene rose. The clot itself, not just the scaffold, is cast as an active player in regeneration.
pmc-10741824:
Shengyuan Zhao and co-authors target a metabolic enzyme in womb cancer in a 2023 study. The enzyme helps cells build DNA letters, and about 38 percent of these tumors overproduce it. Such tumors carry many mutations and unstable chromosomes. Blocking the enzyme, the team reasoned, may stress DNA copying further and push cancer cells over the edge.

High enzyme tumors also often carry faults in their DNA copying machines and grade as aggressive. In their tests, inhibition raised replication linked instability and made the cancer cells more sensitive. A drug that turns a tumor's own copying strain against it is an attractive strategy. The work nominates a patient group for such trials.
pmc-10742124:
Joel Vargas-Ahumada and co-authors compare two scans for staging prostate cancer, in this 2023 study. One scan is a costly PET method; the other is a cheaper SPECT method open to more hospitals. Eighteen men with mid-to-high risk cancer took both.

The PET scan found 257 lesions. The SPECT scan found 229 of them and caught every lesion in the prostate, nearby glands, and organs. Rates were a bit lower in lymph nodes and bone. Size measures agreed closely between the scans. The authors judge the cheaper scan a sound staging option where PET is out of reach.
pmc-10742224:
Charlotte Bauer and four co-authors test two suspect gene changes tied to Alzheimer disease in a 2023 study. The gene SORL1 makes a protein that ferries the amyloid precursor protein inside cells. Changes in the gene turn up in some inherited cases, but whether they drive the disease was unclear.

The team placed the normal gene and two changed forms into human cells that make the precursor protein. They then measured amyloid pieces, cut fragments, and the enzymes that do the cutting. Neither change shifted the processing in a harmful way. The result casts doubt on these two variants as disease causes.
pmc-10742524:
Andrzej Steplewski and co-authors test a gel that carries a scar-fighting antibody, in a 2023 study on healing after injury. Thick scars in joints, tendons, and nerves cause pain and stiff movement. The team's antibody slows the growth of the fibers that form such scars, and it worked in an earlier rabbit study.

Here they load the antibody into a gel that thickens at body heat. They check how fast the drug leaves the gel, whether it stays stable, and whether it still binds its target after release. Early results suggest the gel could deliver the drug to injury sites. That would give surgeons a gentler option than cutting scar tissue out.
pmc-10742624:
María Giménez and six co-authors published a food preservation study in twenty twenty-three on keeping fresh-cut artichokes from browning. Cut artichoke hearts darken fast, and earlier anti-browning treatments only partly work. The team combined the amino acid cysteine with a blend of essential oil components from oregano and thyme family plants.

Hearts of the Blanca de Tudela variety were stored nine days in the cold under four treatments. Cysteine plus the middle oil dose won on every front: least browning, strongest antioxidant measures, best texture, and top sensory scores. Phenolic content, the artichoke's health selling point, was best preserved too. The authors offer the pairing as a natural, eco-friendly shelf-life extender for a finicky product.
pmc-10742724:
Andreea Dumitrescu and six co-authors synthesized four vanadium compounds and tested them against bacteria and tumor cells, in a 2023 paper. Each compound pairs a decavanadate cluster, ten vanadium atoms bound with oxygen, with a guanidine-family partner. The team characterized the crystals with spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction, mapped their structures, and checked how stable they stay in solution and how they react with reactive oxygen species.

All four stopped the growth of four bacterial species, including staph and Escherichia coli, at low concentrations, though they did not break up established biofilms. Against melanoma cells, one compound stood out as most active, while sparing healthy skin cells relatively more. The authors present the family as a lead for antimicrobial and antitumor chemistry, where metal clusters paired with organic partners can tune activity.
pmc-10742824:
Jiantianye Deng and co-authors review compounds from a tea-linked fungus genus in 2023. The genus partners a well-known mold group and holds about twenty species found widely in nature and homes. It drives the fermentation of several traditional foods, from brick teas to fermented bean pastes.

Its compounds span several chemical families, including pigments, ring alkaloids, and scent compounds. Lab studies credit them with effects against oxidation, microbes, tumors, malaria, and inflammation, among others. The review gathers chemistry and activity data for all species in the genus. The authors offer it as a base for future drug hunting.
pmc-10743824:
Plant-pathogenic fungi store fat in lipid droplets inside their spores and threads, and they burn that fat to power infection. The nine authors study a plasma membrane proton pump, CsPMA2, in the fungus Colletotrichum siamense. Deleting the pump gene shrank spores, cut germination, and weakened both the infection pads the fungus builds on leaves and its overall virulence, while thread growth stayed normal.

The mutant also grew more sensitive to phytic and oxalic acids. The pump sits in lipids of the plasma and inner membranes, and without it droplet accumulation fell sharply, with twelve lipid species down and three up. Low pH also suppressed the pump and droplet buildup. The authors conclude the pump governs droplet formation and thereby the fungus's power to infect.
pmc-10744324:
Roberto Zagami and co-authors study how a charged chain speeds a metal step into a ring compound in a 2023 paper. The ring can host zinc ions, and its pace in plain fluid is slow. The chain grabs the ring by charge and shifts shape as acidity changes.

At one acidity point, where the chain sits loose and rich in charge, the pace leapt near a thousand-fold. Salt in the fluid cut the gain back down. The team reads the boost as the chain drawing both parts close, like charge crowding near a charged thread in water.
pmc-10744424:
Konstantinos Dimitriadis and co-authors review what messenger proteins called interleukins do in hepatitis B infection, in a 2023 narrative review. The virus is a leading cause of chronic liver disease and liver cancer worldwide. Immune signals decide whether the virus is suppressed or persists, and drugs that block interleukins for other diseases can wake a sleeping infection, which makes the map clinically urgent.

The review sorts the family by effect. Several inflammation-driving members help suppress the virus, while the calming members IL-10, IL-23, and IL-35 seem to help it copy itself. IL-17 tracks with liver injury. A few members have been tried as treatments with mixed results, and IL-22 remains murky, possibly both copying helper and damage driver. The authors offer the map to clinicians weighing immune therapy in patients with past or present hepatitis B.
pmc-10744924:
Ioanna Aggeletopoulou leads a large team in this 2023 study on a urine test that may flag danger in liver patients who bleed from swollen veins. In cirrhosis, the adrenal glands can underperform, and free cortisol is the truest gauge of that shortfall, yet it is costly to measure directly. The team compared cortisol readings across blood, saliva, and a day's urine in forty bleeding patients.

The urine measure tracked free blood cortisol well. It also ran lower in patients with worse liver scores and higher inflammation. Patients who rebled, caught infection, or died showed lower urine cortisol. Liver stage itself predicted six-week death, and a clotted portal vein predicted early treatment failure. The authors propose urine cortisol as a cheap risk marker worth larger trials in this fragile group.
pmc-10745024:
Hadrian Platzer and co-authors drip bioactive glass on joint-lining cells from worn knees, in a dish study from 2023. Knee wear, osteoarthritis, fires the joint lining, which leaks enzymes that chew gristle. The glass, 45S5, can tune fire, but its touch on this lining was near a blank.

Cells from knee wear souls grew with or sans glass dust. At day one and day seven, enzyme and call-part counts were read. One chew enzyme fell at both reads; its kin rose late. Two fire calls rose at both reads, and two more by day seven. The glass moves the lining, plain — but not in one clean dir, calm or flame. The team calls the tale mixed, and a warn to dose with care.
pmc-10745324:
Cheng Guo and co-authors studied a jet machining method for cutting tiny channels in metallic glass, in a 2023 paper. The glass is a zirconium-based metal with prized traits. The machining method uses a jet of fluid and electric action, with no contact. The fluid used here was alcohol-based rather than water-based.

Channels below a millimeter wide were cut at varied speeds and voltages. Raising voltage made channels much deeper and wider. The effect on depth was especially strong. Raising scan speed made channels shallower, with little change in width. Surface quality stayed high under the method. The authors judge the alcohol-based jet an effective way to shape such glasses. It can also tune surface structures for later use.
pmc-10745724:
Junbo Jung and co-authors build a flexible film that cools objects below the air temperature while using no power at all. Radiative cooling works by reflecting sunlight and beaming the object's own heat out to space through a clear band of the sky. Rigid photonic designs perform well but bend poorly and cost much to make.

Their film mixes titanium dioxide microparticles into silicone rubber. Particle size and loading are tuned so the film reflects the solar range strongly and emits well in the sky window. The result is a bendable sheet that can wrap pipes, tents, or electronics. Zero-energy cooling that ships as a roll could cut air-conditioning demand in hot regions.
pmc-10745824:
Sora Kang and co-authors test a yeast extract against brain inflammation in 2023. Parkinson disease grows where inflammation and oxidative stress meet in the brain. The team studied a patented yeast lysate that mops up harmful aldehydes. Cell tests first showed strong antioxidant action.

Mice dosed with the extract before an inflammatory trigger kept their dopamine neurons. Brain support cells stayed calm instead of flaring. Liver inflammation markers also eased. The extract is offered as a candidate shield for dopamine circuits. Human value remains unproven, but the animal signal is broad and consistent.
pmc-10745924:
Kang Yi and co-authors report a materials study, published in 2023, on a double perovskite ceramic with useful magnetic and electrical behavior. The compound joins lanthanum, iron, chromium, and oxygen in a doubled crystal pattern, and the team made it as a powder using heated water under pressure. The grains came out nearly round and just under a micron wide, in a slanted crystal form.

Spectroscopy confirmed the expected building blocks and mixed charge states of iron and chromium. The material showed weak magnetism at low temperature, a hint of a disordered magnetic phase above its ordering point, and resistance that fell as it warmed, as a semiconductor should. Its electrical response also shifted strongly with frequency, traits of interest for sensor and memory materials.
pmc-10747724:
Kodchakorn Mahasongkram and co-authors built, in a 2023 study, new antibodies meant to wake up T cells against cancer. A surface switch on T cells, called OX40, boosts attack when it is turned on. Drugs that press this switch may add to the gains of checkpoint drugs.

Using phage display and gene craft, the team made fully human antibody pieces fused to an antibody tail. The pieces bind a part of OX40 known to fire its signal. In lab tests, the fused antibodies helped T cells grow, live longer, and release more signal chemicals. They also trended toward stronger killing of ovarian cancer cells. The design offers a fresh set of OX40 tools for cancer therapy work.
pmc-10751624:
The authors pool safety data on wearable sensor patches for a digital medicine system in a study from 2023. The system pairs a drug tablet containing a tiny ingestible marker with a skin patch, an app, and a web portal, so doses can be confirmed. Skin irritation from patches is the main worry, and three patch versions were developed in turn to improve the design.

Data from twelve studies covered 763 adults, patients and healthy volunteers, exposed to at least one patch. Events such as rash, redness, itch, and blisters were grouped as irritation events and counted for each version. The pooled analysis compares irritation across the successive designs.
pmc-10753524:
Janan Hui, Jacob Majikes, and Kathryn Riley adapt capillary electrophoresis to check the purity of DNA origami structures. DNA origami folds DNA into tiny shapes built to order, for use in medicine, computing, and measurement. But misfolded shapes and leftover staple strands are hard to spot fast. The team tuned two modes of the method for this job.

Both modes split folded origami from extra staples cleanly, down to baseline. The transient isotachophoresis mode did better on sharpness, efficiency, and peak shape. Dyes from the SYBR family tagged the structures inside the column, allowing sensitive laser detection. The method also told apart origami of different shapes and split clumps apart. It gives builders a fast quality check for a growing nanomaterial.
pmc-10753724:
Cancer cells often learn to pump out the drugs meant to kill them, using a protein gate called P-glycoprotein. Moralev and co-authors tested a new compound against that pump in 2023. The compound joins a licorice-root acid with a nitrogen-bearing ring, a design chosen to fit how known pump blockers work.

Computer docking suggested the compound grips the pump's inner channel well. In two drug-resistant cell lines, one human and one mouse, harmless doses of the compound let a tracer and a cancer drug build up inside the cells. That buildup made the cells far more sensitive to the drug, matching a known blocker. The authors present the compound as a safe, promising lead for beating drug resistance in tumors.
pmc-10753824:
Stefan Szczepan and co-authors check a sprint swim test for teen swimmers in a 2023 study. The test has swimmers sprint front crawl while tethered to a light load, so coaches can gauge top anaerobic power without a full race. Eight swimmers, four girls and four boys near age thirteen, swam the test twice.

Speed was logged over a fifteen meter stretch by an automated device, and smooth curves gave peak and low speeds and total time. Those three measures repeated with low scatter and strong agreement between trials. Other curve measures were less steady. The authors deem the named three fit for tracking young sprinters.
pmc-10754024:
Joao Presume and co-authors review the mitral valve apparatus in hearts with dilated cardiomyopathy. Their 2023 narrative review explains how a diseased left ventricle can make a healthy valve leak. This secondary leak arises when the ring, leaflets, cords, and muscles that form the valve are pulled out of shape.

The authors describe the normal anatomy first, then the changes seen in ischemic and non-ischemic forms of the disease. They argue for a full multi-part assessment: leak measures alone are not enough. Sizes and shapes of the valve parts and the ventricle carry outlook value, and they predict whether repair will succeed and last. The review guides clinicians who plan valve work in failing hearts.
pmc-10755624:
Trista Benítez and co-authors study wrist fracture care and health coverage in this 2023 paper. Surgery with plates and screws is a common fix for a broken wrist bone. The team asked whether gaps between racial and ethnic groups shrink once patients reach sixty-five. At that age, nearly all United States residents gain Medicare coverage.

Records covered nearly twenty-seven thousand patients in three states. Black and Hispanic patients received the surgery less often than White patients. Reaching Medicare age did not close the gap. In fact, the gap at sixty-five was wider than the trend predicted. The findings suggest that coverage alone does not erase unequal treatment after injury.
pmc-10762524:
Stem cells meant to repair diabetic tissue die quickly in the very sugar-rich environment they are sent to fix. Ejlal Abu-El-Rub and eleven co-authors asked what the sugar does to them, in a 2023 study. They grew human fat-derived mesenchymal stem cells for seven days in normal or high glucose.

The high-glucose cells lost viability and showed disturbed mitochondria, the cell's power plants, in their splitting and fusing balance. Signs of programmed cell death rose. Protein measurements traced a signaling chain, through PI3K, TSC1, and mTOR, that links nutrient sensing to the damage. The authors argue the transplant problem is partly a preparation problem: cells raised or shielded against glucose stress before delivery might survive long enough in diabetic tissue to do their repair work.
pmc-10783824:
Xiaoyang Wang, Fei Gao, Wei Li, and Yijun Zhou read the full chloroplast genome of a desert plant, in a paper dated twenty twenty-three. Zygophyllum brachypterum grows in the deserts of Central Asia, Mongolia, and northwest China. Its green-cell genome runs 104,590 letters with the usual four-part build.

The genome holds 106 genes, split among protein-coding, transfer, and ribosomal types. Eleven genes for one energy complex are missing, a striking gap. Family analysis placed the plant in its expected subfamily, close to two named kin. The data aid study of how this family copes with salty soils.
pmc-10795824:
Lingjun Zhang and nine co-authors build in 2023 a targeted drug aimed only at active T cells that drive disease. T cells fuel many autoimmune ills and graft-versus-host disease. Killing all T cells would leave patients defenseless, so aim matters.

Their drug links an antibody that locks onto CD6, a T cell surface mark, to a toxin that halts cell division. Resting T cells divide little, so they shrug off the toxin. Active, fast-dividing cells take the hit. Lab tests show sharp killing of active human and mouse T cells. In mice, the drug treats two models of eye autoimmunity and one graft model, while sparing normal T cells at the same dose.
pmc-10806124:
Liu and co-authors study children whose epilepsy is caused by new variants in the GABRA1 gene. This gene helps build a receptor that calms brain activity, so faults in it can leave the brain overexcited and prone to seizures. The team asks whether where a variant sits in the gene changes the illness.

They report six patients and compare the position of each variant within the protein with the child's symptoms and severity. Variants in certain subregions were linked to distinct patterns of disease. This kind of mapping helps doctors interpret a genetic result for a newly diagnosed child and may one day guide choices between medicines that act on this receptor system.
pmc-10808624:
Hana Kim, Jessica Obermeyer, and Robert Wiley give the first review of written discourse in brain-based communication disorders. Such disorders come from stroke, from slow cell loss, or from a decline that has not yet fully bloomed. Their review, shown as a 2023 paper, sweeps six databases for work since 2000. It asks four things: how patients split from healthy peers, how groups split, how time shifts the gap, and how written discourse splits from spoken.

Nineteen studies made the cut, some on more than one question. Most set patients next to healthy peers and found clear gaps. Stroke-related language loss gave fewer words and plain clause builds. The big memory disorder gave thin fact loads, which thinned more with time. Written and spoken discourse each show their own side of the loss, the team says, so both earn a place in tests and care.
pmc-10809824:
Three authors present a pilot study published in two thousand twenty-three on tests of the small airways in children with asthma. The outer, peripheral airways matter for asthma control, but it is unclear which test best flags poor control. Several methods estimate resistance, trapped air, and uneven ventilation in that region.

Children with controlled and uncontrolled asthma, thirty-five and twenty-nine of them, took a battery of breathing tests. The set included standard spirometry, a body-box method, oscillation testing, a gas washout test, and exhaled nitric oxide. Most small-airway measures ran higher in the uncontrolled group. Each measure's accuracy was judged by a standard curve method.
pmc-10824924:
Jing-bin Huang, Chang-chao Lu, Zhen-zong Du, Jian-rong Yang, and Jun-jun Li published a study of surgery outcomes in aortic valve endocarditis, focusing on destruction of the valve's supporting ring. This infection of the heart valve is dangerous, and when it eats into the annulus, repair becomes far harder.

The team reviewed 512 surgical patients treated between 2006 and 2022. Eighty had annulus destruction and the rest did not. Overall, 32 patients died during the operation period. Statistical analysis tied ring destruction to higher death rates in hospital and at one year. It also predicted longer time on a ventilator and early leaks around the replaced valve. The authors argue this complication raises both risk and cost, and needs optimized management.
pmc-10832024:
Matilda Aberese-Ako and co-authors studied community engagement in COVID-19 control in two Ghanaian towns in a study published in 2023. Health goals call for strong community roles in fighting disease. The team asked officials and residents how engagement worked during the pandemic and what it taught them.

Talks covered 36 officials from health, information, and civic bodies, plus ten group sessions with 87 residents. All four agencies said they informed and taught communities about control steps and vaccines. Five engagement levels, from informing to empowering, frame the analysis. Data came from mid 2021 fieldwork. The authors draw lessons for later health campaigns in like settings.
pmc-10847324:
Bingqing Xie and colleagues mapped the cell neighborhoods inside ovarian tumors, comparing first tumors with spread tumors across the diseases several forms. Ovarian cancer is not one disease but at least five types with different origins and treatments, and single-cell studies had mostly covered one type. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team sequenced RNA cell by cell from solid tumor samples. The samples came from the ovaries and from spread sites in the belly of a dozen patients. They cover six forms of the disease.

The maps show which cell types live in each form and site, and which marker genes and signaling pairs are active where. Patterns tied to tumor type and location point to routes by which cancers spread and resist care. The authors offer the atlas for sharper patient grouping and better matched treatment choices.
pmc-10870424:
Saba Jalalifar and co-authors offer a 2023 lab study testing a bee venom peptide against drug-resistant staph bacteria. Resistant strains shrug off once-reliable antibiotics and hide inside tough biofilms. Peptides that kill microbes may restore the old drugs' lost power.

Melittin, the main peptide in bee venom, was tested alone and paired with penicillin or oxacillin. Targets were resistant strains that form biofilms, including vancomycin-resistant ones. Lab assays measured bacterial killing and biofilm breakup at several doses. Pairing a peptide with failed antibiotics is the core hope here: reviving cheap, well-known drugs against infections that now outlast them.
pmc-10876024:
Linda Alfano, Ivano Malcotti, and Rosagemma Ciliberti weigh the ethics of artificial intelligence in psychotherapy for adolescents, in an article published in 2023. Chatbot therapists promise wider access to mental health care for teenagers. They also raise hard questions about safety, privacy, and the loss of human contact.

The authors argue that responsible rollout needs rules before scale: accuracy checks, privacy protection, and respect for patient autonomy. Schools carry a special duty, teaching teenagers both knowledge and ethical judgment about online content. Parents matter too, through time, dialogue, and a safe space to share digital experiences. Health and social services, they add, should be redesigned around how adolescents actually live now. Done carefully, the authors conclude, AI could widen care without hollowing it out. Done carelessly, it risks the very people it aims to help.
pmc-10903324:
Negin Esfandiari and co-authors count deaths from salmonella infections across Iran using national health records. Their 2023 study covers 2013 to 2019 and splits deaths by year, season, province, sex, age, and town or country living. Non-typhoid salmonellosis caused 800 deaths in that span, while typhoid caused 32.

Blood poisoning drove most of the non-typhoid deaths. Both forms peaked in spring. Non-typhoid deaths clustered among people in their seventies and eighties and in cities, while typhoid hit children under ten hardest and struck rural areas more. Three provinces carried the heaviest loads of each type. The authors say the patterns should guide food safety policy and warnings aimed at the groups at most risk.
pmc-10915924:
Zahra Alizadeh and six co-authors describe two Iranian patients with a rare immune defect and two new gene variants. Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency is a combined immunodeficiency with a deep cellular fault. Both unrelated patients showed autoimmune hemolytic anemia, low T cells, and high eosinophils. One had mild cortical atrophy, and the other showed developmental delay, low muscle tone, and food allergy.

Genetic testing found a novel variant in exon 3 in one patient and another in exon 5 in the second. Both rated as likely pathogenic under standard guidelines. Since the deficiency carries a poor outlook, the authors stress early diagnosis so stem cell treatment can start in time.
pmc-10994624:
Ali Farag, Wassan Abass, and Hyder Qassem evaluate under-the-tongue glutathione supplements in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, published in 2023. Glutathione is a strong antioxidant and anti-inflammatory compound. The team asked whether adding it to standard therapy improves blood markers of oxidation and inflammation.

Fifty patients were split into two equal groups. One received standard inhaler therapy alone; the other added glutathione tablets twice daily for two months. Blood levels of two inflammatory signals and two antioxidant enzymes were measured before treatment and after one and two months. Inflammation markers fell in both groups, with no significant edge between them. The antioxidant enzymes rose in both groups, but more in the supplement group. The authors discuss what this pattern means for therapy.
pmc-11001324:
Yongqiang Dong and co-authors present a systematic review, published in 2023, comparing drug treatments that calm the immune system in lupus nephritis. In this kidney condition, lupus causes inflammation that can damage the kidneys over time. The review pools randomized trials of induction therapy, the first strong phase of treatment meant to bring the disease under control.

Sixteen trials with more than two thousand patients were combined in a network meta-analysis, which compares drugs that were not always tested head to head. A pairing of voclosporin with mycophenolate mofetil gave the highest rate of complete remission, followed by tacrolimus. That same pairing also carried the highest risk of infection, so the authors stress weighing benefit against safety.
pmc-11018324:
Aydın Yavuz and co-authors test a carbon ball compound in rats in a 2023 study of liver harm. The harm comes when blood returns to a liver that was starved of it, a known risk in liver surgery. A sleep gas used in such surgery adds its own twist to the case.

Thirty-six rats split into six groups, some with the hurt, some with the drug, some with the gas, and some with both. The team gave the carbon balls by weight and then read the liver tissue. The aim was to see if the balls shield the liver. Such rat work can flag a guard worth testing in the clinic.
pmc-11168924:
Abramson, Adler, Dunger, and co-authors introduce AlphaFold 3, a model that predicts how biological molecules fit together. AlphaFold 2 had already changed the field by predicting protein shapes with high accuracy. Many teams then used it to model proteins and design new ones.

AlphaFold 3 extends that power from single proteins to interactions between molecules. It uses a substantially updated design built around a diffusion approach, the same broad family used in image tools. Predicting how drugs and other molecules bind their targets could speed drug discovery and deepen basic biology at once.
pmc-11199424:
Gabriel Furian and five co-authors argue in 2023 that Brazil needs a dedicated program to prevent child sexual abuse by treating people with pedophilic disorder before any offense occurs. Their paper grows out of a case report of one such person, known to psychiatric and forensic services for a past history of concern.

The authors say Brazil's mental health system barely acknowledges this group, leaving a gap in care with serious consequences for children. Awareness among clinicians is the first step, they argue, followed by real prevention and treatment services. The model they point to treats prevention as public health, not only as policing.
pmc-11532424:
Alyssa Overton and a large Canadian team published a genomic surveillance study in twenty twenty-four on sniffing out new coronavirus lineages in airport wastewater. Toronto Pearson, the country's biggest international hub, has sampled its sewage since January twenty twenty-two. Planes deliver both passengers and the variants they carry.

Wastewater from both terminals and pooled aircraft sewage was sequenced with a tiled-amplicon method. The team tracked lineage trends over time and compared them with community data. Because travelers arrive from everywhere, the airport signal can reveal emerging variants before local clinics see them. The study presents airport wastewater as an early-warning layer in national surveillance, complementing Ontario's municipal monitoring programs.
pmc-11534624: Mohd Khairi Othman and co-authors describe how a hospital heart team handled a sudden valve failure, in a short report published in 2024. The patient had chronic rheumatic heart disease, which scars heart valves after repeated infections, and a cord that holds a valve leaflet had snapped. That rupture is an emergency in an already damaged heart. The report stresses public health teaching for patients and families, since preventing the underlying fever protects valves better than late repair can.
pmc-11538224:
Junyong Ou and nine co-authors wrote this 2024 review and network analysis on drug treatment for desmoid tumors that keep growing or resist care. These rare tumors spring from connective tissue and invade locally. Surgery is no longer the default, since drug therapy controls them better, but the best first drug was unclear.

Three studies with 295 patients fed the pooled network. By response rate, one drug class, the gamma-secretase blockers, ranked ahead of two rivals, though the ranges were wide. One rival class led on one-year freedom from growth, and plain chemotherapy led on the two-year mark. Side effects ran highest for the top-ranked class. The authors weigh the trade between control and safety and call the proof base thin.
pmc-11539324:
Ke Zhang and co-authors surveyed psychiatric nurses on violence and sleep in two thousand twenty-four. Psychiatric nurses face frequent workplace violence. The stress can wreck their sleep quality. Emotional labor is part of the pathway studied. Nurses either fake feelings or reshape them deeply. Job identity may buffer the harm done.

Three hundred nurses completed valid online questionnaires. Standard scales measured violence, acting style, and sleep. A modeling macro tested mediation and moderation paths. Surface acting carried part of violence's effect on sleep. Deep acting played a different mediating role. Strong occupational identity softened some links. The findings suggest targeted supports for ward staff. Sleep programs may aid retention in psychiatry.
pmc-11539424:
Lili Dong and colleagues presented two rare immune-deficiency cases in children in 2024. Both children lacked a working defence protein because of paired faulty copies of one gene, a form of chronic granulomatous disease. Both illnesses began with swollen neck glands, yet their later courses diverged sharply, which is the point of pairing them.

One child developed fungal infection of the membranes around the brain, described as an extremely rare site for this disease and not previously reported in this form. The second child followed a distinct course discussed alongside inflammatory lesions. The authors review earlier Chinese cases and urge doctors to consider this deficiency in similar children to cut misdiagnosis.
pmc-11551724:
Ayşe Gümüşler Başaran and co-authors poll health students in a 2024 study on their view of old age. As the share of old people grows, care for them moves to the fore. The students, in their last year of health courses, will soon give much of that care.

More than three hundred students told whether they hold slights against the old, how keen they are to care for them, and how they see aging. Near three in four said they did not want to give such care, a stark start. The team weighed what bends those views. Schools gain a warning: skill with no will to care will not serve an aging land.
pmc-11572624:
Roberta Pajno and seven co-authors report a 2024 case of drug harm in a baby with a hormone disorder. In congenital hyperinsulinism, the body makes too much insulin and blood sugar crashes. The sole approved drug, diazoxide, can cause fluid build-up, so water pills and close watch are advised alongside it.

The baby got the drug without a water pill and fell into sudden breathing distress. Heart checks found fluid around the heart and a thickened heart wall, neither present before. The team tapered and stopped the drug and added a water pill, and the signs cleared. A scan later showed a single focal spot in the pancreas, removed by surgery at four months.
pmc-11574424:
Anna Coughtrey and co-authors published a 2024 study of mental health care delivered inside children's epilepsy clinics by staff who are not mental health specialists. Children with epilepsy often face anxiety, depression, or behavior problems, yet struggle to reach care. A program called MICE trains clinic staff to deliver a flexible talk therapy for these problems, backed by training and supervision. The team checked how faithfully 21 trained staff delivered it.

Records covered 2,269 sessions with 166 young people, and experts rated recordings of 251 sessions. Staff followed the therapy plan closely and delivered it with skill. Where they strayed, they changed the order of steps rather than the content. The authors conclude that clinic staff can be trained to give sound mental health care, and call for work linking this faithfulness to outcomes.
pmc-11575024:
Emine Guzel and co-authors compare three ways of measuring root canal working length, judging them by agreement and by pain after treatment. Their 2024 study starts from a precision need: the canal's end point decides where cleaning and filling stop, and errors there feed post-treatment pain. Which measuring method serves patients best was unsettled.

A hundred patients were randomly assigned to an electronic locator, a simultaneous detection method built into the motor, or the X-ray method. Canals were then prepared and filled the same way. Pain reports and standard records were collected for all. Trials of this kind matter because the measuring step is quick and cheap, yet it shapes comfort for days after the visit.
pmc-11575124:
An eyelid-scrubbing gadget promises lasting relief for inflamed eyelids, and Helena Siegel and six co-authors put it through a placebo-controlled trial in a 2024 paper. Forty-two patients whose blepharitis had resisted standard care were assigned to the BlephEx debridement device or a sham treatment, masked both ways.

Four weeks on, the sham group significantly improved on the Efron grading scale, an awkward result for the device. The treated group improved slightly more on symptom scores, eyelid grades, and tear stability, but none of those edges reached significance. A crossover swap followed as a recruitment sweetener. The authors report the trial straight: a plausible device with a good mechanism story could not beat its own placebo on the pre-set measures, and clinics should price their enthusiasm accordingly.
pmc-11575424:
Azadeh Tahernejad and co-authors review AI use in emergency triage in this 2024 paper. Triage sorts injured people by urgency after disasters and emergencies. As disasters grow worldwide, old triage methods strain, and smart systems are being used to speed and sharpen those calls.

The review searched three databases and a scholar search engine up to September 2024, following standard review rules. From 2,630 records, 19 high-quality studies were kept. AI tools improved care through better resource use and live data transfer, and some vision systems sped work at mass casualty scenes. One tool diagnosed COVID-19 with about 95 percent accuracy. Barriers included trust, training needs, gear shortages, and privacy worries.
pmc-11576324:
Yuhan Yang, Ping Xu, Wei He, and Fei Tao propose using houseflies as living samplers of drug resistance genes in the environment. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Flies are everywhere, pick up germs and genes on their bodies, and move them around, which makes them handy watch tools.

The team read all the DNA on fly body surfaces from five sites tied to human activity. Germ mixes differed by site, and so did the resistance genes found. The gene mix on flies seemed shaped by the genes around each site, and some were enriched on the flies. Genes against several drug classes dominated, above all those for multi-drug resistance. Gene loads also tracked how many people lived near a site and how much they moved. The authors back flies as cheap sentinels for resistance spread.
pmc-11578424:
Hongting Li and co-authors design a family of drug candidates against thyroid cancer in a 2024 paper. Thirty new compounds built on a pyrimidine-hydrazone frame were synthesized and tested on a thyroid cancer cell line that overproduces the signaling protein FAK, a driver of growth and spread.

Most compounds killed the cells at low doses. The best, labeled 14f, stopped cell growth at a tenth of a micromolar and blocked FAK at nanomolar strength. Computer studies showed it fits the target well with favorable drug-like properties. It switched off FAK's activation marks without lowering the protein itself, and slowed both growth and migration of the cancer cells. The authors present the series as a promising start for FAK-targeted thyroid cancer drugs.
pmc-11579324:
An eleven-author team publishes a dataset of tiny RNA fragments in a disease of the lung arteries. Pulmonary arterial hypertension stiffens those vessels and strains the heart, and its molecular basis is still unclear. The fragments, called tsRNAs, are clipped from transfer RNAs and act as regulators. The team collected them from patient blood and from the lungs and hearts of rats bred into the disease state.

They catalogued 2,716 distinct fragments in human blood and 4,733 in rat tissues, with a small overlap between species. A core set of 204 fragments appeared in every sample type. Repeated measurements agreed closely, and pathway analysis tied the fragments to signaling routes including MAPK and cancer pathways. The authors offer the data as a resource for hunting the epigenetic drivers of the disease and new treatment targets.
pmc-11579724:
Parkinson's disease kills the brain cells that make dopamine, and the blood brain barrier that should guard those cells weakens as the disease advances. Muhammad Khalid Iqbal and seven co-authors review in 2024 how that barrier's failure feeds the disease: stray molecules slip in, the protein alpha-synuclein clumps, and inflammation and oxidative stress take hold. A sister barrier in the eye fails alongside it.

Genetic and epigenetic shifts follow the breach, and the damage to DNA repair deepens the spiral. The authors argue that guarding synapses and the barrier could allow earlier diagnosis and slower progression. Patient grown midbrain cells offer truer models for testing such ideas. Personalized care built on a person's genetic form of the disease is their closing hope.
pmc-11580324:
Ann Alex and co-authors explore, in a 2024 study, links between a mother's stress and the microbes living in her mouth during early pregnancy. Gut microbes have already been tied to stress and mood in pregnancy. No study had checked the mouth's microbes for the same link.

Saliva came from 224 women in their second trimester, a group chosen to include many with high stress. The team matched mouth microbe patterns with stress, anxiety, depression, and trauma symptoms. Factors like income, smoking, and dental health were weighed as well. Finding a mouth-brain link would open a simple window on maternal mental health. A saliva sample is easy to collect in routine prenatal care.
pmc-11584624:
Rachel Ainsworth and seven co-authors share two decades of young fish measures from English rivers in a 2024 data paper. Long records help scientists read change in river life over time. The dataset holds body lengths of larval and juvenile fish. Samples came from five river catchments across England.

The set holds more than 380,000 fish of 30 species. Teams caught fish almost monthly for about twenty years. Length data can reveal growth rates and survival odds. It can also show how strong each new year class will be. The authors offer the set as a baseline for climate and pollution studies. Fish size links to swim skill, survival, and breeding output.
pmc-11584924:
Nurse care management is one proven way to get more people treated for opioid use disorder in primary care. The PROUD trial tested the Massachusetts model, in which clinics hire a dedicated nurse, train and support her, and keep several buprenorphine prescribers on staff. Gwen Lapham and a large team now report what happened over three years, using records and claims from six health systems in five states.

The two-year gains held and grew. Over three years, clinics with the program delivered about 19.7 more patient-years of medication treatment per 10,000 primary care patients than usual-care clinics. The analysis suggests the benefit of the model is durable rather than a brief start-up effect, strengthening the case for funding nurse-led addiction care in ordinary clinics.
pmc-11585224:
Rong Yu and co-authors published this heart study in 2024. Diabetic cardiomyopathy is heart harm wrought by diabetes itself, apart from blocked vessels. The team tested tricin, a plant compound from the flavonoid family, known for fighting rust-like cell harm and swelling. They grew rat heart cells in high sugar to mimic the disease, then dosed them with the compound.

Tricin eased the harm in step with dose. Markers of cell stress fell, a guard enzyme rose, and three swelling signals dropped. A chain of proteins that drives swelling, named for its parts TLR4, MYD88, and NF-κB, quieted as well. The authors say tricin guards heart cells by damping both stress and swelling. They call for animal and clinic tests to see if the gain holds in whole hearts.
pmc-11585624:
Ruisheng Ran and co-authors test a screen for autism based on how children look and respond, in this 2024 study. Standard diagnosis leans on rating scales and expert judgment, which can be slow, costly, and swayed by opinion. The team built a filmed social scene and measured what children's faces and eyes did inside it.

Their data set held one hundred eighty-seven children, about half with autism and half developing typically. Software pulled out features such as how long a face stayed in view, where the eyes focused, how fast a child answered a name call, and how well feelings showed. A simple Bayes classifier sorted the children with accuracy above ninety-four percent. The authors offer the method as a fast, cheap aid to doctors, not a replacement for them.
pmc-11586324:
Lijuan Zeng and colleagues make the case that a little-known mucus protein acts as a brake on head and neck cancer, in this study from twenty twenty-four. The protein, FCGBP, was lower in tumors than in healthy tissue across several large datasets, and patients whose tumors kept more of it lived longer. It held up as an independent survival marker in a validation cohort.

Experiments gave the correlation a mechanism. Silencing the gene in two cancer cell lines made the cells migrate and invade more aggressively. It also tilted the immune neighborhood: fewer killer T cells, more suppressor cells. Genes traveling with FCGBP clustered in immune processes, as if its presence keeps the anti-tumor response switched on. The authors name it a tumor suppressor and a candidate for monitoring and drug development.
pmc-11586424:
Cheng and a large team ran an early trial in twenty twenty-four of an immune drug plus chemo as first care for spread pancreas cancer. Such cancer has a grim outlook and immune drugs alone help little. Seventy-two folks got the pair at sites in China.

Mean survival was near nine months, with a third alive at one year. A third of tumors shrank and nine in ten were held in check. No grave drug harms were seen in the trial. A three-cell niche in tumor tissue flagged who gained most. Cell place, not just cell kind, may guide such care.
pmc-11587424:
Majeda Al-Ruzzieh and co-authors spoke with, in 2024, the heads of an oncology center about patient-centered care. It has been tied to sick people staying with their care and to lower costs, yet the views of those in charge had seen little study. Twenty-three middle and senior managers told how they see this care and what stands in its way.

One theme was whole-person care, with partnership with sick people and informed decisions, backed by education and services that work as one. Those in charge told of their part in spreading the word and in giving backing. Blocks from work culture and day-to-day work slowed the spread of the care. The group named the gains they saw and plans to make the care stronger. This gives those in charge a clear map of where the care now stands.
pmc-11587624:
Samuel Spears, Deepak Kalaskar, and co-authors test two scanners for head and neck surface scans, in a 2024 study. One is a pro hand scanner, while the other is a tablet with a scan app. Clinics need cheap, snug scans to fit neck braces and face aids.

Eighteen well folks were scanned three times in three poses on both tools. Face area and scan time matched well across tools and poses. Both tools kept error well under clinic norms for brace fit. The tablet thus works as a low cost stand in, and the team shows pose tricks to hold a dropped head in place.
pmc-11587724:
Maxim Gakh and co-authors read what helped and what blocked joint work in a south Nevada health check of a build plan. The study appeared in 2024. Plans in one field shape health in the next, so joint work can lift town health. Joint health checks oft hit snags, though.

Ten of the twelve group hands gave talks for the case read. Reads broke in themes on the check as a tool, on blocks, and on aids. Care for facts past one's own field was the most named aid. Short time was the most named block. Hands named far more aids than blocks in all, plus gains like new ties.
pmc-11590324:
Chunji Yan and five colleagues set out a plan for a review of baby pain care, in a 2024 protocol paper. Babies under one year often face needle and procedure pain that clinics treat too rarely. Proven comforts exist, such as skin-to-skin contact, sweet solutions, and breastfeeding, yet wards use them only now and then.

The planned review will gather studies on what helps or blocks the use of these comforts. Six databases will be searched without limits on year or language. A standard framework for putting research into practice will sort the findings, and a quality tool will grade each study. A narrative summary will tie the results together. The goal is a clear map of barriers and aids, so hospitals can design fixes that get proven comforts to babies. The protocol is registered in advance for transparency.
pmc-11590524:
Dongeun Lee and co-authors ask when combined chemo and radiation should start in a 2024 study on glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumor. After surgery or biopsy, patients get both treatments together. Whether the wait before that joint treatment changes survival was not settled.

Nationwide insurance records in South Korea covered 3,586 patients treated from 2008 to 2021. Patients were split into early starters, within 21 days, and late starters, past 21 days. Each timing group was split again by surgery type, biopsy alone or fuller removal. Survival was then compared across the groups, giving doctors data for a choice they face in the first weeks after surgery.
pmc-11590824:
Knowing what drives heart disease does not always change daily habits. Barolia and co-authors interview twenty patients at a large public hospital in Lahore, Pakistan, each living with coronary artery disease for at least six months. They ask what the patients understand about risk factors and what changes they have actually made during recovery.

Three themes came out: lifestyle choices and behavior, growing awareness with real change, and a whole-person view of health care. Patients' accounts show both grasp of the risks and uneven follow-through. The authors say the findings support stronger health teaching and prevention, since heart disease risk is a tangle of habits, knowledge, and daily life.
pmc-11590924:
Sabina Ostermeier and co-authors measure stress in young racehorses during a stomach scope exam. Thirty-one two year old thoroughbreds in training had the exam twice, once at the start of their first training season and once six months later. The team tracked a stress hormone in spit and its breakdown products in dung.

Both markers rose after each exam compared with resting levels. The rise was mild but clear in statistical tests at both time points. The results show the routine exam does strain young horses, even when done for their own health. Trainers and vets can use such measures to judge handling and to weigh the cost of repeat checks.
pmc-11591024:
Alessandro Gramenzi, Luana Clerico, Benedetta Belà, Meri Di Leonardo, Isa Fusaro, and Giulia Pignataro wrote a 2024 paper on gut microbes in dogs. They tested three feed supplements: one that feeds helpful gut microbes, one live microbe product, and a mix of both. The work used a lab model of the dog colon rather than live dogs.

The model ran for two weeks with gut material from a healthy dog. The team read microbe DNA to track which groups grew or shrank in each part of the model colon. All three products changed the mix, raising groups often linked with gut health. The findings give pet food makers and vets a base for later tests in real dogs.
pmc-11592324:
Moira Lewitt and co-authors review a blood protein as a possible warning sign for heart disease in a 2024 article. The protein, called IGFBP-1, helps control growth factors that steer metabolism and growth, and it also acts on its own. The liver makes it, insulin holds it down, and inflammation pushes it up.

The review weighs a confusing pattern. Low levels of the protein go with a risky profile of weight, sugar, and blood fats. Yet high levels predict worse outcomes once heart disease is present. Levels also shift with sex and age, which muddy simple readings. The authors suggest richer tests, such as measuring the protein alongside insulin output after a sugar drink, and panels that add inflammation markers, to sort out what a reading really means.
pmc-11593624:
Yasir and five co-authors screened approved drugs against the malaria parasite's shredder in this study from twenty twenty-four. Malaria increasingly resists frontline drugs like artemisinin. The parasite's proteasome, its protein-disposal machine, is a fresh target. The team searched for compounds that block the parasite version while sparing the human one.

Computer modeling, docking, and motion simulations filtered the candidates. Four drugs stood out, led by argatroban and pemetrexed hydrate. In simulation they stayed lodged in the parasite's active site. In the human version, some wandered out or sat unstably. The authors present the hits as starting points for selective antimalarials. Lab testing would be the next step.
pmc-11594324:
