Parveen Akhtar, Ivo van Stokkum, and Petar Lambrev study how a closed reaction center drains glow from special red pigments in photosynthesis, in a paper from 2024. Photosystem I holds pigments that catch light beyond the red edge of vision. Deep cold traps energy on those pigments because the climb back uphill is blocked.

At seventy seven degrees above absolute zero, the team recorded how fast the pigments' glow faded with the reaction center open versus shut. Mid range red glow was unaffected by the center's state. The deepest red glow, past a set wavelength, faded faster when the center was closed and charged. That quenched path shows one escape route for trapped energy in the frozen complex.
pmc-11594724:
Juan Manuel Alcázar-Hernández and two colleagues present a 2024 review of how antidepressant medicines affect the mouth. Use of these drugs is rising, and dentists often see dry mouth and tooth decay in patients who take them. The team gathered observational studies from the past two decades and judged their quality with a standard checklist.

Eleven studies met their bar, and they consistently tied antidepressant use to dry mouth, more cavities, and gum disease. Taste changes and bleeding issues also appeared. Two drug families, the SSRIs and the older tricyclics, were linked most often to dryness and decay. The drugs did not seem to change saliva chemistry or clotting during dental work. The authors urge closer dental monitoring for these patients.
pmc-11594824:
The sodium-potassium pump keeps every animal cell's electrical balance, and one special version of it exists only in sperm. Kazuhiro Abe and co-authors solve that version's structure in a 2024 paper. The isoform, built from alpha4 and beta1 subunits, sits in the sperm's tail and drives the swimming that fertility depends on.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team captured the pump holding ouabain, a plant toxin that jams such pumps, at near-atomic resolution. The overall shape matches the common isoform, but the ouabain pocket and other spots differ in step with its unique sequence. Simulations also found a docking site for fatty sugar molecules that may tune the pump's behavior. The structure explains how this sperm-only machine differs from its household cousins.
pmc-11595224:
Six authors, led by Filipa Campos, report a 2024 case of liver trouble in a man with Graves' disease. Graves' disease drives the thyroid into overdrive, and liver tests often go off in such patients for several distinct reasons. Sorting out which reason applies guides the whole treatment.

The patient was a 42-year-old man whose blood tests showed mild liver dysfunction at his first visit, with very high thyroid hormone levels. He was started on carbimazole, a standard thyroid drug. Over eight weeks, his key liver enzyme climbed far higher, to a peak the report gives in full. The drug was stopped, and urgent radioiodine treatment followed. Within a week off the drug, his liver values fell sharply. The case stands out because drug-linked liver harm from this class usually takes a cholestatic form, while his pattern was hepatitic.
pmc-11595524:
Suchanicz leads a team studying manganese- and iron-doped ceramics in a 2024 paper. The base material is a sodium bismuth titanate ceramic. The team measured stiffness, hardness, toughness, and bending strength in unpoled and poled states, a first for this material.

Adding iron or manganese improved mechanical traits, as did electric poling. The additives also improved piezoelectric behavior. Stress-strain tests showed doping lowered the stress needed to switch domains and raised leftover strain. Poling had the opposite effect. The materials showed large deformation and strong leftover polarization under high stress. The authors suggest they could replace lead-based ceramics in actuators that need high blocking stress.
pmc-11596824:
Xiqian Tan and colleagues characterise a bacterial sugar coating that fights biofilms. Their study from twenty twenty-four works with a pickled vegetable bacterium strain. Such coatings, called exopolysaccharides, can support human health. Biofilms shield harmful bacteria from cleaning and drugs.

The new coating is built mainly from three simple sugars. Its size and ring structures were mapped with standard methods. Antioxidant tests showed strong radical-scavenging power at tested doses. The coating also disrupted biofilms from several pathogens. Staph bacteria were among the biofilm formers tested. Effects grew with dose in the hydroxyl radical tests. Food and health products could use such natural antibiofilm agents.
pmc-11597524:
Shaofang Wu and co-authors study tomato seedlings grown indoors in a 2024 plant paper. In a plant factory, growers control light by the clock, and the length of the light period shapes growth. The team grew one truss tomato type under 12, 16, or 20 hours of light each day and compared the results.

Longer light gave taller, heavier plants with more green pigment and higher rates of food making from light. Mineral levels in the plants changed little across the three settings. A broad chemical scan found shifts in fats, amino acids, and transport pathways as light length grew. The authors say the findings can help growers set light schedules that speed up seedling growth.
pmc-11598024:
Ghozlane Barboucha and co-authors profile a eucalyptus leaf oil from Algeria in a 2024 study. Plant oils are hunted as gentler germ and pest fighters, and this tree's oil had not been mapped from that source.

Steam drawn oil yielded a small share of leaf weight. Its top parts were two plant compounds that made up three quarters of the oil. The oil curbed key bacteria and fungi in dish tests. Against a stored grain beetle, it killed on contact and as fumes, and drove the pests off strongly. Computer docking probes how the top parts grip germ enzymes.
pmc-11598124:
Geon Min, Tae Bok Lee, and Yong Seok Heo (2024) improve a method for repairing damaged face photos with help from a clean reference photo of the same person. Guided diffusion models can do this repair without new training by following gradients from several loss functions, each pushing the result toward a desired trait. The trouble is that these gradients can fight each other, so the repair ends up weaker than it should be.

Their method, called PDGrad, defines losses on both fine detail and high-level features, using the rough repair and the reference photo together. When gradients conflict, one gradient per level is chosen as a pivot and the others are rotated to agree with it; any adjusted gradient that grows too large is scaled back. On the CelebRef-HQ test set, the method beat rival approaches on both measured scores and visual quality.
pmc-11599724:
Annabel Olgo and colleagues checked in 2024 whether the sensors inside a smart battery distort the very chemistry they are meant to watch. Instrumented cells promise early warning of aging by tracking temperature and strain from within, but a sensor is a physical object sitting inside the electrode stack, and it might deform its neighborhood. The team watched a commercial prismatic lithium-ion cell work, using synchrotron X-ray diffraction during charge and discharge to map lithiation in the graphite electrode.

The headline is reassuring at the whole-cell level and cautionary locally. Overall electrochemical performance was untouched by the internal sensors, yet the graphite right around them lithiated at noticeably different rates, especially during fast charging and discharging. The authors conclude that sensor size and the local deformations sensors cause must be engineered deliberately, or smart batteries will report the behavior of a disturbed cell.
pmc-11600824:
Pulse oximeters clip onto a finger and read blood oxygen, but a waving hand can fool them into false alarms. Ting Yang and co-authors compare two meters head to head: Biolight's analog sensor and Masimo's. Their 2024 non-inferiority study ran thirty healthy adults through still, sliding, and waving hand tests.

At rest and under straight-line motion, both meters read alike with only mild disruption. Slow waving at 120 beats per minute caused no alarms on either. Fast tapping at 160 beats per minute split them: the Biolight raised fewer technical alarms but more low-oxygen alarms than the Masimo. The authors judge neither meter inferior overall, and they call for tests on patients with heart and lung disease, where the stakes are higher.
pmc-11600924:
Esther Jie Tian and co-authors reviewed community allied health care and its effect on hospital use, in this 2024 paper. Allied health covers fields such as physio, diet, speech, and social work. The review mixed outcome studies with views from patients, carers, and staff.

Sixty-seven papers met the rules, drawn from wide database and web searches. Proof that these services cut hospital use was mixed, in part because studies varied so much. Patients and carers were largely positive and saw room to build on good experiences. The certainty of proof for patient-level outcomes was rated very low. The authors urge care in reading the results.
pmc-11601124:
Alejandro Rico-Guevara and co-authors show in 2024 that a hummingbird upper bill truly bends while the bird drinks nectar. Past reports of such bending were often dismissed as a trick of the eye.

The team filmed six species as they fed and mapped where the bill bends. The lower bill stayed still through each lick, while the upper bill bent upward near its tip. Scans of bill stiffness helped explain the flex. The authors argue that bending lets the bill wring nectar at the tip while staying shut in the middle. That split of tasks helps the birds drain long, narrow blooms that shut out less skilled feeders.
pmc-11602024:
Upendo Munuo and Fabiola Vincent Moshi surveyed students at colleges in Dodoma, Tanzania about their use of family planning services and what motivates that use. Sub-Saharan Africa has the world's greatest unmet need for contraception, and young people use services less than older groups. Closing that gap is vital for fair access to sexual and reproductive health care.

The team gave a structured questionnaire to 421 randomly chosen students. They measured how many students used family planning and what drove or blocked that use. The results show both the level of use and the reasons students give for seeking care. Health planners can use those motivators to design services that young people will actually visit.
pmc-11603024:
Hartono and co-authors build a tiny probe that lights up aged cells for a sound-based imaging method. Aged, or senescent, cells can suppress tumors early on, yet when they linger they help cancers grow, resist drugs, and return. Their 2024 probe wraps a safe black polymer particle around an approved green dye, making a contrast agent that aged cells take up more readily.

In dishes, cells aged by chemotherapy took up more of the probe than cancer cells did. The probe also held its signal under light better than the free dye and gave a signal about two and a half times stronger. The authors say the probe could help doctors spot senescent cells in the body. That skill could aid early cancer warnings and judging of anti-aging cell therapies.
pmc-11603224:
Chunhui Yao and co-authors present a chip-scale spectrometer that reaches lab-grade precision, in this 2024 paper. Tiny spectrometers suit field and body sensing, but shrinking usually costs resolution and range. The common view held them fit only for rough peak spotting.

Their device rebuilds spectra from coded readings and works across a wide near-infrared band. Its resolution beat eight picometers, giving a record ratio of range to resolution above 65,000. It sorted solid materials and measured liquid strengths at near perfect accuracy. Its detection limit matched bench-top machines, down to a tenth of a percent for glucose. A packaged sensor with electronics was demonstrated.
pmc-11603324:
Gardashli and coauthors test ways to boost stem cell care for worn joints. Knee fat pads hold stem cells that calm swelling well. Those cells may help treat joint wear where no cure drug exists. How cells are grown can change how well they work.

The team grew pad cells in three growth fluids. One fluid met strict rules for use in people. They also primed cells with swelling signals or a hormone. Primed cells were checked for calm-down strength. The aim is a cell batch that calms joints more strongly. Such batches could lift results in joint wear trials.
pmc-11603624:
Ahmad Abdulkareem Alnazzawi and four co-authors test, in 2024 lab work, laser-sintered metal posts against cast ones for fit. Such posts anchor crowns in teeth whose roots have been treated, and each must match its root space just so. The cast route is old and slow; the laser route builds the post layer by layer from a scan.

A clear block with a drilled post space gave the master shape. Ten posts were built each way in a cobalt-chrome mix, and a triple-scan check weighed each against the true form. Both sets strayed from the mark by a like hair's breadth, with no real gap between them. The team calls the laser route a sound swap that saves cost and time.
pmc-11603724:
Chuxin Chen and co-authors grow platelet-producing cells from human embryonic stem cells at high efficiency in a 2024 paper. Platelet transfusions save lives, but supply depends on donors. Stem-cell-derived platelets could become an alternative source if they can be made mature and functional at scale.

Under low-oxygen conditions, the team replayed the natural maturation steps with a tuned sequence of growth factors in a three-dimensional system. The resulting giant parent cells showed the right surface markers at rates above ninety percent, carried many chromosome sets, and shed filamentous arms that release platelets. The platelets bore active markers and were checked by many methods. In mice lacking platelets, the lab-made ones functioned in the body.
pmc-11603824:
Jordan Wickstrom and co-authors set out a plan for a scoping review of how social conditions shape rehabilitation care in the United States. Many adults miss out on fair access to therapy or gain less from it. The causes lie in factors such as race, gender, schooling, and living situation rather than medical need. The review will map studies linking these social determinants of health to access, use, or outcomes across therapy fields.

The team will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute framework, searching five databases for English-language studies from 2013 onward with at least one hundred adults. Two reviewers will screen each record on their own, and three will extract the data, with the process piloted first. Findings will be shared through conferences, professional networks, and a peer-reviewed journal. By mapping what drives unequal outcomes, the review aims to point to fixes in access, training, and care.
pmc-11603924:
Victor Zeng and eight co-authors charted in 2024 road and transport injuries reported in Ghana's Volta Region from 2019 to 2023. Transport harm kills over a million people a year worldwide, and rates climb fastest in poorer countries. Local data are needed before safety money can be aimed well.

The team used monthly clinic reports for injuries and facility records for deaths across the five years. They mapped where injuries cluster, how counts moved over time, and which groups appear most. Patterns in the data point to the roads, seasons, and road users where action should start. The study gives regional planners a factual base.
pmc-11604724:
Zhaoyong Zhang and co-authors describe an antibody against the virus that causes COVID-19 in a 2024 study. The antibody targets a quiet face of the spike protein, a spot veiled by sugar chains that few antibodies reach. Learning how it works may guide better drugs and shots.

Using frozen imaging, the team mapped where the antibody grips the spike. It blocks the spike from latching onto human cells by getting in the way. In animal tests it protected better than other antibodies aimed at the same spike region. Such antibodies seem rare in people who recovered from infection. Readers get a new target spot for future virus defenses.
pmc-11604824:
Jesmeen Maimaris and a large team bring together 149 patients with Griscelli syndrome type 2, a rare immune disorder. The syndrome stems from flaws in the gene RAB27A. It weakens the killing work of immune cells and can trigger a severe overreaction called HLH. The 2024 paper adds eight new patients to those already described in past reports.

Most patients had HLH, and near half had it reach the brain or nerves. Pale skin and hair showed in most cases, but not all. The type of gene flaw shaped how sick patients got and at what age. About a third of the group died. Those who had a stem cell transplant after calm care did far better than those who did not.
pmc-11604924:
Heart failure is the top killer of people on long-term dialysis, and blood markers that warn early could save lives. Xing Qi and co-authors compare long non-coding RNAs in blood cells from dialysis patients in this 2024 study, contrasting those whose hearts pump weakly with those whose pumping holds.

More than fourteen hundred of these RNAs differed between the groups. One candidate stood out because it may serve as the raw material for a small regulatory RNA, and its level tracked heart pumping strength closely in a second group of patients. The authors offer it as a promising early marker for the weak-pump form of failure.
pmc-11605124:
Studying a coronavirus means infecting animals with it, and choosing the right animal model shapes everything downstream. Yue Wu and co-authors built COVID-AMD in 2024, a database gathering coronavirus-infected animal models from the published literature into one searchable platform, covering the SARS, MERS, and SARS-CoV-2 viruses.

The collection holds 869 models across 29 species and 312 virus strains, spanning five diseases and ten infection routes. Each entry details how infection was established, the clinical picture, and phenotype data. Search tools support both simple and advanced queries, plus comparison across models, model recommendation, and omics analysis. The authors offer the open repository as a way to find the right animal model fast, and so speed the development and testing of treatments and vaccines against coronaviruses old and new.
pmc-11605524:
Mansour Khaleel and three co-authors present an illustrative case where a brain tumor bled twice after a fall, and watchful waiting beat the scalpel, in this 2024 case report. Meningiomas are common brain tumors, and bleeding inside one is a rare, dangerous twist. A 78-year-old man with recurrent falls proved to have both a subdural hematoma, blood pooled over the brain, and a hemorrhage inside a left frontotemporal meningioma.

Surgery is the reflex for symptomatic bleeding, and alternatives like focused radiation wait in reserve. This team chose conservative management instead, reasoning case by case. Over six months of follow-up the patient improved significantly. Stranger still, scans showed the tumor itself and the blood within it both shrinking. The authors draw the lesson plainly: hemorrhagic meningiomas deserve individualized plans, and not every bleed demands an operation.
pmc-11605624:
Jeong and co-authors review how one popular vaping brand markets itself on social media. Lost Mary is a favored e-cigarette brand among teens in the United States, and health researchers worry that its ads feed that appeal. Their 2024 study codes 53 brand posts from 2022 and 2023 for features that draw young viewers.

More than a third of the posts named flavors, often fruit or ice types that teens favor. More than two thirds used bright, vivid colors, and the people shown looked like young adults. The team reads this pattern as marketing that fits youth tastes, whether or not that was the stated aim. They call for closer watching of vape brands on social platforms.
pmc-11605824:
Li Zhang and five co-authors tested whether hospital alliances raise the child care capacity of local hospitals in China, in a 2024 study. Child services are scarce and unevenly spread, and alliances between strong and weak hospitals are meant to help. Past evidence on whether they work was mixed.

The team used child service data from 119 local hospitals in 14 cities from 2015 to 2019. Hospitals fell into close alliance, loose alliance, and no alliance groups, and a staggered difference method compared their paths. Both alliance forms lifted outpatient and inpatient visits by firm margins. The loose form gained more than the close form. The authors read the result as support for alliances as a route to fairer child care access.
pmc-11606124:
Kexin Wang and eight co-workers wrote a 2024 registry study on adding a balloon pump after heart-lung machine support in cardiogenic shock. Whether the pump's unloading of the left heart helps was unclear. A Chinese registry held more than five thousand shock patients on the machine. About one in seven also got the balloon pump afterward.

That group died in hospital less often than those without the pump. Survival while on the machine was also higher. Adjusted models kept the pump tied to lower death risk. The pump group had more prior heart procedures and heart attacks at baseline. Complication rates were tracked as secondary outcomes.
pmc-11607824:
Kaisa Cui, Kang Wang, and Zhaohui Huang review ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death, and its role inside tumors, in a two thousand twenty-four review. Since its discovery in two thousand twelve, ferroptosis has become central to thinking about how cancers grow, spread, and resist therapy.

A tumor is an ecosystem of cancer cells, immune cells, stroma, and signaling molecules. The review shows that ferroptosis in the non-cancer cells of that microenvironment matters too: their crosstalk with cancer cells, partly routed through ferroptosis mechanisms, can reprogram the tumor toward resistance or vulnerability. Therapeutic strategies aiming ferroptosis at the microenvironment are catalogued.
pmc-11608224:
David Hymel and co-authors present a light driven route to finishing peptide drugs in a 2024 paper. Many peptide medicines end in a particular chemical cap, called an amide. Installing that cap at production scale is hard.

Their method starts from a longer chain ending in the amino acid cysteine. A light sensitive tag is attached to that end. Light then triggers a break that leaves a special link. A simple acid step, or a ring forming reaction, cuts it to the finished cap. Each step runs efficiently. In a flow reactor lit along its path, the cascade capped a gut hormone analogue and a dual hormone drug precursor at gram scale.
pmc-11608524:
Christoph Zindel and co-authors grade the accuracy of custom guided knee bone surgery in a 2024 study. A steep shin slope plus one sided knee wear can call for a two plane correction. Patient specific guides, planned in three dimensions, steer the cuts. Eighteen patients from one center over four years entered the review.

Average miss between planned and achieved slope was just over two degrees. Closed wedge cuts beat open wedge cuts on accuracy by a wide margin. Error grew as the hinge axis angle rose, with a clear cutoff near thirty-nine degrees. The authors favor closed wedge cuts for combined fixes near that ratio. Guide based planning can hit targets with care.
pmc-11608824:
Cochrane and co-authors present a method to detect hidden oceans inside icy moons in a 2024 paper. Moons such as Europa hide oceans under ice, betrayed by a magnetic signal they generate in response to their planet's changing field. Planned missions to Jupiter's moons make such analysis timely, and the method extends to the Uranus and Neptune systems.

Their approach blends forward and inverse modeling over ensembles of self-consistent interior models, scored by distance to the data. They test it on a hypothetical ocean in Umbriel, a Uranus moon, under a three-flyby mission design. Error analysis shows what ocean thickness and conductivity could be pinned down. The work appears in a theme issue on sensing oceans from afar.
pmc-11609124:
Fajuan Tang, Dongqiong Xiao, Xihong Li, and Lina Qiao review how lactate and a chemical RNA tag interact in disease, in a paper from 2024. Lactate is a by-product of sugar use that also sends signals and fuels cells. The RNA tag, called m6A, is the most common edit made to RNA messages. Each system can alter the other, forming a two-way loop.

Lactate can raise the levels of enzymes that place or remove the RNA tag. Those enzymes, in turn, can change lactate levels by acting on sugar pathways and transporters. The loop appears in cancers, organ scarring, heart injury, and sepsis. The authors map the links as targets for future drugs.
pmc-11609424:
Mehdi Fatahi-Bafghi wrote a 2024 review of rat-bite fever, an infection passed to people by rats. A bite, a scratch, or contact with rat excrement such as urine or oral secretions can transmit it. The most common cause is a group of bacteria in the genus Streptobacillus, which live in the mouth and nose of rats.

The review brings knowledge of this genus up to date. It covers how the bacteria are isolated and identified in the laboratory, the factors they use to cause harm, and the signs the illness shows. It also separates the illness from similar conditions that can be confused with it. The review lists which antibiotics kill the bacteria and which fail, and sets out where cases occur and how they spread. At its center is an analysis of more than two hundred cases from 1915 to 2023.
pmc-11610024:
Dey Hazra and seven colleagues test a new way to rebuild the rim of the shoulder socket in twenty twenty-four. The rim, called the labrum, helps keep the ball of the arm bone in place. Their method wraps the front rim with the long tendon of the biceps muscle. They tried it on ten donor shoulders with a robot arm.

Each shoulder was tested whole, torn, fixed by the new method, and fixed by a standard bone method. The new method restored side shift and force balance to whole joint levels. The bone method restored force but not side shift. The authors say the tendon wrap may suit patients whose rim is worn but bone is intact.
pmc-11610124:
Chunzhen Cheng and co-authors sum ten years of banana gene craft and breed work since the first genome draft. The draft, from a doubled tame stock, opened the field's gene age. Genomes of more kin stocks have since run, and lab tools have grown with them. Their 2024 review walks four fields: source and tame tale, fruit life, stress life, and breed craft.

Gene maps now tie wild and tame stocks in one tale. Fruit ripe rules grow clear at the script tier. Joint trove reads chart heat, cold, and germ stress in one frame. Breed bids lean on gene marks and clean cuts. The review names the hard parts left and the roads out. Bananas feed much of the warm world, so each gain lands wide.
pmc-11610224:
Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors are fast, incurable brain tumors of young children. They offer few gene targets for drugs. Daniel Merk and co-authors search for weak spots in a 2024 study. Their screening switches genes off one by one to see which ones the tumor cannot live without. They then tested the hits against a library of small-molecule drugs.

Drugs that block the cell cycle drivers CDK4 and CDK6 ranked among the strongest. Tumor cells leaned on one or the other of the pair, never both. Wider screens mapped the regulators that steer the first phase of the cell cycle and tune the response to those drugs. The results give a concrete lead for a tumor type that badly needs new treatment ideas.
pmc-11610524:
Marzena Jabczyk and co-authors score heart and metabolic risk in patients with quiet adrenal growths, in work from twenty twenty-four. Non-functioning adrenal adenomas are common growths tied to metabolic upset. They make no hormones, yet patients often show worse metabolic traits. Two European scoring tools estimate ten-year heart risk by age band. The study applies both tools to a clinic group.

Just over a hundred patients are sorted into risk bands by the scores. Waist-to-hip ratio runs higher in the high and very high risk bands. Fasting sugar also runs higher in those bands than in the low band. Fat blood measures and derived indices do not split by risk band. Blood pressure and waist-to-hip ratio stand out as cheap risk clues. Sugar control looks like the key metabolic thread to watch. The scores help target who needs closer heart checks.
pmc-11611124:
Amna Samjeed, Maisam Wahbah, Leontios Hadjileontiadis, and Ahsan Khandoker wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It listens to mother and fetus heartbeats together, asking when the two rhythms lock in step and what breaks their synchrony before birth.

Heartbeat coupling is thought to reflect the maturing fetal nervous system. The team recorded non-invasive heart signals from 105 healthy fetuses between twenty and forty weeks. They sorted fetal behavior into quiet and active states, merging sleep and waking by movement level. Coupling strength was computed for several heartbeat ratios and compared across three age bands. Fetal state mattered: movement changed how tightly the hearts entrained. The mother's breathing rate also steered the coupling, differently by state and age. The authors say the duet of the two hearts could become an early window on fetal development.
pmc-11612024:
Thomas Leclère and Pille Gerhold study whether plant and insect diversity on islands move together when measured along family trees, not just by species counts. Plants and insects depend on each other for pollination, food, and habitat. Island traits like size, age, and distance from land may shape both.

Using species lists from published work, they compared measures of evolutionary diversity for both groups. Recent plant diversity tracked with recent insect diversity, but whole-tree plant diversity did not track with broader insect groupings. Distant and small islands tended to hold high diversity for both. The authors suggest that protecting plant diversity may also shelter insect diversity.
pmc-11612424:
Zhuoran Xia and co-authors engineer, in a 2024 materials study, a copper alloy that is both very strong and an outstanding shield against electromagnetic waves. Such dual-duty materials are needed where electronics face high stress and heavy interference at once.

Tiny magnetic particles of a Heusler alloy were grown inside the copper by a design strategy that balanced many goals at once. The particles are small, dense, and well bonded, pinning the metal's structure for a yield strength of 1.5 gigapascals. At the same time, their magnetism couples with electric fields to block waves almost completely across a wide band. The design route suits other structure-plus-function materials.
pmc-11612524:
Tetsu Sakamoto and co-authors present a 2024 study of trust in AI diagnostic help among Japanese doctors. AI lists can aid diagnosis, but blind trust in them invites error. Their twist: ask doctors in the test group to judge whether the true diagnosis sits inside the AI's list of ten, a trust calibration step.

Twenty doctors each worked twenty cases drawn from real visits. Diagnostic accuracy was much the same in both groups, near the mid forty percent range. Calibration itself was right only about six times in ten. Yet when calibration was right, doctors did far better. Confidence in AI did not explain the pattern. Better calibration tools may matter more than better lists.
pmc-11613724:
Zhuo Jiang and Chaoyan Yuan compare four operations for women who leak urine when they cough, laugh, or lift. Their 2024 study comes from one hospital in China, with records of 243 patients. Each woman got one of four sling or suspension methods that brace the tube that drains the bladder.

A year after surgery, the four groups showed no clear gap in how well the leak was fixed. One method, a single-cut adjustable suspension, stood out for less bleeding, a shorter stay, and a faster operation than two of the others. Two methods cost more in hospital bills than the other pair. The team also set quality-of-life scores and bladder tests beside the surgery records.
pmc-11613924:
Golnaz Kheradkhah and co-authors review how sex hormones affect heart damage caused by cancer drugs, in work published in 2024. Cancer drugs save lives, but some harm heart cells and can weaken the heart over time. Men and women differ in how often and how badly this harm appears.

The review covers the main sex hormones and how each acts on the heart and blood vessels. It explains the signal paths by which they may raise or lower drug harm, and notes that hormone levels change across life stages. Long term harm from one drug family is more common in women, the authors note. They argue that hormone status should be part of how heart risk is judged during cancer care.
pmc-11615024:
Ilka Schmidt-Deubig and co-authors audit breathing tube swaps in children in a 2024 paper. Cuffed tubes seal better and should need fewer exchanges than uncuffed ones. A second-generation pediatric tube with an adapted size chart was their test case.

Zurich records covered 14,188 intubations in children over three kilograms from 2009 to 2015. Most oral placements followed the maker's size chart. When the chart size was used, the need to swap the tube was a fraction of a percent. Off-chart choices carried a far higher exchange risk, above twenty percent in the reported figure. Correct sizing, the audit argues, is where the cuffed tube's advantage is won or lost.
pmc-11615224:
Szymon P Kordon and co-authors show how the outer and membrane parts of an adhesion G protein-coupled receptor move together and shape its function. Published in 2024, the study centers on Latrophilin3, a receptor with a large multi-domain region outside the cell and a seven pass membrane region. How the two parts talk to each other was unclear.

A cryo-EM structure showed the outer GAIN domain sitting parallel to the membrane region, with limited motion. Single molecule tests found three slow swapping states of the outer part. Antibodies and cancer linked mutations at the interface shifted those states and changed signaling. The authors propose the outer region drives activation through this coupling.
pmc-11616324:
Zuomeng Wu and co-authors study, in 2024, why the insulation around nerve fibers fails to regrow after spinal cord injury. After injury, an acid-sensing channel on stem cells in the cord becomes active. The team tested how acid and this channel affect whether stem cells turn into the cells that make that insulation.

When the channel was active, stem cells made more of a fat-like signal and shipped it out in tiny parcels to other cells. That blocked the stem cells from maturing. Turning the channel or its partner gene off in rats and mice eased the block. The pathway may be a target for repair treatments.
pmc-11617124:
Alisha Chuchra and five co-authors compare three digital tools for skull measures used in tooth straightening with hand tracing. Jaw measures guide diagnosis and plans, so new phone and desk tools must prove they match the gold hand method. Films from a mixed patient group were read all four ways.

Most measures matched across tools. Two key angles split, with one web tool high on one angle and all tools high on a second angle versus hand work. Trust scores against hand work were strong for all three. The tools look fit for clinic use with care on those angles.
pmc-11617624:
María Victoria García Espinosa and co-authors tackle false beliefs about pain in primary care in this 2024 paper, written in Spanish. Chronic pain care often lags behind what guidelines recommend. Unhelpful beliefs held by patients and clinicians alike help explain that gap.

Common myths say pain always means tissue damage at the spot felt. Others claim full rest heals best, or that drugs and surgery beat all else. The authors urge clinicians to question their own beliefs first. Brief, plain advice in a normal visit can then correct the patient's myths. Such talks cost little and can prevent years of fear and inactivity. The paper is a practical script for busy family doctors.
pmc-11617724:
Muhammad Siddik and co-authors feed seaweed extract to Nile tilapia in this 2024 study. Hot water stresses farmed fish, sparking harmful oxygen byproducts that hurt health and growth. A red seaweed rich in plant guards may shield the fish, the team tests.

Fish on the extract diet grew better over the ten-week trial, with larger muscle fibers. Harm marks in their tissues ran lower, and red blood cell counts ran higher with fewer cell flaws. Gut wall genes tightened, a guard gene rose, and a stress gene fell. Gut germ sets also grew richer in helpful types. The authors back the extract as a feed aid for hot spells.
pmc-11617924:
Koirala and co-authors report on a mentoring program for refugee and migrant schoolchildren, in a study published in 2024. Newly arrived teenagers must learn English while also keeping up in every other subject. The program paired them with university education students as mentors. Mentors helped with English, with reading and writing across subjects, and with planning the next steps in schooling. The team built and adjusted the program through action research, learning as they went.

Students, teachers, schools, and mentors all reacted warmly. The children's English skills improved clearly, and they began completing work across the whole curriculum. As fluency grew, so did confidence to speak up in class. The article describes how the program was set up and refined. It offers a working model for schools receiving refugee students, built on partnership rather than one-way aid.
pmc-11618424:
Calef Sanchez-Trasvina and co-authors packed a plant compound into silk-based nanoparticles in 2024 to test it against obesity. The compound, called DIM, comes from common vegetables and may curb fat gain, but it needs a carrier. Silk fibroin particles carried it well: they stayed small, even in size, and stable. Loading the compound slightly shrank the particles and changed the silk structure.

The loaded particles fought cell-damaging oxygen far better than empty ones. They did not harm mature fat cells, though they slowed young fat cells at higher doses. Treated cells stored more fat droplets, a mixed signal. The authors still see the silk carrier as a promising delivery route worth more study.
pmc-11618524:
Mirosław Mączka and colleagues squeeze a layered perovskite crystal and watch its light output change. Their materials study from twenty twenty-four examines a lead bromide perovskite. Such layered crystals attract interest for light-based devices. Temperature and pressure both reshape how they glow.

At room temperature the crystal emits a narrow band of light. Cooling reveals extra bands tied to trapped energy states. Pressure triggers three structural changes in sequence. Each change distorts the crystal network further. Light emission first grows much stronger under pressure. Its colour also shifts as the energy gap narrows. The rich set of phases helps designers tune these crystals for devices.
pmc-11619624:
Pohontsch, Stark, and Scherer present a 2024 interview study on how medical students grasp clinical empathy. Empathy improves care for patients and doctors alike, yet schools lack a shared, concrete definition of it. Vague ideas make the skill hard to teach and test. The team asked German students what empathy means to them in daily practice.

They interviewed twenty-four students, half mid-course and half in their final clinical year. Three themes stood out in the accounts. Empathy meant sensing a patient's needs and acting on them. It also felt like an intangible bond between people. Taking time for patients formed the third theme. The authors use the map to sharpen teaching.
pmc-11620024:
Hyacinte Trésor Ghassi and co-authors survey ankle sprain recurrence among athletes in western Cameroon in this 2024 paper. Two hundred fifteen club athletes who train at least three times weekly took part. About seventy-three percent had sprained an ankle before.

Recurrence struck about sixty-two percent of those. Professional status and hand-on-ball sports raised the odds. Fewer than half of the injured had received physiotherapy, and only about a third had fully recovered before playing again. Not knowing about therapy was the main barrier. Physiotherapy and full recovery before return both protected against recurrence. The authors call for education campaigns across the region to spread rehab care.
pmc-11621124:
Haijun Fan wrote a 2024 study of how far a pressure signal reaches in a layered oil or gas reservoir. That reach, called the radius of investigation, guides well tests and reserve counts. Past work dealt mostly with uniform rock, and layered cases lacked a checked method.

Fan gives a pressure solution for a two-zone reservoir and tests how layer contrasts shape the signal's spread. A big flow contrast slows the spread, while a low storage ratio in one zone raises the reach. A new formula matches the full solution well, and both simulations and real cases back the findings.
pmc-11621424:
Bin-Bin Zhang and co-authors built a contactless heart monitor using radio waves in a 2024 paper. Heart disease kills over ten million people a year, and long-term tracking catches trouble early. Standard ECG gear is accurate but needs electrodes on skin. Wrist wearables are easier yet less precise and prone to interference. Their system bounces millimeter-wave radio signals off the body and reads the heartbeat from the reflections.

Breathing moves the chest far more than the heart does, usually drowning the signal. The team found frequency bands far above the heartbeat's own harmonics where heart motion dominates, turning those harmonics from nuisance into signal. Trials with 6,222 outpatients and weeks of home sleep recordings matched clinical ECG systems on heart rate variability and abnormality spotting.
pmc-11622824:
Bronwen Connolly and co-authors build a core outcome set for trials of physical rehabilitation in critical illness. Past trials chose outcomes in unlike ways, which blocks pooling of results and hurts clinical choices. A shared set would let future trials speak to each other.

An online Delphi process ran in two rounds with 329 people from twenty-six countries: researchers, clinicians, and patients and caregivers. From thirty-two starting outcomes, eight reached agreement as critical for all groups. They are physical function, daily living activities, survival, health-related quality of life, exercise capacity, cognitive function, emotional and mental well-being, and frailty. The next step is to pick how each should be measured.
pmc-11623124:
Shaohan Wei proposes a method in a 2024 paper for mapping changing networks into compact number codes. Graphs of linked nodes, such as social or trade networks, shift as new nodes and links arrive. Most coding methods train on the whole graph at once, so they cannot greet new nodes without a full retrain.

His network gathers information from three angles: the node's neighbors, its timing pattern, and its wider setting. Each angle is mined apart, then a gated memory unit blends them into one code. New nodes can thus be coded from their local context alone. The approach suits live systems like fraud detection and recommendation feeds.
pmc-11624824:
Ching-Yi Lee and five co-authors set out a plan for reviewing games in medical training in this two thousand twenty-four protocol paper. Gamification adds game elements, like points and levels, to learning. Teachers hope it boosts engagement and helps students reason through cases. Clinical reasoning is the core skill behind sound diagnosis and care. No map yet shows how games have been used to teach it.

The planned review follows established scoping frameworks. The team will search major databases with terms on games, reasoning, and medical education. They will chart what has been built, how it was used, and what outcomes were reported. The finished map can guide educators who design playful training. It may also reveal gaps where careful trials are still missing.
pmc-11625224:
Williamson and co-authors review what happens when bystanders give chest pushes to a person who turns out not to be in cardiac arrest. Fear of causing harm can make people hold back from this life saving act. Their 2024 review searched three large medical databases.

Five studies with 1,031 patients met the rules for the review. No deaths were blamed on the pushes themselves. Fewer than one in a hundred patients had injuries such as broken ribs or inner bleeding. About two in a hundred felt chest pain. The authors rate the proof as very weak, but the harm rate looks low. The review team also graded how much trust the weak study designs could support.
pmc-11625724:
Ruiqing Di and co-authors gather in this 2024 summary the best evidence on grading exercise risk for patients with implanted heart devices. Pacemakers and defibrillators make rehab safer to offer but riskier to run blind. Searching a dozen databases under an evidence pyramid model, the team screened in sixteen items: guidelines, reviews, consensus statements, and one trial.

From them they distilled thirty-four evidence points in four areas: screening and judging exercise risk, monitoring during sessions, carrying out prescriptions, and preventing trouble. The summary spells out nurses' roles in judging, watching, and teaching, giving clinics a base for rehab plans that fit real patients rather than guesswork. Ward teams can lift the set as written.
pmc-11626524:
Ultrafast lasers cut and shape materials with extreme precision at micron and nanometer scales, but their action is too fast to watch directly. The four authors use molecular dynamics simulations to study how such pulses treat amorphous defects on a nickel-iron alloy surface. The simulations track how deposited energy drives crystal growth within nanoseconds.

They find the temperature for crystal growth rises with the rate of heating, though the final crystal structure stays the same. More deposited energy speeds lattice formation, improves atomic order, and cuts growth time from four point five to three point two nanoseconds. The phase change itself completes within half a nanosecond. A higher incubation temperature shrinks the amorphous share. The authors present the results as a theoretical base for future processing methods built on ultrafast lasers.
pmc-11626824:
Christiana Prestigiacomo, Lindsey Fisher-Fox, and Melissa Cyders present a 2024 systematic review on why people who have had alcohol treatment choose to quit or cut down. Most past research asked people outside treatment. The team searched four databases and kept twenty-one studies of treated patients. Coding the stated reasons produced twenty-one distinct themes.

Common reasons echoed those in general samples: health problems, clashing with personal goals, family influence, and social pressure. Some themes seemed tied to treatment itself, such as hitting rock bottom and fearing disapproval. How reasons were measured changed what people reported, which worries the authors. They urge a standard way to ask, and suggest clinics shape care around each patient's reasons. Tracking reasons across treatment stages is a next step they recommend.
pmc-11627224:
Jung Eun Yu and Jung Yoon Kim mine a large South Korean online mental health community for how its members experience urinary symptoms. Their study came out in 2024. Bladder symptoms and mental illness often occur together and can worsen each other, yet patients' own views are rarely studied.

Nearly a thousand posts mentioning urine were drawn from a community with hundreds of thousands of posts. Topic modeling and close reading showed members blamed psychiatric medication for their symptoms and treated them as unavoidable. Many tried adjusting or stopping medication on their own rather than seeing a urologist, and often failed. Incontinence deepened shame and despair and strained family life. The authors urge proactive urological care and honest risk information for this group.
pmc-11627524:
Yuan Luo and co-authors compare, in a 2024 proof-of-concept study, two large language models on spotting health rumors in Chinese. False health claims spread fast online and can trigger panic or bad choices. The team tested GPT-4 and Baidu's ERNIE Bot 4.0 on the task.

Twenty rumors and ten true statements were fed to both models, which had to judge each and explain why. Each model then wrote a short popular-science essay. Judges scored accuracy, quality, readability, and practical use. The head-to-head shows where chatbots can already help health communicators debunk myths, and where their answers still need a human check before reaching the public.
pmc-11628424:
Jordana Salma and co-authors run an outdoor walking program with older Muslim immigrants in Canada in a 2024 study. Many older newcomers live sedentary lives, and a program must fit their culture and faith to be accepted.

Thirteen participants, with a mean age near sixty seven, were recruited through an Edmonton mosque. After group talks shaped the plan, weekly walks ran for ten weeks in an accessible park with benches and restrooms, led by a fitness instructor. Trackers counted steps, and interviews followed. Three things raised satisfaction: company of peers, the instructor's guidance, and the activity trackers. Transport trouble and thin teaching content were the weak points the authors flag for improvement.
pmc-11628724:
Divine Eli-Cophie, Charles Apprey, and Reginald Annan measure anemia among teenage athletes in Ghana and test how it tracks their physical fitness. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Low hemoglobin is common among adolescents in developing countries. Its cost to young athletes had not been quantified locally.

Nearly two hundred athletes from boxing and football clubs across three regions were tested. About one in seven was anemic, with the youngest group worst hit. Boys carried higher average hemoglobin than girls. Fitness batteries covered grip strength, reaction time, flexibility, and a twelve-minute run. Hemoglobin correlated with endurance and grip measures. Anemia thus predicts fitness even in trained youth. Screening young athletes could catch a fixable drag on performance. Nutrition programs gain a sports argument, not just a health one.
pmc-11630624:
Martha Smith, Elizabeth Yu, and Ghattas Malki lead a team review asking whether exercise alone can treat fatty liver disease in children. Their systematic review appeared in two thousand twenty-four. About one in ten American children carries this liver condition. It raises later risks of cirrhosis, diabetes, and heart disease.

They searched six databases and screened over fifteen hundred records. Sixteen studies covering nearly a thousand children survived the filters. Designs ranged from controlled trials to lifestyle comparisons. Outcomes centered on liver fat and blood chemistry. Bias was scored with standard tools by two independent reviewers. The review maps a literature with real gaps in dose and duration answers. Exercise is already first-line advice, yet prescribing it precisely remains guesswork. The authors set out what trials must measure next.
pmc-11630824:
Kelly Bennion and five colleagues ran five memory experiments testing whether relatedness between study episodes helps or hurts later learning. Memory research has long known later material can strengthen earlier memories after the fact when the two are related. The reverse path was untested. One thousand people learned paired items, with relatedness varied between the first and second pairs' cues, targets, or both.

High relatedness reliably produced proactive help: later pairs were learned faster and held better. Low relatedness produced proactive interference in the same experiments. Memories also became more interdependent, standing or falling together. The 2024 results recast relatedness as scaffolding: what you know props up new learning or trips it, by semantic fit. Teachers who order material face exactly this trade-off.
pmc-11630924:
Suguru Nakagawa and Kiyoshi Ishii report a simple fix for a slipped artificial lens inside its own capsule, in a 2024 case report. Their patient, a 43-year-old man, had received the lens a decade earlier during retinal surgery. The lens, still wrapped in its full capsule, had dropped into the eye's rear cavity. To reuse it, the lens had to be freed of that wrapping.

Working from outside the eye, the surgeons lifted each spring arm of the lens through the wound in turn. They stripped the capsule and its ring from each arm while it sat outside, then tucked it back. The cleaned lens was anchored inside the wall of the eye with a flange method. A week later the eye saw sharply, and its front surface cell count held up well. The authors call the outside route quick and clean.
pmc-11631024:
Ziyuan Huang and six co-authors wrote a data study in 2024 that links long noncoding RNAs tied to COVID-19 with the fate of lung cancer. Sick people with non-small cell lung cancer do worse once they catch the virus, and these long RNAs steer how tumours grow. No one had tried if the shared set could foretell scores.

Data from cancer and group stores fed a screen for RNAs tied to the virus by shared counts. Layered regression built a risk score from four of them. High-risk and low-risk sets split in their sick traits, their shield-cell mix, and how they took drug care. Risk scores also tracked counts of the flesh round the tumour. The team puts the four-RNA plan forth as a tool for fate and drug choice that still needs proof in sick care.
pmc-11631224: Karokh Hama Hussein and eleven co-authors report a 19-year-old man whose Takayasu arteritis hid behind a brucellosis label. His brucella blood tests stayed positive and round after round of anti-brucellosis treatment failed to help. Once the artery inflammation was diagnosed and immune-suppressing therapy began, his symptoms eased and the serology normalized. The case warns that the two diseases can mimic each other, and that treating one can rewrite the other's test results.
pmc-11631624:
Jiao Zhou, Xiang Lu, and Haichuan Wang reviewed work in 2024 on a protein called Fyn and its role in brain harm in newborn babies. This harm occurs when a baby's brain gets too little oxygen and blood around birth, and it can cause lasting damage.

Fyn helps send signals in the brain and guides growth, wiring, and learning links between nerve cells. The review pulls together lab findings that tie Fyn to too much of a brain chemical, swelling in the brain, and nerve cell death from stress. By laying out these paths, the authors hope to point drug makers toward new ways to protect newborns and improve their long term health.
pmc-11632224:
Huan Zhang and co-authors trace how a common yeast moves from gut colonization to bloodstream infection, in a 2024 study. The yeast, Candida albicans, lives quietly in many guts but can turn invasive in hospital patients. The study began with thirty-one patients who had Candida bloodstream infections at a Chinese university hospital. Risk factors for gut colonization were weighed first.

Animal models then reproduced the path from gut settlement to kidney infection. Gene, microbe, and metabolite scans of the colon showed a clear pattern as disease advanced. A brake on immune cells, called PD-1, fell in colon tissue. Helpful gut bacteria and their fatty acid products dropped, while other microbes and compounds rose. The authors say these shifts could serve as warning signs of infection to come.
pmc-11632424:
Ten authors study radiation lung harm in mice in 2024 and test a drug that blocks the STING immune switch. Chest radiation can scar the lungs and cap the dose doctors can give. Mice got a strong chest dose, with the blocker given from day one for four weeks in the test arm.

The immune path lit up in treated lung tissue, and blocking it cut early swelling and later scar by a clear margin. Fluid from harmed lung cells held loose DNA strands that pushed support cells toward scar forms. A stress path inside cells carried that push, the team found.
pmc-11632524:
Emma Mills, Katherine Wollman, and Elizabeth Waring count trash along an Oklahoma river, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. The Illinois River near Tahlequah is a scenic recreation waterway. Litter degrades both its ecology and its visitor experience.

For three months the team monitored litter levels along the river. Aluminum cans proved most abundant in their counts. They also surveyed 170 people about the problem. Respondents ranked cigarette butts as the most visible litter, a mismatch with the counts. Most wanted change, and cooperation with commercial float operators emerged as the practical lever. The data were aimed at local and state management agencies. Small rivers live or die by such unglamorous monitoring.
pmc-11632824:
Five authors report a 2024 case of gut blockage caused by an ameboma in a patient who had weight-loss surgery. An ameboma is a rare growth-like mass from infection with a gut parasite. It can look like Crohn disease or colon cancer on scans, so tissue tests give the surest answer.

The mass sat in the rising colon and blocked the bowel. Care for such masses aims first to kill the parasite, with surgery when there is blockage, a hole, or severe colon swelling. The case warns teams to keep this rare cause in mind after bariatric surgery.
pmc-11632924:
Yanfang Bai and co-authors show a compound from the herb Danshen eases kidney scarring in a 2024 study. Kidney fibrosis, the scarring that ends chronic kidney disease, travels with broken sugar production in kidney cells. Tanshinone I, an active compound from Danshen, is known to fight fibrosis and inflammation, but its metabolic route was unclear.

The team found the compound raises a master regulator called PGC-1 alpha, which restarts gluconeogenesis, the kidney's own glucose making. Restoring that pathway tracked with less fibrosis in their models. The result reframes part of kidney scarring as a fuel problem, not only an inflammation problem, and names a traditional compound that addresses it through a defined molecular lever.
pmc-11633224:
Sawash Mohammed and co-authors tracked hormone patterns in the pancreas of ferrets bred to model cystic fibrosis, in a 2024 study. In these animals, blood sugar swings through set phases before diabetes linked to the disease sets in. First comes a month of normal sugar, then two months of high sugar with loss of hormone-making cell clusters. A calmer phase follows, in which those clusters grow back.

The team stained the clusters to see how three signals changed across the phases. Insulin staining ran high in the first phase, then fell below normal in the third. A second hormone moved the other way, while a precursor form fell across the later phases. Ratios between the signals also flipped between phases. The authors read the shifts as a map of how the disease reshapes the pancreas before diabetes takes hold.
pmc-11634124:
Jiunn-Jye Sheu and co-authors patch stem cell sheets onto the hearts of mini-pigs recovering from old heart attacks. Their 2024 study seeds fat-derived stem cells into a sheet scaffold and lays it on the heart's outer wall. One group of pigs gets cells first zapped with gentle shock waves, a pretreatment meant to wake them up.

Twenty pigs split across four groups, from sham surgery to the full treatment. By day 180 the shock-waved group kept stronger pumping and grew more small vessels near the scar than the plain cell group. Its cells also showed richer energy and growth signals in the lab. Scarring and wall stretch ran lowest where pumping held best. The authors credit the sheet with bracing the wall against its own pressure.
pmc-11634624:
Amelia Hurley-Novatny and co-authors review bone health in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, published in 2024, a fatal inherited disease that wastes muscle. Weak bones, spinal curvature, stunted growth, and frequent fractures add heavily to the burden of the disease. These problems were long blamed on steroid treatment and the loss of walking, the two most visible causes.

The review gathers newer evidence for a wider set of drivers, including low vitamin D, hormone imbalance, body wide inflammation, signals released by sick muscle, and poor blood vessel function. Current treatments are few and blunt. By mapping the full set of causes, the authors aim to guide new therapies and the combined care teams these patients need.
pmc-11635124:
Mohammad Ghorbani and co-authors tested blood cell clumps and a signal protein as markers for heart emergencies, in this 2024 study. Acute coronary syndrome follows the rupture of fatty plaques in heart arteries. Platelets stuck to white cells may drive that process.

The study compared 30 patients with the syndrome and 24 healthy controls. Two kinds of platelet-white cell clumps and the signal protein IL-6 were all higher in patients. A second signal protein did not rise. Clump levels tracked IL-6 levels closely. Curve tests showed all three measures could separate patients from controls. The authors propose them as diagnostic clues.
pmc-11635324:
Andrew O'Malley, Miriam Veenhuizen, and Ayla Ahmed test skin tone spread in AI medical images in a 2024 protocol paper. Image generators learn from textbooks that under-show dark skin, so their medical art may skew light. Students who train on such art risk a skewed eye.

Two standard generators each made one hundred psoriasis images. A tuned setup pushed a third set toward the United States tone spread from survey data. Three raters scored each image on a standard tone scale. Fit tests then compare each set's spread against the national one. The design shows whether a prompt fix can fair the output.
pmc-11635524:
Erming Ouyang and six co-authors turn bamboo waste into biochar that strips quinolone antibiotics from water, in work from 2024. These drugs harm ecosystems and human health once they escape into the environment. Biochar was made at several heating temperatures and tested against three model drugs: moxifloxacin, ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin.

Char made at 700 degrees had the richest pore structure and the strongest uptake, holding roughly 116 to 151 milligrams of drug per gram depending on the compound. Uptake followed the Langmuir isotherm and second-order kinetics, the standard signs of surface-driven capture. The authors pitch bamboo char as a cheap, practical adsorbent for antibiotic cleanup.
pmc-11635724:
Greg Marchand and co-authors pool studies on ovarian torsion surgery in young patients in a 2024 meta-analysis. Ovarian torsion twists the ovary and needs fast care. A gentle laparoscopic approach untwists it and may add cyst removal or ovary fixing. The team searches many databases for studies in children and teens.

Outcomes include recurrence, switch to open surgery, ovary removal, and later ovary function on ultrasound. Recurrence appears in a small share of cases across five studies, they report. Conversion to open surgery is also uncommon. The pooled work aims to show how safe and effective the conservative route is for young patients.
pmc-11636124:
Jaap Jan Boelens and Michael Scordo comment on drug dosing before stem cell transplants in this 2024 article. They discuss a study of a large group of young leukemia patients. The study used a tested population model to estimate each child's exposure to rabbit antithymocyte globulin. That drug calms the immune system.

The study found a sweet spot: children with high exposure before the transplant and low exposure after it fared best. The commentators note warning signs too, such as a high graft rejection rate after chemotherapy based preparation, and they question why exposure was not checked against rejection directly. Their wider point is that model based dosing, tested in simulations, can shape better trials and better survival after transplant.
pmc-11636224:
Reem El-Shenawy and co-authors publish in 2024 a correction to their study of immune markers and liver cancer risk in Egyptian patients with hepatitis C scarring. The original paper weighed blood markers as predictors of liver cancer in cirrhotic and non cirrhotic patients, before and after cure with direct acting antivirals. Two abstract sentences were wrong as first printed, and this notice fixes both.

The corrected result states that the three serum markers did not differ between cirrhotic and non cirrhotic patients still carrying the virus, yet differed sharply between the two groups once cured. The corrected conclusion names the full predictor set the authors stand behind: three blood markers plus two gene expression measures in blood cells. The journal notes the original article itself has been updated to match. Corrections of this kind keep the printed record aligned with the data as the authors intend it read.
pmc-11637424:
Cholesterol-lowering statins were floated as shields against severe viral lung illness long before COVID-19, on hints from flu studies and on theory. Eric Meyerowitz and Arthur Kim weigh the best test of that idea in a 2024 commentary. The test borrows a large heart trial in people with HIV that had assigned one statin or placebo years before the pandemic.

Serious COVID struck less often in the statin arm, about twenty-seven percent less, though the gap could still be chance because vaccines had thinned the events. Nearly all serious cases landed before vaccination. Set beside earlier observational hints, the result keeps the shield idea alive but unproven.
pmc-11637624:
Tu and co-authors adapt a fear avoidance scale into simplified Chinese and test it. The scale gauges thought, feeling, and behavior sides of pain fear. A team of 330 patients with chronic muscle pain took part. They filled the scale twice, one week apart. Other pain and disability surveys were taken for comparison.

Internal consistency hit 0.920 on the alpha scale. Test-retest reliability reached 0.918 as well. A two-factor fit matched the original English version. Scores tied strongly to disability, catastrophizing, and anxiety marks. The authors call the Chinese version sound for clinic use.
pmc-11639824:
Baisch and co-authors measure what soybeans grown in wet lowland fields, once reserved for rice, carry in their grains. Soil there differs from the highlands, so nutrient export may shift. Their 2024 study grows two seasons of crops under two soil preparation styles and six cover crop choices, then assays yield, protein, oil, and minerals.

Average yield came to about 3,830 kilograms per hectare. Loosening the soil lifted yield and pushed protein and oil to their peaks. The oil's two main fatty acids were oleic and linoleic. Most mineral levels matched highland values, while loosened soil raised potassium and zinc uptake, and ryegrass cover raised nitrogen. Oil quality indices all fell within accepted ranges, the authors report.
pmc-11639924:
Flavio Ragni and co-authors built a machine learning tool that predicts, at each clinic visit, whether an eye patient needs another injection, in a 2024 study. The disease, wet age-related macular degeneration, slowly destroys central vision and is treated with repeated injections into the eye, given only when scans show need. That visit-by-visit judgment burdens patients and clinics.

The models used eye scan features such as fluid pockets and retinal thickness, plus vision scores, rather than whole images. Cross-checks that held out whole patients kept the testing honest. The best models called the need for injection with solid accuracy. An explanation method showed fluid under and within the retina, plus central thickness, driving the calls. The authors say such a tool could slot into routine clinics and trim needless visits.
pmc-11640024:
Lazar Karić and co-authors re-examine how inflammation, oxidative stress, and blood fats tangle together in dogs with excess cortisol. Fourteen newly diagnosed dogs were compared with fourteen healthy matches of similar age. The team measured markers of oxidative damage and defence, inflammation ratios from blood counts, and the animals' cholesterol, triglycerides, and lipoprotein patterns.

The sick dogs carried more oxidative damage, and among the defences only glutathione ran higher, while uric acid rose in a way the authors read as pro-oxidative. Several inflammation ratios climbed too, though without a clear tie to inflammation itself. The fat profile shifted markedly, with altered HDL and high cholesterol and triglycerides. Statistical links bound the fat markers to both stress and inflammation indices. The authors offer the pattern as a fuller picture of Cushing's syndrome in dogs.
pmc-11640124:
Manel Albertí-Valls and co-authors review how immune therapy is changing care for cancer of the womb lining. Early cases of this cancer are often cured, but cases that spread or return are hard to treat. Their 2024 review centers on drugs that free the immune system to attack tumors. It asks which patients gain most from these drugs.

A key trait is whether the tumor can fix faults in its own DNA code. Tumors that lack this repair tend to carry more faults and answer better to the drugs. Yet some such tumors stay cold, with few immune cells inside, and resist care. A few repair-fit tumors run hot and do respond. The review also covers cell-based cures now in trials for hard cases.
pmc-11640324:
André Lollert and co-authors linked resting heart scans to exercise tests in patients with a sunken chest in twenty twenty-four. The condition, pectus excavatum, presses the breastbone into the heart. Seventeen patients had both a magnetic resonance scan, with measures of heart wall motion, and a treadmill exercise test before surgery. The team asked whether the resting scan could foretell exercise capacity.

Several resting measures tracked the exercise results. Motion rates at the base of the right ventricle, the spot most squeezed by the breastbone, gave the strongest links. High motion rates there went with higher peak heart rates but lower peak oxygen uptake. The authors read this as a compensation that works only so far: the squeezed base strains harder, yet the most strained hearts cope worst at full effort. Resting scans may thus hint at exercise limits.
pmc-11640424: Judith Millastre and ten co-authors present thermal liquid biopsy as a tool for sorting pancreatic cystic lesions, in a two thousand twenty-four paper. These cysts form a varied group found ever more often, usually by chance on CT, MRI, or endoscopic ultrasound scans. Telling harmless cysts from malignant ones is the clinical problem the title addresses. The hosted abstract is cut short, so the entry is described at this level: a blood-based thermal profiling approach proposed for differential diagnosis of pancreatic cysts and detection of malignancy.
pmc-11640524:
Mehmet Ozemre and co-authors study root canal shape in upper first molars in a 2024 dental imaging study. The front cheek side root often holds extra canals, and canal layout may relate to distances between canal openings and to root lengths. Knowing such links helps dentists plan root treatment.

The team reviewed more than fifteen hundred cone beam scans taken for other reasons between twenty twenty and twenty twenty three. Canal types did not differ by age or sex. Opening distance and root lengths also did not differ between canal types. The authors conclude opening distance does not predict canal type.
pmc-11640624:
Salt land is oft writ off as waste, yet some crops crop there, and what grows may not match its sweet soil kin. Yimin Zhang and co-authors weigh that match in a 2024 study of five peanut kinds. Each kind was grown on shore salt land and on plain land near by, then run through a full food test.

Salt land nuts ran high in ash, zinc, and one more ore, plus some rare fats. Their rust fight score ran low next to plain nuts. Salt and one shield score split the sets most hard. Much else, from fat and flesh build to most rare stocks, sat the same in both. The team says salt land nuts hold their own as food.
pmc-11640724:
Sara Spinelli and co-authors review how red blood cells handle strain from oxygen in a 2024 article. Red cells carry a small set of chemical pathways, since they lack many parts other cells have. Harmful oxygen agents can warp those pathways and damage key enzymes, which then hurts how the cells work.

The review lays out the main pathways of the red cell in plain order. It then traces how each pathway shifts under high oxygen strain. The authors link those shifts to disease states where red cells fail early. The piece aims to give readers a map of where strain and metabolism meet in this simple but vital cell.
pmc-11640824:
Ewa Mirzwa-Mróz and co-authors review the genetics of cucumber resistance to downy mildew. Their 2024 review covers a fungus-like pathogen that devastates cucurbit crops in growing regions worldwide. Chemical control has limits, and the pathogen keeps evolving, so resistant varieties are the sustainable path.

The review maps the resistance genes and genome regions found so far. It then covers breeding tools: marker-assisted selection, genomic selection, and gene editing, each speeding the making of resistant lines. Gene activity and genome studies that reveal how resistance works get their own treatment. The authors also discuss disease management more broadly and how climate change may shift the disease's reach and severity. Prospects for durable resistance close the review.
pmc-11640924:
Katya Stefanova and co-authors test whether three soluble receptors track anemia types in rheumatoid arthritis in a 2024 study. Anemia rides along with this joint disease often, and it comes in two blends: anemia of chronic disease alone, or that plus true iron deficiency. Sorting the blend guides treatment.

Blood levels of two receptors ran clearly higher in the combined-anemia group than in the chronic-only group. A third protein, osteoprotegerin, trended lower there. Correlation webs then split by group. In the chronic-only patients, the receptors danced with inflammation marks, antibodies, and disease activity scores. In the combined group, they tied instead to falling serum iron. The authors propose the receptor set as a fingerprint panel, flagging which patients carry the double burden and why.
pmc-11641024:
Yue and co-authors dissect why high- and low-grade Ninghong black teas taste different. Ninghong is a distinctive black tea, and grade gaps shape its price and fans. The team compared Jinhao, a high grade from unfolded leaves, with Congou, a lower grade from unfurled leaves.

They joined sensory tasting, broad metabolite profiling, and taste activity values for key compounds. Jinhao stood out for sweetness and mellowness with umami depth. Chemical measures showed which metabolites drive those traits. Linking taste panels to molecule data gives tea makers targets for processing and grading that match drinker experience.
pmc-11641224:
A review team surveys what is known about fetuin-A, a blood protein also called alpha-2-Heremans-Schmid glycoprotein, and its part in cancer. The protein already has known roles in mineral balance and inflammation. The reviewers ask how it behaves across cancers of the liver, breast, prostate, bowel, brain, bone, and lung, and whether it could guide diagnosis or treatment.

Across many cancer types, fetuin-A helps tumor cells stick, spread, move, and grow, and it shapes the signals that control cell growth. It also affects the release of inflammatory messengers, which ties it to inflammation inside tumors. Because high levels track with spread and poor outlook in several cancers, the protein looks promising as a marker and a drug target. The reviewers stress that more work is needed to pin down how it acts and how clinics might use it.
pmc-11641424:
Nishank Raisinghani and co-authors coax a famed protein-folding tool into showing more than one shape per protein. Proteins bend when a drug or partner docks, and that bend drives their work. A tool trained to call one best shape can miss the bent forms. Their 2024 study masks parts of the chain at random and trims the kin lists the tool reads, so each run can land on a fresh pose.

Test sets hold matched pairs: each protein in free form and in docked form. The trick yields sound calls for both forms and for the cloud of poses round each. Pose clouds from the two forms share like motion traits. The team reads that match as a sign that a fold's own shape sets its dance, a base drug hunters can use.
pmc-11641524:
Pancreatic cancer often spreads first to nearby lymph nodes, and long noncoding RNAs may help drive that spread. The authors of a 2024 study mine a cancer genome atlas for genes turned up in tumors that had reached the nodes. Their screen flags a cluster in the HOXA region, including a long noncoding RNA called HOXA11-AS. Patients with more of it had later-stage tumors and shorter survival. The team then tests what it does in cancer cells.

Silencing the RNA slowed the cells' growth and movement. It also raised interferon lambda genes and lowered a family called HMGB. Silencing one of those, HMGB3, slowed the cells too. The authors name the RNA a possible drug target.
pmc-11641624:
Martínez-Rodríguez and co-authors read DNA from tiny parcels shed by tumors to foresee hormone therapy failure in metastatic breast cancer, in a 2024 study. They followed fifty-nine patients whose cancers feed on hormones, checking two resistance-linked genes in DNA from extracellular vesicles and in ordinary circulating tumor DNA.

One gene's mutations, in ESR1, appeared in a quarter of patients, and finding them in vesicle DNA at baseline meant faster progression, especially on one drug. The other gene told a different story depending on the source: silent in vesicle DNA, ominous in circulating DNA. The authors argue the two liquid biopsy sources complement each other.
pmc-11641724:
Teenagers with cancer lean on different mental strategies at different stages of the illness. Diego-José Sáez-Rodríguez and four co-authors surveyed 201 patients aged 12 to 17 in three Spanish cities, in a 2024 study, comparing those in active treatment with those in follow-up care. A standard coping questionnaire captured strategies such as worrying, calming down, ignoring the problem, and self-blame.

All four strategies were used more during treatment than afterward, and girls and boys differed on three of them. The authors say emotional needs shift sharply between phases, so support should be retargeted as treatment ends rather than simply stopped.
pmc-11641924:
Wolken and co-authors build a lab test to measure total testosterone with high accuracy. Testosterone levels in blood range widely, from 1 to 1,480 nanograms per deciliter. Fast immunoassays often lose accuracy at low levels, below 100, which matter most for women and children.

Their test uses liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry, run on three instruments of two types. Sample steps start with dilution and conditioning to clean the blood sample. The aim is a test that stays exact across the full range. Care teams could then trust low readings that guide hormone care.
pmc-11642124:
Susanna Vu and co-authors review fibres made from graphene that can sniff gases, in a 2024 paper. Gas sensors guard air quality, workplace safety, and increasingly health, since breath carries disease clues.
