Graphene fibres bring a rare mix to the job: huge surface area, bendability, and strength. Their chemistry can also be tuned to favour one gas over another, which is the heart of a good sensor.

The review explains how such fibres are made, from spinning pure graphene to blending it with other materials. It then walks through how the sensors work and sorts them by the gases they target, comparing sensitivity and performance for each. The authors close by judging where the field stands and what it needs next, such as better stability in humid air, before these thread-like sensors reach daily use.
pmc-11642324:
Chen and five co-authors report a study from twenty twenty-four on a link between curved spine and severe knee arthritis. A curved spine can tilt the pelvis, but ties to knee disease were little studied. The team use Taiwan health insurance records for a case-control study. Cases had knee arthritis treated with first-time knee replacement surgery. Controls were matched peers without replacement surgery. Over ten thousand cases and thirty thousand controls entered the analysis.

People with a prior curved spine diagnosis had notably higher odds of knee replacement. The link held for both sexes and for younger and older patients. The study lacks data on which way each spine curved. The authors still urge clinicians to weigh spine shape in knee care.
pmc-11642424:
Phenylalanine, one of the building blocks of protein, may be a limiting ingredient for milk making in dairy cows. Guo and co-authors feed cow mammary cells a range of doses and watch the milk proteins respond. A mid-high dose raised all three casein proteins and the transporter that pulls the amino acid into the cell, while quieting a starvation signal.

Blocking the cell's growth switch, mTOR, erased the casein gains, which pins the effect on that pathway. Silencing the transporter showed it ferries the amino acid in. The treated cells also drew less of several other amino acids from their medium. The authors lay out the route as a target for feed design.
pmc-11642624:
Laura Rehak and co-authors sum ward tales of own blood cell care for sugar sick folk whose legs face the knife with no path left, in a review from 2024. The cell care seeds the leg with the sick own white cells to wake flow and mend sores. Six ward studies with over two hundred sick feed the pool.

Cut loss ran near a sixth per year in the pool. Sores shut in past three fifths of legs, at a mean of near seven months. Skin air marks rose and pain fell past care. Death ran near a fifth in the pool span. No grave harms tied to the care. Cost and rite notes urge first line use.
pmc-11643424:
Salvatore Raccuia and a large team of co-authors give food-processing waste a full physical and chemical examination. Their 2024 study characterizes pomaces from bergamot, grapes, and olives, in raw and pre-treated forms. These residues are usually discarded. Yet their acid-base, heat, and surface behavior decides whether they can clean polluted water, and those traits were barely documented.

Six lab methods were combined, from gas adsorption and electron microscopy to heat analysis, light-based fingerprinting, and titration. Tests ran at room temperature across several salt levels. Modeling showed one kind of acid group dominates the active surface sites in every pomace, though its amount varied. The particles proved irregular and mixed under the microscope. The data support designing cleanup uses for an abundant waste.
pmc-11643524:
Xiaolong Qiao and co-authors turn bamboo pulp waste into glowing carbon dots. Their 2024 paper starts from black liquor, the dark waste liquid of bamboo pulping in China. The liquor is rich in sugars and lignin that usually go to waste, so finding value in it has clear gains.

Heating the liquor in water produced tiny carbon dots that glow blue-green under light. The team tracked how sugar content in the liquor changed with heat and time. One recipe gave dots whose glow color shifts with the light used to excite them. Those dots were used to print a security code that stayed clear and stable. The work links forest protection, waste use, and anti-counterfeit printing in one chain.
pmc-11643724:
Hyun Woo Lee and co-authors report, in a 2024 trial, a heat killed gut bacterium given to patients with breathing symptoms. Such symptoms are common, and they track with falling lung function and higher death rates. A growing body of work links gut imbalance to lung disease through a gut lung connection. The bacterium used here has shown promise in calming diseases beyond the gut.

The trial was randomized and double blind, run at several centers. Patients with symptoms lasting four to twelve weeks got the preparation or a placebo. The main outcome was change in a breathlessness, cough, and sputum score over twelve weeks. Side measures covered lung function, exhaled nitric oxide, breathlessness scales, and a respiratory quality of life form. The design tests whether a killed microbe can still deliver benefit, without live bacteria.
pmc-11643924:
Angélica Hernández-Moreno and a team of colleagues analyze food security among rural Mapuche elders over sixty near Temuco, Chile. Longer lives are often lived amid inequity and poverty, and being rural, Indigenous, female, and old compounds the risk. Their qualitative study interprets elders' own accounts through a symbolic and complexity lens.

Growing their own food emerged as the main route to food security. Cultural food heritage, preserved especially by women, and community spaces reinforcing that culture both helped. Obstacles included migration to cities for work, declining health, and shrinking production of traditional healthy foods under environmental pressure and ill-fitting public policies. The authors call for policies congruent with the Mapuche territorial worldview.
pmc-11644024:
Tiago Bertola Lobato and co-authors feed omega-3 fish oil to diabetic rats in this 2024 study. Their rats, Goto-Kakizaki rats, develop type 2 diabetes and insulin resistance without obesity, which isolates the sugar problem from the weight problem.

For eight weeks the rats got fish oil rich in two omega-3 fats, or water as a control. Treated diabetic rats handled glucose loads better and responded to insulin more sharply. Their lymph node immune cells shifted toward regulatory T cells and away from inflammatory types, made fewer inflammatory signals, and raised a calming one. Cell growth also slowed. The authors conclude the fats improved glycemic control while cooling lymphocyte driven inflammation.
pmc-11644224:
Jin Qiu and co-authors carve a tiny diving board into an optical fiber to sense vibration in a study from 2024. A femtosecond laser cut a Fabry-Perot cavity into a standard single-mode fiber. The cavity and fiber tail act together as a cantilever beam. Shaking bends the beam and stretches the cavity, shifting its interference fringes.

No external pickup part is needed, which keeps the sensor small. It hears from seventy hertz up to one hundred ten kilohertz. Sensitivity and signal clarity were both strong, with a signal-to-noise ratio near fifty-six decibels. Cavity depth tunes the response. Such hair-thin ears could monitor machines, bridges, and pipes from inside tight spaces.
pmc-11644524:
James Duverger leads a team on textile sensors for breathing in cars. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with respiratory monitoring. Seat based sensors can track driver alertness quietly.

A numeric method rates signal quality to guide placement. A simple setup tested belts and seat backs. The waist gave the best breathing signals overall. Chest came next, then upper back, then lower back. Folding the sensors improved back signal quality. Three design rules came from the analysis. Many sensors and smart placement raise success odds.  Seat belt spots were part of the case.
pmc-11644624:
Hyeon-Ji Kim and co-authors test in 2024 whether a plant extract fraction can fight cell damage and slow aging in tiny worms. The plant is rich in flavonoids, compounds known for guarding cells. Lab-made guards work well but raise safety doubts, so plant sources draw interest.

One fraction of the extract held the most phenols and flavonoids and scored best on three radical tests. Fed to worms, it raised guard enzyme activity in step with dose. Worms handled stress better, built up less harmful oxygen, and lived longer. The results back the fraction as a natural guard worth more study for aging and health foods.
pmc-11644724:
Simone Pietro Garofalo and co-authors predict cotton water stress from satellite images in a 2024 study set in southern Italy. Water is scarce around the Mediterranean, and growers need fast warning when cotton runs dry. The team trained learning models on Sentinel-2 satellite bands to estimate stem water potential, a direct gauge of plant thirst, during the 2023 season.

A random forest model did best, beating two boosting methods on accuracy. Blue and red visible bands and the red edge bands carried the most signal. Explanation tools confirmed which bands drove each call. The trained model then traced the season's ups and downs, spotting spells of sharp and moderate stress. The approach could let growers water by need across whole fields without walking them with handheld gauges.
pmc-11644924:
Can Ersü, Eduard Petlenkov, Karl Janson, and Guangcai Sun systematically review radar technologies for unmanned ground vehicles. Radar enhances autonomy in defense, transportation, and exploration roles, sensing through conditions that defeat cameras and lidar. Searching four databases, the team selected fifty-four studies for full analysis.

The review details advancements in radar perception, machine learning integration, and sensor fusion. It also discusses the challenges of deploying radar in complex environments. Findings reveal both the potential and the limitations of radar for ground vehicles, particularly in adverse weather and unstructured terrain. Radar's all-weather robustness is its selling point, yet resolution and clutter in messy ground environments remain stubborn problems. The authors outline implications for practice, policy, and future research. The review consolidates what radar can do alone, what it should do fused, and where problems lie.
pmc-11645024:
Seckin Oncu and co-authors build a real-time radar classifier on a software-defined radio in this 2024 study. Military listening systems must spot and sort enemy radar signals fast. Modern radios defined by software offer flexible platforms for that job, and each radar pulse can be summed up in a short data word that describes its traits.

Their system sorts those pulse words with a density-based clustering method that needs no preset number of classes. A graphics processor speeds the trait extraction, letting the system keep up with very fast sampling. In tests the setup reached about ninety percent accuracy while running in real time. The authors say the mix of software radio and graphics power suits modern electronic support work.
pmc-11645424:
Kenneth Harrison and co-authors combine studies of walking speed in essential tremor in a 2024 analysis. Essential tremor is a common movement disorder, and walking speed marks mobility and risk of poor outcomes. The team searched for studies that set patients next to healthy controls.

Eight studies with several hundred people were pooled. People with the disorder walked much slower than controls, with a large gap by standard measures. Studies varied a lot, which the authors note as a caveat. They link the slow gait to trouble in the cerebellum. The work argues that gait checks belong in routine care for this group.
pmc-11646124:
Tara Chaplin and five co-authors study how teen brains react to a parent's feelings and how that links to mood and habits. More than one hundred young teens did a talk task with a parent, then watched clips of their own parent and a strange parent while in a brain scanner.

Strong response in key feeling hubs to a parent's bad mood went with more trouble in handling feelings and more sad and tense symptoms. Response to a parent's good mood linked mainly to tense symptoms. The work hints that a keen brain response to parents helps shape teen mental health.
pmc-11646224:
A laser treatment can lower eye pressure in glaucoma without daily drops, and one maker's green laser now offers the mode. Karin Pillunat and co-authors report twelve months of results from four German centers. Twenty-five eyes of twenty-five patients with open-angle glaucoma took part. One hundred laser spots ringed the eye's drainage tissue in a single session. About a quarter of eyes needed extra treatment during the year.

In the nineteen eyes with stable therapy, pressure fell from twenty to about sixteen by six to twelve months. Over half of those eyes cut pressure by at least a fifth. Side effects stayed in the expected mild range. The records support the device as a safe pressure-lowering option.
pmc-11646824: Three doctors report that the drug baclofen eased vertical nystagmus in a patient with an advanced glioma, in a case report published in 2024. Nystagmus makes the eyes move without control, and brain tumors are among its causes, apart from the more common inner ear trigger. In this patient, the eye movements ran up and down. After treatment with baclofen, a drug that acts on a calming signal system in the brain, the vertical nystagmus improved. The brief report adds a documented case for this use of the drug.
pmc-11647524:
Hofmann and co-authors introduce a journal research topic on computer models of language that can be checked against brain and behavior data. The editors argue that plain linguistic theory cannot claim the standing of a natural science, while models that predict neural and behavioral results can. Their call drew seven papers, and the editorial walks through them.

One paper modeled how brain regions interact during reading aloud and found the eye ran closer to the voice when the text hung together. Another proposed a roadmap for brain-computer interfaces that respect each user's language and culture. Other papers took yet other routes into the shared question. The editors frame the collection as one step toward closing the gap between models of language in machines and language in the human mind.
pmc-11647924:
Chutima Kranrod, Hiromi Kudo, and Shinji Tokonami review studies of high background radiation areas in three Asian countries in this 2024 paper. Some regions in India, China, and Indonesia expose residents to far more natural radiation than average, from the ground and from radon gas indoors. People have lived there for generations, which makes these areas natural laboratories. The review gathers what such studies measured and what they taught about dose and risk.

The authors cover the sources of exposure, land based radiation and inhaled radon chief among them. They compare how studies across the three countries were run and what health signals they found. Lessons include how hard low dose risk is to pin down, and how much local geology varies. The review aims to guide future studies and to inform safety rules for such regions.
pmc-11648024:
Zhixiang Gao and co-authors compare laser power levels for prostate surgery in this 2024 trial. Holmium laser enucleation trims an enlarged prostate through the urethra. Whether low power matches high power for small glands was untested in a randomized trial.

Eighty-one men with small glands and strong symptoms took part across centers. Half got the low-power setting and half the high-power one. Symptom and flow scores improved equally in both groups by six months. Low power used well under half the laser energy and caused less pain after surgery. Minor capsule tears occurred only in the high-power group. The authors back low power for small glands.
pmc-11648224:
Yasushi Yabuki, Norifumi Shioda and their co-authors study how RNA structures and calcium ions together push the Tau protein toward aggregation in 2024. Tau clumping is a hallmark of Alzheimer disease and related dementias, and it begins with a phase change in the protein.

In lab tests set to mimic conditions inside cells, Tau formed stable liquid droplets that kept their fluidity for a day. RNA from cells sped the shift from liquid to gel, and a folded RNA form called a G-quadruplex proved crucial. Calcium ions, which build up during degeneration, sped the process further. Together they acted within an hour.
pmc-11648624:
Ying-Fei Li and co-authors trace a giant change in electrical resistance in a europium compound to spin-carrying polarons, in this 2024 paper. The material family broke the usual rules for the effect, showing none of the standard causes. Something else had to carry the response.

Light-based probes and computer models checked the lead compound across heat levels and sister materials. The low-energy signal tracked the resistance peak, yet showed no sharp particle-like features. The spectra looked smeared and weak instead. The team blames tangled magnetic and lattice forces, forming polarons that drag spin through the crystal.
pmc-11649324:
Newsted, Bajin, and You give a short guide in twenty twenty-four to a growth of skin-like tissue in the middle ear. Despite its name, the growth is not a tumour and holds no cholesterol. Poor air flow in the ear and long-term ear infection let shed skin build up, and the mass can eat into nearby bone.

Lasting ear discharge with a bad smell and hearing loss are the key signs, they warn. A close look at the eardrum is needed, with the upper flap checked with care. Drugs can calm discharge, but only surgery can remove the growth. It comes back in many cases, so checks every six to twelve months matter.
pmc-11649724:
Joanna Brokowska, Anna Herman-Antosiewicz, and Aleksandra Hać test cabbage-family compounds on healthy human cells. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses skin fibroblasts and prostate cancer cells. These isothiocyanates trigger cell recycling in cancer cells. Their effects on normal primary cells were less explored.

Both compounds switched on recycling in the healthy fibroblasts. Protein production fell at the same time measurably. A known energy-sensing pathway explained the paired effects. Mutant huntingtin clumps, the Huntington disease protein, were counted. The compounds protected against that toxic aggregation. Effects in primary cells differ from cancer cell lore. Dietary compounds might support recycling-based therapies.
pmc-11649824:
Marlene Reichel and co-authors show that reading a chemical tag on plant messages takes a two-protein team. Their 2024 paper studies m6A, a mark placed on RNA in the model plant Arabidopsis. A reader protein called ECT2 normally grabs marked messages in the cell body and carries out their instructions.

The team finds that ALBA proteins, another message-binding family, grip the reader through a short shared motif. Their binding sites sit right beside the m6A marks, on the same messages. Without the ALBA partnership, the reader binds poorly and its jobs in the plant falter. The pair forms the true working reader of the mark, and that partnership multiplies the ways plants can tune the mark's effects.
pmc-11649924:
David Lau and a large team find that one brain enzyme in a reward hub guards mice against diet-driven obesity, in a 2024 study. The enzyme, ABHD6, breaks down a cannabis-like signal molecule, so removing it should raise that signal and, by the usual logic, boost appetite. The team removed the enzyme in separate spots of the reward circuit using viral tools. The circuit runs from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens and drives motivated behavior.

Against expectation, removing the enzyme in the accumbens, on the receiving side only, fully blocked diet-induced obesity in male mice. Treated mice also sought food and drugs less and moved more. The result redraws the map of how this pathway controls weight, and it flags a drug target worth a closer look.
pmc-11650124:
Bessadok and co-authors built a glowing ceramic that senses cold by its light in a 2024 study. The material mixes silica glass with zinc silicate crystals doped with europium, a rare earth that emits sharp red lines. It was made by a home-adapted gel method and checked for structure and light output.

Microscopy showed the crystals wrapped inside the silica, shielding them. Alongside the strong red emission, faint blue and green bands came from defects in the host material. By comparing the defect bands with the europium lines, the team turned brightness ratios into a thermometer. Sensitivity peaked at about two percent per degree in the deep cold range below room temperature. The authors present the first such study for this material at low temperatures.
pmc-11650724:
Yongfu Zhong and five co-authors map the trends and fronts of work on the risk traits of urine stones, by counts of print. Their study, from two thousand twenty-four, spans more than a decade.

Stone disease in the urine path ties to many traits, but no firm word stood on how to treat those traits. The team drew all works on the theme from a core store over the span. Counts came to more than four hundred works. Ties of lands, labs, writers, and word webs were charted with count tools. Two lands led the field, and one famed clinic led labs. The aim is to show the hot themes and the paths ahead.
pmc-11650824:
Jessica Arnhold and co-authors published this 2024 study on watching wheat roots grow without digging them up. The standard method cuts soil cores, which is slow work and kills the plants at each spot. Clear tubes sunk in the soil let cameras view the same roots all season. The catch is sorting the flood of images fast.

The team adapted an image-learning program to mark roots in tube photos. They grew winter wheat in varied field setups over two years and checked tube results against core samples. Deep in the soil, the two methods agreed well. Near the surface, tube results fell short. The authors also warn that a badly placed tube can itself change root growth, and they show how to avoid that trap.
pmc-11651224:
Benjamin and co-authors (2024) analyzed the work system behind how emergency nurses manage patient flow. Nurses actively move patients through crowded emergency departments, and that work is complex and mentally demanding. The team gathered focus groups and interviews with 27 nurses plus 64 hours of observation across four departments, then organized the findings with a patient safety work-system model.

Flow management was shaped by many factors at once: the nurses' own traits, their tools and technology, outside pressures, and the department's layout and social climate. Nurses raised concerns about clumsy technology, tight capacity, thin resources across the wider system, and uneven teamwork between departments. Roles and titles varied confusingly between sites, and timing targets were enforced in ways that could clash with good flow. The authors call for joint work by administrators, engineers, and nurses, and for studies that measure how these factors affect flow outcomes.
pmc-11652324: Joost Drenth bids farewell to the UEG Journal after six years as its editor-in-chief, in a 2024 editorial. He recalls the daily work of reading papers and making decisions as a source of real joy. He thanks a team of associate editors he calls quick, sharp, and critical. He singles out the journal's trainee editors, young professionals woven into the review process from the start of his time in charge.
pmc-11652524:
Immunotherapy before surgery may extend survival in esophageal cancer, Haibo Cai and co-authors report in a 2024 follow-up study. The question was whether adding a checkpoint inhibitor to chemotherapy before surgery brings real-world survival benefits in locally advanced, resectable squamous cell cancer of the esophagus. Such combinations are moving fast in trials, but routine-practice evidence with mid-term follow-up is thinner.

Patients who had surgery at one hospital over two years were analyzed retrospectively. They split into a combined-treatment group and a surgery-only group by their treatment history. Two-year overall and disease-free survival were the primary endpoints. Safety and efficacy of the pre-surgery regimen were secondary. Readers get practice-based numbers to set beside trial results, from a cancer where recurrence after surgery is common.
pmc-11653024:
An EFSA food enzyme panel redid the dose mathematics for a fat-splitting enzyme used in food plants, in a report published in 2024. The enzyme comes from a modified mold strain and had passed an earlier safety review. A new dose counting method, set in 2016, made the old mathematics stale. The panel realigned the uses to two plant steps and recounted who consumes how much.

In one step the solids of the enzyme wash out, so no dose lands there. In the other, top dose came to about half a unit per body weight each day. Set next to the no-harm dose from past tests, the gap ran near seven hundred times. The panel kept its past call: no safety worry at the set uses.
pmc-11653124:
Two great American health data vaults claim to mirror the public, but their mirrors bend in unlike ways. Nihmath Nasiha Maliq and four co-authors hold the mirrors side by side in 2024. One is a national medical vault; the other, a dental one. Habits, health pasts, and health reading skill are compared across race, roots, and sex.

Some of the gaps between the two are wide. Drink use among Hispanic members reads eighty point six percent in one vault and sixteen point eight in the other. Diabetes among women reads eight point eight against twenty-one point six. Such splits warn any study that borrows a vault as if it were the land itself. The pair of vaults serves mouth and body research; knowing each one's lean is step one.
pmc-11653824:
Ali Amanati and co-authors present a case series, printed in 2024, on a paradox that can mislead doctors treating children with cancer. Four young patients with invasive lung infection from the Aspergillus fungus grew suddenly worse just as their white blood cells recovered, despite proper antifungal drugs. Scans showed spreading lung shadows that looked like the infection winning.

The team recognized immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome: the returning immune system itself was inflaming the battlefield. Steroids, not stronger antifungals, settled the symptoms dramatically in all four children. The authors stress that mistaking this flare for treatment failure invites dangerous overtreatment, and they offer the series as the first map of the syndrome in pediatric cancer care.
pmc-11654024:
Holly Harris and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on a mental health learning college that judged the quality of its own plan-making process. Recovery Colleges teach people living with mental health and addiction challenges, built on peer support and co-production, where lived experience sits beside professional expertise. Yet few of their evaluations are themselves co-produced.

A subcommittee of members with mixed backgrounds agreed on three principles for good collaboration. Each member then wrote a self-narrative judging the process against those principles. The exercise surfaced both trials and triumphs of sharing power in evaluation design. The authors offer the principles-focused method to other programs that preach co-production and want to practice it honestly.
pmc-11654124:
Jintao Ma and co-authors ask whether a hazy tumour component predicts better outcomes after focused radiation, in a 2024 study. Early-stage lung cancer patients who cannot or will not have surgery receive stereotactic body radiotherapy, a few doses aimed at the tumour. Some carry a ground-glass part, a hazy region on scans marking less dense growth.

Of two hundred and thirty-nine patients treated over a decade, sixty-five had partly hazy tumours, the rest solid ones. The hazy group lived longer without the cancer returning: at five years, cancer-specific survival was about ninety-one percent against sixty-four percent, and freedom from progression was higher. Nearby spread came back less often in the hazy group. Adjustment for other factors kept the pattern. The authors conclude the ground-glass part is a favourable sign and should be highlighted for prognosis.
pmc-11654324:
Four days of fatty food can prime the liver for worse injury, Nanizawa and co-authors show in a 2024 mouse study. Fatty liver disease raises clot and heart risks, but how fast diet alone shifts liver clotting was unclear. Mice ate a high-fat diet for four days before a chemical that triggers acute liver injury.

The team traces both clot stages, the platelet plug and the fibrin mesh, in liver tissue. Short fatty feeding boosts clotting and swelling signals before any lasting disease sets in. That early tilt explains why the injury chemical hits fat-fed livers harder. The work warns that even brief diet lapses can leave the liver exposed, a point for patient advice.
pmc-11654824:
Antibiotics fail against resistant bacteria partly because of the cell's metabolic state. Jiao Xiang and co-authors reset that state with pyruvate in a resistant fish germ, Edwardsiella tarda. Feeding pyruvate, to their surprise, flipped that drug-proof trait. The trail led to glutathione, a key antioxidant in the cell. Pyruvate reshaped the amino acid routes that build it, lifting the cell's reactive oxygen output. That oxygen burst is what kills the bacteria.

Knocking out genes in the pathway raised or lowered resistance as predicted, in dishes and in animals. The reversal also worked in lab-evolved resistant strains and in clinical isolates of other species. The authors present this pyruvate route as a new target against drug resistance.
pmc-11655024:
Yaxuan Sun, Xun Zhou, and Xiaohui Hu build a switchable cell model of cancer spread in a 2024 paper. Early in metastasis, cancer cells shed their tidy sheet-like form and gain the loose, mobile form of mesenchymal cells. That shift is called EMT. A model that can start the shift on command lets researchers test which genes drive it.

Their host is a human breast cell line that grows without limit but is not cancerous. They inserted a mouse gene, Twist1, under the control of the antibiotic doxycycline. Adding the drug turned the gene on and drove the shift at a pace like a known natural trigger. Mixed and single-cell lines both shifted in step with marker changes. Removing the drug reversed the shift. The authors offer the model for hunting genes that push metastasis.
pmc-11655224:
Jiaxin Zhu and co-authors link two vitamin levels with survival in fatty liver disease in a 2024 study. The disease, tied to metabolic dysfunction, is common, and both folate and vitamin B12 relate to how often it occurs. Whether the levels also predict death was unclear. The team used a large United States health survey with death records followed for over twenty years.

Both vitamins showed a curved link with death risk. Below the middle level, rising levels meant falling risk; above it, the benefit flattened. People in the higher folate and B12 bands had notably lower death risk than those in the lowest band, by roughly a quarter to two fifths for some groups. The authors say low levels of either vitamin mark higher risk in these patients.
pmc-11655324:
Healthcare workers face needles, falls, and violence as part of the job, and Turkey counted the toll nationwide. İrem Medeni, Mehmet Erdem Alagüney, and Volkan Medeni analyzed 2024 reports covering five years and all eighty-one provinces, more than sixty-eight thousand injuries in total.

Nearly two thirds of the injured were women, and the twenty-to-twenty-nine age group led the counts. Sharps injuries made up over half, then slips, trips, and falls. Hospitals and summer months saw the most cases. Three quarters of workers returned without long absence, but sixty-one died of their injuries over the period. Nurses and midwives were hit most often, a pattern the authors use to argue for targeted prevention.
pmc-11655524:
Chiara Romano, Francesco Branda, Fabio Scarpa, Giovanna Jona Lasinio, and Massimo Ciccozzi present an open data set that pairs measles cases with flight traffic in Europe. Their 2024 resource covers the years 2011 to 2023. It draws case counts and vaccine coverage from world and European health bodies.

Flight passenger flows between countries sit beside the health data in one place. That pairing lets analysts trace how travel may seed outbreaks across borders. Finer spatial work on watch and forecast tasks becomes possible. The authors stress that strong vaccine coverage and steady joint surveillance remain the core guards against spread. The set is offered for public reuse.
pmc-11655824:
Rui Li, Xuanwen Yang, Jun Lou, and Junsong Zhang present a neural model that reads emotion from brain wave records, in work from 2024. The cues sit spread across time, wave bands, and brain sites, and they shift from person to person. A model must catch all three spreads and still work on new people.

Their model treats brain sites as a graph and tracks wave changes across time windows and bands. A special loss term softens clashes between felt ratings and fixed labels. A two-level training trick also pulls new-person data closer to known data, which lifts transfer. Tests on public sets beat prior top methods. Part-removal checks showed each added piece helped the score.
pmc-11655924:
Shrikirti Anand and Trupti Patel review in a 2024 paper the shared circuits of diabetes, obesity, and cancer. Fat rich diets and still lives have made the first two a world health hazard. Their blend, dubbed diabesity, is also tagged as a driver of cancer onset.

The review revisits the molecular paths that link the blend to tumor growth. DNA repair flaws under heavy oxidative damage get close study in the read. Unstable genomes, a cancer hallmark, grow when repair lags behind damage. Warped hormone and fuel settings in diabesity build a setting that favors tumor reprogramming. New marks and targeted drugs may come from mapping those links, the authors argue.
pmc-11656024:
Jennifer Storey, Rhianna O'Brien, and Silvia Fraga Dominguez ask where people draw the line on abuse of older adults, in a study published in twenty twenty-four. How abuse is seen shapes whether it gets reported and stopped. The team also asked whether ageist views color those judgments.

Nearly three hundred people rated fifteen acts, spanning hitting, mental cruelty, sexual and money abuse, and neglect. Each act was aimed at an older adult, an adult, or a child. On average, a quarter of the group did not call the acts abuse. Ratings barely changed by the victim's age group. Stronger ageism did predict softer judgments when the victim was older. The authors call that pattern a serious concern.
pmc-11656224:
A phase diagram from the 1970s does not survive remeasurement, Beata Salamon-Baran and co-authors report in a 2024 study. The system pairs praseodymium bromide with thallium bromide, salts used in scintillator research. Inaccuracies in the old diagram prompted a fresh determination by differential scanning calorimetry. The new results differ significantly from the published version, and the paper discusses where the earlier work went wrong.

Only one congruently melting compound was confirmed in the system, the double salt named in the title. Its heat capacity was characterized across temperature. A CALPHAD assessment checked the internal consistency of the new data. Mixing enthalpy and entropy of the liquid phase were estimated as functions of composition. Inorganic chemists get corrected foundations for crystal growth work.
pmc-11656424:
Md Nasir Uddin and co-authors used computer tools to study variants in the furin gene and COVID-19 risk in two thousand twenty-four. Furin is an enzyme that cuts the spike protein of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, helping it enter human cells. Variants in the gene might change how well that step works in different populations.

The team mapped furin variants with many public databases and prediction tools, and placed spike proteins on a family tree. They report that in some regions, furin variants linked strongly to susceptibility to the virus, while in other regions the effect was very small. Their overall claim is a strong link, and they suggest furin as a drug target to block viral entry.
pmc-11656724:
Kwanwong Boonpitak and five co-authors wrote this 2024 dental study on how to make a repair layer stick to a printed temporary crown. Printed provisionals often need a lining added to fit the mouth well, and the bond between the two materials can be weak. The team tested five ways to treat the printed surface before adding the lining.

Fifteen samples per group were bonded, left a day to set, then pulled apart by a test machine. Plain and alcohol-wiped surfaces bonded weakest. Sand blasting alone and glue alone each helped some. The strongest bond, by a wide margin, came from sand blasting followed by the glue. The authors conclude that surface prep is the deciding step for a lasting repair of this kind.
pmc-11656824:
Élodie Vajda and co-authors (2024) test new anti-mosquito tools in Thailand against a malaria carrier biting by day. The Greater Mekong region aims to eliminate human malaria by 2030, and what remains hides in forest foci. People at risk — farmers, miners, migrants — are bitten outdoors and in open dwellings bed nets do not reach. The local vector, Anopheles minimus, lands on them in daylight. Tools beyond nets are needed, and they must be proven before programs buy them.

The team ran semi-field evaluations: controlled settings mimicking real exposure while measuring landing rates on people, plus secondary endpoints such as how many mosquitoes the tools kill or divert. Semi-field trials are the gate between promising products and deployment. The study supplies local evidence elimination planners need to decide whether these tools deserve a place beside nets in the region's last-mile campaign.
pmc-11657424:
Amri Abas and co-authors present a 2024 study of mosquito disease risk around the Tanzanian seaport of Tanga. Ports move goods worldwide, and Aedes mosquitoes that spread dengue and related diseases hitchhike along trade routes. Locals, though, worry mostly about malaria. The team sampled mosquitoes in the port and at set distances out to five kilometers.

They mapped nearly three thousand breeding sites, and about sixty percent held Aedes larvae, with the port itself the most infested zone. Aedes aegypti adults were also densest inside the port. The pattern suggests trade hubs can seed new outbreaks even while public attention stays on malaria. The authors argue port surveillance deserves a larger place in disease control.
pmc-11657524:
Getachew Birhanu Abera and eight colleagues review how biofilms can improve anaerobic digestion. A biofilm is a group of microbes wrapped in a slime the cells make themselves. Digesters turn organic waste into biogas without air. Biofilms keep microbes in the reactor longer, which makes the process work better. Most past work focused on wastewater treatment.

The review covers newer uses: speeding the breakdown of tough plant matter, improving gas-liquid transfer for biogas upgrading, and standing up to inhibitors and toxic pollutants. It also looks at what shapes biofilm performance, ways to tune it, reactor designs, and the microbe groups involved. A full-scale biofilm reactor in Norway serves as a case from industry. The authors aim to give practitioners a current map of biofilm use in digestion.
pmc-11657724:
Hamidreza Rashidi and co-authors study weak bones in people living with HIV in Iran, in this 2024 paper. Modern HIV treatment has lengthened lives, which brings age-linked problems such as bone loss into view. The team screened patients in Kerman with bone scans, treated those with low density, and followed the rest to see who newly developed the problem.

Ninety-four patients on treatment for at least a year took part. Just over half already had low bone density at the start. Over the follow-up, about sixteen percent of those with normal bones newly developed low density. Among treated patients, only one in eight reached normal density. Thin patients fared worst. The authors stress that bone checks should be routine in HIV care in this setting.
pmc-11657824:
Saleema Mehboob Ali and co-authors study tiny gene regulators in 2024 in pancreatic cancer patients in Pakistan. Pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest cancers, and small RNA molecules help steer the signals that drive it. How four such regulators interact with key proteins in Pakistani patients had not been explored, so the team tested tumor samples from 109 patients.

Forty-three samples had RNA good enough for precise measurement. Three of the four small RNAs ran high in about seventy percent of cases. One of them linked strongly to levels of a well-known repair protein. Stains scored by two pathologists mapped the proteins in the same tumors. The study gives a first local picture of these regulatory pathways.
pmc-11657924:
Chengyu Xia, Yingjun Zheng, Liuxia Ji and Hui Liu compare ways to keep heart patients active after treatment in this 2024 network meta-analysis. Their focus is phase two cardiac rehabilitation, the exercise-based stage that follows a percutaneous coronary intervention, a procedure that opens blocked heart arteries. Many patients drop out, so the team asks which support works best.

They pooled thirty trials with more than four thousand patients and seventeen kinds of support. Home-based rehabilitation paired with mobile health tools ranked first for adherence, with hospital-based care plus mobile health tools a close second. The results give clinics a clear hint: pairing exercise plans with phone-based support helps patients stick with them.
pmc-11659124:
A spinning sense that starts when the head moves is often due to loose crystals in the inner ear. Malene Hentze, Dan Dupont Hougaard, and Herman Kingma tested two ways to spot this fault, called BPPV, in a 2024 trial. One way uses hands-on head moves, and the other uses a motor chair, with eye-move goggles in both.

Their crossover trial enrolled 215 adults at a Danish clinic, and each person got both tests in random order. The chair found more true cases than the hands-on method. Hands-on tests still worked well as a first step for most people. The chair helped most with hard cases, weak teamwork from the patient, and prior missed tests.
pmc-11660924:
Paul Schwerdtner and co-authors (2024) made uncertainty estimates practical for wildfire simulations of record size. Fire managers need to know the error bars on a forecast, but running many high-fidelity simulations is far too costly. The team's trick couples cheap surrogate models with the expensive model in a multifidelity scheme. For this to work, the surrogate only needs to correlate with the real model; its bias does not matter. Cheap related data can therefore train it.

They tested the approach on the 2017 Tubbs fire with a model holding billions of degrees of freedom. Training time fell from three months to under three hours. Burned-area predictions came out at least twice as accurate as using the expensive model alone on the same budget. The authors argue the lesson travels: many fields with costly simulators sit on piles of related, imperfect data that can unlock honest uncertainty numbers.
pmc-11661824:
Joanne Weber and three co-authors studied how deaf aesthetics can reshape university teaching in a 2024 paper. Deaf aesthetics is a design outlook rooted in deaf ways of seeing and signing. Deaf teachers and students want it in their courses, yet most teaching materials lack its supports.

The team redesigned a course, overhauling slide decks and other materials, and evaluated the change with a mixed-method case study. Their guiding question was how designers and educators can build multimodal materials that spark and sustain interaction with deaf and deafblind learners and teachers. The paper reports what the redesign involved and what it changed, aiming to move deaf higher education toward formats built for deaf eyes from the start.
pmc-11662924:
Zexin Zhu and Xiaoxue Wang use gene data to test cause links between a patchy hair-loss disease and cancer, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The disease is driven by the immune system attacking hair roots. Past reports linked it to cancer, but cause was unclear.

Seventeen cancer types were checked against gene data for the hair disease. The disease showed a small protective link to two cancers: one of the bile duct and one of the bowel. No links showed for the other types. Gene pathway work pointed to immune and swelling signals as shared ground. The authors see fresh angles for cancer research.
pmc-11663924:
Karhof and co-authors reviewed two decades of torn diaphragm injuries at a Dutch trauma center, asking whether better scans have eased a stubborn diagnosis, in a 2024 study. A tear in the diaphragm, the breathing muscle, is rare after trauma and easy to miss. A missed tear can kill or maim later. The team pulled every case from 2000 to 2018 at their level one center and traced how each was found and treated.

Forty-seven patients qualified, most hurt by blunt force. One in five died, mostly from their other injuries, though one death traced to a missed tear. Scans caught about six in ten tears before surgery; the rest surfaced during operations. In a third of scanned patients the tear hid from the CT. Complications after surgery were common, mostly chest infections. The authors say suspicion must stay high.
pmc-11665824:
Hanna Helena Schalkwijk, Graciela Andrei, and Robert Snoeck test if a mix of herpes drugs holds back the growth of drug resistance. Their 2024 study passes herpes simplex virus through rounds in the lab. In each round, the dose of drug is raised.

Drugs in use now aim at the viral DNA polymerase. That leads to patterns of cross-resistance in patients whose immune system is weak. The team joined a helicase-primase inhibitor with one of two polymerase drugs. Mutations for resistance showed up fast when one drug was used on its own. With the drugs used as a pair, mutations were not there, or were held to the polymerase drugs. Resistance to the newer drug did not show up at all in one pair, in spite of many rounds. Strains that resisted both drugs came up in time, in one pair with a low dose only.
pmc-11666524:
Quan Chen and thirteen co-authors build a forecast model for lung cancer in a 2024 paper. Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer subtype. A chemical tag on RNA, called m6A, shapes gene activity in tumors. The immune scene around the tumor also steers outcomes.

The team clustered patients by both tag patterns and immune patterns. Seven genes were picked to build a risk score. High score patients fared worse in several data sets. Their tumors held more immune cells yet resisted them better. They also carried more mutations and higher levels of a checkpoint protein. Lab tests tied a tag writing enzyme to the score's genes. Co culture work showed that enzyme shapes T cell attack strength.
pmc-11666824:
Qingting Chen and co-authors used network methods in 2024 to ask how a seaweed sugar might calm a bladder condition marked by swelling and blocked flow. The condition is called cystitis glandularis and can be a step toward worse bladder change. Drug care is the main option when treatment is needed.

Computer maps linked the sugar, named fucoidan, to sixteen genes shared with the condition. Six core targets stood out, most tied to signals that drive or calm swelling. The paths found point to less swelling and better immune balance as the likely ways the sugar acts. The authors stress that the work is a map for lab tests, not proof from patients yet.
pmc-11666924:
Zakareya Gamie and five co-authors wrote a 2024 study on the accuracy of a robotic system for knee replacement surgery. The ROSA robot helps surgeons cut bone to planned thicknesses. This study tested its imageless mode, which works without pre-operative scans, in patients with primary knee osteoarthritis.

One surgeon treated 44 patients between June 2023 and January 2024. Caliper checks compared planned and actual cuts at the thigh bone, shin bone, and back of the kneecap joint. Average gaps ran from about 0.67 to 1.1 millimeters across the six sites. Some gaps reached statistical significance but stayed small in absolute terms. The authors conclude the system hits planned resection thickness with high accuracy. Results apply only to this mode and patient group.
pmc-11667024:
Wenping Zhou, Dongyou Zhang, and Maoli Yang study rain wear on turbine blades in a 2024 paper. Fast rain hits at the blade edge chip the surface, spoil airflow, and raise upkeep costs. Past models treated the edge as flat, which skips how curve shapes the hit.

Their joined fluid-solid model sends a water drop at a set speed onto edges of four curve radii, from tight to flat. Wider curves block the drop more, spray it sideways harder, and pass more energy into the blade. Stress and lasting strain rise with radius. Flat-edge guesses drift most for tight curves. Blade coats and shapes can draw on the split.
pmc-11667624:
Marwan Mezher and co-authors work on welding two unlike metals in a 2024 study: a titanium alloy and a stainless steel. Joints of this kind are prized in industry, and they are made by resistance spot welding, which fuses metal with heat from an electric current. Picking the right settings is hard because the two metals behave so differently.

The team ran welding tests with sheets of equal and unequal thickness. They then trained machine learning and neural network models on the test results to predict joint quality. The models help find the settings that give the strongest joint without wasted trials. Better settings mean fewer weak welds in parts that must join light titanium to tough steel.
pmc-11667724:
Fabian Otte and co-authors report a 2024 chemistry study on joining two plant chemical families into hybrid molecules. One side of each hybrid comes from coumarins or flavonoids, ring systems common in plants. The other side comes from phenylpropanoids, a second plant family. Such hybrids may carry mixed traits worth testing.

The team linked the parts with a palladium-driven coupling that uses diazonium salts and allyl-tagged partners. A guard group near the link point steered the key step to one outcome with high selectivity. A mild oxidation step then turned the linked products into chalcones, the open-chain forms. The route gives chemists a clean path to a library of plant-inspired hybrids for later screening.
pmc-11669524:
Franca Orsini and co-authors test, in a 2024 mouse study, whether boosting a protein-tagging system can shield brain cells from a toxic mutant tau protein. Tau clumps mark Alzheimer's and related dementias, and the tagging system runs low in patient brains. The team used viruses to add the mutant tau, with or without extra tagging protein, in the mouse memory center.

Mutant tau placed only in neurons still hurt nearby support cells too. Extra tagging protein fought the toxicity in both cell kinds. Stains and counts showed rescued cells and calmer support cell shapes. The authors suggest raising this tag is a candidate strategy against tau diseases, pending more work.
pmc-11671524:
Zhaoyan Chen and Fangyuan Tian weighed in 2024 whether a tweaked drug pair is worth its cost for gallbladder cancer in China. The cancer is among the most common bile duct cancers, and it often can not be cut out. Their economic model built on a trial where the pair, gemcitabine with oxaliplatin, beat an older mix on survival. A Markov model rolled costs and health gains over ten years from a societal view.

The pair added health gains but at a cost per year of good life well above China's pay threshold. The chance it counts as good value at that line was nil. Tweaks to side-effect, test, and hospital costs barely moved the call. The pair is not good value there, they find.
pmc-11672424:
Minghua Xie and co-authors cross two catfish from different genera and produce a hybrid that outgrows its mother. Distant crosses usually fail because the species cannot breed together, but the Ussuri catfish mother and longsnout catfish father, both carrying 52 chromosomes, succeeded. The team profiled the offspring with body measurements, chromosome counts, DNA quantity, and inherited markers. The young fish fell between their parents on most measures, though their outer shape leaned toward the mother.

Growth trials gave the hybrids a clear edge over the mother's kind. Chromosome and DNA checks confirmed the hybrid makeup, and the mitochondrial line confirmed the mother. A species-specific DNA marker was built to tell the three apart at a glance. The authors see commercial promise, pending husbandry and welfare studies at larger scale.
pmc-11672624:
Miriam Uzuriaga leads a team on fast bacterial identification and costs. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry. Rapid lab reports can lift clinic and money outcomes.

A three year study ran at a university medical center. Hospital patients with bacterial infections were enrolled. A past control group got reports late in the day. The test group got species names hours earlier. Susceptibility results still came in the evening slot. The early group needed fewer follow up tests. Savings followed the drop in extra testing.  Test counts fell across several lab types.
pmc-11672824:
Luyu Ding and co-authors present a 2024 study of ultraviolet A light as a germ killer for cattle barn air. Airborne germs ride dust out of barns and into lungs, and sunlight is known to wear them down. The team released barn air germs into a small test box and dosed them with set light strengths. Decay sped up steeply as the light rose, from a few percent to over sixty.

Longer or stronger doses killed like shares in swap tests, so time and strength trade off evenly. The top kill rates passed sixty percent. The authors pitch UVA as a barn air aid if dosed with care. Light rigs could cut germ load without chemicals or filters. Farm trials would be the next proof step.
pmc-11673224:
Zhongrui Bai and co-authors present a universal frame for reading heartbeat gaps from mixed touch-free sensors, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Sensors worn lightly or built into furniture give messy signals, and mixing sensor types is harder still. Their frame first finds the average heart rate by summing signal harmonics.

That rate guides band choice, template building, and matching for each beat. A quality score then picks the best gap value per beat. Tests on two data sets, one self-collected, lifted detection by about five to six percent. Timing errors beat past methods at near five milliseconds.
pmc-11673424:
Alexandra Mederle and co-authors reviewed trials of the cancer drug pazopanib across thyroid cancer types, in a paper published in 2024. The drug blocks several growth signals at once and had been tried in differentiated, medullary, and anaplastic forms of the disease. Following standard review methods, the team gathered six studies covering 289 patients. They compared survival without growth, overall survival, tumor shrinkage, and side effects.

Time without progression ranged from about two to twelve months across studies, and survival from under six months to not yet reached. Between five and forty-nine percent of tumors shrank partly. High blood pressure hit up to seventy-two percent of patients, with fatigue and diarrhea also common, and severe side effects stopped treatment in up to fourteen percent. The authors find real benefit in medullary and stubborn differentiated cancers, little in the anaplastic type, and a side-effect load that needs careful handling.
pmc-11673524:
Eye disease that harms the retina affects millions of people, and swelling inside the eye plays a large part in the harm. Bijorn Omar Balzamino and co-authors reviewed how one type of support cell in the retina reacts to injury in this 2024 paper. When stressed, these cells release growth factors and signal molecules that can help or hurt nearby nerve cells.

The review traces how genes, stress, and life habits can set off the reaction, and how blood flow problems can keep it going. It then looks at ways to calm the response and shield nerve cells, using the factors these cells release. Readers get a clear account of how the retina tries to heal itself, and where new treatments might step in.
pmc-11673624:
A trial result can be real and still not matter, and Sadi Elasan writes to remind clinicians of the difference. Statistical significance, judged by the p-value, asks whether a finding is likely due to chance. Clinical significance asks a harder question: does the finding change anything for patients? The two are often confused when results move from journals into practice.

Elasan gives a plain example. A drug that lowers blood pressure by a small margin may pass the statistical test easily. Whether that margin helps anyone needs long follow-up and wider study. Tools like effect size and the minimal clinically important difference help make the judgment. The letter argues that medical decisions deserve both answers, not just the easier one.
pmc-11674124:
Savannah Kozole and Karen Beningo review how myosin light chains help cancer grow and spread. These chains belong to non-muscle myosin II, a force-producing engine inside cells, and their phosphorylation state sets how hard the engine works. Their 2024 review sums up the family members known to promote cancer progression. In fast-growing tumors, phosphorylated chains drive the squeeze that splits one cell into two during division.

During metastasis, signaling pathways line the chains up to power cell crawling, with chains piling up at the leading edge of the moving cell. The same chains also shape the immune response to tumors. In the clinic they serve as biomarkers for staging the disease. Each role turns on the phosphorylation switch, which makes that switch a drug target in its own right, the authors hold.
pmc-11674424:
You Mi Hong and co-authors follow pregnancies from mosaic embryos in a 2024 study. In fertility care, some tested embryos carry a mix of normal and abnormal cells, called mosaic. Clinics still transfer them when nothing better exists, so their outcomes matter. The team reviewed such transfers at a Seoul center from 2021 to 2024.

Eighty-eight mosaic embryos were transferred and seventy-seven implanted. Sixty-seven pregnancies passed eleven weeks, all singletons among fifty-eight patients. The most disordered mosaic type had the lowest ongoing rate, and stronger mosaicism was rarer among lasting pregnancies. Amniocentesis in thirty-three mothers found two abnormal results, neither matching the embryo test. Two ultrasound findings also appeared. The data help counsel patients on what mosaic transfer usually brings.
pmc-11674624:
Aline Ingelson-Filpula and co-authors study how hibernating bats protect their muscles through the winter, in this 2024 paper. Little brown bats spend months in deep torpor, slowing their metabolism to survive. Unused muscles normally waste away, yet bats emerge able to fly. The team sequenced small regulatory RNAs, called microRNAs, in the leg muscle of torpid bats and awake controls.

Ten microRNAs shifted levels during hibernation. Their predicted targets point to slowed cell cycles and damped protein breakdown, plus quieter growth signaling routes. Two themes stand out: blocking myostatin, a muscle-shrinking signal, and muting insulin signaling. The authors read the pattern as a tailored defense that keeps muscle intact while the body runs on minimal energy.
pmc-11675124:
Courtney Caiola and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on how women living with HIV in the southern United States decide about their care. Taking virus drugs on time keeps the virus down, but women in the South face wide gaps in reaching that goal. Race, sex, class, and place all press at once, along with shame tied to the disease.

The team held deep talks with forty women from across the region. Women said distance and poor local care made it hard to stay in care and take their drugs. They also spoke of power gaps with clinics, tied to race and sex. Helps and harms shifted with each woman's setting. Care plans, the team says, must fit each woman's real place in the world.
pmc-11675624:
Regina Ding and Linda Duxbury count in 2024 the health care that Canadian caregivers use themselves. Unpaid care for elders saves the system money but wears on the carer. The study compared people caring only for elders with sandwiched carers who also raise children.

Doctor visits were the most used service, about 3.7 visits in six months among users. Mental health services, emergency visits, and hospital stays followed. The two carer groups used care at similar rates. The clearest pattern was workload: more weekly care hours went with more health care use across most services. The authors frame caregiver health use as a hidden cost of unpaid care that policy should count.
pmc-11675724:
Lucca Ortolan Hansen, Renato Garcia, André Miranda Torricelli, and Samir Jacob Bechara assess whether corneal collagen crosslinking is cost-effective for progressive keratoconus in Brazil. Keratoconus burdens health systems and patients worldwide, and crosslinking had been shown abroad to be cost-effective, but no Brazilian study existed. The authors evaluate it from the public Unified Health System's perspective as payer.

A lifetime microsimulation compared crosslinking against conventional treatment in two simulated groups of five thousand eighteen-year-old patients, one treated at the outset and one untreated. Crosslinking proved highly cost-effective, costing roughly fifty-eight US dollars per quality-adjusted life year gained, with a large positive net monetary benefit. It also significantly reduced required corneal transplants, by roughly nine hundred seventy per ten thousand eyes treated. The analysis gives Brazilian policymakers a local number, not an imported one, for deciding whether the public system should fund the procedure.
pmc-11675824:
Ana Luisa Varrone Sartorao and co-authors reviewed anxiety and depression in medical students during the COVID-19 years, in this 2024 paper. Medical training is stressful, and the pandemic added strain. The review kept studies that used two standard symptom questionnaires.

Of 85 studies kept, pooled results showed high rates of moderate to severe symptoms. About 28 percent passed the anxiety threshold and about 39 percent passed the depression threshold. Rates were higher in students from developing countries and in data gathered after the 2020 lockdown period. Female students faced higher depression risk. The authors call for targeted mental health support in medical schools.
pmc-11676224:
Cristiana Mercê and co-authors ask why balance bikes teach cycling better than training wheels, in a 2024 study. Children on balance bikes — small bikes with no pedals — reach a real bike sooner than children on bikes with side wheels. The likely reason is that balance bike riders must balance from the start, yet proof has been thin.

The team tracked how the child-and-bike system wobbled and settled as children learned on each trainer type. They then watched the same children move to a standard bike and compared the change. Ideas from the math of stable motion, linked to Lyapunov, frame the reading of the data. The findings can help parents and teachers pick the trainer that builds real balance, not false support.
pmc-11676424:
Muhammad Naeem and Dianna Bourassa published a 2024 literature review of feeding strategies against Salmonella in poultry. The bacterium threatens flock health and food safety alike. The review surveys nutritional tools: probiotics, prebiotics, organic acids, and plant chemicals, judging how well each cuts Salmonella colonization in birds. It also examines how these feeds might work inside the gut.

The authors weigh the evidence for each approach and its knock-on effects for the wider food chain. Their aim is to name the most promising dietary strategies for producers. The review frames nutrition as a front-line control that can reduce reliance on antibiotics. It closes by tying flock-level feeding choices to public health outcomes at the table.
pmc-11676624:
Arkadiusz Kocur and colleagues reviewed low-dose methotrexate monitoring in two thousand twenty-four. The drug treats inflammatory diseases at low doses. Blood levels vanish within a day of dosing. Its stored breakdown products last much longer, though. Those products collect inside red blood cells. They signal drug exposure and adherence well.

The review examined studies on measurement methods. Each analysis stage received best-practice guidance. Sample handling before testing matters greatly. Validation steps were summarized for clinical labs. Proper standard procedures were also outlined. This is the first review of its kind here. Clinicians gain help judging whether patients take the drug.
pmc-11676924:
Schizophrenia's deepest disability is often cognitive, and standard drugs barely touch it. Chien-Chen Hung and two co-authors review in 2024 what is known about these deficits and whether brain stimulation can lift them. Medication and talking therapy both leave much of the impairment standing, they note.

Stimulation techniques show real promise in specific thinking domains, though protocols vary and long term results are thin. The reviewers argue the field must first understand the circuits whose tuning produces the gains. That circuit knowledge would turn scattered trials into a strategy. They close with a research agenda: standardize the stimulation, follow patients longer, and target the domains that decide daily function.
pmc-11677024:
Akihiro Nakamura reports a drug pairing case in a young boy. The case from twenty twenty-four deals with risperidone plus high dose melatonin. Melatonin is widely used for sleep disorders.

A boy of ten came in with restlessness and poor sleep. Low doses of both drugs were started by mouth. Daytime focus improved as melatonin was raised stepwise. Night waking did not fully clear with the increases. After a month at high dose, breast budding appeared. It vanished quickly once melatonin was stopped. The pair still cut his restlessness well.
pmc-11677124:
Wei Zhu and co-authors review SHIME, a machine that mimics the human gut and its microbes. The device strings together compartments that copy the stomach and intestines. It runs for weeks with live microbial communities. Sensors track the system in real time, and its settings bend to many study designs.

Newer versions multiply the setup. Twin and triple rigs run side-by-side comparisons. A toddler version models young children's guts. Uses span food science, drug testing, gut health and traditional Chinese medicine. The authors also look at pairing the rig with newer tech. They present SHIME as a workhorse for gut research without human or animal trials.
pmc-11677224:
Anar Zhexembekova and co-authors peel atom-thin oxide skins from liquid metal balloons in this 2024 paper. Blowing air into a droplet of gallium-indium alloy inflates a bubble. A uniform gallium oxide film forms on its surface and can be lifted off. The film then draws carbon nanotubes out of water, building a dense conducting web.

The team turned that web into a chemical sensor. It sniffed out stand-ins for chemical warfare agents at very low levels. The sensor answered reversibly, with detection limits in the tens of parts per billion. The authors present the balloon method as a cheap route to thin-film devices that carry nanotube networks.
pmc-11677524:
Malgorzata Bacmaga, Jadwiga Wyszkowska, and Jan Kucharski sum what weed kill drugs do to soil, water, air, and the life in them, in a review from 2024. The drugs guard crops by blocks on light use, seed goods, and growth calls in weeds. Trade forms mix many act goods, which fogs harm reads.

Pick drugs are traced through each world part in turn, then through man, beast, plant, and germ. Germ and mold rot paths that clear the drugs from soil get their own tale. Loose use has hurt off aim life in print proof, the team finds. Yet gaps in the tale stay wide, and more work is called for.
pmc-11677624:
Grzegorz Suwinski, Izabela Nowak, and Simona Martinotti evaluate an innovative honey-based hand cream using modern biophysical and imaging skin techniques. Their 2024 study tests four honey concentrations against skin parameters and application feel.

Twenty-four volunteers were split into pairs receiving blinded cream combinations for left and right hands. Instruments measured moisture, water loss, elasticity, and wrinkle appearance at baseline, shortly after first use, and after four weeks. Honey creams improved moisturisation by up to about thirty percent and smoothness by about a fifth. Wrinkle area and depth also fell, with some gains significant versus placebo. Sensory scores did not differ, showing the base cream masked honey's usual stickiness.
pmc-11677724:
Huanhuan Liu and co-authors test a new imaging probe that seeks two targets on tumors at once, in a preclinical study from 2024. The probe aims at tumors that carry two markers, called SSTR2 and FAP. Single-target probes are already used to find neuroendocrine tumors, but they can wash out of the tumor too soon.

The team joined parts of two known probes into one molecule and labeled it with a radioactive form of gallium. In cell tests and mouse scans, the joined probe bound both targets about as well as each single probe. It built up far more in tumors that carried both markers than either single probe did. Tumors without the markers showed no such rise, and blocking tests confirmed the dual targeting.
pmc-11677824:
Victor Cuenca, Viviana Pedroni, and Marcela Morini study what DHA, the omega-3 fat, does to a model of the grey matter membrane. Brain membranes are rich in DHA, and its presence shapes how they work. The team built a multi-part lipid mix that mimics the grey matter membrane. They probed it with molecular acoustics, a sound-based method, exact, simple, and cheap.

The fat under study was PDPC, a membrane lipid that carries DHA. As its share in the model rose, the membrane grew harder to compress and more elastic, seen in a falling bulk modulus. The results match what other methods have found. The authors read them through the lipid raft model, in which DHA-bearing lipids slip into raft domains and reshape them. A bench model that ties fat content to stiffness gives cell biologists numbers they can use.
pmc-11677924:
Paula Diez-Roda, Elena Perez-Navarro, and Ruben Garcia-Martin review fat tissue as a main source of small gene scraps carried in blood by tiny vesicles. These scraps, called microRNAs, help organs talk to each other and tune body metabolism. The review came out in twenty twenty-four.

Fat sends out a vast list of such scraps, which act much like hormones. Fresh studies link them to the liver, muscle, pancreas, heart and vessels, gut, and brain. The authors weigh proof for each link and what it means for health and disease. They also cover current and future uses of these scraps to spot or treat illness.
pmc-11678224:
Boone and four co-authors studied how viruses lift off floors in this paper from twenty twenty-four. Everyday acts like walking and vacuuming can stir settled particles back into the air. The team seeded carpet and wood floors with a harmless test virus, plain or mixed with dust. They then measured how far the virus spread.

Vacuuming spread dust-laden virus much farther than walking did. Floor type mattered for both activities. A risk model using norovirus suggested infection odds rose sharply when dust carried the virus. The biggest risk cuts came from cleaning surfaces near the floor after vacuuming bare of dust. The authors call for more work on resuspension as a route of exposure indoors.
pmc-11678424:
Nitin Muchhal and co-authors design a compact satellite band filter in a 2024 paper. C band satellite links need filters that pass one band and firmly block the rest. Their design folds a waveguide into a printed board using the half mode trick. Comb shaped slots create a multimode resonator inside it.

A fractal pattern etched into the ground plane sharpens the blocking. The Minkowski curve's first two iterations supply that pattern. Simulations were followed by fabrication on common board material. The measured filter centered at 4.75 gigahertz with a wide pass band. Insertion loss stayed near one decibel. Rejection beyond the band exceeded twenty eight decibels up to eight gigahertz. Small size plus deep stopband suits crowded satellite payloads.
pmc-11678524:
Dániel Juhász and co-authors report gene guided care for a rare bladder linked cancer in a 2024 case paper. The cancer grows from a leftover cord between navel and bladder. It is most often found late, after it eats into the bladder wall. No trials set its drug care, so gene reads and lab drug tests offer a path for picks.

Their patient, a woman of thirty one, went through three surgeries and five drug plans. Gene reads on her tumor and drug screens on her own tumor cells fed each next pick. Chemo, immune drugs, and targeted pills all played a part in turn. A blood mark tracked how care was doing across the whole course. The team backs this tailored path for such rare cases.
pmc-11678724:
Taegi Kim and co-authors present a transparent gas sensor that merges sensing with a memory element. Their 2024 paper builds the device from tin oxide with a thin hafnium oxide layer, aiming at so-called gasistor applications. The added layer was meant to raise the response and make readings hold steady from day to day.

The device answered strongly to nitrogen dioxide: at fifty parts per million its response reached about eighty-one percent, roughly one and three-quarter times the response of the same sensor without the layer. It also switched at low voltage and used power well. Over ten days of tests at lower concentration, its readings varied by only about two and a half percent. The authors conclude that the layered design gives a clear gain in both sensitivity and reliability for this class of sensor.
pmc-11678824:
Nuno Moura and co-authors test in 2024 whether a silver-bearing dye can lock onto folded DNA knots that cancer cells lean on. The knots, called G-quadruplexes, sit in the telomere and in growth genes such as MYC. Ligands that grip them may slow telomerase and curb gene activity, a route many groups chase for therapy.

The silver complex bound the knots with good selectivity, above all the MYC form, and it raised singlet oxygen output when attached. It also blocked a copying enzyme in a test assay. In skin cells the compound showed low toxicity and reached the cell nucleus, marks the team reads as promise.
pmc-11678924:
Gissel García and co-authors ran a 2024 trial of a probiotic blend sold as Sugar Shift, testing what it does to gut bacteria and blood markers in adults with type 2 diabetes. The blend mixes eight bacterial strains with prebiotics, the foods that help those strains grow.

Sixty-four adults took the blend or a placebo twice a day for twelve weeks. The group on the blend showed lower levels of a bacterial toxin in the blood and better scores for insulin response. Their gut samples also held more bacteria that make helpful fatty acids. The authors say the blend may calm gut swelling and aid blood sugar control, though longer and larger trials are still needed.
pmc-11679224:
Brain scans can support spotting depression, but patient datasets are small and lopsided. Wei Zhang and co-authors build STANet, a network made for that handicap. It reads brain activity scans as both space and time. A first step compresses the signal into components. Convolutions at several sizes then pull out features. A resampling trick balances the classes by faking extra minority examples. A special recurrent unit then follows long patterns over time.

The system reached 82.38 percent accuracy, with an AUC of 90.72 percent. Ablation tests credit both the feature module and the classifier design. The authors aim the tool at earlier, more objective detection of depression.
pmc-11679324:
Kok Ming Goh and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four randomized trial of a supplement mix for dry eye disease and immunity. Eye pigments lutein and zeaxanthin support eye health, but low doses over short periods were little tested. Elderberry extract was added for immune support.

About one hundred ten volunteers took the combined supplement daily for twenty days. Eye symptoms were scored with a standard surface disease index. Immune status came from a questionnaire. Symptom scores in the treated group fell by about half. The trial gives short-course, low-dose evidence for a common, quality-of-life draining condition.
pmc-11679424:
Bitong Li and five co-authors wrote this 2024 review on the hazards of taking apart electronic waste in China. Discarded devices carry heavy metals and plastics that reach bodies through air, food, and skin, and through the food chain over time. The same trash holds gold, silver, and copper worth recovering, so crude dismantling persists despite the risks.

The review traces the history of e-waste in China, its present scale, and where handling is heading. Informal workshops gain the metals while spreading the poisons; formal systems exist but compete on cost. The authors see the fix as a bundle: better recycling technology, government policy, clear laws, and a public that values safe disposal. Their overview is meant to offer other countries lessons from the world's largest e-waste stream.
pmc-11679524:
Shu-Juan Gao and Tan-Lai Yu analyzed a boron-aluminum cluster that reshapes itself as it sits in 2024. The cluster, with eight boron and three aluminum atoms and a single positive charge, settles into a three-layer form: an aluminum pair, a boron ring, and a lone aluminum atom.

Charge analysis casts the cluster as a sandwich of charged parts with double aromaticity, obeying the classic Hückel count in both its pi and sigma clouds. Dynamics simulations show the parts rotate almost freely: the barrier to inner rotation is a fifth of a kilocalorie per mole at top-level accuracy. The boron ring's cloud of shared electrons greases that motion. The cluster is a fresh case of structural fluxionality.
pmc-11679724:
Osama Alharbi and seven co-authors design and test new compounds aimed at type 2 diabetes. Current drugs help many patients but carry limits and side effects, so fresh chemical leads are wanted. Their 2024 study builds molecules that merge quinoline or naphthalene units with a reactive linker tail.

Seven target compounds were made through a short chain of reactions. Each was tested against three enzymes tied to blood sugar and its complications. One compound, labeled 7g, beat the standard drug acarbose at blocking two sugar-processing enzymes. It also topped quercetin, a reference blocker, on the third enzyme, which drives diabetic complications. Computer docking backed the lab results. The lead compound merits animal testing, the authors suggest.
pmc-11679824:
Peanut pods in China often rot from a mould that lives in the soil. Huiling Wang and co-authors hunt in 2024 for the poison the mould uses to do that harm. They pull a compound from the mould and pin down its shape with lab tools.
