The compound showed up only in rotted pods, never in sound ones. It slowed root growth in rice seed at low dose. When the team shot it into sound peanut pods, the pods rotted in the same way as in the field. Those checks mark the compound as a main driver of the rot. Knowing the driver gives growers and breeders a clear target to fight.
pmc-11679924:
Darche and co-authors follow heart transplant patients whose new hearts needed pacing support right after surgery, and compare their fate with patients who did not. Slow heart rhythms are common after transplant, but the meaning of early pacemaker dependency was unclear. The team screened all adult transplants at one German center from 1989 to 2022. Of 699 recipients, 127 needed pacing support immediately after the operation, split between two kinds of conduction fault.

The dependent group fared far worse. More than half died within a year, against about 15 percent of the others, and graft failure caused far more of those deaths. Dependency stood as an independent risk factor in adjusted analysis, and these patients also needed permanent pacemakers far more often. The authors present the early pacing need as a strong warning sign. For transplant teams, it marks a group that merits close watch and early planning.
pmc-11680124:
Yinjie Niu and co-authors study a fish version of the TRIM44 gene in mandarin perch, a farmed fish, and its odd help for one virus. TRIM44 is known from work on cancers, nerve diseases, and viral infections in other species. Its role in this fish was unknown. Their 2024 study first maps the gene's parts and where it is expressed in the body. Then it tests the gene against three fish viruses.

The gene was expressed strongly in immune tissues of the fish. Its levels fell after two of the viruses struck but rose after the third, a rhabdovirus. Raised gene levels helped that virus grow in fish cells, while lowering the gene slowed the virus. The first two viruses were unaffected either way. The help ran through the RIG-I and MDA5 pathways, which trigger interferon signaling. The gene thus aids one foe while it may guard against others.
pmc-11680424:
Second-hand smoke leaves a marker in the body, and it has now been found in a new place: dog semen. Groppetti and co-authors report that first find in 2024. The marker is the ash form of nicotine, and dogs of smoking owners carry it in their seed.

Levels in semen tracked levels in blood and hair, which makes the new read a fair gauge of a dog's smoke load. The team also weighs links to sperm counts and to the shield strength of blood and semen fluids. Whether the marker harms a dog's breeding is not yet shown. The find opens a fresh route to study smoke's reach into animal health, through a fluid no one had thought to test.
pmc-11681624:
Jun Dai and co-authors test how fast and how long a single vaccine shot guards chickens against Marek's disease, a contagious tumor-causing virus of poultry. Their vaccine candidate is a rebuilt virus carrying an inserted gene segment, already shown to weaken the disease strain. Their 2024 study vaccinates day-old chicks, then challenges them with a fierce field strain at set times.

Protection began by day three after the shot and was good by day five. Challenged groups were checked for symptoms and weight gain. Immunity lasted at least one hundred eighty days, the full span tested. Counting the natural resistance older birds gain, the authors argue the shot likely protects for life. The results guide how such a vaccine would be used on farms.
pmc-11681924:
Jay Dave, Ian Hakkinen, and Pengfei Zhang drew up lists of migraine prevention drugs that can be safely combined, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. People with hard-to-treat migraine often need two or more drugs at once, but some pairs clash in the body. Starting from expert guidance lists, the team gathered twenty-six prevention drugs and formed every mix of two, three, and four, then struck out any mix with a known clash.

Out of all mixes, one hundred twenty-four pairs and one hundred forty-six triples had no clash, while no set of four was clean. The full result condenses to one hundred sixty-two distinct safe mixes. Four drugs clashed least of all: a newer class aimed at a migraine-linked protein, botulinum toxin A, melatonin, and candesartan. The lists give clinics a quick check before stacking drugs.
pmc-11683124:
Charlotte Berg and Hannah Vickers study complaints about putting animals to sleep in a 2024 paper from Sweden. They read formal complaints sent to the national board that reviews vets from 2018 to 2022. The team asked how many complaints were upheld, why owners complained, and whether any animal suffered needlessly during the act. Their work ties to a view that human and animal welfare are closely linked.

Wrong treatment or handling was the most common charge, but poor talk between staff and owners lay behind many cases. Only a very small share led to a warning or rebuke, and most vets had acted in line with good care. Readers see why clear talk at a hard moment may prevent most disputes.
pmc-11683424:
Zyani, Mzaalak Tazi, Alkouh, Es-Saad, and Labib report in twenty twenty-four a rare case of stress-type heart failure in a young crash victim. A six-year-old boy arrived with skull, rib, and arm fractures plus bruised lungs after a high-impact collision. Hours after surgery his circulation faltered and a heart damage marker rose, pointing first to a bruised heart.

Heart scans instead showed the classic pattern of takotsubo syndrome: a still tip and an overactive base of the main pumping chamber. Doctors swapped his support drug for one that adds less stress hormone load. Within a week his heart function returned to normal, and he went home stable. The authors stress early scanning to tell this syndrome from bruising in injured children.
pmc-11683624:
Twaha Mohamed, Janusz Kozinski, and Francisco Ramos-Pallares present a 2024 engineering study on equations that predict how pure substances behave. Cubic equations of state are workhorse tools in chemical plants. Each pairs with an alpha function that adjusts for temperature, and the pairing choice affects accuracy.

The team tested four pairings built from two equations, Peng-Robinson and Redlich-Kwong, and two alpha functions, Twu and Soave. They checked saturation pressure, heat of vaporization, and liquid heat capacity for 147 pure components. The set covered nonpolar, polar, and hydrogen-bonding substances below their critical points. They also scored how well each pairing stayed consistent across the phase diagram. The goal was one pairing that engineers can trust broadly.
pmc-11683724:
Jili Long, Jingru Lin, Jia Tao, and Hao Wang test a new heart scan score in a 2024 study of chest pain patients. Doctors need a safe way to tell which narrowed heart vessels truly block blood flow. The team used a sound-wave scan with tiny bubbles to grade how well blood filled the heart wall.

Their score was checked against a wire-free flow measure taken as the standard. The study held 112 patients sent for vessel imaging, and 64 had flow-blocking disease. The new score tracked the standard well for the main front vessel and stood out in joint tests. A clear cut point could help doctors sort who needs more care.
pmc-11684024:
Mona Amrihesari, Joseph Kern, Hilary Present, Sofia Moreno Briceno, Rampi Ramprasad, and Blair Brettmann predict whether polymers dissolve in this two thousand twenty-four paper. How well a polymer dissolves governs its mixing and use, but past datasets were too small and coarse to capture how strength and heat matter. The team built a dataset from Crystal16 cloudiness measures, recording percent transmission for many polymer-solvent pairs across strengths and heat. That signal tells clear solutions from cloudy, partly dissolved ones.

They trained a model predicting the transmission data across conditions. From those predictions, pairs sort into three grades of dissolving, finer than the binary labels of earlier models. Adding many strengths, heat levels, and partly soluble cases extends prediction toward what mixers and designers need. The work shows machine learning can pull out graded behavior, not just class labels, when base measures are dense enough.
pmc-11685024:
Ye Hu and co-authors chart the burden of peripheral artery disease in China from 1990 to 2019. Their 2024 paper uses a global disease study data set. This disease narrows arteries outside the heart and brain, and its rate in China is rising. The team tracks new cases, deaths, and years of healthy life lost.

In 2019, China held nearly a quarter of the world's cases of this disease. New case rates rose until 2005 and then fell, while death rates kept climbing. Women made up most cases and lost years, but men made up most deaths. Smoking hit men hardest, while blood pressure and diabetes hit women more. Forecasts to 2030 see death rates still rising. The authors urge plans matched to these patterns.
pmc-11685224:
Chang-zhan Xie led a team building adenovirus vaccines against a new pig virus strain in a 2024 paper. The virus causes reproductive failure in sows and lung disease in piglets, and a newly emerged strain has challenged control in China. The team built vaccine candidates carrying different viral surface proteins and dosed piglets. Blood tests tracked specific and neutralizing antibodies plus two immune signals.

Vaccinated groups showed strong mixed immune responses by five weeks. After challenge with the virus, vaccinated pigs had no clear symptoms, less virus in blood, and no obvious lung damage, unlike controls. The authors offer the candidates as reserves against new subtypes.
pmc-11685524:
Sayisree Yarlagadda and four co-authors compare two motions of a dental file during root canal work, in a 2024 trial. The patients had painful, inflamed tooth pulp needing single-visit treatment. The file system studied can spin steadily or move adaptively, changing motion with resistance.

Seventy patients with sore molars were split evenly between the two motions, and neither patients nor assessors knew which was used. Pain was scored before treatment and repeatedly up to seventy-two hours after. Sixty-seven patients finished the analysis. Pain faded over time in both groups, but the adaptive motion brought significantly lower pain. The result matters to patients, for whom post-treatment ache is the chief complaint about root canal therapy.
pmc-11686024:
Nancy Allen and colleagues lay out a trial protocol for Share plus, a glucose data-sharing programme for older adults with type 1 diabetes and their care partners. Continuous glucose monitors can stream readings to a partner's phone, which may deepen partner help. Eighty patient-partner pairs will be split evenly between Share plus and a standard follower app plus diabetes education.

The active phase runs twelve weeks, then twelve weeks of watch-only follow-up. The main outcome is time spent in the target glucose range, with diabetes distress second. Surveys and interviews will judge ease of use and acceptance, and partner burden and shared coping are also tracked. A home blood test kit covers long-term sugar control.
pmc-11686224:
Rubén Martín-Escolano and nine colleagues published a 2024 study of people living with both HIV and hepatitis C whose livers stayed stiff after successful hepatitis C treatment. Liver stiffness is a sign of scarring; a reading of at least 12.5 kilopascals counts as persistently high.

The retrospective study covered 39 patients who had advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis before treatment and cleared the hepatitis C virus. The team measured immune checkpoint proteins, immune regulators shed into the blood, one year after treatment. They tested whether those levels were associated with high stiffness five years after treatment. The findings may help explain why some livers fail to recover even after the virus is gone.
pmc-11686524:
Katarina Barbaric Starcevic, Goran Bicanic, and Luka Bicanic present a 2024 journal article on hip replacement in adults whose hips were damaged by childhood disorders. These patients are younger, demand more from the joint, and bring altered anatomy that complicates surgery. The authors set out their preferred approach and the reasoning behind it.

Their plan aims the socket at the ideal rotation center and locks the thigh component with good offset, sparing the abductor muscles. A modified side approach opens a clear view of socket and thigh bone without cutting the trochanter. A socket-shaping step, cotyloplasty, is their choice for the best mechanical position.
pmc-11687124:
Sun and seven co-authors test a steroid drug to prevent sickness after knee replacement, in work from twenty twenty-four. Nausea and vomiting after surgery slow recovery for many patients. Steroid drugs help in breast and heart surgery, but proof for knee surgery was unclear.

More than a hundred patients were split by chance in the trial. One group got betamethasone by vein minutes before anesthesia. The other got plain salt water. Main outcomes tracked nausea and vomiting after surgery, plus safety. A clear result, either way, helps anesthesia teams choose a cheap preventive step with more confidence.
pmc-11687224:
Gabriel and co-authors review, in a 2024 paper, the modern lab methods changing dermatopathology, the diagnosis of skin disease. Skin disorders burden millions, and molecular tools now reveal causes that microscopes alone could not.

The review covers tests that copy genes and find infections such as tuberculosis and Epstein-Barr virus in skin. It also covers sequencing that maps mutations and gene activity, antibody staining, and in-situ methods that locate signals inside tissue. Together they tell apart look-alike skin cancers, flag targets like BRAF mutations, and guide treatment matched to each patient. The authors map where each method earns its place in the testing workflow.
pmc-11688024:
Humza Saeed and co-authors chart emphysema deaths in the United States across two decades, in work from 2024. The lung disease affects millions, yet death trend data by group were thin. Fairness gaps in who dies of it were a central concern.

Death records from 1999 to 2020 held over 484,000 emphysema deaths. The adjusted death rate fell from 18.5 to 7.2 per hundred thousand people. A steep yearly drop ran from 2008 to 2015, then a slight rise followed. Older adults carried the highest rates by far. Men died at higher rates than women. Breakdowns by race, region, and urban status expose where the burden still concentrates.
pmc-11688224:
Hervé Monka Lekuya and co-authors study surgery timing after brain injury in a paper published in 2024. After a traumatic brain injury, inflammation rises, and operating at the wrong moment may add harm. The team tracked blood markers of inflammation around surgery in patients with mild to moderate injury and skull fractures.

The study followed 82 patients, most of them young men, many injured in assaults. About half had surgery within two days of injury and half later. One pro-inflammatory marker ran higher after later surgery. Patients who later developed wound infections showed a rise in an anti-inflammatory marker. The authors aim to guide safer timing of surgery in lower-income settings.
pmc-11688324:
Vasile Valeriu Lupu and a large team review how oxidative stress drives harm in children with diabetes, and how antioxidants may help, in a review from 2024. Diabetes in children, type 1 or type 2, leads in time to damage in many organs. The review centers on the pancreas, eyes, kidneys, nerves, and heart and vessels.

Oxidative stress, an overload of reactive molecules, sits at the core of that slow damage. The authors survey fresh data from global databases on how it builds and spreads harm. They then detail helpful compounds: vitamins, minerals, polyphenols, and other plant actives. Each is described by how it steps into the damage chain. The goal is a full map of the stress-antioxidant-diabetes triangle in children.
pmc-11688724:
Amy Elliot and Katherine Abbott describe an art program that pairs students with people living with dementia, in a paper published in 2024. The program, Opening Minds through Art, began in 2007 at Miami University and runs on person-centered care. It gives people with dementia a way to create and connect, while training students in empathy.

The program now counts over a thousand trained facilitators in more than three hundred communities, with thirty university partners. Thirteen peer-reviewed studies back gains in mood, engagement, and cross-age empathy. This symposium paper compares how three universities adapted the model: health trainees at one, an internship at another, and further variants at a third. Success, the authors say, depends on fitting the program to each campus and its partners.
pmc-11688824:
Ariel Green and five co-authors study, in twenty twenty-four, how people with dementia and their care partners use patient portals to talk about drugs. People with dementia often take drugs whose risks outweigh their gains. Portals could help cut such use, but little was known about real message content. The team read close to four hundred message threads from one health system, spanning twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-two.

Most threads were about logistics, such as how to take a drug. A quarter covered side effects or burden. Others asked for new drugs, or showed openness to stopping a drug. Patients were on average seventy-eight years old. The authors say portals are a live channel for drug talks.
pmc-11688924:
Rajagopal Sekhar and three co-authors test a two-part supplement against meal-driven strain in a 2024 trial. After a meal, the blood carries a wave of oxidative stress and swelling signals, worse in older adults. The supplement, GlyNAC, pairs glycine with a cysteine source to refill the body's own shield.

Twenty older and ten young adults drank a set glucose load, and their two-hour blood shifts were read. Older blood spiked far higher on both marks. After a course of the supplement or a dummy, the test ran again. The paper weighs whether the real supplement blunted the post-meal surge.
pmc-11689024:
Claudia Haase and four co-authors took a closer look at how older adults accept their feelings, in a report published in 2024. Older adults tend to favor plain acceptance, letting a feeling be without judging it, over reframing or mental distancing. Two studies probe the habit. In a laboratory, 129 adults aged 64 to 83 watched sad film clips under varied instructions while their body states were recorded.

Habitual acceptance, alone among the three strategies, tied to stronger nerve calm during the task. It also tied to lower anxiety and depression scores. In an online group of 241, a new scale split in two: acceptance of negative feelings and acceptance of positive feelings stand apart. The authors urge attention to both kinds in work on late life.
pmc-11689324:
Jing Wang and seven co-authors asked what matters most in person-centered dementia care inside low-resource nursing homes. They worked with four long-term care facilities in medically underserved areas, two rural and two urban. Interviews covered administrators, direct care staff, residents living with dementia, and family members, fifty-nine people in all, and the team mapped each group's journey.

Staff described learning dementia care principles, joining daily huddles, and slowly gaining the trust and feel for each resident's routines and past. Residents wanted a home-like place where their voices counted and staff understood them. Families saw their role as easing the move, speaking up for preferences, and keeping communication open. The authors frame these parallel journeys as the groundwork any improvement effort in such homes must build on.
pmc-11689724:
Justin Lam presents, in twenty twenty-four, a guide to age-friendly web design. Most adults over sixty-five now use the internet, he notes. Web tools can help them find health facts and stay in touch. But loss of sight, hearing, thought, or hand skill can make sites hard to use. Rules for disability access do not always give older users a good experience.

Lam reviews frames that aim to help users find facts, read text, and spot links. He covers design for both older adults and their care partners. Tips touch how users click and move, and how to make text clear. The goal is sites that feel easy, not just legal.
pmc-11689824:
Caterina Rosano, Stephen Kritchevsky, and Paul Coen outline in 2024 a symposium on how the brain, muscles, and physical ability hold each other up in old age. Older people differ widely in how well they move, and some stay strong despite clear risk factors, a resilience whose biology is still murky.

The session gathers work from varied ethnic cohorts on the two-way talk between muscle and brain. Much of what is known comes from animals or from patients with wasting diseases, leaving open how the link works in ordinary aging. The symposium aims to firm up that picture and find where resilience comes from.
pmc-11690024:
A 2024 symposium report by Frank Oswald, Johannes Doll, and Lycia Tramujas Vasconcellos Neumann looks at growing old at home in Brazil. Place shapes health in later life, yet how place, ageing, and learning fit together has had little study. The session brought together talks on theory, city design, gardens, and adult learning.

One talk rethinks old theories of place and ageing for new times. A second shares views from residents in Sao Paulo on what they want from their homes and streets. A third shows how older adults helped plan gardens in care homes, with good results. A fourth ties learning to big shifts such as city growth and a warming climate. Together, the talks argue that homes and neighbourhoods should help older people keep learning and stay well.
pmc-11690124:
Alison Rataj and four co-authors ask if childlessness links to loneliness in mid and late life. Their twenty twenty-four study pools data on close to twelve thousand adults aged fifty and older. Data came from two waves of a large United States aging study. The team also asked if friend support, friend strain, and sex change the link.

Adults with no children were notably lonelier than parents. Friend support cut loneliness, and the cut was larger for childless adults. Men were lonelier than women overall. Yet childlessness shaped loneliness more for women than for men. Friend strain made no clear difference. The authors stress both family and friends in later life.
pmc-11690224:
Rona Karasik, writing alone, offers a 2024 editor's view on a long-standing problem in aging education. Programs that train people to work with older adults have long struggled to draw students, even as the older population grows. Funding has been thin for decades, and the need for an age-savvy workforce keeps rising.

Karasik draws on trends in work sent to a leading journal in the field. The piece asks why students pass over gerontology and geriatrics, and what might draw more of them in. It sorts submitted work by the blocks it names, from money to image. The view gives teachers and leaders a map of where to act.
pmc-11690324:
Nasreen Lalani, Bhagyashree Katare, Sampada Wagle, and Siqi Yang studied self-care among rural women who care for frail older relatives, in a 2024 study from the Midwest of the United States. Rural caregivers face wider gaps in help, and women carry most of this unpaid work. The strain can harm their body, mind, and finances.

The team first surveyed 160 women across twelve rural counties, then held deep talks with 20 of them. Early results link more self-care with higher well-being and lower depression. Social support also tied to higher well-being. Themes from the talks included rising burnout, which the authors set against the factors that help some caregivers stay resilient.
pmc-11690424:
Kelli Barton shares lessons from dementia programs for adults with learning limits in a 2024 presentation. Few proven dementia programs serve people with such limits and their care partners. A United States grants scheme let teams stretch two known programs to fit this group across three funded projects.

One program cuts disability through home drills, the other joins a care web around each pair. Mixed tools tracked gains and drew lessons from staff and partner talks. Barton sums what worked, what snagged, and what later programs should copy when they serve this often-missed group.
pmc-11690524:
Sarah Fraser, Andrea Rosso, and Teresa Liu-Ambrose introduce a symposium on aging brains in a 2024 summary. Thinking and movement skills decline together with age, sharing brain resources. Those shared resources are still poorly mapped. The symposium asks what imaging can reveal about them.

Four study groups present their angles. One uses light based brain imaging during a dual task to compare elders with and without felt cognitive decline. Another pairs that method with dopamine scans during dual task walking. A third links dopamine binding to gait changes on uneven ground. The fourth ties muscle energy function to long term brain structure change. Together they probe how dopamine and energy systems support resilience.
pmc-11690624:
Aman Shrestha and co-authors report a 2024 study on kidney markers and the joint path of thinking skill and walking speed in older adults. Kidney health and mind-body function sway each other, yet most work tracks them one at a time. A joint view over years may catch decline that single tracks miss.

The team used a long health study of adults who began with fast gait and high scores. Grouping by both tracks over years gave three paths: one high and steady, one with steady mind but falling gait, and one low and fast falling. A urine marker of kidney strain raised the odds of the two worse paths. A hormone marker from kidney and bone also linked to the worst path. Better kidney filter rates lowered the odds of that path.
pmc-11690724:
Marino Bruce and co-authors study faith, social class, and memory and thinking skills among Black men in a 2024 paper. Black men face higher rates of cognitive impairment, yet faith practices have been linked to protection, at least for those with modest incomes. The team used data from a national retirement study from 2016, covering nearly four hundred Black men.

Men with lower income or fewer years of schooling had far higher rates of impairment. Among men with modest incomes, private prayer and strong beliefs were linked to lower impairment. Prayer also linked to lower impairment among men with more schooling. The authors call for larger studies of Black men to sort out how class shapes these protective links.
pmc-11690924:
Chris Phillipson argues in a 2024 paper that the social side of COVID-19 needs its own sociology, with older people at the center. Most talk about the pandemic has been biomedical: where the virus came from, how vaccines were built, and what to do next time. Phillipson notes that pandemics are also social events, seen through shared values and shaped by inequality in who falls ill and who gets care.

The paper sets challenges and priorities for social gerontology, the study of aging in society. It stresses that the virus hit groups unevenly by age, place, job, and housing. It also looks at how people saw themselves after loss, or after pulling together in crisis. The piece asks researchers to treat care and support as social systems, not just medical ones.
pmc-11691024:
Ellen Lee and co-authors mine free speech for marks of lone life in older folks. Lone life and cut ties lift death risk in old age, yet stock asks are long and miss the felt grain. Their 2024 study runs tongue craft and sound tools on loose talk from old folks in home yards. Word marks, theme sets, talk-part splits, and sound marks form the sieve.

Ties from speech marks to later body, mind, and brain ends are read in a sound San Diego set. Sleep and step marks from wrist bands and a mind test set ride with the talk. Speech is took in day life, so its marks could flag lone risk ere harm lands.
pmc-11691124:
Jane Lowers argued in 2024 that United States aging policy rests too heavily on fortitude, the idea that older people and their families should endure hardship on their own. Policy now pushes the money, physical, and emotional costs of aging onto households. That works only for those who built wealth and support over a lifetime.

When public supports are weak, personal grit cannot make up for fixed incomes, scarce family caregivers, and long years of chronic illness. Drawing on cases of adults aging alone with dementia, Lowers proposes different organizing principles for policy. The aim is a fairer system that does not treat endurance as a substitute for support.
pmc-11691224:
Fats in the blood shift with age, and those shifts may not be the same for males and females. Ziying Xu, Anindita Bhattacharjee, and Xianlin Han charted those shifts in aging mice in this 2024 study. Lipids build cell walls, store energy, and carry signals. Their levels tie to diseases of aging, from artery hardening to diabetes and brain decline.

Blood was drawn from lab mice of both sexes at seven ages, from eight to thirty-two months. A shotgun mass method weighed hundreds of lipid kinds at once. The team tracked which classes rose or fell with age in each sex. Sex-specific aging charts could refine how lipid clues are read in older patients. Mice offer a controlled stand-in for the long human aging span.
pmc-11691424:
Bryce Van Vleet, Heather Fuller, and Andrea Huseth-Zosel report lessons from a survey on vaccine hesitancy among older adults. The survey covered 901 community dwelling adults aged 65 and over. It asked about views and habits for vaccines against shingles, pneumonia, COVID-19, and influenza. The team focused on volatile participants, 59 people whose open-ended replies showed strong anger or mistrust.

Linear regression linked volatile replies to younger age, strong religiosity, and conservative views. Volatile respondents also skipped fewer of the questions they likely saw as controversial, such as items on COVID-19 and influenza vaccines. The authors use these patterns to guide future survey work with distrustful older participants.
pmc-11691524:
Shraddha Shende and Raksha Mudar test a cognition screening tool in older adults with mild hearing loss in a study from 2024. Hearing loss is a changeable risk factor for dementia, so early checks matter. Fifteen adults with mild to moderate hearing loss and fifteen matched peers with normal hearing took the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and a speech-in-noise test.

The hearing loss group scored worse on both the total score and the memory index of the screen. Harder speech-in-noise listening went with lower total scores, even after accounting for basic hearing measures. Self-rated hearing handicap did not track the scores. The authors see early global changes beyond memory alone.
pmc-11691624:
Zachary Gassoumis, Erin Thayer, and Jeanine Yonashiro-Cho track what changed when California widened its adult protection net in 2022. The state cut the age floor from sixty-five to sixty and added homelessness under self-neglect. Their 2024 study reads public case records from late 2019 to late 2023.

Total case growth sped up after the change, with no sharp jump at the switch itself. Cases for ages sixty to sixty-four leapt at once, from about 375 to 550 a month, then kept climbing. Housing service cases also grew faster after the change. The authors say wider nets bring real new load. States weighing like moves should plan staff and funds for it.
pmc-11691724:
Sabine Lohmar and co-authors study burnout among sandwich generation caregivers in 2024. These caregivers look after both their children and their aging parents at once. Low satisfaction, depression, and burnout are common in the group. What drives those outcomes was still poorly mapped.

The team tested whether the quality of family relationships changes the link between burnout and depression. Both warm and strained relationship quality were measured alongside burnout. Strained quality tracked strongly with both burnout and depressive signs. The study is the first to cast relationship quality as a buffer or amplifier in this group.
pmc-11691824:
Kingsley Mbam and co-authors published this 2024 study on grandparents who help raise grandchildren with disabilities. Grandparents often give steady support to such children, from autism to physical disability. How that caregiving shapes the grandparents' own sense of self in later life has drawn little study.

The team recruited eight grandparents through senior centers in Massachusetts and interviewed each in depth by video or phone. Questions covered work, family ties, self-image, and the bond with the grandchild. Themes of resilience and shifting attitudes toward aging emerged from the talks. The study gives a close look at how caring for a grandchild with a disability can remake the identity of an older adult.
pmc-11691924:
Esther Park, Milenko Petrovic, and Gohar Azhar study older adults with COVID-19 in a 2024 paper on delirium and heart disease. Delirium is a sudden state of confusion that can arise during illness. The team looked back at records for three hundred nineteen patients aged sixty-five and older at one medical center in Arkansas.

About four in ten patients had delirium during or after the infection. Most of those patients also had some form of heart disease, such as a fast or slow heart rate or heart failure. Patients with no heart disease were far less apt to have delirium. The authors say good heart care during COVID-19 may also help protect the mind and lead to better results.
pmc-11692124:
Nicole Dalmer and Cal Biruk wrote a 2024 paper on how older adults talk about data in daily life. Phones and home devices turn routines into data, yet people grasp that flow in unlike ways. The authors ask what shared words could help groups talk about data at all. They draw on two linked studies with older Canadians.

One study surveyed seventy older Canadians online about what data means to them. The other visited seven older adults at home to see how data moves through their days. Words like informative, dull, and hard to grasp came up in their accounts. The paper argues for a plain shared vocabulary around data.
pmc-11692224:
Jessica Strong asks whether holding a faith tightly makes people kinder toward the old. Ageism, bias against people for their age, harms memory, mood, health, and even survival. Earlier work hinted that strongly religious cultures view older adults better. Her 2024 study separates the strength of attachment to a belief system from the beliefs themselves, in thirty-one adults aged 21 to 73.

Participants spanned Christian, Buddhist, Muslim, and atheist or agnostic identities, split into attached and unattached groups. With death anxiety held constant, attachment did not move positive attitudes toward older adults. It did significantly reduce negative ageism and the wish to restrict older people's lives, both with large effect sizes. Strong concedes the sample is small and likely underpowered, but argues the size of the effects justifies a fuller study of faith as a buffer against age bias.
pmc-11692424:
Chelsea Leonard and co-authors study in 2024 how veterans affairs staff handle home health agency choice for older veterans. Hospital leavers get skilled home care from community agencies paid by one of two public payers. Who picks the agency and payer was murky from the staff view.

Site visits and interviews at six medical centers gather twenty nine talks with thirty nine staff. Four themes center on doubt in agency and payer choice. Roles sit in silos, network entry rules are opaque, and local sites craft their own quality checks. The veteran's own role in the choice also stays unclear in the accounts.
pmc-11692524:
Xinyuan Peng, Da Jiang, Dwight Tse and colleagues studied how being alone feels across adulthood in 2024. In an experience sampling study, 191 adults aged 19 to 93 answered phone prompts five times a day for a week, reporting whether they were alone and how they felt.

People high in certain mindfulness traits coped better with solitude. Describing feelings and acting with awareness softened the drop in lively positive mood when alone. Nonreactivity to inner experiences strengthened calm positive feelings in solitude, and observing weakened the rise of low-key negative feelings. Age itself did not change these patterns. The findings suggest mindfulness skills help people of all ages use time alone well.
pmc-11692624:
Sleeping too little or too much both track with depression in old age, and Wuyi Dong and co-authors ask whether schooling softens the link. Pooling two waves of a United States health survey, they studied over nine thousand adults past sixty, sorting sleep into short, optimal, and long, and scoring depression on a standard nine-item scale. Both tails of sleep carried heavier symptoms.

The twist is the moderator: a college education significantly blunted the depression tied to long sleep, though not the short-sleep side. Education, usually filed under income and access, here behaves like a psychological reserve against one specific risk.
pmc-11692724:
Michelle Yang and co-authors presented this 2024 trial on helping older patients regain strength after hospital stays. Muscle loss with age, called sarcopenia, deepens during bed rest and raises the risk of decline and death. A past pilot hinted that whey protein or testosterone could help recovery. This phase-one trial tested whether the plan is workable and safe.

Eighty patients aged 65 and up joined during hospital care for acute illness. They were split into four arms mixing real or dummy drinks and shots. Whey was given twice daily in hospital and after discharge. Testing covered leg function at entry and four weeks after leaving. Fifty-two people finished, while fifteen returned to hospital. The study gauges feasibility for a larger trial.
pmc-11692924:
Not having reliable access to food is tied to many health problems in old age, but its link to trouble moving around is less clear. Usha Dhakal, Khalil El Asmar, and Carlos Mendes de Leon follow more than six thousand older Americans from a national retirement study. They track food insecurity scores and a mobility score built from five everyday tasks across waves from 2014 to 2020.

At the start, worse food insecurity went with more mobility limits, even after accounting for income, schooling, illness, and mood. Over time, though, the food score did not predict how fast mobility worsened. The authors suggest that spotting food insecurity early may still protect mobility and delay disability, even if it is not the main driver of decline.
pmc-11693024:
Tricia VanCleef reviews what plant based diets do to heart risk factors in older adults, in a 2024 journal article. Heart disease is the top killer in the world, and it hits older adults hardest. Plant based diets stress foods from plants and cut or drop animal foods.

VanCleef searched three databases for studies in adults aged sixty-five and up and kept seventeen papers. Each study found at least one gain for heart health on such a diet. Gains ran from lower bad cholesterol, blood pressure, and body mass to less calcium in heart arteries and better vessel lining. The author backs the diet as a guard against heart disease in old age. She also calls for larger trials built for this age group.
pmc-11693324:
Fernandez Cajavilca, Lee, and Doan review how rarely aging grants split health data by detailed ethnic groups in a 2024 paper. Broad race categories hide real differences among older adults. Fine-grained reporting is a data equity issue.

Searching a federal grants database across four decades found only a dozen awards proposing such disaggregation. Nearly all were recent, and most named Latino, Asian, Pacific Islander, or Arab groups. Funding came through standard research and training mechanisms. The authors recommend stronger cultural fit and rigor in data collection and reporting. Underrepresented communities stay invisible without it. The review urges funders and researchers to act. Better data is framed as a health equity tool.
pmc-11693924:
Mahdyeh Neghabi Hajigha and co-authors review short protein chains that kill germs and viruses, in a paper from 2024. Such chains draw wide hope as new drugs, since they hit drug proof germs in ways that set drugs do not. The review gathers where the chains occur in nature and how each kind does its work.

Virus chains can break the virus cycle before entry, at the merge step, or once inside the host cell. Germ chains act on the outer skin of the germ or slip in and block inner work. Shape, size, charge, heat, and germ tricks all tune how well a chain works. The authors map those levers so drug teams can build chains that last and hit hard.
pmc-11696424:
Nuray Serginay, Mehmet Bingol, Erkan Karatas, and Mehmet Yilmaz build magnetic core-shell particles topped with gold that destroy dye pollutants and can be reused, in a study from 2024. Textile dyes foul water, and a catalyst that a magnet can fish out solves the cleanup twice over. A sticky polymer shell is the assembly trick.

Magnetite cores were wrapped in polydopamine, whose grip groups held gold particles in tunable amounts, added two ways. The best systems erased crystal violet and malachite green fully within four minutes. Gold amount was the main driver of speed. After five magnet-recovered cycles, activity stayed satisfying.
pmc-11698924:
Camille Siharath, Olivier Biondi, and Sabine Peres build a computer model of energy use in muscle, tested on a muscle-wasting disease, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. Lab work alone struggles here, since so many enzymes act at once. A model can predict how the system rebalances when demand rises or a step fails.

Their model mimics calpainopathy, a dystrophy caused by a faulty protein-cutting enzyme. It confirmed a shortfall in the cell's main energy supply under rising demand. The muscle compensates by burning sugar without oxygen, but too much of that route floods the tissue with lactate. The model points to a fix: moderate exercise training plus more carbohydrates and amino acids in the diet. The authors offer the model for other muscle diseases.
pmc-11703624:
García Martí and three co-authors wrote in twenty twenty-four on deals that share risk when states in Latin America pay for new health tools. Such deals let a drug or device in while its true gain and cost are still unclear. A large forum on health checks met in twenty twenty-three to weigh their use.

Cash-based deals were more common in the zone than deals tied to health results. Blocks named were weak laws, poor data, and lack of trust among the sides. Fixes named were talks from the start and short test deals that can be reworked. The team backs laws and open talks to make the deals work.
pmc-11704224:
Shubashini Mathialagan and Poh Li Lau published a 2024 review of weight discrimination in Asia. Weight bias is widely tolerated there, they argue. It harms body and mind across daily life. Evidence in Asian settings remains thin. The review gathers what is known.

Stigma worsens health habits and care seeking. Paradoxically, it may also fuel the obesity it condemns. The authors push for social unacceptance of weight bias. Practical recommendations target clinics, media, and policy. Cultural context shapes how stigma operates in Asia. Reducing it could support both prevention and treatment goals.
pmc-11704624:
Reading all the genes in a stool sample can show what gut microbes do, but current tools lose much of that detail, above all in shallow samples. Kai Mi and co-authors built a new framework to recover the lost detail in this 2024 paper. Their method blends gene notes from known genomes with the mix of species found in the sample.

The framework also includes a way to measure exact shifts in microbe jobs between two groups. Tests on datasets tied to autism and bowel cancer showed the method sharpened later analyses, such as finding which microbe jobs differ and how they link to host traits. The tool is free and open for others to use. The work matters because function, not just species lists, drives how microbes affect health.
pmc-11709324:
Fahri Küçükali and Kristel Sleegers, with the EADB group, report a 2025 genome-wide study of short tandem repeats and Alzheimer's disease risk. Classic studies of this kind have found many risk loci, but their panels miss some kinds of genetic change, such as repeats that make up a large share of the genome.

Short tandem repeats are motifs of a few base pairs repeated in a row. New panels let the team impute hundreds of thousands of them in a European biobank data set. The study asks how much these repeats add to Alzheimer's risk, past what classic scans have found.
pmc-11709524:
Kanokphong Suparan and co-authors study how the regularity of blood transfusions shapes health in thalassemia, an inherited blood disorder, in a 2025 paper. Lifelong transfusions load the body with iron, which can harm the brain and gut.

The team compared twenty patients who need regular transfusions, twenty who do not, and twenty healthy people. The regular group carried the most iron and scored worst on a thinking test. Their gut germ mixes also differed most from healthy ones. Higher iron went with lower thinking scores across patients. One gut germ group rose alongside thinking decline. The authors suggest tight iron control and gut care could protect the brain.
pmc-11709624:
Pepper Dawes and co-authors share a 2025 conference abstract on herpes virus infection in brain organoids. The common cold sore virus has been tied to Alzheimer's-like molecular changes. The team infected flat and 3D organoid cultures and read gene activity cell by cell, with and without spatial mapping, to compare with older bulk data.

Earlier bulk work found that changed genes in infected cells were enriched for Alzheimer's risk genes alone. Single-cell data sorted infected cells into clusters by their viral gene patterns. The clusters differed sharply in how far the viral program had run. The team uses the contrast to show what each method can and cannot see.
pmc-11709724:
Mohammad Walid and co-authors review nose delivered progenitor cells for Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 paper. Cells from the smell lining can make new nerve cells throughout life and are safely obtained from the upper nose. Such cells have eased markers of brain damage after stroke like injury in past work. The question was whether they could home to the shrinking hippocampus in Alzheimer's disease.

Trials reviewed found the cells migrated close to damaged fibers and cell bodies in injury models, far closer than to random sites. Mouse work showed new relay neurons formed from the cells in injured spinal cords. The authors argue the cells' homing ability makes them promising for hippocampal repair. Readers see a novel delivery route weighed on early evidence.
pmc-11709824:
Grace Terry and co-authors test whether a depression drug might be reused against Alzheimer's disease. Agomelatine, an atypical antidepressant, surfaced from a screening algorithm as a candidate. It boosts melatonin receptors and blocks one serotonin receptor. Their 2025 paper tries the drug in rats bred to develop Alzheimer-like disease.

The rats carry human mutant genes that drive plaque buildup and steady mental decline with age. Treatment began at five months, before symptoms, at about ten milligrams per kilogram daily, and ran to eleven months. The team then tested the rats on a place-avoidance task, measured plaque in brain tissue, and read gene activity. Treated females showed smaller mental deficits, the abstract reports, with the tissue and gene results examined alongside. The study weighs a known drug's promise for a disease short on options.
pmc-11709924:
Soyoung Lee and co-authors published a study in 2025 mapping the brain network behind anxiety in older adults with early Alzheimer's changes. Anxiety is common in this group and tied to faster decline, yet its brain basis is murky. Using data from about eighteen hundred unimpaired adults in a prevention trial, the team built personal maps of cortical thinning for those with high amyloid. A large reference wiring dataset turned those maps into networks.

Anxiety symptoms pointed to one distinct network. It matched a known anxiety network from brain stimulation work, more strongly once depression was set aside. The match beat chance in shuffle tests. The authors propose the network as a stimulation target for anxiety across the Alzheimer's path.
pmc-11710024:
A shed piece of a microglia switch, found in spinal fluid, may tell where Alzheimer's disease stands. Harry Crook and six co-authors read that mark, called sTREM2, in 2025 across healthy folk, folk with mild memory loss, and folk with the full disease. They split each group by brain amyloid and tau signs, using fluid tests and scans. The shed mark runs high when the brain's guard cells wake, a state tied to the disease.

Levels ran highest in disease folk with both amyloid and tau signs. The mark rose with tau load in most groups but tracked amyloid in mixed ways. In full disease it linked to worse test scores and thinner brain rims. The team read the guard cells as helpers early and harmers late, with the fluid mark tracing that turn.
pmc-11710124:
Laura Berkowitz and co-authors test whether raising brain blood flow rescues memory in mice, in a 2025 study. The mice carry gene changes that mimic Alzheimer disease in people. Such mice show weak spatial memory and faulty circuits in the hippocampus, a memory hub. Brief brain bursts there during sleep help lock in new memories, and those bursts shrink in the model mice.

Earlier work found that a treatment lifting blood flow also restored memory. Here the team recorded circuit activity in the memory hub during sleep, before and after field exploration. They sorted cell types and picked out firing groups that reactivate together. The study checks whether circuit patterns return to normal as flow rises.
pmc-11710224:
Facundo Peralta and co-workers test thymulin gene therapy in a rat model of sporadic Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 paper. Thymulin is a thymus peptide with anti-inflammatory effects. The disease model uses a single brain injection of a toxin that impairs memory and behavior.

Rats received a viral vector that raised thymulin levels across the body, given into muscle at two time points. Treated rats behaved much like healthy controls on exploration, anxiety, and mood tests. Recognition memory, impaired in untreated model rats, was restored. At the tissue level, some brain cell effects of the toxin were not reversed. The authors report a partial benefit.
pmc-11710324:
Elizabeth Fisher and co-authors study how microglia shape vessel inflammation through a receptor partner called IL1RAP, in a research paper from 2025. Most Alzheimer patients show vessel damage that comes before memory decline. A gene variant in IL1RAP tracks with higher disease rates and faster amyloid build-up, which hints the pathway may modify the disease.

The team grew microglia and vessel lining cells from human stem cells carrying two APOE forms. Cells were challenged with inflammatory signals. Gene activity, cytokine release, and barrier strength were measured. The setup lets the team test whether microglial signals through IL1RAP weaken the blood-brain barrier. Results may point to a new drug target.
pmc-11710424:
Juliana Acosta-Uribe and co-authors present a genetics study, published in 2025, on Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia in Latin American populations. Most past research came from wealthy countries, leaving the genetic picture in Latin America poorly known. The ReDLat project was built to close that gap across six countries, from Mexico to Brazil.

The team combined whole genome sequencing, exome sequencing, and gene chip data to read the cohort's ancestry and risk variants. Latin American populations blend Indigenous, European, and African roots, which can shift which gene changes matter. Readers get a broad account of how genes and social conditions together shape dementia risk in a region long left out of such studies.
pmc-11710524:
Ethan Loew and co-authors compare gut chemistry and immune cells in Alzheimer's patients who decline fast versus those who stay stable, in a 2025 study. Alzheimer's always brings memory loss eventually, but its pace varies widely between people. Beyond the brain plaques and tangles, the body's wider immune system also drifts with the disease, losing fresh T cells and gaining worn ones.

The team profiled stool chemicals in thirty-five patients and thirty-five matched healthy controls using untargeted screening. One sulfur compound already stood out as elevated in patients. Ongoing work tracks blood immune cells and gut microbes over time in the same people. If gut or immune signatures predict who declines quickly, doctors could spot fast progressors early and perhaps intervene through the gut-immune route.
pmc-11710624:
Tsuneya Ikezu reports a 2025 mouse study of how tau spread can be slowed by cutting parcel release from brain immune cells. Immune cells shed tiny parcels that can carry clumped tau to new sites. A cell machine builds those parcels, and one part of it can be removed in a single cell type.

Mice with a tau disease gene were bred so the part could be switched off in immune cells. Treated mice kept better memory in maze and object tests. Their brains showed less tau build-up, less swelling, and less firing of a harm path. Lab cells with the part off also shed fewer parcels. Ikezu names the cell part a drug target.
pmc-11710724:
Asli Uyar and five co-authors hunt for cell groups tied to cognitive resilience in the face of amyloid in a 2025 mouse study. Genes shape how prone a mind is to Alzheimer's harm. One wild mouse strain keeps its thinking sharp with amyloid plaques in place, while the standard lab strain does not.

The sharp strain also holds a distinct mix of microglia, the brain's immune cells. The team aim to name and grade the microglia and neuron groups in the hippocampus of both strains. The goal is the cell-level base of that gap in resilience.
pmc-11710824:
Michelle Houston and co-authors study paired memory reports in aging in 2025. A person sense of their own memory slipping can warn of Alzheimer disease. A loved one report may add truth, or clash with the self view. The team joined both views into paired patterns and tracked thinking over years.

Hundreds of adults and their informants filled out daily cognition forms. Gaps between self and informant scores were sorted into three patterns. Brain and thinking tests followed the group for years on average. The study asks which pattern of agreement best flags real decline ahead.
pmc-11712124:
Alexander, Alladi and their co-authors test teleneurology for dementia care in a low-resource setting in India in 2025. Remote care could widen access for patients far from specialist centers, if patients and clinicians accept it.

Fifteen patients who had first been seen in person joined follow-up video visits from districts across Karnataka. Patients or caregivers rated the remote visits highly on a satisfaction survey. The neurologist and the local doctors who started most visits also gave positive scores. Agreement was strongest on time saved and willingness to use the method again. The authors see real promise, in a small early study.
pmc-11712224:
Christine Musyimi and five co-authors report lessons from a 2025 scheme that screened older adults in rural Kenya for dementia. The scheme trained health workers and hospital staff to use a short test in the community. It drew on local staff and groups rather than scarce experts.

Over six months, ten health workers offered checks to more than three thousand adults aged sixty or more in one county. The team found signs of the illness in close to one in five of those checked. Talks with staff and partners showed what helped and what blocked the work. Early work on shame, close ties with policy staff, and use of local means all helped. The authors call the scheme a first for rural Kenya.
pmc-11712324:
Hema Chaudhary and Mohit Agrawal report a 2025 animal study on a drug that might shield the brain in Parkinson disease. The disease kills nerve cells that make dopamine, and stress inside cells plays a part. The drug, filgrastim, is known for calming cell stress and swelling in other settings.

The team gave rats a toxin that harms those nerve cells over 35 days, plus one of three drug doses from day seven on. Toxin alone cut movement and body weight and raised stress markers in the brain. Treated rats fared better on these measures, which hints the drug guards nerve cells in this model.
pmc-11712424:
Teresa Leon outlines a case for combination treatment of Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 overview. The disease rarely travels alone: heart disease, diabetes, and depression often come with it. Those added conditions can speed decline and complicate care, Leon notes.

The overview reviews the main companion conditions and the shared drivers behind them, such as inflammation and vessel damage. It also notes that low mood and some calming drugs can cloud thinking on their own. Leon argues that drug plans hitting several targets at once may beat single-target plans. Pairing disease drugs with treatment of companion conditions, she suggests, could improve outcomes for patients.
pmc-11712524:
Rafael Bottos and co-authors report a laboratory study, published in 2025, on a synthetic DNA strand aimed at a failing splice machine in Alzheimer's disease. A complex called U1 snRNP helps cells edit RNA messages, and its breakdown may come before tau tangles form. The team tested the strand in neurons grown from stem cells of healthy and Alzheimer's donors, and in fast aging mice.

A week of treatment lowered tau in the Alzheimer's neurons without harming energy use or signaling chemical release. In the mice, six weeks of infusion into the brain shifted levels of the complex's key parts and related proteins. The authors read the results as early support for repairing RNA splicing as a treatment angle in Alzheimer's disease.
pmc-11712624:
Jude-Patrick Okafor and co-authors test whether a portable, low-field brain scanner can share the work of monitoring Alzheimer's immunotherapy, in a study published in 2025. The antibody drug lecanemab can cause amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, brain swelling or bleeding that regulators require frequent MRI checks to catch. High-field scanners are scarce and scheduling is hard.

Patients with mild impairment from Alzheimer's receive paired scans: the standard three-tesla MRI as reference, and a bedside-style scanner at 0.064 tesla, repeated about five times across twelve months of treatment. The study compares how well the small machine detects the abnormalities and tracks response. If a portable scanner proves adequate, monitoring could move closer to patients and ease a bottleneck in delivering the new therapy.
pmc-11712724:
Phillip A Cantu published a research paper in 2025 on how family members and other informants report memory loss in older adults. Such reports help doctors spot decline, and Cantu asked whether reports differ for men and women, and whether the gap changes from one country to the next.

He drew on large aging studies from the United States and Mexico, with close to three thousand people in one and over seventeen hundred in the other. Informants in both lands more often noted memory slips and trouble with chores for women. Other gaps ran in unlike ways in each land. The paper shows that the sex of the older adult and the place they live both shape what informants say.
pmc-11712824:
Alzheimer's drugs that hunt amyloid can also be turned into measuring tools. Kenjiro Ono and eight co-authors use the antibody lecanemab to fish a specific amyloid form, the soluble protofibril, out of spinal fluid in this 2025 study. Nearly one hundred and fifty people took part, from young healthy controls to patients with full dementia.

The caught protofibril levels ran high in mild impairment and dementia groups, and even stirred upward in symptom-free people whose scans already showed amyloid. That early rise, tracking closely with brain damage markers, sets it apart from plaque-based measures, which mostly report the load of finished deposits. The authors argue the protofibril is the form closest to the injury itself, making it a candidate marker for when treatment should start. A negative-scan patient group showed no such rise.
pmc-11712924:
Stina Saunders and seven colleagues ask Americans over fifty what brain health means to them personally, in their own words. Drugs and lifestyle plans for dementia often measure success by clinic scores, not by what patients say matters. A British program pioneered the personal approach; whether it fits the United States was open.

The online survey drew 764 people and over eleven thousand free-text answers. Most were women, married, and well educated, and few carried a dementia diagnosis. Word patterns shifted by age, sex, and diagnosis status. Confidence in managing personal priorities differed by diagnosis group. The results give trial designers a person-first yardstick for the American setting.
pmc-11713024:
Hernan Hernandez and co-authors present a 2025 study of chronic pain in Latin America and its link to dementia. Pain that lasts more than three months is a known risk factor in European and North American groups. In Latin America, how common it is and what drives it were largely unknown.

The team used two national health surveys from Chile covering more than thirty-six hundred people, plus a short pain survey given to dementia patients in four countries. Pain grew more common between the surveys, rising by about thirty percent. Low mobility, anxiety, low mood, poor diet, and low income or schooling were all tied to pain in the Chilean data.
pmc-11713324:
Helmet Karim and co-authors compare two tau imaging tracers against brain network connectivity in Alzheimer's research. Their 2025 study recruits people across the range of cognitive health and scans them at rest, plus with both tracers, which light up the tau tangles of Alzheimer's disease. The default mode network, a set of regions active at rest, is known to falter as amyloid and tau build.

Tau is thought to strike a belt of memory regions tied to that network, including the amygdala and hippocampal neighbors. The team asks whether network strength links to global tau load the same way under each tracer. A head-to-head read helps trials choose their imaging yardstick.
pmc-11713424:
Casey Allen and seven co-workers wrote a 2024 study on how to involve partners in community-based research. Classic partner mapping is top-down, which can clash with joint research aims. Their center asked partners what they value in such work. The goal was to deepen teamwork and impact.

They interviewed a few dozen partners, from community members to funders. Three themes stood out. True voice and fair partnership build trust and buy-in. Clear talk and shared results keep people engaged over time. Ongoing learning and long-term funds keep the work alive. The study turns those themes into steps for research teams.
pmc-11713524:
Abraham Varghese and four co-authors trained a neural network to predict Alzheimer's disease from brain scans, in a 2025 paper. Their data came from a large public imaging initiative, with scans sorted into classes from healthy cognition through stages of mild impairment to Alzheimer's. The team cleaned the images first, focusing on brain regions, then built a convolutional network with two feature layers and a stack of dense layers.

Training accuracy reached nearly ninety-nine percent, and a small test set of sixty-five images was classified without error. To open the model's reasoning, they applied LIME, a tool that highlights which image regions pushed each decision. The highlighted zones matched the predicted class in the healthy example they detail. The authors argue that pairing accuracy with such explanations is the path to trustworthy diagnostic AI.
pmc-11713624:
Prokopis Prokopiou and co-authors study an early brain site in Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 paper. The locus coeruleus is among the first places where tau protein builds up. Animal work hints that bursts of activity there may guard thinking as disease grows.

The team used data from a Harvard aging study with about ninety older adults who had no symptoms yet. Brain scans gauged resting activity in that site, plus tau and amyloid load, and thinking was tracked for years. Lower burst activity linked to more tau and to decline tied to amyloid. The finding may point to an early marker worth watching.
pmc-11713724:
Jason Flatt and co-authors explore how to engage minority caregivers of people with dementia in research, in this 2025 paper. Millions in the United States live with Alzheimer's and related dementias. Their unpaid caregivers give care worth hundreds of billions each year.

Caregivers from sexual and gender minority groups are rarely reached by studies. The RISE project held focus groups and interviews to learn why. It asks what keeps such caregivers out and what would draw them in. Findings can reshape how trials recruit and support diverse carers. Research that misses whole groups builds care advice on partial ground. The project treats engagement itself as the research question.
pmc-11713824:
Guilherme Povala and co-authors present a shared scale for tau brain scans in a 2025 paper. Different scan tracers measure tau, the second hallmark protein of Alzheimer's, on different scales. Results from one tracer cannot be compared directly with another. The team builds a universal scale that converts each scan type into common units.

The study covers 185 people across the aging and Alzheimer's range. Each person was scanned with one of two common tau tracers. A set formula, anchored on young adults and on patients, converts the images to the shared scale. Common units would let hospitals and trials pool scan data. That pooling speeds research on how tau spreads and how drugs slow it.
pmc-11713924:
Arthur Macedo and a large team of co-authors compare brain scan tracers for staging Alzheimer's disease in the HEAD study, reported in 2025. The tracers bind tau, a protein that clumps in the brain as the disease advances. Braak staging grades how far tau spread has gone, and doing that staging in living patients guides both care and trials.

Different tau tracers vary in how cleanly they image each stage. The study scans patients with competing tracers and checks which ones track the stage pattern best. A clear winner would standardize staging across centers, so trial results and clinic reads can be compared directly. The work serves the push toward scan-based diagnosis of Alzheimer's.
pmc-11714024:
Charles Windon and co-authors describe, in a 2025 paper, two United States data platforms that track Alzheimer's disease care in the real world. Trials alone cannot show how new treatments serve the full range of patients, and research has long missed many communities.

One platform, ALZ-NET, is a national registry following patients being assessed for or treated with newly approved therapies, with imaging and sample stores attached. The other, New IDEAS, follows patients through amyloid brain scanning to judge its value in care. Together they let researchers study who gets reached, who gets left out, and how outcomes differ, aiming at fairer care and more representative science.
pmc-11714124:
Lele Chen and six co-authors test whether a blood protein adds to brain scans for early diagnosis of mild thinking loss, in a 2025 conference paper. Mild loss sits between normal aging and dementia on the path of Alzheimer's disease. Scan signs now in use, such as memory area size, can miss the earliest stage.

The protein, called ASS1, runs high in brain cells of patients and links to a gas that harms tissue. The team signed up twenty patients with mild loss and twenty healthy adults. Each had thinking tests, brain scans, and blood work read by a fine lab method. The authors built a joint model of scan and blood signs and charted how well each split the two groups. They aim for a cheaper, earlier warning.
pmc-11714324:
Ahmed Negida and three co-authors hunt for brain wave signs of the ups and downs in alertness that mark Lewy body dementia, in a 2025 conference paper. These swings in focus and wakefulness hit quality of life hard. Their brain base is still poorly grasped.

The team signed up 35 patients at a Virginia clinic and split them by a standard scale into those with swings and those without. Each had rest brain wave records with eyes open and closed for three minutes each. The team pulled out the main wave speed and how much it wavered. The swing group showed a slower main speed and less of the calm alpha wave. The authors say wave tests may help spot the swings.
pmc-11714424:
Alison Fohner and co-authors searched for blood proteins tied to the pace of mental decline, split by a key gene type, in a 2025 paper. The APOE gene is the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer disease, but whether it changes which proteins track risk was unclear. Blood proteins may reveal the body processes behind the disease. The team drew on a long running heart health study in the United States.

They measured nearly five thousand proteins in blood from more than twenty seven hundred older adults who had no dementia or stroke. Thinking skills were tested each year for up to seven years. For one standard test, dozens of proteins linked to decline at different rates in carriers of one gene form. A second gene form showed its own smaller set. The results point to protein paths that may matter only for certain gene groups.
pmc-11714524:
Stephanie Frilling argues for a national Medicare system to store and share advance care directives, in a 2025 conference paper. An advance directive is a signed form that states the care a person wants at the end of life. With no central store, forms sit lost in files while families and doctors guess.

Medicare held more than 65 million members in 2023, and Alzheimer's care ranks among its costliest loads. Frilling says a shared store would let care honor each person's wishes and guide teams and kin. The federal role would cover wide gaps in state forms and keep health data safe. She notes the gap hits poor and minority groups hardest, where records are weakest. A fair store, she argues, would be a step toward health equity.
pmc-11714624:
Radmila Choate and co-authors pilot a survey of money strain in older adults tied to an Alzheimer research center in Kentucky, in a study from 2025. Care for dementia drains funds through clinic fees, drugs, lost work, and kin care, a load the team calls financial toxicity in the text after its use in cancer care. A twelve item scale, reshaped for mixed levels of thought, scored strain from naught to forty four.

Replies came from 153 adults with a mean age near eighty, most with sound thought and long schooling. Mean scores sat in the low strain zone. Strain showed no link to age, sex, schooling, or thought state in this small, well off group. The authors urge larger, wider studies of cost coping and life grade.
pmc-11714824:
Sophie Lefèvre-Arbogast and four co-authors studied in 2025 whether chemicals eaten in food raise dementia risk in older adults, and whether a fatty diet changes that risk. Food carries pesticides, industrial compounds, and metals, many of which reach the brain. The team followed 1,288 dementia-free French adults who had filled a food survey in 2001 and 2002. Exposures to 167 chemicals were estimated from diet records and national food testing.

Over about ten years, 314 people developed dementia. No chemical tied to risk in the whole group. But for eighty-two chemicals, a high-fat diet flipped the picture: higher intake meant higher risk only among high-fat eaters. Seafood and meat contaminants stood out. A combined model kept thirty-three chemicals, led by a known pollutant and nitrites.
pmc-11714924:
Attention falters in both Lewy body dementia and Alzheimer's disease, but not in the same way. Li Su combined brain scans and scalp recordings in a 2025 study to separate the attention failures of the two diseases while patients played a standard attention task.

Thirty-three Lewy body patients, fifteen Alzheimer's patients, and nineteen healthy older adults took the task during both kinds of recording. Behaviorally, Lewy body patients lost the alerting boost, while Alzheimer's patients stumbled on orienting attention instead. Source analysis tied the alerting loss to frontal-central regions and the orienting loss to lower frontal areas. Both groups over-recruited some regions for conflict handling, which the author reads as compensation.
pmc-11715124:
Jose Luchsinger and the Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group describe a long-running cohort's new dementia project in a 2025 design paper. People with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes face higher risks of memory decline and dementia, yet the shape and causes of that decline in this population remain murky.

The original trial, begun in 1996, showed lifestyle change and metformin could cut diabetes risk, and its follow-up study has tracked the cohort for over two decades across twenty-five centers. The new project adds standard dementia assessments, blood markers of Alzheimer's processes, and brain imaging. A rich stored sample collection supports the work.
pmc-11715324:
Imre Lengyel and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on eye scans in people with Down syndrome. This group faces a high risk of early Alzheimer's disease, and life spans have grown, so early warning signs are in demand.

The team used ultra-widefield imaging, which photographs a broad sweep of the retina at the back of the eye. They compared twenty people with Down syndrome with seventeen matched healthy adults. The scans proved workable in this group, which is not a given for eye tests. Vessel patterns in the retina differed between the groups, above all in those who also had Alzheimer's disease. Deposits once flagged as a sign showed no group gap here. The authors propose that retinal vessel change could help track Alzheimer's risk in Down syndrome.
pmc-11715424:
Maxie Liebscher and co-authors, with the Medit-Ageing Research Group, tied stress hormones in blood to brain health in old age. Stress is a named risk for Alzheimer's disease, yet how its hormones map onto the brain is less clear. The data came from a French study of aging and meditation. Thought, brain fuel use, blood flow, and amyloid were all in the frame.

The group held one hundred thirty-two older adults with sharp thought and no low mood. One stress hormone, epinephrine, stood out in the full group. Higher levels went with lower fuel use in three zones known to fail early in the disease. The same hormone went with lower blood flow in one of those zones. Split by sex, a second hormone tied to weaker memory in men but not in women. The split hints that stress may harm the sexes by unlike paths.
pmc-11715524:
Reem Neal, Zhiyi Yang, and Ihab Hajjar hunt risk factors for thinking loss after COVID in a 2025 study. The virus is tied to fresh cognitive trouble, which can be a step toward dementia, yet who falls prey was unclear. They mined hospital records for more than thirty two thousand patients who had caught COVID in the first three pandemic years.

Mean age sat near sixty. Post COVID thinking trouble ran higher in Black patients than White patients in both share and new case rates. Men carried more of it than women by the same reads. Risk links varied by race and sex in the joint models. The authors say follow up care should watch the hardest hit groups closest.
pmc-11715724:
Christopher G Schwarz and co-authors compare two de-facing programs, MiDeFace and mri_reface, which remove faces from brain scans before the scans are shared. A face left in a scan can be matched to a photograph and re-identify a study participant. MiDeFace ships with a common imaging suite, while mri_reface has often won past comparisons. Their 2025 study ran both tools on two datasets of scans with known photographs.

A face recognition program named the right person in about 98 percent of unmodified scans. That rate fell to about 8 percent with one tool and about 12 percent with the other. Visual checks showed one tool more often removed the whole face while keeping the whole brain. Both tools shifted later brain measurements only slightly, and by nearly the same amount. The authors give the edge to the tool with the lower match rate.
pmc-11715824:
Jin-Tai Yu built in 2025 a biological age score from healthy volunteers in a giant British health bank. The score blends body measures, blood chemistry, gene data, and thinking tests to say how old a body acts, not how many birthdays it has passed. People aging faster than their years were followed for disease and death.

Fast agers faced more circulation disease and higher mortality. Thirty-five changeable factors tied to the gap, with lung power, body mass, and grip strength near the top. One gene stood out as central to the aging rate. The map shows which levers might slow the clock.
pmc-11715924:
Mohamad J Alshikho and ten co-authors published a study in 2025 on reading the texture of bright spots in brain white matter. These spots, seen on MRI scans of older adults, vary in size and brightness because their causes vary, from small vessel disease to inflammation. Lumping them together may hide which kind threatens thinking.

Working with 161 adults from a New York aging project, the team sorted each person's spots into even, middling, and mottled zones by signal texture. They then compared fiber quality and blood flow inside each zone. Fiber and flow measures related differently across zones, with the mottled tissue behaving unlike the smooth. Texture-aware maps could sharpen how doctors judge these common scan findings.
pmc-11716124:
Brianne Breidenbach and co-authors ask in 2025 whether fitness changes how a pulsing brain measure ties to Alzheimer markers. A stiff pulse in brain arteries runs higher in the disease and tracks with more of its hallmark protein. Fitness, in turn, eases that pulse in big vessels. Their group held thirty-three adults, average age sixty-four, with no thinking problems, drawn from two Wisconsin registries.

All met tight study rules, with protein burden and spinal fluid markers in hand. The question was interaction: does a fitter heart soften the link between pulse and disease marks? If so, exercise would count as a brain-vessel lever, not just a heart one. Small, clean samples are the right first step for such a three-way question.
pmc-11716224:
Mahboubeh Motaghi, Olivier Potvin, and Simon Duchesne wrote this 2025 study comparing brain shrinkage in type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. Diabetes is known to raise dementia risk, but whether it wears the brain down in the same places as Alzheimer's was unclear. They built atrophy maps from MRI scans of more than forty-three thousand UK Biobank participants and a second Alzheimer's cohort.

The two maps overlapped significantly across the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes.
