People with diabetes showed extra thinning in regions Alzheimer's hits, including the memory-critical hippocampus. Statistical tests could not tell the diseases' footprints apart. The authors read this as strong evidence that diabetes is a substantial Alzheimer's risk factor, not merely a fellow traveler. If the pathways truly merge, protecting the diabetic brain may borrow strategies from dementia prevention.
pmc-11716324:
Jason Russell and co-authors study brain chemistry and amyloid in adults with Down syndrome in a 2025 paper. Adults with Down syndrome carry the world's highest risk of Alzheimer's disease, since an extra copy of a chromosome raises amyloid production early. A brain system based on acetylcholine also declines early and shapes thinking.

Near two hundred adults from two cohorts had brain scans and anatomy measures. The team tested how amyloid load relates to the health of that chemical system in the basal forebrain. Cross-sectional links are reported in the study. The work may help time interventions in a group where Alzheimer's is near certain with age.
pmc-11716424:
Palpatzis and co-authors study in 2025 why an inner brain area linked to memory shrinks more in women over time. They followed 71 older adults without dementia for about seven years, with brain scans at least three times. At the start they noted signs of low mood and levels of a protein called tau in the same brain area.

The group tested whether low mood and tau worked together to speed shrinkage, and whether that link differed in women and men. They also checked two other brain areas to see if the effect was local. The work may help explain why memory loss and low mood often travel together in later life.
pmc-11716524:
Yue Cai and co-authors ask if school years shield the mind in Alzheimer disease in a 2025 study. Past snapshots hint that more school slows mind loss once the disease starts. The team used a large scan cohort with plaque, tangle, and brain form reads. They split folk by plaque and tangle state and by school years at the mid line of 16. Mind tests ran over time in five fields.

In the group with both plaque and tangles, high school years tied to slow loss in a broad test and in language. Path checks showed how: more gray matter and more sugar burn in set zones carried the shield. Low tangles in two zones also carried the gain. Plaque paths did not. The authors say school gains work through brain bulk and tangles, a clue for guard plans.
pmc-11716624:
Konstantinos Ioannou and co-authors published a study in 2025 on what a lone positive amyloid test really means. Doctors sort patients by two spinal fluid markers, one for amyloid and one for tau. Some people test positive for amyloid alone, and it is unclear whether they have Alzheimer's disease or a mix of other brain conditions.

The team studied 71 people whose brains were examined after death and whose fluid was tested years earlier. Both amyloid-positive groups scored lower and declined faster than the others, whatever their tau status. Brain exams then showed how often other diseases were also present. The study guides how doctors should read a single positive result.
pmc-11716724:
Aparna Lalana Venugopal studies how mild memory loss and dementia differ by sex in Bengaluru, India, in 2025. Worldwide, dementia risk is reported higher in women than men. The reasons are not clear, and urban Indian data were scarce.

A team tested 1,234 city adults aged sixty and over in 2021, going door to door. Tests covered thought, daily tasks, and a risk questionnaire on heart disease and high blood pressure. Six point five percent had mild loss; one point nine percent had dementia. Men had more mild loss, at seven point nine percent against five point three for women. Women had more dementia, at two point seven percent against one point one for men. Heart disease was more common in men, and high blood pressure in women. Men were older and had more years of school, on average. Venugopal concludes that conditions and risk patterns differ by sex here.
pmc-11716824:
Bernadette Fausto and six co-authors weighed genes against life habits as foretellers of an Alzheimer's risk sign in a 2025 study. The sign is how well a person carries past learning into new cases, a skill that fades early in the disease. Their group was older African American adults with no thinking loss, studied in deep detail.

Four hundred seventy two people gave survey answers on health and daily life, plus spit samples for gene checks on known risk genes. A Bayes style learning method, paired with a fix for gaps in the data, ranked which factors foretold the learning score best. The work aims to sort nature from nurture for early risk in a group too often left out of such studies.
pmc-11716924:
Balaji Kannappan and co-authors study a 2025 family-based question in Alzheimer's research. Some Puerto Rican families carry a gene change called G206A that causes early disease, yet carriers fall ill at very different ages. The team asked whether two common gene variants shift that timing.

The study covered 505 people from 87 families. The G206A change raised risk sharply, as expected. One variant added a modest extra risk, while the other leaned protective but not clearly so. Results also varied between ethnic subgroups, and some groups were too small for firm claims. The work shows how background genes can soften or sharpen a strong risk.
pmc-11717324:
John Delgado, Logan Atkins, Micah Pippin, and Jessan Jishu report a case in two thousand twenty-four of a newborn with a cluster of birth defects. The cluster resembles the VACTERL association, a named pattern that links defects of the spine, anus, heart, windpipe-food pipe connection, kidneys, and limbs. Its causes remain an open puzzle.

The full-term baby was found to have a two-leaflet aortic valve, a small hole in the heart, and an abnormal link between the windpipe and food pipe. Further findings included an uneven crying face and genital differences. The authors weigh environmental and genetic factors and compare a similar pattern called CHARGE syndrome.
pmc-11718524:
Samantha Pfiffner, Arif Musa, Ira Winer, and Ali Harb propose burning shut the ureter to treat urinary fistulae in a paper from 2024. Fistulae are abnormal passages that leak urine into nearby organs or skin. They follow infection, radiation, cancer, or surgery and cause deep social distress. Standard fixes include surgery, diversion, and blocking the tube with coils, but each has limits. The authors suggest scoping in and ablating the tube's lining instead.

Laser or radiofrequency burns would scar the tube closed. Early animal and human results look promising. The approach could suit patients too frail for surgery at lower cost. The authors stress that proper trials must come before routine use.
pmc-11721124:
Public health planners need honest forecasts of epidemic death rates, including the worst plausible cases. Oleg Gaidai and co-authors test a reliability method, borrowed from engineering, on Singapore's COVID-19 records. The approach treats a health system like a structure under load. It estimates the risk of extreme death rates over chosen time spans and regions.

They cross-checked the method against a standard statistical rival, the bivariate Weibull model, on the raw clinical data. The authors report that their approach suits multi-region systems watched over long periods. When the underlying pattern is steady, it can project future risks with confidence intervals. The 2023 study offers the method for health planning beyond COVID-19.
pmc-11721524:
Julian M. Burwell, Alejandro Bugarini, and Mathangi Rajaram-Gilkes made a training case in 2024 for an old skull operation. The operation removes the front of the skull on both sides. It once treated midline brain masses often. Modern neurosurgery now uses it far less. The authors argue its teaching value remains high. They demonstrated the full procedure on a preserved cadaver. Steps ran from the scalp cut to keyhole placement. Suturing of the great top vein was included. Part of the frontal lobe was removed under a microscope.

Wide exposure lets teachers discuss tissue handling in detail. Many techniques fit inside one training session. Protecting the great vein teaches risk management directly. The authors say programs undervalue the procedure as teaching. Its clinical role is now narrow and selective. Its classroom role could be much wider, they argue. Residents gain structured practice in a low-stakes setting.
pmc-11725324:
Intekhab Hossain and co-authors report a case of double blockage treated with scopes in this 2024 article. A 53-year-old man with inoperable pancreatic cancer arrived jaundiced and vomiting. His bile duct stent, placed over a year earlier for a stone blockage, had clogged, and a tumor-driven narrowing now also blocked the first part of his small intestine, trapping food.

The team first widened the gut narrowing and placed a metal mesh tube exactly short of the old bile stent. Two days later they passed a scope through the new tube and swapped the clogged plastic bile stent for a metal one. His jaundice cleared, he ate by discharge on day two, and chemotherapy restarted on day twelve. The authors stress order and placement when both passages are blocked.
pmc-11726224:
Igor Łoniewski and co-authors review gut microbe tuning as part of surgical preparation in a 2024 paper. Prehabilitation readies patients for surgery through exercise and diet before the operation. The review argues the gut community belongs on that checklist.

Surgery, stress, antibiotics, and poor diet disturb gut microbes, raising infection risk and slowing recovery. Gathered trials and reviews suggest probiotics and related products can cut wound infections, sharpen immune responses, and speed healing. The authors favor tailoring the mix to each patient and operation type. They also caution that standard regimens and safety proof are still missing, so more trials are needed.
pmc-11726724:
Boris Kos and co-authors published this case series in 2024 on mouth cancer. After surgeons cut out a mouth tumor, they patch the hole with a flap of skin moved from the arm or chest. A new, second cancer can later grow, but growth on the patch itself is rare. The team present three cases where a fresh primary tumor arose on flap skin inside the mouth.

Two cases sat on arm flaps, and one count covers chest flaps used in the series. No known cause yet explains why moved skin would host a new cancer. The cases show the chance is real, if small. The authors' lesson is plain: at follow-up, doctors should examine the flap itself with the same care they give the neck and the first tumor's site.
pmc-11727024:
Researchers compare in 2024 gene activity in blood from heart patients who smoke and who do not smoke. Smoking is a known risk for heart artery disease. How it shifts gene activity in Hungarian patients has had little study so far.

The team pairs eleven samples by age and sex, all free of weight, drink, sugar, and pressure issues. Sequencing finds 58 genes with clear shifts between the groups. Smokers show less healthy fat levels in blood, though some shifts miss firm proof. Heat maps show the two groups split cleanly by gene pattern. No single body pathway stands out, but the work gives a base for care tuned to each patient.
pmc-11727424:
Bárbara Costa and co-authors review a dilemma in treating infections during pregnancy: the drugs that protect mother and fetus may harm their cells. Their 2024 review examines how antiviral medicines, especially those used against HIV and the coronavirus, can raise oxidative stress. Pregnancy already shifts the body's balance, and drug handling changes with it.

Some studies link these drugs to cell stress and mitochondrial strain in pregnancy; others find their use generally safe. The authors map that conflict honestly, including what remains unknown. They survey natural defenses and ways to blunt the damage without weakening antiviral power. The stakes are uneven: untreated infection is certainly dangerous, while drug harms are suspected and long-term. Their call is for research that can weigh both sides, including follow-up of exposed children, rather than reassurance by default.
pmc-11727624:
Hu and colleagues review in 2024 how the Hedgehog signaling pathway drives fibrosis and where drug efforts stand. Hedgehog signaling guides embryo development and tissue repair. When it stays switched on wrongly, tissues lay down excess matrix and scar. The review explains the pathway's machinery, then tracks its role organ by organ, across liver, kidney, airways, lungs, and beyond.

Some effects are shared, but many differ by tissue, which the authors stress as context dependence. Inhibitors aimed at the pathway are in preclinical and clinical trials. The review closes with the challenges of turning those drugs into working anti-fibrotic therapies.
pmc-11727724:
A team including Cristina Arroqui tests whether high-pressure treatment improves a Spanish rice. The rice, Nuovo Maratelli, suits paella because it holds its shape and soaks up flavor. The team pressed the rice at two high levels for ten minutes, then boiled or microwaved it. Pressing changed the look of the starch grains but not how the rice paste behaved when cooked.

Cooking times fell at both pressure levels. Rice pressed at the lower level and then microwaved came out softer and less sticky, tied to starch that leaked in cooking. The paper presents pressing as a useful first step for better cooked rice.
pmc-11728324:
George Kaptay marks the 150th anniversary of Gibbs's phase rule by generalizing it, in a paper published in 2024. The phase rule counts how many variables can change freely in a mixture at equilibrium, and it underpins every phase diagram in materials science and chemistry. Kaptay argues the classic statement hides assumptions worth making explicit.

He separates state variables into compositional and non-compositional kinds, and replaces the rule's fixed number two with the count of independent non-compositional variables. He also adds a component rule for choosing independent components, adjusts the count at special points such as azeotropes, and connects the maximum number of coexisting phases to the diagram's dimensions. Examples run from one-component systems to nano-scale diagrams.
pmc-11728524:
A virus that often harms newborns' brains rarely reaches the brain in adults, and the reason may be age itself. A research team infected mice with the mouse version of cytomegalovirus at several ages. They then checked whether the virus entered the brain and stirred inflammation there.

Infection during the newborn stages did reach the brain and trigger inflammation. In weaned and adult mice, the same infection did neither. The contrast matches the human pattern, where the danger concentrates in babies infected before birth. The 2024 study sets up a base for working out how the virus breaks in early in life, and what could stop it.
pmc-11731924:
Savitri, Rahmawaty, and Minarno study tiny silver particles made with the seaweed Fucus vesiculosus. This brown alga is rich in fucoxanthin, phlorotannin, fucoidan, sterols, and astaxanthin. The team hoped the mix would fight free radicals, block collagenase, and kill germs. Collagenase is an enzyme that breaks down collagen, so blocking it has skin care appeal.

The team checked the size and spread of the grains with a sizing tool. Tests then gauged how well they fought free radicals, blocked collagenase, and killed germs. The results judge if seaweed based silver particles can serve in health or beauty goods. Such use would rest on how strong each of those three actions proves to be.
pmc-11732324:
Ralph Mobbs surveys the rise of scope-based spine surgery in a 2024 review. In this craft, a thin tube with a camera lets surgeons fix spine ills through tiny cuts. Once a fringe craft, it now sits near the core of spine care, with journals logging a surge of studies and surgeon uptake.

Mobbs traces how the tools and skills grew, and why the field's own journal gave it a full special issue in 2020. Gains claimed for the craft span faster heals, less post-work pain, and fewer harms. The review weighs that promise and maps where the craft may head next.
pmc-11732624:
Saim Mahmood Khan, Kamal Huda Khan, and Filzah Imam write in a 2024 letter about using the drug perampanel for children with Dravet syndrome, a rare and severe epilepsy. They respond to a study of the drug's efficacy and tolerability in young patients, and raise points they feel need deeper treatment.

Dravet syndrome usually begins in the first year of life, often involves a mutation in the SCN1A gene, and produces many seizure types that resist standard medicines. The letter writers argue that judging perampanel fairly requires separating its effects by seizure type, since the drug may not act evenly across them. They call for closer study of the syndrome's mechanisms to guide better treatment.
pmc-11742124:
Heart and chest surgery saves lives across Africa, but the money to deliver it safely is chronically short. Cynthia Nwalibe and seven co-authors review the financing gap in this 2024 paper, sifting sixty studies down to fifty that map where funding exists, where it leaks, and what care actually costs. The picture is stark.

Most patients pay out of pocket; insurance coverage is thin, so families face ruinous bills or go without operations. Building a surgical center and staffing it are expensive, and underfunding tracks with worse outcomes and higher deaths. The authors sort the barriers, from budget allocation to donor dependence, and propose routes to steadier support. Their conclusion is that money, more than skill, is the binding constraint on African cardiothoracic care.
pmc-11749024:
Faleh Alyazidi and four co-authors check how well death certificates match family interviews in Saudi Arabia in a 2025 paper. Where certification is weak, a verbal autopsy, in which relatives describe the death, can fill gaps in vital data. The team compare causes of death from medical records with those from interviews for people on a diabetes register who died over a four year span.

Agreement between the two sources was moderate at the population level, but shares for single cause groups differed widely. Record based causes overstated hormone and breathing related deaths and understated circulation deaths, the authors find. Interview based causes looked plausible against past Saudi data.
pmc-11772424:
Anastasia Poliakova and co-authors compare plant silica in fresh palm leaves and old manuscripts in a 2024 paper, per its head. Palm leaf manuscripts served South and Southeast Asia for centuries. Their silica grains, phytoliths, may carry clues of make and age.

Two palm species used for manuscripts anchor the study. Fresh, dried, and herbarium leaves gave the base patterns. Twenty five manuscripts of each palm were read the same way. Manuscripts date from the sixteenth to the early twentieth century. Silica sets split fresh from manuscript leaves in kind and count. Such splits may one day sort true old leaves from new.
pmc-11781224:
Ahmad Shamabadi and co-authors test whether pentoxifylline, a drug that improves blood flow and calms inflammation, can ease the negative symptoms of schizophrenia. Those symptoms, such as flat affect and withdrawal, lack good treatments. The trial enrolled stable outpatients who had taken risperidone for at least two months. Half received pentoxifylline twice a day for eight weeks; the other half received a matched placebo.

The pentoxifylline group improved more on the negative symptom scale, with the gap clear by week four and larger by week eight. Their response rate was also better. Depression scores, movement side effects, and other symptom scores were similar in both groups. Remission came to 37.1 percent on the drug against 14.7 percent on placebo, though that gap was not statistically firm. The authors call the drug safe, tolerable, and helpful for the primary negative symptoms of chronic schizophrenia.
pmc-11788324:
Ashanul Haque and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study of new drug candidates against a brain enzyme tied to Alzheimer's disease. The enzyme MARK4 helps drive the protein tangles behind memory loss. Blocking it is a promising but unproven strategy.

A series of pyrimidine-based compounds was synthesized and fully characterized. Laboratory assays measured how well each blocked the enzyme's energy use. Computer docking and long motion simulations tested binding stability. Drug-likeness and toxicity were screened in software as well. The combined wet and dry work narrows which chemical shapes deserve animal testing next.
pmc-11792724:
Mohammad Reza Khami and co-authors report work from two thousand twenty-four on a questionnaire about COVID-19 for dental patients. During the outbreak, clinics needed to know what patients understood about the virus and how they felt about care. No trusted tool existed for that purpose in both English and Persian.

The team drafted the form from a literature review, then translated it. Experts rated each item, and sixty adults in each language group tested the draft online. Scores for clarity and consistency varied by item, so the team removed, merged, or revised weak questions. The final form holds nine background questions and forty-six items across five sections. The authors judge it valid and reliable for its stated use.
pmc-11806224:
Good management may save hospital patients as surely as good medicine, and a global survey scores Chinese hospitals on that claim. Qinghong He, Gordon G Liu, Jinyang Chen, Luoqi Yuan, Xuezhi Hong, and Zhihua Zhang run the analysis in a 2024 paper. The survey, run from 2014 to 2016, graded management practices in a national sample. Outcomes covered heart attack, heart failure, child pneumonia, and bypass surgery.

Higher management scores tied to lower heart attack deaths and fewer bypass complications. Stays ran shorter in better-managed hospitals as well. Staff turnover and satisfaction ratings joined the outcome set. The authors place China's scores against the world field. Management reform is pitched as a health lever.
pmc-11830924:
Infertility touches many couples, and polycystic ovary syndrome is one of its most common causes. Narges Gholizadeh and co-authors ask, in a 2024 study, whether saliva can reveal the chemical stress linked to the syndrome. Saliva is far easier to collect than blood or follicle fluid.

The team compared forty women with the syndrome, all in fertility treatment, against forty controls. They measured antioxidant enzymes and a key hormone in both saliva and blood. Levels differed clearly between the groups in both fluids, and the hormone ran higher in the syndrome group. Matching saliva and blood patterns could open a gentler way to track these patients.
pmc-11835924:
Wu, Nie, He, Li, and Xu ran a mouse study in twenty twenty-four. They tested a fruit extract against liver fibrosis. The fruit, Fructus Akebiae, is used in Chinese medicine. The team scarred the livers of mice with a toxic chemical. Groups of mice got the extract at three dose levels. Staff tracked tissue change and key scarring markers. They paired gut microbe reads with liver chemical profiles. Computer maps added guesses at the targets hit.

The extract clearly eased liver scarring in treated mice. It rebalanced gut microbes, raising a helpful Akkermansia group. Liver chemical profiles moved back toward normal sugar handling. Some microbes tracked closely with set sugar chemicals. Guessed targets centered on swelling and cell death paths. The team puts it forward as a strong treatment hope.
pmc-11839624:
Rasha Elmeihy and co-authors pair a fungus and a bacterium to fight late wilt of maize in Egypt in two thousand twenty-five. The hosted text dates the work to two thousand twenty-four. Late wilt, caused by a fungus that invades plant vessels, brings heavy losses to Egyptian maize.

The partner fungus attacks the wilt fungus with enzymes, poisons, and scent compounds, and its filtered broth also slows growth. The bacterium likewise slows the wilt and makes plant growth hormones. When the wilt fungus is near, the partner fungus shifts its chemical output in clear ways. A field trial on wilt-prone and wilt-resistant maize types tests the pair under farm terms, as a greener swap for chemical sprays.
pmc-11849024:
Karin Bage and seven co-authors link views on sexual and reproductive rights with people's sense of control over their own fertility, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Data came from the World Values Survey in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Zimbabwe, with just over three thousand adults. The team scored support for these rights and for gender equality, then compared people with high and low reproductive agency.

People with stronger agency tended to hold more supportive views, above all on fair norms for men, on health services in this field, and on gender equality. Links varied more by country than by sex. Schooling, religion, class, and country also tracked with agency. The authors say values and rights support move with real choice in family life, which programs should keep in view.
pmc-11866324:
Ira Chang and co-authors test a robotic ultrasound scanner in a study published in 2024 for stroke workups. A small hole between the heart's chambers lets clots cross and cause strokes, and finding it matters. Standard checks are either insensitive, invasive, or need scarce trained staff.

A robot-guided Doppler scan of the head offers an automated route. Of 212 stroke patients scanned, most could perform the strain maneuver, and just under six in ten showed a right-to-left shunt. Severity scores combine with a risk score to judge whether the hole likely caused the stroke. The authors assess the robot as a feasible screening tool.
pmc-11887824:
Camille Tonneau and co-authors present a case report, published in 2024, on a leftover embryonic cord that blocked an adult's intestine. The omphalomesenteric duct links the gut to the yolk sac before birth and normally vanishes. In this rare case a fibrous band from that duct survived in a man aged eighteen who arrived with fever, belly pain, and flu like symptoms.

A scan suggested a blockage, and surgery found the band stretching from the navel to the colon's supporting tissue, with bowel wrapped around it. Such remnants mostly cause trouble in children and mimic other conditions, so imaging rarely shows the band itself. The authors stress that surgery both settles the diagnosis and treats the blockage in cases like this.
pmc-11888624:
Four dentists led by Malathi report a rare jaw tumour that lacked its namesake trait. The tumour is a slow growth in the jaw bone first named in 1955, and it makes up a tiny share of jaw tumours. Most cases strike adults in their thirties and forties. Its name comes from lime-like flecks it forms, yet this case formed none, which makes it a rare non-calcifying form.

The patient was a 63-year-old man with a sore swelling in his right lower face, grown over four months. Scans showed a tooth-linked bone loss that looked like a plain gum abscess at first read. Tissue tests under the scope gave the true call of tumour. Age and mimicry both mark the case as a warn tale: odd jaw lumps merit full tissue proof.
pmc-11892724:
Omar Khan and Katherine Smith open a journal issue in 2024 with a look back at the pandemic years. They recall how news of a new disease came from China in late 2019. The illness then spread fast across the United States and the world.

The editors trace how care, schools, and work changed under lockdowns. They note telehealth, shots in parking lots, staff burnout, and gaps in broadband access. They also note poor outcomes, slow vaccine uptake, and false claims in the United States. The piece frames the issue that follows on public health lessons learned since then.
pmc-11893324:
Letizia Carrera sketches in 2024 a new kind of travel for older people, past both health trips and the classic sun, sand, and sea package. Rich lands are aging fast, and the image of old age is changing with it. Today's seniors seek company, leisure, and culture as parts of a fuller sense of wellbeing.

A qualitative study sorts senior travelers into types with unlike wants. Those types give the travel trade a map for richer offers. Conditions that make a trip feel complete, not just pleasant, are drawn out. The catalog dates the piece 2025; the head gives 2024.
pmc-11895024:
Chudan Liang and twelve co-authors present fast tests in two thousand twenty-four for counting intact, infectious flu virus. Standard molecular tests cannot tell live virus from dead copies. Their two methods aim to measure only H1N1 virus that can still infect cells.

One method lets cells absorb the virus before running the PCR test, and the other uses a dye that blocks dead virus DNA. Both reached low detection limits, the cell method being far more sensitive. Counts from each tracked the standard infectivity assay closely, so infectivity could be estimated. Tests worked on inactivated samples, wastewater, and biological material. The authors see uses in labs, clinics, and wastewater watch.
pmc-11898624:
Juliane Helm and seven co-authors tracked how starving poplar trees spend their stored carbon in a 2024 study. When drought or leaf loss cuts new carbon, trees live off reserves, but which pools they tap, and when, was poorly known. The team ringed tree stems to cut the flow of sugars from the canopy, creating a lasting shortage below the cut.

Over three growing seasons they measured breathing gases, stored carbon, and the age of the carbon burned. The trees survived long shortages by shifting from fresh sugars to older stores, with fats joining the fuel mix. Carbon dating showed the burned fuel grew older over time. The authors say this slow burn may explain why tree decline can take years before death.
pmc-11959124:
Eve Namisango, Tonia Onyeka, Nafula Esther and colleagues reviewed how Africa can build the research base for palliative care in cancer in 2024. Need is highest where resources are thinnest, and the cancer burden is expected to double by 2050, yet African evidence remains scarce.

Scanning published and grey literature, the team found several working models: community engagement, centres of excellence, knowledge exchange platforms, research networks, and practice-based networks. Partnerships within the Global South, and between South and North, also recur. The models overlap rather than compete. The authors conclude that the evidence base is growing and that these identifiable strategies are steering the growth, offering a map for funders and institutions.
pmc-11971824:
David Ogbolu and five co-authors examined drug resistance in a lung and wound germ collected in Nigeria in a 2024 study. The germ has become a hospital threat, causing severe infections in frail patients. The team tested samples from sick and healthy people against drugs and read their full gene codes.

Every sample resisted many drugs, including the usual first choice for this germ. All carried gene sets that block several drug families, from common antibiotics to sulfa drugs. The samples also held small loops of extra DNA that can move resistance between germs. The authors warn that such spread narrows treatment choices for a germ that already leaves few. They call for tighter watch on resistance in the region.
pmc-11975524:
Wang and co-authors report a 2024 case of hidden breast cancer that first showed as a blocked bowel. Hidden breast cancer means no source lump can be found by touch, scans, or tissue tests. The patient was a woman aged sixty-seven with no past illness, seen at a hospital in Zhuzhou, China.

Scans showed thick bowel walls and swollen nodes near the armpit. Surgery on the narrowed bowel gave tissue that read as a bowel tumor at first. Stain tests then pointed to breast cancer spread, with hormone marks and a breast-linked protein. Node samples found tiny cancer foci, though the breast tissue itself stayed clear.
pmc-11978424:
Guillaume Baille and co-authors present a 2024 case report on a rare muscle disease with brain involvement. The disease packs muscle fibers with dense tube-like clumps. It causes weak upper muscles, cramps with effort, muscle pain, and eye signs. Brain and nerve involvement is rare and poorly mapped. Three genes are often blamed for the condition.

The patient is a 35-year-old man who had floppy muscles at birth, slow motor growth, seizures, and hearing loss. During a covid infection he developed jerks, confusion, and marked weakness. A shoulder muscle biopsy showed the classic clumps. Whole-genome sequencing found no genetic cause. The authors say the case widens the known range of this disease when the nervous system is involved.
pmc-12008324:
Kailas Datkhile and co-authors studied gene variants and chemo side effects in breast cancer, in this 2024 paper. DNA repair genes may shape how patients bear treatment. The team followed 104 patients in India who got two common chemo drugs.

Older age linked to mouth sores and nerve pain. Higher body weight linked to low blood counts, fever with low counts, and nerve pain. One variant in a repair gene tripled the odds of nerve pain. Another variant raised the odds of fever with low counts and of nausea and vomiting. The authors say gene checks could help flag patients who need closer watch during chemo.
pmc-12040224:
Cancer care eats time as well as health, and a 2024 study by Arjun Gupta and co-authors asks patients, caregivers, and clinicians how that time burden feels. The field has lately named this cost the time toxicity of cancer care, but the views of those who live it were little known.

The team ran in-depth interviews at a major cancer center in Minnesota during 2023. They spoke with adults who had advanced gut cancers on drug treatment, the unpaid partners who help them, and the staff who treat them. The talks covered which parts of care feel most time-heavy, who bears the load most, and what the lost time costs people. The study gives the new concept a human grounding.
pmc-12225524:
Vocca and co-authors audit the safety of nerve pain drugs as actually used in an Italian hospital clinic, in a 2023 study. Over two and a half years, 2,370 patients came to the pain clinic, and about a third with confirmed neuropathic pain entered the analysis. Every patient carried at least one other illness and took on average five drugs a day, a fertile ground for bad reactions and interactions.

Reactions were documented in 112 patients on a standard probability scale. No link turned up between reactions and dose or patient traits. The authors stress structured checking for interactions in this heavily medicated group.
pmc-12315724:
Mira Erhart and co-authors read, in a 2024 study, how heart beats in a stress test map to brain work, man by man. Stress replies vary by folk and by hour, which breaks set task-phase reads. The team used each folk's own heart rate as the stress gauge. Eighty-three sound adults did a scan stress task with three phases, each of five one-minute work blocks and rest gaps. Work was mind sums; the stress phase added harsh social grades. Pulse was logged the whole run. Heart rate, as a block mean, rode the task in one math frame for all blocks.

High heart rates tied to low work in the twin hippocampus, amygdala, and insula. Those zones are core stress hubs.
pmc-12384224:
SoYeun Lim and Jun-Ah Song sift world work for the parts of best nurse care for a good death in dementia. Such deaths span home, ward, and care house ground, with kin at the core. Six banks were searched in two tongues to an April 2024 line. Twenty-seven works made the cut for the theme sort.

Four care parts with sixteen sub-parts fell out of the sort. Plan talks held long pre-need, joint calls with kin, care bent to the wants of the ill, and tech aids form the four. Each part breaks into acts ward teams can post as rules. Death care for this group gains a shared parts list.
pmc-12661824:
Carlo Caffarelli and co-authors pick the top child health papers of two thousand twenty-four in a review dated two thousand twenty-five. The picks come from one journal, the Italian Journal of Pediatrics, across the full spread of child medicine. Fields range from allergy and heart care to newborn care, gut health, and social media.

Each chosen paper is read for what it can change in daily care of children. Topics also span lung illness, kidney disease, brain health, feeding, and end-of-life care. The review aims to give busy clinicians a guided tour of the year's most useful work in one place. It flags where care of common and rare child conditions can improve.
pmc-12663124:
Alessia Zinzi leads a team that reviews a pain drug and a grave blood risk. Their study from twenty twenty-five deals with metamizole. The drug was pulled in some lands over agranulocytosis risk.

That risk means a sharp drop in white blood cells. Yet the drug stays in wide use across the world. A Europe safety body began a fresh review of it. The team checked past studies and a Europe report data set. Just a small set of studies met their rules. Proof stays unclear, and reports skew female and adult.
pmc-12666224:
Edwine Barasa and co-authors warn poor countries off tempting shortcuts in a 2025 health financing commentary. Donor money is shrinking, so low- and middle-income governments must fund more of their own health systems, and the authors see four policy turns they call unacceptable.

The list: pushing costs onto patients at the point of care, leaning too hard on contributory insurance, letting basic primary care be displaced, and abandoning community services for facility-only models. Each looks fiscally tidy, they argue, while quietly eroding equity and universal coverage. Their plea is for efficiency and public financing that shields the poorest during the transition.
pmc-12667724:
Chaofan Cao and colleagues trace a three-protein relay by which cigarette smoke makes lung cells burst in inflammatory death, in this study from twenty twenty-five. The death mode is pyroptosis, and the disease is COPD, where smoke-damaged airways inflame and narrow for good. Cell and mouse models of smoke exposure let the team follow the signal.

A stress gene, EGR1, emerged as the pivotal responder. It switches on a second protein, USP44, which stabilizes a third, TRAF6, by stripping off its disposal tags. Stabilized TRAF6 then promotes the fiery cell death. Blocking either of the first two proteins sharply cut pyroptosis in cells. In mice, knocking down USP44 eased the COPD-like lung damage from smoke. The authors name the relay a drug target: interrupt it, and smoke's slow burning of the lung might slow with it.
pmc-12681424:
Mikhail Syromyatnikov led a team that studied a gut microbe in mice in two thousand twenty-five. The microbe is Akkermansia muciniphila. It lives in the mucus layer of the gut. It draws much hope as a probiotic, a live germ taken for health gain. How it works is still not clear, though.

The team used lipopolysaccharide, a toxin from germs, to set off inflammation through the whole body. Then they read the genes of the gut germs to see how the mix changed when mice ate the microbe. Three germ families stood out in all groups. The fed mice had a more mixed gut mix. Paths that build and break amino acids, work on folic acid, and make sugars shifted too. In the end, the microbe cut the harm the toxin did to the gut.
pmc-12690024:
Alain Bicart-See and co-authors track infection debris in septic shock blood in a 2025 study. Sepsis care lacks markers that clearly forecast who will recover. Mannose-binding lectin is an immune protein that grabs most germs and their wreckage. An engineered version coats magnetic beads to fish those patterns from patient blood. Adults in intensive care with septic shock are sampled often across five days.

Pattern levels are mapped against whether sepsis persists past day five and against routine scores, they report. Early sampling runs every six hours, then spreads out. The study tests whether the debris curve can guide care for the critically ill in real time.
pmc-12691824:
Abdulmonem Alsiddiky and ten co-authors survey public views on scoliosis in Saudi Arabia in a study from 2025. Scoliosis, a sideways curve of the spine, is often missed until late. During a national awareness campaign, more than two thousand people answered questions on what they know about the condition, school screening, and treatment choices.

Most people had heard of scoliosis, but fewer than one in five said they understood it well. Support for school screening and early checks was very high, with age eight the favored screening age. Braces and surgery were accepted more than watchful waiting. Lack of knowledge was the main barrier named.
pmc-12693124:
Ziming Zhou and six co-authors engineered in 2025 tougher green quantum dots for display diffuser plates. Quantum dots give displays their rich color, but heat and light degrade them, above all inside the plastic plates that spread backlight. The team built dots with an alloy core and a thick multi-layer shell.

Careful tuning balanced color purity, glow width, and brightness. Swapping the surface coating and thickening the shell raised stability a great deal. The dots were then mixed into plate material as a masterbatch for production. Steadier dots mean screens that keep their color over years of use.
pmc-12693824:
Zhiqiang Cao and co-authors present a 2025 mouse study testing whether a plant fibre added to a low-fat diet helps type 2 diabetes more than the diet alone. Low-fat diets are widely advised but often disappoint and are hard to keep. The fibre, a partly broken-down guar gum, feeds gut microbes that matter in this disease.

Diabetic mice were split into four groups for twelve weeks: a high-fat control, the low-fat diet alone, and the diet plus low or high fibre doses. The diet alone fixed blood fats but not blood sugar. Adding the fibre cut fasting sugar and insulin resistance and raised helpful gut bacteria and their useful by-products.
pmc-12694124:
Kenneth Ladd Seldeen and co-authors study how hard interval exercise affects muscle in old mice. Their 2025 paper looks at a receptor for vitamin D in muscle. Exercise is known to raise levels of that receptor for a short time. The team asks if interval work does the same, and where the rise occurs.

Old male mice did a single ten-minute session, and tissue was taken at set times after. Signs of inflammation peaked at four hours and faded by 24 hours. Receptor protein stayed up at 24 hours, though its gene signal faded. The receptor sat at the edge of fibers, with satellite cells and immune cells. The authors say the rise likely comes from those helper cells, not the fibers.
pmc-12694824:
Hammed Mogaji and co-authors set out a plan in 2025 for a review of how disease-control work is delivered in poor city neighborhoods of poorer countries. Germs thrive where housing is dense, water is unsafe, and clinics are hard to reach. How programs adapt to such settings is little mapped.

The review will follow standard scoping rules and search four large databases for work since the year 2000. Two-stage screening will sort finds by set rules, and data will be pulled into sheets for analysis. The team frames its questions around who is served, what is adapted, and where. They expect to chart the approaches programs have taken and the methods used to study them. Gaps found will guide later programs and trials.
pmc-12695024:
Watching the same neurons fire across days is the only way to see a brain circuit grow up, but matching cells between imaging sessions is painstaking. Jure Majnik and co-authors present Track2p, a tracking method based on registering images session by session. They validated it on calcium imaging from the whisker cortex of mouse pups across the first postnatal week, following several hundred individual neurons.

The tracking held up over the full week, letting the team measure how each neuron's activity and stability evolved. One clear transition emerged: activity statistics shifted as arousal states began to shape the cortex. Beyond that finding, the authors offer Track2p as a general tool for developmental studies, including work on how circuits deviate in neurodevelopmental disorders.
pmc-12695424:
Freda Yang and three co-authors report a girl whose illness looked like cystic fibrosis but proved to be a rarer syndrome, in a 2025 case report. Both conditions cause repeat chest infections and poor pancreas function. The girl, aged six, had a wet cough, fatty stools, and repeat infections. Early tests gave mixed signals.

Her sweat test was borderline, and the cystic fibrosis gene panel was negative. Other signs included odd liver values, faulty white cells, and bone anomalies. Deeper gene analysis found two changes in a gene tied to the rarer syndrome. One change was known to cause disease, and the other was new. Follow-up over forty-two years showed ongoing low white cell counts and chest infections. Milder forms can reach adulthood, the authors note.
pmc-12695924:
Tomoyoshi Kaneko and co-authors describe six new viruses that infect gut bacteria, in a 2025 study. Such viruses shape microbe communities and may serve as tools in biotech, yet few can be grown in the lab. The team drew samples from pig farm waste water and city sewage. They then studied the new viruses through their genes, shapes, and the range of hosts each one can infect.

Five of the six form a tight group inside a known virus family branch. The team proposes that this group is a new genus, and that its members fall into two species. The sixth virus did not fit the new group. Its traits strain the current rules for sorting viruses, a case for more flexible rules. Fine shifts in tail fiber proteins matched shifts in host range, a clue to how these viruses pick their targets.
pmc-12696224:
Warren Clements and co-authors compare the costs of two procedures that prevent repeat stomach vein bleeding in a study from 2025. After a gastric variceal bleed, guidelines offer two fixes: a liver shunt called TIPS, or a vein-blocking route called BRTO. Clinical results get much study; costs get little.

The team priced every case treated from 2017 to 2024. Procedure, ward, and other hospital costs were all counted. Ward costs used elective stays only, to keep emergency noise out. The tally takes the health system's view throughout. Side-by-side costs let doctors weigh money alongside safety when they plan prevention. Such data matter where budgets force hard choices.
pmc-12697924:
Hong Cheng and co-authors built a living, electrically conductive tube to bridge cut peripheral nerves in rats. Nerve grafts from the patient are the standard repair, but they cost a second injury site. Artificial guide tubes often lack the biological and electrical cues nerves want. The team's tube combines carbon nanotubes coated in silk protein, for conductivity, with fat-derived stem cells that steadily release growth factors. Together they form a supportive, signal-rich path for regrowing fibers.

In rats with a ten-millimeter sciatic gap, the loaded tubes matched real grafts: similar counts of new nerve cells, similar fiber regrowth, and nearly identical walking-function scores at twelve weeks. Histology showed the fullest regeneration in the combined group. The authors propose the design as a tissue-engineered stand-in for grafts. Matching the gold standard in animals is the bar for human talk, and this conduit cleared it.
pmc-12698724:
Peng Chen, Qiang Fu, and Chunjie Wang design a many-coil motor for sea solar floats in 2025. Waves tilt sea panels hour by hour, so light takes swing by spot and the feed turns lopsided across the float. Their motor runs many lone buses at split volt grades, one per panel zone, to hold the feed even.

Shape terms and a math model come first, checked by field runs on a bench rig built for the work. The rig holds high work grade and even output while coil power shares stay near set in all runs. Worst share drift sat at 6.7 percent in the tests.
pmc-12699324:
Enrique Lopez-Poveda and co-authors test a new sound method for people with implants in both ears in 2025. Such implants help many people hear speech in quiet rooms. Noise makes speech much harder to follow, even with two implants. The method copies a reflex in the healthy ear that turns down gain when sound comes from the other side.

Each implant changes its sound map based on what the other side hears. Past work with a like method raised speech scores in noise. Here the team presents the two-ear form and tests it. The goal is to give users more of the gain that two ears give people with normal hearing.
pmc-12699524:
Huacheng Tang and co-authors study how to print very fine silver lines for use as electrodes. Their 2025 paper uses a jet printing method driven by an electric field, which steers the ink with great care. Electrodes carry signals in small devices, so the lines must be thin and must conduct well.

Lower drive and bias voltages gave narrower lines, down to under four micrometres wide. Heat treatment after printing cut the resistance of the lines step by step. Hotter treatment bound the silver grains more tightly and drove off leftover organic matter. The best lines reached a low set value for resistance. The team sees strong promise for the method in fine devices.
pmc-12699824:
How long a woman waits between a caesarean birth and the next pregnancy may change the risks, but what the wait means to women is unstudied. Alison M Canty, Hazel Keedle, Annemarie Hennessy, and Angela Makris publish a review protocol in a 2025 paper. Risks after caesarean birth are well logged, from scar rupture to placenta troubles. The coming review asks how women themselves weigh the timing advice.

Five databases plus unpublished sources will be searched with no date or language limits. Mixed methods findings will be merged under a standard framework. The goal is advice that fits women's own decision making. This paper sets the plan, not the findings.
pmc-12700224:
Yongjun Wang and seven co-authors wrote a study in 2025 on the use of a catalyst to add hydrogen to ring compounds with care. Filling the rings with hydrogen makes feed stocks for plastics and drugs, but poor catalysts also snap links to oxygen and spoil the choice of end good. A better held ruthenium catalyst was the aim.

By a finer make, the team made ultra-small ruthenium bits spread in an even way on a base of magnesium and aluminium oxides. The new catalyst turned phenols to ring-full alcohols fast, and it hit the ring more than it broke links. Ring esters and ethers were changed in a clean way to their full forms too. The team says the build fits non-stop work on goods of high worth.
pmc-12700424:
Nailya Ibragimova and co-authors tested the safety and healing power of a new iodine wound treatment in animals, in a 2025 study. Standard iodine antiseptics can harm cells and release their iodine too fast. The new product, Novostron, locks iodine into a polymer complex with dextrin and other ingredients so it releases slowly; lab checks confirmed its makeup, mild acidity, and iodine content.

On rabbit skin, almost no iodine entered the blood, levels stayed in the normal range, and thyroid hormones did not shift. Standard tests in three animal species found no skin irritation, allergy, or poisoning even at high doses. In rats, the treatment shrank inflammatory lumps, and in burned mice it sped wound closing, thickened new skin, and boosted collagen beyond a standard iodine product. The authors call it a promising candidate for human trials.
pmc-12700724:
Swan, McIvor, and Cram report the first video proof of wild brown skuas teaming up to feed. Old accounts claimed pairs of these Antarctic seabirds coordinate to tear meat from carcasses, but no one had filmed it. The authors watch the birds on the Antarctic Peninsula and judge their behavior against four known forms of joint work.

The footage shows partners acting together in space and time. A bird holds the carcass still while waiting for its partner, then both pull in unison; alone, a bird shakes or pecks instead. The authors say lab-style tests are now needed to learn how much the birds grasp their partner's role, and they propose skuas as a strong model for studying bird social thought.
pmc-12701024:
Parkinson's disease kills neurons partly by letting broken mitochondria linger. Ga Hyun Park, Hye In Park, Donghyuk Shin, and Kwang Chul Chung found a guardian of the cleanup crew in a 2025 study. The crew chief is PINK1, a kinase that flags damaged mitochondria for disposal. Its own survival, the team shows, is protected by an enzyme called USP20.

USP20 strips away the specific ubiquitin chains, the Lys48-linked kind, that mark PINK1 for destruction. A mitochondrial poison used to trigger cleanup also speeds USP20 up, so PINK1 accumulates exactly when needed and the disposal of impaired mitochondria accelerates. The authors name USP20 a positive regulator of mitochondrial quality control, filling a gap: enzymes that destroy PINK1 were known, but the one that saves it was not.
pmc-12701324:
Zhang and eight co-authors used gene tools in twenty twenty-five to test whether red wine cuts brain bleed risk, though drink at large is a risk. Gene-based checks split drinks by kind, with a Chinese health set for cross-checks. Plain alcohol came out as a risk in those checks.

Red wine alone tied to lower bleed risk across the checks. Part of that guard ran through lower high blood press-ure rates. In the Chinese set, wine drinkers showed less high press-ure than non-drinkers. White wine showed no such guard, they find.
pmc-12703124:
Simone Giusti and co-authors compare, in a 2025 study, how surgeons and an AI model decide on an added step in knee surgery. The step is a lateral extra-articular procedure, done on the outer side of the knee. It can help when a reconstructed anterior cruciate ligament still leaves the joint rotationally unstable. The team asked which cases truly call for it.

They built 40 hypothetical case profiles spanning patient ages, injury traits, and activity levels. The AI model, trained on published criteria and expert input, gave a yes or no recommendation on each. Twenty-two high-volume knee surgeons, blinded to the AI calls, reviewed the same cases. Agreement ran high where signs were clear, above all when a rotational test came out positive. Surgeons backed the AI more when it said yes than when it said no. Gaps grew in borderline cases and in cases for women.
pmc-12704124:
Seven authors review how athletes should return to sport after a lateral ankle sprain, in this 2025 paper. Such sprains are common, yet return choices mix healing, strength, balance, and sport demands, and no single standard rule is widely used.

The team searched four databases up to March 2024 and scored the studies they found for quality. Twenty papers passed, with a good mean quality score. The authors sort the work into rehab methods, return criteria, tests after return, and the link between criteria and timing. Their message is that return is a staged process shaped by injury severity and like factors, not a single date on a calendar.
pmc-12705824:
Zhimeng Zhang, Fei He, and a large team of colleagues read gene activity across 328 wheat lines, from old landraces to modern elite types bred in China and the United States. Most work on crop traits looks at DNA letters alone. Gene activity varies just as much, and a single reference genome misses genes that some lines carry and others lack.

Using a pan-genome, the team found over twenty-three thousand transcripts the standard reference had missed. They built a map of the DNA spots that tune each gene's activity. That map yielded 299 strong candidate genes for 34 farm traits and for resistance to eight mildew strains. Tests in a mutant library backed most of them. The work shows breeding has reshaped gene activity, not just gene content.
pmc-12706224:
Britzer Vincent and co-authors gather what is known about why Pakistanis, at home and abroad, do or do not agree to donate organs after death. From nearly twelve thousand papers screened, 26 studies from universities, hospitals, religious venues, and workplaces made the cut. Four reviewers handled screening and quality checks, and findings were woven together by themes rather than pooled numbers.

Five themes ran through the studies: what people know about donation, their willingness, family decision-making overriding the individual, religious uncertainty, and trust in the health system. A person's own wish often yields to collective family choice, and unclear religious guidance leaves many hesitant. The authors argue raising registration and consent will take a whole-system approach working with families, faith leaders, and trust-building, not just information campaigns. They call for broader research, since current evidence leaves real gaps about this global population.
pmc-12706524:
Yang and five co-authors mapped how bird communities respond to human pressure in northeastern Inner Mongolia in twenty twenty-five. The Human Footprint Index sums human impacts such as roads, farming, and settlement. Birds, sensitive to change, serve as indicators of ecosystem health.

The team tested the idea that diversity peaks at middle disturbance levels. Using threshold analysis, they found the bird community shifted sharply at a footprint score near fourteen. Individual species had thresholds spread widely. Richness and diversity did peak at middle pressure, near a score of twenty-three point five, then fell. The results support the middle-disturbance idea while showing composition changes earlier. The authors advise conservation plans that track both diversity and which species remain.
pmc-12706724:
Yifei He and co-authors report a new thorium compound in 2025. Thorium chemistry is less mapped than that of many metals, so each new structure teaches something. The team started from a thorium chloride held by a tailored support frame. They swapped in a nitrogen rich group and then applied a strong reducer.

The steps yielded a paired compound with one oxygen atom bridging two thorium atoms. Crystal data show a highly symmetric shape for that bridge. Computer models find a strong shared bond across the bridge, stronger than in akin nitrogen bridged cases. The work adds a rare clear case to actinide bonding studies.
pmc-12706924:
Yiting Li and nine co-authors build a scale for judging food choices in bowel disease in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Diet choices are central to managing inflammatory bowel disease, yet they are hard to make well. No tested tool measured a patient's skill at making healthy dietary decisions. Such a tool would help clinicians spot who needs support. The team set out to create and validate one.

The work ran in two phases: drafting the scale, then testing it. Items were drawn from the real challenges patients face with food. The tests checked whether the scale is consistent and measures what it claims. A sound scale can guide tailored diet programs for each patient. The paper serves gastroenterology teams and dietitians who counsel this group.
pmc-12707524:
Caio Leonardo Faria Andrade and co-authors ask old adults how falls shape their sense of life grade. The study appeared in 2025. Falls can raise frailty and curb free acts in late life. How the old see that tie was the aim here.

Staff spoke with near thirty old adults at a town health post in Brazil. Talk reads fell in four themes, from fall facts to calls for a safe life. Falls fed frailty and weak state, and cut health, free acts, and task skill. Many old folks treat falls as plain fate and shrug them off. The team calls for more warn work on cause and block.
pmc-12707824:
Anna Fijarczyk and co-authors ask how a fungus's way of life shapes its genome in a 2025 study. Fungi live many lives: some rot wood, some live inside insects, and some cause disease. Whether those lifestyles leave a common mark on genome size and gene content was little known. The team gathered and annotated more than five hundred genomes from one large class of fungi.

They tested links between thirteen genome traits and two lifestyle traits, being a pathogen and being tied to insects. Pathogens carried more protein-coding genes, including the effector genes used to attack hosts, and larger non-repetitive genomes. But the pattern bent by group. Insect parasites and symbionts ran small genomes, and insect-carried pathogens held fewer genes. Genes, not repeats, drove most size differences.
pmc-12708724:
Kancsev and co-authors compare thinking skills and inflammation across schizophrenia patients with and without metabolic disease. Metabolic syndrome and diabetes are common in this illness and may deepen cognitive harm. Their 2025 study examines 218 adults in three groups: schizophrenia alone, with metabolic syndrome, or with diabetes, using a standard thinking battery and two blood inflammation markers.

The diabetes group scored lowest on attention and delayed memory, while other skills did not differ. One marker, IL-6, climbed stepwise across the three groups; the other did not differ. Across everyone, higher IL-6 and blood sugar tracked with weaker attention and delayed memory. The authors caution that a one time snapshot cannot prove cause, and call for longer studies with wider marker panels.
pmc-12709024:
Hero Noori Ali and Muhammad Rashid Amen survey how well people with high blood pressure in Iraqi Kurdistan care for themselves. Good self-care keeps blood pressure down and prevents strokes and heart attacks, yet it demands daily habits many patients struggle to keep. Their 2025 study interviewed 393 adults with primary hypertension at public primary care centers.

Most participants, about 72 percent, knew their condition well, but only about 27 percent managed adequate self-care. Stress, money trouble, and lack of time were the top barriers named. Younger age, marriage, and stronger social support raised the odds of good self-care, while more other illnesses and uncontrolled pressure lowered them. The gap between knowing and doing is the paper's central finding. The authors call for care that builds habits and support, not just knowledge, in this region's clinics.
pmc-12709824:
Xuyang Du and co-authors ask whether sons and daughters care for aging parents in different ways in this 2025 study. They used four waves of a long survey of older adults in China. The team compared the body and mind health of parents by the gender of the child who cared for them.

Parents cared for by sons showed better day-to-day function but worse mood. When caregiver and parent shared the same gender, parents' mental health was clearly better. Sons' edge on function showed mainly in low-income homes, while daughters' lift to mood showed in high-income ones. City families varied more than country ones. The authors urge care policy that fits these patterns.
pmc-12710424:
The European Food Safety Authority weighs a request to change residue limits for a mite drug on berry crops, in work from twenty twenty-five. Belgium asks to modify limits for acequinocyl on several small fruits. Crops cover blueberries, cranberries, currants, and gooseberries in many colours. Data sent in support prove sufficient to derive new limit proposals. Lab methods can enforce the limits in high-acid plant samples reliably.

Residue intake is modelled for short bursts and for long daily spans. Both models use the reported farm practices for the drug. Intake at those levels is judged unlikely to risk consumer health. The opinion follows the standard European pesticide law route. National authorities weigh in before the final limit is set. Shoppers gain assurance that berry residues stay within safe bounds.
pmc-12710924:
Li and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a study of gentle microwave heat as an aid to cancer immune therapy in mice. Pancreatic cancer often resists drugs that free the immune system to attack. Mild heat is an approved cancer aid with few side effects. The team heated tumor cells and mouse tumors to about forty-one degrees. They then tested heat alone and heat paired with an immune drug.

Heated cells showed damaged nuclei and signs of failed cell division. A day or two later, a DNA-sensing alarm pathway switched on. In mice, heat plus the immune drug shrank treated and distant tumors and lengthened life. Immune cells entered tumors in greater numbers. Blocking the alarm pathway removed the benefit, showing it was key.
pmc-12711024:
Chia-Heng Lin and co-authors study violent offenders with mental illness in 2025. The catalog creator field repeats one name four times, but the head byline lists four authors. Crime rates for people with severe mental illness match the general public overall, yet violent crime links remain debated.

The study covered six hundred forty-eight offenders sent for court-ordered psychiatric review. Violent offenders were more often male and less often previously assessed. Severe illness, substance disorders, joblessness, and poor treatment adherence did not tie to violent crime. None of the tested moderators changed that picture, the authors report.
pmc-12711624:
Tianwei Chen and co-authors fuse five layers of molecular data to find what drives outlook in colorectal cancer, in a 2025 study. This cancer kills many patients, and its mixed biology blurs prognosis. The team applied a factor method to mutations, RNA, proteins, and their chemical edits from a public cohort. One hidden factor they extracted tracked survival, and it held up across three more cohorts totaling 579 patients.

The factor mostly reflected scar-like matrix laid down around the tumor. Two genes, TNS1 and FERMT2, weighed heaviest, and single-cell maps placed them in myofibroblasts, the muscle-like support cells. Silencing either gene in such cells slowed tumors in animals. The pair raised a sticky protein that switches on integrin signals in cancer cells. The authors name the chain a target for new therapy.
pmc-12712024:
A plastic that cools when voltage is applied could replace gas-based refrigeration, but the champion polymer, PVDF, barely cools at all. Yibo Zhang and co-authors change that verdict in a 2025 paper. Their trick is mechanical: pressing the film in its solid phase under strong pressure before use.

The pressing shatters the polymer's crystals into tiny, loose grains. In that state the film showed a giant electrocaloric effect, a temperature change of up to 12.8 degrees at room temperature, working across a sixty-degree range. The cooling comes from chains rearranging between loose and compact crystal forms and from dipoles flipping in the small grains. Because PVDF is cheap and common, the authors present the method as a scalable route to solid-state cooling.
pmc-12712124:
Christine Ryan and co-authors review the search for biomarkers in progressive supranuclear palsy, a rare brain disease that harms movement, thinking, and eye control. Their 2025 review finds no reliable test yet for early diagnosis or for sorting patients into subtypes. The team surveys recent work on fluid tests from blood and spinal fluid, gene and molecule profiling, and brain scans.

New candidates include protein clumps carried in tiny cell parcels, blood markers, and several scan methods that read chemistry, structure, and blood flow. Because symptoms and brain changes vary a lot between patients, one test alone will not do. The authors argue for a biotyping frame that groups patients by biology to guide trials.
pmc-12712324:
Víctor Vera-Ponce and co-authors estimate how common chronic kidney disease is in Latin America in this 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis. The disease carries extra weight in the region because of inequality and varied health systems. The team searched major databases for observational studies that used standard diagnostic criteria.

They pooled twenty-one studies with more than seventy-two thousand participants across twelve countries. The pooled prevalence came to about seventeen percent, though studies differed greatly from one another. Results are broken down by age, sex, disease stage and country. The authors use the findings to show the scale of kidney disease facing Latin American health systems.
pmc-12713024:
Dong Yun Lee and co-authors look for sleep-test signs that foretell whether throat surgery will help people whose airways collapse at night. Their 2025 study deals with obstructive sleep apnea. Palate surgery is a set treatment, yet its results swing widely from person to person.

The team read the records of 56 adults who had full sleep tests and a drug-sleep scope exam both before and after surgery. Patients were split by how far their hourly pause count moved: a strong fall counted as success, a strong rise as a bad turn. The success group came in with worse apnea and bigger tonsils. They also spent more of their deep sleep in the deepest stage and woke less often, and both signs held up as lone predictors.
pmc-12714424:
Kyung Min Lee and co-authors use genomes to sort out Aletis moths of Africa. Their twenty twenty-five study faces a hard case: these day-flying moths vary hugely in wing pattern, sit in mimicry rings, and yet look alike in the traits taxonomists trust. Fresh moths and caterpillars were gathered in South Africa and Uganda.

Mitochondrial and nuclear data test where species lines truly fall. The team also dates splits and maps population structure across the range. Mimicry can glue false species together or split one into many on looks alone. A genome-backed family tree gives conservation and field guides a firmer footing for this group.
pmc-12714724:
Bukke Bai and seven co-authors move a leaf rust shield from a wild goat grass into bread wheat and map its gene. Leaf rust cuts wheat yield world wide, and shields wear out as the germ evolves. The wild source stood firm against three Indian rust strains in tests.

Crosses show a single strong gene rules the shield. Chip and marker work place it on a known chromosome arm in a small span with a few candidate genes. Close markers flank it on both sides. Breeders can now track the shield with cheap tests and stack it with others.
pmc-12714824:
Xuan Zhou and co-authors review how damage inside the placenta may drive diabetes in pregnancy in a 2025 paper. Gestational diabetes is rising, and its inner causes remain partly hidden. The placenta sits between mother and fetus, burns large amounts of energy, and leaks hormones that blunt insulin. Flooding that organ with sugar sparks oxidative stress, the chemical wear caused by reactive oxygen.

Stressed power plants inside cells then fail, and an iron-driven form of cell death called ferroptosis follows as fats oxidize. The review gathers five years of work tying these three steps into one chain. Seeing the chain whole points to where a drug or diet change might break it before harm spreads.
pmc-12715124:
Junhao Wang, Xi Zeng, Bowen Li, Kaya Xu, and Xu Xu report an unusual repair in this 2025 case report. A middle-aged Chinese man carried a giant bulge in the arteries at the base of his brain. The vessel wall had split along a long stretch, from the left vertebral artery into the basilar artery. The split segment measured about sixty-five millimeters long.

Surgeons threaded four mesh stents, called flow diverters, in a bridged chain through the damaged stretch, working from inside the vessel. The repair sealed the bulge completely and rebuilt the parent artery with steady flow and no major clotting. A year later the man had no new nerve symptoms. The authors offer the case as guidance for giant unruptured bulges at the back of the brain, at least where the partner arteries are well formed.
pmc-12715224:
Michelle Natasha Colin and five co-authors pool past trials of web health tools meant to cut drug faults. Their review, from two thousand twenty-five, matches such tools to plain care.

Drug faults, caught or through, are a grave safe-care care. A caught fault is one spied and stopped, by hand or by screen. The past kind is the fault that lands, soft or harsh. Screen aids, most of all warn-aids at script time, aim to cut both. Four stores were searched for lot-split trials. A dozen works came in; nine stayed past a spread trim. The pool weighs if the tools beat plain care.
pmc-12716524:
Sreeramoju and co-authors poll germ guards in poor and mid lands in a 2025 survey. More than three of four of the world lives in such lands, and germs caught in care run far more rife there. Yet the staff who fight those germs are the least heard from.

The poll, run by mail and web through late 2022 and early 2023, asked of their work, their woes, and what help they lack. It spans five fields, from the staff own roots to their tools. The yield is a call to act for the guards with least. Health chiefs gain a wish list drawn from the front line.
pmc-12717124: Hanna Braaß and co-authors publish a correction carrying a rewritten passage for their study of brain wiring in healthy older adults. The original article had misplaced four figure legends into the body text, and part of the Results had been swapped with the legend of Table 1. The corrected passage reports assessment data for younger and older participants, the older group split into low and high performers. Its significant finding: white matter integrity in the anterior corpus callosum differed between older low and high performers, while behavior did not.
pmc-12717224:
Meda Theodory studies the economics of cassava processing machines in coastal Tanzania, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. New mechanical chippers and graters have been introduced, but their profit for farmers was unclear. Theodory compares them with traditional drying and fermentation methods.

Data came from household surveys, focus groups, and machine trials in the Tanga and Pwani regions. Machines cut drying time from six to twelve days down to one to three days, and made better flour. All machines made a profit, with the grater giving the highest total returns. The manual chipper gave the best return per cost and the highest daily profit per kilogram. Theodory suggests subsidies, shared ownership, and credit to spread adoption.
pmc-12717324:
Lyhne and co-authors test whether ketone bodies can prop up the heart during a lung blood clot. A sudden pulmonary embolism strains the right side of the heart, the usual cause of death. In a blinded pig study, animals with induced clots receive a three-hour infusion of the ketone 3-hydroxybutyrate or a salt solution control, while heart pressures and flows are recorded.

The ketone does not significantly raise cardiac output, the main target. It does ease the balance of resistance between the lungs and the body, and it relaxes isolated lung arteries in the lab. The authors judge the effect promising but early, and call for more work before any human use.
pmc-12717724:
Njoud Alenezi and co-authors survey why asthma patients in one Saudi region skip their inhalers, in a 2025 study. Phone interviews reached adults in Al-Ahsa between May and July 2024. Only about thirty nine percent took their medicine as prescribed. The top reasons were stopping when feeling better and stopping over side effects.

Women, the married, city dwellers, higher earners, and patients with support for their medicine stuck to the plan more often. Regression pinned non adherence on younger age, male sex, lower income, and lack of support. The authors call for education and support programs aimed at the groups most likely to lapse.
pmc-12717824:
Yi Gou and co-authors build a tool to flag heart injury risk in sepsis patients, in this 2025 study. Sepsis, the body's extreme response to infection, often damages the heart muscle. That damage raises the chance of death, so spotting high-risk patients early matters for care. The team set out to build and test a scoring model for this injury.

Patients were split at random into a larger group for building the model and a smaller group for checking it. Statistical sieves picked the traits that predicted injury on their own. Those traits were drawn into a nomogram, a chart that turns patient values into a risk score. The team then checked how well the chart sorted patients, how true its scores ran, and whether it would help in real clinic choices.
pmc-12718224:
Yetunde Omotosho and colleagues assessed a stimulation test for pediatric Cushing's disease in 2025. The test uses desmopressin, also called DDAVP. Doctors need accurate tests to confirm this hormone disorder in children. The team compared DDAVP with the older ovine CRH stimulation test. Patients had peripheral testing or sampling from veins near the pituitary.

Cases were matched one to one by age, sex, and tumor size. In peripheral testing, DDAVP showed high sensitivity for cortisol response. Its sensitivity for ACTH response was somewhat lower than the older test. ACTH rose more strongly after CRH than after DDAVP. Sampling results for DDAVP were also reported for baseline and stimulated states. The study weighs accuracy and safety for both options.
pmc-12719624:
Nong and co-authors test whether a protein called BNIP3L, measured in blood, can help diagnose multiple myeloma and predict its course. The protein helps control cell recycling and death; its levels go astray in several cancers. The team measured serum BNIP3L in 152 myeloma patients and 158 healthy controls with a standard lab assay. They checked how well the levels separated the groups and how they related to survival and treatment response.

Patients had higher BNIP3L than controls; the test showed fair diagnostic value. High levels clustered with worse features, such as disease spread outside the marrow and high-risk genetic changes. Patients responding better to treatment had lower levels, and high levels trended toward shorter survival. The authors propose serum BNIP3L as a marker for tracking disease activity. That link is a trend rather than firm proof, so larger studies are needed.
pmc-12719924:
Mohamed Mahamud and eight co-authors reported in 2025 a Somali child from a displacement camp infected with several gut parasites at once, plus a stomach bacterium. Crowded camps with poor sanitation breed exactly these overlapping infections, and children suffer most through stunted growth and anemia.

The case walks through the worms and microbes found and the treatment given. Shared transmission routes mean one infection flags the likelihood of others. The report urges camp clinics to test broadly instead of treating the first parasite found and stopping, since the hidden companions keep harming the child.
pmc-12721724:
Fernando Sotelo-Díaz and seven co-authors tell, in a 2025 case report, of a swollen pituitary gland in a man who lives with HIV and hidden syphilis. The gland sits at the brain's base and runs the body's hormones. Infection with the syphilis germ can spark such swelling, though it is rare.

The fifty-year-old man came in with headache, deep tiredness, and failing sight. Tests showed hormone failure across the gland's range, and a scan found a mass pressing the nerve crossing for sight, which explained his loss of side vision. He was treated with penicillin through a vein plus hormone top-ups. A later scan showed the gland shrunk, and within a month his sight and nerve signs had much improved. The team urges doctors to keep this cause in mind.
pmc-12722424:
