Mohamed Hany and co-authors present a 2025 case-control study of obesity and the stomach. The team asked how two genes tied to body weight, named FTO and MC4R, act in stomach tissue, and how that action links to three signals in the blood.

The study drew on fifty patients who had weight-loss stomach surgery and fifty people who had a scope exam for other reasons. Tests on tissue and blood showed FTO turned up far more in the obesity group, while MC4R was turned down far more. One blood signal, tied to fat tissue, ran high in the same group and tracked with weight and a good form of blood fat. The authors read the pattern as a sign that stomach gene action may shape weight-linked health risks.
pmc-12722524:
Howard, Jama, and Duangthip wrote a review, published in 2025, on what social science adds to dental research. Teeth and gums are shaped by far more than biology: income, housing, habits, and power all leave marks in the mouth. The review gathers social science work on oral health from 2015 to 2025. It sits inside a longer history of joint work between the fields. The authors searched medical and anthropology databases for studies that use interviews, group discussion, and field observation.

That body of work shows how people understand oral health, why they seek or avoid care, and how services can exclude. The authors find that core social concepts already inform public dental health frameworks. Yet true blending of methods and theory stays rare. The review argues for deeper integration, so dental research can explain outcomes, not just count them. It maps the field for researchers on both sides.
pmc-12722624:
Baxi and eight colleagues set out a protocol for a large bipolar disorder study in twenty twenty-five. Bipolar disorder varies a lot from person to person. Diagnosis is often delayed, and good treatment options are limited. The network aims to follow a diverse group of patients over time in depth.

The study will collect detailed clinical data and repeated biosamples. Samples include whole blood, serum, plasma, and immune cells from blood. Samples will also be shared with other researchers. The team calls it the largest study of its kind in bipolar disorder. Its goal is to map disease paths and find biological drivers of illness. That knowledge should support treatments tailored to each patient and a better quality of life.
pmc-12722724:
A dental crown lasts only as well as the glue beneath it, and the glue's curing style turns out to matter. Nermin Mohieldin Abdelmohssen and co-authors test how adhesive curing modes interact with when the dentin is sealed. Thirty-six human molars received computer-made composite blocks. Adhesives were light-cured, dual-cured, or self-cured. Sealing happened either immediately or after a week of provisional wear.

Delayed sealing won with light-cured and dual-cured adhesives. Immediate sealing won with the self-cure product. Failures mostly occurred at the glue line itself. The practical moral is pairing: the best adhesive depends on the appointment schedule, and vice versa. Dentists choosing products by habit may be leaving bond strength on the table.
pmc-12723724:
Samuel Mouron and co-authors test whether richer landscapes above ground mean richer animal life in the gravel beneath tropical streams. The hyporheic zone, the wet sediment under a streambed, hosts small invertebrates whose diversity should, by one theory, grow as the catchment feeds more food down. Their 2025 study samples 228 sites in New Caledonia and weighs nine local and nine catchment factors at once.

Productivity signs in the catchment, such as plant cover and soil type, tracked closely with sediment oxygen and acidity, which in turn explained much of the species richness. Fast-growing animals drove the pattern: their numbers and kinds rose steadily with catchment productivity. Slow growers answered mostly to local conditions and peaked midway. The authors say extra food helps only those quick enough to grab it, so competition, not just supply, shapes the underground community.
pmc-12723824:
Seven authors pool evidence on mood and survival in blood cancers in this 2025 review. Depression and anxiety are common in patients with leukemia, lymphoma, and related diseases, but whether they shorten life was unsettled.

Following standard review methods, the team searched three databases and gathered twenty-nine studies covering over four hundred thousand patients. Depression came with clearly worse overall survival, with risk about seventeen percent higher. Anxiety's link was weaker and not statistically firm for overall survival. Event free and cause specific survival showed a mixed pattern, which the authors probed with subgroup and bias checks. The message is that treating depression may matter for outcomes, not only comfort.
pmc-12723924:
Leah C Ott and co-authors test fat-derived stem cells for nerve repair in a 2025 mouse study. Cut peripheral nerves heal poorly, above all across gaps longer than three centimeters. The team took neural stem cells from under-skin fat and loaded them into silicone tubes bridging a five-millimeter cut in the mouse sciatic nerve.

The cells survived to day fifty-six and became part of the rebuilt nerve. Most turned into Schwann-like cells, the type that wraps nerves in insulation, and none became unwanted cell types. They joined with the animal's own Schwann cells at both cut ends. Walking tests showed clearly better hind leg recovery than tubes without cells. The authors say fat tissue offers a handy cell source for nerve repair.
pmc-12726824:
The authors hunt for drug targets in a lung-disease bacterium by mapping which genes each strain cannot live without. They profiled eight patient isolates plus the reference strain with a genome-wide knockout screen. Just 131 genes were essential across all of them.

Patient strains leaned harder on sugar-making and secretion genes, the same genes the reference strain needs in low-oxygen biofilms. The patient strains also adapted to low oxygen faster, and mouse lung infections confirmed the pattern. The authors urge drug hunters to test patient strains under host-like conditions, not just lab standards.
pmc-12728424:
Weiwei Ma and co-authors dress graphene oxide in a friendlier coat for cancer therapy. Their 2025 study grafts a biotin-tagged polysarcosine polymer onto graphene oxide, fixing the material's poor stability and biocompatibility while keeping its gifts: huge drug loading and strong light-to-heat conversion.

The coated carrier proved stable and safe in cell and animal tests. Loaded with doxorubicin, it held a quarter of its weight in drug and released it in response to near-infrared light and tumor acidity. Under laser light the combined chemo-photothermal attack shrank tumors in dishes and in animals better than either alone. The authors present the platform as a safer route to dual-mode cancer treatment.
pmc-12729124:
After surgery for a deep anal fistula, many doctors give antibiotics by habit, though the gain is unclear. Xue Li and co-authors test that habit in a 2025 trial in China. Ninety patients got a standard seton procedure and were split by chance into drug and no-drug groups.

The drug group cost far more and stayed in hospital about five days longer. Wound healing time and early return of the fistula did not differ between groups. The drug group also needed more follow-up visits. Total social costs ran higher with drugs in every check the team ran. The authors say routine drugs here waste money without helping wounds.
pmc-12729224:
Sjacky Cooijmans and a large team of co-authors lay out a trial plan to trim drug harm in older hospital patients in a 2025 protocol paper. Many drugs at once raise the odds of harm and fresh admissions, and about half of drug-linked returns could be stopped. Hospitals are split at random into care and control arms.

The care arm gives high-risk patients of seventy and up a four-part drug review that spans the move home. Past work says such blends work best when many hands join, hand-offs are minded, and the frailest are picked. The main score is drug-linked readmission.
pmc-12729324:
Xi Zhou and co-authors probe gene marks behind tooth decay in a 2025 study. Decay is one of the most common mouth illnesses in the world. A chemical mark on RNA, the cell's working copy of genes, shapes many cell tasks, and the team asked if that mark helps drive decay.

They merged gene data from large shared studies with cell-by-cell reads of tooth pulp. Four gene sites stood out, and one gene's activity rose in sore pulp. Cells that guard against germs were most changed in the sore samples. A cause-check method tied 15 immune cell traits to decay risk. One guard cell type raised risk, while a kin type lowered it.
pmc-12729724:
Kaddour Mehiriz and Sara Cherqaoui ask what actually moves vulnerable people to protect themselves during heat waves, in this 2025 study. Older adults and people with chronic illness face the highest heat risk. Three survey waves in the Canadian city of Longueuil tracked risk perception and beliefs about five standard protective actions. A random subset also received heat warnings, giving the team a natural experiment.

Believing an action works raised the odds of doing it. Feeling at risk, by contrast, had no clear effect, alone or combined with belief. Warning exposure backed the main result through a separate statistical route. The authors conclude that campaigns should sell the effectiveness of protective steps rather than raise fear. That flips a common assumption in heat planning.
pmc-12729824:
Eight authors led by Loredana Hurjui build a score that may flag jaw and face strain before symptoms show. The jaw system, which spans teeth, joints, and chew muscles, can slip out of balance in quiet ways first. Low-grade swelling and metabolic drift may show in blood long before pain or stiff joints do. Their score, called BioRisk-S, blends three blood marks into one risk read for that early stage.

The study held 260 healthy adults with no clear jaw disorder at the start. Blood marks were read at entry and again at six months, with jaw checks at the close. Adults with high entry scores showed higher swelling marks and lower vitamin D than low scorers. Gum swelling, joint signs, and muscle soreness at six months are set against the entry score in the report.
pmc-12730024:
Yvonne Peijun Zhou and co-authors review seventeen years of antibiotic stewardship at a Singapore hospital in a 2025 study. Stewardship programs coach doctors to use antibiotics only when needed and to pick them well, which slows drug resistance. The program at Singapore General Hospital began in 2008 and grew through four phases, from launch to new ideas.

The team tracked prescribing and germ sensitivity from 2011 to 2024. Use of three broad intravenous antibiotics fell, and the share of fitting prescriptions for seven such drugs rose and stayed up. Six key gut-type germs grew more sensitive to nearly all tested antibiotics over the years. Two pairings were the exceptions. The authors say a program must keep adapting as medicine changes around it.
pmc-12730124:
Natthaporn Kaewchoothong, Sorracha Rookkapan, Chayut Nuntadusit, and Surapong Chatpun simulate blood flow inside individual patients' aortic aneurysms to read rupture risk from the currents. Their 2025 study builds models from CT scans of one healthy subject and seven patients with abdominal aneurysms over three centimeters, sorted into small, medium, and large.

Flow inside the bulges turned highly turbulent in the resting phase of the heartbeat, more so as size grew. Wall shear stress peaked at systole and sagged in diastole, while the oscillation index ran highest mid-sac and downstream. Low average shear with high oscillation flags the wall zones the authors judge most rupture-prone. The paper argues patient-based simulation shows what a diameter number alone cannot: where the wall is being worried loose.
pmc-12730424:
Alvarez-González and co-authors look for proteins in airway muscle that may drive the twitchiness of airways in asthma. Airway hyperresponsiveness is a hallmark of the disease, but its molecular roots are still unclear. Working in guinea pigs with an induced allergic asthma model, the team measured airway response to histamine and analyzed tracheal tissue proteins with mass spectrometry. One known suspect protein was not found; instead, a peptide from a glycogen-targeting regulatory subunit, RG1, turned up.

Follow-up staining showed RG1 and a partner kinase, ROCK2, were both raised in the airway muscle of the asthma model, and their levels tracked the degree of hyperresponsiveness. The two proteins' levels also correlated with each other. The authors suggest RG1 may help drive the overreaction of asthmatic airways. As an animal study, the work points to a candidate mechanism rather than proving one in patients.
pmc-12730824:
Mengxian Song and three co-authors build a simple heart risk score in a 2025 study. Patients with coronary artery disease face heart attack, stroke, and death. A score from routine clinic data could flag those at highest risk. The team used records from a large hospital in China.

More than seven thousand patients entered the study. They were split into training and testing groups at random. Over about twenty seven months, near seven percent had a major event. Six plain factors made the final score, led by a heart strain marker. Age and blood sugar control also counted. The score sorted patients into risk groups with clear gaps. The authors offer it as a quick bedside tool.
pmc-12731024:
Aneta-Rada Dobrin and co-authors report a 2025 hospital study of lung clots in patients with COVID-19. The mix of lung infection and clotting makes risk hard to judge: clot scores, other illnesses, and swelling markers may not weigh the same. The team reviewed one hundred sixty-one adults at one center with both the virus and a confirmed lung clot.

About one in four patients died in hospital. Wide lung damage on scans strongly raised the odds of death and of needing a breathing machine. Two swelling markers in the blood also tracked higher death risk. A combined pattern of swelling and clotting, drawn from the data, raised risk further. Classic clot scores and past illnesses, by contrast, sorted patients poorly.
pmc-12731924:
Sanja Peršić Kiršić and co-authors compare three denture designs over five years in a 2025 study. Patients missing back teeth on both sides of the upper jaw can wear a removable partial denture held by clasps, by hidden attachments, or by mini implants. Long-term patient views on looks and chewing were little known.

Eighty-eight patients wore one of the three designs and rated looks, quality of life, and chewing before treatment and over five years. Clasp wearers consistently scored worst, and their quality of life declined the most. Attachment and implant wearers scored higher and stayed steadier. The authors note a caveat: patients chose their own design, so the gaps may partly reflect that choice rather than the denture alone.
pmc-12732224:
Bartosz Bichalski, Magda Bichalska-Lach, and Dariusz Waniczek wrote this 2025 review of colorectal cancer diagnosis with a focus on Poland. The disease is the third most common cancer worldwide, and early detection strongly improves survival. The authors survey both the screening pathway and the molecular markers now entering practice.

Polish screening options range from colonoscopy to stool blood tests and combined DNA stool tests, each with its own accuracy and effect on deaths. The review then walks through blood and tissue markers, from classic ones like CEA to circulating tumor DNA and microRNAs. Proteins such as p53 and PTEN add prognostic value. The authors argue for pairing molecular markers with standard methods to sharpen early detection and to tailor treatment.
pmc-12732524:
Anastasia Bougea reviews how faults in one gene help drive Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, in a 2025 narrative review. Both diseases feature clumps of a misfolded protein, alpha-synuclein, in the brain. Changes in the gene, called GBA1, are a major inherited risk factor for both. The gene makes an enzyme that breaks down a fatty substance inside the cell's recycling units.

When the enzyme falls short, the fatty substance builds up, the recycling units falter, and protein clearing slows. Bougea searched four large databases from their start to November 2025, gathering about 1,650 papers. The review updates the chain from gene fault to brain damage. It aims to guide work on treatments that target the pathway.
pmc-12733024:
Smoke residue that clings to walls, dust, and cloth long after smoking ends can expose babies and children who touch or mouth those surfaces. Valentina Vanzi and co-authors mapped what is known about that residue and what it means for nurses in this 2025 review. Babies are at special risk because they crawl and put hands in their mouths.

The review gathered studies on the residue in newborn and child settings and sorted findings on nurse knowledge, ward contamination, and teaching roles. Nurses are well placed to warn parents that cleaning and smoke-free homes protect children even when no one smokes nearby. The authors call for training so nurses can spot the risk and teach families in plain terms.
pmc-12733124:
Fulya Yukcu and co-authors published a case-control genetics study in twenty twenty-five on two clotting gene variants in heart attack patients arriving with chest pain. The prothrombin and factor V Leiden variants raise clotting tendency and are suspected in coronary events. One hundred emergency patients with acute coronary syndrome were compared with one hundred thirty-one healthy controls.

Genotyping used standard DNA cutting methods. Surprisingly, the common GG forms of both variants were more frequent in patients, and carrying the variant A allele was rarer among them. Adjusted odds suggested several-fold higher risk for GG carriers at each site. Age independently added risk as well. The authors flag both variants as relevant to emergency coronary presentations in this population.
pmc-12733224:
Jose Lombana, Maureen Hanson, and Stephane Bentolila present a 2025 review of synthetic PPR proteins, a toolkit for precise RNA control. In plants, natural PPR proteins bind RNA by a readable code, one block per letter. Learning that code lets engineers build proteins that bind chosen RNA on demand.

Fused to editing enzymes, the built proteins convert single RNA letters in bacteria, plants, and even human cells. They can also steady RNA or tune its reading. Small versions from early plant lineages need no helper factors, widening their use. The authors see uses from basic research to RNA disease therapy. Sharper targeting and stronger editing are the next steps.
pmc-12733524:
Ruslan Akhmedullin and co-authors mapped prolonged seizures across Kazakhstan over ten years, in this 2025 study. Status epilepticus is a seizure that will not stop and can kill. National health data from 2014 to 2023 held 14,010 patients.

The age-adjusted rate tripled over the decade, with a sharp rise during the COVID-19 years. Death within 30 days was 2.1 percent, and 8.85 percent by five years. Older age, brain tumors, and cancer drove the survival gap most. Prior epilepsy, by contrast, linked to better outlook. The authors call for better access to rescue medicines, above all for older and tumor patients.
pmc-12733724:
Leyla Schweiger and co-authors tested cheap blood ratios as signals in a stiff-skin autoimmune disease, in a 2025 study. The disease, limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, scars skin and harms vessel linings. The team compared thirty-eight patients with thirty-eight matched people who have a milder vessel condition, then followed the patients for three years.

Several ratios built from blood counts and proteins ran higher in patients than in controls. During follow-up, some ratios climbed further, and one, mixing monocytes with protective cholesterol, tracked with a heart-risk score. The authors judge these simple ratios promising as low-cost markers, while noting the small group size.
pmc-12733824:
Nomy Levin Iaina and co-authors report a trial in two thousand twenty-five of an expanded dialysis filter for kidney failure patients. Standard dialysis clears small toxins but leaves middle-sized molecules that drive inflammation and symptoms. A medium-cutoff dialyzer, Theranova 500, is built to remove those larger toxins.

Forty patients at two Israeli centers were assigned in sequence to the new filter or a standard high-flux one for twenty-four weeks. Dialysis adequacy rose clearly in the new-filter group, from about one point two four to one point four zero on the standard index, while the comparison group barely moved. Inflammation, tracked by C-reactive protein, stayed flat with the new filter but nearly tripled without it. Other measures, including albumin and weight, stayed stable in both groups.
pmc-12734224:
Researchers test fat stem cell secretions against nasal inflammation in mice in a paper from 2025. The secretome is the mix of signals that stem cells release, without the cells themselves. The target disease is a form of chronic sinus inflammation with nasal polyps, driven by allergic-type immune cells. Mice were given the secretion through the nose three times a week for eight weeks.

Treated mice formed fewer polyp-like growths and had less allergic cell buildup. Several inflammatory signals fell toward normal levels. A chemoattractant that draws allergic cells dropped in both gene activity and tissue staining. The authors suggest the secretion as a cell-free therapy candidate. Human studies would be needed to confirm safety and benefit.
pmc-12734524:
Szafran and co-authors test ways to strengthen a steel column and compare two ways of judging the result, in a 2025 case study. When buildings change use or loads grow, columns of square hollow section may need welded stiffeners. Four stiffening layouts were checked twice: once by simulation software that accounts for imperfections, and once by handbook-style analysis from the literature.

All four layouts met the needed capacity under the higher loads. But the critical forces from the two methods disagreed sharply, with buckling simulation and classic Euler theory far apart. The paper weighs what each method sees and misses, a caution for engineers who lean on one alone.
pmc-12734724:
Melanie Namour and colleagues test whether blue laser light helps enamel hold fluoride. Their ex vivo study from twenty twenty-five uses extracted human teeth. Fluoride protects teeth, but enamel can lose it over time. Locking fluoride in longer could strengthen decay prevention.

Hundreds of small enamel discs were cut from healthy teeth. All discs first received a standard fluoride treatment. Half then received low-energy blue diode laser exposure. Samples rested in air or warm water for a week. A physics-based method measured fluoride content at each stage. The design isolates the laser effect from storage effects. Dentists may gain a simple add-on for fluoride treatments if results hold.
pmc-12735224:
Luyu Chen and co-authors build catalysts from lignosulfonate tied to metals, to turn hexose sugars into new forms in a picky way. Their 2025 study looks at the active sites, and at the fluids the reaction runs in. The aim is to turn glucose toward products of value.

Lignosulfonate can be kept in use, and it was tied to more than one metal ion to make the catalysts. Isomerisation of glucose was driven by Lewis acid-base site pairs that worked as one. Brønsted acid sites were the pick for the next step. In that step, fructose lost water to form a platform chemical. Some solvents made that step more strong, but held back isomerisation. A new form was made in its place. One hafnium catalyst, with sites in balance, did best. It did most well at high glucose levels in ethanol.
pmc-12735324:
Greta Mucignat and a large team test a red algae extract against dog mast cell tumors in the lab. The extract comes from the alga Sphaerococcus coronopifolius. Their 2025 study runs the extract on two tumor cell lines and two normal cell lines. Three assays gauge how well it kills cells. Gene reads and cell scans then probe how it acts.

The extract did slow tumor cells, at modest doses. It also harmed normal cells, so its aim was far from clean. In tumor cells it stalled the cell cycle and cut a growth pathway tied to cholesterol build-up. It also pushed cells toward death and left marks of DNA damage. The title's hopes and fears both show up in the results.
pmc-12735424:
Beatriz de Mateo Silleras and co-authors test a body-scan method for spotting nutrition problems in older adults who live in care homes, in a study from 2025. These patients often lose muscle and shift in body makeup, yet standard checks miss it. The method sends a mild electric signal through the body and reads how tissues resist it. No guesswork about body water is needed.

The study covered ninety-five residents with mental health conditions of old age. Two forms of vector analysis on the readings were compared with clinical exams. One form split patients with low muscle and a mixed low-muscle, high-fat state. The other flagged fat gain and the mixed state. Neither form tracked plain weight scores or malnutrition labels. The authors say the scan adds a fast, cheap check for care teams.
pmc-12735524:
Louise Bureller and colleagues review hybrid materials that tuck glowing dyes called BODIPY inside metal-organic frameworks, sponge-like crystals built from metal nodes and organic links. The dyes shine brightly as loose molecules but often fail in solid form, while the frameworks offer order, pores, and tunable structure. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors sort the ways the two parts are joined. The dye can serve as a building link with one, two, or three attachment points, be tied on afterward, or sit inside the pores as a guest.

The hybrids show stronger performance in light harvesting, glowing materials, sensing, light-driven chemistry, and light-based medical treatment. The review stresses careful cooking conditions, thorough checking of the product, and exact measurement of how much dye got in, so the framework stays intact and useful.
pmc-12735624:
Towhidul Tarun and co-authors test an olive compound against an aggressive prostate cancer in a 2025 study. Some prostate cancers change into a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine form after hormone blocking treatment, and that form is hard to treat. A compound from olives, oleocanthal, was a candidate because olive rich diets are tied to lower rates of some cancers.

In lab tests, the compound suppressed the growth of neuroendocrine prostate cancer cells. The team also studied tumors grown in mice, using gene and protein tests to track its effects. A tissue analysis showed that a key enzyme was elevated in cancer tissue compared with normal prostate. The work links the compound to pathways that drive this cancer form, including a receptor and a growth signal.
pmc-12735924:
Thelma Flores and co-authors review a bold idea for treating a deadly brain tumor by aiming at a common virus, in a paper from 2025. The tumor grows fast, resists standard care of surgery, radiation, and drugs, and almost always comes back. Many studies have found traces of the virus, a member of the herpes family, inside tumor tissue.

The review weighs claims that the virus helps the tumor grow, hide from immune cells, build blood vessels, and shrug off drugs. Early trials of virus aimed drugs and vaccines have shown hints of gain for some patients. The authors say the link is not yet proved as cause, but the stakes are so high that the path deserves full and careful testing.
pmc-12736324:
Yuan-Chao Xue, Ping Ren, Jasper Fuk-Woo Chan, and Vivian Huiping Shuai review how laboratories diagnose measles, in a two thousand twenty-five minireview. Measles still outbreaks worldwide as vaccination coverage slips, and with no specific antiviral, fast accurate diagnosis drives outbreak control.

The review traces the field from virus isolation in cell culture through antibody assays to real-time molecular PCR testing. Each method's strengths depend on specimen type, timing, and laboratory capacity, so the authors lay out current strategies side by side. Emerging technologies and persistent challenges get attention too. The piece is a practical map for laboratories facing resurgent measles demand.
pmc-12736424:
Can Wang and co-authors breed, in a 2025 study, wheat lines that carry a blight shield borrowed from a wild grass relative. Head blight is a ruinous wheat disease worldwide, and wild kin hold resistance genes that farm wheat lacks. The team crossed a chromosome arm from the wild grass into wheat using a mutant that lets unlike chromosomes swap parts.

Nineteen swap lines were found among hundreds of offspring, using gene markers and stained chromosome views. Fine genotyping mapped the swap points and found a hotspot near one arm's end. Eleven lines resisted blight far better than the weak control strain. The shield sits in a defined stretch at the arm tip, ready for breeders.
pmc-12736524:
A research team pairs a classic filter with a learning agent to estimate a car's sideways drift angle, in a 2025 paper. The sideslip angle is a core quantity for stability control and active safety. Kalman filters estimate it well, but their noise settings are fixed by hand and degrade on tricky roads.

The team's method lets a deep reinforcement learning agent tune the filter's noise matrices on the fly. The agent watches vehicle motion and filter performance, then adjusts the settings to cut estimation error. A policy optimization algorithm trained the agent across varied speeds, road grip levels, and sensor noise. Root-mean-square error fell by over thirty percent versus the fixed filter. Accuracy held up across the tested conditions. The authors suggest the hybrid approach could extend to other vehicle states that safety systems need.
pmc-12737124:
Byeongkyu Min and three co-authors chart in 2025 where microplastics gather in the seas off Korea and how they get there. The team collected surface seawater and sediment samples during summer in the South Sea and the East China Sea.

Counts were highest in one study area, then fell across the others, in both water and mud. Most particles were fragments, and most were tiny, between two hundredths and three tenths of a millimeter across. The authors trace the pattern to warm currents flowing north from southern waters, which carry light, small plastic bits into the region. The map helps target cleanup and monitoring.
pmc-12737524:
Seraina Müller and co-authors measure botulinum toxin results in facial palsy with artificial intelligence in this 2025 study. Toxin injections ease the tight, uneven faces of non-flaccid palsy, but proof has leaned on impressions. The team paired AI face tools with patient questionnaires.

Eleven patients received tailored injections and were checked three weeks later. Software found real gains in dynamic symmetry: brow raising, smile angle, and lower lip height all improved. Emotion reading software, though, detected no change in expression. Patients reported better social well-being and looks satisfaction after treatment, while daily function scores stayed flat. The authors suggest symmetry improved partly by quieting overactive muscles, which may cap expression gains.
pmc-12738524:
Mousumi Debnath and Dikshita Aneja review how pomegranate peel, a farm waste, can serve skin care. The peel is rich in plant compounds with healing traits. Named examples include quercetin, catechin, punicalagin, and ellagic acid. These compounds can help build tiny particles for creams and can fight germs and swelling. The review maps studies found through a strict search of science data bases.

Drug-like checks show how each compound moves through skin. Punicalagin crosses skin poorly, suiting it for creams that act on the surface. Ellagic acid crosses well, suiting it for goods like sunscreens. Mixes of peel particles may add sun guard and moisture. The authors call for trials in people and for work on scaling the goods for sale.
pmc-12740924:
Xiaoting Yi, Peng Deng, and their co-authors built an ultra sensitive sensor for a lung cancer marker's DNA. Their 2025 study targets CYFRA 21-1 DNA, whose detection aids lung cancer prevention and care. The sensor reads an electric signal and needs no added indicator dye, which simplifies the design.

The sensing surface uses tiny rods made of two iron oxides joined together, coated with gold. Magnets draw the rods into place on the electrode by self assembly. The team checked each building step with standard electrochemical scans. The mixed oxide rods offer both magnetism and a large active surface, which boosts the signal from tiny amounts of target DNA. Such sensors could move tumor marker testing toward quick, cheap formats.
pmc-12741424:
Jiaan-Der Wang and Cheng-Ta Chou report claw hands in a woman with acute intermittent porphyria in work from 2025. The rare disorder causes recurrent attacks and chronic nerve damage that can deform the hands over time.

The 48-year-old woman had years of cramp-like belly pain and limb weakness that moved from hands upward. Nerve tests showed severe axonal damage, and her fourth and fifth fingers showed the classic claw posture with wasted muscles. On a gene-silencing drug in a trial, her yearly attack rate fell from twenty-four to zero. Finger bending and muscle bulk then partly recovered.
pmc-12742124:
Sara Alsuwais, Christopher Wibberley, and Richard Body interview paramedics about child head injuries in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Most such injuries are mild, but a few worsen fast. Paramedics are often first on scene, yet they lack tools made for children and see these cases rarely.

Thirty-seven paramedics from one ambulance service in the United Kingdom took part in interviews. Four themes emerged, covering the child, the clinician, the system, and the decision rules. Respondents described low confidence, training gaps, and strong emotions around safeguarding. They welcomed decision rules for structure and legal cover, but worried the rules were built for hospitals and adult patterns. The authors call for tools shaped to prehospital care.
pmc-12742224:
Carlos Pereira leads a team on two bone drugs and bone repair in rats. Their study from twenty twenty-five uses graft spheres in femur defects. Two bisphosphonate drugs of distinct generations are compared.

Female rats were split into six groups for the tests. Some got graft alone, some drug alone, some both combined. Drugs were given monthly for two months before surgery. A small standard hole was made in each femur bone. After a month of healing, tissue was taken for study. New bone and leftover graft were both measured.
pmc-12742724:
Leprosy still carries heavy stigma in parts of Indonesia, and Ralalicia Limato and co-authors explore what people in South Sulawesi know and feel about the disease. Their mixed-methods study surveyed 402 people — patients, close contacts, community members, and health workers — and added interviews and group discussions. Knowledge scores came out low, above all on symptoms, cause, and spread.

Many believed the disease passes through families by birth, or through animal waste or sexual contact. Stigma scores were highest among general community members. Interviews revealed that the local name for leprosy carries shameful overtones linking it to witchcraft and sin, and patients described rejection and avoidance of touch. Stigma also lived inside the national programme itself. The authors call for education shaped to local beliefs, backed by steady political commitment and funding.
pmc-12743024:
Akiyoshi Nakayama and co-authors weigh the gene risk for raised uric acid in more than nine thousand Japanese participants, in work from twenty twenty-five. Raised uric acid can lead to gout over time. Variants in a transporter gene called ABCG2 are a major genetic cause.

The gene variants accounted for about thirty percent of progression risk at the population level. That share beat classic factors such as excess weight, heavy drinking, and aging. Each factor also raised risk at the personal level, and gene effects could be translated into equal lifestyle terms. The authors map a nurse led, gene aware prevention plan on a behavior change model. Personal risk talks could spur healthy change, they argue.
pmc-12743224:
Chenchen Wu and co-authors build blood tests that predict who will respond long-term to a Crohn's disease drug, in a 2025 study. The drug, ustekinumab, helps many patients, yet doctors cannot tell in advance whose gut will heal.

The team profiled inflammatory proteins in blood from forty patients before treatment, split evenly between later responders and non-responders. Three proteins differed at the start: two ran high in non-responders and one ran low. A follow-up test in twenty more patients confirmed the pattern. A simple model joining the three beat fancier learning methods. One protein alone also predicted fairly well, aiding tailored care.
pmc-12744224:
Hoa Trung Dinh and co-authors linked frailty to falls in 2025 among older Vietnamese outpatients with type 2 diabetes. Frailty and falls both erode health and freedom in this group, yet their tie in Vietnam was unstudied. The team read 740 patients past sixty at a Hanoi geriatric hospital. Fall risk came from a twenty-one-item index and frailty from a clinical scale.

Near a fifth were frail, and a like share had fallen in the past year. Frailty more than quadrupled fall odds after full adjustment. Age, poor sugar control, diabetes complications, and other old-age syndromes added risk. The team urges routine frailty checks in diabetes care so fall plans can target the frailest.
pmc-12744824:
Tzu-Hao Yen and co-authors report long term results for a disc heat treatment for lumbar degenerative disc disease in a 2025 study. The procedure, intradiscal biacuplasty, heats the disc from inside to ease pain. Long term outcomes and predictors of success were underexplored.

A single surgeon treated more than one hundred patients at one center and followed them for two years. Pain and disability scores fell within a week and stayed down. Mean improvements passed three fifths at six months, and over three quarters of patients reported satisfactory outcomes. Disc extrusion on scans was linked to better results.
pmc-12745424:
Zhaoxia Lou and Deng Sun estimate winter wheat yields from space and weather data in this 2025 study. Their region, Huang-Huai-Hai in China, grows much of the country's winter wheat. Good yield forecasts help guard the food supply. The team combined satellite readings with rain and temperature records at county level.

Satellite measures tracked leaf area and how much light the crop absorbed. Patterns were studied across three stages: winter rest, active growth, and ripening. Three model types were built for each stage and compared. A neural network model did best, above all during active growth. A follow-up analysis ranked which inputs shaped each forecast most. County planners gain a tested window for early yield calls.
pmc-12746624:
Xiaoping Liu, Ping Yuan, and Ying Huang link artery-health markers with fatty liver in a 2025 study of Japanese adults. Fatty liver is known to travel with heart and vessel disease, but its tie to standard atherosclerosis indexes was less mapped. The team drew on exam records for just over nine hundred adults who had blood tests, questionnaires, and belly scans.

About twenty-nine percent had fatty liver on ultrasound. Three markers stood out: an atherogenic index, a triglyceride-glucose index, and a pulse-wave speed measure. All three stayed tied to fatty liver after age, sex, weight, and habits were counted. The triglyceride-glucose index sorted cases best of the three. Past a cutoff the authors name, it flagged fatty liver with high sensitivity. They suggest the cheap index can help screen for the condition.
pmc-12747324:
Eric Mishio Bawa and ten co-authors map a new disparity measure for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias across South Carolina. The mortality-to-incidence ratio compares how many die of a disease with how many are newly diagnosed; it is routine in cancer work but new here. Using the state registry for 2017 to 2021, with a pre-pandemic window for comparison, they computed ratios by race, rurality, and county.

Black residents and rural residents consistently showed higher ratios, and the pandemic years widened the gap. Ratios above one, meaning deaths outnumber new diagnoses, appeared only among Black residents. Thirty-one of forty-six counties sat above the state average. The authors offer the maps as a targeting tool, pointing services toward the communities carrying the heaviest burden.
pmc-12747924:
Abdulaziz Shalali, Saad Wali, and Mohammed Aldurdunji survey in 2025 what health workers in Saudi Arabia know about interactions between medicines and food. Such interactions can quietly weaken a drug or make it unsafe, yet little evidence described how well local professionals understand or counsel about them.

Three hundred eighty-five doctors, pharmacists, and other health workers answered a structured questionnaire. The survey covered knowledge, day-to-day counseling habits, and the barriers and training gaps they perceive. The results give educators a map of where teaching on drug-food interactions needs to go.
pmc-12748724:
Orel Levy and co-authors report a 2025 study on how noise and interest shape the brain while people learn from video talks. Staying focused through a long talk is hard, and it is harder still when the room is loud or the talk is dull. The team wanted to know which of these two factors matters more for the brain.

The team tracked brain waves and skin response while people watched talks with or without real background noise. Dull stretches showed weaker tracking of speech, signs of lower focus, and more strain. Noise, by contrast, had small effects. The work suggests that keeping course content engaging may matter more for attention than cutting noise alone.
pmc-12748924:
Gold holding a strongly negative charge sounds impossible, yet pressure plus two pushy partners may force it. Xiaohua Zhang, Sheng Wang, Aitor Bergara, Xin Du, and Guochun Yang propose that state in a 2025 paper. Their recipe pairs lithium, a strong giver of electrons, with fluorine, a strong taker, under high pressure. The result is a crystal where gold sits at a minus-seven charge state.

In that crystal, gold's electron count matches the noble gas radon. Loose electrons pair up in the gaps of the structure. Swapping fluorine for iodine or phosphorus softens the charge step by step. The last swap yields a superconductor in their models. The authors offer the recipe as a route to exotic matter.
pmc-12749124:
JianFu Zhou, YiBing Zhang, Ruiling Li, Yue-Cune Chang, and Niang-Huei Peng model how families, schools, and children jointly block lung infections in two thousand twenty-five. Child lung infections spread through homes and classrooms, so prevention must span all three. A survey of over two thousand parents of children aged three to sixteen fed the model.

Four blocks were measured: parent prevention steps, vaccine concern, school safeguards, and children's own habits. A structural model found parent steps feed all three other blocks directly. School safeguards also carried part of the parent effect onward to vaccine concern and child habits. The map gives health planners a lever chart: strong parent action lifts the whole web.
pmc-12749624:
Jiaxin Zhang and eight co-authors compare breast cancers with several tumor sites against single-site disease in a 2025 study. Multi-site cancers raise questions about spread, treatment, and outlook. Their traits and survival patterns had not been set beside single-site cases at this scale.

Records covered 262 multi-site patients and 1,745 single-site patients, all followed over time. Multi-site patients were more often younger and premenopausal. Their tumors differed in type mix and marker patterns, and fewer received chemotherapy after surgery. Disease-free survival showed no clear gap between the groups. Overall survival results and trait differences are laid out in full. The comparison helps doctors counsel patients facing this less common presentation.
pmc-12750624:
Xia Jin and co-authors chart the learning curve for a two-portal spine surgery in a 2025 study. The endoscopic method treats disc herniation with spinal narrowing through two small channels. New methods take practice, and patients deserve to know the ramp. Records cover 112 cases at one Beijing hospital.

A cumulative sum method split the series into early and late groups at the curve bend. The first 25 cases formed the early group, and 87 followed. Later cases ran faster with shorter incisions. Pain and disability scores and complication rates matched across groups. The study names the case count where the method steadies in trained hands.
pmc-12750724:
Min Gao and co-authors pair mouth drills with mind aid for old folks whose mouth work fades. The study appeared in 2025. Mouth fade curbs chew and gulp, and drags mood and self-trust down with it. Near one hundred old folks split in two arms for a season of care.

One arm got stock mouth care and health tips. The next arm added mouth drills and mind aid on top. At the start the arms sat even on all reads. Past the span, the drill arm chewed and gulped past the stock arm. Its fear and gloom scores sat low, and mouth-life and self-trust scores sat high.
pmc-12751224:
Yan Zhang and co-authors build a tool for judging health care simulation centers, where students and staff train with lifelike practice setups. Such centers cost a great deal in space, gear, and expert staff. Yet most research judges the training itself, not the centers behind it.

Using a structured expert consensus method, heads of centers first proposed many possible items, which were then sorted and voted on. The final tool, called STRIVE, covers six areas from course content and teacher training to resources and effects. It keeps the most supported items in each area. The authors say it can help managers see strengths, spot gaps, and improve their centers.
pmc-12751624:
Rashida Ali, Nimish Tutwala, and Mena Abdalla review ten years of re-exploratory laparotomies in obstetrics and gynecology at a tertiary care hospital in Mumbai, India, from 2014 to 2024. A second open abdominal surgery soon after the first is a serious event with high morbidity and mortality. Their 2025 study collects every such case at one center. Records gave the primary surgery, the indication for return, the time gap, the procedures done, and the outcomes.

The set held 117 cases, with a mean patient age near 32 years. Cesarean section was the primary surgery in about 46 percent of cases, and total abdominal hysterectomy in about 23 percent. Postpartum hemorrhage led the indications for return, then muscle hematoma, then burst abdomen. Return came at a mean of about five days, and nearly half the patients had some complication afterward. The team calls for meticulous technique and swift return when needed.
pmc-12751724:
Seyedeh Batool Hasanpoor-Azghady and co-authors test a support program for fathers of early-born babies, in work from 2025. A preterm birth and a stay in intensive care strain fathers, who often hide their feelings to stay strong. Eighty fathers at an Iranian hospital were split at random into a support group and a standard care group.

The support group got tailored facts and emotional backing at the first meeting with their baby. Three days on, their stress and anxiety scores sat far below the control group. Stress over the parent-child bond stayed highest even in the helped group. The authors urge that such support join standard care.
pmc-12751924:
Ramazan Aslan interviews medical rescue staff who deployed after the 2023 earthquakes in Türkiye in this 2025 paper. Two huge quakes struck Kahramanmaraş in February of that year. Twelve team members described how they prepared, mobilized, and lived in the field. Their accounts were sorted into three themes.

Clear roles and visible leaders helped; mixed training and fuzzy command hurt. Orders often arrived through messaging apps, and winter roads slowed deployment. Short first rotations of three to seven days worked best. Shelter, heat, food, and sanitation started out poor, then improved as logistics scaled. Aslan recommends checklists, set mission orders, and minimum living standards.
pmc-12752024:
Wiem Feki and five co-authors report a rare jaw bone disease in a thirteen-year-old boy from Tunisia. The disease, Garré's osteomyelitis, is a long-term bone infection that lays down new bone along the jaw. It usually starts from a bad tooth or gum sore, and it mostly strikes the young. In this boy, no source of infection could be found, which made the case hard to name.

Scans and tissue tests confirmed the disease and ruled out tumors. Drugs given by vein cleared it without surgery. Ten months later the boy had no symptoms and a balanced face. The case argues for keeping this disease in mind when a teen's jaw swells.
pmc-12752424:
Fahimeh Farzanegan and co-authors surveyed, in a 2025 study, job satisfaction among postgraduate dental students in Mashhad, Iran. Advanced dental training is long and stressful, and mood at work shapes learning. Sixty-four students across ten specialties took part in early 2024.

Two satisfaction scales disagreed: one scored the group above average, the other below. Social support and psychological well-being both scored above average, while stress ran high. Married students reported stronger satisfaction and support than single peers. Satisfaction moved with support and well-being in the data. The authors urge dental schools to build support systems and stress relief into training, since the two travel with how students judge their work life.
pmc-12753324:
Tz-Syuan Su and co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, a surface protein that helps cancers spread by rewiring how tumor cells eat, grow, and hide. The protein, CD147, sits in the cell membrane and partners with many other surface proteins. Through those partnerships it shapes blood vessel growth, drug resistance, and immune behavior. It also helps prepare distant sites where traveling cancer cells can later settle and grow.

The review traces how CD147 works with partners such as CD44 and growth factor receptors to switch on signals inside the cell. Those signals retune the use of sugars, fats, and amino acids, and reshape the tissue around the tumor. By linking this protein network to the seeding of new tumors, the authors mark CD147 as a target worth watching for future anti-spread therapies.
pmc-12753424:
Four researchers measure how daily movement relates to self-control skills in five- and six-year-olds. Executive function covers holding back impulses, shifting between rules, and keeping facts in mind, and it grows fast at this age. The team fitted 170 kindergarten children with motion sensors for a week and asked parents to rate each child's daily executive skills.

The children averaged about 111 minutes of activity a day, and most reached the advised level of moderate-to-vigorous movement. After accounting for body size and family background, more vigorous activity went with better overall executive scores and better impulse control, flexibility, and working memory. The link bent into an inverted U, with the sweet spot near 71 to 83 minutes a day. Boys gained more than girls as activity rose. The authors present movement as a practical support for early thinking skills.
pmc-12753924:
Aneta Szymaszek, Szczepan Iwanski, and Aleksandra Bala open a Research Topic on where the study of mind and brain is heading. Their 2025 editorial says the field is changing fast. It is joining brain science, brain imaging, computer modeling, and clinical practice. The collected articles aim for sharper measures, real-world fit, and findings that carry into care. Topics range from early thinking decline and new blood markers to immersive and AI-based tools for testing.

Other pieces cover targeted stimulation of the brain and the effects of COVID-19 on it. One study links structural changes in a deep brain area in epilepsy to memory problems. Work on resting brain waves ties altered patterns to burnout at work, a possible marker for the condition.
pmc-12754724:
Xiao-yin Lin and co-authors review how ultrasound guidance has changed nerve block practice for older patients. Older adults face higher risks from pain drugs and from surgery itself, so precise, low-dose numbing matters. Their 2025 review covers ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia, in which the doctor watches the needle and the nerves live on a screen while placing the block.

The review reports higher success rates, smaller drug doses, and less whole-body exposure than older landmark-based methods. It links the technique to lower opioid use, calmer recovery, and fewer cases of delirium or mental fog after surgery. The authors also note fits with fast-track recovery plans, which prize early movement. Training gaps and uneven resources still limit use. They call for standard, skills-based training and large trials across many centers to firm up the evidence.
pmc-12754924:
Jiewei Ming and co-authors study the mental and social weight of HPV infection for women in Luzhou, China, in a 2025 survey study. More than four hundred women who tested positive at two large hospitals filled in forms on worry, low mood, and quality of life. The team also recorded income, schooling, infection type, and how long the infection had lasted.

About four in ten women reported signs of worry or low mood. Worry and concern scored worst among the life areas tested. Infection with the highest-risk types and a short time since finding the infection were linked to worse scores. Lower income, by contrast, was linked to lower odds in this group. The authors call for early, kind screening and advice that fits local culture, offered soon after a positive test.
pmc-12757224:
Silvia Carbone studies how a joint research project reshaped local welfare networks in an Italian area, in this 2025 paper. Welfare services are delivered by a web of public bodies, groups, and cooperatives. Carbone asks whether designing services together can strengthen that web rather than leaving it imposed from above.

The study mapped two networks of local actors and how they link to each other. It tracked how the joint design work changed who talks to whom and how plans get made. The project drew organizations into a shared view of community planning. Carbone argues that local welfare grows from such ties, not from top-down orders alone.
pmc-12757324:
Shang Lifeng and co-authors ask in 2025 which traits of a swollen heart artery warn that it will stay swollen a year later. The work deals with Kawasaki disease in children, where such swelling can form. The team looks back at past cases at one site.

The study counts one hundred thirty five children with the disease and a swollen artery. It checks the widest swelling size, its shape, and which side it sits on. A large early size was a strong warn sign on its own. Shape and side added more warn power when joined with size in one combined score.
pmc-12758924:
Betül Gündüz, Elif Kılıç Kan, and Ayşegül Atmaca review how industrial chemicals that mimic hormones can quietly weaken bones, in this 2025 article. Endocrine-disrupting chemicals are everywhere in modern industry. Because they resemble the body's own messengers, they latch onto hormone receptors and tilt the systems those hormones govern. People absorb them through food, water, air, dust, and skin.

Bone is a living, constantly remodeled tissue, and its remodeling is under hormonal management. The review gathers evidence that these chemicals disturb bone formation, skeletal development, and calcium balance. The most sensitive window is early: exposure before birth and in infancy, while the skeleton is being built, carries the largest risk. Osteoporosis research usually blames age, diet, and inactivity. This review adds the chemical environment to the list of suspects worth measuring.
pmc-12764224:
Georgios Tyrikos and co-authors report a rare clot complication in this 2025 case paper. Atrial fibrillation is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder. It often causes strokes or blocked arteries, but spinal cord infarction is a rare result.

A 91-year-old woman was found to have new atrial fibrillation and a large lung clot. After blood-thinning treatment began, she developed sudden limp paralysis of both legs and low blood pressure. A spine scan showed a long infarct in the front part of the cord. Despite strong support care, she declined and died soon after. The authors urge fast spine scans when such patients lose leg function.
pmc-12764824:
Drug-carrying sheets of molybdenum disulfide are simulated by Fatemeh Najafi and Farzaneh Farzad in work dated 2025. The sheets are eyed as taxis for a chemo drug, gemcitabine, that treats pancreatic and other cancers. Three add-on groups dress the sheets to grip the drug harder. Atom-level runs weigh grip strength for plain and dressed sheets. The full dress set gripped far harder than the plain sheet.

Free energy sums backed the grip edge with clear spans. The drug sat tighter, moved less, and hid more from water on dressed sheets. Dressed sheets look like strong drug taxis for hard-to-reach tumors.
pmc-12766024:
A drug-proof gut germ's genes are read by Hong Shen and co-authors in work dated 2025. Among over two thousand hospital samples of Enterococcus faecium, nineteen shrugged off linezolid, a last-line drug. Gene hunts and type reads sorted their tricks. One strain held two resistance sets at once, a first of its kind in clinic. It still fell to vancomycin in tests, an odd split.

Two new variants of one spread gene turned up. A fresh type number joined the books as well. Watch on this germ needs both gene lenses.
pmc-12766124:
Wenyu Yang and ten co-authors studied in 2025 what happens when kidney transplant patients get too much of their main anti-rejection drug in the first week. High blood levels of the drug can harm the new kidney itself. The team matched over two hundred patients into exposed and unexposed groups at one center.

The high-exposure group showed weaker kidney function at one week and at one and three months. Infection rates over the first year were also compared. The authors then built a model that predicts who will overshoot, using a selection method that keeps the model lean. Early warning could let doctors trim doses in time.
pmc-12766824:
Giovanni Innella and eleven co-authors test whether software can flag ovarian cancer patients likely to carry a faulty breast cancer gene, in a 2025 paper. Inherited damage in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes changes treatment and family advice, but gene testing everyone is costly. A good guess from routine chart data could target testing well.

The team fed the records of 648 tested patients into three learning methods. A boosting method did best, calling the overall answer right about eighty-five percent of the time. Family history of ovarian cancer drove the guesses most, then tumor type and the patient's own breast cancer history. Age at diagnosis helped a little; tumor stage added nothing.
pmc-12767224:
Lin Shuang Mao and co-authors test a blood ratio as a sign of poor heart blood flow backup in this 2025 study. Patients had type 2 diabetes and stable heart artery disease, with at least one major heart artery fully blocked. Backup vessels can grow to feed the blocked area, and the team asked whether the ratio predicts weak backup growth.

Data covered 1,558 patients, with backup growth graded on a four-step scale. The ratio, uric acid divided by albumin, was higher in patients with poor backup growth. After adjusting for other factors, a high ratio still predicted poor growth on its own. It predicted better than either blood value alone, mainly in patients with sound kidney function.
pmc-12768624:
Nitza Muniz and co-authors study public input on care rules in a 2025 paper from Brazil. A rare disease that upsets body water balance carries a heavy burden. Adding new health tools to the public system calls for both solid science and public voice, so that access stays fair.

The study looked at a public consultation held while a care protocol for the disease was drafted. It profiles who took part, what patients and other stakeholders said, and how openly each comment was handled. The case shows how public input can be tracked in a clear way, so trust in the final rules can be checked rather than assumed.
pmc-12768724:
Dandiany Sofka and co-authors present a 2025 review of a blood test for sepsis in newborn babies. Sepsis is a severe infection and a major cause of harm and death in this age group. Blood culture is the standard test, but it misses many cases. The review asks how well a marker in blood, called PCT in the paper, finds the disease.

The team searched major sources and pooled 111 studies with 19,175 newborns. The marker caught most true cases and cleared most healthy babies. Tests done a few hours after signs began worked best. The authors judge that the marker has high value for diagnosis. It can support, but not replace, clinical care.
pmc-12768824:
Natália Brandão and co-authors wrote a 2025 study on how long patients with rheumatoid arthritis stay on modern drugs in Brazil. The joint disease is a long-term autoimmune condition. New drug classes, from lab-made antibodies to targeted pills, have changed its care, yet some patients still do not respond.

The team compared how long patients stayed on each drug class in first and second rounds of treatment. Staying on a drug is a real-world sign that it works and is tolerated. Records came from public pharmacies in Minas Gerais state, for patients who first asked for a drug between June 2018 and September 2022. Curves tracked persistence out to 18 months. The study helps officials judge which drugs serve patients best in daily practice.
pmc-12769524:
Zeyu Yu and four colleagues test whether zinc and iron levels causally affect asthma risk, in a 2025 study. They used Mendelian randomization, which treats gene variants as natural experiments, drawing on large genome data sets. Each standard step up in blood zinc came with about five percent lower asthma odds, and iron showed a stronger link in the simple analysis.

When both metals were modeled together, zinc kept a small protective link while iron's faded. Gene analysis pointed at the NRF2 and HO-1 antioxidant pathway and the NF-kappa B inflammation pathway as plausible routes. The authors call the evidence suggestive and ask for direct mechanism studies and trials.
pmc-12770924:
Chloe Hampshire and co-authors set out a study plan, published in 2025, for checking how a phone app for paranoia was used in a large trial. Paranoia means unfounded fears that others mean to harm you, and it can disrupt daily life. The app, called STOP, was tested across sites in England to see if it helped.

The plan mixes counts and interviews to learn how much the app was used, by whom, and in what settings. It also asks what helped or blocked its use during the trial. The team follows national guidance for such checks. Findings should show what would help clinics adopt the app later, and they may guide other digital mental health tools as well. Knowing why a tool is used, or dropped, matters as much as knowing it can work.
pmc-12771724:
Noah Ziff and co-authors follow people whose headaches followed a mild head injury, checking whether tender, over-sensitive skin predicts who stays ill, in a 2025 study. Post-traumatic headache is common after mild brain injury and sometimes lingers for months. Allodynia, pain from light touch, signals a sensitised pain system. The team enrolled 139 adults soon after their headaches began, plus ninety-five healthy controls.

At the first visit and again three to four months later, participants completed a standard allodynia questionnaire. A subset also had heat pain thresholds measured on the skin. The analysis compares men and women with the headache against controls, then asks whether early sensitivity foretells the later course. If it does, a simple checklist at the first visit could flag patients who need aggressive early treatment.
pmc-12775024:
Prakash Sandhya and Venkataramana build an AI scout for fall armyworm, a caterpillar that devastates maize worldwide. Human scouting is slow and error-prone. Their system reads two views of each plant: normal color photos and thermal images. Heat patterns can betray infestation the eye misses.

Two fusion designs get tested. One merges extracted features before a neural classifier. The other stacks both images into six channels for a vision transformer. The fused system hit 98 percent accuracy, with matching precision and recall. Single-view or unfused versions lagged far behind, near 60 percent. The authors argue that paired sensing makes pest detection field-ready and far more robust.
pmc-12775524:
Alta Howells and co-authors argue, in a 2025 commentary, that the search for life beyond Earth should deliberately feed back into caring for this planet. Astrobiology studies how life begins and where else it might live, using extreme Earth sites and organisms as guides to other worlds.

Those same studies, the authors say, yield tools for carbon capture, low-carbon energy, waste cleanup, and biotechnology at home. Field sites and microbes picked for space relevance often sit at the edge of what life tolerates, exactly where green technology needs hardy performers. They call for astrobiology to become a two-way science, exploring outward while sustaining life here.
pmc-12779424:
Makito Miyake wrote a 2025 update on a trial of first treatment for bladder and urinary tract cancer that had spread. The cancer starts in the lining of the bladder, ureter, or kidney outlet. Once it spreads, patients have often lived less than two years on standard drug care.

The update covers a large trial, known as EV-302 or KEYNOTE-A39, that paired two newer drugs as the first treatment. The focus is on patients whose response to care lasted a long time. The report asks what a lasting response means for how long patients live and how they fare over time. Such updates help doctors judge whether a strong early response can turn into years of control, and they guide talks with patients about what to expect from care.
pmc-12779824:
Brain-computer links that read the mind passively, without the user trying, need headsets that work outside the lab. A team of researchers compared two consumer headsets, the Emotiv EPOC X and the Muse S, against a research-grade system across twenty-four volunteers. Each person wore all three in turn while watching videos, juggling tasks under rising load, and driving in a simulator.

The research system gave the steadiest signals, the fewest artifacts, and mental-state scores that tracked both task load and how people said they felt. Cleaning the data helped the consumer sets, but their scores stayed blunter and less in line with self-reports. The team sums up the trade-offs among signal quality, ease of use, and cost for each device.
pmc-12780024:
Akie Shimotohno and co-authors found the plant's fast drought alarm, a tiny peptide that slams the pores shut before the stress hormone arrives, in a 2025 study. Plants close their stomata to save water, yet the hormone abscisic acid builds up only later, leaving the first response unexplained. Mutants missing the peptide CLE5 wilted sooner under drought.

The peptide docks onto a receptor pair in the guard cells around each pore. That switch directly activates the two kinases at the heart of drought response, moving the pores and the drought genes without making more hormone or oxidants. The parts are conserved across land plants. Breeding may borrow the fast lane.
pmc-12780424:
Sota Yoshimine and six co-authors study air leaks after lung surgery in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Wedge resection cuts out a small piece of lung holding a tumor. Surgeons seal the cut with staples, choosing cartridge size by habit and feel. Air leaking past the staple line is a common setback. The team suspected that short staples tear the lung's surface as it expands. The tallest staple cartridge might spare that surface.

They reviewed one hundred forty-five patients treated with a modern stapling device. Most received only the tallest, black cartridge; the rest received a mid-height one, alone or mixed. The comparison tests whether staple height changes leak rates. A simple gear choice that cuts leaks would speed recovery for many patients.
pmc-12780724:
Huixin Ma and co-authors rank targeted drug mixes for advanced pancreatic cancer, in a 2025 review. This cancer offers few good options once it spreads. A standard drug forms the base of most care, often joined with newer targeted agents, yet no one had ranked the mixes head to head.

The team pooled thirteen trials with more than four thousand patients, run between 2010 and 2024. Most mixes failed to beat the base drug alone on survival. One agent that blocks a growth signal did help in set subgroups. The authors chart the whole field, which can steer doctors and trial designers toward the most hopeful paths.
pmc-12781024:
Klevis Mihali and co-authors published a 2025 review of a rare heart defect, an aneurysm of the left atrial appendage. The bulge in this small pouch of the heart is linked to blood clots and uneven heart rhythms. The authors gathered case reports and series from three major databases through September 2025.

In all, 216 cases were included, with an average age at diagnosis of about thirty years. The review covers symptoms, heart tracings, imaging findings, related heart problems, treatments, and outcomes. As the largest such review the authors know of, it gives doctors a single source for a defect most will rarely see.
pmc-12781224:
Zeki Vatansever, Izgi Alniak, and Tonguc Berkol compare heroin patients who also use methamphetamine with those who do not, in a 2025 study. The records cover 166 inpatients with heroin use disorder, split into 80 heroin only and 86 dual use patients. Scales rated addiction depth, psychotic signs, suicide risk, and craving.

The dual use group scored worse on nearly every axis: deeper addiction, more craving, more risk taking and thrill seeking, and more suicidal thoughts. Craving and thrill seeking each predicted methamphetamine use on their own. The dual group also lapsed more in the three months after care. The authors urge teams to target craving head on.
pmc-12781524:
Lea-Noelle Stoehr and co-authors report eye inflammation after injections of a stronger eye drug dose in a 2025 study. The drug, aflibercept at eight milligrams, treats wet macular degeneration and diabetic eye swelling. Reports of sterile inflammation inside the eye after this dose were scarce. Three centers logged twelve eyes with such inflammation between mid-2024 and mid-2025.

The inflammation struck about two days after injection, on average after the second or third dose. Most patients had been treated before with no such event, many with the older two-milligram dose. The middle layer of the eye was hit in two-thirds of cases. The rate worked out to about 1.4 percent per injection at the three centers. The series helps clinics weigh the higher dose.
pmc-12782324:
Waraporn Sutthisa and co-authors test shiitake mushroom extracts against nine harmful bacteria, in a 2025 study. Three solvents pulled the extracts; ethanol gave the biggest yield at 31.16 percent. In disc tests, the ethyl acetate extract hit hardest.

Its widest kill zone, 30 millimeters, struck a test strain of Escherichia coli, with a Salmonella strain next. Dilution assays confirmed its edge, most sharply against a Staphylococcus strain, where the lowest dose that stopped growth was 1.95 milligrams per milliliter. Chemical scans found ergosterol leading one extract and linoleic acid the ethyl acetate one, both known bacteria fighters. The team backs such extracts for food and drug uses.
pmc-12784524:
Qing Xiao and co-authors study how Epstein-Barr virus infection shapes Burkitt lymphoma at the genetic, transcriptomic, and immune levels. Their 2025 paper deals with a highly aggressive B-cell lymphoma whose course is closely tied to virus status.

Targeted sequencing of a large gene panel covered 27 cases, and RNA analyses covered 25. Virus-negative tumors had more chromosomal amplifications at several sites, and novel variants in one gene in adults. Virus-positive tumors were enriched for mutations in a different gene. More than sixteen hundred genes differed in expression between the groups, mostly in key growth pathways. The landscape differs sharply by virus status.
pmc-12784724:
Nari Kim and five co-authors sort a class of tumors by immune heat to find which will answer immunotherapy. Their twenty twenty-five article deals with tumors that lack mismatch repair, a DNA proofreading system. Such tumors often respond to checkpoint inhibitors, but responses vary widely.

Using four cancer types from a large atlas, the team scored tumors on immune cell inflow and on a T-cell inflammation gene profile. The two axes made four subgroups. The hottest group lit up interferon and antigen display pathways. A twenty-gene signature of that group was built and checked in three cohorts. It predicted response to PD-L1 blockade in a bladder cohort and tracked survival trends in high-mutation cases.
pmc-12784924:
Rui Wang and co-authors test how protein level and antibiotics in feed affect piglets just after weaning, in work published in 2025. Weaning is a stressful stage, and diet shapes growth and gut health. The team fed 100 piglets one of four diets for two weeks, crossing low or high protein with the presence or absence of antibiotics.

Piglets on low protein grew more slowly and gained less weight by day fourteen than those on high protein. Their bodies held less protein and water but more fat. Blood levels of several amino acids rose in the low-protein group. After the test phase, all piglets shared one diet until they reached a set weight. The authors also track gut health and microbes to guide feeding practice.
pmc-12785324:
Yulia Vlasova and colleagues test a fire-quenching additive for hotter, denser lithium batteries, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Silicon-graphite anodes store more energy, but silicon swells and shrinks as it charges, wrecking cycle life, and bigger batteries raise fire fears. Their additive, a ring-shaped phosphorus compound called HFEPN, was designed to answer both problems at once.

At fifteen percent of the electrolyte, the mix would no longer sustain a flame. The additive also formed a steadier protective skin on the anode and sped reactions at its surface. Yet the cells did not last longer: after seventy cycles they kept about as much charge as plain cells. The authors blame thicker, slower electrolyte, whose drag cancels the surface gains. The lesson is a trade-off to engineer around, at lower doses or with a redesigned molecule.
pmc-12785424:
Zhu leads a large team mapping chronic gout mechanisms with multi omics, in work from twenty twenty-five. Gout moves from sudden acute attacks to a chronic form that harms joints for good. Past studies used single data types and missed the full picture.

Blood samples came from healthy controls and from acute and chronic gout patients. Deep protein profiling and broad metabolite profiling were combined. Nine proteins stayed altered across stages, holding one that controls urate removal and several tied to immunity. Eleven metabolites also shifted in a steady way. A thyroid hormone and taurine axis stood out as a fresh lead for therapy.
pmc-12785724:
Milagros Lopez-Reynoso and co-authors offer a 2025 overview of corn-based fermented drinks in Latin America. Corn is the most eaten cereal in the region, with deep cultural roots and wide genetic variety. Fermented drinks made from it draw growing interest for their health promise. The review weighs grain color, nutrition, microbes, and safety across studies.

Corn types differ in starch, protein, minerals, and active compounds. Those gaps shape the taste, safety, and health traits of the drinks. Most drinks ferment on their own or with light control, driven by acid bacteria, fungi, and yeasts. Their by-products can raise food value and block harmful germs. Safe practice in making them is stressed. Gaps on variety effects remain open.
pmc-12785824:
Laura Calvillo, Eugenio Caradonna and their co-authors review links among a gut-derived compound, nerve control and heart failure in 2025. The compound, called TMAO, forms when gut bacteria process choline and carnitine from food and the liver oxidizes the result.

High TMAO is tied to artery disease and heart failure and predicts death in heart failure patients. It can trigger inflammation, blunt protective pathways, make platelets more reactive and boost sympathetic nerve activity. The review frames a gut-brain-heart loop where vagal signals and low brain blood flow worsen the cycle. Targeting gut microbes or TMAO is a new frontier, they argue.
pmc-12785924:
Karen Kirkness and Suzanne Scarlata set out a shared molecular frame for how fascia, the body's connective tissue web, senses force. Much work covers how it acts under load, but no shared mechanotransduction frame told how forces become adaptive cell responses. The narrative review pulls in work on mesenchymal cells and fibroblasts, proposing the calcium-hyaluronan axis as a feedback loop.

In the frame, stress from load switches on calcium channels, setting off hyaluronan synthesis by enzymes, and the weight of the hyaluronan then decides the signal outcome. Heavy hyaluronan binds one receptor and backs tissue stability and quiet. Light fragments switch on a different receptor and drive remodeling and repair. It has points for movement, manual therapy, and rehabilitation, but fascia proof is still a need.
pmc-12786324:
Naznin Nahar and a large team show night hormone signs time the shift from nurse to food hunt in honey bees. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The hormone, melatonin, is an old clock part, yet its role in bee task splits was not clear. One shot sped bees out of the hive and brought their first food dance near nine days soon.

Block drugs and gene hush runs flipped the push, which marks the path as the driver. A make gene for the hormone peaked at hunt age, near ten times its young mark. Code reads found clock marks at the catch gene. More hive checks are called for.
pmc-12787424:
Zhang and co-authors score trait spread across 362 chickpea lines. They measured 17 traits tied to growth and seed quality. Diversity scores for five trait groups ran from 0 point 76 to 1 point 20. Scores for twelve count traits ran higher, from 1 point 45 to 2 point 07. Spread values ranged from 7 point 63 to 41 point 69 percent across traits.

Growth span, plant height, and seed weight tracked yield most closely. Five main factors captured 76 percent of the total spread. Sorting split the lines into five groups with clear strengths. Ten lines scored best overall on a combined grade. Those lines are prime picks as parents for new chickpea breeding.
pmc-12787824:
