Liansheng Zheng and co-authors study how strong-field femtosecond laser filaments make micro-nano forms on steel. Their 2025 work looks at stainless steel worked in point, line, and area patterns.

Laser filament work can shape rough and large surfaces with no need for tight focus. That fits uses in aerospace, energy, and defense. The team finds that the way energy is spread in the filament, with a core and a pool round it, plays a key role in how the forms take shape. Ablation, flow of molten metal, and settling of metal vapour drive change at the surface as a set. The forms shift in turn, from patterns that repeat, to ripple-like, crater-like, and honeycomb-like forms, and then to taro-leaf-like forms. The account helps guide smart making of steel surfaces made to do a set job.
pmc-12788024:
Masahito Nakano searches in 2025 for steady reference genes to anchor gene activity tests in the fig tree. Such tests compare a target gene against a housekeeping gene assumed to hold constant. For figs, an important fruit crop, no one had checked which housekeeping genes truly stay steady, above all during infection.

Twelve candidate genes from the fig genome were tested in fruit, leaf, and stem tissue under fungal attack. All twelve amplified cleanly. Four ranking programs, plus a combined ranking tool, judged which genes varied least. A different winner topped each tissue: one gene for fruit, one for leaves, and one for stems. Several classic housekeeping choices, long used by habit, ranked among the least steady in every tissue. Nakano's validated set gives fig researchers a firmer base for gene studies under disease stress.
pmc-12788424:
Reddi Narendra and six co-authors compared saving front teeth with replacing them, in this 2025 study. Sixty patients aged twenty-five to fifty-five had front teeth with deep gum pockets, root damage, and structural harm. Half got joined care from gum, root, and crown specialists aimed at keeping the tooth. Half got the tooth pulled and an implant crown.

After a year, the saved-teeth group scored far higher on pink and white beauty scales for gum and tooth looks. Their satisfaction also ran higher, at about nine against seven and a half on a ten-point scale. The authors back joined specialist planning as the better path for looks and patient contentment in the front of the mouth.
pmc-12788524:
Jaishree Garg and a team of co-authors compare two dressings after gum depigmentation surgery, in two thousand twenty-five. Dark gums can trouble patients with a high lip line, and surgery can remove the excess pigment. What covers the wound afterward affects pain and healing speed.

Twenty patients took part in a split-mouth trial, so each person received both dressings on unlike sides. One side got an active oxygen gel and the other a standard dressing paste. Healing and surface regrowth were scored over a month with index measures and a dye test. The gel side showed lower pain and better regrowth scores, with a firm statistical gap. The authors favor the gel as the better dressing.
pmc-12789024:
Altug Didikoglu and co-authors present a 2025 study on how everyday light exposure shapes thinking. Light is known to sharpen alertness in the lab, but real life mixes light with sleep, weather, and routine. The team tracked personal light exposure and cognition over seven days in British adults.

Fifty-eight volunteers wore light sensors and took phone tests of sleepiness, vigilance, working memory, and visual search. Forty-one also came into the lab for eye response tests tied to the light-sensitive pigment melanopsin. Brighter recent light went with less sleepiness and faster reactions on two tasks. More daytime light and steadier light patterns linked to better scores across all three tests. Early bedtimes strengthened the light-sleepiness link.
pmc-12789424:
Victoria Tsang and co-authors grow a brain ball to watch a fierce cancer creep in a 2025 study. The cancer in view spreads through the brain in fine threads, which is why it so oft comes back.

Their stage joins balls of brain grown from stem cells with cancer lines drawn from patients. Fast film shows the cancer cells crawl down nerve threads straight for the balls, then flood in. Plain stem cells did no such thing. A test of drugs found two that choked the creep, a fresh one for each line. Gene reads of the lines tied creep grade to drug feel in a clear weave. The authors cast the stage as a way to hunt drugs by the creep they stop.
pmc-12796024:
Kazi Soha and fifteen co-authors published a cancer pharmacology study in twenty twenty-five on a zinc complex built as a gentler chemotherapy candidate. Standard chemotherapy is limited by resistance and side effects, so metal-based alternatives are under active study. The team synthesized a zinc compound carrying thiocyanate groups and tested it thoroughly.

Against breast cancer cells in dishes, it blocked growth in a dose-dependent way and pushed cells into programmed death, switching on genes like p53 and Bax. In mice carrying tumor cells, it reduced tumor burden and extended survival. Blood and tissue checks assessed harm to the host. The authors present the compound as effective in both settings with manageable toxicity.
pmc-12796324:
Yusuke Kitagawa and co-authors report breast cancer hiding in the bowel in a study from 2025. Invasive lobular carcinoma spreads to the gut more often than its ductal cousin. There it mimics a primary bowel tumor, with vague symptoms. Two surgical cases show the trap in action.

The first patient, a forty-five-year-old woman, had no known cancer. Scans showed strictures in her duodenum and small bowel. Bone lesions hinted at spread from somewhere. Surgery and tissue study, backed by immune staining, named the breast as the source. Bowel narrowing in a woman with any breast history deserves that suspicion. The cases urge pathologists to stain before anyone calls a gut tumor primary.
pmc-12797524:
Yongkun Li and co-authors report a 2025 hospital study on burning liver tumors through keyhole surgery. Heat ablation works well for many liver tumors, but badly placed ones resist the standard approach. The team borrowed moves from laparoscopic liver surgery to reach and guard such spots, then reviewed 28 patients with 61 tumors treated at their hospital between 2020 and 2023.

Every ablation hit its target. Sessions averaged about twenty-two minutes, blood loss stayed low, and patients went home in about four and a half days. No major complications arose, and only one tumor came back locally during follow-up. The authors call the blend effective for hard cases, while noting limits to address.
pmc-12800224:
Shaheen and co-authors test whether deep learning can forecast cherry prices in India well enough to guide daily choices. Cherries spoil fast and sell for high prices, so wrong guesses hurt growers and traders. The team pulled daily prices from five wholesale markets, covering the years from 2012 to 2024.

Six forecast methods were compared, from classic time-based tools to neural networks. The deep models won across all error scores. The best one was then put live on the web for the 2025 season, taking fresh market reports each day. Its calls landed within a few percent of real prices in the big markets, with over nine in ten calls judged right.
pmc-12800524:
Koh and co-authors report a hard case of a closed pilon fracture, a break near the ankle joint. A 55-year-old man had a severe fracture, and a first external frame did not ease skin pressure on the inner ankle. Ischemic skin damage soon followed.

Within 72 hours, blisters and purple skin gave way to full skin loss. Later steps included staged surgery, a skin flap, and treatment of bone infection, yet chronic infection forced bone removal. Final repair used joint fusion with a tibial nail. At one year, the bone had healed and he walked alone.
pmc-12802124:
Ahmet Doğan Kuday and Nazlıhan Tekin test whether teaching emotional intelligence lowers the job anxiety of paramedic students. These students carry heavy classroom and clinical loads, and worry about the profession can drag down performance and care quality. That skill, the ability to recognize and manage feelings while keeping healthy relationships, was a plausible antidote.

A single group of 110 students took a structured training course, with measurements before and after. Average scores on that skill rose significantly, from about seventy-five point one to seventy-nine point four. Meanwhile, occupational anxiety fell from about fifty-nine point five to fifty-four point six. The two measures were moderately linked: higher scores went with lower anxiety, and the skill predicted anxiety, explaining about twenty-two percent of its variation. The authors recommend weaving such training into their education.
pmc-12802324:
Pilar Barnestein-Fonseca and co-authors present a 2025 study of how new tech tools feel to those in end-of-life care volunteering. When the pandemic barred face-to-face help, tech stepped in to keep patients, kin, and aides in touch. The team asked patients, kin, staff, and aides how useful such tools seem.

Scores on use, gains, blocks, and contentment were paired with a tech outlook profile. Talks and group chats added depth on what helps and what grates. The aim is to guide which tools to offer and how to ease their uptake in care teams.
pmc-12802624:
Maged Hassanein and co-authors pool the small trial literature on stem cells dripped into veins after ischemic stroke. Four randomized studies, ninety-seven patients in all, tested intravenous mesenchymal stem cells against placebo in the acute and subacute window. Outcomes tracked disability, daily-living independence, and neurological scores, plus death and recurrence for safety.

The stem cell groups finished with better modified Rankin scores and clearly higher Barthel Index gains. Neurological scale improvement, though, did not reach superiority. Death and stroke recurrence ran no higher with cells, with risk ratios under one but wide uncertainty. The authors conclude the therapy looks efficacious and acceptably safe in this sliver of evidence, while the tiny patient total begs for bigger trials.
pmc-12803524:
Taki Eddine Sid, Verena Bauer, and Christian Stumpf present a study from two thousand twenty-five on checking a pressure estimate in the lungs. Doctors need the pressure in the lung artery to judge pulmonary hypertension. Ultrasound of the heart gives a painless estimate, while a catheter threaded to the heart gives the true value.

The team looked back at patients who had both tests within seven days. They asked how closely the two readings tracked and agreed. They also tested whether a leaky heart valve or a weak right ventricle made the ultrasound estimate less reliable. Subgroups by type of hypertension were checked as well.
pmc-12804924:
Shatakshi Mishra and co-authors hunt for virus-blocking compounds in a soil bacterium from high-altitude ground. Their study appeared in 2025. The target is the main protease of SARS-CoV-2, an enzyme the virus needs to copy itself. The bacterium, a Streptomyces strain, showed strong protease-blocking power in lab assays, especially against papain- and trypsin-like enzymes. Chemical separation and identification singled out phenyl carbamate as the most abundant active compound.

Computer docking then tested how that compound fits the viral protease, finding strong binding, and motion simulations checked the fit over time. The authors frame the strain as a promising natural source of antiviral leads. They stress the work is computational and early; cell and animal tests would be needed before any drug claim.
pmc-12805324:
Tianmai Zhang and co-authors follow people with long COVID at a low-cost clinic in the United States in a 2025 study. Much past work rests on what patients say they feel, while far less ties those reports to plain measures of how the body moves and rests.

The team gave wrist trackers to one hundred seventy-two patients, most of them women with low incomes, to wear for up to a year. Patients also filled out health surveys at the start and at three and six months. The study maps how steps, rest, and body signs move over time next to the scores patients give. It also hunts for subgroups whose health paths look alike. The aim is a clear view of how the illness plays out day to day.
pmc-12805724:
Feifei Pan and co-authors find that a blood lipid signal can push womb cancer cells into a rust-like death in a 2025 study. Endometrial carcinoma recurs often and resists treatment. Patients carry high levels of a broken-down, inactive form of the signal, called lyso-PAF, yet what the active form, platelet-activating factor, does to this cancer was unclear.

The active factor shrank tumors in dishes and in patient-derived organoids, tiny tumor replicas grown from real patients. Using binding assays and docking models, the team traced its action to a protein that switches off the cell's antioxidant shield, the SLC7A11 and GPX4 axis. With the shield down, iron-driven damage, ferroptosis, kills the cell. A molecule the body already makes becomes a candidate weapon.
pmc-12808124:
Jing Li and co-authors compare four crape myrtle cultivars for cleaning cadmium from soil, in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. Woody ornamentals may serve in phytoremediation, but the cadmium tolerance of Lagerstroemia indica was little studied. Four named cultivars were grown in pots for eighty days at four soil cadmium levels.

The cultivars differed sharply. One grew faster at low cadmium yet died at the highest level. Two others kept growing steadily at the highest dose by locking cadmium in their roots, a phytostabilization strategy. A fourth switched strategy with dose, sharing cadmium between root and shoot at mid levels, then sequestering it in roots under high stress. The results support cultivar choice for polluted sites.
pmc-12808424:
Thirimon Moe-Byrne and a team of co-authors update a review of health video animations, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. The review asks how well short animations teach patients and the public versus other formats. Eighty-seven publications covering eighty-eight trials made the cut.

Half the trials were new to this update, spanning procedures, condition care, and public health. Animations lifted knowledge in four of five trials that measured it. Attitudes and self-perceptions improved in about half. Open questions remain on lasting effects and on viewers with low literacy or another first language.
pmc-12808724:
Seyong Jin and four co-authors present SwinCLNet, a net to cut brain tumors out of scans with more truth. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Tumor edges blur in scans, yet cuts must be sharp for care. Their net builds on a three-space U-Net with window gaze blocks that catch wide context.

A cross-scale fuse in the tail sharpens edge marks, and a large-kernel gaze on skip links widens the view. Tests on two BraTS sets gave top scores on two truth marks for all tumor zones. Gains were most clear in the hard tumor core and growth rim. Edge miss span fell by near a third against past nets.
pmc-12810424:
Amira Salem and co-authors wrote an audit from 2025 of wrong or mismatched findings in two hospital pathology labs in England. The labs serve the towns of Wigan and Salford. When a finding is later shown to be off, the case is logged and talked through at a set meeting. The team read two years of those meeting notes, from the spring of 2022 to the spring of 2024.

More than half of the logged cases were errors made while staff read samples under the microscope. Cases from the gut and the breast came up most often, and small biopsy samples were the type most prone to error. A joint review with the wider care team caught the most errors and put them right. The team urges labs to guard time for talks before those reviews and to use in-lab scans more when they judge treated tissue.
pmc-12812524:
Wei Xiong and co-authors pool studies on a simple body sign that may flag hidden artery disease. The sign pairs a wide waist with high blood triglycerides, a cheap, no-needle test called the hypertriglyceridemic waist. The review, published in 2025 though the catalog lists 2026, searched seven databases for studies tying the sign to early artery thickening or plaque in the neck arteries.

Six studies qualified. People with the sign had well over double the odds of subclinical atherosclerosis, the silent stage before heart attacks and sudden death. The authors back the sign as an inexpensive screen that clinics could apply widely. They are candid that the evidence base is small: six studies cannot settle how well the sign performs across ages and populations. Bigger prospective work is the next step.
pmc-12812624:
Safa Shaheen and Mohammed Ghaly published a scoping review, with the head dated 2025, on the concept of geneticization in the genomic era. The term, coined by Abby Lippman, criticizes the growing weight given to genetic explanations of health and identity. The authors reviewed twenty-five peer-reviewed studies from 2011 to 2024. They asked what themes dominate recent work and whether Lippman's worries still hold.

Recent writing moves away from strict determinism toward ideas of agency, biosociality, and biological citizenship. Risks of reducing people to genes persist in areas such as race, reproduction, and education. The authors conclude the concept remains a sharp lens for judging genetic technologies, and call for ethical vigilance.
pmc-12812724:
Reshaping gut germs is moving from lab talk to clinic trials for bowel disorders. Meng-Ying Zhang, Shao-Yu Chen, Yu-Hua Lin, and Xing-Xing Yuan review that shift in a 2025 paper. Gene and chemistry reads now map germ influence clear to brain and lung.

Probiotics, stool transplants, and fiber fuels lead the toolkit. Phage therapy and built germs wait in the wings. Trial results swing widely between studies, they note. Germ signatures differ by disorder, which complicates one-size care. Standard dosing and strain rules lag the promise. The review charts where proof stands today.
pmc-12812924:
Qiang Wang and co-authors review the rise of METTL1, an enzyme that stamps a chemical mark on transfer RNA, as a driver of cancer and a possible treatment lever. The mark, m7G, steadies tRNA and speeds the making of selected proteins. Tumors from lung to liver show too much of this enzyme.

Excess METTL1 helps cancers grow, spread, resist therapy, and rewire their fuel use. The review traces how the tRNA mark ripples into message stability and protein output. It then turns to immunotherapy, where the enzyme may shape how tumors answer immune attack. A single RNA editor touching so many cancers makes an attractive, if early, drug target.
pmc-12813124:
Lichao Cao and co-authors study a channel gene called TRPM6 in colon cancer in a paper whose head dates it to 2025. The cancer, colon adenocarcinoma, grows from colon lining cells and turns grim in late stages. The team mined public gene data for the TRPM gene family across cancer types. They asked which genes mark outlook and how they act. Lab tests then cut TRPM6 in two colon cancer cell lines.

High TRPM6 levels went with a better outlook for patients. The gene tied to nerve paths and to the immune mix near tumors. When the team cut the gene in cells, the cells grew and moved more. Added magnesium curbed the cells, but that curb faded when TRPM6 was cut. The gene seems to carry the good effect of magnesium. The authors pitch it as a mark for outlook and a drug aim.
pmc-12815824: Diana Manolescu, Emil Robert Stoicescu, and Ariadna Petronela Fildan open a research collection on finding and treating infectious diseases in this 2026 editorial. They describe a field changing fast under pressure from new germs and drug resistance. Gene-based tests, fast bedside checks, and blood markers now let doctors spot infections sooner and treat them more precisely. The collection's twenty studies fall into five groups, from sequencing-based detection to drug stewardship. The editors' theme is the shift from lab breakthroughs to daily care.
pmc-12816724:
Miloud Zerarka, Said Nouri, Assia Nouri and colleagues reinforced a clayey sand with strips cut from recycled PET bottles in 2025. Soils that mix sand and clay lose much of their strength when wet, which threatens shallow foundations and road bases.

In direct shear tests at moisture levels up to 12 percent, plain samples lost up to half their strength. The PET strips raised peak shear stress by 25 to 30 percent and cohesion by 40 percent, and cut vertical settling by about a third. Even at the wettest level the reinforced soil kept higher cohesion than the plain soil. The strips act like tiny traction cables, offering a cheap, low-impact stand-in for cement or lime.
pmc-12816924:
Dunja van der Velde and ten co-authors study how smoking, stress, and negative affect interact in daily life for patients with psychosis, in work published in 2025. Smoking is highly prevalent in this group, and stress and low mood are common as well. Experience sampling tracks these factors many times a day in real settings.

Samples include 158 patients, 136 unaffected siblings, and 117 controls from a Dutch genetic risk study. Across time, smoking status first links to negative affect in patients, but the link fades once psychotic symptoms and cannabis use are counted. Within person tests show negative affect drops right after a cigarette in patients who smoke. The design separates stable group differences from moment to moment effects.
pmc-12817524:
Ran Xue and six co-authors study how long-term grazing changes the viruses living in acidic karst soil, in a 2025 paper. Soil viruses shape bacterial communities and nutrient cycles, yet land use effects on them are little known. The team compared four land regimes after reclamation: unused land, grazed pasture, abandoned pasture, and fertilized grazed pasture. Genome-resolved methods catalogued both bacterial and viral communities in each.

Both communities differed clearly across the regimes. Grazing lowered viral diversity and loosened the links between viruses and their bacterial hosts. The team also profiled the extra metabolic genes viruses carry, which can steer soil chemistry. The findings warn that grazing management reaches deeper than plants and animals, down to the viral layer that helps run the soil.
pmc-12820224:
Hao Zhou and a large team showed in 2025 one way high blood sugar makes osteoarthritis worse: it sabotages the cleanup cells in the joint. Cleanup cells normally swallow dead cells, keeping inflammation down. In high sugar, these joint macrophages burn more sugar and pile up lactate. The lactate chemically tags a surface protein they need to recognize dead cells.

The tag bends the protein out of shape, so cleanup falters, inflammation rises, and joint damage speeds up. The team also found the enzyme that applies the tag. Silencing it in joint macrophages restored cleanup and slowed disease in their experiments. They propose blocking that enzyme as a treatment strategy for osteoarthritis aggravated by diabetes.
pmc-12820324:
Peipei Xin, Haytham Isleem, and Mohammad Khishe build a digital twin for concrete and use it to hunt for stronger, greener mixes without pouring a test batch, in a 2025 study. Construction talks about digital twins often but rarely validates one end to end. The team treated a public dataset as the digital feed. It trained a deep neural network as the virtual twin of the material. Four classical machine learning models served as benchmarks for predicting compressive strength.

The twin predicted held-out results with an R-squared of about 0.90 and an average error near five megapascals. A plain linear model managed only 0.63, showing that the material's nonlinear interactions demand the heavier machinery. The authors present the workflow as a reproducible blueprint: digitalize the data, build the twin, and optimize mixes by simulation. They argue the approach can cut the physical experiments behind low-carbon concrete design dramatically.
pmc-12821724:
Kis and co-authors look in 2025 for early-life factors linked to a tooth flaw that weakens the enamel of first molars and front teeth. The flaw starts before birth or in infancy as teeth form. Mothers of fifty children with the flaw filled a thirty-item survey in early 2024.

Most links seen at first faded once the team adjusted for other factors, they report. Fever illness in the first year of life stayed linked to tooth sensitivity. A mother's drug use in pregnancy tied to early birth in the raw counts. Careful reading matters here: a survey of fifty can hint, not prove. The authors frame their results with that limit up front, which helps parents and dentists weigh the hints fairly.
pmc-12821824:
Planning surgery on a child's liver tumor from flat scans leaves much to imagination, and the hardest cases punish guesswork. Wenli Xiu and thirteen co-authors tested in 2025 whether patient-specific virtual simulation, a rehearsal in software, sharpens surgeons' evaluations beyond ordinary 3D views.

Six children with tumors of rising difficulty anchored the study. Thirty surgeons, half junior and half senior, assessed each case three ways in order: flat scans, 3D reconstructions, then full virtual simulation. The simulations were built from each child's own anatomy in time for real operations. Scores rose at each step, simulation over 3D over flat. Juniors on flat scans trailed seniors badly, but the gap vanished with the richer tools, a leveling effect the authors stress.
pmc-12822024:
Radiation cures many throat cancers, but tumors short on oxygen shrug it off, and a low-oxygen sensor protein sits at the center of that defiance. Bao and Liao test whether that protein, HIF-1α, drives resistance through the Notch1 signal path. They mine a public tumor database, finding both the sensor and the path's genes turned up in resistant tumors, then run cell experiments under low oxygen.

Silencing the sensor gene made cancer cells die more readily after radiation, with more DNA breaks and less growth, while forcing Notch1 back on partly undid the benefit. The authors name the HIF-1α to Notch1 axis as a target for making stubborn tumors radiation-sensitive again.
pmc-12822124:
Aiqi Yin and co-authors published a 2025 study on whether a routine blood marker in early pregnancy warns of preeclampsia. The condition, dangerous high blood pressure in pregnancy, remains a leading killer of mothers and babies. Early warning would let doctors watch and treat the right women. The marker, CA125, is better known in ovarian cancer care; the team tested its first-trimester level as a predictor.

Within a prospective pregnancy cohort, they ran a nested case-control study: seventy women who developed preeclampsia and seventy matched controls. Blood drawn around the twelfth week was compared between the groups. Modeling then assessed how well the marker predicted the disease, and how its level tracked blood pressure across pregnancy. Higher early CA125 went with later preeclampsia, the title reports. A cheap, early blood test that flags risk would fit antenatal care anywhere; the study measures how far this candidate goes.
pmc-12822224:
Shiva Khaleghparast and co-authors measured and then explained nurses' resilience in 2025 at a heart institute in Iran, ending with strategies to raise it. Resilience here means holding mental and bodily balance under stress. Nurses who have it stay in the job and care better, which makes it a workforce issue, not just a personal trait.

The study ran in two phases. First, 149 nurses were scored on a standard resilience scale, so the level and its spread were plain. Then interviews explored what drives the scores and what could lift them, and the two phases were read together, numbers explaining stories and stories explaining numbers. Readers get both a gauge reading and a workshop manual: how resilient these nurses are, and what the nurses themselves say would make them stronger.
pmc-12823724:
Zi-Yu Han and co-authors traced how lactate worsens acute pancreatitis through a gene-control switch in a 2025 study. High lactate levels predict poor outcomes in this sudden, painful inflammation of the pancreas. Lactate also tags proteins directly, a recently found modification called lactylation that can switch genes on or off.

The team focused on lactylation of a histone site and its effect on NCOA4, a protein that drives ferroptosis, an iron-linked form of cell death. That chain helps explain how metabolic stress turns into tissue destruction. Blocking a link in the chain could soften severe attacks. The study connects metabolism, gene control, and cell death in one pathway for a disease with no targeted drug.
pmc-12824424:
Alejandro Hernández-Alejo, Diego Salinas-Rodríguez, Katia Sofía Alatorre-Plascencia, and Guillermo Elizondo-Riojas published this case report in 2025. It tells of a tumor in the head of the pancreas that fooled imaging into the wrong diagnosis. Such growths glow on scans, and tumor types share that glowing pattern.

The patient, a sixty-three-year-old woman, had three months of belly pain and swelling. Scans showed a large bright mass with a dead center, looking like a neuroendocrine tumor. Surgery had to stop when the rich blood supply caused bleeding, so a biopsy was taken. Under the microscope the growth proved to be a gastrointestinal stromal tumor, a rare visitor to the pancreas, and a low-risk one. Offered major surgery plus targeted drugs, she declined and has done well on watchful care. The authors stress tissue proof must settle what scans cannot.
pmc-12826824:
Ethan Waisberg and four co-authors look in twenty twenty-five at a new tool for medical teaching. The tool is Sora, made by OpenAI, which turns written prompts into videos. Video is already used more and more in medical classes, since it can show moving scenes that text cannot. The authors ask what made-up videos could add to that work.

Sora builds its videos with the same kind of large models that sit behind chat tools. That could make good teaching videos much faster and cheaper to produce. A class could get a custom scene made from a short written request. Readers get an early look at the gains, and at the care needed when fake scenes teach real medicine.
pmc-12827124:
Ali Tfaily led a team setting out a trial plan for mild head injury care in a 2026 paper. Emergency rooms see many such injuries, and scans are often ordered even though most find nothing. A quick blood-based test for brain injury markers might help doctors decide who truly needs a scan. Their trial tests that idea at one center.

Hundreds of adults with suspected mild injury will be split at random into two groups. In one group, doctors see the test results in real time; in the other, results are hidden. The main measure is how many patients get scanned. Stay length, cost, and later outcomes are also tracked.
pmc-12827324:
Eight researchers in Iran compare two diet styles for heart risk in adults with excess weight in a 2025 paper. Intermittent fasting on a 5:2 pattern and daily calorie restriction both claim benefits, but head to head real world data are thin. Registry data covered eighty-two adults over three months.

Forty people fasted two days a week at five to six hundred calories; forty-two cut five hundred to a thousand calories daily. Mean age was near thirty-six, and most were women. Mean arterial pressure and rate pressure product fell in both groups by week twelve. The fasting group also cut triglycerides, and ended with lower systolic and pulse pressures. Long term risk scores are compared across the arms.
pmc-12827524:
Wan and co-authors examine in 2025 the research potential of a regulatory enzyme called A20 in psoriatic arthritis, a joint disease tied to psoriasis. The skin disease reaches beyond the skin to joints, bowel, eyes, and heart valves, yet the joint form is hard to study for lack of good models. The enzyme, coded by a gene linked to both conditions in genome wide studies, damps a key swelling pathway and shapes cell death.

Mice that lack the enzyme develop skin lesions like psoriasis and joint swelling on their own. Varied genetic changes give varied disease pictures. The authors argue that systematic study of these models can fill gaps in how the joint disease starts and reveal treatment targets.
pmc-12829224:
Hui Zhang and four co-authors probe how a common preservative in cosmetics and food may feed Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 journal article. The chemical is methylparaben. Past hints tied it to the illness, but the inner path was unknown.

The team mapped the chemical's shape, then hunted its likely protein targets in four databases and matched them with illness genes. One hundred fifty-three shared targets turned up, and ten core ones stood out in network maps. Docking tests showed the chemical can sit on those core proteins. In nerve cells, a tau mark of the illness rose with the chemical's touch, and gene reads backed some picks. The authors frame the chemical as a risk worth tighter watch.
pmc-12830624:
Gulum Yenisehirli and a large team of co-authors hunt for drug targets in eye melanoma in this 2025 study. Uveal melanoma is the most common eye cancer in adults, and in about half of patients it spreads to the liver, where it almost always kills. Loss of a tumor guard gene drives that spread and scrambles gene control.

The team screened a library of gene-control drugs for weaknesses. One drug family, BET blockers, stood out, though members varied widely in strength. The best one halved deaths in mice carrying spread tumors and blocked spread to bone, spine, and brain. Its gene effects closely matched a second drug family already in trials. The authors name this family a potent, overlooked target.
pmc-12831424:
Ali Kutta Celik and six co-authors survey drug-resistant bacteria in intensive care units in Mogadishu, Somalia. Their 2025 study looks back over six years. It covers one tertiary hospital. ICU patients face high risk of these infections. Yet data from Somalia are scarce.

Blood, urine, and airway samples came from adults. They yielded over two thousand isolates. Three quarters were Gram-negative. Over half of them were multidrug-resistant. Rates were much the same in both Gram classes. Most of the Gram-negative ones fell in the possible extensively resistant class. Carbapenem resistance was high. It was highest in Klebsiella species. The team sets their patterns next to data from the region and the world.
pmc-12833724:
Antek Nicklas and co-authors report a two-stage rebuild for returned acne inversa of the penis in a 2025 case paper. This deep skin disease had come back five years after a plain skin graft in a man in his early forties.

Care ran in steps: cleaning the wound, vacuum therapy, a collagen matrix sheet, then a split-thickness skin graft. Antibiotics and close wound care ran alongside. Over nineteen months of follow-up, the area stayed free of disease with good function and looks. The patient life quality score nearly tripled. The authors argue a well-fed wound bed plus matrix and graft can give lasting cover and may delay or prevent new relapse.
pmc-12835524:
Dieisson Martinelli, Andre Schneider de Oliveira, and Vivian Cremer Kalempa put forth an algorithm drawn from slime mould, for mesh networks in systems with more than one robot. Their 2025 study uses coordination with no central control, in a port scene built in a computer.

Three robots that ran on their own found their way and dodged blocks in their path. A module for links held their mesh network in place. The module was drawn from Physarum polycephalum. It let the robots share tasks when a link was in place, and work on their own when no link held. Links formed in less than two seconds, on average. They formed once more, close to at once, after a fault. New robots joined at great speed. Set next to no exchange of data at all, the network lifted efficiency and cut the time to do the work.
pmc-12836924:
Enihomo Obadan-Udoh and Rachel Howard survey United States dentists about diagnostic slips, in a 2025 study. Wrong calls in dentistry draw little research, though they can wound a patient's daily life and trust. The team asked dentists nationwide about slips they had made and slips they had seen in peers. They also logged which diseases get misread, at what stage, and what drives the errors.

Over 600 dentists answered. About four in ten said they saw a peer slip every day or week, yet only about one in eight owned up to slipping that often themselves. Tooth pulp and gum diseases, sinus trouble, and head and neck cancers topped the misread list. Younger dentists and the busiest ones owned up more. The authors say the field needs open talk and training about diagnostic error.
pmc-12837124:
Xianzhi Zheng and co-authors built a deep learning tool to forecast gut infections in a Chinese city in this 2025 study. The illnesses are hand, foot, and mouth disease and other infectious diarrhea cases in Changzhou. Daily case counts from 2014 to 2024 were matched with weather and air pollution records.

Three model designs were tested: two standard deep networks and a hybrid that first splits the case curve into seasonal and trend parts. A search routine tuned each model's settings. The hybrid posted the best scores on held-out days across four error measures. The authors say blending weather, pollution, and past cases can give health teams a short head start on outbreaks.
pmc-12837224:
Rieth and seven co-authors test a parent coaching program inside public early intervention services, in a 2025 study. Project ImPACT teaches caregivers of toddlers with social communication needs. The trial ran across California with a waitlist design.

Forty seven providers and 125 families took part. After training, providers coached parents far better. Parents in the program improved some parts of play and interaction with their children. Parenting stress and confidence did not differ between groups. Children's communication grew in both groups, with no clear program edge in four months. The authors call for bigger samples and longer follow-up.
pmc-12838024:
Eloísa Pajuelo and co-authors check whether helpful farm bacteria could spread drug resistance. Plant growth promoting bacteria boost crops by moving nutrients, making growth hormones, and fighting plant disease. Farmers use them as living fertilizer, yet some strains carry genes that resist antibiotics, which could spread when the bacteria are released.

The team tested 20 strains against 12 antibiotics using three lab methods. Gram-negative strains tended to resist more than Gram-positive ones. The group then sequenced the full genomes of the four most resistant and two most open strains. They matched lab results with the resistance genes found in the DNA. The work gives a way to judge the risk before such bacteria are spread on fields.
pmc-12839024:
A diabetes drug class that spills sugar into urine has outgrown its first job: it now guards the heart and kidneys too. Dana Movila, Daniel Duda Seiman, and Simona Ruxanda Dragan survey the class's next wave in 2025. The first wave's twin stars anchor the tale.

New forms sharpen aim at the sugar gate, stretch how long each dose lasts, or block a sister gate as well, for a dual hit. Dose plans bend to the patient: weak hearts with full squeeze, worn kidneys, and more. The review weighs trial proof for each twist and flags where proof is thin. The class's arc, from sugar aid to organ guard, makes it a model of how a drug can be reborn.
pmc-12844324:
Yujuan Tang and four co-authors build and test a pump with no moving parts, in a 2025 study. The pump moves fluid using electric drag on charged particles, and it draws its power from light rather than wires. A special ceramic turns laser light into the electric field that drives the flow, which suits tiny devices and soft robots.

The team made the pump and ran a series of tests on what helps or hurts its output. Better electrode shapes and channel layouts raised performance, and so did stronger light. The pump needs no contact to receive power, which makes it handy where wires are awkward. The authors offer their results as design guidance for microfluidic tools, flexible robots, and cooling of small devices.
pmc-12844424:
Tae Min Choi, Hwa Rim Lee, and Sung Gyu Pyo characterize stacked metal-insulator-metal capacitors for radio-frequency CMOS chips. Accurate radio-frequency models need careful removal of test fixture effects, a step called de-embedding. The team compared one-step, two-step, and three-step de-embedding recipes on measured stacked capacitors. Two steps proved the floor for stacked parts, with a thru pattern giving the most precise result.

A modified equivalent circuit was built from the cleaned measurements. Capacitance, quality factor, and S- and Y-parameters all lined up well with the new model. Accuracy held into high frequency bands, which suits RF design work.
pmc-12844724:
Jing Zhang and co-authors build a targeted nanoparticle for breast tumor care in a 2025 study. The particle has a core of polydopamine and manganese dioxide. It carries a small RNA that silences survivin, a protein tumors use to stay alive, plus a ring-shaped guide that homes to tumors.

Tests checked the particle's makeup, how well it shielded its RNA cargo in blood serum, and how tumor cells took it up. It heated well under infrared light, so heat therapy could join the gene effect. In animals, the combined treatment shrank tumors more than either part alone, and the particle also lit up on MRI scans.
pmc-12847724:
Yong Tao and co-authors untangle a puzzle about aluminum in cement's main binding mineral. As this mineral loses calcium over time, structures weaken, yet aluminum's role in that decay has been argued both ways. The team mixed computer simulations, quantum calculations, and lab measurements to watch the process atom by atom.

They found the answer depends on what else changes. Adding aluminum while holding the calcium share fixed twists the mineral's chains and loosens calcium, speeding the decay. Adding it while holding a different ratio fixed lengthens the chains instead, pinning calcium down and slowing the loss. Sodium ions wash out first and shield calcium further. Their computed energy barriers matched lab decay rates across temperatures. The results offer a recipe book for minerals designed to degrade at a chosen pace.
pmc-12847824:
Siddharth Umakarthikeyan and Priyadharshini give factory transport robots a learning based path planner for flexible plants, in work from twenty twenty-five. Guided vehicles haul material in automated factories, but fixed routes jam when people and goods move unpredictably. Flexibility is the missing piece.

Their hybrid method models routing as a decision process with path costs that update as travel times change. A timed elastic band planner then steers the vehicle between waypoints. Laser scans sort obstacles into still and moving, so the robot can react live. Simulations and hardware runs checked single vehicle planning. In multi robot work, live network updates kept vehicles apart and lifted floor coordination.
pmc-12847924:
Can an AI model outthink people on hard mental tasks? Ehsan Latif led a team that pitted OpenAI's o1-preview model against human test-takers across seven kinds of higher-order thinking, from critical and creative thinking to logic and data skills. They used standard tests with published human scores at several levels of schooling.

The model beat undergraduates and postgraduates on a critical thinking essay test and scored far above humans on a systems thinking task. It also led on data skills, originality in creative tasks, logic questions, and a near-perfect run on a science reasoning test. Its weak spots were open-ended problem solving and adapting on the fly. The team sees promise for teaching, with care over ethics and oversight.
pmc-12848024:
Xia Liu and six co-authors built a prediction tool for ovarian cancer surgery in a 2025 study. For advanced cases, the best outcome is removing all visible tumor, which surgeons call an R0 result. Knowing beforehand who can reach it would help planning. The team combined scan readings with clinical measures into a scoring chart.

Records came from 209 patients at three hospitals, split into a building group and a check group. Complete removal happened in about two thirds of cases. Three factors predicted it independently: a scan-based score of how widely the cancer had spread in the belly, a blood protein level, and a ratio of two white cell types. The chart built on them scored high accuracy in the building group and fair accuracy in the check group. The authors offer it as decision support, not a verdict, for surgical teams.
pmc-12848324:
Dalal Alhaffar and co-authors report a clot in the brain's veins after a motorcycle crash that seemed, by head injury standards, only moderate. Cerebral venous thrombosis is usually tied to clotting disorders, hormones, or severe trauma. Better imaging now catches it after milder injuries too, even without skull fractures, where nobody thinks to look.

Their patient, a man of thirty-one, arrived confused with small bleeding contusions and a minor occipital fracture. Venography revealed thrombus in the great venous confluence reaching into two major sinuses. Treating clots beside fresh brain bleeds is a therapeutic tightrope. The case argues for venous imaging when a head injury's course stops making sense.
pmc-12849124:
Fang Chen, Dan Liu, Zuoquan Zhu, and Da Chen trace, in 2025, an RNA marking chain that worsens chronic lung disease in cells and mice. The disease brings lasting airflow blockage and inflammation. A fat-carrier protein and a marking enzyme were each known to play a role, but whether they work together was unclear.

In airway lining cells exposed to smoke extract, silencing the carrier protein reduced injury and a form of iron-driven cell death. The enzyme stabilized the carrier's message by adding chemical marks, helped by a reader protein. Blocking the enzyme restored cell health, while restoring the carrier undid that rescue. The chain offers new drug targets.
pmc-12849324:
Junyi Wang and four co-authors study poisoning cases in teens and young adults at one Chinese hospital, hunting marks of intent. Self-poisoning is a grave risk in this age group. Their 2025 review covers 203 cases from 2017 to 2023, all in patients from fourteen to twenty-four.

Most cases, about eighty-five percent, were suicide bids. Women made up three fifths of the cases, and most patients lived in cities. More than half had a past record of depression. Every patient with such a record sat in the suicide group, and that mark outscored age and sex by far as a warning sign. The authors back screening, safe drug storage, and limits on means for at-risk youth.
pmc-12849424:
Yanping Wang and co-authors report a 2025 study of electric needle treatment in mice with a model of multiple sclerosis. In this disease, immune attack inflames the brain and spine and breaks the barrier that guards them. Star-shaped support cells in the brain help drive that inflammation, so the team focused on them.

Treatment at a classic point eased barrier damage and inflammation at the disease peak. It also raised levels of a hormone and its receptor on those support cells. A drug that turns the receptor on copied the benefit, while blockers and gene silencing undid it. The chain gives a clear target for how the treatment works.
pmc-12849624:
Mostafanezhad, Valizadeh, Karami, and Mohammadi test teach-back training for mothers of premature babies in a 2025 study. Mothers leaving the newborn intensive care unit often feel stressed and unready. Teach-back asks learners to repeat instructions in their own words.

Dozens of mothers at an Iranian hospital were split between standard training and teach-back. Nurses prepared through a workshop and pilot run. After training, teach-back mothers scored clearly higher on discharge readiness. Readmission within a month did not differ significantly between groups. The authors recommend adding teach-back to care plans and nursing curricula. They also note nurses need time for such personal teaching. Staffing shortages are the practical barrier.
pmc-12852124:
Aleksander Kołos and three colleagues track efforts to restore a rare swamp willow at a bog lake in northeast Poland, in a twenty twenty-five study. The willow, Salix myrtilloides, is a leftover from colder times and is fading across Europe as the climate warms. The team planted 240 seedlings at Lake Wiejki and watched them for five years.

The count rose to 272 plants, likely because moose browsing spurred the plants to sprout more shoots. Flowering, though, fell from about forty percent of plants to about a quarter over the study. Tall herbs and rival plants around them curbed shoot height. Soil water acidity mattered too: lower acidity aided regrowth but limited flowering. The results guide care of rare plants at range edges.
pmc-12852724:
Angang Cao, Huiting Jin, Wei Li, and Shiquan Jiang built a math model for a wavy metal diaphragm used in flexible couplings, in a 2025 paper. The part, a multiple corrugated diaphragm, flexes when shafts meet at an angle, and its rippled shape makes forces hard to predict with simple formulas. The team applied plate and shell theory, slicing the ripples into segments with sensible edge conditions. From that they derived formulas for how the part bends, where stress peaks, and how stiff it is against twisting.

They checked the model against detailed computer simulations. Bend shapes and stress patterns matched closely, and the stiffness figures agreed within seven percent. The authors conclude the model captures the part's core behavior. They offer it as a fast design tool, letting engineers size high-performance couplings without running a full simulation for every tweak.
pmc-12853824:
Florian Simon and co-authors published this study in 2025. It steadies engineered gut bacteria for long continuous fermentation. Such runs promise efficient bioproduction, but the inserted DNA circles, called plasmids, get lost over time. Mutations and stray early expression also creep in. The team's fix makes cell survival depend on keeping the plasmid. They deleted a gene the cells need, then put that gene on the plasmid alone.

Extra design tweaks curbed plasmid loss and silenced output during seed phases. Small-scale screens confirmed even, stable producer populations. Two best designs then ran in continuous two-stage setups for over a thousand hours. Output, plasmid levels, and cell mass held steady throughout. The authors offer the system as an antibiotic-free platform for durable industrial production.
pmc-12853924:
Body strength in the first year on belly dialysis swings widely, and Liuyan Huang and co-authors set out a study plan to chart those paths, in work from twenty twenty-five. New patients join within a month of tube placement. Strength is checked five times across the year by bike tests, grip, sit-to-stand, and walk pace.

Path-finding math will group patients by how their strength bends. A forecast model will then sort new patients into paths from early data. Path membership gets weighed against bad outcomes. The protocol is the paper: a careful plan, laid out before the first patient is counted.
pmc-12855824:
Král and co-authors report unusual ordered states in a kagome superconductor, a material whose atoms form a woven triangular lattice. Kagome metals host flat bands and frustrated electrons, a recipe for strange phases. In the compound YRu3Si2, the team combined muon spin probes, transport tests, X-ray diffraction, and theory calculations.

They found a charge-ordered state starting at eight hundred kelvin, a record high for kagome systems, with a repeating pattern along one axis. Below twenty-five kelvin the material broke time-reversal symmetry, and near ninety kelvin a magnetic response switched on under field. It turns superconducting below about three kelvin, with a gap structure the data narrow to two full gaps or one uneven gap. The authors present the compound as a prime stage for correlated kagome physics.
pmc-12855924:
Yiwei Gong and co-authors present a 2025 study on a brain circuit that helps epilepsy develop. Temporal lobe epilepsy grows through a process called epileptogenesis, in which seizures become easier to trigger over time. The subiculum, a hippocampus output zone, has upper and lower parts with different jobs.

Using light-based recording in a mouse kindling model, the team found that excitatory neurons in the lower subiculum fire far too much during seizure development. Switching those cells on with light sped up kindling, while switching them off suppressed seizures in three models. Tracing showed the effect runs through a projection to the front of the thalamus. That circuit was both needed and enough for the process, marking it as a target.
pmc-12857124:
Miki Kawaguchi and co-authors evaluate in this 2025 study a one-minute blood machine for malaria in Thailand, where the milder vivax species rules. The analyzer reads cell size and DNA content by flow cytometry and flags species and parasite share. From 349 suspected patients at a Bangkok tropical hospital, samples faced the machine, microscopy, rapid tests, and gene checks.

Against thick-film microscopy, the machine caught 98.4 percent of infections, beating rapid tests, and every positive was confirmed by gene check. Its species flags matched the microscope every time, and its counts tracked thin-film counts closely. The authors endorse it for vivax regions. Field clinics could skip the microscope wait.
pmc-12859124:
Yugo Nagata, Riki Mikami, Nazrene Zafar, and Yasuyuki Nagashima report the observation of positronium diffraction, in a research paper from 2025. Diffraction proves that particles also act as waves. The effect was known for electrons, neutrons, atoms, and molecules, but not directly for positronium, a bound pair of an electron and its antiparticle.

A tuned positronium beam passed through graphene, a sheet one atom thick. Time selection and position sensing revealed a clear first-order diffraction peak. Its place matched the wave prediction for positronium as one unit. The result proves the pair interferes as a single quantum entity. It opens paths to precision tests with positronium.
pmc-12859824:
Mehmet Umut Kutukoglu and seven colleagues test a urine marker for kidney swelling in children, in a prospective study published in two thousand twenty-five. Hydronephrosis, urine backing up into the kidney, has many causes. The dangerous kind involves a blocked junction that can damage the kidney.

Children with the condition were compared with healthy controls and with children whose swelling came from bladder dysfunction. A spot urine ratio of the CA 19-9 marker to creatinine was measured at entry and six months later. Ultrasound grades, kidney size, and function tests accompanied the marker. The question is whether a simple urine test can separate obstructive cases needing surgery from harmless ones needing only watching.
pmc-12859924:
Bakanae, a fungal disease of rice, causes heavy yield losses worldwide. Chen and co-authors ask whether the microbes living on the plant, read together with machine learning, can diagnose the disease and judge its severity.

They found that two bacterial groups track closely with how severe the disease is. Using 88 samples, they trained random forest, support vector machine, and neural network models. The random forest did best, reaching about 89 percent accuracy and a 94 percent F1 score, and a screening step based on community distance improved it further. For grading severity at the family level, accuracy reached about 78 percent. The authors present the approach as a tool for precision farming.
pmc-12860024:
Maram Abbas and co-authors explore gene-based prescribing in UAE insurance in a 2025 paper. Pharmacogenomic testing matches drugs to a patient's genes, but cost and coverage slow its spread. Insurers' views in the Emirates were little studied.

The team interviewed twelve insurance managers and mapped their views with a SWOT analysis. Awareness of the testing varied widely. Benefits were recognized, yet cost worries, thin physician and public awareness, and weak infrastructure blocked uptake. Privacy concerns were minor. Participants urged joint efforts to align testing with national health goals and to prove its value for money.
pmc-12864924:
Xi Sun, Kai-Yuan Zhang, Shu-Zheng Zhou, and Hua-Hua Fu build, in twenty twenty-five, a theory of spin selectivity in knotted molecules. Some twisted molecules let electrons of one spin pass far more easily than the other. That effect is called chirality-induced spin selectivity. Knotted molecules with a twist that comes from their topology, not their shape, showed near ninety percent spin polarization, plus far higher conductivity and heat stability. Why was unclear.

Their math shows a single trefoil knot, the simplest knot, gives spin polarization above sixty percent. The effect survived shrinking the lattice and straining the shape. When the knot was undone into a plain twisted shape, polarization fell sharply. Topology, they conclude, drives the effect.
pmc-12866024:
Haowei Du and co-authors present a software platform from two thousand twenty-five for finding copy number changes in the genome. Such changes delete or duplicate DNA stretches and cause many inherited disorders. Modern sequencing can call them, but families with unsolved rare diseases need tools that show the evidence clearly and rank likely causes.

Their open-source tool, called VizCNV, joins read depth with allele balance to support careful copy number calls. It offers interactive views that combine variant calls with gene notes, and a filter scheme for parent-child trios that highlights new changes. The team tuned it on a public genome project and tested it on a cohort with known changes. The platform also helps assess parent of origin and mosaic cases.
pmc-12866124:
Palida Palahati and five co-authors study autoimmune liver disease in the Kashgar region in this two thousand twenty-five paper. In this condition, the immune system attacks the liver, and scarring can follow. Liver stiffness is a handy gauge of that scarring. The team gathered clinical data on patients from this region of western China. They recorded disease traits and measured stiffness with a scan.

Their cross-sectional analysis asks which factors track with higher stiffness. Such factors may include disease type, blood markers, and patient traits. Knowing them helps doctors judge who needs closer watch or faster treatment. Regional data matter, since this population is rarely studied. The paper gives local clinicians a clearer picture of their patients' disease stage.
pmc-12868624:
Yanan Chen and co-authors report a 2025 study of a myelin disease in mice, with an eye to treatment. Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease comes from faults in a myelin protein gene and kills the cells that wrap nerve fibers. Without those cells, the brain and cord end up short of myelin.

The team used the Jimpy mouse model of the disease. Cells under stress from the faulty protein trigger a pathway called the integrated stress response. Turning off the trigger enzyme of that pathway in male mice extended life and saved more wrapping cells. Small-molecule drugs that act one step later in the pathway did even better, doubling lifespan in the model. The results suggest that tuning this stress pathway could help patients.
pmc-12870824:
Diego Zelada and co-authors study how a rare inherited disease harms the links between brain cells, in a 2025 paper. The diseases in view attack the cell parts that clear fatty waste. Memory and learning often suffer, yet the link level cause was unclear.

The team used a mouse model of Krabbe disease, which lacks a key clearing enzyme. Signals between cells in the memory region were weaker, and the tiny spines that receive signals were fewer. A toxic fat built up in the membranes that release signal packets. Tests showed that this fat blocks the docking and reuse of those packets. The work names a clear target for future treatment ideas.
pmc-12870924:
Five authors present a study from two thousand twenty-five on children with celiac disease and other autoimmune conditions. Celiac disease is triggered by gluten and is known to travel with type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease. Whether worse gut damage in celiac disease goes with higher levels of the related antibodies was a gap in the literature.

The team reviewed two hundred forty-eight children diagnosed over more than a decade and followed for at least two years. The median age was eleven, and about two thirds were girls. They compared antibody levels against the severity of intestinal damage found on biopsy.
pmc-12872524:
Holger Lode and co-authors compare an antibody therapy, dinutuximab beta, with historical controls in relapsed neuroblastoma, in work the head dates to 2025. The therapy is used as maintenance for this childhood cancer when it returns or resists care. Direct comparisons with no such therapy are lacking.

Three studies of the therapy with individual patient data are set against two historical control cohorts. Both simple and population-adjusted comparisons of overall survival are made, using weighting methods. Harmonized entry rules are applied across cohorts. The indirect design estimates benefit where a head-to-head trial is absent.
pmc-12872824:
Francesco Garifalos and co-authors build a care model for young men in a paper whose head dates it to 2025. The condition they target is low testosterone at a young age, a marker of heart and metabolic risk. Care is often split and poorly matched to young patients' needs.

The team screened eight hundred males aged fifteen to thirty-five and found fifty-five cases. They built a sample patient profile and checked it with a panel of experts. Those men's health burden was higher than peers, and their top concerns were sexual health, mood, and body strength. Phone-based tools were shaped around those needs.
pmc-12872924:
Mohamed Ibrahim and co-authors survey substance use in war-torn south-central Somalia in a study the head dates to 2025, though the catalog lists 2026. The region has endured armed conflict, displacement, and climate shocks. Trauma and hardship feed substance use, yet local data stayed scarce.

Fieldwork in late 2021 covered 694 adults across three districts, drawn from both host towns and displacement camps. Over half reported using some substance in their lives, and about the same share used currently. Tobacco led the list, named by about thirty-nine percent of lifetime users. The team used a World Health Organization screening tool and regression to map who uses. Results aim to guide aid and health planning in the camps.
pmc-12873424:
Dan Wu and seven co-authors publish a single-cell atlas of blood immune cells in kidney transplant patients, in a 2025 data paper. Immune cells decide whether a transplanted kidney is accepted or attacked, and blood tests could reveal that battle early. The dataset profiles nearly ninety-nine thousand quality-checked cells from five recipients, with clinical details attached. Samples span different rejection types and the phases before and after suppression treatment.

Major immune cell types were identified for comparison across those conditions. A public dataset of this depth lets other teams hunt for rejection signatures without recruiting their own cohort. Noninvasive immune monitoring is a standing goal in transplant medicine, since the alternative is repeated biopsies of the graft.
pmc-12883824:
Saranya Sankar, Kathirvel Maruthai, Zachariah Bobby, and Bethou Adhisivam study in 2026 how chemical tags on DNA relate to inflammation in newborns with late-onset sepsis. This serious infection of the newborn is a major problem, above all where resources are scarce, and immune signals called cytokines drive much of its harm.

The team compared forty-two sick newborns, some sampled again after three days of antibiotics, with forty-two healthy babies. They found that genes for pro-inflammatory signals carried fewer methyl tags, while genes for calming signals carried more. The pattern suggests the tags help set how strongly a sick newborn's immune system fires.
pmc-12903724:
Cheng-Liang Chang and co-authors test stretchy kinesiology tape on athletes with wobbly ankles, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Thirty college athletes with chronic ankle instability tried tape at two tensions in swap-over sessions. Ankle position sense, balance and hop tests, and brain waves were all measured.

Tape at mid tension sharpened position sense and improved closed-eye balance and side hops. Slack tape made position sense worse and cut a brain response tied to sensing. Sharper position sense tracked with stronger brain responses. The authors say right tension helps at once, while dummy tape can hurt.
pmc-12904324: Miguel Quiñones and co-authors host a 2025 webcast on vascular robotics, recorded as a fifty five minute video conversation. The session serves as the focus piece for a journal issue on the topic. Led by the issue's editors, the discussion brings the issue's authors together to talk through emerging themes in robot assisted vascular care. The panel draws out lessons the authors learned while researching and writing their articles, and the record links readers to the full video.
pmc-12916424:
Neeraj Kumar and five co-authors review how rice copes with heat, in a paper whose text dates to 2025. Rice feeds much of the world, and rising heat from climate change threatens harvests. The crop is most fragile while flowering, when heat can leave grains empty.

The review gathers what is known at three levels: the plant's shape and growth, its inner workings, and its genes. Heat stokes harmful oxygen byproducts that damage leaves and cut sugar production. The authors list gene regions and genes tied to heat tolerance, plus the control pathways behind them. They then weigh breeding, gene transfer, and large-scale data methods for building hardier rice. The paper serves as a guide for researchers racing the warming trend.
pmc-12927224:
Sharing health data speeds science, but in poor countries the ethics of sharing carry extra weight. Paul Kutyabami and six co-authors asked researchers at a Ugandan public university how they see it, in a 2025 study. They interviewed 26 people at Makerere University's health sciences college, from professors to doctoral students.

Views varied widely, and some researchers showed a thin grasp of what data sharing involves. Money rewards and co-authorship stood out as the incentives that would move people to share. Credit in a paper's acknowledgments was welcome, but many felt big contributions deserve co-authorship instead. Control over one's own data mattered deeply to the group. The authors read the mix as a call for clearer rules that respect both open science and the researchers who gather the data.
pmc-12931724:
Ivonne Sagrario Romero-Flores, Jaime García-Mena, and Claudia Perez-Cruz link gut imbalance to hormone disruption in female mice bred for Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 study. Women face higher dementia risk, and falling estrogen after menopause is one suspect.

The engineered mice showed a disturbed gut system for recycling estrogen: helpful bacteria fell, a recycling enzyme weakened, and usable estrogen dropped. Their cycles faltered and memory suffered. Healthy mice given antibiotics developed the same gut pattern, then the same hormone and memory problems. The authors argue gut imbalance may feed female vulnerability to dementia by draining estrogen, adding the gut to the list of treatment targets.
pmc-12935924:
Sandra Gattas and co-authors seek a short math formula for how signals change as they pass from one hippocampal zone to another. The head dates the work to 2025, though the catalog lists 2026. The hippocampus is a brain area tied to memory, and the synapse is the basic unit of signaling there. Too many factors act at once for a step by step account.

Using mouse brain slices, the team fit a second order equation to the response in the apical dendrites, the upper branches of the receiving cells. The formula captured over 94 percent of the response and held on new cases. It also revealed timing rules not seen before. A different branch type needed a higher order form.
pmc-12956724:
Sun and Chen asked in twenty twenty-five whether two tests together can warn of delayed brain swelling after a bleeding stroke. This swelling, arriving days after the bleed, worsens outcomes, yet doctors lack a reliable early alarm.

The study covered eighty patients with spontaneous brain bleeds. A blood enzyme called MMP-9 was measured within the first day, and a scan that reads brain chemistry was done on day three. Twenty-seven patients went on to develop the delayed swelling. Those patients showed higher enzyme levels and lower values of a marker for healthy nerve cells. Each test predicted the swelling on its own, but the pair together did better than either alone. The authors say the combined check could flag high-risk patients early. That warning would let doctors watch and treat those patients more closely.
pmc-13018424:
Mahboob Rahaman and co-authors test a one-visit treatment for young teeth whose roots never finished forming, in a 2025 study. When such a tooth dies, its open root tip cannot seal, so dentists use apexification to grow a hard barrier at the tip. The study asks whether a material called MTA can do the job in a single visit.

Eighty-five patients with immature, non-vital teeth took part. Each tooth received the one-visit procedure, with MTA placed as the barrier material at the root tip. X-ray checks afterward showed a calcified barrier had formed in most cases. The authors conclude that the single-visit method works well and saves time over older multi-visit routines for these teeth.
pmc-13037624:
Qasim Saleem Raza and co-authors test how fungal toxins and a common bacterium harm developing chicks inside the egg, in a 2025 study. The toxins, ochratoxin and aflatoxin, taint poultry feed, and Bacillus cereus bacteria turn up in feed too. Their combined effect on embryos was not well charted.

Fertilized eggs were split into seven groups: plain controls, each toxin alone, both toxins, the bacterium alone, and all three together. Doses went into nine-day-old embryos through the membrane around the chick. The team then tracked embryo deaths, hatching rates, body and organ weights, and tissue damage. Knowing how feed poisons combine can sharpen safety limits for hatcheries.
pmc-13058624:
Afei Qin and co-authors report a 2025 study of caregiver abuse in rural Chinese families coping with severe mental illness. The team surveyed 763 patient-caregiver pairs in Shandong province, grading symptom severity with a standard scale and asking patients about verbal and physical abuse in the past year. They also scored each caregiver's tobacco dependence to test whether it sharpens the link.

About a quarter of caregivers had used verbal abuse and fifteen percent physical abuse. Worse symptoms tied to more of both. Caregivers with moderate to heavy tobacco dependence abused more, and their dependence strengthened the symptom-to-verbal-abuse link in particular. The authors call for caregiver support and quit-smoking help in these homes.
pmc-13059924:
Yulia Lin and a large Canadian team set out a pilot trial in 2025 on giving whole blood before hospital to trauma patients who are bleeding heavily. Major bleeding is the top cause of deaths that trauma care could prevent. Whole blood is gaining ground over giving blood in separate parts, but Canadian travel times to hospital run long.

Patients aged sixteen or older who need a transfusion from the air ambulance service will be split at random between whole blood and standard part-based blood. The main aim is to learn if a full trial can be run well, judged by sign-up, data, and delivery counts. A side aim asks whether whole blood cuts death or huge transfusions in the first day.
pmc-13081424:
Amir Ali Judaki and co-authors hunted for marker genes that forecast survival in colon and rectal cancer, in a 2025 study. Outlook for advanced cases stays poor, in part because single markers miss how tumors and immune cells interact. The team mined a large cancer atlas with just over four hundred sixty tumors. They built gene and protein webs and ranked genes by their place in the web.

Close to one thousand genes differed between tumor and normal tissue. Eight hub genes sat at the web's crossroads. Two of them forecast survival on their own: high levels of either meant a poorer outlook. Both tracked with more innate immune cells but fewer activated helper T cells nearby, a sign of immune shut-out. Tissue data backed the gene reads. The authors present the pair as markers that link scar-like tumor growth to weak immune attack.
pmc-13084324:
Peter Taffo and co-authors follow long-term catheter users for five years in a 2026 study. People who drain their bladders with intermittent catheters for years worry about infections, scarring, and quality of life over time. Most earlier data covered short horizons or new users.

The study enrolled ninety-eight adults at three European sites, all using hydrophilic catheters for at least six years already, with thirteen years of use on average. Half finished the full five years. Infection rates, other urinary complications, and quality-of-life scores stayed flat across the period. Stricture reports edged up without statistical weight. The authors read the steady picture as support for the long-term safety of the method.
pmc-13086624:
Diabetic retinopathy can blind people with diabetes who never learn they are at risk. Parviz Marouzi and five co-authors pool what surveys worldwide say about patients' knowledge, attitudes, and daily practices toward the disease. Their review gathered twenty-nine questionnaire studies covering 14,830 people with diabetes.

Only about forty-three percent had good knowledge, about half held a positive attitude, and forty percent followed good preventive practice. Scores ran higher in rich countries than in poorer ones. A positive attitude nudged practice slightly, while knowledge alone barely moved either attitudes or habits. The authors conclude that awareness programs must be tailored to local conditions, especially where resources are thin, rather than assuming information by itself changes behavior.
pmc-13087124:
Kenan Kaya and fifteen co-authors let a language model write the follow-up plans hidden in radiology reports, and grade it against doctors, in this 2026 study. Real reports recommend future scans inconsistently; two radiologists reading the same findings name different dates and machines. The team asked whether GPT-4o could standardize those calls.

One hundred CT and MRI cases, split across head and neck, liver, lung, and pancreas, were drawn from two centers. GPT-4o, a resident, and a board-certified radiologist each wrote follow-up recommendations from the report text alone. Blinded experts scored completeness, modality choice, timing, and overall quality. The model's median global quality matched both humans at 4 of 5. Its timing was right in 96 of 100 cases, against 75 for the resident and 90 for the senior. Completeness also favored the model over the senior reader, 92 against 80 percent.
pmc-13107024:
Yudi Zhang, Hefei Wang, Chencheng Liu, and Fei-Long Meng review how AI opens up the study of antibody repertoires. Their 2025 review covers the full set of antibodies in a person, shaped by gene shuffling and by cell selection after exposure. That set stores layers of history about past germs.

Fast sequencing now clones repertoire data at scale, and fresh features of adaptive immunity keep surfacing. The review first sets out what an antibody clonotype is and how such families evolve. It then weighs vaccine ideas that steer the repertoire on purpose. Deep learning uses close the survey: predicting binding, designing fresh antibodies, and reading diagnoses from repertoire data. The authors see rich data plus learning models reshaping the field.
pmc-13117524:
Robert and co-authors add shape-based features to a neural network that reads facial expressions. Their 2026 paper argues that standard networks lean on surface appearance, which shifts with lighting and face type. Shape structure, drawn from the outline of features, could add a steadier signal alongside it.

The team built a data set from five public collections plus a new Indonesian one: three thousand six hundred eighty-four images from three hundred twenty-six people across seven expressions. Tests used subject-independent splits so no person appeared in both training and scoring. Their best model reached about eighty-nine percent accuracy, level with strong baselines. It also ran with lower delay and far less graphics memory. The authors present the design as a lean option for real-time use.
pmc-13119424:
Misa Iida and co-authors report a 2026 study of how doctors and nurses support shared choices in kidney care. Patients who need renal replacement therapy face a major life decision, and staff views shape how well that choice is shared. The authors compare what helps, in the words of each group.

A web survey drew free-text answers from physicians and nurses across Japan in late 2024 and early 2025. Valid replies came from 103 physicians and 122 nurses, and the text was mined for themes. Both groups named six factors, with shared ground on patient understanding, staff training, and team work. Physicians stressed systems and time, while nurses stressed patient values and daily support. The split shows where joint training could help.
pmc-13124624:
Penelope Banchi and co-authors review the microbes that colonize newborn dogs and cats in this 2026 paper. Early microbes shape lifelong health in humans, but pet medicine lags behind. The review borrows lessons from human research while stressing what differs in animals.

Evidence does not support live microbes reaching the healthy fetus before birth. Birth itself is the great turning point, with delivery mode and setting seeding the newborn. Milk, mothering, and the home environment then steer the young gut week by week. The authors weigh mother-focused probiotic ideas, note big gaps in pet data, and call for long-term studies that track mother, newborn, and surroundings together.
pmc-13130324:
Holton, Higgins, Brockmeier, and Hall study a brain rhythm fault in early psychosis, published in 2024 per the text head. A forty hertz response to sound is known to run weak in psychosis. Most past work read a few scalp sites only. This team read the whole scalp over time. Machine learning sorted patients from others.

Phase locking between sound and brain beat raw power as a signal. It also tied to thinking skill measures. Early outcome linked to the baseline rhythm at set sites. Group gaps spread widely across the scalp. The authors back the rhythm as a marker of circuit faults. It may also forecast how patients fare.
pmc-13135424:
Vimoltip Luksanapisitakul and Anas Alojayli write a letter adding a case to a recent report on weak Rhesus blood typing in pregnancy, in a letter from 2026. A 37-year-old woman, pregnant for the fourth time, arrived with second-trimester bleeding.
