In three past pregnancies in Canada she had been typed as Rh-positive and never given preventive antibody treatment.

This time, screening showed a weak D reaction. Deeper testing found a partial-D variant, and her type was corrected to Rh-negative. The authors stress that such patients can still form anti-D antibodies, which can cause severe disease in the baby. Guidelines call for the preventive injection after any bleeding event, within 72 hours, for women not yet sensitized. The letter urges care with borderline typing results.
pmc-13135524:
Children in intensive care who cannot speak cannot say when they hurt, and Portefaix and co-authors tested a pupil-based pain gauge for them in work from twenty twenty-six. The gauge reads pupil size shifts with a video tool at the bedside. The study ran in one French unit, with nurses scoring pain by a known scale while blind to the gauge.

Sixty-six children on breathing machines gave more than two hundred paired readings. The gauge sorted pain only fairly, and its match with nurse scores was weak. At a high catch rate for pain, it cleared pain-free states just half the time. Use was hard in tiny babies and in restless children. The authors call the tool a weak stand-alone test.
pmc-13136524:
Tientcheu Noutong Jemimah Sandra and co-authors test, in two thousand twenty-six, a blend of two plants long used together against malaria in Cameroon. Malaria parasites resist standard drugs more and more, so plant extracts draw fresh interest. The pair is Terminalia macroptera and Erythrina sigmoidea, both used as stem bark.

The team mixed the extracts in three ratios and tested them in the lab and on a computer. All three blends worked against both a drug-sensitive and a drug-resistant parasite strain. The blend richest in the second plant worked best and did not harm test cells much. The extracts also mopped up free radicals well. Docking tests named five plant compounds that fit a key parasite protein most strongly.
pmc-13137124:
Alex Moreira Mélo and co-authors present a 2026 pair of case reports on cannabis oil for stubborn facial nerve pain. Two women with trigeminal neuropathic pain, one after injury and one without cause, had failed standard drugs and procedures. Both took a balanced THC and CBD mouth spray, titrated over eight weeks.

Pain scores fell steeply, from near maximum to mild, and the pain's character shifted from electric shocks to burning. Chewing and oral hygiene improved, quality of life rose, and 3D face imaging showed the sensitized skin areas shrinking dramatically, with touch-evoked pain gone by week eight. No serious side effects appeared.
pmc-13137324:
Jake Miller and a large team of co-authors review results in 2026 for a drug shot used to treat Peyronie's disease, a bend in the penis that can cause pain and stress. The drug, made from a bacterial enzyme, softens the scar tissue that causes the bend. The study focuses on men who have sex with men, a group that may feel this burden more.

Records came from five United States clinics, with close to four hundred men in the final group. The bend eased by a median of fifteen degrees, and most men said they were pleased with the care. This group had a higher rate of one injury type, a break in the shaft tissue, but their gains and need for surgery matched other men.
pmc-13138324: MicroRNAs quiet genes by guiding a silencing complex to their targets. Amy Pasquinelli comments in 2026 on new work showing how a whole family of these small regulators gets destroyed together. A long noncoding RNA pairs loosely with them and still manages to trigger their decay, a process called target-mediated microRNA decay. The pairing is weaker than textbooks suggested such decay requires. Pasquinelli explains why that surprise matters for how cells tune gene activity.
pmc-13139524:
Omnia Mousa and five colleagues make a hydrogel from treated orange peel charcoal that soaks up two water pollutants, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. The targets were toxic chromium ions and methylene blue dye. The gel's wide surface and rich chemical groups were confirmed by several scans and tests. Best removal came at set acidity and contact times for each pollutant.

Top capacity reached about 476 milligrams per gram for the dye and 1,250 for chromium. The two pollutants followed different uptake patterns over time. Fine-tuning with two math methods confirmed the best mixes. The authors offer the gel as a cheap, waste-based water cleaner.
pmc-13139624: Syed Shah and co-authors report a pancreas flare as a rare side ill of a liver virus infection. The case report appeared in 2026. The virus is a rare but real cause to weigh next to top causes such as gall stones and drink. The team urges early virus screens when liver and pancreas faults show as one, most of all where the virus runs wide, so care can start fast and spare needless steps.
pmc-13140524:
An expert panel of the European Food Safety Authority assesses a food additive in beverages in a report from two thousand twenty-six. The additive is glycerol, used in slush ice drinks and proposed for de-alcoholised wine. The panel was asked to judge the safety of a single large intake.

From an older study, the panel set an acute reference dose for one consumption event. Estimated intakes from slush drinks at typical volumes would exceed that dose for all age groups. The same held for de-alcoholised wine at the proposed maximum level. The panel calculated safe single volumes and maximum levels for different groups. It recommends that regulators set firm numerical limits for glycerol in drinks.
pmc-13143124:
Yan Yan, Mingxie Chen, Chuanyong Tang, and Sheng Wang present a study dated two thousand twenty-six on soil erosion in the world's karst regions. Karst landscapes, built on dissolving rock, cover about fifteen percent of the land. Their odd geology and water flow make soil loss a special concern there.

Using a standard ecosystem model and robust trend tests, the team mapped erosion from two thousand to two thousand twenty. Erosion fell worldwide, though it stayed intense in southwest Asia, southern Europe, and northwestern North America. Rainfall linked strongly to erosion, while vegetation's role varied by region. Scenario tests weighed each driver's share.
pmc-13144324:
Ying Wang and six co-authors hunt for nonlinear fingerprints in human brain rhythms, in a 2026 paper. Whether large-scale brain signals are organized linearly or nonlinearly is still poorly settled, yet the answer shapes models and disease markers. Standard spectra split signals into background and rhythmic parts but cannot see phase coupling, the signature of nonlinear resonance. The team built a method combining spectral and bispectral analysis to separate those parts and localize the coupling.

Simulations confirmed the separation works. Applied to two large datasets, over seventeen hundred implanted channels and nine hundred sixty scalp recordings, most signals carried nonlinear or non-Gaussian structure. Brain biomarkers read through a purely linear lens may be missing the dominant organization.
pmc-13144824:
Mohammed Al Hashmi and co-authors report on clot removal for stroke patients whose scans show a large area of dead brain tissue. Their conference abstract from 2026 draws on records from two large hospitals in Riyadh. Such patients were left out of early trials, so local data from Saudi Arabia are scarce.

The team reviews adults treated from 2020 to 2025 and compares those who had clot removal with those who had drug care alone. They record function at ninety days, death, and bleeding in the brain. They also seek scan and health signs that go with a better result, to help teams pick patients with care.
pmc-13144924:
Jung Hwa Seo and co-authors judge a regional stroke hotline set up by the Korean government in 2024. Their conference abstract from 2026 compares transfers before and after the hotline began. Patients moved from a small hospital in Geoje, which lacks full stroke care, to a large center at Dong-A University.

Hotline calls before transfer rose a great deal after the change. For patients with blocked vessels, times in and out of the first hospital fell, and total travel time fell too. Use of clot removal and of combined drug and device care also rose. The authors read the hotline as a way to cut delay across a region.
pmc-13145124:
Yuki Sakamoto, Kazunori Toyoda, Shigeru Fujimoto and colleagues describe the design of the LACUNAR-tPA trial, which compares two early treatments for lacunar stroke in 2026. These small, deep strokes cause mild symptoms, and it is unclear whether clot-busting treatment beats strong antiplatelet therapy.

The trial will randomise 500 patients at 43 Japanese sites within 4.5 hours of onset. One group gets dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel for fourteen days. The other gets intravenous alteplase followed by the same drug pair. The main question is whether the drug-only route is not worse for excellent recovery at ninety days, with bleeding and early worsening tracked as safety outcomes.
pmc-13145224:
A China trial of social-network care for people at high stroke risk is set out in a 2026 conference abstract by Dongmei Li and co-authors. Many high-risk patients skip their shield drugs or let risk factors drift after leaving hospital. The trial will sign 720 people at thirty-three hospitals. Half get a year of team care run through the WeChat app, and half get routine follow-up.

The chief score is the share who take at least eighty percent of all five shield drug types at one year. Those types span blood pressure, sugar, fat, and clot drugs. Data are locked and study is in progress, the abstract notes.
pmc-13145324:
Cassady Olson and Clifton Ragsdale study the nerve tracts that run along an octopus arm. Their 2026 paper deals with the axial nerve cord, a structure like a spinal cord that sits in the center of the arm and controls complex movement.

Each arm is highly flexible and holds hundreds of suckers, so coordination is a major task. A large fiber bundle, the cerebrobrachial tract, links the arms and the brain. The authors asked whether the cord also has intrinsic longitudinal connections, like the spinospinal links in vertebrates. With tract tracing and immunohistochemistry, they found that the cord neuropil is enriched in such tracts, supporting coordinated arm and sucker motion.
pmc-13145424:
Pilar Nieto Palomares and co-authors tell of a woman whose bleed near the spine looked at first like a stroke. Their conference abstract from 2026 notes that such bleeds are rare and can fool teams. Wrong early care with blood thinners can then do real harm.

The woman, aged seventy, had sudden neck pain and weakness on her right side. She was already taking a drug that slows clotting. A spine scan showed a blood pool pressing on the cord in her neck. After her blood pressure was controlled and extra platelets were given, surgeons removed part of the bone and cleared the blood. The case stresses a full check when neck pain comes first.
pmc-13145524:
Stroke care has improved for a decade, and an eleven-author team asked whether patients over eighty shared in the gains. In a conference abstract, they analyze 18,434 such patients from a Korean national registry spanning 2011 to 2022, tracking treatments and outcomes over time. Extra checks asked whether trends bent after 2020.

The share of very old patients rose from about 17 to 27 percent of admissions, strokes arrived milder, and preventive treatments such as blood thinners before stroke roughly tripled. Yet outcomes turned: one-year death rates fell from 27.5 percent in 2011 to 19.4 percent in 2019, then climbed back to 23.7 percent by 2022. Functional scores worsened too. Younger patients kept improving after 2019. The authors read the split as a sign that the very old are hit hardest when health systems are strained, as during the pandemic years.
pmc-13145624:
Sławomir Michalak and co-authors test virtual reality rehabilitation in the first days after an ischemic stroke. Their 2026 conference abstract covers 185 patients who trained with virtual reality between day two and day nine after stroke onset. Some also received Cerebrolysin, a drug used as an add-on to support recovery.

Patients tolerated the sessions well, with no worrying changes in symptoms, blood pressure, heart rate, or heart tracings. Stroke severity scores improved substantially over the training period. The virtual scenes let patients practice real self-care tasks safely inside the hospital. A Bayesian analysis suggested those given Cerebrolysin improved more than those without it. The authors call early virtual reality training safe and promising, while the drug effect needs firmer testing.
pmc-13146024:
Bonifacio Pedregosa and Jose Navarro pilot a strikingly simple stroke treatment: raising the legs. In this conference report, fifty patients with moderate strokes from large artery disease, none eligible for clot removal, were randomized to thirty-degree leg elevation within a day or to standard care. The idea is to nudge blood toward the struggling brain without drugs.

Adherence ran high and one patient could not tolerate the position. Adverse events were few and no worse than in controls. At ninety days, about five eighths of the leg-up group had good function against under half of controls, and thirty-day deaths also trended lower. The authors call the pilot feasible and safe enough to justify a full trial.
pmc-13146124:
Anita Arsovska reports a 2026 conference study tracking stroke care quality across one year at a large center, using registry measures. Steady tracking exposes gaps and guides fixes. Records covered every quarter of 2025 at the center.

One hundred seventy-five patients were treated over the year, with the first quarter by far the busiest. Arrival severity eased over time, and time from onset to arrival more than halved after the first quarter. Scans reached every patient, and scan speed improved through the year. Drug use for clot care peaked in the third quarter, while clot removal use crept up. Leaving severity scores improved, and the author backs ongoing registry watch.
pmc-13146224:
Bleeding around the brain from a burst vessel leaves many patients needing long rehabilitation, and Sara Tellroth and Hanna Persson examine how much specialised inpatient rehabilitation helps in Sweden. They drew on a national registry covering the years 2014 to 2024, including 814 patients. Physical function was scored at admission and discharge with a standard independence measure.
