The fused design holds far more active material than vapor routes. It also stands up to extreme volume changes in testing. Strong, loaded fiber mats suit batteries and filters alike. The team frame the method as a general manufacturing strategy, not a one-off trick.
pmc-13186224:
Salad Abdullahi Farah and co-authors describe diphtheria's full wrath in an unvaccinated two-year-old from rural Somalia. The boy arrived with fever, a sore throat, trouble swallowing, and labored breathing. A gray-white membrane clung to his throat, and his neck swelled in the classic bull-neck pattern. The bacterial toxin then struck far beyond the airway.

His heart muscle inflamed and stretched into a dilated cardiomyopathy, and his limbs weakened with the nerve damage diphtheria leaves behind. Doctors gave antitoxin, intravenous erythromycin, heart failure care, and therapy for his limbs, under isolation. A month later he had no signs of heart failure and could walk with slight support. The case pleads for vaccines where coverage is thin.
pmc-13186324:
Julián Gajón and co-authors review cancer stem cells as a root of immune therapy failure in a 2026 paper. A small set of tumor cells can seed growth, renew themselves, and spawn varied cancer cells. Those traits help tumors spread, return, and resist drugs. The review gathers proof on how the cells blunt immune attacks.

Signals, local surroundings, and support tissue form one linked frame in their model. Tumors rich in stem traits track with shorter survival and weak response to immune drugs. The authors propose attacks aimed at the stem core, from vaccines to forced maturation. Combined plans may crack the shield. The frame reframes resistance as a stem cell problem first.
pmc-13188124:
Zhenxing Ding, Mingqing Li, and Yuanyuan Chen published this study in 2026. It was a randomized trial in septic shock, a life threat where infection crashes blood pressure. Patients got norepinephrine, the standard drug that props pressure up. The trial added terlipressin, a second pressure drug, at three starting points. One group got it early, at a low dose of the first drug. The other groups waited for higher doses.

Death rates at 28 days were much the same across groups. But the early group spent more days free of all pressure drugs. Their pressure steadied sooner, and waste cleared from the blood faster. Organs also recovered better, with less time on kidney machines. Side effects were fewer in that group. The authors say adding the second drug early helps, even if it does not cut deaths.
pmc-13189724:
Enli Xie and co-authors review how exercise reshapes the immune cells that live permanently in tissues. Their 2026 review concerns tissue-resident memory T cells, sentries fixed in lung, gut, and skin that answer reinfection on the spot. Exercise science has long counted immune cells in the blood, a view the resident cells make incomplete.

The authors ask whether endurance training, like a vaccine, raises the density of these sentries in the organs they guard. They summarize the cells' biology and its meeting with exercise research. The shift they propose is from counting to mapping: immune fitness as geography, not just numbers.
pmc-13190724:
Chengji Lu and co-authors link two neuron groups and watch them sync in a 2026 study. Lab-grown neuron nets serve as clean models for how the brain codes and adapts. What happens when two sealed groups gain an electric bridge was little known.

The team built a chip with split chambers, a switchable electric link, and many recording channels. With the link on, firing in the two groups can be tracked as it shifts toward shared rhythms. A dynamic model frames those shifts in firing sync and link strength. The setup gives a firm test bed for how split brain circuits join into one working net.
pmc-13191524:
Anna Irto and co-authors studied a plant acid that could serve as a green metal catcher in water, in a 2026 paper. The acid forms in nature, breaks down with ease, and has three arms that can grip metal ions. Standard catchers used to clean metals from water degrade poorly. The team tested how the acid behaves with five metals of concern in the environment, in salt water at a set warmth.

Lab measures and computer models worked side by side to map the acid's grip. It caught copper and magnesium with the most strength. The models also showed how its three arms differ in acidity and how each metal binds. Scores for cleaning power backed the bench results. The authors present the acid as a sound green option for pulling metals from natural and factory waters, and for stopping scale before it forms.
pmc-13191624:
Nematchoua Weyou and eight co-authors published a 2026 study of insecticide-treated bed nets after 18 months of use in a Cameroon refugee camp. The camp houses Central African Republic refugees in a high-malaria area. The team checked 440 nets for physical wear and lab-tested 30 against local mosquitoes. About 61 percent of nets stayed in good shape, while a quarter were deteriorated.

Wear tracked with household size, washing habits, and harsh detergents. The insecticide result was stark: all tested nets failed, killing only about 3 percent of mosquitoes, which appear resistant to standard net insecticides. The authors urge agencies to teach gentler net care, with attention to gender roles, and to switch to next-generation nets. They also call for routine checks of net condition and potency.
pmc-13191824:
Masaki Shinohara is first author on a 2026 case report of kidney surgery in a child with OHVIRA syndrome. OHVIRA is a rare birth condition. It combines a blocked half-vagina with a kidney anomaly on the same side. Some variant cases have a tiny, poorly formed kidney draining into the vagina, causing constant urine leakage, so removing the kidney is required.

At age five, doctors found the misplaced urine tube opening by vaginal scope and threaded a fluorescent catheter, a glowing tube, backward through it. During keyhole surgery, the glow reliably showed the tube and the small kidney remnant, guiding safe removal. The authors present the technique as feasible and useful for selected children with this condition.
pmc-13193924:
Shuai Zhang, Haonan Hu, Jingting Peng, Jianrong Zhai, and Mingfeng Yang published a 2026 crop study asking which weather factor most limits winter wheat yield in Shihezi. Shihezi is a farming region in Xinjiang, China. Extreme weather is growing more frequent under climate change. Local food security planning needs to know which extreme matters most.

The team matched wheat yields from 1980 to 2024 with daily weather records from a local station. They covered rainfall, sunshine, several temperature measures, and wind. Each factor's effect was scored by a yield loss ratio, with extremes defined by a standard anomaly scale. Extreme low temperature, read from the daily minimum, emerged as the key limiting factor. The finding tells local growers where protection efforts pay off most.
pmc-13194424:
More people now give a kidney while still alive, and hospitals need fair ways to judge how well that care is run. Rafael Rodrigo Da Silva Pimentel and co-authors wrote this 2026 scoping review to gather the quality measures used for living kidney donation. A scoping review maps what a field has published rather than testing one claim.

The team searched major health databases and gray sources between March and May 2023, using a set method from the JBI group. They also checked seventeen official sites run by donation, transplant, and quality bodies. Their goal was to sort the measures they found into clear groups. A shared list like that can help hospitals compare their own care and spot weak points in donor safety and follow-up.
pmc-13194824:
Wang and co-authors build in 2026 a blood test model for bile duct cancer based on free DNA fragment patterns. This cancer is usually found late, with poor survival and no good screening tool. Fragment patterns in blood DNA reflect tumor chromatin state and instability.

Shallow genome sequencing of plasma gave three feature types, copy changes, fragment size spread, and promoter fragmentation entropy. A learning model joined them and was trained with cross validation. It beat single features and standard serum markers in validation groups, and split cancer from benign bile disease. Scores tracked disease burden over time in repeat samples, which aids post surgery risk checks.
pmc-13195024:
Leticia Gondim Souto is first author on a 2026 veterinary study of platelet counts as a prognostic sign in dogs with cancer. Thrombocytosis means an abnormally high platelet count, and platelets are known to aid cancer progression. In human oncology it marks poor outlook, but its meaning in dogs was little explored.

The authors reviewed one hundred and sixty-six dogs with malignant tumors and high platelet counts. Dogs with moderate-to-severe elevation survived significantly less long than mildly elevated dogs. In mammary carcinoma, higher elevation more than tripled the risk of death, and a similar trend appeared in mast cell tumors. Prospective studies with larger groups are needed, the authors say, to confirm platelet count as a useful marker.
pmc-13195224:
Yunnan Zhang is first author on a 2026 safety analysis of statin use alongside breast cancer treatment. More breast cancer patients now take statins, cholesterol-lowering drugs, during therapy, yet safety data are sparse. The authors mined the United States Food and Drug Administration adverse event reporting system, covering two decades of reports.

Of nearly two hundred and thirty-eight thousand breast cancer related reports, over eight thousand involved statin co-use. Reporting signals ran lower for liver and blood disorders among statin users, but higher for skin, psychiatric, kidney, muscle, and several other categories. Such reporting patterns cannot prove cause, the authors note, but they argue for individualized monitoring and deeper study of the pathways involved.
pmc-13195424:
Said and co-authors clean heavy metals from oilfield water with mineral powders in this 2026 study. Produced water from oil wells carries toxic cadmium and chromium. The mineral goethite, an iron oxyhydroxide, can grab such metals from water. The team baked versions of it laced with calcium, cobalt, manganese, or aluminum.

The aluminum version worked best, lifting removal capacity for both metals. Its needles came out smaller and more spread, with more surface grab points. Uptake followed patterns that point to chemical binding in a single layer for cadmium. Tests on real produced water reached full removal. The powders could suit low-cost cleanup in oil regions.
pmc-13195524:
Isabella K Jacobs and Nina Peel study a worm gene needed for full breeding in a 2026 paper. The gene makes a helper that lets cells fuse small sacs with their outer skin to ship goods out. Its kin in humans help nerve cells send signals, and faults cause nerve disease.

Tagged copies of the helper sit at the skin of many worm cells, as its shipping role would suggest. Worms that lack it have smaller broods, and mating only partly restores the count. More flaws in the germ line point to roles past sperm, and the worm may model non-nerve roles of the kin.
pmc-13196024:
Amanda Rodriguez Orengo and co-authors study who gets sent from urgent care to a skin specialist, in this 2026 paper. Some patients are referred when they do not need it, while others who need more care never complete the path. The team wanted to learn what drives referral choices and how urgent care staff think access could improve.

They reviewed nearly seven thousand skin-related urgent care visits in one health system. Patients who were not white, lived near a dermatology site, lacked insurance, or needed a procedure or follow-up were more likely to be referred. A staff survey backed three fixes: skin training for urgent care providers, remote skin consults, and urgent-access skin clinics. The authors note the single-system design limits how far the findings reach.
pmc-13196224:
Dan Wang and Litao Guo describe hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis presenting with persistent high lactate as a distinct phenotype. Their 2026 letter deals with a life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome that often mimics septic shock.

High lactate in critical illness is usually blamed on poor tissue perfusion. This syndrome, though, can drive severe lactic acidosis through cytokine effects without low oxygen. The authors searched three databases for such cases, up to September 2025, and added four cases from their own institution. Diagnosis required standard criteria. Clinical traits and prognosis of this presentation were poorly described before. Their synthesis aims to help intensive care teams spot it.
pmc-13196524:
Heloísa Pagnussatt and co-authors test how the mix of fine and coarse limestone in feed affects laying hens. Published in 2026, two trials covered hens at peak lay, 26 weeks old, and aged hens at 66 weeks. Diets varied the ratio of fine to coarse limestone, a calcium source that feeds shell building and bone health.

Across both trials the ratios did not change laying performance, egg quality, or blood measures. In young hens the coarsest mix cut tibia weight and breaking strength. In aged hens that mix raised feed intake and lowered tibia calcium. A middle ratio lowered a kidney protein tied to vitamin D use. The authors conclude shell quality is safe, but bone traits suffer at high coarse shares.
pmc-13196724:
Xue Chen and Zhirun Wang review the fear of steroid creams among people with eczema, in this narrative review from twenty twenty-six. The skin disease at issue, atopic dermatitis, is a common, long-lasting source of itching and rash. Steroid creams are a main treatment, yet many patients worry they will thin the skin or cause lasting harm.

The review pulls together data on how common this fear is and what feeds it, from past side effects to mixed advice online. It weighs what steroids can and cannot do, and shows how fear leads patients to skip doses or stop early, which lets flares drag on. The authors then judge the fixes on offer: clearer teaching, support for anxiety, and care plans shaped to each patient. They close by naming research gaps and steps clinics can take to build trust in a proven treatment.
pmc-13197424:
George Lund and co-authors build a way to find natural antifungal compounds from soil bacteria that attack a wheat leaf disease. The fungus behind the disease has beaten most chemical and genetic controls. The team first tested which bacteria slowed the fungus in a dish, then read their genomes to hunt for the gene clusters behind the attack.

Three strong bacteria shared a gene cluster matching one known to make an antifungal compound. Breaking a key gene in one strain stopped both the compound and the fungus blocking. Fungus strains varied in how much the bacteria hurt them, a trait the team flags as worth watching.
pmc-13198124:
The heart's own wiring carries the spark that times each beat, and disease in that wiring slows or blocks the signal. Syeda Atiqa Batul and Pugazhendhi Vijayaraman review conduction system disease in a 2026 article. They walk through the system's parts. The sinus node starts the beat, the AV node and His bundle pass it down, and the fast Purkinje network spreads it through the ventricles.

Pacemaker cells fire on their own through a balance of potassium and sodium currents, including the so-called funny current. Disease can strike at any level, from inherited faults or from the wear of aging, valve trouble, and heart failure. The review notes that a first-degree AV block shows in 1 to 2 percent of people in ECG-based studies. It sets out how these blocks are recognized and why their level matters for care.
pmc-13198524:
Daha Garba Muhammad and co-authors published a 2026 review on physiotherapy for shoulder joint arthritis. The joint where the arm meets the shoulder blade wears out in this condition, causing pain and stiffness. Physiotherapists often manage it without surgery, or help recovery around an operation. The team asked what trial evidence says about the value of that care.

They searched five databases for randomized trials in adults over forty-five with this arthritis, including a related rotator cuff wear condition. Of 582 papers found, only four trials qualified. All four covered care after surgery, and none used a placebo comparison. The evidence, rated low in certainty, showed no difference in outcomes between therapy starting within six weeks of surgery and therapy delayed beyond six weeks. Other findings were too thin to judge. The authors highlight a stark evidence gap for a very common treatment.
pmc-13199924:
Jana Bartakova and co-authors build a survey tool to weigh what nursing graduates value in an employer, in a 2026 study. Health systems struggle to attract and keep young nurses. Many studies list factors that matter, from pay to team climate. Lists alone do not show how much each factor counts. Policy choices need those weights.

The team developed a discrete choice experiment for Swiss nursing undergraduates. Students pick between job offers that vary across key attributes. Their choices reveal the trade-offs they accept. The paper describes building and pretesting the questionnaire. Clear wording and realistic options were design priorities. Once fielded, the tool can rank what employers should fix first. Nursing schools and hospitals both gain from the results.
pmc-13200024:
Anna Margaretha Smit and co-authors ask clinicians in South Africa why patients with schizophrenia so often relapse. The study appeared in 2026. The team ran three focus groups with 14 public-sector clinicians, all with at least five years of care work in this field. The focus was on causes beyond missed medication, such as poverty and weak services.

Clinicians said missed doses are often the last step, not the root cause. Behind them sit poverty, joblessness, unsafe streets, stigma, and broken services. Drug stock-outs, early discharge for lack of beds, and scarce follow-up care add to the risk. Crime and gang violence can keep patients from clinics. The authors argue that cutting relapse means fixing these wider conditions, not only urging patients to take their pills.
pmc-13200124:
Yasushi Ishigooka and co-authors build a fine-grained daily weather record for Japan to serve farm climate research. Their 2026 paper describes a grid of cells about one kilometer on a side, with daily values back to 1978. Such a record is basic gear for judging how a warming climate will hit crop yields.

The new set adds wind speed and dampness of the air to an older version. The team took care to strip out jumps in the record caused by changed tools or changed math, which are not climate. They also add farm-linked measures, such as heat stress and the water and flower heat of rice paddies, plus season and year scores that hint at yield or at harm from extremes.
pmc-13200324:
Chikara Nakagami and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a rare fatty tumor near a past surgery site. A myelolipoma mixes mature fat with blood-forming tissue. It usually grows on the adrenal glands above the kidneys, so one in the belly wall is extremely uncommon.

Their patient was a 62-year-old man who had chest surgery for a thymus tumor at age thirty-nine, using a breastbone-lifting device. Decades later, a scan for another reason found a slowly growing mass by that device site, in front of the belly lining. Scans showed fat inside, raising worry of a cancerous fatty tumor. Full removal proved it benign. The authors add this tumor to the list for fat masses at old surgical sites.
pmc-13200624:
Li-min Wang and colleagues review cardiac mast cells in heart disease in a 2026 article. Mast cells are immune cells that release inflammatory signals. In the heart they help keep tissue balance but also drive swelling, scarring, and remodeling after injury, with roles that can flip by context.

The review traces where heart mast cells come from and where they sit in cardiac tissue. It covers their part in calming inflammation and reshaping tissue after damage. Animal work suggests they act much like other inflammatory cells, directly and indirectly. Their dual roles could cut both ways in disease. The authors map open questions and possible clinical uses for targeting these cells.
pmc-13200924:
Wenjun Liu and colleagues propose a finer fluid metric for children on continuous kidney therapy in a 2026 study. CRRT slowly cleans blood and removes fluid in critically ill children. The usual removal rate ignores each child's starting overload, so the team coined a clearance percentage: balance removed as a share of the initial overload.

They reviewed 432 children treated at one center from 2012 to 2023. Non-survivors got higher removal rates yet cleared no more overload than survivors. Body weight drove the removal rate strongly. The new percentage barely tracked illness severity or starting overload, making it a cleaner progress gauge. Their three-part framework pairs prescription, safety, and clearance for daily care.
pmc-13201324:
How many operations a surgeon needs before robotic hernia repair becomes routine is the question behind a 2026 scoping review by Francesco Brucchi. The review gathers studies that used cumulative sum analysis, a statistical method for spotting when performance stabilizes, during robotic repair of groin hernias.

Brucchi and colleagues searched five databases and found seven studies covering eight learning curves and 1,361 patients. The point where operating time leveled off ranged widely, from 12 to 138 procedures across the included studies. The authors estimate stabilization after roughly 25 to 35 procedures in structured training, while stressing that the evidence is weak and not a credentialing standard.
pmc-13202524:
Turning a biomass byproduct into a valuable chemical without solvents is the goal of a 2026 catalysis study led by Margi Joshi. The research article anchors a tungsten-rich cluster compound onto zeolite HY and uses it to oxidize levulinic acid into succinic acid with hydrogen peroxide.

The catalyst achieved complete selectivity toward succinic acid at a moderate yield, which the authors present as a first for this reaction setup. Careful tuning of reaction conditions and scavenger experiments revealed a controlled radical pathway that cleaves the target bond while suppressing over-oxidation. The material kept working through four reuse cycles, offering a blueprint for sustainable production of dicarboxylic acids from biomass.
pmc-13203824:
Yunzhen Yang and co-authors trace how a fungus that kills honeybee young uses long non-coding RNA strands during attack. Their 2026 paper deals with chalkbrood, a disease of bee larvae caused by this fungus. The host here is an Asian honeybee, and the team sampled spores plus the guts of infected larvae at three ages. They catalogued the RNA strands in each sample and tracked which ones rose or fell.

More than a thousand such strands were found, in several forms. Shifts grew much larger by the oldest larval age. Some strands may pair with matching message strands, while others sit near genes they may sway. The work maps paths the fungus may use.
pmc-13204524:
Rafter and co-authors present a 2026 scoping review on whether mindfulness practice changes brain structure. Mindfulness programs are known to help mood and thinking, but proof of physical brain change is thin. The team searched for studies from 2010 to 2023 that used structural MRI before and after such training. Nine studies passed their screen, five of them randomized trials.

Training ranged from ten hours to decades of practice. Changes clustered in five regions tied to body sense, self-control, and memory, such as the insula and hippocampus. Longer programs and lifelong practice showed the largest shifts. The authors call the evidence promising but small and mixed, and urge stronger trials.
pmc-13204624:
Xiaochen Yang and colleagues built in 2026 an ultrasensitive biosensor for microcystin-LR, a water toxin that threatens health and the environment. Their platform pairs ultrathin sheets of a three-metal alloy, palladium with molybdenum and copper, with a light-emitting detection scheme. The metal sheets offer many active sites and speed charge transfer.

A programmable aptamer interface holds the light-emitting compound until the toxin arrives, then releases it, so the signal drops in a target-linked way. The sensor responds across a very wide range and can detect the toxin at femtogram levels. It stayed selective against look-alike compounds and gave near-full recovery in tap water tests.
pmc-13205324:
Broccoli stalks and leaves, usually thrown away, carry compounds that fight microbes and oxidation. Iris Gudiño and co-authors profile that waste stream in this 2026 study of two broccoli cultivars, with cauliflower as a yardstick. They counted and named the microbes living on leaves, stems, and heads, and mapped the extracts' chemical makeup.

Leaves held the richest chemistry, though more phenolics did not always mean stronger antioxidant action. All extracts killed foodborne bacteria well at higher doses, Listeria above all. Against fungi the effect was selective, stopping one Alternaria species reliably while two others resisted. The authors pitch these leftovers as natural preservatives for food and crop care. Compound-by-compound work comes next.
pmc-13205624:
Brian Lee and co-authors ask health staff who are also parents how the plague years felt at work. The study appeared in 2026. It draws on talks with near forty front-line staff at a big city hospital in Australia. The talks ran across late 2020 and early 2021.

Fast change at work put a hard strain on staff and chiefs alike. The strain hit body, mind, and home ties. Help from peers and chiefs did guard staff, but it piled more load on chiefs. Many staff felt pride in their work. Some felt less cheer in their career path and feared long mind harm. The team maps what kind of help works.
pmc-13206624:
Yin and seven colleagues track how a fermented herbal mix changes as it brews, and when it best lowers uric acid in twenty twenty-six. The mix pairs a classic root with a medicinal fungus. High uric acid drives gout, so the brew is eyed as a remedy. Mass scans and broad chemical profiling watched the brew over four weeks.

Samples split cleanly by brew day, and dozens of compounds shifted. Sugars and a class of plant compounds tracked with the acid lowering effect. Both peaked on day twenty-one, when the brew worked best. The study is the first to map the brew's chemistry against its power over time.
pmc-13207424:
Diseases like ALS, Parkinson's, and Lewy body dementia steadily damage the brain and nerves, and no cure exists. Chadwick Prodromos and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, a treatment drawn from stem cells: tiny packages called exosomes, sprayed into the nose. Animal work had suggested the packages might slow or partly reverse decline.

The team treated 86 patients with one of the three diseases and tracked them for up to six months. Patients who did not respond to one product were switched to another. Their courses were compared with records of past patients who never got the treatment. The authors frame the study around the molecules that might explain any benefit, and they present the series as early human evidence in a hard field.
pmc-13207724:
Beata Krasińska and co-authors present a study the catalog lists under 2026. Heart failure with weak pumping is now seen as a metabolic disorder. Amino acids in blood may trace its stages. The team studies forty-two patients split by ejection fraction: below forty percent, or forty to forty-nine. The milder group serves as the reference. Cross-sectional metabolic profiling compares amino acid patterns. From the differences, the authors build a composite score, the HASI-40 index.

The index aims to separate the two stages from a blood pattern. Internal testing checks how well it discriminates. Cardiologists get a candidate metabolic staging tool where imaging alone draws the line. A blood index could flag stage drift between echo scans. Biologically readable scores are favored over black boxes, since doctors must explain them to patients. Derivation plus internal testing is the first step before outside validation.
pmc-13207924:
Yao Deng, Minzhang Zhao, Xiaoyu Zhang, Chunjie Mu, and Runwei Ma study when heart defect closure by catheter later needs surgery, in a paper from 2026. Closing simple birth defects with a device avoids open surgery for most children. A small share, though, face severe problems that force a second, surgical fix.

The team reviewed 4,190 patients treated from 2017 to 2022 and tracked checks at one, three, and six months. Only 44 needed surgery for problems after the procedure. For one defect type, size and age mattered most. For the other, device size and heart measures mattered. The authors offer these traits as early warning signs.
pmc-13208824:
Eight authors, led by Kai Zhang, wrote this 2026 paper on how pyrite in stone aggregate can crack concrete from within. Mining leaves behind large amounts of waste rock and tailings. Using them as aggregate would recycle the waste, but pyrite in the material can cause damage that limits such use.

The team made C50 concrete with quarry rock and tailings as coarse or fine aggregate, using standard mix ratios. They found that pyrite exposed on the surface of a stone grain oxidizes first. That reaction forms ettringite, a mineral that swells and pushes the concrete apart. The swelling rate rose with the amount of surface pyrite. The team described the growth of the swelling with the Arrhenius equation and measured how heat speeds it up. The work gives engineers a way to predict deformation and failure in such concrete.
pmc-13209424:
Marek Zdaniewicz and co-authors spin beer wort with a rotary jet head and measure what changes in a 2026 study. Faster fermentation must not wreck flavor, so the trial ran at full industrial scale in huge lager tanks. Yeast byproducts that make aroma were the quarry.

Alcohol level and acidity finished identical between spun and still batches. The jet raised fruity esters and higher alcohols modestly, a trade brewers usually welcome. The green-apple off-note acetaldehyde fell more than threefold, a clear win. Tasters, though, could not reliably tell the beers apart. Speed gains ride free of flavor cost, on this evidence.
pmc-13209724:
Kaja Karakula and co-authors review ways to protect the body from a widely used weed killer, in a 2026 article. Lab studies link the chemical and its products to cell stress, swelling, and organ harm. Many candidate protectors have been tried in single studies. No review had gathered them across test systems.

The team searched four databases for work from 2004 to early 2026. Thirty-seven studies met their rules. They covered 23 compounds, from vitamins and plant extracts to hormone-like agents. Protective effects clustered in a few classes. The authors also stress the limits of moving lab results to people. The review gives toxicology researchers a map of what has been tried and what remains unproven.
pmc-13210024:
Han Lee and co-authors compare two sequencing methods for tracking probiotic bacteria in the gut, in a 2026 study. The standard method reads one stretch of a bacterial marker gene, but primer mismatches and blurry resolution make it bad at counting specific strains, exactly what probiotic trials need. The rival method targets species directly at high resolution. Older adults took a synbiotic supplement over nine weeks while stool samples were collected.

The standard method caught a brief dip in gut diversity and broad genus swings. But agreement between the methods collapsed at species level, to under seven percent, even though it stayed high for broad groups. Only the targeted method could actually count the administered probiotic strain in the samples. The authors conclude the standard method carries heavy counting bias and recommend pairing both: broad screening from the standard, precise strain counts from the targeted.
pmc-13210224:
Jakub Garbarek and co-authors track chemical stress in the blood in 2026 after an ischemic stroke, the kind caused by a blocked vessel. A stroke floods brain tissue with harmful oxygen by-products, and the body's defense system tries to mop them up. How that defense shifts in the first days was not well mapped.

The team tested blood from forty-eight patients on the first and eighth day after stroke. One defense enzyme rose over the week, while two others barely changed. Signs of cell damage stayed flat. Two helpful compounds, melatonin and vitamin D, fell in the same span. The authors read this as a patchy defense that may leave the body out of balance.
pmc-13210724:
Ploutarchos Pastras and co-authors present a 2026 review separating two gut disorders that share a microbial theme. Irritable bowel syndrome and inflammatory bowel disease both involve disturbed gut bacteria, yet the disturbance means different things in each. The review sorts the pathways by where they truly belong.

In bowel disease of the inflammatory kind, microbes tie into immune misfiring, a leaky gut wall, and lasting inflammation, with diversity loss a hallmark. Irritable bowel talks more through the gut-brain axis, mast cells, and bacterial byproducts that stir nerves. Some actors, like an invasive gut bacterium and the gut's Paneth cells, appear only in the inflammatory story. Biomarkers differ accordingly. The authors map what that means for choosing probiotics, antibiotics, or transplants.
pmc-13211324:
Holly Fontenot and seven co-authors explore when parents prefer their children to get the HPV vaccine and why. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. The vaccine, which guards against several cancers, can be given from age nine, within the nine-to-twelve window the team studied.

Forty-three parents of nine-and-ten-year-olds joined four online text focus groups. Three themes shaped their choices. Some felt nine was too young, while others valued early protection. Parents also weighed how many shots a single visit should hold, spreading them out or grouping them. Many simply followed their doctor's advice. The findings can help clinics frame the timing choice so more children are protected before exposure to the virus.
pmc-13213224:
Health records usually lump Asian American patients into one group, which hides differences between ethnic subgroups. Sarah Lee and co-authors set out to split that group more accurately for ovarian cancer patients treated at their center between 2011 and 2023. Alongside the race and ethnicity patients reported themselves, they applied a method that guesses a patient's likely subgroup from their surname: Chinese, Filipino, Indian, Japanese, Korean, or Vietnamese. The surname list was validated and built from Social Security files.

Among the Asian American patients, the surname method assigned a subgroup to more patients than self-report alone did, and the two methods mostly agreed. Combining both raised the share with a known subgroup to about ninety-one percent. The surname check even reclassified a few patients recorded as unknown into the Asian American group. The authors argue that using both sources gives a fuller picture for studying differences in cancer care.
pmc-13213524:
Christian Hendershot leads a team of fifteen authors in 2026 in a randomized trial of the diabetes drug semaglutide for people who smoke cigarettes daily. Smokers face heavy rates of heart and metabolic disease, and early evidence hints that this class of drugs, GLP-1 receptor agonists, might also dull smoking itself.

Participants received a once-weekly shot of semaglutide or a placebo. The team tracked smoking behavior, craving, and body weight. A single drug that both aids quitting and guards the heart would be doubly valuable, and this trial gives the idea a fair clinical test.
pmc-13214524:
Chioma Moneme and a team of co-authors built a glowing tracker for lab grown gut tissue in a 2026 paper. The tissue, grown from human stem cells, mimics the early small gut. Planting it in animals lets labs watch it grow, but checks used to mean killing the animal and cutting the graft out.

They gave the gut cells a red shifted glow gene that did not harm their growth. Grafts went under the kidney skin of ten mice with weak immune systems. Weekly glow scans picked up nine of ten grafts by week two, and the glow grew over twelve weeks. Glow strength matched graft weight at the end with a near perfect fit. The tool lets one animal be tracked over time.
pmc-13215524:
Abdulsalam Al-Shami and co-authors report a 2026 cross-sectional study of blood ferritin levels in Yemeni patients with sickle cell anemia. High ferritin can signal iron overload from repeated transfusions, although inflammation can also push the level up.

The study enrolled 80 patients aged fifteen and older at a clinic in Sana'a between June and December 2024. About 85 percent had ferritin above the threshold used for concern, with a median value of 1,645 nanograms per millilitre. Ferritin rose alongside white blood cell counts, which hints at an inflammation link, while background factors such as age and sex showed no association. The authors back routine screening and want follow-up work with transfusion histories.
pmc-13217024:
Yuanxiang Huang and nine co-authors ask whether insulin resistance worsens the odds after a stroke clot is pulled out, in a paper whose head dates it to 2026. The pull-out procedure is standard for strokes from a blocked big brain vessel, yet many patients stay dependent even when the vessel reopens. The team graded resistance with a blood index that mixes fats and sugar, in 1,305 patients from a shared registry.

Patients in the top quarter of the index faced far higher odds of dependence at ninety days than those in the bottom quarter. Their odds of early decline and of death also ran higher. The links ran stronger in younger patients, women, and those with high blood pressure or diabetes. Swelling in the body explained part of the link, the team found.
pmc-13217724:
Predicting radiation dose in three dimensions could speed up cancer treatment planning, but most models look only at anatomy and assume standard beam layouts. The authors test whether adding beam geometry helps for esophageal cancer, where beam setups vary a lot. They build two models on the same backbone: one anatomy-only, and one that also receives ray-traced maps of beam coverage and overlap, available before planning. The data cover 751 patients treated with intensity-modulated radiotherapy.

On an independent test set, the geometry-aware model cuts average dose error from 2.88 to 2.02 percent, with the biggest gains in the lung and heart dose ranges. It also holds up far better on rare beam setups. In a workflow study, planning with its help takes up to 65 percent less time and needs fewer rounds. The authors call beam geometry a key ingredient for clinical dose prediction.
pmc-13217924:
Shengxin Tong and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, systems that build proteins outside living cells using parts from eukaryotic cells, the cell type of plants and animals. Such cell-free systems can fold complex proteins correctly and add the chemical finishing touches that bacterial systems miss. The review takes a systems engineering view of the field's latest steps.

The authors cover the widening choice of host extracts, the redesign of core reaction parts, and new materials and high-throughput machines that reshape the setup. Uses range from basic mechanism studies to protein design, artificial cells, and bioelectronic links. Costs and weak standards still block factory use. The authors propose design driven by artificial intelligence and synthetic biology as the path past those limits.
pmc-13218024:
Crowns and fillings now come off printers and milling machines, and patients will brush them for years. Yasser Aly, Mohamed Mahmoud El-Kateb, and Nodar Mohamed Ghrebi simulated that brushing in 2026 on three resin materials to see which surface survives.

Ten bar-shaped samples of each material, two printed resins and one milled block, were weighed and tested for hardness and roughness, then run through a brushing machine and tested again. Weight loss measured wear. Standard statistics compared the materials and the before-after changes. The study design speaks to a practical dental question: whether the new printable resins hold their finish as well as milled ones under daily hygiene.
pmc-13218224:
Yogi Sugiawan and Shunsuke Managi present a 2026 study asking whether progress on the United Nations sustainable development goals truly leaves countries better off in the long run. They measure that by inclusive wealth, which adds up made assets, human skills, and natural assets per person. Goal scores alone may hide losses in nature.

Using data from ninety countries over twenty years, they linked all seventeen goals to changes in the three kinds of wealth. Goal progress went with higher total wealth, driven by made and human assets, but natural assets often fell. Their forecasts to 2040 show faster goal progress gives the largest gains, with wide gaps between countries.
pmc-13219424:
Yifang Long and co-authors traced how dust spreads inside a deep bowl-shaped coal mine and how to hold it down. Their test site was the Fushun East mine in Liaoning, China. The team mixed field readings, theory, computer simulation, and lab checks. Trucks on haul roads turned out to be the biggest dust source.

Air inside the pit loops back on itself in a swirling pattern rather than blowing through. Sloped walls create low-pressure pockets where dust gathers and hangs. Around a moving truck, the stirred air reaches about one and a half times the truck's own volume. At low speeds, the outside wind matters more than the truck's pace for how fast dust spreads. The authors use these patterns to lay groundwork for dust control systems fitted to deep open pits.
pmc-13219524:
Lorenz Thurner and colleagues link severe COVID-19 to autoantibodies against two of the body's inflammation brakes in a 2026 study. Some patients' immune systems attack their own proteins, and this work concerns interleukin-1 receptor antagonist and progranulin, blockers of two strong inflammatory signals. When antibodies block those blockers, inflammation can run free.

The autoantibodies appeared with chemically altered, hyperphosphorylated versions of the two proteins, formed complexes with them, lowered their levels in blood, and left the inflammatory signals they usually restrain more active. Using custom antibody fragments, the team tracked the altered proteins and the autoantibodies across a German pandemic cohort. Most positive patients carried both autoantibodies; levels peaked early and faded over twelve months, and the altered proteins disappeared first. Seropositivity tracked with hyperinflammation. Inflammatory signals themselves could force the alteration in blood cells, but at doses up to a thousand times higher than in cells from positive survivors.
pmc-13219924:
Areez Shafqat and colleagues examine how the drug decitabine rewires two different breast cancer cell lines in a 2026 study. Decitabine blocks the enzymes laying down methylation, the marks that silence genes, and cancers carry different marking patterns by subtype. Whether effects follow the subtype, or march to one drum, matters for how it is tested in patients.

Using a dataset, the team compared treated and untreated T-47D, a luminal line, with JIMT-1, a HER2 line resistant to trastuzumab. Decitabine stripped methylation from twelve hundred sites in JIMT-1 and over nineteen hundred in T-47D, switching on hundreds of genes in each. The activated programs diverged, though: immune signaling in one, matrix and collagen pathways in the other. One gene rose while its promoter gained methylation, defying the rulebook. It disturbed the sites used by epigenetic clocks. Survival analyses in cohorts tied 100-plus genes to outcomes in hormone-positive disease.
pmc-13220424:
L. A. Pardo and colleagues measured vibration sense after arm injuries in 2026. Touch guides how we handle surroundings. Amputation and nerve injury disrupt touch badly. Vibration feedback can restore some sensation. Healthy arm data exist in plenty. Patient measurements stayed scarce until now.

Upper arm and forearm sites were tested. Some sensation survived near the injury. Proximal regions kept partial vibration sense. That finding surprised the authors somewhat. Complete disconnection was expected after avulsion. Samples were small and power limited. Findings therefore count as preliminary only. Feedback device design can still learn.
pmc-13221124:
Chuwen Dou and colleagues map world research on simplifying medication regimens in a 2026 bibliometric analysis. Simpler schedules can cut treatment burden for people juggling many drugs. The team charted 468 publications from 2005 through 2025 in a major citation database, tracking who publishes, where, and on what themes.

Output rose over time, led by the United States, with Monash University the most productive institution. Collaboration clustered in a few networks linking North America and Europe. Topics moved from HIV treatment and adherence toward diabetes, heart failure, and long-term care. The map shows a growing field that still needs wider cooperation and clearer priorities.
pmc-13221424:
Karolina Weiner-Gorzel, Lynda McSorley, and Janice M Walshe review unanswered fertility questions in modern breast cancer care, in a 2026 opinion piece. Survival for younger patients keeps improving, yet worries about fertility and pregnancy safety can lead some to refuse or stop treatment. The authors argue counseling belongs in planning from diagnosis onward.

Chemotherapy remains the main threat to ovarian function, and temporary ovarian suppression deserves routine consideration. Hormone therapy does not permanently damage ovaries, though its long course needs personal pregnancy planning. For newer drug classes, human fertility data are largely absent, so the authors urge caution, preservation before treatment, and honest discussion of uncertainty.
pmc-13222524:
Jing Li, Leyi Wei, Henry Tong, and Quan Zou review where quantum computing could fit into early drug discovery, in a 2026 article. Three standard computer methods anchor the review: deep learning screens, docking screens, and simulations of how molecules move. Each method trades speed against steadiness and physical accuracy. Present quantum machines are noisy and mid-sized, which limits what they can do.

The authors argue the best near-term role is not to replace these methods but to plug quantum modules into chosen steps. Such steps include feature building in predictive models, priors in generative models, pose search in docking, and parts of movement simulations. The key test, they stress, is whether a module gives repeatable gains worth its time and cost.
pmc-13222824:
Rheumatic diseases in children rarely cause emergencies, but when they do, minutes matter. Francesca Casini and co-authors survey those emergencies in a 2026 narrative review written for pediatric rheumatology practice. Their aim is practical: help clinicians spot and manage the most relevant and frequent crises in childhood rheumatic disease.

The review is a non-systematic sweep of the literature rather than a formal meta-analysis. It explains that these emergencies are often misread at first, which delays the treatment that limits death and disability. Conditions are organized for quick reference, with signs to watch for and management steps. The authors present the article as a bedside guide for a corner of pediatrics where few clinicians see enough cases to build instinct.
pmc-13223624:
Faith Magut and co-authors test whether community health fairs lowered deaths in rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, in a 2026 longitudinal cohort study. The Vukuzazi program screened residents aged fifteen and older for HIV, tuberculosis, hypertension, and diabetes between 2018 and 2020, with referrals into care. Half of eligible residents attended, and deaths were tracked through household surveillance for a median of four years.

Attendance was associated with a twenty-five percent lower hazard of death from any cause, about a one and a half point absolute reduction over five years. Clinic visits rose briefly among attenders after the fairs but not among non-attenders. Linking screening days to ongoing primary care may explain the survival edge.
pmc-13223824:
Mairi Northcott and co-authors survey intensive care specialists in Australia and New Zealand about bedside tracheostomy practice. Their 2026 survey covers the percutaneous dilatational method, the standard way of opening the windpipe for long-term ventilation in critical care. An anonymous online form went to trainees and specialists of the regional intensive care college.

In all, 321 clinicians replied. Questions covered how often they perform or supervise the procedure, how much hands-on exposure they got in 2024, and whether training keeps skills sharp. Practice surveys like this expose the gap between assumed and actual experience, a patient-safety question for a procedure done on the sickest patients in the hospital.
pmc-13223924:
Echeverri Restrepo and co-authors publish a full recipe for making and testing copper-doped manganese-aluminum ribbons. The alloy family is chased as a rare-earth-free permanent magnet: its tetragonal phase holds hard magnetic character. The protocol covers two series, with copper swapping in for manganese or for aluminum at two low doses.

Steps run from arc melting and melt spinning, flinging molten alloy into thin ribbons, through heat treatment. Checks follow on structure by X-ray diffraction with Rietveld fitting, on makeup and grain by electron microscopy, and on magnetic strength by a vibrating-sample magnetometer. The authors point readers to a companion paper for the results, presenting this document as the bench manual others can repeat.
pmc-13224024:
Chun-Yang Zhang and co-authors designed in 2026 an ozone disinfection system built into the air handling of a hospital pharmacy's clean buffer room. Such rooms prepare intravenous mixtures, where contamination threatens patients directly. Traditional cleaning leaves gaps, so the team piped ozone into the upstream air system instead.

They compared particles, airborne and settled bacteria, and surface microbes between standard areas and the ozone-treated room, then tuned the recipe with response surface modeling. The sweet spot, eight parts per million of ozone for about sixty-seven minutes, clearly improved the room's cleanliness. Medication contamination risk fell with it. The authors present the design as strong support for safe pharmacy operation. It turns the ventilation itself into the disinfecting agent.
pmc-13224724:
Xin Yin and colleagues report a 2026 study of virus-based therapy against carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, a hospital bacterium that shrugs off last-resort antibiotics. Bacteriophages, viruses that kill bacteria, were collected in steps, each round targeting bacteria that survived the previous virus. Three phages from different families formed a cocktail that held bacterial growth down for fifteen hours.

Each virus attacked a different doorway on the cell surface, which explains the teamwork. Bacteria escaping the first phage deleted a large chunk of their sugary coat, and that loss exposed new targets for the others. One phage even killed several unrelated gut bacteria once their coats were gone, a pattern the authors call closing one door while opening another.
pmc-13226924:
Cezary Osiak-Wicha and nine co-authors feed black soldier fly products to broiler pheasants in place of soybean protein. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. Insect protein is a candidate to ease the feed industry's reliance on soy.

Birds were split into five diets: a soy control, and half or full replacement with either insect meal or dried larvae. Growth, thigh muscle, and leg bone quality were measured by density, strength, and shape analysis. Males on insect diets gained more weight and thigh muscle; females changed little. Bone effects split by sex and bone, with males gaining mineral and strength at high replacement. The results support insect feed, with the dose tuned by sex.
pmc-13227224:
Areesha Moiz and co-authors write a 2026 clinical guide to the gains and harms of GLP-1 receptor agonists. These drugs are now widely prescribed for diabetes, obesity, and a growing list of metabolic and kidney-heart conditions. Prescribing increasingly reaches younger and healthier people, where the benefit-risk balance differs from the original trial populations. The guide organises evidence on how the drugs work, who they suit, and what to watch.

Gut side effects receive special attention, with an algorithm for managing early symptoms before patients abandon treatment. Communication strategies aim to support shared decisions, cut stigma around weight treatment, and match therapy to each patient's goals. The authors frame the result as structured, patient-centred guidance for a fast-evolving drug family.
pmc-13229324: The publisher issued a 2026 correction for a study of bird diversity and West Nile virus spread by Culex mosquitoes in Emilia-Romagna, Italy. The notice is a correction only. It states that the author affiliations in the original article were wrong. It then prints the corrected list for the ten authors. Their institutions span London, Brescia, Bologna, Oxford, and Trento. No data, analysis, or conclusions are changed. The publisher apologises for the error.
pmc-13229924:
Majd Abouassi and colleagues trace in 2026 eleven years of repeated spine failure in a sixty-two-year-old woman after lumbar fusion. Her first operation joined three lower back levels for narrowing and instability in 2014. Over time the levels next to the fusion wore out, hardware failed, and bones fractured as deformity grew.

Each setback led to another revision that extended the rods higher, finally reaching the neck area. Surgeons used multi-rod builds, pelvic fixation, and scan-guided screws, yet mechanical failure kept returning. Her last crisis was an unstable chest spine fracture that threatened the spinal cord and needed urgent replacement of a vertebral body. Careful patient choice, bone health, and long follow-up are urged for long fusions.
pmc-13231424:
Yersin and co-authors review silver complexes that glow, spanning the extremes of light emission timing, in this 2026 paper. Some of these compounds shine by phosphorescence, others by delayed fluorescence lit by heat. Telling the two apart takes care, and the review sets out the criteria.

One highlighted material glows for an unusually long 110 milliseconds with about fifty percent efficiency. Its partner compound, reshaped with an electron-rich ligand, answers in just over a microsecond at full efficiency. The difference traces to the energy gap between two excited states. Computer calculations including spin-orbit effects back the assignments. The authors present the pair as design lessons for light-emitting materials.
pmc-13232624:
Wei Yao and co-authors study joint and brain degeneration in an Alzheimer mouse model in this 2026 paper. Alzheimer disease and osteoarthritis are both common in older people. Human and mouse work hints that joint disease may raise dementia risk. The team injured the knee ligament in mice bred to develop Alzheimer like changes.

Injury was done without surgery at seven months of age. Memory and behavior tests ran six weeks later, including maze and object tasks. Knees, brains, and joint tissue were then checked for degeneration and Alzheimer proteins. Female Alzheimer mice with joint injury showed worse outcomes on several measures. The study probes a two way link between joint damage and brain decline.
pmc-13232924:
Jonathan D Mathers and co-authors published a 2026 case report about a breathing emergency during anesthesia in a patient who had earlier weight-loss surgery. The operation, called one anastomosis mini gastric bypass, reshapes the stomach with a single join. A known side effect is bile flowing back into the new stomach pouch.

The patient was being put under anesthesia for planned gallbladder surgery when bile-rich stomach contents entered the lungs, a severe event called pulmonary aspiration. The authors warn that earlier bypass surgery of this type raises aspiration risk in ways standard airway routines may miss. They propose that anesthesia guidelines account for this history when planning how patients are put to sleep.
pmc-13233224:
Jing Yang and colleagues published a 2026 lab study on how the yeast Candida albicans forms biofilms and resists the antifungal drug itraconazole. Biofilms, dense mats of microbes on surfaces, make infections hard to clear. The team compared normal yeast with strains missing the STP1 or MRR2 genes, plus drug-sensitive and drug-resistant strains, measuring growth, gene action, and autophagy, the cell's recycling system.

Resistant strains built stronger biofilms than sensitive ones. Deleting STP1 boosted biofilm growth, while deleting MRR2 weakened it. Autophagy genes switched on in biofilms and resistant strains but fell quiet in both deletion strains. A drug that triggers autophagy raised activity of the SAP2 gene in normal cells only. The findings tie both genes to resistance through the recycling pathway.
pmc-13233524:
Xiaoping Chen sets out a single math theory of how tumors and the immune system act on each other, in a 2026 paper. Chen had built two frames before: one for immune response over time, and one for the tumor as a living system. The two were close kin but still apart, so a shared frame was the next step.

Chen merges the frames through an information based reading of their core equations. Values are reset against a plain background, and the known theory of how tumors and immunity edit each other is put into math form. The result is ten standard equations meant to give doctors and researchers one shared model for the whole system.
pmc-13234024:
Ömür Baysal and three co-authors explain how the bacterium Bacillus velezensis EU07 suppresses the cereal pathogen Fusarium graminearum. The fungus threatens global grain production, and lasting ways to hold it back are needed. Gene work plus microscopy reveal an unusually deep attack rather than a mild stress effect.

EU07 twists the hyphae of the fungus and breaks the wholeness of its cells. More than 35 percent of the altered transcriptome is suppressed, hitting metabolic hubs, secreted effectors, and master regulators. The fungus fights back with a thirty fold rise in toxin export transporters and an eighty fold rise in detoxifying enzymes. Key weak spots are shut down, and docking shows a bacterial lipopeptide binding a fungal target tightly. In short, the attack does not just slow the fungus, but hits how it feeds and grows.
pmc-13234324:
Shaoyi Jiang and co-authors reported in 2026 on bacteria that learn to live by recycling the remains of dead cells. The material, called necromass, can feed later generations when food is scarce. Their question was whether better recycling also helps a whole closed microbial system last longer. Escherichia coli bacteria were kept for sixty days in sealed, nutrient-free salt solution.

Adapted bacteria grew better on several carbon sources, moved less, and formed more biofilm, with patterns shaped by spatial layout. The adapted strains were then paired with a green alga in closed biospheres. Under uneven spatial conditions, those systems lasted about a quarter less time than systems with non-adapted bacteria. The result warns that efficient recycling in one species can weaken wider system persistence.
pmc-13234624:
Jason Fanning and colleagues set out in 2026 the design of a trial testing a remote activity program for older adults with joint pain. Participants will have obesity plus chronic knee or hip osteoarthritis, a leading cause of pain in later life. The program works through group support delivered at a distance. It targets eating habits, daily activity, and time spent sitting.

Two hundred low-active adults will be assigned randomly to the program or to enhanced usual care. Everyone receives the same self-monitoring devices so device effects do not confuse the comparison. Daily step count is the main outcome after six months of intervention. Pain interference, weight, and physical function serve as further outcomes. Follow-up extends twelve months beyond the program to test lasting behaviour change and pathways of benefit.
pmc-13234724:
Six authors link neighborhood disadvantage, cannabis use, and patient reported outcomes in cancer care in this 2026 study. Cannabis use is spreading among cancer patients, yet little was known about whether where patients get it or how they take it ties to the disadvantage of their neighborhood.

The analysis covered 106 patients across levels of neighborhood disadvantage. Regression models tested links with cannabis source, regulated or not, and route, inhaled or eaten, plus outcomes such as pain, mood, sleep, and quality of life. Disadvantage itself predicted none of these. Household income did: lower income came with worse pain, lower quality of life, and more depression, which shifts attention from place to means.
pmc-13234824: Overgaard and colleagues introduce an editorial series on writing scientific articles better. The series targets two linked faults: weak reporting, where key details go missing, and weak method, where the study itself is loosely built. Its stated themes run from transparency and proper presentation to quality improvement and fair peer review. A well-reported study, the editors argue, can be repeated, judged, and used; a poorly reported one cannot, however good its data. The series aims to cut review rounds and raise the share of papers fit to guide practice.
pmc-13235224:
Mohamed Ali Ag Ahmed and co-authors interviewed in 2026 leaders about why drugs fail to reach conflict-hit parts of Mali reliably. Twenty-eight interviews gathered views from health workers, community groups, officials, and aid actors around Mopti and Bamako. Talks were coded by theme with software support. Conflict has disrupted medicine supply across the Sahel for more than a decade.

Four linked problem themes emerged from what people described to the team. Insecurity breaks transport routes and supply chains across the hit areas. Market breakdown drives price swings and repeated gaps of vital products. Weak storage and logistics infrastructure puts medicine quality at risk during distribution. Poor teamwork among public, private, and aid actors deepens every other problem. The authors urge joint teamwork, funding in logistics and information systems, and stronger rules during and after conflict.
pmc-13235324:
Sebastian Lehmann and co-authors checked in 2026 whether skull openings planned in virtual reality match what surgeons actually perform. Eighty-three patients had meningioma surgery planned with interactive headsets from two makers. The planned opening was compared with the real one for position, relative size, and number of drill holes. Meningiomas are common brain tumours where precise opening placement shapes the whole operation.

Average size measures differed only slightly between plan and reality in both directions measured. Drill hole counts changed in under a tenth of the operations performed. Hole position changed in only a small handful of cases in the series. Statistical equivalence tests supported the closeness of planned and real openings. Overall geometric deviation stayed under six percent between the two. The authors say interactive planning transfers faithfully to the operating room.
pmc-13235524:
Tianyi Zhao and co-authors measured in 2026 how efficiently suburban villages near Nanjing use their output, living, and ecological spaces. Rapid urbanization has left many such areas with wasteful, unbalanced land use. An efficiency method compared inputs and outputs across townships over a decade. Geographic mapping, inequality decomposition, and a triangular balance model added views of pattern and teamwork.

Average efficiency across the three space types rose by nearly half between 2011 and 2021. Seventeen townships moved from gap toward teamwork during that decade in the analysis. About half of townships reached at least a basic level of teamwork by the end. Nine townships achieved high-quality teamwork among output, living, and ecological uses. The authors offer their framework to sharpen rural governance and support sustainable countryside development in fast-growing metropolitan regions.
pmc-13236124:
Tareq Al-Jaberi tracks rules for surgery in cancer care, from Al-Zahrawi's Kitab al-Tasrif to modern oncology. His work is a 2026 review of the past. Al-Zahrawi lived from 936 to 1013. He wrote a vast treatise on surgery, in the form of an encyclopedia.

The review sets his rationale, operative techniques, and cautions next to the rules used in surgical oncology now. Al-Zahrawi backed full excision, with healthy tissue round the growth taken too. He saw the risk that cancer could come back, and he stressed early diagnosis. He also urged care in cases that were far gone or deep and hard to reach. Al-Jaberi says these stands match modern rules that have lasted. That holds in spite of the tight bounds on tools in medieval times. The piece gives a close account of what stayed the same, and what changed, over a thousand years.
pmc-13236524:
Yohei Tateishi and colleagues built in 2026 a score to spot a specific stroke cause before clot-removal surgery. Some large vessel blockages arise from fatty narrowing inside the skull rather than travelling clots, and they behave differently during the procedure. Records for more than three hundred thrombectomy patients with brain magnetic resonance imaging were analysed retrospectively. Imaging signs and clinical features were ranked, then combined into a point score.

Four features independently pointed to the narrowing-related cause in the final model. Absence of an irregular heartbeat rhythm carried the strongest weight among them. Multiple infarcts in border zones and mixed-age lesions also raised the score in the system. A missing clot sign on a sensitive scan sequence added further points toward the diagnosis. The score separated the two causes with high accuracy in internal validation checks.
pmc-13236724:
Shi-Jie Wang and co-authors read the mitochondrial genomes of two stingless bees from Hainan, China, in a 2026 study. The bees, both in the Tetragonula group, matter for local ecology. Their full small genomes had not been described in this detail before.

Both genomes show the typical insect layout, yet each has its own rearrangements and changes. Both are rich in the A and T bases, which shapes how their code is used. Family tree analysis places them firmly with other stingless bees, apart from honey bees and bumble bees. The data will aid family studies and plans to guard and use these bees.
pmc-13236924:
Yun Zhang and Tinglei Liu surveyed 1,533 vocational undergraduates at eight universities in China's Hebei Province for a 2026 study of why students stay silent in class. The survey measured how much support students felt from teachers, their confidence about speaking, their speaking anxiety, and their tendency toward silence. A structural model traced paths among the four.

Teacher support showed no direct link to silence. Instead, supported students felt more confident about speaking, and that confidence, partly by easing anxiety, went with less silence. One small path through anxiety alone ran the other way. Because the data were collected once, the authors treat the paths as associations, not proof of cause. Confidence-building teaching is their practical suggestion.
pmc-13237224:
Vamsi and colleagues present HS-RankFormer, a model that rebuilds a full light spectrum from an ordinary colour photo. Hyperspectral images record dozens of narrow colour bands and reveal what eyes cannot see, but the cameras are costly. Rebuilding that data from a normal RGB image is hard: labelled examples are few, and models often fail on new scenes.

Their transformer-based model aims to be both efficient and sturdy across different settings. It tries to keep fine spatial detail while guessing each pixel's spectrum, without the heavy cost of earlier methods. Reliable reconstruction could put spectral imaging into farming, medicine, and inspection using cameras people already own.
pmc-13237424:
Chen and colleagues review how to steer crystal growth in antimony-based solar films. These chalcogenide materials are cheap and promising for thin-film solar cells. Their flaw is structural: their ribbon-like crystals conduct charge well along one direction and badly across it, so the way crystals lie in the film decides performance.

Crystals lying flat create slippery internal walls that block charge flow. Crystals standing upright, the team explains, form clean paths with friendly grain boundaries. The review gathers strategies to favour the upright growth, from seed layers to heat treatments. Mastering crystal direction could lift these films from laboratory promise to real panels.
pmc-13238524:
Xue Ao and six co-authors feed a traditional fermented soup to fat-fed rats and track their livers, in a paper dated 2026. Miao sour soup, a Guizhou staple, carries compounds such as lycopene and capsaicin linked to leaner, calmer metabolism. In obesity, the liver makes too much new glucose, worsening blood sugar.

Rats on a high-fat diet that received the soup stored less liver fat, secreted fewer inflammatory signals, and showed lower blood fats and glucose. Broad metabolite profiling pointed at the glucose-making pathway. Protein blots then showed the soup dampened one inflammatory switch while activating a signaling chain that reins in glucose production. The dish behaves, in rats at least, like a functional food against diet-driven metabolic strain.
pmc-13239324:
Shama Patel and a large working group argued in 2026 that artificial intelligence for global health must move from tech optimism to locally led, equity-centered rollout. Their narrative landscape review, joined with talks from a 2025 pre-conference session, surveyed AI across education, epidemiology, and clinical medicine, with data equity at the center. Benefits so far are unevenly shared and thinly tested in real settings.

Five must-dos structure their plan: oversight rules fitted to context, fair capacity building, careful rollout and cost research, open data stores, and community-centered ethical design. Without those shifts, they warn, AI will reinforce the very gaps it claims to solve. The piece asks who designs the tools, for whom, and under whose oversight, and refuses easy answers.
pmc-13239524:
Reem El Sherif and colleagues compare malpractice lawsuits against doctors trained in different countries in a 2026 Canadian cohort study. Using records from the national medical protective body, they asked whether international medical graduates face civil legal actions more often than peers trained in Canada or the United States.

The analysis covered nearly ninety-nine thousand physicians and thousands of cases across several years. Lawsuit rates per year of practice did not differ significantly between the groups. Raw outcomes slightly favoured patients suing internationally trained doctors, yet that gap vanished once other factors were taken into account. The authors conclude that place of training alone does not predict legal risk.
pmc-13240024:
Govindarajan Karthivashan and co-authors test whether a common drug-carrier material, on its own, can slow Alzheimer's disease in mice. Their 2026 study uses a mouse strain bred to build up amyloid beta, the protein clumps linked to the disease, and treats older mice with steady doses into the brain's fluid spaces.

After treatment, the mice showed better memory scores, lower amyloid levels and deposits, and less nerve cell damage. Gene readouts from brain tissue shifted in pathways tied to waste clearance, cell defense, and immune activity. The authors link the gains to changes in how amyloid is made, cleared, and how cells handle stress. They argue the plain carrier itself may hold promise as a treatment base.
pmc-13240324:
Five food scientists study protein and mucilage conjugates for better food ingredients in a paper from 2026. Plant proteins are popular but often dissolve and foam poorly. The products were checked for structure, heat stability, and working traits.

Longer bonding raised fiber and two key amino acids. The protein's shape shifted, and its heat resistance improved over the plain isolate. Solubility rose across acidity levels, and emulsions and foams grew stronger and more stable. The authors propose the conjugates as novel food ingredients. Longer treatment generally enhanced the morphology as well.
pmc-13240424:
Huishen Yan and Liang He single out a cell membrane pump gene as a survival marker in oesophageal cancer in a 2026 analysis. Tumours rich in the gene showed calmer profiles for invasion and spreading programmes, alongside distinctive immune cell mixes. Single-cell data placed the gene mainly in malignant surface cells but also in support and immune cells. Silencing it in laboratory cells changed behaviour and raised inflammatory gene activity.
pmc-13240924:
Ndengue's team in Douala tested how sample handling distorts breast cancer marker readings in a low-resource lab. One breast tumor from a 34-year-old woman supplied fifty tiny samples. Four cohorts varied the fixing recipe, fixing length, and delay before fixing. Estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and Ki67 were scored by staining.

pmc-13241524:
Tóth and Nagy at the Balaton Limnological Research Institute studied how city life affects common reed along Lake Balaton in Hungary. Reed beds dominate the shallow edges of the lake. Artificial light at night proved much stronger along the shore than over open water. The pair measured vegetative and reproductive traits across sites with different urban pressure.

Reed growth also started later in the season at more urbanized sites. The authors argue that city influence acts as a selective filter, hitting reproduction and timing harder than bulk growth.
pmc-13241924:
Rishi Raj Sinha writes a 2026 letter questioning whether time to plasma exchange is the right focus in suspected thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. This rare blood disorder needs urgent plasma exchange, yet outcomes vary widely even with early treatment. Recent population data link timing to results in a curved, weak pattern.

He also proposes a readiness bundle that readies diagnosis, plasma, and exchange services in parallel, like sepsis care bundles.
pmc-13242224:
Shreena Reddy, Vishaka Hatcher, and Charles Miller tell how a peanut allergy label from childhood was lifted in a 2026 case report. Peanut allergy is often diagnosed young and can stick for life as a label, even when the person outgrows it. For their patient, the label blocked a long-held goal: joining the United States military.

A supervised food challenge, the gold-standard check, was passed with no symptoms at all. The diagnosis was removed and he was cleared to enlist. pmc-13242424:
Claire Munsie and colleagues evaluated a community exercise program built for teenagers and young adults who had finished cancer treatment. Their study appeared in Supportive Care in Cancer in 2026. Participants aged fifteen to twenty-seven joined twice-weekly group sessions for twelve weeks at a local facility. A trained exercise physiologist tailored aerobic, strength, and flexibility work to each person, and the team measured fitness and well-being before and after.

Of 127 starters, 93 finished the program and final testing. Aerobic fitness, leg and chest strength, and everyday physical function all improved, and lean mass rose while fat mass and fatigue fell. Quality of life improved across physical, role, and social domains, and no one was harmed by the training. pmc-13242824:
Xiaoshuang Chen and co-authors publish a 2026 multicenter study of an inflammation index as a prognostic marker in advanced liver cancer. Patients whose cancer progressed after first-line therapy received a three-part second-line combination. A simple blood-based immune-inflammation index was tested as a continuous measure rather than a cut-off.

The pattern held across drug dose and immunotherapy subgroups. The index did not predict tumor shrinkage, yet it did flag higher risk of severe side effects. The authors propose it as a cheap risk-stratification aid alongside liver and tumor measures.
pmc-13243524:
Direct-current microgrids need faults caught fast, but their fault signals are faint and brief. Dai and four co-authors build a detection and early warning method from three parts. A signal-splitting step then cleans the waveform, keeping the parts that carry fault information and dropping noise.

In tests, the method classified faults with about ninety-two percent accuracy in islanded mode and ninety-one percent when grid-connected. It topped ninety-five percent on single-phase grounding faults and stayed above ninety-one percent across network layouts. The authors present it as a robust guard for small DC grids.
pmc-13245424:
Miyazawa and co-authors investigated a patterned pufferfish's origins in this 2026 PeerJ study. Mushifugu, a poisonous pufferfish found only around Japan, wears a striking labyrinth pattern unlike its plain or spotted relatives. Biologists had speculated it might be a hybrid, since blending two spotted patterns can produce labyrinth designs. The team compared its DNA with its closest spotted relative, komonfugu, across both coasts of Japan.

Genome-wide markers, though, showed little split between the two mushifugu populations and a clean separation from komonfugu. The authors use demographic modeling to weigh the hybrid story, treating the fish as its own lineage whose pattern demands explanation beyond simple mixing.
pmc-13246624:
Shaked Farbstein-Yavin and co-authors follow behavioral addictions in young people across the COVID-19 years in a 2026 study. Gambling, shopping, exercise, and eating can all turn compulsive in youth. The pandemic broke routines and raised strain, which may have fed such patterns.
