Dark mood, mental symptoms, and thrill seeking predicted higher symptom levels. Hope, life satisfaction, and secure attachment linked to fewer symptoms, mostly by easing distress. Support from others showed a surprising tie to more symptoms for some habits.
pmc-13246924:
A tick-borne parasite disease drains cattle herds across South Africa, causing fever and lost blood. Thandikhaya Bambeni and co-authors map how common that disease is in a 2026 study. They test cattle blood with a gene test for live parasites and an antibody test for past exposure, at dip tanks and high-risk sites.

In the core Mnisi area, 38 percent of cattle carried at least one of the two parasite species. In the added risk areas, the share hit 60 percent. One species ruled in one province and the other in another. The two tests agreed only slightly, since each reads a unlike stage of infection. Using both gives a fuller watch on herd risk.
pmc-13247224:
Sun, Zhou, Huang, and co-authors describe a camouflage trick for delivering messenger RNA to the lungs, in this 2026 letter in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Inhaled mRNA vaccines could raise immunity right where respiratory viruses enter, but the lung's mucosal barrier blocks the lipid nanoparticles that carry mRNA, and none has finished clinical trials. That binding kept them in the mucosal layer longer and ferried them into and across airway cells. pmc-13248324:
Zhao and co-authors looked for better predictors of cancer drug response in this 2026 Biomarker Research letter. Their patients had advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma treated first with immune therapy plus chemotherapy. The usual marker, PD-L1, alone predicts benefit poorly, so the team stained pretreatment biopsies for several immune cell types.

In one hundred forty-seven patients, high PD-L1 pointed to longer time before the cancer grew. Yet dense PD-1 positive killer T cells pointed the other way, toward shorter control. Combining both markers separated patients sharply, from under four months to nearly nine. The authors propose the pair as a practical guide for treatment choices.
pmc-13248424:
Florence Cook and co-authors map in 2026 how head and neck cancer patients are fed after flap reconstruction surgery. After such surgery patients start on tube feeding with nothing by mouth, then transition back to eating, a phase few reviews had charted. The scoping review screened over five thousand records and kept thirty-six papers.

Tubes went in before, during, or after surgery, as nose tubes or stomach tubes, with feeds ideally starting within a day. Stomach tube placement hinged on tumor site and stage, age, and prior treatment. The synthesis lays out transition practices and where the nutritional evidence runs thin.
pmc-13249124:
Miller and a U.S. team describe a trial protocol aimed at caregivers who sit too much, published in 2026. Caring for a relative with Alzheimer's disease raises a caregiver's own health risks, and long sitting is part of that load. The goal is a habit: four hourly walks a day, each adding a modest burst of steps, held for a week straight. Wrist trackers record movement passively while surveys probe whether the walking becomes automatic. Forty percent of the planned sample had enrolled by August 2025, with data collection expected to finish in mid 2026.
pmc-13250224:
Beauchamp and co-authors lay out a trial testing whether activity-based coaching can prevent depression after stroke. Their 2026 BMJ Open protocol targets low-income adults aged fifty-five and older, within three months of a stroke. Poststroke depression affects about a third of survivors and worsens recovery, yet no standard prevention approach exists.

Trained community health workers will run an orientation, five weekly sessions, and two monthly booster calls. Depression scores over nine months form the main outcome, with anxiety, quality of life, and hospital visits also tracked. The team will share deidentified data and code through a national archive.
pmc-13250324:
Mohmmed Margni and co-authors set out a technique paper in 2026 on treating painful knee arthritis from inside the blood vessels. Blocking overgrown small arteries around the knee can ease pain, and the entry point is usually the groin artery.

Drawing on more than ten years of practice, the team instead enters through a foot artery, checking it first with ultrasound. They report faster walking after the procedure, plus lower radiation and dye use, making foot entry a practical option.
pmc-13250724: Feyza Nur Topcu Yenercag, Sule Ozturk, and Gunay Kaya Tarhan published this 2026 correction to their study of premarital spinal muscular atrophy screening in northern Türkiye. The notice is a correction only: it replaces the article's ethics statement with a fuller version. The corrected text names the Samsun University ethics board decision. It adds a second approval from the Samsun Provincial Health Directorate dated July 2024, and confirms that the records review rested on earlier written consent. No findings, data, or conclusions of the study change.
pmc-13251524:
Vlasov and Manley review enhancer RNAs, short-lived transcripts copied from the genome's enhancer switches. Their 2026 RNA Biology paper sorts what these RNAs do and how they blur the line between coding and non-coding RNA. Enhancer RNAs are usually destroyed quickly, yet several roles in switching genes on have been proposed.

The review covers current models of enhancer RNA function and the discoveries behind them. It highlights a surprise: some enhancer RNAs contain readable protein recipes, and a few are actually translated. Proteins from supposedly non-coding transcripts tend to be small and may carry their own jobs. The authors argue these findings reshape thinking about how both enhancer RNAs and ordinary messenger RNAs evolved.
pmc-13253424:
Dongmei Gou, Maomei He, and Jiaquan Zhuo test an acupoint injection for chronic heart failure in a 2026 randomized, double-blind trial. The treatment injects astragalus extract, a traditional herbal preparation, into the Neiguan point on the forearm, which Chinese medicine links to heart function. After treatment, the injection group showed better symptom scores, lower levels of the heart strain marker BNP, and stronger pumping function. They also walked farther in six minutes and reported better quality of life. Readmissions did not differ, and no adverse events occurred in either arm. The authors conclude the add-on is safe and helpful for this patient pattern.
pmc-13253924:
Francesca Alfieri and many colleagues test an AI model that warns of kidney injury in a 2026 study. Acute kidney injury is a sudden loss of kidney function common in intensive care. Their model gives hourly risk scores for moderate and severe injury, and was upgraded to cope with missing data.

Past records covered 70,107 ICU admissions in three countries across 176 units, with strong scores above 0.89 on a key accuracy measure. A live test in three European hospitals with 329 patients scored from 0.82 to 0.96. Warnings came about 14 hours early on average, which the authors say could aid care.
pmc-13254424:
Xiaobin Tang and co-authors run a pilot study of facial microbes in rosacea in a 2026 paper. Rosacea is a chronic facial skin disease with redness and bumps. Skin samples from six patients and two healthy controls, across three skin oil types, were sequenced for bacteria and fungi.

pmc-13256224: A short 2026 retraction notice in Open Forum Infectious Diseases withdraws an IDWeek conference abstract by Monirujjaman Biswas on acute viral hepatitis among dengue patients in northern India. The journal says the abstract overlapped significantly with a previously published paper by Jain and others, without giving credit to it. It also says the authorship of the publication cannot be verified. pmc-13256324:

pmc-13256824:

pmc-13257324:
Marija Ratković-Janković and co-authors test urine and blood markers in children with urine reflux in a 2026 study. pmc-13257624:

pmc-13257724:

pmc-13257924:

pmc-13258024:

pmc-13258124:

pmc-13258424:

pmc-13258524:

pmc-13258824:

pmc-13258924:

pmc-13259224:

pmc-13260124:

pmc-13260224:

pmc-13260324:

pmc-13260724:

pmc-13260824:

pmc-13261024:

The authors say scan changes can help sort patients by outlook.
pmc-13261124:

pmc-13261324:

pmc-13262424:

pmc-13262724:

pmc-13262824:
Cosmas Zyambo leads a national survey study of HIV treatment adherence in Zambia in a 2026 journal article. Antiretroviral therapy, the drug regimen that controls HIV, works only when taken as prescribed. The team surveyed people living with HIV at 193 clinics across all ten provinces, using a 2023 national survey, and modeled which factors tracked with missed treatment.

Of 5,204 people surveyed, 7.1 percent were not adhering, with higher rates in men than women. Among those not adhering, 60 percent drank alcohol and 22 percent smoked tobacco. Drinking and smoking each raised the odds of non-adherence roughly two to three times. Older age and more schooling lowered the odds. The authors suggest targeted support around alcohol and tobacco use.
pmc-13263224:
Takeshi Yamashita and co-authors report a relapsing neck spine infection in an 88-year-old man in a 2026 case report. The infection, called spondylodiscitis, attacks a spinal bone and its disc, and neck cases are uncommon. Blood cultures found a strain of Streptococcus gallolyticus, a normal gut germ rarely blamed for spinal infections.

A standard 90-day course of antibiotics first cleared his fever, neck pain, and blood markers. Yet symptoms returned on day 174, even though repeat scans showed no clear active inflammation. Doctors resumed oral antibiotics for nine months, reaching lasting remission without surgery. To their knowledge, no earlier case caused by this strain described a return. They suggest longer, patient-matched treatment and long follow-up for such cases.
pmc-13263624:
Laila Shakhtour and co-authors check whether a lateral perforator flap keeps breast shape after cancer surgery in a 2026 study. These chest wall flaps fill the gap left by wide tumor removal, a decade-old conservation method still lacking shape proof.

All flap patients at one Swedish hospital over ten years were measured before surgery and one year after. The untreated breast served as each woman's own control. Volume held steady, while nipple distance and droop shrank slightly. Photo scoring rated most results excellent or good, close to the pre-surgery rate. Radiation followed surgery for many patients. The authors conclude the flap is surgically and oncologically safe, with breast features largely preserved.
pmc-13264024:
Bilguun Mend and colleagues publish a 2026 dataset on cement made with waste-derived ferrous sulfate in place of natural gypsum. Gypsum normally controls how Portland cement sets, so a waste-based substitute needs careful testing. The collection records how the materials were made and how the hardened cement behaved over time and at different curing ages.

Included files cover crystal structure, heat-based analysis, microscope images, chemical composition and setting times. Strength results, soluble hexavalent chromium measurements and life-cycle inventory inputs are also provided. Both raw instrument output and processed tables are organized by method and sample. Engineers and researchers can reuse the data to compare sulfate sources, model hydration and judge environmental trade-offs.
pmc-13264424:
Long Wang and co-authors published a 2026 study of a heat-sensitive gel built to fight gum disease on three fronts at once. Gum disease is fed by bacteria that shun oxygen, by too much inflammation in the gum, and by slow bone regrowth in the jaw. Single-purpose materials cannot meet all three needs. The gel is designed to do so in one package.

The gel holds tiny particles: an oxygen-releasing core wrapped in a dark coating, inside a base that gels at body heat and thins when pressed. In dish tests the particles released oxygen and magnesium ions bit by bit. Two key gum bacteria were held back. Immune cells produced fewer of their inflammatory signals. Bone cells moved, matured, and laid down mineral at a high rate. In rats with gum disease, the gel reduced inflammation, restrained the bacteria, and raised bone regeneration markers.
pmc-13264824:
Katie de Luca led a 2026 commentary on the role of chiropractic care in rehabilitation, the care that restores daily function after illness or injury. About 2.4 billion people live with conditions that could gain from such care. Chiropractors train in muscle and joint health and person-centered care, and the paper argues they can strengthen health systems.

The authors describe chiropractic work after surgery, in sports injury recovery, and in nerve rehabilitation. They show how chiropractors join team-based care, public systems, and hospitals. Gains in low- and middle-income countries and for fair access are weighed. Barriers include uneven laws, low recognition by other professions, and patchy team integration. The paper ends with a call for better training links and advocacy.
pmc-13264924:
Lars Dijk and colleagues published a 2026 interview study on how sudden worsening events shape daily life for people with COPD, a long-term lung disease. Such events were defined by drops in breathing measures, more reliever use, or worse symptoms. The team asked patients in five countries how they spot and handle these turns.

Nineteen patients with moderate to severe disease took part, with interviews right after an event and again six weeks later. Patients described bad days in varied ways, from lost ability to do tasks to needing extra treatment. Events under two days often went unnoticed, while longer ones were usually recognized. Most said they would seek care if needed, but hard-to-get appointments and a wait-and-see habit held some back. The authors link low awareness to under-reporting.
pmc-13265224:
Xiaoxiong Wang and colleagues examine a protein called DKK4 across colorectal growths, in a 2026 study. Colorectal cancer develops stepwise from normal lining through benign adenomas. Markers for early precancerous stages are scarce. Tissue staining and data analysis tracked DKK4 at each stage.

DKK4 was low in normal tissue, rose in adenomas, and peaked in high-grade precancerous lesions. Levels then fell notably in invasive cancer. Expression linked to mutation burden and to a growth pathway called Wnt. A risk model built with DKK4 showed modest predictive accuracy. The pattern may help flag lesions needing closer attention.
pmc-13266024:
Mushrin Malik and colleagues pool evidence on AI-read heart artery scans for predicting major cardiac events, in a 2026 meta-analysis. Automated plaque measurement promises consistency beyond simple narrowing grades. Ten studies covering about twenty thousand patients were included. Searches ran through October 2025.

Plaque burden measured by AI predicted major events with roughly doubled risk. Soft, low-density plaque showed the strongest link. Event rates for death, heart attack, and repeat procedures were pooled across cohorts. Results held when restricted to one AI platform. The authors argue plaque character adds prognostic value beyond stenosis severity alone.
pmc-13266224:
Younghee Park and the team ask whether nodal radiation can be omitted in certain breast cancers after chemotherapy (2026). Patients had small tumours with initial node spread and residual node disease after chemotherapy. Surgery meant full node clearance. The Korean study group evaluated radiation benefit in this niche.

Highlights report no added survival benefit from regional nodal irradiation here. Omission may therefore be considered for selected patients. Decisions after chemotherapy are tricky because response changes risk estimates. Prior registry work supports risk-adapted de-escalation plans. The findings add Korean data to an active international debate on tailoring radiation.
pmc-13266824:
Kun Zhang and colleagues pool in 2026 the results of freezing therapy for early-stage lung cancer, for patients who often cannot face major surgery. Their meta-analysis gathered seven small studies covering 353 patients, most with stage IA disease. They tracked survival, cancer control, local return of tumor, spread, and procedure harms.

Survival stayed high through three years, then fell by year five, a pattern the authors report without a direct surgery comparison. Local recurrence and spread were uncommon in the pooled data. Collapsed lung was the most frequent harm, affecting about a quarter of patients, while no deaths occurred within thirty days. Stage IA patients fared best, supporting freezing as an option for carefully chosen cases.
pmc-13266924:
Li and Noble couple aldehydes with electron poor olefins using light and a Hantzsch ester in twenty twenty-six. Both partners are cheap feedstocks, and their union yields prized alcohols. Past routes needed harsh reducing power that let side paths win. Aliphatic aldehydes failed most often. Their setup skips any photocatalyst.

Light wakes the ester anion under mild base, and it reduces the olefin. Water as an additive lets the charged olefin attack the aldehyde. Tests back the olefin radical anion as the key middle step. The simple recipe widens who can play, they argue.
pmc-13267024:
Xinjing Shen and colleagues report a 2026 study of a drinkable drug carrier aimed at scarred liver tissue. Liver fibrosis builds up when star-shaped liver cells switch on and lay down excess matrix. The team loaded a plant compound called morin into tiny oil droplets marked with vitamin A, which those cells tend to take up.

In rats with chemically induced liver scarring, the oral carrier crossed the gut wall intact and reached the liver through the lymph route. Treated rats showed less scarring, less of a scar marker, and lower levels of a key scar-driving signal. Liver function also improved. The authors offer the system as a long-term oral option for fibrosis care.
pmc-13267424: Shah and colleagues' letter on lung blood pressure in chronic lung disease is the subject of a 2026 correction notice. The original letter argued that male sex is linked to severe pulmonary hypertension and worse outcomes in COPD patients sent for a heart catheter test. A publisher's error left the published title incomplete. The correction restores the words Letter to the Editor at the start of the title, marking it as a letter. The notice apologizes for the error. No findings or conclusions change.
pmc-13267824:
Yuhao Fu, Jiajie Qian, Yang Zhang, and Fuhai Ji built and validated a machine learning model that predicts kidney injury after heart surgery in older adults, in a 2026 study. This complication is frequent and devastating in this age group, and early warning would let clinicians act preventively. Data from two centers trained the models; a third center's patients were held back for a truly external test.

Four feature-selection methods agreed on a predictor set, and six learning algorithms were compared. A gradient boosting model, LightGBM, performed best, with an accuracy score of about 0.78 on the standard curve measure. The strongest predictors were lactate level, operation length, two clotting times, and transfusion volume, a clinically sensible list. Explanation plots showed how each factor pushes risk up or down, including nonlinear effects. The authors present the model as a practical risk-stratification tool, while noting it needs prospective testing.
pmc-13267924:
Min Xu and colleagues report a 2026 survey of fear of movement after pacemaker surgery in China. Kinesiophobia, an excessive fear that movement will cause harm, can keep patients from rehab exercise. The team surveyed 211 patients at one large hospital in Yinchuan between October 2025 and January 2026. They measured family functioning, pain, worst-case thinking about pain, and movement fear.

About 60 percent of patients showed kinesiophobia. Stronger family functioning went with less fear, less pain, and less worst-case thinking. Pain and worst-case thinking each went with more fear. The chain analysis showed family support linked to lower fear partly through lower pain and calmer thinking about pain, in that order. The authors caution that a one-time survey cannot prove cause and urge follow-up studies.
pmc-13268724:
Jooyun Kim and co-authors review in 2026 how clinicians can judge tissue starvation in shock without leaning only on blood pressure. Shock means the circulation fails to match oxygen delivery with the body's needs. Large vessels may look restored while the tiny vessels that feed cells stay poorly perfused, a split the authors call hemodynamic incoherence.

The review walks through clinical signs, blood chemistry markers, and device-based measures that reflect both levels of circulation. Each indicator is explained in terms of what it says about the body and where it helps decisions. Their framework supports checking several signals at once when diagnosing shock, estimating outlook, and guiding treatment for critically ill patients.
pmc-13268924:
Qian Chen and colleagues follow in 2026 the paths of a urine protein marker over time in Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes, asking which paths warn of kidney damage ahead. They studied 3,101 patients whose starting albumin-to-creatinine ratios were still in the normal range, with records from 2018 to 2024 at a metabolic center in Ningbo. Modeling sorted patients by how their marker moved over the years.

Three paths appeared: low-normal, mid-range normal, and a rising path with swings. Both higher paths carried far greater risk of developing protein in the urine than the low path, with the rising, swinging path the most dangerous by a wide margin. Machine learning singled out baseline marker level, body measures, and blood values as key clues. Tracking the path, not just one reading, could sharpen early screening.
pmc-13270724:
Manouri Wimalasekera is lead author of a 2026 narrative case study on bringing community engagement and involvement into research in Sri Lanka. That approach, shortened to CEI, means involving local people in shaping and guiding studies, and the work was coordinated by a Sri Lankan research institute between 2018 and 2025.

Drawing on stakeholder activities, workshop results, and programme records, the authors describe how CEI became part of the national research system. Success, they argue, needs tackling structural inequality, matching engagement to local culture, and backing from ethics rules and leaders. They present Sri Lanka's foundation as a model other lower- and middle-income countries could adapt.
pmc-13271424:
Jingyan Zhang is lead author of a 2026 single-centre survey on whether Chinese breast cancer patients would consider corrective surgery. The patients had breast deformity after breast-conserving surgery. They had finished radiation at least a year earlier. Deformity was graded with a standard scale. Willingness meant openness at survey time, not a booked operation.

Among 306 patients, 123, or 40.2 percent, were willing, and 183 declined. In simple analyses, willingness linked to home area, income, travel time to care, deformity grade, and other factors. Those declining most often cited fear of complications or failure, cost, acceptance of their look, or not wanting another operation. Better body image and self-belief motivated those willing.
pmc-13271924:
Haiqing Wang and coauthors report in 2026 a case of fixing a small broken piece of ankle joint cartilage and bone with thin metal wires. Such osteochondral fractures of the talus are rare and easy to miss. Left unfixed, the loose piece can wear the joint and lead to arthritis.

The patient also had an unmoved break of the inner ankle bone, which surgeons opened to reach the fragment. After setting the piece back in place, they passed two thin wires from the front and drew them back so the ends sat flush with the joint surface. Both breaks healed within two months, and later imaging confirmed sound repair.
pmc-13272324:
Endzhe Takemura and Hirotaka Matsuoka ask in 2026 why sports fans at times cheer for the team that knocked out their favorite. The authors framed that switch as a way to cope when a fan's group pride feels under threat and the rivalry is over. Fans of Japanese pro baseball teams filled in surveys on team loyalty and self-esteem.

The results tied loyalty and group self-esteem to support for the winning team, yet they did not back the coping idea. Stronger loyalty went with higher self-esteem after the favorite lost. The authors say fan loyalty repairs pride in other ways than simply backing the winner, which refines how such behavior should be read.
pmc-13272524:
Konstantinos Ouranos leads a 2026 database study of sepsis, a life-threatening response to infection, paired with very high ferritin in the blood. That pattern is called macrophage activation-like syndrome, or MALS. The authors used the TriNetX database and a ferritin cutoff to define the group.

From 2017 to 2025, 10,169 patients met the MALS pattern, against 214,338 without it. After matching, MALS patients died more often at 28 and 90 days and needed breathing tubes, intensive care, and blood pressure drugs more often. Higher ferritin cutoffs meant worse outcomes, and the drug anakinra showed no survival gain.
pmc-13273124:
Xue Li and colleagues pooled evidence on rheumatoid arthritis and thyroid cancer risk in a 2026 meta-analysis. Rheumatoid arthritis raises the risk of some cancers but not others, and studies on thyroid cancer have disagreed. No earlier review had focused on this single link.

The team gathered fourteen cohort studies covering nearly two million people. Overall, patients with rheumatoid arthritis faced a modestly higher risk of thyroid cancer than the general population. The link was clear in Chinese populations but absent in other groups studied. Adjustment choices also changed results, with fuller adjustment weakening the link. The authors say their findings can inform cancer watch strategies for these patients while noting the mixed picture.
pmc-13273224:
Pamungkas Rizki Ferdian and co-authors tested the safety of leaf extract from Taxus sumatrana in a 2026 study. This Indonesian tree yields anticancer compounds, but stripping its bark kills slow growing trees. Leaves regrow, so the team asked whether leaf extract is safe enough to use instead.

Mice given the extract by mouth showed no deaths within a day, even at the highest dose tested. Computer predictions for the one hundred compounds found in the leaves also pointed to low toxicity. Organ weights and blood chemistry barely shifted across dose groups. Liver and kidney changes under the microscope stayed minor. The authors support leaf use as a safer and more sustainable source, while calling for longer toxicity studies.
pmc-13273524:
Emily Ravenhill and William Farr present a 2026 review of hikikomori, long social withdrawal first described in 1990s Japan. Debate persists over whether this is a disorder, a response to stress, or a coping strategy. Their two-stage review looks at overlap with autism traits and at cultural context.

They find overlap in social talk differences, sensory sensitivity, and narrow interests, though life paths differ. School pressure, family dynamics, and norms in Japan can worsen withdrawal. They also frame withdrawal as sometimes protective, aiding rest and coping. Harm arises when isolation lasts long with no support. They urge flexible, culturally aware help.
pmc-13273624:
Charlotte Naslund-Koch leads a 2026 study of fatty liver disease with fibrosis in patients with psoriasis, a chronic skin disease. The prevalence in this group is unknown and no screening consensus exists. Patients from a Copenhagen skin biobank program were examined with transient elastography, a scan that measures liver fat and stiffness, plus blood markers.

Of 403 patients, 40 percent had liver steatosis and 5 percent had fibrosis. Nearly all steatosis cases fit metabolic dysfunction-associated disease by reported alcohol use. Against the scan as reference, the FIB-4 index and the ELF test performed best, with accuracy measures of 0.92 and 0.90, while a collagen marker scored 0.77.
pmc-13273724:
Obesity and unsound food systems feed each other, Zahra Namkhah and co-authors argue in a 2026 paper. Diets rich in cheap, heavily processed foods raise obesity risk and carry a heavy environmental cost. Rules that prize volume and ease lock farms and shops into that pattern.

The authors map feedback loops across supply chains, food settings, and social gaps. They propose a health-in-all-policies frame that joins health and green goals across government sectors. Policy bundles span farm aid, taxes, city planning, school food, and trade. Shared scorecards would track diet quality, price fairness, and emissions together. The aim is double-duty wins without shifting harm onto the poor.
pmc-13274024:
Carla Bellinghausen and co-authors report a 2026 journal article from the CCHROMO study of long-lasting illness after COVID-19. The study follows patients at a post-COVID clinic with lung tests, exercise tests, and blood samples for up to three years. Its exact causes and course are still poorly understood.

This interim report covers 253 patients across 561 visits, a median of 273 days after diagnosis. Fatigue hit about eighty-five percent, with breathlessness, headache, and thinking problems each near seventy percent. Standard breathing tests were mostly normal, yet over half of visits showed weak breathing muscles and nearly a third showed poor exercise capacity. Links between symptoms, test results, and blood markers were weak overall.
pmc-13276324:
Jennifer Robblee and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on brain size during status migrainosus, a migraine attack lasting more than three days. These long attacks disable patients and resist treatment. Whether the brain itself swells during them was not known.

Eleven participants had MRI scans both during an attack and later at a pain-free baseline. Ten were women, and attacks had lasted a median of about twenty-five days. Total brain volume measured higher during attacks than at baseline. The cortex and deep gray matter trended slightly smaller, while white matter under the cortex trended larger, though neither shift was clear-cut. The authors suggest hidden cell swelling could explain the volume gain. They call for larger studies to pin down the mechanism and what it means for patients.
pmc-13276524:
Ruth Harvey and co-authors report a 2026 journal article testing human immunity to a new flu strain that emerged in 2025. The strain, a subclade K version of A/H3N2 flu, carried many changes in its surface protein, raising fears it might dodge vaccines. Yet the season in Britain looked fairly normal.

The team mapped how the new virus relates to recent strains, then tested blood from two hundred forty-three people in Britain and Norway. Cohorts spanned ages one to over one hundred. The seasonal vaccine, though built for an earlier strain, boosted antibodies against all tested viruses, including the new subclade. People of every age group already showed some reactivity to the emergent virus, with no age band standing out as unprotected. The authors urge including blood profiling in future flu risk assessments.
pmc-13276724:
Virginie K.E. Duvat presents a 2026 framework for assessing what blocks ecosystem-based adaptation on tropical islands. Such projects use nature, like mangroves or reefs, to soften climate risks. Practitioners often lack a structured way to name and track the barriers that stall them.

The framework sorts barriers by type, origin, impact, and timing, and revisits them as projects run. It was applied to twenty-four projects in French tropical island territories across three oceans. Awareness, knowledge, and technical gaps formed the largest barrier group, followed by institutional and legal problems. More than half of all barriers were never overcome during the projects. Knowledge sharing and better coordination worked best as remedies.
pmc-13277124:
Chen Zhang and nine co-authors set out a trial protocol in 2026 for swallowing training in older adults. Swallowing difficulty raises the risk of food entering the airway and harms nutrition and quality of life. Their simple training program is designed to be safe and easy for daily use, but its long term effects are unknown.

The trial will enroll four hundred seventy two community dwelling adults aged sixty and over with mild swallowing difficulty. Half will train for a full year and half will get an active control program. Main outcomes are swallowing function and airway protection at twelve months. Nutrition risk, quality of life, coughing episodes, and pneumonia rates will also be tracked.
pmc-13277424:
Wei Lee and co-authors present the case of a 64-year-old woman who came to an emergency room with fever and hard breathing, reported in 2026. She had high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and she had just had hip surgery. Her blood pressure was low, her pulse was fast, and the first checks found no clear source of infection.

A bedside ultrasound showed a moving mass in the right side of her heart. A deeper scan confirmed a blood clot that had reached her lungs, a blockage doctors call pulmonary embolism. She was treated with clot-busting drugs sent through a thin tube. The case shows how a fast bedside scan can spot a deadly clot.
pmc-13277824:
Fatemeh Sarani Rad leads a 2026 scoping review of digital twin systems for diabetes care. A digital twin is a virtual copy of a patient, updated with real data, that can be used to test or guide treatment. The review mapped studies published up to April 2025 across four databases, screening more than two hundred records.

Twenty-eight studies met the rules. Most covered type 1 or type 2 diabetes and used data-driven or simulation models. Common uses were glucose prediction, treatment control, and decision support. Inputs leaned on glucose monitors, wearables, lifestyle logs, and health records. The review sorts the field by design, personalization, and validation so future builders can see where evidence is thin.
pmc-13278424:
Lisa Graham leads a 2026 pilot study of a handheld device that measures a tiny eye tremor in people with Parkinson's disease. The tremor, called ocular microtremor, is an involuntary eye movement linked to brainstem activity and may be reduced in Parkinson's. Older methods were invasive and slow. The team tested the iTremor ONE device in 33 patients and 31 matched healthy controls.

Repeated measures in patients were highly reliable. Average tremor frequency was lower in patients than in controls, and the measure separated the groups fairly well. Frequency tracked with age in both groups and with speech, facial expression, and gait features in patients. Medication state made no difference. The measure may support screening, with more work needed.
pmc-13279024:
Phillip A Williford and colleagues published a 2026 conceptual article proposing that measures of epigenetic aging could help counsel patients toward healthier habits. These clocks estimate biological age from chemical marks on DNA, and the number can move with lifestyle. The authors map that feedback onto the Transtheoretical Model, a framework that sorts behavior change into stages from precontemplation through maintenance and relapse.

Within their model, a biological-age result is introduced differently at each stage: gently for someone not yet considering change, and as reinforcement for someone sustaining new habits. Repeat testing is reserved for moments where it could re-engage a patient after a lapse, alongside tools like motivational interviewing and wearable trackers. The authors stress the framework is untested and needs real trials before clinics use it. It recasts a research measure as a stage-matched teaching aid for prevention.
pmc-13279224:
Ayse-Gul Ozturk and co-authors follow a large Swedish group in 2026 of patients with a Fontan circulation, a surgical setup for hearts born with one working chamber. Blood thinning care is a key open question for these patients.

National registers held data on eight hundred sixty four patients born between 1970 and 2017, followed for about fourteen years on median. About a third got no blood thinning treatment, and death rates in that group were very high over the follow up. Most treated patients got antiplatelet drugs, with far lower death rates. Stroke rates, by contrast, were about the same with and without treatment, a contrast the authors report in full.
pmc-13279524:
Mengmeng Liu and Tong Liu published a 2026 cost-effectiveness analysis comparing two first-line drug combinations for inoperable liver cancer, judged from the viewpoint of payers in China. One pairing joins atezolizumab with bevacizumab; the other joins rivoceranib with camrelizumab. The authors built a three-state survival model from the two regimens' trial curves, extended with fits. Costs and quality-of-life weights came from published sources.

The atezolizumab combination was projected to cost about 109,556 dollars per patient against about 15,265 dollars for the rivoceranib combination. It also produced slightly fewer quality-adjusted life years, 1.47 against 1.59 in the model, a measure combining length and quality of life. A regimen that costs more while delivering less health is dominated. The authors conclude the rivoceranib pairing is the cost-effective choice for advanced disease in China. Such verdicts depend on local prices and trial populations, which readers should keep in view.
pmc-13279824:
Juliette Vivien and colleagues present a 2026 toolbox paper on DBSsync for Parkinson disease research. Deep brain stimulation devices can now record brain signals for long spans while they stimulate. Such records could reveal disease marks and guide adaptive stimulation, which tunes itself by brain feedback. To find sound feedback marks, brain records must align in time with outside data like motion or heart signals.

DBSsync joins a study design with an open source Python toolbox and a graphic interface. It syncs brain records with outside streams at a precision of eight milliseconds. Heart artifact removal tools clean the brain signal as a first step. The setup lets labs run multimodal protocols, where many signal types run at once. Precise sync is the base for new biomarker hunts in Parkinson care.
pmc-13280124:
L Velur Prasuna and colleagues published a 2026 diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis of nerve monitoring during surgery for ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament. In this condition a spinal ligament turns to bone and squeezes the cord. Surgeons use transcranial motor evoked potentials, stimulating the brain and watching muscle responses, to warn of cord injury during decompression. Searching three databases through January 2026, the team kept five studies with usable data covering 990 patients. Of those, 6.9 percent woke with new neurological deficits.

Pooled sensitivity was 54.8 percent and specificity 90.0 percent, meaning the monitor missed many injuries it should catch but rarely cried wolf. The overall diagnostic odds ratio was a consistent 13.75 across studies. Alarm thresholds varied widely between centers, distorting summary curves and agreement for specificity. The authors call the tool useful but incomplete. They argue level-specific alarm criteria and combined methods must come before the numbers can be trusted in operating rooms.
pmc-13281424:
Wajahat Mirza and colleagues pooled trials on wound suction after stoma reversal surgery in a 2026 review. A stoma is an opening that lets waste leave the body after bowel surgery. Reversal closes it, but the wound gets infected in a large share of cases. A suction dressing pulls fluid from the closed wound and may cut infection. Seven strict trials with four hundred twenty-nine patients met the review's rules. The team split results by how skin was closed, gathered or straight.

The review rated proof quality with a standard grading tool. It tracked infection in the first weeks, hospital stay, healing time, and blood loss. Two reviewers screened and scored each trial on their own to cut bias. The authors frame the work as a check on whether suction helps in all closure styles or just some. Their design aims to guide surgeons who face this common, costly setback.
pmc-13281524:
Ken S Lee and colleagues published a 2026 synthetic chemistry study turning simple alkoxyallenes into versatile three-carbon building blocks carrying a TEMPO group and an aldehyde, which they call linchpins. Allenes invite chemists to decorate all three carbons, but oxidation methods have relied on awkward reagents and produced unstable intermediates that cannot be stored or steered. Their route installs the two handles cleanly, yielding an intermediate reactable at each carbon in turn.

From these linchpins the team built a gallery of nitrogen- and oxygen-containing rings prized in drug discovery, including quinoxalines, imidazoles, oxazoles, and thiazoles. As a proof of the strategy's reach, they completed a short metal-free synthesis of the natural product clathrodin. The authors present the linchpin concept as a general platform: park a stable, multifunctional intermediate, then diverge into many scaffolds from one starting material rather than redesigning each route.
pmc-13281624:
Sunil Thakali and colleagues reviewed eye injections at a community hospital in Nepal in a 2026 paper. The drug, bevacizumab, is shot into the eye to treat leaking or overgrown blood vessels at the back of the eye. The hospital serves a poor area with few resources. The team read charts of patients treated from 2019 to 2022. More than four hundred shots were given to two hundred forty-seven patients. Vision and retina thickness were tracked over follow-up visits.

The swollen center of the retina thinned a great deal after treatment. Overall sight scores, though, held flat across the whole group. Gains in sight did show in four subgroups, covering diabetes swelling, age-related damage, and two kinds of vein block. Most patients needed just one or two shots. The authors say the drug gave real gains even in a low-resource clinic, where repeat visits are hard to secure.
pmc-13281824:
Tobias Sägesser and colleagues built a single-atom probe that scans in three dimensions in a 2026 study. Stray fields from surfaces blur fine measurements and shorten quantum device life. Trapped ions, single charged atoms held in place, are superb field sensors. Past traps could only slide the ion along a line. Their new trap holds the ion with steady fields alone. That frees it to move through a block of space near a metal surface.

The probe mapped still and flickering electric and magnetic fields. It worked from close up to about half a millimeter away. Maps revealed charge patches and the texture of surface noise. By their pattern, the team could tell noise sources apart. The authors say the probe can serve surface science broadly. Any field where surface grit limits tools, from gravity tests to quantum chips, could gain.
pmc-13282324:
Kyriakos Psarakis and co-authors describe a 2026 computer systems paper presenting Styx, a runtime for stateful cloud functions. Cloud functions are small programs that run on demand. Many real tasks also need stored state, strict consistency, and low delay, which current tools handle poorly. Styx organises work as a flowing graph of functions and promises each transaction, a set of linked steps, runs exactly once and in a consistent order.

Three additions cut delay: detecting where a transaction ends, caching function results, and replying before full commit when safe. Styx can also move state between machines to balance load as demand shifts. Standard benchmark tests showed at least ten times the throughput of rival approaches, with near-linear scaling and low delay. Migration tests beat a stop-and-restart method. The authors aim at workflows and microservices that need speed without giving up correctness.
pmc-13282424:
Suey Yee Low and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their study of zoonotic gut parasites in public spaces in Malaysia. The original study surveyed small animal faeces and soil for parasites that can pass from animals to people. Several figures in the abstract, main text, and a table were wrong. The correction replaces them and leaves the study's topic and setting unchanged.

The corrected count is fifty-six positive samples, about seventy-nine percent, not sixty-three. Cat faeces carried parasites more often than dog faeces, at ninety percent against about sixty-five percent. The risk findings also change direction. Lacking a dustbin, not having one, was linked to higher hookworm infection in dogs. Cat samples from apartment playgrounds carried more hookworm than those from residential parks. Soil from dog-friendly parks showed higher odds of one hookworm type than soil from residential parks.
pmc-13283324:
Children's dental work needs materials that bond well and survive years in a wet mouth. Szu-I Lin and six co-authors compare three strong plastics for that job in this 2026 study: a milled high-grade polymer called PEEK, a ceramic-filled printed resin, and a milled acrylic. They test water uptake, surface traits, and how strongly cements grip each material after aging.

Discs of each plastic were soaked in water and fake saliva under a standard test rule, and all stayed well below the allowed limits for water uptake and dissolving. Surfaces were left plain, sandblasted, or blasted and primed, then joined with one of two cements. Bond strength was measured after a day in water, after heat cycling, and after harsh aging. The results show which surface treatment and cement pairing suits each plastic for lasting children's restorations.
pmc-13283424:
Noya Doolman and co-authors ran a 2026 proof-of-concept study on freezing human embryos with a shorter soak in protective fluid. Freezing by vitrification, meaning ultra-fast cooling, needs a timed soak in an equilibration fluid first. Shorter soaks worked in eggs and mouse work, but embryos lacked evidence, and no licence covers their use in embryos.

One IVF lab froze 45 blastocysts, 49 early embryos, and 102 abnormally fertilised eggs used as early-stage stand-ins. Groups used either the standard soak or the short soak, in full or tiny fluid volumes. After warming, survival, growth, and re-expansion rates looked much the same across methods. The authors present the short soak as workable in the lab, pending wider checks.
pmc-13283624:
Jeffrey Nepple led a multicentre team in 2026 asking whether loose joints change hip surgery results in teenage girls. The surgery treats femoroacetabular impingement, where hip bones pinch during motion. Generalised joint hypermobility, scored by the Beighton flexibility test, may feed hip instability and pain. The study followed girls aged fourteen to nineteen having first-time keyhole hip surgery across centres.

Ninety-seven patients were grouped by Beighton score: normal in 45 percent, mildly raised in 31 percent, and clearly raised in 24 percent. After about a year, outcome scores for pain, hip function, and sport were gathered, and failure was counted as reoperation or missing set gain marks. Higher Beighton scores did not tie to worse results, and final scores did not differ across the groups.
pmc-13284024:
Over half of men awaiting penile implant surgery report strong pre-surgery anxiety in a 2026 survey by Fayez T Hammad and colleagues. Worry may run high due to the foreign device and partner expectations afterward. No earlier study had measured anxiety in this exact group.

A total of 123 men at one institute answered a standard anxiety scale before surgery. Mean age was about 56 years across the survey group. Just over half scored in the clinically significant anxiety range. Past surgical problems and internet searching predicted high anxiety after adjustment. Top concerns were device failure, trouble activating the device, and size changes. Longer consults also tracked with worry.
pmc-13284324:
Fatma M. Talaat and colleagues present GreenAid, a plant disease detection system described in a 2026 research article. GreenAid combines three image models, VGG16, ResNet50, and InceptionV3, and weights each model by its class-level F1 scores. The system pairs the models with a phone app, a web dashboard, and a chat tool for farmers.

On the PlantVillage set of 87,000 images in 38 classes, the combined system reached high accuracy and beat five other ways of merging model outputs. A small phone version kept most of that accuracy while running offline in 127 ms per image on a mid-range phone. The work matters because plant disease causes large crop losses, and small farms often lack fast expert diagnosis.
pmc-13284424:
T. D. A. Stindt and co-authors report a nationwide Dutch cohort study, published in 2026, on local breast cancer return after mastectomy. Even after full removal of breast tissue, cancer can return at the chest site, yet trials often merge local and regional return. The team used the Netherlands Cancer Registry for women treated from 2012 to 2016.

Among more than 22,000 patients split by whether systemic therapy came first, local return stayed low, near 2 percent in both groups after long follow-up. Lower risk linked to screening detection, radiation, and some drug treatments, while higher stage and missed hormone therapy linked to higher risk. The patterns could help tailor follow-up and added treatment after mastectomy.
pmc-13284524:
Jin-Tao Lí and colleagues tested in 2026 whether soil microbes toughened by one climate stress withstand a different one. Microbes drive soil carbon handling, and their recovery after shocks keeps ecosystems working. The team exposed soil communities to frost or drought, then hit them again with either stress, tracking growth recovery and how efficiently microbes used carbon.

Prior exposure to either stress made microbes more resilient to both stresses afterward, not just the one they had met. Carbon use efficiency also held up better. The authors reason that frost and drought both squeeze microbes through water potential, so the training transfers. Repeated shock cycles added nothing beyond a single event, and the lag phase before growth resumed proved decisive. They call this cross-stressor resilience an overlooked climate factor.
pmc-13285624:
Diabetes more than doubles the odds of severe dengue and nearly quadruples death odds, Jingjing Lin and co-authors pool in a 2026 review. Dengue spreads fast by mosquito bite while diabetes climbs worldwide, and its chronic swelling and weak defenses may deepen dengue harm. Three databases plus hand checks yielded twenty-seven studies with 734,123 patients.

Patients with diabetes faced clearly higher odds of severe dengue than those without, and higher odds still of dying from it in the pooled results reported here. Both gaps held across the varied study set. The authors urge early flagging and tight watch of diabetic patients where dengue thrives, plus care plans that treat both ills together.
pmc-13285824:
A Shreenivas and a large team of colleagues map HER2 changes across solid cancers in a 2026 real-world analysis. HER2, a growth signal protein, can be copied too often, mutated, or simply present at high levels on tumor cells. Using a huge profiling database, the team asked how these forms line up with each other and with survival.

The set held more than 200,000 tumors with gene data and a smaller group with protein stain results. Gene copies often, but not always, matched high protein levels, and some mutated tumors showed raised protein without extra copies. Patients whose tumors stained strongest lived longest on median, though the edge came mostly from breast and stomach cancers with known HER2 drugs. The mixed picture argues for testing each tumor on its own terms.
pmc-13285924:
Kien Trung Nguyen and colleagues describe late-pregnancy preeclampsia care at a large hospital in Vietnam in a 2026 retrospective study. The blood pressure disorder can turn severe fast and endangers both mother and baby. The team reviewed one year of cases to map how the disease looked, how staff handled it, and which signs warned of poor outcomes for newborns.

The review covered 154 women who gave birth at the hospital between August 2022 and July 2023, and severe disease made up well over half the cases. Older mothers, first pregnancies, past stillbirth, and assisted conception each came with higher odds of severe illness. Every woman with severe disease gave birth by cesarean, and early birth struck more than a third of the group. Birth before 34 weeks stood as the strongest warning sign for harm to the baby.
pmc-13286324:
Tri Budiati leads a 2026 quasi-experimental study of breastfeeding support after caesarean birth in Indonesia. Mothers who deliver by surgery often start nursing late and doubt their milk supply, and local myths feed that doubt. A culture-aware support model was tested against usual care in 116 mothers, with belief in milk adequacy and newborn weight tracked before and after.

Mothers receiving the model gained more confidence in their milk supply than the control group did. Their babies also put on more weight across the study window. After myths and family support entered the math, the model more than doubled the odds of a mother rating her milk as very sufficient. Nurses gain a ready option for coaching surgical-birth mothers through the shaky first days of nursing.
pmc-13286524:
Christina Ping and colleagues run a randomized trial on paid invitations to research through patient portals in a 2026 study. Portal messages recruit cheaply, but the same groups missing from trials also use portals least, so the tool might widen the gap it promises to close. Twelve hundred cancer patients, half from historically underrepresented groups, got a message about a fictitious survey study, with a third randomly offered twenty dollars to respond.

Only about four in ten patients even opened the message, and 13.3% answered with interest. White patients responded at 18%, against 7% for Black patients, and patients over 65 engaged far less than younger ones. The twenty-dollar offer moved nothing: response rates with and without it sat within noise of each other. Portal recruiting, the authors conclude, mirrors the very disparities it was meant to heal.
pmc-13286924:
Yunzhang Zhao and colleagues ask whether taking aspirin and a statin together improves survival when sepsis injures the heart muscle. Their 2026 study mines a large intensive care database covering 1,884 patients with this complication, which carries high death rates and few proven drug treatments. Only 119 patients received both medicines.

Those patients died far less often at twenty-eight days, ninety days, and one year than patients on neither drug. The gap was large, with risk cut by well over half at each point. A separate intensive care cohort of about four thousand patients confirmed lower early mortality, though the advantage shrank. Subgroups behaved consistently. The authors call the pairing promising for a condition short on options.
pmc-13287224:
Martin Pingel and colleagues mapped farming systems across Germany in 2026 so that payments for wildlife-friendly practice can be fitted to local conditions instead of applied uniformly. They grouped districts using land cover, field patterns, farming intensity, climate, and terrain, then refined the grouping with specialists from farming, conservation, and public agencies.

Eight system types emerged, ranging from cash-crop dominated areas to livestock dominated areas and mixed mosaics. Each type carries its own pressures on farmland wildlife, from heavy inputs to loss of varied habitat. The authors outline where tailored schemes could relieve each pressure and note that the grouping method could be repeated in other countries.
pmc-13288724:
Ismail Cifci, Bilal Durmaz, and Esra Meltem Koc test a muscle screen in Turkey in 2026. The screen is the five-question SARC-F. Records covered 396 adults. All were aged sixty-five or more. Two family health centers in Izmir took part. Blood tests joined the screen data.

Risk hit 16.9 percent of the group. Women showed risk more often than men. Older age raised the odds. Female sex and higher body weight also raised them. Lower ferritin tracked with more risk. Lower albumin did the same. When time blocks the screen itself, blood values may help. They can flag patients worth a full check.
pmc-13289224:
Elsa Martins and a large team report a 2026 phase Ib trial of mosunetuzumab given under the skin in systemic lupus erythematosus. Mosunetuzumab is a lab-made antibody that links T cells to B cells so T cells can remove B cells. The open-label study tested safety, drug levels in blood, and effects on immune cells across several centers.

Fifteen adults with active, antibody-positive lupus joined between January 2022 and December 2023. Some got one fixed dose, while others got a small first dose then a larger dose on day 8, up to 60 mg in the highest group. Two people stopped care because of side effects during treatment. No severe cytokine release events or nerve toxicity linked to immune cells were reported, which supports further careful study.
pmc-13289324:
Flávio Fidêncio de Lima headed a 2026 systematic review on whether poor diet links to painful temporomandibular disorders. These disorders cause jaw joint and muscle pain, and interest in lifestyle drivers of chronic pain is growing. The team searched five major databases for clinical and observational work through November 2025, then rated bias with a standard tool.

From 7,760 records, only seven studies passed with low risk of bias for synthesis. Birth and teen diet quality did not predict later jaw pain in cohort work. Cross-sectional work hinted that some eating patterns track with symptoms, and women with muscle-based jaw pain ate fewer key nutrients than controls. One lab test found a flavor enhancer raised pain, while the sole trial found no clear vitamin D benefit.
pmc-13289424:
Abdulkadir Calavul reports in 2026 on surgery for pale patches left after burns heal. Deep burns can leave skin without color and with poor scar quality. A common fix sands the scar surface and then lays on a thin skin graft.

The study followed thirty-six patients at two hospitals whose patches were stable. Scar quality was scored later by both patients and trained observers, and the two scores matched very closely. Age, sex, and burn size did not shape the scores. Problems after surgery, by contrast, went with clearly worse scars. The author notes the scale scores scars, not color, so color checks are still needed.
pmc-13290124:
Plant compounds packed into tiny carriers are reviewed as weapons against drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus by Neha Gupta and a large team in 2026. The bacterium is a leading cause of hospital-acquired infection, and standard antibiotics increasingly fail against it.

Plant chemicals alone disappoint, the authors note, because they dissolve poorly, break down fast, and miss their targets. Loading them into nanoscale carriers fixes much of that. The loaded particles attack on several fronts: they jam efflux pumps, break membranes, make reactive oxygen species, and stop biofilms from forming. Curcumin particles broke MRSA membranes in the studies reviewed, and quercetin in liposomes entered biofilms better than the free compound. Gains also appeared when such particles were paired with standard antibiotics.
pmc-13290624:
Priyanka and colleagues report in 2026 that the gel inside the eye clings to the retina more often in diabetes, though how much sticks does not clearly differ. Their prospective study comes from central India. Vitreomacular adhesion is a normal stage of vitreous separation that may steer how diabetic retinopathy advances.

The team used optical coherence tomography scans at four angles. They measured the share of retinal surface still attached in 68 eyes of 40 diabetic patients without proliferative disease and 50 eyes of 25 matched controls. Adhesion was present in 96% of diabetic eyes against 84% of controls, a significant gap. The attached percentage, though, averaged 65% versus 58% without reaching significance, and early retinopathy stages did not separate either. The authors call for studies in advanced disease with newer scanners.
pmc-13290724:
Each drug in one leukemia family carries its own danger signature, Yong Wang and colleagues find in a study from 2026 of the FDA's adverse event database. Anthracyclines anchor acute myeloid leukemia treatment, but their harms differ by drug and by patient.

Mining reports from 2004 to 2024, the team analyzed 1,079 cases and 3,622 adverse events. Epirubicin showed the strongest heart-toxicity signal, doxorubicin the most pregnancy-related events, daunorubicin blood-vessel disorders, and idarubicin marrow suppression and infections. Most events arrived within 180 days of treatment. Idarubicin's onset ran late in older patients, and timing differed by sex for two drugs. Wang and colleagues argue the distinct profiles should steer drug choice and monitoring in leukemia care.
pmc-13290824:
Speed, prior revision, and mixed germs decide whether an infected hip implant can be saved, Ernesto Muñoz-Mahamud and colleagues report in a long-term study from 2026. Debridement with implant retention is a main option for acute prosthetic joint infection, but reported success swings wildly, from 16 to 92%.

The retrospective series covered 115 patients treated between 1999 and 2018 and followed a mean 7.1 years; by five years, 30.4% had failed. Failure roughly doubled when surgery waited past the first week after diagnosis, when the infected joint was a revision rather than a primary implant, and when infections were polymicrobial rather than single-organism. No other traits mattered significantly. The authors urge fast action while flagging the timing result as needing confirmation.
pmc-13291024:
Abel Trujillo-Ocampo heads a 2026 laboratory study of a calming immune cell type called NKT10, grown from cord blood invariant natural killer T cells. Such cells can steer immune responses toward control rather than attack, yet their medical use in stem cell transplantation had barely been tested before this work.

Cord-derived cells held many cells with a regulatory profile and produced calming signals when triggered, and gene checks set them apart from adult donor cells, which leaned toward attack-ready programs. Single-cell analysis confirmed a distinct NKT10-like group rich in control pathways. In dishes the cord cells slowed other immune cells from multiplying, and in mice they eased graft-versus-host disease, supporting their promise as a cell therapy.
pmc-13291224:
Growing onions in very dry soil takes smart feeding. Abeer Abd EL Moiez Ahmed Bakr leads a 2026 field study in Upper Egypt. Poor soil, scant water, and storage losses cut profits. The team paired organic waste with tiny mineral sprays.

Sugarcane filter mud was spread as organic feed. Sprays held copper or calcium particles at varied doses. Trials ran over two growing seasons. Best yields beat plain controls by a wide margin. Low copper with high calcium worked best. Too much copper with too little calcium harmed plants. Storage quality also improved under good mixes. Balanced pairing is the core lesson for dry farms.
pmc-13291324:
A learning agent can design light gear faster than old searches. Nada Yazeed M. Dawood leads a 2026 study of fiber modulator design. The part switches light using a phase-change film layer. Low signal loss was the design goal.

The agent learned by trial inside a physics simulator. No pre-made training set was needed. Repeated runs with varied seeds found the same best design. It took just twelve steps and about three minutes. Rival methods needed far more steps each. Loss fell well below the target value. Stable, fast search is the main win here. Photonics design may gain from such self-driving tools.
pmc-13291424:
Masab Mansoor writes a 2026 editorial on large language models in children's diagnostic reasoning. His starting point is a study that pitted four models against seventy-eight clinicians on fifty real cases from a Barcelona children's hospital. Half the cases were common conditions and half were rare diseases. Two models, o1-preview and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, beat the clinician group by a wide margin. The edge grew largest on the rare diseases, where diagnosis often takes years.

For rare cases, one model's top-five odds reached six times the clinicians' level. Clinician experience, strikingly, did not predict accuracy across seniority levels. Mansoor argues that such results demand a place for these tools in the diagnostic workflow. He also weighs where the evidence falls short, including the limits of testing on already gathered case data. The piece calls for responsible integration rather than adoption on accuracy scores alone.
pmc-13291524:
Tian Gao and colleagues wrote a commentary in twenty twenty-six questioning a claim that desert planting in China has turned part of the Taklamakan Desert into a carbon store. A recent study credited the Three-North shelter forest program with that change and extended the claim to the whole desert. Gao and coauthors argue that water limits make the claim doubtful. Rain in the region is very low, while water loss to the air is extremely high, so plants face dry conditions all year.

They also fault the seasonal comparison behind the claim, since the so-called dry season falls in midwinter when plants are inactive. Comparing winter with summer then shows little about growth. The authors warn that a weak carbon claim can lead to planting policy that wastes effort in a hyperarid region where trees can hardly survive.
pmc-13291924:
Brenig and Pach reported in 2026 a rare case of haemophilia A in a female German Shepherd dog. The bleeding disorder stems from a fault in the F8 gene on the X chromosome, so females are usually only carriers. Mating a mildly affected male with a carrier can produce daughters carrying the fault on both copies. Their patient bled heavily from minor injuries from puppyhood, starting with swelling after microchip placement at three months.

Clotting tests showed a greatly prolonged clotting time with factor VIII activity at only about six percent of normal, while related factors were normal. Whole-genome sequencing found the same fault on both gene copies, changing one building block in a region vital to the factor's stability. The variant had been seen once before in an unrelated German Shepherd over a decade earlier. The authors stress full genetic workups in rare disease with odd inheritance.
pmc-13292024:
Mohammad Hosein Taziki Balajelini and co-authors pool a 2026 systematic review and cumulative meta-analysis on how often fluid returns in children's ears after ventilation tube surgery. Otitis media with effusion is common in childhood, and recurrence after tubes fall out worries clinicians. Their August 2024 search covered eight databases under PRISMA guidance.

From 1,117 articles, 21 studies qualified, and the pooled recurrence rate came to 30 percent of children worldwide. Tubes alone gave 31 percent recurrence, against 20 percent when antibiotics were added, though the authors urge caution about that comparison. Children who also had cleft palate surgery fared worst, at 45 percent recurrence in the analysis. Year-by-year pooling showed recurrence easing from 39 percent in 2005 to 24 percent by 2019.
pmc-13292424:
Heikki Opoku Ofori and Emre Debreli dig into a 2026 classroom question in Ghana: what actually decides whether English teachers use AI tools well? Working in senior high schools, they combined teacher interviews, classroom observations, and stimulated recall sessions. The study leans on the Technology Acceptance Model and self-efficacy theory to explain reading and writing instruction.

Teachers generally saw AI tools as useful and fairly easy, yet those views alone did not predict classroom practice. Confidence was the hinge: self-assured teachers built structured, meaningful AI activities, while less confident colleagues stuck to shallow uses. Positive attitudes also collided with thin infrastructure and scarce time. The authors argue teacher psychology is the missing middle layer between what AI could do and what lessons actually deliver.
pmc-13292924:
Graeme C. Hays leads a 2026 study tracking how green turtles steer across open ocean between nesting beaches and feeding grounds. How sea animals find distant targets far from land has puzzled scientists for over a century.

New tags sent compass headings by satellite during trips over 1000 kilometers that lasted about 27.5 days on average, a span the authors report. Turtles often held one steady heading for long stretches, even when that path drifted off course, then turned to correct it. Steady legs with rare fixes fit the idea that turtles use magnetic signposts or rough maps, rather than constant fine tuning.
pmc-13293124:
Abhineet Sheoran and colleagues test a lab-made antibody treatment for a dangerous gut infection in mice, in research published in 2026. The target is Shiga toxin made by certain E. coli bacteria, which can damage the kidneys and cause hemolytic-uremic syndrome, a leading cause of kidney failure in young children. No specific treatment exists, and antibiotics can make matters worse.

The team built a mouse version of the infection using a related bacterium engineered to produce the toxin, which caused gut lesions and kidney damage much like human disease. A single injection of the toxin-blocking nanobody product, given as late as four days after infection, protected the mice completely. The result supports developing the treatment for people during the short window between diarrhea and kidney illness.
pmc-13293824:
Ning-chen Wang and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective cohort study on early breast cancer care. Their focus is why some people who choose breast-conserving surgery later need full mastectomy because tumor remains at the cut edge. Records cover operations from January 2015 through December 2024.

Among 290 patients, 31 needed the larger operation while 259 kept the smaller one. Four traits stood out as independent predictors: low body mass index, disease in more than one spot, larger tumor size, and a ductal carcinoma in situ part. Spotting these traits before surgery could help teams plan better and counsel patients more honestly.
pmc-13294124:
Abdullah, Zulaikha Fatima, and José Luis Oropeza Rodríguez present ApneaSense in 2026, a home-friendly system for spotting sleep apnea without a costly lab study. Standard overnight testing can cost over $6,000 per unit and reaches few people. Their setup fuses heart, oxygen, breathing effort, and motion signals on a low-power Raspberry Pi unit with a phone app for live viewing and telehealth sync.

Validation mixed a public database of 25 people with a clinic set of 61 people. On a held-out group of 17, the EvoApneaFormer model scored near 99.9% on accuracy, precision, and recall across six event classes. Home accuracy reached 96.9%, even with movement and signal dropouts.
pmc-13294224:
