Four databases were searched through January 2026 for randomized trials of manual-based therapies in ages 12 to 18. Twelve trials held 844 teens, mean age 15.8 years and 81% female, covering dialectical, mentalization-based, and other structured programs.

Therapy gave small but clear gains for core symptoms, emotion control, and general mental health scores. No clear effect appeared for depressive symptoms or quality of life, though quality data came from just two trials. Variation between studies stayed low and no publication bias showed. Gains are real but modest, so expectations should stay measured.
pmc-13294324:
Yu Huang and colleagues grade two MRI methods for facial pain surgery planning in a 2026 retrospective study. In primary trigeminal neuralgia, a vessel pressing the nerve is the usual target for decompression surgery. Records covered 412 patients whose surgical findings served as truth, comparing vessel angiography imaging, a steady-state sequence called FIESTA-c, and both together.

Surgeons found a culprit vessel in 407 of 412 patients, most often the superior cerebellar artery at 60.68% in the reported share. Simple presence checks scored near 91% for each scan alone and 96.36% combined. Exact vessel matching also favored pairing both scans. Preoperative confidence rises when the two views agree.
pmc-13294424:
Feng Xu and colleagues hunt scan signs of tumor spread through air spaces in early lung cancer for a 2026 study. Such spread worsens outlook even in stage IA disease, yet it is usually confirmed only after surgery. Records for 765 resected patients fed group comparisons and a prediction model, checked in an outside cohort, with tissue and mutation profiles compared as well.

Four scan signs independently flagged spread: high solid share, cut-off airways, pleural pulling, and satellite dots. Model accuracy areas reached 0.823 in training and 0.829 outside in the reported figures. High-risk patients relapsed sooner. Spread-positive tumors favored solid growth patterns and KRAS or ALK changes.
pmc-13295224:
Jordana Chaves and co-authors pool the evidence on artificial intelligence for timing orthodontic treatment, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Growth-modifying braces work best around the pubertal growth spurt, and judging that moment from head or hand X-rays takes expertise. Following a registered protocol, the team searched four databases through December 2025 for studies where AI read cephalometric or hand-wrist films in patients up to twenty-one years old.

Twenty-one studies entered the pooled analysis. Overall accuracy sat in the low eighties in percentage terms, with hand-wrist models more sensitive and head-film models more specific. Deep learning and combined-input approaches generally outperformed older machine learning, while large language model attempts looked shaky. Wide variation between studies and thin external testing temper the promise, and the authors call for multicenter work before clinics rely on these tools.
pmc-13295324:
Andrzej Falniowski, Aleksandra Jaszczyńska, and Sebastian Hofman describe a new snail genus and species from the Dominican Republic in a 2026 article. Minute freshwater snails were found in 2001 in the Dudu cenote, a pond formed where a cave roof partly fell in. Island snail life remains poorly studied despite its rich history.

Body features and DNA evidence placed the snails in the family Cochliopidae but apart from every known genus. The new genus honours Robert Hershler, a leading specialist on that family. The snails still live in the same pond today, underlining how much hidden diversity small island waters may hold.
pmc-13295424:
Andrea Briceño and colleagues study a brain toxin linked to Parkinson's disease in a 2026 laboratory article. Aminochrome forms inside dopamine neurons and is suspected in their loss. Its effects on the cell's waste clearing system, beyond known stress and skeleton damage, were poorly mapped.

In neuron-like cells, the toxin delayed the meeting of waste sacs with the digestive sacs that should clear them. Protein clumps marked by vimentin and ubiquitin piled up near and even inside the nucleus. Boosting the clearing process partly saved cells from death. The authors point to skeleton steadying and waste system support as joint treatment directions.
pmc-13295524:
Nan Wang and colleagues link how long pregnant women sleep with how they feel, in a 2026 survey of 1,035 women across ten counties in rural northwest China. Professional mental health care is scarce in such areas, so finding household-level levers matters. Women reported their nightly sleep, sorted into short, medium, and long bands, and completed a standard scale for depression, anxiety, and stress.

About a fifth slept short and another fifth slept long, while roughly a third scored in the moderate-to-severe range on each symptom measure. Both tails of sleep carried extra stress risk, with short and long sleepers each showing clearly higher odds than the middle band. The links grew stronger when husbands skipped prenatal visits, when relations with mothers-in-law were poor, or when women distrusted counseling. Helping families guard a healthy sleep window, the authors suggest, is cheap, practical mental health care.
pmc-13296024:
Antonio Farina and colleagues follow, in 2026, long-term nerve damage after cancer immunotherapy at a French national centre. Such side effects can be severe, yet how often they leave lasting problems was unclear, so records for 164 patients treated between 2015 and 2024 were reviewed.

Half the patients had recovered well by three months, but among those alive at one year, two in five still had notable nerve problems. Little improvement came after the first year. Relapses affected about one in seven patients, while restarting immunotherapy rarely triggered one. Cancer-linked nerve syndromes and early relapse predicted lasting harm.
pmc-13296224:
Thomas J. Nicholl and Maree J. Abbott interview professional classical musicians who perform without crushing anxiety, in a 2026 qualitative study. Performance anxiety is often treated as part of the job, and most work studies those who suffer it. Six ensemble players, three women and three men, told how they think and feel before and during concerts, and the team sorted the talks into themes.

All six knew anxiety early in their careers, then built calm through repeated playing and the good pull of others. They lean on firm technical, performance, and mental skills, plus a strong sense of why they play. On stage they describe feeling bound up with the music itself, close to fellow players, and turned outward toward the hall. The authors urge training that grows such values-led preparation in anxious players.
pmc-13296324:
Sergio Navas-León and Jon Andoni Duñabeitia test, in 2026, whether Easy-to-Read formatting, designed for readers with cognitive needs, also helps university students. Twenty-four young adults without disabilities read passages in hard, standard and easy formats while eye movements were tracked.

Comprehension scored highest in the easy format and clearly beat the hard format. Easy text also brought shorter fixations and longer jumps between them, hinting at lighter mental load. Hard text drew the most fixations overall. The authors suggest plain formatting may ease reading for everyone, not just its target group.
pmc-13297324:
Fabián Leonardo Barreto and colleagues test a cannabis extract that does not intoxicate against relapse-like behaviour in cocaine-trained mice, in a 2026 study. No approved drug treatment exists for cocaine use disorder, so memory-based routes draw interest. Mice learned to link one chamber with cocaine, then received the extract, rich in cannabidiol with little THC, around memory tests.

The extract weakened the return of cocaine seeking triggered both by a small cocaine dose and by stress. Given after memory recall sessions, it also seemed to disrupt the re-saving of the drug memory, with effects lasting at least two weeks. The extract alone caused neither liking nor dislike of a place. The work supports more study, in both sexes and other test setups.
pmc-13297424:
Kidney function might one day be read from a light scan of blood serum rather than a chemistry lab, propose Diogo Serrano and colleagues in a 2026 methods paper. They tested whether vibrational spectroscopy can estimate the markers clinicians use to stage chronic kidney disease.

The team prepared 54 serum-like solutions mimicking five disease stages and measured creatinine, urea, and albumin with mid- and near-infrared light. Mid-infrared scans, taken after a simple drying step, predicted urea best, while chosen near-infrared regions excelled for creatinine and albumin, with top models above R2 of 0.9. Classification separated healthy from diseased profiles with AUC above 0.93, supporting point-of-care potential.
pmc-13297624:
A simple ratio from two routine blood tests may warn which heart attack patients risk poor blood flow after stenting. pmc-13297724:

pmc-13297824:

pmc-13298024:
Computer modeling can rank which gene variants deserve laboratory attention for heart disease in Serbia, argue Tamara Drljača and colleagues in a 2026 in silico study. pmc-13298124:
Talia Costa Rodrigues and co-authors simulate opinion dynamics on directed random networks, in a 2026 statistical physics study. pmc-13298224:

pmc-13298524:

pmc-13298924:
Yingyue Xing, Siyuan Zou, and Guohua Liu build a machine learning framework for predicting carbon allowance prices across China's regional markets, in a 2026 study. Removing feature groups showed predictor importance varies by market, with no universal best set. pmc-13299224:
Timothy Pittaway, Leanne Townsend, and Claire Hardy analyse European urban treescape projects by working backward from benefits to the weak spots beneath, in a 2026 study. pmc-13300024:
Shinnosuke FUKAMI and co-authors report delayed lung flooding after a burst brain aneurysm, in a 2026 case report. pmc-13300824:
Shortened telomeres mark aging cells, but do they warn of trouble ahead in lupus? Telomere length in white blood cells was measured by qPCR at entry, and fifty healthy women served as a comparison group.

pmc-13301224:
K De Silva and co-authors test a mapping catheter design meant to care less about which way an electrical wave is traveling, in a 2026 experimental study. After normalizing each setup to its own maximum, the perpendicular pairing showed the least shortfall across directions, beating the ultra close and the two millimeter spacings. The authors present the geometry as a step toward direction fair mapping inside a clinical catheter, with consequences for how scar and block lines get read.
pmc-13301324:
Alessia Pennacchi and co-authors review three decades of attempts to reshape a bent nasal septum with energy instead of the scalpel, in a 2026 systematic review. Laser reshaping worked within a narrow temperature band around fifty-five to seventy-five degrees, but higher doses injured cartilage cells and broke down the matrix. pmc-13301824:

Fairness came from matching decision thresholds to the scale's own operating points.

pmc-13302324:
K Tokutake and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether pulsed field ablation can be used safely in lung veins already narrowed by an earlier heat-based ablation. Narrowing, called stenosis, is a feared side effect of thermal treatment, and redo procedures might worsen it. The new energy source mainly harms heart muscle while sparing nearby tissue.

CT scans measured vein openings before treatment and three months afterwards, slice by slice. Average narrowing stayed essentially unchanged after the new procedure, and no vein with severe pre-existing narrowing got worse. Nobody developed symptoms or major complications, supporting the redo approach in this small group.
pmc-13302824:
Lei Wang, Peng Tan, and Rantao Zuo introduce, in a 2026 editorial, a journal special issue gathering six studies on fish nutrition, gut microbes, and metabolic balance. Two studies test feed additives that mobilise fat and enrich helpful gut bacteria in bass and yellow drum. Another shows a crayfish by-product supplement easing the strain of low-fishmeal diets in shrimp. Two more compare rice-paddy rearing with ponds, finding better antioxidant defences and flesh quality in carp. A final study profiles bone ageing with untargeted metabolite screening.
pmc-13303124:
A dietitian in a box beat general chatbots at writing medical diets, Yanan Wang and colleagues test in a 2026 evaluation of their Med-Diet system. pmc-13303224:

Some suit single-port and natural-orifice surgery. Early trials of remote surgery over 5G networks are also reported. pmc-13304424:

Magnetic pull slowed the flow while melting sped it. Heat rose with the heat source but fell with radiation and melting. Microbe levels dropped with one transport ratio and rose with another.
pmc-13304924: Indriya Laras Pramesthi and co-authors issue a 2026 correction to a study of Indonesia's national school feeding program. The study looked at effects on child nutrition and school settings. One Ghana finding in the discussion was credited to the wrong source; the reference now points to Abizari and colleagues from 2014, with the full reference restored in the list. The notice states that results and conclusions stand, no discussion wording needed change, and the article has been updated with editor approval.
pmc-13305424:
Claudio Ucciferri and co-authors test adding an immune booster drug to HPV vaccination for men with stubborn infections in a 2026 pilot study. Vaccines prevent new infections well, but whether they help clear existing ones faster is unsettled.

pmc-13305524:

Semi-structured interviews with 20 bereaved caregivers who lost an adult family member to chronic illness grounded the analysis. Fitting into the caregiver role and bracing for loss formed the twin adaptation work, with awareness of the illness gravity opening grief itself. Information access, satisfaction with care, recognition of effort, and feelings of abandonment all colored the process.
pmc-13305924:

One group had navigation help with non-anatomical removal, while two groups had standard anatomical or non-anatomical surgery. Starting traits were similar across groups in the reported checks. Navigation cases finished faster and lost less blood, with median loss of 125ml in that group. Follow-up ran to 36 months, and the authors present navigation as a useful aid for orientation and precision.
pmc-13306224:

pmc-13306824:

pmc-13307124:

pmc-13307924:

pmc-13308324:

pmc-13308624:

pmc-13308724:

pmc-13310624:

pmc-13310824:

pmc-13310924:

pmc-13311124:

pmc-13311324:

pmc-13311624:

pmc-13311924:

pmc-13312024:

pmc-13312824:

pmc-13312924:

pmc-13313024:

pmc-13313224:

pmc-13313524:

pmc-13313824:

pmc-13314324:

pmc-13316024:

pmc-13316224:

pmc-13316624:

pmc-13316824:
Xuejie Shao and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, a refined herbal blend called ECC-BYF against the broken air sac barrier in COPD, the chronic lung disease where that barrier drives decline. The blend comes from the Bufei Yishen formula, a traditional prescription.

Rats made ill with smoke and repeated infection breathed and healed better on the blend, with tidier air sac cells and stronger barrier proteins. Lung wash fluid showed more of a calming signal and less of three inflammatory ones. In dish-grown lung cells, the blend likewise restored barrier proteins and blocked a key inflammatory switch, p38 MAPK; a compound that reopens that switch erased the benefit. The pathway anchors the formula's claim.
pmc-13317224:
Kelebie and co-authors compare two short screening tools for thinking problems linked to HIV, in adults receiving care in Ethiopia. Full testing is the reference standard but is slow and needs trained staff, so clinics rely on brief screens whose local accuracy was unclear. The team enrolled 290 adults at three hospitals. Each person took both the International HIV Dementia Scale and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, judged against standard criteria.

About 43 percent of participants met the criteria for HIV-linked cognitive disorder. The dementia scale caught more true cases, with sensitivity of about 85 percent at its best cut-off. The Montreal test was somewhat more specific but missed more cases. The authors argue the dementia scale is the better first screen in this setting. For programs with few specialists, the study gives cut-off scores backed by local data.
pmc-13317324:
Kim Frederik Gundrosen and co-authors track how daily movement changes over one year in patients at a memory clinic, in a 2026 study. Twenty-seven patients wore a small thigh sensor for four days at the start and again a year later. The device logged upright time, standing, walking, step counts, and how often people got up.

Patients averaged about 69 years old, and just over half were women. Almost every measure held steady across the year. The one clear change was the longest single stretch spent upright, which shrank from about 84 minutes to about 59. The authors read this as a shift in how activity is spread through the day rather than a drop in its total amount.
pmc-13318624:
Junnan Chen and colleagues review, in 2026, how pancreatic cancer spreads across the lining of the abdomen, a pattern that sharply worsens survival and quality of life. Their account follows the step-by-step route cancer cells take from the main tumour to new growths.

Key steps covered include cells breaking away, changing character, resisting death signals, escaping immune attack, sticking to the abdominal lining, and growing new blood vessels. Four linked drivers get special attention: altered energy use, tiny vesicles that carry messages between cells, stem-like cancer cells, and a reshaped immune setting. The review closes with treatments delivered inside the abdomen, in normal, heated, or pressurised forms, and their possible pairing with immunotherapy.
pmc-13318824:
Anteneh M. Feyissa writes a 2026 commentary on sleep, thinking, and dementia risk in focal epilepsy. He discusses a Neurology study by Tai and co-workers using the UK Biobank cohort. Sleep disruption and cognitive problems are common partners of this epilepsy type. Whether sleep changes long-term dementia risk was unclear.

The discussed study followed 482,207 participants without dementia at baseline. Sleep of six to eight hours counted as optimal. That pattern linked to better executive function in epilepsy, stroke, and control groups alike. The benefit was significantly stronger in focal epilepsy than in controls. People with epilepsy and poor sleep faced a fivefold dementia risk against well-sleeping controls. Their hazard ratio was 5.15 in the reported model. Feyissa presents better sleep as a promising protective target.
pmc-13320024:
Gustavo Armando Tafoya-Arreguín and four co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether the shape of a shoulder fracture can predict how well the arm will work later. They study breaks near the top of the upper arm bone that were treated without surgery. A newer sorting system, the Mayo-FJD system, groups these breaks into nine types by shape.

The team followed 149 patients for at least two years and scored arm use, motion, and pain. Outcomes differed sharply by fracture type. One type, a valgus impacted break, healed best, while a type with a detached neck did worst and always went on to a joint replacement. Shape beat age, sex, and which arm was hurt as a guide to success.
pmc-13320424:
Brandy T. Cervantes and co-authors describe twenty six years of ocean buoy data from a marine sanctuary off Washington State in a 2026 data article. The sanctuary, named in 1994, sits in a rich cold current system rocked by heat waves, warm phase years, low oxygen, and acid seas. Four coastal treaty tribes hold protected rights to sea goods there, so sound local sea records carry legal as well as science weight.

Buoys at fifteen sites on five cross shelf lines have logged water heat, salt, oxygen, pressure, and flow since 2000, chiefly in the summer upwelling season. Two sites also log winter heat all year in recent runs. Cleaned joined series now sit in a public store for free reuse in climate and care of the sanctuary.
pmc-13321024:
Yu-Yang Sha and a large team map the state of medical large language models in a 2026 review. Such models now help with decision support, note writing, patient messages, image plus text analysis, and remote care. Fast growth has raised hard questions about reliability and safe use in real clinics.

Clinical value, the authors argue, cannot rest on test scores alone. Models must rest on sound evidence, stay in line with current medical knowledge, and fit daily workflows. Gaps remain in how models are judged, kept up to date, and kept safe once deployed. Stronger clinical trials and careful rollout across settings are presented as the way forward.
pmc-13321224:
Jyoti Lama and a large team search, in 2026, for genetic variants that predict eye pressure rises after steroid treatment. Some patients develop ocular hypertension from glucocorticoid medicines, including eye injections used for diabetic macular swelling. Knowing who is vulnerable could guide monitoring.

Discovery data came from 530 participants in fluocinolone implant trials, with pressure measured repeatedly during six months after exposure. Genotyping and exome sequencing were combined with a replication cohort of 588 clinic patients. One variant near a gene involved in protein tagging reached genome-wide significance, and a second variant in the same region held up in the combined analysis. Tissue data linked the region to regulation of that gene in several organs including the aorta. A rare-variant analysis flagged one further gene after correction.
pmc-13321524:
Yuya Mawarikado and co-authors compare daily activity in men with a bleeding disorder, split by whether their joints are already damaged. In this disorder, repeated joint bleeds destroy the joint over time. Damaged joints cut activity and quality of life, but activity in those without damage was unclear.

Forty-six males wore a wrist motion sensor for seven straight days. Nineteen had joint damage, twelve had the disorder without damage, and fifteen had no disorder. The team counted minutes of moderate-to-hard activity in bouts of at least ten minutes. The comparison shows how much activity joint health alone explains. Keeping activity up is a goal of modern care for this disorder. Wearable data give a truer picture than memory-based surveys.
pmc-13322724:
Deepak Ranade, Apurva Satish Lachake, and Ramis Aziz wrote a 2026 review on surgery for burst fractures where the chest and lower back meet. The title calls the work a prospective study, but the head describes a systematic review with the authors' own case series. Surgeons can rebuild the spine from the front or fix it from the back, and no consensus exists.

Tradition holds the front route costs more blood and time, with no better nerve outcomes. Biomechanics studies, though, give the front route some edges, renewing interest in it. The authors weigh that evidence and add their cases. Reviews like this help trauma teams choose an approach by injury pattern rather than habit.
pmc-13323224:
Mahmoud Albashier leads a review comparing two enoxaparin doses after bariatric surgery, published in 2026, for preventing venous blood clots. Obesity changes how this blood thinner behaves in the body, so the standard 40 mg dose may under-protect surgical patients.

Following PRISMA guidance, the team searched five databases to September 2025 for trials and cohort studies of 40 mg against 60 mg dosing. Ten studies with 1,276 patients qualified. The main outcome was reaching target anti-factor Xa levels, with clots, bleeding, deaths and other complications also tracked. Random-effects pooling compared drug levels and clinical events, aiming to judge whether higher dosing protects without added bleeding harm.
pmc-13323724:
Aarthi and Kannimuthu published this 2026 study on classifying autism from resting brain scans by listening to several atlases at once. Autism reshapes how brain regions synchronize, but every atlas slices the brain differently, and single-map models miss what the others catch. Their network takes functional connectivity maps from six atlases and projects each into a shared space.

A transformer then fuses the maps with attention that weighs how the atlases inform each other, instead of a fixed average. The fused picture feeds a neural classifier. On the ABIDE-I benchmark the system reached 88.46 percent accuracy with an area under the curve of 0.9546. The authors argue context-aware fusion across parcellations is the honest way to read a connectome.
pmc-13324524:
Wei Mao and colleagues compare how astringency unfolds in green, black, and oolong teas in a 2026 sensory study. The drying, puckering feel shapes whether buyers like a tea, yet most past checks scored it at one moment only.

Six teas were tracked with time-intensity scoring, dominance tracking, an electronic tongue, and LC-MS chemistry. Green tea hit a higher peak, lasted longer, and started faster than the others. Tasters called green tea harsh and grainy, black tea smooth and dry, and oolong tea rough and dry in turns. Chemistry tied strong astringency to anthocyanins, quercetin forms, and catechin products. The type and structure of polyphenols seem to set both strength and character.
pmc-13325124:
Hongyi Cheng and co-authors show that a skin channel boosts the nerve signal from electroacupuncture in a 2026 mouse study. The channel TRPV4 senses pressure and stretch, but it sits in skin cells rather than in nerves themselves.

Calcium imaging in living mice watched sensory neurons at the fourth lumbar ganglion during hindpaw stimulation. Stronger current at 2 mA recruited more neurons than 0.5 mA stimulation did. Staining found TRPV4 in skin macrophages, not in the sensory neurons. A drug that opens TRPV4 raised neuron activity, while a blocker cut the acupuncture response. The results cast skin immune cells as early partners in how acupuncture signals begin.
pmc-13325324:
Xin-Xiang Lim and co-authors survey interdisciplinary learning in a forensic science program in a 2026 education study. Forensic work joins science with law, so graduates must blend fields and judge evidence across them.

Across six semesters from 2022 to 2024, 260 undergraduate and postgraduate students rated their skills on an 18-item survey. Interdisciplinary skills scored highest, at a mean of 4.33 on the five-point scale. Reflective behavior lagged at 3.89, and grasp of other fields views trailed at 3.83 on the same scale. Students felt strong at merging knowledge but weaker at weighing the limits of each field. The authors advise more direct coaching in reflection.
pmc-13325724:
Rahul S. Nanduri and colleagues recount an eye tumor that hid behind a wrong diagnosis for three years in a 2026 case report. Medulloepithelioma is a rare tumor of the ciliary body that can invade nearby eye tissues.

A 54-year-old woman came in with falling vision in her left eye and signs read as a vasoproliferative retinal tumor. She received freezing treatment, a scleral buckle, and several vitrectomies without success. When the blind eye turned painful, it was removed, and pathology revealed a malignant teratoid medulloepithelioma invading iris, choroid, retina, and beyond. Radiation followed, with no spread found. The authors urge ultrasound checks of the ciliary body in such cases.
pmc-13326124:
Saba Alyas and co-authors interview asthma patients in Malaysia about managing their own care in a 2026 qualitative study. Daily self-management keeps asthma in check, but habits and beliefs shape how well it works.

Nineteen adults spoke in semi-structured interviews held from February to May 2025, online and in person. Patients understood their disease and most care tasks well, yet self-monitoring habits lagged. Confidence, faith in traditional remedies, and views on inhalers all steered practice. Work hazards and passive smoke stood out as barriers. The authors suggest counseling seminars and personal action plans as supports, plus policy action on smoke exposure at work.
pmc-13326424:
Ozan Tuysuz and co-authors read more than three thousand sinus CT scans in 2026 to count the anatomical traps that can turn routine sinus surgery dangerous. Thin bone walls near the eye and two great structures, the carotid artery and the optic nerve, sometimes bulge into the sinus or lack their bony cover.

The eye wall gap appeared in about two percent of patients, mostly on one side and near the front. Artery bulging showed in about eight percent, half of them on both sides. The team graded each variant by depth. Two radiologists read the scans blind to each other. The authors stress a careful scan review before any sinus operation.
pmc-13326524:
Tina Burkhard and co-authors review how small blood vessel cells reshape the tissue around them in a 2026 paper. The cells, called pericytes, sit against the cells that line vessels, inside a shared sheet of matrix. They help keep vessels sound, guide new vessel growth, and can turn into other cell types.

The review covers how these cells both build and cut down the matrix around vessels in health and disease. The authors also compile an atlas of matrix parts these cells produce, drawn from recent gene and protein data sets. They note the atlas cannot be read in isolation, since vessel cells interact closely. Grasping this reshaping role may clarify diseases such as stroke and cancer.
pmc-13327424:
Asher Park and co-authors mapped in 2026 where nose and sinus specialists practice in the United States against neighborhood social vulnerability. If specialists cluster in well-off areas, patients in struggling areas must travel farther for care. The team used a national index that scores each census tract on themes like income, household makeup, minority status, and housing and transport.

Practice addresses came from the national rhinology society directory. For every tract they computed the distance to the nearest specialist and grouped index scores into quarters. Regression models then linked distance with vulnerability, overall and by theme. Readers get an access map for a small specialty: who lives near a rhinologist and who does not, sorted by the hardships of their neighborhood.
pmc-13327524:
Yajing Zhou and co-authors propose a new statistics method in a 2026 article on causal mediation with continuous treatments. Standard tools handle yes-or-no treatments well, but dose-like treatments plus thousands of possible background factors strain them. Their framework joins variable selection with propensity modeling in a weighted semiparametric design.

Tests in simulation showed better variable picking and more efficient estimates than rival regularization methods, because outcome-linked factors were kept and noise factors dropped. The team then applied the method to UK Biobank data, measuring how much of the link between diabetes risk and cancer runs through apolipoprotein B levels. The approach offers a steadier balance of accuracy, clarity, and strength for large biomedical datasets.
pmc-13328024:
Ashit Kumar Dutta and co-authors review AI and eye-tracking methods for screening dyslexia in a 2026 article. Formal reading assessments take much time and staff, limiting how many children can be checked early. The team searched four databases for studies from January 2015 to March 2026 that used eye movement data, with or without predictive models.

Twenty-three papers qualified, including fourteen on machine learning prediction models, and samples ranged from under twenty people to over three hundred. Dyslexic readers consistently showed longer fixations, more backward eye jumps, and weaker forward jump efficiency while reading. Models built on those signals could sort readers well, pointing to low-cost screening that flags risk before failure sets in.
pmc-13328524:
Shuo Li and co-authors study in 2026 how lighting changes contact-free heart rate checks that use face video. Such methods read tiny colour shifts in skin as blood flows. The team split the face into 15 regions based on anatomy. They tested each region on two public video sets with four different signal methods.

Three areas held up best under hard lighting: the space between the brows, the bridge of the nose, and the cheeks. Using several regions together beat using one region alone or the whole face. The findings offer practical guidance for building camera-based heart rate tools that stay accurate when light is uneven or weak.
pmc-13328724:
Hyun Kwon, Joo Bon Maeng, and Dae-Jin Kim present a two thousand twenty-six method for detecting adversarial examples crafted to fool image classifiers. Tiny invisible tweaks flip model predictions, endangering medical and driving systems. Detectors must catch inputs that look normal to humans.

Their system trains a decoder to rebuild a frozen network's internal features from clean images only. Attack inputs distort those features, so reconstruction fails measurably. Statistical distance checks add a second alarm. Tests on photo and skin-image datasets against five attack families reached strong detection scores, advancing practical AI safety screening.
pmc-13329924:
To stop atrial fibrillation, doctors seal off the veins entering the heart's upper chamber, and they can burn, freeze, or zap the tissue to do it. Marina Marins and three co-authors compare those energy sources in 2026. The newest, pulsed field ablation, uses short electric pulses that kill heart cells while sparing nearby structures.

Trials show the pulse method works as fast or faster than heat or cold, with lower risk to the food pipe, nerves, and veins. It brings its own hazards, though, such as blood cell damage and spasm of heart arteries. Heat still serves better for lines beyond the veins. The authors see the methods as partners for now, not rivals.
pmc-13332024:
Waleed and co-authors apply in 2026 neural network modeling to the question of what makes heritage tourism sustainable in Pakistan. Six UNESCO listed destinations anchor the study, from the ruins of Moenjodaro and Taxila to Lahore's Fort and Shalamar Gardens. More than four hundred domestic tourists rated their satisfaction and the sites' sustainability on survey scales.

Four families of factors were fed to the network: economic, perceptual, ecological, and socio-cultural. All four tied positively to sustainability in the results. The ecological factor carried the most weight, the authors report, with tourists' own perceptions next in line. The modeling flips the usual survey analysis: a neural net can rank fuzzy human factors by influence without assuming straight line relationships. For site managers, the message is that green stewardship is not decoration but the strongest lever visitors themselves reward.
pmc-13332124:
Mengru Yang and co-authors argue in a 2026 review that cancer treatment should stop trying to simply dissolve the stiff tissue around tumors. In cancers such as pancreatic and breast tumors, the extracellular matrix can grow five to ten times stiffer than normal tissue, shutting immune cells out and teaching them to tolerate the tumor.

Breaking that matrix down wholesale has failed in trials and may even help cancer spread, so the authors propose rebuilding a healthy stiffness instead. They define a mechano-therapeutic window, a stiffness range where immune entry and drug response peak without raising spread risk. Smart nanoparticles could soften tissue in a controlled priming step before immunotherapy, chemotherapy, or radiation, and future carriers might sense stiffness and adjust in real time. The framework targets scar-like solid tumors where physical barriers block treatment.
pmc-13332224:
Yuxi Wang and four co-authors wrote this 2026 study testing a graphene heating cape for office workers in cold rooms. Heating whole buildings is wasteful; warming the person may be smarter. Thirty volunteers sat in a chamber held at winter-office cold while the cape ran at four settings, or stayed off. Skin temperature, heart rate, and comfort votes were tracked throughout.

The cape clearly helped, and forty degrees was the sweet spot. At that setting, overall sensation moved from slightly cool to near neutral, and comfort reached a slightly comfortable level, with the belly and lower back gaining most. Heart rate barely moved, showing the warmth cost the body little. People differed sharply in their favorite temperature, though. The authors recommend personal, adjustable heating over one-size settings, and give building managers evidence that local warmth can substitute for hotter rooms.
pmc-13333624:
Lucinda Grummitt and co-authors describe a 2026 mixed-methods study of the KidsXpress School Partnership Program in Australian primary schools. The program places creative expressive therapists and trauma consultants inside schools to support children affected by trauma.

Five primary schools took part, and the team gathered surveys and interviews from teachers, therapists, and consultants. They also tracked wellbeing scores for students referred to therapy, using the Child Outcome Rating Scale from first to last session. The evaluation used the RE-AIM framework to judge reach, uptake, and delivery in real school settings. Early evidence on how such whole-school, trauma-informed support works in practice can guide schools planning similar partnerships.
pmc-13333824:
Shakiba Sharifi Tashnizi and co-authors study acid activation of nitrogen generating chemicals for oil fields in this 2026 paper. Sodium nitrite and ammonium chloride react to make nitrogen gas inside a well. That gas can lift oil recovery and clear blockages. Acids speed the reaction, but acid choice and strength matter.

Five acids were compared, from acetic to trichloroacetic acid. Acetic acid made the most nitrogen, about twenty percent more than the others at top settings. Gas output rose almost linearly with reactant concentration. Heat helped, with the best range between 70 and 90 degrees Celsius. Careful pH control limited harmful nitrogen oxide byproducts. The results guide field dosing for this recovery method.
pmc-13334124:
So Young Lim wrote a 2026 narrative review of syndromic craniosynostosis, where several skull sutures fuse early alongside facial and neurological problems. The review centers on raised pressure inside the skull, skull base pathology, and surgical management.

Older thinking blamed high pressure mainly on a too-small cranial vault. Newer evidence spreads the blame: faulty spinal fluid circulation, venous hypertension, blocked upper airways, and early fusion of skull base joints all contribute. In Crouzon syndrome especially, premature skull base fusion lines up with returning pressure problems and repeat vault surgery. Many patients keep near-normal skull volume through compensating growth, so pressure symptoms can be vague and easy to miss. The review gathers clinical, imaging, and institutional experience to guide monitoring and operations.
pmc-13335324:
Kaustubh Kishor Jadhav and colleagues study 2026 metabolite patterns in adolescent depression using a focused approach. Depression ranks among the top causes of death around the world and keeps growing as a public health worry. Most past work has centered on adults, even though evidence shows the teen years often mark the start of mental health problems. Metabolite profiling reflects ongoing bodily chemical processes, offering a promising avenue to find possible signs of disease state.

The study aims to find early occurring blood patterns linked to teen depression. The study compared 204 teens with clinical depression against 78 healthy peers, using focused nuclear magnetic resonance scans on serum samples. In total, 250 blood measures were counted, including absolute levels and percent measures.
pmc-13335924:
Johannes Jungwirth and co-authors identify a human cell protein that holds back herpes simplex virus type 1, in a 2026 paper. The virus infects most people worldwide and is growing resistant to standard drugs. It needs the host cell's building blocks and repair systems to copy itself, so host factors that block it are prized targets for new treatments.

The protein, a part of the phosphatase PP2A called PR130, cut virus growth in both skin-like and nerve-like cells, against lab strains and fresh patient isolates. Infection in turn lowered PR130 levels. Wide scans of proteins and their switches showed PR130 steering cell-cycle and DNA repair controls, including the brake protein p21. Blocking a second protein that destroys p21 steadied that brake and lowered virus levels. Removing PR130 also made the virus depend on a damage-checkpoint pathway it normally avoids.
pmc-13336024:
Takuya Kuwahara and colleagues study 2026 shear-induced appearance of ring-shaped ultra-low-friction contact layers in glassy carbon, foreign atoms and atomic-scale workings. Mismatched graphite contact layers represent a classic friction system to achieve ultra-low friction. Another route uses shear-induced ring-forming of glassy carbon.

This process occurs right at surface rough contacts, relying on foreign atoms like hydrogen and oxygen. To address these gaps, the authors undertake a careful computer study with 1,000 1-ns-long quantum molecule motion runs of sheared glassy carbon with and without foreign atoms. No ring-shaped contact layers emerge for four-valent systems like pure or silicon-doped glassy carbon, while shear-induced ring-forming is always observed for foreign atoms with valency lower than four.
pmc-13336224:
Marina Melo Martin and co-authors profiled young adults treated in intensive care for COVID-19 in São Paulo in a 2026 retrospective study. Most pandemic ICU research centered on older patients, leaving the young adult picture thinner.

The longitudinal study covered 105 patients aged 20 to 40 admitted between April 2021 and December 2022 at a university hospital. Mortality reached 27.6 percent. Sex, ethnicity, arriving from the emergency room, hemodynamic instability, and use of vasoactive drugs, ventilation, heparin, and corticosteroids all associated with death, as did C-reactive protein, lactate, and lymphocyte levels. Raised lactate and longer time on vasoactive drugs emerged as risk factors. The profile helps intensivists spot which younger patients are sliding toward danger.
pmc-13336424:
Luxiang Zhao and co-authors built a fully flexible cold plasma patch for skin cancer treatment in a 2026 device study. Plasma devices promise noninvasive therapy with reactive species, but rigid hardware touches skin poorly and flexes not at all.

The All-Flex Plasma Patch stretches, runs on ambient air, and presses reactive oxygen and nitrogen species through skin better than rigid sources. In a mouse melanoma model, one week of treatment shrank tumors to one nineteenth of the control volume in their comparison. Proteomic work showed the treatment rewires tumor metabolism and disturbs calcium balance through several newly reported protein targets. The team also mapped an exposure window, since excessive dosing provoked adverse responses, and reported minimal systemic burden at tuned settings.
pmc-13337124:
Liping Yang and colleagues traced a gene that drives escalating cocaine use to a brain reward hub, in a 2026 rat study. The gene ANKS1B had already surfaced as a shared risk factor for heroin, methamphetamine, and alcohol dependence in human genetics. Here the team asked what it does in the nucleus accumbens as cocaine intake grows out of control.

Long-access cocaine lowered ANKS1B in that hub, and tuning its level changed escalation and later drug seeking without touching baseline intake. ANKS1B binds the acetyltransferase CBP, steering histone acetylation that represses the factor FoxO3. The chain marks ANKS1B and its epigenetic partners as candidate targets for curbing compulsive drug use.
pmc-13337424:
Zsuzsanna Szőke and colleagues describe a first-of-its-kind deer case in a 2026 report from Hungary. A middle-aged fallow deer hind, aged 6–7 years and in good condition, was legally culled and examined after death. The team found retained fetal skull bones in the front vagina and a smooth-muscle tumor, a leiomyoma, in the left uterine horn.

Tissue study and a desmin stain backed the tumor diagnosis, claimed as the first published uterine leiomyoma in this species. Gene sequencing compared microbes from the healthy horn, the tumor tissue, and feces; the tumor sample resembled feces, with more Bacteroides and Escherichia–Shigella. As a single case with no treatment, it can only hint that blockage and retained material may reshape local microbes.
pmc-13337624:
Aleigha Lawless and colleagues gave real world results in 2026 for immune drugs given around surgery for melanoma that can be cut out. Trials favour giving immune drugs before surgery over after surgery alone, yet the best plan around surgery and sound blood markers remain unsettled. The team looked back at care, outcomes, and safety in patients treated in routine clinics.

Whether small surgery after pre surgery drugs is safe and whether tumour DNA in blood can flag relapse were key questions. Real world data of this kind help doctors judge whether trial gains hold in day to day care and which patients need close watch. The findings back refining surgery plans while stronger blood marker proof is awaited.
pmc-13338224:
Chang Zhao and seven co-authors propose that variety among urban trees shapes the microbes people breathe and touch, with effects on health. Past work links total green richness to immune health but ignores how habitats differ across a city. The team surveys plants and microbes across 72 neighborhoods in Shanghai.

Samples cover soil, leaf surfaces, and airborne microbes that move indoors. Higher variety among trees tracked with higher variety in airborne and soil microbe communities. Patterns of respiratory disease linked most to variety in the airborne microbes. The authors build a planting model with a threshold score and give templates that use distant tree families to keep microbe variety high across a city.
pmc-13338424:
Thystere Matondo Bantidi and colleagues tested a traffic light warning idea in 2026 for volcanic eruptions at eight well watched volcanoes. Eruptions often follow rock failure around magma paths, and a falling b value in quake data tends to precede failure, signalling rising stress. The team asked whether that signal can sharpen near real time forecasts.

They flagged red light when b values fell more than 10 percent below background and checked whether eruptions followed within 10 days. Sites spanned Iceland, Hawaii, and Japan, giving varied tectonic settings. The system offers a simple, testable rule for eruption priming, though local calibration will decide its worth at each volcano.
pmc-13339024:
Gonzalo Gomez-Munoz and a large team write periodic patterns on conductive glass with ultrafast lasers in a 2026 study. Fluorine-doped tin oxide films gain rippled structures that split electrical behavior by direction. Such surfaces could serve as clear heaters, sensors, or switchable wetting bases.

Films were scanned with high-rate femtosecond pulses at 1030 nm under varied power, pulse length, and overlap. Good pattern spread depended on how fluorine content evolved during writing as reported. Uneven fluorine in starting films caused problems the authors discuss frankly. Still, strongly directional surfaces formed at scan speeds above 1.0 m per second in the reported runs.
pmc-13341324:
Ping Jin and colleagues tested a new drug, BGM0504, in 2026 in Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes, comparing it with semaglutide. The multicentre, randomised, placebo controlled trial assigned 64 adults to BGM0504 at 5, 10, or 15 milligrams, placebo, or semaglutide 1 milligram, each once weekly for twelve weeks. Safety, drug levels, drug effects, and efficacy were all tracked.

The main endpoint was change in HbA1c from baseline, with fasting glucose, two hour glucose, and body weight as secondary endpoints. Early phase trials of this kind test whether a new drug merits larger trials. The comparison with semaglutide gives a first read on relative potency and tolerability.
pmc-13341424:
An eyebrow cyst that lingered 29 years is reported by Yanpeng Zhu and coauthors in their 2026 case report. Pilonidal sinus usually appears near the tailbone; facial cases number only about 10 worldwide, all on the cheek, and none had formed a bridging scar before.

The 56-year-old man's trouble began with a school injury, leaving swelling and drainage beside his right eyebrow plus a scar band toward the nose that tugged at his vision. Staged surgery, tissue expansion, and scar revision, followed by three injection sessions, cleared the lesion. Tissue study confirmed chronic pilonidal sinus. At one year, appearance and visual field had improved without recurrence.
pmc-13341524:
Screening dialysis patients for depression with machine learning is developed by Yugang Cao's team in a 2026 multicenter study. The project enrolled 601 peritoneal dialysis patients from two hospitals, counting a Self-Rating Depression Scale score of 53 or more as high symptoms.

Six factors survived selection: age, peritonitis, catheter problems, anxiety score, social support score, and time on dialysis. Among nine models, XGBoost did best with an outside testing AUC of 0.869. The team built an online visualization tool for bedside use and confirmed subgroup differences. Early flagging could connect kidney patients with mental health help sooner.
pmc-13341624:
Healthcare workers' willingness to screen for dormant tuberculosis is surveyed by Yalan Liu's team in a 2026 Chongqing study. Staff at 46 named institutions across 31 districts answered a structured form on knowledge, attitudes, and acceptance of screening and preventive care.

Of 1,022 respondents, 39.7% had limited knowledge and 67.4% had never been screened, yet most would accept screening (78.7% of them) and preventive treatment (93.3% of them). Fear of drug side effects dominated refusal of treatment at 79.4% of those who refused. Prior screening experience raised screening acceptance odds fivefold, with an odds ratio of 5.145 in the model. Department, job type, and years on the job each shaped willingness, pointing to focused staff training.
pmc-13341724:
Expert consensus on safe teen technology use is built by Andrés Arana-Rodríguez's team, in their 2026 Delphi study. A mixed expert panel worked through three rounds between November 2024 and June 2025, proposing, voting on, and rating measures for schools and families.

Of 100 invited experts, 38 joined, with round replies falling from 28 to 17. Consensus was set at 80% agreement and very high agreement at 95%, and a composite score ranked measures into three relevance levels. Risks covered span problem use, health misinformation, cyberbullying, and unsuitable content. The resulting framework aims to give policy and practice shared, evidence-based priorities.
pmc-13341824:

pmc-13341924:
A celebrated gut microbe cuts both ways in heart disease, in a 2026 review by Shihao Li and colleagues on Akkermansia muciniphila. The authors call for strain-level clarity, safe dosing, and smarter delivery before clinical use.
pmc-13342124:

pmc-13342324:
André Pontes-Silva and colleagues probed missing data methods in 2026 for fibromyalgia drug trials, with hands on guidance for linear mixed models. pmc-13342424:

pmc-13343524:

pmc-13346824:

pmc-13348024:

pmc-13353924:

pmc-13355324:

pmc-13356724:

Within the tumor setting, steady activation shapes links among cancer, immune, and support cells. The authors survey drugs that block the pathway's kinases or its STAT proteins directly. They also discuss gene based approaches still in development.
pmc-13372524:
Imman Qadri and co-authors tell of stiff jaw disease in a 2026 case report. A man aged 52 in Pakistan, a keen gardener who had no shots for the ill, hurt his foot. He grew stiff in the jaw, had trouble swallowing, and then had body spasms.

pmc-13373224:

Sensitivity checks tested how firm the pooled result was.
pmc-13374224:
Jiahua Du and co-authors used deep cold to make double pollen in poplar trees in a 2026 study. Double pollen has twice the gene set, and crosses with it give trees with three sets. Such trees can grow fast and strong, a prize for wood and paper work.

Cold snaps broke the last split step in male cells, which left the gene set whole. Stage of growth, cold depth, and cold span each swayed the yield. The best run froze buds at one set stage for five hours and got double pollen in near one in three grains. Crosses with the pollen gave 26 three-set young trees.
pmc-13374324:

pmc-13374824:

pmc-13376424:
Jun Li and co-authors uncover a protease-gated immune checkpoint on the locust body surface, in a 2026 paper. Insects must tell dangerous fungi from harmless ones living on their skin. How the surface immune system makes that call was largely unknown.

pmc-13376624:

pmc-13376924:

pmc-13377824:

Healthy vaginal microbiota are dominated by Lactobacillus, while shifts raise illness risk and worsen reproductive results. Swabs were cultured for germs and lactobacilli, and a diamine assay quantified diamines, byproducts of bacterial breakdown linked to dysbiosis. The study tracks how hormone therapy changes microbiota and diamine levels and whether those changes track with embryo implantation. Diamines could become a simple, objective check for vaginal health during IVF preparation.
pmc-13378624:
Víctor Jiménez Yuste and co-authors surveyed unmet needs among people with haemophilia worldwide, in a 2026 paper. Haemophilia is a bleeding disorder where blood clots poorly. Modern preventive treatments have cut bleeds and improved outcomes. Still, the daily burden patients face with these treatments was poorly documented, so the team drew on a large global survey program.

Doctors reported on more than two thousand patients across many countries. Most patients took their preventive doses as planned, yet doctors were unhappy with the plan for over half of them. Worries centered on how doses are given, how often, and how well they work. Nearly half the patients had joint problems, and quality of life suffered on every treatment type. The authors call for care shaped around patients' lives.
pmc-13379324:
Chaowapong Jarasvaraparn and two co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary on liver harm in children and adults who lose much of their small bowel. With too little gut, patients rely on vein feeding, and the liver often suffers over time. The cause was once blamed on vein feeding and stalled bile alone. It is now seen as a break in the gut-liver axis.

Their remaining gut also shifted toward an upper-gut pattern of genes. The writers link this to a receptor pathway in the gut-liver axis.
pmc-13379424:

The yeasts came from kombucha and beetroot kvass. Zinc oxide can kill bacteria, but making it usually needs harsh chemicals and high energy use.

Films made this way are of interest for food packaging and medical surfaces that resist bacteria. The study links how the films are structured to how well they fight germs.
pmc-13379524:
Yancy S Wu and colleagues present a 2026 Norwegian case study on making drug funding decisions earlier, before the largest trials finish. The drug in question treats a rare, gene-defined form of lung cancer as a first treatment. Decision makers had only mid-stage trial evidence at the time.

The study compares two ways of filling the evidence gap: structured questioning of experts, done in a formal way, and other outside evidence. Both were fed into a model that estimates long-term health gains and costs against standard chemotherapy plus immunotherapy. The aim was to see whether such methods can support an earlier, conditional funding decision without waiting years for final trial results.
pmc-13380024:
Tyson Tetoff, Jasmin Kaur, and Carlos Zambrano present a 2026 case report on diagnosing and treating suspected bone infection in a medically complex patient. Their patient was a 51-year-old man with several other illnesses, skin ulcers, anaemia, and reduced kidney function. Blood tests showed signs of infection.

Scans supported a diagnosis of long-standing bone infection, but key confirming tests were missing, including detailed imaging, a bone sample, and wound cultures. Treatment therefore rested on clinical judgement. Kidney problems also shaped the antibiotic choice, ruling out a standard drug in favour of two others. The case shows how doctors must act on incomplete evidence when a patient cannot undergo every test.
pmc-13380524:

Four labs, with eight trained staff, measured clotting times by a shared manual method.

pmc-13380724:

pmc-13381024:

pmc-13381724:
Ruoxin Chen and co-authors test electroacupuncture for sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength, in patients on maintenance haemodialysis. The treatment group received twenty-four thirty-minute sessions over eight weeks, three times weekly. One participant dropped out, leaving thirty-five in the analysis. Walking speed over six metres rose in the treated group and fell in controls, and handgrip strength showed the same pattern. Muscle mass index also increased significantly with treatment while controls did not change. No serious adverse events occurred. pmc-13382024:

Consistency was tested over time and within the questionnaire itself, and statistical analysis explored its structure. Nine preference groups emerged, covering fruit, vegetables, snacks, and grain-based foods among others. Ratings ranged from moderate to excellent, supporting the Persian version as a usable research tool.
pmc-13382524:

pmc-13382724:

pmc-13383224:

pmc-13383724:

pmc-13385324:

pmc-13385424:

pmc-13385524:

pmc-13386924:

pmc-13388424:

pmc-13389324:

pmc-13390024:

pmc-13390424:

pmc-13390824:

pmc-13390924:

pmc-13391124:

pmc-13391224:

pmc-13392424:

pmc-13392624:

pmc-13393524:

pmc-13393724:

pmc-13394024:

pmc-13394924:

pmc-13396224:

pmc-13396424:

pmc-13396724:

pmc-13397324:

Doses of the two antibody drugs were delivered at over 93 percent of the planned intensity. Real-world safety and effect in older, frailer patients are the study's reason to exist.
pmc-13397524:
Qingfeng Fu and colleagues present a room-temperature route for breaking down Teflon waste, a plastic famed for resisting almost everything. Their 2026 paper uses a liquid sodium-potassium alloy that reacts with the material and keeps the reaction going on its own. The strong carbon-fluorine bonds in these plastics normally demand harsh heat to break.

Less than a tenth of plastic waste gets recycled, and Teflon-type waste mostly ends up burned or buried. Here the alloy strips fluorine away in a self-heating reaction sparked by contact charging, turning the waste into fluorine-doped carbon plus metal fluorides. The products could serve as useful materials, offering a fresh path for a waste stream that today has almost none.
pmc-13398524:
Yanjuan Hou and co-authors pin a kidney gene behind a genome-scan signal. Their 2026 study names ELF3 as the effector gene at a locus tied to kidney function, out of more than a thousand such loci still unexplained. In injured kidney tubules, ELF3 switches on and marks cells caught in a transitional, inflamed state ringed by immune cells.

Deleting the gene in mice after injury thinned those stuck cells, cut cytokine output and reduced immune cell gathering. ELF3 drives the effect by switching on parts of a noncanonical NF-κB pathway and escorting its key protein into the nucleus. The work frames ELF3 as an amplifier worth blocking in chronic kidney disease.
pmc-13398724:
Giulio Magrin calls for shared standards in microdosimetry in this 2026 paper. The field measures how radiation deposits energy at tiny scales, which matters for therapy and protection. Labs, though, read and report their data in widely unlike ways.

Those gaps distort shared quantities and cloud clinical use. A 2024 workshop of specialists urged progressive standardization. With experiments and simulations mixing more each year, a coherent frame grows urgent. No neutral world body exists to lead, so Magrin proposes open debate on the disputed points. The paper maps where agreement is needed first. It is a roadmap toward comparable results across labs.
pmc-13398824:
Meng Zhang and co-authors uncover a two-factor module that arms millet and wheat against drought and salt while lifting yield. Their 2026 study works in foxtail millet, where the transcription factors TAF10 and ERF109 team up to switch on flavonoid-making genes. Flavonoids, plant pigments with protective chemistry, sit at the heart of the stress shield the pair builds.

Spraying the flavonoids themselves (apigenin, naringenin or hesperetin) rescued plants whose module was silenced. Field protocols for apigenin then raised wheat yields by 12.3 to 19.6 percent and millet yields by 15.8 to 23.9 percent under dry and salty field conditions in the trials reported. A spray-on shield beats breeding timelines where climates are already turning.
pmc-13399124:
Yuya Ueno, Shota Yamazaki, Hiromichi Hoshina, and Masahiko Harata report in 2026 that terahertz radiation can speed up repair of broken DNA in living cells. Double-strand breaks are the most dangerous kind of DNA damage. Slow or faulty repair can lead to cancer and other diseases. Terahertz waves sit between microwaves and infrared light and cannot ionize molecules, which makes them attractive as a gentle tool.

In their experiments, exposing cells to terahertz waves lowered the amount of chemically induced double-strand breaks. The effect size depended on the wave frequency used. Heating the samples instead raised the number of breaks, which told the team the benefit was not a simple warming effect. Earlier work showed terahertz exposure promotes actin polymerization, a process also involved in break repair inside the nucleus. The authors suggest such exposure might one day support treatments for diseases tied to genomic instability.
pmc-13399424:
Rafael Mathias Pitta and colleagues followed Brazilian men over time to see whether changing their own physical activity habits changed their risk of erectile dysfunction, in a 2026 longitudinal study. Earlier studies linked leisure exercise to lower risk, but they mostly froze people at one moment and came from wealthy countries. The effect of real-world habit change stayed untested.

The cohort drew on employer-sponsored health checkups at a São Paulo hospital between 2008 and 2022. The analysis included 925 men over 39 who had no erectile dysfunction at their first visit and who returned for a second assessment 300 to 800 days later. Each man was classed by how his activity pattern moved between visits: persistently inactive, becoming inactive, becoming active, or persistently active. Erectile function was scored with the standard international index questionnaire at both visits. The authors expected men who became or stayed active to fare better than those who stayed inactive.
pmc-13400224:
Nelson-Georges Dengo and colleagues report two years of a French national emergency committee that advises, within twenty-four hours, on pregnant and postpartum women with thrombotic microangiopathy, in a 2026 article. The committee, under the national TMA reference center since October 2023, convenes experts from eight specialties per case.

The first 76 reviewed women were most often in a preeclampsia context, 47 percent, or peripartum hemorrhage, 40 percent. Thirty-eight percent were first-time mothers. Acute kidney injury appeared in 62 percent, including nine women with renal cortical necrosis, the extreme phenotype the authors highlight. True TTP accounted for only thirteen cases, 17 percent, and none was judged atypical HUS. The committee changed management in 26 percent of cases, most often by de-escalating therapy, sparing women plasma exchange or costly drugs they did not need. The authors advocate real-time multidisciplinary conferences as standard support.
pmc-13400624:
Behnam Taherizadeh and colleagues apply, in 2026, an eagle-inspired search algorithm to place solar panels and batteries in local power networks. Adding solar generation and storage can cut losses and steady voltage, but only if units are sized and sited well. The team framed it as an optimization problem.

Their enhanced Bald Eagle Search was tested on two standard networks with 33 and 69 connection points, under solar-only and solar-plus-battery plans. It beat a genetic algorithm and a whale-inspired method on every run. On the larger network, daily energy losses fell by up to roughly half depending on setup, the weakest voltage improved, and operating costs were lowest. The authors claim the method scales across network layouts.
pmc-13400724:
Zakiur Rehman Ansari and colleagues present, in 2026, a man whose heart stent, placed years earlier, fractured and seeded a slowly draining chest fistula. Delayed inflammatory complications of stents are exceptionally rare, and a skin-draining tract years later can masquerade as a simple chest wall infection. Untangling it required several imaging methods.

The 53-year-old, who had diabetes and heart disease, had a right coronary stent placed in 2018 and later developed months of intermittent fever and a draining pit near the breastbone. Scans revealed the broken, blocked stent wrapped in inflamed tissue reaching through the diaphragm. Surgeons removed the stent, the inflamed tissue and the tract after antibiotic cover. The case shows how cross-sectional imaging guides such operations.
pmc-13401324:
Inês Martins Esteves wrote a 2026 cohort study of a programme-level revamp in specialist eye nursing training in the United Kingdom, asking whether structural reform of a whole curriculum lifts student grades. Post-registration programmes often stay fragmented across results, assessments, and workload even when theory favours joined-up design.

Nine cohorts of registered nurses, 106 students in all, were compared. Six cohorts, 73 students, finished the traditional structure between 2018 and 2021, while three cohorts of 33 students took the redesigned programme in 2022 and 2023. The revamp drew on constructive alignment, programmatic assessment, competency-based education, and cognitive load theory. Esteves also introduces the Integrated Programme Reform Model as a framework for programme-level reform. Tests whether the new structure was linked to measurable gains in achievement.
pmc-13401524:
Lidiane Araujo Cezário and co-authors wrote a 2026 study of long-term cancer survivors in Brazil moving from oncology follow-up back to primary health care. After five years at a major cancer centre, survivors are referred onward, and the study asks how that transition actually works.

At the National Cancer Institute, 91 survivors answered a structured phone questionnaire about demographics, lifestyle, nutrition, prevention, and surveillance. Their average age was about 69 years. The most reported late effects were cognitive difficulties, hormonal symptoms, sleep problems, and chronic pain. Fewer than half said they had been referred to a primary care unit after treatment ended. Only 11 members, about 12 percent, recalled receiving a discharge summary to hand to their primary care provider, exposing a weak handover.
pmc-13402324:
A pyramid solar still uses sunshine to distill fresh water, a clean answer to water scarcity in sunny regions, but its output is capped by how heat and vapor move inside it. Ramesh Kumar and co-authors redesigned the still's absorber plate to expose about twenty percent more surface to heat. They studied the standard and modified designs with computer simulations of heat flow and structure, then built the stills and checked the results by experiment.

The modified still ran hotter, moved more heat, and lifted efficiency from sixty-eight to seventy-two percent. Stress levels stayed far inside safe limits in both designs. The experiments matched the simulations closely, within five percent on temperature and eight percent on heat flow. The authors conclude that plate geometry is a powerful lever on performance, and that their validated simulation approach is a dependable base for further improvements to solar desalination.
pmc-13402424:
Amouzadeh and co-authors study, in 2026, what makes mobile banking hard for older adults. They test six widely used Iranian banking apps through expert review and hands-on trials with 1,200 users aged 60 and above. Five human-computer interaction experts applied smartphone usability rules, while the older users completed tasks, rating scales, and interviews in a mixed-methods design.

The experts logged 135 usability problems, with error blocking the most severe category at a mean severity of 2.27, followed closely by visibility of system status at 2.22 on their scale. Usability scores diverged widely between apps, from 27.50 for the worst to 59.02 for the best on the hundred-point System Usability Scale. Age mattered within the older group too: users aged 60 to 63 averaged 54.2, while those aged 72 to 75 averaged 45.3 in the comparisons. Talks blamed cultural mismatches and cognitive overload as key barriers to handling money alone.
pmc-13402624:
Souad Kartti and co-authors map the drug-response genes of a Moroccan cohort, in a 2026 study aimed at a gap in global data. How a person responds to many medicines depends on their genes. North African populations are missing from most pharmacogenomic databases, despite wide genetic diversity that can strongly shift drug response and safety.

Whole-genome sequencing of 109 Moroccan individuals found about 129,000 new variants across thousands of candidate genes. In seventeen genes with firm clinical guidance, several common variants stood out, including ones tied to statin handling and blood thinner dose. Immune gene typing added variants linked to bad drug reactions. The data seed precision medicine for the region.
pmc-13402824:
Chenglin Wang and colleagues searched for blood-cell gene markers that separate sepsis from systemic inflammatory response syndrome, or SIRS. Their 2026 study addresses a hard bedside distinction: both conditions inflame the body, but sepsis stems from infection and needs urgent antimicrobial care. Lysosome genes, tied to cell cleanup and immune signaling, offered a promising discriminator.

Sequencing blood from 12 SIRS and 20 sepsis patients yielded 21 overlapping lysosome-linked genes enriched in autophagy and vacuolar transport. Meta-analysis narrowed them to four core genes in total: CD1C, RNASE6, and SNCA fell in sepsis, while DRAM1 rose. All four showed good discrimination, with DRAM1 strongest at an AUC of 0.888. Single-cell data pinpointed the immune cells expressing them. The markers need larger clinical validation before diagnostic use.
pmc-13402924:
Qing Li and Mario Plebani argue that machine learning in laboratory medicine needs two kinds of traceability kept distinct. One is the metrological kind that anchors a measurement to reference standards. The other is an algorithmic kind that lets auditors rebuild how a model turned data into output. Labs now use learning models to interpret tests, predict outcomes, and run operations, and each use carries different proof burdens.

A model can eat perfectly traceable lab values yet transform them in ways that leak information, hide uncertainty, or drift after deployment as methods and populations shift. The authors propose a functional framework aligning calibration thinking with model documentation, plus traceability dossiers and tiered rules backed by international teamwork. Their aim is reproducibility and comparability strong enough for clinical trust, without pretending a training set is a reference material.
pmc-13403024:
Tierra L Mosher leads a team reporting a 26-month-old girl whose acute liver failure traced to HHH syndrome. It is a rare urea cycle disorder named for its three blood and urine markers: high ornithine, high ammonia, and homocitrullinuria. The condition can bring lethargy, unsteadiness, seizures, coma, and liver failure, and newborn screening does not catch it. She was diagnosed one week into her admission.

Liver tissue showed an acute hepatitis-like injury with many acidophil cells and glycogen-filled nuclei, a pairing the authors say is rarely discussed. Acute care used intravenous dextrose and intralipids; long-term care restricts protein, adds glycerol phenylbutyrate to mop up nitrogen, and supplements citrulline to support the cycle. A telling clue was the child own avoidance of protein. The authors urge early metabolic labs and biopsy in pediatric liver failure.
pmc-13404624:
Cia Sin Lee and co-authors examine, in 2026, how health workers in Singapore viewed the OPTIMUM remote monitoring system for diabetes. The system was rolled out in primary care across the country after a trial showed good health outcomes. Knowing what helped or hindered its use matters for keeping it running.

Staff involved in the trial gave individual semi-structured interviews, which were transcribed, coded and analysed for themes. Analysis followed the CFIR framework, which sorts influences into the tool itself, outside pressures, clinic setting, individual staff and process. Workers said remote monitoring helped patients change habits and that its treatment algorithm allowed steady monitoring with tailored advice. Other setting and workload factors also shaped how the system landed.
pmc-13404924:
Muna Al-Daihani, Hisham Al-Abri, and Syed Rizvi compared two forms of tear duct surgery, in a 2026 study. The surgery opens a new path from the tear sac to the nose when the normal duct is blocked. One form adds a soft silicone tube during healing. The team studied a front-flap form of the operation at a specialist eye hospital.

Records covered operations from 2017 to 2023, and just under half the files met the study rules. In all, one hundred seventy-seven patients were included. Success was judged by free flow on flushing and by a dye test. Rates of success were high in both groups. No clear gap appeared between surgery with the tube and surgery without it. The finding lets surgeons weigh the tube's costs and fuss against no proven gain.
pmc-13405024:
Shahana Singh and colleagues describe a 2026 quality project to strengthen child health checks at a Delhi primary care centre. Young children often arrive with one complaint while other problems stay hidden. The IMCI approach, a standard method for assessing sick children, covers danger signs and common illness together.

Age-specific checklists were introduced for children from 2 months to 5 years, backed by a dedicated children's clinic room and better measuring equipment. Two six-week improvement cycles followed. Complete assessment rose from low levels to 50 percent by the second cycle in the reported figures. Checking for danger signs reached 97.2 percent, and screening for cough, fever and diarrhoea all climbed.
pmc-13406324:
Yunjiao Shen and co-authors test the plant Centella asiatica against diabetic liver and fat problems in mice, in 2026 work. Diabetic mice were created with a fatty diet plus streptozotocin, then treated with plant extract or its component asiatic acid. A standard diabetes drug served as comparison.

Fasting glucose fell by about half in both treatment groups, 51.01 and 53.01 percent in the reported figures, with better glucose tolerance and blood fats. Liver fat and insulin resistance eased as well. The mechanism traced to pyrimidine metabolism: liver uridine and related compounds rose, supporting glycogen storage. A protein called UPP1 sits at the centre of the proposed pathway.
pmc-13407324:
Barbora Mechúrová and co-authors review what builds trust when a patient meets a doctor for the first time. While trust in long-term relationships is well studied, the very first encounter is not. Their 2026 scoping review searches PubMed for studies where trust was measured around that first visit.

From 2,825 initial records, ten studies passed full screening for thematic analysis. Trust was shaped in three phases. Before the visit, reputation, care coordination, and past good experiences helped. During the consultation, warmth, visible technical skill, information sharing, participation, listening, and empathy built trust. Afterward, symptom relief reinforced it, and apologising for errors proved crucial. Barriers included little chance to ask questions, time pressure, unmet expectations, and stigmatising language. The authors conclude trust formation starts before the door opens.
pmc-13407724:
Keng Siang Lee and co-authors set out, in a 2026 protocol, to build expert consensus on using artificial intelligence to measure vestibular schwannomas, benign tumours of the hearing nerve. Growth decides treatment for these tumours. Volume measurement beats simple diameters for sensitivity. Yet hand segmentation is slow and variable. AI tools can now outline tumours on MRI automatically.

The plan runs in three phases. First comes a systematic review of how tumours get measured. That drafts candidate indicators. A steering committee then refines them into questionnaire items. Last comes a two-round Delphi survey plus a consensus meeting. Experts come from British and European skull-base societies. The resulting core reporting set will be spread through journals, funders, and conferences, aiming to standardise how AI-assisted measurement enters routine care.
pmc-13407924:
İlker Akyıldız and co-authors reviewed surgery for an inner-ear problem caused by a benign ear growth, in work published in 2026. The growth, a cholesteatoma, can eat into the balance canals of the inner ear and form a leak called a fistula. Surgeons must clear the growth while trying to save hearing. The team studied cases treated at one large referral hospital.

Of 230 patients operated on for the growth, thirty-nine had such a leak, most often in the side balance canal. Hearing stayed steady six months after surgery for early and middle stage leaks. Late stage cases varied more, with some loss on average. In five hard cases, surgeons removed part of the inner ear, yet every patient kept some hearing and none lost it fully. Passing dizziness faded with rest and medicine in all cases.
pmc-13408624:
Homayouni-Rad and co-authors review, in 2026, the psychobiotic potential of postbiotics, the metabolic leftovers of probiotic bacteria, for depression, psychosis, and mania, a little-studied corner of gut-brain research. Their search covered PubMed, Medline, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library for English-language studies from January 2015 to January 2025, covering mood control, brain inflammation, and neurotransmitter tuning.

The surveyed evidence shows postbiotics raising serotonin and GABA signals, damping neuroinflammation, and tuning the body's stress axis. One cited mix, a Lactobacillus brevis strain from Thai fermented sausage, carried a GABA content of 2.85 milligrams per milliliter in the reported assay, showing how potent these metabolites can be. The clinical need is large: depression was about 50 percent more common among women than men in 2023, one of the gaps the review cites. The authors conclude postbiotics are promising drug candidates but insist on proper trials to pin down how they work and dosing.
pmc-13408724:
Saud Alsaleh, Mariam Shikshok, Ahmed Abdel-Aal, and Ammar Almehmi review in 2026 how to perform a kidney biopsy through the skin safely and well.
