Tomasz Bugajski, Derek Lichti, and Payam Zandiyeh test, in a 2026 proof-of-concept study, a simpler X-ray setup for tracking bones in motion. The standard method uses two source-detector pairs, which forces a long distance that blurs and magnifies images. Field of view shrinks as a result.

Their configuration fires two sources at a single detector instead. The shorter distance should sharpen images and widen the view. A pseudo-dynamic experiment checked whether bone positions stayed accurate under the new geometry. Multi-joint motion studies stand to gain most from the simpler rig. Proof-of-concept results decide whether the design deserves wider adoption in biomechanics labs.
pmc-13459924:
Yating Lv and colleagues map shared and plan-specific brain effects of repeat skull-crossing magnet zaps in a 2026 study. Zap plans vary widely in target and pattern, leaving unclear whether they act through common brain-surface principles. Resting-state working MRI before and after single-session zaps across nine plans was mapped by local wobble size, with key results checked in two multi-session datasets.

After-effects moved as one across plans along wiring and working links, and a shared spatial pattern tracked the brain's sense-link ladder. Shared and own effects both matched messenger spreads, and side-brain and motor zaps drove links to thinking domains and to faults in depression and Parkinson's disease. Experts gain a unified framework for guiding brain zaps, with the side-brain area as a possible cross-illness target.
pmc-13460024:
Wenguang Lai and colleagues test swelling and insulin trouble indices against death in heart-kidney-fuel syndrome in a 2026 study. The CRP-fat-sugar index marks insulin trouble and swelling, yet its pairing with waist-based measures was untested for death prediction. A total of 10,941 people from the NHANES records were followed for about 13 years, with all-cause and heart death as outcomes.

During follow-up, 20.3 percent died, including 6.3 percent from heart causes. Higher index values raised both all-cause and heart death risk, and the body-shape-index pairing predicted best. Links ran stronger in early syndrome stages 0 to 2 than in advanced stages 3 to 4. Doctors gain a handy early-warning marker, most useful before disease advances.
pmc-13460224:
Junyi Chen and colleagues describe in 2026 a fully camera-guided way to redo mitral valve surgery on a beating heart, using high potassium to slow the heart rather than stop it. Repeat valve surgery usually means reopening the breastbone, a hazardous route through scar tissue. Their retrospective review compared 43 patients treated through a small right chest incision with 68 treated by conventional reopening, in cases from 2020 into 2026.

The camera group finished bypass and surgery faster, lost far less blood, and needed much less transfused blood and plasma. Drainage, ventilation time, intensive care stay, hospital stay, and total cost all fell, and pneumonia occurred less often. No deaths, strokes, or reoperations for bleeding occurred in the camera group, supporting the technique as safe in experienced hands.
pmc-13460824:
Daniel G Foster and co-authors chart how three lung fibroblast types behave while scar tissue forms and then resolves. Their 2026 paper uses a mouse model where a single drug dose injures the lung, mimicking the repair seen after severe human lung injury. Fibroblasts drive scarring, but their role in the repair phase was understudied.

Using lineage tracing, the team followed collagen-making cells, alveolar support cells, and contractile cells over time. All three groups grew during scarring and shrank back as the lung healed. Gene activity profiling showed each group shifted heavily during scarring, then converged in distinct ways during resolution. Knowing which subsets aid repair could let therapies target scarring cells while sparing the healers.
pmc-13461324:
Liu and co-authors ran a 2026 training study combining blood flow restriction with eccentric exercise, which lengthens muscles under load, in college sprinters. Cuffs on the upper thigh partly restrict blood flow during training to amplify gains. Sixteen male sprinters were split randomly into cuff and non-cuff groups of eight.

Both groups trained eccentrically three times weekly for six weeks, with the cuff group held at a set pressure during sessions. Liu measured hip strength, thirty metre sprint, vertical jump, anaerobic capacity, and leg circumference before and after. Both groups improved across the board, but the cuff group gained more hip extensor strength and jumping power. Cuff training also strengthened the weaker side, reducing imbalance between legs.
pmc-13461624:
Jiahao Dong, Zhongyu Peng, and Tao Chen offer a 2026 reinterpretation of an old idea in Chinese medicine: that the kidney governs the bone. Older readings stressed hormones alone, which cannot explain effects under stress, inflammation, or nerve injury. They recast the idea around a brain-bone axis: brain, hormone, and immune systems as one network. Herbal and hands-on treatments are then read as working at several network levels.

Their model has three tiers, from brain control through body-wide signals to the local bone setting. Kidney-tonifying herbs steady a key hormone control loop. Blood-activating methods and acupuncture link to nerve tone and blood flow near bone. Acupuncture and moxibustion tie to calmer immune activity inside bone. Hard problems remain, including timing differences and lab-to-clinic gaps. They suggest tools such as light-based nerve control and multi-layer gene studies for testing.
pmc-13462224:
Xin Wei, Siqin Hu, and Chen Lin present a 2026 model predicting spots where a chemical tag, crotonylation, lands on proteins. The tag, attached to lysine, helps control cell signaling and metabolism, and appears widely beyond the histones that package DNA. Finding spots in the lab is slow and costly, and few prediction tools exist for non-histone proteins. Their model, DFN-Kcr, reads sequences two ways at once.

One branch uses embeddings from a protein language model, the other reads the raw amino acid code. Filters in one branch catch short local patterns, and an attention design in the other tracks long-range links. A gating step blends both branches. In tests the model beat leading methods on sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and a quality score. The team offers a web server so researchers can run predictions at scale and guide lab checks toward likely tag sites.
pmc-13462324:
Zhicheng Tan and colleagues present a 2026 method for steering groups of driverless surface boats that must hold shape while dodging obstacles at sea. Older steering rules can stall in dead ends, miss the goal, or react late to moving hazards. The new method builds on a force-field style planner that pulls boats toward goals and pushes them from hazards.

Added escape pushes, turning terms, and speed-aware terms let follower boats chart safe paths that keep the group intact in both still and shifting obstacle scenes. In computer trials, the method cut arrival times by 34.52% against classic rules and by 25.13% against recent force-field variants. The work suits sea survey, rescue, and patrol tasks where boats must act as one team without a crew on board.
pmc-13463024:

Carolyn Galbraith, Tonia Gray, and Marion Sturges explore nature walks for Australian parents of autistic preschoolers. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses an ecological framework. Walking in nature benefits parents and young children broadly. Autistic children join physical activity and nature less often, though.

Twenty parents of autistic preschoolers completed a qualitative survey. Twelve parents of non-autistic children formed a comparison group. Five themes emerged from the parents answers. Barriers and joys both differed from typical family accounts. The lens used views child, family, and environment together. Nature programmes can adapt walks to sensory needs. Small changes may open big developmental benefits.
pmc-13479624:
Ali Aboklaish and co-authors assess macrolide resistance in preterm infants in the AZTEC trial, in a 2026 paper. The trial tested whether ten days of early azithromycin helps babies born too soon survive without chronic lung disease. Because drug resistance is a worldwide concern, these resistance checks were planned from the start.

The team tracked six common resistance genes in airway samples, taken before treatment and on days five, ten, and fourteen. They also grew bacteria with and without the drug to confirm how resistance works. The study asks whether treatment changes which resistance genes show up, and whether the resistant germs also shrug off other common drugs used in newborn care.
pmc-13481324:
Takeshita and colleagues reported in 2026 a minimally invasive fix for a rare kidney blood-vessel malformation in a man in his forties. A renal arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal direct link between an artery and a vein. His lesion had one feeding artery, one draining vein, and a ballooned vein segment with a narrowed outflow, a type I layout. The goal was to seal the shunt while sparing healthy kidney tissue.

Through catheters, the team blocked flow with a balloon and injected warmed, diluted medical glue using a triple-layer catheter system. Coils were then placed to reinforce the block. The shunt disappeared completely, with no kidney dysfunction or complications. The authors suggest this balloon-occluded glue technique is a useful option for selected fistulas of this shape.
pmc-13481424:
Darja Popkova and co-authors offer a 2026 scoping review of why valproic acid, a mainstay drug for seizures and mood care, so often adds weight. The team searched four databases and mapped fifteen studies with 1,339 adults in total. Study types ranged from snapshots and follow-ups to gene studies, and quality checks used a standard scale.

Proof clustered into three lanes. Hormone shifts led, covering raised insulin, raised leptin, and insulin resistance. Fat measures shifted too, with higher total cholesterol and triglycerides plus mixed readings for protective cholesterol. Gene lanes stayed young, pointing to a drug-processing gene variant and a methylation mark, yet small groups demand larger checks. Bipolar patients were scarce in the pool. The map argues for personal watch plans that track weight, hormones, and lipids from the start.
pmc-13482324:
Song and colleagues build an explainable risk model in 2026 for a dangerous turn in intensive care, pneumonia patients who go on to develop bloodstream infections after admission. They trained the model on the MIMIC-IV critical care database and tested it externally on patients from Dazhou Central Hospital in China. Six predictors survived the selection process, mixing illness severity scores with sputum culture results and how long the patient had already spent in intensive care.

The best algorithm scored 0.753 on the discrimination curve in internal testing, respectable but far from perfect for spotting who will develop the infection. On the external hospital's patients it slipped to 0.703 on the same measure, and charts of feature importance showed stay length and culture results driving most predictions. A version restricted to admission-day data fell to 0.632 externally, which the authors read as a warning that early warning, before cultures return, remains genuinely hard.
pmc-13483624:
Ontas, Güçlü, and Aydın Son built in 2026 a cheap web system, named SALGINTR, that lets doctors in Türkiye report their own flu like illness each week. Such crowd reporting can back up the classic sentinel network of clinics. Their tools were free cloud forms and sheets, with a total build cost near one hundred dollars. Doctors joined through peer invites and filed weekly symptom forms through the flu season's first three months.

Of 243 doctors who signed up, 197 gave data fit for study, near fifteen hundred person weeks in all. About half of them caught a flu like illness in the span. Weekly rates from the new system rose and fell in step with the national sentinel figures, and matched them most tightly before the peak weeks. Alarm tools in both systems fired in fair accord, and neither led the other in time.
pmc-13483724:
Pin-Jui Kung and co-authors map tiny protective RNAs in developing human germ cells and find a surprising address pattern. Their 2026 study collects fetal testes from weeks 12 to 22 of gestation in Taiwan and compares profiles with United States material. These piRNAs normally guard the genome against jumping genetic elements while the germline resets its marks.

Many of the human fetal piRNAs matched enhancers, the DNA switches that boost gene activity, including both super-enhancers and ordinary enhancers. The same enhancer link appeared in mice and chickens, marking it as deeply conserved across warm-blooded vertebrates. Notably, many switches involved normally serve body tissues rather than germ cells. The authors propose that piRNAs police those switches, dampening body-program genes at the wrong moment to protect germ cell identity.
pmc-13483824:
Stephina Adjoa Yanney measures how strongly malaria mosquitoes in Ghana now resist the insecticides used to control them. Published in 2026, the study raises mosquitoes from larvae collected at eight sites across coastal and northern savannah zones. Standard intensity tests, species identification, and resistance gene checks are paired with a household survey on home and farm pesticide use.

Coastal mosquitoes showed high-intensity resistance to pyrethroid sprays, surviving even tenfold test doses at notable rates, while northern samples showed only moderate resistance. One organophosphate also met high resistance at two coastal sites. A key nerve-channel mutation sat near fixation at every site sampled. Heavy domestic and agricultural chemical use is examined as a driver in the full report. Control programs relying on standard nets and sprays face a shrinking margin.
pmc-13486424:
Gregorich and colleagues reviewed how protein-level studies are rewriting the story of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a disease where heart muscle thickens dangerously. The condition was long blamed on single gene defects in the sarcomere, the heart cell's contracting engine. Yet only about one third of patients carry a known defect, and severity varies wildly among those who do. Their 2026 mini-review gathers recent work using mass spectrometry, which weighs proteins to identify and count them.

The protein surveys show broad remodeling far beyond the sarcomere, touching energy factories, the cell's skeleton, calcium stores, and the nucleus. Different genetic causes seem to converge on similar protein-level end states inside the heart muscle. That convergence hints at shared drug targets downstream of the varied genes. Gregorich argues protein profiling can reveal disease modifiers that gene tests alone will never show.
pmc-13486824:
Yang and co-authors tackled resource waste in blockchain-secured federated learning, where phones and sensors train shared models without sending raw data. Adding blockchain removes the single central server that could fail or cheat, but consensus and training compete for scarce wireless resources. Their 2026 framework splits work among client devices, a consensus step, and edge servers, and picks which clients join each round while allocating computing power and bandwidth jointly.

Simulations showed the scheme improved final model accuracy while cutting delay compared with the baselines examined. Screening out low-quality clients protected training from devices with poor data or weak connections. The joint allocation beat schemes that set client choice and resources separately in the scenarios tested. Yang presents the approach as practical groundwork for trustworthy learning on crowded wireless edge networks.
pmc-13487324:
Notaristefano and a French led team ran in 2026 a pilot test of a new heart catheter for persistent atrial fibrillation, a lasting faulty heart rhythm. The tool can switch between two burn types: heat based radiofrequency and pulsed field, a newer electric pulse method. Forty patients got vein isolation plus burn lines across the heart's upper chamber. Half had heat alone, and half had the switchable tool.

First try success for the full burn set came far more often in the mixed group than in the heat only group. By the end of each case, though, block rates were close in both arms, and total time in the lab was much the same. One patient in the pulse group had a brief spasm of a heart artery. The team notes the pulse mode shone on the back wall, but shared heat's limits at one tough line.
pmc-13487924:
Andrea J. Chow leads a large Canadian team describing family care for children with inherited metabolic diseases in a 2026 survey. These rare conditions often need strict diets, medicines, and close daily management at home. Seventy-one caregivers of children aged twelve or younger answered an online questionnaire about supports used, time spent, missed work, and quality of life for child and caregiver.

Dietary supports were the most common help reported. Many families gave several extra hours each week to care tasks, and many caregivers missed work days in the past year. Every respondent reported some fulfillment, yet most also reported mental strain. Children with progressive, multisystem disease fared worst, and the authors call relief for families a policy priority.
pmc-13488224:
Xiuli Zhang and co-authors review a shortened chemotherapy schedule for malignant ovarian germ cell tumors in a 2026 single-center study covering 2004 to 2024. These rare tumors strike mostly teenagers and young women and respond very well to the three-drug BEP combination. The modified plan packs the drugs into three days instead of five, repeated every four weeks, aiming to cut side effects and hospital time. Records covered eighty-one patients at a women's hospital in Zhejiang.

After a median follow-up beyond nine years, five-year freedom from progression reached about ninety-eight percent in the reported figures, with no treatment-related deaths. Lung irritation from one drug affected a few patients and settled with supportive care. Most patients kept fertility, and nine in ten of those trying conceived.
pmc-13490024:
Mubarek Tuna and colleagues measure satisfaction with psychiatric outpatient care in public hospitals of Ethiopia's Harari Region in a 2026 multicenter survey. The team interviewed 422 outpatients chosen by systematic random sampling with a structured questionnaire and standard tools. Satisfaction matters in mental health care because it tracks with staying in treatment and using services again, yet eastern Ethiopian data were scarce before this work.

Just over half of participants said they were satisfied with the care received. Satisfaction ran higher among patients with major depression, strong social support, reliable access to prescribed medicines, and insurance payment in adjusted models. Waits under thirty minutes also linked with higher satisfaction. The authors urge steadier drug supply and shorter waits.
pmc-13490424:
Jillian L. King and colleagues challenge a standard mouse test for psychedelic activity in a 2026 pharmacology study. The head-twitch response, a rapid head shake in mice, is widely used to flag hallucinogenic potential through a serotonin receptor. Two related drugs were compared across movement, coordination, stress, cognition, and brain wave measures in the front of the brain, with and without a blocker of that receptor.

Lisuride caused no head twitches, yet it impaired movement and thinking, spiked stress responses, and cut brain wave power broadly in the reported results. LSD caused strong head twitches with little effect elsewhere. Blocking the serotonin receptor changed neither drug's wider profile. The authors argue the twitch test alone cannot judge psychoactivity.
pmc-13490524:
Sanjana Dutt and colleagues link satellite images to forest ecology in Poland's Tuchola Forest in a 2026 study. The reserve was divided into structural zones using a foreground density measure that captures how fragmented the canopy is. Sentinel-2 satellite images from 2016, 2020, and 2024 supplied seventeen vegetation indices. Cluster checks showed heavy overlap, so the indices were pruned to a distinct few. They were then fed to interpretable tree-based learning models alongside field records.

Prediction errors stayed under one degradation class, with stand age the loosest target in the reported test results. One red-edge index predicted most consistently across outcomes, while rare zones showed stronger stress signals and wobblier moisture patterns than stable core zones. The authors offer the recipe for open-data monitoring of fragmented forests.
pmc-13491724:
Jiaye Du and four colleagues grade in 2026 the quality of snakebite first-aid videos circulating on TikTok and Bilibili, two major Chinese short-video platforms. Snakebite is a medical emergency where bad advice can cost lives, and short videos now shape what the public learns. The reviewers scored 220 eligible videos with three standard rating tools, working independently and blind to each other's judgments.

Most videos explained causes, symptoms, and treatment, while prevention and basic disease patterns were rarely covered. Overall quality landed in the middle range, with trustworthiness scores lower still. Videos from health professionals and nonprofit groups scored clearly higher than those from individual users. Popularity signals such as likes and shares barely tracked quality, so the authors urge platforms to surface professional content more prominently.
pmc-13491824:
Kohei Ikeda and Tsunehisa Tsubokawa evaluate in 2026 an on-screen alert meant to stop blood pressure checks from lapsing during surgery. Guidelines call for readings at least every five minutes, yet gaps happen when teams are busy. Their hospital's anesthesia system began flagging any chart silent for five minutes in February 2021, and the authors compared over thirty-four thousand cases before and after.

Cases with a gap of ten minutes or longer fell from about one in fifteen before the alert to fewer than one in twenty afterward. Adjusted models confirmed lower odds of long gaps, slightly shorter worst intervals, and fewer large pressure swings across the longest gap. The authors conclude that a simple vendor-built reminder measurably tightened monitoring discipline.
pmc-13492324:
Nitin Kulkarni, Curtiss Moore, Kiara Agosto, and Theodore Takata report in 2026 a heart ablation done under an unusual blood thinner. Their patient lacked clotting factor XII from birth, a defect that makes the standard clotting-time test unreadable even though real clotting is normal. Heparin dosing guided by that test would be unsafe.

The team used bivalirudin, a thinner that works without factor XII, clears in about twenty-five minutes, and cannot be reversed. Because of that last trait they chose pulsed-field ablation over heat-based burning. The case, which the authors believe is the first of its kind, went successfully.
pmc-13493824:
Osuna-Mascaró and co-authors asked whether Goffin's cockatoos can learn that something is permanently broken, not just temporarily unrewarding. Recognising lasting loss of function matters for animals that forage on perishable food and use breakable tools. Some researchers see it as a building block toward grasping death. In the 2026 touchscreen experiments, the parrots pecked icons for rewards, and certain icons were made to stop working for good after one bad outcome.

The cockatoos learned to skip the dead icons and treated them as a lasting category rather than re-testing them hopefully. They adjusted after a single negative event with each one. Performance improved markedly across sessions at group level, though individuals varied a lot, which the authors link to differences such as age and personality. They call the patterns preliminary, since the sample was small, and propose larger studies.
pmc-13493924:
Debkumar Chakraborty leads a seven-author team studying in 2026 how to ferment mixed kitchen waste into hydrogen and useful acids without chemical crutches. Their two-stage system pairs a leached bed reactor with an airlift reactor, feeding it either food waste alone or a blend weighted toward fibrous vegetable waste, whose tough plant fibers slow digestion. Enzyme activity and the broth's natural buffering were tracked through the acid-making stage.

Both feeds buffered themselves impressively, peaking within the first five days with no additives needed. The fibrous blend tamed hydrolysis speed, steadied acidity, and nearly doubled acetate yield, though plain food waste won on hydrogen output and climate footprint in the life cycle check. Recirculating the second reactor's effluent replaces chemicals, pointing to cheaper waste-to-resource plants.
pmc-13494624:
Tsuji and colleagues report an ultrasound clue for men with nonobstructive azoospermia, the severe infertility where no sperm appear in semen because production itself fails. Finding any sperm requires microdissection surgery, hunting through testicular tissue under a microscope, and success is far from guaranteed. Their 2026 study covered 975 men who had the operation at two Japanese clinics between 2003 and 2025, classifying their pre-surgery scans by the pattern of tiny calcium specks called microlithiasis.

Six men showed the diffuse snowstorm pattern, where specks blanket the testicle, and sperm were found in every one of them, a perfect record in that small subgroup. The limited and classic speck patterns carried no independent link to success. A microscope-based tissue score remained the strongest predictor. The authors read the snowstorm pattern as a sign that pockets of sperm production survive, worth flagging in counselling.
pmc-13495224:
Begüm Özcan and Emine Mustafaoğlu study, in a 2026 paper, the link between stress and jaw joint trouble among dentistry students at a Turkish health sciences university. Jaw joint disorders, called TMD, cause pain and clicking where the jaw meets the skull, and stress is a known driver. The team surveyed 250 students, fifty from each year, split between preclinical and clinical stages.

Face-to-face questionnaires paired a jaw index with a standard stress scale. The two scores moved together strongly: students with worse jaw trouble reported higher stress. Stress also ran higher in clinical-stage students, women, smokers, and those living away from family or not exercising. A deeper analysis tied clinical stage and stress score to jaw trouble on their own. The authors note stress management may deserve a place in dental training, while the one-time survey cannot prove which came first.
pmc-13495324:
Ya Wen and colleagues test, in a 2026 rat study, whether vesicles from human bone marrow stem cells can guard both lung and diaphragm during long ventilation. Breathing machines save lives in intensive care, yet days on one wound the lung and waste the diaphragm, the main breathing muscle, delaying weaning. The team kept rats on controlled ventilation for five days in a lab intensive care model.

Ventilation alone left severe lung damage and cut diaphragm fiber size and force by about half. A single vein dose of the tiny cell-shed vesicles eased both: lung tissue looked better and fibers worked stronger. Deep molecular reads across lung, airway fluid, and diaphragm showed wide disturbance from ventilation, most of which the vesicles reversed. The authors read the paired rescue as proof the two injuries travel together, and as a case for vesicle therapy in critical care.
pmc-13495524:
Runfeng Wang leads a large team mapping, in a 2026 genetics study, the DNA regions that set peanut seed quality. Oil content, the balance of oleic and linoleic acids, and protein level drive both food value and breeding goals. The team built a dense linkage map of nearly 4,750 markers from whole-genome resequencing and scored seed traits across four years of field data.

They found 48 trait regions covering eight quality measures, and twenty clusters where one region steered several traits at once. Twenty candidate genes in fat-building pathways emerged. One gene, AhFATB1, carried a working DNA variant whose forms traded off oil level and acid mix without touching protein. The authors offer the map and markers as tools for breeding peanuts that are richer in oil and in the heart-friendlier oleic acid.
pmc-13495624:
Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a leg wound infected with Wohlfahrtiimonas chitiniclastica, an emerging bacterium carried by flies that can pass to humans.  The patient had type 2 diabetes and a sprained leg wound; poor blood sugar control early in the hospital stay let the wound progress into active infection.

Poor hygiene and chronic wounds are known risk settings for this germ, and diabetes adds poor healing and weak defenses. Lab pathogen detection confirmed the culprit, which matters because rare germs are easily missed by routine assumptions. The authors warn the bacterium can cause severe local and body-wide infection in diabetic patients. Early identification and treatment, plus tight sugar control, are their prescription for avoiding amputations and sepsis in similar wounds.
pmc-13498524:
Alessandra Dei Cas leads a 2026 Italian trial testing whether four diabetes drugs given together by mouth can push newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes into remission better than standard care. Remission here means blood sugar below the diabetes threshold after all glucose-lowering drugs have been stopped. Six outpatient clinics took part in the open, practical trial, with treatment lasting 16 weeks before drugs were withdrawn where sugar had regressed.

A total of 108 patients joined, with 60 assigned to the four-drug plan and 48 to standard care. More patients on the combined plan reached sugar regression during treatment, yet remission rates after stopping drugs were similar in both groups, at roughly two in five patients. The authors conclude the combined plan was not superior, and any true advantage would be modest at most.
pmc-13498624:
Mariana Henriques Ferreira and co-authors report four cases in a 2026 brief paper on side effects of a myeloma drug. Talquetamab works well against relapsed multiple myeloma, but it often distorts taste and dries the mouth, which can hurt nutrition and quality of life, and no proven supportive treatment existed.

The team treated four adults with photobiomodulation, a low-level light therapy, alongside the drug, using two wavelengths adjusted to each patient's symptoms. All four developed taste problems during treatment, ranging from partial loss to complete loss of taste. The series focuses on whether the light sessions were feasible and tolerable.
pmc-13498724:
Thaiza H T Fernandes and veterinary colleagues describe a zoo case in which a whole-body scan done for gut symptoms revealed severe bone disease in a red-handed howler monkey. The eight-year-old male, kept at a zoo in Recife, Brazil, had two days of foul watery diarrhoea, low energy, and poor appetite. Blood tests were normal and a stool check found no parasites, so imaging was arranged to look deeper.

Quantitative scans of the lower spine showed very low bone density, mineral loss, and weakened internal bone structure, read as metabolic bone disease found by chance. The team linked the condition to long-standing care problems, chiefly a badly unbalanced diet and too little sunlight in captivity. The case shows how scans ordered for one problem can expose hidden nutrition and housing failures in zoo animals.
pmc-13499024:
Buse Ceyda Öncel and others test whether parental tetracycline contact harms water flea offspring across generations. In 2026, the study exposes Daphnia magna parents to concentrations from 25 to 400 milligrams per litre for one to three days, choosing sublethal doses that still damage DNA. It then tests lives, reproduction, growth, and DNA damage in parents and offspring.

Contact impaired parental fertility, reduced lives and reproductive capacity, and stunted offspring growth, with shorter maximum body length in exposed generations. Animals appeared to recover from DNA damage, but repeated tetracycline use in water could raise concentrations and contact times for many organisms. The work highlights a One Health risk from antibiotic contamination.
pmc-13499624:
Bushra Rehman and eleven co-authors report outcomes for babies caught by newborn thyroid screening in Pakistan, in a 2026 study. Congenital hypothyroidism is the commonest congenital hormone disorder and a leading preventable cause of intellectual disability. Pakistan has no national screening program, though local incidence looks higher than the global average.

One Karachi hospital screened dried blood spots from 53,799 babies between 2019 and 2024. Forty cases were confirmed. Thirty-nine children were followed, most of them girls, nearly all of normal birth weight. Prolonged jaundice was the commonest early sign. By age three, growth measures sat within the normal range for nearly all. Of thirty-four children with developmental records, thirty-two developed normally. The single case of global delay was blamed on a separate suspected metabolic disorder. The authors argue for expanding screening nationwide.
pmc-13499724:
Ariel Weiming Dong and Mark Bounthavong evaluate two migraine prevention immune proteins against topiramate from a United States payer perspective. In 2026, the hybrid choice tree and Markov model simulates response in the first six months. It then follows patients over two years through states of on treatment, off treatment, and death, with costs in 2025 dollars.

Eptinezumab and erenumab cost about twenty-one thousand dollars each with similar quality-adjusted life years, yielding incremental ratios near 118,000 and 155,000 dollars per life year gained versus topiramate. Erenumab was eliminated by extended dominance, and eptinezumab became cost-effective only at a 150,000-dollar threshold in most models. Policymakers must weigh uncertain benefits against price when setting coverage.
pmc-13500824:
Baoji Lu leads a twelve-author team reporting a 2026 rat study of placental hydrolysate as a pain reliever. The extract mixes amino acids, peptides, and nucleotides from human placenta. It was tested in rats given capsaicin, the hot compound in chili peppers, which produces heightened pain sensitivity called hyperalgesia. The team measured pain responses with fine filaments. They imaged activity in spinal cord slices with a voltage-sensitive dye and stained tissue for two activity markers, c-Fos and phosphorylated PKC epsilon.

The extract reduced both primary and secondary hyperalgesia in step with the dose. It calmed overactive spinal cord neurons and lowered the two marker signals. With a low dose of the steroid dexamethasone, it matched a high steroid dose for pain relief while causing less weight loss. The authors propose the extract as an add-on that could let clinicians use lower steroid doses for inflammatory pain.
pmc-13501424:
Therapeutic antibodies carry chemical decorations that regulators want cataloged, but one tough region of the molecule resists the standard cutting enzyme. Nanna Eskesen and co-authors automate a multi-enzyme workaround in a 2026 methods paper.

Robots run digestion with up to three enzymes mounted on magnetic beads, each cutting the protein at different points. The overlapping pieces give the mass spectrometer a far clearer read than any single cut. In the stubborn region, the combined approach revealed six distinct attachments on an engineered site, including an unexpected process impurity later confirmed. Peptide overlap between methods stayed low, proving the pools truly complement each other. Automation makes the deep check routine rather than heroic.
pmc-13501624:
An-Qi Cai and others systematically review acupuncture for vessel mild mental impairment, a transitional state between normal aging and vessel memory loss. In 2026, the review searches six databases and two trial registries for randomized trials against sham acupuncture, drugs, or usual care, including add-on designs, and assesses bias with Cochrane tools. Forty-nine trials with 3,555 people met rules.

Acupuncture added to usual care improved Mini-Mental State scores by about two points across seven trials and Montreal Mental Assessment scores by two and a half points across five trials. Only one trial carried low risk of bias, most others raised some or high concerns, and only two found adverse reactions. The authors call acupuncture hopeful but limited by heterogeneity and trial quality.
pmc-13501724:
Ugur Sozlu leads a three-author team reporting a 2026 comparison of ChatGPT against expert physiotherapists at judging posture from photographs. Thirty-nine young adults who each had at least one visible posture flaw were photographed from the front, back, and side under controlled conditions. Two physiotherapists scored seven body regions on a form, and the same anonymized images went to ChatGPT-5.1 through its web interface on 15 and 16 November 2025, using a fixed prompt.

The two experts agreed almost perfectly, with kappa values from 0 point 84 to 0 point 94 across regions. ChatGPT matched the trunk at a kappa of 0 point 85 and the knee at 0 point 83 in the reported statistics, and it reached substantial agreement on head and neck position. Agreement sagged to moderate for the scapula, shoulder girdle, pelvis, and feet, where angular judgement matters. Percentage agreement ran from about 64 to about 92 percent. The authors see a support tool, not a replacement.
pmc-13501824:
Hui Qu leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 study of how blocked upper airways relate to face and jaw growth in children. The study enrolled 177 children with symptoms such as congestion, snoring, and mouth breathing between April 2024 and April 2025. Guardians completed the OSA-18 questionnaire, and cone-beam CT scans supplied craniofacial measurements covering jaw angles, facial heights, and tooth tilt. Children were grouped by age: three to six, seven to ten, and eleven to fourteen years.

The links changed with age. In the youngest group, mouth breathing scores rose alongside steeper jaw angles and taller faces, and every symptom tracked with front height. In the middle group, longer symptoms tied to jaw and tooth angles in mixed directions. In the oldest group, only an apnoea-to-lower-tooth link stood out. The authors identify ages three to ten as the sensitive window and urge age-tailored assessment.
pmc-13502924:
Kirtikar Ghorela leads a four-author team with a 2026 study testing whether ultrasound of the eye can track brain dysfunction in sepsis. Sepsis-associated encephalopathy clouds the brain without direct infection, and the optic nerve sheath diameter, measurable at the bedside, is proposed as a stand-in for raised pressure inside the skull. Eighty intensive care patients were treated at Indraprastha Apollo Hospitals in New Delhi. Enrolled between May 2021 and October 2022, they had sheath measurements and Glasgow Coma Scale scores recorded at diagnosis, 24 and 72 hours, day five, and any deterioration.

The two measures did not move together: no significant correlation appeared at time points, and baseline diameter ignored illness severity scores and length of stay alike. Twelve patients, 15 percent, died within 28 days. Non-survivors did average a wider baseline sheath, 5.35 versus 5.20 millimetres, yet splitting patients at a 5.5 millimetre threshold erased the mortality difference. The authors label the signal exploratory.
pmc-13503124:
Thorsten Rudroff wrote a 2026 letter about a hidden flaw in brain scan models that predict Alzheimer's disease. Alhasan and colleagues built a model on FDG-PET scans from 4,732 people in a large cohort. The model forecasts mental decline and conversion to Alzheimer's. Rudroff praises its rigor, including careful cross-checks and calibration.

His worry is sex balance. Women made up 52 percent of the healthy group but only about 42 to 46 percent of the impaired groups. Sex itself shifts brain glucose patterns, by one analysis far more than diagnosis does in some regions. If models never test sex as a factor, they may mistake sex effects for disease effects. He urges that check before the models guide care.
pmc-13503824:
Zhiyong Yang and seven colleagues build a system to spot faults in belt conveyor rollers, in a 2026 paper. Rollers carry heavy loads in harsh plants and fail often, which stops whole lines. Sound and shake data hold clues, but past smart tools read the signals too coarsely and adapted poorly.

Their system first reshapes the sound spectrum to sharpen the bands where faults speak loudest. A time-aware network then tracks patterns across long spans. A special layer with flexible curve functions reads tangled links between tones. Under real plant conditions the system reached fault accuracy above 81 percent. The authors say the design suits live plant use where loads and speeds shift.
pmc-13504624:
Luhao Han and co-authors lay out the plan for a study that will predict pregnancy problems caused by a failing placenta, in a protocol published in 2026. Such problems include blood pressure crises, slow fetal growth, early birth, and stillbirth. Current screening based on background risk alone is weak.

More than twelve hundred women at an Australian hospital joined at three points in pregnancy. Each visit gathers clinical data, ultrasound and blood flow measures, and stored blood and urine samples. Separate prediction models will be built for each stage and tested by cross checks. Most participants had delivered by the time of writing. The authors aim for models that also guide delivery timing.
pmc-13504824:
Mobina Karimi leads a team listening to Iranian teens with ADHD and their parents about treatment, in a 2026 interview study. Care mixes drugs with therapy, yet sticking with either can falter. Lived experience in non-Western settings is rarely recorded.

Nine teens aged twelve to sixteen and ten parents from Tehran clinics took part in long interviews. Parents stressed barriers: drug side effects, late diagnosis, and the grind of keeping to schedules. They also praised better focus and trust in their providers. Teens weighed gains like sharper concentration against harms like stigma and tiredness. Both sides valued combined care, though teens prized independence while parents prized system support. The authors call for care shaped to each family and culture.
pmc-13505024:
Maria Llaine J. Callanta and Patrick R. Relacion chart research on rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease in Southeast Asia, in a 2026 bibliometric study. These strep-driven conditions still disable many people in poorer settings, yet the region's research footprint had never been mapped.

A database search found 333 papers from 1900 to 2024. Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and the Philippines led regional output, but the region still supplies under 2.5 percent of world papers on the topic. Only a fifth of papers reported funding. Topics clustered on diagnosis, surgery, registries, and blood-thinning care. Themes like social drivers, cost value, and patient-centered care were thin. Output tracked with country wealth measures and foreign co-authorship, which the authors say deserves investment.
pmc-13505124:
Samet Can Demirci and co-authors studied 226 young inpatients treated for substance use disorders, asking whether remembered childhood ADHD symptoms relate to how severe their addiction had become. They also tested whether time perspective, meaning how people view past, present, and future, helps explain that link. Participants were aged eighteen to twenty-five.

The team measured childhood and adult ADHD symptoms, five time-perspective scales, distress, and addiction severity with standard questionnaires. Patients whose main problem was stimulants scored higher on childhood ADHD measures and on addiction severity than the cannabis or pregabalin groups. In their models, four time-perspective scales carried part of the link, and the model explained a large share of severity differences. Because all measures came from one point in time, the authors caution against reading the pattern as cause and effect.
pmc-13505324:
Floriane Etheve and colleagues describe a 56-year-old woman with widespread melanoma who developed a rare immune side effect one week after her first combined immunotherapy cycle. She arrived with fever, an itchy rash, and loss of vision in both eyes. Eye examination showed fluid lifting the retina in both eyes, matching a Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada-like syndrome, where the immune system attacks pigment-bearing cells.

Spinal fluid testing confirmed inflammation around the brain, and a skin sample showed the rash pattern with fewer pigment cells than normal. Doctors stopped the immunotherapy and gave high-dose steroids followed by methotrexate, and she improved quickly. Over two and a half years later her scans still show cancer remission with no further immunotherapy. The authors use the case to stress fast, joint care across specialties to protect sight, and they note such pigment-directed reactions may mark a strong anti-cancer response.
pmc-13507024:
Jung-Eun Kim, Byoung-Cheol Lee, and Byung-Chang Suh study, in 2026 cell work, how a membrane protein called TMEM16E helps cells survive in acid conditions. The protein shuffles membrane fats and also acts as an ion channel. The team tracked a cell drinking process, macropinocytosis, where cells gulp fluid and membrane in large bubbles.

At a strongly acid level, uptake tied to the marker annexin V rose, while total bubble counts stayed flat across acid levels. Sudden acid exposure quickly shut down protein activity, and calcium inside cells cleared faster. Cells with the protein grew and survived better under acid stress. The pathway may protect membrane health in tumors and muscle disease.
pmc-13507124:
Liangjie Niu and co-authors search in 2026 for genes tied to oxidative stress that mark the start and progress of diabetic eye disease. The disease grows through many interacting factors, and the role of such genes was unclear. The team combined two public data sets on the disease with a list of nearly one thousand stress related genes, then used network and learning methods to narrow the field.

Four genes passed checks across data sets and scored well as diagnostic markers. A combined score built on them predicted the disease well. The genes clustered in pathways for protein building and RNA processing, and they linked to shifts in certain immune cell types in the eye tissue.
pmc-13507224:
Fabien Garces and co-authors show how cellar treatments change the vitamin content of grape must and shape the wine, in a 2026 study. Fining agents clear the must, and yeast foods feed the ferment. The team tracked B vitamins through these steps and into the yeast's work.

Bentonite and carbon fining stripped several B vitamins from the must, while yeast based foods gave some back. Vitamin B1 stood out: must rich in it fermented harder and made more aroma compounds. Adding B1 back to a bentonite treated must restored the aroma profile of the untreated batch. The findings name a hidden lever in wine style.
pmc-13508124:
Gil and co-authors reported a 2026 food allergy study on making cow's milk proteins less allergenic by binding them to plant polyphenols. Casein, the main milk protein, triggers IgE antibodies in allergic patients and can cause life threatening reactions. Changing casein's shape could hide the spots those antibodies grab.

Gil tested the bonded formula against blood serum from patients allergic to cow's milk proteins in preclinical assays. IgE binding fell significantly, though the size of the drop varied between patients. Computer modelling showed polyphenols sitting on antibody binding spots across three casein types, with fewer such spots on the fourth type. A related milk protein also responded well, and the authors argue the approach could support personalised oral immunotherapy.
pmc-13508224:
Michael Gonzalez leads a ten-author team hunting the gene locus that sets potassium levels inside sheep red blood cells, in 2026 work. Some sheep carry low potassium cells and others high, and the trait passes down as if controlled by one locus. Genome scans across sheep pointed to a large repeated stretch of a gene family called MYADM. The repeat appears in sheep, goats, cattle, and pigs, but not in horses.

Closer mapping in more sheep tied the trait most strongly to a handful of genes within that repeat. Protein models suggest one family member can grip a potassium transporter and hold its control section in the off position. That offers a route by which the repeat could set cell potassium. The same gene has been linked to human blood pressure, which widens the interest in this sheep finding.
pmc-13508324:
Tsung-Yang Lee and six co-authors hunt factors that predict long hospital stays and sickness after weight-loss surgery, in 2026 work. The study reviewed 476 patients who had one of two operations, a gastric band or a gastric bypass, between 2022 and 2023. A stay over three days counted as prolonged. Statistical models weighed patient traits and care details together to find independent predictors.

Just under a quarter of patients stayed beyond three days, and the typical stay was exactly three days. Longer anesthesia time was the strongest predictor of a long stay. Higher fluid rates during surgery, asthma, and post-surgery sickness each added independent risk. The type of operation itself did not predict stay length once other factors counted. Sickness struck nearly half of patients, more often women and younger patients. The authors advise tightening anesthesia time, fluids, and sickness control to speed discharge.
pmc-13508824:
Chenglong Yao and co-authors built a prediction model in 2026 for a dangerous heart rhythm that newly strikes people with long-term heart failure. The rhythm, atrial fibrillation, may grow out of both body-wide swelling and poor sugar handling. The team joined two cheap blood markers, one for each force, inside a learning model.

Records of nearly five thousand patients from two hospitals trained the model, and a fresh group tested it. The best of nine methods scored well at home and fairly abroad. Each marker's risk rose in its own bent shape past a threshold, and the pair together sorted patients better. One marker seemed to carry much of the other's link to the rhythm. The authors offer the pair as a low-cost early warning.
pmc-13509424:
Mingliang Gong and Shuanghong Chen study how depressive tendency changes the place of one's mother in the self. Published in 2026, the work starts from a pattern in East Asia, where close others such as mothers are often folded into the self-concept. People with strong depressive tendencies draw that boundary more narrowly.

Across three experiments, people with low depressive tendency recalled mother linked items better than items linked to others, an effect the authors call the mother-reference effect. People with high depressive tendency showed no such gain, or a weaker and later one. Brain wave measures told the same story, with a delayed response. The results suggest low mood shrinks the self's reach.
pmc-13514924:
Aliki Karkala leads a ten-author team investigating morning headaches in obstructive sleep apnoea, in a 2026 retrospective study of 3,227 adults treated at a sleep clinic between 2013 and 2023. Waking headaches are a recognised apnoea symptom. The researchers split patients by headache frequency, comparing those with at least one episode weekly against the rest.

About thirty-five percent reported frequent morning headaches. Simple comparisons tied them to female sex, larger waist size, worse oxygen dips, sleepiness, and insomnia complaints. A tighter analysis of patients with complete sleep-study data reshaped the picture. Being female, waist size, and the rate of brief brain arousals during sleep predicted frequent headaches, while standard breathing-severity measures did not. Karkala's team argues that fragmented sleep, more than apnoea severity itself, drives these headaches, especially in women.
pmc-13515824:
Madalina-Ianca Suba leads a nine-author team asking whether past COVID-19 leaves a lasting inflammatory mark in people living with HIV, in a 2026 retrospective study. Modern therapy holds HIV undetectable, yet low-grade inflammation often persists and drives later illness. The team reviewed 286 adults on treatment at one centre from 2023 to 2025. They compared those with and without a documented past SARS-CoV-2 infection, and repeated the check in the 231 patients whose virus stayed fully suppressed.

Patients with past COVID-19 carried clearly higher levels of several inflammation markers, from C-reactive protein to interleukin-6 and cell-ratio scores. Among the suppressed group, high inflammation also tracked lower CD4 counts, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and fatty liver. Past infection stayed an independent predictor after adjustment. Suba's team stresses that a records study shows association, not cause. They point to long-term host and metabolic factors as the deeper drivers worth prospective study.
pmc-13516324:
Li and colleagues report a 2026 study of nanoparticles that both burn tumors with light and block their spread, tested in bowel cancer models.  The team linked a light-sensitive dye to a peptide that blocks uPA, an enzyme cancers use to invade tissue, and the linked molecules assembled themselves into nanoparticles.

The particles gathered in tumors, produced reactive oxygen under light, and kept the enzyme-blocking action of the peptide, which normally clears from the body too fast to help. In mice, they shrank implanted tumors and curbed lung spread, the pattern this cancer follows when it travels.  Packaging a short-lived peptide with a light drug makes the pair attack growth and spread together.
pmc-13517024:
Augustine Saiz and co-authors test whether a peptide adds anything to a gel injection for damaged sheep knees, in a 2026 study. Removing part of the meniscus sets a knee on the road to osteoarthritis, and hyaluronic acid gels are a standard cushioning injection. A proline-rich peptide, P6, was hoped to boost the gel's repair effects.

Sheep knees were left intact, injured only, or injured and injected with gel alone or gel plus peptide over the first month. Three months after surgery, scans and tissue analysis showed the gel itself improved the bone patterns under the cartilage. The peptide, however, added no significant benefit on the main comparison. Honest null results like this save clinics money and steer developers to strengthen the gel rather than decorate it.
pmc-13517224:
Noszczyk-Nowak and colleagues published a 2026 report on heart rhythm ablation in dogs in Poland. Fast, stubborn heart rhythms can weaken a dog's heart muscle over time. Catheter ablation burns the tiny faulty spot through a vessel, sparing open surgery. The procedure remains rare in veterinary care, offered at few centers.

The center performed fourteen ablations across dogs of many breeds and sizes. Half the dogs arrived with heart muscle weakened by the fast rhythm. Three dogs needed a second procedure to finish the job fully. No major or lasting complications followed any of the cases treated. Newer three-dimensional mapping systems joined the toolkit over the years covered. The cases span both upper and lower heart chamber rhythm faults.
pmc-13517424:
Kate S Rawlings, Olga Kim, and Anne Huvos argue in a 2026 article that one flu treaty already solves the vaccine-equity problem COVID-19 exposed. Rich countries bought early and deep while poorer nations waited months, and the delay prolonged spread and bred variants. The Pandemic Influenza Preparedness Framework works differently: binding advance deals hand the World Health Organization a real-time slice of world flu vaccine output.

Allocation then follows public-health risk and need, not wealth. The authors say this design attacks both axes of unfairness at once, who gets doses and when. No country queues behind richer buyers, so vaccine reaches the hotspots where it cuts transmission fastest. Equity and efficiency, usually traded off, here point the same way. Rawlings and colleagues offer the framework as a working model for future pandemic deals beyond influenza, having operated quietly since long before COVID-19.
pmc-13517524:
Roa Al-Osaimi leads a ten-author study of drug resistance in newly diagnosed HIV patients in Saudi Arabia in a 2026 paper. Resistance passed on at infection can blunt first-line therapy, so baseline gene testing guides drug choice. Three hospitals contributed six hundred fourteen untreated patients diagnosed in 2023 and 2024, whose viral genes for three drug targets were sequenced and checked against a standard database.

The patients were mostly men aged twenty-five to forty-four, and most arrived with high virus levels. The virus itself was strikingly diverse, led by subtype C and two recombinant and G forms. Raw mutation counts looked alarming, above eighty percent in some genes, yet nearly all were harmless subtype quirks. Mutations that truly matter sat near three percent overall, and none touched the newest drug class. Al-Osaimi's team backs continued baseline testing to catch any rise early.
pmc-13518224:
Hao Zhang and nine co-authors study spin waves in a quantum magnet with two non-perturbative methods in a paper from 2026. In ordered magnets where excitations interact strongly, standard approximations fail to explain the broad signals seen in neutron tests. The team examine a triangular-lattice magnet held in a one-third plateau state by a magnetic field.

Two methods, one exact within a trimmed space and one based on matrix product states, agree with each other and with neutron data. They confirm bound pairs of spin waves and show that the odd broad signal is a resonance where a bound pair mixes with free pairs. The approach should transfer to other magnets.
pmc-13518824:
Takao Yoshida and co-authors report a 2026 test of whether deep-sea water pumped to shore can reveal which fish live below. Checking deep-sea life with nets or cameras takes much effort and gear. DNA shed into water offers a simpler route, but it was not clear if a long pipe trip to a shore station would damage that signal.

The team compared pumped water with water caught near the intake in two Japanese bays, and checked results against baited cameras. Both methods found a like range of fish, and the depths of those fish matched the intake depth. The pumped route found fewer kinds in one bay, yet the overlap was large. Pumped samples can thus serve as a workable way to track deep-sea fish.
pmc-13518924:
Mingfu Tian and a large team explain in 2026 why interferon drugs, stars in lab antiviral tests, fall short once a real infection is underway. Given before infection, interferons protected well. Given later, they failed to help while causing harsh side effects, and the team's sleuthing points at lactic acid made by the host itself.

Lactic acid blunted interferon signaling through a SIRT1 route, helped viruses evade, and teamed with interferon to overactivate the NF-kB inflammation switch, feeding cytokine storms. Pairing interferon with a licensed lactate-blocking drug undid the suppression and calmed inflammation, working even in late-stage infection. Tian's team frames lactic acid as a broad-spectrum antiviral target.
pmc-13519024:
Yongqiang Zhang and four colleagues rank five coastal marine pollution monitoring systems in 2026 using expert judgment and robust decision methods. Choosing among underwater sensor networks, cabled observatories, mobile platforms, and satellites means weighing detection power, coverage, cost, sturdiness, and energy limits at once. A panel of 120 experts supplied judgments, with 110 responses passing consistency checks.

Detection capability earned the highest weight at 0.29, followed by coverage at 0.24. The underwater sensor network ranked first with a closeness score of 0.56, ahead of the cabled observatory and mobile platforms. Shifting weights by 20 percent barely moved the order, and score-jitter simulations stayed tight, supporting a stable verdict.
pmc-13519424:
Padma Panni and colleagues tested a combined gum and braces treatment for patients whose front teeth had drifted forward as gum disease weakened their support. Published in 2026, the study treated 28 people with 56 enlarged upper front teeth and horizontal bone defects. Care paired braces with a fiber-cutting gum procedure, then used guided tissue regrowth surgery to rebuild bone shape where defects were angular.

X-ray checks showed new bone filling in, while gum attachment loss and pocket depth improved markedly from start to finish. The authors conclude that moving teeth inward after the fiber procedure can reshape bone defects into a form where regrowth surgery works better. Readers gain a staged recipe for saving drifted front teeth, with the caveat that the group was small and follow-up details remain thin.
pmc-13519524:
Samuel Stenz, Franziska Zúñiga, Kornelia Kotkowski, and Carla Meyer-Massetti test a new tool for home care nurses in Switzerland, in a research paper from 2026. The tool checks how well patients understand their own medicines. Nurses at two home care firms helped plan how to bring it into daily work.

Small nurse teams then tried the tool with patients and shared their views. Barriers included weak talk skills with patients, unclear roles in team care, and a long instruction manual. Nurses who saw clear benefit for patients were more willing to use it. The authors say short, clear guides and defined roles would help wider use.
pmc-13519924:
Antonio Licheri and eight colleagues published a sensor study in two thousand twenty-six on improving biochar for electrochemical biosensors. Biochar is a carbon-rich char made from plant waste. It can carry the catcher molecules a sensor needs, but its messy surface lets proteins stick and block signals.

Working with char from spent coffee grounds, the team added chemical groups step by step. A click reaction attached a molecular spacer that holds catcher molecules out into the liquid. Tests confirmed each step of the build. A test enzyme sensor on the new surface resisted fouling better and measured more cleanly than one on plain char. The authors present the spacer design as the key gain.
pmc-13520224:
Cevher İlhan Cevheri leads a ten-author field trial in 2026 pitting organic against chemical fertilizers on cotton under semi-arid conditions at Harran University. Cotton supports the textile industry worldwide, and growers lean on both fertilizer families. Plots drawn by lot got differing doses, and leaves were checked for pigments, protein, carbohydrates, and antioxidant defenses.

The top chemical dose, 300 kilograms of DAP per hectare, gave the highest chlorophyll and protein values. Heavy farmyard manure, at 100 tonnes per hectare, led instead on carbohydrates and antioxidants. Signs of membrane damage stayed fairly stable across treatments. Cevheri's team advises blending organic amendments with targeted mineral fertilizer for healthier plants and steadier yield.
pmc-13520424:
Ayşe Sena Şişman and colleagues chart in 2026 yeast bloodstream infections in intensive care by their likely source, a view missing from earlier literature. Breakthrough infections that appear despite antifungal treatment received special attention.

The study included 141 adults whose blood grew Candida more than two days after intensive care admission. Abdominal sources and primary infections each made up roughly four in ten cases, while line-related cases made up about one quarter. Feeding and steroid patterns differed by source, whereas death rates at two and four weeks did not. Breakthrough cases clustered in the abdominal group and arrived with higher severity scores.
pmc-13521024:
Monika Lamba Saini and colleagues compare in 2026 digital slide file formats from two scanner brands for cancer tissue images, asking whether format conversion alone changes image analysis results. Hospitals mix scanner brands, so hidden format effects could undermine automated readings.

Ten colon cancer and ten lung cancer slides were scanned on both systems at the stated magnification. Converted files stayed highly similar to their native versions in pixels, colour and algorithm predictions. Native files from the rival scanner differed widely in size and colour, reflecting hardware plus format together. Small numbers make findings exploratory, while the authors anticipate a shared enterprise standard for pathology images.
pmc-13521824:
Zheng-ri Zhu and co-authors lay out a behavior-based support plan for people living with ulcerative colitis, a gut disease that flares and calms in cycles. Daily self-care is key, yet many support programs lack a steady theory of behavior change. Their 2026 paper builds a plan on a well-known behavior wheel frame.

Five habits anchor the plan: taking medicine, managing food, watching symptoms, handling stress, and keeping follow-up visits. Each habit is checked against what a person can do, what chances they get, and what drives them. Support steps and feedback loops then adapt the plan over time. The frame is still a concept, the authors stress, and needs real-world testing before clinic use.
pmc-13521924:
Yuki Ashino and Noriyuki Kida follow in 2026 the careers of 179 Japanese college decathletes from 2000 to 2024. Each athlete held scores for at least three school years. The study tests a trade-off rule. Gains in some skills may cost gains in others over time.

Path groups split athletes into high, upper-middle, lower-middle and low total score bands. Speed, jump and throw scores rose with total points in gaining groups. Running stamina showed little tie with total growth. A repeat check on cleaner data matched that pattern. Coaches may gain more from speed and power work when total score is the goal.
pmc-13522024:
Hung Chang and colleagues test in 2026 a blood protein as a risk flag for lymphoma patients with low standard scores. The protein is beta2-microglobulin. The rival flags are tumour bulk and a liver enzyme. Cohort data came from one hospital for diagnoses in 2015 to 2019.

The full cohort held 523 patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. A total of 238 patients sat in the low score band. Full data allowed class calls for 234 of them. Median age was 64 years. High risk meant tumours over the size cut-off or enzyme over its limit. Survival splits then judge which flag finds true poor outlook in a low-risk group.
pmc-13522124:
Emanuele Bizzi and a large team of co-authors report a case where one disease seemed to turn into another in a 2026 paper. Their patient, a 42-year-old woman, had years of recurring pericarditis, inflammation around the heart, that depended on steroids and resisted standard drugs. A drug blocking interleukin-1 kept her fully well for nearly thirty months.

As the drug was tapered, she relapsed hard, and this time wider signs appeared: mouth and genital ulcers, skin lumps, and a positive pathergy test. Together they met the criteria for Behçet's disease, a body-wide vessel inflammation. The authors argue the two conditions share one IL-1-driven root, and that tapering unmasked the fuller disease.
pmc-13522224:
Xiu-yun Chen and co-authors surveyed operating room nurses in 2026 about moral sensitivity, the ability to spot the ethical side of care choices. They questioned 579 nurses from eighteen top hospitals in Jiangsu Province, China. Alongside moral sensitivity, they measured how nurses saw their work setting and how clear their role felt. A profile method sorted nurses into hidden groups.

Two groups emerged: one lower in moral sensitivity, at about forty-three percent, and one higher. Male nurses, older nurses, and those with mid-length experience were more likely in the high group. Clearer roles also linked to higher sensitivity. The authors urge ethics training aimed at younger, less seasoned nurses, plus clearer role definitions.
pmc-13522424:
Biruk Shalmeno Tusa, Rosa Alati, Getinet Ayano, and Berihun Dachew investigate depression in mothers around pregnancy and birth in a 2026 study. They ask whether it relates to how the children later perform at school. Linked health and education records from New South Wales supplied the data. National literacy and numeracy results in grades three, five, and seven were checked against minimum standards.

Children whose mothers had a perinatal depressive disorder were more likely to fall below the standard in reading, spelling, writing, and grammar, though no clear link appeared for numeracy. Patterns were strongest for depression during pregnancy, while depression after birth related mainly to reading and writing. The authors argue for earlier identification and treatment during pregnancy to support later learning.
pmc-13522524:
Sinan Wang and co-authors build a drought prediction system for the Ordos region of Inner Mongolia in a 2026 study. Ordos is an important mining and economic area that suffers frequent drought. A regional comprehensive drought index was first constructed for 2001 to 2020 from temperature, rainfall, vegetation, soil moisture, land use, and elevation, using an established drought measure as the reference.

Three deep learning models were then trained to forecast the new index, using data through 2016 for training and later years for testing. A hybrid model combining convolutional and memory networks performed best, with clearly lower errors than either model alone. The index matched known drought conditions and tracked standard measures closely. The work offers a technical reference for drought monitoring in the region.
pmc-13522624:
Joyonta Kumar Nath and colleagues compare deep learning models for reading sign language alphabets from images in a 2026 study. Recognizing single-letter hand signs is a basic step toward accessible communication tools for people with hearing or speech impairment. Four pretrained image networks were tested under one protocol on a benchmark American Sign Language alphabet dataset.

The largest modern network reached the highest accuracy, just under ninety-nine point nine percent, with the other three close behind. Transfer learning, meaning reuse of networks pretrained on general images, proved effective at capturing fine hand shape differences. The comparison offers practical guidance for choosing models when building reliable, scalable sign language interpretation systems for real-world use.
pmc-13522924:
Hanna Ziąbska and co-authors report a 2026 case of stroke care that added a brain-support drug very early. Their patient was an 88-year-old woman with weakness on her right side and loss of speech from a blocked brain artery. She already lived with fair disability before the stroke struck.

She first got a clot-busting drug through a vein, then a procedure that pulled the clot out in three passes and fully reopened the artery. Even so, she showed no quick gain. The team then started a short course of cerebrolysin, a mix of small proteins meant to limit harm and aid early recovery. The case shows one team's timing and dose choices for study by others.
pmc-13523224:
Li-bing Liang and co-authors pool trial evidence on exercise for type 2 diabetes in a 2026 systematic review with network and dose-response analyses. One hundred twenty-seven randomized trials with nearly nine thousand people compared eight exercise types for their effect on glycated hemoglobin, a long-term blood sugar marker. Blood factors released during exercise, called exerkines, were studied as well.

A combined mind-body and resistance program ranked highest for lowering the marker, followed closely by high-intensity interval training. Benefit rose steeply up to a moderate weekly dose and then plateaued, with most gain reached well before the plateau. Exercise types showed distinct exerkine patterns, with interval training raising one protective factor and resistance work tending to lower inflammatory factors. The authors advise aiming for the effective dose rather than ever more exercise.
pmc-13523324:
Martha M Lyke leads a team tracking how colony management changed the genetics of captive rhesus macaques in a 2026 study. Macaques are central to biomedical research, and mixing between Indian and Chinese origins can affect study suitability. Whole exome sequencing covered four hundred eighty-eight founding and colony-born animals at a large United States primate center, alongside targeted sequencing of immune genes in more than a thousand animals.

Founder analysis found one Chinese-origin animal and several dozen admixed animals, with structure reflecting their source centers. Chinese ancestry in the colony fell over time, while overall diversity stayed high. Immune gene management reduced a virus-protective variant that can distort research, without sacrificing immune diversity. Genome scans also found many regions where allele frequencies shifted, suggesting short-term adaptation under captive conditions.
pmc-13523424:
Faris Alotaibi and co-authors examine how frailty interacts with patient traits to shape hospital safety incidents in older adults in a 2026 study. More than one hundred fifty-eight thousand acute admissions with a recorded frailty score were analyzed. Safety incidents were defined as staff-reported events with potential to cause harm, and frailty was scored at the emergency department with a standard clinical scale.

Risk of at least one incident rose with frailty. Statistical interactions appeared between frailty and age, emergency waiting time, and length of stay. In the final multivariable model, only the interaction with length of stay improved the fit. The authors conclude that frailty assessment can help flag patients at higher risk of reported incidents, while stressing that the length-of-stay interaction does not prove causation.
pmc-13523524:
Omer Boshra Mohamedsalih Shmed and Waleed Abdelateif Hussein present a 2026 pilot case-control study in Sudan on immune gene variants in patients with end-stage kidney disease and hepatitis B infection. People on maintenance dialysis face higher risk of lasting hepatitis B infection. Variants in two cytokine genes, one promoting and one restraining inflammation, might influence that course.

The study compared 31 patients with both kidney failure and hepatitis B against 37 with hepatitis B alone. Genotyping used a primer-based PCR method, and blood cytokine levels were measured by ELISA. Genotype frequencies for both genes did not differ significantly between groups, nor did levels of the first cytokine. Levels of the second, IL-10, were higher in the kidney group, and within that group one genotype carried higher levels. Small size limits firm conclusions.
pmc-13523624:
Taryn Lubbers and four co-authors reviewed trials of green tea extract on aging faces in a 2026 systematic review. Demand for natural anti-aging products is rising, and the extract's strong antioxidant action makes it a candidate against sun damage. The team followed standard review methods and kept only controlled trials that used the extract's key compound on facial aging, not tea drinks.

From 481 papers, seven trials qualified. All five that measured elasticity found some gain. Four of five wrinkle studies found fewer fine lines. Effects on redness, irritation, and dryness were mixed. Tone, texture, glow, and firmness also improved in reports. The authors call the promise real but the evidence base thin and uneven.
pmc-13524424:
Francesco Cecere and others present, in a 2026 methods paper, scGraphVerse, a software workflow for mapping gene networks in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Such data are sparse, wide, and noisy, making network reconstruction hard. Tools rarely combine several data sets or support thorough follow-up.

The R package joins five algorithms with shared inputs and outputs, plus tools for group detection, pathway enrichment, and mining of past papers. It supports early, late, and joint ways for merging data sets. Benchmarks on test data showed model-based methods doing well with small samples, while a joint forest method did best as networks and data sets grew. A blood cell case study found regulatory groups backed by past papers across donors. The package is shared through Bioconductor.
pmc-13524724:
Marta Paszkiewicz-Gawron and co-authors join two plant alcohols using sound and light in a 2026 paper. The starting alcohol comes from wood like plant matter. Pairing two of its units makes a product valued by drug and chemical makers. Older routes need harsh heat, pressure, or toxic helpers.

Sound waves plus light drove the pairing at room conditions instead. Plant based and zinc catalysts each reached full conversion in the tests. The pair product formed with high selectivity and stayed stable over a day. Tuning the sound energy steered which products formed, the team reports.
pmc-13525024:
Martin Korpan leads a large Austrian team in a 2026 real-world analysis of treatment for resectable stomach and esophagus junction cancers with a DNA repair defect called mismatch-repair deficiency. These tumors carry a favorable prognosis yet gain little from standard chemotherapy, while immune checkpoint drugs looked promising in early studies. Optimal combinations and nonoperative paths were unclear.

The multicenter study included 55 patients split among chemotherapy, combined chemo-immunotherapy, immunotherapy alone, or surgery first, and 82 percent ultimately had resection. Complete disappearance of tumor in removed tissue occurred in about a quarter of chemotherapy-based groups but in all five resected patients given dual immunotherapy. Among patients managed without surgery, one third reached clinical complete response. Responses clustered with a high PD-L1 score.
pmc-13526524:
Cheon and colleagues find the sensor that lets a worm taste and reject a green tea compound. Their 2026 paper studies epigallocatechin gallate, the main catechin in green tea, and shows the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans actively avoids it. The work identifies both the receptor and the nerve cells involved, answering how plant chemicals shape nematode behaviour at molecular level.

Only catechins carrying a galloyl group triggered strong avoidance. The response ran through the ASH pain-sensing neurons and depended on a receptor called SRXA-7. Worms lacking it showed specific avoidance defects and blunted calcium responses in those neurons. Restoring the receptor just in ASH rescued both. Avoidance also varied across species and wild strains, and shifted with feeding state and prior experience. The authors identify SRXA-7 as a dedicated sensory receptor for this class of plant compounds.
pmc-13527224:
Ruth Ann Marrie and a large team compare two data sources for tracking mental illness in home care and long-term care in Canada, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. One source is billing and hospital records; the other is a standard assessment form filled in for each resident. The team linked both sources across three provinces for care given between twenty twelve and twenty twenty-three.

Depression was the most common illness in both care settings. The assessment forms always gave lower rates than the billing records.
