The two sources agreed only to a fair degree for depression and anxiety. Younger age, dementia, and more doctor visits made disagreement more likely. The authors warn that counts of mental illness depend on which source a study uses.
pmc-13527324:
Forte and a team of colleagues measured in twenty twenty-six how many Italian patients have difficult-to-manage axial spondyloarthritis. The condition is chronic spinal inflammation. A new consensus label marks patients who still suffer despite proper treatment, and a stricter label marks treatment-refractory cases.

Two specialist centers studied two hundred fifty-two patients. Sixteen, about six percent, met the difficult-to-manage definition, and eight met the refractory one. These patients had higher disease activity scores, more spinal pain, and worse self-rated health. Fibromyalgia, eye inflammation called uveitis, and current anti-inflammatory drug use were independently linked to the label. A comparison with an Argentine cohort added consistent links to psoriasis, smoking, and structural spine damage. The authors describe the hard cases as multifactorial.
pmc-13527524:
Saikat Mandal and two co-authors mine drug safety reports for skin side effects of a class of cancer antibodies, in a 2026 study. The drugs bind two targets at once and pull T cells onto cancer cells. Rash and severe skin harm are less charted for them than other side effects. The team searched United States and Canadian report banks from 2016 onward, covering ten drugs grouped by target.

Among exposed reports in the United States bank, about six percent noted a skin event, and severe skin reactions were rare. No clear class-wide excess of severe reactions stood up after matching by disease. One drug, aimed at a skin-linked target, drew far more skin reports than the rest. Another showed a hint of very early skin onset on thin data. The authors urge target-aware skin watch in care.
pmc-13527924:
C. Vanlalhriata and nine colleagues document a 2026 shift in malaria patterns in Mizoram, a state in northeast India bordering Bangladesh and Myanmar. Using national program data plus health-center records from Mamit district for 2021 to 2025, the team mapped cases over time and place against environmental factors.

The share of infections caused by Plasmodium vivax climbed from 23 percent in 2021 to 47 percent in 2024, overtaking the historically dominant falciparum species. In Mamit district vivax caused most cases in 2025, including the great majority among children under five, and it circulated all year rather than peaking with the monsoon. Because drug-resistant vivax has been reported in Myanmar, the authors urge urgent drug efficacy testing.
pmc-13528024:
Husein Mufaddal Hassanali and six colleagues recount a 2026 case from Tanzania of many complications in a row after heart bypass surgery. The patient was a 63-year-old man with triple-vessel heart disease. He also had diabetes, high blood pressure, obesity, and asthma. His chest wound split open after a fall on day six. Emergency surgery reclosed the sternum with a reinforced technique.

He then developed severe nerve and muscle weakness from critical illness. Later a deep chest infection with Pseudomonas bacteria set in. Care included long antibiotics, repeated washouts, suction wound therapy, wire removal, and a chest muscle flap. Heart rhythm trouble, kidney injury, and fluid on the lung also appeared. After eight months of team care and rehab, he healed fully and regained function. The authors stress early action and teamwork.
pmc-13528224:
Sreenija Yarlagadda and co-authors test whether moving a saliva gland before radiation still helps when the beams are protons, in a study from 2026. Dry mouth is a lasting harm of head and neck radiation. Surgeons can move one gland under the chin to dodge the beam path. Proton therapy already spares tissue with care, so the added gain was in doubt.

The team reviewed seventeen patients with throat cancer who had the move. They rebuilt each plan as if the gland had stayed in place. The moved gland took a far lower dose in the reworked plans. Target coverage and doses to other organs stayed the same. Moved plans also met the gland dose cap far more often. The authors say the old surgery still earns its place beside proton beams.
pmc-13528524:
Daniël W. Groefsema and five colleagues watch catalyst heat from inside a methane reaction in a 2026 study. The reaction joins methane into ethylene, a prized building block. It runs hot and gives off fierce heat, which has stalled factory use. The team used glowing particles as tiny thermometers during operation. The method is called luminescence thermometry.

Even without reactive gas flowing, catalyst spots ran nearly 250 degrees Celsius above the oven setting. Heat from the reaction itself pushed local readings further. Airflow, bed size, and catalyst amount all swayed the readings strongly. Oven dials, in short, hide the real working heat. The authors say such inside views are vital for taming the process. Better heat control could finally make methane coupling practical at scale.
pmc-13528724:
Eyüp Sari and colleagues checked whether emergency transport worsens inflammation in newborns with breathing distress. Published in 2026, the retrospective study reviewed 117 infants with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome moved to a tertiary intensive care unit between 2019 and 2023. Transport complications can harm fragile newborns, so the team compared inflammation markers before and after transfer.

Babies averaged about thirty-five and a half weeks of gestation at birth. About two fifths were intubated, two fifths needed breathing machines during transport, one eighth received CPR, and about one ninth died. Ratios tracking neutrophils, platelets, and lymphocytes showed no meaningful change across transport. The authors read the stability as a sign that careful stabilization during transfer limited inflammatory harm. Readers get reassurance for transport teams, with retrospective limits noted.
pmc-13528824:
Johnson and co-authors survey how Australian mental health clinicians actually use general-purpose AI tools at work, in a 2026 mixed methods study. Little was known about how these off-the-shelf systems fit into daily therapy practice. The team first interviewed 12 clinicians between June and August 2025 about uses, benefits, limits, and workplace rules. Those findings then shaped a national survey that drew 278 responses.

The survey tracked how often clinicians use AI for client-facing work versus admin and support tasks, and what predicts daily use. It also recorded perceived usefulness and concerns about safety and governance. Together, the two phases give a grounded picture of a fast-spreading practice that policy has yet to catch up with.
pmc-13529324:
Manuel Rodriguez-Concepcion and co-authors argue in a 2026 review that metabolic cues drive plant plastids to change type. Plastids range from green, sugar-making chloroplasts to pigment-storing chromoplasts. Ripening fruit makes that switch in full view. Gene programs rewrite the plastid contents during the change.

The triggers of that rewrite were poorly understood. Using tomato as the model case, the review lines up the event order. Molecular, structural, and metabolic steps unfold in sequence. Engineered systems that force the switch add proof. The authors place metabolic signals, not genes alone, in the driver seat.
pmc-13530024:
Marie Jönsson comments on a study of nursing students mentored by nurses fresh from graduation themselves, in a 2026 commentary. With a world shortage pushing new graduates into mentor roles early, their worth needed a test. The study under review spoke with twelve students in an Australian program. Their young mentors, barely past the classroom, left a strong mark.

Students felt they belonged: the near-peer mentors built safe, warm rooms where questions cost nothing. The teaching held up too, with joint work, room to reflect, and independence handed over in steps. Confidence, reasoning, and craft all grew, the students said. The brake was the system: heavy loads, thin staffing, and mentors' own thin experience and support. Jönsson ties the tale to her work on person-centered leadership, arguing that support is a structure, not a mood, and must be built for the mentors as well.
pmc-13530224:
Fazle Rabbi Chowdhury leads a 2026 study of specialist immune cells in acute melioidosis, a severe tropical infection common in Thailand. These MAIT cells help fight bacteria, yet their role in this illness was unknown. Lab cultures and blood from 120 patients and local controls supplied the data.

The bacterium did trigger the cells to release a key defense signal in culture. During acute illness, circulating cells were fewer, highly activated, and poor at responding, with recovery restoring their function. Patients who died showed weaker responses, while diabetes deepened the deficit, hinting these cells guard against severe disease.
pmc-13530524:
Haskell and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 157, a validation study of the Universal Pain and Function score. This two-question outcome measure, built from a pain rating and a single function rating, is meant to replace long questionnaires that burden patients and clinics after common sports surgeries.

Scores were collected prospectively from 1,648 patients before and after rotator cuff repair, meniscus trimming, or ligament reconstruction, alongside the standard long instruments. The two-question score tracked the shoulder and knee gold standards closely. Its correlations ran from the low seventies up to the low nineties in the study's own reporting of its convergent validity checks. It barely correlated with mental health scores, as a physical measure should not, and it matched the long forms' ability to detect change after surgery. The authors conclude two questions deliver valid, responsive measurement.
pmc-13530724:
Reviews that overstate a treatment benefit in their summaries can mislead surgeons, and a study hunted for that spin in reviews of a blood product used to boost knee cartilage repair. Christina Im and co-authors carried out the hunt in this 2026 paper. The product, plasma rich in platelets, is injected or applied during meniscus repair surgery.

Following standard review-finding rules, the team gathered the systematic reviews and meta-analyses on the topic. Each abstract was then rated for spin patterns, such as claiming benefit the full results did not support. Spin matters because many clinicians read only abstracts. Naming how often spin appears, and in what forms, pressures review authors and journal editors to keep summaries honest.
pmc-13530924:
Ahsein Addloli and co-authors examine in 2026 how low thyroid hormone reshapes fat-burning organelles called peroxisomes inside rat fat tissue. A drug induced the hormone shortage for 7, 15, or 21 days. Fat pads from under the skin and three belly sites were compared by microscopy and protein measurement.

Peroxisome numbers rose gradually everywhere, yet the timing differed by depot. Production pathways shifted from the standard route toward building fresh organelles. Belly fat alone sprouted odd finger-like structures reaching into fat droplets, possibly from unbalanced fat burning. Under-skin fat never showed them, revealing sharp regional differences.
pmc-13531224:
Daiki Nagayama and co-authors report a chest cancer first mistaken for tuberculosis, in a 2026 case report. Their patient was an eighty-three-year-old man. Fluid around his lung was rich in immune cells. A tuberculosis test came back positive. A camera inspection showed pus-like fluid, but biopsies found no answer. Standard tuberculosis treatment began anyway. The fluid persisted despite therapy.

A surgical biopsy showed scarring with scattered spindle cells. Two months later a chest wall mass grew fast and invaded bone. A needle biopsy then found abnormal spindle cells. A genetic probe test confirmed sarcomatoid mesothelioma. This cancer type is aggressive and hard to catch. The authors warn that stubborn pleurisy demands suspicion. Repeat biopsies should come quickly when treatment fails. Pathologists should consider probe testing earlier. The case shows how a rare cancer can hide behind a common infection's mask.
pmc-13531824:
Gordon Abekah-Nkrumah leads a 2026 study of whether health facilities in Ghana will keep using a digital medicine supply platform called Med4All. Surveys from 124 staff plus 56 interviews measured usefulness, ease, approval, and intention to continue. The system orders medicines and offers interest-free loans to facilities.

Intention to continue scored high, near four on a five-point scale. Usefulness, ease, and positive attitude each fed that intention, while fast deals and the loans stood out as prized features. Delivery delays, weak supplier contact, payment snags, and some staff holding back threatens long-term survival.
pmc-13531924:
Mathieu Megevet and colleagues report in 2026 a rare lung reaction to the myeloma drug pomalidomide in a 67-year-old man. He was receiving a three-drug regimen for relapsed blood cancer when breathlessness, cough, sweating, and chills built over a week. Symptoms had first flickered three months earlier, weeks after the regimen began.

Washing fluid from the lungs was rich in eosinophils, a hallmark white cell of allergic-type lung injury. Antibiotics failed to help, while stopping the drug and starting steroids brought fast clinical and scan improvement. Lung function stayed recovered at twelve months.
pmc-13532124:
Marvin Domanski, Michael Fuhrmann, Nils Hacket, Heike Hausmann, and Peter Schreiner use a molecular balance to weigh a faint force between benzene rings. Two rings can pull on each other weakly, a force that helps shape how molecules fold and bind. The team's balance is a ring-shaped molecule that can fold so two benzene-like parts meet, or open so they part. They read the fold balance in many solvents with magnetic scans.

The folded form won in every solvent by a small, steady margin. Computer work traced the pull to a broad, weak force between the rings. The study gives a clean measure of a force that is hard to pin down.
pmc-13532324:
Sylvain Meyer, Thomas Lafon, and Olivier Barraud present two cases from 2026 where gene tests missed key facts in Staphylococcus aureus blood infections. In one case at Limoges, a rapid test found no sign of the germ in a man with septic shock. Culture still grew the germ, and full gene reading showed a small loss in the target gene.

In the second case the rapid test called the germ drug resistant, while culture tests showed it was drug sensitive. Gene reading found a small loss that stopped a resistance protein early. The cases show why culture and drug tests still matter beside fast gene tests.
pmc-13534424:
Ewelina Lange and colleagues propose in 2026 a quantum battery design where light-driven jumps help rather than hurt charging. In most designs, random jumps drain stored energy and blur the stored state. Their battery uses groups of three-level atoms that hold energy in a long-lived middle state.

When jumps are limited to fall from the excited state into that middle state, with decay to the ground state blocked, jumps drive the battery to full charge. All stored energy stays extractable, and the second charging stage runs faster. Readers see a route to turn a loss channel into a charging aid.
pmc-13534724:
Jianxi Liu and colleagues develop in 2026 an electronic trigger system to flag sedative-hypnotic drug misuse in a large hospital. Such drugs carry dependence risk, yet passive reporting misses most cases. The team first reviewed over 16,000 outpatient prescriptions, then ran a ten-day live pilot.

A trigger dictionary inside the hospital system produced 200 automated alerts during the pilot. Phone screening of high-risk patients found 17 meeting criteria for suspected dependence, while the passive system found none in the same span. Benzodiazepine use, older age, and longer therapy stood out. Pharmacists can use the alerts to triage cases and curb diversion risks in busy clinics.
pmc-13534824:
Getu Abeje and a large team report a five year review in 2026 of gut parasite infections among students in northwest Ethiopia. Such infections are a major health problem, in part because students live in shared housing. The team reviewed stool test records from a university clinic for the years 2021 through 2025.

After removing incomplete records, more than seven thousand five hundred tests remained. About thirty percent came back positive for a parasite, and most of those were single celled organisms rather than worms. The study gives clinic leaders a clear picture of how common these infections stayed over five years. That record can guide testing, treatment, and hygiene efforts on campus.
pmc-13535424:
A peanut variety bred to resist root-knot worms still throws off occasional susceptible plants, and growers blame mixed seed, but the plant genome itself may be unstable. Samuele Lamon and co-authors tested those rival explanations in this 2026 study. The variety carries a resistance segment borrowed from a wild peanut relative.

Recent work showed cultivated peanut DNA reshuffles at a surprising rate, which could shed the resistance segment spontaneously. The team grew foundation seed in worm-infested conditions to watch how often susceptibility appears and in what pattern. The answer matters for seed certification and for farmers who trust the variety protection. If instability is the cause, breeders need new checks, not just cleaner seed handling.
pmc-13536024:
Giulia Maiocco and co-authors lay out a plan to gather all evidence on catheter lock therapy for newborns, in a 2026 protocol paper. Babies in intensive care often need central lines, and those lines invite bloodstream infections that can kill. Lock therapy fills the idle catheter with an antimicrobial solution to keep germs out or clear them. It works reasonably in adults and older children, but newborn evidence is scattered.

The review will follow Cochrane and PRISMA standards for rigor. Its main question is how infection rates compare between locked catheters and placebo or standard care in neonatal units. Safety outcomes matter as much as efficacy at this fragile age. A firm synthesis should guide practice in units worldwide.
pmc-13536124:
Brittany Dennis and the REVISE trial team probed acid block care in aired patients who had COVID-19. Plain look checks had hinted acid block drugs might make fates worse in SARS-CoV-2 cases. The sub study sat in a trial picked at random of pantoprazole to stop stress sores in the gut. Its aims were three. Name the sick group, set them next to a matched group with no such ill, and test if the drug acted in a split way by ill state.

Match steps lined up sick and well patients for fair checks. Traits and fates were then set side by side by group. The team checked if the drug's acts on bleeds and next ends shifted in sick patients. Proof picked at random counts here, since sick men both catch ills and get more drugs. The 2026 sub study splits the drug's act from the virus's act.
pmc-13536724:
Melike Buşra Atar and co-authors examine what raises the chance of newborn eye inflammation in a 2026 case-control study at a referral center. Records for babies born between 2022 and 2024 were reviewed, comparing 203 newborns who developed conjunctivitis in the first 28 days with 355 newborns who did not. Maternal, birth, newborn, and lab details were tested together to find independent links.

Affected newborns were more often male and born slightly earlier, with lower health scores at birth. Mothers of affected babies were older on average and showed higher diabetes rates and higher inflammation marker levels. After adjustment, older maternal age, maternal diabetes, higher inflammation levels, and male sex each stayed linked to the condition. The authors suggest closer early eye checks for babies with these features.
pmc-13536824:
Xingyu Sun and colleagues develop a prediction tool for urinary infection after surgery in older adults in a 2026 study at a teaching hospital in southwest China. Infections after surgery prolong stays and raise costs, yet early flagging is hard. Patients aged 65 years or older who had inpatient surgery between 2019 and 2024 supplied routine care data. Cases were split into training and validation groups, and a chart for personal risk estimates was built.

About one in five training patients developed a urinary infection after surgery. Six factors formed the final model, covering diabetes, intensive care stay, catheter time, repeat catheter use, hospital stay length, and return within a month. Accuracy stayed good in validation, and risk estimates matched observed rates well. The authors frame the tool as ongoing risk tracking during recovery, not a pre-surgery forecast.
pmc-13536924:
A fatty liver in a child with severe obesity was once dismissed as a passenger; ten years on, its shadow on the arteries can be measured. Anne-Sophie Stroes and nine co-authors follow fifty-two such children into young adulthood in this 2026 study. They sort them by whether liver fat was present at the start, at the end, both, or neither.

The surprise is timing. Childhood liver fat alone did not predict thicker artery walls in adulthood, but adult liver fat did, firmly, after adjustments. Across the four paths, from never to persistent, the wall thickness rose in step, and childhood metabolic markers fed into its growth. The authors argue the liver's insult is current, not ancient: clear the fat by adulthood and the artery risk seems to fade with it. Small numbers, they note, counsel care.
pmc-13537124:
Koffi Barnabé Kegbevi and co-authors run a trial asking whether babies need three hepatitis B vaccine doses, or whether two can do the job. Two doses are known to protect children over one year old, but data in infants were thin. Their 2026 trial enrolls children at two months of age and randomizes the schedules.

One group got two doses of the same vaccine, another got two doses mixing brands, and a control group got the standard three. A challenge dose three years later tested the memory of each schedule. A month after the main series, protection rates ran above ninety percent in all three groups. Antibody levels were lower after two doses, which the later challenge helps judge. Vaccine planners get infant data for a schedule that saves a visit.
pmc-13538024:
Ryoichi Kitamura comments on a glue-based fix for a stubborn urine leak after kidney injury in a 2026 editorial. The case behind it: a teenager whose torn kidney leaked for over sixty days. Stents and drains had failed. The treating team sealed the fistula with coils and surgical glue, sparing the kidney.

Kitamura praises the persistence and sets the case in wider practice. Most high-grade kidney leaks settle on their own or with stents. Hard cases invite segment shutdown, freezing, or direct sealing, each with trade-offs. The comment frames glue closure as a worthy salvage step before removing the kidney.
pmc-13538224:
Ahmed Mohamed and colleagues review nanoparticle strategies for diffuse midline glioma in a 2026 synthesis. These deep brain tumors mostly strike children and teens, spread through tissue, resist drugs, and sit behind a tight blood-brain barrier. Survival past five years stays extremely low. The review covers current care and then sorts tiny carrier designs by material and targeting method, including paired imaging and therapy options.

Carriers can cross or bypass the barrier through receptor shuttles or local delivery, concentrating drugs at tumors while sparing the body. Metal particles can also boost radiation damage inside tumors. Imaging-linked carriers promise live tracking of treatment. Lab results look strong, yet barrier entry, spread inside tumors, and large-scale making still block patient use. The authors set four research priorities.
pmc-13538324:
Ming Zhou and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six study rescuing aged hamsters from lethal viral pneumonia with a late multi-part intervention. Ageing itself drives deadly outcomes in respiratory virus infections worldwide. Old hamsters infected with the coronavirus showed distinct lung damage patterns.

Gene profiling revealed widespread cell death, weak antiviral responses, and inflammation-driven clotting in aged lungs. Adult animals pushed toward the same aged pattern when infected with the virus. A combined late intervention targeting several of these dimensions reversed the lethal course. Multi-angle treatment, started late, may matter most for elderly patients.
pmc-13538524:
Jian Yun and Tao Liu propose a blockchain framework for asynchronous federated learning in a 2026 design study. Federated learning trains shared models without moving private data, yet waiting for slow nodes stalls sync versions and ledgers add storage strain. The design stores bulky parameters off-chain, boosts local adaptation while compressing updates, verifies updates by shared information while discounting stale ones, and elects committees by stake-weighted chance.

Simulations showed steady global accuracy with lower communication load than rival schemes. Oscillations from delayed updates were damped, and poisoning plus Byzantine attacks were resisted. Scaling to three hundred nodes brought no sharp rise in agreement delay. The authors present the stack as a secure, efficient base for decentralized learning among uneven devices.
pmc-13538724:
Angela Zanfardino and colleagues report first real-world results for a tubeless automated insulin system in young people with type 1 diabetes in a 2026 observational study. Seventy-six children and adolescents starting the patch pump with its adaptive learning algorithm were followed for six months across centers. Glucose monitor metrics and blood sugar averages were tracked at one, three, and six months.

Time spent in the target glucose range jumped within the first month and stayed higher through six months. Time above range fell while low time held steady, and average glucose plus variability declined. Blood sugar averages dropped meaningfully by three months and held. Over half the group met the international target range goal at six months. No severe low events or acid crises occurred, supporting safety in routine care.
pmc-13540124:
Yesim Ozkaya Ucar and Taner Turan present a 2026 study on sexual quality of life after cervix procedures. Two methods remove early abnormal tissue from the cervix: a heated wire loop and a cold knife cut. Their effect on later sexual life was unclear. The team surveyed 185 sexually active women at least six months after treatment in 2022 to 2024.

Average scores on a validated 18-item scale were nearly the same for both methods. In adjusted models, the surgical method still did not matter. Age, marital status, and how often a woman had sex did matter. So did family setup, prior views of her sex life, hopes after surgery, and body image. The design cannot prove cause, the authors note.
pmc-13540824:
Li Xiaonan and colleagues search health records from northern China in a 2026 study. They wanted the ages when three health risks start to climb fast. The risks were high blood pressure and raised fasting blood sugar. Abnormal blood lipids were the third. Sharp turning points could guide screening by age and sex.

The records numbered 263,824 health examinations. They spanned January 2020 to May 2025. Blood pressure turned upward near age forty. It turned earlier in men than in women. Blood sugar turned later, above all in women. Lipid problems turned strikingly early in men, near age thirty-one. Having several risks at once predicted more than any one alone.
pmc-13540924:
Myuri Ruthirakuhan and colleagues hunted blood-fat clues to who gains from methylphenidate for Alzheimer's apathy. Published in 2026, the study drew on ADMET 2 trial members with baseline blood-fat profiles. Apathy, a loss of drive, is common in Alzheimer's and drags down daily life, yet methylphenidate helps only some patients.

Among 43 treated people, 28 counted as better on an apathy scale and 10 on a clinician global scale. A lipid model told improvers from others well on both scales, with scores above eight tenths. Fat-pathway breaks in ceramide and related lipids marked drug responders, while placebo responders showed only one shared pathway break. The authors read ceramide-linked breaks as drug-only and the shared pathway as tied to apathy shifts in general.
pmc-13541124:
An eight-author team tests how well people judge where someone else is looking, and how mental health traits change that skill. Reading gaze direction is a basic social ability that weakens in conditions such as schizophrenia, social anxiety, and autism. The team asked 106 adults to view faces with nine gaze angles, varied noise, and two head positions, and to say whether each face seemed to look at them.

Precision dropped as autism traits rose but improved slightly with social anxiety, suggesting the two traits pull in opposite ways. Added noise and mismatched head and gaze directions made judgments less precise and more likely to feel self-directed, a pattern also seen in patients with schizophrenia. The authors read that self-directed bias as a default the brain uses when a social signal is unclear.
pmc-13541224:
Claudia Maddren and co-authors wrote a protocol paper from 2026 for a pilot program that aims to head off chronic disease in rural Australia. The program, named Wellness my Way, runs in South West Queensland, a region with a heavy load of such disease. It was built by a state health body with local services and many partner groups, shaped by joint design with the community.

The paper sets out how the pilot was built and how it will be judged, by reach, effect, uptake, delivery, and staying power. The main gauge is how many people it reaches. Side gauges cover user gladness and staff views. The pilot ended in the first month of 2026, with findings due late that year, on what a joint program can do in a place of high unmet need.
pmc-13541624:
Linda L Magnusson Hanson and five colleagues review, in a 2026 systematic review, longitudinal evidence on whether working conditions raise the risk of suicidal behaviour. Research on employment as a mental health determinant had never been gathered this comprehensively.

Searches across four databases for studies from 1995 to 2024 found twenty-seven eligible papers, fourteen fit for pooling. Part-time work, job loss, job insecurity, high demands, low control, job strain, and workplace bullying each associated significantly with suicide, with job loss more than doubling relative risk. Certainty was moderate only for job loss and low for insecurity, and evidence on suicide attempts was thin. The authors call for many more studies.
pmc-13541824:
Lucy Taylor and co-authors review how fatty liver disease talks to the heart and kidneys, in a 2026 paper. In metabolic liver disease, fat in the liver rarely stays a liver problem: heart failure and kidney disease often follow. The review traces that three-way axis and the liver-born signals that carry it.

Fat overflow, inflamed fat around the heart, and clot-prone blood drive the cardiac damage, the authors argue. Two nerve growth signals from the liver stand out: one protective signal fades, shielding the heart and kidneys less, while growth factors from the liver play double roles in metabolism. New diabetes drugs that also protect heart and kidney fit the same story. Shared targets may treat the whole axis at once.
pmc-13542124:
Reshmi Debbarma and colleagues test a natural powder in a 2026 study. The powder comes from de-oiled moringa seeds. It serves as a clumping agent for biofloc fish farming. In biofloc systems, microbial flocs clean the water. Synthetic clumping chemicals work, yet they cost more. They also sit poorly with green production.

Lab checks showed strong clumping by the powder. It removed over ninety percent of suspended solids at its best dose. A forty-five-day trial used young Clarias magur catfish. Tanks held eighty fish each. One dose stood clearly ahead of the rest. Ammonia and nitrite fell, while nitrate rose. Fish gained more biomass, with better survival and feed use.
pmc-13542424:
Lena Capern and colleagues tested two feed germs against harmful dairy germs in lab dishes. Published in 2026, the study mixed Bacillus licheniformis 809 and Bacillus subtilis 810 with gut, rumen, and womb germs. Harmful germs threaten cow and calf health and output, and these feed germs already show herd benefits.

The Bacillus pair eased growth of a varied set of harmful germs, from gram-negative to gram-positive types. Gains showed even when the harmful germs outgrew the Bacillus pair, a striking result. The findings help explain field reports of better dairy health and output with Bacillus feeds. Readers get lab backing for a feed plan that curbs harmful germs without germ-killers.
pmc-13543324:
Nayeli Gonzalez-Gomez and colleagues report a proof-of-concept study adapting low-cost parent-child activity packs, first made in the United Kingdom, for vulnerable families in Argentina. Early childhood is a key window for language, thinking, and social development, and parents in economic hardship lack access to rich activities. The packs were reworked for local culture, materials, and daily routines with help from a local health worker, then given to 73 families at early childhood centres.

Parents filled in surveys and joined feedback sessions, while infants were checked with the Bayley-III developmental scales. Families said they did more varied activities, and the home learning setting improved. Parents spoke of enjoyment, stronger bonds, and greater confidence in playing with purpose. Developmental scores did not change, as foreseen in a short pilot. The authors present the packs as a welcome way to support early learning in poorer settings.
pmc-13543424:
Liming Shi and colleagues reported in 2026 on building a scorecard for judging the quality of lung cancer diagnosis and treatment. Lung cancer is China's commonest and deadliest cancer, yet hospitals lacked a shared, weighted set of quality indicators. The team used the Donabedian model, which splits quality into structure, process, and outcome, and ran two rounds of a Delphi consultation, where experts rate items until they converge. An analytic hierarchy process then converted expert judgements into weights.

The finished system holds three top-level indicators, fifteen secondary ones, and fifty-five detailed measures. Structure covers staff, rules, and facilities; process runs from diagnosis and team review through surgery, drugs, radiation, and follow-up; outcomes cover effectiveness, safety, and timeliness. Expert participation stayed above ninety-six percent across rounds, and their agreement strengthened. The authors offer the weighted system as a credible shared yardstick for hospitals.
pmc-13543524:
Maria Paes and co-authors asked in 2026 whether grapevine cells grown in flasks can stand in for whole leaves when studying defence chemistry. Cell cultures are tidy and repeatable, but disease research in the end concerns real plants. Cells from two vine types, Cabernet Sauvignon and Chambourcin, were dosed with jasmonic acid, a plant stress hormone. Their chemistry was read two and five days later with an ultra-precise mass spectrometer, side by side with detached leaves.

Cultures and leaves kept clearly unlike chemical profiles, and responses varied by type and time in both systems. Yet on chosen ground the two met, above all in oxidative-stress defence, stress signalling, and secondary metabolite output. Flask cells can thus serve as a partner platform for switch-on responses, the authors conclude. Findings still need checking in intact plants, with key chemicals firmly named, before the stand-in is trusted.
pmc-13544624:
Farzad Fereidouni and co-authors study a light-based tool for cancer surgery in a 2026 paper. Surgeons removing head and neck tumours must judge where cancer ends, yet checks during surgery are limited. A method called fluorescence lifetime imaging reads how long tissue glows after a flash, and cancer glows differently from healthy tissue.

The team measured tissue from 75 patients both in the body and after removal, at three sites in the throat area. Removal changed the glow patterns, but not in the same way everywhere. Contrast fell for tongue and tonsil samples after removal, while it improved for the tongue base. The authors warn that diagnostic rules must be trained separately for use during surgery and on removed tissue.
pmc-13545024:
Julia Gomes do Vale and co-authors report a 2026 field study of ghost crabs on sandy beaches in southern Brazil. The crab Ocypode quadrata is a common gauge of beach health, yet its numbers shift with season and beach shape, and those natural swings can muddy readings. The team tracked burrow counts, body mass, shell size, and body condition across beaches and seasons.

Mass and shell size peaked on the steep reflective beach in summer, but on flatter beaches in winter. Body condition peaked in autumn everywhere. Burrow counts stayed steady, yet every measure rose where beach vegetation spread wider. The authors urge that beach shape and season be counted before the crab is read as a warning sign.
pmc-13545124:
Jen-Hao Wu and colleagues published a 2026 population pharmacokinetic study of bosutinib, a targeted leukaemia drug, in children with Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukaemia. Dosing children by shrinking adult rules is unreliable, and the phase one dose-finding trial behind this work enrolled only twenty-six young patients. The team therefore borrowed strength from a published adult model, using its knowledge as a prior while fitting 235 blood samples from the children.

A two-compartment model with a brief absorption lag described the children's data well. Clearance, scaled to body size, ran higher in children than the reported adult value, a difference that matters for keeping blood levels in range. Simulations from the fitted model were used to judge the recommended phase two dose for children. Sparse paediatric data, the authors show, can still yield firm dosing science when adult knowledge is formally folded in.
pmc-13546524:
Emad Aljohani and co-authors chart pancreatic cancer across the Middle East and North Africa from 1990 to 2023 in a 2026 study. The cancer kills fast and leaves a narrow window for care, so tracking its spread guides where scarce help should go.

World burden data for twenty one countries feed the counts. Age adjusted rates of the illness rose by more than half across the span. Men carried a higher load than women in the latest year. Death and lost healthy years are tracked as well. The team urge early spotting and comfort care where the load runs highest.
pmc-13546724:
Rakhmad Perkasa Harahap and colleagues tested in 2026 whether chitosan, a compound made from shrimp shells, can preserve mixed livestock rations and improve how rumen microbes handle them. Rations were stored for 30 days with no additive, raw shell, chitin, or chitosan, under conditions with and without air. Afterward the team measured storage losses and ran laboratory rumen fermentations.

Storage without air preserved feed better overall, and chitosan gave the strongest protection, with the least dry matter loss and the best appearance and smell scores. Chitosan rations also digested best in the laboratory and produced the least methane. The authors present shrimp shell waste as a useful feed additive that turns a disposal problem into a benefit.
pmc-13547324:
Panpan He, Shouyang Yu, and Jingjing Wang proposed in 2026 a system that reads college students' facial expressions and then learns, by trial and feedback, which support strategy to offer each person. Questionnaires and manual counseling are slow and subjective, the authors argue. Their pipeline cleans and aligns face images and extracts texture features tied to states like stress and anxiety. Those features feed a reinforcement learning agent that picks relaxation exercises, cognitive prompts, or motivational messages.

Tested on a public dataset of about ten thousand records, the combined system beat traditional techniques on accuracy and related scores, all landing near or above ninety percent. The authors offer the design as a framework for adaptive, personal mental health support on campus.
pmc-13547424:
Saini, Fidler, Boffito, and colleagues ask why people on HIV prevention pills still seroconvert. Their 2026 paper reviews new HIV diagnoses at a London clinic. The clinic, 56 Dean Street, serves many PrEP users. PrEP is medication taken beforehand to block HIV infection. Records covered diagnoses from 2017 through 2024.

Among 1,080 newly diagnosed people, 210 had used PrEP before. That share climbed steeply across the study years. It rose from about four percent in 2017 to sixty percent in 2024. Prior users tested more often and caught infections earlier. Over a third of them had stopped PrEP entirely. Among those still nominally on it, most reported poor adherence. Running out of pills was the top reason for stopping. Monogamy and stomach side effects followed behind. One resistance mutation, M184I/V, appeared far more in PrEP-exposed patients. Support for staying on PrEP is the clear unmet need.
pmc-13548324:
Qizheng Wang and co-authors published this study in 2026. It builds a tool to predict genetic interactions, pairs of genes whose joint loss kills a cell or, oddly, saves it. Such pairs point to drug targets, since a tumor with one gene lost may die when the second is blocked. Testing all pairs in the lab is impossible, so prediction matters. Their network model, GiGCN, learns from a signed web of known interactions and gene similarities.

The model splits gene features into separate strands, so opposite interaction types do not blur. On benchmarks it beat rival tools on both accuracy measures. Case studies surfaced known and new lethal pairs around a famous cancer gene. Viable pairs clustered near cell clean-up pathways. The authors offer the tool as a map for target hunting in cancer and other diseases.
pmc-13548624:
Marie Emilie Hjorth Lutambi and colleagues review what is known about intoxication among injured patients arriving at emergency departments, in a 2026 systematic review. Alcohol and other psychoactive drugs alter judgment and behavior, so they may change both how badly people get hurt and how they fare afterward. The team searched two major databases and kept eighteen prospective studies of patients aged fifteen and older.

Intoxication was common but varied enormously: alcohol involvement ranged from under ten percent to nearly two thirds of patients across studies. Nine studies found worse injury severity scores among intoxicated patients, while others found no difference or even milder injuries. Hospital stays and death rates also swung between studies. Intoxicated patients were consistently younger and mostly male. The authors call the severity evidence inconsistent and point prevention efforts at those groups.
pmc-13549524:
Jinyoung Jeong and colleagues track depression and suicidal thinking among South Korean adolescents by school grades, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Strong pressure to do well at school is suspected of driving these problems. Their data come from a nationwide youth risk survey from two thousand six to twenty twenty-two. Over one point one million adolescents were included.

Next to high achievers, moderate achievers had a modestly higher depression risk. Low achievers faced about one and a half times the risk of both depression and suicidal thinking. Both problems fell before the pandemic, then rose steadily during it. Girls showed higher depression rates in every grade group. The authors argue that grade pressure leaves real marks on mental health. Their long trend gives policymakers a base line for judging new steps.
pmc-13549624:
A two-stage surgery for a rare infant spine tumor is told by Tae-Kyun Kim and co-authors in work dated 2026. The tumor, a teratoma, ran from mid-back to waist and into the chest. The baby was one month old. Stage one took the spine part through a door-like cut that spared back muscles. Stage two, a month on, took the chest part by scope through three small ports.

Tissue reads called it a mature teratoma. Scans showed all of it gone, and the baby kept full nerve function. No return or spine bend showed at sixteen months.
pmc-13550824:
Peiji Yao and co-authors chart blood eosinophil counts across the Chinese general public. Their 2026 study uses health check data from more than 680,000 people gathered over thirteen years. These white blood cells guide allergy and asthma care, yet clinic cutoffs often ignore age and sex splits, and Asian data were scarce.

Counts lean right, with a median near one hundred cells per microliter. Men run higher than women at every age, and the age curve bends like a U. Smoking, higher body weight, and the youngest and oldest ages tie to higher counts. Asthma and chronic lung disease also track with higher counts. Age- and sex-matched ranges are proposed.
pmc-13551924:
Sivan Cukerman and Orli Grinstein-Cohen published a 2026 survey of emergency nurses in Israel. The topic was forensic nursing, the work of saving evidence from injured patients. An online survey reached 438 nurses from November 2023 to April 2024. It asked how often they do set forensic tasks. It also asked how important they judge those tasks.

Nurses said they do such tasks rarely. Yet they rated the tasks as highly important. Few had any forensic training in their studies. Close to nine in ten wanted such training. Older nurses and those with a master's degree rated the tasks higher. So did nurses with more years on the job. The pair urge schools to add forensic content and hospitals to back the role.
pmc-13552024:
Serizawa and co-authors link bowel urgency in ulcerative colitis to ultrasound signs of deep gut wall inflammation. Urgency is a key symptom that drags down daily life. The team ran a single-center study of patients set for colonoscopy in 2023. Ultrasounds through the belly and pelvis measured wall thickness layer by layer. Blood flow signals in the sigmoid colon and rectum were also read. Urgency was scored by a standard clinical index.

Of 59 patients, 33, or 56%, reported urgency. The team compared ultrasound traits against scope findings and blood markers. Deep wall changes may explain urgency better than surface inflammation does. That link could guide treatment aimed at the full wall.
pmc-13552724:
Seon-Hye Won and co-authors interview Korean women with breast cancer about the colors they choose to wear, in a 2026 study. Color can shape mood and self-image, yet little was known about what these patients prefer and why. Fourteen patients and survivors at a university hospital spoke for an hour each with an art therapist.

Every woman had strong color memories and favorites. Four themes ran through the talks: how colors shape social contact and public image, how they flatter or hide the body's shape, and the good feelings a loved color brings. A fourth theme covered shifts in taste after diagnosis. Social image led the reasons, named in about two-fifths of key statements. The authors suggest testing whether guided color use could lift quality of life.
pmc-13552824:
Ng and co-authors report a quality campaign that raised HPV vaccine starts among nine- and ten-year-olds. HPV shots prevent infections and cancers, and starting at nine improves uptake and finish rates. The campaign worked through a care system's records from 2021 to 2024. Children needed at least one well visit a year to count. Baseline rates came from early 2021 to mid 2022. Steps included provider training and a system-wide Start at 9 policy.

Family handouts and record tweaks put the shot on every nine-year-old's order list. Monthly rates were tracked on a control chart. The cohort held 9,315 patients. The project shows how defaults, not lectures, move vaccine rates.
pmc-13554024:
Xiang Shi and three colleagues check how well a thin-needle test sorts swollen lymph nodes in a 2026 single-centre study. Needle sampling is quick and gentle, yet final proof still comes from surgery. The team reviewed 133 cases from 2023 and 2024 where both tests were done. Four kinds of disease were covered: harmless overgrowth, two forms of lymph cancer, and cancer spread from elsewhere.

The needle test matched the surgical answer in close to nine cases out of ten. It was sharpest for spread cancer, catching most cases, and never falsely named the rarer lymph cancer. Cell shapes and patterns differed clearly between the four groups. The authors call the test a sound first screen that helps doctors plan next steps.
pmc-13554424:
Safia Arbab and co-authors test whether extracts from five plants used in folk care can kill germs taken from livestock wounds, in work from 2026. Wound infections in farm animals are a growing problem as drug resistance spreads.

From 250 wound samples the team found 216 germs, most often Staphylococcus aureus. Extracts of Withania somnifera, Achyranthes aspera, Verbascum sinaiticum, Aloe vera, and Capparis zeylanica were screened for plant chemicals and tested on agar plates. Screening found alkaloids, flavonoids, tannins, and like compounds in most extracts. Withania somnifera hit Staphylococcus aureus hardest, and Gram-positive germs were in most cases easier to kill. The plants look like good sources for new wound care.
pmc-13554524:
Alessandro Rossi and ten co-authors present a cheaper way to make gratings for a special kind of X-ray imaging, in a research paper from 2026. Phase contrast imaging reveals soft details that normal X-rays miss, but its gratings are costly, fine-lined devices made by long multi-step processes with gold.

The team instead molds soft microchannels and fills them with liquid mercury, which blocks X-rays well. Their test grating matched the image quality of a solid gold equivalent. The process uses fewer, cheaper, and more scalable steps. The authors say higher, finer structures are within reach with known methods, which could speed the spread of this imaging type.
pmc-13554724:
Ammar AbuMostafa and co-authors test how root canal rinsing methods affect tooth strength, in a 2026 lab study. Rinsing disinfects the canal during root treatment, but activation tools may weaken the root dentin. Forty pulled human premolar teeth were split into four groups. Each group got a different final rinse style.

The four styles were plain needle rinsing, ultrasonic rinsing, negative-pressure rinsing, and a flexible finisher tool. All teeth shared the same cleaning chemicals and volumes. Hardness, stiffness, and bending strength of the dentin were then measured. Plain needle rinsing left the hardest dentin, while ultrasonic rinsing left the softest. Dentists get data for balancing clean canals against tooth strength.
pmc-13554924:
Ayşe Yaşar and three colleagues study heterozygous TSHR variants in childhood idiopathic subclinical hypothyroidism. The condition in childhood is often idiopathic and usually benign. Heterozygous TSHR variants cause isolated high TSH, but long-term outcomes and care lack data. Their 2026 study reviews children aged 1 to 18 with the condition.

The cohort held 51 patients followed for a mean of 4.9 years. TSHR variants appeared in 18 patients, about 35 percent, including one novel missense variant. Variant-positive patients mostly kept a stable thyroid picture without progression to overt disease. Levothyroxine stopped in 6 of 11 treated patients after genetic diagnosis, though five later restarted. No patient developed overt disease.
pmc-13555024:
Hui Zhang and nine co-authors link age-friendly surroundings to lower pre-dementia risk in a 2026 paper. The syndrome pairs slow gait with memory complaints. It forecasts dementia, falls, and early death in older adults. Age-friendly environments follow a World Health Organization frame.

The cohort held 7,608 older adults free of the syndrome at start. Over a median four years, 801 new cases appeared. The friendliest areas cut risk by over a third at the top end. Each step up in friendliness score lowered risk a bit more. The dose-response pattern held across the full range. Building such neighborhoods may delay dementia, they suggest.
pmc-13555124:
Diego Velasco-Rodríguez and twenty-one colleagues test thrombin assays in healthy adults across Spain and Portugal. Fully automated thrombin assays ease the move from research to clinical use. Their 2026 multicenter study runs plasma from healthy adult volunteers in 12 labs under one harmonized protocol. It uses the ST Genesia analyzer with STG-ThromboScreen, with and without thrombomodulin.

Within-run and intra-day precision were high, with variation under 10 percent for all measures except velocity index. Normalization cut interlab variation for measures such as endogenous thrombin potential and peak height. Good interlab performance held in 96 to 98 percent of results. In 252 adults, median ETP was 131 percent and peak height 116 percent, with median ETP inhibition of 47.2 percent with thrombomodulin.
pmc-13555724:
Andrew S Handel leads a four-author team reporting a lone star tick rash illness in an eight-year-old New York girl in a 2026 case report. The illness, called STARI, mimics Lyme disease with an expanding round rash after a tick bite. Two weeks before her visit she had developed a five-centimetre ring with a central bump on her upper back. Fever, swollen neck glands, and muscle aches came with it.

The tick, removed from the very spot and kept, tested positive for Borrelia lonestari, a disputed suspect for this illness. Suspecting early Lyme disease, her doctor prescribed two weeks of amoxicillin. Rash and symptoms cleared within one week, and she stayed well at follow-up. Lone star ticks are spreading north, sharpening the Lyme look-alike problem.
pmc-13555824:
Yan presents ClinAgent in twenty twenty-six, an AI layer for clinical trial programming. Statistical programming for a large trial can take one to two years of staff time. AI coding agents reason well but lack tools for clinical data formats and standards. ClinAgent adds those tools through a standard protocol.

Its design splits data access from domain logic. Skills package prompts, rule engines, and decision trees that encode expert knowledge. Tools handle statistical data sets, specification sheets, and log files. Nine skills were tested on artifacts from a real Phase two heart study. All passed functional validation on synthetic data. Deterministic checks found errors and warnings with no false positives. Draft specifications from prompts were strong in simple domains and weaker in complex ones, so expert review is still needed.
pmc-13555924:
Xueying Bai leads a seven-author team stress-testing two collagen membranes used in jaw bone rebuilding in a 2026 lab study. Guided bone regeneration lays a membrane over graft material to hold space for new bone. One membrane comes from cow heart sac tissue, the other from pig skin. Wet tests stretched, inflated, and compressed both materials.

The cow-derived membrane proved far stiffer and stronger under pulling and compression loads. The pig-derived membrane stretched much further before failing and expanded slightly wider under air pressure. Surgeons thus face a trade-off: strength and load bearing against flexibility and give. The authors frame the results as a mechanical basis for choosing membranes in horizontal bone rebuilding around implants.
pmc-13556024:
Shengnan Kong and six colleagues examined in 2026 whether a simple nutrition score predicts death in patients whose severe infection brings on delirium. The prognostic nutritional index combines blood albumin with a white cell count, and its value in sepsis-associated delirium was unclear. Using the MIMIC-IV intensive care database, they split 2,160 patients into low and high score groups and tracked survival to one year.

Patients with low scores died far more often at three, six, and twelve months than patients with high scores. The link held after statistical adjustment and after weighting methods that balance the groups, and the score predicted death about as well as a standard organ failure score. The relationship was curved rather than straight. Clinicians could use this cheap, routine measure to spot high-risk patients early.
pmc-13556124:
Stefan Weber, Berthold Stoger, and Maren Podewitz make a family of iron compounds held in a stiff ring-shaped frame. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The frame forces the iron's other partners into a seesaw shape, side by side rather than opposite. Frames of this kind usually use soft nitrogen donors; this one mixes in phosphorus donors, which bind more strongly.

Starting from an iron salt, they built several charged variants by pulling off halide partners or adding new ones. Structures were checked both as crystals and in solution. One compound drove a carbon-carbon coupling reaction with high speed. It needed just one percent catalyst and finished within an hour at room temperature. Such iron catalysts could replace costlier metals in fine chemical work.
pmc-13556424:
Sp Konara Mudiyanselage and co-authors study loneliness in bipolar disorder in 2026. They compare patients with psychotic features, patients without them, and healthy controls. Early hardship, social support, and loneliness are all measured.

Loneliness adds to illness burden and to the risk of self-harm. Early hardship is linked to mood problems and to weak social ties later in life. Patients with psychotic features often face worse thinking and social problems than other patients. The team asked whether support protects each group in the same way. Readers see why support may need to be shaped to fit the type of bipolar disorder a person has.
pmc-13556524:
Melatonin may shield lung cells from the damage that hits when blood flow returns, and a 2026 study by Zehra Yilmaz and co-authors tests that shield in a dish. The harm, called lung ischemia-reperfusion injury, follows events such as bypass surgery and lung clots, and a form of cell death named necroptosis plays a part.

The team grew human airway cells and put them through a low-oxygen stretch, then a return to normal air, with or without a small dose of melatonin. They measured cell survival, death markers, cell-cycle state, and the health of the cells' energy centers. They also tracked a death-pathway protein called MLKL and levels of harmful oxygen byproducts. The study asks whether melatonin's known calming of oxidative stress extends to blocking this death route.
pmc-13556724:
S Pallanti leads a 2026 symposium paper on full remission in obsessive-compulsive disorder. Many patients gain only partial relief from standard drug and talk care. The paper argues that full remission should be the main goal of treatment.

Lasting symptoms leave people with poor function and low quality of life. The authors review what remission means and why it matters in the clinic. They look at early drug choices and other factors that shape the chance of remission. Secondary forms of the disorder and brain-based groupings are also covered. Readers learn how care might be tailored to push past partial gains toward full recovery.
pmc-13556824:
H-S Suh and co-authors set out expert agreement on anxiety care in Korea in 2026. The work supports the 2024 Korean guidelines for generalized anxiety disorder. The focus is on what to do when treatment falls short or other conditions are present.

A panel of sixty-five experts in anxiety care took part. They answered a survey built from Korean and world guidelines and past studies. Their answers were used to shape drug treatment advice for hard cases. Cases with added illness were given special care in the questions. Readers see how expert consensus fills gaps where trial evidence is thin in daily practice.
pmc-13557824:
Kotaro Takeshita and co-authors describe a rescue method for hard cases of bile duct access during an endoscopic procedure, published in 2026. When wire-guided methods fail, doctors need another way in. A common fallback cuts with a needle knife, but loose mucosa can hide the duct opening after the cut.

Their method first cuts away, cold and without electric current, the protruding tissue at the duct mouth. Only then is the needle-knife cut made. They report the case of a frail older woman with jaundice from pancreatic cancer, where both standard methods had failed. Folds, a diverticulum, and redundant mucosa made the cut hard. The case sets out each step, with images, as a guide for similar rescues.
pmc-13558424:
Veerasingam and a team of co-authors review radionuclide levels across Qatar's environment, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Their sources span papers from nineteen eighty to September twenty twenty-five. They gathered measures from soil, sediment, groundwater, seawater, building materials, and sea life.

Natural radionuclides such as radium-226, uranium-238, thorium-232, and potassium-40 varied moderately across sites. Human-made cesium-137 and strontium-90 showed only trace levels, in line with global fallout. Risk measures pointed to minimal danger for most soils and common building materials. Higher levels appeared in factory by-products, oil-field waste, and residues, which mark local hazards. The team urges steady monitoring and strict control of factory waste.
pmc-13558524:
Siyu Li and co-authors read tumor maps that split a mouth cancer into zones by water flow traits. Their 2026 study scans eighty-four patients with a diffusion MRI method that splits true spread from blood drift. Whole-tumor averages hide inner variety, so the team grades each tiny cube of tissue on its own.

Four zones emerge from set cut lines for spread and blood share. Zone traits track with lab reads of stroma share, immune cell entry, and neck node spread. Stroma-rich tumors lit up in sparse zones, and node-positive tumors grew one zone in size. Zone models beat whole-tumor scores at calling stroma and immune states. Such maps could sharpen risk calls before surgery.
pmc-13558624:
Konosuke Takashima and four colleagues proposed in 2026 a damage detector for structures that computes with the structure itself. Physical reservoir computing treats a physical system's response as the computer, needing only a thin trained readout. Their version splits a structure's vibration into frequency bands. Each band passes through a nonlinear function. The results are summed and fed back into the structure, creating virtual nodes from one sensor and one actuator pair.

Tests used a thin plate plus a thin-walled tube, in simulation and in the laboratory, classified damage about as accurately as ordinary neural networks. Training and running costs fell sharply by comparison, since only the small readout layer learns. The authors present the scheme as a cheap route to continuous structural health monitoring for bridges, pipes, and similar assets where many sensors are impractical.
pmc-13558724:
Yang Yu and six colleagues traced in 2026 how liver cancers escape lenvatinib, a first-line targeted drug whose benefit usually fades as resistance grows. A ubiquitin-trimming enzyme, USP32, turned up overactive in these tumours and tied to aggressive spread and drug failure. Silencing it in cells and in mouse grafts slowed growth and movement and restored the drug's bite, while forcing it higher did the opposite.

The enzyme protects a partner protein, a helicase called DDX17, by snipping off the tags that mark it for destruction. Stabilised DDX17 silences a small tumour-suppressing RNA, which unleashes a growth signalling pathway at the heart of the resistance. Adding a blocker of that pathway to lenvatinib overcame resistance in grafts from already resistant tumours. The authors propose the whole chain as a target sequence for refractory liver cancer.
pmc-13559024:
Ackim Munthali and co-authors reviewed blood test records of COVID-19 patients in three central hospitals in Malawi, in a 2026 study. Blood and chemistry markers are used in routine care to judge how sick a patient is. Malawi had little published data of this kind. The team read records for just under three hundred seventy confirmed patients admitted from 2020 to 2022. Each record was checked against standard healthy ranges.

The median age was forty-six, just over half the patients were men, and about three in five survived. Most markers sat in the normal range. Red cell measures and several liver and stress markers stood out as off range. Low oxygen tracked with high white cell counts. Non-survivors were older, with lower oxygen and higher breathing strain. The authors offer the profile as a base for triage rules tuned to local data.
pmc-13559124:
Liqin Ke and three colleagues present two cases of endobronchial inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor in children, a rare growth inside the airway that is often mistaken for asthma or a swallowed foreign body. Their 2026 report shows treatment guided jointly by where the tumor sat and by its molecular profile, especially ALK status, a gene change that can drive growth.

One boy, aged eight, had an ALK-negative tumor in the right lower lobe bronchus and received a robot-assisted sleeve resection that spared working lung tissue. The other boy, aged six, had an ALK-positive tumor at the airway fork that badly narrowed breathing. He had endoscopic removal followed by crizotinib, a drug aimed at ALK. Neither child showed recurrence at follow-up, though those checks came at only six and three months. The authors urge early molecular testing in children with unexplained airway blockage.
pmc-13559324:
Surgeons at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center reflect on esophageal diversion, an operation that reroutes the food passage after a catastrophic injury to the esophagus. Writing in reply to a Mayo Clinic commentary, Yota Suzuki, Evan Alicuben, James Luketich, and Omar Awais stress that diversion is a bailout, not a first choice. Their center now favors stents with drainage, or direct repair when patients arrive early with favorable anatomy.

Diversion still matters when tissue is destroyed, infection is uncontrolled, or gentler fixes fail. It controls the leak without risking a fragile new join. The team also maps what follows: recovery, quality of life, and later reconstruction.
pmc-13559924:
Xiang-Yu Pei and seven co-authors show that a common flame retardant and plastic nanoparticles scar mouse hearts through one shared pathway. Their 2026 study tests TBBPA, a brominated flame retardant found widely in the environment, alone and with polystyrene nanoplastics, which can carry it. Direct evidence for heart fibrosis from this chemical in mammals had been missing.

In mice, realistic doses impaired heart function and drove inflammation and scarring; the plastic partner alone produced fibrosis. In heart cells the pair acted together, worsening every marker. Tracing the signal, the team found an estrogen receptor switch flipping on a long RNA, H19, which then fires the Wnt pathway. Blocking the receptor or the RNA cut the damage. The axis they name is both a warning and a drug target.
pmc-13560024:
Hay fever and depression travel together in surveys, and Shaojie Zhang and co-authors ask which one causes the other in this 2026 study. They use Mendelian randomization, a genetics trick that treats inherited variants as a natural experiment. Data came from two large genome studies of each condition, all in European ancestry groups.

Genetic liability to hay fever raised depression risk slightly and consistently, by about one percent. The reverse path showed nothing: depression genes did not raise hay fever. Sleep length and anxiety symptoms may carry part of the effect, though those links were fuzzy. A companion molecule, IgE, tied strongly to hay fever liability. Loneliness stood out as the strongest side factor for depression in joint models.
pmc-13560124:
Ümit Karabulut and colleagues investigate duodenogastric reflux, the backward flow of intestinal contents into the stomach, in patients with indigestion. Their 2026 retrospective case-control study covers 524 patients who had upper endoscopy between January 2017 and December 2022. Endoscopic signs such as bile pooling sorted 287 patients into the reflux group, with 237 serving as controls.

Chemical gastropathy, stomach lining injury from bile exposure, appeared significantly more often in the reflux group. Intestinal metaplasia and Helicobacter pylori rates, however, did not differ between the groups. Reflux patients showed higher bilirubin and lower albumin in blood tests. Gallbladder removal and gallstones stood out as strong independent risk factors, while age added a modest effect. The authors describe the condition as multifactorial and leave open whether reflux itself drives precancerous change, calling for prospective research.
pmc-13560824:
Julia Marie Stewart and colleagues present the chromosomal genome of the maze coral, Meandrina meandrites, together with sequences from its microbial partners. Their 2026 genome note describes a stony coral of the western Atlantic, ranging from Bermuda and Florida through the Caribbean to Brazil in shallow water. Its ridged, valleyed surface gives the species its maze and brain coral names.

The assembly spans 551.16 megabases, with 99.25 percent arranged into fourteen chromosomal pseudomolecules, plus a mitochondrial genome of 17.2 kilobases. Annotation by Ensembl identified over thirty thousand protein-coding genes. The team also recovered two bins from the specimen's metagenome, capturing symbiont microbes. The coral grows slowly, laying calcium bands by day, and reproduces both by broadcast spawning and asexually. The authors offer the resource for reef biology and symbiosis research.
pmc-13561024:
Diana Summanwar and co-authors set out a study protocol on finding hidden dementia in primary care in a 2026 paper. More than half of older adults with Alzheimer's disease or related dementias never get a formal diagnosis. A computer tool called the Passive Digital Marker can flag high-risk patients from health record data alone.

The INCLUDE study will run in twelve clinics of one health system. Flagged patients will receive patient-informed secure messages inviting them to a memory assessment. The pilot tests whether this quiet, record-based approach brings more people to testing without adding work for busy clinicians. If it works, the same design could spread to other clinics.
pmc-13561324:
Lijuan Zhao, Shijie Yang, Yadong Wang, and Xin Jin present a faster way to build moving machine models, in work from twenty twenty-six. Old hand building of such models takes much time and invites errors. Their method works with the RecurDyn program and a coal cutting machine as the test case.

The method pulls shape data from design files and names each part with word and sense checks. Code then sets up the parts, joints, drives, and gear contact on its own. Tests on three cutting units matched real trials well. The top speed error was very small, and build time fell to less than one part in a hundred. The plan can move to other complex machines.
pmc-13561524:
Norah Emrich and four co-authors map, in a 2026 study, how distance to a central egg-tissue bank tracks with who uses fertility preservation in Germany. Freezing ovarian tissue can save fertility for girls and women facing harsh treatments. Past work tracked return and pregnancy rates, while who reaches the service at all was less known.

The cohort held 2,426 patients from 124 centres who banked tissue between 2000 and 2021. Children under fifteen lived closest to the bank, with a median of about 136 kilometres, and the distance grew with age group through adolescents to adults. The authors suggest that doctor-led counselling and local referral paths may serve the youngest patients in a more guided way, while adults must travel further or push harder themselves.
pmc-13562124:
Hiroyuki Umegaki and co-authors offer, in a 2026 study, a four-question score, taken at admission, that flags older patients likely to leave hospital less able than they entered. Hospital-associated disability is common and hard to reverse. Prevention works but costs staff time, so targeting matters.

The rule checks age over eighty, a frailty grade, a thinking test score, and whether admission was an emergency. It sorted risk well in their data, with fair accuracy. Low scorers proved very unlikely to decline, sparing them needless intervention. High scorers can receive full geriatric assessment early. A pocket rule that triages fairly beats both blanket programs and guesswork.
pmc-13562224:
Alejandro Lopez-Bezanilla and colleagues use frustrated magnets shaped like fullerene cages to stress-test quantum annealers. Their 2026 study builds Ising models on these closed carbon-like shapes, where magnetic moments cannot all please their neighbors at once, leaving a huge set of equally good layouts. Quantum fluctuations must do the choosing.

The team saw quantum swings lift that tie, favoring certain coherent setups through tunneling between states. Since the models have no edges and high symmetry, they make clean test cases for quantum hardware. Scores rose sharply across successive generations of superconducting annealers on these problems. The authors argue that hitting the shared ground state exactly is where quantum rigs prove themselves. Frustrated cages, they conclude, offer a sharp benchmark for the young field.
pmc-13562524:
Sudenur Ozkan and two colleagues show that the spacing of footstep sounds can change how fast a walking figure seems to move. Earlier work used simple flashes and clicks, leaving open whether sound timing also bends the perceived speed of real human motion. The 2026 experiments used point-light walkers, figures made of dots on the joints, shown one after another with identical visuals. Only the gap between footstep sounds differed. Viewers judged the walker with shorter sound gaps as walking faster, every time.

Shifting the first or last sound did not remove the effect, so the whole interval mattered rather than any single alignment moment. Mismatched sounds worked too, which points to timing itself as the driver. The authors argue that hearing supplies a strong timing cue that vision borrows, helping the brain keep a moving, sounding world in step.
pmc-13562724:
Jingjin Li and five colleagues study what moves Chinese herders to turn grassland ecology into income, selling the value of pasture rather than only livestock. Policy wants those green hills to pay, and herders must act. Working from an ecological-ethics lens, the 2026 study names five factors. They span how herders see their bond with nature, what they know of grassland functions and laws, their pro-environment attitudes, and their husbandry knowledge. Survey data was modelled two ways, with structural equations and with fuzzy-set comparison.

All five factors shaped both intention and behaviour, and intention carried part of the effect. Government policy support strengthened the step from intention to action. Six combinations of conditions sufficed to produce the behaviour, showing there is no single recipe. The authors advise policy that works on beliefs, knowledge, and legal awareness, rather than paying for outcomes alone.
pmc-13562924:
Vladimir Krivtsov, Peter M. Hollingsworth, and a Darwin Tree of Life consortium publish the genome sequence of common heather, Calluna vulgaris. Heather dominates heathlands and moorlands across the British Isles and much of Europe, yet lacked a reference genome. The 2026 assembly covers both copies of the plant's genome, its two haplotypes, at about 522 and 520 million bases. Nearly all of each copy is organised into eight chromosome-scale scaffolds. The team also assembled the mitochondrial genome at about 441 thousand bases and the plastid genome at about 208 thousand bases.

The work sits inside the Darwin Tree of Life project, which is sequencing every eukaryotic species in Britain and Ireland. Background notes trace heather's history: mainly outcrossing, pollinated by bees and flies, with little population structure in Scotland and a likely French refuge after the ice age. A chromosome-level reference now lets researchers probe how this landscape-defining shrub adapts and spreads.
pmc-13563024:
Defei Yin and co-authors present a 2026 review of ferroptosis, an iron-linked form of cell death, in gut cancers. The death path runs on iron overload and fat damage inside cells. In tumors of the food pipe, stomach, liver, and bowel, the same path can cut both ways: it can kill tumor cells or help them resist care. The review gathers the known switches of the path.

Iron handling, fat damage, and one shield system of the cell form the core trio. Shared patterns run across gut tumors, with local twists per organ. Plant extracts that spark the death path get a full survey as candidate drugs. The authors also list what blocks clinic use so far. Clearer rules for when to spark or block the path could sharpen care choices.
pmc-13563124:
Cristian Wulkop-Gil and Michael Petrascheck propose a unifying idea for why brains age: homeostatic conflict. Healthy tissue balances two cell classes with opposite needs. Dividing cells must be pruned when damaged, while post-mitotic cells such as neurons can never be replaced, so they must be protected at all costs. Aging pushes both classes the wrong way at once.

In the brain, support cells called glia multiply and slip into inflammatory senescent states, while neurons lose their molecular identity and die. Maintenance then demands two contradictory actions simultaneously. The authors suggest combination therapies that resolve the conflict: shield irreplaceable neurons from a death pathway called ferroptosis while clearing maladaptive senescent cells. They argue this framework explains age-related dysfunction better than lists of separate causes.
pmc-13563724:
Meo Nguyen and seven colleagues test, in dishes, whether adding a collagen membrane changes how a blood-derived material treats gum ligament stem cells. Advanced platelet-rich fibrin, spun from a patient's blood, is a staple of gum regeneration, and collagen membranes partner it in surgery. Whether the pairing helps or hinders the cells was unclear. The 2026 study soaked the materials into extracts at full strength and at 20 percent, using fibrin from four donors, then fed them to periodontal ligament stem cells.

Only the full-strength combined extract met the toxicity bar, while full-strength fibrin alone wobbled near it, unevenly across donors. Growth activity peaked around day five for all groups. In a scratch test, diluted extracts closed the gap better than full-strength ones, and fibrin beat the pairing at 20 percent. The authors call the pairing's profile mixed and in need of tuning, not an upgrade.
pmc-13563824:
Maiko Kobayashi and two colleagues benchmark GPT-4o's emotional reading of photographs against human raters, and test two tricks meant to make the machine more culturally Polish. Models inherit cultural biases, and vendors suggest persona prompts or native-language prompts as fixes. Their 2026 study had the model rate 1,276 standardised pictures on pleasantness, arousal, and approach-avoidance, fifty-five times per image, under three setups: plain, a Polish-student persona, and Polish language.
