The human yardstick came from 204 raters, sixty percent Polish.

Every setup tracked human ratings, with correlations from 0.525, up to 0.809 at best. Neither trick helped consistently. Polish prompting matched humans better on arousal yet drifted further on approach-avoidance. Pleasantness agreed best overall; landscapes were the easiest category, reaching 0.933, and faces the hardest, dropping to 0.253. Distribution shapes differed in all nine comparisons. The authors advise validating each fix dimension by dimension before trusting machine judges across cultures.
pmc-13563924:
The authors present a fast way to tell which mining area a bauxite ore sample came from, using a laser technique plus machine learning. Traditional composition testing is slow and needs complicated sample preparation. Their method fires a laser inside a small cavity, which strengthens the light signal from the ore; a five-millimeter cavity gave the best boost for aluminum, iron, and titanium. Spectra from nine mining areas were reduced to their most informative features, and a boosted decision-tree classifier, tuned by Bayesian search, did the sorting.

The final system reached about ninety-eight and a half percent accuracy, with matching precision and recall. It beat both untuned versions and rival models. The authors propose the technique for rapid source identification of bauxite in mining, where knowing an ore's origin quickly can guide processing and quality control.
pmc-13564224:
Zeno Guardini and six co-authors pinpoint which light-harvesting parts stack the membranes inside plant cells, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Green plant cells fold their inner membranes into stacks called grana. The stacks keep the two photosystems apart, which balances the flow of light energy between them.

By removing parts of the antenna family that serves the second photosystem, the team could test each part's role. Removing the whole antenna erased the stacks entirely. Removing single subgroups cut stacking by up to two-fifths. One part alone could partly restore stacks, while another made oversized stacks that fell apart in light. Energy spill between the systems tracked antenna loss more than stack shape.
pmc-13564624:
Ching-Kai Lin and four co-authors built an AI helper for lung biopsies in a 2026 study. A scope passed through the airways can sample lung spots, and a quick stain check during the procedure helps doctors judge what they found. Telling a lung-born cancer from one that spread there is hard on the spot, yet it shapes treatment.

The team trained a model on just 346 cell images from forty-one patients. Their design learns from very few examples by borrowing a pretrained network and mixing two model types. The task was to sort three cancers: lung adenocarcinoma and spread from breast and colon tumors. In a test where the model saw five examples per class, it scored about forty-nine percent, beating other few-example methods. The scores are modest, but labeled samples in this setting are scarce, and the authors frame the tool as early decision support.
pmc-13564724:
In cats, an immune attack on their own red blood cells is uncommon but often deadly, and treatment data are thin. The authors review 37 cases seen at one center over ten years, all meeting standard diagnostic criteria. Fifteen cats receive prednisolone alone, and 22 receive it with cyclosporin A added, with the choice left to the treating clinician. The study records clinical findings, side effects, relapses, and long-term outcomes for both groups.

Overall mortality is 24.3 percent, and every death comes within four weeks. Most cats survive the acute phase but need long suppressive treatment, and lasting remission without drugs is rare, seen in just two cats. Five cats relapse, mostly while still on treatment. Because the added drug goes mainly to sicker cats, the authors stress that the two groups cannot be fairly compared for efficacy. They call for prospective studies to settle the question.
pmc-13565224:
Haoliang Chai and co-authors compare five soybean protein feeds for newly weaned piglets. Weaning stress and harsh parts of plain soybean meal can harm the gut and slow growth. Processed feeds may ease both problems, but they differ in cost and effect.

Two trials ran side by side for four weeks with weaned piglets in pens. One trial fed a single diet, and the other let piglets choose between feeds. The team tracked growth, feed choice, protein uptake, blood markers, and colon microbes. One hydrolyzed feed gave the best protein uptake and weight gain. It also raised some immune and growth markers in blood. Gut microbe range did not differ across feeds.
pmc-13565924:
Jolanta Krupa, Jędrzej Blaut, Mariusz Warzecha, Mateusz Kozioł, and Łukasz Breńkacz test 3D-printed polymers for water-lubricated sliding bearings. Their 2026 paper uses fused filament fabrication to make candidate bearing materials.

Specimens from four materials were analyzed for surface profile and mechanical properties by instrumented indentation. Tribological behavior was checked with a pin-on-disc setup. Harder material is usually thought to resist wear better. Yet the material with the lowest wear in their tests had the lowest hardness of all. Wear mechanisms, wear products, and tribolayer formation seem to matter as much as hardness. The findings guide material choice for printed bearings.
pmc-13566324:
Shaza Alkhatib wrote a 2026 study that re-examines old data on how fiber in food shapes gut microbes. No new animals or lab tests were used. Instead, the author reworked gene data from fifteen female mice that had been shared in public archives. The mice had eaten diets with fiber, without fiber, or without fiber but with added short-chain fatty acids.

Those acids are made when gut microbes ferment fiber, and they help feed the gut lining. Mice on the fiber diet had the richest mix of microbes. Their guts held more of the kinds linked to fiber use. Mice without fiber had a clearly different mix, with more of one other kind. Adding the acids alone did not restore the fiber pattern. The re-analysis maps dozens of gene features that differ between the diets. It shows how removing fiber reshapes the gut community and its expected work.
pmc-13566524:
Aina Bellver-Sanchis and six co-authors review how a tiny worm can model Alzheimer's disease research, in a 2026 paper. The worm, Caenorhabditis elegans, lives briefly, has a clear body, and has a fully mapped nervous system. The review centers on a defense pathway that guards cells against oxidative stress. In worms the pathway runs through a protein called SKN-1, the counterpart of a human regulator named Nrf2.

The authors explain how that pathway changes in Alzheimer's disease and how plant compounds switch it on. They describe worm strains built to mimic parts of the disease, from protein clumps to tangles. They then discuss how findings in worms carry over to mammals and to human trials. The review also touches on tailoring treatments to each patient, a growing aim in the field.
pmc-13566824:
Lanjie Xu and co-authors present a 2026 study that pairs body measures with gene activity to tell apart the growth stages of a safflower aphid. Knowing a pest's stage guides when to strike. They measured eight body traits under a microscope and tracked six genes across five young stages and adults.

Body length alone split most young stages. Antenna and tail lengths helped in the middle stages. Leg and head widths overlapped too much to help. Gene patterns filled the gaps: three genes peaked in the first stage, one marked adults, and a pair shift flagged the fourth stage. The combined kit offers farms a fast screen plus a lab check.
pmc-13567124:
Mounir Maafi published a research paper in 2026 on predicting the speed of reactions driven by light between two molecules. Chemists often borrow the order rules of heat-driven reactions for light-driven ones, but light and heat enter molecules differently, and most light rate laws cannot be solved exactly. That gap has held the field back.

Maafi proposes a general formula for the whole course of two basic bimolecular light reactions, covering pairs that share or swap partners. The formula was tested against exact numerical simulations on more than two hundred cases, fitting full reaction traces and matching starting rates. The validated model gives photochemistry a predictive tool it previously lacked.
pmc-13567724:
Frederick Ferguson and co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, a Los Angeles program that hands out free produce at safety-net clinics. Food insecurity shadows the patients these clinics serve. Free distribution days are a direct, popular response.

The team examined repeat attendance at sixteen health center sites. They asked whether regulars ate all the produce they took home, versus only some. Surveys intercepted participants at distribution events. The analysis adjusted for personal, household, and program traits. It also hunted reasons some produce goes uneaten. Distribution programs often count pounds delivered; this one asks what fraction nourishes. The answers can guide how much to give, how often, and with what storage advice.
pmc-13568324:
Yemao Zhang and Xijuan Zhao screen in 2026 the climate cost of road binder made with plant oil and old tire crumbs. The blend could cut the load of plain oil based binder. Yet plant oil chains and tire split rules can swing the full count a lot.

Eight blends were scored from raw goods to plant gate for one ton of binder. Ten thousand dice runs spread the doubt across stock, haul, and energy counts. The top blend, with most crumbs and oil, cut the mean mark next to plain binder. How tire waste is split can flip the gain, so rules must be named.
pmc-13568824:
Marella and seven co-authors present MeTime, a free software package for studying how body chemistry changes over time, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-six. Metabolomics measures hundreds of small molecules, and following them across repeated samples is powerful but messy to analyze.

Written for the R language, MeTime stores datasets, their background details, and results together in one container, so a whole analysis can be rerun and checked. Steps chain together in order, from cleaning data to models and network analysis, and the package wraps many trusted methods, from dimension reduction to mixed-effects models. It can also write up results automatically as web or PDF reports, helping teams keep long studies reproducible.
pmc-13569824:
Feifei Huang, Zhongyi Tong, and Yi Jiang review, in a 2026 retrospective study, 265 patients with invasive breast cancer tested for inherited BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene variants. These variants raise cancer risk and open the door to targeted PARP inhibitor drugs. Tumor features, immune markers, and outcomes were compared by variant status.

Inherited faulty variants clustered with distinct tumor traits, enrichment for triple-negative breast cancer, and worse outlook. Adding standard tissue markers, including an immune marker used in triple-negative disease, may sharpen risk grouping. The authors argue that pairing genetic testing with routine marker panels can guide more personal treatment choices for patients carrying these inherited variants.
pmc-13570024:
Shao-Hsuan Chang and five co-authors hunt for a tear-based molecular signature of keratoconus, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The disease slowly thins and bulges the cornea. Whether tiny RNA strands in tears mirror the cornea's molecular changes was unknown.

The team mined three public corneal gene datasets and found immune-linked shifts in diseased tissue. In a small tear cohort they profiled the tiny RNAs and picked a five-member signature. The signature separated patients from controls in an independent dataset, and one member was consistently lowered across all sources. A combined index mixing that RNA with corneal steepness tracked disease shape closely. The authors say tear RNAs may add molecular detail to eye exams, pending more work.
pmc-13570124:
Kim Birnie-Gauvin and co-authors measure sprinting in migrating salmon in a 2026 study. Sockeye in British Columbia's Fraser River swim up to eleven hundred kilometers to spawn, spending a fixed energy budget on steady cruising and short anaerobic bursts. Tags that record motion were fitted at the river mouth, and sixteen were recovered at the spawning grounds, giving full-trip records for the first time.

Bursts filled only 1.2 percent of the journey on average, but the Fraser Canyon, just over a third of the distance, demanded three quarters of all burst effort. In the canyon, fish averaged about four and a half bursts per kilometer. Fish avoided bursting at night early in the trip. Burst styles varied along the route but not consistently per fish.
pmc-13570524:
Sophie Maiwald, Ferdinand Maiwald, and Tony Heitkam hunt for overlooked jumping genes in sugar beet, in a 2026 study. Plant genomes teem with retrotransposons, DNA stretches that copy themselves around the genome. Short, non-autonomous versions lack full copying machinery and often hide from standard searches. The team knew the sugar beet element landscape well and used it to size the blind spot.

A structure-based search with hand checks found over one hundred hidden families. Some were tiny trimmed versions, others stretched past fifteen thousand letters with shuffled parts. Only some families could be tied to a full autonomous parent element. The rest show the hidden fraction varies far beyond known templates. The authors propose fixes so genome catalogues stop missing this large share of plant DNA.
pmc-13570824:
Danzeng Awang and colleagues tested whether salidroside, a Rhodiola compound, protects the heart from low-oxygen injury, publishing the study in 2026. High-altitude hypoxia strains the oxygen-hungry heart, driving oxidative stress, mitochondrial failure, and cell death, while current drugs carry notable side effects. The team combined network pharmacology and docking with experiments in cobalt-chloride hypoxia models in cells and rats.

Salidroside improved cell survival, cut reactive oxygen species, restored mitochondrial energy output, and curbed cell death, while in rats it eased ECG abnormalities, heart-muscle injury, hypertrophy, and lung and liver damage. Mechanistic tests showed it steered a protective GSK-3β switch largely without Akt. The work supports salidroside as a candidate shield against hypoxia-related heart injury.
pmc-13570924:
Yiyao Fu and colleagues compared gut microbes and blood chemistry in young and aged mice whose ovaries had failed. Ovary failure goes with ageing of the reproductive system and body-wide metabolic upset, but the microbial causes are poorly mapped. Their 2026 study read gut-microbe genes from faeces and scanned blood serum from 7-week-old and 12-month-old female mice.

Old mice had a changed gut community, with fewer Firmicutes and more Bacteroidetes, plus more Alistipes and Akkermansia. Their blood held 246 differing metabolites, mostly tied to amino-acid and energy pathways. Tryptophan metabolism stood out as the link between gut imbalance and metabolic change. The authors point to those microbes and blood markers as targets for future care in ovary failure.
pmc-13571124:
Moath Bani Salem and five co-authors report a 2026 case of lung scarring tied to burst breast implants. A 77-year-old woman came in short of breath. Her silicone implants, placed at age 35, had both ruptured. Two years earlier a chest scan had shown early lung disease next to that rupture, with few symptoms.

The new scan showed the disease much advanced: hazy patches, a net of scars, warped airways pulled by the tightening tissue. Silicone that leaks can reach the lungs and stir slow harm, from clots to pneumonia-like patches to this scarring kind. The case warns that the fuse can burn for years.
pmc-13571324:
Joint replacement parts that get infected are hard to treat, and a 2026 study by Jesper Ericsson and co-authors reviews how one antibiotic, clindamycin, performed at low dose. The drug is a backup option when first-line drugs do not suit, but a partner drug, rifampicin, is known to lower its levels in the body.

The team looked back at patients treated at one center from 2010 to 2022, given clindamycin alone or with other antibiotics. Cure meant no return of the same germ after two years of follow-up. Just under half the group received clindamycin alone. The study weighs how well each route worked and how well patients tolerated the drug in real practice.
pmc-13571524:
Yuan Tian and co-authors test whether steroid shots after stretching a narrowed esophagus help patients whose narrowing keeps returning. Their study appeared in 2026. The team reviewed thirty patients treated at one Beijing hospital between 2012 and 2021. Eleven received a modified steroid injection after dilation; nineteen had dilation alone. The new technique aims a short needle into the layer under the tear edge left by stretching.

The combined treatment did not clearly delay the next dilation, and session counts matched. But total time on dilation therapy was shorter, and swallowing difficulty eased more. Bleeding and other risks did not differ. A pooled analysis with earlier studies accompanies the review. The authors read the modified shot as a modest but real aid for a stubborn condition.
pmc-13571724:
Yun-Fei Lin and co-authors study how stem cells from umbilical cords calm lung immune cells in a model of aspiration pneumonia, in work published in 2026. Aspiration pneumonia follows when mouth germs reach the lungs. A toxin from a gum germ can push lung immune cells into an inflamed state that harms the lung.

The team combined gene data, single-cell analysis, and lab and animal tests. The toxin pushed all lung immune cell types toward the inflamed state. The stem cells reversed that shift, and in animals they restored the main lung immune cells to a calm state. The change ran through the cells' power units, which the stem cells reprogrammed. The findings hint at a cell-based route to restore balance in this severe lung disease.
pmc-13571824:
Laila Ahmed Abdelhamid and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of major harms tied to emergency breathing tube placement in adults. Placing a tube outside the operating room is one of the riskiest acts in acute care. Yet reports of harm vary widely across places and studies. The team set out to pull the recent proof together.

They searched five large databases for studies from 2021 onward. Only primary studies of non-elective cases in adults were kept. Reviews, letters, and plans were left out. Data were pulled twice to check for errors. The review maps how often major harm occurs and what drives it. The aim is safer practice in emergency care.
pmc-13572024:
Mohamed Riad and co-authors looked for signs that predict dangerous heart rhythms in patients with tumors inside the heart's lower chambers, in work published in 2026. Thirty four patients from a heart center registry were followed for a median of three years. Eleven had a serious rhythm event or sudden death.

Those patients were older and more often had fainting and palpitations. Their tumors were much larger, always single, and more often of certain types. One common childhood tumor type appeared only in the calmer group. Heart pumping strength did not differ. The authors caution that tumor type itself may explain much of the pattern.
pmc-13572524:
Constance Denoyelle, with 16 colleagues, reports a 2026 survey of a gut protozoan in French broiler chickens. Blastocystis is the most common such organism found in people, and birds may pass it to humans. No French farm survey had been done, so the team sampled birds at one slaughterhouse from 66 farms.

A total of 967 gut samples covered three farm systems, from free-range label birds to standard indoor flocks. The organism turned up in 49.7 percent of samples and on 83.3 percent of farms. Farm type and season shaped how often it appeared. Subtype 7 led by far, with subtype 6 next, and near a fifth of positive birds carried two or more subtypes. Gene reads showed wide variety within subtype 7. The authors flag flocks as a real source of human exposure.
pmc-13572624:
Why do some people suffer in the midst of success? Swapan Samanta argues in 2026 that common well-being models share a hidden flaw: they let a surplus in one part of life cancel a lack in another. Rich total scores then fail to predict how a person truly feels, a gap the author sees in wealth, love, and even in those who give up worldly life.

The essay sets out a candidate model where balance matters more than totals, so a deep lack in one area cannot be bought off by gains elsewhere. It ties that frame to Buddhist contemplative practice, which the author casts as a path that works on balance itself. The piece is a theory proposal, offered to link two fields that have talked past each other.
pmc-13572724:
Sahar Nouri and six co-authors read the full set of viruses in birch pollen by its gene text. Their study, from two thousand twenty-six, shows a rich mixed crowd.

Viruses are now seen as part of plant life, yet the seed dust of trees was bare of study. Birch pours out vast wind-borne pollen that can roam far. It may bear viruses from the tree or its clinging microbes. The team took pollen from trees in and round a great city. Pooled dust from a past year was read in depth. Single-tree dust from a fresh year was checked by a quick test. One virus's text was walked out to near full length.
pmc-13572824:
Curcumin making in engineered microbes is lifted by Jianbin Chen and co-authors in work dated 2026. Curcumin is a prized plant compound, but one step in its path rots fast in air. With pH and air control in stages, a five-litre vat run hit the best yield yet for one-strain making from scratch. The same frame lifted a kin compound's yield by near seventy percent and cut browning. Flux guard may travel to kin paths.
pmc-13572924:
Mitreski and a team including Chan and Kamba tested in twenty twenty-six if a smart chat tool can translate live talks on consent for scans and treatments. Tongue gaps can lead to mix-ups and poor care, and trained speakers are often not at hand. They ran fake consent talks in nine tongues with the tool GPT-4o.

Thirty-six talks were scored on a long list of points for clear and true word swaps. Most talks passed the set bar, with a mean near nine-tenths of the top score. Seven tongues passed each time, while two tongues lagged well behind. Speed was high in all tongues, but the lagging two still need a human speaker in charge.
pmc-13573524:
Hongbin Zhou and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six observational study of body composition markers in sleep apnea among heavier adults. Obesity raises apnea risk, yet many obese people never develop it. Simple ratios of muscle to fat might separate those who do.

Patients with full body composition and sleep study records were divided by apnea status. Three muscle-to-fat ratios were compared between the groups. Statistical models and diagnostic curves weighed each ratio's value. The aim was markers that flag apnea risk beyond weight alone. Sleep clinics get candidate measures that a body scan already provides.
pmc-13573624:
Dan Ding and co-authors map a rare plant-sterol disease across China, adding one unusual case. Their 2026 paper concerns sitosterolemia, a gene fault that lets plant sterols build up in blood. Their young patient also carried a second gene fault that destroys the kidneys.

The boy was first misread as having an immune storm condition. Gene tests settled both diagnoses at once. A review of 131 Chinese cases found fatty skin lumps and high cholesterol in most patients. Blood and organ damage grew commoner in adults. One of the two genes caused most cases. The authors stress gene testing when the picture clashes.
pmc-13573724:
Clarisa Bencomo, Terry McGovern, and Oriana López Uribe argue that strong, specialized United Nations bodies remain vital for sexual and reproductive rights. The drivers they name are expert agencies with matched mandates, civil society voice in norms and watch, and consensus rule. Each driver, they warn, is now being undercut, and the hard-won gains have begun to slide back.
pmc-13573924:
Haohong Zhang and co-authors review foundation models for microbiome science in a 2026 paper. Sequence data on microbes pile up faster than sense made of them, and most studies stay locked to one cohort. Foundation models learn reusable codes from vast unlabeled sets, which may loosen that lock.

The review stacks the field by scale: sequence models that read DNA and protein grammar, community models that learn from abundance maps, and mixed models that add host and habitat context. Design picks on tokens, training aims, and tests get a hard look. The path ends at world models that can simulate interventions.
pmc-13574224:
Ernesto Sánchez-Llanos and co-authors study healing of a leak after throat surgery in work from 2026. The leak, called a pharyngocutaneous fistula, can follow removal of the voice box and is often treated without more surgery.

Among 194 patients treated from 2010 to 2025, about half developed the leak, and about two thirds of those healed on their own with conservative care. Size was the strongest factor: tiny leaks almost always closed, while large ones rarely did. Low hemoglobin, a high blood ratio marker, and prior radiation also lowered or slowed healing.
pmc-13574324:

They also weigh ways to raise acid levels, from diet to targeted microbes. Gaps are flagged honestly, since much of the chain is still inferred from separate studies. pmc-13574724:
Cynthia Russell Lippincott and co-authors analyze, in 2026, whether a habit-building program helps transplant patients take immune-suppressing drugs on schedule. The program links pill-taking to existing routines or builds new cues. Data came from trials in the United States and Türkiye, with adherence measured by electronic bottle caps.

Habit strength rose during the program in both the intervention and comparison groups, then settled. Turkish participants showed stronger habits than American ones. Statistical analysis confirmed habit as the pathway: the program strengthened habit, and stronger habit improved adherence. The authors say designing for habit, not just reminders, is the transferable lesson.
pmc-13575124:
Narek Abelyan introduces PocketMaster, a 2026 software tool for comparing the pockets in protein structures where molecules bind. Small shape changes in these pockets can alter how a protein works and how a drug fits. Comparing many structures by hand is slow, so the tool automates lining up, grouping, and charting pockets.

For the estrogen receptor, it caught a known shift in one helix between active and inactive states. Results come with automatic reports and visuals. Abelyan positions the tool for early drug design, with code shared openly online.
pmc-13575424:

pmc-13575624:
Hannah Al-Yousuf and co-authors report a rare fusion gene behind acute myeloid leukaemia in a young adult. Their twenty twenty-six case report covers a nineteen-year-old woman. The fusion joins HNRNPH1 with ERG, and such ERG fusions make up under one percent of these leukaemias.

RNA sequencing found the fusion at diagnosis, though standard chromosome tests can miss it. At relapse, a second form of the fusion appeared that the first tracking test could not see. That miss shows why fusion shape matters for watching leftover disease. The team argues for care tracking of transcript shifts, since they can change prognosis and guide treatment choices in rare subtypes.
pmc-13576124:
Wu Weiwei and five colleagues test a spiral form of arc radiotherapy for bulky tumours in a 2026 planning study. GRID therapy aims high dose at peaks inside a tumour while keeping valleys between them low. Standard linear accelerator methods struggle to keep that contrast sharp.

Twenty patients' plans were rebuilt three ways: the spiral method, standard arc therapy, and helical tomotherapy. The spiral approach pairs couch movement with gantry rotation to trace a helical path. It produced the steepest dose fall-off and the highest peak-to-valley ratios under both measures used. Healthy organ limits were met by all three methods with no meaningful gaps. Beam time for the spiral method sat between the other two. The authors judge the spiral method dosimetrically strongest for single-session GRID work.
pmc-13576224:
Szymon Kuliś and three colleagues test whether brief targeted cooling calms the tremor that follows hard exercise in young swimmers, in a 2026 crossover trial. Tremor rises after intense effort as muscles tire. Cold therapy is common in sports medicine, yet its effect on exercise tremor had not been directly tested.

Thirty-four competitive teenage swimmers each completed both conditions: 60 seconds of localised cooling on tender muscle trigger points, and a no-treatment control. Tremor in both legs was recorded before and after a 30-second maximal tethered swim, with a set recovery gap. Exercise raised tremor power as expected. Cooling blunted that rise in the 9 to 14 hertz band, the frequency range tied to nerve-driven tremor. Frequency shifts were less tidy. The authors note the value for actual performance is still unknown.
pmc-13576324:
Andrea Stašek leads a 2026 study mapping how problem gaming and problem social media use connect to teenage wellbeing across ten European countries. Most past work scored each habit as a single total. This team used symptom networks on survey data from 33,586 adolescents aged 11 to 15, gathered in 2021 and 2022.

One symptom sat at the centre of both habits: escapism, using games or feeds to dodge feelings. It was the most common symptom and the main bridge to loneliness in both sexes, and to overall wellbeing and nervousness in girls. Symptoms reflecting fallout, such as conflict, deception, and trouble with others, linked tightly across the two habits, hinting at a shared condition rather than separate ones. The authors argue prevention should target single symptoms, starting with escapism.
pmc-13576424:
John Holland and co-authors argue that a major kidney care trial teaches as much about how a treatment is delivered as about the treatment itself. Kidney disease is now largely a disease of older age, bringing frailty, many conditions at once, and heavy medication loads. Comprehensive geriatric assessment promises care fitted to that whole picture.

Reading the GOAL trial closely, the authors ask whether the assessment was actually delivered with fidelity in every site. A complex service tested loosely can look weak even when the idea is sound. Their commentary urges nephrology teams to measure delivery quality before judging results, and to plan that measurement into future trials.
pmc-13576624:
Ruanlin Li and co-authors trace why a pinch of cerium improves aluminum in a 2026 study. Adding rare-earth cerium to plain aluminum raises both strength and electrical conductivity, a rare pairing, since most strengtheners hurt conductivity. The team added a tiny share of cerium to a standard pure aluminum and asked which inner changes drive the double gain.

Conductivity, strength, and stretch all rose, while grains shrank by more than a third. Microscopy showed iron and silicon, the usual impurities, pulled out of the main metal into small round particles that also held cerium. With fewer stray atoms in the matrix, electrons met less resistance. Inside those particles, a cerium-rich layered phase bonded to the aluminum in a set alignment. Atom-level math showed that bond is stable. The authors link the gains to this cleaning and bonding.
pmc-13577124:
Gan and nine colleagues profile the gut effects of a keratin digesting enzyme in mice in twenty twenty-five. The enzyme, kerZJ, might serve as a feed additive. Safety and gut impact needed checking before such use. The team combined gene, protein, microbe, and metabolite profiling.

The enzyme was well tolerated, with no sign of body wide toxicity. Gut lining stayed intact, and barrier proteins such as collagen increased. Mucosal immunity strengthened without triggering inflammation. Digestive enzyme levels and short chain fatty acid output rose. Gut microbes shifted toward helpful families without falling into imbalance. High doses changed community makeup more strongly. The authors support developing kerZJ as a safe additive.
pmc-13577824:
Bernadett Szögi-Tatár and co-authors document natural etiolation in spearmint: shoots growing pale and undeveloped because they rise through dark soil from underground rhizomes. The team found the inner structures of true darkness growth, including etioplasts with prolamellar bodies, in the leaves and stems of these soil-grown shoots.

Shoots forced in darkness in water matched the soil shoots in symptoms, plastid structure, and chlorophyll building, so lab-grown dark shoots make a fair model of the natural process. Dark shoots had slightly smaller leaves and smaller oil glands, though gland counts were unchanged and always higher on the leaf underside. Their scent and phenolic profiles also shifted, with fewer compounds in the dark-grown tissue.
pmc-13577924:
Ximing Ran leads a 2026 study hunting blood proteins that foretell when a healthy carrier of an ALS gene fault will develop the disease. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal nerve disease, and prevention trials are blocked by not knowing who will convert, or when. The team used a high-throughput protein platform on stored blood samples.

The collection held 516 samples from 33 people who later developed ALS, 35 patients, 10 symptom-free carriers, and 59 controls. Ninety-two proteins shifted in level before symptoms began. A core panel of 19 predicted conversion with ranking scores between 0.80 and 0.89 across half-year to five-year windows, and estimated the timing to within a mean of 1.6 years. Checks in UK Biobank data backed several of the signals. The authors say the panel beats the single best-known marker used alone.
pmc-13578124:
Joseph Wishart and three co-authors wrote this 2026 paper fixing a known method for checking MRI scanner fields. A scanner's main magnetic field should be perfectly even; unevenness warps images. One check compares images taken at two bandwidths, but the published version of that check rests on an error, which the team proves on paper and in practice.

Their fix measures how far fixed points shift between the two images, instead of measuring widths. In a test block filled with fluid pins, they bent the field on purpose and compared methods against a trusted reference scan. The fixed method matched the reference closely, while the old width-based method badly understated the unevenness. A round test object confirmed the fix within a small margin. Scanner teams gain a corrected recipe for routine quality checks.
pmc-13578224:
Mikolaj Rogalski and eight co-authors present a lens-free three-space scan that maps vast blocks at fine grain and heeds multi-scatter. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Lens scans are capped in view width and depth, which blocks high-flow work. Lens-free scans widen the view but past ones failed on thick, clouded goods over depth.

Their set uses multi-tone slant light and auto angle checks for true builds. A slice-by-slice solver tracks multi-scatter, which beats plain first-pass math. Test builds spanned vast depth and view at gigavoxel scale. A thick mouse brain slice was mapped with no dye, a first for this rig. Wide life and goods work is the aim.
pmc-13578324:
Xiaoyu Zhang and colleagues test whether hemoglobin, the oxygen carrying protein in blood, can calm inflamed vessel lining cells, in a 2026 lab study. Vessel diseases grow from long term injury and oxidative stress, a state where reactive oxygen overwhelms cell defenses. The team stressed human vein cells with peroxide, then added hemoglobin and watched stress and inflammation markers.

Hemoglobin lowered three key inflammatory signals and cut cell death, along with the waste markers of oxidative damage. The gain ran through a defense pathway that switches on protective genes. Blocking that pathway largely erased the benefit, which ties the effect to the pathway itself. Since the anti-inflammatory effect followed the drop in stress, the authors frame stress control as the root of the gain.
pmc-13578424:
Temesgen Debas Awoke, Semu Mitiku Kassa, and Gizaw Mengistu Tsidu model short, sharp control bursts against visceral leishmaniasis, a deadly parasite disease spread by sandflies, in a 2026 study. Heat and rain drive sandfly numbers, so spread swings with the seasons. Steady year round control is too costly for many poor regions, which pushed the team toward brief, well timed pushes.

Their model folds weather into the spread math and tests spray rounds, breeding site clearing, and culling of infected host animals. Sandfly linked factors drove cases far more than host factors, so fly control won priority. Two one week pushes a year cut human cases by about ninety five percent in the model. Starting six weeks after the infection peak worked best, and pairing fly control with culling beat either alone.
pmc-13578724:
Haelim Yoon and colleagues test an old drug, emetine, against liver cancer cells that learn to spread, in a 2026 lab study. Spread starts when cancer cells loosen their neat sheet form and gain a wandering form, a shift driven by a protein called Twist1. The drug, long used for other ills, had never been checked for this anti-spread role.

At doses that spared cell life, the drug slowed migration and invasion across five liver cancer cell lines. Twist1 levels fell, sheet markers rose, and wandering markers dropped. Rescue tests showed the drug shortens the life of the Twist1 protein itself. A mutant form that cannot take a key chemical tag resisted the drop. Two stress pathways that place that tag went quiet under the drug, tying the pieces together.
pmc-13578924:
Masaki Tanaka and co-authors report three cases from 2026 of amyloid in the lung, a rare build-up of firm protein threads. The disease can pose as cancer or as wide lung scarring on scans, so tissue proof is a must. All three patients were called by a plain forceps biopsy through a scope, a gentler path than surgery.

Two patients held lumps that mimicked cancer. The biopsy named amyloid, and full checks found no spread past the lung. The third had weight loss and wide wall thickening in the lung. Her biopsy find sparked body-wide checks that found a blood cancer driving the build-up. The team shows one test can serve two ends: clear a lump, or flag a whole-body disease.
pmc-13579524:
Prabhakar and co-authors review in 2026 a class of holey materials built to trap pollution. The materials, porous organic polymers, are light nets with permanent pores and surfaces that can be tuned by design. That tuning lets builders aim them at one pollutant over others, and reuse them many times.

The review sorts the main families, from cross-linked nets to crystal-like frames, and ties pore shape and surface charge to results. Uses cover carbon capture, solvent vapors, heavy metals, dyes, drug waste, and farm sprays, across water, air, and soil. Working rules cover how trapping works, how well the nets survive damp and time, and how they are refreshed. Such a map helps pick the right net for each clean-up job.
pmc-13579824:
Xue Huang, Xingya Liu, Huibo Dai, and Mei Xu report a benign cyst that made an early ovarian cancer look far advanced, in a 2026 case report. A 58 year old woman past menopause carried a large belly and pelvis tumor of a clear cell type. Scans showed odd patches in the gut lining membrane, and a blood marker ran high, both hinting that cancer had seeded widely.

Surgery told another story. The membrane patches were one blood filled cyst, not spread at all. Lab work confirmed the ovarian tumor was still early stage, and the cyst was harmless. Twelve months after surgery she remained free of disease. The authors warn that scans and markers alone can overstage such cases, and that eyes in the operating room plus lab proof should settle the stage.
pmc-13579924:
Yuxin Jiang and co-authors review how gut microbes steer uric acid, the waste product behind gout. High uric acid is rising worldwide, and current lowering drugs carry safety limits. The gut both makes and expels a share of uric acid, so its microbes are natural suspects and natural levers. Their 2026 review gathers a decade of work from two major databases.

Microbes push uric acid up or down by handling its building blocks, degrading urate itself, adjusting the gut's export pumps, and stoking or calming inflammation. The review sorts microbe-based remedies into four families, from live strains and their products to natural compounds, fibers the microbes eat, and active peptides. The authors argue these offer safer templates for drug design than simply blocking one transporter, since they regulate the whole system at once.
pmc-13580024:
Linghan Kong, Stephen Eichhorn, and Richard Bryce use molecular dynamics simulations to test whether folded chain ends fit the cellulose-II fibril structure. Their 2026 study inserts short folded glucosyl turns into a crystal model of that fibril.

Ten candidate turn models were ranked by semiempirical quantum mechanical energies. Across many long simulations, the crystalline core kept its unit cell, diffraction pattern, hydrogen bonding network, and ring conformation. Perturbation stayed localized near the folded ends, where higher-energy conformations appeared. Five-residue turns were more flexible, but the authors judge the three-residue turn more plausible. The result suggests chain folds need not destroy bulk crystalline order.
pmc-13581024:
Thomas Muehlbauer leads a team on balance training for young soccer players. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with interlimb asymmetry. Single mode versus combined training had not been compared.

Young male players were split by chance in three groups. One did balance drills alone on the weak leg. One added jump training to the balance work. A control group kept its usual active routine. Training ran nine weeks in season, twice weekly. Still and moving balance were tested on both legs. Tests ran before and after the program.  Ages sat in the early teen years.
pmc-13581524:
Jingyi Peng and co-authors review how a family of protein tags links metabolism to liver inflammation in this 2026 paper. The disease in view is fatty liver tied to metabolic dysfunction, a slow condition of fat buildup, low-grade inflammation, and immune change. Beyond fat itself, chemical edits to proteins may steer its course.

The tag family is lysine acylation, small groups attached to a common protein building block. What tags get written depends on the cell's fuel supply and on the enzymes that add and remove them. The review follows the tags through four liver cell types, from fat-storing cells to the immune sentries and scarring cells. Gut-derived chemicals and disturbed sugar and fat handling shape which tags appear. The authors weigh the tags as possible blood markers and drug targets, and propose tracing and gene-editing tools to pin down which single sites matter.
pmc-13581724:
Women who had diabetes in pregnancy often keep extra weight afterward, which raises their long-term health risks. Jiahui He and co-authors study 141 such women living one to three years past delivery in Dali, a moderately high-altitude region of China. They score each woman's diet quality from a food questionnaire and record how much weight she kept.

Better diet quality went with clearly less kept weight, even after adjusting for many other factors. Each extra point of diet score meant roughly a tenth of a kilogram less, so ten points meant about a kilogram. Activity looked helpful at first glance but lost its link once other factors were counted. Lower starting weight and bigger babies predicted more kept weight. The authors back diet advice tailored to the region.
pmc-13581824:
Zunyuan Li and five co-authors map in 2026 the clinical trials of bispecific antibodies for non-small cell lung cancer. This common lung cancer often learns to resist targeted drugs, and many tumors shut out the immune-based drugs known as checkpoint inhibitors.

Bispecific antibodies grab two targets at once, which can block escape routes and wake up the immune response inside the tumor. The authors systematically reviewed the trial record to chart which designs are being tested and how the field is developing. Their survey shows where this approach stands and which strategies drug developers are betting on next.
pmc-13581924:
Nixuan Wang, Mingxia Ji, Junfeng Wang, and Chenyu Ma published a study in 2026 on a nutritional risk score in sepsis-associated lung failure. They tested its prognostic value for twenty-eight-day mortality. Nutritional and metabolic derangements are common in these patients and may contribute to adverse outcomes. The NUTRIC score was designed to flag nutritional risk in critical illness.

The researchers analyzed 152 patients admitted to intensive care at one hospital between December 2023 and January 2025. About a third of the patients died within twenty-eight days. Each one-point rise in the score was associated with higher odds of death, after adjustment for other characteristics. The relationship ran close to a straight line. The score distinguished patients who died from survivors with fair accuracy, and held up in internal validation. Compared with two other nutritional indices, it is a sound tool for flagging patients needing prompt attention.
pmc-13582024:
Dengke Ou, Jie Song, and Mingyang Tang report a case where a heart device slipped into the wrong chamber and was retrieved in the same session, in a 2026 case report. Closing the left atrial appendage is a stroke-prevention option for patients with atrial fibrillation who cannot take blood thinners long term. In rare cases the device comes loose and moves, which can be life-threatening. In this case it landed in the left ventricle.

The patient was a sixty-eight-year-old woman with lasting fibrillation, heavy bleeding on blood thinners, chronic heart failure, and high stroke risk. Imaging showed a wide appendage opening. On the first try, the device did not anchor well. The team retrieved it through the aorta by catheter and then redid the closure in the same session.
pmc-13582224:
Kiril Trpkov and Abbas Agaimy introduce a journal issue on new ideas in kidney tumor classification in a 2026 article. Kidney tumors are biologically diverse and their classification has shifted much over two decades, as the World Health Organization guides show. The issue gathers studies and reviews on several tumor types whose place in the scheme is being rethought.

One thread argues that a tumor long listed on its own is really a pattern inside a related family. It bases the claim on shared looks, stains, and gene traits, and says the two should be merged. Another thread covers a tumor tied to a gene that, when faulty from birth, causes a syndrome with skin and lung signs. The editors frame the issue as part of an ongoing cleanup of kidney tumor taxonomy.
pmc-13582324:
A sow that returns to heat promptly after weaning keeps a pig farm efficient, and her gut fungi may have a say in the timing. The authors profile fecal fungi with metagenomics in 85 sows and compare those that return to estrus on schedule with those that do not. Twenty-two fungal species differ between the groups. On-time sows carry more of one yeast, Arxiozyma slooffiae, and less of two others.

The fungi do not act alone: the favored yeast tracks with Prevotella bacteria also enriched in on-time sows, and the pair are predicted to swap metabolites such as iron and thiamine. A panel of fungal markers separates the groups well, and adding bacterial markers sharpens it further. Links to hormones run through the data too, with the yeast tied to plant estrogens and steroid pathways. The authors present the gut mycobiome as an overlooked player in sow fertility.
pmc-13583024:
Two doctors in Brazil ran a small pilot study of Botox treatment to lift the eyebrows, in work published in 2026. Brow position shapes how young a face looks, and the muscle that rings the eye pulls the brow down. Most Botox routines treat that muscle only in part. The team tested blocking its upper portion completely in ten women unhappy with their brow position.

Nine women finished the study and were photographed before and fifteen days after treatment. About eighty-nine percent saw their brows improve, and none saw them worsen. Most felt only mild pain from the injections, and no serious side effects such as drooping eyelids appeared. Every participant said she was satisfied and would recommend the treatment. The authors offer the fuller block as a promising add-on to standard brow routines.
pmc-13583124:
Junya Wang and co-authors use alternating current to unlock a new bond making path in a 2026 chemistry paper. Joining carbon chains to ring carbons is a staple move, but one classic route needs the chain part pre built in a fixed way.

Their scheme frees a fleeting charged chain fragment with electric current, then a metal catalyst guides it to a ring carbon with sharp aim. The flipped route yields chain topped stilbene frames across a broad set of starts. Signal hunts and computer models point to a metal path in two high states. The work widens what electric synthesis can do.
pmc-13583224:
Yujia He and co-authors test a probiotic bacterium against allergic asthma, tracing its effect through the gut. Their 2026 study starts from growing evidence that gut microbes shape lung immunity through their chemical products. The strain studied, a Lactiplantibacillus plantarum called GUANKE, was tested for both prevention and treatment of airway allergy.

In models, the bacterium eased airway overreaction and the Th2-type inflammation behind allergy, while partly restoring regulatory T cells. Wiping out gut microbes, or transferring them, showed the protection rides on the resident community. A microbial product, indole-3-acetic acid, fell in patients' blood and proved to be a key messenger in the chain.
pmc-13583324:
Kei Kimura and eleven co-authors map wiring between two brain hubs in monkeys, in this twenty twenty-six study. A front brain area that steers mood and feeling talks closely with the amygdala, the brain's alarm center. The fine layout of that wiring was not known.

Using tracer dyes and viruses in macaques, the team traced fibers both ways between three parts of the front area and two parts of the amygdala. Each link came from a distinct mix of shallow and deep cell layers. A clear wiring map helps explain how the brain steadies mood, and where that control may fail in illness.
pmc-13583524:
Callum Stephenson, Jazmin Eadie, Mohsen Omrani, and Nazanin Alavi survey mental health clinicians about AI in care in a paper from 2026. Sixty-two United States professionals answered in late 2024. Most were not yet using AI in practice. The most welcomed uses were clerical: coding, billing, intake, and documentation. Discomfort with AI touching direct patient care was widespread.

Top worries were wrong outputs, bias, and lost accessibility. Barriers named included clinician resistance, weak validation, and integration trouble. Nearly nine in ten wanted dedicated training in AI ethics and use. Open answers stressed fears of dehumanized, culturally blind care. The authors frame AI as an adjunct, not a replacement.
pmc-13583724:
Vidya Lalloo, Jan Heystek, and André du Plessis review ECG training in South African teaching hospitals in a paper from 2026. Emergency clinicians often misread electrocardiograms, with risks for patients. The authors view the problem through a framework about how people live inside institutions. Consultants sit between national rules and the daily pressures of trainees they supervise.

The review proposes accredited ECG workshops as a middle path. A framework for sustainable workshops balances regulator demands, university training duties, hospital quality goals, and clinicians' negative attitudes. Local realities, including curriculum change, are built in. The authors call for trials that test whether the workshops improve skill and patient outcomes.
pmc-13583824:
Shanti Narayanasamy and co-authors track rule following in at risk groups during COVID in a 2026 study. The work sits in Victoria, Australia, inside a long cohort study that ran from 2020 to 2023. It compares two month long windows, one calm and one in lockdown, for people from diverse language roots or low income homes.

Measures split into advice, lockdown limits, and standing mandates. Of 782 recruits, most filled a survey or diary in at least one window. Groups were classed as diverse, low income, or neither, and rates of adherence were set side by side. The design shows how crisis rules land unevenly across a city.
pmc-13583924:
Faizal Manrapi and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a fifteen-year-old boy with several cysts in his jaws. Such cysts, called odontogenic keratocysts, can appear alone, but many at once in a young patient point to an inherited syndrome. His left jaw had been swelling for nine months before he reached a dental hospital in Indonesia.

Scans showed cysts in both upper and lower jaws, with teeth trapped inside the bone. A chest image showed a split rib, and a head scan showed hardened tissue in the brain's midline fold. Tissue tests confirmed the cyst type, and the full picture fit Gorlin-Goltz syndrome. Surgeons removed the cysts in stages, and early scans showed new bone forming. The authors stress careful checks for the syndrome whenever teens show many jaw cysts.
pmc-13584024:
Waleed Mohammed Abdelfattah and five co-authors model a reactive nanofluid flowing over a sensor plate, in a 2026 paper. The fluid carries heat-hungry nanoparticles and swimming microbes, a mix pitched at chips, biosensors, and fuel cells.

Rather than solve the tangled equations head-on, the team trains a neural network with a Bayesian regularization method. The model handles blowing at the surface, heat radiation, and an activation energy for the chemistry. Stronger blowing lifted the flow profile. A stronger chemical reaction thinned the concentration field. The authors frame the setup for reactor design. The same scheme might aid wastewater treatment and biofuel reactors, where microbes and heat must be managed together.
pmc-13584124:
A bacterium that normally lives quietly in the urinary tract turned destructive in a man whose immune defenses were lowered by leukemia treatment. Benandi and Blanton report the first such infection tied to obinutuzumab, a newer antibody drug.

The patient, a 70-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia, suffered months of worsening shoulder pain as the joint rapidly broke down. Early fluid samples and cultures found nothing, and repeated surgical washouts revealed pus and abscesses around the joint. Only extended culturing named the culprit: Mycoplasma hominis, a wall-less bacterium that standard tests and common antibiotics miss. Six weeks of levofloxacin and doxycycline cleared the infection, and his shoulder slowly recovered. The authors warn that such germs deserve early thought when antibody therapy empties the B cells.
pmc-13584324:
Haodong Cai and co-authors report a puzzling blood case in a 2026 paper. A gene defect called ALAS2 usually causes anemia with small red cells, passed down the X chromosome in males. Girls and women who carry one copy sometimes show the opposite pattern, big red cells, which can be mistaken for a vitamin lack or a bone marrow disease.

A 15 year old girl had lived with stubborn big cell anemia for eight years. Blood tests, iron studies, and marrow checks narrowed the search. Whole exome sequencing then found a new variant in the gene. The report pairs her case with past cases to explain how the odd pattern arises.
pmc-13584424:
Xiaoling Wang and a large team trace a brain circuit that links lasting pain with memory loss in mice in this 2026 study. Long-term pain often brings both sharp sensitivity and foggy memory, yet the shared wiring was unclear. The team used a nerve injury model and tested the animals on mazes and object tasks while recording activity in a front brain region called the prelimbic cortex.

One set of calming nerve cells in that region stayed overactive after injury, which threw off the balance between go and stop signals and dulled memory. Quieting those cells eased both pain sensitivity and memory faults. Switching them on in healthy mice created the same faults. A protein named ATF4 sat upstream of the shift, which gives drug hunters a concrete target to test.
pmc-13584724:
Swollen gums in people wearing braces may involve an allergic role for mast cells, and a 2026 study by Amal Ali Ibrahim and co-authors counts those cells in gum tissue. Mast cells sit in soft tissue and release signals such as histamine that draw in other immune cells.

Thirty patients were split into three groups of ten: healthy gum tissue, swollen gums from plaque without braces, and swollen gums during brace treatment. The team stained the samples three ways, one with a marker that tags mast cells, and compared the counts. The aim is to learn whether brace-related swelling carries a mast cell pattern that sets it apart from plain plaque swelling.
pmc-13584824:
Navneet Kumar, Sudeep Tanwar, and Anurag Singh introduce a research collection in a 2026 editorial on AI in food making. Food production once ran on trial and error and broad dietary rules. The editors argue it is shifting toward prediction, live optimisation, and meals tailored to each person.

The editorial surveys five contributions in the collection, from framework reviews to restaurant decision support and cereal product tuning. One review maps AI tools such as computer vision and live monitoring across factory work. Another tracks the move from population diet rules to personal frameworks fed by body data and wearable sensors. The editors stress that value comes from joining many data kinds into workable, repeatable products, not from any single algorithm.
pmc-13584924:
Venema and co-authors report a 2026 study on heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, a form of heart failure that is hard to diagnose. Two scores in wide use, called HFA-PEFF and H2FPEF, rest on heart ultrasound scans that staff read by hand. The team asks whether a deep learning program that reads the scans on its own can score patients as well as manual reading.

The group tested the program in three patient groups, one with 102 patients and two larger groups used for checks. Scores from the program matched the hand-read scores well, and both tracked a pressure measure from heart tests in much the same way. The authors conclude that automated scoring is workable and could speed up diagnosis.
pmc-13585224:
Irene Deftereos and co-authors listen to patients describe eating through curative treatment for upper gut cancers, in work from 2026. Thirteen patients, mostly with esophageal cancer, were interviewed before surgery and again three months after going home.

Four themes emerged: the lived experience of nutritional change, views of the dietitian's role, feeding tubes and supplements as a necessary evil, and the daily-life impact of it all. Patients praised the structured dietetics care and called dietitians essential; one kept the number on speed dial. Nutritional struggles, though, weighed heavily on daily life and mood. The authors recommend intensive, individual nutrition pathways, plus peer support, in similar services.
pmc-13585324:
David Hohenschurz-Schmidt and a large team test a combined therapy for painful diabetic nerve damage in a 2026 feasibility trial. People with this condition lack treatments that work well and are easy to tolerate. Hands on therapy, exercise, and psychological support might help, above all in combination.

Thirty six adults were split among three arms: five sessions of the combined program, five sessions of a look alike control with the same therapists, or usual care. Targets for recruitment, retention, blinding, and data quality were met, and attendance and satisfaction in the program arm were high. Pain, disability, and quality of life were tracked for sixteen weeks as early signals. The authors conclude a full scale trial is workable.
pmc-13585424:
Deborah Maus and co-authors screened a box of candidate drugs against the dormant stage of a common parasite, in a study published in 2026. They found a weak spot in its power plant. The parasite infects a quarter to a third of humanity. It hides in brain and muscle cysts, causing grave illness when immunity fails. Existing drugs kill only its fast-growing form.

Using human muscle cells grown in the lab, the team tested compounds against cyst-stage parasites. The test strains were bred to resist standard care. Several compounds hit both stages at once. Chemical tracing then showed the active ones strike a key complex in the parasite's energy machinery. The data suggest even dormant forms lean on that machinery to live. Drug hunters can exploit that dependence.
pmc-13585524:
Massoud Boroujerdi writes a primer that brings control theory to hormone systems in this 2026 paper. Hormone networks oscillate, respond in bursts, and filter noise; these are engineering behaviors. The paper models endocrine axes as chains of second order negative feedback loops. Loop settings come from a measurable quantity: how fast each hormone is cleared from blood. Two loop types cover the range, from fast responsive control to stable noise rejecting control. Standard frequency tools then yield readings like bandwidth and phase margin.

The cortisol stress axis serves as the worked example. Its model matches the roughly ninety minute rhythm of cortisol pulses, responses to stimulation tests, and suppression by a standard drug. A table gives clearance derived settings for thirty-six hormones and substrates. Boroujerdi argues that dose timing, not just dose size, decides replacement therapy outcomes. Control language can turn such puzzles into testable questions.
pmc-13585824:
Einat Ritter and co-authors describe the range of illness seen in a rare inherited condition called PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome. People with the condition grow benign lumps in the gut and face a high lifetime risk of cancer. The team reviewed adults followed at special high-risk clinics to map the condition's full picture.

The study covered sixty-two adults, most of them men, with a median age near forty. A harmful change in the PTEN gene was found in about four out of five. Growths in the colon appeared in forty patients. Cancer had occurred in sixty-one percent, most often in the breast and thyroid. Three people had rare soft tissue tumors. The authors stress that the condition's reach is broad. They advise doctors to consider hidden gene changes when tests on blood come back negative but suspicion stays high.
pmc-13586224:
