The team compared health risks from fire-made particles with risks from other particle sources. They used records across 20 states from 2006 to 2019, with each person acting as their own control. Per unit rise, fire-made particles linked to clearly higher hospital risks. The study asks whether fire smoke is more toxic than city air particles. The answer shapes how health warnings are set on smoky days.
pmc-13586324:
Chuan Gao and colleagues report a genetic puzzle in a 94-year-old man that mimicked Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a hereditary cancer syndrome. The same TP53 hotspot variant, Arg175His, appeared in both his blood and his tumour, initially raising concern for an inherited syndrome. Given his atypical presentation, the team tested multiple tissues to pin down the variant's origin. This 2026 case report shows why that extra step matters.

Bladder and skin samples carried just a faint trace of the variant, while fingernail DNA showed none. Those results support two independent somatic acquisitions of the same hotspot mutation, one in blood-forming cells and one in the tumour, rather than an inherited variant. The authors stress multi-tissue testing to avoid mislabelling older cancer patients with hereditary syndromes.
pmc-13586624:
Prajowl Shrestha and co-authors measure what tuberculosis costs Nepali households in a 2026 national survey. Diagnosis and drugs are free under the national program, yet families still pay for travel, food, and lost work. Interviewers questioned one thousand patients, six hundred with drug-susceptible disease and four hundred with the drug-resistant form, using a standard cost survey.

Costs were split into medical, non-medical, and indirect parts, with lost income valued by the human-capital method. A household faced catastrophe when the total passed a fifth of its yearly income. The survey, Nepal's first of its kind, sizes the hidden bill that free treatment leaves behind and names the factors that push families under.
pmc-13586824:
Deyu Zhu and ten co-authors trace how polystyrene microplastics harm blood vessels in mice, in this 2026 paper. These tiny plastic bits are widespread pollutants, already linked to heart and vessel disease. The team suspected ferroptosis, a cell death in which iron and oxidized fats kill cells from within.

Mice got saline or three dose levels of particles for five weeks. One group also got a drug that blocks ferroptosis. In exposed mice, stress markers, oxidized fat, cholesterol, and triglycerides rose, while antioxidants fell. Two defense proteins dropped and iron deposits rose, the clear sign of that cell death. Vessel lining damage markers rose, and nitric oxide, the vessel relaxant, fell. Blood profiles shifted for folate, amino acids, and energy paths. The blocker undid much of the harm. The authors conclude the particles harm vessels through stress, that cell death, and disturbed body chemistry.
pmc-13587324:
Benjamin Wee Y and colleagues map gene networks that help hemp cope when phosphorus runs short. Phosphorus is a core plant nutrient, and hemp, shaped by centuries of human selection for fiber and seed, handles poor soils better than many crops. Their 2026 study grew hemp under rich and poor phosphate supply and read gene activity across roots, leaves, and other organs, then grouped genes that rose and fell together.

Twelve gene groups appeared, tied to jobs such as root growth, fiber making, and flowering. Two groups, one in leaves and one in roots, tracked the plant's phosphorus state closely, and both overlapped with genes marked by domestication. A gene called SPX3 sat at the hub of the leaf response, while root shape changes ran through known regulator families. Hormones called strigolactones also steered the root response.
pmc-13587424:
Sun-Young Kim and a team of co-authors describe a home air monitoring campaign in a 2026 paper. Most studies of air pollution and health use outdoor readings, yet people at risk spend most of their time indoors, where levels can differ a lot. Long indoor records are rare, so this campaign was built to gather them properly.

The team monitored 130 older adults with a lung scarring disease in the Seoul area from 2021 to 2023. Small samplers measured fine particles and their makeup for five days in each season, indoors and out. Repeat visits were handled by mail to avoid contact. Early results show hourly indoor levels swinging widely around a modest mean.
pmc-13587524:
Khulud K Alharbi and co-authors asked home care providers in Saudi Arabia what blocks their work, in a 2026 study. Sixty providers joined by open invitation and sat for interviews between late 2023 and spring 2024. Most were under forty, and the group spanned four regions of the country. The team read the talks for shared themes, cross-checking as codes formed.

The study gathers these unseen barriers straight from the people who meet them daily, across roles from nursing to family medicine and physiotherapy. Home care for older adults in private houses carries strains that clinic work does not. Naming the barriers gives planners a ground view for fixing staffing, training, and support in a growing service.
pmc-13587824:
Julianna Bernardi and colleagues build a new early-warning index for hospitals in financial trouble. Closures and distressed hospitals stretch care thin across the United States, yet the standing public scores were designed for narrow hospital types or demand complete data, which shaky hospitals often lack. Their 2026 measure, the integrated vulnerability measure, extends a rural model to every general acute-care hospital filing Medicare cost reports between 2017 and 2022.

The index sorted checked hospitals into four risk bands, with about half called low risk and under one in ten high risk. Higher bands were far more likely to land in real financial distress within two years. Because the model stays readable and forgiving of missing data, the authors pitch it for targeting help and oversight before a closure is on the table.
pmc-13588124:
Pili annulati is a rare inherited hair condition in which light and dark bands alternate along each shaft, like rings. Daxing Wu, Jianzhong Xu, Danni Hua, and Lifeng Wu report a case in a black-haired Asian woman in this 2026 paper. The banding shows easily in blond hair but hides in dark hair, where heavy pigment masks the pattern, so cases like this one are seldom spotted.

The woman had carried the trait for thirty years. A skin-scope exam of the hair showed the typical bright and dark bands, though without the white nodes sometimes seen. Her family history also fit the condition, which usually passes from parent to child, though the authors note family history alone cannot prove the pattern of inheritance. They stress the scope exam as the key tool for dark-haired patients.
pmc-13588224: James Young and Arvind Bhimaraj honor a surgeon who shaped their practice in a 2026 essay. The subject is George Noon, a cardiovascular surgeon at Methodist Hospital. Two partners trace his reach across trainees, referring doctors, leaders, and patients. They tell how his example marked their own careers at unlike stages. The essay stands beside a formal memorial in the same journal issue.
pmc-13588924:
Phoenix Wong, Fanny Yeung, Patrick Chung and Kenneth Wong wrote a 2026 study on liver scarring in children fed by vein for long stretches. Gut failure forces such feeding, which can harm the liver over time. A stiffness scan checked for scarring without biopsy. Thirty-seven children fed for over three months were traced across two decades.

Nineteen had the scan; most had lost large parts of bowel. Gut tissue death in infancy was the commonest cause. About one in five scanned children showed liver scarring. That rate tops older reports, the team notes. Two deaths occurred in the scarring group and none outside it.
pmc-13589524:
Jamal Hassan Mohamoud, Mohamed Hussein Adam, and Ahmed Mahad Sheikh Mohamed argue that Somalia's health system must move from crisis response to sturdy primary care, in this 2026 perspective. Decades of conflict, weak governance, drought and flood, and deep poverty have left services fragmented and donor-driven. The country fights infectious disease and rising chronic illness at once, with high deaths among mothers and children.

The authors define resilience as the power to foresee shocks, absorb them, adapt, and recover while keeping care fair. Their prescription covers stronger public stewardship, joined-up federal and state planning, steadier funding, and a workforce that stays and spreads evenly. Linked labs, referral chains, and water systems complete the picture.
pmc-13589924:
Yilun Qu heads a large team in a 2026 study of a kidney disease marked by fast growth of cells in the filters of the kidney. That growth, driven by swelling and irritation, can end in kidney failure. The team tested chlorogenic acid, a natural plant compound, and asked how it protects the kidney. Their work used a rat model of the disease plus lab tests on the compound.

Qu and the team found that the acid binds a protein called RAC1 and blocks its action. That step lowered signals that spur cell growth and calmed immune cells called macrophages. Levels of key irritant signals fell as well. The authors propose the acid as a lead for a new drug, though human tests lie ahead.
pmc-13590824:
Vanessa Herranz Muñoz and co-authors census mangrove mammals in Cambodia in a 2026 study. Mangroves shelter shy, threatened mammals, yet long baselines for them are scarce. Camera traps ran from 2017 to 2023 at two coastal protected sites, building to 156 stations in all. A joint model estimated how often each of eight species used the sites and how those rates moved over time.

An endangered macaque and a vulnerable fishing cat showed the highest occupancy of the set. Habitat links and human pressure effects came out of the same model. A six year baseline turns later change into measurable trend, which is what protection funding needs to see.
pmc-13590924:
Wasif Majeed Chaudhry and three co-authors present a 2026 case report on stubborn high blood pressure. Their message is simple: in a young patient whose blood pressure resists treatment and whose blood potassium runs low, doctors should suspect overactive adrenal glands. That disorder, called primary hyperaldosteronism, makes the glands release too much of a hormone that raises blood pressure.

Blood tests and scans of the glands can find a small growth that makes the extra hormone. Removing that growth through surgery can cure the problem in such cases. The report notes that after surgery, blood pressure and potassium can return to normal and symptoms clear. The case is a reminder to look for a fixable cause before adding more pressure drugs. Young patients with this pattern deserve the full workup.
pmc-13591124:
Kishan Reddy and co-authors reported in 2026 a cocaine-linked lung clot that mimicked a major heart attack. Cocaine can cause both a true heart attack and a clot in the lungs, and the lung clot can at times copy the heart attack pattern. Sorting the two quickly decides the treatment, so the trap matters.

A man aged 54 years with polysubstance use was found unresponsive and revived with naloxone. He then had chest pain, a heart tracing with raised segments, and raised troponin, all pointing to a blocked heart artery. A bedside heart scan instead showed a strained right heart, and a CT scan found large clots in both lungs. Blood thinners were given, and a later artery check found only mild disease. Readers get a sharp reminder to image before assuming a heart attack in cocaine use.
pmc-13591424:
Jaysan Janabel and Tynchtyk Amatov review persistent organic radicals and their talent for moving single electrons. Most molecules guard their electrons in pairs. Persistent radicals hold an unpaired electron yet stay stable, and they can gain or lose one electron reversibly. That gives them three reachable states, a rare and useful trait.

The review covers how these compounds drive single-electron transfer reactions, both as one-off reagents and as catalysts that cycle. Most fame has gone to nitroxide radicals such as TEMPO. The authors deliberately spotlight other families that deserve wider use. Their pitch: persistent radicals form a platform for predictable electron shuttle catalysts in synthesis.
pmc-13592324:
Xiao Wang leads a 2026 team building a flow battery with no membrane at all, pairing lithium metal with an organic liquid cathode. Membranes usually keep the two fluids apart yet add cost and resistance. Their cell stacks two liquids that refuse to mix. A deep eutectic lithium fluid sits below, while a chlorine solvent floats above it. The upper fluid holds a sulfur nitrogen dye that stores charge and stays in its own layer.

The stack reached about 3.6 volts, high for this class. After 100 cycles it kept most of its charge with near perfect charge recovery, and a flowing version ran ten days with little self drain. Cost estimates undercut vanadium systems, and both fluids resist flame. Wang and the team credit the eutectic lithium mix for the wide, stable window.
pmc-13592424:
Qian Zhang and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, a score set to grade follow-up care for vein clot patients. Care after such clots lacks a set form and a full grade frame. The team used the Donabedian frame, which grades care by build, act, and result. A first draft came from past reads and group talks. A tweaked Delphi path then ran: 20 experts from many fields, in two rounds. A rank math set the weight of each mark. Both rounds drew full replies.

Expert accord sat sound, and judge weight ran high. The end set holds 3 top marks, 8 mid marks, and 37 leaf marks. The team casts it as a guide to make follow-up care even and strong.
pmc-13593424:
Sydney Fearnley and co-authors test in a 2026 mouse study what breaks when a single sticky spot on the Kirrel3 adhesion protein is swapped out. The protein glues smell-sensing axons into tidy balls in the accessory smell system, which steers social behavior. Mice with the swap form scrambled maps, like mice missing the gene entirely.

Males with the swap attacked other males less, and females lacked maternal aggression while still retrieving and nesting pups normally. Both sexes needed stronger urine scents to notice them, yet other smells stayed sharp. Social novelty, oddly, survived the swap though not the full deletion.
pmc-13593924:
Diabetes, blood vessel disease, and heart failure travel together so often that treating them in separate silos fails patients. Zachary Bloomgarden and Yehuda Handelsman synthesize a meeting on joining that care in this 2026 report. The tenth Heart in Diabetes meeting gathered in Philadelphia. Its theme: the cardio-renal-metabolic patient whose conditions interact and increasingly share drugs.

The report is a critical synthesis, not a practice guideline, and says so plainly. A formal framework from the heart association gives the shared biology a structure. The meeting's practical push was coordinated management over organ-by-organ referral. Shared biology and shared outcomes do not erase organ-specific diagnosis, the authors stress. Clinicians get a map for team-based care of tangled chronic disease.
pmc-13594224:
Mo Yan leads a fourteen-author team that mined thirty years of published experiments on making methanol from carbon dioxide to find operating lessons hidden across two hundred papers. Their 2026 study assembled the results into one dataset on copper and zinc oxide catalysts, then trained six machine learning models and used an explanation tool to rank what actually drives performance.

The models pointed to combinations of catalyst makeup, preparation, and reaction settings that deliver high methanol output at milder pressures than plants usually assume. A smaller dataset on activation energy, a measure of how strongly temperature drives the reaction, revealed patterns tied to the operating regime. A follow-up experiment on commercial catalysts confirmed one predicted link between flow speed and activation energy. The authors pitch the approach as a way to squeeze guidance out of legacy data for mature technologies.
pmc-13594324:
Gizem Vural, Sarina Drexler, Daniel Keeser, and Alexander Soutschek tested whether stimulating the striatum changes how hard people are willing to think. The striatum is a deep brain hub for weighing rewards against costs. They used a new technique that sends interfering electrical fields through the head to reach deep tissue, while volunteers performed an effort-based decision task inside a brain scanner.

Under stimulation, participants grew more sensitive to both sides of the bargain: bigger rewards pulled them more, and higher effort demands pushed them off more sharply. Brain recordings matched, with effort demands represented more strongly in the striatum and tighter coupling to the anterior cingulate, a region where motivation meets cognition. The authors suggest such targeted stimulation could one day inform treatments for the loss of motivation seen in several mental disorders.
pmc-13594524:
Mohamed Abdirahman Mohamud and Tabu Geoffrey report the case of a young boy with a deep neck infection that was found and drained late. Their 2026 paper comes from a setting with few resources, where such infections in children can turn grave fast. The boy was four years old.

He arrived after four days of fever, a swelling neck, a muffled voice, and hard breathing. A scan was read as a different illness, a needle draw found no pus, and the needed scan and surgery did not happen then. He worsened, and surgeons opened his airway and drained about 20 milliliters of pus. A later X-ray showed a second pocket of infection, and a wider draining followed. He left the hospital on day twenty.
pmc-13594724:
Rafaella Italiano Peixoto and co-authors study fatty liver disease in older people living with HIV, in this 2026 paper. Liver disease is now a leading cause of death not tied to HIV itself in this group. HIV, its drugs, aging, and body fat risks may combine to raise rates of fat buildup in the liver. The team measured how common and how severe that buildup was at one center in northeast Brazil.

Ninety-two older patients were checked with ultrasound scans, and stiffness tests gauged liver scarring. Just over half had fat in the liver, and about half of those cases were moderate to severe. A wider waist stood out as the trait most tied to the condition. Scarring of note appeared in about one in ten of those with fatty liver.
pmc-13595124:
Gohar Azbekyan, Anahit Shirvanyan, Nicoletta Guaragnella, and Karen Trchounian stress baker's yeast with vinegar acid and watch strains cope differently, in a paper dated 2026. Weak acids plague industrial fermentation, where yeast must work in sour conditions. Tolerance varies by strain, and the metabolic reasons were the target here.

Two laboratory strains grew at very low pH with graded doses of acetic acid. A mild dose barely mattered. A middle dose tripled oxygen use, as cells burned more fuel to fight the stress. A high dose crushed growth and gas production, nearly a hundred-fold under still conditions. One strain kept breathing and recycling acetate better; the other exhausted itself. The lesson for industry is that keeping respiration strong is what buys acid tolerance.
pmc-13595624:
Catriona Connell, David Griffiths, Jessica Greenhalgh, and Morgan Torrance mapped the social networks of fifty people. All were in contact with the criminal justice system. The team wanted to understand why they do or do not seek help for mental health and substance use problems. Their 2026 mixed-methods study combined network mapping with interviews about stigma and the perceived value of support.

Five distinct network types emerged, differing in structure, membership, and culture. What the people around someone knew and believed about mental health, substance use, and asking for help proved to shape the individual's own choices, as did attitudes in the wider community. The authors advise services to design outreach around network type rather than the isolated person. Adding diverse contacts with different perspectives can shift a network's culture. Messages also need tailoring. People should know when, where, and how to get help.
pmc-13596824:
Koray Samet Altınçekiç and co-authors ran a randomized trial in 102 male youth basketball players. They tested whether how long each body region is rolled changes the benefit of foam rolling for reaction speed. Players rolled thirty seconds per region, sixty seconds per region, or rested quietly, with reaction time for the dominant hand measured before and after.

The shorter rolling dose beat the longer one on every scoring method, by roughly twenty-two milliseconds on the best-trial measure. Against rest, the short dose looked better on the best-trial analysis but not on average-based ones, and the long dose actually scored worse than rest in the extended model. Because the comparisons shifted with baseline speed and scoring choice, the authors decline to crown a best duration: brief rolling never hurt, and longer rolling may dull the quickness players want.
pmc-13597124:
Jorge and colleagues introduced hicream, a software framework for finding regions where genome folding differs between conditions, in a 2026 bioinformatics paper. Genome folding, measured by the Hi-C technique that counts contacts between DNA segments, shapes gene control, and its disruption contributes to cancer and birth defects. Existing comparison tools mostly hunt one preset structure type, such as loops or domains, or return local hits that are hard to interpret.

Jorge built hicream to detect changed regions of any shape. It first tests contact differences pixel by pixel across the interaction matrix, then clusters neighboring signals into candidate regions using the data. It attaches a strength measure to each region through after-the-fact inference. Results can be explored in an interactive visualization interface. The authors argue this frees researchers from preset structure definitions and can surface complex folding changes, and the package is available through the R archive.
pmc-13597224:
Ran and co-authors track if lone life lifts death odds for growth hosts. Lone states tie to death in broad past work on hosts. Their mark on cause-wise death post growth stayed dim. The set drew from UK Biobank hosts with growth at start. Hosts were tracked from 2006 to the fall of 2024. Self-fill forms set lone state and lone feel for each host.

In sum, 32,524 hosts sat in the set, most of them women. Mean age was 60.3 years at the start of the track. Near 15.7 years of track saw 5,945 deaths in the set. Lone state tied to more deaths from all causes in fits. It tied to growth deaths and heart deaths as well. Lone feel tied to heart deaths but not to all deaths.
pmc-13597424:
Kumar Selvarajoo argues that drug discovery should join network biology with artificial intelligence. His 2026 paper notes that drug development still suffers high failure rates, long timelines, and weak translation from molecular findings to working therapies. Single-target approaches have delivered major drugs, yet patient outcomes often depend on whole biological networks.

Systems biology mapped those networks, but its forecasts were limited by tangled biology, partial mechanism knowledge, and data that show links rather than causes. New AI tools can blend large, varied biomedical data sets at a scale not seen before. Selvarajoo proposes models that are both predictive and testable, aimed at disease mechanisms and treatment failure. He also warns that adding mechanism detail will not lift every prediction.
pmc-13597624:
Ori Meir Komemi and Yaniv Efrati sorted porn use in 608 young adults aged eighteen to twenty-seven by two styles: use to fill a gap, and use to tune out of life. The model grew from game-use work, where a short shift from stress differs from a deep cut from real life. Folks scored use style, past harm, mood signs, rash acts, lone feel, mood control, and basic needs.

Group sorts gave low, mid, and high gap-and-tune-out groups. The high group fared worst in mind and mood, the low group best. Past sex harm went with more out-of-hand use and more use in all, yet the mid group, oddly, used most of all. Help should thus fit each use style and past harm, not just count hours of use.
pmc-13597824:
Moses Kpum and Velisiwe Gasa argue for fairer tests of learning in Africa in 2026. Many African tests follow Eurocentric models for scoring learning. One set form and mold rule those models. Indigenous know-how and group ways of knowing are often pushed aside.

The paper takes a qualitative, conceptual path grounded in decolonial thought. English-taught and Southern African higher education frames the talk. Tests are framed as shaped by past and power, not mere tools. Talk passed down by mouth, hands-on learning, and group-shared proof fit ill in set forms. Those misfits raise whose knowledge counts. The authors propose tests that fit local lives and let locals help shape them. Real school cases show the other ways at work. Multiple forms of competence deserve to count, they argue. Reform should value group-shaped proof of learning. The paper speaks to rule setters and university leaders alike.
pmc-13597924:
Myriam Liz Aponte and co-authors argue that artificial intelligence in schools should be judged by whether it strengthens teachers' working relationships, not just by speed or scale. AI tools are spreading in education faster than schools can guard teacher wellbeing. Debates swing between cheerleading for the tools and fearing them outright.

They sort AI tools by function, from scheduling systems to chat agents and emotion-sensing tools, and weigh the risks of each. Special care goes to guarding feelings data, the money side of school AI, and language and culture fit. Better ties among teachers, they note, also lift the climate students learn in.
pmc-13598424: An announcement from the Alzheimer's Association, published in 2026, for a two-day meeting on unfair gaps in brain health. The meeting, AAIC Advancements: Reducing Disparities in Brain Health, is set for October 30 to 31, 2026, in Charlotte, North Carolina, with online attendance also offered. It follows the association's large summer conference held the same year.
pmc-13598524:
Christopher Husson and co-authors report a toddler whose swallowed button battery silently infected his spine, in a 2026 case report. Button batteries burn the food pipe when lodged inside. Infection of the spinal discs is a rare late complication. Only about a dozen cases are published. Delayed removal is the shared pattern.

The two-year-old had vague breathing symptoms for five months. No imaging was done during that expectant period. Films then revealed the battery, its negative pole facing backward. Emergency removal uncovered several battery injuries. Scans confirmed disc infection across three thoracic levels. Clinicians gain warning signs and an imaging clue. The review gathers the scattered prior cases for comparison.
pmc-13599024:
Jan Estoppey and co-authors published this heart study in 2026. In cardiogenic shock, the heart fails so badly that machines must help pump blood for a time. Failure of the right side of the heart is common in such cases and is tied to worse odds. The team drew on a Swiss registry to ask how much that right-side weakness matters for patients on pump support.

They counted 745 patients, most on a left-side pump and the rest on a heart-lung machine. Right-side weakness showed in a third of pump patients and in three-fifths of the rest. Among pump patients, those with the weakness died more by six months and steadied more slowly. On the heart-lung machine the gap was less clear. The authors say right-side checks should guide device choice and care.
pmc-13599424:
Richell Booijink and her team tested a closed-loop glucose system in teens with type one diabetes in two thousand twenty-six. The system gives two hormones on its own, with no input from the user. Teens with this disease often have the worst glucose control of any age group.

Twenty teens joined the trial, and data from fifteen were used. Each teen used the system for two weeks and their usual care for two weeks, at home. Time in the target glucose range rose from 61.3 to 74.9 in a hundred. Time spent too high fell as well. No safety problems were seen, but the authors call for longer, larger trials.
pmc-13599524:
Yafang Luo, Jiani Wu, and Yeting Xie tested marker-guided care for sudden hearing loss in this 2026 study. The condition, where hearing drops fast in one ear, links to swelling and stress inside cells. The team asked whether tracking blood markers could sharpen treatment.

A total of 102 patients were split at random between routine care and marker-guided care. Blood levels of five markers tied to swelling and cell stress were checked before and after care. Hearing levels and life quality scores were tracked at the same time. The head of the study sets up the test of whether close marker checks lead to better hearing results than routine care alone.
pmc-13599924:
McClarty leads a large team setting out a study protocol from twenty twenty-six in Nairobi, Kenya. The study looks at infections passed by sex or blood, and at how place shapes risk. Past HIV work focused on personal behavior and split groups into silos.

Sex work sites shape risk and safety for young women, sex workers, and men who gather there, the team notes. Risk levels vary a lot by site. Their mixed methods study will map places, gather both counts and stories, and rank place based prevention steps with local input. The protocol aims for plans that fit real sites, not just broad groups.
pmc-13600924:
Valerie Sticher and a large team of co-authors argue for satellite data in conflict research in this 2026 paper. War studies lean on text reports and death counts, which miss much and arrive unevenly. Satellite images of damage offer a second lens, flawed in different ways, which makes the two sources stronger together.

The authors lay out three ways to merge them: sharpen text data with images, enrich images with context, and fuse both into new measures. Case studies from Ukraine and Myanmar show each route in practice and the fresh insights that follow. The team urges a shift away from death counts toward the full spectrum of violence, including destruction of homes and infrastructure.
pmc-13601524:
Teresa Bonserio and co-authors warn in 2026 that power trade across Africa faces a near term rise in political risk. Wars and unrest hurt power supply in many states and slow the shift to clean energy. Most large plans use least cost math and skip unrest risks.

Six low cost paths for the continent are scored for trade linked unrest risk. The first half of this decade rates as the most weak span. Risk hot spots sit in the west, south, and center east. Shifts in births, weather, and water flows move the risk map. Plans, the team says, must build unrest in from the start.
pmc-13601724:
Azhar and Al-Salam review how silent RNA molecules steer a cleanup process inside heart cells after blood flow returns. The cleanup process, autophagy, protects during the blockage yet can harm during the return.

Non-coding RNAs, which never build proteins, tune the cleanup machinery at many points. The review maps how these RNAs touch key cleanup genes and shape whether heart cells live or die. Most evidence comes from mouse studies so far. The authors see these RNAs as targets for drugs that could soften reperfusion damage.
pmc-13601824:
Qiuyu Xu and co-authors review a fiery form of cell death in heart disease in a 2026 article. Pyroptosis is programmed cell death that spills inflammatory signals, and one pathway runs through the NLRP3 inflammasome, a protein complex that senses danger. Heart disease remains the world's top killer, and inflammation inside vessel walls and heart muscle drives much of it.

The review gathers evidence on how this death pathway works and where it matters, above all in artery clogging, heart attacks, and heart failure. It then surveys drug strategies that block the pathway at various points. The authors argue that trials built around the mechanism, rather than broad anti-inflammatory shots, offer the best path to new heart therapies.
pmc-13602324:
Mehmet Bahadır Savaş, Tülay Dikencik, Füsun Özkaya, Yusuf Doğan, and Ayşe Yılmaz describe a phone app for cardiac arrest care in this 2026 letter. Fresh European guidelines stress the road from evidence to bedside, yet arrest teams labor under extreme mental load, and most teaching apps fail quality checks.

Their app turns the advanced life support algorithm into a timed, interactive workflow. A two minute cycle timer ticks with a metronome, drug reminders fire on schedule, and a stubborn rhythm pathway opens after three failed shocks. Entries are time stamped into standard Utstein records automatically. Big glove friendly buttons, spoken confirmations, and double checks for irreversible steps suit the arrest room. A simulation trial of the app is in preparation.
pmc-13603524:
Rusu and Delcea compare early maladaptive schemas in homicide convicts and community adults. Schemas are deep patterns formed early in life. The study held 492 people, split evenly by group. A short Young schema survey scored 18 patterns. Models tested group, sex, and their joint effect. Each group held 246 people, convicts in one and community adults in the other.

All three effects came out strong in the joint model. Convicts scored higher on emotional deprivation and abandonment. Community adults scored higher on several autonomy-linked schemas. Sex reshaped which gaps appeared between the groups. Age and schooling were held as controls in the models.
pmc-13603924:
Cristina Dragomir and six co-authors probe a vessel enzyme in new mothers in a 2026 study. The enzyme, eNOS, makes a gas that keeps blood vessels relaxed. Under stress it can make a harmful form of oxygen instead. Its blood levels right after birth had not been described.

The study took place at one center in Romania with 40 mother-newborn pairs. Blood was drawn on the first day after delivery. Higher enzyme levels linked to lower cholesterol in the mothers. pmc-13604024:

pmc-13604724:

pmc-13604924:

pmc-13605824:

pmc-13605924:

pmc-13606424:

pmc-13606824:

pmc-13607224:

pmc-13607424:

pmc-13608424:

pmc-13608524:

pmc-13608724:

pmc-13609424:

pmc-13609724:

pmc-13610724:

pmc-13610924:

pmc-13611024:

pmc-13611124:

pmc-13611224:

pmc-13618924:

pmc-13619424:

pmc-13620224:

pmc-13620324:
Yinchen Wu and co-authors built a scoring chart from special CT scans to predict a tumor trait and patient outlook without tissue tests, in a 2026 study. The cancer sits where the food pipe meets the stomach. A trait pair called MSI and dMMR guides treatment choices, but it normally needs a biopsy. The team instead used spectral CT, which measures how tissue absorbs X-rays at set energies.

Their chart combines sex, the cancer's nodal stage, and two scan measures. It was built and checked across five patient groups totaling five hundred and eleven people, holding strong accuracy in each, including a group tested before treatment began. In one group it caught cases a biopsy had misread. The chart also split patients into risk groups with clearly different survival without the disease returning.
pmc-13620424:
Fatmanur Çimen and İsmail Seçer adapt a trauma screening tool for Turkish children and teenagers. The tool, called CATS-2, asks about trauma symptoms after hard life events. Before doctors can trust a translated version, it must be shown to measure what it claims to measure.

The authors report that the Turkish version proved both valid and reliable for judging trauma-related symptoms in young people. They also mapped how symptoms connect to one another. Trouble managing emotions sat at the center of the network, linking strongly to reliving the event and to feeling constantly on alert. Anxiety and problems in relationships also tied closely to many other symptoms. The authors suggest that care for traumatized youth should pay special attention to emotion control, anxiety, and relationships. A checked screening tool gives Turkish clinicians and researchers a firmer base for spotting these patterns early and planning support.
pmc-13621124:
Zhigang Chen and five co-authors published a review in 2026 on how treatment itself reshapes the support cells around stomach tumors. Fibroblasts near a cancer are often sorted into fixed types, but therapy bathes them in injury signals, low oxygen, and stress. The authors argue these cells take on changing states under treatment pressure, and those states help leftover tumor cells survive.

The review walks through four stages, from the untreated tumor to full drug resistance. Some fibroblast programs are brief and stir the immune system, for good or ill. Others harden into lasting shields of matrix and blood supply signals. The authors urge studies that track patients over time and pair tissue samples with blood tests for matrix wear.
pmc-13621524:
Deepak Subramani and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how fermenting legumes in a moist solid state can unlock better food properties from them. Legumes are rising stars in plant-based foods, but their tight inner structure limits how they foam, gel, and mix. Harsh splitting methods fix some of that while wasting parts and harming function.

Fermentation lets microbes and their enzymes remodel the bean in place, gently and with less waste. The review maps changes at cell, microstructure, and molecule levels. Freed starch and protein hydrate better, broken protein clumps dissolve and coat surfaces better, and starch crystals shift heat behavior. Gaps in the process-structure story are named as next steps.
pmc-13621624:
Yasmeen Mohamed Mohamed Shehata and five colleagues tested a structured study routine, the modified KWHLAQ strategy, on critical care nursing students at Alexandria University. The routine walks learners through what they know, want, and learned, then how to apply it and what questions remain. One hundred third-semester students split into two groups: fifty learned through the framework for twelve weeks, fifty through standard lectures.

Both groups took thinking and self-direction tests before and after. The framework group finished with clearly higher critical thinking scores, a moderate-to-large advantage, while the lecture group's scores actually slipped. The sharpest gains landed in the evaluating subskill. Self-directed learning jumped dramatically in the framework group, improving across all four measured dimensions. The authors recommend weaving the low-cost, copyable routine into nursing curricula, arguing it builds the reflective reasoning and decision-making that high-acuity wards demand from new nurses.
pmc-13623224:
Ahmad Rizky Mardhatillah Umar, writing alone in two thousand twenty-six, gives a new frame for how Indonesia acts toward the world. He argues the land is not best read as a middle power.

That tag rests on size, strength, name, or rank. Umar's frame is a state of being in-between, born of a freed land's past. It springs from a pull: on one side, the wish to remake the world order and end rule by others; on the next, the press of great-power strife. The state takes a stance of not-belonging. Umar traces that pull from the land's free birth through the cold clash of blocs.
pmc-13623524:
Mehmet Baysal and Seval Akpınar write from Türkiye about the uneven spread of progress in multiple myeloma, in this 2026 article. This blood cancer has seen faster advances in five years than in the previous twenty. New antibody drugs, engineered cell therapies, and drug combinations have all reached patients. Reading the trial results, the authors feel both admiration and unease.

One gap troubles them most: the new treatments have never been compared head-to-head in a large randomized trial. Doctors must choose among options that differ in cost, logistics, side effects, and the facilities they demand, with no direct evidence on which is best. A second gap is access. Sophisticated therapies pile up in wealthy centers while patients at the periphery wait. The piece argues that trial design and commercial rivalry, not just science, decide who benefits from the myeloma revolution.
pmc-13623624:
Umezaki and six co-authors propose a model for how a deadly ovarian cancer evolves, in this two thousand twenty-six hypothesis paper. Ovarian clear cell carcinoma often grows out of endometriosis, in tissue rich in iron and low in oxygen.

The authors argue these two stresses act together as a selection filter. Repeated iron-driven damage, of the kind that triggers the cell death called ferroptosis, kills off sensitive cells and enriches tougher ones that learn to lock iron away safely. Those survivors also adapt their oxygen and antioxidant pathways. Over years this weeding could produce the cancer's known traits. The model, they stress, is a framework to test, since tolerance of this stress is not yet directly proven.
pmc-13624024:
Linus Alexander Völker and colleagues test a get-fit-before-surgery programme for patients aged sixty-five and older facing oesophagus removal for cancer. This operation carries heavy complication rates, and older patients start with less reserve. The programme mixed home exercise, breathing training, balance work, and a geriatric review with medication tidying, run over four weeks.

Twenty-six patients enrolled and twenty-two finished, then were matched against forty-two historical controls. Early check-ins showed most patients following the programme fully or mostly, though paperwork thinned by the second check. Complications, leaks at the surgical join, deaths, and hospital stay matched the control group. Readmission to intensive care looked lower after the programme, but that gap vanished once the surgical approach was taken into account. Controls were fitter at baseline. The authors call the approach feasible and safe, and ask for a proper randomised trial.
pmc-13624124:
Lulu Hu and co-authors build a 2026 machine learning model to tell cancer from harmless nodules in patients with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. In that gland disease, swelling blurs ultrasound images, so papillary thyroid cancer hides easily. The team gathered records for 1,200 patients at one hospital, plus 550 more at a second hospital, and fed 38 measures into seven learning methods.

Six measures carried the most weight, led by a blood swelling index and a thyroid antibody level. A random forest model scored best, with strong accuracy in training and fair accuracy on the outside hospital's patients. An explanation tool showed which inputs drove each call, and the team put the model online as a risk calculator.
pmc-13625024:
Miki Scaravaglio and a large multi-center team build a bedside model to tell two look-alike bile duct diseases apart. Primary sclerosing cholangitis scars the ducts slowly, while secondary forms follow other causes, and no single test separates them cleanly. Reviewing records of 234 adults, the team found six facts that leaned toward the primary form, from younger age and bowel disease to no past duct surgery and no pancreas changes.

Those six facts became the PSC-DM score, and on a fresh group of 142 patients the score sorted the diseases with an AUROC of 0.95, a value near the top of the scale. The score also lifted non-expert doctors' accuracy in a trial run. A simple checklist could shorten the long road to a firm diagnosis.
pmc-13625224:
Yue Hu and co-authors map the chemistry of a parasitic worm, Angiostrongylus cantonensis, across its whole life cycle. The worm, spread through snails and rats, can invade the human brain lining and cause a rare meningitis. Using liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry, the team profiled five life stages, from early larvae to adult males and females, in both mouse and rat hosts.

Thousands of chemical signals shifted across stages, with the jump from the infective larva to the next stage the largest, and 127 compounds could be named, spanning fats, steroids, and purine pieces. Certain compounds peaked at single stages, such as xanthosine in adult females. Such stage fingerprints may expose weak points for drugs or tests that catch infection earlier.
pmc-13626524:
Mourão and Juliasse argue that health care lacks clear accountability when large language models cause harm. Such models are entering clinical work faster than hospitals can assign blame for failures. Responsibility can scatter across clinicians, institutions, and vendors, leaving a vacuum. Their 2026 piece proposes a standard they call earned delegation.

Under that standard, authority passes to a model only when proof matches the clinical risk. Real human oversight must be staffed and funded, and blame for foreseeable failures must be named in advance. A pre-deployment charter would spell out intended and banned uses, proof, oversight, and escalation paths. The authors say poorer countries face the sharpest gaps, since their digital health rules are still forming.
pmc-13626624:
Rajkumar Meshram, Sagar Chopde, and Ashma Rashid looked for hidden heart dysfunction in Indian children who depend on blood transfusions. Children with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia receive blood regularly, and iron overload damages the heart over time. Heart complications are their leading cause of death. Tissue Doppler imaging can catch dysfunction before symptoms appear. The twenty twenty-six comparative study enrolled fifty affected children aged two to eighteen.

Fifty children with minor illnesses served as matched controls. Both groups received standard and tissue Doppler heart scans, blood tests, and ECGs. Ferritin levels, a marker of iron load, were correlated with the imaging findings. Finding subclinical dysfunction early matters because chelation and treatment can still change course. The study reports experience from a tertiary center in central India.
pmc-13626924:
Kai Wang reviews whether oxidative stress in Sertoli cells is the shared harm point where many pollutants damage male fertility, in a systematic review from twenty twenty-six. These nurse cells sustain sperm production and guard the blood-testis barrier. Wang organized the evidence around a harm pathway: pollutants stir reactive oxygen in the cells, which then triggers cell death and barrier breakdown.

Ninety-six studies fed the synthesis and twenty-nine the pooled analysis. All six chemical classes studied, from air particles to metals, raised oxidative stress significantly. Metals hit hardest, air pollutants second. Every pooled study pointed the same way. Statistical links tied the oxygen surge to cell death, supporting the pathway. Wang urges formal use of this endpoint in safety testing.
pmc-13627024:
Dan Zeng and co-authors pool studies on combined liver cancer therapy in 2026. Unresectable liver cancer is often treated by blocking its blood supply while delivering chemo locally. Adding focused radiation may extend that benefit. The team ran a systematic review and meta analysis of head to head studies.

Five databases were searched for trials comparing the pair against the vessel treatment alone. Survival with and without progression were the main outcomes, with severe side effects as the safety check. Pooled ratios summed the evidence across studies. The verdict helps oncologists judge whether the added radiation earns its risks.
pmc-13627324:
Norermi Firzana Alfian and co-authors present a study dated 2026 on how the fluid an embryo grows in can shape lifelong health. The days before implantation are a sensitive window when nutrition sets metabolic paths. Glutamine is a key fuel in embryo culture media, and the team asked whether doubling it harms later development.

Mouse embryos were grown in standard fluid or in fluid with extra glutamine, with or without a carrier protein. Embryos in the rich mix made fewer cells, mostly in the outer layer, and showed more cell death. Their energy organelles and recycling systems shifted, and one chemical mark on DNA packaging fell. Pups born from these embryos grew unevenly, died more often, and handled glucose poorly.
pmc-13627724:
Mian Wang and co-authors build tiny layered shells in 2026 from chain-like molecules that fold together on their own. The shells are hollow, stacked in layers, and pierced by neat rows of pores. Such structures could gate flow, release cargo in steps, or run chained reactions, but making them in a stable form has been hard.

Two added compounds tune how the chains pack inside a tight space, and weak bonds between parts open the pores in chosen regions. Tests and computer models show the tight space and the weak bonds work together. The finished shells soak up iodine well, can be reused, and take it up faster than solid layered shells.
pmc-13627824:
Muhunthan and co-authors tell of a kidney growth with a fat clot in two veins. A dame of 53 came in for a full kidney cut by plan. She bore a known growth, AML, in her left kidney. Scans showed a 5.3 cm fat growth at its top pole. Fat stuff also sat in the left kidney vein in the scans. It ran to the big vein at its first tier there.

Fear of a lung clot drove the cut choice in her case. A bot-aided full cut and big-vein clot pull were done. In-cut views bore out the growth and the fat clot. Post-cut reads showed pure AML growth with no ill marks. The fat clot matched the growth in the lab read.
pmc-13628224:
Li-Bin Zhou and eleven co-authors package a plant compound into tiny particles aimed at injured kidneys, in a paper dated 2026. Acute kidney injury strikes fast and lacks targeted drugs. The compound, naringenin from citrus, blocks a master inflammation switch, but it dissolves poorly and clears from the body before reaching the kidney.

The team built ultra-small iron-based particles under ten nanometers across, small enough to slip through the kidney's filters and linger where vessels leak after injury. In two mouse models of the condition, the particles delivered far more drug to the kidney than the free compound. Kidney function recovered better, tissue damage eased, and inflammation quieted. The design turns a weak natural product into a guided therapy.
pmc-13630524:
Chen and Yao study a rare form of blood cancer in a 2026 paper from a hospital in Anqing, China. Some patients with multiple myeloma carry two abnormal proteins instead of one. The team asked whether the timing of the second protein matters. They split 21 patients into two groups: those with both proteins at diagnosis, and those where the second one showed up after treatment began.

The two groups started with similar protein levels. In the later group, the protein level fell sharply by the time the second one appeared, a sign of treatment effect. Age at study start had a median of 66 years across the group. All tests were early stage and meant to guide later work. The paper sets out two forms of the disease that doctors may need to track in distinct ways.
pmc-13632024:
Chao Fu and co-authors study how a liver virus slips its genes into one host gene in liver cancer. The study appeared in 2026. That host gene is a known hot spot for such inserts. Yet how the insert drives cancer growth was not clear.

The team read virus inserts and gene use in tumor and near tissue from fifty patients. The insert at this gene was the second most common of all. It cut full gene output and made a short form of the protein. Both the cut and the short form sped cell growth, spread, and move, and held back cell death. Gene marks shifted in ways that fit a worse cancer.
pmc-13632924:
Levi Kadiri, Anthony Maher, and Andy Bridgen reviewed how well two lab tests on bone samples agree in diabetic foot bone infection. The infection, called diabetic foot osteomyelitis, can lead to amputation when missed. A bone biopsy is the surest test, and labs can study the sample two ways: growing microbes from it, or examining its tissue structure under a microscope. The team searched five databases for studies that ran both tests on the same patients.

Five studies covering three hundred eight patients qualified. The two methods agreed only modestly, both positive in well under half of cases on average. Tissue examination was more specific, while microbe growing caught more true infections but picked up more contamination. A positive tissue result also predicted later revision surgery or longer antibiotics more strongly. The authors advise reading both results together with the clinical picture.
pmc-13633524:
Amirreza Peyrovinasab and his team sift in a set way the use of resveratrol in small beast tests of spine cord harm. Their 2026 pooled study joins tests in rats, mice, and rabbits. It checks the shield acts of this plant good found in the wild.

Twenty-six studies met the bar from hunts through April twenty twenty-five. Resveratrol made move skill much more good than in check sets in the pooled finds. More than one burn mark fell sharp with care. They took in tumour death part and two interleukins. Guards from air harm rose, with strong rises in shield enzymes and in glutathione. Ends took in air stress, cell death, and nerve cell life too. Study grade and fit were checked with known bias and spread tools for beast work.
pmc-13633824:
Mya Ya Minn and co-authors study recurrent urinary tract infections in patients with type 2 diabetes, in this 2026 Europe PMC paper. Recurrent infection is a common, costly complication that also drives antibiotic resistance. The team reviewed records from a hospital in Lahore, Pakistan, covering more than four hundred adults with culture-confirmed infection.

About forty-three percent had recurrent infections. Those patients were older, more often female, had diabetes longer and showed higher blood sugar control markers. Kidney damage from diabetes, kidney stones, prior antibiotic use and catheter use were all more common in the recurrent group. Escherichia coli was the leading microbe, as the study's microbial profile details.
pmc-13633924:
David Dallas-Orr, Gregory J Harbison, Samuel K Simister, Shannon Tse, and John Meehan report a hip liner shattered for a preventable reason. Cross-linked polyethylene liners resist wear but forgive concentrated stress less, and failures follow trauma. Their patient, a sixty-two-year-old woman, arrived twenty months after hip replacement with groin and hip pain, a squeaking joint, and a hip unable to bend past ninety degrees.

Scans showed the ball sitting off-center in the socket and the locking ring displaced. At revision, the liner lay in fragments amid metal debris. The cause stood out: an off-center socket screw poked through the shell's inner surface where the liner's back side had worn. The team removed the screw and exchanged the liner. Eight years later she walks without difficulty or pain. The authors urge surgeons to confirm screws sit flush before liner placement.
pmc-13635224:
Ingvild E Bjerke and nine colleagues published this 2026 image collection tracking two calcium-handling proteins across the developing mouse brain. The proteins, calbindin and parvalbumin, sit inside neurons that help control excitability, navigation, and memory. Nobody had mapped when and where these neurons appear across the whole brain. The team stained brain sections from five age groups, from nine-day-old pups to adults, and aligned every image to age-matched brain atlases.

The collection can be browsed interactively online or downloaded for analysis. It gives researchers a brain-wide view of how these neuron populations emerge region by region, instead of the single-area snapshots that dominated earlier work. Because calcium control goes wrong in several developmental and psychiatric disorders, knowing the normal timetable matters. The authors tailored the images for counting workflows, so others can measure change across ages without redoing the staining work themselves.
pmc-13636324:
Isha Iqbal and co-authors analyze, in twenty twenty-six, patient satisfaction with general practice in Scotland, and how it varies with deprivation, rurality, and practice size. They used a national health and care experience survey run every two years from twenty ten to twenty twenty-two. Data were linked to public national data sets. Six hundred thirty-two practices were analyzed, about two-thirds of those that took part. Practices were dropped for closure, merger, reclassification, or missing size data. Response rates ranged from sixteen to thirty-eight percent.

Outcomes were practice-level shares of positive replies to seven survey items on patient-centred care and continuity. The team used relative importance methods and regression to weigh how much urban-rural class, deprivation band, and practice size band each contributed to satisfaction.
pmc-13638724:
Flávia Alessandra Maciel and eleven colleagues report a 2026 rat study on how low protein intake during pregnancy and nursing affects lungs. The work covers both the mothers and their female pups, a pairing the authors note has rarely been studied for lung outcomes.

Rats fed a diet with six percent protein were compared with a control diet of seventeen percent. In mothers, low protein raised collagen and mast cells in lung tissue. In female pups it shrank air sacs and changed proteins tied to muscle and energy use. The study links poor early nutrition to lasting lung changes.
pmc-13639024:
Yassine Guennoun and seven colleagues describe a 2026 deep learning system that outlines brain tumors on MRI scans while also reporting how unsure it is. Clinicians hesitate to trust automated tumor outlines that give no sense of their own uncertainty.

Trained on 1,655 scans from 788 patients, the system segmented meningiomas with a median Dice score of 0.93 on held-out scans, and its doubt maps matched areas that radiologists found ambiguous. A separate group of 353 patients confirmed the accuracy. The authors argue that honest uncertainty estimates can make medical imaging software safer to use in daily practice.
pmc-13641824:
Nese Unver and nine co-authors probed why blind mole-rat stem cells resist cancer in a 2026 study. The burrowing rodent almost never gets cancer, even when provoked. Its marrow stem cells and skin cells were dosed with a strong carcinogen and compared with mouse, rat, and human cells.

The chemical killed or stalled the human and mouse stem cells, but the mole-rat cells kept growing, dividing, and maturing normally. Gene reads showed the mole-rat cells flexing their signaling while guarding a tumor-suppressor circuit. One node in that circuit stood out across species and human cancer data. In mole-rat skin cells the same chemical shut a growth pathway and retuned energy production. The authors see a layered defense worth mining for therapy ideas.
pmc-13642924:
Runlai Xu and eight colleagues present a 2026 field study on how wheat roots recruit microbes that fight Fusarium crown rot, a soil fungus that can halve yields. Plants under attack are thought to cry for help chemically, yet how wheat varieties differ in that call was unclear.

In diseased fields, plant variety and health together shaped root-zone microbe communities and chemistry. Healthy roots favored Bacillus, while a susceptible variety also leaned on Pseudomonas, and both microbes fought the fungus in lab and pot tests. The tolerant variety kept more complex microbe networks. The work ties root chemistry to disease suppression.
pmc-13644424:
Cancers of the ovary, cervix, and womb are often found late and shrug off standard drugs, which is why tiny drug carriers draw so much interest. Xinyun Tu and co-authors review dual-targeted nanotechnology for these cancers: particles built to home in on two markers at once. Two locks, in principle, mean fewer keys opening healthy doors.

The evidence so far comes mostly from lab dishes and animal models, where the carriers do sharpen tumor selectivity. Human trials are only beginning, so clinical proof remains thin. The review names the hurdles plainly: making the particles at scale, proving long-term safety, and clearing regulation. It also covers the sheer variety of tumor biology. The authors see individualized, precisely aimed therapy as the prize if those hurdles fall.
pmc-13645924:
Geraldine Lafeber and her team sift in a set way models that tell of a grave blood-force ill when a child is on the way. The models take in help to bear young as a mark. Their 2026 review judges if models in hand can serve folk in care to bear young. The risk of that group is more high.

From more than fifteen thousand files, twenty-six models that fit the bar were put as one. Right scores swung  twixt models. Just seven had been tested on data from out side at all. Risk of skew was not clear in most studies. That flaw came in the main from weak points in the math work, judged with stock grade tools. No model was built for folk in help-to-bear-young care as its aim. The team calls for a high-grade model made fit for that group.
pmc-13646124:
Jinbiao Han and three colleagues pool randomized trials of omalizumab, an antibody drug, for allergic asthma in children and teenagers. Six trials with 1,835 participants aged six to twenty met their rules, most of them under eighteen. The team compared the drug with placebo or standard therapy. Outcomes covered asthma attacks, lung function, symptom control scores, and harms, under a registered review plan.

The drug cut asthma attacks by about a third and hospital admissions by roughly two thirds. Serious side effects were also less frequent in the drug groups, while overall side effects matched the control groups. Evidence on lung function and day-to-day control was too thin to pool. The authors support omalizumab as an add-on for young patients whose moderate to severe allergic asthma stays uncontrolled on standard treatment, while flagging the gaps that remain.
pmc-13647424:
Gabriela Carrasco-Torres and six colleagues pair the dietary compound quercetin with a thiol-reactive agent to overwhelm cervical cancer cells' antioxidant defenses. Cancer cells lean on glutathione, a protective molecule, to survive treatment stress. The strategy primes cells with quercetin first, then strikes with the partner agent, called DMAB. Effects were mapped across a grid of combined doses in dishes, then tested in mice carrying a lymphoma model.

The pairing acted synergistically, draining glutathione and wrecking the cells' redox balance. Treated cervical cancer cells mostly died by apoptosis, with survival down to under a quarter and movement blocked. Healthy epithelial cells were hurt far less. In mice, the combination cut tumor burden by about two thirds and lengthened survival without obvious toxicity. The authors offer redox sensitization as a template for combinations that attack cancer's chemical safety net.
pmc-13647624:
Xiaoli Xu led a 2026 cohort study of whether lifetime estrogen exposure and heart health together shape kidney disease risk in postmenopausal women in China. Life after menopause itself raises kidney risk, possibly as sex hormones fall, but how lifetime estrogen from reproductive history interacts with heart health was unexplored. The team followed 33,700 women past menopause from the China Cardiometabolic Disease and Cancer Cohort, enrolled in 2011 to 2012 and followed for a median of 3.1 years.

Shorter lifetime estrogen exposure, measured three ways, raised kidney disease risk by roughly 28 to 42 percent. Risk fell steadily as the number of optimal heart health measures rose, and women with short estrogen exposure but five or more optimal measures no longer carried excess risk. The authors urge women past menopause to protect heart health as kidney prevention. Readers should note the short follow-up and study design, which limit causal claims.
pmc-13648224:
Sebastian Hilscher and twelve colleagues ask if a new-found histone mark can be wiped off by the enzymes that clear such marks. Histones are spools that wind DNA, and their marks help switch genes on and off. The new mark carries two tags at once on the same spot, an acetyl tag and a methyl tag, long thought to bar each other.

The team built short protein chains with the dual mark and fed them to two enzyme families. The plain chains lost their tags as expected. The dual-mark chains did not lose theirs at all. The methyl tag also blocked most side acts of the enzymes. Crystal views showed the tag twists the chain so the cut point sits wrong. The mark may last a long time on DNA spools.
pmc-13648824:
Francesco Citiulo and co-authors report, in a 2026 preclinical study, a three-in-one vaccine aimed at invasive salmonella disease and typhoid fever together. Non-typhoidal salmonella bloodstream infections kill many children under five in sub-Saharan Africa, and no vaccine exists for them; antibiotics are the only tool. Typhoid, by contrast, already has licensed shots.

Their candidate fuses membrane vesicle technology covering the two invasive strains with the established typhoid conjugate vaccine. In mice it raised stronger anti-typhoid antibodies, with a distinct subclass mix, and greater bacteria-killing power in serum than the typhoid vaccine alone. Human immune cells in dishes also answered robustly to the vesicle parts. The work moves a combined shot toward trials for regions hit by both diseases.
pmc-13649124:
Jie Ren and five colleagues show how gut fat handling steers defence in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans. A gene switch called NHR-68, set in the gut, keeps a fat called linoleic acid in balance. Worms must split scarce fuel between growth and two kinds of defence: fleeing germs and fighting them inside.

Without the switch, worms lost the fat balance and stopped shunning germ food. Feeding the fat back brought the shunning back. Gut signals reached a smell circuit through gut-to-nerve talk, which steered the flight. The switch also held two inside fight paths in check. The team frames this as one gut-brain loop that tunes both arms of defence at once.
pmc-13649324:
Johnson and co-authors measure a protein PD-L2 in throat tumors, comparing HPV-tied cancers with those that are not. Virus-linked cases of this cancer are rising fast in the United States. The team had earlier found a small RNA raised in virus-positive tumors and predicted to target the gene for PD-L2. That protein matters because it binds a brake receptor on T cells; it can quiet the immune attack on a tumor.

Using tumor samples from two patient groups, the authors found lower PD-L2 levels in the virus-positive tumors. The pattern fits the small RNA story: more of the RNA, less of its target protein. The authors say the result justifies deeper study of PD-L2 control in this cancer type. The finding may matter for immunotherapy planning, since virus-positive and virus-negative tumors are known to behave differently.
pmc-13649424:
Yueyao Zhao and seven colleagues checked if a low heart stress marker can rule out early heart strain in people with type 2 diabetes. The marker can run low in people with more body fat, which may hide real problems. The team studied 191 adults in hospital who had both the blood test and a heart scan within two days.

Among those with a low marker score, one in nine still had a stiff heart pattern, and one in four had some heart change. Extra weight strongly raised the odds of these hidden changes. Blood fat and sugar scores also tracked with how well the heart's upper and lower chambers worked as a pair. The authors warn that a low marker alone is not a clean bill of health.
pmc-13649724:
Manuela Iglesias and six colleagues asked if the chance a neighbourhood offers shapes how toddlers grow and learn. They studied children born in Northern Virginia from 2020 to 2023 and tested them at age two to three with a standard development scale. Home zip codes gave each child a neighbourhood chance score.

Higher chance scores tied to stronger thinking and language scores, in a steady step pattern. The social and money part of the score drove the link most. Motor scores showed no such tie. A mother's schooling explained a bit more than the score did, though not by a firm margin. Gaps ran widest for Hispanic and Latino children in areas weak on health and surroundings. The authors urge focused help for such areas.
pmc-13651624:
Petr Rozhin and seventeen colleagues stack two atom-thin semiconductors to make one of them glow six times brighter. Layered materials called transition metal dichalcogenides emit light from excitons, bound electron-hole pairs, but most of that energy usually leaks away as heat instead of photons.

Placing a palladium selenide layer against a molybdenum selenide monolayer created a type-I alignment that funnels excitons into the brighter channel. The main emission line strengthened roughly sixfold at room temperature, reaching a quantum yield several times the bare monolayer's. The competing higher-energy exciton dimmed, evidence that populations were being redirected rather than merely added. Power and temperature sweeps showed fewer exciton collisions and a reshaped energy landscape, and excitation scans found the boost spanning a broad wavelength range. No chemistry or heavy strain was needed. The authors present interlayer coupling as a clean dial for emission efficiency.
pmc-13652424:
Isabella Montealegre and co-authors report a rare heart case from Colombia in this 2026 paper, the first of its kind in that country. A woman had a hole between the upper heart chambers closed with a device placed through a vein. Three years later, a routine scan found a mass growing on that device.

Heart tumors are very rare, and myxomas are the most common benign kind in adults. A mass on a closure device can be a blood clot, an infection, or a tumor, so care is needed. The team describe how the case was found and assessed. Their report alerts heart doctors to a late risk after device closure.
pmc-13652924:
Samuel Tschopp and co-authors check whether one night of home sleep testing tells the truth about children's breathing, in a 2026 study. Pediatric sleep apnea is often diagnosed from a single night at home. Breathing, though, can vary from night to night, and the first night in a test setup may skew results. The team analyzed two consecutive nights of recordings from children suspected of disordered breathing.

Records came from routine care rather than a hand-picked trial group. The main measure was the apnea-hypopnea index, the standard count of breathing pauses per hour. Comparing nights showed how stable that index really is. The analysis also tested how often the diagnosis itself would flip between nights. Such evidence helps doctors decide when a second night is worth ordering.
pmc-13654124:
Wei and co-authors build a scoring chart that tells two breast tumor types apart before surgery. One type is a rare, leaf-like growth that is often harmless. The other is breast cancer. Their scans look much alike, so the wrong call is a real risk.

The study covered 92 patients whose tumors were proven by lab tests after removal. Thirty-one had the leaf-like growth and 61 had cancer. All had detailed magnetic scans before surgery. The chart joins shape, blood flow, and water-motion measures from the scans. It also probes whether the water measure hints at the leaf tumor's grade. A sound pre-surgery call can spare women either needless wide surgery or a missed cancer.
pmc-13654524:
Ito and co-authors test a score that aims to predict dangerous acid build-up in a baby during birth. Heart rate tracing alone predicts it poorly. The score sums the stress shown in the heart pattern over time.

Past checks ran where the acid problem was rare, which flatters a test. This study nested cases in 272 full-term vaginal births, enriched for bad outcomes. The score sorted babies well across a range of acid cut-offs. It tracked most strongly with cord blood acid and its buffer measure. Its forecasts ran a bit high, overshooting true acid levels. The authors weigh where the score can be trusted. A validated score could help teams decide when to speed a birth.
pmc-13655424:
Ye-Jun Han, Hyun Ahn, Sea-Hyun Bae, and Kyung-Yoon Kim test a hamstring exercise program for high school baseball pitchers, in a study from 2026. The exercise is the Nordic hamstring curl, done here with air pressure help from a Keiser device. Strong and supple hamstrings matter for young pitchers even though the arm does the throwing.

Sixteen pitchers trained for ten weeks. Before and after, the team measured hamstring tone, stiffness, and stretch with a handheld device. They also checked strength, trunk and shoulder motion, ball speed, and spin rate. After training, tone and stiffness fell while strength and a slow stretch measure rose. The authors report gains in several of the pitching and body measures as well.
pmc-13655824:
Kang and co-authors look back at patients with cancer of the food pipe whose disease grew worse during a first course of immune therapy. The question was whether giving the same kind of immune drug again, as a second course, could still help. All patients came from one hospital in China.

Each patient had at least three months of the first treatment and at least two rounds of the second. Half of the group lived ten months or more after the second course began. About one third saw their tumors shrink, and about two thirds kept the disease in check for a time. Patients whose first course held the disease for over six months did best. Side effects were manageable, and no deaths were tied to the treatment.
pmc-13656324:
Wei Chen and co-authors compare cells from swollen prostates with cells from sound tissue in a 2026 study. The swell is the most common ill of older men, and male hormones feed its growth more than they feed the sound gland.

The team grew support cells from both tissues of the same men and dosed them with hormones. Gene reads showed the swollen cells answer hormones with a louder voice. Their switched-on genes steer cell motion, vessel growth, and signals sent to the gland's skin cells. Fluid from hormone-dosed swollen cells made those skin cells breed faster in a dish, while fluid from sound cells did not. The authors read the gap as part of why the swell grows under hormone push.
pmc-13657524:
Sara Mirzamohamadi and co-authors compare surgery and non surgery care for belly injuries in Iran in a 2026 study. The injuries came from hard blows that hurt solid organs such as the liver, spleen, and kidney. Choosing between an operation and watchful care is a key call in trauma wards. The data come from a national trauma registry that spans seven years.

Single organ injuries were more often cared for without surgery than with it. The same held for some multi organ injury mixes in the records. In matched groups, a low alertness score sharply raised the odds of intensive care. Heavy blood loss raised the odds of death by a wide margin as well.
pmc-13657624:
Nabil Almouaalamy studies muscle loss during cancer drug treatment in a 2026 paper. Muscle loss, called sarcopenia, can weaken patients and make treatment harder to bear. The study used a short survey and a hand grip test as simple signs of muscle health. Data came from outpatients with advanced cancer at a center in Jeddah.

One drug stood out in the checks: patients on it scored worse on the survey and gripped far less strongly. That link held after other factors were weighed in the model. A second drug showed a link in simple checks but not after adjustment. The number of treatment rounds showed no link to either muscle sign.
pmc-13657824:
Jian Wu and co-authors review engineered immune cells for solid tumors in a 2026 paper. The cells are macrophages, immune cells that can enter tissue and eat tumor cells. They can also show tumor parts to other immune cells and release alarm signals. The catch is that tumors can bend these cells toward helping the tumor instead of fighting it.

The review sorts tumor defenses into five layers that block cell therapy. Layers include thick tissue, low oxygen, harsh fuel use, and signals that stop eating of tumor cells. Each design idea is matched to the layer it aims to beat. The authors also weigh what blocks the move from lab work to patient care.
pmc-13658524:
Helen Hong and three co-authors timed cell-cycle genes in mussels against the tide in a 2026 paper. Mussels on the shore swing between breathing water at high tide and air at low tide, a daily metabolic roller coaster. The team asked when the mussel's cyclin genes, which drive cell division, switch on, and how heat stress in air changes the timing.

They expected division genes to peak when oxygen stress is lowest, or right after a heat shock. In simulated tides, heat-stressed mussels pushed cyclin levels clearly above unstressed ones. A growth proxy assay ran alongside the gene measures. The study links the cell cycle to tidal cues in an animal that must budget DNA safety against a punishing shore.
pmc-13658924:
Ingrid Larsson and co-authors explore how women live with chronic widespread pain, a condition that touches about one adult in ten and strikes women more often. Rather than test a treatment, the team interviewed nineteen women and mapped the different ways they cope, using a method that groups outlooks rather than people.

Four broad ways stood out. Some women took control, adjusting plans and guarding rest. Some carried on as usual, downplaying the pain. Some leaned on professional guidance and set routines. Others coped by resting and cutting demands when pain and fatigue peaked. The same woman might switch ways as her body and day demanded. Knowing this range, the authors say, helps clinicians tailor support to each woman's current needs.
pmc-13659524:
Meghana Singh and Anwaar Saeed discuss vaccine hopes for a rare liver cancer in a 2026 paper. The cancer strikes mostly teens and young adults and lacks a standard drug plan. Surgery can cure early cases, but advanced disease has a poor outlook. A fused gene found in most tumors drives the cancer, yet the fused protein cannot be blocked safely.

The fusion creates new protein bits that the immune system can spot as foreign. Those bits appear in nearly all tumors of this type, which makes them a shared target. A vaccine could train the immune system to attack cells that carry them. The authors present this path as a new direction for a cancer long called undruggable.
pmc-13661224:
Junchi Liu and co-authors identify a blood metabolic fingerprint of frailty and test how much of frailty's link to heart disease runs through it. Their data come from over two hundred twenty thousand UK Biobank participants. Frailty was scored from five physical features. Metabolite measurements in a large subgroup were distilled into a signature of thirty-six molecules.

Frail people developed coronary disease at much higher rates over about fifteen years. The metabolic signature accounted for roughly a fifth of that excess risk. The signature's danger varied with inherited genetic risk, and people high on both had about three and a half times the risk of the lowest group. The authors argue that combining frailty, metabolism, and genetics sharpens risk understanding.
pmc-13662224:
Gyuzel Y Mitronova and co-authors review drugs that hit several targets at once in a 2026 paper. Heart diseases arise from many tangled pathways, so one target drugs often fall short. A single compound that acts on several pathways could work better and cut pill counts. It could also lower dose linked side effects and slow drug resistance.
