The review covers fresh advances in building such compounds for heart care. It focuses on a few compound families and how their shapes drive their effects. Links between structure and strength, safety, and healing promise are traced for each family. The authors frame the field as a bridge between chemistry craft and clinical need.
pmc-13666224:
Sara Habouria and co-authors study small RNA regulators during parasite infection in this 2026 paper. Leishmania major is a parasite that lives inside human macrophages, the cells meant to kill it. It tweaks host microRNAs to aid its own survival.

The team tracked four microRNAs in lab-grown human macrophages over the first forty-eight hours of infection. Two of them rose early and fell by the second day. Blocking those two freed several immune genes from restraint. Network analysis found hundreds of target genes, including key immune signals. The pair act as early brakes on the immune response, which marks them as possible drug targets.
pmc-13668624:
Phan Duy and many co-authors (2026) link a gene carried by microglia to congenital hydrocephalus. Microglia are the brain's immune cells. In this condition, fluid builds up and enlarges the brain's ventricles in infants. It is a leading reason for brain surgery in children, yet its causes are poorly understood. The team found recurring damaging changes in GRB2, a gene for an adaptor protein, in unrelated patients. The changes cluster in one binding region of the protein.

In the developing brain, GRB2 is co-expressed with its partner receptor, CSF1R. This happens especially in a subtype of microglia. The study shows these cells are needed for the ventricles to form properly. They also keep the brain's fluid in balance. The findings recast a condition long treated as a plumbing problem. At least in part, it is a disorder of brain immune cells during development.
pmc-13669024:
Tewodros Fentahun Jember, Mark Edward Westman, Sameer Dinkar Pant, and Seyed Ali Ghorashi test a cheap way to ready milk samples for bacteria hunting. The target germ, Escherichia coli, is a common cause of udder infection in cows, and fast detection guides treatment. Complex DNA extraction slows molecular tests in the field. Their 2026 study tries a simple hot-shot preparation method with two kinds of test.

Spiked pasteurized milk set the sensitivity floor, and seventeen culture-proven clinical samples checked real-world use. The simple method let PCR match the best store-bought kits, while a color-change LAMP test ran ten to a hundred times less sensitive than the best kits. Plain boiling without spinning performed far worse. On clinical samples, LAMP caught fifteen of seventeen and PCR caught all. The authors see a workable base for field tests in low-resource settings.
pmc-13669324:
Louise Klem and a large team test a first-in-human dementia drug that raises progranulin. Their phase one trial from twenty twenty-six covers the oral drug VES001. Low progranulin from a gene fault causes frontotemporal dementia. Blocking the sortilin receptor lifts progranulin without removing the receptor.

Animal work first showed rises in blood, spinal fluid, and brain fluid. Seventy-nine healthy adults then joined the randomised human trial. Single and week-long dosing schedules were both tested. Safety goals were met with no serious drug-linked harms. Headache was among the common minor complaints reported. Patient trials can now test whether raising progranulin helps. Early human data justify that next step.
pmc-13669624:
Ali Al-Fatlawi and Michael Schroeder warned that database pruning hides proteins in two thousand twenty-six. UniProt, the main protein catalog, reorganized itself massively. Tens of millions of entries moved to an archive tier. More tens of millions face removal soon. Curated and structurally known proteins were kept. The rest fade from everyday view.

The authors call the fading set the dark proteome. Navigation gets easier with less clutter, they grant. But unstudied proteins vanish from routine searches. Discovery pipelines train on what remains visible. Bias toward the already-known deepens quietly. The piece urges care in how pruning proceeds. Archives should stay searchable, not forgotten.
pmc-13670324:
Ilker Sengul and Demet Sengul write a letter on a rare thyroid cancer case in 2026. The case they discuss involves papillary thyroid cancer that spread to the skin years after surgery. Such spread is rare and hints at more active disease than the first tumor suggested. The letter questions parts of the first report, from lab test results to the choice of a small local surgery.

The authors note a clash in the lab signs found in the skin growth. They also question whether hormone control played the role the first team claimed. They urge gene tests on such tumors to spot high risk traits early. Closer follow up could then catch odd returns of the disease sooner.
pmc-13671724:
A fungus that attacks the brain, Cladophialophora bantiana, kills sixty to seventy percent of the people it infects. Maria Nelson and co-authors report in 2026 on cases detected at a single United States reference laboratory. Their field notes cover January 2009 to July 2026.

The lab confirmed 48 cases and one probable case, most from brain and nervous system tissue, sent in from twenty-two jurisdictions. Detections rose roughly fourfold between 2023 and 2025. Why cases are climbing is unknown: there is no national surveillance, and even how people catch the fungus is unclear. The authors urge systematic reporting, faster antifungal treatment, and consideration of surgery, and they ask clinicians to think of this fungus when a patient has a brain abscess.
pmc-13671824:
How children learn to walk, run, and climb depends in part on the culture around them. Jessica Silveira and co-authors map that evidence in a 2026 scoping review of gross motor development in children from birth to age five. Caregiving routines, parent beliefs, and the spaces children can move in all vary across cultures.

Searching seven databases for studies from 1994 to 2025, the team gathered 166 publications from more than eight thousand screened. They recorded how each study defined typical development, what it counted as culture, and which motor outcomes it measured. The review also lists the supports and barriers studies reported. Its aim is to show where the field agrees, where definitions drift, and what future studies should standardize.
pmc-13672824:
Ending tobacco sales outright is one endgame strategy for cutting smoking, but shops that sell cigarettes have a say in how it would land. Joshua Trigg and co-authors surveyed licensed tobacco retailers in South Australia in 2026. Their exploratory survey, run in April 2025, drew responses from seventy retailers across the state.

Retailers said legal duties, falling profits, and shrinking demand would most drive them to stop selling tobacco, while community health barely registered. A third said they would need lead time to adjust, and they asked for compensation, planning help, and chances to stock other products. Many feared a boom in illegal tobacco sales and the losses and safety risks that could follow. Views on a phased ban were mixed.
pmc-13673324:
Paula López-García and co-authors test a way to block traumatic memory in mice in 2026. Post-traumatic stress has no real cure beyond easing symptoms. A brain protein that clumps into an amyloid form helps lock in long-term memory, and it is also a risk gene for the disorder.

A small peptide that blocks such clumping was studied first on the human protein in a dish. The peptide's active core stopped clumping while leaving other assembly behavior intact. Mice bred to make the peptide throughout life then showed impaired memory locking. The work frames a path toward a drug for the disorder.
pmc-13674924:
Vanaja Jain and co-authors review copy versions of eye drugs for swelling at the center of the retina in diabetes. Their article from 2026 deals with a common diabetes harm and a main cause of sight loss. Shots of drugs that block a vessel growth signal are the gold standard care.

The high cost and thin access to the first drugs have pushed interest in copies built to match them in effect, safety, and immune response. As patents ran out, several copies were made and cleared for use. Real world studies and trials named in the review found the copies matched the first drugs in eye care for this disease. The authors also set out rule paths and the hard parts of daily use.
pmc-13675224:
Tahereh Sabouri Aghbolagh Rostam Khan and co-authors draft Iran's first rules to grade the graders of medical schools. School grade boards vouch for care training, yet few check the boards' own work. Their 2026 study blends talks with a score of home experts, a scan of six world grade frames, panel deals, and a land-wide poll of just under one hundred stake holders.

A first pool of near two hundred draft rules is honed to a final set of just over fifty. Poll scores for use, need, and clarity top the set bar for each rule. Three realms sort the set: form, grade steps, and answer-and-grow duties. The frame can lift trust in Iran's care schools and set a case kin lands can ape.
pmc-13676224:
Aaron Nagiel and Lamberto Rondoni model, in a 2026 fluid study, what sets the flow rate when surgeons inject therapy under the retina. Slow injection spares the fragile cell layer beneath, yet surgeons often tweak the setup blindly. The team wrote the physics of the whole injection line, from console to fine cannula, as a flow model.

One factor ruled: the cannula's inner width, where tiny widenings unleashed large flow gains. Console pressure raised flow in a straight line. Trimming the tip by three millimeters added a modest bump, while beveling or eye pressure barely mattered. Their free web app lets surgeons test changes before touching an eye.
pmc-13676624:
Anaïs Havet and nine co-authors published a study in 2026 on how robot-assisted keyhole surgery spread across France. Robotic operating has been available for nearly two decades, but no national map covered every specialty, including ear, nose, and throat surgery. The team used the national health data system to track its rise.

They counted more than nine hundred thousand keyhole operations from twenty seventeen to mid twenty twenty-three. From mid twenty twenty the robotic share reached about nineteen percent overall. Urology led at nearly two thirds robotic, while digestive surgery sat near six percent. Use grew steadily each quarter but varied widely by department. The map gives planners a base for fairer access.
pmc-13676724:
Manabe and co-authors report a study, published in 2026, on how sugar tags help a prostate protein fold into shape. Many proteins carry sugar chains at set points, and those chains guide folding and movement inside the cell. Gene errors that remove a sugar site can cause disease, but the role of each single site is rarely clear. The team studied one prostate protein that carries sugar at three sites.

Tests showed that two sites carry large, complex sugars, while the third carries a simpler type. Removing the first two sites did little harm. Removing the third site broke the protein's folding and its function. The work ranks the three sites by importance and shows that one plain-looking sugar does the heavy lifting. It helps explain how a single gene error at that site can lead to disease.
pmc-13677024:
Wentong Jia wrote a commentary, published in 2026, on how brown fat handles fat during fasting. Brown fat is a special tissue that burns fuel to make heat. White fat, by contrast, mainly stores fuel. When an animal fasts, white fat breaks down and sends fatty fuel into the blood. Brown fat then takes up much of that fuel. What it does with the fuel next was not well understood.

Jia discusses a mouse study by Song and colleagues that tracked brown fat over a fast. The tissue did not simply burn more fuel as more arrived. After a short early phase of breaking down its own stores, it began to store the incoming fuel instead. By about 20 hours, it held a large pool of stored fat. The commentary explains why storing, rather than burning, may help the whole body manage a long fast.
pmc-13677424:
Sabina Karačić and six co-authors study leaf decay in 2026, asking whether microbe films protect or destroy. Films of microbes coat most surfaces in nature, wrapped in a self-made slime. They are often blamed for decay, yet they can also seed mineral growth that preserves tissue.

The team rebuilt leaf microbe mixes in the lab and varied the salts and metals around them. With extra calcium, film-covered leaves formed minerals on their surface and decayed far less, judged by retained green pigment. One iron-eating bacterium laid down varied iron minerals. Heavy metals helped or hurt depending on which microbes were present.
pmc-13677624:
Braida Thom and co-authors assess the social side of coffee production in Brazil and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Most coffee sustainability work stresses environment and cost, yet social factors shape producers' lives most directly. The team applied a social life cycle method to nine case studies.

They used only firsthand, site-specific data and gathered views from many actors early in the supply chain, through a large set of interviews. Social scores varied widely within each country, not just between them, showing that how a farm is organized matters. Cooperatives in Brazil scored above large plantations. Low pay and weak livelihoods were the worst areas, and most workers did not earn a living wage.
pmc-13677724:
Bei Jin and ten co-authors traced how tiny packages from blood vessel cells help cancer settle in the liver in a 2026 study. The work focuses on two cancers that often spread to the liver, uveal melanoma and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. For both, settling in the new organ is a key step and a main cause of death.

The team found that packages called exosomes, released by the cells lining blood vessels, carry a signal into cancer cells. That signal switches on a factor named KLF4. The factor then opens up packed DNA and reshapes booster regions, turning on two genes that drive growth, movement, and spread. In patient data, high levels of the signal's parts each tracked with shorter survival. That pattern points to a chain that drugs might one day block.
pmc-13678324:
Laura Samet, Zainab Ali, and Habib Haider report a 2026 case in which a cancer drug's farewell gift arrived twelve days after the last dose: a full adrenal crisis. The patient, a man in his fifties with metastatic lung cancer, had just finished two years of pembrolizumab.

Routine bloods first flagged a critically low morning cortisol. He then arrived at hospital with malaise, vomiting, and blood pressure crashed to dangerous levels. Infection was considered and set aside for lack of signs. Fluids and high-dose intravenous steroids rescued him, and he settled onto daily replacement tablets under endocrine supervision. The authors warn that immune side effects ignore the treatment calendar, and patients must be taught the symptoms.
pmc-13679224:
When to start steroid drugs in children hospitalized with mycoplasma pneumonia is unsettled. Lei Yang, Hu Liu, Jiangang Leng, and Jiali Tong compared early and late starts at one Chinese children's hospital. Records from twenty twenty-three to twenty twenty-five held nine hundred two children who got steroids between days three and fourteen of illness. Matching balanced the groups on many starting factors, leaving two hundred ninety-nine pairs. A severe outcome bundle served as the main measure.

All children also received standard antibiotics. Secondary measures covered fever length, hospital days, oxygen use, and intensive care. Earlier starts are often assumed better, but timing studies are rare in this disease. The matched design aims to give that question a fair test.
pmc-13679924:
Po-Hsiang Chen and colleagues built a coating analysis platform in 2026. Medical surfaces often hide thin coatings beneath them. How buried coating shape drives function was hard to measure. Soft, curved surfaces resist standard inspection. The team chose silicone hydrogel contact lenses as the test case. They formed sturdy woven nanocoatings on the lenses. Three advanced tools then mapped the buried layers. Chemical gradients, layer thickness, and stiffness were all charted. Precision reached below one hundred nanometers.

The maps revealed even, conformal buried coatings. A tuned surface layer then covered most of the lens. Wetting improved, and protein deposits dropped sharply. Cell fouling also fell markedly. Oxygen flow, clarity, and strength stayed fully intact. Sun protection survived the coating as well. Extra building blocks enabled light-triggered drug release. The authors offer the platform for many medical interfaces.
pmc-13680324:
Antonio Tovar Faro and co-authors compare river health checks in Portugal and Spain in this 2026 paper. European law requires member states to grade the ecological status of surface waters. Rivers that cross the border are graded by both countries. Different national methods could give different grades for the same river.

The team compared grades for 32 water bodies across five shared river basins. Data from 2019 to 2021 covered fish, plants, small invertebrates, and diatoms. Fish grades matched fairly well between the two countries. Other groups matched less well, and some showed weak or no link. The work shows where harmonized methods work and where they still drift apart.
pmc-13680424:
Gereon Schnellbacher and eight co-authors predict test performance from ultra-sharp brain scans in a 2026 study. Drug therapy for mental illness has barely improved in decades, which pushes the search for personal markers of who will do well on what. The team bets that brain shape itself carries such signals.

Scans came from a 7-tesla MRI machine, far stronger than clinic standard. The group held 74 patients with varied diagnoses and 41 healthy controls. Measures of gray matter volume, cortex thickness, and folding were drawn from a 100-region brain atlas. A deep learning model then used those measures to predict scores on a trail-making test of attention and mental speed. Success would link brain form to thinking in a usable way.
pmc-13680524:
Gianmaria Rausch and a large team of co-authors study how fast surgery should follow blunt belly injury in patients with many injuries at once, in a paper from 2026. Blunt hits to the belly are common in major trauma. Bleeding from solid organs or a torn gut calls for an emergency open operation, but the cost of delay was not firmly known.

The team drew on one top trauma center's registry, covering cases from 1996 to 2020. Adults with severe overall injury who had the emergency operation were split by time to surgery: within one hour, or between one and three hours. Stay length, intensive care time, breathing support, repeat operations, and deaths were compared. Adjusted models then tested whether the timing itself drove any gap in outcomes.
pmc-13680624:
Laura Sherwood and co-authors grow working salivary gland organoids from human stem cells, in work from 2026. Dry mouth from gland failure lowers life quality, and current care is limited and often harsh. Their plan copies the steps the gland takes in early development.

First they coax stem cells into gland starter cells, marked by a glowing tag gene. Those cells then form three-dimensional organoids with hollow cores that can secrete, much like real glands. Planted into the jaw gland of mice with weak immunity, the organoids settled in and matured into the gland's main cell types. The authors see uses in studying gland growth, testing drugs, and future cell therapy.
pmc-13680724:
Ruijie An, Ningning He, and Wendong Gu review, in a 2026 paper, how signal proteins called chemokines help pair heat-based tumor killing with immunotherapy. Microwave ablation burns a tumor directly, but it also reshapes the immune scene around the tumor and can spark wider attacks on cancer cells.

Chemokines direct where immune cells travel and how they behave, so they mediate much of that teamwork. The review sums up how ablation changes the tumor's immune surroundings, which chemokine networks matter most, and how combined treatments are progressing in clinics. It closes with open problems and design ideas for making the pairing prevent recurrence and spread more reliably.
pmc-13681124:
Jin Li and co-authors tested whether combining three ultrasound methods improves prostate cancer detection. Each method sees the tissue differently: standard transrectal imaging shows structure, shear wave elastography maps stiffness, and contrast-enhanced imaging follows blood flow. Eighty-five men received all three scans plus biopsy, the reference standard, at one hospital.

Each single method performed respectably, with contrast imaging the strongest alone. The combined multimodal approach beat them all, reaching about ninety-eight percent sensitivity and ninety-four percent specificity, with the best overall discrimination score. The advantage was clearest for tumors whose single-scan appearance is atypical. The authors recommend combined imaging as a reliable basis for telling benign from malignant prostate lesions.
pmc-13681724:
Archith Rajan leads a team of eleven authors in 2026 in showing how detailed MRI measurements can track one brain tumor patient's response to a vaccine therapy over time. The patient, a long-term survivor of glioblastoma, received a dendritic cell vaccine made from their own tumor material.

Measuring whether immunotherapy works in the brain is notoriously hard, since scans can flare misleadingly. The team used multiparametric MRI, combining several kinds of scan signal into numbers that can be followed month by month. Their illustrative case argues such measures could become the sensitive, practical biomarker that vaccine trials for this cancer still lack.
pmc-13682724:
Yan Ma and a team of co-authors compared two mind-body programs for cancer survivors in a 2026 trial. Poor sleep, fatigue, and pain often linger after cancer treatment. The trial tested a mindfulness-based cancer recovery course against Tai Chi and Qigong, and let patients help choose their path.

The 587 participants picked a program or agreed to be assigned one, then were split into starting now or waiting. Both programs eased fatigue by over three points on their scale, and Tai Chi also improved sleep, an edge that held after adjustments. Pain improved by more than a point. Changes in the three symptoms moved together, and having a choice did not warp the results.
pmc-13682824:
Long Xu and four co-authors review the state of diagnosis and treatment for psittacosis, in work from 2025. The disease is passed from birds by the bacterium Chlamydia psittaci, and its burden is understated because symptoms are vague and testing is scarce. The review gathers evidence from 1879 to 2024 on spread, symptoms, tests and therapy.

Cases span mild pneumonia to severe disease of the brain, heart or pregnancy. Culture and antibody tests are slow or unreliable, while gene-based tests are sensitive but costly and unstandardized. Tetracyclines stay the main treatment, with macrolides for pregnant women and children. The authors urge surveillance, wider testing and clinician awareness.
pmc-13688124:
Eun Seon Chung shows that a pathogen's past climates shape its drug survival in a 2026 solo paper. The bacterium causes tuberculosis and meets shifting host conditions. Nutrients and acidity swing as infection moves through the body. Adaptation to single conditions is well studied by contrast.

Chung passaged the bacteria six times under set or shifting regimes. Carbon sources and acidity were held steady or swapped each round. Growth and drug survival hinged on that history. Stable pasts bred higher survival on two key drugs. Fluctuating pasts limited such tuning despite more varied cells. Drug tests should use dynamic host-like settings, Chung argues.
pmc-1794324:
Achard and Bullmore examine how well human brain networks work compared with what they cost. Brain wiring is sparse yet complex, with economical small-world traits that keep signals fast without endless links. The authors used brain scans that track activity over time.

They compared functional networks in two groups of healthy older adults, weighing efficiency against connection cost. A brain that achieves high efficiency at low cost can share information widely without wasting resources. Their results help explain how ageing brains stay organised, and give a baseline for spotting costly breakdowns in disease.
pmc-3214824:
Lee, Macfarlane, Lam, and co-authors review studies testing the International Physical Activity Questionnaire Short Form. The short questionnaire had been recommended as a cost-effective way to assess physical activity in surveys. Several validation studies had been run, with differing results, and no systematic review had gathered them.

The team weighs how well the questionnaire matches objective measures across those studies. Their verdict helps survey designers judge when the cheap tool is good enough and when it misleads. National health monitoring depends on such checks, since policy rests on the numbers.
pmc-4290824:
Li, Xu, Xiao, and their team presented MAGeCK in 2014 for CRISPR screening data. Genome-scale knockout screens switch off genes one by one across a whole library of cells. Finding which genes are truly essential in that flood of data takes a strong statistical method.

MAGeCK models the data to rank guide RNAs, genes, and pathways by importance. In tests it performed better than existing methods and found both positive and negative selection signals. Essential genes point to a cell's weak spots, which matters for cancer drug research. A robust ranking method helps labs trust the short list a huge screen produces.
pmc-4668324:
Sørensen, Pelikan, Röthlin, and their colleagues reported health literacy results for Europe in 2015. Health literacy means how well people can find, grasp, and act on health information in daily life. European policy makers wanted firmer facts on its status across countries.

The European health literacy survey measured these skills in a comparative way across nations. Results showed wide gaps, with many people struggling to find, understand, and use health information. Such findings guide programs that make health systems easier to navigate. The survey gave Europe a shared baseline for tracking progress on a skill that shapes care and outcomes.
pmc-5039924:
Ewels, Magnusson, Lundin, and their colleagues built MultiQC in 2016. Studies built on next-generation sequencing stand or fall on fast, accurate quality control. Numerous tools exist to quantify quality metrics, but there was no common way to combine their outputs flexibly.

MultiQC summarizes analysis results for multiple tools and samples in a single report. Instead of opening dozens of files, a researcher gets one clear view of a whole run. That makes it easy to spot a failing sample hiding among hundreds of good ones. MultiQC became a standard final step in sequencing pipelines across genomics labs.
pmc-5051824:
Shen, Le, Li, and their team presented SeqKit in 2016, a toolkit for sequence files. Nearly every lab stores sequences in FASTA or FASTQ, the two basic formats for nucleotide and protein data. Daily chores on such files range from format conversion and search to filtering, removing duplicates, splitting, shuffling, and sampling.

Existing tools each implemented only some of those manipulations, forcing users to chain many programs. SeqKit is cross-platform and ultrafast, covering the common tasks in one toolkit. It is built for the huge file sizes of modern sequencing. A single reliable tool for file chores removes friction from nearly every genomics workflow.
pmc-6324024:
Sara El-Gebali, Jaina Mistry, Alex Bateman, and coauthors reported the Pfam database in 2019. Pfam groups protein regions into families that share ancestry and often share a job. Recent years brought big growth and change to the resource.

The release described here holds close to eighteen thousand families. Work focused on refining older families and sharpening domain boundaries, not only on adding new ones. Users scan a new protein against Pfam to learn its likely parts at a glance. The database remains a first stop for interpreting unknown protein sequences.
pmc-7145624:
Brian Alcock, Amogelang Raphenya, Tammy Lau, and coauthors described CARD, a shared database on drug resistance in germs, in its 2020 form. CARD gathers the genes and changes that let germs survive drugs meant to kill them. It pairs those records with search models and free software tools.

The update reports growth in curated entries and in the tools that scan whole genomes for them. Health programs use CARD to read resistance straight from the DNA of a germ sample. Shared names let labs in many lands compare what they find with ease. As resistance spreads, such shared records support the work of tracking it across the globe.
pmc-7402624:
Divij Mathew and many co-authors profiled the immune systems of patients with COVID-19 in unusual depth in 2020. At the time it was still unclear how a person's immune response shapes whether the illness stays mild or turns severe. The team used high dimensional methods that can measure many immune cell types and states in a single blood sample.

Their work grouped patients into distinct immunotypes, patterns of immune activity that lined up with different disease courses. Some patterns hinted at which treatments might help which patients, rather than giving everyone the same drug. The atlas they built helped other researchers compare results across hospitals, and it showed how much the immune response differs from one patient to the next.
pmc-8005924:
Matthew Page and a team of methods experts issued the PRISMA 2020 statement in 2021, an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. The original statement, published in 2009, taught reviewers to say plainly why the review was written, how the work was carried out, and what came out of it. Over the following decade, both review methods and the expectations around them moved forward.

The update refreshes the checklist of items every review report should include, from search details to how results were combined. It also reflects new topics such as judging certainty in the evidence. Journals and funders around the world point authors to this guideline, so its wording shapes how thousands of evidence summaries are written each year.
pmc-8728224:
Mihaly Varadi and co-authors introduced the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database in 2021, a free archive of predicted protein shapes. The database is powered by DeepMind's AlphaFold system, which computes a protein's folded structure from its sequence. Before it appeared, known structures covered only a modest fraction of the proteins scientists study.

The archive opened with models for a vast range of organisms, including the full human set, and kept expanding from there. The authors explain how the models are made, how confidence scores guide their use, and how to search and download them. By putting a plausible shape for nearly any protein a click away, the database changed the starting point of countless studies.
podcast-dannyjones-ZC3Rr_UKJ24:
Aaron Smith-Levin, a former member of Scientology, joins Danny Jones to argue the church is near collapse. The episode title says the group is on the verge of ruin. Smith-Levin now spends his time reporting on the church he left.

Smith-Levin points to shrinking numbers, lost staff, and bad press as signs of deep trouble. He tells stories from inside the group and from his years of reporting since he left. Jones asks what would prove the church can still bounce back. Listeners get an insider's view of a secretive faith under strain. The library keeps the talk as an archive record.
podcast-tuckercarlson-rpQop5vPm24:
Preparing for nuclear war is the grim subject of this Tucker Carlson episode, explained by a chemical engineer. The guest lays out the practical steps a family can take if the sirens ever sound. The talk treats the unthinkable in plain, calm terms.

The engineer covers fallout, shelter, water, and how long to stay inside. He explains which supplies matter most and which myths could get people killed. Carlson asks how likely such an attack now is, given world tensions. Preppers and the merely worried get a clear guide to the worst day imaginable.
procopius-wars-gothic-2-dewing-1924:
Books six and seven of the Wars of Procopius, in H. B. Dewing's Loeb volume of 1924, carry the Gothic War into its brutal second act. Ravenna falls by guile, Belisarius is recalled in disgrace, and Italy slips back into fire. Procopius wrote from reports and from his own years in the country.

Under their new king Totila, the Goths rise again and take Rome itself, twice. Plague, famine, and the wreck of the Italian cities fill these books. Procopius counts the cost of Justinian's dream of a restored empire with open doubt. The war that began in triumph becomes a warning. Dewing's notes guide readers through the tangled campaigns.
proust-budding-grove-moncrieff-1924:
Within a Budding Grove is the second volume of Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time. Proust published it in French in 1919, and C. K. Scott Moncrieff translated it into English in 1924. The young narrator leaves Paris for the seaside resort of Balbec with his grandmother.

At Balbec he watches a band of lively girls on the beach and falls in love more than once. Albertine, the most vivid of them, enters his life for good here. First love, snobbery, and the sea air fill long, drifting scenes. The volume won Proust the Prix Goncourt in France. It deepened his great theme: how time and desire change all we see.
res-gestae-divi-augusti-shipley-1924:
Before his death in 14 CE, Augustus wrote a short account of his own deeds and had it cut in stone at his tomb. Copies were set up across the empire, and the best one survives on a temple wall in Ankara. Frederick W. Shipley's Loeb version of 1924 gives the text with a full study of that monument.

The emperor lists the offices he held, the wars he won, the games he gave, and the gold he spent on Rome. It is cool, plain, and masterful self-praise. No single paper tells us more about how Augustus wished to be seen. Historians call it the queen of inscriptions.
robertson-works-vol-1-1824:
Volume one opens the 1824 Works of William Robertson, the nine-volume gathering of Scotland's great Enlightenment historian. Robertson published his histories from 1759 and rose to lead the historical writing of his age. The Works collect his History of Scotland, his reign of Charles V, his History of America, and his Historical Disquisition on India.

Robertson wrote history as philosophy teaching by examples, in prose of unusual grace. His Scotland made him famous; his Charles V made him Europe's historian. The collected edition of 1824 fixed his full achievement between covers for the Victorian reader. Volume one begins that monument, the life's work of Edinburgh's royal historiographer in full.
robertson-works-vol-2-1824:
The Works of William Robertson continue into volume two of the nine-volume edition of 1824. Robertson, who issued his histories from 1759 onward, wrote the past of nations as a single, connected advance. His History of Scotland, his Charles V, his America, and his Disquisition on India make up the gathered set.

In each field Robertson joined archives to argument, telling not only what happened but how society itself had changed. His calm, elevated style won readers far beyond Britain. The Works were the standard shelf form of his achievement for a century. Volume two holds its share of that achievement, from northern kingdoms to southern empires, in one historian's steady hand.
robertson-works-vol-3-1824:
Volume three of Robertson's Works, in the collected edition of 1824, carries on the nine-volume set. William Robertson published his first history in 1759 and soon stood in the front rank of European letters. The Works bind his Scotland, his Charles V, his America, and his study of ancient India into one uniform whole.

Robertson's histories trace how manners, laws, and commerce grow together across the centuries. He was the Scottish Enlightenment's great popularizer of that broad view of the past. Students of America and India still cite his volumes as starting points in their fields. Volume three keeps the set's wide world in view, told with its usual poise.
robertson-works-vol-4-1824:
Robertson's Works reach volume four in the nine-volume edition of 1824. William Robertson, whose writing career in history began in 1759, became the model of the philosophical historian in Britain. The set gathers the fruits of that career: Scotland, the Emperor Charles V, America, and the Historical Disquisition on India.

His pages move from Highland clans to Mexican temples with the same inquiring calm. Robertson asks in each place how peoples lived, traded, believed, and were governed. That method, history as the study of society, shaped generations of writers after him. Volume four stands mid-set, holding its portion of one of the Enlightenment's widest historical minds.
robertson-works-vol-5-1824:
Volume five stands at the center of the 1824 Works of William Robertson, nine volumes in all. Robertson issued his histories from 1759 and won a European name beside Hume and Voltaire. The Works collect the History of Scotland, the History of Charles V, the History of America, and the Historical Disquisition on India in one edition.

Across those fields Robertson practiced a single art: clear narrative steered by reflection on manners and causes. His America taught Britain about the Spanish conquests; his India opened ancient eastern trade to his readers. The middle volume of the set holds that range in balance. Robertson's calm authority fills every part of it.
robertson-works-vol-6-1824:
William Robertson, the Scottish historian, stands with Hume and Gibbon among the masters of Enlightenment history. Volume six here forms part of the nine-volume Works of 1824. The Works gather his History of Scotland and his History of Charles V. His History of America and his Historical Disquisition on India stand with them. Robertson wrote with a broad, philosophical sweep across nations and ages.

His histories joined deep research to a clear, elevated style that readers across Europe admired. The Charles V made his name; the America and the India carried his reach worldwide. A single volume of the Works holds a cross-section of that range. Volume six keeps the set's portrait of its author whole: Scotland's great practitioner of philosophical history.
robertson-works-vol-7-1824:
The Works of William Robertson reach volume seven in the nine-volume edition of 1824. Robertson, principal of Edinburgh University and royal historiographer, published his famous histories from 1759 onward. His books on Scotland, on the Emperor Charles V, on America, and on India form the core of this collected set.

Robertson's gift was scope joined to calm judgment: he wrote the history of continents as one connected story. His account of Charles V opened a new era in English history writing. The Disquisition on India showed his range reaching to Asia's ancient trade. Volume seven carries its share of that wide, ordered vision. The set preserves Enlightenment historiography in full dress.
robertson-works-vol-8-1824:
Volume eight of the 1824 Works of William Robertson stands one volume from the end of the nine-volume set. Robertson's histories, issued from 1759, made him a leader of the Scottish Enlightenment's historical school. Scotland, the reign of Charles V, America, and India all came under his pen, and the Works bind them together.

His method joined narrative grace to a philosopher's search for causes in society and manners. Readers in his day placed him beside Hume, and the comparison still instructs. This volume holds part of that achievement in the standard collected form. To read through the Works is to watch history become a science of human progress, in one master's hands.
robertson-works-vol-9-1824:
Volume nine completes the Works of William Robertson in the edition of 1824. Robertson, publishing from 1759, had gathered his histories of Scotland, Charles V, America, and India into a single fame. The nine uniform volumes of 1824 gave that fame its lasting shelf form for the century that followed.

The closing volume ends the set as Robertson's work deserves, in the company of all his great subjects. His school of history, calm, connected, and alive to society's growth, ruled British taste for decades. Readers finishing the Works hold the Enlightenment's historical project nearly entire. Robertson taught his age to see the past whole, and volume nine sets the last stone.
russell-icarus-1924:
Icarus, published in 1924 in the To-day and To-morrow pamphlet series, is Russell's dark little prophecy about the future of science. Written against J. B. S. Haldane's sunny Daedalus, it warns that knowledge multiplies power faster than wisdom.

Russell foresees science used to sharpen war, tighten propaganda, and extend the reach of governments and great firms. He doubts that ordinary human nature will improve to match its new tools. The pamphlet is brief, bleak, and often quoted, a founding text of the debate about technology's dangers. Its title is the whole argument: wings, wax, and the sun.
scott-hermetica-vol-1-1924:
Walter Scott spent years building his monumental edition of the Hermetica, published from 1924. The Hermetica are Greek and Latin writings ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage. Volume one gives the texts with facing English translation.

Readers find the Corpus Hermeticum, the Latin Asclepius, and excerpts preserved by Stobaeus. A long introduction untangles the writings' tangled history and authorship. These dialogues treat God, the soul, and the cosmos in mystical terms. They shaped Renaissance magic and later spiritual movements deeply. Scott's first volume became the standard English Hermetica of its age.
spr-proceedings-vol34-1924:
Volume thirty four binds parts eighty nine through ninety two, dated 1924. The SPR Proceedings are in their fifth decade, and the format holds. Experiments in thought reading appear with their chance scores computed. Long trance reports, checked line by line, fill the center.

Spontaneous experiences, from hauntings to death bed visions, arrive in steady flow. The society's committees sift them by rules set in the census years. Physical phenomena stay rare and closely watched in these parts. Volume thirty four is a late brick in the central archive. It documents a debate that shaped how Britain argued about survival. The record stays, as ever, open.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5024:
Abraham Lincoln gives four yearly addresses, from December 3, 1861, to December 6, 1864, in a set parted by three stars. The first opens in the midst of political troubles past all past measure. Still, Lincoln says, there is cause for great thanks: the folk have known rare good health and the most plenteous harvests. Dealings with foreign nations have been held in deep care, chiefly as they turn on home affairs.

A disloyal part of the American people, he reports, has spent the whole year in a bid to split and wreck the Union. A nation torn by factious strife at home lies open to slight abroad, and one side, if not both, is sure in time to call in foreign help. The rebels, though, have won less backing and cheer from abroad than they likely hoped for, Lincoln notes, a point he takes up with grave care.
suess-face-of-earth-vol5-sollas-1924:
Volume 5 of Sollas's translation of Suess's Face of the Earth appeared in 1924, completing the English set. Eduard Suess had died in 1914, and his great synthesis closed with this volume. Sollas's translation project had run for twenty years by its end.

The final volume draws the threads together into a completed global geology: continents, oceans, and mountain systems in one account. Suess's Earth, cooling and contracting, ordered the facts his age possessed. Within decades, continental drift and then plate tectonics replaced that frame, yet his terms and maps endured. The volume completes the most ambitious work of geology written by a single author in the nineteenth century.
t-mann-buddenbrooks-vol-1-of-2-1924:
The Buddenbrook family of Luebeck rises through trade in the first half of Thomas Mann's great saga. The text is Helen Lowe-Porter's 1924 English translation, Volume One of two. Wealthy merchants across the early 1800s fill its drawing rooms: consuls, senators, and their carefully married children. Mann was twenty-five when the novel made him famous.

Mann traces the firm's prosperity and the family's vitality together, with ironic tenderness for both. Christenings, weddings, and business deals mark the generations as the century turns. Seeds of decline already hide inside the success, for readers who watch closely. The novel that eventually won Mann the Nobel Prize begins with this confident ascent. Few family sagas open at such full stretch.
t-mann-buddenbrooks-vol-2-of-2-1924:
Decline governs the second half of Buddenbrooks, in Lowe-Porter's 1924 English translation, Volume Two of two. As the nineteenth century wears on, the Buddenbrook energy drains away into art, illness, and introspection. The firm's grip loosens as each generation finds commerce less natural than the last.

Thomas Buddenbrook holds the house together by will until the effort consumes him. His son Hanno, frail and musical, closes the line with his early death. Mann renders a bourgeois dynasty's fall with love rather than scorn, which gives the book its ache. The portrait stands among the most moving in European literature. Readers finish the two volumes feeling they have lived a whole family's century.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
The Indiscreet Confession, The Contract, and The Quid Pro Quo, or The Mistakes, fill the twenty-fourth volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. Parisian love and its written bonds govern the three tales.

The first opens on Aminta, whose lot of magic charms famed Paris never matched within its walls: youth, beauty, temper, and fortune, all that should render a husband blessed. Her mother still kept her beneath her wing, while her father's riches drew lovers, and whatever his daughter wished he would provide, amusements, jewels, and dress. Blithe Damon won her heart and became her lord and master by Hymen's right. What an indiscreet confession then undoes, and how contracts and mistaken identities finish the volume, is La Fontaine's usual dance of candor and cost.
taylor-mystical-hymns-orpheus-1824:
Thomas Taylor published his translation of the Orphic Hymns in a second edition in 1824. The hymns are ritual songs of the Orphic mysteries of ancient Greece. Taylor first issued his rendering in 1792 and later revised it.

Each short hymn calls upon a god with offerings and storied titles. Night, the Stars, Sleep, and Death all receive their invocations. Worshippers chanted these hymns at secret rites two thousand years ago. Taylor's verse keeps a strange, solemn music in English. He believed in the hymns' spiritual power, not merely their antiquity. His version became the classic English Orpheus for later occult and literary readers.
temple-word-of-lalla-1924:
Richard Carnac Temple gave English readers his own rendering of the sayings of Lalla in The Word of Lalla the Prophetess, printed at Cambridge in 1924. Lalla, or Lal Ded, was the fourteenth-century mystic of Kashmir whose vakhs passed by mouth for five centuries. Temple's edition stands independent of the Grierson and Barnett version of 1920.

Short, fierce verses tell of her leaving home, her guru, her dance of joy in the self, and her scorn for rite without love. Temple adds an introduction, notes, and an index to guide the reader. He reads her as a prophetess of the inner life for all faiths. The two English Lallas of the 1920s still frame her for the West.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: No. 24 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It, dated April 22, 1897, is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and one advertisement, for The Sportsman's Magazine of New York. That magazine is an 80-page monthly, written and published by sportsmen, for sportsmen. A copy costs twenty cents, and a year two dollars. Its premium list offers guns, pistols, bicycles, and fishing-rods for new subscriptions. Readers may send five two-cent stamps for a sample copy.

The issue of June 16, 1898 is number 24 of volume 2 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It. Its whole-run number is 84. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a publisher's notice of rates. A year's subscription costs $1.50, and six months seventy-five cents. Foreign subscriptions cost two dollars and a quarter. The publisher is at 3 and 5 West 18th Street, New York. Remittances go to the Great Round World Publishing Company.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
The Ormsby Don Quixote, Cervantes' tale in English, opens Volume 2, Part 24 here. Chapter twenty-one continues Camacho's wedding, with other delightful incidents. Don Quixote and Sancho are deep in the discussion set out in the last chapter when loud shouts and a great noise break in.

Men on mares ride at full gallop, shouting, to receive the bride and bridegroom. Music, pageantry, the priest, kin of both sides, and the chief people of the place surround the pair. Cervantes fills the road with noise and show, as a rich wedding draws the knight and his squire into village rivalry and display.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Bolsover Castle in Derbyshire is described in No. 566 of The Mirror, dated September 15, 1832. Bolsover is a populous village on the county's eastern edge near Chesterfield. The castle stands on the flat top of a rocky hill rising sharply from meadows, a landmark for the country around.

A castle has stood there since the Norman Conquest, though nothing of the first building survives. At the Domesday survey the place belonged to William Peveril. King John ordered its governor, Bryan de L'Isle, to fortify Bolsover against the rebellious barons or demolish it if it could not be held. Later owners included the Howard dukes of Norfolk and a fifty-year grant to Sir John Byron. Gilbert Talbot sold it in 1613 to Sir Charles Cavendish.

No. 584 of The Mirror, marked as a supplement to volume 20, is present here only as a title page followed by the single heading Preface. No preface text and no article text appear. The title page gives the magazine's full name, The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, with London and the year 1832 below.

What the title page promises is the magazine's usual range. Original essays stand first, followed by historical narratives, biographical memoirs, and sketches of society. Topographical descriptions, novels and tales, anecdotes, and poetry follow. Extracts from new and expensive works, the spirit of the public journals, discoveries in the arts and sciences, and useful domestic hints complete the printed list.
theodori-kerckringii-doctoris-medici-anm: Theodor Kerckring, a doctor of medicine, is named on a badly garbled title page dated by the record to 1724. His notes concern Basilius Valentinus and other spagyric writings, the old chemical medicine tradition. Much of the German title survives only in broken lettering. What can be read gives the author, his profession, and his subject, plus a note that some material was translated into German. The page shown here is the title alone, in damaged form, so Kerckring's annotations themselves are not present.
tob-0144-54824:
Blavatsky called The Secret Doctrine, published in 1888, her masterwork, and volume one bears the subtitle Cosmogenesis. She claimed its core came from the secret Stanzas of Dzyan, an ancient text few others have seen. The volume explains how the universe unfolds in great cycles.

Worlds appear, evolve through rounds, and dissolve, again and again, over spans too vast to picture. Matter and spirit are two faces of one reality. The style is dense and demands patience, with long quotes from science and scripture. For Theosophists, Cosmogenesis stands as the movement's deepest account of where everything came from.
tob-10024:
Thomas à Kempis, a fifteenth-century monk, wrote the devotional guide known in English as The Imitation of Christ, here in an alternative translation as The Following of Christ. Only the Bible has been read more widely among Christian devotional books. Its chapters are short and direct, meant for daily use.

Kempis urges humility, warns against vanity and idle learning, and teaches readers to imitate Christ in ordinary life. Much of it reads like quiet counsel from a wise friend rather than formal theology. Saints and skeptics alike have carried the book for six hundred years, returning to its plain call to turn inward.
tob-10824:
William Q. Judge's American Theosophical magazine The Path, in its first volume for 1886-87, shows the movement's work in the United States. Contributions by various Theosophists mix practical spiritual advice with defenses of Blavatsky and reports from the lodges. Compared with Blavatsky's Lucifer, the tone is less flamboyant and more workmanlike.

Theosophy appears here as a lived discipline: study, meditation, ethics, and organized local work. News from branches shows a young occult movement building itself month by month. Readers interested in how ideas travel will value the volume as a record of American Theosophy finding its own voice beside the louder London center.
tob-13324:
A different edition of Brother Lawrence's classic presents the lay brother's method of turning kitchen work into prayer. Letters from Lawrence and the recollections of those who knew him carry the teaching. He was a Carmelite lay brother in seventeenth-century Paris, assigned to the kitchen and later to sandal repair.

Lawrence's method needs no retreat: return the mind to God, again and again, in the middle of ordinary tasks. Short enough to finish in one sitting, the account is deep enough to practice for a lifetime, as generations of readers testify. Comparing editions shows how stable the core of his conversations and letters has remained.
tob-4024:
René Descartes put out his Discourse on the Method in 1637. In it he sets rules for the search for sure truth. Doubt all that can be doubted. Split hard tasks into small parts. Move from the plain to the hard. Take as true only what is clear and plain.

In the course of the tale comes the most famed line in all thought: I think, therefore I am. From that one firm point Descartes builds back out to God, the world, and the sciences. The short book stands as the birth deed of modern rational thought. A reader can finish it in an afternoon and argue with it for life.
tob-4224:
Francis Barrett published The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer, in London in 1801, and English occultism revived around it. Barrett compiled natural magic, magnetism, Kabbalah, alchemy, and the evocation of spirits into one grand summa, much of it drawn from Agrippa and older masters. His school of magic taught from the book.

Plates of talismans, circles, and spirit forms give the volume its famous look. Bulwer-Lytton studied it for his novels; the founders of the Golden Dawn studied it for their rites. Verified from the 1919 edition, Barrett's Magus remains the great English grimoire-compilation of the Romantic age.
un-ga-res-24:
When the League of Nations died, its work had to go somewhere. Resolution 24, passed by the General Assembly on 12 February 1946, maps the handoff. Under a web of treaties and deals, the League and its arms had long held tasks that some states wished the new UN to keep alive. League members told the Assembly they would move, at the League's last meeting, to bless the steps set out here.

The Assembly keeps a free hand. It may refuse any one task after fair study. For each task it takes, it will name the UN arm or linked agency fit to hold it. Out of this dry text grew the UN's quiet grip on old League work, from drug pacts to refugee files.
un-ga-res-a-69-24:
Jerusalem's status stands at the core of Resolution A/69/24, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the 1947 partition vote and its terms for the city. It recalls a long chain of later votes as well. In them, the Assembly held that all steps by Israel, the occupying power, to change the face or status of the Holy City are void and must be undone.

One target is named: Israel's so-called Basic Law on Jerusalem, and its claim of the city as its capital. The Security Council in 1980 chose not to accept that law. The world court in 2004 ruled on the wall built in the held land. Through all these cites, the stance holds firm: the city's fate must be settled by talks, not by one side's acts.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 24, adopted on 12 February 1946, arranged the handover of League of Nations work to the United Nations as the League was wound up. The Assembly stated that the United Nations was willing, in broad terms, to take over certain duties and powers the League had held under treaties and other agreements.

The plan split the work three ways. The Secretariat would keep custody of treaty texts and handle filings and notices. Technical and non-political duties would pass after review by the Economic and Social Council. Political duties would be judged case by case. The League's library, archives, health and opium work, and its assets were also to move over.

Resolution 69/24 of the General Assembly (2014) is devoted entirely to Jerusalem. It recalls the 1947 partition plan's provisions for the city. It recalls the Assembly's earlier rulings. Under them, Israeli measures changing Jerusalem's character and status are null and void. Those measures include the 'Basic Law' proclaiming it Israel's capital.

The Assembly repeats that any Israeli action imposing its laws, jurisdiction, and administration on the city is illegal and without validity. It calls for an immediate stop to such measures. It voices grave concern at settlement activity, home demolitions, evictions, and excavations around religious sites. It stresses that a final solution must protect both sides' legitimate concerns. It must guarantee freedom of religion and free access to the holy places for people of all faiths.
un-sc-res-1024:
The Golan Heights force won its usual renewal in November 1995. On 28 November 1995 the Security Council extended UNDOF until 31 May 1996. The Secretary-General had reported on the force earlier that month. The decision follows the mission's standard wording. UNDOF has watched the Israel-Syria separation line since 1974.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 at once. A report from the Secretary-General was due at the end of the term. It would cover events in the area. It would also list steps taken to apply 338. The Council treated the renewal as routine business. The calm it guarded was anything but guaranteed.
un-sc-res-1224: Catalogued with a 1999 date, Resolution 1224 forms part of the Security Council's official record at the United Nations. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording.
un-sc-res-124: Ghana became the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence in March 1957. Days later, on 7 March 1957, the Security Council considered its membership application. The Council recommended to the General Assembly that Ghana be admitted to the United Nations. The vote was unanimous. The whole text is one sentence. Ghana's entry opened the door to the great wave of African admissions that followed.
un-sc-res-1324:
The wait for a referendum in Western Sahara stretched on in the autumn of 2000. On 30 October 2000 the Council extended MINURSO until 28 February 2001. The Secretary-General's envoy was still trying to bridge the parties. Deep differences over the Settlement Plan remained open. The plan promised the people of the territory a free vote on their future.

The Council voiced full support for the envoy's work. It expected the parties to keep trying to solve the plan's problems. It also held out the hope of an agreed political solution to the dispute. The Secretary-General had to assess the situation before the new term ended. The deadlock in fact outlasted many such renewals.
un-sc-res-1424:
Prevlaka's observers won a further term in the summer of 2002. On 12 July 2002 the Security Council authorized UNMOP to keep monitoring the peninsula. The demilitarized zone sat between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The Secretary-General's June report guided the vote. Ties between the two governments kept improving. A joint border commission was at work.

Both sides had to stop breaking the demilitarized regime. They had to work with the observers and ensure their safety and free movement. The Council urged faster progress toward a negotiated settlement of the dispute. It also encouraged steps to build confidence. The mission's quiet watch was nearing its end. The two states settled the issue later that year.
un-sc-res-1524: Security Council Resolution 1524 is held in this collection as a transcription of the United Nations official record. The Wikisource source line is part of its identity: this is the record text, not a retelling. Inside, opening clauses frame the problem and numbered paragraphs deliver the Council's answer, in the order the members agreed.
un-sc-res-1624:
Resolution 1624, adopted in 2005 at a summit of world leaders, targets the preaching that leads people to terrorism. Rather than weapons or money, it focuses on words: calls to carry out attacks and praise for those who do. The Council asked states to outlaw such incitement.

Inside, members are urged to keep suspected terrorists from crossing borders and to share information with each other. The text also warns states to respect free speech and refugee law while acting. It stands out among terror resolutions because its subject is propaganda, and how far governments may go to silence it.
un-sc-res-1724: Resolution 1724 is one of the Security Council's numbered formal acts, preserved in official wording through Wikisource. The text speaks with the combined voice of fifteen states, five of them permanent members. What that voice said on this occasion is kept entire in the entry, from the first recalling clause to the last decided paragraph.
un-sc-res-1824: The Council adopted Resolution 1824 on the Rwanda war crimes tribunal on 18 July 2008. Judges' terms were set to end that December, yet trials would run into 2009. Fresh arrests of senior accused in late 2007 and early 2008 had pushed the timetable back. The Council extends the terms of nine permanent judges and seventeen temporary judges to 31 December 2009. Two appeals judges serve to the end of 2010. The step keeps the completion plan on track.
un-sc-res-1924: Resolution 1924, adopted in 2010, is preserved here as a Security Council decision in official-record form. The transcription comes from English Wikisource. Inside the text, the members recall their earlier steps in the matter before taking the next one, and the entry keeps that continuity visible, which is how the Council's practice actually accumulates.
un-sc-res-24: Security Council Resolution 24, adopted in April 1947, concerned applications by states seeking to join the young United Nations. In the council's second year, membership bids from states on both sides of the late war raised hard questions. The text deals with how such bids were to be handled and passed on. Hungary was among the states whose hopes were tangled in this early bargaining; it in fact waited until 1955 for its seat. The record shows admission becoming an early Cold War contest.
un-sc-res-324:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force won a further six months in December 1972. On 12 December 1972 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 June 1973. The Secretary-General had reported that the force was still needed for peace. Cyprus's government agreed it should stay past 15 December. Conditions on the island, as his report described them, left little choice.

The Council restated its Cyprus resolutions back to 1964. It urged all sides to act with restraint. It also pressed them to speed up work toward the Council's goals. The text voices hope that progress would soon allow a cut in the force. That hope framed many renewals of a mission now decades old.
un-sc-res-424:
Rhodesia's armed invasion of Zambia on 6 March 1978 was condemned on 17 March 1978. Zambia's letter and its foreign minister set out a long list of hostile acts. Innocent people had been killed and hurt, and property destroyed. Three days earlier the Council had condemned the regime's aggression against its neighbors.

The Council strongly condemned the recent armed invasion by the illegal racist minority regime in Southern Rhodesia. It praised Zambia and the other front-line states for backing the Zimbabwean people's struggle for freedom. The liberation of Zimbabwe and Namibia and the end of apartheid were restated as the price of justice and lasting peace in the region. Britain, as the administering power, was called to take prompt and effective steps to end the regime. The Council decided that any further violation of Zambia's sovereignty would bring it back to weigh measures under the Charter, sanctions among them.
un-sc-res-724: Formal action by the Council in its numbered series produced Resolution 724, which the catalog dates to 1991. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Another routine but vital Golan Heights renewal came on 28 November 1995. Resolution 1024 passed unanimously that day. The UN Disengagement Observer Force had stood between Israel and Syria since 1974. Its mandate was about to expire. The Secretary-General's report of 17 November 1995 informed the decision.

Members renewed the force for six additional months, through 31 May 1996. They paired the extension with a call on both sides. Both were urged to act on Resolution 338 of 1973. The Secretary-General was asked to report when the period closed. His report would cover events and progress toward that older resolution.

Security Council resolution 1224 (1999) briefly extends the mandate of MINURSO, the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, until 11 February 1999. It asks the Secretary-General to keep the Council informed of all significant developments. The developments are in putting the Settlement Plan and the agreements between the parties into effect. Where appropriate, he is to report on whether MINURSO's mandate remains viable.

Ghana led black Africa into the UN with this vote of 1957. On 7 March, the Council adopted Resolution 124 without dissent. Ghana had won freedom from Britain the day before. It was the first sub-Saharan colony to do so after the Second World War. The new state applied to the United Nations at once.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Ghana. Ghana took its seat the next day. Its leaders pledged that Ghana's freedom meant little without Africa's full liberation. The pledge set the tone for the years ahead. Within three years, seventeen more African states passed through the same door.

Four more months for the Sahara vote mission came in October 2000. On the thirtieth, the Council adopted Resolution 1324 without dissent. The Secretary-General had just sent his October report. His Personal Envoy won warm praise in the text. The mission, MINURSO, had sought since 1991 to run a vote on the territory's future.

The text extends the mandate to 28 February 2001. It voices the hope that the parties keep trying under the envoy. Their deep gaps over the vote plan still had to close. A deal both sides could accept was the stated goal. The Secretary-General must assess the state of play before the term ends.

The Prevlaka cape watch gained a short new lease in 2002. UN men had kept eyes on the demilitarized cape since 1992. Croatia and Yugoslavia both claimed the small point of land. Peace there had held firm and calm. The chief's report of 28 June 2002 told a bright tale. Resolution 1424 passed with no dissent on 12 July 2002.

The watch ran to 15 October 2002. Both sides had to end breaches of the no-arms zone. The UN men needed safe, free range to do their work. Warm words marked the thaw in ties. A joint border team had been set up. The Council told both sides to speed a deal on the cape. If word of a pact came, the watch's length would get a fresh look.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended on 30 January 2004, and the Abkhazia peace process is pushed into a more structured form. High-level meetings of the Group of Friends in Geneva had given the talks new momentum. Georgia also had new leadership after presidential elections that month.

The lack of progress on a settlement is again called unacceptable, and those who shot down a UNOMIG helicopter in 2001 remain unidentified, the Council notes. Both sides are urged to work steadily in the Geneva task forces on economic cooperation, refugee return, and political and security questions. Those talks rest on a paper setting out how powers might be divided between Tbilisi and Sukhumi.

Incitement to terrorism is the target on 14 September 2005, during the World Summit in New York. World leaders were gathered at the United Nations for the summit. The text builds on the binding counter-terrorism duties of resolution 1373 and on later measures against listed terrorist groups.

All states are called on to pass laws banning incitement to commit terrorist acts, to prevent such conduct, and to deny safe haven to anyone credibly linked to it. States are also asked to strengthen border security and document checks, and to deepen dialogue among civilizations to undercut extremist propaganda. Steps taken are to be reported to the Counter-Terrorism Committee, and all counter-terrorism action must respect human rights and refugee law.

Somalia's arms embargo Monitoring Group is set up again on 29 November 2006, for a further period. The transitional federal institutions still struggled to build effective national government, and fighting between them and the Union of Islamic Courts sharpened the need for oversight. The embargo itself dated from 1992 and kept being breached.

The Secretary-General, working with the sanctions committee, is asked to set the group up again with its standing task of tracking arms flows and reporting violations. The African Union, the regional development authority, and the Arab League are praised for backing reconciliation in Somalia. Somali leaders are urged to take real steps in political dialogue, and the transitional institutions to keep building national governance.

The Rwanda tribunal's judges are kept on to finish their trials in Resolution 1824, adopted on 18 July 2008. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda was working to its Completion Strategy. Remaining trials were now projected to run to December 2009. Its president had written to the Council on 6 June 2008 about judicial terms.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the two Appeals Chamber permanent judges until 31 December 2010, or until the appeals finish if sooner. The Trial Chamber permanent judges and the ad litem judges, serving and not yet appointed alike, are extended until 31 December 2009 on the same condition. It also amends Article 11 of the Statute. The amendment caps the Chambers at sixteen permanent and nine ad litem judges. It lets Trial Chambers sit in sections of three judges with full powers.

Côte d'Ivoire was still divided after years of crisis when the Council adopted Resolution 1924 on 27 May 2010. The United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, known as UNOCI, was waiting for a review of its mandate. A new report had just set out recommendations for how the mission's work should change.

Acting under Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter, the Council extended UNOCI's mandate until 30 June 2010. The mission kept the tasks set out in an earlier resolution. For the same short period, French forces kept their permission to support UNOCI, within the limits of their deployment and abilities. The brief renewal held everything in place. The Council could then decide on a fuller redesign of the mission.

Botswana stepped out of British protection in September 1966. The arid southern African territory had been called Bechuanaland. Its leaders applied quickly for a UN seat. Resolution 224 was adopted unanimously on 14 October 1966. The vote came two weeks after independence day.

Members recommended Botswana's admission to the General Assembly. Admission followed within days. Botswana was poor, landlocked, and ringed by white-minority regimes. Its founding president, Seretse Khama, chose steady democracy. The country later became a model of stable governance in the region. Diamonds, found soon after independence, transformed its economy. This single-line resolution records the quiet legal moment when Botswana joined the community of states.

Hungary applied to join the United Nations on 22 April 1947. The country was emerging from the Second World War on the losing side. Its application reached the Council eight days later. Resolution 24 was adopted on 30 April 1947 by ten votes to one. Australia cast the only no vote.

The text does not admit Hungary or reject it. Instead, it sends the application to a specialist body. The Committee on the Admission of New Members would study it. That committee would then report back at the proper time. The resolution captures one early step in the UN's slow, political process for judging would-be members after the war.

The last calm Cyprus renewal before the storm came in December 1972. On the twelfth, the Council adopted Resolution 324. Fourteen members voted yes and none voted no. China held back. The Secretary-General reported that the force was still needed. Cyprus agreed it should stay past mid-December.

The text restates the whole Cyprus series through June 1972. It urges the parties to speed up joint work in the hopeful climate. The posting then runs to 15 June 1973. The standing hope closes the text once more. Progress by then might let the force shrink or go home. Eighteen months later, a coup and an invasion split the island for good.

Rhodesia's armed raid into Zambia is condemned in Resolution 424. It passed by a full vote on 17 March 1978. Zambia's foreign chief told of raid after raid by the white-led rebel regime. The raids broke Zambia's skies and soil, killed and hurt the blameless, and wrecked homes and goods. They peaked on 6 March 1978 with troops crossing the border in force.

The Council's wrath had a long past, which it spelled out. Texts from 1973 and 1977 had condemned the same regime for the same acts, in Zambia and in two more states. It restated the right of Zimbabwe's people to rule their own land. Freeing Zimbabwe and Namibia, and ending South Africa's race laws, were named as the roots of true peace in the region.

Arms still reached Yugoslavia despite the embargo of 1991, and the Council moved to make the ban work better in December that year. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 11 December, had found that conditions for sending peacekeepers did not yet exist. Resolution 724 followed that report. Its adoption date is given as 14 December 1991 in the chain of later resolutions.

The Council approved the report and agreed that the time for a peacekeeping force had not come. All states were told to report within twenty days. Their reports had to set out the steps taken to enforce the embargo. A committee made up of the whole Council was created. It would collect those reports and follow up claims that the embargo was being broken. It would also recommend ways to make the ban bite harder.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s21-24: Section 21.24 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers references to the 1938 edition of the Code in documents prepared for codification. It sits in Part 21 of Title 1, in the electronic Code as of October 2026. The evidence shown is brief. For material codified in the 1938 edition of the Code of Federal Regulations or a supplement to it, set forms may be used, as fitting. The section thus gives drafters approved forms for citing that early edition.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s304-24:
Section 304.24 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations gives a denied records requester a right of appeal. It belongs to the disclosure rules of the Administrative Conference of the United States. A person who asked for records and was refused may not be satisfied with the answer.

The appeal goes to the Chairman of the agency. It may challenge the adverse determination in any respect. The appeal must be made in writing, by email or letter. It must reach the agency within sixty days of the denial. The letter should give reasons and supporting information showing why the first decision was wrong. It should also clearly identify the particular determination under challenge. The rule turns a flat refusal into a decision that a named senior official must reconsider.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s601-24:
Section 601.24 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers the Final Environmental Impact Statement for the National Capital Planning Commission. It sits in Part 601, the part that carries out the National Environmental Policy Act. The final statement comes after the public comment span and the public meetings on the draft statement.

The final statement must respond to the spoken and written comments got in the draft comment span. The Commission may take final action on an application only after a thirty day review span of the final statement. That span starts when the Environmental Protection Agency prints a notice of availability for it in the Federal Register. The rule ties the timing of a decision to that public notice.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1724:
Section 1724 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets the responsibilities of the National Recording Preservation Board. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the sound recording preservation chapter, in the board subchapter. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. The board advises on the National Recording Registry.

The Board shall review nominations of sound recordings sent to it for inclusion in the registry, the text states. It advises the Librarian of Congress on those choices, as the opening goes on to provide. Further duties on study and public awareness of recorded sound follow in the section. Expert review thus stands between public nominations and a national honor.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1824:
Section 1824 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers energy and green measures in the Capitol Complex Master Plan.
